units.la: QUOD Clementiæ Vestræ Opus istud nuncupare audeam, facit Usseriani Nominis dignitas; quæ ratione summi, quem in Ecclesiis Britannicis tenes, loci à te potissimùm Patrocinium quæreret; si tanto nomini quærendum esset. Ille quidem in cœlos jamdiu receptus, extra omnes invidiæ ictus collocatur ; & præclarâ pietatis, eruditionis, atque omnifariæ virtutis famâ, ipsorum etiam, quos Persecutores olim expertus est pessimos, venerationem meruit : tibi tamen, cui Operum ejus posthumorum in lucem protrahendorum tanta fuit cura, gratias quàm maximas debet, & quantum Opus istud efficere potest, agit. In tuto quidem est Usserius : Mihimet autem Patrocinium necessariò quærendum sentio ; ne Illustrissimi Heroïs Manibus injuriam fecisse videar ; dum Lucubrationem illius aliquam ad incudem revocare ; id quod Vir Maximus imperfectum reliquit, supplere ; quod confusum, digerere ; quod minùs accuratum, emendare ausus fuerim. Unicum id mihi refugium ; quòd tuis mandatis opus suscepererim, tuis consiliis persecutus, tuis demum auspiciis absolverim. Factum id à me quidem obedientiæ debito ; à te autem Ecclesiæ Orthodoxæ causam adversùs errores & impetus Pontificios propugnandi animo, eo præsertim tempore ; quùm Pontificiorum injuriis & violentiâ Ecclesia Anglicana in summum adducta discrimen nutaret. Et forsan nutando prorupisset; nisi Clementissimum Numen in haec tempora Te, aliosque aliquot tui Suffraganeos Episcopos, reservâsset; quorum prudentiâ, zelo atque invictâ constantiâ res nostrae starent. Istud enim mihi muneris dedisti, paulò ante Gloriosum illum Carcerem; quo Leges Patrias asseruistis, fidem confirmâstis, Adversariorum impetus fregistis. Atque utinam is essem; qui & tuis in hac re votis, & Usseriani Nominis amplitudini satisfacere potuissem! Cùm verò neutiquam id sperare licuerit (neque enim facilè reperiendus est aliquis, qui Usserio succedaneus fiat) id mihi solummodo restabat; ut apud te in humanitate tuâ, illâque quâ me semper immeritum dignatus es benevolentiâ; apud alios autem in patrocinio tuo refugium quaererem. Faxit Deus Optimus Maximus; ut in Religionis incrementum, in Orthodoxae Fidei tutelam, in fidelium solamen, Ecclesiae Anglicanae Clavum diu incolumis teneas; ut quae nobis imminent procellae, te praesidente, dente, dissipentur; ne quod à malevolo olim Gallo in opprobrium nostræ Gentis causâ S. Edmundi decessoris tui, scriptum est [Consuetudinis est Terræ illi bonis Prælatis injurias inferre] nostris temporibus renovetur. Ita vovet ex animo, Clementiæ Vestræ, Devotissimus Sacellanus, & Cliens humillimus, Hen. Wharton.
units.tr: That I dare to dedicate this work of yours to Your Grace is owed to the dignity of the name of Ussher. If that name needed a patron, it would seek one above all from you, because of the very high position you hold in the British Churches. He has long since been received into heaven and stands beyond every stroke of envy, and he has earned reverence for his outstanding reputation for piety, learning and every kind of virtue, even from those who, as he once found, were his worst persecutors. Yet he owes you the greatest thanks, since you took such great care to bring his posthumous works to light, and this work does what it can to repay that debt. Ussher is indeed safe. I, however, feel that I must seek a patron, so that I may not seem to have wronged the spirit of that most illustrious hero. I have dared to call back to the anvil some of his writings, to supply what that great man left unfinished, to arrange what was confused, and to correct what was less accurate. My only refuge is this: I undertook the task at your command, pursued it under your counsel, and at last finished it under your auspices. I did this from a sense of duty owed in obedience, and you did it from a desire to defend the cause of the Orthodox Church against the errors and assaults of the Papists, especially at a time when the English Church, pressed by the injuries and violence of the Papists, was brought to the brink of extreme peril and seemed about to fall. Perhaps it would have collapsed in its wavering, had not the most merciful Deity kept you and a few other of your suffragan bishops for these times, whose prudence, zeal and unconquered constancy kept our affairs standing. For you gave me this service a little while ago, in that glorious prison, where you upheld the laws of our country, confirmed the faith and broke the attacks of our adversaries. Would that I were the man who could have satisfied both your wishes in this matter and the greatness of Ussher's name! Since I could by no means hope for this (for it is not easy to find anyone who could stand in for Ussher), there remained for me only this: to seek refuge with you, in your humanity and in that goodwill with which you have always deigned to regard me, though I did not deserve it, and with others under your patronage. May God, the best and greatest, grant that you may long hold the helm of the English Church, unharmed, for the increase of religion, the protection of the Orthodox faith and the comfort of the faithful; and that, with you presiding and God favouring, the storms that threaten us may be scattered. May what the malicious Frenchman once wrote in reproach of our nation in the cause of St Edmund, your predecessor, [It is the custom of that land to inflict injuries on good prelates], not be renewed in our times. This is the sincere prayer of Your Grace's most devoted chaplain and most humble client, Hen. Wharton.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: NON opus esse arbitror; ut quod Usseriano nomini inscriptum prodit, Lectori datâ operâ commendem. Nôrunt quotquot literas meliores colunt, nôrunt & semidocti; quanta fuerit Usserii & quàm diffusa eruditio, quàm infinita lectio, quanta judicii gravitas. Inter tot certè literaturæ Instauratores & Orthodoxæ Religionis Pugiles, quos Sæculo postremo tulit Orbis Britannicus; illum præ aliis habemus, quem nobismetipsis gratulemur, & in re literariâ Ducem statuamus.
units.tr: I do not think it necessary to recommend to the reader, with deliberate effort, what this work bears on the title-page under Ussher's name. All who cultivate better letters know it, and even the half-learned know it: how great and how wide-ranging Ussher's learning was, how boundless his reading, how weighty his judgment. Among the many restorers of letters and champions of the orthodox religion that the British world produced in the last century, we have him above others, whom we may congratulate ourselves on and set up as our leader in literary matters.

units.la: Neque magis etiam necessarium duco eam, quam in isthoc Opere Author iniit, Controversias pertractandi Methodum commendare. Jamdiu est, quòd Eruditis comprobari cœperit. Cùm Pontificii enim in Traditione refugium quærant; & erroribus suis Ecclesiæ Primitivæ auctoritatem prætexant; id potissimum nobis agendum, ut Erroris originem investigemus, ut adversantem Patrum autoritatem in medium proferamus, & uniuscujusque Sæculi sententiam ordine exquiramus. Quod quidem unico aut altero testimonio sive laciniâ ex Patrum scriptis adductâ atque hinc inde prolatâ parùm efficitur. Ejusmodi flosculi Scriptoris forsan alicujus sententiam exhibent, neque id quidem indubiè; erroris autem fontem nequaquam indicant. Unicum id igitur nobis faciendum restabat; quùm & his & illis rationibus solutiones jamdudum utrinque excogitatæ fuerint; quin & suas Scripturarum interpretationes mordicus teneant Pontificii, suas & Refor-
units.tr: Nor do I think it any more necessary to commend the method which the author has adopted in this work for handling controversies. It has long since begun to win the approval of the learned. For since the Papists seek refuge in tradition, and pretend that their errors have the authority of the Primitive Church, our chief task is this: to investigate the origin of the error, to bring forward the testimony of the Fathers that opposes it, and to trace the opinion of each century in order. This is hardly accomplished by one or two testimonies, or by a scrap taken from the writings of the Fathers and produced here and there. Such little flowers may perhaps show the opinion of some writer, and not even that with certainty, but they nowhere indicate the source of the error. This alone, therefore, remained for us to do, since answers to both kinds of argument have long been devised on both sides; and the Papists, and our Reformers too, cling stubbornly to their own interpretations of the Scriptures.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Reformati ; ut arbitri adhibeantur Patres ; ut sepositis utrinque sive ex Scripturâ, sive ex ratione ductis argumentis, Veterum Oracula consulantur ; ut Ecclesiæ praxis continuo Historiæ filo demonstretur : cujusmodi argumentis non ita facilè inveniri possunt effugia. Quas enim admittit Dialectica tricas & argutias, excludit Historia. Illi litem movere potest subtile atque acre ingenium ; huic sola frontis impudentia.
units.tr: Reformed; that the Fathers be called in as arbiters; that, with arguments drawn on both sides either from Scripture or from reason set aside, the oracles of the ancients be consulted; that the practice of the Church be demonstrated along the continuous thread of history. Against arguments of this kind, escape is not easily found. For Dialectic admits of tricks and subtleties, but History excludes them. Dialectic can be contested by a subtle and keen wit; History is met only by brazen impudence.

units.la: Atque utinam integram Controversiarum, quæ inter Orthodoxos & Pontificios agitantur, Historiam aut ab Usserio aut ab Ussérii non absimili conscriptam haberemus. Tunc in angustos fines redacta Controversia integram hominum ætatem non exerceret ; neque subtili disputantium calliditate in ævum continuari posset. Id Operis olim in animo habuit Ussierius ; quod quidem illi per temporum injuriam absolvere non licuit.
units.tr: Would that we had a complete history of the controversies debated between the Orthodox and the Papists, written by Ussher or by someone not unlike Ussher! Then the controversy, reduced to narrow limits, would not occupy the whole span of men's lives, nor could it be prolonged for ages by the subtle cunning of the disputants. Ussher once had this work in mind; but the injury of the times did not allow him to complete it.

units.la: Unica tanti Operis, quod meditatum esse diximus Ussefrium, pars restat iste, quem nunc demum evulgamus, Commentarius de Scripturis & Sacris Vernaculis. In isthoc enim argumento vires suas experiri cœpit, atque ideo nomen illi indidit ; Specimen Historiæ Dogmaticæ Quæstionum inter Orthodoxos & Pontificios controversarum. Verùm ne Specimen quidem suum finire illi datum est. Innumera etenim congesserat Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum testimonia ; totam lectionis suæ vim coacervaverat ; multa quidem secundùm temporis seriem disposuerat ; plurima autem prout in animum venerunt, aut legenti sese obtulerunt, sine ullo ordine, ullo partium contextu in Adversaria sua retulerat. Manebat adhuc Opus rudis indigestaque moles, ab Authore concinnandum & disponendum ; quod utinam fata dedissent. Quod quidem illi præ ingruentibus Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ turbis nunquam præstare licuit.
units.tr: The only part of so great a work, which we said Ussher had planned, is this commentary, On Scripture and the Vernacular Sacred Books, which we now at last publish. For in this subject he began to test his powers, and therefore gave it the title: A Specimen of a Dogmatic History of the Questions Controverted between the Orthodox and the Papists. But it was not granted to him to finish even this specimen. For he had gathered countless testimonies of ecclesiastical writers; he had heaped up the whole force of his reading; many things indeed he had arranged in chronological order, but most he had entered into his notebooks as they came to mind or presented themselves to him while reading, without any order or connection of parts. The work remained a rough and undigested mass, to be put together and arranged by its author; which, would that the fates had granted him. But the pressing troubles of the Church and the State never allowed him to accomplish this.

units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Autographum demum ab Authoris Hæredibus in Illustrissimi Primatis & colendissimi Patroni mei Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis potestatem devenit: qui perlectum Opus luce non indignum & Ecclesiæ non inutile judicabat, quamvis ultimum præstantissimi Authoris manum non expertum. Mihimet itaque operam dedit; ut rem conficerem, fœtumque imperfectum obstetricante manu in lucem producerem.
units.tr: The autograph at last came into the power of the author's heirs, and into that of the most illustrious Primate and my most revered patron, the Archbishop of Canterbury. He judged the completed work worthy of publication and not useless to the Church, although the most distinguished author had not himself applied the final touch. I therefore undertook the task myself: to put the thing in order and bring the unfinished offspring into the light, with a midwife's hand.

units.la: Principio itaque integrum Autographum manu propriâ descripsi; membra inordinata in sua quæque loca reposui; lacunas, prout potui, supplevi; omnia methodo continuâ disposui; testimonia quamplurima, ad quæ indicatis duntaxat Authorum locis Lectorem Usserius remiserat, conquisivi & appposui: singula cum vulgatis Authorum libris contuli, errata emendavi; denique Græca Latinis addidi. Neque enim in citandis Patrum Græcorum testimoniis Græca protulerat Author Illustrissimus (si pauculas demas lacinias, quas in ipso Opere expressas habes) neque in multis viderat. Plurima enim nondum Græcè erant edita.
units.tr: First, then, I copied out the whole autograph in my own hand; I put the disordered members back in their proper places; I filled the gaps as well as I could; I arranged everything in a continuous method; I gathered and inserted very many testimonies, to which Ussher had merely referred the reader by indicating the places in the authors. I compared each one with the printed editions of the authors and corrected the errors. Lastly, I added the Greek passages alongside the Latin. For the most illustrious author had not given the Greek when citing the testimonies of the Greek Fathers (apart from a few scraps which you find set out in the work itself), nor had he seen them in many cases, since most of them had not yet been published in Greek.

units.la: Historiæ Dogmaticæ de Scripturis & Sacris Vernaculis, comites dedi Dissertationes ejusdem Authoris binas, hactenus ineditas; alteram prolixiorem de Pseudo-Dionysii scriptis, breviorem alteram de Epistolâ ad Laodicenses. Utriusque copiam mihi fecit Reverendissimus in Christo Pater ac Dominus, Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis; qui posteriorem ex Usserii Adversariis manu propriâ olim descripserat; priorem etiam ab alio quodam mendosissimè exaratam, & sæpiùs hiulcam, Conjecturis suis in margine additis, plurimis in locis restituerat. Aderant & aliæ ejusdem Dissertationes de Ignatii & Clementis Romani scriptis. Cùm istæ autem nil haberent, quod in Notis editis ad Ignatii Epistolas Cl. Usserius non uberius tractaverit; rejiciendas duxi.
units.tr: To the Historia Dogmatica de Scripturis et Sacris Vernaculis I have added two dissertations by the same author, hitherto unpublished: the one, longer, on the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius, and the shorter one on the Epistle to the Laodiceans. The Most Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, the Archbishop of Canterbury, supplied me with copies of both. He had himself long ago copied out the latter in his own hand from Ussher's Adversaria, and had restored the former, which another hand had written very faultily and often with gaps, in very many places by means of his own conjectures added in the margin. There were also other dissertations by the same author on the writings of Ignatius and of Clement of Rome. Since these contained nothing that the learned Ussher had not treated more fully in his published notes on the Epistles of Ignatius, I decided to leave them out.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: Preface.

units.la: Ista de Illustrißimi Primatis Historiâ Dogmaticâ nunc recens editâ præfari necesse erat; ne famæ ejus injuria fieret, si (quod facilè auguror) Lector assis illius scriptis assuefactus, solitam eruditionem, nitorem, & judicium inibi desideraverit.
units.tr: These remarks had to be made before the Most Illustrious Primate's Dogmatic History, now newly published, is put forward; otherwise an injury would be done to his reputation if (as I easily foresee) the reader, accustomed to his writings, should miss there the usual learning, polish and judgement.

units.la: Quod Auctarium meum attinet; de eo nil magnum sentio: lucis tamen nonnihil argumento præsenti additurum spero. In eo quatuor præcipue præ oculis habui; ut Versionum Scripturæ Vernacularum Historiam (quod argumentum minimè exhauserat Usserius) perfectiorem darem; ut Ecclesiæ praxin ampliùs illustrarem; ut testimonia Veterum Patrum ab Usserio aut per incuriam omissa, aut illi incognita (scriptis quippe nondum evulgatis) exhiberem; & ut recentiorum testimonia è Codicibus Manuscriptis repræsentarem; quæ quidem Orbi Erudito minimè ingrata fore confido; cùm quòd argumentum præ manibus spectent; tum quòd plurimorum Authorum memoriam aut monumenta ab interitu vindicent. Si quæ ex vulgatis sequioris ævi Authoribus testimonia adhibeam; ejusmodi sunt, quæ legendi fastidium suâ gravitate facilè compensent.
units.tr: As for my own Appendix, I have no great opinion of it; yet I hope it will add something of light to the present subject. In writing it I kept four aims chiefly before my eyes: to give a fuller history of the vernacular versions of Scripture (a subject Ussher had not exhausted); to illustrate more fully the practice of the Church; to present the testimonies of the ancient Fathers which Ussher had either omitted through oversight or did not know (since their writings were not yet published); and to set out the testimonies of more recent writers from manuscript codices. I am confident these will not be unwelcome to the learned world, both because they concern the matter at hand and because they rescue the memory or the monuments of many authors from oblivion. If I adduce any testimonies from the printed authors of a later age, they are of a kind whose weight will easily compensate for any tedium in reading them.

units.la: Disputatio de primâ veritate {Καλλασκδαςικὴ / Αναςκευαςικὴ Historia, in quâ de Ethnicis (thesaurum hunc prorsus aspernantibus) Veteribus (inter quos & Christianos veteres eadem fuit differentia, atque inter nos & Pontificios) {Sua mysteria celantibus. Nostram Scripturam suppriment-ibus. Posterioribus, Turcis scilicet, simul cum Papistis haeresi natis. Judaeis, (quibus commissa primum sunt τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ) Videamus igitur nunc abscónderint sub modio aut serâ. Ita quidem Pharisaei. Nobis tamen favent veteres Rabbini ante Christum, & qui proximè Christo successerunt. Reliquios non moramur: quibus velum obductum. Veteribus {Ante Christum. / Post Christum (ubi de Pharisaeis usque ad Justinianum.) Posterioribus (quibus velum planè obductum est) ubi de Saadiae Gaonis Arabicâ versione & recentiorum Rabbinorum vulgaribus. Christianis Veteribus, à nato Christo ad natum Antichristum, primis ꝛc. 600 annis (in quorum fine Gregorii restimonium notetur de verbi Dei contemptu; & subjiciatur Authorum γεγενλογικὴ διαχυσεαλαίωσις) Orthodoxis {Ad annum 300. / à 300 ad 600. ubi horum notandae Sententiae hàc de re, & praxis. Haereticis, ubi nota Pontificios imitari non Ecclesiam, sed hostes Ecclesiae illis temporibus, tam Haereticos, quàm Ethnicos. Posterioribus {A nato Antichristo ad eundem adultum, à Greg. I. vel II. usque ad Greg. VII. sive ab anno 600. ad 1080. / Ab adultâ aetate Antichristi usq; ad senectam ejusdem ab anno 1080. ad nostra usque tempora, ubi de Haeretici (quos hîc praeter Turcas, imitandos sibi proposuerunt Pontificii) sunt Gnosimachi. Orthodoxi (ubi incipiendum à sententiâ tributâ Eusebio Emeseno. Orientalibus, communionis Graecanicae {Graecis. / Armenis, &c. Occidentalibus, qui {A Romanâ Ecclesiâ secessionem fecerunt {Waldens. Lollardis, Bohemis. In ejus communione permanserunt. Quae Historia perexenda est, ut intelligatur nondum ipsam Ecclesiam Romanum hic erroribus penitus corruptam esse.
units.tr: Disputation on the first truth. The history is either constructive [Κατασκευαστικὴ] or refutative [Ἀνασκευαστικὴ], and in it we treat of the following: of the Gentiles, who utterly despise this treasure; of the ancients, among whom the same difference existed between the ancient Christians as between us and the Papists, namely those who hide their own mysteries and suppress our Scripture; of the later ones, namely the Turks, together with the Papists, who were born of heresy; and of the Jews, to whom the oracles of God [τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ] were first entrusted. Let us see, then, whether they have hidden it under a bushel or behind a bolt. The Pharisees certainly did so. Yet the ancient rabbis before Christ, and those who came closest after Christ, favour us. We do not dwell on the rest, over whom a veil has been drawn. Of the ancients: before Christ; after Christ, where we treat of the Pharisees down to Justinian. Of the later ones, over whom the veil has been plainly drawn: where we treat of the Arabic version of Saadiah Gaon and of the common views of more recent rabbis. Of the early Christians, from the birth of Christ to the birth of Antichrist, that is, the first six hundred years (at the end of which the testimony of Gregory is to be noted concerning the contempt of the Word of God, and the genealogical dissolution of the authors is to be appended). Of the orthodox: up to the year 300; from 300 to 600, where the opinions and practice of the orthodox on this matter are to be noted. Of the heretics, where it is to be noted that the Papists imitate not the Church but the enemies of the Church of those times, both heretics and Gentiles. Of the later ones: from the birth of Antichrist to his adulthood, that is from Gregory I or II down to Gregory VII, or from the year 600 to 1080; from the adult age of Antichrist to his old age, from the year 1080 down to our own times, where the heretics (whom the Papists have proposed for themselves to imitate, besides the Turks) are the Gnosimachi. The orthodox, where one must begin with the opinion attributed to Eusebius of Emesa. Of the Orientals, in communion with the Greek church: the Greeks; the Armenians, etc. Of the Westerners, who seceded from the Roman Church: the Waldensians, the Lollards, the Bohemians, who remained in its communion. This history must be worked through so that it is understood that the Roman Church itself has not yet been wholly corrupted by errors here.

units.la: Ben Sira à quibusdam putatur esse Jesus Filius Sirach, ab Hebræis nepos Hieremiæ Prophetæ fuisse putatur. In sententiis ejus moralibus ita legimus: Cùm penès præceptorem suum sederet discendi gratiâ, dixit ad eum, Rabbi, doce me legere; Qui respondit ei, Nondum es capax disciplinæ, eò quòd adhuc pusillus es. [Atqui sapientes nostri piæ memoriæ dixerunt, puerum quinque annorum idoneum esse ad discenda Biblia] Videtur glossema Judæi ex Bag Bag, de quibus infra. Dixit illi Ben Sira: Nescis quod dici vulgò solet, Dies brevis est, & opus multum? Et tu dicis ad me; Quiesce, ne discas, adhuc enim pusillus es. Certè ego video in loco, ubi mortui sepeliuntur, me juniores mortuos esse. Quis novit, quid sit futurum, an diu sim superviciturus, an brevi moriturus?
units.tr: Some think Ben Sira is Jesus son of Sirach; the Hebrews think he was a grandson of the prophet Jeremiah. In his moral sayings we read as follows: When he was sitting with his teacher to learn, he said to him, Rabbi, teach me to read. He replied to him, You are not yet fit for instruction, because you are still small. [But our wise men of blessed memory have said that a boy of five is fit to learn the Bible.] This seems to be a gloss by a Jew from the Bag Bag, of whom below. Ben Sira said to him: Do you not know what is commonly said, The day is short and the work is great? And you say to me, Be quiet, do not learn, for you are still small. Surely I see that in the place where the dead are buried, the younger ones die before me. Who knows what will happen, whether I shall live long, or die soon?

units.la: Hillel, celeberrimus ille Hebræorum Doctor, anno 100. ante Templi secundi eversionem floruit; ut est in Talmud, ord. 2. Mașsécheth, Schalbath, & Elia præfat. in Methurgeman. Hujus sunt illæ sententiæ in Pirke Aboth, cap. 2. Qui multiplicat legem, multiplicat vitam; Qui comparat sibi verba legis, comparat sibi vitam futuri seculi.
units.tr: Hillel, that most celebrated of the Hebrew teachers, flourished a hundred years before the destruction of the second Temple, as is found in the Talmud, order 2, Massechet Shabbath, and in Elijah's preface to the Methurgeman. These are his sayings in Pirke Aboth, ch. 2: He who multiplies the law multiplies life; he who acquires for himself the words of the law acquires for himself life in the age to come.

units.la: Ex LXXX. Discipulis, quos excellenti ingenio ac doctrinâ præditos post se reliquit Hillel, (inter quos etiam fuisse dicitur Simeon Justus, qui Christum infantem suscepit in ulnis) maximus Jonathas Uzzielis filius extitit; minimus verò omnium Johannes Zacchæi filius, sacerdos, quem Judæi Raban Johanan Ben Zaccai vocant; ut habet P. Galatinus de Arcanis Catholicæ Veritatis, lib.1. cap. 2.
units.tr: Of the eighty disciples whom Hillel left behind after him, endowed with excellent talent and learning (among whom Simeon the Just, who took the infant Christ in his arms, is also said to have been), the greatest was Jonathan son of Uzziel; but the least of all was John son of Zaccheus, a priest, whom the Jews call Rabban Johanan ben Zaccai; as Galatinus has it in his De arcanis catholicae veritatis, book 1, ch. 2.

units.la: Et quidem Jonathas , ut Prophetici libri à vulgo Hebræorum commodiùs intelligi possent , Vetus Testamentum in Chaldaicam Linguam transtulit. Tantæque est apud Judæos authoritatis illius Paraphrasis, ut in ipsorum Synagogis, cum ipso Hebraeo textu perpetuo quodam more ad hunc usque diem legi consueverit. Ita quidem Tremellius Præfat. in Jonathæ Paraphr. 12. minor. Proph. à se Latinè conversi. Sed Onkelon solum legi ita solitum apparet ex Eliæ præfatione in Methurgeman. Authorem hujus paraphrasis longè antiquiorem putat Joannes Dinckelius ; cui suffragatur, quod in Talmud in Massécheth Megilah legitur, Jonathanem Prophetas Chaldaicè convertisse ex ore Haggæi, Zachariæ, & Malachiæ.
units.tr: Indeed Jonathan translated the Old Testament into the Chaldean language, so that the prophetic books might be more easily understood by the common people of the Hebrews. That Paraphrase has such authority among the Jews that, along with the Hebrew text itself, it has been customarily read in their synagogues in a continuous manner down to this day. So Tremellius says in the preface to his Latin version of Jonathan's paraphrase of the twelve minor Prophets, which he himself rendered into Latin. But it appears that only Onkelos was customarily read in this way, according to Elijah's preface to the Methurgeman. John Dinckel thinks the author of this paraphrase is much older; and this is supported by what is read in the Talmud, in tractate Megillah, that Jonathan translated the Prophets into Chaldean from the mouths of Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.

units.la: Johannis Zacchæi filii est illa sententia, cap. 2. Pirke Aboth. Si didicisti multam legem; non est bonum tibi ipsi adscribas; ad hoc enim creatus es. Ibidem etiam trium discipulorum illius (qui circa tempora Servatoris nostri vixerunt) sequentes habentur sententiæ.
units.tr: The following saying is from the son of Johanan Zaccai, ch. 2 of Pirke Aboth: If you have learned much law, do not ascribe it to yourself, for to this end you were created. In the same place are found the following sayings of three of his disciples, who lived around the time of our Saviour.

units.la: R. Josè dixit: Præpara teipsum ad discendam legem; non enim ea hæreditate tibi contingit.
units.tr: R. Jose said: Prepare yourself to learn the law, for it does not come to you by inheritance.

units.la: R. Eleazar. Da operam ad discendam legem; ut habeas quod respondeas Epicureo.
units.tr: R. Eleazar: Apply yourself to learning the law, so that you may have something to answer the Epicurean.

units.la: R. Simeon. Non teneris opus perficere; neque sic liber es, ut prorsus abstineas ab eo. Si didiceris multam legem; dabitur tibi multa merces. Fidelis enim est Dominus laboris tui, qui reddet tibi præmium laboris tui. Et scias, quòd merces justorum est in futuro seculo. Sensus est, (ut Judæi exponunt) hominem non teneri, ut totam legem edisca t, neque ut ab illâ penitus abstineat; sed præstet quantum potest. Hoc tamen sciat, quòd si multùm in discendâ lege sudaverit, multum & præmii à Deo reportabit, non quidem in præsenti, sed in futuro seculo.
units.tr: R. Simeon: You are not bound to finish the work, nor are you free to abstain from it altogether. If you have learned much law, you will be given great reward. For the Lord of your labour is faithful, who will repay you the reward of your labour. And know that the reward of the righteous is in the age to come. The sense is (as the Jews explain it) that a man is not bound to learn the whole law, nor to abstain from it entirely, but to do as much as he can. Yet he should know this: if he has laboured much in learning the law, he will also obtain much reward from God, not indeed in the present age, but in the age to come.

units.la: Ex ore R. Eleazaris & R. Josuæ (discipulorum Johannis Zacchæi filii) legem Chaldaicè interpretatus est Onkelus (ut ait R. Jeremias, sive R. Hija Abbæ filius in Talmud Massécheth Megilah) qui sororis
units.tr: Onkelos, who was the son of a sister of ..., translated the Law into Chaldee from the mouth of R. Eleazar and R. Joshua (disciples of John son of Zakkai), as R. Jeremiah, or R. Hija son of Abba, says in the Talmud, tractate Megillah.

units.la: {d} Vid. Strauchum in Psalm. 109. sol. 214. & in Psal. 102. f. 189. {e} Galatinus, lib. 1. cap. 3. & lib. 8. cap. 24. {f} Orat. de Linguâ Chaldaicâ & Syrâ. {g} Apud Masium Præfat. in Josuam. Titi filius fuisse dicitur (in ninakin, & Elia praefat. in Methurgeman.) Hunc vero totam Bibliam in Chaldaeum vertisse dicit Galatinus: Sed ejus editionem nunc, praeterquam in Pentateuchum, vix alicubi reperiri. Postea autem Munsterus retulit penes Johannem Dernschnammum fuisse Onkeli Paraphrasin in Prophetas, ex Budensis Bibliothecae spoliis.
units.tr: {d} See Strauchius on Psalm 109, p. 214, and on Psalm 102, p. 189. {e} Galatinus, book 1, chapter 3, and book 8, chapter 24. {f} Oration on the Chaldee and Syriac Language. {g} Cited by Masius, Preface to Joshua. He is said to have been the son of Titus (in ninakin and Elijah, Preface to Methurgeman). Galatinus says he translated the whole Bible into Chaldee, but his edition can now scarcely be found anywhere except for the Pentateuch. Later, however, Munster reported that Johann Dernschwam had possession of Onkelos's paraphrase of the Prophets, taken from the spoils of the Buda library.

units.la: Flavius Josephus, lib. 2. contra Apionem. 5 In unaquaque septimana ad legem audiendam conveniunt universi. Nostrorum quilibet de legibus interrogatus, facilius quam nomen suum recitat. Universas quippe mox a primo sensu discentes in animo velut inscriptas habemus.
units.tr: Flavius Josephus, book 2, Against Apion: Every week all people come together to hear the Law. If anyone of our people is asked about the laws, he recites them more readily than he gives his own name. For we learn them from the first use of reason and hold them as if inscribed in our minds.

units.la: Idem lib. 4. Antiquit. cap. ult. (De Mose verba faciens ad Deut. VI.) 6 Pueri etiam ante omnia leges edisce.nt; qua disciplina nec honestior est alia, nec ad felicitatem conducibilior. Et paulo ante [ex Deut. XI.] Septimo quoque anno, quando per Scenopegia festa apud Sanctam urbem sacrorum causa convenitur; Pontifex e sublimi suggesto, unde a tota multitudine exaudiri possit, legem pro concione legat; neque mulieres, & neque pueri ab audiendo arceantur: immo ne mancipia quidem. Nam bonum est legem ita animis impressam teneri, ut nunquam oblivione deleri possit. Sic enim neque peccabunt; cum ignorantiam rerum, quae in legibus definitae sunt, praetexere nequeant, &c.
units.tr: The same, book 4, Antiquities, last chapter (speaking of Moses, on Deuteronomy 6): Children also learn the laws before anything else; no discipline is more honourable or more conducive to happiness. And a little earlier [from Deuteronomy 11]: Every seventh year, at the Feast of Tabernacles, when people gather in the holy city for sacred purposes, the High Priest is to read the Law publicly from a high platform, where he can be heard by the whole multitude. Neither women nor children are to be kept from hearing it, nor even slaves. For it is good that the Law be so impressed upon the mind that it can never be erased by forgetting. Thus they will not sin, since they cannot plead ignorance of what has been defined in the laws, etc.

units.la: Idem, lib. 2. contra Apionem [de Mose agens.] 7 Jussitque filios literis erudiri propter leges, & nosse progenitorum actiones, ut actus imitentur; & cum legibus educati neque transgrediantur, neque cogitationem 8 ignorationis habere judicentur.
units.tr: The same, book 2, Against Apion (speaking of Moses): He also commanded that their sons be educated in letters for the sake of the laws, and to know the deeds of their forefathers, so that they may imitate the deeds; and that, brought up with the laws, they neither transgress them nor are judged to have an excuse of ignorance.

units.la: Ipsum Josephum ab infantia sacris literis eruditum esse confirmat Hieronymus, Tom. 2. Epist. 84. ad Magnum.
units.tr: Jerome confirms that Josephus was instructed in sacred letters from infancy, Vol. 2, Letter 84 to Magnus.

units.la: 8 Melius excusationem seu praetextum ignorantiae, ... (Greek note, right column) in jejunio propitiationis faciunt, ostendit Galatinus . Hujus est sententia illa in Pirke Aboth, cap. 3. Duo qui accumbunt mensæ, & non colloquuntur de lege; ecce iste est confessus irrisorum, de quo dicit Scriptura , & in concessu irrisorum non sedit. Veruntatem duo qui assident mensæ, & colloquia habent de lege; divinitas quiescit super eos.
units.tr: 8 It is better to make excuse, or a pretext, of ignorance ... [Melius excusationem seu praetextum ignorantiae ...] (Greek note, right column). They do this in the fast of atonement, as Galatinus shows. Of this is that saying in Pirke Aboth, chapter 3: Two who sit at a table and do not talk about the Law: this is the seat of scoffers, of which Scripture speaks, "and he has not sat in the seat of scoffers." But two who sit at a table and converse about the Law: the Divine Presence rests upon them.

units.la: Similis est ibidem sententia R. Simeonis . Tres qui edunt in unâ mensâ, neque loquuntur in eâ verba legis; perinde est ac si comedissent de sacrificiis mortuorum. Cæterum tres, qui cibum capiunt in unâ mensâ, & conferunt in eâ verba legis; perinde est ac si comedissent de mensâ ipsius Dei.
units.tr: A similar saying in the same place is that of R. Simeon: Three who eat at one table and do not speak words of the Law over it are as if they had eaten of the sacrifices of the dead. But three who take food at one table and discuss words of the Law over it are as if they had eaten at the table of God himself.

units.la: R. Meir in Pirke Aboth, cap. 4. Minue negotia, & vaca legi. Si vacare velis à lege, multa erunt, quæ te avocabunt; sed si laboraveris in lege, multa merces tibi dabitur.
units.tr: R. Meir, in Pirke Aboth, chapter 4: Lessen your business and devote yourself to the Law. If you wish to be free from the Law, there will be many things that call you away; but if you labour in the Law, a great reward will be given you.

units.la: R. Eleazar Jacobi filius . Qui legem discit in pueritiâ, cui similis est? Ei qui scribit in chartâ novâ. Qui verò legem discit in senectute, cui similis est? Ei qui scribit in chartâ veterè.
units.tr: R. Eleazar son of Jacob: Who learns the Law in childhood, to what is he like? To one who writes on fresh paper. But who learns the Law in old age, to what is he like? To one who writes on used paper.

units.la: R. Jehoschua filius Levi: Omni die filia vocis (i. e. vox cœlitus sonans) egreditur de monte Horeb, & præconizat: Væ hominibus ob ignominiam legis. Quicunque enim non exercet se in Lege, culpabilis vocatur. Nullus verò sive liber, sive nobilis, habendus est; nisi is qui exercet se in studio legis. Pirke Aboth cap. 6.
units.tr: R. Joshua son of Levi: Every day a voice (that is, a voice sounding from heaven) goes forth from Mount Horeb and proclaims: Woe to men for the reproach of the Law. For whoever does not exercise himself in the Law is called guilty. Nor is anyone to be considered free or noble unless he exercises himself in the study of the Law. Pirke Aboth, chapter 6.

units.la: Ibid. cap. 5. adducitur sententia בן בן בן (ita appellatus est Rabbinus magni nominis ex Paganismo ad Judaismum conversus, quasi בן גל ובן גלח) de meditatione legis divinæ: Verte eam, & iterum verte eam: omnia enim in eâ sunt. In eâ item totus esto, neque unquam discedas ab eâ: non enim habes melius eâ exercitium.
units.tr: In the same place, chapter 5, a saying is cited of ben Bag Bag (so called after a rabbi of great renown who was converted from paganism to Judaism, as if ben Gal ve-ben Galach) concerning meditation on the divine Law [בן בג בג]: Turn it, and turn it again, for all is in it. Be wholly in it, and never depart from it, for you have no better occupation than this.

units.la: In Talmud Hierosolymitano, Tractatu Suta: Quùm R. Levi Cæsaream venîsset, audivit aliquos recitantes שמע audi (precatio est, quæ incipit: Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus, &c.) Græcè, Volebat itaque interdicere. Quod cùm audivisset R. Joses; iratus dixit: Quicumque eam Syriacè recitare nescit, ne recitet; sed reciter eâ linguâ quam intelligit. Hoc patto suo muneri satisfacit. Verba Hebræa extant apud Angelum Caninium de locis N. T. p. 13.
units.tr: In the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Sotah: When R. Levi had come to Caesarea, he heard some reciting the Shema [שמע, "hear"] (a prayer beginning, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God," etc.) in Greek. He therefore wished to forbid it. But when R. Jose heard this, he was angry and said: Whoever cannot recite it in Syriac, let him not recite it; but let him recite it in the language he understands. In this way he fulfils his duty. The Hebrew words are found in Angelus Caninius, On the Places of the New Testament, p. 13.

units.la: Omne quod egressum est ab ore Domini, divisum est in LXX. linguas; inquiunt Talmudici in Tract. Sabbath, cap. 9. (Prolegom. Bibl. Polar. pag. 68. col. 2.) ut Anastasius Sinaita, & Theodoretus.
units.tr: Everything that has gone forth from the mouth of the Lord was divided into seventy tongues, say the Talmudists in tractate Sabbath, chapter 9 (Prolegomena to the Polyglot Bible, p. 68, col. 2), as also Anastasius of Sinai and Theodoret.

units.la: Circa annum Domini 552. inter Hebraeos magna exorta est controversia; eo quod nonnulli Hebraica tantum lingua in sacrorum librorum lectione uti vellent; nec Graecam tradere dignarentur. Re vero ad Justinianum Imp. delata, illorum sententia confirmata est, qui Graecam etiam assumendam putarunt , & linguam omnem simpliciter, quam locus aptiorem & magis cognitam audientibus faceret. Ciutumque est, ut neque damnis aliquibus subjicerentur omnino, qui Graecam vocem & alias traderent; neque ab alio quovis prohiberentur; neque licentiam haberent Rabbini illorum anathematismis aliquibus hoc prohibere; corporalibus alioqui poenis, & privatione facultatum castigandi. In Authenticis Collat. 9. tit. 28. est Novell. Constitut. 46.
units.tr: Around the year of the Lord 552 a great controversy arose among the Hebrews, because some wished to use only the Hebrew language in reading the sacred books, and did not deign to deliver them in Greek. The matter was referred to the Emperor Justinian, and the judgement of those was confirmed who thought that Greek should also be adopted, and every tongue simply, which would make the place more suitable and better known to the hearers. It was decreed that those who rendered the Greek word and others should not be subjected to any penalties at all, nor be forbidden by anyone; and that the rabbis should not have the licence to forbid this by any anathemas of theirs, under bodily punishments and loss of property otherwise. See the Authentic Collation 9, title 28, and Novel Constitution 146.

(vol. 8, 9, 20, pp. 37–38). See Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 12, chapters 2, 12 and 14; and Chrysostom (vol. 2, 3, 14, p. 261); and Aben Ezra; and Ribera, cited by T. Morton, part 2, Apology, p. 56; and Elpenaeus, ibid., p. 60. See Masius on Joshua, p. 157, from Sotah (against p. 159), and p. 25, from Bereshit Rabbah.

units.la: IN Epistola ad Philadelphios, quæ huic tribuitur, ita legimus: Patres educate filios vestros in disciplina & admonitione Domini, & docete eos sacras literas & artes, ut non dedant se otio & inertiæ. Honestè (inquit) educat justus pater liberos; in filio sapienti lætabitur cor ejus. Οι πατέρες εκτρέφετε τὰς ἑαυτῶν παῖδας ἐν παιδείᾳ ἢ νουθεσίᾳ κυρίου. Καὶ διδάσκετε αὐτὰς τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, ἢ τεχνὰς πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀργὰ χαίρειν. Καλῶς ᾖ, φησὶν, ἐκτρέφει δίκαιος, ὅτι ἐμοὶ συνέταξεν ἀπεργάσασθαι ἡ χαρὰ αὐτοῦ. Ibidem de Virginibus agens, pudicitiam servandam monet, ἀλλ' ἵνα τῶν νόμων μελέτῃ. h. e. (ut vertit Sylvius) non in calumniam matrimonii, sed ut liberioribus animis divinæ legis meditationi vacent. 1
units.tr: In the Epistle to the Philadelphians, which is attributed to him, we read as follows: Fathers, bring up your children in the discipline and admonition of the Lord, and teach them the sacred letters and the arts, so that they do not give themselves over to idleness and sloth. "Honourably," he says, "a righteous father brings up his children; his heart will rejoice in a wise son." [Οι πατέρες εκτρέφετε τὰς ἑαυτῶν παῖδας ἐν παιδείᾳ ἢ νουθεσίᾳ κυρίου. Καὶ διδάσκετε αὐτὰς τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, ἢ τεχνὰς πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀργὰ χαίρειν. Καλῶς ᾖ, φησὶν, ἐκτρέφει δίκαιος, ὅτι ἐμοὶ συνέταξεν ἀπεργάσασθαι ἡ χαρὰ αὐτοῦ.] Speaking of virgins in the same place, he urges that chastity be kept, not as a slander on marriage, but so that with freer minds they may devote themselves to meditation on the divine law [ἀλλ' ἵνα τῶν νόμων μελέτῃ], that is (as Sylvius translates it) 1

units.la: Atque hoc nomine, Epist. 1. Mariam Cassoboliten commendat propter 2 crebrò ab ipsâ citata Scripturarum loca: Eandemque in fine Epistolæ ad Heronem exemplar sanctissimarum fœminarum facit. Vid. Epist. ad Smyrnæos.
units.tr: For this reason, in Epistle 1, he commends Mary the Cassobolite, because of the passages of Scripture that she often cites. At the end of the Epistle to Hero, he also holds her up as a model of most holy women. See the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans.

units.la: 1 Sic etiam vertit Vetus Interpres Latinus. 2 Ἰλαρὸν δέ με ἴσως αἱ συνεχῶς σε τ' γεραιῶν χρείαν μνῆναι. 3 Ἐντυχὼν ᾧ δέλεας τῆς περιπτῶν ἰσοείαις, ἡ γνῶναι παρ' αὐτῆς τ' ἀληθῆ διόδευσιν——τὸ ἄριον πνεῦμα τοῦ τ' ἀληθῆ διδάσκειν παρδάσκειν βουλομένη δι' αὐτῆς διδάσκειν πεπληρωμένη. libris, & ex eis veram addiscere religionem, non dicendi artes profitentibus, neque verbis ad permovendum atque persuadendum compositis utentibus (hoc enim eorum est proprium qui veritatem suffurari studio habent) verum qualiacunque simpliciter nomina & verba usurpantibus, & eas vobis res annunciantibus, quas descendens in eos Spiritus Sanctus religionem veram discere volentes, per illos docendos esse statuit. Et paulo post; 4 Reliquum fuerit, ut remisso majorum vestrorum errori nuncio sanctorum virorum legatis vaticinia (non splendorem orationis ab eis petentes: Quod non in dictis sed in factis res nostrae religionis consistant) & ex ipsis ea percipiatis, per quae vitam possitis consequi sempiternam.
units.tr: 1 So also the Old Latin translator renders it. 2 I am glad, perhaps, that you often recall the need of the elders. 3 Having fallen in with a certain ... wishing through her to learn the true teaching ... books, and from them to learn the true religion, not from those who profess the arts of speaking, nor from those who use words composed to move and persuade (for this belongs to those who are eager to steal the truth), but from those who simply use plain names and words, and announce to you those things which the Holy Spirit, descending upon them, decided should be taught through them to those who wish to learn the true religion. And a little later: It remains that, having set aside the error of your forefathers, you should receive from the messengers of holy men the prophecies (not seeking from them the polish of oratory, since the matters of our religion consist not in words but in deeds), and from them learn those things through which you can attain eternal life.

units.la: In Epistola ad Zenam & Serenum de vita Christiana. Quocirca vigilare debemus, responsis Salvatoris navantes [operam] ac nihil de quoquam mali vel dicentes vel audientes. Διὰ τοῦτο χρηγορητέον τοῖς λόγοις τῆς σωτηρίας ... Et paulo post. Quaerendum autem de divinis oraculis; ac si quidem prudenter, pulchrum id fuerit; sin secus, ad instar tamen idiotarum & imperitorum [id faciemus.] Insipienti namque sapientiam inquirenti sapientia imputabitur. Ζητητέον ... σοφίαν σοφία λογισμός.
units.tr: In the Epistle to Zena and Serenus, on the Christian life: Wherefore we ought to be watchful, devoting ourselves to the answers of the Saviour, and saying or hearing nothing evil of anyone. [Διὰ τοῦτο χρηγορητέον τοῖς λόγοις τῆς σωτηρίας ...] And a little later: We ought to inquire into the divine oracles; and if we do so wisely, it will be fine; if otherwise, nevertheless we shall do it in the manner of the unlearned and inexperienced. For to one who foolishly seeks wisdom, wisdom will be imputed. [Ζητητέον ... σοφίαν σοφία λογισμός.]

units.la: In Apologia II. Pro Christianis ad Antoninum Pium, ordinem sacrorum Christianorum ita describit. 5 Solis, qui dicitur, die, omnium, qui vel in oppidis vel ruri degunt, in eundem locum conventus fit, & commentaria Apostolorum aut scripta Prophetarum, quoad tempus fert, leguntur. Deinde Lectore quiescente, Praesidens orationem, quâ populum instruit, & ad imitationem tam pulchrarum rerum cohortatur, habet. Sub hæc consurgimus communiter omnes. Et precationes profundimus. En horum temporum venerandam simplicitatem. I. In conventu fratrum S. Scripturæ legebantur. II. Sequebatur concio continens ... quâ sc. admonebatur populus, ut bona illa imitarentur, quæ ex lectione sacra audiverant. Unde intelligitur scripta Apostolica & Prophetica nequaquam in peregrinâ linguâ fuisse recitata. Atque hinc illud in Patrum concionibus solenne c: Au-
units.tr: In the Second Apology for the Christians, addressed to Antoninus Pius, he describes the order of the Christian sacred assemblies thus: On the day called Sunday, all who live either in the towns or in the countryside gather in one place, and the memoirs of the Apostles or the writings of the Prophets are read, as long as time allows. Then, when the reader has finished, the president gives an address, in which he instructs the people and exhorts them to imitate such excellent things. After this we all rise together and send up our prayers. Behold the venerable simplicity of those times. I. In the assembly of the brothers the Holy Scriptures were read. II. There followed a sermon, in which, namely, the people were admonished to imitate those good things which they had heard in the sacred reading. Whence it is clear that the Apostolic and Prophetic writings were by no means recited in a foreign tongue. Hence that customary formula in the sermons of the Fathers: Au-

units.la: {a} Nullâ re. {c} Vid. Chrysost. init. Homil. 1. ad populum Antioch.
units.tr: {a} By no means. {c} See Chrysostom, at the beginning of Homily 1 to the people of Antioch.

units.la: 4 Λεγὼν ... ἐντυγχάνειν ... 5 Τῇ τε ... ἡμέρᾳ ... (Greek notes in two columns) divisis vocem Apostoli, &c. III. Preces ab omnibus κοινὴ habebantur. Erat actio communis, non Sacerdotis propria. Et quidem intellectâ linguâ conceptas fuisse preces illas ex præcedenti narratione intelligitur; ubi docet quòd preces & supplicationes communes à fratribus peractæ essent ὁμοθυμαδὸν animo intento; precibusque absolutis, πᾶς ὁ παρὼν λαὸς ἐπευφημεῖ λέγων Ἀμήν. Populus, qui aderat, omnis faustâ approbatione acclamaverit, Amen dicens.
units.tr: 4 Saying ... to meet/encounter ... 5 On the ... day ... (Greek notes in two columns) the voice of the Apostle divided, etc. III. Prayers were offered by all in common [κοινὴ]. It was a common action, not the proper action of the priest. And indeed, from the preceding narrative it is understood that those prayers were composed in an intelligible language; where he teaches that the common prayers and supplications were performed by the brothers with one accord [ὁμοθυμαδὸν] with minds intent; and when the prayers were finished, all the people present acclaim, saying Amen [πᾶς ὁ παρὼν λαὸς ἐπευφημεῖ λέγων Ἀμήν]. All the people who were present acclaimed with a favourable assent, saying Amen.

units.la: Oratione contra Græcos. 6 Hoc in singulis rebus intelligi potest ab illo, qui non superbè respuerit divina eloquia: quæ paulatim è sacris libris observata, prorsus Deo acceptos reddunt illos, qui animum eis applicaverint. Item 7 Nostræ verò omnes pudicæ sunt, & intentæ lanificio virgines divinos sermones edisserunt, multo honestiore, quam vestra Puella, studio.
units.tr: From the Oration against the Greeks, 6: "This can be understood in every matter by anyone who does not proudly reject the divine words; which, gradually observed from the sacred books, make those who apply their minds to them wholly acceptable to God." Likewise, 7: "But our virgins, all of them chaste and devoted to wool-working, expound the divine discourses, with a far more honourable zeal than your girl (Puella)."

units.la: 184. Theophilus, Antiochenus Episcopus
units.tr: 184. Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch

units.la: Lib. 1. ad Autolycum, Christianæ Religionis calumniatorem, in fine. 8 Verùm tu ipse, si placet, consule sacras literas. Hæ etenim majore evidentiâ te instituere possunt, quo pacto possis evitare sempiternas pœnas, & nancisci perpetua bona; quæ suis cultoribus pollicetur Deus.
units.tr: Book 1 to Autolycus, a calumniator of the Christian religion, near the end. But you yourself, if you please, consult the sacred letters. For they can instruct you with greater clarity how you may escape everlasting punishments and obtain the perpetual goods which God promises to his worshippers.

units.la: Lib. 2. ad eundem. Ad quid necesse est multitudinem enumerare Prophetarum, qui plurimi extitere; & omnia inter se consona, adeò ut nulla contrarietas deprehendi possit, protulere. 9 Si quis ea scire gestit, Prophetarum januæ patent. Hos legat accedens mente purâ, & exactè veritatem ipsam cognoscet.
units.tr: Book 2 to the same. Why is it necessary to list the multitude of the Prophets, who were very many, and who set forth everything in agreement with one another, so that no contradiction can be detected? If anyone wishes to know them, the gates of the Prophets lie open. Let him read them with a pure mind, and he will know the truth itself exactly.

units.la: Et in fine ejusdem libri, 10 Oportet te, si es discendi cupidus, frequentius accedere Scripturam sacram, ut vivas; & audiens vocem Dei, ad unguem (quod aiunt) veritatem consequêre.
units.tr: And at the end of the same book: You ought, if you are eager to learn, to come more often to the sacred Scripture, that you may live; and hearing the voice of God, you will attain the truth to a nicety, as they say.

units.la: 6 Τὰς ἁγιωτάτας ἐρμηνείας, αἱ χρὴ χρόνον διαγεγραφὰς ἐξελληνισμέναι πάντα σοφιλὴς τοῦ περιέχοντας αὐτῆς ἀποποίησιν. 7 Ἰάσου δ᾽ αἱ παρ᾽ ἡμῖν σωφροσύναι, ᾗ οἱ τὰς ἱλαρότητας αἱ παρθένοι τὸ μὴ ὅσον λαλεῖν ἐκφωνήματα. 8 Εἰ δ᾽ βούλει ᾗ οὖ, ἵνα χρῇ φιλοπάμως ἢ περιπ-φρπικαῖς γεγραφὰς, ᾗ αὐταί σι τεγυβτιτιερ ὀλλ-γήσομ, &c. 9 Οἱ γὰρ βουλόμενοι λύναι ἐπιγεγόντες τῆς ἀληθείας αὐτῆ ἐρημίας, ἀκριβῶς γνῶναι τὸ ἀληθὲς, &c. 10 Χρὴ ἐν ἡ φιλομαθὴς ᾗ φιλομαθῶν, πεποίηται ἐν πυκνότερον συμβαλεῖν, &c.
units.tr: 6 The most holy translations, which have been written down over time and rendered into Greek, reject every wise ... [Τὰς ἁγιωτάτας ἐρμηνείας, αἱ χρὴ χρόνον διαγεγραφὰς ἐξελληνισμέναι πάντα σοφιλὴς τοῦ περιέχοντας αὐτῆς ἀποποίησιν.] 7 Among us, the chastity of the virgins who are intent on wool-working and who expound divine words is far more honourable [Ἰάσου δ᾽ αἱ παρ᾽ ἡμῖν σωφροσύναι, ᾗ οἱ τὰς ἱλαρότητας αἱ παρθένοι τὸ μὴ ὅσον λαλεῖν ἐκφωνήματα.] 8 And if you wish ... [Εἰ δ᾽ βούλει ᾗ οὖ, ἵνα χρῇ φιλοπάμως ἢ περιπ-φρπικαῖς γεγραφὰς, ᾗ αὐταί σι τεγυβτιτιερ ὀλλ-γήσομ, &c.] 9 For those who wish to loosen ... to know exactly what is true [Οἱ γὰρ βουλόμενοι λύναι ἐπιγεγόντες τῆς ἀληθείας αὐτῆ ἐρημίας, ἀκριβῶς γνῶναι τὸ ἀληθὲς, &c.] 10 It is necessary ... to come together more often [Χρὴ ἐν ἡ φιλομαθὴς ᾗ φιλομαθῶν, πεποίηται ἐν πυκνότερον συμβαλεῖν, &c.]

units.la: 184. Irenæus, Lugdunensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 184. Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons

units.la: Lib. 2. adv. Hæreses, cap. 46. Universæ Scripturæ, & Propheticæ & Evangelicæ, II in aperto, & sine ambiguitate, & similiter ab omnibus audiri possunt.
units.tr: Book 2 against the Heresies, ch. 46. All Scripture, both prophetic and evangelical, can be heard openly and without ambiguity, and in the same way by all.

units.la: Lib. 5. cap. 17. (vel 20. ut est in Feuardentii editione) Confugere [oportet] ad Ecclesiam, & in ejus sinu educari, & Dominicis Scripturis enutriri. Plantata est enim Ecclesiæ Paradisus in hoc mundo. Ab omni ergo ligno Paradisi escas manducabis, ait Spiritus Dei, i.e. ab omni Scriptura Dominica manducate.
units.tr: Book 5, ch. 17 (or 20, as in Feuardent's edition). [We ought] to take refuge in the Church, to be brought up in her bosom and nourished on the Lord's Scriptures. For the Paradise of the Church has been planted in this world. Therefore, "of every tree of the garden you may freely eat," says the Spirit of God; that is, eat from every Scripture of the Lord.

units.la: Lib. 3. cap. 12. Hæc autem omnia contulit eis [Hæreticis] Scripturarum & dispositionis Dei ignorantia.
units.tr: Book 3, ch. 12. But ignorance of the Scriptures and of the dispensation of God brought all these things upon them [the heretics].

units.la: 198. Clemens Alexandrinus
units.tr: 198. Clement of Alexandria

units.la: In λόγῳ προτρεπτικῷ πρὸς Ἕλληνας, p. 56. edit. Parisi. 1629. Sunt 12 verè sacræ literæ, quæ sacros faciunt & deificant. Ex quibus literis & sacris syllabis compositas Scripturas & opera Paulus Apostolus appellat divinitus inspiratas; ut quæ sint utiles ad docendum, &c. prout 2 Tim. 3. habetur. Et post. Ἀκούσατε οἱ μαχεταὶ, ἀκούσατε δὲ ἐγγυς. Οὐκ ἀπεκρύβη τινας ὁ λόγος. Φῶς γὰρ κοινὸν, ἐπιλάμπει πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις. Οὐδεὶς ἀμμυνεῖς ἐν λόγῳ. Ἐπιδυσόμεθα εἰς σωτηρίαν, ὅτι τὸ παλιγγενεσίαν. Audite ergo qui estis longè; audite qui prope. Nullis celatum est verbum; lux est communis, omnibus illucescit hominibus. Nullus est in verbo Cimmerius: festinemus ad salutem, ad regenerationem.
units.tr: In the Exhortation to the Greeks, p. 56, Paris edition of 1629. There are truly sacred letters, which make sacred and deify those who read them. From these letters and sacred syllables, the Apostle Paul calls the Scriptures and the works composed from them divinely inspired, as profitable for teaching, etc., as is found in 2 Tim. 3. And afterwards: Ἀκούσατε οἱ μαχεταὶ, ἀκούσατε δὲ ἐγγυς. Οὐκ ἀπεκρύβη τινας ὁ λόγος. Φῶς γὰρ κοινὸν, ἐπιλάμπει πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις. Οὐδεὶς ἀμμυνεῖς ἐν λόγῳ. Ἐπιδυσόμεθα εἰς σωτηρίαν, ὅτι τὸ παλιγγενεσίαν. Hear then, you who are far off; hear, you who are near. The Word has been hidden from no one. It is a common light, shining on all men. No one is a Cimmerian in the Word. Let us hasten to salvation, to regeneration.

units.la: Lib. 1. Stromatum, p. 288. 13 Propterea Græcâ voce expositæ sunt Scripturæ; ut nullum unquam ignorantiæ possint prætextum afferre; cùm possint quæ sunt apud nos audire, si tantùm voluerint.
units.tr: Book 1 of the Stromata, p. 288. 13 Therefore the Scriptures were expounded in the Greek language, so that they can never plead ignorance as a pretext, since they can hear what is among us, if only they are willing.

units.la: Lib. 7. Strom. p. 728. Vitam Christiani hominis describens, Universa ejus vita, inquit, est tanquam quidam celebris ac sanctus dies 14
units.tr: Book 7 of the Stromata, p. 728. Describing the life of a Christian man, he says: The whole of his life is like a certain celebrated and holy day. 14

units.la: d Christum, opinor, intelligit.
units.tr: I think he means by this Christ.

units.la: 11 Φανερῶς γὰρ ἀναμφιςβόλως, apud Damascenum in parallelis.
units.tr: 11 For clearly and without doubt [Φανερῶς γὰρ ἀναμφιςβόλως], in Damascene's Parallels.

units.la: 12 Ἐκκλησία γὰρ ὡς ἀληθῶς τὰ ἱερογραφικὰ στοιχεῖα γεγεννημένα, ἐξ ὧν γεγεννημένων ἐκ συλλογῶν τῶν ἱερῶν τῶν συγγεγραμμένων γραφῶν ἐκ συντάγματα ὁ ἐποτὸν, &c.
units.tr: 12 For the Church, truly, having been begotten from the hieroglyphic elements, from which, having been begotten from collections of the sacred written Scriptures, ... [Ἐκκλησία γὰρ ὡς ἀληθῶς τὰ ἱερογραφικὰ στοιχεῖα γεγεννημένα, ἐξ ὧν γεγεννημένων ἐκ συλλογῶν τῶν ἱερῶν τῶν συγγεγραμμένων γραφῶν ἐκ συντάγματα ὁ ἐποτὸν, &c.]

units.la: 13 Διὰ τοῦτο τὸ Ἑλλήνων γραφὴ ἐμφυλῶν ἐπ' αὐτοῦ, οὐ μὴν πεφασμένην ἀγνοίας περὶ ἐκ... ἐκ ... &c.
units.tr: 13 For this reason the writing of the Greeks ... among them, but not made known from ignorance ... [Διὰ τοῦτο τὸ Ἑλλήνων γραφὴ ἐμφυλῶν ἐπ' αὐτοῦ, οὐ μὴν πεφασμένην ἀγνοίας περὶ ἐκ... ἐκ ... &c.]

units.la: 14 Θυσίαι ὡς αὐτῶν, αἱ πι ἐκ λόγου, καὶ αἱ ὑμνοι ... ἐπὶ ἐσιαν, &c. festus. Atque ei quidem sacrificia sunt ipsæ preces & laudes, & quæ ante cibum fiunt, Scripturarum lectiones; Psalmi autem & hymni, dum e cibus sumitur; antequam eatur cubitum. Quinetiam nocte rursus orationes.
units.tr: 14 Sacrifices, as they say, are the prayers and hymns ... [Θυσίαι ὡς αὐτῶν, αἱ πι ἐκ λόγου, καὶ αἱ ὑμνοι ... ἐπὶ ἐσιαν, &c.] For to him, indeed, sacrifices are the prayers and praises themselves, and the readings of Scripture which are made before food; the Psalms and hymns while the food is taken; and before going to bed. Moreover, at night again, prayers.

units.la: Lib. 6. Stromatum, non utilem solum, verùm etiam necessariam esse, Scripturæ lectionem confirmat. 15 Tum alia doctrina est utilis, tum Scripturarum lectio est necessaria.
units.tr: Book 6 of the Stromata confirms that the reading of Scripture is not only useful but also necessary. 15 Other teaching is useful, but the reading of the Scriptures is necessary.

units.la: 100. Leonides Martyr.
units.tr: 100. Leonides Martyr.

units.la: Ab eo attentâ curâ laboratum est, ut filius Origenes sacras literas à primo tempore ætatis edisceret. 16 Omnino enim ante liberalium artium & politioris doctrinæ studium, eum sacris literis instituendum exercendumque tradidit. Ac sententias aliquot, quas ei cùm ad verbum addiscendas, tum memoriter coràm ipso recitandas præscripserat, ab illo in dies singulos exegit. [Eusebius, lib. 6. Hist. cap. 2.
units.tr: His father took careful pains to have his son Origen learn the sacred letters from his earliest years. 16 For indeed, before the study of the liberal arts and of more refined learning, he handed him over to be instructed and trained in the sacred letters. And some sentences, which he had ordered him to learn by heart and to recite from memory in his presence, he required of him day by day. [Eusebius, Hist. lib. 6, cap. 2.

units.la: 240. Origenes Adamantius
units.tr: 240. Origen Adamantius

units.la: In Genes. XXIV. Homil. 10. Animarum est eruditio, & spiritalis doctrina, quæ te instituit; & decet quotidie venire ad puteos Scripturarum, ad aquas Spiritūs Sancti, & haurire semper, ac plenum vas domum referre: sicut faciebat & Sancta Rebecca. Ibid. Christiani omni die carnes Agni comedunt; i. e. carnes verbi Dei quotidie sumunt.
units.tr: In Genesis, Homily 10 on chapter 24: It is the instruction of souls and a spiritual teaching that trains you; and one ought to come every day to the wells of the Scriptures, to the waters of the Holy Spirit, and always draw and carry home a full vessel, as holy Rebecca did. Ibid.: Christians eat the flesh of the Lamb every day; that is, they receive the flesh of the Word of God daily.

units.la: In Genes. XXVI. Homil. 12. Tentemus facere illud, quod Sapientia commonet, dicens f; Bibe aquas de tuis fontibus, & de tuis puteis; & sit tibi fons tuus proprius. Tenta ergo & tu, o auditor, habere proprium puteum & proprium fontem; ut & tu, cùm apprehenderis librum Scripturarum, incipias etiam ex proprio sensu proferre aliquem intellectum: & secundùm ea quæ in Ecclesiâ didicisti, tenta & tu bibere de fonte ingenii tui.
units.tr: In Genesis, Homily 12 on chapter 26: Let us try to do what Wisdom advises, saying: Drink waters from your own cisterns and your own wells, and let your own spring be yours alone. So you too, hearer, try to have your own well and your own spring, so that when you take up the book of the Scriptures you too may begin to bring forth some understanding from your own sense; and, according to what you have learned in the Church, try to drink from the spring of your own mind.

units.la: In Exod. XXXIV. Homil. 12. Si studio, actibus, mente, sollicitudine verbo Dei operam demus, & in lege ejus die ac nocte meditemur, omissis omnibus Deo vacemus, exerceamur in testimoniis ejus; hoc est conversum
units.tr: In Exodus, Homily 12 on chapter 34: If we devote ourselves to the Word of God with zeal, with action, with mind and with care, and meditate on his law day and night, setting aside everything else, and give ourselves to God, and exercise ourselves in his testimonies; this is to be turned
