units.tr: <bl>e</bl> Compare Cyprian at the end of his second letter to Donatus, and his reply to Praesul of Reims, section 2.

units.la: f Proverb. V.
units.tr: f Proverbs V.

units.la: 15 "Ητι ἄλλη παιδεία χρήσιμος, ἢ τὴν γεγραμμένων ἀναγνῶσις ἀναγκαία.
units.tr: Nothing else is useful as education but the reading of the Scriptures is necessary [Οὐδεμία ἄλλη παιδεία χρήσιμος, ἢ τὴν γεγραμμένων ἀναγνῶσις ἀναγκαία].

units.la: 16 Περὶ τῶν ἑλληνικῶν μαθημάτων μελέτης, ἱστορίας ἱεροῖς ἐναςκεῖσ παιδεύματ. Ἐπιμαθήσεις ἐπαγγελίας ἡμέρας ἐχέτης ὡσὴν εἰσπεπλόμεθα. esse ad Dominum. Et post, Aliqui vestrum ut recitari audierunt, quæ leguntur, statim discedunt. Nulla ex his, quæ dicta sunt, inquisitio ad invicem, nulla collatio, nusquam memoria mandati illius, quo te divina lex commonet: Interrogo patres tuos, & dicent tibi; Presbyteros tuos, & annuntiabunt tibi. Alii ne hoc ipsum quidem patienter exspectant; usquequo lectiones in Ecclesia recitentur. Alii vero nec, si recitantur, sciunt; sed in remotioribus dominicæ domûs locis secularibus fabulis occupantur. De quibus ego ausus sum dicere, quia cùm legitur Moses, jam non velamen super cor eorum, sed paries quidam & murus est positus. Si enim ille, qui adest, qui audit, & intentus est, & quæ audit retractat & discutit, & quæ assequi non potest, percontatur & discit; vix potest ad libertatem scientiæ pervenire; ille qui abscondit aures suas ne audiat, & terga in faciem legentis obvertit; quomodo dicendus est velamen habere superpositum cordi; ad quem ne ipsum quidem velamen literæ, quo sensus velatur, qui est sonus vocis, accessit?
units.tr: Concerning the study of Greek learning, the history of the sacred writings… [Περὶ τῶν ἑλληνικῶν μαθημάτων μελέτης, ἱστορίας ἱεροῖς ἐναςκεῖσ παιδεύματ. Ἐπιμαθήσεις ἐπαγγελίας ἡμέρας ἐχέτης ὡσὴν εἰσπεπλόμεθα.] …to be with the Lord. And afterwards: Some of you, as soon as you hear the passages read, go away at once. There is no questioning of one another about what has been said, no comparing, nowhere is there any memory of that command by which the divine law admonishes you: Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; ask your elders, and they will declare it to you. Others do not even wait patiently until the readings are recited in the Church; others, even when they are read, do not understand them, but are occupied with worldly tales in the more remote parts of the Lord's house. Of these I have dared to say that when Moses is read, a veil is not over their heart, but a kind of wall and barrier is placed there. For if he who is present, who listens, and who is attentive, examines and discusses what he hears, and asks about and learns what he cannot grasp, he can scarcely attain to the freedom of knowledge; but how is he to be said to have a veil laid over his heart, who stops his ears lest he hear, and turns his back on the face of the reader? To him not even the veil of the letter, which veils the sense and is the sound of the voice, has come near.

units.la: In Levit. VI. Homil. 4. Ego si possem die ac nocte in lege Domini meditari, & omnes Scripturas memoriâ retinere; memoriale sacrificii mei Domino obtulissem. Certè si non omnia possumus; saltem ea, quæ nunc docentur in Ecclesiâ, vel quæ recitantur, memoriæ commendemus.
units.tr: In Leviticus, Homily 4 on chapter 6: If I could meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, and retain all the Scriptures in memory, I would have offered a memorial sacrifice to the Lord. Certainly, if we cannot do everything, at least let us commit to memory those things that are now taught in the Church or read aloud.

units.la: In Levit. XVI. Homil. 9. Optamus, ut vel his auditis operam detis, non solùm in Ecclesiâ, audire verbum Dei; sed & in domibus vestris exerceri, & meditari in lege Domini die & nocte: & ibi enim Christus est, & ubique adest quærentibus se. Propterea namque mandatur in lege, ut meditemur eam, quùm imus in viâ, & quùm sedemus in domo, & quùm jacemus in cubiculo, & quùm surgimus.
units.tr: In Leviticus, Homily 9 on chapter 16: We wish that, having heard these things, you would take pains not only to hear the Word of God in the Church, but also to be exercised in your houses and to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night; for Christ is there, and he is present everywhere to those who seek him. For this reason it is commanded in the law that we meditate on it when we walk on the road, when we sit in the house, when we lie down in our chamber, and when we rise.

units.la: In Numer. XXXIII. Homil. 27. Dæmonibus super omnia est tormentorum genera, & super omnes pœnas; si quem vident verbo Dei operam dare, scientiam divinæ legis & mysteria Scripturarum intentis studiis perquirentem. In hoc eorum omnis flamma est; in isto uruntur incendio. At Pontificii tam diligenter eis operam navârunt; ut hoc tormento eos magnâ ex parte liberaverint, hanc flammam & incendium restinxerint.
units.tr: In Numbers, Homily 27 on chapter 33: For the demons there are kinds of torment and punishments above all others, if they see someone giving himself to the Word of God, eagerly seeking the knowledge of the divine law and the mysteries of the Scriptures. In this is all their flame; by this they are burned with fire. But the Papists have so diligently kept them from this that they have, for the most part, freed them from this torment and quenched this flame and fire.

units.la: In Josu. XV. Homil. 20. Dici potest; Scripturæ difficiles sunt. At nihilominus si eas legeris, profuerint tibi. Nam ipse Dominus noster Jesus Christus, si nos inveniat hus [verbis Divinæ Scripturæ] vacantes, & hujusmodi studiis & exercitiis operam dantes; non solùm pasci & refici dignatur in nobis; verùm etiam si has epulas viderit apud nos apparatas, Patrem secum conatur adducere.
units.tr: In Joshua, Homily 20 on chapter 15: It may be said: the Scriptures are difficult. Nevertheless, if you read them, they will profit you. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself, if he finds us free for these words of the divine Scripture and busy with such studies and exercises, deigns not only to feed and refresh himself in us; but even if he sees these feasts prepared among us, he tries to bring the Father along with him.

units.la: s Deut. VI.
units.tr: s Deuteronomy VI.

units.la: In Prologo lib. Job. (vel quisquis Author ejus fuit.) Sicut olim Moses librum illum in Ægypto ex Syro in Hebræum transtulit; ita LXX. sub Ptolomæo ipsum ex Hebræo in Græcum transtulerunt; & inde per universas gentes Beati Job scriptura divulgata est; primùm quidem Syriacè scripta in Arabiâ, ubi & Job habitabat; postea verò & in Hebræis & in Græcis & in omnibus gentibus interpretata.
units.tr: In the Prologue to the book of Job (or whoever its author was): Just as Moses once translated that book in Egypt from Syriac into Hebrew, so the Seventy, under Ptolemy, translated it from Hebrew into Greek; and from there the writing of Blessed Job was spread through all nations: first indeed written in Syriac in Arabia, where Job also lived; afterwards, however, also translated into Hebrew, into Greek, and into all the nations.

units.la: In Isai. I. Homil. 2. Utinam omnes faceremus illud, quod scriptum est: Scrutamini Scripturas.
units.tr: In Isaiah, Homily 2 on chapter 1: Would that we all did what is written: Search the Scriptures.

units.la: In Isai. VI. Homil. 6. verba illa explicans; Et auribus suis graviter audierunt; & gravitudinem auditionis exponens, quæ non ceat animæ hominis: Quid est, quod faciat auditum non graviter audire, sed leviter? Pennæ verbi, pennæ virtutis. Etenim pennæ verbi multùm levitatis asserunt, &c. Si autem peccaverimus, & negligentes fuerimus circa alas; & defluxerint pennæ nostræ: gravabimur, & graviter audiemus. Et post. Usque hodie autem, quotquot audientes scripturas, non audiunt sermonem spiritualiter, qui levis est; sed literam, quæ est gravis & occidens, graviter audiunt. Atque ita dupliciter auditur Scriptura. Ab eo, qui non intelligit quæ dicuntur, graviter auditur: ab eo, qui intelligit eam, non solùm auditur non graviter, sed potiùs acutè? Unde qui sit intelligens, sit auditor.
units.tr: In Isaiah, Homily 6 on chapter 6, explaining those words: And they have heard heavily with their ears; and explaining the heaviness of hearing, which does not befall the human soul: What is it that makes hearing not heavy but light? The wings of the word, the wings of virtue. For the wings of the word bring great lightness, etc. But if we sin, and are negligent about the wings, and our feathers fall out, we will be weighed down, and will hear heavily. And afterwards: Yet to this day, all who hear the Scriptures do not hear the word spiritually, which is light; but they hear the letter, which is heavy and kills, heavily. And so the Scripture is heard in two ways. By one who does not understand what is said, it is heard heavily; by one who understands it, it is heard not only not heavily but rather sharply. Therefore let him who is intelligent be the hearer.

units.la: In Jerem. Homil. 9. Percurramus universas Scripturas; & probati nummularii effecti, dicamus: Hęc audite; debemus hęc auribus percipere.
units.tr: In Jeremiah, Homily 9: Let us run through all the Scriptures; and, having become approved money-changers, let us say: Hear these things; we ought to receive these things with our ears.

units.la: In Levit. X. Homil. 9. Infœlix anima, cujus fidei ignis extinguitur, & refrigescit charitatis calor; ad quam cùm venerit cœlestis Pontifex noster, quærens ab eâ ignitos & ardentes carbones, super quos incensum offerat Patri; invenit in eâ aridos cineres & frigidas favillas. Tales sunt omnes, qui subtrahunt se, & longè faciunt à verbo Dei, ne audientes sermones divinos accendantur ad fidem, incalescant ad charitatem, igniantur ad misericordiam. Vis tibi ostendam, quomodo de verbis Spiritûs Sancti ignis exeat, & accendat corda credentium? Audi dicentem David in Psalmis ; Eloquium Domini ignivit eum. Et iterum in Evangelio scriptum est: Postquam Dominus locutus est ad Cleopham; Nonne cor nostrum, inquit, erat ardens intra nos, cùm aperiret nobis Scripturas? Tu ergo unde ardelis? Unde invenientur in te carbones ignis, qui nunquam Domini igniris eloquio? nunquam verbis Spiritûs Sancti inflammaris? Audi & alibi ipsum David dicentem ; Concaluit cor meum intra me; & in meditatione meâ ex-
units.tr: In Leviticus, Homily 9 on chapter 10: Unhappy is the soul whose fire of faith is extinguished and whose warmth of love grows cold; when our heavenly High Priest comes to it, seeking from it burning and glowing coals on which he may offer incense to the Father, he finds in it dry ashes and cold embers. Such are all those who withdraw themselves and keep far from the Word of God, lest, hearing divine words, they be kindled to faith, warmed to love, and set afire to mercy. Do you want me to show you how fire comes out of the words of the Holy Spirit and sets the hearts of believers alight? Hear David saying in the Psalms: The word of the Lord has set him on fire. And again it is written in the Gospel, after the Lord spoke to Cleophas: Was not our heart, he says, burning within us, while he opened the Scriptures to us? Where, then, do you catch fire from? Where will coals of fire be found in you, who have never been warmed by the word of the Lord? Never inflamed by the words of the Holy Spirit? Hear also David himself saying elsewhere: My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a

units.la: {h} Joan. V. {i} Psalm XVII. {k} Luc. XXIV. {l} Psal. XXXVIII. ardescit ignis. Unde tu concalescis? Unde ignis accenditur, qui nunquam in divinis meditaris eloquiis? imò, quod est infœlicius, concalescis in spectaculis circi, concalescis in equorum contentionibus, in certamine athletarum. Hæc omnia etiam ex Origene transtulit Cyrillus Alexandrinus in Lib. 9. in Leviticum.
units.tr: {h} John 5. {i} Psalm 17. {k} Luke 24. {l} Psalm 38. fire blazes up. Where do you grow warm? Where is a fire kindled in you, who never meditate on the divine words? Indeed, what is more unhappy, you grow warm at the spectacles of the circus, you grow warm at the contests of horses, in the struggle of the athletes. All these things Cyril of Alexandria also translated from Origen in book 9 on Leviticus.

units.la: In Matth. cap. 13. 17 Omnibus modis comandum est; ut congregemus in corde nostro, attendentes lectioni, exhortationi & doctrinæ, & in lege Dei meditando die ac nocte: non solum nova Evangeliorum oracula & Apostolorum, & horum explanationes; verum etiam vetera legis, umbram habentis futurorum bonorum, ac Prophetarum, qui his consentanea prædixerunt.
units.tr: In Matth. cap. 13. 17 On every account we must take care to gather them into our heart, attending to the reading, the exhortation and the teaching, and meditating on the law of God day and night: not only the new oracles of the Gospels and the Apostles and their explanations, but also the ancient things of the law, which have the shadow of the good things to come, and of the Prophets, who foretold things agreeing with these.

units.la: In Luc. IV. Homil. 31. Scrutamini Scripturas; ut & in his, quæ putantur esse simplicia, reperiatis non minima sacramenta. Scrutemur principium Evangelicæ lectionis, quotquot hodie audivimus; & id quod latebat, procedit in medium.
units.tr: In Luc. IV. Homil. 31. Search the Scriptures, so that in those things which seem to be simple you may also find no small sacraments. Let us search the beginning of the Gospel reading that we have heard today, and what was hidden will come forward into the open.

units.la: In Johannem, Tom. 13. Introductiones ergo sunt Scripturæ, à quibus accuratè intellectus, & nunc nominatis fons Jacob, ascendendum est ad Jesum, ut nobis largiatur fontem aquæ salientis ad vitam æternam. Cæterùm non similiter omnis haurit è fonte Jacob: nam etiamsi bibebat Jacob & filii ejus & pecora ejus, atque etiam Samaritis illa venit ad fontem ipsum & haurit; vide ne aliter & prudenter biberit Jacob cum filiis, aliter & simpliciùs moreque magis pecuino biberint pecora ejus, rursus biberit etiam aliter quàm Jacob & filii & pecora ejus, Samaritis illa. Qui enim docti sunt in Scripturis, bibunt sicut Jacob & filii ejus; rudiores verò & simplicires, qui dicuntur oves Christi, bibunt perinde atque oves Jacob; tum aliqui laudantes Scripturas, & quædam constituentes malè dicta, prætextu quod eas intellexerint, non secus bibunt, atque bibebat Samaritis illa, antequam crederet in Jesum.
units.tr: In Johannem, Tom. 13. The Scriptures therefore are introductions, and by them we must go up accurately to an understanding of Jesus, the well of Jacob just mentioned, so that he may bestow on us the spring of water welling up to eternal life. However, not everyone draws from the well of Jacob in the same way. For although Jacob drank, and his sons and his cattle drank, and that Samaritan woman came to the well itself and drew water, take care lest Jacob drank one way with his sons, prudently, and his cattle drank another way, more simply and in the manner of beasts, and again that Samaritan woman drank in yet another way than Jacob and his sons and his cattle. For those who are learned in the Scriptures drink as Jacob and his sons did; but the cruder and simpler folk, who are called the sheep of Christ, drink just as the sheep of Jacob do; then some who praise the Scriptures, and set up certain things as badly said, on the pretext that they have understood them, drink no differently from that Samaritan woman before she believed in Jesus.

units.la: In Epist. ad Roman. lib. 9. explicans illud cap. 12. Reformamini in novitate sensûs vestri.] Renovatur sensus nostER per exercitia sapientiæ & meditationem verbi Dei, & legis ejus intelligentiam spiritualem: & quantum quis quotidie ex Scripturarum proficit lectione, quantò altiùs intellectus incedit; tanto semper novus magis & quotidie novior efficitur. Nescio
units.tr: In Epist. ad Roman. lib. 9. explaining that verse of chapter 12. "Be transformed by the renewing of your mind." Our sense is renewed through the exercises of wisdom and the meditation on the Word of God and the spiritual understanding of his law; and the more anyone advances daily in the reading of the Scriptures, the higher his understanding rises, so much the more new, and daily newer, it becomes. I do not know.

units.la: 17 Σωάζειν δὲ πεπὶ τεῖχον περιεχλίον ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ἡμῶν διὰ τὸ ἀεὶ ἔχειν τὴν ἀπαγγελίαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ἐμελέτων ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός, ἃ μόνον τὰ καινὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, καὶ τὰ ἀπόστολον, &c. ἀλλὰ ὅτι, τὴν παρακλήσιν, τὴν διδασκαλίαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ καὶ παλαιά, &c. autem si potest renovari sensus, qui piger est erga Scripturas divinas, & intelligentiae spiritualis exercitia; quibus possit non solùm intelligere quae scripta sunt, verùm ea applicare apertius, & manifestare diligentius.
units.tr: 17 Σωάζειν δὲ πεπὶ τεῖχον περιεχλίον ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ἡμῶν διὰ τὸ ἀεὶ ἔχειν τὴν ἀπαγγελίαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ἐμελέτων ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός, ἃ μόνον τὰ καινὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, καὶ τὰ ἀπόστολον, &c. ἀλλὰ ὅτι, τὴν παρακλήσιν, τὴν διδασκαλίαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ καὶ παλαιά, &c. [Greek, garbled in the scan; the sense is: "to be occupied, always having the message in our heart, and meditating on the law day and night, not only the new things of the Gospel and of the Apostles, but also the consolation, the teaching, and the old things."] But if the sense that is slow toward the divine Scriptures can be renewed, and the exercises of spiritual understanding, by which one may not only understand what is written but apply it more clearly and make it manifest more diligently.

units.la: Lib. 10. in cap. XVI. ejusdem Epistolæ. Dominus in Evangelio o dicit: Attendite vobis ab iis, qui veniunt ad vos in vestimentis ovium, intus autem sunt lupi rapaces. Et ideo vigilans sensus & mens intenta requiritur, quæ probare noverit vel ovis in propatulo simplicitatem, vel lupi latentem rapacitatem. Unde vide quàm proximi periculis fiunt hi, qui exerceri in divinis literis negligunt; ex quibus solis hujusmodi examinationis agnoscenda discretio est.
units.tr: Lib. 10. in cap. XVI. ejusdem Epistolæ. The Lord says in the Gospel: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves." And therefore a watchful sense and an attentive mind is required, one that knows how to test either the simplicity of the sheep in plain view or the hidden ravening of the wolf. See then how close to danger those are who neglect to be exercised in the divine letters, since only from them is the discernment of such examination to be recognised.

units.la: Lib. 8. contra Celsum. 18 Deinde oblitus in Christianis se agere soli Deo per Jesum preces offerentibus, admisçet aliena temerè cum rebus Christianorum confundens & dicens: Quos si barbaricis nominibus quis appellet, virtutem habebunt; sin Græcis aut Romanis, non item. Quem enim nos invocamus nomine barbaro? Quare persuasum fit omnibus Celsum hæc nobis objicere immeritis; sciantque quòd germanè Christiani ne usitatis quidem in Sacrâ Scripturâ Dei nominibus utantur inter precandum; sed Græci Græcis, Romani Romanis; singulique precentur propriâ linguâ, Deumque celebrent pro viribus. Et omnium linguarum Dominus omnibus linguis precantes exaudit, tam variè loquentes haud secus quàm consonos (ut ita dicam) & unius vocis homines intelligens. Non est enim Deus maximus unus eorum, qui certam aliquam linguam sortiti sunt, sive Græcam, sive Barbaram, cæterarum ignari, nec solliciti de alienæ linguæ hominibus.
units.tr: Lib. 8. contra Celsum. Then, forgetting that we Christians are those who offer prayers to God alone through Jesus, he rashly mixes foreign things with Christian matters and says: "If anyone calls on them by barbarian names, they will have power; but if by Greek or Roman names, not so." For what barbarian name do we invoke? Therefore let it be clear to everyone that Celsus objects these things to us undeservedly; and let them know that genuine Christians do not even use in prayer the names of God that are customary in Sacred Scripture; but Greeks pray to God in Greek, Romans in Roman, and each prays in his own tongue and celebrates God as far as his powers allow. And the Lord of all tongues hears those who pray in all tongues, understanding men who speak so variously just as if they were in agreement, and of one voice, so to speak. For God the greatest is not one of those who have been allotted some particular language, whether Greek or barbarian, ignorant of the others and unconcerned with men of a foreign tongue.

units.la: 18 ——Δεικνύτω γὰρ τινα ἡμῖν Καισάρας ὀνομάζομεν, ὡς καλῶς ἔχει αὐτὸν ὅπι ἐοίκειν, ἡ πυθέσθαι, μᾶλλον καὶ ἡμῖν τοῦ τὰ εἰρηκέναι τὴν Κίλσον, ἐφ' ᾧ ὅτι οἱ λοιποὶ τῆς χειστιανῶν ἐκ τῆς ἐπ' ἐκ θείας γεγονάσι κευῶφοις ὀνόμασιν, ἡ πλαγιώσοις ὅτι τὸ θεὸς, χρὴν ἐν ἐπ' ἐυχαῖς, ἀλλ' ὡς ἀπὸ Ἕλληνες Ἑλληνικοῖς, οἱ δ' Ῥωμαῖοι Ῥωμαϊκοῖς, ἢ ἕτοιμος ἴσος κ?! ἡ ἑαυτῶν διάλεκτον εὐχέσθαι τοῦ θεοῦ, ἡ ὑμνεῖ αὐτὸν ὡς Λίναι). Καὶ ὁ πάσης διαλέκτῳ χωρεῖ ἡ ἀπὸ πάσης διαλέκτῳ ἐυχομένων ἀκούει, &c.
units.tr: 18 "For let him show us some [...] whom we call Caesars, as it is fitting for him to suppose or to ask, rather than for us to have said with Celsus that the rest of the Christians, from the [...] of the divine, have names that are [...], or are sidelong to [...] that God ought not to be prayed to in any tongue, but as Greeks in Greek and Romans in Roman, and each one prays in his own dialect to God or praises him as he can. And the Lord of every language hears those praying in every language, &c." [Δεικνύτω γὰρ τινα ἡμῖν Καισάρας ὀνομάζομεν, ὡς καλῶς ἔχει αὐτὸν ὅπι ἐοίκειν, ἡ πυθέσθαι, μᾶλλον καὶ ἡμῖν τοῦ τὰ εἰρηκέναι τὴν Κίλσον, ἐφ' ᾧ ὅτι οἱ λοιποὶ τῆς χειστιανῶν ἐκ τῆς ἐπ' ἐκ θείας γεγονάσι κευῶφοις ὀνόμασιν, ἡ πλαγιώσοις ὅτι τὸ θεὸς, χρὴν ἐν ἐπ' ἐυχαῖς, ἀλλ' ὡς ἀπὸ Ἕλληνες Ἑλληνικοῖς, οἱ δ' Ῥωμαῖοι Ῥωμαϊκοῖς, ἢ ἕτοιμος ἴσος κ?! ἡ ἑαυτῶν διάλεκτον εὐχέσθαι τοῦ θεοῦ, ἡ ὑμνεῖ αὐτὸν ὡς Λίναι). Καὶ ὁ πάσης διαλέκτῳ χωρεῖ ἡ ἀπὸ πάσης διαλέκτῳ ἐυχομένων ἀκούει, &c.]

units.la: 19 ——τῆς ἀναγκαίσμα εὐσεβὼν, ἡ ὧς αὐτῶν ὠφέλειαν ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἀντιτάξει. ea quæ legebantur auscultans, utilitatem præceptorum vitæ institutione servabat. Hinc intelligitur sacra apud Ægyptios lingua Vernaculâ peracta esse. Antonius enim Ægyptiacè tantùm intellexit; siquidem interprete uti solitus, qui verba ejus Græco formone exprimeret; ut ex eodem libro apparet.
units.tr: 19 "...of necessary piety, or in its place sets [...] 'listening to what was read, he kept the usefulness of the precepts for the ordering of his life.' Hence it is understood that the sacred rites among the Egyptians were performed in the vernacular language. For Antony understood only Egyptian; indeed he was accustomed to use an interpreter who would express his words in Greek, as appears from the same book." [τῆς ἀναγκαίσμα εὐσεβὼν, ἡ ὧς αὐτῶν ὠφέλειαν ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἀντιτάξει.]

units.la: 300. Ofroeni in Mesopotamiâ.
units.tr: 300. Ofroeni in Mesopotamia.

units.la: Apud hos Eusebius Emisenus 20 ab ineunte ætate sacris literis institutus est; ut in ejus vitâ tradit Georgius Laodicenus à Socrate q citatus: Et notandum est quod hic scribit r Sozomenus 21, Eusebius cognomento Emisenus, genere oriundus ex Edessâ nobili civitate Ofroenorum, ab ineunte ætate (ut mos Patrius fert) sacris in literis educatus, deinde disciplinis humanioris literaturæ institutus est. At Colonienses Jesuitæ s hoc nomine adolescentes nostros reprehendunt; quòd priusquam Grammaticam probè calleant, & alias disciplinas à limine salutârint; vestigio illotis (quod aiunt) pedibus sacras literas adoriantur.
units.tr: Among these, Eusebius of Emesa, 20 "from early age was instructed in the sacred letters," as Georgius of Laodicea, cited by Socrates, relates in his Life. It should be noted that Sozomen here writes: 21 "Eusebius, surnamed Emesenus, born of a family from Edessa, a noble city of the Ofroeni, from early age (as the custom of his fathers brings) was educated in the sacred letters, and then instructed in the disciplines of humane literature." But the Jesuits of Cologne reproach our young men on this account: that before they have mastered grammar well, and have greeted the other disciplines from the threshold, they attack the sacred letters with feet unwashed, as they say. [20 Ἐκ τίας τε ἡλικίας τὰ ἱερὰ μαθὼν γεγέμμαῖα. 21 Ἐκ τέν ἡ χρ πάτερ τὸν ἱερὸν ἱν- μαθὼν λόγως, μὲ ταῦτ᾽ ἡ τὰ παρ᾽ Ἑλλησιν, &c.]

units.la: 300. Pamphilus Martyr.
units.tr: 300. Pamphilus, Martyr.

units.la: Scripturas sanctas non ad legendum tantùm, sed & ad habendum tribuebat promptissimè, nec solùm viris, sed & fœminis, quas vidisset lectioni deditas: Unde & multos codices præparabat, ut cùm necessitas poposcisset, volentibus largiretur. Eusebius in 3. libro de Vitâ Pamphili citatus ab Hieronymo in lib. 1. Apologiæ adversùs Ruffinum.
units.tr: "He readily gave the holy Scriptures not only to be read but also to be kept, not only to men but also to women whom he saw devoted to reading. Hence he also prepared many codices, so that when need demanded he might give them freely to those who wished." Eusebius, in book 3 of the Life of Pamphilus, as cited by Jerome in book 1 of his Apology against Rufinus.

units.la: 311. Gregorius Armeniæ majoris Episcopus.
units.tr: 311. Gregory, Bishop of Greater Armenia.

units.la: Ludos literarios constrvxit per omnes civitates; eisque Doctores & magistros constituit, Rege ita jubente, & ad hæc adjuvante, & Pontificis animo magnam opem ferente. Publicè quidem per civitates prædicatum fuit à Pontifice, ut filii Armeniorum undique ad eos ventitarent, & sacras docerentur literas. In Actis Gregorii Armeniæ Episcopi apud Sym. Metaphrasten Septemb. 30.
units.tr: "He built schools of letters in all the cities, and appointed teachers and masters for them, the king so commanding, and helping in this, and the Pontiff bringing great aid with his zeal. Publicly indeed, throughout the cities, it was proclaimed by the Pontiff that the sons of the Armenians should come to them from everywhere and be taught the sacred letters." In the Acts of Gregory, Bishop of Armenia, in Symeon Metaphrastes, September 30.

units.la: 330. Constantinus Magnus Imp.
units.tr: 330. Constantine the Great, Emperor.

units.la: Hujus pia exercitia ita describit Eusebius in Orat. de laudibus illius, ante med. 22 Ille ipse sibi praeceptionum salutarium doctor factus, in ipsius regiae penetralibus Servatorem suum veneratur; & interdum precibus divinos cultus exequitur, interdum sacris literis audiendis mentem suam erudit. Et lib. 4. de Vita illius, cap. 17. 23 Sumptis in manus libris, vel sacrarum literarum contemplationi diligenter animam adhibebat, vel constitutas cum universo Ecclesiae coetu preces reddebat. Ibid. cap. 36. (quemadmodum etiam apud Socratem, lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. cap 6. & Theodoretum, lib. 1. Hist. cap. 16.) habetur exemplum Epistolae ejus ad Eusebium, qua praecipit eidem, ut 50. volumina ad usum Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae in membranis pararet; in quibus eos libros S. Scripturae describi curaret, 24 quorum & apparationem & usum maxime Ecclesiae necessarium cognosceret; descriptosque ad se Constantinopolin transmitteret. Illius denique diligentia effectum esse prodit Eusebiust; ut 25 mulieres & innumerabiles virorum multitudines corporis alimenta cum rationalibus alimentis, quae ex sacris literis perlegendis depromta animis rationis participibus admodum conveniunt, commutarent.
units.tr: Eusebius describes his pious exercises thus, in the Oration on his praises, shortly before the middle: 22 "He himself, made the teacher of his own salutary precepts, reveres his Saviour in the innermost chambers of his palace; and at times he performs the divine worship with prayers, at times he instructs his mind by hearing the sacred letters." And in book 4 of his Life, ch. 17: 23 "Taking books into his hands, he diligently applied his mind to the contemplation of the sacred letters, or rendered the prayers appointed with the whole assembly of the Church." Also in ch. 36 (as also in Socrates, Church History book 1, ch. 6, and Theodoret, History book 1, ch. 16) there is an example of his letter to Eusebius, in which he orders him to prepare fifty volumes on parchment for the use of the Church of Constantinople, in which he should have those books of holy Scripture copied, 24 "knowing both their preparation and their use to be most necessary to the Church"; and to send the copies to him at Constantinople. Finally, Eusebius reports that by his diligence it was brought about that 25 "women and countless crowds of men exchanged bodily food for rational food, which, drawn from the perusal of the sacred letters, is most suited to souls that share in reason."

units.la: 335. Eusebius Caesariensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 335. Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea.

units.la: In Orat. de laudibus Constantini, paulo ante sin. Quid tam eximium ad ejus (Christi) divinitatem evidenter declarandam, quam non solum promittere se eos (Apostolos) facturum piscatores hominum; quod uti verbo protulerat, sic reipsa praestitit: verum etiam tantam virtutem, tantamque facultatem illis tribuere, 26 ut monumenta scriptis mandarent, librosque ederent; iisque tam magnam apud omnes haberent & authoritatem
units.tr: In the Oration on the praises of Constantine, shortly before the end: "What is so remarkable for clearly declaring his (Christ's) divinity as that he not only promised that he would make them (the Apostles) fishers of men, which as he had said in words, so he actually did in deed; but also gave them such virtue and such ability, 26 that they committed monuments to writing and published books, and had such great authority and esteem among all"

units.la: t Orat. de laudibus Constantini, paulo ante sin. & existimationem; ut in omnes tam Barbarorum quàm Græcorum linguas, quæ in toto orbe terrarum existunt, converterentur; omnesque gentes in illis perdiscendis studium & operam ponerent, proque certo crederent divina eloquia in illis esse tradita comprehensaque ?
units.tr: t Oration on the praises of Constantine, shortly before the end: "...and esteem; so that they were translated into all the languages of the barbarians as well as of the Greeks which exist in the whole world; and all nations applied zeal and effort to learning them, and believed for certain that the divine oracles were delivered and contained in them?"

units.la: Hist. Eccles. lib. 2. cap. 16. populum Christianum 27 festum passionis Domini, non jejuniis solùm & vigiliis, sed & attentâ Scripturarum auditione excolere ac celebrare consuevisse indicat.
units.tr: Church History, book 2, ch. 16, indicates that the Christian people were accustomed 27 "to celebrate the feast of the Lord's passion not only with fasts and vigils, but also with attentive hearing of the Scriptures."

units.la: 28 De Præparat. Evangel. lib.8. cap.1. Cùm jam Salvatoris nostri tempora viderentur propius advenire; conducebatque maximè saluti omnium gentium, quaecunque à Prophetis scripta fuerant, intelligere, per linguam Græcam, quam ferè omnes gentes intelligunt, Judaicam Scripturam universis propositit.
units.tr: 28 From the Preparation for the Gospel, book 8, ch. 1: "When the times of our Saviour seemed to be drawing nearer, and it was most conducive to the salvation of all nations to understand whatever had been written by the prophets, he set out the Jewish Scripture before all, through the Greek language, which almost all nations understand."

units.la: 28 Ibid. lib.12. cap.1. Nonne multò ante Platonem divinæ literæ fidem cæteris præposuere virtutibus, cùm inquit u, Nisi crediderit, non intelligetis: ac rursum x; Credidi, propterea locutus sum. Unde apud nos quoque incipientibus ac imperfectioribus quasque secundùm animum infantibus simpliciùs Scripturæ leguntur. Credendum enim omnibus est, omnia quæ in eâ feruntur, sicuti Dei verba, verissima esse. Illis autem, qui ad majorem jam habitum Scripturarum pervenerunt, altiora petere, ac rationem singulorum quærere conceditur. Vid. cap. 22.
units.tr: 28 Ibid., book 12, ch. 1: "Did not the divine letters, long before Plato, place faith above all the other virtues, when they say: Unless you believe, you will not understand; and again: I believed, therefore I spoke? Hence among us too, the beginners and the more imperfect, as infants in mind, read the Scriptures more simply. For all must believe that everything contained in them, as the words of God, is most true. But to those who have come to a greater familiarity with the Scriptures, it is allowed to seek higher things and to inquire into the reason of each point." See ch. 22.

units.la: 7 Sine ullà scientià literarum Scripturas divinas & memoriter audiendo tenuisse, & prudenter cogitando intellexisse prædicatur. [Augustin de Doctrin. Christ. in Prologo. ]
units.tr: 7 It is said of him that, without any knowledge of letters, he held the divine Scriptures by hearing them and remembering them, and understood them by thinking about them wisely. [Augustin de Doctrin. Christ. in Prologo.]

units.la: 350. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Episcopus.
units.tr: 350. Cyril of Jerusalem, Bishop.

units.la: Catechef. 4. de Sacr. Script. 29 Diligenter ab Ecclesiâ disce, qui sint Veteris, & qui Novi Testamenti libri; ut nihil Apocryphum legas. Cùm enim ne ista quidem, quæ omnes confitentur, scias; quid in dubiis discere laboras? Lege Sacras Scripturas, nempe XXII. Veteris Testa-
units.tr: Catech. 4, on Holy Scripture, 29: Learn diligently from the Church which books belong to the Old and New Testament, so that you read nothing apocryphal. For since you do not even know those things which all acknowledge, why do you labour to learn what is in doubt? Read the Sacred Scriptures, namely the twenty-two books of the Old Testament, which were translated by the Seventy-two interpreters. — Study these alone with care, which we also recite in the Church securely and safely.

units.tr: 29 A diligent learner (?) ... the books of the Old Testament are those which we read openly in the Church [Φιλομαθὴς διδάγμα ἐπ' ἐκκλησίας, μίαι εἰσιν αἱ τ' παλαιᾶς διαθήκης βίβλοι, τὰς ἡ ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ μετὰ παρρησίας ἀναγινώσκομεν.] ... books, which were translated by the Seventy-two interpreters. — Study these alone diligently, which we also recite in the Church securely and safely.

units.la: Catechef. 9. Vade ad Apem, & disce quàm laboriosa sit ; quomodo per flores omnis generis oberrans congerit tibi mel in usum ; 30 ut & tu circuiens divinas Scripturas, tuam ipsius salutem apprehendas, & illis satiatus dicas : ² Quàm dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua? super mel & favum ori meo.
units.tr: Catech. 9: Go to the bee and learn how laborious it is: how, wandering over flowers of every kind, it gathers honey for your use; so that you too, going round the divine Scriptures, may grasp your own salvation, and, satisfied by them, say: How sweet are your words to my throat, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth. Psalm 119.

units.la: 360. Athanasius Alexandrinus Episcopus.
units.tr: 360. Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria.

units.la: In Apologiâ pro fugâ suâ. ² Diacano mandavi, ut XXXI. Psalmum legeret, populusque attentè auscultaret ; cùm recitaret hanc particulam : Quoniam in seculum misericordia ejus.
units.tr: In the Apology for his Flight: I ordered the deacon to read Psalm XXXI, and the people to listen attentively, when he recited this clause: For his mercy endures for ever.

units.la: In Exhortat. ad Monachos. Has (Orationes) si fieri potest, sola intercapedo disrumpat. Cujus rei cura in canonicis ponenda est salubriter monumentis. Non quòd Apocrypha debeamus, præsertim ignorata, damnare ; sed quòd ad scientiam Dei digestam canonis seriem putemus posse sufficere. Illa enim, si consentiunt, supervacua sunt. Si dissentiunt, vitanda sunt. Sine legendi studio nemo ad Dominum valebit esse intentus. Primùm, quòd hujusmodi opera ab aliis actibus caducæ occupationis abducunt ; & diversorum exemplorum insinuata cognitio, vel bonorum appetentiam, vel malorum factam esse cautelam. Neque enim aliàs Petrus Apostolus admoneret nos, dicens : Parati semper estote ad rationem reddendam ad omnes poscentes vos de verbo spei vestræ & fidei. Et Apostolus : Non cessamus pro vobis orantes ; ut impleamini agnitione ejus in omni sapientiâ & intellectu spirituali. Et rursus : Verbum Christi habitet in vobis abundanter omni sapientiâ. Nam & in veteri Testamento similem hominibus curam sacræ præceptionis inculcavit eloquium. Sic enim David ait : Beatus vir, qui non abiit in consilio impiorum, & in viâ peccatorum non stetit, & in cathedrâ pestilentiæ non sedit : Sed in lege Domini voluntas ejus meditabitur die ac nocte. Et ad Jesum Nave Deus loquitur: Non recedet liber iste de manibus tuis ; & meditaberis in eo die ac nocte. [Habetur Tomo 2. editionis Commelinianæ p. 435. sed annotat Petrus Fleckmannus hoc omnino scriptum Latinum videri.]
units.tr: In the Exhortation to Monks: These (readings), if it can be done, let only an interval interrupt. The care of this matter must be wisely placed in the canonical writings. Not that we should condemn the Apocrypha, especially those that are unknown; but because we think that the ordered series of the canon is enough for the knowledge of God. For those, if they agree, are superfluous; if they disagree, they are to be avoided. Without zeal for reading, no one will be able to be attentive to the Lord. First, because such works draw us away from other actions of fleeting occupation; and the acquaintance with various examples has either made us eager for good things or wary of evil. For otherwise the Apostle Peter would not admonish us, saying: Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you about the word of your hope and faith. And the Apostle: We do not cease praying for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of him in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. And again: Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly in all wisdom. For also in the Old Testament the utterance inculcated a similar care for sacred precept in men. For thus David says: Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his will is in the law of the Lord, and he meditates on it day and night. And God speaks to Joshua the son of Nun: This book shall not depart from your hands; and you shall meditate on it day and night. [This is found in volume 2 of the Commelin edition, p. 435, but Peter Fleckmann notes that this seems to have been written originally in Latin.]

units.la: ¹ Psalm. CXIX. ² Citatur à Theodoreto, lib. 2. Hist. cap. 13.
units.tr: Psalm CXIX. Quoted by Theodoret, Church History, book 2, ch. 13.

units.tr: 31 Having taken ... the reading as teaching ... that the people obey, for ever, etc. ["Περίστασιν, ἡ ὡς διδαχὴν ἀναγνώσεως ... λαμὼν, πού ἡ λαὸς ὑπακούειν, ὅπ εἰς ἡ αἰῶνα, &c."]

units.la: In lib. de Virginitate sive de Meditatione [Tom. 1. edit. Commelinianæ, quanquam non videatur Athanasii.] 32 Non abscedat ab ore tuo verbum Dei. Sit autem illud opus tuum omni tempore. Meditare in S. Scripturis: habe Psalterium, & Psalmos disce. [p. 828.] 33 In Ecclesia tace; ne quicquam loquaris; sed lectionibus duntaxat intende. [p. 834.]
units.tr: In the book On Virginity, or On Meditation [Tom. 1, Commelin edition, though it does not appear to be by Athanasius]: 32 Let the word of God not depart from your mouth. Let this be your work at all times. Meditate on the Holy Scriptures; have a Psalter, and learn the Psalms. [p. 828.] 33 In church be silent; say nothing, but attend only to the readings. [p. 834.]

units.la: In disceptatione adv. Hæreticos [Tom. 2. edit. Commelin. p. 248.] 34 Vis Scripturas negligam? Unde ergo cognitio? Vis cognitionem relinquam? Unde fides? &c. Romanas leges sine periculo nemo ignoraverit. Quas ergo parant insidias, qui magnorum cœlestis Regis oraculorum curâ studioque volunt interdictum? Scriptura est animæ cibus. Define verò, o homo, fame internum hominem necare; diramque non panis & aquæ, sed audiendi Verbum Domini, famem attrahere, ——Reverere Eunuchum illum, sermonis amatorem, qui ne in itinere quidem lectionem neglexit; cujus propositum comprobans Deus, statim Doctorem illi dedit. ——Atque hinc est, cur ipse præceperit, Scrutamini Scripturas; 35 scrutationem vocans diligentem attentamque abstrusorum inquisitionem de Scripturâ sanctâ.
units.tr: In the Disputation against the Heretics [Tom. 2, Commelin edition, p. 248]: 34 Shall I neglect the Scriptures? Whence then will knowledge come? Shall I give up knowledge? Whence then faith? etc. No one can be ignorant of the Roman laws without danger. What snares, then, do they lay who wish to forbid the care and study of the great oracles of the heavenly King? Scripture is the food of the soul. Stop, O man, starving the inner man, and do not draw on yourself a dreadful hunger, not for bread and water, but for hearing the Word of the Lord. ... Revere that Eunuch, lover of the word, who did not neglect reading even on the road; God, approving his purpose, at once gave him a teacher. ... And hence it is that he himself commanded, Search the Scriptures; calling the searching a diligent and attentive inquiry into the abstruse things of holy Scripture.

units.la: Turrianus in Defens. Epist. Pont. lib. 2. cap. 2. libellum hunc gravissimum appellat, & tanto auctore dignum. A Gennadio autem Scholario, p. 385. edit. Græcæ (Tom. 4. Biblioth. Patrum col. 1446.) dicitur Disputatio S. Maximi cum Theodosio Cæsareæ Episcopo. 36
units.tr: Turrianus, in the Defence of the Letter of the Pontiff, book 2, ch. 2, calls this book most weighty and worthy of so great an author. But Gennadius Scholarius, p. 385 of the Greek edition (Tom. 4 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, col. 1446), says it is the Disputation of St Maximus with Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea.

units.la: Ibid. pag. 259. 37 Egone verbum audiam, & convenientem sensum non inquiram? Ubi igitur aut sermonis consequentia, aut audientis utilitas? Forte & in brutorum animantium naturam mutari homines præcipiunt? Siquidem verborum sonum auribus arrepturi; ex sensu verò fructum nullum animo sunt percepturi. Non hoc nobis Paulus, qui de hujusmodi rebus docuit, mandavit: non amplexandum aliquid sine ratione, sine judicio, censuit, &c.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 259. 37 Shall I hear a word and not inquire into its fitting sense? Where then is the coherence of the discourse, or the usefulness to the hearer? Perhaps men also teach that we are to be changed into the nature of brute animals? For they would indeed catch the sound of the words with their ears, but would receive no fruit of meaning in their minds. This is not what Paul, who taught about such matters, commanded us: he judged that nothing should be embraced without reason and judgement, etc.

units.la: Vid. eundem (si idem Author est) initio epistolæ ad Episcopos ad Dioeceses suas proficiscentes, apud Fr. Torrensem de Resid. Episcop. sol. 446.

[Μὴ ἀποστήτω ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκ τῆς στόματός σε· ἀλλ᾽ ἢ τὸ ἔργον σε διαπαντὸς μελέτα τὸν Θεὸν γεγραφῶν· ψαλτήριον ἔχε ἐν τῷ ψαλμὸς μάνθανε.]

units.tr: 33 But attend only to the hearing. [Ἀλλὰ τῇ ἀκροάσει μόνον πρόσεχε.]

units.tr: 36 Learned men have long ago observed that this work is owed to Etherius of Tyana.

units.la: 37 ἀκούσω ἢ ῥήματος, εἰ μὴ ζητήσω τὸ εὐαρεστὲς ἢ φεσήματος. ——γὰρ ἢ σοφὸς ἀλλήλων ἔξεις μεδισμὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπους φεσφάλπισον, εἰ τὸ μέλλουσι ῥόξον ὡς ῥημάτων τῇ αἰσθῇ δίδωσι, κέρδος ἢ νοημάτων μηδὲν τὴν ψυχὴν σεσωσμένης; ἐχ ἵνα Παῦλος, &c.

Not thus did Paul, etc. [ἀκούσω ἢ ῥήματος, εἰ μὴ ζητήσω τὸ εὐαρεστὲς ἢ φεσήματος. ——γὰρ ἢ σοφὸς ἀλλήλων ἔξεις μεδισμὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπους φεσφάλπισον, εἰ τὸ μέλλουσι ῥόξον ὡς ῥημάτων τῇ αἰσθῇ δίδωσι, κέρδος ἢ νοημάτων μηδὲν τὴν ψυχὴν σεσωσμένης; ἐχ ἵνα Παῦλος, &c.]

units.la: 370. Macarius Ægyptius.
units.tr: 370. Macarius the Egyptian.

units.la: Homil. 6. 38 Qui accedunt ad Dominum, debent preces suas in tranquillitate, pace, & sedatione multâ fundere; non ineptis, aut confusis clamoribus uti, sed attentione cordis & cogitationibus sobrius attendere Domino. Item 39 Verum orationis fundamentum hoc est, attendere nimirum cogitationibus, & in multâ tranquillitate & pace precari. Et post: 40 Sunt alii, qui cogitationibus attendunt, & prælium internum committunt. Hique propter intellectum ac discretionem possunt dirigere & amoliri insurgentes cogitationes, & secundum voluntatem Domini ambulare.
units.tr: Homily 6. 38 Those who approach the Lord ought to pour out their prayers in tranquillity, peace, and great calm, not using foolish or confused shouting, but attending to the Lord with an attentive heart and sober thoughts. Likewise 39 The true foundation of prayer is this, namely to attend to one's thoughts and to pray in great tranquillity and peace. And afterwards: 40 There are others who attend to their thoughts and wage an inner battle. These, by reason of understanding and discernment, are able to direct and drive off the thoughts that rise up, and to walk according to the will of the Lord.

units.la: Homil. 33. 41 Oportet nos non ex more corporeo, nec pro more vociferandi, nec ex consuetudine silendi, aut genua flectendi, preces facere; verùm sobriè animum attendentes exspectare Deum, quando aderit & visitabit per omnes egressiones animam, per semitas ejus ac sensuum organa; & ita quando conveniat tacere, & quando conveniat clamare, & cum vociferatione precari, 42 modò mens fit firmata in Deum. Perinde enim ac corpus, cùm operatur quippiam, totum penitus occupatum incumbit operi, & omnia ejus membra se invicem adjuvant; 43 sic quoque anima tota prorsus consecretur postulationi & charitati Domini, quæ nec vagis occupetur, aut circumferatur cogitationibus, & spem atque exspectationem omnem collocatam habeat in Christo. Atque hoc pacto illucescet ille, purum docens petendi modum; & suggerens orationem puram, spiritualem, Deo dignam; & quæ fit in spiritu & veritate, adorationem.
units.tr: Homily 33. 41 We ought not to make our prayers after the manner of the body, nor in the custom of shouting, nor in the habit of keeping silent or bending the knees, but attending to the soul soberly, to wait for God, who will be present and will visit through all the soul's goings-out, through its paths and the organs of the senses. Thus, when it is fitting to be silent and when it is fitting to cry out, one should pray with vociferation, 42 provided the mind is fixed upon God. For just as the body, when it is working at something, leans wholly and entirely occupied upon the work, and all its members help one another, 43 so also the whole soul must be entirely consecrated to the petition and love of the Lord, not occupied or carried about by wandering thoughts, and must have all its hope and expectation placed in Christ. In this way that one will shine forth, teaching the pure manner of asking, and suggesting a pure, spiritual prayer, worthy of God, and the adoration which is in spirit and truth.

units.la: 370. Ephræm Syrus.
units.tr: 370. Ephraem Syrus.

units.la: De armaturâ generali. Studeamus jugiter lectioni sanctarum Scripturarum, ut nos doceant, quomodo laqueos Diaboli possimus effugere, æternamque adipisci vitam.
units.tr: On the General Armour. Let us constantly apply ourselves to the reading of the holy Scriptures, so that they may teach us how we can escape the snares of the Devil and obtain eternal life.

units.la: De patientiâ & consummatione seculi, &c. (quæ quidem Homilia & inter Chrysostomi & inter Ephræmi Opera habetur. Vid. Savil. & Vossii
units.tr: On Patience and the Consummation of the Age, etc. (This homily is found both among the works of Chrysostom and among those of Ephraem. See Savile and Vossius

units.la: 38 Οἱ προσδοκῶντες τὸν Θεὸν, ὀφείλουσι τὰς ψυχὰς ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ καὶ εἰρήνῃ καὶ γαλήνῃ πολλῇ πνεῦμα ... (Greek note, left column)
units.tr: 38 Those who wait for God ought to pour out their souls in quietness and peace and much calm, spirit ... [Οἱ προσδοκῶντες τὸν Θεὸν, ὀφείλουσι τὰς ψυχὰς ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ καὶ εἰρήνῃ καὶ γαλήνῃ πολλῇ πνεῦμα ...] (Greek note, left column)

units.la: 43 ... ἡ ψυχὴ ὅλη ... (Greek note, right column). edit p. 165.) 44 Vide, ne negligas animam tuam, sed lectioni ac precibus sedulo incumbe, ut mens tua illuminetur, fiatque perfectus ac integer, in nullo deficiens. Gloriantur alii de Magnatum Principumque ac Regum familiaritate atque colloquio: at tu coram Angelis Dei gloriare, colloquens & cum Spiritu S. per sacras literas conferens. Nam Spiritus S. est, qui loquitur per eas. Da operam igitur, ut divinarum Scripturarum lectionem familiarem tibi reddas, & perfistas in oratione. Et post. Quod si legere forte nescias; adhibe eum, a quo audire queas atque proficere. Vid. pag. 165. edit. Vossii, ubi hoc pluribus persequitur Ephraem, & p. 166. Non studeas duntaxat libri folia evolvere; sed si opus fuerit, 45 non pigeat etiam bis terve ac saepius eundem repetere versum, ut vim orationis intelligas.
units.tr: 43 ... the whole soul ... [ἡ ψυχὴ ὅλη ...] (Greek note, right column). See edition p. 165.) 44 Take care not to neglect your soul, but devote yourself diligently to reading and to prayers, so that your mind may be enlightened and become perfect and whole, lacking in nothing. Others boast of their familiarity and conversation with magnates, princes, and kings; but you should boast in the presence of the Angels of God, conversing and conferring also with the Holy Spirit through the sacred letters. For it is the Holy Spirit who speaks through them. Take pains, therefore, to make the reading of the divine Scriptures familiar to you, and persevere in prayer. And afterwards: But if perhaps you do not know how to read, seek out someone from whom you can hear and profit. See p. 165 of Vossius's edition, where Ephraem pursues this at greater length, and p. 166: Do not be content merely to turn over the leaves of a book; but if it is necessary, 45 do not be ashamed to repeat the same verse two or three times, or even more often, so that you may understand the power of the prayer.

units.la: In Encomio in Psalmos. Psalmus, infantium tutela, ornamentum senilus, majorum natu consolatio, mulieribus aptissimum ornamentum. Rudibus est instructio, proficientibus incrementum, perfectorum firmamentum. Ubi sacri libri adsunt & lectiones: ibi justorum est laetitia, & auscultantium salus. Ubi autem cithara & tibiarum cantus atque tripudia perstrepunt; ibi virorum pariter ac mulierum sunt tenebrae, diabolique festum celebratur. p. 13.
units.tr: In the Encomium on the Psalms. The Psalm is the protection of infants, the ornament of the old, the consolation of the elders, and a most fitting adornment for women. It is instruction for the untrained, growth for those making progress, and the firm support of the perfect. Where the sacred books and readings are present, there is joy for the righteous and salvation for those who listen. But where the lyre, the music of pipes, and dancing resound, there is darkness alike for men and women, and the festival of the devil is celebrated. p. 13.

units.la: De Panoplia sive Armatura generali (p. 480, 481.) Vere arcus aereus est contra inimicos, expansae in oratione manus in scientia orantis; sicut etiam sagitta directe emissa ab eo, qui arcum vibrat, &c. Ejusmodi est quod dico, fratres, cum quis in scientia orat, nec sinit evagari cogitationes suas: sed intelligit, quem interpellet, quem alloquatur: & tunc oratio illius Deo appropinquat. Et tunc vehementer contristatur inimicus, veluti acerrimo spiculo in corde percussus. Nam quanto per gratiam anima amplius proficit; tanto ipse, tanquam pulvis ante faciem venti effectus, magis profugit: persequitur enim illum Angelus Dei. Ecce quam in re illum acriter vulnerat: quia sc. orat in scientia, roboraturque, quia cogitationem captivat, nec evagari permittit. Et tu ergo, mi frater, etiam in scientia orationes funde.
units.tr: On the Panoply, or General Armour (pp. 480, 481). Truly the bronze bow against enemies is hands stretched out in prayer with knowledge on the part of the one praying; just as also an arrow shot straight from the one who draws the bow, etc. This is what I mean, brothers: when someone prays with understanding, and does not allow his thoughts to wander, but knows whom he is entreating and whom he addresses, then his prayer draws near to God. And then the enemy is greatly distressed, as if struck in the heart by a very sharp spike. For the more the soul advances through grace, the more he himself, become like dust before the face of the wind, flees away; for the Angel of God pursues him. See how sharply he wounds him in this matter: because he prays with understanding, and is strengthened, and because he takes his thought captive and does not permit it to wander. And you therefore, my brother, pour out your prayers also with understanding.

units.la: Porro notandum est ex. Hieronymo in Catalogo Scriptor. Ecclesiast. Syriaca lingua Ephraemum sua scripta edidisse, eaque tantam authoritatem
units.tr: Moreover, it should be noted from Jerome in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers that Ephraem published his writings in the Syriac language, and that these gained such authority

units.la: b Psalm. XXXIV. tatem adepta esse, ut post lectionem Scripturarum (linguâ etiam Syriacâ editarum c) publicè in quibusdam Ecclesiis recitarentur. Unde intelligimus, 1. Syros in suâ liturgiâ homilias vernaculâ linguâ scriptas usurpâsse, non peregrinâ, & minimè intellectâ, ut apud Pontificios fit. 2. Scripturas (ad quas legendas suos hortabatur Ephraem) Syrorum vernaculâ linguâ extitisse. Nam nec ipse Ephraem (in Scripturis exercitatissimus) sacras literas Græcâ linguâ legere potuit; quippe cujus ignarum fuisse, tum ex ipsius Encomio in Basilium M. tum ex Theodoreto, lib. 4. Hist. Eccles. cap. 29. d colligitur.
units.tr: b Psalm 34. that after the reading of the Scriptures (also published in the Syriac language c) they were read publicly in certain Churches. From this we understand, 1. that the Syrians used in their liturgy homilies written in their own language, not a foreign and little understood one, as happens among the Papists. 2. that the Scriptures (which Ephraem urged his people to read) existed in the vernacular language of the Syrians. For Ephraem himself, most thoroughly practised in the Scriptures, could not read the sacred letters in the Greek language; indeed, that he was ignorant of it is gathered both from his own Encomium on Basil the Great and from Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 29. d

units.la: Syriacè etiam divinos hymnos composuit Ephraem e, à Syris cantari solitos f in Martyrum celebribus festis; quos ad sua usque tempora ab Ecclesiæ cantoribus retentos fuisse 46 innuit Nicephorus Callist. lib. 9. cap. 16.
units.tr: Ephraem also composed divine hymns in Syriac, which the Syrians were accustomed to sing at the solemn festivals of the Martyrs; Nicephorus Callistus, book 9, chapter 16, implies that these were retained by the cantors of the Church down to his own time. 46

units.la: 370. Basilius Magnus Cæsareæ in Cappadociâ Episcopus.
units.tr: 370. Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

units.la: Procemio in Psalmos (quod quidem idem est cum Prologo præfixo Augustini enarrationibus in Psalmos, initio Tomi 8. Operum ejus: sed Basilii est, non Augustini.) 47 Scriptura omnis divinitus inspirata, & utilis, ob eam rationem à Spiritu S. conscripta est, ut velut è communi curandarum animarum officinâ, universi mortales, quisque pro morbi sui ratione medelam deligeremus. Medicamentum enim, inquit, magna sedat delicta. Et post de Psalmis. Melodiæ jucunditatem dogmatis immiscuit Spiritus Sanctus; ut aurium oblectatione deliniti, sermonis utilitatem latenter suscipieremus; more Medici sapientis, qui pueris medicinas aliquanto austeriores daturus, ut volantibus nauseam discutiat, melle poculum circumlinit. 48 Propterea nobis hæc apta Psalmorum modulamina offeruntur; ut qui ætate aut omnino etiam moribus adhuc pueri sunt, in speciem quidem concinant ac modulentur, re autem verâ animas suas erudiant. Nec enim ul-
units.tr: Preface to the Psalms (which is the same as the Prologue prefixed to Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms, at the beginning of volume 8 of his Works, but it is Basil's, not Augustine's). 47 All Scripture, divinely inspired and profitable, was written by the Holy Spirit for this reason: that, as from a common workshop for the healing of souls, all mortals might each choose a remedy suited to the nature of his own sickness. For, he says, medicine greatly calms transgressions. And afterwards, about the Psalms: The Holy Spirit mingled the pleasantness of melody with the doctrine, so that, soothed by the delight of the ears, we might take in the usefulness of the discourse without noticing; in the manner of a wise physician, who, about to give boys medicines somewhat harsher, smears the cup with honey so that the children, flying from it, do not feel nausea. 48 Therefore these fitting measures of the Psalms are offered to us, so that those who are still boys in age, or altogether in their character, may indeed seem to sing and modulate, but in truth instruct their souls. Nor indeed ul-

units.la: 46 Ὠδὰς παραδίδωσι, εἰς λύγον Σύρης παρέδωκε φάλλειν.
units.tr: 46 He hands down odes; he handed them to the Syrians to be sung [Ὠδὰς παραδίδωσι, εἰς λύγον Σύρης παρέδωκε φάλλειν].

units.la: 47 Πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος ὠφέλιμος, διὰ τοῦτο συγκατεσκευάσθη πρὸς τὸ πνεῦμα, ἵνα ὥσπερ ἐν κοινῇ τῇ ψυχῶν ἰατρείᾳ, πάντας ἀνθρώπους τὸ ἴαμα τῶν οἰκείων πάθους ἴκας ἐπιλεγόμενα, &c.
units.tr: 47 All Scripture is God-breathed and useful; for this reason it was fitted together with the Spirit, so that, as in a common healing of souls, all people, taking to themselves the remedy for their own passions, &c. [Πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος ὠφέλιμος, διὰ τοῦτο συγκατεσκευάσθη πρὸς τὸ πνεῦμα, ἵνα ὥσπερ ἐν κοινῇ τῇ ψυχῶν ἰατρείᾳ, πάντας ἀνθρώπους τὸ ἴαμα τῶν οἰκείων πάθους ἴκας ἐπιλεγόμενα, &c.]

units.la: 48 Ταῦτα μάλιστα ἡμῶν ὑπηνέμον, ἵνα οἱ παῖδες ἡλικίαν, ἡ ἐν ὅλαις οἱ τάξεσι τὸ ἦθος, τὰ μὲν δὲ ἐν μελῳδίαν, τῆ δ' ἀληθείᾳ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐκπαιδεύων — τὰ δ' τ' ψαλμῶν λόγια ἡ κατ' ἐκεῖνο μελῳδεῖσαι, ἡ ὅτι ἡ ἀρετὰς παιδεύεται, &c. lus ex iis, qui tardiore præsertim sunt ingenio, reperitur, quin apostolicum seu propheticum aliquod præceptum statim edifcat; Psalmorum verò protinùs reminiscuntur: hos & domi cantant, & foris obmurmurant, & in agro circumferunt. Unde exclamat ibidem, 49 O sapiens Doctoris inventum, qui excogitavit quo pacto unâ eâdemque operâ & caneremus, & quæ utilia sunt cognoscceremus; unde & quæ discun'ur, animis nostris magis insigantur. Nihil enim violentum durat; quod verò cum voluptate & gratiâ acquiritur, durabilius animis nostris insidet.
units.tr: 48 These things especially, for our sake... so that children, according to their age, and others according to their character, might be trained, the one in melody, the other in the truth of the soul; and the sayings of the Psalms, whether they sing them in that way or because they are learning virtues, &c. [Ταῦτα μάλιστα ἡμῶν ὑπηνέμον, ἵνα οἱ παῖδες ἡλικίαν, ἡ ἐν ὅλαις οἱ τάξεσι τὸ ἦθος, τὰ μὲν δὲ ἐν μελῳδίαν, τῆ δ' ἀληθείᾳ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐκπαιδεύων — τὰ δ' τ' ψαλμῶν λόγια ἡ κατ' ἐκεῖνο μελῳδεῖσαι, ἡ ὅτι ἡ ἀρετὰς παιδεύεται, &c.] There is hardly anyone, even of slow wit, who does not at once learn some apostolic or prophetic precept; but they immediately remember the Psalms: they sing these at home, murmur them abroad, and carry them about in the fields. Hence he exclaims in the same place, 49 "O the wise invention of the Teacher, who devised how we might at once sing and learn what is useful; so that what is learned is impressed more deeply on our minds. For nothing violent endures; but what is acquired with pleasure and grace settles more durably in our souls."

units.la: In Psal. XXVIII. 50 Homines miserabiles relictis ædibus suis ad templum concurrunt, quasi emolumenti quicquam inde lature; cùm tamen nec oracula Dei attentè audiant, nec naturæ suæ sensum accipiant, &c. 51 Psalmos habes, Prophetas, Evangelica præcepta, Apostolicas prædicationes; quæ corde oreque voluta, lingua psallat, mens sensum eorum, quæ dicuntur, scrutetur; ut psallas spiritu, psallas & mente. Nn enim gloriâ Deus indiget; sed ut laudéris te dignum reddere cupit.
units.tr: On Ps. XXVIII. 50 Wretched men, leaving their houses, run to the temple as if they would carry off some profit from it; yet they neither listen attentively to the oracles of God, nor receive the sense of their own nature, &c. 51 You have the Psalms, the Prophets, the evangelical precepts, the apostolic preachings; let these, turned over in heart and mouth, be sung by the tongue, and let the mind search out the sense of what is said; so that you sing with the spirit, and sing also with the mind. For God does not need glory; but he wishes you to make yourself worthy of being praised.

units.la: In Psalm. XXIX. Homil. 18. 52 Non si quis ore profert Psalmi verba, hic Domino psallit; sed qui à puro corde emittunt psalmodias; & qui sancti sunt, servantes justitiam ad Deum; hi psallere possunt Deo spirituales hymnos convenienter assequentes. Vid. eundem Epist. 1. ad Gregorium Theologum.
units.tr: On Ps. XXIX, Homily 18. 52 It is not the case that whoever utters the words of the Psalm with his mouth sings to the Lord; but those who send up psalmody from a pure heart, and who are holy, keeping justice toward God, these can sing to God, fittingly attaining spiritual hymns. See the same author, Epistle 1 to Gregory the Theologian.

units.la: Homil. in Psalm. LIX. 53 Ideo nostra sunt divina hæc oracula, & in Ecclesiâ Dei tanquam dona divinitus emissa, in unoquoque conventu relegutur; perinde ac animabus alendis à Spiritu Sancto administrata quædam alimonia, &c.
units.tr: Homily on Ps. LIX. 53 Therefore these divine oracles are ours, and in the Church of God, as gifts sent forth by God, they are read in every assembly, just as a certain nourishment administered by the Holy Spirit for feeding souls, &c.

units.la: Orat. Moral. 9. à Simeone Logothetâ ex Basilii scriptis collecta. 54 Neque enim per se verba orationis prosunt; sed cum diligenti mentis intentione emissa tunc demum prosunt, &c.
units.tr: Moral Discourse 9, collected by Simeon the Logothete from the writings of Basil. 54 For words of prayer do not profit by themselves; but when they are uttered with diligent attention of mind, then at last they profit, &c.

units.la: Sermon. in Martyrem Julittam. Oratio est boni petitio à piis mentibus ad Deum facta. 55 Petitionem autem non verbis tantùm definimus.
units.tr: Sermon on the martyr Julitta. Prayer is the petition of good made to God by pious minds. 55 Moreover we do not define petition by words alone.

units.la: 49 Ω σοφῆς ἐπινοίας τῷ διδασκάλῳ, ὁμῶς τ' ἀλίσθειν ἡμᾶς ἡ τὰ λυσιτελῆ μανθάνειν μηχανωμένῳ, &c.
units.tr: 49 O wise device of the Teacher, who contrived that we should be led to learn what is profitable, &c. [Ω σοφῆς ἐπινοίας τῷ διδασκάλῳ, ὁμῶς τ' ἀλίσθειν ἡμᾶς ἡ τὰ λυσιτελῆ μανθάνειν μηχανωμένῳ, &c.]

units.la: 50 Ἐπὶ τ' γὰρ ὑπὸ ἐξεταζόμενοι, ὡς δὲ τι ἑαυτοὺς ὠφελήσοντες, ὑχ' ἑαυτοῦ τὰς ἀκοὰς λόγοις δεῖ, &c.
units.tr: 50 For those who are examined, as if they would benefit themselves in some way, ought not to have their ears filled with words, &c. [Ἐπὶ τ' γὰρ ὑπὸ ἐξεταζόμενοι, ὡς δὲ τι ἑαυτοὺς ὠφελήσοντες, ὑχ' ἑαυτοῦ τὰς ἀκοὰς λόγοις δεῖ, &c.]

units.la: 51 Ψαλμῶν ἔχω, προφητείαν ἔχεις, εὐαγγελικὰ παραγγέλματα, τὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων κηρύγματα, ἡ γλῶσσα ψάλλειν, ὁ τῆς ἐρμηνείας τῇ διάνοιαν τῶν εἰρημένων, ἵνα ψάλλῃς τῷ πνεύματι, ψάλλῃς ἡ ψυχῇ, &c.
units.tr: 51 You have the Psalms, you have prophecy, the evangelical precepts, the proclamations of the apostles; let the tongue sing, and let the mind interpret the meaning of what is said, so that you sing with the spirit, sing also with the soul, &c. [Ψαλμῶν ἔχω, προφητείαν ἔχεις, εὐαγγελικὰ παραγγέλματα, τὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων κηρύγματα, ἡ γλῶσσα ψάλλειν, ὁ τῆς ἐρμηνείας τῇ διάνοιαν τῶν εἰρημένων, ἵνα ψάλλῃς τῷ πνεύματι, ψάλλῃς ἡ ψυχῇ, &c.]

units.la: 52 Οὐκ εἴ τις τῶν ῥημάτων περιοίσει τὰ ψαλμῶν ῥήματα, ἐσθ' ψάλλει τῷ κυρίῳ, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἀπὸ καρδίας καθαρᾶς ἀναπέμπουσι τὰς ψαλμῳδίας, &c.
units.tr: 52 Not if someone merely carries the words of the Psalms about in his mouth does he sing to the Lord; but because they send up psalmody from a pure heart, &c. [Οὐκ εἴ τις τῶν ῥημάτων περιοίσει τὰ ψαλμῶν ῥήματα, ἐσθ' ψάλλει τῷ κυρίῳ, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἀπὸ καρδίας καθαρᾶς ἀναπέμπουσι τὰς ψαλμῳδίας, &c.]

units.la: 53 Οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς τὰ ῥήματα ἡ προ-θήκη ὠφελεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸ μετὰ σπουδῆς διαθέσεως ἀναπέμπειν, &c.
units.tr: 53 For the bare words do not profit by being uttered, but the sending up with eager disposition does, &c. [Οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς τὰ ῥήματα ἡ προ-θήκη ὠφελεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸ μετὰ σπουδῆς διαθέσεως ἀναπέμπειν, &c.]

units.la: 54 Διὸ τὴν ἡμετέραν δεῖ τὰ θεῖα λόγια, τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ὡς θεόπνευστα δώρα, καθ' ἕκαστον σύλλογον ἀναμιμνήσκει, &c.
units.tr: 54 Therefore we must remind the Church of the divine oracles, as gifts breathed by God, in each assembly, &c. [Διὸ τὴν ἡμετέραν δεῖ τὰ θεῖα λόγια, τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ὡς θεόπνευστα δώρα, καθ' ἕκαστον σύλλογον ἀναμιμνήσκει, &c.]

units.la: 55 Τὴν δ' αἴτησιν οὐκ ἐν ῥήμασιν δεικνύομεν πίστεως. Τί οὖν ἐστὶν ὁ φαμέν, ὅτι χρὴ μὴ ἐν συλλαβαῖς ἡμᾶς ἡ ψυχὴ ἀπαπληρῶν, ἀλλὰ πεφυκότας μᾶλλον ψυχῆς, &c. Non enim Deum putamus verborum admonitione indigere, sed ea quæ utilia sunt satis vel nobis non petentibus videre. Quid igitur est quod dicimus? quòd oportet nos orationem non in syllabis perficere, sed magis animi proposito, tum actione secundum virtutem in omni vitâ perseverante, vim orationis implere. Non enim simplicia verba orationis prosunt (ut alibi idem 8) sed illud demum, quod ex seriâ animi affectione proficiscitur μετὰ σπουδαίας διαθέσεως. Hoc itaque illud est quod ait in Homiliâ in Psalm. XXVIII. Preces cujuslibet Deo manifestæ sunt. Alius ex affectu tantùm orat, alius scitè ac prudenter cælestia quærit; quidam perfunctorie nec acri attentione summis labris verba loquitur; cor autem ejus procul à Deo est. Ἡ προσευχὴ ἐκάστου προφανέρωσις θεῷ, τῆς ἐκ διαθέσεως (ex animo) τῆς ὑπερμένως ἐπιζητεῖ τὰ ὑπερφνια, τῆς ἀφωνοποιένως ἄχρις τοῖς χείλεσι τὰ ῥήματα φθέγγεται. ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτοῦ πόρρω ἀπέχει ἀπὸ θεοῦ.
units.tr: 55 We show petition not in words of faith. What then is it that we say, that we must not fill up the soul with syllables, but, being by nature more of the soul, &c. [Τὴν δ' αἴτησιν οὐκ ἐν ῥήμασιν δεικνύομεν πίστεως. Τί οὖν ἐστὶν ὁ φαμέν, ὅτι χρὴ μὴ ἐν συλλαβαῖς ἡμᾶς ἡ ψυχὴ ἀπαπληρῶν, ἀλλὰ πεφυκότας μᾶλλον ψυχῆς, &c.] For we do not think God needs to be reminded by words, but he sees what is useful even when we do not ask. What then is it that we say? That we ought to complete prayer not in syllables, but to fulfil the power of prayer by the purpose of the mind, and then by action according to virtue persevering through the whole of life. For simple words do not profit prayer (as the same author says elsewhere, 8), but only that which proceeds from an earnest disposition [μετὰ σπουδαίας διαθέσεως]. This therefore is what he says in the Homily on Ps. XXVIII: "The prayer of each is manifest to God. One prays from feeling alone; another wisely and prudently seeks heavenly things; another utters the words perfunctorily, without keen attention, only with the lips; but his heart is far from God." [Ἡ προσευχὴ ἐκάστου προφανέρωσις θεῷ, τῆς ἐκ διαθέσεως (ex animo) τῆς ὑπερμένως ἐπιζητεῖ τὰ ὑπερφνια, τῆς ἀφωνοποιένως ἄχρις τοῖς χείλεσι τὰ ῥήματα φθέγγεται. ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτοῦ πόρρω ἀπέχει ἀπὸ θεοῦ.]

units.la: De Spiritu S. cap. 1. Nobis præscriptum est, ut similes efficiamur Deo, saltem quatenus humanæ naturæ fas est. 56 Porrò similitudo non est absque cognitione, cognitio verò è doctrinâ paratur. Doctrinæ autem initium est oratio, orationis partes syllabæ ac dictiones. Proinde syllabas (S. Scripturæ) excutere non est aberrare à scopo.
units.tr: On the Holy Spirit, ch. 1. It is prescribed for us to become like God, as far as human nature allows. 56 Moreover, likeness is not without knowledge, and knowledge is acquired from teaching. The beginning of teaching, however, is prayer; the parts of prayer are syllables and words. Therefore to examine the syllables (of Holy Scripture) is not to stray from the goal.

units.la: . In Regulis contractioribus Quæst. 45. Si quis audito Domino, qui dixit, Servus sciens voluntatem Domini sui, & non faciens, neque parans se ad illius voluntatem, vapulabit multis; qui verò illam ignorat, & facit digna plagis, vapulabit paucis: hujus gratiâ cognitionem divinæ voluntatis studio negligat; an quid habet solatii? Respondeo. 57 Manifestum est, quòd qui ejusmodi est, ignorantiam falsò prætexat, & inevitabile habeat peccati judicium. Si enim non venissem, inquit Dominus, & non locutus illis essem, peccatum non haberent; nunc verò excusationem de peccato suo non habent. Cùm sacra Scriptura omnibus ubique voluntatem Dei denuntiet. Itaque qui talis est, non cum ignorantibus minore judicio, sed vehementiore cum illis damnabitur, de quibus scriptum est; Instar aspidis surdæ & obturantis aures suas, ne audiat vocem incantantium & venefici, dum ab illo incantatur sapienter.
units.tr: In the Shorter Rules, Question 45. If someone, having heard the Lord who said, "The servant who knows his master's will and does not do it, nor prepares himself for his will, shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who does not know it, and does things worthy of blows, shall be beaten with few," neglects for this reason the study of learning the divine will; does he have any consolation? I answer. 57 It is clear that one of this kind falsely pretends ignorance, and has an inescapable judgment for sin. For if I had not come, says the Lord, and had not spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin, since Holy Scripture proclaims the will of God to all people everywhere. Therefore whoever is such will be condemned not with the lesser judgment of the ignorant, but with a heavier one, along with those of whom it is written: "Like the deaf asp that stops its ears, so as not to hear the voice of the charmers and the enchanter, though he is skilfully charmed by him."

units.la: Ibid. Quæst. 95. An conducat, ut qui recens accesserunt, confestim scripturas discant? Respondeo. Et de istâ quæstione ex prædictis sta-
units.tr: Ibid. Question 95. Is it advantageous that those who have only recently come should at once learn the Scriptures? I answer. Concerning this question, from the things stated above...

units.la: {8} Orat. Moral. 9. supra cit.
units.tr: Oration on Morals, 9, cited above.

units.la: 56 Ὁμοίωσίς ἡ ἐκ ἀνὰ γνῶσιν, ἡ ἡ γνῶσις ἐκ διδαγμῶν· λόγῳ δὲ διάσωσις ἀρχὴ, λόγῳ δὲ μέρη συλλαβαὶ καὶ λέξεις, ὥστε ἐν ἐξ ὧν ὁ ... ἀγνοεῖ, ... ἀλλά, &c.
units.tr: 56 Likeness comes from knowledge, and knowledge from teaching. Speech is the beginning of salvation, and the parts of speech are syllables and words, so that ... [Ὁμοίωσίς ἡ ἐκ ἀνὰ γνῶσιν, ἡ ἡ γνῶσις ἐκ διδαγμῶν· λόγῳ δὲ διάσωσις ἀρχὴ, λόγῳ δὲ μέρη συλλαβαὶ καὶ λέξεις, ὥστε ἐν ἐξ ὧν ὁ ... ἀγνοεῖ, ... ἀλλά, &c.] ...

units.la: 57 Δῆλον δὲν ὁ τοῦτο σημαινόμενον ... tuatur. 58 Necessarium enim est & consonum, ut ex sacra quisque Scriptura quod necesse fit discat, tum ad pietatis plerophoriam, tum ne adsuescat humanis traditionibus.
units.tr: 57 It is clear that this means ... [Δῆλον δὲν ὁ τοῦτο σημαινόμενον ...] ... 58 For it is necessary and fitting that each person learn from holy Scripture what he needs to know, both for the full assurance of piety and so that he does not grow accustomed to human traditions.

units.la: Ibid. Quæst. 278. Quomodo spiritus alicujus precetur, mens vero fructu careat? Respondeo. 59 Hoc de illis dictum est, qui in lingua audientibus ignota preces faciunt. Dicit enim, Si oro lingua, spiritus meus quidem orat: mens vero sine fructu est. Nam quando præsentibus verba precationis incognita sunt; sine fructu est mens, quia nihil utilitatis redit ad precantem. Quando vero qui adsunt, precationem intelligunt, quæ utilis potest esse audientibus; tunc qui precatur, fructum habet, ædificationem sc. eorum qui inde juvantur. Consimiliter autem & de quacunque verborum Dei pronuntiatione sentiendum est. Scriptum enim est: Sed si quis bonus est ad ædificationem fidei.
units.tr: Ibid., Question 278. How can someone's spirit pray while his mind is without fruit? I answer: This is said of those who pray in a language unknown to the hearers. For he says, "If I pray in a tongue, my spirit indeed prays, but my mind is without fruit." When the words of the prayer are unknown to those present, the mind is without fruit, because nothing of benefit returns to the one praying. But when those present understand the prayer, it can be useful to the hearers; then the one who prays has fruit, namely the edification of those who are helped by it. The same must be thought of any recitation of the words of God. For it is written: "But if anyone is good for the edification of faith."

units.la: In proœmio de Judicio Dei, inter Ascetica (si is Author eorum est) in init. Jam olim ab initio à Christianis parentibus educatus, 60 ab illis quidem à puero sacras literas didici, quæ me ad veritatis cognitionem adduxerunt.
units.tr: In the preface to On the Judgment of God, among the Ascetica (if he is the author of them), at the beginning: "From the start I was brought up from childhood by Christian parents, and from them I learned the sacred letters from boyhood, which led me to the knowledge of the truth."

units.la: Epist. 63. ad Clericos Neocæsar. 61 Ad id vero quòd propter Psalmodias accusamur (qua re po'issimùm simpliciores perterrefaciunt, qui nos traducunt) hoc habeo quod dicam: quòd qui jam obtinuerunt ritus omnibus Ecclesiis Dei concordes sunt & consoni. De nocte siquidem populus consurgens antelucano tempore domum precationis petit; inque labore & tribulatione ac lachrymis indesinentibus facta ad Deum confessi ne, tandem ab oratione surgentes ad psalmodiam instituuntur. Et nunc quidem in duas partes divisi alternis succinentes psallunt; atque ex eo simul eloquiorum Dei exercitationem ac meditationem corroborant; & cordibus suis attentionem, & rejectis vanis cogitationibus mentis soliditatem suppeditant: deinde uni ex ipsis hoc munus dato, ut quod canendum est prior ordiatur, reliqui succinunt: atque ita psalmodiæ varietate precibusque subinde interfertis noctem
units.tr: Epistle 63, to the clergy of Neocaesarea. "As to the charge that we are accused because of the psalmody (which chiefly frightens simpler people who slander us), I have this to say: those who have already adopted the rites are in agreement and harmony with all the Churches of God. For the people rise at night and, at the time before dawn, go to the house of prayer; and, in labour and tribulation and unceasing tears, after making confession to God, they rise from prayer and are instructed in psalmody. Now they sing in two parts, chanting alternately; and thereby they strengthen both the practice and the meditation on the words of God, and supply attentiveness to their hearts and steadiness to their minds, with empty thoughts cast aside. Then one of them, who has been given this office, begins what is to be sung, and the rest respond; and so, with the variety of psalmody and with prayers interspersed from time to time, they pass the night

units.la: 58 Τὰ δὲ εἰς ἡ χρείαν ἕκαστον ἐμμαρθάνειν ἐν τῇ Θεοτόκῳ... [Greek note, lower left column]
units.tr: 58 But that each one should learn what is needful for use ... in the Theotokos ... [Τὰ δὲ εἰς ἡ χρείαν ἕκαστον ἐμμαρθάνειν ἐν τῇ Θεοτόκῳ...]

units.la: 61 — τὰ γὰρ κατεχόμενα ἔθη παίδεις τῆς Θεοῦ ἐκκλησίας... [Greek note, lower right column] superant. Illucescente jam die pariter omnes velut uno ore ac corde uno confessionis Psalmum Deo offerunt; ac suis quisque verbis resipiscentiam prositentur. 62 Horum gratia si nos fugitis; fugietis simul & Ægyptios, sugietis Libyam utramque, Thebaeos, Palaestinos, Arabes, Phoenicas, Syros, & qui ad Euphratem habitant; &, ut semel dicam, omnes, apud quos vigiliae & preces communesque psalmodiae in pretio sunt.
units.tr: 61 For the customs that prevail are children of the Church of God ... [— τὰ γὰρ κατεχόμενα ἔθη παίδεις τῆς Θεοῦ ἐκκλησίας...] are superior. As the day now dawns, all together, as with one mouth and one heart, they offer to God the Psalm of confession, and each professes repentance in his own words. 62 For their sake, if you flee from us, you will flee also from the Egyptians; you will flee from both Libyas, from the Thebans, Palestinians, Arabs, Phoenicians, Syrians, and those who dwell by the Euphrates; and, to say it once for all, from all those among whom vigils, prayers and common psalmody are held in high esteem.

units.la: 370. Gregorius Nyssenus Episcopus, Basilii frater.
units.tr: 370. Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, brother of Basil.

units.la: Tractatu I. in Psalmos, cap. 3. 63 Principio causam indagabimus, ob quam cum adeo vita ex virtute acta difficilis sit & ardua; mysteriorum tamen & divinorum secretorum aenigmaticam & umbratilem doctrinam, & inexplicabilibus involutam tegumentis Theologicam institutionem, tam facilem captu & jucundam (ἡ διὰ τῆς Ψαλμῶν διδασκαλίας) effecerit: ut non modo viri perfecti, & quibus jam animi sensa perpurgata sunt, eruditionem hanc assequantur; sed ut eandem & mulieres sibi tanquam propriam vendicent: infantibusque, crepundiorum instar, voluptatem pariat; & decrepitis baculi & quietis loco obtingat: illi vero, quibus aetas viget, hujus doctrinae donum suum esse existiment: is autem, qui tristi est animo, & male affecto ob eventum quenpiam, propter se Scripturae hujus gratiam divinitus missam esse credat. Adhaec qui iter seu terra seu mari faciunt, quique sedentarias artes exercent, & (ut rem in pauca conferam) omnes tam viri quam mulieres, quodcunque vitae genus sectentur, aegri simul ac firmi, damnum se pati arbitrantur; si non semper in ore divinam hanc institutionem circumferant. Jam vero & convivia & nuptiales hilaritates Philosophiam hanc, ut partem laetitiae, suis jucunditatibus adscisc unt; ut taceamus divinam illam in nocturnis pervigiliis per psalmos instituti solitam hymnodiam, Ecclesiaeque in his decantandis accuratam sedulitatem.
units.tr: Treatise 1 on the Psalms, ch. 3. 63 At the outset we shall inquire why it is that, although a life lived in virtue is so difficult and arduous, the teaching of the Psalms (ἡ διὰ τῆς Ψαλμῶν διδασκαλίας) has made the enigmatic and shadowy doctrine of mysteries and divine secrets, and the theological instruction wrapped in inexplicable veils, so easy to grasp and so pleasant. The result is that not only perfect men, whose minds are already purified, attain this learning, but women also claim it as their own. It gives delight to infants like a rattle, and it serves the aged as a staff and a source of rest. Those in the vigour of life think this gift of doctrine is their own. The man who is sad at heart, and troubled by some misfortune, believes that this Scripture was sent by God for his sake. Furthermore, those who travel by land or sea, those who follow sedentary trades, and (to speak briefly) all men and women, whatever way of life they follow, sick and healthy alike, think they suffer loss if they do not always have this divine instruction on their lips. Indeed, feasts and wedding celebrations also take this philosophy into their pleasures as a part of their merriment, not to mention the hymn-singing of the Church, which was customary at night vigils through the psalms, and the careful devotion of the Church in chanting them.

units.la: De Vita Macrinae sororis, paulo post init. 64 Proinde quae ex divino spiritu dictata Scriptura primae illi aetatulae (Macrinae) faciliora aptioraque
