units.la: Lib. 2. ad Uxorem. Quid maritus suus illi, vel marito quid illa cantabit? Audiat sanè, audiat aliquid de Dei cænâ, de taberna, de gehenna. Quæ Dei mentio? Quæ Christi invocatio? Ubi fomenta fidei de Scripturarum interleCtione? Ubi spiritûs refrigerium? Ubi divina benedictio? Ibid. Sonant inter duos (maritum sc. & uxorem) psalmi & hymni; & mutuò provocant quis melius Deo suo canat. His pacem suam Christus mittit.
units.tr: Book 2 to his wife: What will her husband sing to her, or she to her husband? Let him hear, to be sure, something of the Lord's Supper, of the tavern, of hell. What mention of God? What invocation of Christ? Where are the supports of faith drawn from the reading of the Scriptures? Where is the refreshment of the Spirit? Where is the divine blessing? Ibid.: Psalms and hymns resound between the two of them (that is, the husband and the wife), and they mutually challenge one another as to who sings better to their God. Christ sends his peace upon these two.

units.la: 250. Cyprianus Carthaginiensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 250. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage.

units.la: De Oratione Dominica, Sect. 3. Et quando in unum cum fratribus convenimus, & sacrificia divina cum Dei sacerdote celebramus; verecundiæ & disciplinæ memores esse debemus; non passim ventilare preces nostras inconditis vocibus, nec petitionem commendandam modeste Deo tumultuosâ loqua-
units.tr: On the Lord's Prayer, sect. 3: And when we come together with the brethren, and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God, we ought to remember modesty and discipline; we ought not to fling our prayers about carelessly in uncontrolled voices, nor to hurl our petition, which ought to be commended to God with restraint, with a noisy loquacity

units.la: {1} In Edit. Rhenani & Pamelii, Coimus. loquacitate jactare. Quia Deus non vocis sed cordis auditor est. Nec admonendus est clamoribus, qui cogitationes hominum videt, &c.
units.tr: {1} In the editions of Rhenanus and Pamelius, "Coimus." with loquacity. For God is a hearer not of the voice but of the heart. Nor is he to be reminded by shouts, he who sees the thoughts of men, etc.

units.la: Ibid. sect. 20. Cùm Dei sermo Dominus noster Jesus Christus omnibus venerit, & colligens doctos pariter & indoctos, omni sexui atque ætati præcepta salutis ediderit; Præceptorum suorum fecit grande compendium; ut in disciplinâ cœlesti discentium memoria non laboraret; sed quod esset simplici fidei necessarium, velociter disceret.
units.tr: Ibid., sect. 20: Since our Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God, has come to all, and, gathering together the learned and the unlearned alike, has given the precepts of salvation to every sex and age, he has made a great summary of his precepts, so that the memory of the learners in the heavenly teaching should not be burdened, but that what was necessary for simple faith might be learned quickly.

units.la: Ibid. sect. 22. Quando autem stamus ad orationem, fratres dilectissimi, vigilare & incumbere ad preces toto corde debemus. Cogitatio omnis carnalis & sæcularis abscedat; nec quidquam tunc animus quàm id solum cogitet, quod precatur. Ideò & Sacerdos ante orationem præfatione præmissâ parat fratrum mentes dicendo; Sursum corda: ut dum respondet plebs; Habemus ad Dominum: admoneatur nihil aliud se quàm Dominum cogitare debere. Claudatur contra adversarium pectus, & soli Deo pateat; nec ad se hostem Dei tempore orationis adire patiatur. Obrepit enim frequenter, & penetrat, & subtiliter fallens preces nostras à Deo avocat, ut aliud habeamus in corde, & aliud in voce, quando intentione sincerâ Dominum debeat non vocis sonus, sed animus & sensus orare. Et paulò post. Quomodo te audiri à Deo postulas, cùm te ipse non audias? Vis esse Deum memorem tui cùm rogas, quando tu ipse memor tui non fis? Locus iste à Gratiano in Decretum transfertur, par. 3. de Consecrat. Dist. 1. cap. Quando autem.
units.tr: Ibid., sect. 22: When we stand to pray, dearly beloved brethren, we ought to be watchful and to give ourselves to prayer with the whole heart. Let every carnal and worldly thought depart; and let the mind think of nothing else than what it prays for. Therefore the priest also, before the prayer, prepares the minds of the brethren by a preface, saying: "Lift up your hearts," so that when the people respond, "We have them lifted up to the Lord," they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing but the Lord. Let the breast be closed against the adversary, and open to God alone; and let it not permit the enemy of God to come near itself at the time of prayer. For he often creeps in, and penetrates, and subtly deceiving, diverts our prayers from God, so that we have one thing in the heart and another in the voice, whereas with sincere attention it is not the sound of the voice but the mind and the understanding that ought to pray to the Lord. And a little later: How do you ask to be heard by God, when you do not hear yourself? Do you want God to remember you when you ask, when you yourself are not mindful of yourself? This passage is transferred by Gratian into the Decretum, part 3, De Consecratione, dist. 1, ch. Quando autem.

units.la: Epist. 2. ad Donatum. Sit tibi vel oratio assidua vel lectio: nunc cum Deo loquere, nunc Deus tecum. Ille te præceptis suis instruat, ille disponat: quem ille divitem fecerit, nemo pauperem faciet. Penuria esse nulla jam poterit, cùm semel pectus cœlestis sagina saturavit.
units.tr: Letter 2 to Donatus: Let there be for you either constant prayer or reading: now you speak with God, now God with you. Let him instruct you by his precepts and order you; whomever he has made rich, no one will make poor. There will be no want at all, once the breast has been filled with heavenly fodder.

units.la: De zelo & livore sect. 14. Sit ante oculos divina lectio, in manibus bona operatio, in sensibus dominica cogitatio.
units.tr: On Jealousy and Envy, sect. 14: Let the divine reading be before your eyes, good work in your hands, and the Lord's thought in your senses.

units.la: 316. Lactantius Firmianus.
units.tr: 316. Lactantius Firmianus.

units.la: Institut. divin. lib. 5. cap. 1. Prophetæ communi & simplici sermone, ut ad populum, sunt locuti.
units.tr: Institutes, Divine, book 5, chapter 1: The prophets spoke in a common and simple speech, as to the people.

units.la: Lib. 6. cap. 21. Num igitur Deus, & mentis & vocis & linguæ artifex, disertè loqui non potest? Immò verò summâ providentiâ carere fuco voluit ea quæ divina sunt; ut omnes intelligerent, quæ ipse omnibus loquebatur.
units.tr: Book 6, chapter 21: Does God then, the artificer of mind, voice and tongue, be unable to speak eloquently? Rather, by his supreme providence he willed that the things of God be free of ornament, so that all might understand what he himself spoke to all.

units.la: 360. Hilarius.
units.tr: 360. Hilarius.

units.la: 360. Hilarius Pictavorum Episcopus.
units.tr: 360. Hilarius, Bishop of Poitiers.

units.la: In Psalmum I. Meditatio legis non solùm in verbis legentis est, sed & in operis religione : neque ut libros tantùm & Scripturas recenseamus, sed ut ea quæ Scripturis & libris continentur, gestis rebusque meditemur.
units.tr: In Psalm I. Meditation on the law lies not only in the words of the reader but also in the religious practice of the work. We should meditate not merely on reviewing the books and Scriptures, but on the deeds and things contained in the Scriptures and books.

units.la: In Psalm LXV. Audiat orantis populi consistens quis extra Ecclesiam vocem, spectet celebres hymnorum sonitus, & ante divinorum quoque Sacramentorum officia responsionem devotæ confessionis accipiat.
units.tr: In Psalm LXV. Let whoever stands outside the Church hear the voice of the praying people, look upon the famous sounds of the hymns, and receive, even before the rites of the divine sacraments, the response of a devoted confession.

units.la: In Pfalm. CXVIII. ad finem Zain. Utile est justificationes Dei sine aliquâ temporis intermissione scrutari ; quia per exquisitionem earum memoriam nos perpetim continemus in Jesu Christo. Ibid. ad literam Caph. Utinam cordis clamore loqueremur. Labia tantùm nostra sensu peregrinante quod nesciunt murmurant ; & officium corporis mens in res alias occupata non sequitur.
units.tr: In Psalm CXVIII, at the end of Zain. It is useful to search out the justifications of God without any interruption of time, since through the seeking of them we continually keep their memory in Jesus Christ. Ibid., at the letter Caph. Would that we spoke with the clamour of the heart. Our lips alone murmur what they do not understand, our sense wandering abroad, and the mind, occupied elsewhere, does not follow the office of the body.

units.la: In Psalm. CXXVI. Sermo divinus secundùm intelligentiæ nostræ consuetudinem naturamque se temperat, communibus rerum vocabulis ad significationem doctrinæ suæ & institutionis aptatis ; nobis enim non sibi loquitur, atque ideo nostris utitur in loquendo.
units.tr: In Psalm CXXVI. The divine word adapts itself to the custom and nature of our understanding, using common words of things fitted to signify its teaching and instruction. For it does not speak to itself but to us, and therefore it uses our language in speaking.

units.la: In Psalm. CXXXV. Plerunque, immo semper, vitio nostro accidit, ut quæ legi in Ecclesiâ audimus, auribus atque animis nostris longè ab his peregrinantibus negligamus ; ut per audiendi incuriam vilescat apud nos dictorum cœlestium dignitas ; cùm in lectionis tempore rationes supputamus, iras concipimus, injurias cogitamus, luxus recolimus. Tunc ad hæc occupatis nobis surdæ aures sunt, & hebes mens est. Et si quid fortè in aures nostras eorum quæ leguntur inciderit ; virtutem tamen dictorum obrutus sæculi curis animus non sentit ; & quorum intelligentiam non sequitur, levem existimabit authoritatem. Omnia autem, quæ in libris Propheticis sunt, maximum humanæ & salutis & doctrinæ profectum in se habent ; nostrique causâ universa scripta sunt, &c.
units.tr: In Psalm CXXXV. It very often, indeed always, happens through our fault that we neglect what we hear read in the Church, our ears and minds wandering far from these things; so that through carelessness in hearing, the dignity of heavenly words grows cheap among us. While the reading is going on we reckon accounts, conceive anger, brood over wrongs, and recall luxuries. Then, with us occupied with these things, our ears are deaf and our mind is dull. And if anything of what is read happens to enter our ears, the mind, buried under the cares of the age, does not perceive the power of the words; and whatever it does not follow in understanding, it will think of little authority. Yet all the things that are in the prophetic books hold the greatest advance of human salvation and teaching within themselves; and they have all been written for our sake, etc.

units.la: 370. Ulphilas Gothorum Episcopus.
units.tr: 370. Ulphilas, Bishop of the Goths.

units.la: Hic primus γεγράμματα ἐφηύρε Γοτθικὰ, ᾗ τὰς θείας γραφὰς εἰς τὴν Γοτθῶν μεταβαλὼν, τὰς βαρβάρες μανθάνειν τὰ θεῖα λόγια παρεσκεύασεν, Gothicas literas excogitavit ; & sacris Scripturis in Gothorum sermonem conversis, effecit ut Barbari divina eloquia perdiscerent. Ut habet Socrates lib. 4. Hist. Eccl. cap. 33. [juxta edit. Græc. nam in Latin. est 27.] cui consentit Sozomenus lib. 6. Hist cap. 37. edit. Lat. & Nicephorus lib. 11. cap. 48. Atque hinc est quòd Walafridus Strabo de rebus Ecclesiasticis cap. 7. de Gothis ita scribat. Et (ut historiæ testantur) postmodum studiosi illius gentis divinos libros in suæ locutionis proprietatem transtulerunt, quorum adhuc monumenta apud nonnullos habentur. Quin & hodie translationis Ulphilæ exemplar MS. idque vetustissimum Gothicis literis majoribus scriptum in aliquâ Germaniæ Bibliothecâ delitescere dicitur, (B. Vulcanius præfat. in lib. de linguâ & moribus Getarum.)
units.tr: He was the first to devise Gothic letters, and by translating the divine Scriptures into the language of the Goths he enabled the barbarians to learn the divine oracles [Οὗτος πρῶτος γράμματα ἐφεῦρε Γοτθικά, καὶ τὰς θείας γραφὰς εἰς τὴν Γοτθικὴν μεταβαλὼν γλῶτταν, τοὺς βαρβάρους μανθάνειν τὰ θεῖα λόγια παρεσκεύασεν]. So Socrates reports, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 33 [according to the Greek edition; in the Latin it is chapter 27]. Sozomen agrees, History, book 6, chapter 37 (Latin edition), and so does Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 48. This is why Walafrid Strabo, in his book on ecclesiastical matters, chapter 7, writes of the Goths as follows: "And (as the histories bear witness) afterwards the scholars of that people translated the divine books into the proper idiom of their own speech, and some still keep the monuments of this work." Indeed, it is said that a manuscript of Ulphilas' translation, very ancient and written in large Gothic letters, is still hidden away in some library in Germany (B. Vulcanius, preface to his book on the language and customs of the Getae).

units.la: Matthæus Parker de Archiep. Cantuar. pag. 42. ex Roffensi Historiâ. Ado in Chronico ætat. 6. A. D. 364. Isidorus in Chron. Goth. Æra 415. Galfilam dicunt Gothorum Episcopum Gothicas literas adinvenisse & Scripturas sacras in eandem linguam convertisse. Petrus Equilinus in Catalogo Sanctorum de S. Gulphilâ agens, (sic enim appellat) Testamentum (inquit) vetus ac novum in linguam transtulit propriam. Sixtus Senensis lib. 4. Biblioth. Sanct. Omnes (inquit) divinas Scripturas è Græco in Gothicam linguam à se conversas Gothis tradidit, & Catholicè explicavit, diu multumque adversus Arianos decertans. Simeon etiam Metaphrastes in Martyrio S. Nicetæ (quod habetur 15. die Septembris) de Ulphilâ ita scribit. Hic cùm esset vir prudens & doctus, invenit figuras literarum & sonos Gothicæ voci convenientes: & cùm in eis sacram nostram & divinitus inspiratam Scripturam è Græcâ in linguam Gothicam vertisset; omni studio & diligentiâ effecit, ut eam discerent, qui erant suæ gentis. Quamobrem magnum incrementum accipiebat pietas apud Barbaros, & indies proficiebat. Vid. Sigebertum.
units.tr: Matthew Parker, On the Archbishops of Canterbury, p. 42, from the Rochester history. Ado, in his Chronicle, age 6, A.D. 364. Isidore, in the Gothic Chronicle, Era 415. They say that Galfila, bishop of the Goths, invented Gothic letters and turned the Holy Scriptures into that language. Petrus Equilinus, in his Catalogue of the Saints, speaking of St Gulphilas (for so he calls him): "He translated the Old and New Testament into his own language." Sixtus of Siena, Bibliotheca Sancta, book 4: "He (he says) handed over to the Goths all the divine Scriptures, translated by himself from the Greek into the Gothic language, and expounded them in a Catholic manner, struggling long and hard against the Arians." Simeon Metaphrastes too, in the Martyrdom of St Nicetas (which is found on the 15th day of September), writes thus of Ulphilas: "Since he was a prudent and learned man, he discovered letter forms and sounds suited to the Gothic voice; and when with these he had translated our holy and divinely inspired Scripture from Greek into the Gothic tongue, he took every pains and care to make those of his own nation learn it. Therefore piety received a great increase among the barbarians, and advanced day by day." See Sigebert.

units.la: Sixtus Senensis, & Rhemenses in Præfat. Nov. Testam. fatentur translationem hanc ab Ulphilâ factam, antequam esset Arianus: factumque id probat Angelus Roccha in Biblioth. Vatic. p. 152. ut salsum esse appareat, quod scribit Bellarminus lib. 2. de Sacram. in genere cap. 31. & Johannes Magnus lib. 15. histor. Gothor. cap. 1. Ulphilam, ut suam insignem impietatem efficacius stabiliret, primum omnium divinarum literarum sacratissimum thesaurum in Gothicam linguam transfudisse, immixto, quod imbiberat, perniciosò veneno.
units.tr: Sixtus of Siena and the Rhemists, in the preface to the New Testament, admit that this translation was made by Ulphilas before he became an Arian; and Angelus Roccha, in the Vatican Library, p. 152, proves the fact, so that what Bellarmine writes, book 2, On the Sacraments in general, chapter 31, and John Magnus, History of the Goths, book 15, chapter 1, is shown to be false: that Ulphilas, "in order the more effectively to establish his notorious impiety," was the first of all to pour the most sacred treasure of the divine letters into the Gothic language, "mixing in, along with what he had imbibed, a pernicious poison."

units.la: Gothi temporibus Valentis Aug. Wulfilâ Episcopo Authore, Christiani quidem facti sunt, sed Ariani: atque adeò etiamnum in iisdem regionibus degunt sub Præcopensi Tartarorum Dynastiâ; & utrumque Testamentum iisdem literis, quas excogitavit Wulfila, conscriptum, & eadem linguâ, quâ tempore Ovidii utebantur, interpretatum legunt. Josephus Scaliger lib. 3.
units.tr: "In the times of the Emperor Valens, the Goths, under their bishop Wulfila as author, became Christians, but Arians; and even now they live in the same regions under the Tartar dynasty of Perekop; and they read both Testaments, written in the same letters that Wulfila devised and translated into the same language that was used in the time of Ovid." Joseph Scaliger, book 3 of his Isagogic Canons, p. 138.

units.la: Canonum Isagogicorum pag. 138. De Ulphilæ translatione vid. Paulum Diaconum lib. 12. 2
units.tr: On Ulphilas' translation, see Paul the Deacon, book 12.

units.la: 370. Hilarius Romanus Diaconus, 3 vel quicunque author fuit Commentariorum, qui Ambrosii nomine feruntur, in Pauli Epistolas.
units.tr: 370. Hilary the Roman Deacon, or whoever was the author of the Commentaries that go under the name of Ambrose on the Epistles of Paul.

units.la: Authorem hunc sancti Hilarii nomine citat Augustinus lib. 4. contra 2. epist. Pelagian. cap. 4. Alii Hilarium, qui Romæ Diaconus fuit temporibus Damasi, esse suspicantur. In Commentariis ad 1 Tim. III. mentionem factam legimus Damasi Rectoris Ecclesiæ; quem locum cùm Pontificii Doctores, Hardingus a, Sanderus b, Bellarminus c, Stapletonus d, & alii e passim ad Primatum Pontificium stabiliendum citare soleant; ejusdem Authoris explicationem 14. capitis prioris Epistolæ ad Corinthios aspernari non debeant. Hinc autem sententiæ sequentes deductæ sunt.
units.tr: Augustine cites this author under the name of St Hilary, in book 4 against the second letter of Pelagius, chapter 4. Others suspect that he was Hilary, who was a deacon at Rome in the time of Damasus. In the commentary on 1 Tim. 3 we read of Damasus as ruler of the Church. Since the Papist teachers, Harding, Sanders, Bellarmine, Stapleton and others, commonly cite this passage everywhere to establish papal primacy, they ought not to scorn this same author's explanation of chapter 14 of the first letter to the Corinthians. From it the following statements are drawn.

units.la: Nam qui loquitur linguâ ] Hoc est quod dicit; quia qui loquitur incognitâ linguâ, Deo loquitur, quia ipse omnia novit; homines verò nesciunt; ideoque nullus est ex hâc re profectus. Si igitur nesciero virtutem vocis, &c. ] Non utique id studendum monet, ut invicem per incognitam linguam barbari sibi videantur: sed quia concordiæ res est, his nitendum est, ut per unanimitatem intellectûs communi lætitiâ, glorientur. Id ibid. Exemplis commendat, per quæ facilè assequantur non debere illos loqui linguis, qui interpretari non possunt; ut quid enim loquatur, quod nemo intelligit? Si oravero linguâ; spiritus meus orat, mens autem est sine fructu. ] Manifestum est ignorare animum nostrum, si linguâ loquatur quam nescit: sicut assolent, non autem in Ecclesiâ, Latini homines Græcè cantare, oblectati sono verborum, nescientes tamen quid dicant. At quem potest habere fructum, qui ignorat quæ loquatur? Cæterùm si benedixeris spiritu ] Hoc est si laudem Dei linguâ loquaris ignotâ audientibus. Quis supplet locum Idiotæ? Quomodo dicet Amen super tuam benedictionem? quia nescit quid dicas ] Imperitus enim audiens, quod non intelligit,
units.tr: "For he who speaks in a tongue." This is what he means: he who speaks in an unknown tongue speaks to God, because God knows all things, but men do not understand, and so no one is edified by it. "If then I know not the meaning of the voice, etc." He does not advise that they should strive to make barbarians seem to one another through an unknown tongue, but because it is a matter of harmony, they must strive for this, that they may rejoice together in unity of understanding. The same, on the same place. He commends by examples, by which they may easily grasp, that those who cannot interpret ought not to speak in tongues; for why should he speak what no one understands? "If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful." It is plain that our mind does not understand if it speaks in a language it does not know, just as Latin men are wont to sing in Greek, delighted by the sound of the words but not knowing what they say, and that not in church. But what fruit can there be for one who does not know what he is saying? "But if you bless with the spirit." That is, if you praise God in an unknown tongue to those who hear. "Who fills the place of the unlearned?" How will he say Amen to your blessing? "Because he does not know what you say." For the unskilled listener, since he does not understand, does not know the end of the prayer, and does not answer Amen, that is, "True," so that the blessing may be confirmed. For the prayer is confirmed through those who answer Amen, so that everything said may be confirmed in the minds of the hearers by the testimony of truth.

units.la: a Artic. 4. contra Juel. b De visib. Monarch. lib. 7. c De Roman. Pontif. lib. 2. cap. 16. d In epist. dedicat. Princip. doctrinal. ad Gregor. XIII. e Rhemenses in 1 Tim. III. 15.
units.tr: a Article 4, against Jewel. b On the Visible Monarchy, book 7. c On the Roman Pontiff, book 2, chapter 16. d In the dedicatory epistle of the Principles of Doctrine to Gregory XIII. e The Rheims commentators on 1 Tim. 3:15.

units.la: 2 Gothicam IV. Evangeliorum Versionem antiquam cum Glossario & notis Junius & Marefchallus ediderunt Dordraci, 1665. 4to.
units.tr: 2 The old Gothic version of the four Gospels, with glossary and notes, was published by Junius and Marshall at Dordrecht, 1665, quarto.

units.la: 3 Hilario Diacono deberi hosce Commentarios apud omnes fere eruditos receptum est. intelligit, nescit finem orationis; & non respondet Amen, i. e. Verum, ut confirmetur benedictio. Per hos enim impletur confirmatio precis, qui respondent Amen; ut omnia dicta veri testimonio in audientium mentibus confirmentur. Citatur locus iste postremus Ambrosii nomine ab Amalario Fortunato Ecclesiast. Offic. lib. 3. cap. 9.
units.tr: 3 It is generally accepted by almost all the learned that these Commentaries are owed to the deacon Hilary. He understands, but the other does not know the end of the prayer; and he does not answer Amen, that is, "True," so that the blessing may be confirmed. For the confirmation of the prayer is fulfilled through those who answer Amen, so that all that is said may be confirmed in the minds of the hearers by the testimony of truth. This last passage is cited under the name of Ambrose by Amalarius Fortunatus, Ecclesiastical Offices, book 3, chapter 9.

units.la: Nam tu quidem bene gratias agis] De eo dicitur, qui cognita sibi loquitur, quia scit quid dicat. Sed alius non aedificabitur] Si utique ad aedificandam Ecclesiam convenitis, ea debent dici, quae intelligant audientes. Nam quid prodest, ut quis lingua loquatur, quam solus scit; ut qui audit, nihil proficiat? Ideo tacere debet in Ecclesia, ut ii loquantur, qui prosint audientibus. Per sensum meum, ut & alios aedificem, &c.] Utilius dicit paucis verbis in apertione sermonis loqui, quod omnes intelligunt, quam prolixam orationem habere in obscuro. Hi ex Hebraeis erant, qui aliquando Syra lingua, plerunque Hebraea in tractatibus aut oblationibus utebantur ad commendationem. Gloriabantur enim se dici Hebraeos propter meritum Abrahae. Si intret aliquis infidelis vel Idiota, &c.] Cum enim intelligit & intelligitur, addiens laudari Deum, & adorari Christum; pervidet veram esse & venerandam religionem; in qua nihil fucatum, nihil in latebris videt geri; sicut apud Paganos, quibus velantur oculi, ne quae sacra vocant perspicientes, variis se vanitatibus cernant illudi. Omnis enim impostura tenebras petit, & falsa pro veris ostendit. Ideo apud nos nihil astute, nihil sub velamine; sed simpliciter unus laudatur Deus, ex quo sunt omnia, & unus Dominus Jesus Christus, per quem omnia. Si enim nullus sit qui intelligat, aut a quo ipse discutiatur, poterit dicere seductionem esse quandam & vanitatem, quae ideo linguis canitur, quia pudoris est, si reveletur. Omnia ad aedificationem fiant.] Conclusio haec est, ut nihil incassum in Ecclesia geratur; hocque elaborandum magis, ut & imperiti proficiant, ne quid sit corporis per imperitiam tenebrosum. Quòd si non fuerit interpres, taceat in Ecclesia; sibi autem loquatur & Deo.] Hoc est, intra se tacite oret aut loquatur Deo, qui audit muta omnia. In Ecclesia enim ille debet loqui, qui omnibus prosit.
units.tr: "For you indeed give thanks well." This is said of one who speaks in a tongue that is known to him, because he knows what he says. "But the other is not edified." If indeed you assemble to build up the Church, those things should be said that the hearers understand. For what good is it if someone speaks in a tongue that only he knows, so that the hearer gains nothing? Therefore one should keep silent in church, so that those who benefit the hearers may speak. "Through my understanding, that I may also edify others, etc." He says it is more useful to speak a few words that everyone understands at the opening of the sermon, than to have a long prayer in obscurity. These were Hebrews, who sometimes used the Syriac tongue, but mostly Hebrew, in their discourses or offerings, for commendation; for they boasted that they were called Hebrews because of the merit of Abraham. "If any unbeliever or unlearned person enters, etc." For when he understands and is understood, and God is praised and Christ worshipped in his hearing, he sees that the religion is true and to be venerated, in which he sees nothing feigned and nothing done in hiding; as among the Pagans, whose eyes are veiled, lest, seeing what they call sacred things, they should be deceived by various vanities. For all imposture seeks darkness and presents falsehoods as truths. Therefore among us there is nothing crafty, nothing under a veil; but simply the one God is praised, from whom are all things, and the one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. For if there were no one who understood, or by whom it could be examined, he could say that it is a certain deception and vanity, which is sung in tongues for this reason, that it would be shameful if it were revealed. "Let all things be done for edification." This conclusion is that nothing is done in vain in the Church; and this should be worked at more, so that even the unskilled may profit, lest anything in the body be dark through lack of skill. "But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in church; but let him speak to himself and to God." That is, let him pray or speak silently within himself to God, who hears all things in silence. For in church he ought to speak who benefits all.

units.la: Idem in Ephes. cap. IV. Pastores (quorum sc. Apostolus meminit, Ephes. IV. 11.) Possunt esse Lectores, qui lectione saginent populum audientem: quia non in pane tantum vivit homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit ex ore Dei.
units.tr: The same, on Ephesians chapter 4. Ministers (of whom the Apostle speaks, Eph. 4:11) may be readers, who feed the hearing people with reading, because man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

units.la: 375. Turonensis Ecclesia.
units.tr: 375. The Church of Tours.

units.la: Cùm S. Martinus ad Turonensis Ecclesiæ Episcopatum à populo eligeretur; inter Episcopos qui affuerant, præcipuè Defensor quidam nomine, dicitur restitisse: unde animadversum est, graviter illum lectione prophetica tunc notatum. Nam cùm fortuitò Lector, cui legendi eo die ossicium erat, interclusus à populo defuisset, turbatis ministris, dum expectatur qui non aderat, unus è circumstantibus sumpto Psalterio, quem primum versum invenit, arripuit. Psalmus autem hic erat: f Ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudem, propter inimicos tuos, ut destruas inimicum & defensorem: quo lecto clamor populi tollitur, pars adversa confunditur. Hæc Severus Sulpitius lib. 1. de vitâ Martini: ex cujus narratione intelligimus Scripturas linguâ à populo intellectâ recitatas fuisse in Gallicanis quoque Ecclesiis. Eandem historiam habes apud Venantium Fortunatum lib. 1. de vitâ Martini cap. 11. & Paulinum Nolanum lib. 2. de vitâ Martini.
units.tr: When Saint Martin was being chosen by the people to the bishopric of the Church of Tours, a certain Defensor, among the bishops who were present, is said to have opposed it in particular. For this, it is noted, he was severely rebuked by a prophetic reading. For when the reader, whose duty it was to read that day, happened by chance to be absent, kept back by the crowd, the ministers were thrown into confusion. While they waited for the man who was not there, one of the bystanders took up a Psalter and seized on the first verse he found. The psalm was this: Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have brought forth praise, because of your enemies, that you might destroy the enemy and the defender. When this was read, a shout went up from the people, and the opposing party was confounded. Sulpicius Severus tells these things in book 1 of his Life of Martin. From his account we understand that Scriptures were read aloud in a language the people understood, in the Gallican churches too. You will find the same story in Venantius Fortunatus, book 1 of his Life of Martin, chapter 11, and in Paulinus of Nola, book 2 of his Life of Martin.

units.la: 377. Ambrosius Mediolanensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 377. Ambrose, Bishop of Milan.

units.la: In Psalm. CXVIII. Serm. 1. Si quis in viâ ambulat, scrutetur testimonia Domini. Ibid. Et tu lege Prophetam, ut videas: lege, ut aperiat oculos tuos. Et paulò post. Quòd si fugias lectionem Propheticam, si domi non legas, in Ecclesiâ audire nolis; nonne sicut ille qui averso connivet obtutu, ne videat quod possit videre, claudit oculos ne aspiciat, cui potestas videndi est; aut sicut in furore plerique injecere manus oculis suis: ita & tu primò averteris conniventi magis [dissimulatione] quàm refragatione præruptâ. Nam cum ad Ecclesiam venis, & Christianum te asseris, sanus videris; aperis oculos, quibus possis videre: sed dum audire dissimulas quæ leguntur; claudis ne videas tibi, etsi aliis videre videris. Injicis etiam quasdam perfidiæ & intemperantiæ manus oculis animæ tuæ, & cæcitatem infers cordi tuo (quod est gravius) voluntariam; ut videns non videas, audiens non audias.
units.tr: On Psalm 118, Sermon 1. "If anyone walks on the way, let him search out the testimonies of the Lord." Ibid.: "And you, read the Prophet, that you may see; read, that he may open your eyes." And shortly after: "But if you shun the reading of the Prophets, if you do not read them at home, and are unwilling to hear them in the Church, are you not like the man who, with his gaze turned away, half-closes his eyes so that he may not see what he could see; who shuts his eyes so as not to look, though he has the power of sight; or like the many who in a frenzy have thrust their hands into their own eyes? So you too first turn away, with a pretended indifference rather than an open refusal. For when you come to the Church and call yourself a Christian, you seem healthy; you open the eyes with which you could see; but while you pretend not to hear what is read, you shut them so that you do not see, although you seem to others to be seeing. You also thrust certain hands of faithlessness and intemperance upon the eyes of your soul, and you inflict on your heart a blindness (which is worse) that you have chosen; so that, seeing, you do not see, and hearing, you do not hear."

units.la: Ibid. Serm. 19. Noctibus ac diebus sine ullâ cessatione recenseto Scripturas divinas; quia & siquid aliud seniorem interrogaveris; nescit nisi Scripturæ divinæ seriem resultare. Vacat illic sermo de sæculo: sola illic Scriptura contexitur: singulorum sibi per vices ora succedunt, &c.
units.tr: Ibid., Sermon 19. "Night and day, without any pause, go over the divine Scriptures; for if you ask an elder anything else, he knows only how to recite the sequence of the divine Scripture. There talk of the world has no place: only Scripture is woven there. The voices of individuals take their turns in succession, etc."

units.la: {f} Psalm. VIII. Ibid. Serm. 21. Inveni Heptateuchum, inveni Regnorum libros, &c. inveni sapientem auditorem, populum Christianum, qui novit ea, quæ leguntur, audire. Ille enim audit, qui ea, quæ audit, intelligit. Lex enim spiritualis est. Non eam audit Judæus, qui audit corporaliter: sed ille audit, qui audit in spiritu.
units.tr: Psalm 8. Ibid., Sermon 21. "I have found the Heptateuch, I have found the books of the Kings, etc.; I have found a wise hearer, the Christian people, who know how to hear the things that are read. For he hears who understands what he hears. The Law is indeed spiritual. The Jew does not hear it, who hears only in the flesh; but he hears who hears in the Spirit."

units.la: Offic. lib. 1. cap. 22. de colloquiis agens. Sit igitur sermo hujusmodi de Scripturis maximè.
units.tr: On Duties, Book 1, chapter 22, dealing with conversation. "Let therefore such talk be about the Scriptures above all."

units.la: De Abraham lib. 2. cap. 5. Mens igitur nostra cum ipso (Jesu) semper sit: ab ejus templo, ab ejus verbo nunquam recedat. Semper in lectione Scripturarum sit, meditationibus, orationibus; ut sermo ejus, Qui est, semper operetur in nobis; & ut quotidie procedentes in Ecclesiam, vel de mesticis incubantes orationibus, ab ipso incipiamus, & in ipso finiamus.
units.tr: On Abraham, Book 2, chapter 5. "Let our mind therefore always be with him (Jesus); let it never withdraw from his temple, from his word. Let it always be in the reading of the Scriptures, in meditations and prayers; so that his word, which is, may always work in us; and so that, as we go daily into the Church, or lie down in evening prayers, we may begin with him and end in him."

units.la: 4 De Jejunio Domini in Deserto serm. 35. Quàm bene autem jejunium tempore verbum Dei dixit, eò quòd reficit; ut ostenderet jejunia nostra non debere sæculi actibus occupari, sed sacris literis exerceri. Negligit enim famem corporis, qui pabulo lectionis intendit; nec ventris curam habere poterit, qui alimenta verbi cœlestis acquirit. Ipsa est enim refectio, quæ saginat animam, quæ impinguat viscera; cùm de divinis Scripturis cibium eloquii perennis accipimus. Ipsa est esca, quæ vitam æternam tribuit; & insidias à nobis diabolicæ tentationis excludit. Quòd autem sacrarum literarum lectio vita sit, Dominus testatur dicens: h Verba quæ ego locutus sum vobis, spiritus & vita est.
units.tr: 4. On the Lord's Fasting in the Desert, Sermon 35. "How well did the word of God speak of fasting in relation to refreshment; so as to show that our fasts ought not to be occupied with the affairs of the world, but exercised in the holy letters. For he who attends to the food of reading neglects the hunger of the body, and one who gains the nourishment of the heavenly word can have no care for the belly. For that is the refreshment which feeds the soul and fattens the inner parts, when we receive the food of the everlasting word from the divine Scriptures. It is the food which gives eternal life and shuts out from us the snares of diabolical temptation. That the reading of the sacred letters is life, the Lord bears witness, saying: 'The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.'"

units.la: De Virginitate lib. 3. Maxima est virtus tacendi, præsertim in Ecclesiâ. Nulla te divinarum fugiet sententia lectionum, si aurem admoveas, vocem premas, &c. i Conservabat enim Maria, ut legimus, omnia in corde suo, quæ de filio dicebantur; & tu, cùm legitur aliquid, quo Christus aut venturus annunciatur, aut venisse ostenditur; noli fabulando obstrepere, sed mentem admove. An quicquam est indignius, quàm divina oracula circumstrepi, ne audiantur, ne credantur, ne revelentur; circumsonari Sacramenta confusis vocibus, ut impediatur oratio pro salute deprompta omnium: cùm Gentiles idolis suis reverentiam facendo deferunt?
units.tr: On Virginity, Book 3. "The greatest virtue is silence, especially in the Church. No sentence of the divine readings will escape you, if you lend your ear and hold back your voice, etc. For Mary, as we read, kept all the things that were said about the Son in her heart; and when something is read by which Christ is announced as to come, or shown to have come, do not strike up a chatter and drown it out, but attend with your mind. Is there anything more unworthy than that the divine oracles should be shouted down, so that they are not heard, not believed, not revealed; that the sacraments should be drowned in a confused noise, so that the prayer for the salvation of all, offered up, is hindered; when the Gentiles pay reverence to their idols by making a sacrifice?"

units.la: In Luc. lib. 7. cap. 15. Hæc est symphonia; quando concinit in Ecclesiâ diversarum ætatum atque virtutum velut variarum chordarum indiscreta concordia. Psalmus respondetur: Amen dicitur. Hæc est sym-
units.tr: On Luke, Book 7, chapter 15. "This is the symphony: when in the Church there sounds the undivided harmony of different ages and virtues, like varied strings. A psalm is answered; Amen is said. This is the symphony which Paul also knew, and therefore he says: 'I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind.'"

units.la: t Apoc. I. h Joan. VI. i Luc. II.
units.tr: Rev. 1. John 6. Luke 2.

units.la: 4 Vide annon Maximo Taurinensi potius debeatur. phonia, quam scivit & Paulus; & ideo ait: Psallam spiritu, psallam & mente.
units.tr: 4 See whether it is rather to be attributed to Maximus of Turin. symphony, which Paul also knew; and therefore he says: "I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind."

units.la: Hexaemer. lib. 3. cap. 5. Ecquid aliud ille concentus undarum, nisi quidam concentus est plebis? Unde bene mari plerunque {1}comparatur Ecclesia; quae primo ingredientis populi agmine totis vestibulis undas vomit; deinde in oratione totius plebis tanquam undis refluentibus stridet: tum responsoriis Psalmorum, cantu virorum, mulierum, virginum, parvulorum, consonus undarum fragor resultat.
units.tr: Hexaemeron, Book 3, chapter 5. "What else is that harmony of the waves, but a certain harmony of the people? Hence the Church is fittingly often compared to the sea; which, at the first coming in of the people's throng, pours out waves through all its porches; then in the prayer of the whole people it roars as with receding waves; then with the responses of the Psalms, the singing of men, women, virgins and little children, the consonant crash of waves resounds."

units.la: Praefat. in Psalmos. Psalmus benedictio populi est, Dei laus, plebis laudatio, plausus omnium, sermo universorum, vox Ecclesiae, &c. institutio incipientium, perfectorum confirmatio, &c. Psalmum Reges sine potestatis supercilio resultant: Psalmus cantatur ab Imperatoribus, jubilatur a populis. Certat in Psalmo doctrina cum gratia simul. Cantatur ad delectationem, discitur ad eruditionem.
units.tr: Preface to the Psalms. "A psalm is the blessing of the people, the praise of God, the commendation of the populace, the applause of all, the speech of everyone, the voice of the Church, etc.; the instruction of beginners, the confirmation of the perfect, etc. Kings too join in the psalm without the haughtiness of power; the psalm is sung by emperors and shouted by the peoples. In the psalm, teaching and grace contend together. It is sung for delight, it is learned for instruction."

units.la: 380. Ruffinus Aquileiensis.
units.tr: 380. Ruffinus of Aquileia.

units.la: In Psalm. XLI. Si veraciter volumus orare, valde attendendum, & memoriae commendandum est quod dicitur; Apud me oratio mea Deo vitae meae. Saepe quando oro, mens mea vagatur exterius: non intelligo quod dico. Tunc oratio mea non est apud me; neque ipse ego sum apud me. De talibus Dominus ait; Populus hic labiis me honorat; cor autem eorum longe est a me. Quomodo autem intendit Deus orationi meae, cui non intendo.
units.tr: On Psalm 41. If we truly wish to pray, what is said must be heeded closely and committed to memory: "My prayer is with me, the God of my life." Often when I pray, my mind wanders outside, and I do not understand what I say. Then my prayer is not with me, nor am I with myself. Of such people the Lord says: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." But how does God attend to my prayer, when I do not attend to it?

units.la: In Psalm. LX. Sic Psalmum dicam, ut vota reddam, i.e. sic psallam voce, ut vox oris cum animi concordet devotione. Psallentium enim Deo vox concordare debet cum corde, ut impleatur illud Apostoli. Psallam spiritu, psallam & mente. Non enim placet Deo laus illorum, de quibus dicitur: Hic populus labiis me honorat; cor autem eorum longe est a me. Tunc est autem Deo acceptabilis nostra psalmodia; quando sic ore psallimus, ut corde accendamur: quando in laude Dei simul conveniunt lingua, vita, & conscientia.
units.tr: On Psalm 60. I will sing the psalm so that I may pay my vows, that is, I will sing so that the voice of my mouth agrees with the devotion of my mind. For the voice of those who sing to God ought to agree with the heart, so that that saying of the Apostle is fulfilled: "I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also." For God does not take pleasure in the praise of those of whom it is said: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." Our psalmody is then acceptable to God when we sing with the mouth in such a way that we are kindled in the heart: when tongue, life and conscience come together in one praise of God.

units.la: In Psalm. LXIV. Est etiam Scriptura sacra cibus nobis paratus a Domino, quo quotidie reficimur, ne deficiamus in hujus peregrinationis deserto. Unde scriptum est: Non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit ex ore Dei.
units.tr: On Psalm 64. Holy Scripture is also food prepared for us by the Lord, by which we are refreshed every day, lest we faint in the wilderness of this pilgrimage. Hence it is written: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God."

units.la: {k} 1 Cor. XIV. {l} Psalm. XXIII. & LXXIX. {m} Esai. XXVI. & Matth. XV. {n} 1 Cor. XIV. {o} Deut. VIII. & Matth. IV.
units.tr: {k} 1 Cor. XIV. {l} Psalm. XXIII. & LXXIX. {m} Esai. XXVI. & Matth. XV. {n} 1 Cor. XIV. {o} Deut. VIII. & Matth. IV.

units.la: Lib. 2. Apologiæ, seu Invectivæ potius in Hieronymum. Puellis quoque & mulierculis scribens, quæ non utique nisi de nostris Scripturis ædisicari & cupiunt & debent, exempla eis Flacci sui & Tullii vel Maronis intexit.
units.tr: From Book 2 of the Apology, or rather Invective, against Jerome. Writing also to girls and little women, who ought above all to desire and be built up by our Scriptures alone, he wove in for them examples from his Flaccus and from Tully or Virgil.

units.la: 390. Hieronymus Stridonensis.
units.tr: 390. Jerome of Stridon.

units.la: Epist. 7. ad Lætam de Institutione filiæ. Reddat tibi pensum quotidie de Scripturarum floribus carptum. Et post, Pro gemmis & serico divinos codices amet; in quibus non auri & pellis Babylonicæ vermiculata pictura, sed ad fidem placeat emendata & erudita distinctio. Discat primò Psalterium; his se Canticis avocet; & in Proverbiis Solomonis erudiatur ad vitam. In Ecclesiaste consuescat, quæ mundi sunt, calcare. In Job virtutis & patientiæ exempla sectetur. Ad Evangelia transeat, nunquam ea depositura de manibus. Apostolorum Acta & Epistolas totâ cordis imbibat voluntate. Cumque pectoris sui cellarium his opibus locupletaverit; mandet memoriæ Prophetas, Pentateuchum, & Regum & Paralipomenon libros, Esdræ quoque & Hester volumina, &c. Ibid. Adhuc tenera lingua Psalmis dulcibus imbuatur. Item. Quærant eam in itinere sæculi inter turbas & frequentiam propinquorum, & nusquam alibi reperiant nisi in adyto Scripturarum: Prophetas & Apostolos de spiritualibus nuptiis sciscitetur.
units.tr: Letter 7, to Laeta, on the education of her daughter: Let her pay you back each day a task gathered from the flowers of the Scriptures. And afterwards: Let her love the divine codices instead of jewels and silk, in which the gold, the Babylonian leather and the coloured pictures are not to please, but a correct and learned arrangement faithful to the text. Let her first learn the Psalter; let her turn from these to the Canticles; and let her be instructed for life in the Proverbs of Solomon. Let her accustom herself in Ecclesiastes to trample underfoot the things of the world. Let her seek out examples of virtue and patience in Job. Let her move on to the Gospels, never to lay them down from her hands. Let her soak herself with all her will in the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles. And when she has enriched the storeroom of her heart with these treasures, let her commit to memory the Prophets, the Pentateuch, the books of Kings and Chronicles, and the volumes of Ezra and Esther, etc. Also in the same letter: While her tongue is still tender, let her be steeped in the sweet Psalms. Likewise: Let them seek her on the road of this world, amid the crowds and the throng of relatives, and let them find her nowhere else but in the sanctuary of the Scriptures. Let her inquire of the Prophets and Apostles about spiritual marriage.

units.la: Epist. 8. ad Demetriadem. Unum illud tibi nata Deo, præque omnibus unum, prædicam, & repetens iterumque iterumque monebo; ut animum tuum sacræ lectionis amore occupes; nec in bonâ terrâ pectoris tui sementem lolii avenarumque suscipias, &c. Et post, Statue quot horis sanctam Scripturam ediscere debeas, quanto tempore legere, non ad laborem, sed ad delectationem & instructionem animæ. Et in fine, Finem jungo principio, nec semel monuisse contentus sum. Ama Scripturas sanctas; & amabit te sapientia: dilige eam, & servabit te: honora illam, & amplexabitur te. Hæc monilia in pectore & in auribus tuis hæreant.
units.tr: Letter 8, to Demetrias: One thing I proclaim to you, daughter dedicated to God, and above all others one thing; and repeating it again and again I will advise you: that you occupy your mind with love of sacred reading, and that you do not admit the seed of tares and wild oats into the good soil of your heart, etc. And afterwards: Decide how many hours you ought to learn the holy Scripture by heart, and how long you ought to read it, not as a labour but for the delight and instruction of your soul. And at the end: I join the end to the beginning, and I am not content to have given this warning only once. Love the holy Scriptures, and wisdom will love you; cherish her, and she will keep you; honour her, and she will embrace you. Let these ornaments hang on your breast and in your ears.

units.la: Epist. 9. ad Salvinam viduam. Semper in manibus tuis sit divina lectio.
units.tr: Letter 9, to Salvina, a widow: Let the divine reading always be in your hands.

units.la: Epist 10. ad Furiam viduam. Quando comedis, cogita quòd statim tibi orandum, illicò & legendum sit. De Scripturis sanctis habeto fixum versuum numerum; illud pensum Domino tuo redde; nec ante quieti membra concedas, quàm calathum pectoris tui hoc sub tegmine impleveris. Post Scripturas sanctas doctorum hominum tractatus legè, &c. Amorem monilium atque gemmarum sericarumque vestium transfer ad scientiam Scripturarum.
units.tr: Letter 10, to Furia, a widow: When you eat, think that you must at once pray and read. Set yourself a fixed number of verses from the holy Scriptures; pay that task to your Lord, and do not let your limbs rest until you have filled the basket of your heart under this covering. After the holy Scriptures, read the treatises of learned men, etc. Transfer your love of jewels and necklaces and silken garments to the knowledge of the Scriptures.

units.la: Epist. 12. ad Gaudentium de Pacatulæ infantulæ educatione. Cùm autem virgunculam rudem & edentulam septimus ætatis annus exceperit, & cœperit erubescere; scire quid taceat, dubitare quid dicat; discat memoriter Psalterium, & usque ad annos pubertatis libros Solomonis, Evangelia, Apostolos, & Prophetas sui cordis thesaurum faciat.
units.tr: Letter 12, to Gaudentius, on the upbringing of the little girl Pacatula: When the seventh year of her age has received the little virgin, still unskilled and toothless, and she begins to blush; let her know what to keep silent about and to doubt what to say; let her learn the Psalter by heart, and up to the years of puberty the books of Solomon, the Gospels, the Apostles and the Prophets; let her make them the treasury of her heart.

units.la: Epist. 22. ad Eustochium. Crebrius lege, disce quamplurima. Tenenti codicem somnus obrepat, & cadentem faciem pagina suscipiat. Ibidem Monachorum sui temporis instituta describens. Dominicis diebus orationi tantùm & lectionibus vacant: quod quidem & omni tempore completis opusculis faciunt. Quotidie aliquid de Scripturis discitur.
units.tr: Letter 22, to Eustochium: Read more often, learn very many things. Let sleep creep over you while you hold the codex, and let the page catch your face as it falls. In the same letter, describing the customs of the monks of his time: On the Lord's days they give themselves only to prayer and readings; and they do this at every time too, once their little tasks are finished. Something is learned from the Scriptures every day.

units.la: Epist. 27. ad Eustochium de Paulâ matre, Cumque à nobis crebrius moneretur, ut parceret oculis, & eos servaret Evangelicæ lectioni, aiebat. Turpanda est facies, quam contra Dei præceptum purpurissâ & cerussâ & stibio sæpe depinxi.
units.tr: Letter 27, to Eustochium, on her mother Paula: When we often advised her to spare her eyes and keep them for reading the Gospel, she said: "The face must be defiled, which I have often painted, against God's command, with rouge, white lead and antimony."

units.la: In Ecclesiast. cap. 3. Porrò quia caro Domini verus est cibus, & sanguis ejus verus est potus, juxta ἀναγνωσιν: hoc solum habemus in præsenti bonum; si vescamur carne ejus cruoreque potemur, non solum in mysterio, sed etiam in Scripturarum lectione. Verus enim cibus & potus, qui ex verbo Dei sumitur, scientia Scripturarum est.
units.tr: On Ecclesiastes, chapter 3: Moreover, since the flesh of the Lord is the true food and his blood the true drink, according to the reading [ἀνάγνωσιν], we have this one good thing in the present: if we eat his flesh and drink his blood, not only in the mystery but also in the reading of the Scriptures. For the true food and drink, which is taken from the word of God, is the knowledge of the Scriptures.

units.la: In Isai. lib. 4. cap. 11. Frequenter evenit, ut homines sæculi, mystica nescientes, simplici Scripturarum lectione pascantur.
units.tr: On Isaiah, book 4, chapter 11: It often happens that men of the world, not knowing mystical things, are fed by the plain reading of the Scriptures.

units.la: In Isai. lib. 16. cap. 57. Possumus terram & montem Domini, quem sancti possessuri sint; & Scripturas sanctas intelligere, &c. de quo & in Michea legimus. Erit in novissimis diebus manifestus mons Domini. Et ipse Dominus præcepit Apostolis, cunctisque Doctoribus Ecclesiæ, ut quicquid asperum videretur atque difficile, suâ interpretatione dissolvant, & intelligentiæ viam præbeant, omniaque tollant de medio scandala; ut populus Domini absque ullo impedimento, quod legit, intelligat, & in Dei timore proficiat.
units.tr: On Isaiah, book 16, chapter 57: We can understand the land and the mountain of the Lord, which the saints are to possess, as the holy Scriptures, etc. Of which we also read in Micah: "In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be made manifest." And the Lord himself commanded the Apostles and all the teachers of the Church that whatever seems rough and difficult they should resolve by their interpretation, and offer a way of understanding, and remove every stumbling-block from the midst; so that the people of the Lord may understand what they read without any hindrance, and grow in the fear of God.

units.la: Lib. 14. in Ezechielem cap. 47. Quòd cubitos genere masculino, & non neutrali cubita dicimus, (in versione) juxta regulam Grammaticam, & in superioribus docui, non nos ignorantiâ hoc facere, sed consuetudine, propter simplices quosque & indoctos, quorum in congregatione Ecclesiæ major est numerus.
units.tr: Book 14, on Ezekiel, chapter 47: That we say cubitos in the masculine gender, and not cubita in the neuter, in the version, according to the grammatical rule, and as I have shown above, we do not do this through ignorance but through custom, on account of the simple and unlearned, of whom the number in the congregation of the Church is greater.

units.la: Lib. 2. adv. Ruffinum cap. 7. [de LXX. Versione] Tam stultus eram, ut quod in pueritiâ didici, senex oblivisci vellem.
units.tr: Book 2, against Rufinus, chapter 7 [on the Septuagint version]: I was so foolish that I wished, as an old man, to forget what I had learned in boyhood.

units.la: In Nahum cap. 3. In adventu Christi & sermonis Dei, & doctrinæ Ecclesiasticæ & consummationis Ninivæ speciosissimæ quondam meretricis, elevabitur & properabit populus, qui sub magistris ante fuerat confusus, & & ibit ad montes Scripturarum, ibique inveniet montes Moysem & Jesum filium Naue; montes Prophetas; montes Novi Testamenti, Apostolos & Evangelistas: & cum ad tales montes confugerit, & in huiusmodi montium lectione fuerit versatus; si non invenerit qui eum doceat (P Messis enim multa, operarii autem pauci.) tunc & illius studium comprobabitur, quia confugerit ad montes; & magistrorum desidia coarguetur.
units.tr: On Nahum, chapter 3: At the coming of Christ and of the word of God, and of ecclesiastical teaching, and at the destruction of Nineveh, once a most beautiful harlot, the people who had earlier been confused under teachers will be lifted up and hasten, and will go to the mountains of the Scriptures, and there they will find the mountains of Moses and Joshua the son of Nun; the mountains of the Prophets; the mountains of the New Testament, the Apostles and Evangelists. And when they have fled to such mountains, and have been occupied in reading such mountains, if they do not find someone to teach them (the harvest is indeed great, but the labourers are few, Matth. 9.), then their zeal too will be proved, because they have fled to the mountains; and the negligence of the teachers will be convicted.

units.la: In Agge. cap. 1. Igitur quia haec mandata sunt nobis, ut ponamus corda nostra in viis nostris; ascendamus in montem rationabilem, & ad singula problemata, congrua de testimoniis Scripturarum ligna quaerentes, praecidamus ea, & aedificemus domum sapientiae in nobis. Et paulo ante, De omni Scriptura sanctae monte, in quo varia virtutum & Paradisi ligna plantata sunt, praecidamus ea, & aedificemus domum sapientiae in nobis.
units.tr: On Haggai, chapter 1: Therefore, since these commands have been given to us, that we should set our hearts on our ways, let us ascend the rational mountain, and, seeking suitable wood from the testimonies of the Scriptures for each problem, let us cut it down and build the house of wisdom in ourselves. And a little earlier: From the whole mountain of Scripture, in which the various trees of virtues and of Paradise are planted, let us cut them down and build the house of wisdom in ourselves.

units.la: Proem. in 3. lib. Commentar. ad Galat. Quotusquisque nunc Aristotelem legit? quanti Platonis vel libros novere vel nomen? Vix in angulis otiosi eos senes recolunt: Rusticanos vero & piscatores nostros totus orbis loquitur, universus mundus sonat. Itaque sermone simplici simplicia eorum verba pandenda sunt.
units.tr: Preface to book 3 of the Commentary on Galatians: How few now read Aristotle? How many know the books of Plato, or even his name? Scarcely do the idle old men in corners recall them. But our rustics and fishermen the whole world speaks of, the entire earth resounds with. Therefore their plain words must be unfolded in plain speech.

units.la: Proem. Commentar. in Epist ad Ephes. in ipso initio. Si quicquid est (Paula & Eustochium) quod in hac vita sapientem teneat, & inter pressuras & turbines mundi aequo animo manere persuadeat; id esse vel primum reor meditationem & scientiam Scripturarum. Cum enim a caeteris animantibus hoc vel maxime differamus, quod rationale animal sumus, & loqui possumus: ratio autem omnis & sermo divinus libris contineatur; per quos & Deum discimus, & quare creati sumus non ignoramus; miror quosdam extitisse, qui aut ipsi se inertiae & somno dantes, nolunt quae praeclara sunt discere; aut caeteros qui id studii habent, reprehendendos putent.
units.tr: Preface to the Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, at the very beginning: If there is anything (Paula and Eustochium) that holds a wise man in this life, and persuades him to remain calm of mind amid the pressures and whirlwinds of the world, I think it is first of all the meditation and knowledge of the Scriptures. For since we differ from other living creatures chiefly in this, that we are rational animals and can speak, and since all reason and divine speech are contained in books, through which we learn God and do not ignore why we were created; I wonder that some have arisen who, either giving themselves over to sloth and sleep, do not wish to learn what is excellent, or think that others who have this zeal should be rebuked.

units.la: In Epist. ad Ephes. lib. 3. cap. 5. Et canere igitur & psallere & laudare Dominum magis animo quam voce debemus. Hoc est quippe quod dicitur, Cantantes & psallentes in cordibus vestris Domino. Audiant haec adolescentuli; audiant hi quibus psallendi in Ecclesia officium est; Deo non voce sed corde cantandum: nec in Tragoedorum modum guttur & fauces dulci medicamine colliniendas, ut in Ecclesia theatrales moduli audiantur & cantica; sed in timore, in opere, in scientia Scripturarum. Quamvis sit aliquis (ut solent illi appellare) κωμῳδὸς, si bona opera habuerit, dulcis apud Deum cantor est. Sic cantet servus Christi, ut non vox canentis, sed verba placeant, quae leguntur, &c.
units.tr: On Ephesians, book 3, chapter 5: And so we ought to sing and psalm and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice. For this is what is said: "singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord." Let the young men hear this; let those hear it whose office it is to sing psalms in the Church: God is to be sung to not with the voice but with the heart; nor should the throat and jaws be smeared with sweet medicine after the manner of tragic actors, so that theatrical tunes and songs are heard in the Church; but sing in fear, in work, and in the knowledge of the Scriptures. Although there may be someone (as those people are wont to call him) a comedian [κωμῳδὸς], if he has good works, he is a sweet singer before God. Let the servant of Christ so sing that it is not the voice of the singer that pleases, but the words that are read, etc.

units.la: P Matth. IX.
units.tr: Matth. IX.

units.la: In fine Commentar. in Epist ad Galat. Quod autem Amen consensum significet audientis, & sit signaculum veritatis, ad Corinthios quoque prima nos docet: in quâ Paulus ait, Caeterùm si benedixeris spiritu, quis supplet locum idiotæ? quomodo dicet Amen super tuâ benedictione: quoniam quidem nescit quid dicas? Ex quo ostendit idioten non posse respondere verum esse quod dicitur, nisi intellexerit quod docetur. Universum autem populum Amen acclamare solitum idem indicat proœmio in 2. lib. Comment. in candem Epist ubi de Romanæ plebis devotione differens: Ubi, inquit, sic ad similitudinem coelestis tonitrui Amen reboat, & vacua idolorum templa quatiuntur.
units.tr: At the end of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians: That Amen signifies the assent of the hearer, and is the seal of truth, the first Epistle to the Corinthians also teaches us. In it Paul says: "Otherwise, if you give thanks in the Spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the unlearned say Amen to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?" From this he shows that the unlearned cannot respond that what is said is true unless they have understood what is taught. That the whole people used to shout Amen, the same writer shows in the preface to the second book of his Commentary on the same Epistle, where, speaking of the devotion of the Roman people, he says: "There, in the likeness of heavenly thunder, the Amen resounds, and the empty temples of the idols are shaken."

units.la: In Epist. ad Titum cap. 3. [De stultis quæstionibus] Exerceatur sensus, mens quotidie divinâ lectione pascatur: & quæstiones nostræ stultæ non erunt quæstiones.
units.tr: On the Epistle to Titus, chapter 3 [On foolish questions]: Let the mind be exercised, let the intellect be fed every day by divine reading, and our questions will not be foolish questions.

units.la: Epist. 3. ad Heliodorum. Epitaphium Nepotiani. Bellorum feritas, & pellitorum turba populorum, qui mortuorum quondam in eriis hominês immolabant, stridorem suum in dulce crucis fregerunt melos, & totius mundi una vox est Christus.
units.tr: Letter 3 to Heliodorus, the Epitaph of Nepotianus: The savagery of wars and the crowd of skin-clad peoples, who once sacrificed men on their altars among the dead, have broken their shrill noise into the sweet melody of the cross, and the whole world has one voice, Christ.

units.la: Epist. 4. ad Rusticum Monachum, de vivendi formâ. Dicas Psalmum in corde tuo, in quo non dulcedo vocis, sed mentis affectus quaeritur; dicente Apostolo: Psallam spiritu, psallam & mente: & Cantantes in cordibus vestris Domino. Legerat enim esse praeceptum, Psallite sapienter.
units.tr: Letter 4 to Rusticus the monk, on the form of living: Say the Psalm in your heart, in which what is sought is not the sweetness of the voice but the disposition of the mind, since the Apostle says: "I will sing with the spirit, I will sing with the mind also," and "Singing in your hearts to the Lord." For he had read that this is the command: "Sing wisely."

units.la: Epist. 7. ad Laetam, de Institut. filiae. Humni discunt Psalterium.
units.tr: Letter 7 to Laeta, on the education of her daughter: Let them learn the Psalter as hymns.

units.la: Epist. 18. ad Marcellam. In Christi villâ (Bethlehem intelligit) tota rusticitas est. Extra Psalmos sientinm est. Quocunque te verteris, arator ferrum tenens, alleluia decantat. Sudans messor psalmis se avocat; & curvâ attondens vites falce vinitor, aliquid Davidicum canit. Haec sunt in provinciâ carmina, hæ (ut vulgò dicitur) amatoriæ cantiones.
units.tr: Letter 18 to Marcella: In Christ's villa (he means Bethlehem) everything is rustic. Apart from the Psalms there is silence. Wherever you turn, the ploughman holding his iron sings Alleluia. The sweating reaper beguiles his labour with psalms, and the vinedresser pruning the vines with his curved sickle sings something of David. These are the songs of the countryside; these are, as the saying goes, the love songs.

units.la: Epist. 27. ad Eustochium. Epitaph. Paulae: funus Paulae describens, ad quod tota Palaestinarum urbium turba convenit: Hebraeo (inquit) Graeco, Latino, Syroque sermone Psalmi in ordine personabant.
units.tr: Letter 27 to Eustochium, the Epitaph of Paula, describing the funeral of Paula, to which the whole crowd of the Palestinian towns came together: In the Hebrew, Greek, Latin and Syriac tongues the Psalms rang out in turn, he says.

units.la: Ex Commentariis in Psalmos & Paulinas Epistolas, quæ inter Opera Hieronymi habentur.
units.tr: From the Commentaries on the Psalms and the Pauline Epistles, which are found among the Works of Jerome.

units.la: In Psal. V. Ego cupio intrare in domum tuam, & volo intrare per viam tuam rectam, &c. Quæ est autem ista via? lectio Scripturarum.
units.tr: On Ps. 5. I desire to enter your house, and I want to enter by your straight way, etc. What, then, is that way? It is the reading of the Scriptures.

units.la: 1 Cor. XIV.

In Psal. LXXXVI. Dominus narrabit in Scripturis populorum: in Scripturis sanctis. Quæ Scriptura populis omnibus legitur, hoc est, ut omnes intelligant. Quod dicit, hoc est. Sicut scripserunt Apostoli, sic & ipse Dominus, h. e. per Evangelia sua locutus est, non ut pauci intelligerent, sed ut omnes. Plato scripsit in Scripturâ: sed non scripsit populis, sed paucis. Vix enim intelligunt tres homines. Isti verò, h. e. principes Ecclesiæ, & principes Christi, non scripserunt paucis, sed universo populo.
units.tr: On Ps. 86. "The Lord will declare it in the Scriptures of the peoples": in the holy Scriptures. The Scripture that is read to all peoples is so that everyone may understand it. When he says "this is", he means: just as the Apostles wrote, so the Lord himself also spoke, that is, through his Gospels, not so that a few might understand, but so that all might. Plato wrote a book, but he did not write for the people, only for a few; for hardly three men understand it. But those, that is, the leaders of the Church and the leaders of Christ, did not write for a few, but for the whole people.

units.la: In Psal. CXXXIII. Solent & viri, solent & monachi, solent & mulierculæ hoc inter se habere certamen, ut plures edissent Scripturas; & in eo se putant meliores, si plures edidicerint. Et paulò ante, Scripturas legimus, Psalmos edisimus, Evangelia tenemus, Prophetas edisserimus.
units.tr: On Ps. 133. Men, monks and little women are all in the habit of competing with one another to see who has memorised more Scriptures, and they think themselves better if they have learned more by heart. And a little earlier: "We read the Scriptures, we have learned the Psalms by heart, we hold the Gospels, we expound the Prophets."

units.la: 440. Primasius Uticensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 440. Primasius, Bishop of Utica.

units.la: Sequentia hominis sunt Pelagiani. Eadem tamen habet & Primasius.
units.tr: The following sayings belong to the man, and they are Pelagian. Yet Primasius also holds the same views.

units.la: In 1 Cor. XIV. Tamen ea quæ sine animâ sunt, &c.] Cùm hæc inanimata, nisi distinctionem habeant, non possunt reddere cantilenam, & ut superflua respuuntur: quantò magis vobis, qui spirituales estis, suavitas non aures debet mulcere sed mentes? Si igitur nesciero, &c.] Omnis sermo, qui non intelligitur, barbarus judicatur. Mens autem mea sine fructu est, &c.] Quia non intelligo quod loquor. Quis supplet locum Idiotæ?] Laicum significat, qui nullo gradu Ecclesiastico fungitur. Quomodo dicet Amen super tuam benedictionem? &c.] Quomodo tuæ perhibet benedictioni testimonium vel consensum? Nam si orem lingua, spiritus meus orat.] Hoc dicit, quoniam si quis incognitis aliis linguis loquatur; mens ejus non ipsi efficitur sine fructu, sed audienti: quicquid enim dicitur, ignorat. Hæc omnia habentur etiam in Primasii Commentariis: conferantur ergo.
units.tr: On 1 Cor. 14. "Yet those things which are without life, etc.": Since these inanimate things cannot produce a melody unless they have distinction, and are rejected as superfluous, how much more ought sweetness to delight your minds, not your ears, you who are spiritual? "If then I know not, etc.": every speech that is not understood is judged barbarous. "But my mind is without fruit, etc.": because I do not understand what I say. "Who fills the place of the unlearned?": He means the layman, who holds no ecclesiastical rank. "How will he say Amen to your blessing? etc.": How does he bear witness or give consent to your blessing? "For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays": He says this: if anyone speaks in other tongues that are unknown, his mind is made without fruit not for himself but for the hearer; for he does not know what is said. All these things are also found in the Commentaries of Primasius; let them therefore be compared.

units.la: In Coloss. III. Verbum Christi habitet in vobis abundanter.] Hic extenditur verbum Christi non sufficienter, sed abundanter etiam Laicos habere debere, & docere se invicem vel monere. Eadem verbatim habet Primasius; & paulò ante: Ut sapienter & rationabiliter proferatur. Item, ut non solùm ore sed etiam in corde cantetis, ut cor cum voce concordet; vel intelligatis quod cantatis.
units.tr: On Col. 3. "Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly": Here the word of Christ is extended to mean that not merely sufficiently but abundantly even the laity ought to have it, and to teach or admonish one another. Primasius has the same words verbatim; and a little before: That it may be set forth wisely and reasonably. Likewise: that you may sing not only with the mouth but also in the heart, so that the heart agrees with the voice; or that you may understand what you sing.

units.la: 410. Pelagius Hæreticus.
units.tr: 410. Pelagius the Heretic.

units.la: Epist. ad Demetriadem de Virginitate (quæ r. est in Tomo 4. Operum Hieronymi editionis Basileensis, vel 9. in editione Mariani Victorii.) Nihil in hoc secreto magis agere debes quàm animam divinis eloquiis pascere; & quantum ei per totam sufficere possit diem, hoc eam veluti cibo pinguiore satiare. Ita Scripturas sacras lege, ut semper meminneris Dei illa verba esse, qui legem suam non solum sciri, sed etiam impleri jubet. Nihil enim prodest facienda didicisse & non facere. Optimè uteris lectione divinâ, si eam tibi adhibeas speculi vicè; ut ibi velut ad imaginem suam anima respiciat; & vel fœda quæque corrigat, vel pulchra plus ornet. Lectionem frequenter interrumpat oratio; & animam jugiter adhærentem Deo grata vicissitudo sancti operis accendat, &c.
units.tr: Letter to Demetrias on Virginity (which is the 4th in the 4th volume of the Basel edition of Jerome's Works, or the 9th in the edition of Marius Victorius). In this retreat you ought to do nothing more than feed your soul on divine words, and to satisfy it, as with richer food, for as much of the whole day as it can bear. Read the holy Scriptures in such a way that you always remember those words to be God's, who commands that his law be not only known but also fulfilled. For it profits nothing to have learned what should be done and not to do it. You will use the divine reading best if you apply it as a mirror, so that the soul may look into it as at its own image, and either correct whatever is foul or adorn whatever is beautiful. Let prayer interrupt the reading often, and let the pleasant change of holy work stir up the soul that clings continually to God, etc.

units.la: 390. Paula & Eustochium.
units.tr: 390. Paula and Eustochium.

units.la: Epist. ad Marcellam (quæ 17 est Tomo 1. Operum Hieronymi) postquam dixissent Bethlehemum (vel Hierosolymam potiùs & reliqua loca sancta) convenisse Gallos, Britannos, Armenos, Persas, Indos, Æthiopas, Ægyptios, &c. addunt: Vox quidem dissona, sed una religio: tot pene psallentium chori, quot gentium diversitates. Posteaque illud adjungunt, quod habet etiam Hieronymus in Epist. 18. ad eandem Marcellam. In Christi villulâ tota rusticitas, & extra Psalmos silentium est. Quocunque te verteris, arator stivam tenens Alleluia decantat. Sudans messor Psalmis se avocat; & curvâ attondens vitem falce vinitor, aliquid Davidicum canit. Hæc sunt in hâc provinciâ carmina: hæ, ut vulgò dicitur, amatoriæ cantiones, hic pastorum sibilus, hæc arma culturæ.
units.tr: Letter to Marcella (which is the 17th in the first volume of Jerome's Works). After saying that Gauls, Britons, Armenians, Persians, Indians, Ethiopians, Egyptians, and others had gathered at Bethlehem (or rather at Jerusalem and the other holy places), they add: The voice indeed is discordant, but the religion is one: almost as many choirs of singers as there are differences of nations. Then they add what Jerome also has in his letter 18 to the same Marcella: In Christ's little farm all is rustic, and outside the Psalms there is silence. Wherever you turn, the ploughman holding the plough sings Alleluia. The sweating reaper beguiles himself with the Psalms; and the vinedresser, trimming the vine with a curved sickle, sings something of David's. These are the songs in this province: these, as is commonly said, are the love songs, here the whistling of shepherds, these the implements of tilling.

units.la: 410. Author Operis Imperfecti in Matthæum.
units.tr: 410. Author of the Incomplete Work on Matthew.

units.la: Homil. 42. in illud, Nescitis Scripturas, neque virtutem Dei.] Sapienter primùm arguit stultitiam eorum, quia non legebant. Secundò ignorantiam, quia non cognoscebant deum, quia ex diligentiâ lectionum nascitur scientia Dei. Ignorantia autem negligentiæ filia est. Si enim nec omnes qui legunt, cognoscunt Deum; quomodo cognoscet qui non legit? Quòd autem diximus non omnes legentes cognoscere veritatem Dei; tunc est si nolentes invenire legant.
units.tr: Homily 42, on the words, "You know not the Scriptures, nor the power of God": First, he wisely rebukes their folly, because they did not read. Secondly, their ignorance, because they did not know God, for knowledge of God is born from diligence in reading. But ignorance is the daughter of negligence. For if not all who read know God, how will he know who does not read? Now when we said that not all who read know the truth of God, that is so if they read unwilling to find it.

units.la: Homil. 42. in illud, Cùm videritis abominationem desolationis stantem in loco sancto; tunc qui in Judæâ sunt, fugiant ad montes.] Montes autem sunt Scripturæ Apostolorum aut Prophetarum; de quibus dictum est: Illuminas tu mirabiliter de montibus æternis. Et iterum de Ecclesiâ dicit; Fundamenta ejus in montibus sanctis. Et quare jubet in hoc tempore omnes Christianos conferre se ad Scripturas? Quia ex tempore hoc, ex quo obtinuit hæresis illas Ecclesias, nulla probatio potest esse veræ Christianitatis, neque refugium potest esse Christianorum aliud, volentium cognoscere fidei veritatem, nisi Scripturæ divinæ. Antea enim multis modis ostendebatur, quæ esset Ecclesia Christi, & quæ Gentilitas; nunc autem nullo modo cognoscitur, volentibus cognoscere quæ sit vera Ecclesia Christi, nisi tantummodo per Scripturas. Quare? quia omnia hæc, quæ sunt propriè Christi in veritate, habent & hæreses illæ in schismate; similiter Ecclesias, similiter & ipsas Scripturas divinas, similiter Episcopos, cæterosque ordines Clericorum, similiter Baptismum, similiter Eucharistiam, & cætera omnia, denique ipsum Christum. Volens ergo quis cognoscere quæ sit vera Ecclesia Christi, unde cognoscat in tantæ confusione similitudinis, nisi tantummodo per Scripturas? ——Sciens ergo Dominus tantam confusionem rerum in novissimis temporibus esse futuram; ideò mandat ut Christiani qui sunt in Christianitate, volentes firmitatem accipere fidei veræ, ad nullam rem fugiant, nisi ad scripturas. Alioqui si alia respexerint, scandalizabuntur, & peribunt, non intelligentes quæ sit vera Ecclesia. Et per hoc incident in abominationem desolationis; quæ stat in sanctis Ecclesiæ locis.
units.tr: Homily 42, on the words, "When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, then let those who are in Judaea flee to the mountains." The mountains are the Scriptures of the Apostles or of the Prophets, of which it is said: "You wondrously illuminate from the everlasting mountains." And again, of the Church he says: "Its foundations are upon the holy mountains." And why does he command all Christians at this time to betake themselves to the Scriptures? Because from this time, since those heresies have prevailed over those churches, no proof of true Christianity can exist, nor can there be any other refuge for Christians wishing to know the truth of the faith, except the divine Scriptures. For formerly it was shown in many ways which was the Church of Christ and which was the Gentile world; but now it cannot be known in any way, to those wishing to know which is the true Church of Christ, except only through the Scriptures. Why? Because all these things which are properly Christ's in truth, those heresies also have in schism: likewise churches, likewise the divine Scriptures themselves, likewise bishops and the other orders of clergy, likewise baptism, likewise the Eucharist, and all the rest, finally Christ himself. Therefore if anyone wishes to know which is the true Church of Christ, how will he know it amid so great a confusion of likenesses, except only through the Scriptures? ——The Lord, therefore, knowing that such great confusion of things would come in the last times, commands that Christians who are within Christianity, wishing to receive the firmness of the true faith, should flee to nothing but the Scriptures. For if they look to other things, they will be scandalized and will perish, not understanding which is the true Church. And through this they will fall into the abomination of desolation, which stands in the holy places of the Church.

units.la: [Tom.I.] Confession. lib.6. cap.5. Cùm essemus infirmi ad inveniendam liquida ratione veritatem, & ob hoc nobis opus esset autoritate sanctarum literarum; jam credere cœperam nullo modo te fuisse tributurum tam excellentem illi Scripturæ per omnes jam terras authoritatem; nisi & per ipsam tibi credi & per ipsam te quæri voluisse. Jam enim absurditatem, quæ me in illis literis solebat offendere, cùm eis probabiliter exposita audissem, ad sacramentorum altitudinem referebam; eòque mihi venerabilior & sacrosanctâ fide dignior apparebat authoritas, quò & omnibus ad legendum esset in promptu, & secreti sui dignitatem in intellectu profundiore servaret, verbis apertissimis & humillimo genere loquendi se cunctis præbens, & exercens intentionem eorum qui non sunt leves corde: ut exciperet omnes populari sinu, & per angusta foramina paucos ad te trajiceret; multò tamen plures, quàm si nec tanto apice autoritatis emineret, nec turbas gremio sanctæ humilitatis hauriret. Cogitabam hæc, & aderas mihi: suspirabam, & audiebas me: fluctuabam & gubernabas me: ibam per viam seculi latam, nec deserebas me.
units.tr: [Vol. I.] Confessions, book 6, ch. 5. When I was too weak to find the truth by clear reasoning, and for that reason needed the authority of the holy Scriptures, I had already begun to believe that you would never have given such an excellent authority to that Scripture, spread through all the lands, unless you had also wished to be believed through it and sought through it. For when I heard those passages in them explained in a plausible way, I used to refer the absurdity that had offended me in those writings to the depth of the sacraments. The authority of the Scriptures then appeared to me more venerable and more worthy of holy faith, because it lay open for everyone to read, yet kept the dignity of its hidden meaning for a deeper understanding.
