It offers itself to all in the plainest words and in a most humble style, and it exercises the attention of those who are not light of heart; it takes all into its popular embrace, and it leads a few through its narrow openings to you, yet many more than would have come if it had stood out with no such lofty authority and had not drawn the crowds into the bosom of holy humility. I thought these things, and you were with me; I sighed, and you heard me; I wavered, and you guided me; I walked the broad road of the world, and you did not forsake me.

units.la: Lib. 8. cap. 6. Quodam die, non recolo causam, quâ erat absens Nebridius, cùm ecce ad nos domum venit, & ad me & ad Alypium Politianus quidam civis noster, in quantum Afer, præclarè in palatio militans, nescio quid à nobis volebat. Et consedimus ut colloqueremur, & forte super mensam lusoriam quæ ante nos erat, attendit codicem, tulit, aperuit, invenit Apostolum Paulum, inopinatò sanè; putaverat enim aliquid de libris, quorum professio me conterebat. Tum verò arridens, meque intuens, gratulatoriè miratus est; quòd eas & solas præ oculis meis liberas repentè comperisset. Christianus quippe & fidelis erat; sed sæpe tibi Deo nostro prosternebatur in Ecclesiâ crebris & diuturnis orationibus. Cui ego cùm indicâssem illis me Scripturis maximam curam impendere, ortus est sermo ipso narrante de Antonio Ægyptio Monacho, &c. Vid. etiam cap. 12.
units.tr: Book 8, ch. 6. One day, I do not recall why Nebridius was absent, a certain Ponticianus, a fellow countryman of ours from Africa and a distinguished officer at court, came to our house to see me and Alypius, and wanted something from us. We sat down to talk, and by chance he noticed on the game table before us a book. He took it up, opened it, and found the Apostle Paul, which was quite unexpected; for he had supposed it would be one of those books whose profession had troubled me. Then he smiled, looked at me, and expressed his delight in surprise that he had suddenly found that I had these Scriptures before my eyes and nothing else. For he was a Christian and a believer, and he often prostrated himself before you, our God, in the Church with frequent and lengthy prayers. When I told him that I was devoting the greatest care to these Scriptures, a conversation arose, as he himself related it, about Antony the Egyptian monk, etc. See also ch. 12.

units.la: Lib. 10. cap. 33. Cùm reminiscor lachrymas meas, quas fudi ad cantus Ecclesiæ tuæ in primordiis recuperatæ fidei mæ; & nunc ipso commoveor, non cantu, sed rebus quæ cantantur, cùm liquidâ voce & convenientissimâ modulatione cantantur; magnam instituti huius utilitatem rursus agnosco. Ita fluctuo inter periculum voluptatis, & experimentum salubritatis; magisque adducor, non quidem irretractabilem sententiam proferens, cantandi consuetudinem approbare in Ecclesiâ; ut per oblectamenta aurium infirmior animus in affectum pietatis assurgat. Tamen cùm mihi accidit, ut me amplius cantus, quàm res quæ canitur, moveat; pænaliter me peccare confiteor, & tunc mallem non audire cantantem.
units.tr: Book 10, ch. 33. When I recall the tears I shed at the songs of your Church in the early days of my recovered faith, and when I am now moved, not by the singing but by the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and a most fitting melody, I again acknowledge the great usefulness of this practice. So I waver between the danger of pleasure and the experience of wholesome benefit. I am inclined, not indeed pronouncing an unalterable opinion, to approve the custom of singing in the Church, so that a weaker mind may rise to devotion through the delights of the ears. Yet when it happens that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I sin grievously, and then I would rather not hear the singer.

units.la: Lib. ii. cap. 3. Si (Moses) Hebræâ voce loqueretur, frustra pulsaret sensum meum, nec inde mentem meam quicquam tangeret.
units.tr: Book 11, ch. 3. If Moses spoke in the Hebrew language, he would beat in vain upon my senses, and my mind would be touched by nothing from it.

units.la: Retractat. lib. 2. cap. 38. Libri de fide & operibus conscribendi occasionem explicans, Interea, inquit, missa sunt mihi à quibusdam fratribus laicis quidem, sed divinorum eloquiorum studi-{ }is scripta nonnulla, quæ ita distinguerent à bonis operibus Christianam fidem, ut sine hac non posse, sine illis autem posse perveniri suaderetur ad æternam vitam. Quibus respondens librum scripsi, cujus nomen est de fide & operibus.
units.tr: Retractations, book 2, ch. 38. Explaining the occasion for writing the book On Faith and Works, he says: "Meanwhile, some brothers, indeed laymen but students of the divine oracles, sent me some writings which so distinguished the Christian faith from good works as to persuade that one cannot attain eternal life without the former, but can attain it without the latter. In answer to them I wrote a book, whose title is On Faith and Works."

units.la: [Tom.II.] Epist.3. ad Volusianum. Modus ipse dicendi, quo sacra Scriptura contexitur, quàm omnibus accessibilis, quamvis paucissimis penetrabilis, ea quæ aperta continet, quasi amicus familiaris sine fuco ad cor loquitur indoctorum atque doctorum. Ea verò quæ in mysteriis occultat, nec ipsa eloquio superbo erigit, quò non audeat accedere mens tardiuscula & inerudita, quasi pauper ad divitem: sed invitat omnes humili sermone; quos non solùm manifestà pascat, sed etiam secretà exerceat veritate, hoc in promptis quod in recnditis habens. Sed ne aperta fastidirentur, eadem rursus operta desiderantur, desiderata quodammodo renovantur, renovata suaviter intimantur. His salubriter & prava corriguntur, & parva nutriuntur, & magna oblectantur ingenia. Ille huic doctrinæ inimicus est animus, qui vel errando eam nescit esse saluberrimam, vel odit ægrotando medicinam.
units.tr: [Vol. II.] Letter 3, to Volusian. The very manner of speaking in which holy Scripture is woven together is as accessible to all as it is penetrable by very few. It speaks to the heart like a familiar friend, without pretence, to the unlearned and to the learned alike, with what lies open. Yet the things it hides in its mysteries it does not raise up with a proud eloquence, lest a slow and untaught mind should dare to approach, as a poor man approaches a rich one. It invites all with a humble speech; it nourishes them not only with what is manifest but also trains them with a hidden truth, having in its open parts what it keeps in its recesses. But lest the plain things be despised, the hidden things are again desired; the things desired are in a manner renewed, and the things renewed are sweetly brought home. By these things the perverse are wholesomely corrected, the small are nourished, and the great minds are delighted. That mind is hostile to this teaching which either, by erring, does not know it to be most wholesome, or, by being sick, hates the medicine.

units.la: Epist. 109. Psalmis & Hymnis cùm oratis Deum; hoc versetur in corde, quod profertur in voce.
units.tr: Letter 109. When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is uttered with the voice be what dwells in the heart.

units.la: Epist. 119. ad Januarium cap. 18. de Psalmodiâ loquens. De hâc re tam utili ad movendum piè animum & accendendum divinæ dilectionis affectum, varia consuetudo est, & pleraque in Africâ Ecclesiæ membra pigriora sunt; ita ut Donatistæ nos reprehendant, quòd sobriè psallimus in Ecclesiâ divina cantica Prophetarum: cùm ipsi ebrietates suas ad canticum Psalmorum humano ingenio compositorum quasi tubas exhortationis inflamment. Quando autem non est tempus, cùm in Ecclesiâ fratres congregantur, sancta cantandi, nisi cùm legitur aut disputatur, aut antistites clarâ voce precantur, aut communis oratio voce Diaconi indicitur. Aliis autem particulis temporum quid melius à congregatis Christianis fiat, quid utilius, quid sanctius, omnino non video.
units.tr: Letter 119 to Januarius, ch. 18, speaking of psalmody. There is a varied custom concerning this matter, so useful for moving the heart to piety and kindling the affection of divine love, and most of the members of the Church in Africa are rather sluggish about it. So much so that the Donatists reproach us for singing the divine canticles of the prophets soberly in the Church, while they themselves inflame their drunken revels, as if with trumpets of exhortation, to the songs of the Psalms composed by human wit. But when there is no time for holy singing in the Church, when the brothers are gathered, except when the Scriptures are read or disputed over, or when the presiding ministers pray with a clear voice, or when the common prayer is announced by the voice of the deacon, then I do not at all see what better, what more useful, what holier thing could be done by Christians assembled at other times.

units.la: Epist. 121. ad Probam cap. 9. Qui verbis orare cupit, verba quæ intelligit convenienter adhibet; ut seipsum ad orationem internam excitet.
units.tr: Letter 121 to Proba, ch. 9. He who wishes to pray with words uses fitting words that he understands, so that he may stir himself to inner prayer.

units.la: Epist. 166. ad Donatistas. In Scripturis didicimus Christum, in Scripturis didicimus Ecclesiam. Has Scripturas communiter habemus: quare non in eis & Christum & Ecclesiam communiter retinemus?
units.tr: Letter 166 to the Donatists. We learned Christ from the Scriptures; we learned the Church from the Scriptures. We hold these Scriptures in common; why, then, do we not also hold Christ and the Church in common through them?

units.la: Epist. 178. De vocabulo ὁμοούσιος differens. Si minimè licet Patris & Filii & Spiritus S. unam substantiam lingua exeri Græcā; ergo nec Deum laudari decet & Barbarā. Sicut enim Græcā lingua quod est homusion, una dicitur vel creditur à fidelibus Trinitatis omnino substantia; sic una rogatur ut misereatur à cunctis Latinis & Barbaris unius Dei natura; ut à laudibus Dei unius nec ipsa lingua Barbara fit nullatenus aliena. Latinè enim dicitur, Domine miserere. Sola ergo hæc misericordia ab ipso uno Deo Patre & Filio & Spiritu Sancto linguâ debet Hebraeâ vel Græcâ & ipsâ ad postremum postulari Latinâ, non autem & Barbarâ. Si enim licet dicere non solum Barbaris linguâ suâ, sed etiam Romanis, Sihora armen t, quod interpretatur, Domine miserere: cur non liceret in Conciliis Patrum in ipsâ terrâ Græcorum (unde ubique destinata est fides) linguâ propriâ homusion confiteri, quod est Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti una substantia?
units.tr: Letter 178, discussing the word homoousios [ὁμοούσιος]. If it is by no means permitted to express the one substance of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in the Greek tongue, then it is not fitting to praise God in the barbarous tongue either. For just as, in the Greek language, homusion is what the faithful say, or believe, to be the one substance of the Trinity, so the one nature of the one God is asked by all, Latins and barbarians alike, to have mercy; so that the barbarous tongue is in no way alien from the praises of the one God. For in Latin one says, Domine miserere ("Lord, have mercy"). This mercy, then, should be asked of the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, in the Hebrew or Greek tongue, and finally in Latin too, but not also in a barbarous one. For if one may say not only in their own tongue but even among the Romans, Sihora armen t, which means "Lord, have mercy", why should it not be permitted in the Councils of the Fathers, in the very land of the Greeks (from which the faith has been sent everywhere), to confess in their own language homusion, which is the one substance of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

units.la: [Tom.III] De Doctrinâ Christ. lib.2. cap.5. Ex quo factum est, ut etiam Scriptura divina quâ tantis morbis humanarum voluntatum subvenitur, ab unâ linguâ profecta, qua opportunè potuit per orbem terrarum disseminari, per varias interpretum linguas longè lateque diffusa innotesceret gentibus ad salutem; quam legentes nihil aliud appetunt, quàm cogitationes voluntatemque illorum, à quibus conscripta est, invenire, & per illas voluntatem Dei; secundùm quem tales homines locutos esse credimus.
units.tr: [Vol. III.] On Christian Doctrine, book 2, ch. 5. From this it has come about that divine Scripture, by which such great diseases of human wills are remedied, having proceeded from one tongue, which could fittingly be spread through the whole world, has become known to the nations for salvation, spread far and wide through the various tongues of the translators. Those who read it seek nothing else than to discover the thoughts and will of those by whom it was written, and through them the will of God, according to whom we believe such men to have spoken.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 8. Erit igitur divinarum Scripturarum solertissimus indagator, qui primò totas legerit, notasque habuerit; etsi nondum intellectu, jam tamen lectione duntaxat eas quæ appellantur Canonicæ. Nam cæteras securius leget fide veritatis instructus, ne præoccupent imbecillem animum, & periculosis mendaciis atque phantasmatibus eludentes præjudicent aliquid contra sanam intelligentiam.
units.tr: Book 2, ch. 8. He, therefore, will be the most skilful investigator of the divine Scriptures who has first read them all through and become familiar with them, even if not yet with understanding, at least by reading those that are called canonical. For he will read the others more safely, instructed in the faith of truth, lest they forestall his weak mind, and, by deluding him with dangerous lies and phantasms, prejudice him against sound understanding.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 9. In his omnibus libris timentes Deum & pietate mansueti quærunt voluntatem Dei; cujus operis & laboris prima observatio est (ut diximus) nôsse istos libros, etsi nondum intellectu, adlegendo tamen vel mandare memoriæ vel omnino incognitos non habere.
units.tr: Lib. 2. cap. 9. Among all these books, those who fear God and are gentle in godliness seek the will of God. The first step in this work and labour, as we have said, is to know these books, even if not yet by understanding: by reading them, at least, and committing them to memory, and not leaving them wholly unknown.

units.la: ¹ Gothicam linguam Roma capta didicit.
units.tr: The Gothic language was learned after Rome was captured.

units.la: Lib. 3. cap. 1. Homo timens Deum, voluntatem ejus in Scripturis sanctis diligenter inquirit.
units.tr: Lib. 3. cap. 1. A man who fears God diligently searches out his will in the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 15. Divina dispensatione factum scribit, ut libri, quos gens Judæa cæteris populis vel religione vel invidiâ prodere nolebat, creditu-ri per Dominum gentibus, ministrâ regis Ptolomæi potestate, tantò ante proderentur.
units.tr: Lib. 2. cap. 15. He writes that it came about by divine arrangement that the books which the Jewish nation, either out of religious scruple or out of envy, did not wish to make known to other peoples, were to be entrusted by the Lord to the nations, and so, through the power of King Ptolemy's minister, were made public so much earlier.

units.la: Lib. 4. cap. 10. Quid enim prodest locutionis integritas, quam non sequitur intellectus audientis; cùm loquendi omnino nulla sit causa, si quod loquimur non intelligunt, propter quos ut intelligant loquimur?
units.tr: Lib. 4. cap. 10. For what good is the integrity of speech if the understanding of the hearer does not follow it? Since there is no reason at all for speaking if those for whose sake we speak do not understand what we say.

units.la: De Trinitate lib. 14. cap. 16. Apostolus ad Corinthios dicit, Si autem oravero linguâ; spiritus meus orat, mens autem mea infructuosa est. Hoc enim ait, quando id quod dicitur, non intelligitur.
units.tr: De Trinitate lib. 14. cap. 16. The Apostle says to the Corinthians: "If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful." For he says this when what is said is not understood.

units.la: De Genesi ad literam lib. 12. cap. 8. Si intellectum mentis removeas; nemo ædificatur audiendo quod non intelligit.
units.tr: De Genesi ad literam lib. 12. cap. 8. If you remove the understanding of the mind, no one is edified by hearing what he does not understand.

units.la: [Tom. IV.] De Catechizandis rudibus cap. 9. Ita enim non irridebunt [Rhetores.] Si aliquos antistites & ministros Ecclesiæ forte animadverterint vel cum barbarismis & solœcismis Deum invocare, vel eadem verba, quæ pronuntiant, non intelligere, perturbatéque distinguere? Non quia ista minimè corrigenda sunt, ut populus ad id quod planè intelligit, dicat Amen: Sed tamen piè toleranda sunt ab eis qui didicerunt, ut sono in Foro, sic voto in Ecclesiâ benedici.
units.tr: [Vol. IV.] De Catechizandis rudibus cap. 9. For will they not mock [the rhetoricians] if they notice that some bishops and ministers of the Church invoke God with barbarisms and solecisms, or do not understand the very words they utter, and divide them up in confusion? Not that these things ought not to be corrected, so that the people may say Amen to what they fully understand; but they must still be patiently borne by those who have learned that, as one is praised in the forum by sound, so one is blessed in the Church by prayer.

units.la: [Tom. V.] De Civitate Dei lib. 2. c. 28. Populi confluunt ad Ecclesias castâ celebritate, honestâ utriusque sexûs discretione, ubi audiant, quam bene hîc ad tempus vivere debeant, ut post hanc vitam beatè semperque vivere mereantur. Ubi sanctâ Scripturâ justitiæque doctrinâ de superiore loco in conspectu omnium personante, & qui faciunt audiant ad præmium; & qui non faciunt, audiant ad judicium.
units.tr: [Vol. V.] De Civitate Dei lib. 2. c. 28. The people flock to the churches in chaste assembly, with honourable separation of the sexes, there to hear how they ought to live well for a time here, so that after this life they may deserve to live blessedly and forever. There, with holy Scripture and the doctrine of justice resounding from a raised place in the sight of all, those who do what is commanded hear of their reward, and those who do not hear of their judgment.

units.la: Lib. 18. cap. 43. Editionem LXX. tanquam sola esset, sic recipit Ecclesia, atque utuntur Græci populi Christiani, quorum plerique utrùm alia sit ignorant.
units.tr: Lib. 18. cap. 43. The Church receives the edition of the Seventy as though it were the only one, and the Greek Christian peoples use it, most of whom do not know whether there is another.

units.la: Lib. 22. cap. 8. de miraculis loquens, quæ in sacris libris conscripta sunt: Leguntur, inquit, in populis ut credantur, nec in populis tamen nisi credita legerentur. Et statim: Canon quippe sacrarum literarum, quem diffamatum esse oportebat, illa facit ubique recitari, & memoriæ cunctorum inhærere populorum.
units.tr: Lib. 22. cap. 8, speaking of the miracles recorded in the sacred books: They are read among the peoples, he says, so that they may be believed; nor would they be read among the peoples unless they had been believed. And immediately: For the canon of the sacred letters, which ought to have been made known everywhere, causes them to be recited everywhere and to cling to the memory of all peoples.

units.la: [Tom. VI.] De utilitate credendi ad Honoratum. Quicquid est, mihi crede, in Scripturis illis, altum & divinum est. Inest omnino veritas, & reficiendis instaurandisque animis accommodatissima disciplina; & planè ita modificata, ut nemo inde haurire non possit quod sibi satis est, si modò ad hauriendum, devotè ac piè, ut vera religio poscit, accedat.
units.tr: [Vol. VI.] De utilitate credendi ad Honoratum. Whatever it is, believe me, in those Scriptures is lofty and divine. Truth is wholly present in them, and a discipline most suited to restoring and renewing souls; and it is so tempered that no one can fail to draw from it what is enough for himself, provided he approaches to draw from it devoutly and piously, as true religion requires.

units.la: Epist. 109. ad Sanctimoniales (Monachas) ex quâ fecerunt regulam tertiam Monachorum. Psalmis & hymnis cum oratis Deum, hoc versetur in corde, quod profertur in voce. Et post, Cùm accedéritis ad mensam, donec inde surgatis, quod vobis secundùm consuetudinem legitur, sine tumultu & contentionibus audite. Nec solæ vobis fauces sumant cibum, sed & aures percipiant Dei verbum.
units.tr: Epist. 109, to the nuns (monks), from which they made the third rule of the monks. When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is uttered with the voice be what dwells in the heart. And after: When you come to the table, listen until you rise from it, without tumult and quarrels, to what is read to you according to custom. Let not only your throats take food, but let your ears also receive the word of God.

units.la: Epist. 137. ad Clerum, seniores, & universam plebem Ecclesiæ Hipponensis. Utinam Scripturæ Dei solicitâ mente intendentes, in quibusque scandalis adjutorio nostri sermonis non egeretis.
units.tr: Epist. 137, to the clergy, elders, and the whole people of the Church of Hippo. Would that you, attending to the Scriptures of God with a careful mind, had no need of the help of our speech in any stumbling-blocks.

units.la: De Magistro cap. 1. Non opus est locutione cùm oramus, id est, sonantibus verbis, nisi forte sicut sacerdotes faciunt, significandæ mentis suæ causâ, non ut Deus sed ut homines audiant, & consensione quadam per commemorationem suspendantur in Deum.
units.tr: De Magistro cap. 1. There is no need for speech when we pray, that is, for sounding words, unless perhaps, as priests do, for the sake of signifying their mind, not so that God but so that men may hear, and by a certain agreement, through recollection, be lifted up into God.

units.la: [Tom.VII.] Contra Julianum Pelagianum lib.4. cap.14. Movetur certè animus ad pietatis affectum, divino cantico audito: tamen etiam illic si sensum, non sensum libido audiendi desideret, improbatur.
units.tr: [Vol. VII.] Contra Julianum Pelagianum lib. 4. cap. 14. Certainly the mind is moved to an affection of piety when a divine canticle is heard; yet even there, if the desire of hearing seeks sense rather than nonsense, that is disapproved.

units.la: [Tom.VIII.] In Psal.XVIII. Expositio 2. Deprecati Dominum, ut ab occultis nostris mundet nos, & ab alienis parcat servis suis, quid hoc sit intelligere debemus: ut humanâ ratione, non quasi avium voce cantemus. Nam & merulæ & psittaci & corvi & picæ, & hujusmodi volucres sæpe ab hominibus docentur sonare quod nesciunt. Scienter enim cantare naturæ huminis divinâ voluntate concessum est. Et quàm multi mali & luxuriosi sic cantant, digna auribus suis & cordibus, novimus & dolemus. Eò enim pejores sunt, quò non possunt ignorare quod cantant. Sciunt enim sc. cantare flagitia, & tamen cantant tantò liberiùs, quantò immundiùs: quoniam tantò se putant lætiores, quantò fuerint turpiores. Nos autem qui in Ecclesiâ divina eloquia cantare didicimus, simul etiam instare debemus esse quod scriptum est: u Beatus populus, qui intelligit jubilationem. Proinde charissimi quod consonâ voce cantavimus, sereno etiam corde nosse ac tenere debemus.
units.tr: [Vol. VIII.] In Psal. XVIII. Expositio 2. When we ask the Lord to cleanse us from our hidden faults and to spare his servants from strangers, we ought to understand what this means: that we sing with human reason, not with the voice of birds. For blackbirds and parrots and crows and magpies, and birds of that kind, are often taught by men to sound what they do not know. For it has been granted by divine will to human nature to sing knowingly. And how many evil and debauched people sing in such a way, worthy of their own ears and hearts, we know and we grieve. For they are the worse, because they cannot be ignorant of what they sing. For they know they sing shameful deeds, and yet they sing all the more freely the more filthy they are, since they think themselves the happier the more disgraceful they are. But we, who have learned to sing the divine utterances in the Church, must also strive to be what is written: "Blessed is the people that understands the jubilation." Therefore, dearly beloved, what we have sung with one voice we ought also to know and hold in a serene heart.

units.la: In Psal. XXXIII. Legite Scripturas. Ideo voluit Deus ut scriberentur, ut nos consolaremur.
units.tr: In Psal. XXXIII. Read the Scriptures. God willed that they be written so that we might be comforted.

units.la: In Psal. XLIV. Hæc scriptum est, & ubi sit scriptum commemoravimus. Qui meminerunt, recognoscant; qui non meminerunt, legant; qui non legerunt, credant.
units.tr: In Psal. XLIV. This is written, and we have recalled where it is written. Let those who remember recognise it; let those who do not remember read it; let those who have not read it believe it.

units.la: u Psal. LXXXVIII.
In Pfal. LXIV. Misit inde (ex civitate sc. cœlesti) ad nos epistolas pater noster; ministravit nobis Scripturas Deus: quibus epistolis fieret in nobis redeundi desiderium.
units.tr: In Psal. LXIV. Our Father sent letters to us from there (namely, from the heavenly city); God ministered the Scriptures to us, by which letters a desire to return might be kindled in us.

units.la: In Pfal. LXVI. Vide formicam Dei; surgit quotidie, currit ad Ecclesiam Dei, orat, audit lectionem, hymnum cantat, ruminat quod audit, apud se cogitat, recondit intus grana electa de area.
units.tr: In Psal. LXVI. See God's ant: it rises every day, runs to the Church of God, prays, hears the reading, sings the hymn, chews over what it hears, thinks it over within itself, and stores up inside the chosen grains from the threshing floor.

units.la: In Pfal. XCIII. Sicut intentissimè audivimus, cùm Psalmus iste legeretur, ita intentè audiamus cùm revelat Dominus, quæ hîc dignatus est opacare mysteria. Ad hoc enim claunduntur quædam Sacramenta Scripturarum: non ut denegentur, sed ut pulsantibus aperiantur. Et post, Modò lectio necessaria est, quamdiu ex parte cognoscimus & ex parte prophetamus, sicut dicit Apostolus: Cùm autem venerit quod perfectum est, auferetur quod ex parte est. Non enim liber necessarius est, neque legemus in illâ civitate Hierusalem, ubi angeli vivunt, &c. Sed tamen ipsa lex quæ scripta est, firmamentum nobis est: ibi si fit cor nostrum, non impellitur iniquitatibus hominum.
units.tr: In Psal. XCIII. As we have listened most attentively while this Psalm was read, so let us listen attentively when the Lord reveals the mysteries which he has deigned to veil here. For certain sacraments of the Scriptures are shut up for this purpose: not that they may be denied, but that they may be opened to those who knock. And after: Reading is necessary now, for as long as we know in part and prophesy in part, as the Apostle says: "But when what is perfect has come, what is in part will be taken away." For a book will not be necessary, nor shall we read in that city of Jerusalem where the angels live, etc. But still the law that is written is a firmament for us; if our heart is fixed there, it is not driven headlong by the iniquities of men.

units.la: In Psalm. XCVIII. Audistis cùm Hieremias legeretur ante Apostolicam lectionem, si aurem appostuistis; vidistis ibi tempora præsentia quæ nunc agimus. Ibid. Quanta mirabilia Deus fecit per manum Moysi, noverunt omnino qui istas Scripturas libenter audiunt in Ecclesiâ, vel apud se legunt, vel quo quo modo didicerunt.
units.tr: In Psalm. XCVIII. You heard, when Jeremiah was read before the Apostolic lesson, if you lent an ear; you saw there the present times which we now live. Ibid. Those who gladly hear these Scriptures in the Church, or read them at home, or have learned them in whatever way, know altogether what great wonders God wrought by the hand of Moses.

units.la: In Pfal. XCIX. Beatus populus qui intelligit jubilationem. Curramus ergo ad hanc beatitudinem, intelligamus jubilationem, non eam sine intellectu fundamus. Quid opus est jubilare, & obtemperare huic Psalmo dicenti; Jubilate Deo omnis terra; & non intelligere jubilationem, ut vox nostra sola jubilet, & cor non jubilet? Sonus enim cordis intellectus est.
units.tr: In Psal. XCIX. "Blessed is the people that understands the jubilation." Let us run, then, to this blessedness; let us understand the jubilation, and not lay it down without understanding. What need is there to jubilate and obey this Psalm when it says, "Jubilate to God, all the earth," and yet not to understand the jubilation, so that only our voice jubilates and our heart does not? For the sound of the heart is understanding.

units.la: In Pfal. CIII. Nos sub cælo, tanquam sub pelle divinarum Scripturarum legimus modò cùm tenditur, &c. Prophetas vivos sola Judæa habuit, mortuos omnes gentes. Cùm enim viverent, nondum erat extensa pellis; nondum erat extensum cælum, ut tegeret orbem terrarum.
units.tr: In Psal. CIII. We read under heaven, as under the skin of the divine Scriptures, now that it is stretched out, etc. Judaea alone had living prophets; all the other nations had dead ones. For while the prophets lived, the skin was not yet stretched; the heaven was not yet extended to cover the orb of the lands.

units.la: In Psal. CV. Audiamus Scripturam divinam humiliter excelsa dicentem, cùm & parvulis nutriendis sumenda porrigit, & majoribus exercendis perscrutanda proponit.
units.tr: In Psal. CV. Let us hear divine Scripture, which speaks lofty things in humble terms, offering what is to be taken up to nourish the little ones, and setting before the greater ones what is to be searched out and exercised.

units.la: In Psal. CXVIII. Conc. 23. Quod hîc ait, Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, & lumen semitis meis, verbum est quod Scripturis sanctis omnibus continetur.
units.tr: In Psal. CXVIII. Serm. 23. What he says here, "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths," is the word contained in all the holy Scriptures.

units.la: : Matth. VII. ✓ 1 Cor. XIII.
units.tr: Matth. VII. ✓ 1 Cor. XIII.

units.la: In Psal. CXLVI. Non intelligis, parùm intelligis, non consequeris. Honora Scripturam Dei, honora verbum Dei, etiam non apertum : differ pietate intelligentiam. Noli protervus esse, accusare aut obscuritatem, aut quasi perversitatem Scripturæ. Perversum hic nihil est, obscurum autem aliquid est ; non ut tibi negetur, sed ut exerceat accepturum. Ergo quando obscurum est ; medicus illud fecit, ut pulses. Voluit h ut exercereris in pulsando ; voluit, ut pulsanti aperiret.
units.tr: In Psal. CXLVI. You do not understand, you understand little, you do not attain it. Honour the Scripture of God, honour the word of God, even when it is not open to you: defer understanding through piety. Do not be wilfully obstinate, and do not accuse the Scripture of obscurity or, as it were, of perversity. Nothing in it is perverse; something in it is obscure, but not so that it is denied to you; rather so that it may exercise you, who are going to receive it. Therefore, when it is obscure, the physician has made it so that you may knock. He willed that you be exercised by knocking; he willed to open to the one who knocks.

units.la: [Tom. IX.] In Evangelium Joannis, Tract. 96. Omnia quæ post ascensionem Domini canonica veritate atque authoritate conscripta sunt, quis fidelis vel etiam Catechumenus, antequam Spiritum Sanctum baptizatus accipiat, non æquo animo legit atque audit, etiamsi nondum sicut oportet intelligit ?
units.tr: [Vol. IX.] On the Gospel of John, Tract. 96. Whoever is faithful, or even a catechumen, before being baptized and receiving the Holy Spirit, does not read and hear with an equal mind all that has been written after the Lord's ascension with canonical truth and authority, even if he does not yet understand it as he ought?

units.la: In Epist. Joan. Tractat. 2. Omnia quæ leguntur de Scripturis sanctis, ad instructionem & salutem nostram intentè oportet audire. Maximè tamen memoriæ commendanda sunt, quæ adversùs hæreticos valent plurimùm : quorum insidiæ infirmiores quosque & negligentiores circumvenire non cessant. Et post, Audistis cùm Acta Apostolorum legerentur, quot millia crediderunt ex interfectoribus Christi. Si crediderunt postea, qui occiderant ; non erant credituri, qui paululùm dubitabant ? Et ipsis tamen (quòd maximè debetis animadvertere & memoriæ vestræ mandare, quia contra insidiosos errores Deus ponere voluit firmamentum in Scripturis, contra quas nullus audet loqui, qui quoquo modo se vult haberi Christianum) cùm se palpandum præbuisset, non illi sufficit ; nisi de Scripturis confirmaret cor credentium : prospiciebat enim nos futuros. In quo palpemus, nos non habemus ; sed quod legamus, habemus.
units.tr: On the Epistles of John, Tract. 2. Everything that is read from the holy Scriptures we ought to hear attentively, for our instruction and salvation. Yet those passages are especially to be committed to memory which are most effective against heretics, whose snares never cease to ensnare the weaker and more careless. And after: You heard, when the Acts of the Apostles were read, how many thousands believed from among the killers of Christ. If those who had killed him believed afterwards, were those who had doubted a little not going to believe? And yet he himself (which you must especially notice and commit to your memory, because against insidious errors God willed to set a firmament in the Scriptures, against which no one dares to speak who wishes in any way to be considered a Christian), when he had offered himself to be touched, was not enough for them unless he confirmed the hearts of believers from the Scriptures; for he foresaw that we would come. We do not have him to touch, but we have what we read.

units.la: De Pastoribus cap. 11. Constituit montes Israel, authores Scripturarum divinarum. Ibi pascite, ut securè pascatis, &c. Colligite vos ad montes Scripturæ sanctæ. Ibi sunt deliciæ cordis vestri : ibi nihil venenosum, nihil alienum, &c.
units.tr: On the Shepherds, chap. 11. He set up the mountains of Israel, the authors of the divine Scriptures. Feed there, so that you may feed securely, etc. Gather yourselves to the mountains of holy Scripture. There are the delights of your heart; there is nothing poisonous there, nothing foreign, etc.

units.la: [Tom. X.] De Verbis Domini secundùm Matthæum Serm. 11. cap. 7. In omni copiâ Scripturarum sanctarum pascimur apertis, exercemur obscuris. Illic fames pellitur, hic fastidium.
units.tr: [Vol. X.] On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew, Serm. 11, chap. 7. In the full abundance of the holy Scriptures we are fed by what is open, and we are exercised by what is obscure. There hunger is driven away, there distaste.

units.la: De Verbis Domini secundùm Joan. Serm. 45. cap. 3. Caput nostrum Dominus Christus locutus est ad Judæos ea quæ audivimus cùm Evangelium legeretur. Caput ad inimicos suos loquatur ; & corpus, i. e. Ecclesia, ad inimicos suos loquatur, &c. Hoc ergo illis dicamus, voce Ecclesiæ loquor : O fratres, filii dispersi, oves errantes, rami præcisi, quid mihi calumnia-
units.tr: On the Words of the Lord according to John, Serm. 45, chap. 3. Our head, the Lord Christ, spoke to the Jews those things we have heard when the Gospel was read. Let the head speak to his enemies; and let the body, that is the Church, speak to its enemies, etc. Let us therefore say this to them, speaking in the voice of the Church: O brothers, scattered sons, straying sheep, cut-off branches, why do you accuse me

units.la: h Matth. VII. mihi? Quid me non agnoscitis? Scrutamini Scripturas, in quibus vos putatis vitam æternam habere; ipsæ testimonium perhibent de me. Judæis dicit caput nostrum, quod vobis corpus dicit. Quæretis me, & non invenietis. Quare? Quia non scrutamini Scripturas, quæ testimonium perhibent de me.
units.tr: Matth. VII. me? Why do you not recognise me? Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life; they bear witness to me. Our head says to the Jews what the body says to you. You will seek me, and you will not find me. Why? Because you do not search the Scriptures, which bear witness to me.

units.la: De Verbis Apostoli Serm. i. Sancta & divina eloquia, fratres, jugiter, immo quotidie, nobis salubriter recitantur; ut animæ nostræ pascantur, in futuro autem seculo æternis epulis saginentur.
units.tr: On the Words of the Apostle, Serm. 1. Holy and divine utterances, brothers, are recited to us continually, indeed daily, for our good, so that our souls may be fed, and in the future age be filled with eternal feasts.

units.la: Serm. 39. de Tempore. Divinarum Scripturarum multiplicem abundantiam latissimamque doctrinam, fratres charissimi, sine ullo labore comprehendit, & sine ullo labore custodit; cujus cor plenum est charitate.
units.tr: Serm. 39, On the Time. Dearest brothers, he who has the heart full of charity comprehends without any labour, and keeps without any labour, the manifold abundance and very wide teaching of the divine Scriptures.

units.la: 7 De Tempore Serm. 55. Nec solum vobis sufficiat, quod in Ecclesiâ divinas lectiones auditis; sed etiam in domibus vestris aut ipsi legite, aut alios legentes requirite, & libenter audite. Et circa initium. Si Scripturas divinas aut ipsi non legimus, aut legentes alios non libenter audimus; ipsa nobis medicamenta convertuntur in vulnera, &c.
units.tr: Sermon 55, On the Time. It should not be enough for you that you hear the divine readings in the Church; but also in your homes either read yourselves, or ask others who read, and listen gladly. And near the beginning: If we do not ourselves read the divine Scriptures, or do not gladly listen to others reading them, those very medicines are turned into wounds for us, etc.

units.la: Serm. 56. Lectiones divinas & in Ecclesiâ, sicut consuestis, audite; & in domibus vestris relegite. Si aliquis ita fuerit occupatus, ut ante refectionem Scripturæ divinæ non possit insistere; non eum pigeat in convivio suo aliquid de Scripturis divinis relegere: ut quomodo caro pascitur cibo, sic reficiatur anima Dei verbo: ut totus homo; i. e. & exterior & interior, & de sancto & de salubri convivio satiatus exurgat. Nam si sola caro reficitur, & anima Dei verbo non pascitur; ancilla satiatur, & domina fame torquetur. Et hoc quàm sit injustum, sanctitas vestra non potest ignorare. Et ideo sicut jam dixi, lectiones divinas illo desiderio legere & audire debetis; ut de ipsis in domibus vestris, & alibi ubicunque fueritis, etiam loqui & alios docere possitis.
units.tr: Serm. 56. Hear the divine readings in the Church, as you are accustomed; and reread them in your homes. If anyone has been so occupied that he cannot apply himself to the divine Scripture before his meal, let him not be reluctant to reread something of the divine Scriptures at his table: so that as the flesh is nourished by food, so the soul of God may be refreshed by the Word of God; so that the whole man, that is, both outer and inner, may rise up satisfied from a holy and healthful feast. For if only the flesh is refreshed, and the soul is not fed by the Word of God, the maidservant is satisfied and the mistress is tormented by hunger. Your holiness cannot be ignorant how unjust this is. And therefore, as I have already said, you ought to read and hear the divine readings with that desire, so that you may be able to speak of them and teach others about them in your homes and wherever you may be.

units.la: Serm. 85. [in Quadragesimâ habitus.] Quamvis, fratres charissimi, omni tempore verbum Dei cum grandi desiderio nos oporteat fideliter semper audire; in istis tamen diebus specialiter lectioni divinæ insistere, & de salute animæ nostræ debemus attentius cogitare.
units.tr: Serm. 85, [delivered in Lent]. Although, dearest brothers, we ought always to listen faithfully to the Word of God with great desire at all times, yet in these days we should especially apply ourselves to the divine reading, and think more attentively about the salvation of our souls.

units.la: Serm. 91. Et ideo, fratres charissimi, quantum possumus, cum Dei adjutorio lectioni divinæ studeamus insistere; ut legem Dei spiritaliter mereamur agnoscere, &c.
units.tr: Serm. 91. And therefore, dearest brothers, as far as we can, with the help of God let us be eager to apply ourselves to the divine reading, so that we may deserve to recognise the law of God spiritually, etc.

units.la: Serm. 112. Adhuc ergo bonum habemus solatium, divinarum lectionem Scripturarum: quia sacrarum lectio Scripturarum divinæ est præcognitio non parva beatitudinis. In his enim quasi in quodam speculo homo seipsum
units.tr: Serm. 112. So we still have a good comfort, the reading of the divine Scriptures; because the reading of the holy Scriptures is no small foretaste of blessedness. For in them, as in a certain mirror, a man can consider himself

units.la: 7 Sequentes omnes de Tempore Sermones spurios esse censent Benedictini Parisienses. consM derare potest, qualis fit, vel quò tendat. Lectio assidua purificat omnia, timorem incutit gehennæ, ad gaudia superna cor instigat legentis. Qui vult cum Deo semper esse, frequenter debet orare & legere. Nam cùm oramus, ipsi cum Deo loquimur; cùm verò legimus, Deus nobiscum loquitur. Geminum confert donum lectio sanctarum Scripturarum; sive quia intellectum mentis erudit, seu quia à vanitatibus mundi abstractum hominem ad amorem Dei perducit. Labor honestus est lectionis; & multis ad emendationem animi proficit. Sicut enim ex carnalibus escis alitur caro; ita ex divinis eloquiis interior homo nutritur & pascitur: sicut Psalmista ait: Quàm dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua, Domine, super mel & favum ori meo. Et ideo, fratres charissimi, quicunque ex vobis lectiones sacras legere & intelligere possunt; in his studium impendant, ut earum frequenter meditatione atantur. Qui verò sensum locutionis sacræ ex lectione non possunt percipere, attentius audiant interpretantem, & recipiant saltem inde ædificationem.
units.tr: The Parisian Benedictines judge all the following sermons On the Time to be spurious. what he is like, or whither he tends. Constant reading purifies all things, strikes fear of hell, and stirs the heart of the reader to heavenly joys. Whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray and read. For when we pray, we ourselves speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us. The reading of the holy Scriptures bestows a twofold gift: either because it instructs the understanding of the mind, or because it draws a man away from the vanities of the world and leads him to the love of God. The reading is an honest labour, and it profits many for the improvement of the soul. For just as the flesh is nourished by carnal food, so the inner man is nourished and fed by the divine utterances, as the Psalmist says: How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth. And therefore, dearest brothers, whoever among you can read and understand the holy readings, let them devote their zeal to these, so that they may be occupied with frequent meditation on them. But those who cannot grasp the sense of the sacred discourse from reading should listen more attentively to one who interprets it, and at least receive edification from that.

units.la: Serm. 38. de Sanctis. Modò cùm Evangelica lectio legeretur, audivimus dicentem Dominum: Venite benedicti, percipite regnum, &c. Ut ergo istam vocem desiderabilem audire, & ab audito malo possitis per Dei gratiam liberari; totis viribus Deo auxiliante contendite lectionem divinam in domibus vestris frequenter legere, & in Ecclesiâ libenter & obedienter audire.
units.tr: Serm. 38, On the Saints. Just now, when the Gospel reading was being read, we heard the Lord saying: "Come, blessed, receive the kingdom," etc. So that you may be able to hear that desirable voice, and be delivered by God's grace from the evil that you have heard; strive with all your strength, with God helping you, to read the divine reading frequently in your homes, and to hear it in the Church gladly and obediently.

units.la: Author Libri 8 de Vitâ Christianâ, tomo 9. Operum Augustini.
units.tr: Author of the eighth book De Vita Christiana, vol. 9 of Augustine's Works.

units.la: In fine libri ita sanctam quandam viduam affatur. Ante omnia incessabiliter Domini meditare mandata; orationibus & Psalmis instanter incumbe; ut si possibile est, nemo te aliquando nisi aut legentem inveniat aut orantem.
units.tr: At the end of the book he addresses a certain holy widow in this way: Above all, meditate without ceasing on the commandments of the Lord; apply yourself earnestly to prayers and Psalms, so that, if it is possible, no one may ever find you except reading or praying.

units.la: ¹ Psal. CXVIII.
8 Fastidio, Episcopo Britanno, circa ann. 420. hunc librum deberi notum est.
units.tr: 8 It is well known that this book was dedicated to Fastidius, bishop of Britain, around the year 420.

units.la: Author Libri 9 de Salutaribus Documentis, tomo 4. Operum Augustini.
units.tr: Author of the Book 9 on Salutary Teachings, Tome 4 of the Works of Augustine.

units.la: Cap. 9. Omnis librorum sanctorum series ad nostram salutem scripta est; & hoc maximè auribus nostris intonat, & iterum atque iterum replicat, quid fit homini cavendum vel quid sequendum. In quibus libris tua dignitas (ad Laicum loquitur) optimè exerceri solet; quia per illos nobis loquitur Deus ipse & Dominus noster, & piæ nobis voluntatis demonstrat afsectum.
units.tr: Chapter 9. All the series of the holy books is written for our salvation; and this above all thunders in our ears, and again and again repeats what must be avoided by a man or what must be followed. In these books your dignity (he speaks to a layman) is wont to be exercised most excellently; because through them God himself and our Lord speaks to us, and shows us the affection of a loving will.

units.la: Cap. 38. Grandis confusio est animabus laicorum, qui dicunt; Quid pertinet ad me legendo libros Scripturarum audire vel discere, vel etiam frequenter ad sacerdotes & Ecclesias sanctorum recurrere? Dum Clericus fiam, faciam ea quæ oportet Clericos facere.
units.tr: Chapter 38. There is great confusion among the souls of laymen, who say: What does it matter to me to hear or learn by reading the books of Scripture, or even to have frequent recourse to the priests and the churches of the saints? While I am becoming a cleric, I will do what clerics ought to do.

units.la: Author Præfationis præfixæ Augustini Commentariis in Psalmos, in principio Tomi 8. Recentior est Anony- mus, ut rectè notat Gesnerus.
units.tr: Author of the preface prefixed to Augustine's Commentaries on the Psalms, at the beginning of Tome 8. He is a more recent anonymous writer, as Gesner rightly observes.

units.la: Cùm intelligenter Deo psallendum sit; quomodo debitè Deo psallere poterit, qui quid psallit ignorat? Jubet namque sanctus Psalmista noster, ut psallentes Deo intelligenter psallant. Quoniam rex (inquit) omnis terræ Deus, psallite sapienter, b. e. intelligenter, ut alia litera habet.
units.tr: Since God must be sung to with understanding, how will he be able to sing to God duly who does not know what he sings? For our holy Psalmist commands that those who sing to God should sing with understanding. For, "God is king of all the earth, sing wisely," that is, with understanding, as another reading has it.

units.la: 420. Paulinus Nolanus Episcopus.
units.tr: 420. Paulinus of Nola, Bishop.

units.la: Epist. 42. ad Cytherium de institutione filii agens.
units.tr: Letter 42, to Cytherius, dealing with the instruction of a son.

units.la: In carne vivens vitâ carnis exulet, | Fœcunditatis congerens, In lege mentis ambulans; | Exuberantum dives annorum bonis: Totamque regni creditî terram sibi | Jejuna pavit tempora: Peragret in libris sacris. | Sic iste noster in sacratis literis, Et sicut ille vir Joseph Dei pius | Perambulet regnum Dei. Memphiticos fines obit; | Scriptura namque sancto flata Spiritu, Et ampliatis horreis lætas opes | Regui perennis mater est, &c.
units.tr: Living in the flesh, let him go into exile from the life of the flesh, / gathering the fruit of fertility, walking in the law of the mind; / rich in the goods of abundant years, and feeding himself with the land of the kingdom entrusted to him / through fasting times; let him range through the books of the Holy Scriptures. / So let our man, in the sacred letters, and like that man Joseph, pious toward God, / range through the kingdom of God. He goes through the Memphian borders; / for Scripture, breathed by the Holy Spirit, and with its barns enlarged, is the mother of the joyful riches of an everlasting kingdom, etc.

units.la: Eidem tribuitur Epistola ad Celantiam Matronam, quæ 14. est in 1. Tomo Operum Hieronymi. Illic de institutione matris familiæ agens.
units.tr: The same author is credited with the letter to the matron Celantia, which is the 14th in the first volume of Jerome's works, dealing there with the instruction of the mistress of a household.

units.la: 9 Paulinus, Patriarcha Aquileiensis is fuit plurium Codicum MSS. quibus usi sunt Benedictini Parisienses, qui exeunte Seculo octavo floruit, ex fide Præcipua (inquit) tibi cura sit, legem nosse divinam; per quam possis quasi præsentia cernere exempla sanctorum; & quid faciendum sit, quidve vitandum, illius consilio discere. Maximum enim ad justitiam auxilium est implere divinis eloquiis animum; & quod opere exequi cupias, semper corde meditari. Et paulò post, Sint ergo divinæ Scripturæ semper in manibus tuis, & jugiter in mente volvantur. Item. Eligatur tibi opportunus, & aliquantulum à famil'iæ strepitu remotus locus; in quem tu velut in portum, quasi ex multâ tempestate curarum te recipias, & excitatos foris cogitationum fluctus secreti tranquillitate componas. Tantum ibi sit divinæ lectionis studium, tam crebræ orationum vices, tam firma & pressa de futuris cogitatio; ut omnes reliqui temporis occupationes facile hac vacatione compenses.
units.tr: 9 Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia, who flourished at the end of the eighth century, according to several manuscript codices used by the Parisian Benedictines, says: Your chief concern should be to know the divine law, through which you may see, as if present, the examples of the saints, and learn from its counsel what is to be done and what is to be avoided. For the greatest help to righteousness is to fill the mind with divine utterances, and always to meditate in the heart on what you desire to carry out in deed. And a little later, Let the divine Scriptures therefore always be in your hands, and be constantly turned over in your mind. Likewise: Let there be chosen for you a convenient place, somewhat removed from the noise of the household, into which you may withdraw as into a harbour, as if out of a great storm of cares, and there calm the waves of thoughts stirred up outside by the stillness of solitude. Let there be there such zeal for divine reading, such frequent turns of prayer, and such firm and settled thought about the future, that by this leisure you may easily make up for all the occupations of the rest of your time.

units.la: 430. Sedulius Hyberniensis. 10
units.tr: 430. Sedulius Hyberniensis. 10

units.la: Annotat. in 1 Corinth. XIV. ver. 2. Qui loquitur linguâ] i. e. ignota qualibet linguâ. Non hominibus loquitur] Dum non intelligunt, quia barbara est. Sed Deo] Qui intelligit, sive dum per hoc ipse magnificatur. Nemo enim audit.] i. e. intelligit. Spiritu loquitur mysteria] Spiritualí dono præditus, vel suo Spiritu loquitur. v. 4. Seipsum ædificat] Dum solus ipse intelligit, vel glorificatur. Ecclesiam ædificat] Dum multis proficit. ver. 5. Nisi interpretetur] Ex ignotâ linguâ in aliquam notam. Major enim est qui prophetat, quàm qui loquitur linguâ] Sicut profectu, sic & merito major est, v. 6. Nunc autem, fratres, si venero ad vos linguâ loquens] Suo exemplo hortatur eos illud non pro magno quærere, quod non prodest Ecclesiæ, v. 9. Eritis enim in aera loquentes] b. e. si etiam tam multa loquamini, ut genera sint linguarum; quid proderit? cum omnia in aera solvantur, & nulli proficiant. v. 10. Et nihil eorum sine voce est] Proprium est uniuscujusque linguæ habere vocem. v. 11. Ero, cui loquar, barbarus] Omnis enim sermo, qui non intelligitur, barbarus judicatur. v. 13. Et ideò qui loquitur linguâ] i. e. ignotâ. Oret ut interpretetur] Oratio hoc loco oris elocutio intelligitur. Sic ergo loquatur; ut grammatica verba, quæ dicturus sit, intelligantur: vel oret, ut illi interpretandi gratia donetur, v. 14. Nam si orem linguâ] mihi ignotâ. Sine fructu est] Mens in ipso homine, si absente mente & intellectu spiritus oret: quantò magis quæ ignorantur ab auditoribus, dici
units.tr: Notes on 1 Corinthians 14, verse 2. "He who speaks in a tongue," that is, in some unknown language. "Speaks not to men," since they do not understand it, because it is foreign. "But to God," who understands it, or in whom he is magnified by this. "For no one hears," that is, understands. "He speaks mysteries in the Spirit," endowed with a spiritual gift, or speaks by his own spirit. Verse 4. "He edifies himself," since he alone understands it, or is glorified. "He edifies the Church," since he benefits many. Verse 5. "Unless he interprets," that is, turns the unknown language into a known one. "For he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks in a tongue": as he is greater in profit, so he is greater in merit. Verse 6. "But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in a tongue," by his own example he urges them not to seek after that which does not profit the Church. Verse 9. "For you will be speaking into the air," that is, even if you speak so many things that they are kinds of languages, what good will it do, since everything is dissolved into the air and benefits no one. Verse 10. "And none of them is without voice": it is characteristic of every language to have a voice. Verse 11. "I shall be a barbarian to him whom I speak to": every speech that is not understood is judged barbarous. Verse 13. "And therefore he who speaks in a tongue," that is, an unknown one. "Let him pray that he may interpret": here prayer is understood as the utterance of the mouth. So let him speak in such a way that the words he is going to say are understood grammatically, or let him pray that the gift of interpreting may be granted to him. Verse 14. "For if I pray in a tongue," unknown to me. "It is without fruit": if, while the mind and understanding are absent, the spirit prays in the man himself, how much more are things that are unknown to the hearers said without fruit.

units.la: 10 Rectius ætatem ejus posuit Cl. Usserius | fuit; & siqua Hepidanno fides, circa an. 818. in primor. Eccl. Britan. Bedâ enim posterior | claruit. non prodest ? Mens autem mea sine fructu est ] Dum non intelligo quod loquor. Est autem spiritus vis quaedam animae mente inferior, ubi corporalium rerum similitudines exprimuntur. 15. Orabo Spiritu ] Oratio hoc loco oris narratio intelligitur. Ergo orabo Spiritu] h. e. ignota lingua in spiritu meo expressa eloquar. Orabo & mente] Id est, intellectu mentis meae aliis praedicabo. Qui enim interpretatur, necesse est, ut ipse prius intelligat, quod aliis dicturus est. Non ergo sufficit, ut quis solo spiritu alienâ linguâ loquatur, nisi mens & intellectus accesserit, quatenus ipse cognoscat, quid loquatur, aut aliis interpretando patefaciat. 16. Caeterum si benedixeris spiritu ] id est, sine interpretatione, quatenus aliis clarescat quod loqueris. Qui supplet locum Idiotae] Quod ipse diceret Idiotae, i.e. nuper baptizati, & qui nullam praeter propriam intelligit linguam, quod proprium est auditoribus. Quomodo dicet Amen] Hoc est, quomodo tuae benedictioni perhibebit testimonium vel consensum, cum ignoret ipsius linguae qualitatem ? 17. Nam tu quidem bene gratias agis] Quod superius dixe-at, Si benedixeris spiritu, hoc ipsum exponit. Nam benedicere spiritu est gratias agere, licet ignota idiotis lingua. 19. Sed in Ecclesiâ volo sensu meo quinque verba loqui ] Mavult pauca verba lucida sensu recto loqui, quàm innumerabilia obscura & incognita, quae auditores non aedificant; quia meliora sunt pauca verba quae prosunt, quàm multa quae non prosunt.
units.tr: 10 Ussher the distinguished has rightly placed his age; he flourished, if any trust is to be put in Hepidannus, about the year 818, in the Primordia of the British Church, for he was later than Bede. Is it not profitable? But my mind is without fruit: while I do not understand what I say. Moreover, the spirit is a certain power of the soul lower than the mind, in which likenesses of bodily things are expressed. 15. I will pray in the Spirit. Here prayer is understood as the narration of the mouth. So, I will pray in the Spirit, that is, I will speak in an unknown tongue expressed in my spirit. I will pray with the mind also: that is, I will preach to others by the understanding of my mind. For he who interprets must first understand what he is going to say to others. It is therefore not enough for someone to speak in a foreign tongue by the spirit alone, unless the mind and understanding are added, so that he himself knows what he is saying, or makes it clear to others by interpreting. 16. Otherwise, if you bless in the spirit, that is, without interpretation, so that what you say may become clear to others. He who fills the place of the layman: that is, what he himself would say to the layman, that is, a recently baptized person, who understands no language but his own, which is the custom of hearers. How will he say Amen? That is, how will he bear witness to or assent to your blessing, since he does not know the quality of that very language? 17. For you indeed give thanks well: what he had said above, "if you bless in the spirit," he now explains. For to bless in the spirit is to give thanks, even though the language is unknown to the laymen. 19. But in the Church I would rather speak five words with my sense: he prefers to speak a few clear words with a right sense, rather than countless obscure and unknown ones, which do not edify the hearers; because a few words that profit are better than many that do not profit.

units.la: In Ephes. V. 17. Sed intelligentes quae sit voluntas Domini ] Id est, Scrutamini legem, in quâ voluntas ejus continetur.
units.tr: On Ephesians 5, verse 17. But understanding what the will of the Lord is: that is, search the law, in which his will is contained.

units.la: In Coloss. I. 9. Ut impleamini agnitione voluntatis Dei] Quia aliter voluntatem ejus non poteritis facere : quod Propheta intelligens dicebat ad Dominum : m Doce me facere voluntatem tuam, quia Deus meus es tu.
units.tr: On Colossians 1, verse 9. That you may be filled with the knowledge of the will of God: because otherwise you will not be able to do his will, which the prophet understanding said to the Lord: m Teach me to do your will, for you are my God.

units.la: In Operis Paschalis 11 Praefatione ad Macedonium. Nec Hieronymi divinae legis interpretis, & coelestis Bibliothecae cultoris, exempla te pudeat imitari, atque ad generosas quoque feminas & praeclarae indolis famâ subnixas, in quarum mentibus sacrae lectionis instantia sobrium sapientiae domicilium collocavit, propriae disputationis documenta transmittere.
units.tr: In the Preface to the Paschal Work to Macedonius: "Nor let it shame you to imitate the examples of Jerome, the interpreter of the divine law and the cultivator of the heavenly library, and to transmit the instances of your own disputation even to noble women, supported by the fame of their distinguished character, in whose minds he has placed the diligence of sacred reading as a sober home of wisdom."

units.la: m Psal. CXLIII.
units.tr: m Psal. CXLIII.

units.la: 11 Author hujusce Operis alius à Sedulio Hiberno fuit, sc. Coelius Sedulius, poeta, qui vixit circa an. 440.
units.tr: 11 The author of this work was other than Sedulius the Irishman, namely Coelius Sedulius, a poet, who lived about the year 440.

units.la: 450. Arnobius Junior.
units.tr: 450. Arnobius the Younger.

units.la: In Psal. CXXXV. Venimus ad alleluia, quod duplex scribitur : in quo illud considero, quòd nec caro sine animâ, nec anima sine carne poterit Domino confiteri. Duo ergo in unum duo alleluia decantent, ut dum sunt in uno vitæ hujus transitu, confitendi ordinem teneant ; dicat caro alleluia suum, dicat anima suum. Duplex homo est, duplex alleluia est.
units.tr: In Psalm 135: We come to the alleluia, which is written twice. In it I consider this: that neither flesh without soul nor soul without flesh can confess to the Lord. Let the two therefore sing the two alleluias as one, so that, while they are in the one passage of this life, they keep the order of confessing. Let the flesh say its alleluia, and let the soul say its own. Man is double; the alleluia is double.

units.la: 450. Leo I. Romanus Pontifex.
units.tr: 450. Leo I. Roman Pontiff.

units.la: De Passione Domini Serm. 19. Sacram Dominicæ passionis historiam Evangelicâ, ut moris est, narratione decursam, ita omnium vestrûm arbitror inhæsisse pectoribus ; ut unicuique audientium ipsa lectio quædam facta sit visio.
units.tr: On the Passion of the Lord, Sermon 19. I think the sacred history of the Lord's passion, run through in the Gospel narrative as is customary, has so fixed itself in the breasts of all of you that for each of the hearers the very reading has become a kind of vision.

units.la: Serm. 1. De Passione Domini. Sacratissimum, dilectissimi, Dominicæ passionis diem tam planè ac lucidè Evangelicus sermo reseravit ; ut religiosis ac piis cordibus non aliud sit audisse quæ lecta sunt, quàm vidisse quæ gesta sunt.
units.tr: Sermon 1, On the Passion of the Lord. Beloved, the most sacred day of the Lord's passion has been unfolded by the Gospel account so plainly and brightly that, for devout and pious hearts, hearing what was read is no different from seeing what was done.

units.la: Serm. 13. Evangelica lectio, dilectissimi, quæ sacratissimam Dominicæ passionis reseravit historiam, ita universæ Ecclesiæ nota est de communi frequenter auditu ; ut rerum gestarum ordinem, tanquam sub vestris habitum oculis, singuli quique recolatis.
units.tr: Sermon 13. Beloved, the Gospel reading which unfolded the most sacred history of the Lord's passion is so well known to the whole Church from frequent hearing that each of you can recall the order of events as if it lay before your eyes.

units.la: Serm. 3. De Epiphaniâ Domini. Quamvis sciam, dilectissimi, quòd sanctitatem vestram hodiernæ festivitatis causa non lateat, eamque secundùm consuetudinem Evangelicus vobis sermo reseraverit.
units.tr: Sermon 3, On the Epiphany of the Lord. Although I know, beloved, that the reason for today's festival is not hidden from your holiness, and that the Gospel account has, as usual, set it out for you.

units.la: Serm. 2. De Resurrectione Domini. Notum quidem, dilectissimi, Paschale sacramentum Evangelica nobis narratio præsentavit ; & ita per aurem carnis penetratus est mentis auditus, ut nemini n strum rerum gestarum imago defuerit ; cùm divinitus inspiratæ textus historiæ evidenter ostenderit.
units.tr: Sermon 2, On the Resurrection of the Lord. Beloved, the Gospel narrative has set before us the Paschal mystery, as is well known; and the hearing of the mind has so penetrated through the ear of the flesh that the image of the events was lacking to none of us, since the text of the divinely inspired history has shown it clearly.

units.la: Serm. De Transfiguratione Domini. Evangelica lectio, dilectissimi, quæ per aures corporis interiorem mentium nostrarum pulsavit auditum, ad magni sacramenti nos intelligentiam vocat.
units.tr: Sermon, On the Transfiguration of the Lord. Beloved, the Gospel reading, which has struck the inner hearing of our minds through the ears of the body, calls us to an understanding of the great sacrament.

units.la: 450. Maximus Taurinensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 450. Maximus, Bishop of Turin.

units.la: Homil. 5. de Natali Domini. Hodie igitur nobis, sicut decursâ Evangelii lectione cognovimus, secundùm carnem natus est Christus. Homil. 2. in Epiphaniâ Domini. Audistis, fratres, lectionem Evangelii salutaria præsentis diei sacramenta recitantem. Audistis qualiter Christus Dominus, qui in hunc mundum latenter advenit, paulatim dignatus est suam aperire mortalibus majestatem, &c. Homil. 4. Ait Prophetarum præcipuus Esaias, sicut audistis, fratres charissimi, Illuminare, Illuminare Hierusalem, &c. ibid. Judæus Christum videt & invidet, sicut lectum est: In sua venit, & sui eum non receperunt. (Ubi nota Esai. LX. & Joan. I. simul lecta in Epiphaniâ. Vid. an ita hodie 12) Ibid. Et cum perambularent Magi, stella, sicut lectum est, quam viderant in Oriente, antecedebat eos. (Ergo tres lectiones.)
units.tr: Homily 5, on the Nativity of the Lord: Today, then, as we have learned from the reading of the Gospel just read, Christ is born according to the flesh. Homily 2, on the Epiphany of the Lord: You have heard, brethren, the reading of the Gospel setting forth the saving mysteries of the present day. You have heard how Christ the Lord, who came secretly into this world, gradually deigned to reveal his majesty to mortals, etc. Homily 4: The chief of the prophets, Isaiah, as you have heard, most beloved brethren, says: Arise, shine, O Jerusalem, etc. Ibid.: The Jew sees Christ and envies him, as was read: He came to his own, and his own received him not. (Here note that Isaiah 60 and John 1 were read together at the Epiphany. See whether it is so today, 12.) Ibid.: And as the Magi went on their way, the star, as was read, which they had seen in the East, went before them. (So, three readings.)

units.la: 460. Prosper, Rhegiensis Episcopus. 13
units.tr: 460. Prosper, Bishop of Rhegium. 13

units.la: In libro Sententiarum ex Operibus Augustini excerptarum, sent. 8. Doctrina Apostolica salubris atque vitalis est; ut pro capacitate utentium neminem sui relinquat exortem. Quia sive parvuli, sive magni, sive infirmi, sive fortes, habent in eâ unde alantur, & unde satientur. Hanc sententiam in libro Epigrammaton ita explicat. Exueret Deus ut tetrâ caligine mundum, Doctrinæ accendit lumen Apostolicæ. Quæ nullis animis, nullis non congruit annis, Lacte rigans pueros, pane cibans validos. Non tempus, non sexus huic, non causa resistit, Omnes curat, alit, justificat, vegetat. Sumite quæ magnæ appositit sapientia mensæ, Et variis pasci discite deliciis. Quarum pars totum est epulum quo quisque juvatur: Inde capit vitam, quam parit una fides.
units.tr: In the book of Sentences excerpted from the works of Augustine, sentence 8: "Apostolic doctrine is wholesome and life-giving, so that, according to the capacity of those who use it, it leaves no one without a share. For whether they are little ones or grown, weak or strong, they find in it that by which they may be nourished and satisfied." He explains this sentence in the book of Epigrams thus: "God, to strip the world of its foul darkness, kindled the light of apostolic doctrine. It suits every age and every soul: it waters infants with milk and feeds the strong with bread. Time, sex and circumstance do not resist it; it cares for, nourishes, justifies and invigorates all. Take up the dishes that the wisdom of a great table sets out, and learn to feed on its varied delights. Each part of it is a full feast by which each person is helped; from it he draws the life that one faith brings forth."

units.la: Sentent. 67. Bonæ sunt in Scripturis sanctis mysteriorum profunditates, quæ ob hoc teguntur, ne vilescant; ob hoc quæruntur, ut exerceant; ob hoc autem aperiuntur, ut pascant. Id in Epigrammaton libro sic exprimit.
units.tr: Sentence 67: "The depths of the mysteries in the holy Scriptures are good. They are hidden for this reason, lest they become cheap; they are sought for this reason, that they may exercise us; and they are opened for this reason, that they may feed us." He expresses this in the book of Epigrams thus.

units.la: Esai. LX. Joan. I. Mat. II.
units.tr: Isaiah 60. John 1. Matthew 2.

units.la: 12 Cum Esai. LX. legitur hodie Matth. II. in Epiphaniâ, quæ tertia fuit Veterum Lectio.
units.tr: 12. When Isaiah 60 is read today, Matthew 2 is read at Epiphany, which was the third reading of the Ancients.

units.la: 13 Prosperum nequaquam clero transcriptum fuisse, multo minus infulas adeptum, verior est eruditorum sententia.
units.tr: 13. The more accurate opinion of the learned is that Prosper was by no means enrolled among the clergy, and still less obtained the mitre.

units.la: Quamvis in sacris libris, quos nosse laboras, Plurima sint, Lector, clausa & opaca tibi; Invigilare tamen studio ne desine sancto. Exercent animum dona morata tuum. Gratior est fructus, quem spes productior edit. Ultrò objectorum vilius est pretium. Oblectant adoperta etiam mysteria mentem. Qui dedit, ut quæras; addet, ut invenias.
units.tr: "Although in the sacred books, which you labour to know, reader, there are many things closed and dark to you, do not cease to keep watch with holy zeal. Gifts that are delayed exercise your mind. The fruit is sweeter which a more prolonged hope brings forth. Things readily obtained are of lesser worth. Even mysteries that are covered delight the mind. He who gave you the means to seek will add the means to find."

units.la: Sentent. 271. ex Augustino de Doctr. Christ. lib. 2. cap. 6. Qui in Scripturis sanctis non inveniunt veritatem quam quærunt, fame laborant: qui autem non quærunt quod in promptu habent, fastidii languore marcescunt: & par utrorumque periculum est; dum sapientiæ cibum & illis obcæcatio & bis inedia subtrahit.
units.tr: Sentence 271, from Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 6: "Those who do not find in the holy Scriptures the truth they seek suffer hunger; but those who do not seek what lies ready to hand wither with the languor of disgust. The danger of both is equal, since blindness and a kind of double starvation deprive both of the food of wisdom."

units.la: Sentent. 309. Ignorantia in eis qui intelligere noluerunt, sine dubitatione peccatum est; in eis autem qui non potuerunt, pœna peccati. Ergo in utrisque non est excusatio, sed justa damnatio. [Ex Augustini epist. 105.]
units.tr: Sentence 309: "Ignorance in those who were unwilling to understand is without doubt sin; in those who could not understand, it is the punishment of sin. Therefore in both there is no excuse, but only just condemnation." [From Augustine's letter 105.]

units.la: 490. Gennadius Massilienfis.
units.tr: 490. Gennadius of Marseilles.

units.la: In Catalogo Virorum Illustrium. Musæus Massilienfis Ecclesiæ Presbyter, hortatu sancti Venerii Episcopi excerpsit ex sanctis Scripturis lectiones totius anni festivis aptas diebus; responsoria etiam Psalmorum capitula tempori & lectionibus congruentia; quod opus tam necessarium à Lectoribus in Ecclesiâ probatur, ut expetitum, & sollicitudinem tollat & moram, plebique ingerat scientiam, celebritatem & decorem.
units.tr: In his Catalogue of Illustrious Men: Musaeus, presbyter of the Church of Marseilles, at the urging of holy Venerius, bishop, excerpted from the holy Scriptures readings suited to the festival days of the whole year, and also responsories and Psalm verses fitting the season and the readings. This work is so necessary that it is approved by readers in the Church: it satisfies a desire, removes anxiety and delay, and gives the people knowledge, solemnity and decorum.

units.la: 510. Fulgentius Ruspensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 510. Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe.

units.la: Ad Thrasimundum lib. 1. Equidem erroris hujus qualitatem Dominus ipse Salvatorque noster, dum Saducæos increparet, ostendit, dicens, Erratis nescientes Scripturas, neque virtutem Dei. Propterea utique miserabiliter errabant, quia illum, qui Dei virtus est, nesciebant. Sicut ergo virtutis Dei scientia tenax est cœlestis itineris; sic est insciitia mater erroris: quod etiam beatus David ostendit dicens de quibusdam: {q}Nescierunt neque intellexerunt; in tenebris ambulant.
units.tr: In his letter to Thrasimund, book 1: "Indeed, our Lord and Saviour himself showed the nature of this error when he rebuked the Sadducees, saying, 'You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God' (Matt. 22:29). They were therefore wretchedly going astray because they did not know him who is the power of God. Just as the knowledge of the power of God is the firm guide of the heavenly way, so ignorance is the mother of error; which blessed David also shows, speaking of certain people: 'They have not known nor understood; they walk in darkness.'"

units.la: {q} Psal. LXXXI.
Epist. 2. ad Gallam viduam. Nunquam cesses à divinis eloquiis; & totam delectationem cordis tui Scripturis sanctis indulge.
units.tr: From letter 2 to Galla the widow: "Never cease from the divine words, and give all the delight of your heart to the holy Scriptures."

units.la: Serm. de Confessoribus & dispensatoribus Domini. Scripturæ, ut ditissima fercula, habent quod omni ætati congruat, omni professioni conveniat. In verbo Dei abundat quod perfectus comedat; abundat etiam, quod parvulus sugat. Ibi est enim simul & lacteus potus, quo tenera fidelium nutriatur infantia; & solidus cibus, quo robusta perfectorum juventus spiritalia sanctæ virtutis accipiat incrementa. Ibi prorsus ad salutem consulitur universis, quos Dominus salvare dignatur: ibi est, quod omni ætati congruat; ibi, quod omni professioni conveniat.
units.tr: From the sermon On Confessors and Stewards of the Lord: "The Scriptures, like the richest dishes, have something that suits every age and fits every calling. In the word of God there is abundance that the perfect may eat; there is also abundance that the little child may suck. For there is both the milky drink by which the tender infancy of the faithful is nourished, and the solid food by which the strong youth of the perfect receives the spiritual increase of holy virtue. There, indeed, is provision for the salvation of all whom the Lord deigns to save: there is what suits every age, there is what fits every calling."

units.la: 520. Cæsarius Arelatensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 520. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles.

units.la: Homil. 20. Quando aliquid de utilitate animæ proferimus, fratres charissimi, nemo se excusare conetur, ut dicat; non mihi vacat legere, & ideo non possum Dei præcepta vel agnoscere vel implere; nec dicat aliquis vestrûm: Non novi literas, ideo mihi non imputabitur quicquid minus de Dei præceptis implevero. Inanis est & inutilis excusatio ista, fratres charissimi. Primum est, quòd lectionem divinam etiamsi aliquis nesciens literas non potest legere, potest tamen legentem libenter audire. Qui verò literas novit, nunquid potest fieri quòd non inveniat libros, quibus possit scripturam divinam legere? &c. Quando noctes longiores sunt, quis erit qui tantùm possit dormire, ut lectionem divinam vel tribus horis non possit aut ipse legere aut alios legentes audire. Illi enim lectionem divinam legere non possunt, qui se usque ad medium noctem inebriare contendunt. Et post, Si illi qui literas nesciunt, conducunt sibi mercenarios literatos, ut acquirant terrenam pecuniam; tu quicunque es, qui literas non nosti, quare etiam non cum pretio & mercede rogas, qui tibi debeat Scripturas divinas relegere, ut ex illis possis præmia æterna acquirere? Pro certo, fratres, qui hoc studiosè requirit, credit, quòd ille in æternum prodesse possit. Qui verò lectionem nec ipse vult legere, nec legentem libenter audire; omnino non credit, quòd possit aliquid boni acquirere. Vos ergo, fratres, rogo & admoneo, ut quicunque literas scitis, Scripturam divinam frequentius relegatis. Qui verò non scitis, quando alii legunt, intentius auribus audiatis. Lumen enim animæ, & cibus æternus, non est aliud, nisi verbum Dei, sine quo anima non vivere potest nec videre: quia quomodo caro nostra moritur, si non capiat cibum, ita & anima nostra extinguitur, si non accipit divinum verbum. Sed dicit aliquis; Ego homo rusticus sum, & terrenis operibus jugiter occupatus sum; lectionem divinam nec audire possum nec legere. Quàm multi rustici, & quàm multæ mulieres rusticanæ; & tamen cantica diabolica, amatoria, & turpia ore decantant ? Ista possunt tenere atque parare quæ Diabolus docet; & non possunt tenere quod Christus ostendit. Quando celeriùs & meliùs quicunque rusticus, vel quæcunque mulier rusticana, poterit utiliùs & Symbolum discere & Orationem Dominicam, & aliquas Antiphonas, & Psalmum quinquagesimum vel nonagesimum & parare & tenere & frequentiùs dicere; unde animam suam & Deo conjungere & Diabolo liberare posset. Nam quomodo cantica turpia in tenebras Diaboli mittunt; sic cantica sancta Christi lumen ostendunt. Nemo ergo dicat: Non possum aliquid de hoc, quod in Ecclesiâ legitur, retinere. Sine dubio enim, si velis, poteris. Incipe velle, & statim intelliges.
units.tr: Homil. 20. When we speak of what is useful for the soul, dearly beloved brethren, let no one try to excuse himself by saying: "I have no time to read, and so I cannot know or fulfil the commandments of God." Nor let any of you say: "I do not know letters, so I shall not be held accountable for whatever commandments of God I fail to keep." That excuse is empty and useless, dearly beloved brethren. First, although someone who does not know letters cannot read the divine lesson, he can still gladly listen to someone reading it. But one who does know letters: can it really be that he cannot find books from which he might read Holy Scripture? And so on. When the nights are long, who is there who can sleep so much that for even three hours he cannot either read the divine lesson himself or listen to others reading it? For those who strive to get drunk until midnight cannot read the divine lesson. And afterwards: If those who do not know letters hire literate men for themselves in order to gain earthly money, you, whoever you are, who do not know letters, why do you not also ask, for a price and a wage, someone who ought to reread the divine Scriptures for you, so that from them you may gain eternal rewards? Surely, brethren, whoever seeks this eagerly believes that it can profit him for eternity. But whoever neither wishes to read the lesson himself nor gladly listens to someone reading it, certainly does not believe that he can gain anything good. I therefore beg and urge you, brethren, that whoever of you knows letters should reread Holy Scripture more often; and whoever does not know them should listen more attentively with his ears when others read. For the light of the soul and the eternal food is nothing other than the word of God, without which the soul can neither live nor see: just as our flesh dies if it does not take food, so our soul is extinguished if it does not receive the divine word. But someone will say: "I am a country man, and I am constantly busy with earthly work; I can neither hear nor read the divine lesson." How many country men there are, and how many country women; and yet they sing with their mouths diabolical, amorous and shameful songs! They can hold and retain what the Devil teaches; but they cannot hold what Christ shows. When any country man, or any country woman, will be able to learn more quickly and better, and more usefully, both the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, and some antiphons, and the fiftieth or ninetieth Psalm, and to prepare them, hold them and say them more often, by which he could join his soul to God and free it from the Devil.
