For just as shameful songs send men into the darkness of the Devil, so holy songs show the light of Christ. Let no one therefore say: "I cannot retain anything of what is read in the Church." For undoubtedly, if you wish, you will be able to. Begin to wish, and you will immediately understand.

units.la: Homil. 5. de Divin. Myster. (apud Pamel. Tom. 1. Liturg. p. 616, 617, 618.) Sunt plures minùs de salute suæ animæ cogitantes; qui lectis divinis Lectionibus, statim de Ecclesiâ foràs exeunt; cùm tamen etiam dum ipsæ lectiones leguntur, aliqui ex illis ita otiosis & sæcularibus fabulis occupentur; ut eas nec ipsi audiant, nec alios audire permittant. Ibidem. Si enim diligenter attenditis, cognoscitis, quia tunc non fiunt Missæ, quando divinæ lectiones in Ecclesiâ recitantur, sed quando munera offeruntur, & corpus vel sanguis Domini consecratur. Nam lectiones, sive Propheticas, sive Apostolicas, sive Evangelicas, etiam in domibus vestris vel ipsi legere, vel alios legentes audire poteslis. Consecrationem verò corporis & sanguinis Christi, non alibi nisi in domo Dei audire vel videre poteritis. Est Homil. 12. in Biblioth. Patr. Tom. 2. ubi in 3. Editione col. 597. e. in margine ponitur: Isto modo fieri debet in Ecclesiâ tantùm: cùm in 2. Editione col. 1069. d. alia nota haberetur: Consecratio corporis & sanguinis Domini fit in Ecclesiâ tantùm.
units.tr: Homil. 5. de Divin. Myster. (apud Pamel. Tom. 1. Liturg. p. 616, 617, 618.) There are many who think little about the salvation of their souls; who, as soon as the divine lessons have been read, go straight out of the Church, although even while the lessons themselves are being read some of them are so idle and so occupied with worldly tales that they neither listen to them themselves nor allow others to listen. Ibidem. For if you attend carefully, you will recognise that Mass is not celebrated when the divine lessons are recited in the Church, but when the offerings are made and the body or blood of the Lord is consecrated. For the lessons, whether prophetic, apostolic or evangelical, you can both read yourselves or listen to others reading in your own houses. But the consecration of the body and blood of Christ you can hear or see nowhere else but in the house of God. It is in Homil. 12. in Biblioth. Patr. Tom. 2., where in the 3rd edition, col. 597 e, a marginal note reads: It must be done in the Church only; whereas in the 2nd edition, col. 1069 d, a different note stands: The consecration of the body and blood of the Lord takes place in the Church only.

units.la: 530. Benedictus Abbas.
units.tr: 530. Benedict, Abbot.

units.la: In Regulâ Monachorum (citat. à Walafrido Strabone de rebus Ecclesiast. cap. 12.) Consideremus qualiter in conspectu divinitatis & sanctorum Angelorum esse oporteat: & sic stemus ad psallendum, ut mens nostra concordet voci nostræ.
units.tr: In the Rule of the Monks (cited by Walafrid Strabo, On Ecclesiastical Matters, ch. 12.) Let us consider how we ought to stand in the sight of the divinity and of the holy Angels; and so let us stand to sing the psalms that our mind may agree with our voice.

units.la: 533. Athalaricus Rex.
units.tr: 533. Athalaric the King.

units.la: In Epistolâ ad Senatum Romanum apud Cassiodor. lib. 9. Variarum cap. 25. virum commendans, cui Præfecturæ Prætorianæ dignitatem obeundam tribuit. Hos mores lectio divina solidavit; quando semper bene bene geritur, si cœlestis metus humanis motibus opponatur. Hinc enim virtutum omnium sumitur manifesta cognitio; hinc sapientia veritatis sapore conditur: Sic ad omnia redditur humilis, quem imbuit doctrina cœlestis.
units.tr: In his letter to the Roman Senate, in Cassiodorus, Variae book 9, ch. 25, commending a man to whom he gave the office of Praetorian Prefect: Divine reading has strengthened these morals, since good conduct is always carried on well when the fear of heaven is set against human impulses. For from it comes a clear knowledge of all virtues; by it wisdom is seasoned with the savour of truth. Thus he whom heavenly teaching has imbued is made humble in all things.

units.la: 550. Aurelius Cassiodorus.
units.tr: 550. Aurelius Cassiodorus.

units.la: Prologo in Psalterium. Cantus, qui aures oblectat, & animas instruit, fit vox unâ psallentium.
units.tr: In the Preface to the Psalter: Song, which delights the ears and instructs the souls, becomes the one voice of those who sing the psalms.

units.la: In Psal. XLVI. Non solùm cantantes, sed etiam intelligentes psallere debemus. Nemo enim sapienter quicquam facit, quod non intelligit.
units.tr: On Psalm 46: We ought to sing the psalms not only with our voices but also with our understanding. For nobody does anything wisely that he does not understand.

units.la: 570. Venantius Fortunatus, Pictaviensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 570. Venantius Fortunatus, Bishop of Poitiers.

units.la: Lib. 2. Poematum in laudem Parisiaci Cleri. Pontificis monitis clerus, plebs psallit, & infans. Unde labore brevi fruge replendus erit.
units.tr: Book 2 of the Poems, in praise of the clergy of Paris: At the bidding of the bishop the clergy, the people and the children sing the psalms. Hence the field will be filled with a plentiful harvest from a short labour.

units.la: S. Servulus.
units.tr: S. Servulus.

units.la: Pauper is quidam apud Romanos mendicus fuit. De illo hæc habet Gregorius Homil. 15. in Evangelia. Nequaquam literas noverat, sed Scripturæ sacræ sibimet codices emerat; & religiosos quosque in hospitalitatem suscipiens, hos coram se legere sine intermissione faciebat. Factumque est, ut quantum ad mensuram propriam attinet, plenè sacram Scripturam disceret; cùm, sicut dixi, literas funditus ignoraret. Eadem habet, Dialog. lib. 4. cap. 14.
units.tr: There was a poor beggar among the Romans. Gregory says this of him in Homily 15 on the Gospels: He knew no letters at all, but he had bought copies of Holy Scripture for himself; and receiving into his lodging all the religious men he could, he made them read to him without interruption. And so it came about that, as far as his own capacity went, he learned Holy Scripture fully, although, as I said, he was utterly ignorant of letters. He says the same in Dialogues, book 4, ch. 14.

units.la: 595. Gregorius I. Romanus Episcopus.
units.tr: 595. Gregory I, Bishop of Rome.

units.la: Lib. 4. Epist. 40. ad Theodorum Modicum. Quid est Scriptura sacra, nisi quædam Epistola omnipotentis Dei ad creaturam suam? Et certè sicubi esset gloria vestra alibi constituta, & scripta terreni jam Imperatoris acciperet; non cessaret, non quiesceret, somnum oculis non daret, nisi prius quid sibi Imperator terrenus scripsisset, agnovisset. Imperator cœli, Dominus hominum & angelorum, pro vitâ tuâ tibi suas Epistolas transmisit; & tamen, gloriose fili, easdem epistolas ardenter legere negligis. Stude ergo quæso, & quotidie creatoris tui verba meditare. Disce cor Dei in verbis Dei, ut ardentius ad æterna suspires, ut mens vestra ad cœlestia regna majoribus desideriis accendatur.
units.tr: Book 4, letter 40, to Theodore Modicus: What is Holy Scripture but a letter of almighty God to his creature? And certainly, if your glory were placed elsewhere and you received a letter from an earthly emperor, you would not cease, you would not rest, you would not give sleep to your eyes until you had learned what the earthly emperor had written to you. The Emperor of heaven, the Lord of men and angels, has sent you his letters for the sake of your life; and yet, glorious son, you carelessly neglect to read those same letters eagerly. Study then, I beg you, and meditate daily on the words of your Creator. Learn the heart of God in the words of God, so that you may long more fervently for eternal things, and that your mind may be kindled with greater desire for the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Epist. ad Leandrum, in Moralem Expositionem Job cap. 4. Divinus sermo, sicut mysteriis prudentes exercet, sic plerumque superficie simplices refovet. Habet in publico unde parvulos nutriat: servat in secreto unde mentes sublimium in admiratione suspendat. Quasi quippe fluvius (ut ita dixerim) planus & altus; in quo & agnus ambulet, & elephas natet.
units.tr: Letter to Leander, prefaced to the Moral Exposition on Job, ch. 4: The divine word, as it exercises the wise with its mysteries, so for the most part it refreshes the simple with its surface. It has in public whereby it may nourish the little ones; it keeps in secret whereby it may hold the minds of the lofty in wonder. For it is like a river (so to speak) level and deep, in which both a lamb may walk and an elephant swim.

units.la: Expos. Moral. in Job lib. 15. cap. 8. Sed quia haec ipsa sacra eloquia ad aeternam damnationem sunt eis, qui illa vel scire nolunt, vel certè sciendo contemnunt; rectè de hoc volumine dicitur: ᶻ Haec est maledictio, quae egredietur super faciem universae terrae.
units.tr: Moral Exposition on Job, book 15, ch. 8: But because these very holy utterances become an eternal condemnation to those who either are unwilling to know them or certainly, knowing them, despise them, it is rightly said of this volume: This is the curse that shall go out over the face of the whole earth.

units.la: In fine lib. 19. Quae tamen tempora jam nunc inchoâsse ingemiscimus; cùm multos intra Ecclesiam positos cernimus, qui aut nolunt operari quod intelligunt, aut hoc ipsum quoque, sacrum eloquium intelligere ac nosse, contemnunt. A veritate etenim avertentes auditum ad fabulas convertuntur: dum omnes quae sua sunt, quaerunt, non quae sunt Jesu Christi. Scripta Dei ubique reperta opponuntur oculis; sed haec cognoscere homines dedignantur. Penè nullus quaerit scire quod credidit. Horum temporum ingratitudo postulabat ut vindicta illa subsequeretur, de quâ Apostolus: ª Propterea quòd amorem veritatis non susceperunt, ut salvi fierent; ideò mittit eis Deus efficaciam erroris, ut credant mendacio.
units.tr: At the end of book 19: Yet we groan that these times have already begun, since we see many placed within the Church who either are unwilling to do what they understand, or despise even to understand and know this holy utterance. For, turning away their hearing from the truth, they are turned to fables, while they seek all that is their own, not what is of Jesus Christ. The writings of God, found everywhere, are set before their eyes; yet men disdain to know these things. Almost nobody seeks to know what he has believed. The ingratitude of these times demanded that that vengeance should follow of which the Apostle speaks: Because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, therefore God sends them a working of error, that they should believe a lie.

units.la: In principio libri 20. Omnem scientiam atque doctrinam Scriptura sacra in aliquâ comparatione transcendit: ut taceam, quòd vera praedicat, quòd ad coelestem patriam vocat, quòd à terrenis desideriis ad superna amplectanda cor legentis immutat, quòd dictis obscurioribus exercet fortes, & parvulis humili sermone blanditur; quòd nec sic clausa est, ut pavesci debeat; nec sic patet, ut vilescat: quòd usu fastidium tollit, & tantò amplius diligitur, quantò amplius meditatur: quòd legentis animum humilibus verbis adjuvat, sublimibus sensibus levat; quòd aliquo modo cum legentibus crescit; quòd à rudibus lectoribus quasi recognoscitur, & tamen doctis semper nova reperitur.
units.tr: At the beginning of book 20: Holy Scripture surpasses all knowledge and learning by some comparison: not to mention that it preaches true things, that it calls to the heavenly fatherland, that it changes the heart of the reader from earthly desires to embracing things above; that it exercises the strong by its more obscure sayings, and caresses the little ones with humble speech; that it is not so closed that it ought to be feared, nor so open that it becomes cheap; that by use it removes loathing, and is loved the more, the more it is meditated upon; that it helps the mind of the reader with humble words and lifts it with lofty senses; that in some way it grows along with its readers; that it is as it were recognised by unlearned readers, and yet is always found new by the learned.

units.la: Tho. Hybernicus in Doctorum floribus, titulo de Oratione, ex homiliâ quadam Gregorii hanc sententiam citat. Illam orationem Deus non exaudit; cui homo, quando psallit, non attendit.
units.tr: Thomas the Irishman, in the Flowers of the Doctors, under the title On Prayer, quotes this saying from a homily of Gregory: God does not hear that prayer to which a man does not attend when he sings the psalms.

units.la: Vid. Confessionem Gregorianam, apud Pamel. Liturg. Tom. II. pag. 80, 81, 82, &c. ubi frequentes & prolixae Responsiones plebi praecipiuntur.
units.tr: See the Gregorian Confession in Pamelius, Liturgica, vol. II, pp. 80, 81, 82, etc., where frequent and lengthy responses are prescribed for the people.

units.la: ᶻ Zach. V. ª 2 Thess. II. 10, 11. Temporibus Gregorii I. ita collapsum esse bonarum literarum cultum, ut facile reperiri non posset, qui utriusque linguae peritus esset, ostendit Baronius ad An. 593. Sect. 62. Certè Gregorius in Epistola ad Eusebium Thessalonicae Episcopum, se nunquam Graecum sermonem didicisse; & in alia ad Anastasium Presbyterum, se Graecae linguae nescium, liberè profitetur. Latinam tamen linguam à populo Romano tum vulgò intellectam fuisse, ex Homiliis ejusdem constat. Homilias enim 22. in Ezechielem, à notariis exceptas & tandem recognitas, ad populum habuit. (Vid. utriusque libri harum Homiliarum Praefationem, & finem totius Commentationis.) In Evangelicas etiam lectiones ad emendationem aedificationemque fidelium Homilias 40. partim dictavit, ut plebi assistenti per notarium iterum dictarentur; partim coram populo ipse vivâ voce, Notario excipiente, explanavit: ut ex Prologo Homiliarum, & epist. 53. lib. 7. [ad Secundinum] apparet. Denique epist. 22. libri 10. Joanni Subdiacono Ravennae scribens: Dic ei, inquit, ut commenta Psalmorum legi ad vigilias faciat; quae mentes saecularium ad bonos mores praecipuè informent.
units.tr: Zach. V.; 2 Thess. II. 10, 11. That the cultivation of good letters had so collapsed in the times of Gregory I that it could hardly be found who was skilled in both languages, Baronius shows at the year 593, section 62. Certainly Gregory openly confesses, in a letter to Eusebius, Bishop of Thessalonica, that he never learned the Greek language; and in another to Anastasius the presbyter, that he is ignorant of the Greek tongue. That the Latin language, however, was then generally understood by the Roman people is clear from his Homilies. For he delivered the twenty-two Homilies on Ezekiel to the people, which were taken down by notaries and afterwards revised. (See the preface to each book of these Homilies and the end of the whole commentary.) He also dictated forty Homilies on the Gospel readings, partly for the correction and edification of the faithful, so that they might be dictated again by a notary to the people standing by; partly he himself explained them before the people by living voice, a notary taking them down; as appears from the Prologue of the Homilies and from letter 53 of book 7 [to Secundinus]. Finally, in letter 22 of book 10, writing to John the subdeacon at Ravenna: Tell him, he says, to have the commentaries on the Psalms read at the vigils; for these chiefly shape the minds of worldly people towards good morals.

units.la: 610. Livinus & Benignus Hiberni.
units.tr: 610. Livinus and Benignus, Irish

units.la: Bonifacius in eorum vitâ, pag. 238. refert, quomodo Livinus aetate tenerâ Benigni, Presbyteri Scoti, curae commissus, & Davidicis Psalmorum melodiis, & sanctorum Evangeliorum mellifluis lectionibus, atque caeteris divinis exercitationibus perfectissimè instructus fuerit.
units.tr: Boniface, in their life, p. 238, relates how Livinus, while still young, was entrusted to the care of Benignus, a Scottish presbyter, and was thoroughly instructed in the melodies of David's Psalms, in the honeyed readings of the holy Gospels, and in the other divine exercises.

units.la: 620. Furseus Hibernus, vir nobilis.
units.tr: 620. Fursey the Irishman, a man of noble birth.

units.la: Ab ipso tempore pueritiae suae curam non modicam lectionibus sacris, simul & monasticis exhibebat disciplinis. [Beda lib. 3. Hist. cap. 19.]
units.tr: From the very time of his boyhood he devoted no small care to sacred reading, and at the same time to monastic discipline. [Bede, Hist. book 3, ch. 19.]

units.la: 630. Isidorus Hispalensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 630. Isidore of Seville, Bishop.

units.la: De summo bono lib. 1. cap. 18. Sanctarum Scripturarum altitudo, quasi montes pascuae sunt, ad quos dum quisque justorum contendit, se pascuae indeficientis refectionem invenisse congaudet. In Scripturis sanctis quasi in montibus excelsis & viri perfecti habent sublimia intelligentiae, quibus gressus contemplationis quasi cervi erigant; & simplices quasi parva animalia inveniunt modicos intellectus, ad quas humiles ipsi refugiant. Scriptura sacra infirmis & jensu parvulis secundùm historiam humilis videtur in verbis; verbis ; cum excellentioribus autem viris altius incedit, dum eis sua mysteria pandit : ac per hoc utrisque manet communis manna, quae populo veteri pro singulorum delectatione varium dabat saporem. Juxta sensuum capacitatem singulis sermo congruit.
units.tr: On the Highest Good, book 1, chapter 18. The depth of the holy Scriptures is like pasture mountains: when any of the righteous strives toward them, he rejoices to have found the refreshment of a pasture that never fails. In the holy Scriptures, as on lofty mountains, the perfect men find sublime understanding, by which their steps of contemplation rise like stags; and the simple find, like little animals, modest meanings, to which the humble themselves may retreat. Holy Scripture, according to the history, seems lowly in its words to the weak and to those little in years; but it proceeds more deeply with the more eminent men, as it opens its mysteries to them. And so the same manna remains common to both, which gave the old people a varied flavour according to each one's delight. The word fits each according to the capacity of their understanding.

units.la: .Lib. 3. cap. 8. Qui vult cum Deo semper esse, frequenter debet orare, frequenter & legere. Nam cum oramus, ipsi cum Deo loquimur ; cum vero legimus, Deus nobiscum loquitur. Omnis profectus ex lectione & meditatione procedit. Quae enim nescimus, lectione discimus : quae autem didicimas, meditationibus conservamus. Geminum confert donum lectio sanctarum Scripturarum : sive quia intellectum mentis erudit, seu quod a mundi vanitatibus abstractum hominem ad amorem Dei perducit,
units.tr: Book 3, chapter 8. Whoever wishes to be always with God ought to pray often, and to read often as well. For when we pray, we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us. All progress comes from reading and meditation. For what we do not know we learn by reading, and what we have learned we keep by meditation. The reading of the holy Scriptures brings a twofold gift: whether it trains the understanding of the mind, or whether, drawing a man away from the vanities of the world, it leads him to the love of God,

units.la: Ibid. cap. 7. Oratio cordis est, non labiorum. Neque enim verba deprecantis Deus intendit, sed orantis cor aspicit. Quod si tacitè cor oret, & vox sileat ; quamvis homines lateat, Deum latere non potest, qui conscientiae praesens est. Melius est autem cum silentio orare corde sine sono vocis, quam solis verbis sine intuitu mentis. Et post, Non in multiloquio exaudiuntur homines a Deo, quasi plurimis eum verbis conentur inflectere. Neque conciliat eum multiplex orantis sermo, sed pura sinceraque orationis intentio. Bonum est corde semper orare, bonum etiam & sono vocis Deum spiritualibus hymnis glorificare. Nihil est sola voce canere sine cordis intentione ; sed sicut ait Apostolus : Cantantes in cordibus vestris, h. e. non solum voce, sed & corde psallentes. Unde & alibi : Psallam spiritu, psallam & mente. Sicut orationibus regimur, ita Psalmorum studiis delectamur. Psallendi enim utilitas tristia corda consolatur, gratiores mentes facit, fastidiosos oblectat, inertes excitat, peccatores ad lamenta invitat. Nam quamvis dura sint carnalium corda; statim ut Psalmi dulcedo insonuerit, ad affectum pietatis animum eorum inflectit. Dum Christianum non vocis modulatio, sed tantum verba divina, quae ibi dicuntur, debeant commovere. Nescio tamen quo pacto modulatione canentis major nascitur compunctio cordis.
units.tr: Ibid., chapter 7. Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips. For God does not attend to the words of one who pleads, but looks upon the heart of the one who prays. If the heart prays in silence, and the voice is still, God cannot be hidden, though he may be hidden from men, for he is present to the conscience. Yet it is better to pray with the heart in silence, without the sound of the voice, than with words alone and no attention of the mind. And after: men are not heard by God through much speaking, as though they tried to bend him with many words. Nor does the manifold speech of the one praying win him over, but the pure and sincere intention of the prayer. It is good always to pray in the heart, and good also to glorify God with spiritual hymns by the sound of the voice. There is nothing in singing with the voice alone without the intention of the heart; but, as the Apostle says: singing in your hearts, that is, psalming not only with the voice but also with the heart. Hence also elsewhere: I will sing with the spirit, I will sing with the mind also. As we are ruled by prayers, so we are delighted by the study of the Psalms. For the usefulness of psalmody consoles sad hearts, makes minds more gracious, delights the weary, rouses the sluggish, and invites sinners to lamentation. For although the hearts of carnal men are hard, as soon as the sweetness of the Psalm sounds, it turns their minds toward feelings of piety. The Christian ought to be moved not by the modulation of the voice, but only by the divine words that are spoken there. Yet I know not by what means, a greater compunction of the heart is born from the modulation of the singer.

units.la: De Officiis Ecclesiast. lib. 1. cap. 10. Lectiones pronunciare, antiquae institutionis esse Judaeorum traditio docet. Nam & ipsi legitimis praefinitis diebus, ex lege & Prophetis lectione in Synagogis utuntur, & hoc de veteri Patrum institutione servantes. Est autem lectio non parva audientium aedificatio. Unde oportet, ut quando psallitur, psallatur ab omnibus ; cum oratur, oretur ab omnibus ; cum lectio legitur, facto silentio, aeque audiatur a cunctis. Nam & si tunc superveniat quisque, cum lectio celebratur, adoret tantum Deum ; & praesignatâ fronte, aurem sollicitè accommodet. Patet tempus orandi, cum omnes oramus ; patet, cum voluerit orare privatim. Obtentu orationis ne perdideris lectionem; quia non semper eam quilibet paratam potest habere, cùm orandi potestas in promptu fit. Nec putes parvam nasci utilitatem ex lectionis auditu. Siquidem oratio ipsa fit pinguior; dum mens recenti lectione saginata, per divinarum rerum, quas nuper audivit, imagines currit. Nam & Maria soror Marthæ , quæ sedens ad pedes Jesu, sorore neglectâ verbum intentius audiebat, bonam partem sibi elegisse Domini voce sirmatur. Ideò & Diaconus clarâ voce silentium admonet; ut sive dum psallitur, sive dum lectio pronuntiatur, ab omnibus unitas conservetur; ut quod ab omnibus prædicatur, æqualiter ab omnibus audiatur.
units.tr: On the Ecclesiastical Offices, book 1, chapter 10. The tradition of the Jews teaches that reading aloud is of ancient institution. For they too, on fixed days, use readings from the Law and the Prophets in their synagogues, and in this they keep the ancient institution of the Fathers. Moreover, the reading is no small edification of the hearers. Hence it is fitting that when psalms are sung, they be sung by all; when prayer is made, it be made by all; when the lesson is read, with silence kept, it be heard equally by all. For even if someone comes in while the reading is being done, let him adore God alone, and, having signed his forehead, attentively apply his ear. There is time for prayer when we all pray; there is time when one wishes to pray privately. Do not, under the pretext of prayer, lose the reading; for not everyone can always have it ready, when the power of praying is at hand. Nor think that little benefit arises from hearing the reading. Indeed the prayer itself becomes richer, while the mind, fed by a fresh reading, runs through the images of the divine things it has lately heard. For the Lord's voice affirms that Mary, the sister of Martha, who sitting at the feet of Jesus, while her sister was neglected, listened more intently to the word, had chosen the better part. Therefore also the deacon with a clear voice admonishes silence, so that, whether the psalm is sung or the lesson is pronounced, unity is kept by all, and what is proclaimed by all is heard equally by all.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 11. de Lectore agens. Sic expeditus, vim pronunciationis tenebit; ut ad intellectum omnium mentes sensusque promoveat; discernendo genera pronuntiationis, atque exprimendo omnium sententiarum proprios affectus. Et post, Auribus & cordi consulere debet Lector, non oculis; ne potiùs ex seipso eos spectatores magis quàm auditores faciat.
units.tr: Book 2, chapter 11, speaking of the reader. Thus equipped, he will keep the force of pronunciation, so as to advance the minds and senses of all toward understanding, by distinguishing the kinds of delivery and by expressing the proper feelings of all the sentences. And after: the reader ought to consult the ears and the heart, not the eyes, lest he make them spectators rather than hearers by himself.

units.la: EX Patrum, quos hucusque produximus, sententiis illud manifestum fecimus, prioribus sex à Christi ascensione saeculis linguam peregrinam in Sacris nondum fuisse receptam, neque etiam populo Scripturae lectioni interdictum. Jam verò ad nati Antichristi tempora pervenimus, qui potestatem septicollis bestiae (urbis sc. illius magnae, quae habet regnum super reges terrae) exerciturus erat in conspectu ejus (in ipsâ sc. Romanâ urbe) & effecturus ut omnes characterem haberent aut nomen bestiae, aut numerum nominis ejus, h. e. Romanae potestati subditos se profiterentur. Atque in hunc sanè finem adeò soliciti fuerunt Romani Pontifices; ut Latina Liturgia quantumvis incognita & non intellecta ubique in ditione suâ obtineret: in eo ipso potestatem prioris bestiae, i. e. Romani imperii sedulò imitati. Opera enim data est, ut imperiosa civitas non solum jugum, verùm etiam linguam suam domitis gentibus per pacem societatis (sociatis legendum censet Lipsius, vel certè speciem societatis) imponeret, inquit Augustinus. Curabant ergo Romani (ut in eum locum observat Vives) ut & in Provinciis plurimi Latinè loquerentur; ita ut Hispanias & Gallias Latinas prorsus fecerint, veteribus illarum gentium linguis abolitis: & in Senatu nullos audierunt nisi Latinè verba facientes. Ita Valerius Maximus. Magistratus, inquit, prisci quantopere suam populique Romani majestatem retinentes se gesserint, hinc cognosci potest; quòd inter caetera obtinendae gravitatis indicia, illud quoque magnâ cum perseverantiâ custodiebant, ne Graecis unquam nisi Latinè responsa darent; quin etiam ipsâ linguae volubilitate, quâ plurimùm valent, per interpretem loqui cogebant, non in urbe tantùm nostrâ, sed etiam in Graeciâ & Asiâ: quò sa Latinae vocis bonos per omnes gentes venerabiliter diffunderetur. Atque hinc est quòd Cicero lib. 4. Accusationis in Verrem sibi objectum commemorat: indignum facinus esse quòd in Senatu Graeco verba secisset, quódque apud Graecos Graecè locutus esset; Id terri nullo modo
units.tr: From the opinions of the Fathers that we have cited so far, we have made it clear that for the first six centuries after Christ's ascension, a foreign tongue had not yet been adopted in worship, and the people were not forbidden to read Scripture. We have now come to the time of the Antichrist's birth, who was to exercise the power of the seven-hilled beast (that is, of the great city which has dominion over the kings of the earth) in its sight (that is, in the Roman city itself), and to bring it about that all would bear the mark or the name of the beast, or the number of its name, that is, would profess themselves subject to Roman authority. And the Roman bishops were indeed so eager for this end that the Latin liturgy, however unknown and unintelligible, held sway everywhere in their dominions. In this they carefully imitated the power of the earlier beast, that is, of the Roman empire. For the imperious city took care not only to impose its yoke on the subdued nations, but also its tongue, by means of a peaceful association (Lipsius thinks we should read sociatis, or at least the appearance of association), as Augustine says. So the Romans, as Vives observes in that passage, took care that in the provinces too very many should speak Latin; so much so that they made Spain and Gaul entirely Latin, the old languages of those peoples having been abolished; and in the Senate they heard none but those who spoke in Latin. So Valerius Maximus: How greatly the magistrates of old maintained their own dignity and that of the Roman people may be seen from this, that among the other signs of maintaining gravity, they also kept it up with great persistence that they never gave answers to the Greeks except in Latin; indeed, they even compelled them, though the Greeks were very strong in the fluency of their own tongue, to speak through an interpreter, not only in our city but also in Greece and Asia, so that the good repute of the Latin word might be spread venerably among all nations. Hence Cicero, in the fourth book of his Accusation against Verres, recalls the charge brought against himself: that it was a disgrace for him to have spoken in the Senate in Greek, and to have spoken Greek among the Greeks. Plutarch, however, relates that Cato, among the Athenians, spoke everything through an interpreter, although he knew Greek well enough to have no need of an interpreter's help.

units.la: {e} Lib. 2. cap. 1. posse. Contra vero Catonem apud Athenienses per interpretem omnia locutum esse narrat Plutarchus; quanquam ita Graecè sciret, ut interpretis opera minimè indigeret. Atque hinc Tryphonius J. C. in Digestis: Decreta à Prætoribus Latinè interponi debent. Postea verò Constantinopolin translato imperio; ab Arcadio & Honorio Imp. decretum est, ut Judices tam Græcâ quàm Latinâ linguâ sententias proferre possent. Verùm de hâc re vide egregiam dissertationem Pauli Merulæ in Cosmograph. p. 795, 796. necnon Glareanum Annot. in lib. 1. Comment. Cæsar.
units.tr: {e} Book 2, chapter 1. Yet this could in no way be allowed. Plutarch, however, relates that Cato, among the Athenians, spoke everything through an interpreter, although he knew Greek well enough to have no need of an interpreter's help. And hence Tryphoninus the jurist says in the Digest: Decrees must be issued by the praetors in Latin. Later, however, when the empire was transferred to Constantinople, the emperors Arcadius and Honorius decreed that judges might pronounce their sentences in either Greek or Latin. On this matter, see the excellent dissertation of Paolo Merula in his Cosmography, pp. 795–796, and also Glareanus's notes on the first book of Caesar's Commentaries.

units.la: Romani Pontifices, quos in collapso imperio restaurando omnem operam collocare oportuerat, eandem ingressi sunt viam: ut Romanæ linguæ in Ecclesiasticis Officiis receptus usus Romanæ authoritatis in gentibus propagatæ esset indicium. Ita tempe Romanum Imperium esse videbatur, ubicunque Romana lingua dominabatur. Sed quærit hîc à nobis Alanus, utrùm subitò lingua in Liturgiâ usurpata mutata fuerit. Cui cum Erasmo respondemus linguam vulgarem populo nequaquam subtractam esse, sed populum ab eâ recessisse. Barbaris enim cuncta occupantibus, effectum esse, ut Latina lingua, quæ nationibus Romano imperio subditis communis erat, variè corrumperetur, & in diversas dialectos degeneraret. Ita Italiam oppresswhen Longobardi; de quibus Gregorius ad Phocam Imp. Indictione 6. anno sc. 603. ita scribit. Qualiter quotidianis gladiis, & quantis Longobardorum incursionibus ecce jam per 35. annorum longitudinem premimur, nullis explere vocibus suggestionis valemus. Posteaque anno 755. Aistulphus, cum universo regni sui Longobardorum populo, Romanam urbem per trium mensium spatia oppugnabat, omnia extra Urbem posita ferro & igne devastans. Neque quietem nacta est Italia, donec Desiderio Rege à Carolo M. devicto, regnum à Longobardis ad Francos esset translatum circa an. 773. Hispaniam Athaulpho Duce occupârunt Gothi, anno 4. à captâ ab iisdem Gothis urbe Româ, qui fuit Christianæ Epochæ 414. Altero ante Urbem captam anno Hispaniæ sub Gunderico occupârant Wandali; quorum regnum devicto à Belisario Justiniani Duce Gilimere finem sortitum est anno 533. Gothorum verò regnum ad annum 713. duravit, quo devicto Roderico Hispaniâ potiti sunt
units.tr: The Roman bishops, who had to devote every effort to restoring the collapsed empire, entered the same path, so that the accepted use of the Roman language in ecclesiastical offices would be a sign of Roman authority spread among the nations. Thus the Roman empire seemed to exist wherever the Roman language held sway. But Alanus asks us here whether the language used in the liturgy was suddenly changed. To him we reply, with Erasmus, that the vernacular was by no means taken away from the people, but that the people themselves had drifted away from it. For when the barbarians occupied everything, it came about that the Latin language, which had been common to the nations subject to the Roman empire, was variously corrupted and degenerated into different dialects. Thus Italy was oppressed by the Lombards, of whom Gregory, writing to the emperor Phocas in the sixth indiction, that is, in the year 603, says: "How we are pressed by daily swords and by the great raids of the Lombards, now for a span of thirty-five years, we are unable to express in any words of report." Then in the year 755 Aistulf, with the whole Lombard people of his kingdom, attacked the city of Rome for a space of three months, devastating everything outside the City with fire and sword. Italy did not gain rest until King Desiderius was defeated by Charlemagne and the kingdom was transferred from the Lombards to the Franks, about the year 773. The Goths under their leader Athaulf occupied Spain in the fourth year after the same Goths had captured the city of Rome, which was the year 414 of the Christian era. Two years before the capture of the City, the Vandals under Gunderic had occupied Spain; their kingdom was overthrown by Belisarius, the general of Justinian, and Gelimer's rule came to an end in 533. The Gothic kingdom, however, lasted until the year 713, when Roderick was defeated and the Saracens seized Spain.

Linguas enim Italicam, Hispanicam, & Gallicam Latini sermonis propagines esse, & ex ejus corruptione paulatim natas, in confesso est. Sermo (inquit Marineus Siculus ) quo nunc utuntur Hispani, Latinus est, quem a Romanis acceperunt, ideoque Romancium vocant; qui propter adventum Barbarorum aliquantulum degeneravit a lingua Latina. Quod si neque Gothi, neque Mauri, Barbariae gentes in Hispaniam venissent; tam Latinus esset nunc Hispanorum sermo, quam fuit Romanorum tempore M. Tullii. His addam Ottonis Frisingensis verba. Videtur mihi Francos, qui in Galliis morantur, a Romanis linguam eorum, qua usque hodie utuntur, accommodasse. Nam alii, qui circa Rhenum ac in Germania remanserunt, Teutonica lingua utuntur. Paria habet Godfridus Viterbiensis. Rem vero totam confirmant Erasmus declarat. 41. ad censuras Parisiensium, Henr. Glareanus annotat. in lib. 1. Comment. Caesaris. Conr. Gesnerus in Mithridate. The Saracens. Baronius confirms that the kingdom of the Franks in Gaul began in the year 456; Baronius, vol. 6 of the Annals, year 456, section 6; see Hotman's Franco-Gallia, p. 26. ᵖ On the Affairs of Spain, book 5. ʳ Book 4, chapter 32. ˢ Part 17, chapter 1. ᵗ Chapter 17. ᵘ See the Capitularies collected by Ansegisus, book 1. And so, with the barbarians holding the chief power, it came about that the Gauls and the Spaniards, among whom the Roman speech had been in use (as Strabo testifies), gradually adopted another tongue, variously mixed from Roman and barbarian elements. For it is agreed that the Italian, Spanish and French languages are offshoots of the Latin speech, and gradually arose from its corruption. The language which the Spaniards now use (says Marineo Siculo) is Latin, which they received from the Romans, and therefore they call it Romance; it has degenerated somewhat from the Latin tongue because of the coming of the barbarians. If neither the Goths nor the Moors, barbarian peoples, had come into Spain, the speech of the Spaniards would now be as Latin as the speech of the Romans was in the time of Marcus Tullius. I shall add the words of Otto of Freising: It seems to me that the Franks who dwell in Gaul adopted from the Romans the language which they use to this day. For the others who remained near the Rhine and in Germany use the Teutonic tongue. Godfrey of Viterbo has similar things. Erasmus, in his Declaration 41 on the Censures of the Parisians, Henricus Glareanus in his notes on the first book of Caesar's Commentaries, Conrad Gesner in his Mithridates, Angelo Rocca in the Vatican Library, and Robert Bellarmine in book 2, On the Word of God, chapter 15, all confirm the whole matter.

units.la: Hinc est, quod in Synodo Turonensi III. anno 813. Caroli M. jussu habita provisum est. Ut Homiliae aperte transferrentur in rusticam Romanam linguam aut Theotiscam (seu Germanicam, quia Germania sub ditione fuit Caroli) quo facilius cuncti possent intelligere quae dicerentur. Unde intelligitur ita depravatam fuisse Romanam linguam, quae apud vulgus tunc temporis obtinebat, ut prisca & purior illa vix jam posset intelligi. Ideoque in Moguntiaco Concilio eodem anno decretum est, ut filios suos docent ad scholam (verba sunt cap. 45. quae etiam libro 5. Capitularium a Benedicto Levita collect. cap. 95. habentur) sive ad Monasteria, sive foras Presbyteris, ut fidem Catholicam recte discant, & orationem Dominicam; ut domi alios edocere valeant. Et qui aliter non potuerit, vel in sua lingua hoc discat. Illud nimirum Carolo in votis erat maxime; ut Latina lingua ubique retineretur (quam nec penitus a vulgi intellectu remotam fuisse, ex testimoniis Conciliorum & Patrum horum temporum, quae suo loco a nobis producentur, videtur constare) licet aliam potius usurpari voluerit, quam ut populus quid
units.tr: Hence it is that at the Third Council of Tours, held in the year 813 by the command of Charlemagne, provision was made that homilies should be translated openly into the rustic Roman tongue or the Theotisca (that is, German, since Germany was under the rule of Charlemagne), so that all might more easily understand what was being said. From this it is understood that the Roman language which then prevailed among the common people had been so corrupted that the older and purer speech could scarcely be understood any longer. Therefore at the Council of Mainz in the same year it was decreed that they should send their sons to school (these are the words of chapter 45, which are also found in chapter 95 of book 5 of the Capitularies collected by Benedict the Levite) either to the monasteries, or to the presbyters outside, so that they may rightly learn the Catholic faith and the Lord's Prayer, and so be able to teach others at home. And whoever could not do otherwise should learn this in his own language. It was clearly Charlemagne's greatest wish that the Latin language be retained everywhere (which, from the testimonies of the Councils and Fathers of these times, which we shall produce in their place, seems to be established as not having been wholly remote from the people's understanding), although he would rather have it that another language be used, rather than that the people should not know what...

Quanquam verò Regis studio undecunque adductis magistris, tam legendi quàm cantandi studium, necnon mundanarum & divinarum intelligentia literarum, citius quàm credi poterat, coaluit, ut habet ille Author x qui vitam filii ejus Ludovici Pii descripsit.) Illud tamen negari non potest, Carolum Romani Antichristi conatum plurimùm promovisse, illudque effecisse, ut Ordo Romanus in linguâ Latinâ, quantumvis non intellecta, à posteris retineretur. Offensus enim dissonantiâ Ecclesiastici cantûs inter Romanos & Gallos, & Judicans justius esse de puro fonte, quàm de turbato rivo bibere (verba sunt Sigeberti Gemblacensis y) duos Clericos Romam misit, ut authenticum cantum à Romanis discerent, & Gallos docerent: z & primò per hos Metensis Ecclesia, & per illam omnis Gallia ad auctoritatem Romani cantûs revocata est. Ita anno 805. Saxonas ab eo devictos Romanam religionem accepisse coactos prodit in Chronico Jo. Tilius. Et anno 806. in Concilio in Theodonis villâ habito, ab eo constitutum notat Benedictus Levita a, 1. Ut lectiones distinctè in Ecclesiâ legantur, 2. De cantu, ut secundùm ordinem & morem Romanæ Ecclesiæ fiat cantatus. Carolus M. (inquit Fr. Hotomannus b) Galliæ regnum Papæ Zachariæ ope consilioque adeptus, in tanti beneficii gratiam edixit, ut Romano more ritus Ecclesiæ servarentur, & cantiones haberentur: quæ lex ipsius, cùm in Capitulari c, tum in legibus Francicis his exstat verbis: Ut cantum pleniter discant & ordinabiliter per nocturnale vel gradsuale officium peragant; d secundùm quod beatæ memoriæ genitor nostèr Pipinus Rex decretavit ut fieret, quando Gallicanum cantum tulit, & ob unanimitatem Apostolicæ sedis, & sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ pacificam concordiam. Quæ res dici non potest quantum & Gallicis Ecclesiis caliginem offuderit, & Pontificibus Romanis authoritatem in negotiis religionis tribuerit.

Capitular. ab Ansegiso collect. lib. 1. cap. 70. from God he might seek, he would not know it. Yet although, with the king's zeal, teachers were brought in from every quarter, the zeal both for reading and for singing, and the understanding of worldly and divine letters, grew up sooner than could be believed, as that author x says who described the life of his son Louis the Pious. It cannot, however, be denied that Charles greatly promoted the attempt of the Roman Antichrist, and brought it about that the Roman Order was retained by later generations in the Latin language, however little it was understood. For, offended by the discord of ecclesiastical chant between the Romans and the Gauls, and judging it more right to drink from the pure spring than from a muddied stream (these are the words of Sigebert of Gembloux y), he sent two clerics to Rome to learn the authentic chant from the Romans and teach the Gauls. z And first through these men the church of Metz, and through it all Gaul, was brought back to the authority of the Roman chant. So in 805 Tilius, in his Chronicle, reports that the Saxons, conquered by him, were compelled to accept the Roman religion. And in 806, at the council held at Theodo's villa, Benedict the Levite notes that the following was established by him: a, 1. that the lessons be read distinctly in the church; 2. concerning the chant, that the singing be done according to the order and custom of the Roman Church. Charles the Great (says Fr. Hotman b) obtained the kingdom of Gaul with the help and counsel of Pope Zachary, and in gratitude for so great a benefit he decreed that the rites of the Church be observed in the Roman manner and that the chants be kept. This law of his is found both in his Capitulary c and in the Frankish laws in these words: That they learn the chant fully and carry out the office in an orderly way at the nocturnal or gradual office, d as our father of blessed memory, King Pepin, decreed should be done when he adopted the Gallican chant, for the unanimity of the Apostolic See and the peaceful concord of the holy Church of God. It cannot be said how much this darkened the Gallican churches and conferred authority on the Roman Pontiffs in matters of religion.
