units.la: ERroris origine explicatâ, superest, ut Historiam hanc ad nostra usque tempora perducamus: quò planum fiat nunquam veritati testes defuisse; merasque nugas esse, quæ de omnium ætatum consensu in dogmatis Papisticis stabiliendis jactitare solent Pontificii. Primo autem loco collocabimus testimonium desumptum ex Homiliis illis in Evangelia totius anni, quæ perperam Eusebio Emeseno ascribuntur; quia de tempore, quo Autor ille vixit, nihil adhuc constat. Canisius ᵃ asserit post Gregorium M. scripsisse; Surio ᵇ homo doctissimus, sed non admodum vetustus fuisse videtur. [Mortonus in 2. parte Apologiæ Catholi. p. 72. locum sequentem citat ex Gregorio Nazianzeno hom. 4. Dom. Epiphan. In Catalogo testium Veritatis citatur Gregorii Nysseni nomine.]
units.tr: Having explained the origin of the error, it remains to bring this history down to our own times, so that it becomes plain that witnesses to the truth never failed, and that the claim the Papists habitually make, that all ages agree in establishing their dogmas, is mere nonsense. First, however, we shall cite the testimony taken from those Homilies on the Gospels for the whole year, which are wrongly ascribed to Eusebius of Emesa, because nothing is yet certain about the time when that author lived. Canisius asserts that he wrote after Gregory the Great; Surius, a very learned man, seems to have judged him not very ancient. [Morton, in the second part of his Apology for the Catholics, p. 72, cites the following passage from Gregory Nazianzen, Homily 4, on the Feast of the Epiphany. In the Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth it is cited under the name of Gregory of Nyssa.]

units.la: Homil. in Evang. Dominic. 4. post Epiphaniam. Hanc consuetudinem Christiani perpetuam habere debent; ut quotidie ad Ecclesiam veniant, quotidie legant ipsi, vel (si hoc non valent) alios legentes audiant.
units.tr: Homily on the Gospel for the fourth Sunday after Epiphany. Christians ought to keep this custom constantly: that they come to the church every day, that they read for themselves every day, or, if they cannot do this, that they listen to others reading.

units.la: 634. Aidanus Episcopus nostrâs, ex Hiberniâ ad Anglos instituendos missus.
units.tr: 634. Aidan, Bishop of our people, sent from Ireland to instruct the English.

units.la: De eo ita scribit Beda lib. 3. Hist. cap. 5. In tantum vita illius à nostri temporis segnitie distabat; ut omnes qui cum eo incedebant, sive adtonsi sive laici, meditari deberent, i. e. aut legendis scripturis aut Psalmis discendis operam dare. Illi erant religiosorum apud nos olim mores; quippe qui tantùm ea quæ in Propheticis, Evangelicis & Apostolicis literis discere poterant, pietatis & castitatis opera observare sategerunt: quemadmodum in præcedente capite notavit idem Beda.
units.tr: Bede writes of him thus, in Book 3 of his History, chapter 5: His manner of life was so far removed from the sloth of our own time that all who went about with him, whether tonsured or laymen, were bound to meditate, that is, to give themselves either to reading the Scriptures or to learning the Psalms. Such were the customs of religious men among us in former times, who, as far as they could learn from the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic writings, strove to observe the works of piety and chastity, as the same Bede noted in the preceding chapter.

units.la: ᵃ Chronolog. præfix. Catechismo. ᵇ Præfat. in Homil. Patrum ad Maximilianum Imp.
units.tr: a Chronology prefixed to the Catechism. b Preface to the Homilies of the Fathers, addressed to the Emperor Maximilian.

units.la: 650. Thalassius Monachus.
units.tr: 650. Thalassius, a monk.

units.la: Hecatontad. 1. sect. 57. Scrutatur verba Dei, qui eum colit. Hecantontad. 2. sect. 28. 2 Scrutare eloquia Dei, & doce scientiam Dei eos, qui piè ac desideranter veritatem inquirunt. Hecatontad. 4. sect. 18. 3 Verbis divinis continuè vaca: nam diligens in eis studium affectiones absumit. Sect. 19. 4 Lectio & vigiliae precesque cum Psalmodiis mentem sistunt; ne circa affectiones vagetur. Sect. 54. 5 Scrutare Scripturas; & invenies mandata; quod si feceris quae dicunt, ab affectionibus liberaberis.
units.tr: Hecatontas 1, sect. 57: He who worships God searches the words of God. Hecatontas 2, sect. 28: 2 Search the sayings of God, and teach the knowledge of God to those who seek the truth piously and eagerly. Hecatontas 4, sect. 18: 3 Devote yourself continually to the divine words; for diligent study of them wears away the passions. Sect. 19: 4 Reading, vigils and prayers, together with the psalmody, keep the mind steady, so that it does not wander about the passions. Sect. 54: 5 Search the Scriptures, and you will find the commandments; if you do what they say, you will be freed from the passions.

units.la: 650. Maximus Abbas.
units.tr: 650. Maximus, Abbot.

units.la: In locis Commun. Serm. 17. ex Chrysostomo hanc sententiam profert. "Ὥσπερ γὰρ μὴ βρεχομένην ὗδε ... ὅταν ψυχὴν ἐκ ἔχῃ ... " Quemadmodum terra imbre non irrigata, licèt infinitam seminis copiam accipiat, segetem proferre non potest; sic neque fructum aliquem producere anima, divinis Scripturis non illuminata prius, etiamsi innumeros sermones quis effundat.
units.tr: In the Loci Communes, Sermon 17, he gives this saying from Chrysostom: "Just as the earth, not watered by rain, though it receives an endless quantity of seed, cannot bring forth a crop, so the soul too cannot produce any fruit unless it is first illumined by the divine Scriptures, even if someone pours forth countless sermons." [Ὥσπερ γὰρ μὴ βρεχομένην ὗδε ... ὅταν ψυχὴν ἐκ ἔχῃ ...]

units.la: 670. Cednomus, Poeta Anglicus.
units.tr: 670. Caedmon, English poet.

units.la: Hic divinâ gratiâ specialiter insignis, carmina religioni & pietati apta facere solebat; ita ut quicquid ex divinis literis per interpretes disceret, hoc ipse post pusillum verbis poeticis maximâ suavitate & compunctione compositis, in suâ, i.e. Anglorum linguâ, proferret. Canebat autem de creatione mundi, & origine humani generis, & totâ Genesis historiâ, de egressu Israel ex Ægypto, & ingressu in terram repromissionis, ac de aliis plurimis sacrae Scripturae Historiis. [Beda lib. 4. histor. cap. 24.]
units.tr: This man, specially marked by divine grace, used to make songs fit for religion and piety, so that whatever he learned from the divine writings through interpreters, he himself, a short while later, would set forth in his own language, that is, English, in poetic words composed with the greatest sweetness and compunction. He sang of the creation of the world, the origin of the human race, the whole history of Genesis, the departure of Israel from Egypt and entry into the land of promise, and many other histories of Holy Scripture. [Bede, Book 4 of the History, chapter 24.]

units.la: 1 Ἐρευνᾶ λόγως Θεοῦ ὁ συζήτων αὐτόν.
units.tr: 1 He who searches the words of God, who worships him. [Ἐρευνᾶ λόγως Θεοῦ ὁ συζήτων αὐτόν.]

units.la: 2 Ita quidem Interpres Latinus in Orthodoxographis Basil. pag. 901. locum reddidit, quasi legisset, ἐρεύνα λόγως Θεοῦ. Paulo aliter edidit GL. in Auctuario Bibliothecae Patr. Parisiensi 1624. Tom. 2. p. 1185. "Ἐρεύνα λόγων Θεοῦ, διδάσκει γνῶναι Θεόν, ἐν ἀληθείᾳ ζητοῦντα, ἐν εὐλαβείᾳ καὶ πόθῳ. Inquisitio eloquiorum Dei docet scientiam Dei eos qui pie ac desideranter veritatem scrutantur.
units.tr: 2 The Latin translator in the Basel Orthodoxographa, p. 901, rendered the passage as though he had read "ἐρεύνα λόγως Θεοῦ". GL, in the Auctarium of the Bibliotheca Patrum of Paris, 1624, vol. 2, p. 1185, edited it somewhat differently: [Ἐρεύνα λόγων Θεοῦ, διδάσκει γνῶναι Θεόν, ἐν ἀληθείᾳ ζητοῦντα, ἐν εὐλαβείᾳ καὶ πόθῳ.] "Inquiry into the sayings of God teaches the knowledge of God to those who seek the truth piously and eagerly."

units.la: 3 Ῥήματα θεῖα διαλαλοῦντος φιλάζει· ἡ γὰρ σὺ αὐτὰ φιλοπονία καλλιαλίας τὰ πάντα.
units.tr: 3 [Ῥήματα θεῖα διαλαλοῦντος φιλάζει· ἡ γὰρ σὺ αὐτὰ φιλοπονία καλλιαλίας τὰ πάντα.] Devote yourself constantly to the divine words, for diligent labour on them wears away all the passions.

units.la: 4 Ἴσως δὲ νῦν ἐκ τὰ πάντα πλάνης ἀναγνώσεως ἐν ἀχρηστίᾳ ἐν σπουδῇ ἐν ψαλμῳδίᾳ.
units.tr: 4 [Ἴσως δὲ νῦν ἐκ τὰ πάντα πλάνης ἀναγνώσεως ἐν ἀχρηστίᾳ ἐν σπουδῇ ἐν ψαλμῳδίᾳ.] Reading, vigils and prayers, together with the psalmody, keep the mind fixed, so that it does not wander about the passions.

units.la: 5. Ἐρεύνησον τὰς γραφὰς, ἐν ἀνείσκεις τὰς ἐντολὰς, ἐν τὰ λεγόμενα ποιήσεις· ἐν ἀπ' αὐτῶν ἀπαλλάξῃ.
units.tr: 5. [Ἐρεύνησον τὰς γραφὰς, ἐν ἀνείσκεις τὰς ἐντολὰς, ἐν τὰ λεγόμενα ποιήσεις· ἐν ἀπ' αὐτῶν ἀπαλλάξῃ.] Search the Scriptures, and you will find the commandments; if you do what they say, you will be freed from the passions.

units.la: 660. Wilgis Nordhumbranus.
units.tr: 660. Wilgis Nordhumbranus.

units.la: Infantulum suum Willibrordum statim ablactatum tradidit Riponensis Ecclesiæ fratribus, religiosis studiis & sacris literis erudiendum; ut fragilior ætas validioribus invalesceret disciplinis: ubi nihil videret nisi honesta, nihil audiret nisi sancta. [ Alcuinus in Vita Willibrordi. ]
units.tr: He handed over his little son Willibrord, weaned at once, to the brothers of the church at Ripon, to be educated in religious studies and sacred letters, so that his more fragile age might grow strong under stronger disciplines, where he would see nothing but honourable things and hear nothing but holy things. [Alcuinus in Vita Willibrordi.]

units.la: 685. Alfridus Rex Nordamhumbrorum.
units.tr: 685. Alfred, King of Northumbria.

units.la: Successit Ecgfrido in regnum Alfrit, vir in Scripturis doctissimus. Beda lib. 4. hist. cap. 26. & eum secuti Florentius Wigorn. anno 685. item Henricus Huntingdon. lib. 4. Vide etiam Bedam in Carm. de Cuthberto, tom. 5. Antiqu. Lect. Henr. Canisii part. 2. pag. 710.
units.tr: Alfrith succeeded Ecgfrith in the kingdom, a man most learned in the Scriptures. Bede, book 4 of the History, chapter 26, and those who followed him: Florence of Worcester, under the year 685; likewise Henry of Huntingdon, book 4. See also Bede in his poem on Cuthbert, vol. 5 of the Antiquae Lectiones of Henry Canisius, part 2, page 710.

units.la: 686. Julianus Toletanus Episcopus.
units.tr: 686. Julian, Bishop of Toledo.

units.la: Lib. 1. adv. Judæos. Audite jam o impietatis operarii, o filii scelerati, non me, sed ipsum Christum Dominum, quem expugnare nitimini; audite eum respondentem patribus vestris. Ait enim tentantibus se Judæis in Evangelio, & dixit: Erratis nescientes Scripturas, neque virtutem Dei. Etenim virtus & sapientia Dei secundum Paulum Christus est: ergo ignorantia Scripturarum ignorantia Christi est. Quid jam mirum, si error corda vestra possideat, quos ignorantia Scripturarum objurgat? Scrutamini ergo Scripturarum latentes campos; & tunc intelligetis cæcos oculos vestros.
units.tr: From Book 1 against the Jews. Hear now, you workers of impiety, you wicked sons, not me but Christ the Lord himself, whom you strive to overthrow; hear him answering your fathers. For when the Jews tested him in the Gospel, he said: You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God. For the power and wisdom of God, according to Paul, is Christ; therefore ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. What wonder is it if error possesses your hearts, when ignorance of the Scriptures rebukes you? Search, therefore, the hidden fields of the Scriptures, and then you will understand that your eyes are blind.

units.la: 680. S. Kilianus Hibernus.
units.tr: 680. S. Kilianus, the Irishman

units.la: A puerili ætate magnum habet studium sacras discere literas, & in eis tam perfectè proficiens; ut exinde Pontificale didicit regere culmen. Author Vitæ Kiliani tomo 4. Antiqu. Lect. Henr. Canisii pag. 642.
units.tr: From boyhood he had a great zeal to learn the holy letters, and made such perfect progress in them that he afterwards learned to rule the summit of the pontifical office. The author of the Life of Kilian, in volume 4 of the Antiquae Lectiones of Henricus Canisius, page 642.

units.la: 706. Aldhelmus, Balduinus, & Guthlacus Croilandensis.
units.tr: 706. Aldhelm, Baldwin, and Guthlac of Croyland.

units.la: Aldhelmum Psalterium in linguam Anglosaxonicam transtulisse scribit Jo. Baleus. Psalterii S. Guthlaci Ingulphus in Historiâ suâ meminit;
units.tr: John Bale writes that Aldhelm translated the Psalter into the Anglo-Saxon language. Ingulf, in his History, mentions the Psalter of St Guthlac,

units.la: * Matth. XXII. d 1 Cor. I, e De Scriptor. Britann. Cent. 1. cap. 83. meminit; & ad nostra tempora inter reliquias Croilandensis Monasterii conservatum est. Quod quidem vulgari Saxonicâ linguâ exaratum fuisse, ex testimonio Joannis Lamberti, qui illud vidit, apparet. Et etiamnum in publicâ Academiæ Cantabrigiensis Bibliothecâ Psalmi Latinè & Saxonicè versi cernuntur. Et in Bibliothecâ D. Roberti Cottoni extat Psalterium Romanum vetustissimum cum versione interlineari Saxonicâ: character idem cum chartâ Æthilbaldi Anglorum Regis anno 736. datâ.
units.tr: * Matt. XXII. d 1 Cor. I, e in *De Scriptoribus Britanniae*, cent. 1, cap. 83, and it was preserved among the relics of the monastery of Croyland until our own times. That it was written in the common Saxon tongue appears from the testimony of John Lambert, who saw it. Even now, in the public library of the University of Cambridge, Psalms translated into Latin and Saxon can be seen. And in the library of Sir Robert Cotton there is a very ancient Roman Psalter with an interlinear Saxon version, in the same script as a charter of Ethelbald, King of the English, dated 736.

units.la: 710. Bonifacius.
units.tr: 710. Boniface.

units.la: De eo Gregorius II. Comperimus te ab infantiâ sacras literas didicisse: & Wilibaldus in vitâ Bonifacii cap. 3. Ab infantiâ suâ usque ad decrepitam ætatis senectutem, præteritorum non mediocriter patrum sapientiam imitatus est; dum Prophetarum jugiter & Apostolorum verba stylo sanctitatis conscripta, & gloriosam Martyrum Passionem literarum apicibus insertam, sed & Evangelicam Domini Dei nostri traditionem quotidie commendabat memoriæ, &c. In tantum enim Scripturarum exarsit desiderio; ut omni se intentione earum imitatione & auditione sæpius conjungeret. Et quæ ob doctrinam populorum conscripta sunt; ipse quippe populis mirâ eloquii disertitudine & solertissimâ Parabolarum assertione efficaciter prædicando retexuit. Vide locum tomo 4. Henr. Canisii par. 2, pag. 350, 351. collat. cum Othlono de Vitâ Bonifacii lib. 1. cap. 2. (in Serario de rebus Mogunt. pag. 330.) Sed duo egregia testimonia Bonifacii vide in Epistola ejus 57. de Virginibus sacris, & in Vitâ ejus per Wilibaldum cap. 2. pag. 349, 350. Edit. Canisii; dignissima prorsus quæ subjiciantur.
units.tr: Gregory II says of him: We have learned that you have studied the holy letters from infancy. And Willibald, in the life of Boniface, chapter 3: From his infancy until the decrepit old age of his years, he imitated not a little the wisdom of the fathers who had gone before; while he continually committed to memory the words of the Prophets and Apostles, written in the style of holiness, and the glorious Passion of the Martyrs, inscribed in letters, and also the Evangelical tradition of our Lord God, every day, etc. For he burned with such desire for the Scriptures that with his whole attention he often joined himself to their imitation and hearing. And what had been written for the instruction of the peoples, he himself unfolded to the peoples, preaching effectively with wonderful eloquence and most skilful exposition of the Parables. See the passage in volume 4 of Henry Canisius, part 2, pages 350 and 351, compared with Othlo, On the Life of Boniface, book 1, chapter 2 (in Serarius, On the affairs of Mainz, page 330). But for two excellent testimonies about Boniface, see his Letter 57, on consecrated virgins, and his Life by Willibald, chapter 2, pages 349 and 350 of Canisius's edition; they are altogether most worthy of being quoted below.

units.la: Epist. 57. ad Virginem sacram [quæ quidem ab Aldhelmo Abbate scripta est, ex mente autem Bonifacii jam Antistitis, quod ex initio constat.] Saluto te diligenter, Ofigegyth, ex intimo cordis cubiculo subnexis precibus obsecrans; ut assiduâ Scripturarum meditatione mentem tuam occupare non desistas; quatenus Psalmigraphi sententiam compleas dicentis: In lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte. Et idem Psalmista hoc idem testatur dicens, Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua? & reliqua.
units.tr: Letter 57, to a consecrated virgin [which was indeed written by Abbot Aldhelm, but in the mind of Boniface, then already a bishop, as is clear from the beginning]. I greet you warmly, Ofigegyth, begging you from the inmost chamber of my heart, with prayers joined together, that you not cease to occupy your mind with constant meditation on the Scriptures, so that you may fulfil the saying of the Psalmist: "In his law he shall meditate day and night." And the same Psalmist bears witness to this, saying: "How sweet are your words to my taste?" and so on.

units.la: In vitâ ejus per Wilibaldum, cap. 2. Tanta in eo affabilitatis erga fratres & cœlestis doctrinæ succrevit magnitudo; ut rumore sanctæ exhortationis,
units.tr: In the life of Boniface by Willibald, chapter 2: In him there grew such a great affability towards the brothers and such a greatness of heavenly teaching that, by the report of his holy exhortation,

units.la: {f} in respons. ad 26. Artic. Episc. {g} Lib. 1. Vitæ Bonifacii ab Othlono descriptæ cap. 12. in Serario & Surio. tationis, ejus crebescente fama, multis per Monasteria tam virorum quàm etiam virginum Christi apertissimè claruit; quorum quidem quamplurimi virili sexûs robore confortati, & lectionis instantia incitati, ad eum confluxere, & suluberrimum scientiæ fontem potantes, numerosa Scripturarum volumina legendo recensuere. Quibus ergo sexus infirmioris 6 imbecillitatis inerat, & assidua pergendi abnegabatur facultas; tantæ sibi sapientiæ virum, divini inflante spiritu amoris, præsentari fecerunt; paginarumque seriem transcurrentes, cælesti instantes scrutinio inhæsere; & sacramentorum arcana mysteriorumque abdita jugiter meditantur.
units.tr: {f} In the reply to the 26 Articles of the Bishop. {g} Book 1 of the Life of Boniface, described by Othlo, chapter 12, in Serarius and Surius. ...by the report of his exhortation, his growing fame became very clear among many monasteries of men as well as of virgins of Christ. Very many of them, strengthened by the vigour of the male sex and stirred by the eagerness of reading, flocked to him, and drinking from that most abundant fountain of knowledge, they went through numerous volumes of Scripture by reading them. But those of the weaker sex, who lacked strength and were denied the ability to continue to come, caused the man of such great wisdom to be presented to them, inspired by the breath of divine love; running through the sequence of the pages, they clung to a heavenly examination, and continually meditate on the hidden mysteries of the sacraments and the secrets of the mysteries.

units.la: 710. Eadfridus Lindisfarnensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 710. Eadfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne.

units.la: A sermone Latino in Anglosaxonicam linguam vertit plures Bibliorum libros; ut habet Guilhelmus Butler in suo libello contra translationem vulgarem. Hujus Eadfridi Saxonica Evangelistarum editio (secundùm Eusebii Canonem, non capitulis distincta) jam in manibus Roberti Bowyer Angli habetur; unde Orationem Dominicam transcripsit M. N. (in his Remains of a greater Work, p. 15.)
units.tr: He translated several books of the Bible from the Latin language into the Anglo-Saxon tongue; as William Butler has it in his little book against the common translation. The Saxon edition of the Evangelists by this Eadfrith (arranged according to Eusebius's Canons, not divided into chapters) is now in the hands of Robert Bowyer, an Englishman; from it M. N. copied out the Lord's Prayer (in his Remains of a greater Work, p. 15).

units.la: 730. Beda Anglo-Saxo.
units.tr: 730. Bede the Anglo-Saxon.

units.la: In Historiæ Eccl. proœmio commendat Ceodvulphum Regem, ut Scripturæ studiosum.
units.tr: In the preface to his Ecclesiastical History he commends King Ceolwulf as a student of Scripture.

units.la: Prolog. super Samuel. lib. 1. Quæcunque enim scripta sunt ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, &c. Et mox. Si ad nostram correptionem, doctrinam, vel consolationem omnia scripta sunt, &c. insistendum nobis summopere est, & pro suo cuique modulo Christi juvante gratiâ nitendum; ne ea quæ propter nos scripta sunt, nostro nos torpore vel incuriâ quasi aliena prætereant, &c.
units.tr: Prologue on the first book of Samuel: For whatever things have been written, have been written for our teaching, etc. And soon after: If all things have been written for our correction, teaching, or consolation, etc., we must very much devote ourselves to them and, with Christ's help and grace, strive according to each one's measure; lest we pass over those things which were written on our account, as though they were foreign to us, through our own sluggishness or carelessness, etc.

units.la: In Ezram lib. 1. cap. 1. Christus Scripturas sanctas universum misit in mundum; quibus fidem sui nominis, ac spem salutis cunctis, qui ad regnum suum pertinent, hoc est, electis omnibus prædicaret.
units.tr: On Ezra, book 1, chapter 1: Christ sent the holy Scriptures into the whole world; by them he might preach the faith of his name and the hope of salvation to all who belong to his kingdom, that is, to all the elect.

units.la: Lib. 3. in Ezram cap. 28. Quo exemplo reor in Ecclesiâ morem inolevisse 7, ut per singulas diurnæ (al. divinæ) psalmodiæ horas lectio una de Veteri sive Novo Testamento cunctis audientibus ex corde dicatur; & sic
units.tr: Book 3 on Ezra, chapter 28: By this example, I think, a custom has grown up in the Church, that at each of the hours of the daily (or divine) psalmody, a reading from the Old or New Testament be recited from the heart, all listening, and thus

units.la: Rom. XV.
units.tr: Rom. XV.

units.la: 6 Rectius imbecillitas in editione Serarii, p. 258.
units.tr: 6 More correctly "weakness" in Serarius's edition, p. 258.

units.la: 7 Pulcherrimum, addit Amalarius locum citans. Apostolicis sive Propheticis confirmati verbis ad instantiam orationis genua flectant. Hoc idem ab Amalario Treverensi producitur lib. 4. de Divinis Officiis cap. 3.
units.tr: 7 A most beautiful passage, which Amalarius adds when he cites it: strengthened by the apostolic or prophetic words, let them bend their knees to the urgency of prayer. The same thing is quoted from Amalarius of Trier, book 4 on the Divine Offices, chapter 3.

units.la: Lib. 1. in Luc. cap. 4. Si quis non vescitur verbo Dei, ille non vivit.
units.tr: Book 1 on Luke, chapter 4: If anyone does not feed on the word of God, he does not live.

units.la: 8 In 1 Corinth. XIV. Nemo aedificatur audiendo id quod non intelligit.
units.tr: 8 On 1 Corinthians XIV: No one is edified by hearing what he does not understand.

units.la: In Homiliis Quadragesimalibus, Dominica 2. in Quadrages. Notandum quod haec orandi pertinacia ita solum meretur esse fructifera; si quod ore precamur, hoc etiam mente meditemur; neque alio clamor labiorum quam cogitationum scindatur intuitus. Sunt enim qui intrantes Ecclesiam, multis orationem vel psalmodiam sermonibus perlegant (rectius prolongant in Homiliis in Evangelia totius anni a Surio editis pag. 243.) sed alibi corde intendentes, nec ipsi quid dicunt, recolunt: ore quidem orantes, sed mente foris vagantes, omni se orationis fructu privant; putantes a Deo precem exaudiri, quam nec ipsi, qui fundunt, audiunt. Quod antiqui hostis instinctu fieri nemo est qui animadvertere nequeat. Haec Beda in dicta Homilia, quae etiam ex eis una est, quas Alcuinus vel Paulus Diaconus Caroli M. jussu in Evangelia totius anni collegit.
units.tr: In the Lenten Homilies, second Sunday in Lent: It should be noted that this persistence in prayer deserves to be fruitful only if we meditate in our mind on what we pray with the mouth; nor let the outcry of the lips be separated from the gaze of the thoughts. For there are some who, entering the church, go through prayer or psalmody with many words (more correctly prolong, in the Homilies on the Gospels for the whole year, edited by Surius, p. 243) but, directing their hearts elsewhere, recall neither what they themselves are saying; praying with the mouth but wandering abroad in the mind, they deprive themselves of all the fruit of prayer; thinking that the prayer is heard by God, which they who pour it out do not hear themselves. That this is done at the prompting of the ancient enemy, no one is unable to perceive. Thus Bede in the said Homily, which is also one of those that Alcuin or Paul the Deacon gathered, at the command of Charlemagne, into homilies for the whole year.

units.la: In Homiliis Aestivalibus de Tempore, Dominica, Vocem jucunditatis. Quia supervacuis cogitationibus ad integrum carere non valemus; has, in quantum possumus, immissione bonarum cogitationum, & maxime frequenti scripturarum meditatione fugemus, juxta exemplum Psalmistae, qui dicit; ¹ Quomodo dilexi legem tuam, Domine; tota die meditatio mea est.
units.tr: In the Summer Homilies for the season, Sunday, Vocem jucunditatis: Because we cannot entirely be free of useless thoughts, we shall flee them, as far as we can, by admitting good thoughts, and above all by frequent meditation on the Scriptures, following the example of the Psalmist, who says: "How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day."

units.la: In illud 1 Petr. 2. Sicut modo geniti infantes rationabile & sine dolo lac concupiscite; ut eo crescatis in salutem. Sicut infantes lac maternum naturaliter desiderant, ut ad salutem crescere, atque ad panem comedendum pervenire valeant; ita & vos simplicia fidei rudimenta primo de Ecclesiae matris uberibus quaerite, hoc est, de utriusque Testamenti Doctoribus, qui divina eloquia vel scripsere, vel etiam vivi vobis voce praedicant; ut bene discendo perveniatis ad refectionem panis vivi, qui descendit de coelo, &c. Item. Praecepto concupiscendi lac verbi tangit eos, qui ad audiendas lectiones sacras inviti & fastidiosi adveniunt, ignari illius
units.tr: On 1 Peter 2: "As newborn babes, desire the reasonable and sincere milk, that by it you may grow up to salvation." As infants naturally desire their mother's milk, so that they may grow up to salvation and be able to come to eating bread, so you too should first seek the simple rudiments of faith from the breasts of the Church, our mother, that is, from the teachers of both Testaments, who either wrote down the divine words or still preach them to you with the living voice; so that by learning well you may come to the refreshment of the living bread which came down from heaven, etc. Likewise: By the precept to desire the milk of the word he touches those who come unwillingly and with distaste to hear the sacred readings, ignorant of that

units.la: ¹ Psal. CXIX.
units.tr: ¹ Psalm CXIX.

units.la: 8 Commentaria in Epistolas S. Pauli dubiae sunt fidei. Sunt qui Floro Magistro, qui saeculo sequenti claruit, ea deberi non male censent. fitis & esuriei, de quâ Dominus ait: Beati, qui esuriunt & sitiunt justitiam: Ideoque tardius ad perfectum salutis crementum pervenientes, quò possint solido verbi cibo refici, i. e. arcana cognoscere divina, vel majora facere bona.
units.tr: 8 The commentaries on the Epistles of St Paul are of doubtful authorship. Some not unreasonably think they should be assigned to Florus the Teacher, who flourished in the following century. hunger and thirst, of which the Lord said: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness." Therefore, arriving more slowly at the full growth of salvation, so that they may be refreshed with the solid food of the word, that is, to know the hidden divine things or to do greater good works.

units.la: Gulielmus Malmsburiensis de Bedæ obitu agens, Evangelium (inquit) Johannis, quod difficultate sui mentes legentium exercet, his diebus linguâ interpretatus Anglicâ condescendit minùs imbutis Latinâ. Similiter etiam Evangelium Johannis in Anglicum transtulisse Bedam refert Johannes Trevisa. l In vitâ etiam ejus à Cuthberto Dunelmensi descriptâ habetur (ut est in Dunelmensis Ecclesiæ Historiâ) Evangelium Johannis paulò ante obitum in linguam Anglicanam eum transtulisse. m Hoc nimirum illud est, quod in Epistolâ de obitu Venerabilis Bedæ (ad calcem Operum ejus) legimus. A Capite Evangelii S. Johannis usque ad eum locum, in quo dicitur: Sed hæc quid sunt inter tantos? in vostram linguam ad utilitatem Ecclesiæ Dei convertit. Sed & ex Prologo ante vetera Biblia commemorat Jo. Foxus, n Bedam integra Biblia in linguam Saxonicam transtulisse. Baleus o ait, Evangelium Johannis, Psalterium, & alios Bibliorum libros in patriam linguam eum transtulisse. Illum denique universam ferè Bibliam in linguam Britannicam convertisse ex Præfatione docti inprimis viri in Vetus Testamentum Anglicè ante annos 300. conscriptum refert Jo. Caius lib. 1. de Antiq. Cantab. pag. 150.
units.tr: William of Malmesbury, speaking of Bede's death, says: "The Gospel of John, which exercises the minds of its readers by its difficulty, was in these days interpreted into English speech, to come down to those less versed in Latin." John Trevisa likewise reports that Bede translated the Gospel of John into English. l In the life of Bede written by Cuthbert of Durham (as it appears in the History of the Church of Durham), it is said that shortly before his death he translated the Gospel of John into the English tongue. m This is surely what we read in the letter on the death of the Venerable Bede (at the end of his Works): "From the beginning of the Gospel of St John down to the place where it says, 'But what are these among so many?' he turned it into our language for the benefit of the Church of God." But John Foxe also records, from the preface before the old Bibles, that Bede translated the whole Bible into the Saxon language. n Bale says that he translated the Gospel of John, the Psalter, and other books of the Bible into the native tongue. o Finally, John Caius, in the first book of his work on the antiquities of Cambridge, page 150, reports from the preface to a learned man's English translation of the Old Testament, written more than 300 years ago, that he turned almost the whole Bible into the British tongue.

units.la: 740. Johannes Damascenus
units.tr: 740. John of Damascus

units.la: Orthodoxæ fidei lib. 4. cap. 18. 9 Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata utilis est omnino. Quare optimum & animæ conducentissimum est divinas scrutari Scripturas. Nam quemadmodum arbor plantata secus decursus aquarum, sic anima divinâ irrigata Scripturâ impinguatur, & maturum fructum affert fidem orthodoxam, & semper virentibus foliis decoratur, i. e. Deo placentibus actionibus. Ad actionem enim studiosam & contem-plationem
units.tr: Orthodoxæ fidei lib. 4. cap. 18. 9 Every Scripture divinely inspired is altogether useful. Wherefore it is the best course, and most conducive to the soul, to search the divine Scriptures. For as a tree planted beside the course of waters, so the soul watered by divine Scripture is made fat and bears the ripe fruit of the orthodox faith, and is adorned with ever-green leaves, that is, with actions pleasing to God. For to studious action and contemplation

units.la: k De gestis Reg. Angl. lib. 1. vid. cap. 47. l In Dialogo præfixo Ranulphi Cestr. Polychronico. m Vid. Holinglhed. pag. 130. & Fox. in Evangelia Saxonica. n Præfat. in Evang. Anglo-Saxon. ad Eliz. Reginam. o Cent. 1. cap. 1.
units.tr: k On the Deeds of the Kings of England, book 1, see chapter 47. l In the dialogue prefixed to the Polychronicon of Ranulph of Chester. m See Holinshed, p. 130, and Foxe on the Anglo-Saxon Gospels. n Preface to the Anglo-Saxon Gospels, addressed to Queen Elizabeth. o Century 1, chapter 1.

units.la: 9 Πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος ὠφέλιμος πρὸς διδασκαλίαν... Ἐν τούτοις διείχομεν... ἐὰν ἐν ἅμῳ φιλομαθὴς, ἐπίμενε ... πολιμαθὴς, &c. πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτὸν ... ἐν ἀρετῆς ... γραφῶν, &c. platonem sinceram ex divinis Scripturis apti evadimus. Nam virtutis omnis exhortationem, & omnis vitii aversionem in illis comperimus. Si igitur fuerimus discendi cupidi; erimus & multa discentes. Nam diligentia & labore, & indultoris Dei gratia diriguntur omnia; qui enim petit, accipit; & qui quærit, invenit; & pulsanti aperitur. Pulsemus igitur ad pulcherrimum hortum Scripturarum, suavissimum, dulcissimum, venustissimum, &c.
units.tr: 9 Every Scripture divinely inspired is profitable for teaching [Πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος ὠφέλιμος πρὸς διδασκαλίαν...]. In these matters we differ... if you are eager to learn, persevere... much learned... [...] in virtue... [...] of the Scriptures, etc. We truly become fit from the divine Scriptures. For we find in them the exhortation to every virtue and the aversion from every vice. If therefore we are keen to learn, we shall also become very learned. For all things are achieved by diligence and labour, and by the grace of the bountiful God; for he who asks receives, he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it is opened. Let us knock, then, at the most beautiful garden of the Scriptures, most sweet, most delightful, most lovely, etc.

units.la: 740. Johannes Hispalensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 740. John, Bishop of Seville.

units.la: Hic Saracenis Hispaniam obtinentibus in solatium captivorum in Hispania, Scripturam in Arabicam linguam convertit, uti notat Genebrardus p. De eodem Vasæus q in Chronico Hispaniæ ita scribit. Claruit hoc tempore præter alios Episcopos viros religiosos Hispali Johannes Episcopus, sanctitate vitæ, sacrarum literarum peritia, miraculis celebratus; qui ad doctrinam posterorum sacram Scripturam in linguam Arabicam transtulit. Hic ab Arabibus Cadit Almatran vocabatur, & sacras Scripturas Catholicis expositionibus declaravit; quas ad informationem posterorum Arabicè conscriptas reliquit, ut habet Rodericus Toletanus. r Habeo ego manu descriptum Geneseos librum cum Arabicis Commentariis; qui in numeris annorum Patriarcharum cap. 5. & 11. non sequuntur Hebraicam veritatem aut vulgatam Latinam, sed LXX. Interpretum editionem; quam ad sua usque tempora omnes Doctores Ecclesiasticos tenuisse, & in hac præcipuè annorum supputatione secutos esse confirmat Julianus Toletanus Episcopus. s Ego certè existimo hunc esse illum Johannem Hispalensem, qui circa an. 1142. ex Arabico in Latinam linguam transtulit Alfraganum, itemque Akhabitium, ac alios nonnullos Arabicos Astrologos. Quanquam Jo. Mariana t Jesuita sub Favita Hispaniæ Rege circa an. 738. claruisse velit.: qui de eo ita scribit. Johannes, Hispalensis Præsul, divinos libros lingua Arabica donabat, utriusque gentis saluti consulens, quoniam Arabicæ linguæ multus usus erat Christianis æque ac Mauris: Latina passim ignorabatur. Ejus interpretationis exempla ad nostram ætatem conservata sunt, extantque non uno loco in Hispania.
units.tr: At a time when the Saracens held Spain, he translated Scripture into the Arabic language for the comfort of the captives in Spain, as Genebrard notes. Vasaeus writes about the same man thus in his Chronicle of Spain: At this time there flourished, besides other bishops, religious men: at Seville, John, bishop, celebrated for holiness of life, skill in sacred letters, and miracles; who translated Sacred Scripture into the Arabic language for the instruction of posterity. Among the Arabs he was called Cadit Almatran, and he explained the sacred Scriptures with Catholic expositions, which he left written in Arabic for the instruction of posterity, as Rodericus Toletanus has it. I myself have a manuscript copy of the book of Genesis with Arabic commentaries, which in the numbers of the years of the Patriarchs in chapters 5 and 11 do not follow the Hebrew truth or the Latin Vulgate, but the edition of the Seventy Interpreters; Julian, bishop of Toledo, confirms that all the ecclesiastical teachers held to this edition up to their own times and followed it especially in this reckoning of years. I certainly think this is that John of Seville who, around the year 1142, translated Alfraganus from Arabic into Latin, likewise Akhabitius and several other Arabic astrologers. Yet the Jesuit John Mariana wishes him to have flourished under King Favila of Spain, around the year 738, and he writes of him thus: John, Bishop of Seville, gave the divine books in the Arabic language, consulting the salvation of both peoples, since the Arabic language was in great use among Christians as well as Moors; Latin was everywhere unknown. Examples of his translation have been preserved down to our age, and survive in more than one place in Spain.

units.la: p Chronograph. lib. 3. an. 741. q Ad an. 717. r De rebus Hispan. lib. 4. cap. 3. s Lib. 3. contra Judæos. t De rebus Hispan. lib. 7. cap. 3.
units.tr: p Chronograph, book 3, year 741. q At the year 717. r On the affairs of Spain, book 4, chapter 3. s Book 3, against the Jews. t On the affairs of Spain, book 7, chapter 3.

units.la: 780. Alcuinus Anglus.
units.tr: 780. Alcuin the Englishman.

units.la: In Ecclesiast. cap. 3. Lætari debemus in lectione sanctarum Scripturarum, ubi pascamur, & potemus de ligno vitæ, quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum.
units.tr: On Ecclesiastes, chapter 3: We ought to rejoice in the reading of the holy Scriptures, where we are fed and drink from the tree of life, which is planted beside the course of the waters.

units.la: De virtutibus & vitiis ad Guidonem cap. 5. (Isidorum imitatus lib. 3. de summo bono cap. 8.) Sanctarum Scripturarum lectio divinæ est cognitio beatitudinis. In his enim quasi in quodam speculo homo seipsum considerare potest qualis sit vel quò contendat. Lectio assidua purificat animam, &c. (ut supra, & Serm. 112. de Tempore tomo 10. Operum Augustini.
units.tr: On Virtues and Vices, to Guido, chapter 5 (imitating Isidore, On the Highest Good, book 3, chapter 8): The reading of the holy Scriptures is the knowledge of divine blessedness. For in them a man can consider himself as in a kind of mirror, what he is and whither he is heading. Constant reading purifies the soul, etc. (as above; and Sermon 112 On the Time, in volume 10 of Augustine's Works).

units.la: In 10 lib. de Divinis Officiis. Lector dicitur à legendo, eo quòd ministerium legendi habeat in Ecclesiâ. Illi traditus est codex apicum divinorum, ut distinctè ad intelligendum divinas lectiones pronuntiando, populo placeat.
units.tr: In book 10 of On the Divine Offices: A reader is so called from reading, because he has the ministry of reading in the Church. The codex of divine letters is handed to him, so that by pronouncing the divine lessons distinctly, for the sake of understanding, he may please the people.

units.la: In Psalmos Pœnitential. Expos. Psalmi CI. Hunc verò modum sanctæ orationis devotissimus Christianus servandum intelligat; ut ipsam cogitatione prosequatur, & quùm verba effundit, ipsum respiciat mente cui supplicat, omnes superfluas cogitationes excludat, quæ ab inimico ingeruntur; ut efficax oratio ex cordis charitate perveniat ad Deum, sicut Apostolus ait: Orabo spiritu, orabo & mente; psallam spiritu, psallam & mente. Tunc enim à Deo accepta est oratio canentis; si pura mens idem gerit quod explicat ore. Consentit hìc cum Bedæ sententiâ in Homiliâ Quadragesimali supra à nobis citatâ; quam etiam Alcuinus vel Paulus Diaconus Homiliario suo inseruit.
units.tr: On the Penitential Psalms, Exposition of Psalm 101: A most devout Christian should understand that this manner of holy prayer is to be observed: that he pursue it in thought, and as he pours out the words, that he regard in his mind the one to whom he prays, excluding all superfluous thoughts which the enemy throws in; so that effective prayer may come to God from the love of the heart, as the Apostle says: "I will pray in the spirit, I will pray also with the mind; I will sing in the spirit, I will sing also with the mind." For the prayer of one who sings is accepted by God only when a pure mind does in its heart what it expresses with the mouth. Here he agrees with the opinion of Bede in the Lenten Homily cited above by us, which Alcuin or Paul the Deacon also inserted into his Homiliary.

units.la: Epist. 23. ad Wiorenses Fratres, pag. 54 Tom. I. lect. Antiq. Hen. Canisii. Adsuescant pueri adstare laudibus superni Regis: Discant nunc Scripturas sanctas, ut ætate perfectâ veniente, alios docere possint. Qui non discit in pueritiâ, non docet in senectute. Recogitate nobilissimum nostri temporis magistrum, Bedam Presbyterum; quale habuit in juventute discendi studium, &c.
units.tr: Letter 23, to the Brothers at Wiorenses, p. 54, vol. I of Henry Canisius's Lectiones antiquae: Let boys become accustomed to standing by the praises of the heavenly King. Let them now learn the holy Scriptures, so that when they come to mature age they may be able to teach others. He who does not learn in boyhood does not teach in old age. Consider the most noble teacher of our time, Bede the Priest; what zeal for learning he had in his youth, etc.

units.la: Pfal. I.
units.tr: Psal. I.

units.la: 10 Spurius est iste liber, post annum à Christo millesimum scriptus.
units.tr: 10 This book is spurious, written after the year 1000 from Christ.

units.la: 792. Author Librorum Carolinorum de Imaginibus.
units.tr: 792. The author of the Caroline Books on Images.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 30: In divinæ Scripturæ libris & animæ perpetuus cibus, & præsentis vitæ doctrina, & sapientia, quæ decor est vitæ, & vitæ perpetuæ documenta continentur. Est enim thesaurus nullo bono carens, omnibus bonis abundans; ad quem quisquis devotus accedit, quicquid fideliter quærit, feliciter se adquisisse gaudet. Et post, Tu qui fidei tuæ puritatem in imaginibus conservare te dicis, supplex eis adstare memento cum thymiamatibus: nos præcepta Domini solerti indagatione perquiramus in divinæ legis codicibus. Tu luminaribus perlustra picturas; nos frequentemus divinas Scripturas.
units.tr: Lib. 2. cap. 30: In the books of divine Scripture is contained both the soul's perpetual food, the teaching of the present life, and wisdom, which is the adornment of life, and the lessons of eternal life. For it is a treasure lacking in no good thing and abounding in all good things; whoever comes to it devoutly, whatever he seeks faithfully, he rejoices to have obtained happily. And after: You who say that you keep the purity of your faith in images, remember to stand before them as suppliants with incense. Let us seek out the Lord's precepts with careful inquiry in the codices of the divine law. You go over the pictures with lamps; let us frequent the divine Scriptures.

units.la: Lib. 4. cap. 3. Multis honoribus locus iste sublimandus est, ubi à fidelibus populis undique convenitur, &c. ubi crebro suavisonus psallentium reboat concentus, ubi divinæ lectionis arentia corda irrigantes personant fluctus.
units.tr: Lib. 4. cap. 3. This place is to be exalted with many honours, where the faithful peoples gather from every side, &c. where the sweet-sounding harmony of those who sing echoes again and again, where the waves resound, watering hearts parched for the divine reading.

units.la: 807. Carolus Magnus Imp.
units.tr: 807. Charles the Great, Emperor

units.la: Cæsari Baronio planè miraculum videtur hoc sæculo rudi inventum esse Regem adeò excultum sacris literis, & in procinctu semper positum Principem veluti otiosum de rebus divinis Philosophantem. Eginhardus in vitâ ejus de eo notat Latinam linguam ita eum didicisse, ut æquè illâ ac patriâ linguâ (Teutonicâ sc.) orare fit solitus. Sanè illum omnium primum Latinis literis Germanicam linguam conscripsisse refert Johannes Stumpfius in Chronicis Helvetiorum. Idem Eginhardus: Legendi (inquit) atque psallendi disciplinam diligentissimè emendavit. Erat enim utriusque admodum eruditus; quanquam ipse nec publicè legeret, nec nisi submissim & in commune cantaret. Sigebertus etiam in Chronographiâ ita scribit. Carolus Imperator per manum Pauli Diaconi sui decerpens optima quæque de scriptis Catholicorum Patrum, Lectiones unicuique festivitati convenientes per circulum anni in Ecclesiâ legendas compilari fecit. Similiter de Paulo Diacono refert Trithemius, eum jussu Caroli ordinavisse historias & lectiones per totum annum singulis festivitatibus sanctorum congruentes; quanquam receptum est homilias illas ab Alcuino Caroli M. præceptore collectas esse. Illud verò mirum Homiliarum hujusmodi
units.tr: Caesar Baronius thinks it a plain miracle that a king so learned in Holy Scripture, always ready for battle, should have appeared in such a rude age, like a prince who philosophises about divine matters in his leisure. Eginhard, in his Life of him, notes that he learned Latin so well that he was accustomed to pray in it as well as in his native tongue, German. Indeed, John Stumpf, in his Chronicles of the Swiss, reports that he was the first to write the German language in Latin letters. Eginhard again: He carefully reformed the teaching of reading and of singing. For he was thoroughly learned in both, although he himself did not read aloud in public, and sang only in a low voice and together with the congregation. Sigebert also writes in his Chronography: The Emperor Charles, through his deacon Paul, gathered out the best passages from the writings of the Catholic Fathers and had lessons suited to each feast of the year compiled, to be read in the Church. Trithemius reports likewise of Paul the Deacon that at Charles's command he arranged histories and lessons for the whole year, fitting each feast of the saints; although it is commonly held that those homilies were collected by Alcuin, the teacher of Charles the Great. What is truly remarkable is that a collection of homilies of this kind was instituted in the Churches by wise men, if the people at that time were entirely ignorant of the Latin language. For what other use of these sermons can be imagined than the instruction of the people? And who would think it sensible for a man to preach to the people in a foreign tongue? But more has been noted about the decrees of Charles the Great, both above, where the origin of the error was discussed, and below, where the ecclesiastical decrees on this matter will be treated. Let it suffice to mention here only this: Charles was not only himself most devoted to the divine Scriptures (a praise Trithemius also gives him), but also (if we listen to Franciscus Junius) took care that the Scriptures were rendered into the vernacular tongues, so that the people might understand them. Hence Vitus Amerbach (in his dedicatory preface to the Emperor Charles V and King Ferdinand on the Constitutions of Charles the Great) says: He saw to it that the New Testament was turned into the Frankish tongue, which, as the monuments show, is our own (that is, German). Thus he. Espencaeus has similar words: Charles the Great (he says) saw to it that the New Testament was translated into the Frankish and German tongue. As for his study of the sacred letters, Charles never let a day pass in which he did not read something in histories, or in the sacred letters, or in other disciplines; so Henricus Mutius has it, German Chronicle, book 8. Hence Alcuin writes to him in a certain letter: Nothing of these things can escape your wisdom: we know you to be most learned in the holy Scriptures as well as in secular histories. A full knowledge has been given to you from all these sources, etc.

units.la: {x} Tomo 9. Annal. an. 778. sect. 19. {y} Apud Suffridum Petrum. {z} Ad an. 807. {a} De Scriptor. Eccles. in Paulo. hujusmodi collectionem in Ecclesiis à viris sapientibus institutam; si populus illo tempore Latini sermonis prorsus fuerit ignarus. Quis enim alius horum sermonum usus, quàm populi instructio, fingi potest? Hominem verò linguâ peregrinâ populo concionantem quis putet sobrium? Sed de Caroli M. constitutionibus plura annotata sunt, tum supra ubi de erroris origine actum est, tum infra ubi de Ecclesiasticis hâc in re decretis erit agendum. Illud tantùm hîc admonendum sufficiat, Carolum non modò ipsum in Scripturis divinis fuisse studiosissimum (quæ laus illi etiam à Trithemio tribuitur) sed etiam (si Franciscum Junium audiamus) Scripturas linguis vernaculis reddi curavisse, ut populus intelligeret. Unde de eo Vitus Amerbachius (Præsat. dedicatoriâ ad Carolum V. Imp. & Ferdinandum Cæsarem in Constitutiones Caroli M.) Curavit Novum Testamentum in Francicam linguam converti; quæ, ut monumenta indicant, nostra est (Germanica sc.) Hæc ille. Paria habet Espensæus . Carolus Magnus (inquit) Novum Testamentum in linguam Francicam & Germanicam converti curavit. Quod ad sacrarum verò literarum studium attinet, Carolus nullum unquam intermisit diem, quo non aliquid in historiis, vel in sacris literis vel aliis disciplinis legerit; uti de eo habet H. Mutius German. Chronic. lib. 8. Unde in epistolâ quadam sic ad eum scribit Alcuinus: Nihil horum tuam latere poterit sapientiam: ut puta in sanctis Scripturis vel sæcularibus historiis te apprime eruditum esse novimus. Ex his omnibus plena tibi scientia data est, &c.
units.tr: {x} Tom. 9 Annal., an. 778, sect. 19. {y} Cited by Suffridus Petrus. {z} At the year 807. {a} On Paulus, in De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis. Such a collection was instituted in the churches by wise men, if the people at that time were wholly ignorant of the Latin tongue. For what other use of these sermons can be imagined than the instruction of the people? Who would think a man sane who preached to the people in a foreign language? But much has been noted about the enactments of Charlemagne, both above, where the origin of the error was discussed, and below, where the ecclesiastical decrees on this matter will be treated. It is enough to remind the reader here of this alone: that Charles was not only himself most devoted to the divine Scriptures (a praise Trithemius also gives him), but also (if we listen to Franciscus Junius) took care that the Scriptures should be rendered into the vernacular tongues so that the people might understand. Hence Vitus Amerbach, in his dedicatory preface to Charles V and the Emperor Ferdinand on the Constitutions of Charlemagne, says: "He took care that the New Testament be converted into the Frankish language, which, as the monuments show, is ours" (that is, German). So he. Espensaeus has similar words: "Charlemagne took care that the New Testament be converted into the Frankish and German language." As for his zeal for sacred letters, Charles "never let a day pass without reading something in histories, or in the sacred letters or other disciplines," as H. Mutius reports in German Chronicle, book 8. Hence Alcuin writes to him in a certain letter: "Nothing of these things can escape your wisdom, for we know you to be especially learned in the holy Scriptures and in secular histories. From all these a full knowledge has been given to you," etc.

units.la: Cæterum Francicam & Germanicam eandem olim fuisse linguam, hisce verbis confirmat Vitus Amerbachius in Præfatione supra laudatâ. Verum est Caroli Magni temporibus unum quoddam regnum fuisse bonam & Germaniæ & Galliæ partem, ac deinde inter successores factam ejus divisionem, procedentibusque temporibus magis ac magis & ipsos homines inter se alienatos ac separatos esse moribus & linguâ. Sunt enim & multa & magna indicia, Caroli temporibus ut in eâ parte Italiæ quæ Gallia Togata vocatur, sic etiam longè latéque in Galliis Germanicam linguam in usu fuisse: ac ut Longobardi paulatim peregrinam linguam, sive propter vicinitatem, sive pudore quodam, aut affectatione adsciverunt, ita fecisse totam Galliam. Quod autem vera Francia, & tanquam caput, aut sive domicilium, sive arx Francorum, fuerit ea pars Germaniæ, quam nunc tenet Episcopus Virtspurgensis, vel hoc testatur; quòd sola nomen de vetere Franciâ perpetuum,
units.tr: Moreover, that Frankish and German were formerly the same language, Vitus Amerbach confirms in the preface cited above, in these words: "It is true that in the times of Charlemagne there was one kingdom comprising a good part of Germany and of Gaul, and afterwards division was made among his successors, and as time went on the peoples themselves became more and more estranged and separated from one another in customs and language. For there are many and great indications that in Charlemagne's times, just as in that part of Italy called Cisalpine Gaul, so too the German language was in use far and wide in the Gauls; and just as the Lombards gradually adopted a foreign language, whether from proximity or from some shame or affectation, so did all of Gaul. That true France, and as it were the head, or the seat or citadel, of the Franks was that part of Germany which the Bishop of Würzburg now holds, is attested by this alone: that it alone has kept the name of ancient France constant and perpetual"

units.la: {b} Catalog. virorum illustr. Germaniæ. {c} In Animadvers. ad 1. Controv. Bellarm. de Verbo Dei lib. 2. cap. 15. sect. 44. {d} Tract. quòd Principem literæ deceant, ad Consess. Regium, sol. 98. {e} Epist. 4. tom. 1. Antiqu. Lect. ab H. Canisio edit. p. 19. constans & unum huc usque retinuerit. Quanquam non paulo fuit longior & latior, quam nunc est, olim. Praeterea qui familiam Caroli Germanis adimunt, vehementer falluntur. Praeter enim ea, quae jam dicta sunt, quid (obsecro) volunt sibi nomina Pipini, Berthradae, Caroli, Ludovici, Ruothrulis, Berthae, Theoderatae; quae manifeste omnia sunt Germanica, etsi nonnihil a scriptoribus detorta? Huc facit, quod & nomina mensibus impositi Carolus, quibus adhuc utimur ex magna parte, idque (ut est in historiis) lingua patria, quae, cum nomina sint nostra (i. e. Germanica) sine dubio nostra est: & curavit Novum Testamentum in Francicam linguam converti; quae, ut monumenta indicant, nostra est. Vehementer autem ineptiunt, qui vocant hoc in dubium, Germanicane sint vocabula, quae ita inveniuntur, an Francorum; quasi diversa gens fuerit a Germanis: aut putant veterem Germanorum linguam prorsus aliam fuisse, quod jam non fit paulo, quam olim fuerit, alia. Quasi vero desierit esse Latina lingua propterea, quod longe aliter vetustissimi Latini sunt locuti, aliter Ciceronis tempore; aut Suevi non loquantur Germanice, quod aegre a Saxonibus intelliguntur, vel contra Saxones eandem ob causam. Hactenus Vitus Amerbachius.
units.tr: {b} Catalogue of Illustrious Men of Germany. {c} In the Animadversions on the first controversy of Bellarmine, On the Word of God, book 2, chapter 15, section 44. {d} Treatise that letters befit a prince, addressed to the royal confessor, p. 98. {e} Letter 4, vol. 1, Antiquae Lectiones, edited by H. Canisius, p. 19. "...constant and has retained one name up to now, although formerly it was not a little longer and wider than it is now. Furthermore, those who deprive Charlemagne's family of its German character are gravely mistaken. For besides what has already been said, what (I beg you) do the names Pippin, Bertrada, Charles, Louis, Hruodrud, Bertha and Theoderata mean? Are they not all manifestly German, although somewhat distorted by writers? To this point also: the names Charles given to the months, which we still largely use, and that (as is in the histories) in the native tongue. Since these names are ours (that is, German), they are without doubt ours; and he took care that the New Testament be converted into the Frankish language, which, as the monuments indicate, is ours. But those who call into doubt whether these words, found in this form, are German or Frankish are very foolish, as if the Franks were a different people from the Germans, or as if they think the old German language was entirely different from what it was then, which has not changed by a little since it was used. As if Latin had ceased to be Latin because the most ancient Latins spoke quite differently from the time of Cicero, or as if the Swabians did not speak German because the Saxons scarcely understand them, or conversely the Saxons for the same reason." Thus far Vitus Amerbach.

units.la: 810. Ludovicus Pius Imp. Caroli M. filius.
units.tr: 810. Ludovicus Pius, Emperor, son of Charlemagne.

units.la: Imperator iste Pius non fuit ipse solum in omnibus Scripturis diligentissime versatus (quod in ejus gestis prodit Theganus) sed etiam in Germanicam linguam ligata oratione easdem curavit verti, ut rudiorum memoriae consuleretur. Ita enim de eo Praefatio f in librum antiquum lingua Saxonica conscriptum commemorat. 11 Cum divinorum librorum (inquit Praefationis Author) solummodo literati atque eruditi prius notitiam haberent (hinc non videtur Caroli M. jussu Scriptura translata, ut narrat Junius, nisi Francica & Theotisca diversae sint linguae, quod verisimile est) ejus studio atque imperii tempore, sed Dei omnipotentia atque inchoantia mirabiliter actum est nuper, ut cunctus populus suae ditioni subditus, Theudisca loquens lingua, ejusdem divinae lectionis nihilominus notionem acceperit. Praecepit namque cuidam viro de gente Saxonum, qui apud suos non ignobilis vates habebatur; quatenus non solum literatis, verum etiam illiteratis sacra divinorum praeceptorum lectio pan-
units.tr: This Emperor Louis the Pious was not only himself most diligent in all the Scriptures (as Thegan reports in his deeds), but he also saw to it that they were translated into the German language in verse, so that the memory of the less learned might be served. For so the preface of an ancient book written in the Saxon language records it, in this way: When formerly only the literate and learned had knowledge of the books of the divine law (here it does not seem that Scripture was translated by the command of Charlemagne, as Junius relates, unless the Frankish and Theotisc are different languages, which is likely), it was done wonderfully, recently, by the zeal and in the reign of Charlemagne, but by the omnipotence and inspiration of God, so that the whole people subject to his rule, speaking the Theudisc tongue, likewise received knowledge of the same divine reading. For he instructed a certain man of the Saxon people, who was held among his own as no ignoble poet, that the holy reading of the divine precepts should be spread abroad not only to the literate but also to the illiterate.

units.la: f In 9. libro Catalogi Testium Veritt.
units.tr: f In the 9th book of the Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth.

units.la: 11 Eandem edidit Andr. Quercetanus, Tom. 2. Scriptor. Franc. pag 326. deretur. Qui jussis Imperialibus libenter obtemperans, nimirum eò facilius, quò desuper admonitus est prius, ad tam difficile tamque arduum se statim contulit opus; potius tamen confidens de adjutorio obtemperantiæ, quàm de suæ ingenio parvitatis. Igitur à mundi creatione initium capiens, juxta historiæ veritatem quæque excellentiora summatim decerpens, & interdum quædam, ubi commodum duxit, mystico sensu depingens, ad finem totius Veteris ac Novi Testamenti interpretando more poetico satis facetà eloquentiâ perduxit. Quod opus tam lucidè tamque eleganter juxta idioma illius linguæ composuit, ut audientibus atque intelligentibus non minimam sui decoris dulcedinem præstet. Juxta morem vero illius poematis omne opus per vitteas distinxit, quas nos lectiones vel sententias possumus appellare. Ferunt eundem Vatem, dum adhuc artis hujus esset penitus ignarus, in somnis esse admonitum, ut sacræ legis præcepta ad cantilenam propriæ linguæ congruâ modulatione coaptaret. Quam admonitionem nemo veram esse ambigit, qui hujus carminis notitiam, studiumque ejus compositoris, atque desiderii anhelationem habuerit. In eandem sententiam habentur versus de Poetâ & interprete hujus Codicis.
units.tr: 11 Andreas Quercetanus published the same, vol. 2 of the Scriptores Franci, p. 326. Obeying the imperial commands willingly, and all the more easily because he had first been admonished from above, he at once turned to this task, so difficult and so arduous; trusting, however, rather in the help of obedience than in the smallness of his own talent. Beginning, therefore, from the creation of the world, and briefly picking out whatever is more excellent according to the truth of history, and sometimes depicting certain things with a mystical sense where he thought fit, he brought the interpretation down, in poetic manner and with fairly graceful eloquence, to the end of the whole Old and New Testament. He composed this work so clearly and so elegantly in the idiom of that language that it offers no small sweetness of its beauty to those who hear and understand it. Indeed, following the custom of that kind of poem, he divided the whole work into verses, which we may call lessons or sentences. They report that this same bard, while still wholly ignorant of this art, was admonished in his sleep to fit the precepts of the sacred law to the song of his own language with a suitable melody. No one who has known this poem, and the zeal of its composer, and his longing, doubts that this admonition was true. To the same effect there are verses about the poet and interpreter of this codex.

units.la: Mox divina polo resonans vox labitur alto;O quid agis Vates! cur cantûs tempora perdis? Incipe divinas recitare ex ordine leges, Transferre in propriam clarissima dogmata linguam. Nec mora post tanti fuerat miracula dicti, Qui prius agricola, mox & fuit ille poeta. Tunc cantûs nimio Vates perfusus amore, Metrica post doctâ dictavit carmina linguâ. Cæperat à primâ nascentis origine mundi, Quinque relabentis percurrens tempora secli, Venit ad adventum Christi, qui sanguine mundumFaucibus eripuit tetri miseratus Averni.
units.tr: Soon a divine voice sounding from the high heaven slipped down: "O Bard, what are you doing? Why do you waste the time for singing? Begin to recite the divine laws in order, to transfer the most brilliant doctrines into your own tongue." Nor after the miracle of so great a word was there delay: he who had been a farmer soon became also a poet. Then the bard, drenched with excessive love of song, afterwards dictated metrical songs in his learned tongue. He began from the first origin of the newly born world, running through the five times of the slipping age, and came to the coming of Christ, who with his blood snatched the world from the jaws of the foul Avernus, having taken pity on it.

units.la: Ludovicus Imp. anno 842. moriturus filio Lothario coronam, ensem, Evangelium auro gemmisque redimitum legavit; quemadmodum testatur Author qui illius temporibus vixit, in Annalibus à Justo Reubero editis, pag. 65.
units.tr: Louis the Emperor, about to die in the year 842, bequeathed to his son Lothair the crown, the sword, and the Gospel adorned with gold and gems; as the author who lived in his times testifies, in the Annals edited by Justus Reuber, p. 65.

units.la: * In 3. Lib. Regum, cap. 19. Sicut corpus sine alimento corporali subsistere nequit; ita nec anima vivere potest sine verbo Dei.
units.tr: On the 3rd Book of Kings, chap. 19. Just as the body cannot subsist without bodily food, so neither can the soul live without the word of God.

units.tr: 834. Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt.

units.la: In Psal. XXII. Sicut animalia in pascuis reficiuntur; ita fideles animæ divinis Scripturis impinguantur.
units.tr: On Psalm 22. Just as animals are refreshed in pastures, so the faithful souls are fattened on the divine Scriptures.

units.la: In Psal. XXXII. Sicut aquæ, quæ sunt in utre, coarctantur ne exeant; sic justi positi in Ecclesiâ divinæ paginæ instructione coarctantur, ut nomisi eo permittente, qui posuit, egredi valeant.
units.tr: On Psalm 32. Just as waters that are in a bottle are confined lest they go out, so the righteous, placed in the Church, are confined by the instruction of the divine page, so that they cannot go out except by the permission of him who placed them there.

units.la: In Psal. CL. Frequenti meditatione Scripturarum supervacuæ fugantur cogitationes.
units.tr: On Psalm 150. By frequent meditation on the Scriptures, idle thoughts are put to flight.

units.la: In 1 Corinth. XIV. 12 Profero symbolum Græcè, quia sic reperi illud scriptum; & sum Latinus, non Græcus; barbarus tibi sum. Iterum. Si tu Græci Sermonis aliquid didicisti, & cæperis similiter loqui; qui primùm tibi videbar barbarus, cerno te quasi barbarum mihi. Item, Dicitur idiota propriam linguam tantummodò sciens in qua natus & nutritus est. Si igitur talis astiterit tibi, dum aut mysterium missæ solenniter celebras, aut sermonem facis, aut etiam benedictionem tribus; quando respondebit verbum confirmatorium, quod dicitur Amen; cùm ille tantùm linguæ propriæ peritus, ignoret, quod tu barbarè illi loquaris.
units.tr: On 1 Corinthians 14:12. I bring forward a symbol in Greek, because I found it so written; and I am a Latin, not a Greek; I am a barbarian to you. Again: If you have learned something of the Greek speech, and have begun to speak similarly, I who at first seemed to you a barbarian, see you as a barbarian to me. Likewise: The idiot is one who knows only his own language, in which he was born and brought up. If, therefore, such a man stands by you, while you either celebrate the mystery of the Mass solemnly, or preach a sermon, or even give the blessing to the three; when the confirming word, which is called Amen, is to be answered, since he, skilled only in his own tongue, does not know that you speak barbarously to him.

units.la: In Coloss. III. In gratiâ cantantes.] i. e. semper reddite Deo gratias; ita ut quod ore canitis, corde intelligatis, & mens concordet voci.
units.tr: On Colossians 3. Singing in grace: that is, always give thanks to God; so that what you sing with the mouth, you understand with the heart, and the mind agrees with the voice.

units.la: 810. Rabanus Maurus.
units.tr: 810. Rabanus Maurus.

units.la: De Institutione Clericorum lib. 1. cap. 11. de Lectore agens, Iste doctrinâ & libris debet esse imbutus, sensuumque & verborum scientiâ perornatus; ut distinctè & apertè sonans audientium corda possit instruere. Lib. 2. cap. 52. ea omnia habet, quæ supra produximus ex Isidoro de Officiis Ecclesiast. lib. 1. cap. 10. & lib. 2. cap. 11. Lib. 3. cap. 3. eandem prorsus habet sententiam, quam supra ex Augustino protulimus de doctr. Christ. lib. 2. cap. 5. Cap. 6. sententiam habet Augustini lib. 2. de doctr. Christ. cap. 8. cap. 9. ait: Si ipsius linguæ nostræ, i. e. Latinæ, aliqua verba locutionesque ignoramus; legendi consuetudine audiendique innotescunt.
units.tr: In De Institutione Clericorum, book 1, chapter 11, where he treats of the reader, he writes: He ought to be steeped in teaching and in books, and adorned with knowledge of meanings and words, so that, speaking distinctly and clearly, he can instruct the hearts of his hearers. In book 2, chapter 52, he has all the things that we have quoted above from Isidore, On the Offices of the Church, book 1, chapter 10, and book 2, chapter 11. In book 3, chapter 3, he holds exactly the same opinion that we quoted above from Augustine, On Christian Teaching, book 2, chapter 5. In chapter 6 he holds the view of Augustine, On Christian Teaching, book 2, chapter 8. In chapter 9 he says: If we do not know some words and phrases of our own language, that is, Latin, they become known through habitual reading and listening.

units.tr: In a letter to a certain abbot: The divine wisdom that shines forth in holy Scripture is a healing medicine for all, for the powerful as well as the weak, for the wise as well as

units.la: Idem lib. 5. de Sermonum proprietate, cap. 1. & lib. 3. de Institutione Cleric. cap. 7. citatur à Magdeburgensibus Centur. 9. col. 301. quod conferatur cum Anastasii sententia de 72. linguis. (anno 560.)
units.tr: The same work, On the Proper Meaning of Words, book 5, chapter 1, and On the Institution of Clerics, book 3, chapter 7, is cited by the Magdeburg Centuriators, Century 9, column 301, where it should be compared with the view of Anastasius on the seventy-two languages (in the year 560).

units.la: Lib. 5. de sermonum proprietate, scribit Rabanus, Libros S. Scripturæ esse numero septuaginta duo. Et quomodo septuaginta duae linguae in hoc mundo erant diffusæ; congruè providit Spiritus Sanctus, ut tot libri essent, quot nationes; quibus populi & gentes ad percipiendam fidei gratiam ædificarentur. Notatu digniora sunt quæ lib. 3. de Institut. Cleric. 8 cap. 7. habentur In his omnibus libris (sc. S. Scripturæ) timentes Deum & pietate mansueti, quærunt voluntatem Dei; cujus operis & laboris prima observatio est, ut diximus, nosse istos libros, & si nondum ad intellectum; legendo tamen vel mandare memoriæ, vel omnino incognitos non habere. Deinde illa, quæ in eis aperte posita sunt, vel præcepta vivendi, vel regulæ credendi, solertius diligentiúsque inveniganda sunt: quæ tanto quisque plura invenit, quanta est intelligentia capacior. In his enim quæ aperte in Scripturis posita sunt, inveniuntur illa omnia, quæ continent fidem, morecque vivendi, spem scilicet atque charitatem. Cùm verò 13 factâ quâdam familiaritate cum ipsâ linguâ divinarum Scripturarum; in ea, quæ obscura sunt, aperienda & discutienda pergendum est, &c.
units.tr: In On the Proper Meaning of Words, book 5, Rabanus writes that the books of holy Scripture number seventy-two. And just as seventy-two languages were spread through this world, the Holy Spirit fittingly provided that there should be as many books as there are nations, by which peoples and gentiles might be built up to receive the grace of faith. More worthy of note are the things in On the Institution of Clerics, book 3, chapter 7: In all these books (namely of holy Scripture) those who fear God and are gentle in piety seek the will of God. The first step of this work and labour, as we have said, is to know these books, and, if not yet to understand them, at least to commit them to memory by reading, and not to leave them altogether unknown. Then what is plainly set down in them, whether precepts for living or rules of belief, must be sought out more diligently and skilfully; and each person finds more of these in proportion as his understanding is greater. For in what is plainly set down in the Scriptures, all those things are found which contain the faith and the manner of living, namely hope and charity. But when, by a certain familiarity already gained with the very language of the divine Scriptures, one proceeds to open up and examine what is obscure in them, etc.

units.la: 830. Amalarius Lugdunensis Diaconus.
units.tr: 830. Amalarius of Lyons, Deacon.

units.la: De Ecclesiast. Offic. lib. 2. cap. 8. Episcopus in oratione suâ ad Lectorem dicit; ut assiduitate lectionum sit aptus pronunciare verba vitæ, & mentis ac vocis distinctione populo monstrare intelligibilia.
units.tr: On Ecclesiastical Offices, book 2, chapter 8. The bishop, in his prayer to the reader, says that he should be fit, through constant reading, to pronounce the words of life and, by distinguishing mind and voice, to show the people what is intelligible.

units.la: Ibid. lib. 3. cap. 9. Hàc salutatione Episcopi & responsione populi intelligimus unum debere esse affectum Episcopi & populi, sicut hospitum unius domus, &c. De benedictione dicit Apostolus, Si benedixeris spiritu, qui supplet locum idiotæ, &c. Hanc benedictionem vocat Ambrosius orationem, dicens, Imperitus enim audiens quod non intelligit, nescit finem orationis, & non respondet Amen, id est, verum, ut confirmetur benedictio. Per hos enim impletur confirmatio precis, qui respondent Amen.
units.tr: Ibid., book 3, chapter 9. From this greeting of the bishop and the people's response we understand that the bishop and the people should have one feeling, like the members of one household, etc. The Apostle speaks of the blessing: "If you bless with the spirit, how shall he who fills the place of the unlearned man..." Ambrose calls this blessing a prayer, saying: "For the unskilled listener, who does not understand what he hears, does not know the end of the prayer, and does not answer Amen, that is, 'true,' so that the blessing may be confirmed. For the confirmation of the prayer is completed by those who answer Amen."

units.la: De rebus Ecclesiast. cap. 7. de Gothis loquens. Et, ut historiae testantur, postmodum studiosi illius gentis divinos libros in suae locutionis proprietatem transtulerunt; quorum adhuc monumenta apud nonnullos habentur. Et fidelium fratrum relatione didicimus, apud quasdam Scytharum gentes, maximè Tomitanos, eâdem locutione divina hactenus celebrari officia.
units.tr: On Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 7, speaking of the Goths. And, as the histories bear witness, afterwards the studious men of that nation translated the divine books into the proper form of their own speech; some monuments of which are still kept by some people. And from the report of faithful brothers we have learned that among certain tribes of the Scythians, especially the Tomitani, the divine offices have hitherto been celebrated in that same language.

units.la: Glossa Ordinaria in I. Paralipom. cap. 16. Hodie orantibus sacerdotibus respondetur Amen; ut concordet in precibus pia sacerdotum intentio, & populi sana devotio; secundum illud, Amen, Amen, dico vobis, quia si duo ex vobis consenserint super terram; ex omni re quamcunque petierint, fiet illis.
units.tr: Gloss on 1 Chronicles 16. Today, when the priests pray, the response Amen is given, so that the devout intention of the priests and the sound devotion of the people may agree in their prayers, according to the saying: "Amen, amen, I say to you, that if two of you agree on earth concerning anything they shall ask, it shall be done for them."

units.la: Eadem in 1 Cor. XIV. Qui enim loquitur linguâ. ] 14 Incognitâ & peregrinâ. Hoc autem fiebat; quando linguâ loquens, se non intelligebat, &c. Dum verò non intelliguntur (verba prolata) dicuntur in spiritu, non in mente. Non hominibus loquitur. ] Non intelligentiae hominum. Sed Deo. ] Cujus laudes dicit. Nemo enim audit. ] Intelligit. ——Eritis enim in aera loquentes. ] Non ad corda hominum, quasi diceret, Inutiliter agetis. Si ergo nescio virtutem vocis. ] Interpretationem significationis, quam profero. Ero ei, ] quem instruere debeo, Cui loquor, barbarus. ] Non intellectus. Et qui loquitur. ] Instruitur vel audit. Mihi barbarus. ] Non intellectus. Quia nec ipse me, nec ego ipsum intelligo. Orabo ] loquar. Spiritu] Voluntate, vel linguâ per spiritum datâ. Orabo & mente. ] Intelligentiâ mentis. Caeterum si benedixeris spiritu. ] Linguâ per spiritum datâ; i. e. sine interpretatione, quatenus aliis clarescat quod loqueris. Quis supplet locum idiotae. ] Illiterati & rudis; qui nullam praeter propriam intelligit linguam.
units.tr: The same on 1 Corinthians 14, "For he who speaks in a tongue." 14 Unknown and foreign. This happened when a man speaking in a tongue did not understand himself, etc. But when the words uttered are not understood, they are said in the spirit, not in the mind. "Does not speak to men": not to the understanding of men, "but to God," whose praises he speaks. "For no one hears": understands. "For you will be speaking into the air": not to the hearts of men, as if he were saying, "You will be acting in vain." "If therefore I do not know the power of the voice": the interpretation of the meaning that I utter. "I shall be to him" whom I ought to instruct, "to whom I speak, a barbarian": not understood. "And he who speaks": is instructed or hears. "To me a barbarian": not understood, because neither does he understand me nor do I understand him. "I will pray" (or speak) "with the spirit": by will, or by the tongue given through the spirit. "I will pray also with the mind": by the understanding of the mind. "But if you bless with the spirit": with the tongue given through the spirit, that is, without interpretation, so that what you say may be made clear to others. "Who fills the place of the unlearned": the untaught and rude man, who understands no language except his own.

units.la: Eundem ad annum 560. Cl. Usserius supra reposuit. cap. 2. Verùm opus istud posterioris aevi est; quippe in quo Nicephorus Patriarcha CP. citatur. suo nova & vetera. 16 Resp. Scribam dicit, eum qui per laboriosam divinarum Scripturarum lectionem sibi recondit thesaurum Veteris & Novi Testamenti, & ex eo expromit tempore disputationis. Quamobrem quicunque sunt imperiti divinarum Scripturarum, non possunt esse patresfamilias, ut qui neque à se habeant, neque ab aliis accipiant, sed seipsos decipiant, pereuntes fame ignorationis. Nam quomodo fieri non potest ut terra non irrigata, etiamsi millies in eam dejiciantur semina, spicas ferat: ita etiam fieri non potest, ut animus divinis Scripturis non irrigatus, etiamsi quisquam mille verba effundat, ullum fructum ostendat. Magnum est ergo malum ignorare Scripturas, & sicut bruta animantia circumferri. Etenim oriuntur mala innumerabilia ex ignoratione Scripturarum. Hinc germinavit magna pestis haeresum, hinc vita neglecta, labores inutiles, animae caecitas, deceptio Daemonis. Quomodo enim qui hac luce sunt privati, recta non possunt ingredi; ita etiam qui divinis sunt privati Scripturis & ad earum radios non aspiciunt, saepe offendunt, & coguntur assiduè peccare; ut qui tenebras difficulter probent & examinent, &c.
units.tr: Ussher placed the same author in the year 560, above, chapter 2. But this work is of a later age, since Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, is cited in it. His new and old things. 16 Answer: he means the scribe who, through laborious reading of the divine Scriptures, stores up for himself a treasure of the Old and New Testaments, and brings it out at the time of disputation. Therefore whoever is unskilled in the divine Scriptures cannot be a householder, since they have nothing of their own and receive nothing from others, but deceive themselves, perishing from the hunger of ignorance. For just as no seed sown in unwatered ground can bear ears of grain, however often it is cast into it, so a mind not watered by the divine Scriptures cannot show any fruit, however many words it pours out. Therefore it is a great evil to be ignorant of the Scriptures, and to be carried about like brute beasts. For countless evils arise from ignorance of the Scriptures. From it has sprung the great plague of heresies; from it come a neglected life, useless labours, blindness of soul, and the deception of the devil. For just as those who are deprived of this light cannot walk straight, so those who are deprived of the divine Scriptures, and do not look toward their rays, often stumble and are constrained to sin continually; as those who with difficulty test and examine the darkness, etc.

units.tr: Concerning him, Hincmar of Reims, at the beginning of a letter written to him, cited by Flodoard in book 3 of the History of Reims, chapter 15: We give thanks to God, who has kindled your heart to his love, and has set on fire in you the knowledge of the truth and of the orthodox faith and a zeal for it. He has also given you prudence and understanding in the Scriptures inspired by God; and through your meditation upon them and practice of them, so far as the affairs of the commonwealth allow you, he will advance the eagerness of your devotion, with daily growth, to the benefit of his holy Church.
