units.la: 1 Inter Scriptores rerum Bohemic. à Frehero edit. pag. 20. & Carenthanorum scripsit, narrat Adaluinum (suo tempore Juvanienfem Archiepiscopum) Orientalis Pannoniæ Richbaldum constituisse Archipresbyterum. Qui multum tempus ibi demoratus est, (inquit) exercens suum potestative officium, sicut illi injunxit Archiepiscopus suus, usque dum quidam Græcus, Methodius nomine, noviter inventis Slavinis literis linguam Latinam doctrinamque Romanam atque literas auctorabiles Latinas Philosophicè superducens, vilescere fecit cunctò populo ex parte Missas & Evangelia, Ecclesiasticumque Officium illorum, qui hoc Latinè celebraverunt. Quod ille ferre non valens sedem repetivit Juvamensem. Idem habet Bernardus k Monachus in Krembsmonster, qui circa ann. 1180. de origine Bavarorum scripsit. Post hunc (Osbaldum) inquit, interjecto tempore aliquo supervenit quidam Slavus ab Histriæ & Dalmatiæ partibus, nomine Methodius; qui adinvenit Slavinicas literas, & Slavicè celebravit divinum officium, & vilescere fecit Latinum. Tandem sugatus à Charentanis partibus intravit Moraviam, ibique quiescit. Similiter Jo. Aventinus lib. 4. Annalium l Boiorum. Eâdem tempestate (inquit) Methodius Philosophus Venedas invenit literas, vertitque divina oracula in vernaculum Sclavorum sermonem, persuafitq; populsribus Dalmatiam incolentibus, ut explosâ linguâ Latinâ, exhibilato ritu Romano, suum consecraret eloquium. Posthæc in regnum Boiariæ perrexit, in Liburniâ, Noricò, Pannoniisque Venedis habitantibus idem persuasurus. Richovalda sacrificulus Pontifex, Adeluinus Archimyftes Salisburgensis, item Juvanenses Sacerdotes, qui hactenus in superioribus regionibus ex decreto Caroli M. per quinque & octoginta annos rebus divinis præfuerant, sacrificia privata, publica procurârant, religionem interpretati fuerant; reges adeunt, concionibus, epistolis, populum concitant adversus Methodium; qui regno Boiariæ factione Juvanensium Mystarum pulsus, in Moraviam aufugit. Hactenus Aventinus. Martinus Cromerus m à Methodio & Cyrillo Episcopis illud effectum esse scribit, assentiente Pontifice Maximo, ut Slavis suâ linguâ in sacris uti liceret. Quâ de re narrationem hujusmodi habet Æneas Sylvius n. Ferunt Cyrillum, quùm Romæ ageret, Romano Pontifici supplicâsse; ut Sclavorum linguâ, ejus gentis hominibus, quam baptizaverat, rem divinam faciens uti posset. De quâ re dum in sacro senatu disceptaretur; essentque non pauci contradictores, auditam vocem tanquam de cælo in hæc verba missam o: Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum, & omnis lingua confiteatur ei; indeque datum Cyrillo indultum. units.tr: 1 among the writers of Bohemian and Carinthian history edited by Freher, p. 20, relates that Adaluinus (at that time Archbishop of Salzburg) appointed Richbaldus archpriest of Eastern Pannonia. He stayed there a long time, (the author says), exercising his office with authority, as his archbishop had commanded him, until a certain Greek named Methodius, having invented Slavonic letters and bringing in the Latin language, Roman doctrine and the authoritative Latin writings in a philosophical manner, made the Masses and Gospels and the Church office of those who celebrated them in Latin fall into contempt among all the people, in part. Unable to bear this, he returned to his see at Salzburg. Bernard, a monk at Krems-Münster, who wrote about the origin of the Bavarians around the year 1180, says the same: After this Osbald, (he says), some time passed, and there arrived a certain Slav from the parts of Istria and Dalmatia, named Methodius; he invented Slavonic letters, celebrated the divine office in Slavonic, and made the Latin office fall into contempt. At last, driven out from the regions of the Carinthians, he entered Moravia and rests there. Likewise John Aventinus, in book 4 of his Annals of the Bavarians: At that same time, (he says), Methodius the philosopher invented letters for the Wends, and translated the divine oracles into the Slavic vernacular, and persuaded the peoples living in Dalmatia that, having cast out the Latin tongue and abandoned the Roman rite, they should consecrate their worship in their own speech. Afterwards he made his way into the kingdom of Bavaria, intending to persuade the Wends living in Liburnia, Noricum and Pannonia likewise. The priest Richovald, the high priest Adeluinus, archbishop of Salzburg, and likewise the priests of Juvavum, who until then in the upper regions, by decree of Charlemagne, had presided over the divine rites for eighty-five years, had arranged private and public sacrifices and had interpreted religion; they approached the kings, and stirred up the people by sermons and letters against Methodius, who, driven out of the kingdom of Bavaria by the faction of the Juvavian mystics, fled into Moravia. So far Aventinus. Martin Cromer writes that this was brought about by the bishops Methodius and Cyrillus, with the Supreme Pontiff agreeing, that the Slavs might be permitted to use their own language in sacred things. Æneas Sylvius gives an account of this matter in this form: They say that Cyrillus, while he was at Rome, begged the Roman Pontiff that he might be allowed to perform the divine rites in the Slavic language for the men of that nation whom he had baptized. While this matter was being debated in the sacred senate, and there were not a few objectors, a voice was heard as if sent from heaven in these words o: Let every spirit praise the Lord, and every tongue confess to him; and thereupon the permission was granted to Cyrillus. The voice truly came from heaven.

XIV. 11. stis. Unde igitur profecta illa vox Tridentini Conciliabuli, tantùm tribus linguis Ecclesiam contentam esse debere? Eandem historiam explicatiùs proponit Jo. Dubravius Olomuzensis Episcopus. Nascitur Borivorio (Boemiae Duci) ex Lugmillà filiolus nomine Boleslaus, Methodioque praesuli tingendus ungendusque offertur. Ibi Boiemi Methodium adoriuntur, ab ipso exigentes, ne sermone Latino, quem non intelligerent, sed Boiemo sibi usitato sacra & sacramenta perageret. Hanc rem ille Romam ad Cyrillum collegam, atque is ad Nicolaum Romanum Pontificem retulit. Ambo collegae ob eam relationem non Pontifici modò sed frequenti etiam Patrum Concilio deridendos se propinaverunt: cùm ecce tibi de improviso vox haec sua sponte in tali frequentiâ sonuit: Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum, & omnis lingua confiteatur eum. Quâ voce perculsus Romanus Pontifex secundùm petitionem Boemorum respondendum Cyrillo duxit. Caeterùm non intra multos annos mos ille vernaculâ linguâ inter sacra cantandi viguit, abolente illum rursus Pontifice Romano, cùm daret Boiemis antistitem, (Nam diu saltem Boiemi à privatis sacerdotibus sacrorum religionisque disciplinam percipiebant) eidemque praescriberet, ne à ritu caeremoniisque & cantu Romano ullam in partem devium ageret. Hactenus Dubravius. Paulò aliter rem gestam narrat Matthias de Micovià in hunc ferè modum. Cirullus & Methodius missi à Michaele Graecorum Imperatore, ad postulationem Principum Slavorum, in Moraviam; cùm fundamenta jecissent ibi Christianae fidei; Evocati tandem Romam, & inquisiti quare in linguâ Slavicà divina celebrarent, & non in Latinâ, responderunt, eò quòd scriptum esset; Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum. Post altercationes ergo Romanus Pontifex permisit, ut linguâ Slavicâ celebrando laudaretur Deus, perinde atque Latinâ & Graecâ. Qui mos ad tempora mea circa Cracoviam in Ecclesiâ sanctae Crucis in Clepardiâ observatus, sed jam extinctus est; inquit ibi Michovius. Hinc Hosius de sacro vernaculè legendo; Ac ne nunc quidem fortasse desunt (ait) qui meminisse queant etiam in templo S. Crucis, quod in Clepardiâ est, Slavorum linguâ sacerdotes sacris operantes usos fuisse. Michovius quinetiam in Ecclesiis Ruthenorum linguâ Serviorum, quae est Slavonica, divina celebrari, legi, & cantari commemorat. Et Aventinus; Sacerdotes Liturniae, quae Archiduci Noricorum nostro aevo paret, adhuc ignari sunt Romanae linguae; sacrificia patrio sermone, nempe Slavorum, procurant. Azorius Jesuita : Cyrillus ante sexcentos annos à Romano Pontifice impetravit (ut refert Ae-
units.tr: {k} In the Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth, book 9. {l} p. 434, Ingolstadt edition. {m} On the affairs of Poland, book 3. {n} Bohemian History, chap. 13. {o} Ps. 67.4; 117.1; 150.6; Isa. 45.23; Rom. 14.11. Whence, then, came that voice of the Tridentine conciliabulum, that the Church ought to be content with only three languages? John Dubravius, bishop of Olomouc, sets out the same story more fully: To Borivoj, Duke of Bohemia, a little son named Boleslaus was born of Lugmilla, and he was brought to Bishop Methodius to be baptized and anointed. There the Bohemians attacked Methodius, demanding of him that he not perform the sacred rites and sacraments in the Latin language, which they did not understand, but in Bohemian, which was familiar to them. He referred this matter to Rome, to his colleague Cyrillus, and he to Pope Nicholas. Both colleagues, because of this report, exposed themselves to ridicule not only before the Pontiff but also before a large council of the Fathers, when suddenly, as if by chance, that voice sounded of its own accord in such a gathering: Let every spirit praise the Lord, and every tongue confess him. Struck by this voice, the Roman Pontiff judged that Cyrillus should be answered according to the request of the Bohemians. Yet within not many years that custom of singing in the vernacular during sacred rites flourished, until the Roman Pontiff again abolished it, when he gave the Bohemians a bishop (for for a long time at least the Bohemians received the order and discipline of sacred things from private priests), and prescribed to him that he should not depart in any part from the rite, ceremonies and chant of Rome. So far Dubravius. Matthias of Miechów relates the event somewhat differently, in roughly this way: Cyrillus and Methodius, sent by Michael, Emperor of the Greeks, at the request of the Slavic princes, into Moravia; when they had laid the foundations of the Christian faith there; were at last summoned to Rome and asked why they celebrated the divine rites in the Slavic language and not in Latin, and they answered, because it is written: Let every spirit praise the Lord. After disputes, therefore, the Roman Pontiff permitted God to be praised in the Slavic language, just as in Latin and Greek. This custom was observed in my time near Kraków, in the church of the Holy Cross at Klepardia, but is now extinct; so Miechów says there. Hence Hosius, on reading sacred texts in the vernacular: Perhaps even now (he says) there are those who can recall that in the church of the Holy Cross at Klepardia, priests performing sacred rites used the Slavic language. Miechów also records that in the churches of the Ruthenians the divine rites are celebrated, read and sung in the language of the Serbs, which is Slavonic. And Aventinus: The priests of Liburnia, which in our age obeys the Archduke of Noricum, are still ignorant of the Roman language; they perform the sacrifices in their native speech, namely Slavonic. units.la: Exhortat. ad Leonem filium cap. 17. O fili, quemadmodum teneræ plantæ fontibus irrigatæ virescunt, floresque & fructus ferunt; ita mens tua sacrarum literarum studiis irrigata magis ac magis augescet, ac pro fructibus egregias virtutes producet. Nam corpus quidem saginatur cibis, qui alius super alium infarciuntur: animus verò sanctis sermonibus alitur ac vegetatur.
units.tr: Exhortation to his son Leo, chap. 17. O son, just as tender plants watered by springs grow green and bear flowers and fruit, so your mind, watered by the study of the sacred letters, will grow more and more and will produce excellent virtues as its fruit. For the body is indeed fattened with food, heaped one dish upon another, but the soul is nourished and strengthened by holy words.

units.la: 19 Ταῦτα τὰ ἐντολὰς παραγγελίας, ἀγαπητοί, διὰ τῆς ἀγεωπήτων μὲν πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δὲ τῆς ὑμῶν τὸ Χριστῷ μαθητῶν ἢ ἀγγελιῶν, &c. γραμμάτα εἰς ἡμᾶς, &c. hoc Gratiam Dei Theotiscè præscripsit. Versionis penè in omnibus Bibliothecis fragmenta reperiri testatur Illyricus, qui etiam Præfationem illius integram Catalogo Testium Veritatis inseruit; unde sequentia excerpsimus. A quibusdam memoriâ dignis fratribus rogatus, maximeque cujusdam venerandæ matronæ verbis nimiùm flagitantis, nomine Judith, ut partem Evangeliorum eis Theotiscè conscriberem, ut aliquantulum hujus cantûs lectione ludum secularium vocum delerem; & ut in Evangeliorum propriâ linguâ occupati 20 dulcedine, sonum intulium rerum noverint declinare, &c. Scripsi eorum precum suffultus juvamine Evangeliorum partem Francicè compositam, interdum spiritualia moraliaque verba permiscens, ut qui in illis alienæ linguæ difficultatem horrescit, hic propriâ linguâ cognoscat sanctissima verba. Denique legem suâ linguâ intelligens, inde se vel parum quid deviare mente propriâ pertimescat. Et circa finem. Est tamen conveniens, ut qualicunque modo, sive corruptâ linguâ, sive integræ artis auxilio humanum genus authorem omnium laudet; qui plectrum ei dedit linguæ, verbum in eâ suæ laudis sonare; qui non verborum adulationem politorum, sed in nobis pium cogitationis affectum, operumque pio labore congeriem, non labiorum inanem servitutem requirit. Cæterùm Otfridi Wissenburgensis ad Solomonem Episcopum Constantiensem Præfatio Evangeliorum citatur à Goldasto part. 1. Script paraenetic. pag. 390. ibid. pag. 364. ejusdem præfatio ad Hludovicum Regem, ut & pag. 372, 400. Jo. Trithemius asserit se nullum antiquius vidisse scriptum Germanicum, quam Monachi cujusdam Otfridi, Theotisci nomine, circa annum Dom. 820. idque Rythmis, ut vocant, conditum. Ipse Otfridi Evangeliorum liber (veteri Francico sermone Rythmicè conscriptus) impressus est Basileæ anno 1571. 8°. hoc titulo: Evange- licu Buch in alt Frenchischen Reimen durch Otfridum von Weistuberg Munchu S. Gallen, vor sieben hundert Jarn beschrieben, jetzt aber in den Truck verfertigt. Etiam Alamannicæ Ecclesiæ confessionem cum interlineari explicatione Germanicâ Achilles Gassarus unà cum Otfridi Evangeliorum Expositione evulgavit. [Goldastus tom. 2. Antiqu. Alaman. pag. 165.] Vid. Serarium de rebus Mogunt. pag. 655, 656.
units.tr: 19 "These commandments and injunctions, beloved, ... first through the ... and then through your Christ's disciples, or messages, etc., letters to us, etc." [Ταῦτα τὰ ἐντολὰς παραγγελίας, ἀγαπητοί, διὰ τῆς ἀγεωπήτων μὲν πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δὲ τῆς ὑμῶν τὸ Χριστῷ μαθητῶν ἢ ἀγγελιῶν, &c. γραμμάτα εἰς ἡμᾶς, &c.] He wrote this under the title Gratiam Dei Theotiscè. Illyricus testifies that fragments of this version are to be found in almost all libraries, and he also inserted its whole preface into his Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth; from it we have excerpted the following: Asked by certain brothers worthy of remembrance, and especially by the words of a certain venerable matron, excessively insistent, named Judith, that I should write down for them in German a part of the Gospels, so that by reading a little of this song I might blot out the game of secular voices, and so that, occupied with the sweetness of the Gospels in their own language, they might learn to avoid the sound of worldly things, etc. Supported by the help of their prayers, I have written a part of the Gospels composed in Frankish, mixing in now and then spiritual and moral words, so that whoever shudders at the difficulty of a foreign language in them may recognise the most holy words in his own tongue. Finally, understanding the law in his own language, he may fear to stray even a little from it in his own mind. And near the end: It is nevertheless fitting that, in whatever way, whether with a corrupted language or with the aid of a finished art, the human race should praise the author of all things; who gave to it the plectrum of language, that the word should sound his praise in it; who seeks not the flattery of polished words, but in us a devout affection of thought and a heap of works done with pious labour, not the empty servitude of lips. Moreover, the preface of Otfrid of Weissenburg to Bishop Salomon of Constance is cited by Goldast, part 1 of the Scriptores paraenetici, p. 390; the same, p. 364; his preface to King Ludwig is cited likewise at pp. 372 and 400. John Trithemius asserts that he has seen no German writing older than that of a certain monk, Otfrid, called by the name of German, from about the year of the Lord 820, and composed in what are called rhythms. The book of Otfrid's Gospels itself (written in rhyme in the old Frankish speech) was printed at Basel in 1571, in octavo, under this title: Evangelicum Buch in alt Frenchischen Reimen durch Otfridum von Weissenburg Munch zu S. Gallen, vor siebenhundert Jaren beschrieben, jetzt aber in den Druck verfertigt. Achilles Gassarus also published the Confession of the Alemannic Church, with an interlinear German explanation, together with Otfrid's Exposition of the Gospels. [Goldastus, tom. 2, Antiqu. Alaman., p. 165.] See Serarius, De rebus Moguntinis, pp. 655, 656.

Literas Sclavonicas à Constantino quodam Philosopho repertas, quibus Deo laudes debitas resonent, jure laudamus; ut in eâdem linguâ Christi Dei nostri praeconia & opera enarrentur, jubemus. Neque enim tribus tantùm, sed omnibus linguis Dominum laudare authoritate sacrâ monemur, quae praecepit dicens: Laudate Dominum omnes gentes, & collaudate eum omnes populi; & Apostoli repleti Spiritu S. locuti sunt omnibus linguis magnalia Dei. Hinc & Paulus caelestis quoque tuba insonat monens; Omnis lingua confiteatur, quia Dominus noster Jesus Christus in gloriâ est Dei patris. De quibus etiam in primâ ad Corinthios Epistolâ satis & manifestè nos admonet, quatenus linguis loquentes Ecclesiam Dei aedificemus. Nec sanae fidei vel doctrinae aliquid obstat, sive Missas in eâdem Slavonicâ linguâ canere, sive Evangelium vel lectiones divinas Novi & Veteris Testamenti, bene translatas & interpretatas legere, aut alia officia horarum omnia psallere; quoniam qui fecit tres linguas principales, Hebraeam sc. Graecam & Latinam, ipse creavit & alias omnes ad laudem & gloriam suam. Jubemus tamen ut in omnibus Ecclesiis terrae vestrae propter majorem honorificentiam Evangelium Latinè legatur, & postmodum Slavonicâ linguâ translatum in auribus populi Latina verba non intelligentis annuntietur; sicut in quibusdam Ecclesiis fieri videtur. Et si tibi & judicibus tuis placet, Missas Latinâ linguâ magis audire; praecipimus ut Latinè Missarum tibi solemnia celebrentur. Data mense Junii, Indictione 13. Quod verò ad Constantinum illum Philosophum attinet, cujus hîc fit mentio, Augustinus author Catalogi Olomucensium Episcoporum (qui subjicitur historiae Bohemicae Dubravii) hoc nomine priùs appellatum esse annotat Cyrillum Methodii Collegam; qui etiam in Inscriptione Bibliothecae Vaticanae Illyricarum literarum auctor traditur; unde & lingua ea Chiurilizza, hoc est, Cyrilliana nuncupatur, ut scribit Angelus Roccha . Quanquam Me-
units.tr: In letter 247, addressed to Sfento-pulchrum, Prince of the Moravians, which Angelus à Roccha produces from the register kept in manuscript in the Vatican Library (Appendix to the Vatican Library, p. 316), and which Baronius also gives (Annals, year 880, sect. 19): We rightly praise the Slavonic letters devised by a certain philosopher Constantine, in which praises due to God resound; and we order that in that same language the proclamations and works of Christ our God be recounted. For we are admonished by sacred authority to praise the Lord not only in three tongues but in all tongues, as the psalm commands: Praise the Lord, all nations, and let all peoples extol him together; and the Apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke the mighty works of God in all tongues. Hence Paul, too, sounds forth as a heavenly trumpet, warning: Every tongue should confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. Concerning these matters he also admonishes us, in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, sufficiently and plainly, that by speaking in tongues we should build up the Church of God. Nor does anything stand in the way of sound faith or doctrine, whether one sings the Masses in that same Slavonic language, or reads the Gospel and the divine lessons of the New and Old Testaments, well translated and interpreted, or chants all the other offices of the hours; since he who made the three principal languages, Hebrew, namely, Greek and Latin, also created all the others for his own praise and glory. Nevertheless we order that in all the churches of your land, for greater honour, the Gospel be read in Latin, and afterwards be proclaimed in the Slavonic tongue, translated, to the ears of the people who do not understand the Latin words; as seems to be done in some churches. And if it pleases you and your judges to hear the Masses in Latin rather, we direct that the solemn Masses be celebrated for you in Latin. Given in the month of June, Indiction 13. As for that philosopher Constantine, who is mentioned here, Augustine, author of the Catalogue of the Bishops of Olomouc (which is appended to the Bohemian history of Dubravius), notes that he was earlier called by this name, the colleague of Cyril and Methodius; he is also said to be the author of the Illyrian letters in the inscription of the Vatican Library, and for this reason that language is called Chiurilizza, that is, Cyrilline, as Angelus Roccha writes. units.tr: 890. Ælfred, King of the West Saxons.

units.la: 24 Præfat. in Pastorale Gregorii Saxonicum ad Wulfigeum Episcopum. Tum verò venit mihi in mentem legem Dei primò in Hebræo sermone fuisse inventam; atque postea Græcos, cùm eandem didicissent, eam universam & alios insuper omnes libros in suam linguam vertisse; necnon Latinos etiam, quamprimùm ipsi eam intelligentiâ comprehendissent, per prudentes interpretes suo sermone eandem expressisse; eodemque modo omnem undique Christianam plebem partem ejus aliquam in linguam domesticam transtulisse. Quapropter optimum censeo, si tu quoque sic existimas, ut nos libros aliquos, quos maximè necessarios arbitrabimur, qui ab omnibus intelligantur, eosdem in linguam, quam omnes intelligunt, convertamus. Hæc Ælfredus. De ejus studio sacrarum literarum vide Ingulphi Historiam pag.495. In divinis, inquit, libris, & sacrâ lectione tam assiduus erat, quòd Davidicum Psalterium vel aliquem alium librum ædificatorium in sinu suo semper secum ferret; & viros literatissimos de terris exteris ad se accersens, aliquamdiu in palatio suo secum pro sacris literis addiscendis retentos, demum diversis prælatiis & dignitatibus promoveret. Paria habet Ailredus Abbas Rievalensis y. Portionem quandam Psalterii (inquit) in qua maximè delectabatur, parvo volumine scriptam in sinu semper circumferebat; ut quod illud interius ruminabat, ab interioris hominis sui pectore non recederet. Item. In diebus pacis, non otio torpuit, aut vanis spectaculis otiosisve discursibus tempus perdidit; sed legere, & scribere, & sacros apices in linguam Anglicam vertere laborabat. Psalterii magnam partem ab eo ex Latino Anglicè conversam esse apud Joannem Trevisam z legimus. Gulielmus verò Malmsburiensis, a illumque secutus Ranulphus Ceslrensis b, de eo scribunt, Psalterium transferre aggressum, vix primâ parte explicatâ, vivendi finem fecisse. Hinc Genebrardus c & Gulielmus Eysengrein d Alfredum Psalterii versionem inchoâsse referunt; & Joannes Caius e Psalmos eundem transtulisse ex Præfatione
units.tr: 24 Preface to the Saxon translation of Gregory's Pastoral Care, addressed to Bishop Wulfsige. Then it came into my mind that the law of God was first found in the Hebrew language; and afterwards the Greeks, when they had learned it, translated the whole of it and all the other books into their own tongue; likewise the Latins too, as soon as they had grasped it with understanding, rendered it through wise interpreters into their own speech; and in the same way every Christian people throughout the world has translated some part of it into its native tongue. Therefore I think it best, if you also judge so, that we turn into the language that everyone understands certain books which we shall judge most necessary for everyone to know. So Ælfred. On his zeal for Holy Scripture see Ingulf's History, p. 495. He was, it says, so devoted to the divine books and sacred reading, that he always carried the Psalter of David, or some other edifying book, in his bosom; and summoning men most learned from foreign lands, he kept them for a while in his palace to learn the sacred letters, and at last promoted them to various prelacies and dignities. Ailred, Abbot of Rievaulx, has similar things. He always carried about in his bosom, he says, a certain portion of the Psalter in which he most delighted, written in a small volume, so that what he meditated on within would not depart from the depths of his inner man. Likewise: In days of peace he did not grow sluggish in idleness, nor waste time on vain spectacles or idle chatter; but he laboured to read, and to write, and to turn the sacred letters into the English tongue. We read in John Trevisa that a large part of the Psalter was translated into English by him from the Latin. William of Malmesbury, and Ranulf of Chester who followed him, write that he undertook to translate the Psalter, but, having scarcely explained the first part, he came to the end of his life. Hence Genebrard and William Eysengrein report that Alfred began a version of the Psalter; and John Caius says that he translated the Psalms, from the preface

units.la: 24 Habetur in Spelmanni Concil. Angl. Tom. I. pag. 380. doćti inprimis viri in Vetus Testamentum Anglicè ante annos 300. conscriptum narrat. At in Historiâ Eliensi (lib. 1. sub fine, prout citatur in præfatione præfixâ Assero de rebus gestis Ælfredi, & Caio de Antiq. Cantab. lib. 1. ubi historiæ hujus initium esse notat: Cùm animadverterem excellentiam Eliensis Insulæ) de eodem sic habetur. Aluredus acerrimi ingenii princeps per Grimbaldum & Johannem doctissimos Monachos tantum instructus est; ut in brevi librorum omnium notitiam haberet, totumque Novum (& Vetus, deest id in editis, sed habetur in Codice MS.) Testamentum in eulgiam Anglicæ gentis transmutari fecerit. Et etiamnum Cantabrigiæ in Collegii S. Benedicti Bibliothecâ Novum Testamentum Saxonicè versum habetur. Quatuor autem Evangeliorum vetus Saxonica translatio Anno 1571. Londini excusa prodiit: ubi etiam lectiones pro ratione feriarum & dierum Dominicorum distinctæ inveniuntur.. Denique Bostonus Buriensis in suo Scriptorum Catalogo (quem MS. penes me habeo) de Elfredo inquit: Totum fere Testamentum in linguam Anglicam transtulit.
units.tr: 24 It is found in Spelman's Councils of England, vol. I, p. 380. A learned man especially relates that the Old Testament was written in English about 300 years ago. But in the History of Ely (bk. 1, near the end, as cited in the preface prefixed to Asser's account of the deeds of Alfred, and in Caius, On the Antiquities of Cambridge, bk. 1, where he notes that this history begins with: Since I had observed the excellence of the Isle of Ely) the matter is stated thus: Alfred, a prince of the keenest intellect, was instructed by the most learned monks Grimbald and John, so that he had a brief knowledge of all books; and he caused the whole New (and Old, which is missing in the printed editions but is found in the manuscript) Testament to be translated into the vernacular of the English people. And still at Cambridge, in the library of St Benedict's College, a New Testament translated into Saxon is found. An old Saxon translation of the four Gospels was published in London in 1571, in which lessons are also arranged according to the feasts and Sundays. Finally, Bostonus of Bury, in his Catalogue of Writers (which I have in manuscript), says of Ælfred: He translated almost the whole Testament into the English language.

units.la: 890. Waldo Episcopus Frisingensis.
units.tr: 890. Waldo, Bishop of Freising.

units.la: Beatus Rhenanus scribit se Frisingæ in Bibliothecâ Divi Corbiniani librum insignem Evangeliorum Francicè, h. e. Germanicè versum inspexisse compositum jussu Waldonis Episcopi scriptum à Sigefrido Presbytero ante sexcentos fermè annos (ut ille inquit) quando Franci Orientales primùm ⁸ Christo dedere nomen. Titulus libri erat, Liber Evangeliorum in Theodiscam linguam versus; eratque rythmicè conscriptus. Incipit autem Author in præfatione hoc modo. Nu wil ich schreiban unser heil, Evangeliono depl: So wir nu hiar bigunnon In Frenchisga zungun.
units.tr: Beatus Rhenanus writes that at Freising, in the library of St Corbinian, he examined a notable book of the Gospels translated into Frankish, that is, into German, composed by order of Bishop Waldo and written by the priest Sigefrid some six hundred years ago (as he says), when the Eastern Franks first gave their name to Christ. The book was titled The Book of the Gospels translated into the Theodiscan tongue, and it was written in verse. The author begins his preface in this way: "Now I will write down our salvation, the Gospel's deeds. Since we have now begun, in the Frankish tongue..."

units.la: Versus hos scriptos esse primo tempore ut Franci Christo nomen dedere, colligit non levibus conjecturis Beatus Rhenanus (ait Bibliander h) Gretserus i autem spiritu Jesuitico Beatum Rhenanum reprehendit, quòd hâc notâ veteres illos Germanos seu Francos laudaret, novosque perstringeret. Perpetua laus Francorum veterum est, qui sacros libros in su-
units.tr: That these verses were written at the first time when the Franks gave their name to Christ, Beatus Rhenanus infers from no slight conjectures (says Bibliander h). Gretser i, however, with a Jesuit spirit, rebukes Beatus Rhenanus for praising those ancient Germans or Franks on this ground and disparaging the moderns. The ancient Franks have a constant praise, in that they had the sacred books

units.la: 930. Æthelstanus Anglorum Rex.
units.tr: 930. Æthelstan, King of the Angles.

units.la: Scripturas Divinas, teste Malmesburio, verti fecit in Anglosaxonicum idioma ex purissimis Hebræorum fontibus per quosdam Hebræos ad Christianismum (ut credere par est) in suo regno conversos. Ita Balæus k. Sed in Malmesburio de gestis Regum Anglorum hoc non invenitur. Forte est in libro 5. de Pontificibus, quem rarum admodum esse nostrâ ætate refert Joannes Caius.
units.tr: According to Malmesbury, he had the Divine Scriptures translated into the Anglo-Saxon language from the purest Hebrew sources, through certain Hebrews who had been converted to Christianity in his kingdom (as it is fitting to believe). So Bale. But this is not found in Malmesbury's history of the deeds of the English kings. Perhaps it is in the fifth book of his work on the Bishops, which John Caius reports to be extremely rare in our age.

units.la: 936. Arabes.
units.tr: 936. Arabs.

units.la: Natus sum (inquit Clenardus in epistolâ ad Rutgerum Rescium anno 1536. datâ) Evangeliorum Arabicorum codicem descriptum & versum abhinc annis 600. Habeo & aliud exemplar ex eâdem translatione descriptum. Reperio pleraque omnia sic se habere, ut hodie legimus in Græcorum codicibus, quos secutus est Erasmus, &c. Addit etiam reliquos sacros codices apud Arabas jam olim versos esse. Vetustissimos Codices Evangeliorum ante 500. annos Arabicè scriptorum se habuisse indicat Postellus l in epistolâ ad Giambullarium anno 1549. datâ.
units.tr: I have (says Clenardus in a letter to Rutger Rescius, dated 1536) a copy of the Arabic Gospels, written out and translated six hundred years ago. I also have another copy from the same translation. I find that almost everything stands as we now read it in the Greek manuscripts, which Erasmus followed, etc. He adds that the other sacred books were also long ago translated among the Arabs. Postel indicates that he had very ancient manuscripts of the Gospels written in Arabic more than 500 years earlier, in a letter to Giambullari dated 1549.

units.la: 940. Elias 25 Cretensis Episcopus
units.tr: 940. Elias, Bishop of Crete.

units.la: In Orationem 7. Nazianzeni, de moderandis disputationibus. Sunt igitur in fide communia, lex illa Vetus; quam priore loco posuit, ut multa comprehendentem, & antiquiorem vatibus sexdecim. Nimirum quæ comprehenduntur his, sunt universis ex æquo communia. Et paulò post, de Vetere & Novo Testamento, quatuor Evangeliis, &c. affirmat, ad omnes hæc spectare, omnibus ex æquo patere.
units.tr: In the Seventh Oration of Nazianzen, on moderating disputes: Therefore the old law is common to all in faith; which he placed first, as comprehending much and older than the sixteen prophets. Clearly, what is comprehended in these is equally common to all. And a little later, concerning the Old and New Testament, the four Gospels, etc., he affirms that these pertain to all and are open to all alike.

units.la: 950. Smaragdus Abbas. {26}
units.tr: 950. Smaragdus, Abbot. {26}

units.la: In praefat. explicationum Evangeliorum Dominical. Lectionis sacrae cognitio imbecillis baculum, nervosis arma ministrat, hostium subdolas fortiter premit insidias, & victoribus aeternas promittit coronas.
units.tr: In the preface to the explanations of the Sunday Gospels: The knowledge of sacred reading supplies a staff to the weak and arms to the strong; it bravely crushes the treacherous snares of enemies, and promises eternal crowns to the victors.

units.la: In Epist. ad Romanos, cap. 12. Renovatur sensus noster per exercitia sapientiae, & meditationem verbi Dei, & legis ejus intelligentiam: & quanto quis quotidie ex Scripturarum lectione proficit, quanto altius intellectus ejus ascendit; tanto semper novus & quotidie novus efficitur.
units.tr: On the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 12: Our mind is renewed through the exercise of wisdom, the meditation on the Word of God, and understanding of his law; and the more anyone advances each day from the reading of the Scriptures, the higher his understanding rises, so much the more is he always made new and new each day.

units.la: In Diademate Monachorum cap. 2. Sicut orationibus regimur; ita Psalmorum studiis delectamur, &c. ut supra ex Isidoro lib. 3. de summo bono, cap. 7. quae verbatim huc transtulit Smaragdus.
units.tr: In the Garden of Monks, chapter 2: As we are ruled by prayers, so we delight in the study of the Psalms, etc., as above from Isidore, book 3, On the Supreme Good, chapter 7, which Smaragdus transferred here word for word.

units.la: 954. Bosso Merseburgensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 954. Bosso, Bishop of Merseburg.

units.la: De eo Ditmari Chronicon lib. 2. pag. 24. haec habet. Hic, ut sibi commissos eo facilius instrueret, Slavonica scripserat verba; & eos Kyrie eleison cantare rogavit, exponens eis hujus utilitatem. Qui vecordes hoc in malum irrisorie mutabant.
units.tr: Of him, Ditmar's Chronicle, book 2, page 24, has this: He, so that he might more easily instruct those committed to him, had written out Slavonic words, and asked them to sing "Kyrie eleison," explaining its usefulness to them. These fools, mocking, turned it into an evil.

units.la: 975. Ædgarus Rex Angliae.
units.tr: 975. Edgar, King of England.

units.la: Semper cum Episcopis, virisque doctissimis de lege Dei & sacris literis conferebat; & quod ipse dicere poterat, subditos docere non solum verbo, sed etiam exemplo satagebat. Cumque diligenter Episcoporum, Clericorum, Monachorum vitas & mores investigatione prudentissimâ didicisset; vocatis ad se Ecclesiarum & Monasteriorum presbyteris, cum eis hujusmodi sermonem habuit, &c. [Ailredus Rivallensis in geneal. Davidis.]
units.tr: He always conferred with bishops and the most learned men about the law of God and the sacred letters; and he took pains to teach his subjects not only by word but also by example what he himself could say. And when he had diligently learned, by most prudent investigation, the lives and morals of the bishops, clergy and monks, he summoned to himself the elders of the churches and monasteries and gave them an address of this kind, etc. [Ailred of Rievaulx, in the genealogy of David.]

units.la: 980. Notkerus Labeo, Abbas S. Galli.
units.tr: 980. Notker Labeo, Abbot of St. Gall.

units.la: Transtulit in linguam Alamannicam Psalmos Davidis, & librum Job: quorum meminit in libro Benedictionum Ekkehardus Junior, S. Galli Monachus, citatus à Goldasto in fine 2. Tomi Alamannicarum Antiquitatum: ubi etiam notat Translationem istam Job periisse, Psalmorum vero apud se extare. (Vid. infra ad An. 1020. in Cunegunde
units.tr: He translated the Psalms of David and the book of Job into the Alemannic language. Ekkehard the Younger, a monk of St. Gall, mentions these in his Book of Blessings, as cited by Goldast at the end of the second volume of the Alemannic Antiquities. There Ekkehard also notes that the translation of Job has perished, but that the Psalms are still extant with him. (See below at the year 1020, under Cunigunde

units.la: {26} Illum anno 810. floruisse[?] sententia est verisimilior. Imperatrice) Atque hæc est illa Translatio, cujus meminit Joannes Stumpfius in Chronic. Helvet. ubi scribit: Notgerum S. Galli Monachum sub Abbate Bernardo Psalterium in linguam Francicam rudem adhuc & inconditam convertisse: & Joach. Vadianus lib. 2. de Collegiis & Monasteriis Germaniæ veteribus, ita scribens: Extat apud nos Sangalli Psalterium à Notkero Monacho, quem ob linguæ tarditatem Balbulum cognominárunt, in nostram (i.e. Germanicam) linguam translatum, Arnolpho imperante; tantâ verborum difficultate, ut nonnisi ab attento & immorante lectore accipi & intelligi queat. Tam dura olim & anhelans vetus illa Francorum & Alemannorum lingua fuit. Hæc ibi Vadianus: ubi etiam Orationem Dominicam & Symbolum Apostolicum, sicut in eodem Notkeri Codice Germanicè versa habebantur, describit (sicut etiam Jo. Stumpfius in Chronico) De Notkeri verò Psalterio in notis ad illum Vadiani locum Barthol. Schobingerus: Est nunc penès me in meâ Bibliothecâ; quod vulgare & publicum in usum dare recepit noster Goldastus, cum amplissimâ prisco rum verborum expositione. Nota verò Notkerum Labeonem, qui sub Burchardo Abbate S. Galli floruit, cum Notkero Balbulo, qui sub Abbate Bernardo claruit, à Joach. Vadiano, & Jo. Stumpfio perperam hic confundi.
units.tr: {26} The view that he flourished in 810 is more likely. Empress.) This is the translation mentioned by Johannes Stumpf in his Chronicle of Helvetia, where he writes that Notker, a monk of St. Gall under Abbot Bernard, translated the Psalter into the Frankish language, which was still rough and unpolished. Joachim Vadian, in book 2 of his work on the old colleges and monasteries of Germany, writes thus: "There is extant among us at St. Gall a Psalter translated into our (that is, German) language by Notker the monk, whom they nicknamed the Stammerer because of his slow speech, under the emperor Arnulf. The words are so difficult that it can be received and understood only by an attentive and patient reader. So harsh and gasping was that old language of the Franks and Alemanni." Thus Vadian. There he also describes the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed, as they were held in German in the same codex of Notker. Johannes Stumpf does likewise in his Chronicle. On Notker's Psalter, in his notes to that passage of Vadian, Bartholomew Schobinger writes: "It is now in my library, and our Goldast has undertaken to publish it for public and common use, with a very full explanation of the old words." Note, however, that Notker Labeo, who flourished under Abbot Burchard of St. Gall, is here wrongly confused by Joachim Vadian and Johannes Stumpf with Notker the Stammerer, who flourished under Abbot Bernard.

units.la: Porrò Jacobus etiam Gretserus citat antiquissimas orationis Dominicæ in Germanicam linguam Translationes: quarum duæ formulæ extant apud Vadianum lib. 2. de Collegiis Monasteriisque Germaniæ veteribus, una ex libro Notkeri descripta, altera ex libello in Sacello pervetusto Leprosorum urbis S. Galli à se reperto, quem ante annos plus minus 300. scriptum esse colligebat, tersiore jam & mitiore sermone. Aliam ab utraque diversam longè antiquiorem ipse se habere scribit Gretserus ex S. Galli Monasterio, descriptam ex Manuscripto Codice. Kero Monachus Alamannus Symbolum Apostolicum & Orationem Dominicam (circa An. 1000.) interpretatus est sermone vernaculo: quem libellum in Bibliothecâ D. Magni apud Gallopolitanos vidimus; ait Goldastus par. 1. Script. Parænetic. pag. 487. Vetus etiam Germanicus Interpres Psalmorum (circa An. 900.) alius à Notkero, citatur à Lipsio, Centur. 3. ad Belgas, epist. 44. ad Henricum Schottium: (& Goldasto part. 1. Script. Parænetic. pag. 366, 370, 372, 373, 388. (ubi notat esse Arnoldi Wachtendonkii.) 392, 397, 413, 414, 423, 453.) Psalterium vetus inquit ibi Lipsius se vidisse apud insignem & optimarum artium virum, Arnoldum Wachtendonckium, circa tempora Ludovici
units.tr: Moreover, Jacob Gretser also cites the most ancient German translations of the Lord's Prayer. Two of these forms are extant in Vadian, book 2 on the old colleges and monasteries of Germany: one copied from Notker's book, and the other from a little book that Vadian himself found in the very old chapel of the lepers in the city of St. Gall, which he judged to have been written about 300 years earlier, in a smoother and milder style. Gretser writes that he himself has another translation, quite different from both and far older, copied from a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Gall. "Kero, an Alemannic monk, translated the Apostles' Creed and the Lord's Prayer into the vernacular around the year 1000. We saw this little book in the library of St. Magnus among the people of Gallopolis," says Goldast, part 1 of the Scriptores Parænetici, p. 487. There is also an old German interpreter of the Psalms (around 900), different from Notker, cited by Lipsius in Centuria 3 ad Belgas, letter 44 to Henry Schott. (Goldast, part 1 of the Scriptores Parænetici, pp. 366, 370, 372, 373, 388, 392, 397, 413, 414, 423, 453, where he notes that it belonged to Arnold Wachtendonck.) Lipsius says there that he saw an old Psalter at the house of the distinguished man and master of the liberal arts, Arnold Wachtendonck, dating from about the time of Louis and Charles

units.la: Append. 2. ad lib. 2. Defens. Bellarm. de verbo Dei, col. 1054. & Caroli (filiorum Ludovici Pii) scriptum ante annos circiter 700. Latinum quidem, sed inter lineas ad singula verba Germanicâ interpretatione superscriptâ.
units.tr: (sons of Louis the Pious), written about 700 years ago. It was indeed in Latin, but with a German interpretation written above each word between the lines. (Appendix 2 to book 2 of the Defence of Bellarmine on the Word of God, col. 1054.)

units.la: 1000. Ælfricus Abbas Malmesburiensis 27, & eum secuta Anglosaxonum Ecclesia.
units.tr: 1000. Ælfric, Abbot of Malmesbury 27, and the Church of the Anglo-Saxons who followed him.

units.la: 28 Epistola de Clericis, seu sermone ad Clericos MS. in Bibliothecâ S. Benedicti Cantab. Ipse (Presbyter) debet dicere populo fidem Catholicam & sensum Evangelii propriâ linguâ; ne fit canis mutus sicut dixit Propheta: Canes muti non possunt latrare.
units.tr: 28 Letter on Clergy, or sermon to the clergy, manuscript in the Library of St Benet's, Cambridge. The priest must tell the people the Catholic faith and the sense of the Gospel in their own language, so that he is not a dumb dog, as the Prophet said: "Dumb dogs cannot bark."

units.la: Præfat. in Homilias de Sanctis Anglosaxonicè à se versas, in Bibliothecâ D. Rob. Cottoni, in fine. Non mihi imputetur, quòd divinam Scripturam nostræ linguæ infero. Quia arguet me precatus multorum fidelium; & maximè Æthelwerdis ducis (ealdorman) & Æthelmeri nostri; qui ardentissimè nostras interpretationes amplectuntur legitando. Sed decrevi modò quiescere post quartum librum à tali studio.
units.tr: Preface to the Homilies on the Saints, translated by him into Anglo-Saxon, in the Library of Sir Robert Cotton, at the end. Let it not be imputed to me that I render Holy Scripture into our tongue. For many faithful people will reproach me, and especially Æthelweard the duke (ealdorman) and our Æthelmer, who most eagerly embrace our translations by reading them. But I have now decided to rest from such study after the fourth book.

units.la: Incipit Præfatio Genesis Anglicè (ex Collectionibus Josselini) Ælfric munuc gnet æþelpeand ealdorman eadmodlice, þu bæde me leof þ ic rceolde þe apendan of ledene on englisc þa boc generir þa þuphte nie hepig tyme þe to tiþigenne þær, ȝ þu cpæde þa þat ic ne ponþte na mape apendan þæpe bec. &c.
units.tr: The Preface to Genesis in English (from the collections of Josselin). Ælfric, monk, greets Æthelweard the ealdorman humbly. You asked me, dear friend, to translate for you the book of Genesis from Latin into English. That task seemed to me a heavy one at the time, and you then told me that I should not think of translating any more of that book, etc.

units.la: 29 In fine verò ejusdem Epistolæ dedicatoriæ sic ait: 30 ic cpeþe nu þ ic ne deapp ne ic nelle nane boc æþteþ þirre of leden on englisc apendan.
units.tr: 29 At the end of the same dedicatory letter he says thus: 30 "I say now that I do not dare, and will not, translate any further book out of Latin into English." [ic cpeþe nu þ ic ne deapp ne ic nelle nane boc æþteþ þirre of leden on englisc apendan.]

units.tr: Written in Anglo-Saxon. Something should be said plainly, in some words of good teaching and in the meaning of the faith, for the English people, and about the Father, and about the Son, and also about the Holy Spirit, so that they may teach men to believe and to keep their Christian profession. The priest on Sundays and feast days shall declare to the people in English the meaning of the Gospel-

units.la: 27 Postea Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis. 28 Vide Auctarium. 29 Ælfricus Monachus Æthelwardo Duci salutem supplicitér precatur. Præcepisti mihi, Domine, ut librum Geneseos ex Latino sermone in Anglicum converterem. Quod opus mihi factu difficile videtur. Dixisti itaque mihi non ampliorem libri partem ver tendam, quam, &c. Vide Auctarium.
units.tr: 27 Afterwards the Archbishop of Canterbury. 28 See the Auctarium. 29 Ælfric the monk humbly prays for health to Æthelweard the duke. "You commanded me, my lord, that I should turn the book of Genesis from Latin speech into English. That work seems to me difficult to do. You therefore told me that I should not translate more than a part of the book, etc." See the Auctarium.

units.la: 30 Dico igitur, me nullum, post hanc, librum ex Latino in Anglicum converfurum. sum: pari modo orationem Dominicam & Symbolum explicabit, quotiescunque commodè potest, ad hominum contritionem; ut fidem suam cognoscant, & Christianitatem firmè retineant: seu ut ipse Ælfricus in (31) libro Canonum (citato à D. Fulcone in libro Anglicè contra Stapletonum scripto) exprimit, Constitutum est, ut Sacerdotes diebus Dominicis & festis Evangelii illius interpretationem populo in linguâ Anglicanâ proponerent. Hoc enim decretum inter Canones & Ecclesiasticas Constitutiones ex Conciliis & Patribus ad Ecclesiarum suarum administrationem à se collectas retulerunt insequentes Episcopi; quemadmodum in vetustis Canonum Codicibus, qui ad Ecclesias Cathedrales in Angliâ pertinebant, videre licet. Etsi igitur usus linguæ Latinæ in sacris jam ubique invaluerit; nondum tamen tyrannis illa obtinuit, ut populus in brutâ illâ ignorantiâ detineretur. Sed ut totus ordo divinorum officiorum tam ab indoctis quàm à doctis intelligeretur, Missalia Latino-Saxonica sunt edita; quorum unum adhuc Cantabrigiæ in Collegii S. Benedicti Bibliothecâ habetur n, cui hæc nota Anglicè præfixa cernitur. Communiter appellabant hunc Librum, Rubrum Librum Darbeiensem in montanis Provinciæ Darbeiensis partibus; ubi tantâ veneratione atque honore habitus est, ut vulgariter crederetur, quòd quicunque datâ super istum librum fide perjeraverit, mente excideret. Quinetiam Pamelius o habuisse se Sacramentorum Gregorii miræ vetustatis codicem ex Bibliothecâ Ecclesiæ Cathedralis D. Bavonis Gandavensis refert; qui officia quædam Anglis peculiaria, & quædam Missæ cantica in eam linguam interpretata continebat.
units.tr: 30 I say, therefore, that after this book I shall not translate anything more from Latin into English. In the same way he will explain the Lord's Prayer and the Creed, as often as he conveniently can, for the breaking down of people's ignorance, so that they may know their faith and firmly keep their Christianity: or as Ælfric himself expresses it in (31) the Book of Canons (cited by Dr Fulke in his book written in English against Stapleton): It is ordained that the priests should set out the interpretation of that Gospel to the people in the English tongue on Sundays and feast days. For the following bishops reported this decree among the Canons and Church Constitutions, which they had gathered from the councils and the Fathers for the government of their churches; as may be seen in the old codices of the Canons which belonged to the cathedral churches in England. Although, therefore, the use of the Latin tongue in sacred matters had already prevailed everywhere, that tyranny had not yet taken hold so that the people were kept in that brutish ignorance. But so that the whole order of the divine offices might be understood by the unlearned as well as the learned, Latin-Anglo-Saxon missals were published. One of these is still held at Cambridge in the Library of St Benet's College, with this note prefixed in English: They commonly called this book the Red Book of Derby, in the mountainous parts of the province of Derby, where it was held in such veneration and honour that it was commonly believed that whoever had sworn falsely upon this book would fall dead in mind. Moreover, Pamelius reports that he had a manuscript of the Sacraments of Gregory of great antiquity from the library of the cathedral church of St Bavo at Ghent, which contained certain offices peculiar to the English and certain Mass canticles translated into that language.

units.la: Porrò Ælfricum Genesin in linguam Saxonicam transtulisse author est Baleus. p Cantabrigiæ in Bibliothecâ S. Benedicti capita quædam Geneseos Saxonicè translata vidimus, eique præfixam exhortationem ad Scripturarum lectionem Saxonicè item exaratam; quæ ab hoc Ælfrico profecta videtur. Libri etiam quinque Mosis, Josue, & Judic. habentur in Bibliothecâ D. Rob. Cottoni ab Ælfrico Anglosaxonicè versi hoc initio, Ælfric munoc (Ælfricus Monachus) &c. uti supra ex Josselini Collectionibus retulimus.
units.tr: Moreover, Bale is the authority that Ælfric translated Genesis into the Saxon tongue. I have seen in the Library of St Benet's at Cambridge certain chapters of Genesis translated into Saxon, with an exhortation to the reading of Scripture, likewise written in Saxon, prefixed to them, which seems to have come from this Ælfric. There are also the five books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges, in the Library of Sir Robert Cotton, translated into Anglo-Saxon by Ælfric, with this opening, "Ælfric the monk" etc., as we related above from the Collections of Josselin.

units.la: Epist. ad Eberhardum Præsulem. Inter varios rerum eventus, qui humanæ solent fragilitati accidere, potentissimum ac speciale quoddam reor esse solatium, sanctarum meditationem Scripturarum: quod & Apostolica testari videtur authoritas, dum dicit Quæcunque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, &c. Hæc est illa mensa, cælestium dapium ferculis referta; quæ lassis requiem, infirmis sanitatem, lapsis recuperationem, stantibus in fide confert fortitudinem.
units.tr: Letter to Eberhard, the Prelate. Among the various events that tend to befall human frailty, I think the most powerful and special consolation is the meditation on the holy Scriptures. The apostolic authority also seems to attest this when it says: "Whatever things were written, were written for our learning," etc. This is that table, laden with the dishes of heavenly food, which gives rest to the weary, health to the sick, recovery to the fallen, and strength to those who stand in faith.

units.la: 1020. Chunegundis Imperatrix, & Confugiensis Cœ- nobii Virgines.
units.tr: 1020. Kunigunde, Empress, and the Virgins of the Convent of Confugium.

units.la: Ekkehardus junior Monachus Moguntiæ (Aribonis Archiepiscopi temporibus) commorans mandatu Imperatricis descripsit Psalterium in linguam Barbaricam, i.e. Germanicam, à Notkero Labeone Physico translatum, in privatos nimirum Imperatricis usus. Quod Opus nunc in nostrâ manu est, ait Melchior Goldastus . Imperatrix autem illa procul dubiò fuit Chunegundis, Sigefridi Comitis Palatini Rheni filia, quæ post mortem mariti Henrici Imp. anno 1025. depositis ornamentis Imperialibus vitam Monasticam professa, operabatur manibus suis, sciens scriptum esse: Qui non operatur, non manducet: quemadmodum Vitæ illius Author habet; qui de eâdem etiam hæc addit: Sponso suo [Christo] aut orans loquebatur aut psallens. Item, Semper eam legere, vel legentem audire vidisses. Et paulò post, Cùm post orationis frequentiam inter lectionis lassitudinem ancilla Christi in lecto, non plumis extructo, sed cilicio strato membra sapore gravata remisisset; puella sacrata, quæ de more illi assidebat, sacros codices legens, cùm ferè ad medium noctis lectionem extenderet, caligantes oculos clausit; lumenque è manibus illius prolapsum paleas corripiens suo fragore circumjacentes sorores excitavit, &c. [in Surio, & Gretseri etiam editione pag. 115.]
units.tr: Ekkehard the Younger, a monk dwelling at Mainz in the time of Archbishop Aribo, by the Empress's command wrote out a Psalter translated into the barbarian, that is German, tongue by Notker Labeo the physician, plainly for the Empress's private use. "This work is now in our hands," says Melchior Goldast. The Empress was without doubt Kunigunde, daughter of Siegfried, Count Palatine of the Rhine. After the death of her husband, Emperor Henry, in 1025, she laid aside her imperial ornaments, professed the monastic life, and worked with her own hands, knowing that it is written: "He who does not work, let him not eat." So her Life's author relates, and he adds of her: "She spoke to her Spouse [Christ] either in prayer or in psalm-singing." Likewise: "You would have seen her always reading, or listening to someone reading." And a little later: "When, after frequent prayer, amid the weariness of reading, the handmaid of Christ had let her limbs, heavy with sleep, rest on a bed not built of feathers but spread with haircloth, a consecrated girl who sat beside her, as was customary, reading the sacred codices, extended her reading almost to midnight, and her dim eyes closed. The lamp slipped from her hands and, catching the straw around it with a crash, woke the sisters lying nearby, etc." [in Surius, and also in the Gretser edition, p. 115.]

units.la: Lege 27. (in Codice MS. Cottoniano, & Regio, & aliis harum legum MSS. in historiâ autem Jornalensi MS. lex est 23.) Omnes Christianos sedulò commonemus, ut puro corde semper deum diligant, & Catholicæ Christianitatis fidei digne a deserviant: sanctis Ecclesiæ Doctoribus devotè pareant; Dei leges & doctrinam subtiliter investigent, x sæpius & assiduè sibimet ad utilitatem & y quicunque Christianus addiscat; ut saltem sanæ fidei rectam intelligentiam habeat, & sciat Pater Noster, & Credo in Deum: quia per illud Deum exoramus, per aliud fidem declaramus. (Seu fidem in Deum rectâ declaramus; uti habet Historia Jornalensis.) Verba autem Saxonica in exemplari Saxonico sunt hujusmodi. units.tr: Law 27 (in the Cotton and Royal manuscripts and the other manuscripts of these laws; in the Jornal history manuscript it is law 23). "We diligently admonish all Christians always to love God with a pure heart and worthily to serve the faith of the Catholic Christianity; to obey devoutly the holy teachers of the Church; to investigate God's laws and doctrine carefully, and to learn them often and constantly, for their own benefit and that of every Christian; so that at least they may have a right understanding of sound faith, and know the Pater Noster and the Credo in Deum: for by the one we entreat God, by the other we declare our faith." (Or "we declare our faith rightly in God", as the Jornal history has it.) The Old English text in the Saxon exemplar is of this form.

Horum enim altero Christianâ fide tincti divinum implorant numen; altero puram honestamque de numine Dei profitentur opinionem. Cæte-
units.tr: In the Archaionomia edited by William Lambarde at London in 1568, 4to, there is extant a decree which Cnut, king of the English, Danes and Norwegians, enacted at Winchester, by the counsel of the wise, for the glory of immortal God, the ornament of the royal majesty and the benefit of the commonwealth, on the days of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ. The twenty-second enactment begins thus, in the Old English, which says that every Christian man should learn to know the true faith and the Pater Noster and the Creed, for with the one he calls upon God and with the other he professes a true belief. Lambarde translates it thus: "We exhort moreover that every Christian should so learn that at least he may be well acquainted with sound faith; and let him learn the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed. For by the one, the Christian, dipped in the faith, implores the divine power; by the other he professes a pure and honest opinion concerning the divinity of God." The rest

Roberti Cottoni. Liber scriptus est anno 1049. Habetur enim computatio annorum ad finem libri: & in Kalendario ad 15. Kal. April. ascribitur, Sol in Ariete, ad 12. Kal. Æquinoctium.
units.tr: A Psalter, together with other canticles of the Old and New Testament, the Lord's Prayer, the Apostles' Creed and the Athanasian Creed, in Latin with an interlinear Anglo-Saxon version, is extant in the library of Sir Robert Cotton. The book was written in the year 1049: for a reckoning of years is given at the end of the book, and in the calendar, at the 15th day before the Kalends of April, is written the sun in Aries, and at the 12th day before the Kalends, the equinox.

units.la: In Luc. XVI. 35 Nunc nihil tam utile est, ut Scripturarum diligens scrutatio, &c. Illis enim, qui scrutantur divinas Scripturas, nihil potest illudere. Illæ enim sunt lucerna & lumen; quo lucente fur deprehenditur & manifestatur.
units.tr: On Luke 16. Nothing is now so useful as the diligent scrutiny of the Scriptures, etc. For nothing can deceive those who search the divine Scriptures. They are a lamp and a light; by whose shining the thief is detected and revealed.

units.la: In Ephes. VI. 36 Si vis obedientes habere filios tuos; institue eos divino verbo. Neque dicas Religiosorum tantùm esse legere Scripturas. Quicunque enim Christiani est, maximè eorum qui in mundo versantur; quanto majore auxilio ipsi indigent, ceu in tempestate agentes: proinde pro te est, quòd liberi tui audiant Scripturam: discent enim inde patrem & matrem venerari.
units.tr: On Ephesians 6. If you want your sons to be obedient, instruct them in the divine word. Do not say that reading the Scriptures belongs only to monks. For every Christian, especially those who live in the world, needs this help all the more, like those sailing in a storm. Therefore it is good for you that your children hear Scripture: for from it they will learn to honour father and mother.

units.la: In 1 Corinth. XIV. Chrysostomi verba usurpat (de quibus supra) Si linguâ ignotâ oraveris; quomodo indoctus, i.e. 37 Laicus, respondebit, aut ullum profectum à precibus accipiet? &c. Et mox. 38 Necesse est ut mente intelligamus quæ oramus. Item & de Psalmis intelligendum.
units.tr: On 1 Corinthians 14, he uses the words of Chrysostom (mentioned above): If you pray in an unknown tongue, how will the uneducated, that is, the layman, answer, or receive any profit from the prayers? etc. And soon after: It is necessary that we understand with the mind what we pray. The same must be understood of the Psalms.

units.la: 35 Nῦν ἢ ὑςἶν ἔπος ὠφελεῖ, ὡς ἡ τῶν γραφῶν ἐκρίσις ἰσχυρα. ἢ γραφῶν ὑμῶν ἐπιδιωκμῶν, ὡς ἂν ἰσχύσῃ τῶν τῶν σοφισμάτων, αὖ τα χάρ εἰσι λύχνοι & φῶς, &c. 36 ἐκίφιφος αὐτοῦ τῆς Σἰοις λόγοις ἢ μὴ εἶπας, ὅτι μοναζόντων δεῖ τὸ ἀναγινώσκειν τὰς γραφὰς· ποντὸς δ᾽ χεῖσιανῶ τῶτ᾽ ἐτι, ἡ μάλιστα τῶν κοσμικῶν, &c. ὥστε ἴαρ σὺ γίνη ἡ ἐκείνων αὐτοῦ ἢ γραφῆς, &c. 37 Τυτίσιν, ὁ λαικὸς. 38 Χρὴ τὴ διανοία σωμίσται τὸ ἡ δίγῆς, ὁ μάλιστα ἡ δεῖ τὸ φάλμωκ.
units.tr: [35] Now nothing is so useful as the diligent searching of the Scriptures, which is powerful, etc. [Νῦν οὐδὲν οὕτως ὠφέλιμον ὡς ἡ τῶν γραφῶν ἐκζήτησις ἰσχυρά, ... αὗται γάρ εἰσι λύχνοι καὶ φῶς]. [36] Do not say that it belongs only to monks to read the Scriptures; for it is necessary for every Christian, and most of all for those who live in the world, etc. [μὴ εἴπῃς ὅτι μοναχῶν τὸ ἀναγινώσκειν τὰς γραφάς· πάντων γὰρ χρεία τοῦτο, μάλιστα τῶν κοσμικῶν]. [37] Laikos: the layman. [38] It is necessary to understand with the mind what we read, as much as also the Psalms [Χρὴ τῇ διανοίᾳ συνιέναι τὸ ἀναγινωσκόμενον, ὡς μάλιστα ἐπὶ τοῦ ψαλμοῦ].

units.la: In 1 Corinth. XIV. Qui loquitur linguâ, seipsum œdificat.] 39 De his loquitur, qui noverunt quidem ea, quæ loquuntur, sed aliis interpretari non norunt. Nam si orem linguâ] Nam si loquar (inquit) linguâ, & non etiam interpreter, Spiritus quidem meus, h. e. animus ipse quoad seipsum utilitatem percipit, at mens mea sine fructu invenietur, ex hoc quòd aliis non afferat utilitatem. Mentis enim fructus est per varias ac omnigenas cogitationes utilitatem proximi excogitare. Deinde subjungit ex Photio : Spiritus meus orat] b. e. donum spirituale, nempe ipsum loqui linguis. Verba Orem & Orat accepit pro eo quod est linguis loqui aliquid quod honestum sit & studiosum. Nam & precatio genus quoddam est sermonis. Et postea ex Theodoreto : Psallam spiritu] 40 Spiritum vocat spirituale donum, mentem verò manifestationem ac interpretationem eorum quæ dicuntur. Dicit autem quòd expediat eum, qui aliâ linguâ loquitur, sive in psalmo diâ, sive in oratione, sive in doctrinâ; aut ipsum interpretari & intelligere quid dicat ad utilitatem auditorum; aut alium hoc facere convenit, qui possit operationem doctrinæ suscipere. Alioqui si benedixeris spiritu] Nam si tu solus (inquit) scis quid benedicis aut quid precaris, & anima tua hoc dicit spiritu; reliqui verò ignorant, eo quòd tu non noveris interpretari, sive non noveris vim eorum quæ dicuntur; qui agit idiotam, non poterit dicere Amen ad tuam orationem: non enim novit quid dicas, neque scit quando oportet te audire Amen. Idiotam autem dicit cum, qui in ordine laico sive plebeio constitutus est, &c.
units.tr: On 1 Corinthians 14. "He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself." This is said of those who indeed know what they say, but do not know how to interpret it for others. "For if I pray in a tongue," he says, "and do not also interpret, my spirit indeed, that is, my soul itself, gains benefit for itself, but my mind will be found without fruit, because it does not bring benefit to others. For the fruit of the mind is to devise, through various and manifold thoughts, the good of one's neighbour." Then he adds, from Photius: "My spirit prays," that is, the spiritual gift, namely speaking in tongues itself. He took the words "pray" and "prays" for speaking in a tongue about something honourable and earnest, for prayer too is a kind of speech. And afterwards, from Theodoret: "I will sing with the spirit." He calls the spiritual gift "spirit", but the mind the manifestation and interpretation of what is said. He says that it is expedient for one who speaks in another tongue, whether in a psalm, in prayer or in teaching, either himself to interpret and understand what he says for the benefit of the hearers, or that it is fitting for another to do this, who can receive the working of the teaching. "Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit," he says: "For if you alone know what you bless or what you pray, and your soul says this in the spirit, but the others do not know it, because you do not know how to interpret, that is, do not know the force of what is said, the one who plays the layman cannot say Amen to your prayer, for he does not know what you say, nor does he know when he ought to hear you say Amen." He calls "layman" the one who is placed in the lay or common order, etc.

units.la: 39 Περὶ τῆς ἀδότων μὲν αὐτῶν ἃ λαλεῖ-ν, ἐκ εἰδότων δ' ἑτέρας ἐμμηνεύσαι, διαλαλεῖ. — ἐὰν γὰρ, φ. σι, λαλῶ γλώσσῃ, ὁ μὲν νοῦς μου ἐκ ἐρμηνεύω, τὸ μὲν πνεῦμά μου ἔστιν ὁ ψυχὴ αὐτῆ.
units.tr: Concerning those who, indeed, know what they say, but do not know how to interpret it for others, he speaks. [For if, he says, I speak in a tongue, my mind does not interpret, but my spirit is her soul.] [Περὶ τῆς ἀδότων μὲν αὐτῶν ἃ λαλεῖ, ἐκ εἰδότων δ' ἑτέρας ἐρμηνεύειν, διαλαλεῖ. ἐὰν γάρ, φησί, λαλῶ γλώσσῃ, ὁ μὲν νοῦς μου οὐκ ἐρμηνεύει, τὸ μὲν πνεῦμά μου ἔστιν ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτῆς.]

units.tr: He calls the spiritual gift "spirit", but my mind is unfruitful. [Πνεῦμα τὸ πνευματικὸν χάρισμα καλεῖ, ὁ δὲ νοῦς μου ἄκαρπός ἐστιν.]

units.la: Præfat. in Psalmos. Hic liber (Psalmorum) commune est quoddam medicinæ promptuarium, & passionum omnium certissimum remedium; illiusque verba omnibus congruunt atque aptantur hominibus. Nulla est igitur inter homines actio, nulla ratio, nulla cogitatio; cujus medicinam hic invenire non possis. Cumulus enim & acervus quidam rerum est, omni plenus vitæ conversatione, omni contemplatione; ac veluti penu quoddam doctrinæ publicum, unicuique apta & convenientia distribuit; nam & antiqua purgat vulnera, & nuper illatis celerem liberationem præstat. Insuper quod integrum est, sanum sincerumque conservat; multitudinem verò ipsam prorsus allicit, ac suadet suavi quadam cum delectatione & honestâ voluptate; adeò ut per blandam & lenem illam voccm, utilitatem & commodum latenter etiam reportemus, juxta prudentum medicorum præcepta, qui in austerioribus pharmacis poculum inungi jubent melle: ita & nos apparenter quidem dulce & suave melos canimus; reipsa verò animas erudimus, & divinorum eloquiorum memoriam indelebilem conservamus. Psalmus, sermo & conversatio est cum Deo, Angelorum allectio, alacer animæ ordo ac status, diurni laboris quies, nocturni timoris propulsatio, juvenum & nuper introductorum regula, proficientium adjumentum, perfectorum solidatio: clypeus insuperabilis, ornamentum decentissimum, regibus, privatis, principibus, populis, militibus & belli ignaris, sapientibus & rudibus, monachis & crvibus, sacerdotibus & plebibus, habitatoribus continentis atque insulanis, agricolis, nautis, artificibus & artium ignaris, viris, mulieribus, senibus, adolescentibus; omni denique naturæ, ætati, fortunæ, & proposito, & communiter, & privatim, & semper, tam domi quàm in foro, in Ecclesiis, in agris, in solitudinibus, in itineribus, & omnibus in locis: & est deni-
units.tr: Preface to the Psalms. This book (of Psalms) is a common storehouse of medicine and the most certain remedy for all sufferings. Its words suit and fit all people. Therefore there is no human action, no plan, no thought, whose remedy you cannot find here. It is a heap and store of things, full of every way of life and every kind of contemplation. Like a common pantry of teaching, it distributes to each person what fits and suits them. It cleanses old wounds and gives quick relief for recent ones. Moreover, it keeps what is whole healthy and sound, and it draws the multitude itself and persuades them with a certain sweet delight and honourable pleasure. Thus, through that gentle and soft voice, we also quietly gain usefulness and advantage, following the precepts of wise physicians, who order that the cup be smeared with honey for harsher medicines. So we too sing what seems a sweet and pleasant song, but in fact we teach souls and keep the memory of God's words indelible. The psalm is speech and conversation with God, the attraction of angels, the lively order and state of the soul, rest from the labour of the day, the driving away of night-time fear, a rule for the young and newly admitted, a help to those who advance, a strengthening of the perfect; an invincible shield, a most fitting ornament for kings, private persons, princes, peoples, soldiers and those ignorant of war, the wise and the unlearned, monks and laymen, priests and common folk, dwellers on the mainland and islanders, farmers, sailors, craftsmen and those ignorant of the arts, men, women, old people, young people; in short, for every nature, age, fortune and purpose, both in common and in private, always, at home and in the marketplace, in churches, in fields, in deserts, on journeys, and in all places; and it is of the same kind as

units.la: b Ad calcem Jornandis, p. 57, 58. c Catal. p. 154, 267. que sicuti aeris, spiratio, aut lucis effusio, aut usus ignis, aut quodcunque aliud eorum, quae valde communia sunt & utilia.

units.la: Ibid. Cantorum quatuor erant principes, quatuor choris praefecti (à Davide) ob totidem mundi climata, ad quae psalmorum voces perventurae erant. Unusquisque autem chorus ex duobus & septuaginta Cantoribus constabat, ut quidam retulerunt se apud Hebraeos legisse, juxta proportionem ac numerum linguarum, quae in Babylonicae turris aedificatione confusae, seu potius divisae erant. Futurum enim erat, ut omnis lingua hujusmodi psalmos decantaret.
units.tr: Ibid. There were four chief singers, set over four choirs (by David) on account of the four climates of the world, to which the voices of the psalms were to reach. Each choir consisted of seventy-two singers, as some have reported that they read among the Hebrews, in proportion to and according to the number of the languages which were confused, or rather divided, at the building of the Tower of Babel. For it was to happen that every language would sing such psalms.

units.la: 1080. Uratislaus Boemorum Dux.

units.la: Hic totius gentis suae nomine à Gregorio VII. postulavit; ut secundum Sclavonicam linguam apud ipsos divinum celebrari annueret ossicium. Cui Gregorius rescribens 41 (ut est in 7 libro Registri Epistolarum ejus MS. citat. à Jac. Ledesma , Turriano , & Baronio ) Scias (inquit) nos huic petitioni tuae nequaquam posse favere. Ex hoc nempe saepe volventibus liquet, non immeritò sacram Scripturam omnipotenti Deo placuisse quibusdam locis esse occultam; ne si ad liquidum cunctis pateret, forte vilescéret & pateret despectui, aut pravè intellecta à mediocribus in errorem induceret. Neque enim ad excusationem juvat, quòd quidam religiosi viri hoc, quod simpliciter populus quaerit, patienter tulerunt, seu incorrecta dimiserunt: cùm primitiva Ecclesia multa dissimulaverit; quae à sanctis Pastoribus postmodum, firmatâ Christianitate, & religione crescente, subtili examinatione correcta sunt. Rem totam hisce verbis enarrat Olaus Magnus & Gregorius VII. Vladislao Bohemorum Duci scripsit, ac prohibuit; ne (ut optavit) scriptura sacra verteretur in linguam vulgarem: quoniam tam secreta majestas est in eâ, ut difficulter translatae sensus secretorum Dei poterit in eâ postmodum deprehendi; immò nunquam devotior fieret populus, quando sciens facilitatem in contemptum verteret, quod in reverentiâ consueverat admirari; & jam in cervisiariâ tabernâ irrisorìè decantatur. Observetur hic discrimen temporum & Pontificum Romanorum. Ante 200. annos Johannes Papa nihil obstare intellexit, quo minùs officia divina vel lectiones sacrae in
units.tr: He asked Gregory VII, in the name of his whole nation, that he would grant that the divine office be celebrated among them in the Slavonic language. Gregory, replying to him (as it stands in the seventh book of his Register of Letters, in manuscript, cited by Jacob Ledesma, Turrianus and Baronius), wrote: Know (he says) that we can by no means favour this request of yours. Those who often reflect on this will see clearly that it was not without reason that Almighty God willed Holy Scripture to be hidden in some places; lest, if it were laid open plainly to all, it should perhaps become cheap and be exposed to contempt, or be misunderstood by the ordinary people and lead them into error. For it is no help in excuse that some religious men have patiently borne, or left uncorrected, what the people simply seek; since the primitive Church overlooked many things which were afterwards corrected by holy ministers with careful examination, once Christianity was established and religion had grown. Olaus Magnus relates the whole matter in these words. Gregory VII wrote to Vladislaus, Duke of the Bohemians, and forbade that (as he had wished) Holy Scripture be turned into the vernacular tongue, since there is such a hidden majesty in it that the sense of God's secrets could hardly afterwards be found in a translation; indeed the people would never become more devout, since, knowing the ease of it, they would turn into contempt what they used to admire with reverence; and now it is sung mockingly in the beer-tavern. Here note the difference of the times and of the Roman Pontiffs. Two hundred years earlier Pope John understood that there was no obstacle to the divine offices or sacred readings being given in the Slavonic language, since he who made the three principal languages also created all the others for his praise and glory. Now indeed Hildebrand, that monstrous man, declared that this could by no means be allowed. Clearly at this time Antichrist has been brought to his full height, and the world has been buried in such ignorance that, the true reason for calling upon God being neglected, that babbling [βατταλογίᾳ] condemned by Christ has been received: the Angelic Salutation, the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed repeated by counting on beads a fixed number of times. For around this time (about 1090, under Pope Urban), Polydorus reports that Peter the Hermit, a citizen of Amiens, invented a way of praying by wooden rolls, which the common people now call Prayer-beads, now Paternosters. These, fifty-five in number, are arranged in order so that after every ten a larger one is attached to the thread (for they are pierced), and as many times as these there are, so many times they recite the Lord's Prayer, and as many times as those, the Angelic Salutation, repeating the number three times, and three times they insert the creed. And they call it the Psalter of the Blessed Virgin Mary. So Polydorus. But what he adds there about these beads, that they are the chief instrument of hypocrites for a painted goodness, the censors order to be deleted. Indeed, on the ignorance of God's Word introduced at this time by pseudo-monks, see Waltram's Apology on the Unity of the Church, in volume 1 of the German Writers, edited by Marquard Freher, pp. 228, 40, 50.

units.la: 41 Concil. Labb. Tom. X. pag. 234. Slavonicâ linguâ haberentur: quoniam qui fecit tres linguas principales, ipse creavit & alias omnes ad laudem & gloriam suam. Jam verò Hildebrandus, monstrum illud hominis, hoc nullo modo admitti posse statuit. Scilicet hoc tempore ad ἀκμὴν perductus est Antichristus; tantâque ignorantiâ sepultus est mundus; ut verâ ratione Deum interpellandi neglectâ βατταλογίᾳ illa h à Christo condemnata recepta sit; Salutatione Angelicâ, Oratione Dominicâ, & Symbolo Apostolico ad calculos certo numero repetitis. Nam circa hæc tempora (circa an. 1090. sub Urbano Papâ) refert Polydorus à i Petro Eremitâ, cive Ambianensi, modum orandi inventum esse per rotulos ligneos; quos vulgus modò Preculas, modò Paternostros appellat. Ii numero 55. ita ordine distinguuntur, ut post denos singuli majusculi affigantur filo (sunt enim perforati) & quot hi sunt, toties Dominicam precem, quot illi, toties Angelicam salutationem, ter numerum iterando recitent, terque symbolum inserant. Et id D. Mariæ Virginis Psalterium nuncupant. Hæc Polydorus. Sed quod ibidem de calculis istis addit, hypocritis esse præcipuum fucosæ bonitatis instrumentum, deleri jubent Censores. Verùm de ignorantiâ verbi Dei à Pseudomonachis hoc tempore introductâ, vid. Waltrami Apologiam de unitate Ecclesiæ tom. 1. Script. German. à Marquardo Freher edit. pag. 228. 40, 50.
units.tr: 41 Council, Labbe, vol. X, p. 234. Since he who made the three principal languages also created all the others for his praise and glory. Now Hildebrand, that monstrous man, declared that this could by no means be admitted. Clearly in this age Antichrist has been brought to his full height [ἀκμὴν], and the world has been so buried in ignorance that, the true reason for calling upon God being neglected, that babbling [βατταλογίᾳ] condemned by Christ has been received: the Angelic Salutation, the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed repeated to a fixed number by counting. For around these times (about 1090, under Pope Urban), Polydorus reports that Peter the Hermit, a citizen of Amiens, invented a way of praying by wooden rolls, which the common people now call Prayer-beads, now Paternosters. These, fifty-five in number, are arranged in order so that after every ten a larger one is attached to the thread (for they are pierced), and as many times as these there are, so many times they recite the Lord's Prayer, and as many times as those, the Angelic Salutation, repeating the number three times, and three times they insert the creed. And they call it the Psalter of the Blessed Virgin Mary. So Polydorus. But the censors order deleted what he adds there about these beads, that they are the chief instrument of hypocrites for a painted goodness.

units.la: In Sermone habito in Synodo, De excellentiâ sacrorum ordinum. Hic quidem, qui ad hunc gradum [Lectorum] provehitur, literarum scientiâ debet esse instructus; ut & sensum verborum intelligat, vim accentuum sciat, distinctè legat; ne confusione pronuntiationis intellectum auditoribus auferat. Attendat quid sit indicativè legendum, quid sub interrogatione; ubi sit in oratione subdistinctio, media distinctio; quia & hæc malè servata intellectum perturbant, & Grammaticorum typhum ad risum provocant. Auribus enim & cordi consulere debet Lector.
units.tr: In a sermon delivered at a synod, On the excellence of the sacred orders: The man who is advanced to this rank [of reader] ought to be instructed in the knowledge of letters, so that he understands the sense of the words, knows the force of the accents, and reads distinctly, lest by a confused delivery he take the meaning away from the hearers. Let him take care what must be read as a statement and what as a question, where the principal pause falls in a sentence and where the middle pause falls; for these things, if badly observed, both disturb the meaning and provoke the grammarians' contempt to laughter. For the reader ought to attend to the ears and the heart alike.
