units.la: 42 Spuria sunt ista in Epistolas S. Pauli Commentaria, aut Anselmo Laudunensi, aut Herveo Dolensi, aut Gulielmo Parisiensi ascribenda. pretandi, ut proficiat cæteris studium ejus. Oret non labiis tantùm, sed affectu cordis; ut exaudiri mereatur. [Nam si] Etiam ego, qui tantus sum [orem linguâ] i. e. voce solâ [spiritus meus] i. e. flatus oris mei [orat] dum loquor in oratione; [sed mens mea est sine fructu] i. e. non capit fructum ex ipsâ oratione. Hoc sæpe nobis accidit, dum Psalmum vel orationem labiis proferimus; & mente, quod os profert, non cogitamus. Et quandoquidem mens, quæ intus pio affectu non orat, quod os loquendo foris precatur, fructum orationis non habet.
units.tr: 42 These Commentaries on the Epistles of St Paul are spurious, and should be ascribed either to Anselm of Laon, or to Hervaeus of Déols, or to William of Paris. ...that his zeal may benefit the others. Let him pray not only with his lips but with the affection of his heart, so that he may deserve to be heard. [For if] I too, though I am so great, pray in a tongue, that is, by voice alone, [my spirit], that is, the breath of my mouth, prays while I speak in prayer; [but my mind is without fruit] that is, it gains no fruit from the prayer itself. This happens to us often, when we utter a psalm or a prayer with our lips, and do not think in our mind what the mouth utters. And since the mind that does not pray inwardly with devout affection, while the mouth outwardly prays by speaking, does not have the fruit of prayer.

units.la: Ibidem. Si benedixeris spiritu] i. e. si benedictionem dederis ignotâ linguâ, ut nec tu sensum dictorum tuorum intelligas, nec aliis exponas; quis loco idiotæ respondet Amen in fine sermonis? Nec sapiens hoc facere novit, nedum idiota. Imperitus enim & absque literis, audiens quod non intelligit, nescit finem orationis, & non respondet Amen, i. e. Verum: ut confirmetur benedictio. Per hoc enim completur confirmatio precis, qui respondent Amen; ut omnia dicta veritatis testimonio in audientium mentibus confirmentur. Non poterit idiota respondere benedictioni tuæ quam non intelligit. Nam tu quidem bene gratias agis] Deo in illâ benedictione: & bonum est quod loqueris. Sed alter non ædificatur] ex verbis tuis, quæ non intelligit. Ideo cùm ad Ecclesiam propter ædificationem conveniatis; ea debent in Ecclesiâ dici quæ intelligantur ab hominibus [omnibus] & præstent ædificationem audientibus. Propterea qui loquitur ignotâ linguâ, debet in Ecclesiâ tacere; ut hi loquantur qui prosint audientibus.
units.tr: Ibid. If you bless with the spirit: that is, if you give a blessing in an unknown tongue, so that you neither understand the sense of what you say nor explain it to others, how will the unlearned man in his place say Amen at the end of the discourse? A wise man does not know how to do this, much less an unlearned one. For the unlearned man, without letters, hearing what he does not understand, does not know the end of the prayer, and does not say Amen, that is, "true," so that the blessing may be confirmed. For the confirmation of a prayer is completed by those who answer Amen, so that all that is said is confirmed in the minds of the hearers by the testimony of truth. The unlearned man will not be able to answer your blessing, which he does not understand. For you indeed give thanks well to God in that blessing: and it is good that you speak. But the other is not built up by your words, which he does not understand. Therefore, since you come together into the Church for the sake of edification, those things should be said in the Church which are understood by men [all] and which afford edification to the hearers. For this reason, he who speaks in an unknown tongue ought to keep silent in the Church, so that those who speak may be of use to the hearers.

units.la: In Ephes. VI. Si vis habere filios eruditos, institue eos in verbo divino; nec dicas Religiosorum esse tantum divina eloquia legere. Cujuslibet enim Christiani hoc munus est, & maximè eorum, qui versantur in mundo; qui majore auxilio opus habent, utpote ii qui tempestate agitantur.
units.tr: On Ephesians 6. If you wish to have learned sons, instruct them in the divine word; and do not say that reading the divine oracles belongs only to the religious. For this duty belongs to every Christian, and most of all to those who live in the world, who need greater help, as those who are tossed about by the storm.

units.la: In Leviticum lib. 17. cap. 5. Quid ad hæc dicitis vos, qui labiis Deum honoratis, cor autem vestrum longè ab ipso est? Vos aerem ipsum verbis impletis, corde vacui: cantica omnia divina sine sensu percurritis. Et
units.tr: On Leviticus, book 17, ch. 5. What do you say to this, you who honour God with your lips, while your heart is far from him? You fill the very air with words, empty in heart: you run through all the divine canticles without sense. And

units.la: 43 Illum medio Sæculo sequenti floruisse evicit Labbæus, Dissert. de Script. Eccles. Tom. 1. p. 799. cùm multus labor in ore vestro fit, anima tamen vestra fraudatur bonis: Culmus stans, dicit Osee non est in eis germen, non facit farinam. Vestra quippe farina nec spiritalem affectum germinat, nec sacræ meditationis farinam creat. Meditatio tamen sola est, quæ mentem mutat, spiritui vires præstat. Ex similâ namque (ut dictum est) panis coquitur, quia exercitatione interiori robur mentis acquiritur. l Beatus enim vir, qui in justitiâ meditabitur, & in sensu cogitabit circumspectionem Dei. Cibabit illum Dominus pane vitæ & intellectûs. Sicut ergo de vite amputantur palmites, qui infructuosi videntur, ut fructuosis spaciofitas amplior relinquatur: paucorum namque fæcunditas sterili multitudini longè antefertur: sic juxta Apostolicam sententiam longè utilius esset pauca ædificatione proferre, quàm reverendi sancti Spiritûs oracula sine fructu mentis imò cum Dei contemptu brevi temporis spatio confusè transcurrere. Nunquid enim vobis excidit, quod ait idem Apostolus , volo in Ecclesiâ quinque verba sensu meo loqui, ut & alios instruam, quàm decem millia verborum in linguâ. Linguam autem dicit linguam peregrinam; quæ si audiatur, non intelligitur. Inde enim est quòd ibidem præmittitur: Si incertam vocem det tuba, quis parabit se ad bellum? ita & vos per linguam nisi manifestum sermonem dederitis; quomodo scietis id quod dicitur? Eritis enim in aera loquentes. Ac deinde: Si ergo, inquit, nesciero virtutem vocis; ero ei, cui loquor, barbarus; & qui loquitur mecum, barbarus. Videtis quia in verbis nostris intelligentiam nostram requirit; quæ autem sine intellectu proferuntur, ea parvipendit: unde & B. Augustinus in Psal. XVIII. Psallentes, inquit, intelligere debemus, quæ proferimus; ut humano more, non quasi avium voce, cantemus. Nam & meruli & psittaci & corvi & picæ & hujusmodi volucres sæpe ab hominibus docentur sonare quæ nesciunt. Scienter autem cantare naturæ hominis divinâ voluntate concessum est. Quod & ipse Psalmista commendat dicens: Psallam & intelligam. Vos quàm multa dicatis, attenditis; nec qualiter dicatis, perpenditis: quasi non melius homini sit, qui unum panem in manibus habet, & illo vescitur, quàm asino, qui centum sorsitan portat, & nullo refícitur. Respexistis ad majus, & ecce factum est minus: prophetica exprobratio est ista. Intulistis, inquit, in domum, & dixistis, Ecce de labore; & exsufflavi istud, dicit Dominus exercituum. Quod enim pretium ponendum existimatis stipulæ, quæ spicam non habet? Quomodo placituram Deo putatis Psalmediam, in quâ vox quidem orantis pertendit speciem, mens autem sine fructu est? {k} Hose. VIII. {l} Eccl. XIV. {m} Eccl. XV. {n} 1 Cor. XIV. {o} Ibid. {p} Ibid. {q} Psal. C. {r} Hagge. I. Secus vos sensu vestro agimini, & neque rationi acquiescere vultis, neque sanctorum patrum authoritati. Quid enim? Nonne qui psallendi formam nobis tradiderunt, hoc commonuerunt nos, ut serviamus Domino cum timore, ut psallamus sapienter, & sic stemus ad psallendum, ut mens nostra concordet voci nostrae? Sub Haereticorum persecutione à patre nostro beatissimo Ambrosio Mediolanis psalmodia legitur instituta ad relevandum tribulationis illius pondus; ne sc. populus Christianus maeroris taedio contabesceret. Hanc enim psallendi utilitatem etiam Jacobus Apostolus nobis ostendit dicens: f Tristatur aliquis vestrum? Oret æquo animo, & psallat. Vestra vero psalmodia non solum mœstos non relevat, sed etiam alacribus nimietate suâ fastidium importat. O quantis bonis animas vestras fraudatis, quantâ privatis dulcedine; dum sapienter psallere contemnitis, nec reperire poteritis quod canitis? quia dulcia, inquit, t faucibus meis eloquia tua, super mel ori meo. Inde quippe faucibus ejus dulcia erant divina eloquia; quia voci mens concordabat: & quod sonabat in faucibus, hoc cum magnâ voluptate interius ruminabat. Hoc enim idem alibi testatur dicens: u Quomodo dilexi legem tuam, Domine? totâ die meditatio mea est. Et meditatus sum, inquit, x nocte cum corde meo, & exercitabar, & scopebam spiritum meum. Hoc enim cordis nutrimentum est; sic à vitiis purgatur conscientia; sic divinus ignis in nobis succenditur; quia Dei sapientia non verbis sine sensu sonantibus, sed eruditis se testatur y interesse cogitationibus. Sic denique juxta Apostoli sententiam z, homo noster interior renovatur de die in diem, secundùm imaginem ejus, qui creavit nos.
units.tr: 43 Labbé proved that he flourished in the middle of the following century, On the Writers of the Church, Dissertation, vol. 1, p. 799. Although much labour is done with your mouth, your soul is nonetheless defrauded of good things: the stalk standing, says Hosea, has no shoot in it, and does not make flour. For your flour neither sprouts a spiritual affection, nor produces the flour of sacred meditation. Meditation alone, however, is what changes the mind and gives strength to the spirit. For bread is baked from fine flour (as has been said), because strength of mind is acquired by inward exercise. Blessed is the man who shall meditate in justice, and think with understanding on the watchfulness of God. The Lord will feed him with the bread of life and understanding. Just as, therefore, the shoots that seem fruitless are cut away from the vine, so that a wider space is left for the fruitful: for the fruitfulness of a few is far preferred to a barren multitude: so, according to the Apostle's judgment, it would be far more useful to utter a few things to edification, than to run through the venerable oracles of the Holy Spirit in a confused way, in a short time, without fruit of mind, indeed with contempt for God. For has it escaped you what the same Apostle says: I would rather speak five words in the Church with my understanding, that I may teach others, than ten thousand words in a tongue. But he calls it a foreign tongue, which, if it is heard, is not understood. For this is why it is said just before: If the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless by the tongue you give clear speech, how will you know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. And then: If, says he, I shall not know the power of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to him to whom I speak, and he who speaks with me will be a barbarian. You see that he requires our understanding in our words; but what is uttered without understanding he holds in little regard. Hence also Saint Augustine, on Psalm 18: "When we sing psalms, we ought to understand what we utter, so that we sing in a human manner, not with the voice of birds." For thrushes and parrots and ravens and magpies and birds of this kind are often taught by men to sound what they do not know. But to sing knowingly was granted to human nature by the divine will. This the Psalmist himself commends, saying: I will sing and understand. You attend to how much you say; you do not weigh how you say it: as if it were not better for a man who has one loaf in his hands, and feeds on it, than for an ass, which perhaps carries a hundred and is nourished by none. You looked to the greater, and behold it became less: this is a prophetic reproach. You carried, says he, into the house, and you said, "Behold, from the labour"; and I blew upon it, says the Lord of hosts. For what price do you think should be set on the stubble which has no ear? How do you think the psalmody will please God, in which the voice of the one praying indeed stretches out an appearance, but the mind is without fruit? {k} Hosea 8. {l} Ecclus. 14. {m} Ecclus. 15. {n} 1 Cor. 14. {o} Ibid. {p} Ibid. {q} Ps. 100. {r} Haggai 1. Otherwise you act according to your own sense, and you are unwilling either to yield to reason or to the authority of the holy Fathers. For what? Did not those who handed down to us the form of psalmody remind us of this, that we should serve the Lord with fear, that we should psalm wisely, and so stand to psalm that our mind agrees with our voice? Under the persecution of heretics, psalmody was instituted at Milan by our most blessed father Ambrose, to relieve the weight of that tribulation, so that the Christian people might not waste away from the weariness of grief. For the apostle James also shows us this use of psalmody, saying: f Is any of you sad? Let him pray with an even mind, and sing psalms. But your psalmody not only does not relieve the sorrowful, but by its very excess brings weariness even to the cheerful. O what great goods you defraud your souls of, how much sweetness you deprive them of, while you scorn to psalm wisely, and cannot find what you sing? For, says he, t your words are sweet to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth. Indeed, the divine words were sweet to his throat because his mind agreed with his voice; and what sounded in his throat, this he inwardly chewed over with great delight. For the same man testifies this elsewhere, saying: u How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day. And, says he, x I meditated in the night with my heart, and I was exercised, and I swept my spirit clean. For this is the nourishment of the heart; thus the conscience is purged of vices; thus the divine fire is kindled in us; because the wisdom of God declares that it is present not to words sounding without sense, but to thoughts that are instructed. Thus at last, according to the saying of the Apostle, z our inner man is renewed day by day, according to the image of him who created us.

units.la: Glossa interlineari in 1 Corinth. XIV. Quomodo tu qui linguâ loqueris, supples locum idiotæ? scilicet, ut Ecclesiæ minister, illum ædificans? quoniam quod dicas, nescit: & quomodo idiota ipse respondebit Amen, super tuam benedictionem? Siquidem, nec si multum intentus sit, te intelligit.
units.tr: Interlinear gloss on 1 Corinthians 14: "How can you who speak in a tongue fill the place of the layman?" That is, as a minister of the Church, building him up; "for he does not know what you say, and how will the layman say Amen to your blessing?" Indeed, even if he is very attentive, he does not understand you.

units.tr: Book 1 on the Glorification of the Trinity, and on the Procession of the Holy Spirit, chapter 2: Holy Scripture is rightly called a field, because it is truly a public thing, a thing set out in the open,

units.tr: ᶠ Jac. V. ᵗ Psal. CXVIII. ᵘ Ibid. ˣ Psal. LXXVI. ʸ Prov. VIII. ᶻ 1 Cor. IV. and it is offered to all men, indeed to all peoples who wish to read or hear it.

units.la: De Operibus Spiritus Sancti lib. 4. cap. 9. Dicuntur in Psalmo Scripturae populorum; quia non ut Platonis literae, verbis grandisonae, sensibus pauperculae, paucis intelligibiles sunt, vel in angulis susurrant; sed cunctis populis propositae sunt, & palam omni mundo loquuntur de salute omnium gentium, quae in unâ gente conditae sunt, in quâ & prius abscónditae fuerunt.
units.tr: From On the Works of the Holy Spirit, book 4, chapter 9: They are called in the Psalm the Scriptures of the peoples; because they are not like the letters of Plato, grand in words, poor in meaning, intelligible to a few, or whispering in corners; but they are set before all peoples, and speak openly to the whole world about the salvation of all nations, which were founded in one nation, in which they were also first hidden.

units.la: In Joan. cap. 5. Proinde recte dicimus ignorationem Scripturarum ignorationem Christi esse. Quia videlicet absque Scripturis Novi pariter ac Veteris Testamenti impossibile est hominis animam stare, ut nullo circumferatur vento doctrinae.
units.tr: On John, chapter 5: Therefore we rightly say that ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. For clearly, without the Scriptures of the New and likewise of the Old Testament, it is impossible for a man's soul to stand firm, so that it is not carried about by every wind of doctrine.

units.la: De divinis Officiis lib. 1. cap. 11. Praedictas lectiones ideo oratione praevenimus; quia rogare debemus dominum messis, ut mittat operarios in messem, & ut aperiat cor nostrum in lege suâ & in praeceptis suis; ne semen verbi Dei, quod audituri sumus, aut volucres comedant, aut spinae suffocent, aut duritia petrae frustratâ radice supplantet.
units.tr: On the Divine Offices, book 1, chapter 11: We say a prayer before the readings in question because we ought to ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into the harvest, and to open our heart to his law and his precepts; lest the seed of the word of God, which we are about to hear, be eaten by the birds, or choked by thorns, or, through the hardness of the rock, its root be frustrated and overthrown.

units.la: Lib. 3. cap. 8. Sciendum quoque, quod cum sabbato (jejunii sc.) sex tantum legendae sint, duodecim in titulis quaestiones eâ de causâ praenotantur; quia cùm Romana Ecclesia de Latinis & Graecis esset permixta, singulae lectiones in utrâque linguâ recitabantur. Nam in unâ linguâ recitatae ab utriusque linguae populis intelligi non poterant.
units.tr: Book 3, chapter 8: It should also be known that, since only six lessons are to be read on the Sabbath (of the fast, that is), twelve questions are noted in the headings for this reason: because when the Roman Church was mixed with Latins and Greeks, each lesson was recited in both languages. For a lesson recited in one language could not be understood by the peoples of both languages.

units.la: Lib. 10. cap. 17. Quomodo gentium magistri fierent (Apostoli) wist per scientiam linguarum copiam habuissent conferendi cum eis sermonem? Quomodo, inquam, saltem respondissemus Amen super benedictionem illorum; cùm quid dicerent, nescíremus?
units.tr: Book 10, chapter 17: How would the Apostles have become teachers of the Gentiles, unless they had possessed the ability to speak with them through knowledge of languages? How, I say, could we at least have answered Amen to their blessing, when we would not have known what they were saying?

units.la: 1120. Drogo Hustiensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 1120. Drogo, Bishop of Hustia.

units.la: De Sacramento Dominicae Passionis. Non excidat tibi lex de ore cordis tui; volve, revolve, versa & reversa; & tunc intelliges quid sapiat Manna. Sic faciebat ille qui dicebat: Quàm dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua, Domine? super mel & favum ori meo.
units.tr: On the Sacrament of the Lord's Passion: Let not the law depart from the mouth of your heart; turn it over, turn it again, turn it over and back again; and then you will understand what the manna tastes like. So did he who said: How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord! sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.

units.la: In Regulam D. Augustini cap. 3. Psallentium in Ecclesia mens concordare debet cum voce; ut impleatur illud Apostoli, psallam spiritu, psallam & mente. Orandi perseverantia ita solum meretur esse fructifera; si quod ore precamur, hoc mente meditemur. Saepe namque oramus, & alibi mentem intendimus; nec ipsum, quod dicimus, recolimus. Sed illam Deus non exaudit orationem, cui qui orat non intendit: quod instinctu diaboli saepe fieri solet. Sciens enim utilitatem orandi, & nobis invidens gratiam impetrandi, immittit orantibus cogitationum tumultus; ut mentem ab oratione dividat, & fructum orationis tollat. Contra cujus malitiam debemus habere mentis constantiam; ut quanto plus cogitationum turba nos impugnat; tanto robustius mens nostra in sui status rectitudine fixa permaneat. Multum enim juvat ad orationis puritatem, si in omni loco & tempore nos ab artibus illicitis temperemus; si semper ab otiosis sermonibus auditum pariter castigemus & linguam; si in lege Dei ambulare, & testimonia ejus assuescamus toto corde scrutari.
units.tr: On the Rule of St Augustine, chapter 3. "In the Church the mind ought to agree with the voice when we sing psalms, so that that saying of the Apostle is fulfilled: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also. Perseverance in prayer can only be fruitful if what we pray with the mouth we also meditate in the mind. For we often pray and direct our mind elsewhere, and we do not even recall what we are saying. But God does not hear that prayer in which the one praying does not attend; and this often happens through the prompting of the devil. For knowing the usefulness of prayer, and grudging us the grace of obtaining it, he sends tumults of thoughts upon those who pray, so that he may divide the mind from prayer and take away the fruit of prayer. Against his malice we ought to have constancy of mind, so that the more the crowd of thoughts assails us, the more firmly our mind remains fixed in the uprightness of its condition. For it greatly helps the purity of prayer if we refrain at all places and times from unlawful arts; if we always likewise restrain both hearing from idle talk and the tongue; if we accustom ourselves to walk in the law of God and to search out his testimonies with the whole heart."

units.la: De modo orandi cap. 4. Sed in illa, quae ad Deum fit, oratione narratio necessaria non est, nisi forte homo ad hoc narret, ut ipse suam petitionem melius intelligat; ut & per narrationem suam admonitus, quid petat, consideret; & per considerationem petitionis suae excitatus devotius oret, &c. Sola ergo cordis devotio quantum ad Deum sufficere poterat; nisi ad hoc etiam in voce formaretur oratio; ut mentem orantis ad majorem devotionem accendat. Nam, sicut diximus, si petitioni inserta narratio est; non Deus docetur, sed orans admonetur considerare quid petat, ut devotius oret. Si vero sola supplicatio est; quia devotionem intus in corde esse significat, ad majorem devotionem animum inflammat.
units.tr: On the manner of praying, chapter 4. "But in that prayer which is made to God, narration is not necessary, unless perhaps a man recounts it in order that he may understand his own petition better; so that, reminded by his own narration of what he is asking, he may consider it, and, roused by the consideration of his petition, may pray more devoutly, etc. Therefore devotion of heart alone would have been sufficient before God; but prayer is also shaped in the voice so that it may kindle the mind of the one praying to greater devotion. For, as we have said, if a narration is inserted into the petition, God is not being taught, but the one praying is reminded to consider what he asks, so that he may pray more devoutly. But if it is only supplication, since it signifies that devotion is within, in the heart, it inflames the soul to greater devotion."

units.la: Ibid. cap. 5. Unusquisque ergo cum in oratione vel psalmos vel alias quascunque Scripturas decantat; diligenter consideret, cui affectui serviant; & ad illum affectum toto nisu cor suum excitet; ad quem, id quod loquitur, magis pertinere videt: quia si verborum, quae loquitur, affectum habuerit, per affectum ipsum melius verborum virtutem cognoscet, & intelligentiam capiet, & per verborum intelligentiam in majorem devotionem affectum accendet.
units.tr: Ibid., chapter 5. "Each one, therefore, when in prayer he chants either the psalms or any other Scriptures, should carefully consider to which feeling they serve; and he should stir his heart with all effort toward that feeling to which he sees what he is saying pertains more closely. For if he has the feeling of the words he is speaking, through that very feeling he will better know the power of the words and grasp their meaning, and through the understanding of the words he will kindle the feeling into greater devotion."

units.la: De Sacramentis fidei lib. 2. part. 3. cap. 7. de Lectoribus agens; Isidorum sequitur lib. 2. de Offic. cap. 11. & iisdem utitur verbis, quae infra in Petro Lombardo Anno 1150. proponentur.

units.la: 1140. Richardus Victorinus.
units.tr: 1140. Richard of St Victor.

units.la: In Apocalypsin lib. 2. cap. 3. Sacra Scriptura lex ignea est. Lex, quia nos refrænando ligat. Ignea, quia ad amorem creatoris ardenter inflammat. Intus scriptus est liber iste per allegoriam, foris per historiam: intus per spiritualem intelligentiam, foris ad simplicium & minorum eruditionem: Intus ut secretum sapientiæ immundis occultetur, foras ut veritas mundis reveletur.
units.tr: In Apocalypsin, book 2, chapter 3: Holy Scripture is a fiery law. It is a law because it binds us by restraining us. It is fiery because it kindles us ardently with love of the Creator. This book is written within by allegory and without by history: within through spiritual understanding, without for the instruction of the simple and the lesser ones; within so that the secret of wisdom may be hidden from the unclean, without so that the truth may be revealed to the clean.

units.la: Lib. 7. cap. 8. Sciendum est, quod Sacræ Scripturæ verba & secundum aliquid sunt significanda, & secundum aliquid non sunt significanda. Sunt quippe significanda, quia sunt inimicis occultanda; non sunt significanda, quia sunt amicis revelanda. Utrumque autem sanctus Johannes, & quod prohibitum, & quod præceptum sibi fuit, cavit & observavit: qui & quædam per obscura figurarum velamina malis studuit occultare, & quædam vel absque figuris scribendo, vel per semetipsum figuras exponendo, & sic sub aliis velaminibus latentia mysteria fore quærenda subtiliter insinuando, bonis curavit revelare. Sed quamvis Sacræ Scripturæ mysteria obscuritatibus figurarum significentur, ut bonos exerceant, malos lateant; nequaquam tamen ipsi mali de ignorantia suâ habent excusationem: quia & manifestiora sacræ paginæ verba possunt intelligere; & si vellent vitia deserere & virtutes exercere, possunt ad occultiora quoque cognoscenda adjuvante gratia Dei pervenire.
units.tr: Book 7, chapter 8: It must be understood that the words of Holy Scripture are in some respects to be signified and in some respects not to be signified. They are to be signified because they are to be hidden from enemies; they are not to be signified because they are to be revealed to friends. Holy John took care to observe both what was forbidden him and what was commanded him, and he both strove to hide some things from the wicked under the obscure veils of figures, and took care to reveal some things to the good, either without figures in his writing or by himself expounding the figures, and so, subtly hinting that the mysteries lying hidden under other veils are to be sought, he took care to reveal them to the good. But although the mysteries of Holy Scripture are signified by the obscurities of figures, so that they may exercise the good and lie hidden from the wicked, the wicked themselves have by no means any excuse for their ignorance. For they can understand the plainer words of the sacred page, and if they were willing to forsake vices and practise virtues, they could, with the help of the grace of God, also attain to knowing the more hidden things.

units.la: 1140. Bernardus Claræuallensis Abbas.
units.tr: 1140. Bernard of Clairvaux, Abbot.

units.la: In Meditationib. cap. 6. Cùm ad orandum sive ad psallendum Ecclesiam intraveris; fluctuantium cogitationum tumultus exterius relinque, curamque exteriorum penitus oblivisce; ut soli Deo possis vacare. Fieri enim non potest, ut aliquando cum Deo loquatur, qui cum toto mundo etiam tacens fabulatur. Intende ergo illi, qui intendit tibi; audi illum loquentem tibi, ut ipse te exaudiat loquentem sibi. Ita fiet, si divinis laudibus solvendis debitâ reverentiâ & sollicitudine assistas, super singula verba divinæ Scripturæ diligenter intendas; [ Habetur etiam hoc inter Opera Hugonis Victorini lib. 1. de Animâ cap. 7. ]
units.tr: In Meditations, ch. 6. When you enter the church to pray or to sing psalms, leave outside the tumult of wavering thoughts and utterly forget external cares, so that you may be free for God alone. For it is impossible that he should ever speak with God who, even while silent, chatters with the whole world. Attend, therefore, to him who attends to you; listen to him speaking to you, so that he may hear you speaking to him. This will happen if you stand by to offer divine praises with due reverence and care, and if you attend diligently to each word of divine Scripture; [This is also found among the works of Hugh of St Victor, book 1, On the Soul, ch. 7.]

units.la: De interiori domo, cap. 48. Oratio cordis est, non labiorum. Neque enim verba deprecantis Deus intendit, sed orantis cor aspicit. [ Habetur etiam inter Opera ejusdem lib. 3. de Animâ cap. 29;
units.tr: On the Inner House, ch. 48. Prayer is of the heart, not of the lips. For God does not attend to the words of one who pleads, but looks upon the heart of the one who prays. [This is also found among the same author's works, book 3, On the Soul, ch. 29;

units.la: In Cantica, Serm. 7. Laudem ergo cum cœli cantoribus in commune dicentes, utpote cives sanctorum & domestici Dei, psallite sapienter. Cibus in ore, psalmus in corde sapit. Tantum illum terere non negligat fidelis & prudens anima quibusdam dentibus intelligentiæ suæ; ne si forte integrum glutiat & non mansum, frustretur palatum sapore desiderabili & dulciore super mel & favum. Offeramus cum Apostolis in cœlesti convivio & in Dominicâ mensâ favum mellis. Devotio in cerâ, mel in litera est. Alioquin litera occidit, si absque spiritûs condimento glutiatur. Si autem cum Apostolo psallas spiritu, psallas & mente; cognosces & tu de illius veritate sermonis, quem dixit Jesus: Verba, quæ locutus sum vobis, spiritus & vita sunt.
units.tr: In Canticles, Sermon 7. So, singing praise together with the singers of heaven, as fellow citizens of the saints and members of God's household, sing wisely. Food tastes in the mouth; a psalm tastes in the heart. Let the faithful and prudent soul not neglect to grind that food thoroughly with the teeth of its understanding, lest, if it perhaps swallows it whole and unchewed, the palate be deprived of its desirable savour, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Let us offer, with the Apostles, at the heavenly feast and at the Lord's table, the honeycomb of honey. Devotion is in the wax, honey is in the letter. Otherwise the letter kills, if it is swallowed without the seasoning of the Spirit. But if you sing with the Apostle in spirit, sing also with the mind; you too will know the truth of that saying of Jesus: The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.

units.la: Ibid. Serm. 47. Unde vos moneo dilectissimi, purè semper ac strenuè divinis interesse laudibus. Strenuè quidem, ut sicut reverenter, ita & alacriter Domino assistatis, &c. Purè verò, ut nil aliud, dum psallitis, quàm quod psallitis, cogitetis. Nec solas dico vitandas cogitationes vanas & otiosas: vitandæ sunt & illæ illà duntaxat horâ & illo loco; quas Ossiciales fratres pro communi necessitate quasi necessariò frequenter admittere compelluntur. Sed ne illa quidem profectò recipere tunc consuluerim; quæ fortè paulò ante in claustro sedentes in codicibus legeratis; qualia & nunc me vivâ voce differente ex hoc auditorio Spiritus Sancti recentia reportatis. Salubria sunt; sed minimè illa salubriter inter psallendum revolvitis. Spiritus enim sanctus illâ horâ gratum non recipit quicquid aliud quàm debes, neglecto eo quod debes obtuleris.
units.tr: Ibid. Sermon 47. Therefore I admonish you, most beloved, always to take part in divine praises purely and vigorously. Vigorously indeed, so that as you attend the Lord with reverence, so also you attend with eagerness, etc. Purely, so that while you sing you think of nothing but what you are singing. Nor do I speak only of vain and idle thoughts to be avoided: those too are to be avoided at that hour and in that place, which the officiating brothers are often compelled to admit, as if of necessity, because of common need. But I would certainly advise you not to admit even those thoughts which perhaps, a little earlier, sitting in the cloister, you had read in books, or such fresh things as you now carry away from this hearing of the Holy Spirit, while I speak to you with a living voice. They are wholesome; but by no means should you ruminate on them wholesomely while singing. For the Holy Spirit in that hour does not accept with favour anything other than what you ought to offer, if you neglect what you ought to offer.

units.la: De modo bene vivendi ad Sororem, 44 Serm. 49. Oratio cordis est, non labiorum. Melius est cum silentio cordis orare, quàm solis verbis sine intentione mentis.
units.tr: On the Good Way of Living, to a Sister, 44 Sermon 49. Prayer is of the heart, not of the lips. It is better to pray with the silence of the heart than with words alone without attention of the mind.

units.la: Ibid. Serm. 50. Soror charissima, si vis cum Deo semper esse; semper ora, & semper lege. Valde nobis est necessaria lectio divina. Nam per lectionem discimus, quid facere, quid cavere, quo tendere debeamus. Unde dicitur: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, & lumen semitis meis. Per lectionem sensus & intellectus augentur. Lectio nos ad orationem instruit, & ad operationem. Lectio nos informat ad activam & contemplativam vitam: ideo dicitur in Psalmis: Beatus vir, qui in lege Domini meditabitur die ac nocte. Lectio & oratio sunt arma, quibus Diabolus expugnatur: hæc sunt instrumenta quibus æterna beatitudo acquiritur. Per ora-
units.tr: Ibid. Sermon 50. Dearest sister, if you wish always to be with God, always pray and always read. Divine reading is very necessary for us. For through reading we learn what to do, what to avoid, and toward what we ought to strive. Hence it is said: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. Through reading, sense and understanding are increased. Reading instructs us to prayer and to action. Reading forms us for the active and the contemplative life; therefore it is said in the Psalms: Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. Reading and prayer are the weapons by which the Devil is overcome; these are the instruments by which eternal blessedness is acquired. Through prayer-

units.la: 44 Spurii vulgò censentur isti Sermones. tionem & lectionem vitia destruuntur, & virtutes in animâ nutriuntur. Ancilla Dei semper debet orare & legere. Unde legitur in Psalmis: Tunc non confundar, cùm perspexero in mandatis tuis. Igitur dilecta mihi soror in Christo, insiste orationi frequenter: persevera in meditatione Scriturarum; in lege Dei esto assidua; habeto studium in divinis legibus; usus legendi sit tibi frequens, lectio sit tibi quotidiana legis meditatio. Lectio demit errorem vitæ, subtrahit hominem à vanitate mundi. Per lectionem sensus & intellectus crescunt. Lectio enim docet, quid facias; discernit quid caveas; ostendit quò tendas: multum proficis cùm legis: tamen si facis ea quæ legis. Soror venerabilis, adaperiat Deus cor tuum in lege suâ, & in præceptis suis.
units.tr: 44 These sermons are commonly regarded as spurious. tion and reading, vices are destroyed and virtues are nourished in the soul. The handmaid of God should always pray and read. Hence it is read in the Psalms: Then I shall not be confounded, when I have looked upon your commandments. Therefore, dear sister in Christ, pray frequently; persevere in meditation on the Scriptures; be assiduous in the law of God; have zeal for the divine laws; let your reading be frequent, let your reading be a daily meditation on the law. Reading removes error from life and withdraws a person from the vanity of the world. Through reading, sense and understanding grow. For reading teaches what you should do, discerns what you should avoid, and shows where you should aim: you make much progress when you read, provided you do what you read. Venerable sister, may God open your heart in his law and in his precepts.

units.la: Lib. de scalis Paradisi (qui Bernardo tribuitur, & Tomo 9. Operum Augustini habetur) cap. 11. Lectio sine meditatione arida est; meditatio sine lectione erronea est: oratio sine meditatione tepida est. Cap. 2. Lectio quasi solidum cibum ori apponit, &c.
units.tr: From the book On the Ladders of Paradise (which is attributed to Bernard and is found in volume 9 of the works of Augustine), ch. 11. Reading without meditation is dry; meditation without reading is erroneous; prayer without meditation is lukewarm. Ch. 2. Reading, as it were, places solid food before the mouth, etc.

units.la: 1150. Petrus Lombardus, Magister Sententiarum.
units.tr: 1150. Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences.

units.la: Sentent. lib. 4. Distinct. 24 (secutus Isidorum lib. 2: de Officiis cap. 11. & Hugonem Victorinum de Sacramentis lib. 2. part. 3. cap. 7.) de Lectoris officio verba faciens. Qui ad hunc gradum provehitur, literarum scientiâ debet esse instructus; ut sensum verborum intelligat, vim accentuum sciat, distincte legat; ne confusione prolationis intellectum auditoribus auferat. Attendat, quid indicativè, quid interrogativè sit legendum; ubi sit in oratione facienda distinctio. Hæc enim malè servata intellectum turbant, & alios ad risum provocant. Auribus & cordi consulere debet vox lectoris.
units.tr: In Sentences book 4, distinction 24 (following Isidore, On the Offices book 2, chapter 11, and Hugh of St Victor, On the Sacraments book 2, part 3, chapter 7), he speaks of the office of the reader: "One who is advanced to this rank ought to be instructed in literary learning, so that he understands the sense of the words, knows the force of the accents, and reads distinctly, lest by confused pronunciation he take the meaning away from the hearers. Let him consider what is to be read indicatively and what interrogatively, and where the division is to be made in speaking. For when these things are poorly observed, they disturb the meaning and provoke others to laughter. The voice of the reader ought to please the ears and the heart."

units.la: In Epistola ad Henricum II. Anglorum Regem: quà suadet Henricum filium, regni hæredem, litteris esse instituendum [Est autem inter Petri Blesensis Epistolas à Joanne Busæo editas num. 47.] Rex, cui omne judicium in populo datum est, quomodo judicabit populum in lege Domini, si legem Domini non cognovit? De Rege scriptum est in hunc modum . Postquam sederit Rex in solio regni sui, describet sibi Deuteronomium legis in volumine. In quo manifestissimè liquet, quòd de Rege scientia literarum exigitur; ut sit in lege Domini voluntas ejus, & meditetur in eâ die ac nocte.
units.tr: In his Letter to Henry II, King of the English, in which he urges that Henry's son, the heir of the kingdom, be instructed in letters. [This letter is number 47 among the Letters of Peter of Blois, edited by John Busaeus.] A king, to whom all judgment over the people has been given, how will he judge the people by the law of the Lord, if he has not known the law of the Lord? Concerning the king it is written in this manner: After he has sat on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book, the Deuteronomy. From which it is most clearly evident that knowledge of letters is required of a king, so that his will may be in the law of the Lord, and he may meditate on it day and night.

units.la: 1170. Petrus Waldus, cum Pauperibus de Lugduno.

units.la: Suasit omnibus Petrus, ut Biblia legerent, atque ex ipso fonte libentius haurirent aquam salutarem, quam ex hominum impuris lacunis. Soli enim Bibliæ Scripturæ tot divinis testimoniis ornatæ atque confirmatæ conscientias tutò inniti posse. Et ut cuivis esset potestas cognoscendi fundamenta salutis nostræ; Biblicos libros in vernaculam Galliæ linguam transfundit, ac potestatem describendi cuilibet præbet. Multi igitur magno studio sacros libros evolvunt, & scrutantur rerum amplissimarum fundamenta. Eratque horum communis sententia: Sacrarum Scripturarum lectionem & cognitionem omnibus hominibus, tum laicis tum sacratis viris, liberam & necessariam esse; immò potius Prophetarum & Apostolorum monumenta legenda esse, quam hominum commenta. Ita ex antiquo Manuscripto libro
units.tr: Peter urged everyone to read the Bibles, and to draw the saving water more willingly from the very fountain than from the foul pools of men. For the Scriptures alone, adorned and confirmed with so many divine testimonies, could safely be relied upon by consciences. And so that anyone might have the power of knowing the foundations of our salvation, he translated the biblical books into the vernacular language of Gaul, and gave anyone the power of copying them. Many therefore study the sacred books with great zeal, and search out the foundations of the most weighty matters. And the common opinion of these men was this: that the reading and knowledge of the Holy Scriptures is free and necessary for all men, both laymen and consecrated men; indeed, that the writings of the Prophets and Apostles ought to be read rather than the inventions of men. Thus the Magdeburg historians report from an ancient manuscript book

units.la: g Deut. XVII. 18. h Psal. I. referunt Magdeburgenses Historici i. Unde in libro k à Pontificio quodam Doctore Germano ante annos 300. de Waldensium doctrinâ & moribus exarato ita legimus. Secta Pauperum de Lugduno orta est hoc modo. Cùm cives majores essent in Lugduno pariter; contigit quendam mori ex eis subitò coram eis. Unde quidam de majoribus inter eos tantùm fuit territus, quòd statim magnum thesaurum pauperibus erogavit: & ex hoc maxima multitudo pauperum confluxit ad eum; quos habere voluntariam paupertatem instituit, & esse imitatores Christi & Apostolorum. Cùm enim esset aliquantulùm literatus, Novi Testamenti textum docuit eos vulgariter. Pro quâ temeritate cùm fuit ab Episcopo reprehensus; (erat tunc Joannes Bellomais Archiepiscopus Lugdunensis, ut ex Reynerio intelligitur) contempsit, & incœpit instare doctrinæ suæ, dicens discipulis suis: Quòd clerus pro eo quòd malæ vitæ esset, invideret sanctæ vitæ ipsorum & perfectæ doctrinæ. Cùm autem propter hoc sententiam excommunicationis tulisset in eos, pertinaciter contempserunt; & sic usque hodie in omnibus terminis illis proficit doctrina ipsorum. Similiter Jo. Trithemius in Monasterii Hirsaugiensis Chronico l, de eodem cive Lugdunensi (P. Waldo) refert; quòd translatis ex Latino quibusdam S. Scripturæ libris in Sermonem Gallicanum, officium sibimet Apostolorum assumpsit; & tam per se quàm per suos in errore complices, Scripturas male intellectas ubique prædicavit. Rectores & Prælatos Ecclesiarum unà cum eorum constitutionibus contemnebant, Ordines sacros nihili pendentes: qui dum ut resipiscerent, admonerentur respondere solebant, Deo plùs obediendum esse quàm hominibus. Nota hîc ex testimonio Pontificii Doctoris (veteris sc. Scriptoris Germanici) & Trithemii, ipsum Petrum Waldum sacras literas in vulgarem Gallicam linguam transtulisse. Fuit enim homo doctus (inquit Illyricus m) ut ex vetustis membranis cognosco: & non curavit sibi ab aliis verti, ut quidam veritatis inimici mentiuntur: quales sunt Jo. Laziardus, & Raph. Volaterranus n de Valdone ita scribens: Is enim idiota, sacrorum voluminum degustationem ex aliis deprehenderat. De eodem Wernerus in Fasciculo Temporum o, (& post eum Nuslienfis Monachus in Magno Chronico Belgico, à Pistorio edito p) Scribi fecit aliquos libros Bibliorum in vulgari, cum nonnullis Sanctorum auctoritatibus: quas minùs satis intelligens, suo inflatus sensu, Apostolorum officium usurpavit, prædicando ubique, & suos ad prædicandum mittendo, &c. Similiter Bernardus Lutzemburgh q, (& post eum Gabriel Prateolus) Utique cùm idiota esset, quosdam vulgares libros cum quibusdam sanctorum dictis sibi conscribi fecit; quos non sanè intelligens, suo inflatus Spiritu, prædicando Apostolorum officium sibi usurpavit, &c. Haud dissimilia refert Robertus Gaguinus r Ordinis S. Trinitatis generalis Minister. Hic cum literarum ignarus esset (inquit) obtinuit ab eruditis libellos aliquot Gallos sibi conscribi; ubi nonnullæ doctorum sententiæ insertæ essent. Quod postquam adeptus est, easque suo sensu homo idiota interpretatus est, docendi officium apud sui similes usurpans: multis se atque discipulos erroribus implicavit. Pari modo Thuanus s: Prophetarum atque Apostolorum scripta popylari linguâ vertenda curaverat; antiquorum etiam Patrum aliquot testimoniis adjunctis: quibus in animum defixis, ingenio suo & sensu fretus, prædicationis munus sibi sumpserat; perque plateas ac vicos Evangelium plebi interpretabatur. Nec abludit Jo. Massonus t: Abjectissimam paupertatem est professus; ac totum se Evangelicæ lectioni devovit. Et quia literarum ignarus erat, Prophetarum Apostolorumque scripta Gallicè vertenda curavit, populoque nova avidè appetenti in vicis & plateis perversè interpretabatur, & sic plurimorum animos subvertit. Addam denique Andreæ Favini u verba: Un Lyonnois nommè Valdon, tresriche & opulent en biens [lequel] attirant chez luy un tas de gens ramassez, souffreteux & miserables, les nourilsoit de ses biens, leur expliquant la Bible en langue vulgaire selon sa fantasie. Lugdunensis quidam, cui Waldus nomen erat, vir prædives & opulentus valdè, collecto sibi cœtu hominum infimæ sortis, paupertate & miseriâ obrutorum, illos proprio sumptu sustentavit, & S. Scripturam linguâ vernaculâ pro arbitrio illis explicavit. Vide paria narrantes Nauclerum generat. 39. Philippum Bergomatem supplem. Chronic lib. 12. An. 1158. Severtium de Archiepisc. Lugdunens. & Gretserum defens. Bellarm. de Scriptur. Vernac.

And in a book k written by a certain German Papist teacher about 300 years ago, on the doctrine and morals of the Waldenses, we read as follows: The sect of the Poor Men of Lyons arose in this way. When the leading citizens of Lyons were together, it happened that one of them died suddenly before their eyes. Whereupon one of the leading men among them was so terrified that he at once distributed a great treasure to the poor; and from this a very great crowd of poor people flocked to him. He set them up in voluntary poverty, and made them imitators of Christ and the Apostles. For since he was somewhat learned, he taught them the text of the New Testament in the vernacular. When he was rebuked by the bishop for this rashness (at that time John Bellomais was archbishop of Lyons, as is gathered from Reiner), he despised the rebuke and began to press his doctrine, telling his disciples that the clergy, because of their wicked lives, envied their holy life and perfect teaching. When the bishop, on account of this, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against them, they obstinately scorned it; and so to this day their teaching has progressed in all those regions. Similarly John Trithemius, in the Chronicle of the Monastery of Hirsau l, reports of the same citizen of Lyons (Peter Waldo) that having had some books of Holy Scripture translated from Latin into the French tongue, he assumed for himself the office of the Apostles; and both himself and his fellow adherents in error preached the Scriptures, misunderstood, everywhere. They scorned the rulers and prelates of the churches together with their constitutions, holding the sacred orders in no esteem; and when they were admonished to repent, they used to reply that God must be obeyed rather than men. Note here, from the testimony of the Papist doctor (the older German writer) and of Trithemius, that Peter Waldo himself translated the sacred letters into the common French tongue. For he was a learned man (says Illyricus m), as I learn from old parchments; and he did not take care to have them translated by others, as certain enemies of the truth lie: such as John Lasiardus and Raphael Volaterranus n, who writes of Valdo thus: For he, being an unlearned man, had gained a taste of the sacred volumes from others. Werner, in his Fasciculus Temporum o (and after him the monk of Nuys in the Great Belgian Chronicle, edited by Pistorius p), writes of the same man: He caused some books of the Bible to be written in the vernacular, with some authorities of the saints; which, understanding them imperfectly and puffed up with his own sense, he usurped the office of the Apostles, preaching everywhere and sending his followers to preach, etc. Similarly Bernard of Luxembourg q (and after him Gabriel Prateolus): Since he was indeed unlearned, he caused certain books in the vulgar tongue to be written for him with some sayings of the saints; which, not understanding them rightly and puffed up with his own spirit, he usurped the office of the Apostles by preaching, etc. Robert Gaguin r, general minister of the Order of the Holy Trinity, reports things not much different: He (he says) being ignorant of letters, obtained from learned men some little French books to be written for him, in which some sayings of the teachers were inserted. When he had got them, this unlearned man interpreted them according to his own sense, assuming the office of teaching among those like himself; he entangled himself and his disciples in many errors. In the same way de Thou s: He had arranged for the writings of the Prophets and Apostles to be translated into the popular tongue, with some testimonies of the ancient Fathers added; and having these fixed in his mind, relying on his own talent and sense, he had taken up the work of preaching; and through the squares and streets he expounded the Gospel to the common people. John Masson t does not differ: He professed the most abject poverty, and devoted himself wholly to the reading of the Gospel. And because he was ignorant of letters, he arranged for the writings of the Prophets and Apostles to be translated into French, and he expounded them perversely to the people, who eagerly sought new things in the streets and squares, and so he overturned the minds of very many. Finally I will add the words of Andreas Favyn u: A man of Lyons named Valdon, very rich and wealthy in goods, drawing to himself a crowd of gathered folk, needy and wretched, fed them from his goods, explaining the Bible to them in the vernacular according to his fancy. For accounts that agree, see Naucler, generation 39; Philippe de Bergame, Supplementum Chronicorum, book 12, year 1158; Severt on the Archbishops of Lyons; and Gretser, Defence of Bellarmine, on Scripture in the vernacular.

units.tr: On the Sacrament of the Altar, chapter 2. Readers ought to read the canonical Scriptures and, having read them, to pronounce them distinctly, and to understand what they have pronounced piously and faithfully. For those who read and pronounce distinctly prepare their hearers for understanding; but those who read confusedly disturb their sense.

units.la: In principio lib. de divinis Officiis. 84 In primitivâ Ecclesiâ prohibitum erat, ne quis loqueretur, nisi esset qui interpretaretur. Quid enim, obsecro, prodesset loqui, si non intelligeretur? Certè nihil. Hinc illa laudabilis inolevit consuetudo in quibusdam Ecclesiæ partibus; ut pronunciato secundum literam Evangelio, statim vulgari illud populo exponeretur. Quid verò de nostris temporibus dicemus, si vix (ac ne vix quidem) inveniatur quis, qui quæ legerit aut audierit intelligat; quisque satis animadvertat quæ viderit aut egerit? Unde profectò illud verè dicere possumus, quod olim Propheta conquestus est: Perit sacerdos, quasi è populo unus.
units.tr: At the beginning of the book on the Divine Offices. 84 In the primitive Church it was forbidden for anyone to speak unless there was someone to interpret. For what, I ask you, would it profit to speak if it were not understood? Certainly nothing. Hence that praiseworthy custom took root in certain parts of the Church: that, once the Gospel had been read according to the letter, it was at once explained to the common people in their own tongue. But what shall we say of our own times, when hardly anyone (and scarcely anyone at all) is found who understands what he has read or heard, and each one barely notices what he has seen or done? Whence we can truly say what the Prophet once lamented: The priest perishes, as one of the people.

units.la: 48 Vulgatis Beleth exemplaribus usus est Usserius. Mirum, quantùm ab iis discrepent Codices Manuscripti. Locum itaque ex Codice MS. Bibliothecæ Lambethanæ repræsentabo. In Primitivâ Ecclesiâ prohibitum erat, ne quis loqueretur linguis, nisi esset qui interpretaretur. Quid enim prodesset loqui, nisi intelligeretur? Inde etiam inolevit mos vel usus laudabilis in Ecclesiâ in quibusdam partibus; ut pronunciato literaliter Evangelio, statim in vulgari populo exponeretur. Quid in temporibus nostris est agendum; ubi nullus vel rarus invenitur legens vel audiens, qui intelligat; videns vel agens vel audiens, qui animadvertat? Iam vix letur esse completum, quod a Propheta dicitur: Et erit sacerdos, quasi unus ex populo. Videtur ergo potius esse tacendum quam loquendum, potius esse silendum quam tripudiandum; [addunt impressi Codices] si in hanc temporum infelicitatem incidimus.
units.tr: 48 Ussher used the printed editions of Beleth. It is remarkable how much the manuscript codices differ from them. I shall therefore set out the passage from the manuscript codex of the Lambeth Library. In the primitive Church it was forbidden for anyone to speak in tongues unless there was someone to interpret. For what would it profit to speak if it were not understood? Hence also there grew up a praiseworthy custom or usage in the Church in certain parts, that once the Gospel had been read literally, it was at once explained to the common people in the vernacular. What is to be done in our times, where no one, or hardly anyone, is found who reads or hears so as to understand, who sees or does or hears so as to take notice? Now it scarcely seems that what is said by the Prophet has been fulfilled: And the priest will be as one of the people. It seems therefore better to be silent than to speak, better to keep quiet than to rejoice, [the printed codices add] if we have fallen into this unhappy age.

units.la: Paulus ad Romanos scribens, inquit, An Judæorum tantùm Deus? num & Gentium? certè & Gentium. 48 Qui igitur rectè in omnibus de fide sentiunt, etsi sint Græcæ linguæ omnino expertes, propriâ dialecto sacra conficient, exemplaria consuetarum sacrarum precum habentes non evariantia, utpote 49 desumpta ex contaciis Græcanicis literis eleganter descriptis. Balsamonis Responsum confer cum Lateranensis Concilii Constitutione circa idem tempus factâ. Vide & Gretserum Defensi Bellarm. col. 881.
units.tr: Paul, writing to the Romans, says: Is God the God of the Jews only? Is He not also of the Gentiles? Certainly He is also of the Gentiles. 48 Those therefore who think rightly in all matters of faith, even if they are wholly unacquainted with the Greek language, will celebrate the sacred rites in their own dialect, having copies of the customary sacred prayers that do not vary, being taken from the Greek letters elegantly written out. 49 Compare Balsamon's answer with the constitution of the Lateran Council made about the same time. See also Gretser, Defence of Bellarmine, col. 881.

units.la: 1199. Metenses, & Innocentius III.
units.tr: 1199. The Metz people, and Innocent III.

units.la: 2 Piis illis, qui P. Waldo adhæserunt, Pontificiorum violentiâ Lugduno expulsis, & in varias Galliarum partes secedere coactis: duo qui in Monte Pessulano consederant, inde etiam ejecti, ad civitatem Metensem pervenerunt. Ubi adjuncto sibi viro quodam literato, cum Bertramo Episcopo, in festivitate quadam populo in Ecclesiâ prædicanti, publicè resistitilent, multitudini populi circa se congregatæ doctrinam suam proposuerunt. Indeque factum est, ut tam in urbe Metensi, quàm in diœcesi, laicorum & mulierum multitudo non modica tracta quodammodo desiderio Scripturarum, Evangelia, Epistolas Pauli, Psalterium, moralia Job, & plures alios libros sibi fecerit in Gallicum sermonem converti: translationi hujusmodi adeò libenter intendens; ut secretis conventionibus talia inter se laici & mulieres erudiare præsumant, (sunt enim ista verba querelæ Metensis Episcopi ad Papam Innocentium) & sibi invicem prædicare. Eorum insuper aspernabantur consortium, qui se talibus non immiscerent; & à se reputabant alienos, qui aures & animos talibus non apponerent. Et cùm eos aliqui parochialium sacerdotum super his corripere voluissent; ipsi eis in faciem restiterunt; conantes rationes inducere de Scripturis, quòd non ab his deberent penitus inhiberi. Res ista ubi ex Bertrami literis ad Innocentium III. esset perlata: rescripsit ille ad universos tam in urbe Meten. quàm in ejus Diœcesi constitutos, judicium suum hàc de re ita proponens: Licèt desi-
units.tr: 2 Those pious men who had adhered to Peter Waldo, having been driven out of Lyons by the violence of the Papists and forced to withdraw into various parts of France, two of them, who had settled in Montpellier, were also expelled from there and came to the city of Metz. There, having joined to themselves a certain learned man, they publicly opposed Bishop Bertram, when on a certain feast day he was preaching to the people in the church, and set out their teaching to the crowd of people that gathered about them. As a result, in the city of Metz as well as in the diocese, a not inconsiderable multitude of laymen and women, drawn in some way by a desire for the Scriptures, had the Gospels, the Epistles of Paul, the Psalter, the Moralia of Job and several other books turned into the French language for themselves; they applied themselves so eagerly to such a translation that laymen and women presumed to be instructed in such things among themselves in secret gatherings (for these are the words of the complaint of the Bishop of Metz to Pope Innocent), and to preach to one another. Moreover, they scorned the company of those who did not mix themselves up in such things, and counted as strangers those who did not give their ears and minds to such things. And when some of the parish priests wished to rebuke them for these things, they resisted them to their faces, attempting to bring arguments from the Scriptures that they ought not to be wholly forbidden from them. When this matter had been reported to Innocent III from Bertram's letters, he replied to all who were established both in the city of Metz and in its diocese, setting out his judgment on the matter thus: Although

units.la: 48 Οἱ γὰρ ἐμπεδοξαῖοι ἐν πᾶσιν, καὶ ὢν ἐπ' ἀλλη ἢ ζωῆς πάντως ἀληθοῖ, μὴ τὰ ἰδίας διαλεκτα ἱερουργήσουν, ἀντὶ γε ἐρᾶς ἐχρῆσθαι τῷ συνῳδὼν ἀρᾶν ἐν ἐμπαντ ἀπαρέλλακτα, ὡς μεταγεγραφῆναι ἐν κοινῷ ἑλληνικῶν; 49 Rettius, translata. Centaurum est opus seu volumen chartarum. Τὸ δὲ ἐν τὸ κοινὸν. Marcus Ephes. expos. Eccles. ἀκκλησιας. c. 17. p. 39. derium intelligendi divinas Scripturas, & secundùm eas studium adhortandi, reprehendendum non sit, sed potiùs commendandum: in eo tamen apparent quidam Laici merito arguendi, quòd occulta conventicula celebrant, officium prædicationis Christi sibi usurpant, sacerdotum simplicitatem eludunt, & eorum consortium aspernantur qui talibus non inhærent. Hæc ille, quemadmodum in libro 5. Decretalium tit. 7. de Hæreticis, cap. 12. videre licet. Ubi illud animadvertatur, desiderium intelligendi divinas Scripturas, & secundùm eas studium adhortandi, ex Innocentii sententiâ reprehendendum non fuisse, sed potiùs commendandum. Unde etiam Innocentius à Jo. Francisco Pico Mirandulano in eorum numero ponitur, qui assiduè monent huic divinorum studio incumbendum omnibus, cujuscunque gradùs & ordinis extiterint. At verò cùm consideraret illud, vix tutum fore, ut doctrina Pontificia à Laicis ad Sacræ Scripturæ canonem examinaretur; tacitè eosdem ab illâ inquisitione conatur avertere; cùm in iisdem literis commemorat recte fuisse olim in lege Divinâ statutum, ut bestia, quæ montem tetigerit, lapidetur; ne videlicet simplex aliquis & indoctus præsumat ad subtilitatem sacræ Scripturæ pertingere. Quod terriculamentum si ad Laicos à Scripturæ sacræ meditatione arcendos valeat; valebit etiam ad Sacerdotes ab eodem studio deterrendos. Quicquid enim tetigerit montem, sive jumentum sive homo fuerit, lapidibus erat obruendum, aut jaculis conficiendum: denuntiatumque est interdictum, ne aut sacrorum administri aut populus perrumperent terminum ascendendo ad Jehovam in montem. Sed quid hisce literis apud Metenses effecerit Innocentius, audiamus. Nonnulli mandatis Papalibus obedire prorsus recusabant: quibusdam eorum clanculò, quibusdam verò publicè dicentibus obediendum esse soli Deo: & prædictæ translationi usque adeò insistebant; ut se nec Episcopo, nec Metropolitano suo, nec Papæ ipsi allererent parituros, si eam decrevissent abolendam. Hæc omnia ubi per literas suas Innocentio significâssel Bertramus; irritatus ille, ad Abbatem Cisterciensem & collegas ejus scribit ; ut ad civitatem Metensem pariter accedentes, cum Metensi Episcopo convocarent coram se talia sapientes, & adhærentes translationi prædictæ; & (si fieri poterit) quæ in eis reprehensibilia fuerint, authoritate freti Apostolica, sublato appellationis obstaculo corrigerent. Cùm enim in hoc (inDe studio divin. & human. philosophiæ, l. 2. c. 1. Pag. 686. edit. Parif. ut supra. Exod. XIX. 13, 24 Ex Innocentii III. literis citatis à Jacobo Ledesmâ in lib. de divinis Scripturis quâvis linguâ non legendis, cap. 15. & Turriano contra Magdeburg. lib. 1. pro Canon Apost. cap. 24. Habentur hæ literæ ad calcem Directorii Inquisitorum edit. Romæ 1585. ex Registro Innocentii lib. 2. sol. 409. quit) universalis Ecclesiæ vertatur negotium, & agatur causa fidei Christianæ; ad exequendum Apostolicæ sedis mandatum, cum summa diligentia & cautela, vos studiosos & promptos esse volumus & mandamus. Hactenus Innocentius: qui tamen pios illos viros omni suo conatu opprimere non valuit. Cùm enim in Cæsarii Heisterbachensis Dialogis i legimus Hæreses Waldosianas (ita enim de Christi doctrinâ sensit Antichristianus Monachus) suo tempore nondum fuisse in civitate Metensi prorsus extinctas; apparet eos temporibus Honorii, qui Innocentio in Papatu successit, adhuc remansisse. Illis enim temporibus g scripsisse Cæsarium, ex proximè sequentis Capitis initio intelligimus. Extant in Regesto Innocentii III. lib. 2. tres de hac materia scriptæ Epistolæ. I. ad Metenses; cujus initium: Cùm ex injuncto (pag. 468, 469. edit. Colon. Anno 1606. item pag. 799, 800. ibid. ponuntur fragmenta ejusdem Epistolæ, ut extant in 5. libro Decretalium Collectionis Gregorianæ: integra verò Epistola extat in 3a. antiquâ Collectione Decretal. edit. Paris. Anno 1609. pag. 404, 405.) II. Ad Episcopum Metensem, eodem tempore scripta (ic. IV. Idus Julii, Pontificatus Anno 2.) cujus initium: Sicut Ecclesiarum (pag. 471. edit. Colon.) III. Ad Cisterciensium Morinmundensium & de Christâ Abbat. scripta eodem anno, V. Id. Decembr. cujus initium: Ea est in fovendis. (pag 537, 538. edit. Colon.) & in Bullario Fr. Pegnæ, p. 2, 3.) De rei eventu ita scribit, qui in Magno Chronico Belgico, h, à Jo. Pistorio edito, citatur, Albericus Monachus Trium Fontium (in Chronico, quod ad Annum 1240. perduxit, ut est ibid i Anno 1200. ineunte sc. in urbem Metensem (pullulante secta, quæ dicitur Waldensium) directi sunt ad prædicandum nonnulli Abbates; qui quosdam libros de Latino in Romanum (i. e. Gallicum, vid. Claud. Fauchet. k de orig. lingu. Francic. cap. 4.) versos combusserunt, & prædictam sectam extirpaverunt. Hoc tempore etiam (anno sc. 1200.) apud Merindolienses propagatum est à Waldensibus Evangelium; ubi ad nostra usque tempora conservatum est.
units.tr: 48 For those who are steadfast in all things, and who, whatever their way of life, are in every respect true, should not perform the sacred rites in their own dialect, but should use the common language, agreeing in everything without variation, so that it is set down in the common Greek [Οἱ γὰρ ἐμπεδοξαῖοι ἐν πᾶσιν, καὶ ὢν ἐπ' ἀλλη ἢ ζωῆς πάντως ἀληθοῖ, μὴ τὰ ἰδίας διαλεκτα ἱερουργήσουν, ἀντὶ γε ἐρᾶς ἐχρῆσθαι τῷ συνῳδὼν ἀρᾶν ἐν ἐμπαντ ἀπαρέλλακτα, ὡς μεταγεγραφῆναι ἐν κοινῷ ἑλληνικῶν]; 49 Rettius, translated. A centaur is a work or volume of papers. "The common" [Τὸ δὲ ἐν τὸ κοινὸν]. Marcus of Ephesus, Exposition of the Church [Marcus Ephes. expos. Eccles. ἀκκλησιας], ch. 17, p. 39: the desire to understand the divine Scriptures, and to urge study of them according to their teaching, is not to be blamed but rather commended; yet in this some laymen are rightly to be accused, because they hold secret conventicles, usurp to themselves the office of preaching Christ, mock the simplicity of the priests, and despise the company of those who do not cling to such things. Thus he; as may be seen in the fifth book of the Decretals, title 7, on heretics, chapter 12. Here it should be noted that the desire to understand the divine Scriptures, and to urge study of them according to their teaching, by Innocent's judgment, was not to be blamed but rather commended. Hence Innocent is also placed by Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola among those who constantly urge that this study of the divine things should be taken up by all, of whatever rank or order they may be. But when he considered that it would hardly be safe for the doctrine of the Papists to be examined by laymen against the canon of Holy Scripture, he tried secretly to turn them away from that inquiry, since in the same letters he recalls that it was rightly laid down of old in the divine law that a beast which touched the mountain should be stoned; lest, plainly, any simple and unlearned person should presume to reach the subtlety of Holy Scripture. If this scarecrow is enough to keep laymen away from meditation on Holy Scripture, it will also be enough to frighten priests from the same study. For whatever touched the mountain, whether beast or man, was to be stoned or killed with missiles, and a prohibition was proclaimed that neither the ministers of the sacred things nor the people should break through the boundary by climbing up to Jehovah on the mountain [Exod. 19.13, 24]. But let us hear what Innocent achieved with these letters among the people of Metz. Some utterly refused to obey the papal commands, some secretly and some openly saying that only God was to be obeyed; and they persisted so stubbornly in the aforesaid translation that they declared they would not obey either their bishop, their metropolitan, or the Pope himself, should he decree its abolition. When Bertram had reported all these things to Innocent by his letters, Innocent, roused, wrote to the Abbot of Cîteaux and his colleagues, that going together to the city of Metz, along with the bishop of Metz, they should summon before them those who think such things and cling to the aforesaid translation; and (if it can be done) correct, by the authority of the Apostolic See, whatever in them is blameworthy, the obstacle of appeal being removed. For since in this matter (in the work De studio divinae et humanae philosophiae, book 2, ch. 1, p. 686, Paris edition as above) the business of the universal Church is concerned, and the cause of the Christian faith is at stake, we wish and command you to be zealous and prompt, with the greatest diligence and caution, in carrying out the mandate of the Apostolic See. Thus Innocent; yet he was not able to crush those pious men by all his efforts. For when we read in the Dialogues of Caesarius of Heisterbach that the Waldensian heresies (for so the Antichristian monk judged the doctrine of Christ) were not yet utterly extinguished in the city of Metz in his time, it appears that they remained until the times of Honorius, who succeeded Innocent in the papacy. For we understand from the beginning of the immediately following chapter that Caesarius wrote in those times. Three letters written on this matter are extant in the Register of Innocent III, book 2: I. To the people of Metz, beginning: Since by the injunction (pp. 468, 469, Cologne edition of 1606; likewise pp. 799, 800 of the same, where fragments of the same letter are set out as they stand in the fifth book of the Gregorian Collection of Decretals; the whole letter stands in the third ancient Collection of Decretals, Paris edition of 1609, pp. 404, 405). II. To the bishop of Metz, written at the same time (on the fourth of the Ides of July, in the second year of his pontificate), beginning: As of the churches (p. 471, Cologne edition). III. To the Cistercian abbots of Morimond and of Cîteaux, written in the same year on the fifth of the Ides of December, beginning: This is in cherishing (pp. 537, 538, Cologne edition; and in the Bullarium of Fr. Pegna, pp. 2, 3). Concerning the outcome, Albericus, monk of Trois-Fontaines, who is cited in the Great Belgian Chronicle published by Johann Pistorius, writes thus, in his Chronicle which he brought down to the year 1240, as it stands there: In the year 1200, at the beginning (that is, when the sect called Waldensian was springing up), several abbots were sent to the city of Metz to preach; they burned some books that had been translated from Latin into Romance (that is, French; see Claude Fauchet, On the origin of the French language, ch. 4) and extirpated the aforesaid sect. At this time also (namely in the year 1200) the Gospel, spread by the Waldensians, was preserved among the people of Mérindol, where it has been kept down to our own times.

units.la: De Sacramento Ordinis cap. 3. de Lectoribus agens. Duo (inquit) dederunt causam huic Ordini; viz. sanctitas ipsa verborum, & ædificatio populi seu eruditio. Cùm enim populo non sit ædificatio seu eruditio salutaris, nisi per verba vitæ; hæc autem recitare sive annuntiare propter eorum venerandam sanctitatem non decet nisi sanctos (sicut legitur in Psalmis: Peccatori autem dixit Deus, quare, &c.) coegit ipsa religiositas Ecclesiæ, ut sanctificaretur ad hoc ministér.
units.tr: In De Sacramento Ordinis, chapter 3, treating of readers, he says: "Two things gave cause to this Order: namely the very holiness of the words, and the edification or instruction of the people. For since there is no saving edification or instruction for the people except through the words of life, and since it is not fitting to recite or announce these, on account of their venerable holiness, except to the holy (as is read in the Psalms: 'But to the sinner God said, why...'), the very piety of the Church compelled that this ministry be sanctified for this purpose."

units.la: ¹ Vetus Instrumentum rogatu & jussu Conradi regis, filii Frederici II. Cæsaris Augusti, versibus Germanicis redditum est à Rodolpho quodam oriundo ex familiâ, quæ nomen habet ab eminente arce in Rhetiâ, quam vulgus nominat Hohen Emf. quod se legisse testatur Theod. Bibliander de ratione communi omnium linguarum pag. 49. & Melch. Haiminsfeldius Goldastus tomo 1. rerum Alamannicarum Scriptorum pag. 393. Ibidem pag. 198. elegantissimam hanc Veteris Testamenti paraphrasin in Bibliotheca Schobingerorum S. Galli haberi notat. Est enim ea Paraphrasis Poetica Anonymi, quam se habere scribit Bartholomæus Schobingerus in Additionibus ad Vadiani farraginem Antiquitat. Alaman. tom. 3. p. 145. ubi notat Goldastum habere Christophori ab Helmsdorff Compendium Bibliorum Germanicâ lingua ante annos 300. scriptum: qui idem est ille Chunrat von Helmsdorff, cujus
units.tr: An old document, at the request and command of King Conrad, son of Frederick II, Augustus Caesar, was rendered into German verse by a certain Rudolf, from a family named after the lofty castle in Rhaetia which the common people call Hohen Ems. Theodor Bibliander attests that he had read this in De ratione communi omnium linguarum, p. 49, and so does Melchior Goldast (Haiminsfeld) in volume 1 of Rerum Alamannicarum Scriptores, p. 393. On p. 198 of the same work Goldast notes that this most elegant poetic paraphrase of the Old Testament is held in the library of the Schobingers of St Gall. It is the anonymous poetic paraphrase which Bartholomew Schobinger writes that he possesses, in his Additions to Vadian's Farrago of Alemannic Antiquities, volume 3, p. 145, where he notes that Goldast has a Compendium of the Bible in the German language, written more than 300 years ago by Christoph von Helmsdorff, who is the same as that Chunrat von Helmsdorff whose

units.la: ¹ Vid. Illyrici præfat. in Otfridi librum Evangeliorum. collatio Novi Testamenti cum veteri Historia ab ipso Goldasto parte 1. Script. Paraenetic. pag. 370. citatur.
