units.la: 1252. Waldenses.
units.tr: 1252. The Waldenses.

units.la: De his Raynerius, qui hoc tempore Pontificiae fidei Inquisitor extitit, in Catalogo errorum Waldensium (Parisf. Anno 1548. à Claudio Couffardo edito, ex libro membranaceo ante 296. annos per fratrem Reynerium conscripto) ita scribit: Dociles inter alios complices & facundos decent verba Evangelii, dictaque Apostolorum, & aliorum Sanctorum in vulgari linguâ corde formare; ut sciant & alios informare, & fideles allicere, ac demum suam sectam pulchris Sanctorum verbis polire; quò salubria putentur, quae persuadent. Atque hinc est, quòd alius ejusdem farinae Doctor (si modò alius, nam Illyricus eundem esse putat, perperam tamen) de Waldensium Doctrinâ & moribus circa haec tempora scribens; m tertiam causam illius haeresis (ut appellat) assignat hanc: quòd Novum Testamentum & Vetus vulgariter transtulerunt, & sic docent & discunt. Et addit se vidisse & audivisse rusticum idiotam; qui Job recitavit de verbo ad verbum; & plures alios, qui Novum Testamentum totum sciverunt perfecte. Idem etiam Author inter Waldensium dogmata recenset: Quòd oratio Latina laicis non prosit: quòd Sacra Scriptura eundem effectum habeat in vulgari, quem habet in Latino; unde conficiunt in vulgari, & dant Sacramenta. Textum verò Novi & Veteris Testamenti magnam partem vulgariter sciunt memoriter. Haec ille de secta (ut vocat) Leonistarum sive Lugdunensium; quam ita generalem esse asserit; ut nulla ferè esset terra, in quâ ea non serpat. Superfuerunt autem isti in Galliis etiam ad nostra usque tempora; curâruntque Biblia suâ dialecto eleganter imprimi. Horum enim sumptibus Neocomi anno 1535. prodierunt in magno sol. & magnis characteribus excusa Biblia Gallica ex Hebraicis & Graecis archetypis per Petrum Robertum Olivetanum translata. [Gesnerus in Partitionibus Theologicis, sol. 15. Beza in Iconibus, Genebrardus Chron. lib. 4. An. 1535.]
units.tr: Of these, Raynerius, who at this time was Inquisitor of the Papist faith, writes thus in his Catalogue of Waldensian Errors (published at Paris in 1548 by Claude Couffard, from a parchment book written 296 years earlier by Brother Reynerius): Among their other associates, the clever and eloquent are skilled at forming in the heart the words of the Gospel and the sayings of the Apostles and other saints in the vernacular, so that they may know how to instruct others, attract the faithful, and finally polish their sect with the beautiful words of the saints, so that what they persuade may be thought wholesome. Hence it is that another teacher of the same stamp (if indeed another, for Illyricus thinks it is the same man, though wrongly), writing about the doctrine and morals of the Waldenses around this time, assigns a third cause of that heresy (as he calls it): that they have translated the New Testament and the Old into the vernacular, and so teach and learn. He adds that he saw and heard an uneducated peasant who recited Job word for word, and many others who knew the whole New Testament perfectly. The same author also lists among the Waldensian doctrines: that prayer in Latin does not profit laymen; that Holy Scripture has the same effect in the vernacular as it has in Latin, whence they consecrate and give the sacraments in the vernacular; and they know by heart for the most part the text of the New and Old Testaments in the vernacular. So he writes of the so-called sect of the Leonists, or Lyonese, which he asserts was so widespread that there was hardly any land in which it did not creep. These people survived in Gaul even down to our own times, and they took care to have their Bibles elegantly printed in their own dialect. For at their expense there appeared at Neuchâtel in 1535 a French Bible, printed in large folio with large characters, translated by Pierre Robert Olivétan from the Hebrew and Greek originals. [Gesner in Partitiones Theologicae, fol. 15; Beza in Icones; Genebrard, Chronicon, book 4, year 1535.]

units.la: Alexander IV. cùm videret quantum periculum Romanae Ecclesiae immineret, quamdiu laicis esset integrum in ejus fidem inquirere; ut huic malo tempestivè occurreretur, decretum hujusmodi edidit; quod in 6. Decretalium lib. 5. tit. 2. de Haereticis, cap. 2. videre licet. Inhibemus quoque, ne cuiquam laicae personae liceat publice vel privatim de
units.tr: Alexander IV, seeing how great a danger threatened the Roman Church as long as laymen were free to inquire into its faith, issued a decree of this kind, which may be seen in the Sixth Book of the Decretals, book 5, title 2, On Heretics, chapter 2: We also forbid that any lay person be permitted to dispute publicly or privately concerning the Catholic faith. Whoever acts contrary to this shall be bound with the noose of excommunication.

units.la: m Inter Scriptores rerum Bohemic. à Marq. Frehero edit. pag. 222. fide Catholicâ disputare. Qui verò contra fecerit, excommunicationis laqueo innodetur. At quaenam ista est tyrannis, prohibere homines ne de fide inquirant; quae universalis est, quae omnium communis est, quae non solùm ad Clericos, verùm etiam ad laicos & ad omnes omnino pertinet Christianos? ut ipse Nicolaus Pontifex {n} ad Michaelem Imp. quondam scripsit. Sed praevaluit conatus Antichristi. Vid. an. 1170. ad sin. & Crispinum in Actis Martyrum, sol. 83, 104, 112. Laicus (inquit Martinus ab Aspilcueta Navarrus in Enchrid. de X. praeceptis, cap. 11.) disputans de fide, peccat mortaliter.
units.tr: m Among the Bohemian writers edited by Marquard Freher, p. 222. But what tyranny is this, to forbid men to inquire into the faith? It is a tyranny that is universal and common to all, and pertains not only to clergy but to laymen and to all Christians without exception, as Pope Nicholas himself once wrote to the Emperor Michael. But the attempt of Antichrist prevailed. See the year 1170, near the end, and Crispin in Acts of the Martyrs, fol. 83, 104, 112. A layman (says Martín de Azpilcueta, called Navarrus, in his Enchiridion on the ten commandments, chapter 11) who disputes about the faith sins mortally.

units.la: 1280. Alfonsus Rex Castellae
units.tr: 1280. Alfonso, King of Castile

units.la: Sacros Bibliorum libros in maternam linguam vertendos curavit. Ex eo tempore in regiis diplomatibus ac publicis tabulis Latina lingua, cujus antea usus erat, desiit usurpari. Unde pudenda literarum ignoratio in nostram gentem, atque utrumque ordinem invasit [inquit Jo. Mariana Jesuita de rebus Hispan. lib. 13. cap. 7.
units.tr: He had the holy books of the Bible translated into the mother tongue. From that time on, Latin, which had been used before, ceased to be employed in royal documents and public records. Hence a shameful ignorance of letters spread among our people and invaded both orders [says Juan de Mariana, Jesuit, On the Affairs of Spain, book 13, chapter 7.

units.la: 1280. Jacobus de Voragine, Genuensis Archie- piscopus,
units.tr: 1280. James de Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa,

units.la: Utriusque Testamenti divina volumina primus omnium in Italicam linguam summâ fide ac diligentiâ transtulit; ut habet Sixtus Senensis {o}. Sed monet hîc Possevinus {p} Jesuita, sanè & cautè in his translationibus incedendum esse; quandoquidem validissimae rationes sint, quae Ecclesiam moverint, cur non passim sive hae sive aliae editiones vulgares tractentur ab omnibus. Ubi vides, sapientiorem evasisse nunc Romanam Ecclesiam, quàm ante annos 300. fuerat. In Catalogo librorum prohibitorum Romae Anno 1559. ex decreto Romanae Inquisitionis edito, primùm in Italiâ vetitum esse, ne versio divinarum in Linguam Vernaculam literarum esset in usu, observat in Annotationibus ad illum Catalogum Vergerius.
units.tr: was the first of all to translate both Testaments of the divine volumes into the Italian language with the greatest faithfulness and care; as Sixtus of Siena records. But the Jesuit Possevinus warns here that one must proceed wisely and cautiously in these translations, since there are very weighty reasons that have moved the Church not to allow these or other vernacular editions to be read by everyone without distinction. Here you see that the Roman Church has now become wiser than it was 300 years ago. Vergerius notes, in his annotations to that catalogue, that the Catalogue of Prohibited Books, published at Rome in 1559 by decree of the Roman Inquisition, first forbade in Italy the use of a version of the divine writings in the vernacular.

units.la: {n} Tom. 3. Concil. p. 915. ed. Venet. & apud Gratianum Dist. 96. cap. 4. Ubinam.
units.tr: {n} Vol. 3 of the Councils, p. 915, Venice edition, and in Gratian, Dist. 96, cap. 4. Where?

units.tr: {o} Bibliotheca Sancta, book 4. {p} Bibliotheca Selecta, book 2, chapter 12.

units.la: 1290. Nicolaus Cabasilas. 50
units.tr: 1290. Nicolaus Cabasilas. 50

units.la: In Expositione Liturgiæ, cap. 1. 51 Sacrarum Scripturarum lectiones Dei benignitatem & humanitatem annuntiant; & rursus justitiam & judicium & ejus metum in animas nostras immittunt, & dilectionem in eum accendunt, & ita ad ejus mandata servanda multam promptitudinem & animi alacritatem afferunt.
units.tr: In his Exposition of the Liturgy, chapter 1. 51 The readings of the holy Scriptures proclaim the kindness and goodness of God; and in turn they place in our souls justice, judgment and the fear of him, kindle love for him, and so bring great readiness and eagerness of mind to keep his commandments.

units.la: 1290. Anglicanus Interpres.
units.tr: 1290. The English Translator.

units.la: Longè ante Wiclevi translationem (100 annis, ut conjicit Thomas Jamesius) prodiit universorum Bibliorum Anglicana Translatio: cujus tria in Oxoniensis Academiæ Bibliothecis MSS. extant exemplaria; unum in Bodleianâ (publicâ) alterum in Ædis Christi, tertium in Reginalis Collegii Bibliothecâ. [T. Jamesius lib. vernaculo de Corruptione Patrum part. 2. loc. 24.]
units.tr: Long before Wycliffe's translation (about 100 years earlier, as Thomas James conjectures), an English translation of the whole Bible appeared. Three manuscript copies of it survive in the libraries of the University of Oxford: one in the Bodleian (public) library, another in Christ Church, and a third in the library of Corpus Christi College (Regina's College). [Thomas James, in his vernacular work On the Corruption of the Fathers, part 2, loc. 24.]

units.la: 1300. Nicolaus Lyranus
units.tr: 1300. Nicholas of Lyra

units.la: In 1 Corinth. XIV. Si populus intelligat orationem seu benedictionem sacerdotis; melius reducitur in Deum, & devotius respondet Amen. Ideo dicit [Paulus] Si benedixeris, [tu Sacerdos vel Episcope] Spiritu: i. e. alsque hoc quod populus intelligat; quid proficit populus simplex & non intelligens? quasi dicat; nihil aut modicum; quia nescit se conformare tibi, qui es minister Ecclesiæ, respondendo Amen. Propter quod in Primitivâ Ecclesiâ benedictiones & cætera communia fiebant in vulgari. Ibid. Latinas horas Canonicas non intellectas alteri recensens, Barbarus erit.
units.tr: On 1 Corinthians 14: If the people understand the prayer or the blessing of the priest, it is better directed towards God, and they answer Amen more devoutly. Therefore [Paul] says, If you bless, [you, priest or bishop] in the Spirit, that is, without what the people understand; what good does the simple, uncomprehending people get from it? As if he were saying: nothing, or very little; because they do not know how to join in with you, who are the minister of the Church, by answering Amen. For this reason, in the primitive Church, blessings and other common prayers were said in the vernacular. Ibid. One who recites the canonical hours in Latin to another who does not understand them will be a barbarian.

units.la: 1301. Armeni.
units.tr: 1301. The Armenians.

units.la: Acta Apostolorum scripta Anno 1301. Et Epistolæ Catholicæ in linguâ Armenicâ MSS. habentur in Bibliothecâ Cardinalis Ascanii Columnæ [In Catalogis MSS. ad calcem Apparatus Possevin. p. 133.]
units.tr: The Acts of the Apostles, written in the year 1301, and the Catholic Epistles in the Armenian language, are held in manuscript in the library of Cardinal Ascanio Colonna. [In the manuscript catalogues at the end of Possevinus' Apparatus, p. 133.]

units.la: 1330. Ludolphus Carthusianus
units.tr: 1330. Ludolphus Carthusianus

units.la: In Psalm. 64. Sacra Scriptura est cibus noster, ac panis vitæ & intellectus; quo quotidie reficimur, ne deficiamus in hujus peregrinationis deserto. Unde scriptum est: Non in solo pane vivit homo; sed in omni verbo, quod procedit ex ore Dei.
units.tr: On Psalm 64. Holy Scripture is our food and bread of life and understanding, by which we are refreshed daily, lest we faint in the wilderness of this pilgrimage. Hence it is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

units.la: 1340. Brigitta Suecica
units.tr: 1340. Brigitta of Sweden

units.la: Sacra Biblia, quæ Gothico idiomate sibi scribenda curárat, legebat: ut est in Vita ejus (apud Surium tom. 4. Julii XXIII.)
units.tr: She read the holy Bible, which she had caused to be written for herself in the Gothic language, as is stated in her Life (in Surius, vol. 4, July 23).

units.la: 1358. Richardus Armachanus Archiepiscopus
units.tr: 1358. Richard, Archbishop of Armagh

units.la: Novum Christi Testamentum in Hybernico Sermone (à se fortassis translatum) anno uno aut altero ante suam mortem, in quodam Ecclesiæ suæ muro occultavit: in cujus fine, quasi prophetizans, hæc scripsit: Cùm hic liber inventus fuerit; veritas toti mundo manifestabitur, vel Christus orbi mox apparebit. Et repertus est iste liber circa annum à nato Servatore 1530. in reparatione ejusdem Ecclesiæ. (Jo. Balæus, Osforiensis quondam in Hiberniâ Episcopus, in Scriptorum Britan. Centur. 14. pag. 246.) Joannes etiam Foxus Richardum nostrum censet Authorem Translationis Bibliorum in linguam Hibernicam; quorum vetusta exemplaria à se conspecta esse Angli quidam probatæ fidei homines eidem confirmarunt. Hujusmodi Bibliorum fragmenta in Hiberniâ passim extant. Sed nec illud omittendum est, quod Armachanus in Defensorio Curatorum Fratribus objicit; tantam per eos librorum penuriam esse factam; ut cùm ex Hiberniâ quatuor ex Presbyteris suis Oxonium ipse misisset; rescripserunt se neque Biblia, neque alium ullum Theologicum librum studiis suis accommodum invenire potuisse. Quod etiam postea Galfridus Chaucer iis objecit, his verbis : Freer, what charitye is this, to gather up the bookis of holy write, and put them in treasorye, and so cumpulsion them from Seculat Prestes and Curatts, and by this councell lett them to preach the Gospell freely to the People? Quænam verò, Fratercule, charitas illhæc est, Sacræ Scripturæ libros undique colligere, eosque clanculum recondere, atque
units.tr: Richard's New Testament in the Irish language (perhaps translated by himself) he hid in a certain wall of his church a year or two before his death, and at its end he wrote, as if prophesying: When this book is found, the truth will be made manifest to the whole world, or Christ will soon appear to the world. This book was found around the year 1530 after the birth of the Saviour, during the repair of the same church. (John Bale, formerly Bishop of Ossory in Ireland, in Scriptorum Britan. Centur. 14, p. 246.) John Foxe also judges our Richard to be the author of the translation of the Bible into the Irish language, and certain Englishmen of approved faith confirmed to him that they had seen old copies of it with their own eyes. Fragments of such a Bible are found here and there in Ireland. Nor must it be omitted that the Archbishop of Armagh objects to the Friars in his Defence of the Curates: there has been such a shortage of books through them that, when he himself had sent four of his priests from Ireland to Oxford, they wrote back that they could find neither a Bible nor any other theological book suited to their studies. Geoffrey Chaucer later also objected this to them, in these words: "Friar, what charity is this, to gather up the books of Holy Writ from everywhere and put them in a treasury, and so compel them away from secular priests and curates, and by this counsel stop them from preaching the Gospel freely to the people?" Indeed, little friar, what charity is this, to gather up the books of Holy Scripture from everywhere, to hide them away secretly, and

units.la: Matth. IV. Act. & Monument. pag. 381. Londini 1596. In Jack. Upland, ap. Fox, p. 240. ita à Secularibus Sacerdotibus & Curatis incarceratos subtrahere, & ejusmodi artificio illos impedire, quò minùs Evangelium populo liberè prædicent ?
units.tr: Matth. IV. Acts and Monuments, p. 381, London 1596. In Jack Upland, in Foxe, p. 240. so to withdraw them from secular priests and curates who had locked them up, and by such a contrivance to hinder them from preaching the Gospel freely to the people?

units.la: 1360. Joannes Cantacuzenus, Constantinopolitanus Imp.
units.tr: 1360. John Cantacuzenus, Emperor of Constantinople

units.la: Apologiâ 4. Nos omnes indigemus Scripturarum auxilio propter infirmitatem nostram.
units.tr: In his Apology, book 4: "We all need the help of the Scriptures because of our weakness."

units.la: 1360. Anglus quidam doctus.
units.tr: 1360. A certain learned Englishman.

units.la: Præfationem docti in primis viri in sacrum Vetusque Testamentum, Anglicè antè annos trecentos conscriptum citat Jo. Caius lib. 1. de Antiqu. Cantab. Academ. pag. 150. ubi Aluredum tradit Author transtulisse Psalmos, & Bedam universam ferè Bibliam in linguam Britannicam convertisse.
units.tr: John Caius, in the first book of his De Antiquitate Cantabrigiensis Academiae, p. 150, cites a preface by a learned man, above all, to the Old and New Testament, written in English about three hundred years ago, where the author relates that Alfred translated the Psalms and that Bede translated almost the whole Bible into the British tongue.

units.la: 1360. Johannes Trevisa,
units.tr: 1360. John Trevisa,

units.la: Ad petitionem Domini sui Thomæ de Barkeley, in Anglicanum idioma transtulit totum Bibliorum opus, utrumque sc. Testamentum; præfatione præfixâ, cujus initium: Ego Johannes Trevisa sacerdos, &c. ut habet Balæus Centur. 7. cap. 18. ubi etiam notat eum Polychronicon continuâsse ab anno à Christi Incarnatione 1342. usque ad annum ejusdem 1397. in quo (inquit) ipsemet Trevisa claruit sub Richardo II. Anglorum Rege. Verùm ipse in fine Translationis Polychronici, tempus, quo scripsit, his verbis proponit: Versio ista finita est die Jovis (lege potiùs die Martis) die 18. Aprilis, Anno Domini 1357. Anno autem 35. ætatis Patroni mei Thomæ Domini de Barkeley, qui me versionem istam adornare fecit, atque Anno 31 Regni Regis Edwardi post conquestum Angliæ III. Diem Martis pro die Jovis ideo legendum censui, quòd se Trevisa versionem feriâ quintâ Paschalis Hebdomadis finivisse ibidem attestrat. Anno autem 1357. dies 18. Aprilis in feriam 3. Paschalem incidit. Anno quidem 1397. dies 18. Aprilis est feria 5. sed incidit is in annum 20 Richardi II. In MS. Codice, qui penès M. Forsterum Collegii D. Johannis Cantab. habetur, sic lego: die Jovis, Aprilis octavo, Anno 1387. decimo Richardi II. in Codice MS. Cottoniano die Jovis, Aprilis decimo octavo, Anno 1387. duodecimo Richardi II.
units.tr: At the request of his lord Thomas de Barkeley, he translated the whole work of the Bible, both Testaments, into the English language, with a preface prefixed beginning "I, John Trevisa, priest," etc., as Bale has it in Centuria 7, chapter 18. There Bale also notes that he continued the Polychronicon from the year of Christ's Incarnation 1342 to the year 1397, "in which" (he says) "Trevisa himself flourished under Richard II, King of the English." But at the end of his translation of the Polychronicon Trevisa himself states the time when he wrote, in these words: "This translation was finished on Thursday" (read rather "Tuesday") "the 18th day of April, in the year of the Lord 1357, in the 35th year of the age of my patron Thomas, Lord de Barkeley, who had this translation made, and in the 31st year of the reign of King Edward III after the conquest of England." I judged that "Tuesday" should be read for "Thursday," because Trevisa attests in the same place that he finished the translation on the fifth day of Easter week. In 1357, the 18th of April fell on the third day of Easter week. In 1397, the 18th of April is indeed the fifth day of the week, but that falls in the 20th year of Richard II. In the manuscript copy that is held by Master Forster of St John's College, Cambridge, I read: "on Thursday, the eighth of April, in the year 1387, the tenth of Richard II." In the Cotton manuscript it reads: "on Thursday, the eighteenth of April, in the year 1387, the twelfth of Richard II."

units.la: 1370. Carolus V. cognomento Sapiens, Francorum Rex,
units.tr: 1370. Charles V, surnamed the Wise, King of the French,

units.la: Biblia sacra Gallico idiomate, tum Lutetiæ Parisiorum, tum in Galliâ Belgicâ, Normannia, & aliis Regni partibus evulgavit; ut quisque nativâ linguâ suâ sacris literis frueretur. Veteres illæ interpretationes etiamnum extant, cum inscriptione, De mandato Regis Caroli V. non modò nomine, sed reipsâ principis sapientissimi. Hæc Carolus Molinæus in libro (Anno 1561. scripto) de Monarchiâ Francorum, sect. 133. (tomo 3. Operum ejus edit. Lutetiæ An. 1612. par. 2. col. 612. Latin.) In Gallico sic est (ibid. col. 574.) Aussi feit translater toute la Bible en Francois, non seulement en Paris, mais aussi en Picardie, Normandie, & autres provinces du Royaume; à ce que chacun eust la saincte escripture en son language maternel. Les vieilles translations se treuvent encores intitulees, du mandement du dit Charles le quint, qui estoit non seulement de nom, mais aussi de conseil & effect Sage. Hæc Molinæus. Similiter Antonius Molinæus in Bibliothecâ Gallicâ, tit. Bibles (pag. 137.) Or quant à la translation de la S. Bible en la langue Francoise, le Roy Charles V. dit le Sage, la feit translater au langage vulgaire de son tems. Y en ay une escripte en parchemin, qui est en language Picard. 52 Vid. Plesseï Mysterium Iniquitatis, edit. in 8o. pag. 1071. ubi hujus Translationis auctorem Nicolaum Oremum facit. Ut ad Carolum autem redeam: Jussit sacros Bibliorum libros diligenter & verè in linguam Gallicam transferri, rei ecclesiasticæ literarumque sacrarum perquam studiosus; ut habet Jo. Tilius, f & Anglo-Remenses. t Sed cùm hoc ab illo factum innuunt isti; ut Waldensibus occurreretur, & aliis, qui pro libidine eosdem vertebant: Fr. Hotomannus illum tyrannidi Pontificum infensum Translationem hanc procurâsse affirmat: ad quam etiam reprimendam, ab eruditis librum, qui inscribitur Somnium Viridarii, eundem componi curavisse testatur Carolus Molinæus u. Porro Translationem hanc multis etiam nunc locis in Galliâ videre licet, cum hâc inscriptione: DE MANDATO ET JUSSU REGIS CAROLI QUINTI: camq; in Regiâ Bibliothecâ Fontanebleæi Anno 1563. iterumque Anno 1567.
units.tr: He had the Holy Bible published in the French language, both at Paris and in Gallia Belgica, Normandy and other parts of the kingdom, so that each person might enjoy the sacred letters in his own native tongue. Those old translations still exist, bearing the inscription, By the command of King Charles V, who was a most wise prince not only in name but in fact. So Charles Molinaeus in his book on the Monarchy of the French (written in 1561), sect. 133 (vol. 3 of his Works, Paris edition of 1612, part 2, col. 612, in Latin). In French it reads thus (ibid., col. 574): He likewise had the whole Bible translated into French, not only at Paris but also in Picardy, Normandy and other provinces of the kingdom, so that everyone might have Holy Scripture in his mother tongue. The old translations are still found with the title, By the command of the said Charles V, who was wise not only in name but also in counsel and in deed. So Molinaeus. Similarly Antoine Du Moulin, in Bibliotheca Gallica, under the heading Bibles (p. 137): As for the translation of the Holy Bible into the French language, King Charles V, called the Wise, had it turned into the vernacular of his time. I have one written on parchment, which is in the Picard language. 52 See Plessis, Mysterium Iniquitatis, octavo edition, p. 1071, where he names Nicolas Oresme as the author of this translation. To return to Charles: He ordered the sacred books of the Bible to be carefully and faithfully translated into the French language, being most devoted to ecclesiastical and sacred letters; as John Tillius has it, and the Anglo-Remenses. But when these writers imply that this was done by him so as to counter the Waldenses and others who translated the Scriptures at their own whim, François Hotman affirms that he, being hostile to the tyranny of the Popes, procured this translation; and Charles Molinaeus testifies that, to check it, he had learned men compose the book entitled Somnium Viridarii. Moreover, this translation may still be seen in many places in France, with this inscription: BY THE COMMAND AND ORDER OF KING CHARLES V; and it was in the Royal Library at Fontainebleau in 1563, and again in 1567.

units.la: f Chronic. Reg. Francor. t Præfat in Nov. Testam. Sect. 4. u In Senatusconsf. Franciæ contra abusus Paparum, pag 125. & ad Styl. Parl. part. 4. pag 235.
units.tr: f Chronicle of the Kings of France. t Preface to the New Testament, sect. 4. u In the Senatus-consultum of France against the abuses of the Popes, p. 125, and on the Style of Parliament, part 4, p. 235.

units.la: 52 Quantum autem ad translationem S. Scripturæ in linguam Gallicam, Carolus Rex, Sapiens ille, cum in linguam vulgarem sui temporis con- verti fecit. Habeo exemplar, cui membrana cum, lingua Picardica familiari conscriptum. se vidisse meminit Fr. Hotomannus . Similiter Genebrardus hujus editionis primum exemplar ostendi dicit in Bibliothecâ Regiâ, nempe ab Anno 1374. Claud. Espensæus Tract. ad Confess. Regium. Quòd principem literæ decant: Carolus (inquit) Rex V. sacra Biblia in linguam Francicam Gallicam converti curavit. De eâdem translatione vide Mat. Beroaldum Chronic. lib. 4. pag. 265. Porrò inventa etiam tum sunt Missalia, Breviaria & Psalteria in veterem Francicum sermonem conversa: ut notant Genevenses in Præfat. ad Biblia Gallica postremò à se edita.
units.tr: 52 As for the translation of Holy Scripture into the French language, that wise King Charles V caused it to be turned into the vernacular of his time. I have a copy written on parchment in the familiar Picard dialect, which Fr. Hotman recalls having seen. Similarly Genebrard says he was shown the first copy of this edition in the Royal Library, dated from the year 1374. Claude d'Espence, in his Tract on the Royal Confession: Since letters praise the prince: Charles V, he says, caused the sacred Bibles to be turned into the French tongue. On this same translation see Matthieu Beroalde, Chronicle, book 4, p. 265. Moreover, Missals, Breviaries and Psalters turned into the old French speech were also found at that time, as the Genevans note in the Preface to the French Bible which they lately published.

units.la: 1380. Joannes Wiclefus
units.tr: 1380. John Wycliffe

units.la: Reprehendit hic Papam & suos complices, ut Scribas & Pharisæos claudentes regnum cœlorum, qui nec ipsi intrarent, nec alios intrare permitterent. Eandem querelam etiam alius vir pius apud Anglos circa hæc tempora usurpavit in libello , quem Agricolæ precationem & querimoniam inscripsit (à Joanne Oldcastell dispersum putat Balæus, eidemque tribuit pag. 557.) ita loquens: 53 Thilk that have the key of coming, have y lockt the trewth of thy teaching under many wardes, and y hid it from thy childzen. But Lorde, sith thy teaching is y come frome heaven above; our hope is, that with thy grace, it shall breaken these wardes, and showe hym to thy peple, to bele both the hunger and the thurst of the soul. And then shall no shepeard ner no false hyrid man begile thy peple no moze. For by thy law I write, as thou hightest (promised) sometime, that from the lest to the most all they shullen knowen thy will, and wetem (know) how they. Shullen pleasf thee evermoze in certayne. Ista erat miseranda horum temporum facies; quas tenebras ut dispelleret magnus ille Wiclevus (inquit Balæus) Biblia tota in Anglicum ser-
units.tr: He here rebukes the Pope and his accomplices, as the Scribes and Pharisees, shutting up the kingdom of heaven, who neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter. Another godly man among the English around this time used the same complaint in a little book which he entitled The Plowman's Prayer and Complaint (Bale thinks it was spread abroad by John Oldcastle and attributes it to him, p. 557), speaking thus: 53 Those that have the key of knowing, you have locked the truth of your teaching under many wards, and hid it from your children. But Lord, since your teaching has come from heaven above, our hope is that by your grace it shall break these wards and show itself to your people, to relieve both the hunger and the thirst of the soul. And then no shepherd nor false hired man shall beguile your people any more. For by your law I write, as you promised once, that from the least to the most they all shall know your will, and know how they shall please you evermore in certainty. Such was the wretched face of these times; and to dispel these shadows the great Wycliffe (says Bale) translated all the Bible into the English

units.la: x Franco-Gall. cap. 2. y Chron. lib. 4. ad An. 1535. z Apud Tho. Waldenum in Fasciculo Zizaniorum, (quem MS. apud me habeo) & Orth. Gratium in Fasciculo rerum Expetend. sol. 137. a. a A Gulielmo Tindall edit. est in Fox, p. 369, 370.
units.tr: x Franco-Gallia, ch. 2. y Chronicle, book 4, at the year 1535. z Quoted by Thomas Walden in the Fasciculus Zizaniorum (which I have in manuscript), and by Ortuinus Gratius in the Fasciculus rerum expetendarum, p. 137a. a Published by William Tyndale in Foxe, pp. 369, 370.

units.la: 53 Qui clavem scientiæ habent, doctrina tua veritatem multis seris obscuratam clauserunt; easque à filiis tuis occultatrunt. Cum vero, Domine, doctrina tua cœlitus advenerit; speramus illam tandem aliquando ceras istas gratiâ tuâ effracturam, seipsamque populo tuo ostensuram, ad profligandam ... anima famem & sitim. Et tunc nullus Pastor, neque fallax conabitur ut populum tuum amplius decipiet. Ex authoritate enim tuo tua scripto; ut eum promisisti, quòd omnes à minimo usque ad maximum voluntatem tuam scierint, edocti quomodo tibi in æternum sine errore placere possint.
units.tr: 53 Those who hold the key of knowledge have, by your teaching, locked up the truth, obscured by many bolts; and they have hidden it from your sons. But when your teaching, Lord, has come from heaven, we hope that at length by your grace it will break those bolts and show itself to your people, to banish the hunger and thirst of the soul. And then no shepherd nor deceiver will try to deceive your people any more. For by the authority of your writing, as you promised, all from the least to the greatest shall know your will, taught how they may please you forever without error.

units.la: manem monem transtulit. [Vid. infra An. 1407, 1416.] Extant etiamnum varia veterum Bibliorum Anglicorum exemplaria, quæ translatione differunt: unde manifestum est, præter Wiclevum, alios etiam idem opus persecisse. Ex his 2. exemplaria Evangeliorum, 3. Novi Testamenti, 5. utriusque Testamenti commemorat Tho. Jamesius b. Versionis quinetiam Wiclevianæ meminit M. N. in his Remainder of a greater Work, p. 17. atque idem Jamesius Tractatu vernaculo de Corruptione Patrum. Certè Wiclephum Biblia in Anglicanum sermonem transtulisse testatur etiam Hussus c in quadam suâ Replicâ. Transtulit (inquit Balæus d) in Anglicum sermonem Biblia tota, adhibitis præfationibus atque argumentis cuique libro suis. Vertit & libros duodecim Clementis Lanthoniensis Ecclesiæ Presbyteri de Concordiâ Evangelistarum. Hæc Balæus. In Operis posterioris præfatione Scripturarum Vernacularum prohibitionem Antichristianam esse confirmat Author. Hoc pluribus in Ostiolo suo urget Wiclevus; quod consule. Ejus Translationem Novi Testamenti MS. apud D. Robertum Cottonum Equitem Auratum vidimus.
units.tr: tongue. [See below, under the years 1407 and 1416.] Various old copies of the English Bibles still exist, which differ in their translation; whence it is plain that, besides Wycliffe, others also undertook the same work. Of these, Thomas James records two copies of the Gospels, three of the New Testament, and five of both Testaments. He also mentions the Wycliffite version in M. N.'s Remainder of a greater Work, p. 17, and James himself in his vernacular treatise on the Corruption of the Fathers. Certainly Hus also testifies, in a certain Reply of his, that Wycliffe translated the Bibles into English. He translated (says Bale) the whole Bible into English, with prefaces and arguments suited to each book. He also translated the twelve books of Clement of Lanthony, presbyter of the Church, on the Harmony of the Evangelists. So Bale. In the preface to his later work the author affirms that the prohibition of Scriptures in the vernacular is Antichristian. Wycliffe presses this at length in his Ostiolum; consult it. We have seen his translation of the New Testament in manuscript with Sir Robert Cotton, Knight.

units.la: Ejusdem Speculi Sæcularium Dominorum (quod habetur MS. in Bibliothecâ Regiâ Westmonasteriensi) cap. 1. ita incipit. Cùm veritas fidei eò plus rutilat, quò plus planè cognoscitur: & satrapæ (Episcopi) damnant fidelem sententiam ex invidiâ personæ in auribus sæcularium Dominorum: ut veritas sit nota planiùs atque diffusiùs, necessitantur fideles sententiam, quam promunt, enucleare tam in Latinâ linguâ quàm in vulgari. Dictum est à Prospeculo sæcularium Dominorum in lingua vulgari, quomodo se debent regulare in toto conformiter legi Christi. Nec sunt audiendi Hæretici, qui singunt, quòd seculares non debent legem Dei cognoscere; sed sufficit eis notitia, quam sacerdotes & prælati eis dixerint vivâ voce. Nam Scriptura est fides Ecclesiæ; & quanto est nota planiùs in sensu orthodoxo, de tanto est melior. Ideo sicut seculares debent fidem cognoscere; sic in quacunque linguâ plùs nota fuerit, est docenda. Similiter cùm veritas fidei sit clarior & rectior in Scripturâ, quàm sacerdotes sciunt exprimere: cùm multi etiam Prælati (si fas est dicere) sunt Scripturæ nimis ignari; & alii celant puncta Scripturæ, quæ sc. sonant in humilitatem & paupertatem Cleri; & multi tales defectus sunt in vocibus Sacerdotum; utile videtur esse, fideles sensum fidei taliter referare. Similiter juxta fidem, quam decuit Apostolus Hebr. XI. Sancti per fidem vicerunt regna; & maximè ex stimulo fidei ad patriam properàrunt. Quare igitur non debet fons fidei notificari populo per media, per quæ homo potest scire clarius? Qui igitur
units.tr: Of his Mirror of the Secular Lords (which is held in manuscript in the Royal Library at Westminster), chapter 1 begins thus: Since the truth of the faith shines the more brightly the more plainly it is known, and the satraps (bishops) condemn the faithful opinion out of envy of the person in the ears of the secular lords, so that the truth may be known more plainly and widely, the faithful are compelled to set forth the opinion they hold, both in Latin and in the vernacular. It has been told by the Mirror of the Secular Lords in the vernacular how they ought to conduct themselves in everything in conformity with the law of Christ. Nor are heretics to be heard, who pretend that secular people ought not to know God's law, but that the knowledge which priests and prelates have given them by word of mouth is sufficient. For Scripture is the faith of the Church; and the more plainly it is known in the orthodox sense, the better it is. Therefore, just as secular people ought to know the faith, so it is to be taught in whatever language it is best known. Similarly, since the truth of the faith is clearer and more correct in Scripture than priests know how to express it; since many prelates too (if it is lawful to say so) are too ignorant of Scripture, and others hide those points of Scripture which sound against the humility and poverty of the clergy; and many such defects are in the words of priests, it seems useful for the faithful to refer the sense of the faith in this way. Likewise, according to the faith which the Apostle praises, Heb. XI: "By faith the saints conquered kingdoms," and most of all, from the spur of faith, they hastened to their homeland. Why then should the fountain of faith not be made known to the people by the means by which a man can know more clearly? Who therefore

units.la: b Eclog. Oxonio-Cantab. l. 2. p. 60. c Inter Opera ejus Tom. I. sol. 108, b. d Cent. 6. cap. 1. hoc impedit, vel contra illud remurmurat, procurat quòd populus manet damnabilis & infidelis. Non igitur capiendæ sunt ut fides leges [quas] Prælati fabricant; nec credendum est suis vivis vocibus, nisi de quanto fundatæ fuerint ex Scriptura: cùm secundum crebram doctrinam Augustini lib. 2. de doctrinâ Christianâ, in fine Epistolæ 2. ad Volusianum. Omnis veritas est Scriptura. Hoc igitur bonum faceret ista Scripturæ enucleatio; quòd redderet sacerdotes & prælatos in verbis quæ referant insuspectos. Prælati autem, ut Papæ, & Fratres, & alii medii, possunt in isto deficere. Similiter Christus & sui Apostoli converterunt gentem plurimam per detectionem Scripturæ in linguâ, quæ fuit populo magis nota. Ad hoc enim Spiritus Sanctus dedit eis omnium linguarum notitiam. Quare igitur non debent moderni Christi discipuli de eadem pane fragmenta colligere, & clarius quo sciverunt populo detegere, sicut illi? Non enim est filtio nisi infidelis, volentis Spiritui Sancto resistere. In duplici igitur linguâ, cujus Spiritus Sanctus dedit notitiam, est fides Christi populo referanda. Similiter cùm ex fide, quam docet Apostolus, 2 Cor. V. Oportet omnes Christianos stare ante tribunal Christi, & sibi pro omnibus bonis, quæ illi dederat, respondere: necesse est cunctos fideles bona illa & usus illorum cognoscere, ut responsio tunc patescat; cùm responsio per prælatum vel attornatum tunc non valebit: sed oportet quòd tunc quilibet in propriâ persona respondebit. Cùm igitur Deus dederit tam Clericis quàm Laicis notitiam fidei ad hunc finem, ut clarius doceant, & fideliter operentur per eam: clarum est quòd Deus in die judicii requiret certum computum de usu istorum bonorum, quomodo dabantur fideliter ad usuram, &c.
units.tr: b Eclog. Oxonio-Cantab. l. 2. p. 60. c Inter Opera ejus Tom. I. fol. 108, b. d Cent. 6. cap. 1. He hinders this or murmurs against it, and brings it about that the people remain damnable and unbelieving. Therefore the laws which the prelates devise are not to be received as faith, nor are their living voices to be believed, except insofar as they are founded on Scripture, since according to the frequent teaching of Augustine (Book 2 of On Christian Teaching, and at the end of Letter 2 to Volusianus), "All truth is Scripture." This explanation of Scripture would therefore do this good: it would make priests and prelates unsuspected in the words they report. Prelates, however, such as the Pope, the Friars, and the other intermediaries, can fail in this. Likewise Christ and his Apostles converted very many nations by unfolding Scripture in the language that was better known to the people. For the Holy Spirit gave them knowledge of all languages for this very purpose. Why, then, should the modern disciples of Christ not gather up the fragments of the same bread and disclose them more clearly to the people, as those men did? For no one but an unbeliever, one who wishes to resist the Holy Spirit, is opposed to this. Therefore the faith of Christ is to be reported to the people in the twofold language of which the Holy Spirit gave knowledge. Likewise, since from the faith which the Apostle teaches (2 Cor. 5), all Christians must stand before the judgment seat of Christ and answer for all the good things he has given them, it is necessary that all the faithful know those goods and their use, so that the answer may then be made plain; for an answer given through a prelate or an attorney will then avail nothing, but each one will answer in his own person. Since, then, God has given knowledge of the faith to clergy and laity alike for this end, that they may teach more clearly and work faithfully by it, it is clear that God on the day of judgment will require a certain account of the use of these goods, how they were faithfully entrusted for trading, etc.

units.la: 1390. Anna Regina Angliæ, & Thomas Arundel Eboracensis Archiep.
units.tr: 1390. Anne, Queen of England, and Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of York.

units.la: Soror hæc Wenceslai Regis Bohemiæ, & Richardi II. Angiorum Regis conjux, anno 1394. (ut habet Polydorus Virgilius) mortem obiit. In cujus funere Westmonasterii de laudibus ejus concionem habuit Thomas Arundel, tum temporis Eboracensis Archiepiscopus, & Regni Cancellarius; in quâ non alio nomine eam magis laudavit, quàm quòd quamvis advena esset & peregrina (nempe Bohemica) tamen quatuor Evangelia in linguam Anglicam versa & Doctorum Commentarius declarata assiduè meditaretur. [Ex fragmento libri cujusdam Wigorniensis Ecclesiæ citat. à Matth. Parkero in Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum historiâ pag. 310. & Jo. Fox. Act. & Monument. p. 467.] Hinc Jo. Wiclefus in libello de Triplici vinculo Amoris (citante Jo. Hussio in Replicâ contra Jo. Stokes.) Ex eodem (inquit) patet eorum stultitia qui volunt damnare scripta tanquam hæretica, propter hoc quòd scribunt in Anglico, & acuta tangunt peccata, quæ conturbant illam provinciam. Nam possibile est quòd nobilis Regina Angliæ, soror Cæsaris, habeat Evangelium in linguâ triplici exaratum: sc. in linguâ Bohemicâ, Teutonicâ, & Latinâ; & hæreticare eam propterea foret Luciferina stultitia. Et sicut Teutonici volunt in isto ratinabiliter defendere linguam propriam; sic & Anglici debent de ratione defendere linguam suam.
units.tr: This sister of Wenceslaus, King of Bohemia, and wife of Richard II, King of the English, died in 1394 (as Polydore Vergil has it). At her funeral at Westminster, Thomas Arundel, then Archbishop of York and Chancellor of the realm, preached a sermon in praise of her, in which he praised her for nothing so much as this, that although she was a foreigner and a stranger (namely a Bohemian), she nevertheless assiduously meditated on the four Gospels, which had been translated into the English tongue and explained by the commentary of the teachers. [From a fragment of a certain book of the Church of Worcester, cited by Matthew Parker in his history of the Archbishops of Canterbury, p. 310, and by John Foxe, Acts and Monuments, p. 467.] Hence John Wycliffe, in his little book On the Threefold Bond of Love (cited by John Hus in his Reply against John Stokes), says: From this it is plain how foolish those are who wish to condemn writings as heretical because they are written in English and touch on sharp sins that trouble that province. For it is possible that the noble Queen of England, sister of the Emperor, has the Gospel written in a threefold language, namely in Bohemian, German and Latin; and to charge her with heresy on that account would be Luciferian folly. And just as the Germans wish to defend their own language reasonably in this matter, so the English ought to defend their language with reason.

units.la: 1390. Joannes Gandavensis, Dux Lancastriæ.
units.tr: 1390. John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster.

units.la: Parlamento Richardi II. Regis Angliæ temporibus habito, libellus exhibitus est de tollendis Bibliis in linguam Anglicanam translatis: qui à Nobilibus & inferioris Domûs Congregatione prorsus rejectus est. Et acriter respondit Johannes Dux Lancastriæ in hanc sententiam: Nolumus fæx esse omnium hominum; quandoquidem aliæ nationes legem Dei (quæ nostræ fidei lex est) suâ linguâ exaratam habent: idque magno interposito jurejurando, (ut habet Historia) adversùs eos asseruit, quicunque tandem essent, qui libellum istum primi porrexerunt. Addiderunt alii: Si Evangelium in linguâ Anglicanâ admissum hominibus errandi ansam sit præbiturum; scitote inter Latinos plures inveniri Hæreticos, quàm ex aliâ quacunque linguâ. Decreta namque 66. Hæreticos Latinos recensent. [Historiam hanc translulit Jo. Foxus in Præfationem à se præhixam Evangeliorum Saxonicorum editioni Anno 1571.]
units.tr: In the time of Richard II, King of England, when Parliament was held, a petition was presented for the removal of the Bibles translated into English. It was utterly rejected by the Nobles and by the lower House of Commons. And John, Duke of Lancaster, replied sharply to this effect: "We do not wish to be the dregs of all men, since other nations have the law of God (which is the law of our faith) written in their own tongue." He asserted this with a great oath (as the history has it) against those, whoever they were, who first put forward that petition. Others added: "If the Gospel admitted in the English tongue is going to offer men an occasion for error, know that more heretics are found among the Latins than in any other language, for the Decrees list sixty-six Latin heretics." [John Foxe translated this history into the preface he prefixed to his edition of the Saxon Gospels in the year 1571.]

units.la: De Canonum observantiâ propositi. 9. Cavendum est ne maledictionem incurramus Prophetæ, dicentis: c Maledictus omnis, qui opus Dei facit negligenter. Dignum quippe est, ut mens nostra concordet cum voce, quando ad divinum opus assistimus; & cum diligentiâ à præsentibus universis quisque se retrahat, & divinus inhæreat; ut cælestia ei dona revelentur.
units.tr: On the observance of the canons, proposition 9. We must take care not to incur the curse of the Prophet, who says: "Cursed is everyone who does the work of God negligently." It is indeed fitting that our mind should agree with our voice when we attend the divine work; and each one should withdraw himself from all distractions with diligence, and cleave to the divine, so that heavenly gifts may be revealed to him.

units.la: Anno 1401. Gulielmus Butler Franciscanus scripsit Determinationis nomine libellum contra Translationem (Wiclevianam, uti nos docet
units.tr: In the year 1401 William Butler, a Franciscan, wrote under the title of a Determinatio a little book against the translation of Scripture into the vernacular, the Wycliffite one, as we learn from (c Jerem. XVII. Jamesius, book on the Corruption of the Fathers, part 2, loc. 24).

units.la: c Jerem. XVII. Jamesius lib. de Corruptione Patrum part. 2. loc. 24.) Scripturæ in linguam vulgarem : postquam essed in Angliâ (ut testis est Purvæus) generale mandatum ut comburéretur. Extat adhuc libellus iste Oxonii in Mertonensis Collegii Bibliothecâ vol. 143. Ex eo sequens fragmentum desumptum est. Nec debent Prælati hoc admittere, quòd singuli ad libitum eorum legant Scripturam in Latinum translatam; quia (sicut experientia satis docet) hoc fuit multis modis occasio incidendi in hæreses & errores. Non est ergo politicum, ut quicunque ubicunque quandocunque voluerit, se det ferventi studio Scripturarum. Eodem ferè tempore Scillius quidam Fraterculus, coram Londinensi Episcopo ad Crucem Paulinam contra easdem Translationes concionem habuit; cui alii se oppositerunt, verba illa Pauli ad Elymam Magum, Act. XIII. de Fratre Scillio usurpantes: O plene omni dolo & omni fallacià, quare Episcopum à verâ fide avertere conaris? Objiciebatur etiam ei cùm aliorum Doctorum authoritas, tum Richardi Hampul Eremitæ, qui Psalterium in linguam Anglicanam translulit, & in versum illum Davidis [Ne auferas de ore meo verbum veritatis usquequaque] judicium suum de necessitate Scripturarum Vernacularum propositum. Tandem verò Anno 1407. (sic, opinor, Fox loco citato; at Mat. Parkerus ad Annum 1406. refert. Linvodus verò ad An. 1408.) in Concilio Oxonii habito Thomas Arundel Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis (quem ante annos 13. piæ Reginæ in Scripturâ Vernaculâ perlegendâ diligentiam prædicâsse audivimus) pro authoritate suâ controversiam diremit: septimam ibi Constitutionem in hæc verba sanciens: 54 Periculosa res est (testante B. Hieronymo) textum sacræ Scripturæ de uno in aliud idioma transferre: eò quòd in ipsis translationibus non de facili idem sensus in omnibus retinetur; prout idem Beatus Hieronymus, etsi inspiratus fuisset, se in hoc sæpius fatetur errâsse. Statuimus igitur & ordinamus, ut nemo deinceps textum aliquem sacræ Scripturæ auctoritate sua in linguam Anglicanam vel aliam transferat, per viam libri vel libelli aut Tractatus, nec legatur aliquis hujusmodi liber, libellus aut Tractatus, jam noviter tempore Johannis Wickliff, sive citra, compositus, aut in posterum componendus, in parte vel in toto, publicè vel occultè, sub pœnâ maioris excommunicationis; quousque per loci Diocesanum, seu (si res exegerit) per Concilium provinciale, ipsa transla-
units.tr: After it had been ordered throughout England (as Purvey witnesses) that it be burned. The booklet still survives at Oxford in the library of Merton College, vol. 143, and the following fragment is taken from it. Prelates ought not to allow that individuals read, at their pleasure, Scripture translated into the vernacular; for (as experience teaches well enough) this has in many ways been an occasion of falling into heresies and errors. It is therefore not expedient that whoever, wherever and whenever he wishes, should give himself with eager zeal to the Scriptures. About the same time a certain friar, Scill, preached a sermon at St Paul's Cross before the Bishop of London against these same translations. Others opposed him, applying to Friar Scill the words of Paul to Elymas the magician, Acts 13: O full of all guile and all fraud, why do you try to turn the bishop away from the true faith? He was also confronted with the authority of other teachers, and with that of Richard Hampole the hermit, who translated the Psalter into English, and with his judgment, set out on that verse of David [Do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth], concerning the necessity of vernacular Scriptures. Finally, in 1407 (so I think Foxe has it in the place cited; but Matthew Parker refers it to 1406, and Lyndwood to 1408), in a council held at Oxford, Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury (whom we heard some thirteen years earlier to have preached diligence in reading Scripture in the vernacular under the pious Queen), settled the dispute by his authority, enacting there the seventh constitution in these words: 54 It is a dangerous thing (as Blessed Jerome testifies) to transfer the text of holy Scripture from one language into another, because in translations the same sense is not easily kept in all cases; as Blessed Jerome himself, though he was inspired, often confesses he erred in this. We therefore decree and ordain that no one henceforth, on his own authority, translate any text of holy Scripture into English or any other language, by way of book, booklet or treatise; nor let any such book, booklet or treatise, newly composed in the time of John Wycliffe or since, or to be composed hereafter, be read, in part or in whole, publicly or secretly, under penalty of the greater excommunication; until the translation has been approved by the diocesan of the place or, if the matter requires it, by a provincial council.

units.la: {54} Concil. Labb. Tom. XI. pag. 2095. tio fuerit approbata. Qui vero contra hoc fecerit, ut fautor hæresis & erroris similiter puniatur. Ex eo, quod in hac constitutione dicitur [Noviter compositus] colligit Guilhelmus Lindwodus k, quòd libros, libellos, vel tractatus in Anglicis vel alio idiomate prius translatos de textu Scripturæ legere non est prohibitum. Unde intelligimus ante Wiclevi tempora Scripturas in linguam vernaculam translatas extitisse; neque etiam earum lectionem prohibitam esse (vid. Dialog. Tho. Mori lib. 3. cap.16. cum respond. Tindalli) quod quantopere à sublequentium temporum moribus alienum fuit, ex hujus Historiæ serie post apparebit. Et de Constitutione quidem Tho. Arundelii satis: de cujus vitæ exitu ita scribit Thomas Gascoign l in Dictionario suo Theologico MS. Anno 1411. Tho. Arundel Cant. Archiepiscopus sic linguâ percussus erat; ut nec deglutire, nec loqui per aliquot dies ante mortem suam potuerit, divitis epulonis exemplo, & sic 55 tantum obiit. Atque tunc multi fieri putabant; quia verbum alligâsset, ne suo tempore prædicaretur. Hisce etiam temporibus Alexander V. Scripturas in sermonem vulgarem translatas damnâsse dicitur: m de quo prophetiam edidisse fertur Jacobus de Theramo n; quòd Anno Domini 1409. surget unus, qui Evangelium & Epistolas & fidem Christi persequetur. Nota hic tempus ingredientis erroris, idque cum contradictione.
units.tr: {54} Council of Labbe, Tom. XI, p. 2095. Whoever acts contrary to this shall likewise be punished as a supporter of heresy and error. From the fact that this constitution says [newly composed], William Lyndwood infers that it is not forbidden to read books, booklets or treatises in English or another language translated earlier from the text of Scripture. Hence we understand that before the time of Wycliffe there were Scriptures translated into the vernacular, and that their reading was not forbidden either (see Thomas More's Dialogue, book 3, cap. 16, with Tyndale's reply). How far this was alien to the customs of later times will appear afterwards in the course of this History. Enough about Thomas Arundel's constitution. Of the end of his life Thomas Gascoigne writes thus in his manuscript Theological Dictionary, in the year 1411: Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury, was so struck in the tongue that for some days before his death he could neither swallow nor speak, after the example of the rich glutton, and so died 55 only. And then many thought it had happened because he had bound the word, so that it would not be preached in his time. In these same times Alexander V is said to have condemned Scriptures translated into the common tongue; of him Jacobus de Theramo is reported to have published a prophecy: that in the year of the Lord 1409 one would arise who would persecute the Gospel, the Epistles and the faith of Christ. Note here the time at which the error came in, and that it did so with opposition.

units.la: ◦ In Bibliothecâ Collegii S. Benedicti Cantabrig. habetur Transcriptum Determinationis cujusdam Doctoris in S. Theologiâ, contra eos qui dicunt nefas esse habere S. Scripturam aut alios libros in linguâ Anglicanâ. Tractatus iste à Joanne Foxo evulgatus est in primâ Actorum & Monument. editione pag. 452. titulo Brevis antiqui Tractatus demonstrantis S. Scripturam in linguâ Anglicanâ habendam esse. Initium ejus Latinè versum subjiciam. Contra illos, qui dicunt S. Scripturam Anglicè vertendam non esse, ejusmodi argumenta proferam, &c. Sanctus etiam Paulus in primâ ad Corinthios Epistola cap. 14. dicit: Vellem vos omnes peregrinis loqui linguis, sed magis ut vaticinemini: Dicit etiam: Orabo spiritu, orabo & mente; i. e. cum affectu & intellectu. Idque multò satius est quàm devotionem in verbis tantùm non in intellectu habere. Istud
units.tr: In the library of St Benedict's College, Cambridge, there is a transcript of a determination by a certain Doctor of Sacred Theology, against those who say it is wrong to have Holy Scripture or other books in the English tongue. John Foxe published this treatise in the first edition of his Acts and Monuments, p. 452, under the title A Brief Treatise of an Ancient Writer, Showing That Holy Scripture Ought to Be Had in the English Tongue. I will add its opening, translated into Latin: Against those who say that Holy Scripture is not to be translated into English, I will put forward arguments of this kind, etc. Saint Paul also says in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 14: I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied. He also says: I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also; that is, with feeling and with understanding. And this is far better than having devotion only in words and not in the understanding. That

units.la: 55 Tandem legendum videtur. quinetiam textus demonstrat, istiusmodi verba subiiciens: Quomodo ille dicet Amen super benedictionem tuam, qui quid dicis non intelligit? His addi potest Doctoris Lyrani sententia: Si populus intelligat orationem seu benedictionem Sacerdotis; melius reducitur in Deum, & devotius respondet Amen. S. Scriptura itaque in Hispanicam, Gallicam, & Germanicam linguam conversa est; atque aliae gentes Biblium in vernacula lingua legunt, &c.
units.tr: 55 It seems better to read: Indeed the text itself shows this, by adding these words: How will he who does not understand what you say say Amen to your blessing? To this may be added the opinion of the Doctor Lyra: If the people understand the prayer or blessing of the priest, it is more beneficially directed to God, and they respond Amen more devoutly. Holy Scripture has therefore been turned into the Spanish, French and German tongues; and other nations read the Bible in their vernacular language, etc.

units.la: Huic affine docet lacerum quoddam Bibliothecae Wigorniensis fragmentum 55 circa idem tempus scriptum: quod Latine pariter conversum repraesentabo. Auditum est a Germano quodam fide digno, olim Belgam, cui nomen erat Jacobus Merland, integram Bibliam Belgice vertisse. Propterea Interpres magno a quibusdam odio habitus sese coram Papa judicandum sistere jussus est: liberque examini submissus; qui tandem magnopere approbatus, illi in manus remissus est ad inimicorum confusionem. Quin & Venerabilis Beda Spiritu Dei inductus, Bibliam, saltem majorem ejus partem, in linguam Anglicanam translulit: cujus versionis exemplaria adhuc in multis Angliae Monasteriis supersunt. Porro Cestrensis libro 5. cap. 24. Evangelium Johannis Anglice ab eodem Beda conversum esse prodit: quod quidem Evangelium Johannis, aliaque Evangelia multis in locis adhuc asservantur, in vetustam Anglicae linguae dialectum conversa, quam vix ullus hodie Anglus perlegere potest, &c. Praeterea penes civem quendam Londinensem, nomine Wering, Biblium erat in Septentrionalem Angliae dialectum redditum; quod a multis inspectum est, & ducentorum annorum aetatem prae se tulit, &c. Adhaec magnus ille Theologus Lincolniensis in Sermone, cui initium est [Scriptum est de Levitis] haec habet: Si quis Sacerdos se praedicare non posse dicat; unum praesto est remedium, ut Beneficium suum abdicet; alterum (si forte istud nolit) ut singulis septimanis nudum Evangeliorum Dominicalium textum perdiscat; cumque plebi suae enarret, &c. Itidem vir genere nobilis Richardus Hampole Psalterium Anglice convertit, & prolixa satis glossa illustravit, &c. Frater autem Scillius, qui coram Episcopo Londinensi centenisque aliis auditoribus dixit, Hieronymum agnovisse se S. Scripturam vertendo erravisse, similis est Elymae, qui Episcopum seu Judicem a fide avertere conatus est, &c. Multis etiam constat, tempore Richardi Regis (cujus animae propitius sit Deus) libellum Parlamento oblatum esse duorum Archiepiscoporum totiusque Cleri assensu, ad abrogandam Bibliae aliorumque librorum Evangelicorum versionem Au-
units.tr: Related to this, a torn fragment from the library of Worcester, written about the same time, teaches the same thing; I will give it in Latin as well. It was heard from a certain trustworthy German, once in Belgium, whose name was James Merland, that he had translated the whole Bible into Flemish. For this reason the translator, held in great hatred by some, was ordered to appear for judgement before the Pope; and, submitted freely to examination, he was at last greatly approved and handed back to his enemies to their confusion. Moreover the Venerable Bede, moved by the Spirit of God, translated the Bible, or at least the greater part of it, into the English tongue; copies of this version still survive in many monasteries of England. Further, Chester, in book 5, chapter 24, reports that the Gospel of John was turned into English by the same Bede; this Gospel of John, and other Gospels, are still kept in many places, converted into an old dialect of the English tongue, which scarcely any Englishman today can read through, etc. Besides, a certain citizen of London named Wering had a Bible rendered into the northern dialect of England; many have looked at it, and it showed an age of two hundred years, etc. Moreover that great theologian of Lincoln, in the sermon which begins [It is written concerning the Levites], says this: If a priest says he cannot preach, there is one ready remedy: let him give up his benefice; the other (if perhaps he is unwilling to do this) is that every week he learn by heart the bare text of the Sunday Gospels, and recite it to his people, etc. Likewise Richard Hampole, a man of noble birth, turned the Psalter into English and illustrated it with a rather lengthy gloss, etc. But Friar Scillius, who said before the Bishop of London and a hundred other hearers that he had recognised that Jerome had erred in translating Scripture, is like Elymas, who tried to turn the bishop or judge away from the faith, etc. It is also established by many that in the time of King Richard (may God be merciful to his soul), a petition was presented to Parliament, with the assent of two archbishops and the whole clergy, to abrogate the version of the Bible and of the other evangelical books into English, etc.

units.la: 55 Anglice tantum Fragmentum istud (pariter ac superius) dedit Ulterius, adeoque quae | inibi reperies aliorum fragmenta, non sunt authentica, sed ex versione nieā. glicam. Denique Thomas Arundel, qui sedi Cantuariensi nunc præest, in Ecclesiâ Westmonasteriensi, frequenti auditorum turba præsente, in exequiis Annæ Reginæ concionatus est, &c.
units.tr: 55 Only this fragment (like the one above) is given in English. Further, the fragments of others that you will find there are not authentic, but from my own translation. Finally, Thomas Arundel, who now presides over the see of Canterbury, preached in the church of Westminster at the funeral of Queen Anne, with a large crowd of hearers present, etc.

units.la: 1410. Johannes Huss, & Bohemi.
units.tr: 1410. John Huss and the Bohemians.

units.la: De Johanne Husso ita scribit Jo. Cochlæus: Instituit pellifices, sartores, sutores, & id genus alios Mechanicos; qui crebris concionibus operam dantes, & sacras literas in vernaculam linguam translatas fervidè legentes, cum Sacerdotibus coram plebe disputarent. Et non solum viri, sed & Beguttæ aliæque mulieres, eò audaciæ & inverecundiæ proruperunt; ut de sacris literis disserere, & Presbyteris certamina movere præsumerent.
units.tr: Of John Huss, John Cochlaeus writes thus: He set up furriers, tailors, cobblers and other mechanics of that sort, who, giving their efforts to frequent sermons, and eagerly reading the sacred writings translated into the vernacular, disputed with the priests before the people. And not only men but also beguines and other women broke out into such boldness and shamelessness that they presumed to discourse on the sacred writings and to stir up contests with the presbyters.

units.la: 1416. Radulphus Munginus.

units.la: In Synodo Londini habitâ sub Henrico Chichesley, Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo, Radulpho inter alia objectum est, quòd Evangelia Johannis Wickleffi in civitate Londinensi sparsisset; unde ad perpetuos carceres ab Archiepiscopo damnatus est. Ibidem ad Palinodiam adactus est J. Gallus Presbyter Londinensis, quòd librum Anglicum qui Novæ Legis inscriptus erat, habuisset. [Ex Registro Henrici Chichesley.]
units.tr: In the synod held at London under Henry Chichele, Archbishop of Canterbury, Ralph was charged among other things with having scattered the Gospels of John Wycliffe in the city of London; for this he was condemned by the Archbishop to perpetual imprisonment. At the same place John Gall, a London presbyter, was compelled to recant, because he had possessed an English book entitled The New Law. [From the Register of Henry Chichele.]

units.la: 1420. Johannes Purvey.
units.tr: 1420. Johannes Purvey.

units.la: Ex libello ejus sententias sequentes ut hæreticas & erroneas collegit adversarius ejus Richardus Lavinham Carmelita (quas MSS. habeo) Christianus populus habet grandem causam refutandi leges & statuta mundialium Clericorum, qualia vocat leges Papales & Episcopales factas propter cupiditatem & voluptatem: sine quibus Ecclesia possit currere securè versus cœlum per jugum suave mandatorum Domini; sicut fecit per mille annos, antequam dictæ leges mitterentur Universitatibus; & retraxerunt homines à sacrâ Scripturâ propter cupiditatem beneficiorum & bonorum sæcularium. Item. Simplices homines recipiunt revereniter sententias doctorum, & alias leges, in quantum fundantur super Scripturam sacram expressè vel bonam rationem. Cùm autem leges Paparum & suorum insciorum Clericorum sint contrariæ sibi ipsis, absque fundamento Scripturæ vel rationis; debent simplices homines permittere eas ire dormitum.
units.tr: His adversary Richard Lavenham, a Carmelite, gathered from his little book the following sentences as heretical and erroneous (which I have in manuscript): The Christian people has great cause to refute the laws and statutes of the worldly clergy, which he calls the papal and episcopal laws, made on account of greed and pleasure; without which the Church could run safely towards heaven by the sweet yoke of the Lord's commandments, as it did for a thousand years before those laws were sent to the universities; and they have drawn men away from holy Scripture on account of the greed for benefices and secular goods. Likewise: Simple people receive reverently the opinions of the teachers, and other laws, insofar as they are founded upon holy Scripture expressly or on sound reason. But since the laws of the popes and of their unlearned clergy are contrary to themselves, without foundation in Scripture or reason, simple people ought to allow them to go to sleep.

units.la: {g} Fox, pag 590. {q} Fox, pag 593.

Circa hoc tempus claruit Lupus de Oliveto; quem vide in Regulâ Monachorum, cap. de contemplat. orat. & lectione, tom. 9. Operum Hieronymi, edit. Victorii, rem fusè persequentem. Pauca quædam describam. Ama scientiam Scripturarum, & carnis vitia non amabis. — Orationi lectio, lectioni succedat oratio. — Crebrius lege, & disce quamplurima; & tenente te codicem somnus obrepat, &c. Quotidie de Scripturis sanctis aliquid dicatur. — Sæpe in manibus tuis divina sit lectio, & crebræ orationes. — De Scripturis sanctis habeto fixum versuum numerum. Illud pensum Domino tuo redde. — Scientia pietatis est, nosse legere Scripturas, Prophetas intelligere, in Evangelio credere, Apostolos non ignorare. Nec putemus in verbis Scripturarum esse Evangelium, sed in sensu: Non in superficie, sed in medullâ: Non in sermonum foliis, sed in radice rationis. Si quid autem ignoras, si quid de Scripturis dubites, interroga eum; quem vita commendat, excusat ætas, fama non reprobat, &c. Quæ enim potest esse vita sine scientiâ Scripturarum, per quam etiam ipse Christus agnoscitur? Qui cili, quæ mella sunt dulciora, quàm Dei nosse prudentiam?
units.tr: About this time flourished Lupus de Oliveto, whom see in the Rule of the Monks, chapter on contemplative prayer and reading, vol. 9 of the Works of Jerome, edition of Victorius, where he discusses the matter at length. I shall set down a few things. Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. — Let reading be followed by prayer, and prayer by reading. — Read more often, and learn very many things; and let sleep creep upon you while you hold the codex, etc. Let something be said daily from the holy Scriptures. — Let divine reading and frequent prayers often be in your hands. — Have a fixed number of verses of the holy Scriptures; render that task to your Lord. — The knowledge of godliness is to know how to read the Scriptures, to understand the Prophets, to believe in the Gospel, not to be ignorant of the Apostles. Nor let us think that the Gospel is in the words of the Scriptures, but in the sense: not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of the discourses, but in the root of reason. But if you are ignorant of anything, if you doubt anything about the Scriptures, ask him whom his life commends, his age excuses, his reputation does not condemn, etc. For what life can there be without knowledge of the Scriptures, through which Christ himself is recognised? What honeys are sweeter than to know the wisdom of God?

units.tr: 1425. Valentines in Spain.

units.la: 1429. Norwicenses.
units.tr: 1429. The Norwich people.

units.la: Guilhelmus Wrightus coram Norwicensi Episcopo jurejurando interposito confirmavit, quòd I. Richardus Fletcher de Beckles Anglicè habuit librum Novæ Legis, qui prius Hugonis Pii fuerat. II. Nicolaus Belwardus Novum Testamentum habit, quod Londini pretio 4. marcarum & 40. denariorum (quo pretio nostris temporibus 40. ejusmodi libri coemi possunt) sibi comparavit; eundemque Wrightum & uxorem ejus per anni spatium docuit, & Novo Testamento diligenter studuit. III. Hugo Pius Testamento legavit Aliciæ ancillæ W. Whiti Novum Testamentum (quem librum Novæ Legis tum appellabant) quod in custodiâ extitit Oswaldi Godfrey Colcestrensis. [Ex Registro Norwicensi r.]
units.tr: William Wright, before the Bishop of Norwich, confirmed on oath that: I. Richard Fletcher of Beckles had an English book of the New Law, which had previously belonged to Hugh Pye. II. Nicholas Belward had a New Testament, which he bought for himself at London for the price of 4 marks and 40 pence (at which price 40 such books can be bought in our times); and he taught the same Wright and his wife for a year, and studied the New Testament diligently. III. Hugh Pye bequeathed by will to Alice, the maidservant of W. Whit, a New Testament (which they then called the book of the New Law), which was in the custody of Oswald Godfrey of Colchester. [From the Norwich Register.]

units.la: In Destructorio Vitiorum, part. 4. cap. 40. Quod considerans B. Augustinus in Epistola ad Julianum Comitem ita scribit; Grandis (inquit) confusio est animabus laicorum, qui dicunt, Quid pertinet ad me libroc Scripturarum legendo audire vel discere; vel etiam frequenter ad Sacerdotes & ad Ecclesiam Sanctorum recurrere? Cum Clericus fiam, ea quae oportet Clericus facere, faciam. Sed quare non intelligit, quia panem & vinum atque alia hujusmodi terrae bona, & regni felicitatem aequaliter vult participare, & aequali labore jugum Christi ferre non vult. Et sequitur: Similiter enim mandata Dei servantibus Laicis coeleste palatium patet, veluti & Clericis. Item Augustinus super Johan. Homil. 51. Cum audistis (inquit) fratres, Dominum dicentem: Ubi ego sum, illic & minister meus erit; nolite tantummodo bonos Episcopos & Clericos cogitare: sed etiam vos laici pro modo vestro ministrate Christo bene vivendo, eleemosynas faciendo, nomen & doctrinam ejus quibus potueritis praedicando: ut unusquisque etiam paterfamilias hoc nomine agnoscat paternum affectum suae familiae se debere, pro Christo & pro vita aeterna suos omnes moneat, doceat, hortetur, corripiat, impendat benevolentiam & exerceat disciplinam: & ita in domo sua Ecclesiasticum & quodammodo Episcopale impleat officium ministrans Christo, ut in aeternum sit cum ipso. Item idem super Psalm. L. Quomodo (inquit) ad nos pertinet loqui vobis in Ecclesia; sic ad vos pertinet in domibus vestris agere, ut bonam rationem reddatis de his, qui vobis subditi sunt. Item idem in Epistola ad Julianum Comitem: Quaeso (inquit) mi frater; quaeso cum ..ibus tibi subjectis, & bonae voluntatis, in domo tua a majore usque ad minorem, amorem & dulcedinem regni coelestis, amaritudinem etiam & timorem gehennae annuncies; & de eorum salute sollicitus atque vigil existas; quod pro omnibus tibi subjectis, qui in domo tua sunt, rationem Deo reddes. Annuncia, praecipe, impera, suade eis; ut caveant a superbia, a detractione, ab ebrietate; a fornicatione, a luxuria, ab ira, & a perjurio, a cupiditate, quae est radix omnium malorum. Haec ille: unde dicit Apostolus 1 Timoth. 5. Si quis suorum, & maxime domesticorum, curam non habet; fidem negat, & est infideli deterior. Unde, sicut narrat Eusebius in de Ecclesiasticis Historiis libro 2. cap. 15. Marcus Evangelista Romae scripsit Evangelium Christi: & ad preces & regiones
units.tr: In the Destructorium Vitiorum, part 4, chapter 40: "Blessed Augustine, considering this, writes in his Letter to Julian the Count as follows: 'There is great confusion among the souls of the laity, who say, What does it matter to me to hear or learn by reading the books of Scripture, or even often to have recourse to the priests and the Church of the saints? When I become a cleric, I will do what clerics ought to do. But why does he not understand that he wishes to share equally in bread and wine and the other good things of the earth and in the happiness of the kingdom, yet does not wish to bear the yoke of Christ with equal labour?' And he goes on: 'For when the laity keep God's commandments, the heavenly palace is open to them just as it is to clerics.' Again, Augustine on John, Homily 51: 'When you have heard, brethren, the Lord saying, Where I am, there also shall my minister be, do not think only of good bishops and clerics. You laity too, according to your measure, must minister to Christ by living well, giving alms, and preaching his name and teaching as far as you are able, so that every head of a household also recognises that by this name he owes a fatherly affection to his family. For Christ and for eternal life he should admonish, teach, exhort, correct, bestow goodwill on all his own, and exercise discipline; and so in his own house he fulfils the ecclesiastical and in some measure the episcopal office, ministering to Christ, that he may be with him for ever.' Again the same on Psalm 50: 'Just as it belongs to us to speak to you in the Church, so it belongs to you to act in your houses, so that you may render a good account of those who are subject to you.' Again the same in the Letter to Julian the Count: 'I ask, my brother, I ask that you proclaim to those under you who are of good will, in your house from the greatest to the least, the love and sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, and also the bitterness and fear of hell; and that you be anxious and watchful for their salvation, since you will render account to God for all who are subject to you in your house. Announce, command, enjoin, and persuade them to beware of pride, backbiting, drunkenness, fornication, lust, anger, perjury, and covetousness, which is the root of all evils.' Thus far Augustine. Hence the Apostle says, 1 Timothy 5: 'If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.' Hence, as Eusebius relates in his Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 15: Mark the Evangelist wrote the Gospel of Christ at Rome, and at the prayers and exhortations of that people he handed down what Peter had preached in word, so that they might keep it as a permanent reminder; so that they might remain at home and abroad in meditation on this word. When Peter heard this, he rejoiced at their faith, seeing their devotion in it; he confirmed the deed and gave them Scripture to be read for ever."

units.la: 56 Eadem habet Beda Prolog. in Comment. in Marc. gationes populi illius tradidit; qui exorabat, ut ea quæ ille verbo prædicabat, ad perpetuam eorum commonitionem habendam Scripturæ traderet; quò domi forisque in hujuscemodi verbi meditationibus permanerent. Quo audito Petrus gavisus est de fide illorum, per hoc devotionem eorum considerans; factumque confirmat, & in perpetuum legendam Scripturam eis tradidit. Hæc ibi. Item laici adulti, ut patet ex supradictis, tenentur sub pœnâ mortis æternæ scire Orationem Dominicam & Salutationem Angelicam, & præcepta Decalogi; & omnia hæc continentur in Evangelio. Erubescant igitur infideles Hæretici, & Christianæ fidei inimici; qui dicunt, quod Laici non tenentur scire, addiscere, aut cognoscere, vel se intromittere de Evangelio Christi. Nam idem est sic dicere & afferere, quod Laici non debent Christum cognoscere, sed semper manere ut Judæi & Pagani sine veritatis notitia. Unde Apostolus 2 Corinth. IV. Si opertum est Evangelium; in his qui pereunt est opertum; in quibus Deus hujus seculi excæcavit mentes infidelium, ut fulgeat illuminatio Evangelii gloriæ Christi. Item Hieronym. & ponitur in ca. dist. 39. Si juxta. Si juxta (inquit) Apostolum Paulum Christus Dei virtus & Dei sapientia est; ignoratio ergo Scripturarum est ignoratio Christi. Sed quàm periculosa sit ista ignoratio, ostendit beatus Bernardus; & ponitur 6°. Florum, cap. 26. ubi sic scribit: Omnis (inquit) peccati consummationem parit desperatio: desperatio de Dei ignorantiâ venit. Si enim nos Dei ignorantia tenet; quomodo sperabimus in eum quem ignoramus? Scimus autem desperatis partem vel societatem non esse in sorte sanctorum, &c. Item Gregorius, & ponitur in ca. dist. 38. Qui ea. Qui ea (inquit) quæ Dei sunt, sapiunt, sapiuntur à Domino: & qui ea quæ Dei sunt, nesciunt, nesciuntur à Domino: Paulo testante, qui ait: Si quis ignorat, ignorabitur: & quicunque stultus est in culpâ, sapiens erit in pœnâ. Hæc ibi. Laici igitur informandi sunt per Sacerdotes, quod libenter Scripturam sacram audiant, & humiliter addiscant; & cum omni humilitate, timore, & reverentiâ, de veritate quam addidicerunt & clarè intelligunt, loquantur; & non pompent de illis, quæ sciunt; nec alios ignorantes despiciant; nec arroganter putent se scire quæ forte nesciunt nec intelligunt.
units.tr: 56 Bede has the same in the Prologue to his Commentary on Mark: "Hence, since the laity who have come of age are bound under pain of eternal death to know the Lord's Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, and the precepts of the Decalogue, and all of these are contained in the Gospel, let the unbelieving heretics and enemies of the Christian faith blush, who say that the laity are not bound to know, learn, or understand the Gospel of Christ, or to concern themselves with it. For to say and assert this is the same as saying that the laity ought not to know Christ, but always remain, like Jews and pagans, without knowledge of the truth." Hence the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 4: "If the Gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the light of the glorious Gospel of Christ should shine." Likewise Jerome, quoted in Distinction 39, chapter "Si juxta": "If, according to the Apostle Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, then ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ." But how dangerous this ignorance is, blessed Bernard shows, in the Flowers, chapter 26, where he writes: "Despair brings forth the completion of every sin; despair comes from ignorance of God. For if ignorance of God holds us, how shall we hope in him whom we do not know? We know that the despairing have no part or fellowship in the lot of the saints, etc." Likewise Gregory, quoted in Distinction 38, chapter "Qui ea": "Those who savour the things of God are savoured by the Lord, and those who do not know the things of God are not known by the Lord, as Paul bears witness, who says, 'If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored'; and whoever is foolish in guilt will be wise in punishment." Thus far these authorities.
