The laity, therefore, are to be instructed by the priests that they should gladly hear the holy Scripture and humbly learn it, and speak with all humility, fear, and reverence about the truth they have learned and clearly understand; and they should not boast of what they know, nor despise others who are ignorant, nor arrogantly think that they know what perhaps they do not know or understand.

units.la: 1438. Bohemi, Thaboritæ.
units.tr: 1438. Bohemians, Thaborites.

units.la: Ex petitionibus f, quas regni Bohemiæ Oratores hoc tempore Basileensi Synodo proposuerunt, septima his verbis concipitur. Quatenus vestræ
units.tr: The seventh of the petitions which the envoys of the kingdom of Bohemia put forward at this time to the Council of Basel is worded thus: That your

units.la: {f} In Orth. Gratii Fasciculo rerum Expetend. sol. 160. b. vestræ paternitates dignentur permittere ad minus Evangelia, Epistolas & Symbolum in vulgari in Missis & Ecclesiis coram populo ad excitandam devotionem libertari, legi & decantari. Nam in nostro linguagio Sclavico ex indulto Ecclesiæ olim ab antiquo in vulgari suo exercetur, etiam in nostro regno. Unde & ad nostra usque tempora Bohemorum Sacerdotes in sacrificiis Epistolam & Evangelium lingua domestica canunt; & huic consuetudini pertinacissimè adhærent; asserentes se illud literis Concilii Basileensis (quas vocant Pactionis) confirmatum & approbatum habere: quemadmodum testatur Johannes Slechta Bohemus in literis ad Erasmum Roterodamum Anno 1519. datis t. Huc etiam pertinet sententia illa Æneæ Sylvii u (qui Concilio Basileensi interfuit) Pudeat Italiæ Sacerdotes; quos ne semel quidem Novam Legem constat legisse: apud Thabritas vix mulierculam invenias, quæ de Novo Testamento & Veteri respondere nesciat. Isti vero nec quicquam furente Antichristo ad nostra tempora duraverunt, fideique suæ confessionem x nobiscum ediderunt, in cujus primo capite ita legimus. Unusquisque divina sanctorum Prophetarum & Apostolorum scripta maximi facere, eisque in omnibus fidem prorsus habere, religiosèque assentiri, diligenter ea legere, salutarem doctrinam ex his assumere, & secundum hæc se instituere & dirigere debet; & imprimis ii, qui sanctæ Ecclesiæ Dei præpositi sunt. Quibus de causis in nostris Ecclesiis & conventibus hæc sacra Scriptura auditoribus communi & vernacula lingua, quam universi intelligunt, recitatur, &c. Illud vero quod de Italiæ sacerdotibus narrat Sylvius nequaquam mirum videri debet: cum de Sorboniistis sui temporis referat Robertus Stephanus, y interrogatos à se quo loco Novi Testamenti aliquid esset scriptum, respondisse, se illud apud Hieronymum, aut in Decretis legisse; quid vero Novum Testamentum esset, ignorare. Item alium ejusdem Sorbonæ Theologum subinde dicere solitum: Miror quod isti juvenes allegant in his Novum Testamentum; per diem, ego habebam plusquam quinquaginta annos, quod nesciebam, quid esset Novum Testamentum. Vide Hyperium de Scripturæ Lectione quotidianâ, lib. 1. pag. 123. & Eipenlæum in Epist. ad Tit. pag. 105. t Lib. 14. Epistolarum Erasmi. u Comment. de dictis & factis Alfonsi R. lib. 2. x In Harmonia Confess. sect. 1. y Responsi ad Theologorum Parisi. censuras, edit. Genevæ Anno 1552.
units.tr: {f} In Orth. Gratii Fasciculo rerum Expetend. sol. 160. b. Fatherhoods would deign to permit at least the Gospels, Epistles and Creed to be freed, read and sung in the vernacular at Masses and in churches before the people, to arouse devotion. For in our Slavonic language it has long been practised in the vernacular by indulgence of the Church, even in our kingdom. Hence even to our own times the priests of the Bohemians sing the Epistle and Gospel in the sacrifices in their domestic tongue, and they cling most stubbornly to this custom, asserting that they have it confirmed and approved by the letters of the Council of Basel (which they call of Agreement), as Johannes Slechta, a Bohemian, testifies in a letter to Erasmus of Rotterdam dated 1519. t To this also belongs the saying of Aeneas Sylvius u (who was present at the Council of Basel): It is a shame for the priests of Italy, of whom it is established that they have not once even read the New Law. Among the Thaborites you can scarcely find a little woman who cannot answer about the New Testament and the Old. But those men, though Antichrist raged, have lasted to our own times, and they have published with us the confession of their faith x, in the first chapter of which we read as follows: Each person ought to hold the divine writings of the holy Prophets and Apostles in the highest esteem, to have complete faith in them in all things, and to assent to them with reverence, to read them diligently, to take from them saving doctrine, and to instruct and direct themselves according to these; and especially those who are set over the holy Church of God. For these reasons in our churches and assemblies this holy Scripture is recited to the hearers in the common and vernacular language, which all understand, etc. But what Sylvius relates about the priests of Italy ought not to seem at all surprising, since Robert Estienne reports of the Sorbonnists of his time y that, when he asked them in what place of the New Testament something was written, they replied that they had read it in Jerome or in the Decretals, but what the New Testament was, they did not know. Likewise another theologian of the same Sorbonne used to say from time to time: I wonder that these young men cite the New Testament in these matters; for a day, I had more than fifty years, and I did not know what the New Testament was. See Hyperius on the daily reading of Scripture, book 1, p. 123, and Eipenlaeus on the Epistle to Titus, p. 105. t Book 14 of the Letters of Erasmus. u Commentary on the sayings and deeds of Alfonso the King, book 2. x In the Harmony of the Confessions, section 1. y Reply to the censures of the theologians of Paris, Geneva edition 1552.

units.la: 1440. Henricus VI. Rex Angliæ.
units.tr: 1440. Henry VI, King of England.

units.la: De eo Joannes Blackman Carthusianus in Collectario mansuetudinum & bonorum morum Regis Henrici VI. Aut in orationibus, aut in Scripturarum vel Chronicarum lectionibus, assiduè erat occupatus; ex quibus non pauca eloquia hauserat ad ipsius aliorumque consolationem spiritualem. — Nonnullis etiam solebat Clericis destinare epistolas exhortatorias, cœlestibus plenas sacramentis & salubberrimis admonitionibus, in stuporem multorum. — Cæteros dies (seminus solemnes) aut in regni negotiis cum Consilio suo tractandis, prout rei exposcerat necessitas, vel in scriptis aut Chronicis legendis, non minus diligenter expendit. Unde & de eo testatus est mihi quidam honorandus quondam sibi Camerarius fidelissimus, Dominus Richardus Tunstall, verbis & scriptis suis testimonium de eo dedit dicens; In lege Domini fuit voluntas ejus die ac nocte. In hujus etiam rei testimonium ipse Dominus Rex graviter conquestus est mihi in camerâ suâ apud Eltham, quando solus cum eo ibidem essem in sanctis suis libris cum eo laborans, ejus salubribus monitis & profundissimæ devotionis suspiriis intendens: dato pro tunc interim sono super ostio regio à quodam potentissimo Regni Duce; Rex ait: Sic inquietant me, ut vix raptim per dies & noctes valeam sine strepitu aliquorum sacrorum dogmatum lectione reficí. Simile etiam quoddam huic semel contigit, me præsente, apud Wyndesor.
units.tr: Of him John Blackman, a Carthusian, writes in his Collectarium of the gentleness and good morals of King Henry VI: "He was constantly occupied either in prayers or in reading Scripture and the chronicles, from which he drew not a few sayings for his own and others' spiritual comfort. He was also in the habit of sending exhortatory letters to some of the clergy, full of heavenly sacraments and most wholesome admonitions, to the astonishment of many. On the remaining days (less solemn ones), he gave no less careful attention either to the affairs of the kingdom, to be handled with his Council as the need of the matter required, or to reading writings and chronicles." Hence a certain honourable man, Lord Richard Tunstall, once his most faithful chamberlain, bore witness to him, and in his words and writings gave testimony about him, saying: "In the law of the Lord was his delight day and night." In confirmation of this, the king himself complained to me sharply in his chamber at Eltham, when I was alone with him there, labouring with him over his holy books and attending to his wholesome counsels and the sighs of his most profound devotion. At that moment a sound was made at the royal door by a certain most powerful Duke of the realm. The king said: "They so disturb me that I can scarcely, by snatches, through days and nights, be refreshed by reading some holy doctrines without noise." A similar thing once happened to him in my presence at Windsor.

units.la: 1440. Johannes II. Legionis & Castellæ Rex.
units.tr: 1440. John II, King of Leon and Castile.

units.la: Scripturis sacris delectabiliter vacabat; adeò ut plerunque nocumento foret, quòd plus quàm Regi expediret, lectioni operam daret. (Rodericus Sancius Hist. Hispan. par. 4. cap. 34.) Audio, Biblia Castiliana linguâ jussu Regis Johannis II. olim reddita, adhuc extare (Conradus Gesnerus in Partitionib. Theologic. lib. ult. Pandect. tit. 2. sol. 15. a.)
units.tr: He devoted himself with delight to the holy Scriptures, so much so that it was often harmful to him, since he gave himself to reading more than was fitting for a king. (Rodericus Sancius Hist. Hispan. par. 4. cap. 34.) I hear that a Castilian Bible, translated into the Castilian language long ago by command of King John II, still survives (Conradus Gesnerus in Partitionib. Theologic. lib. ult. Pandect. tit. 2. sol. 15. a.)

units.la: 1450. Reginaldus Peacock, Ciceftrenfis Episcopus.
units.tr: 1450. Reginald Peacock, Bishop of Chichester.

units.la: Vid. Stow.
units.tr: See Stow.

units.la: 1450. Alphonsus V. cognomento Magnanimus, Aragoniæ, Siciliæ, & Neapolis Rex.
units.tr: 1450. Alphonsus V, surnamed the Magnanimous, King of Aragon, Sicily and Naples.

units.la: Gloriatum assiduè Regem scimus, quòd Biblia quater & decies cum glossis & commentariis perlegisset: proinde illa memoriâ ita tenere, ut non solum res sed & verba etiam ipsa pluribus locis sine scripto redderet. Hæc Antonius Panormita lib. 2. de dictis & factis Alphonsi; in quem Jacobus Spiegelius, Mirum est (inquit) plantopere delectatum occupatissimum Regem toties repetitâ lectione sacrorum voluminum. Genebrardus lib. 4. Chronographiæ suæ Anno Christi 1261. annotat, Alphonsum X. cognomento Sapientem, quaterdecies universa Biblia cum suis glossis inter tot negotia legisse. Sed quod de Alphonso Aragonum Rege est dictum, perperam ille transtulit ad Alphonsum Castellæ & Legionis Regem, qui Astronomicas tabulas ad An. 1252. edidit. Porro nec id omittendum est, quod in ultimo libro Pandectarum Gesneri, legimus, per Alphonsum Aragonum Regem proverbia Solomonis Hispanicè esse reddita; necnon Joannem Aragonum Regem (quem Alphonsi V. fratrem & in regno Anno 1458. successorem intelligo, quem ut Christianæ religionis præcipuum assertorem praedicat Fr. Tarapha & L. Marineus Siculus) inter divinæ Scripturæ Translatores numerari à Sixto Senensi b, & Antonio Possevino c.
units.tr: We know that the king constantly boasted that he had read through the Bible fourteen times, with its glosses and commentaries, and that he had so fixed it in his memory that on many occasions he could recite not only the matter but the very words, without a text before him. So Antonius Panormita, book 2 of his Sayings and Deeds of Alphonsus. On this, Jacobus Spiegelius remarks: "It is remarkable that a king so busy took such delight in reading the sacred volumes so often." Genebrardus, in book 4 of his Chronography, notes at the year of Christ 1261 that Alphonsus X, surnamed the Wise, read through the whole Bible with its glosses fourteen times amid his many affairs. But what was said of Alphonsus, King of Aragon, he wrongly transferred to Alphonsus, King of Castile and León, who published the Astronomical Tables for the year 1252. Nor should we omit what we read in the last book of Gesner's Pandects: that the Proverbs of Solomon were rendered into Spanish by Alphonsus, King of Aragon. Likewise John, King of Aragon (whom I take to be the brother of Alphonsus V and his successor in the kingdom in 1458, and whom Fr. Tarapha and L. Marineus Siculus praise as a chief defender of the Christian religion), is counted among the translators of divine Scripture by Sixtus of Siena b and Antonius Possevinus c.

units.la: 1460. Dionysius Carthusianus
units.tr: 1460. Dionysius the Carthusian

units.la: In 1 Corinth. XIV. Si tu benedixeris spiritu] i. e. non verbis, quæ ab aliis intelligantur, sed tantùm linguâ.
units.tr: On 1 Corinthians XIV: "If thou shalt bless with the spirit" — that is, not with words that others may understand, but only with the tongue.

units.la: 1470. Dalmatæ.
units.tr: 1470. Dalmatians.

units.la: Paulus II. concedit illis, ut divinas preces suâ celebrent linguâ. (Victorius in Indice in 6. posterior. tomos Hieronymi, verb. Illyricum.)
units.tr: Pope Paul II granted them that they might celebrate the divine prayers in their own language. (Victorius, in the Index to the last six volumes of Jerome, s.v. Illyricum.)

units.la: ¹ Vid. Espenseum (apud Morton. par. 2. p. 63.) ² De Theol. tit. 2. sect. 6. pag. 26. ᵇ Biblioth. Sanct. lib. 4. ᶜ Biblioth. Select. lib. 2. cap. ult.
units.tr: ¹ See Espenseus (in Morton, part 2, p. 63). ² De Theol., tit. 2, sect. 6, p. 26. ᵇ Bibliotheca Sanctorum, lib. 4. ᶜ Bibliotheca Select., lib. 2, last chapter.

units.la: 1478. Ludovicus XI. Francorum Rex.
units.tr: 1478. Louis XI, King of the French.

units.la: Quemadmodum jus unum per totam Galliam lingua vulgari comprehensum constituere propositurat, si vita superesset; ita illud effecisse videtur, ut jus divinum lingua Vernacula expositum ad communem omnium usum ederetur. Johannes enim Lambertus in responsione ad 26. Articulum Episcoporum Angliæ, quam Anno 1532. edidit, asserit 54. ad minimum annos Biblia in sua lingua habuisse Gallos, cum Regis Francorum atque etiam Imperatoris privilegio; quæ quidem Ludovici Regis rogatu translata fuerint, quantum ex privilegio meminit, quod in libri frontispicio cernebatur.
units.tr: Just as he proposed to establish one law for all of France, drawn up in the vernacular, had life been granted him, so he seems to have brought it about that divine law, set forth in the vernacular, was published for the common use of all. For John Lambert, in his reply to the 26th Article of the Bishops of England, which he published in 1532, asserts that for at least 54 years the French have had Bibles in their own language, under the privilege of the King of the French and even of the Emperor. These were indeed translated at the request of King Louis, as far as I recall from the privilege, which could be seen on the title page of the book.

units.la: 1483. Carolus VIII. Francorum Rex, & Johan- nes de Rely.
units.tr: 1483. Charles VIII, King of the French, and John de Rely.

units.la: Genevenses, in Præfat. ad suam Bibliorum versionem Gallicam, notant, Carolum ejus nominis Octavum curasse, ut Novum Testamentum in linguam Gallicam transferretur. Similiter Antonius Verderius in Bibliothecā Gallicā, tit. Bibles, pag. 137. Par apres & du regne de Charles VIII. Jean de Rely Chanoine de Noftre Dame de Paris en feit une translation en meilleur langage, toutesfois encores rude. De Johanne de Rely vide eundem pag. 751.
units.tr: The Genevans, in the Preface to their French version of the Bible, note that Charles, the eighth of that name, had the New Testament translated into French. Similarly Antoine Verdier, in the Bibliothèque Gallique, under the title "Bibles," p. 137: "Later, in the reign of Charles VIII, Jean de Rely, canon of Notre Dame de Paris, made a translation in a better language, though still rough." On Jean de Rely see the same work, p. 751.

units.la: 1485. Richardus Hilminus
units.tr: 1485. Richard Hilmin.

units.la: Ad Johannem Coventriensem & Lichfeldiensem in Anglia Episcopum delatus est; quòd Orationem Dominicam, Salutationem Angelicam, & Symbolum in linguâ Anglicanâ habuerit; itemque alium librum, qui Epistolas & Evangelia Anglicè continebat, viderit & habuerit; asserens se secundùm illa victurum, indeque salutem expectare [Ex Registro Diœcesfeos .]
units.tr: He was denounced to John, Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield in England, because he had the Lord's Prayer, the Angelic Salutation and the Creed in English; likewise, he had seen and possessed another book which contained the Epistles and Gospels in English, and he affirmed that he would live by them and expect salvation from them. [From the Register of the Diocese.]

units.la: {d} Jo. Tilius in Chron. Reg. Franc. {e} Fox, pag. 714.
units.tr: {d} John Tillius, in the Chronicle of the Kings of France. {e} Foxe, p. 714.

units.la: 57 Postea etiam regnante Carolo VIII. Joannes de Rely, Ecclesiæ Cathedralis Parisiensis Canonicus, meliori stylo, rudiusculè tamen adhuc, versionem adornavit.
units.tr: 57 Afterwards also, in the reign of Charles VIII, John de Rely, canon of the cathedral church of Paris, prepared a version in a better style, though still rather rough.

units.la: 1496. Jo. Franciscus Picus Mirandula
units.tr: 1496. Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola.

units.la: De studio divinæ & humanæ Philosophiæ, lib. 2. cap. 1. Ad hanc notitiam divinorum capessendam veteres Theologi omnes exhortantur. Huic juniores, Innocentius, Joannes Gerson, aliique nonnulli assiduè monent incumbendum: & non modò his qui ex officio ad id negotii sunt obnoxii, ut sacerdotes & clerici; sed omnibus cujuscunque gradùs & ordinis extiterint. Et jure quidem; quoniam nullus ab hoc officio immunis est, quòd sc. pro suâ ingenii viriumque facultate & sibi & aliis non debeat esse adjumento.
units.tr: On the study of divine and human philosophy, book 2, chapter 1: "All the ancient theologians exhort us to lay hold of this knowledge of divine things. Among the more recent, Innocent, John Gerson and several others constantly urge that we apply ourselves to it; and not only those who are bound to this business by their office, such as priests and clergy, but all of whatever rank and order they may be. And rightly so; for no one is exempt from this duty, since each should, according to his talent and the powers he has, be a help both to himself and to others."

units.la: Exam. Vanit. Gent. lib. 2. cap. 37. In iis itaque divinarum literarum testamentis quærenda est veritas, quæsitu proculdubio facilis, &c. Nullus sexus excluditur; & anus decrepita & puer ejus rei tam capaces, quam est satis ad fœlicitatem.
units.tr: Examen vanitatis gentium, book 2, chapter 37: "In those testaments of the divine letters, therefore, truth is to be sought, a thing doubtless easy to seek, etc. No sex is excluded; and a decrepit old woman and a boy are as capable of this matter as is enough for happiness."

units.la: 1500. Georgius Florus Baldinus
units.tr: 1500. Georgius Florus Baldinus.

units.la: In Compendio de Oratione & precib. Quomodo se à Deo exaudiri postulat; qui seipsum non audit, & quid loquatur ignorat? Nunquam enim orare dicitur, qui flexis genibus orat; si vagatione distrahatur. Nihil igitur aliud cogitare debet animus orantis, quàm quod precatur.
units.tr: In the Compendium on Prayer and Prayers: "How can he who does not hear himself ask to be heard by God, and what does he say, not knowing what he says? For he is said never to pray who prays with bended knees if he is distracted by wandering thoughts. Therefore the mind of the one praying ought to think of nothing else than what he prays for."

units.la: 1506. Johannes Trithemius, Spanheimensis Abbas
units.tr: 1506. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

units.la: In Epist. familiar. lib. 2. epist. 28. hanc cujusdam sententiam citat:
units.tr: In the Familiar Letters, book 2, letter 28, he cites this saying of someone:

units.la: Nil homini melius, quàm si divina legendo: Figat ibi mentem, quò sibi vita venit.
units.tr: Nothing is better for a man than, by reading divine things, to fix his mind there, whence life comes to him.

units.la: Lib. 2. Epist. 1. ad Jacobum Trithemium fratrem suum, ita de divinâ scriptura scribit. Mirabilis iste fluvius est, in quo simplex & sine literaturâ Christianus, pedibus (ut ita dixerim) siccis ad salutem securus transfire poterit; & magnus subtiliterque literatus & natare p teft sobriè sapiendo, & si nimium scrutatus fuerit, submergi. Habet enim in publico, unde parvulos nutriat; & servat in occulto, unde mentes sublimium in admirationem ducat.
units.tr: In book 2, letter 1, to his brother Jacob Trithemius, he writes thus about Divine Scripture: "This is a wonderful river, in which a simple Christian without learning may cross safely to salvation with dry feet, as it were; and a great and subtly learned man may swim, wisely and soberly, yet if he has searched too deeply, be submerged. For it has in plain view whence it may nourish little ones, and it keeps in its depths whence it may lead the minds of the lofty into wonder."

units.la: Idem etiam studium Scripturarum à multis sui temporis Sacerdotibus & Claustralibus omnium pene Regularum contemptum queritur. Atque inde de Sacerdote quodam Curiensi fertur; quòd circa hæc tempora prophetico quodam spiritu crebrò sacrificulis dictitare solitus sit; Vos jam Paulum sub scamnum abjecistis; veniet aliquando tempus, cùm ipse inde prorepens, vicissim vos sub scamnum protrudet.
units.tr: The same complaint is made about the neglect of the study of Scripture by many priests and monks of his time, of almost all religious orders. And so it is reported of a certain priest of Chur that about this time, with a certain prophetic spirit, he was accustomed often to say to the little priests: "You have now cast Paul under the bench; the time will come when he himself, creeping out from there, will in turn thrust you under the bench."

units.la: 1512. Jacobus Faber Stapulensis
units.tr: 1512. Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples

units.la: In 1 Corinth. XIV. Maxima pars hominum, cùm nunc orat, nescio st spiritu, tamen mente non orat: nam in linguâ orat, quam non intelligit. Attamen maximè Paulus probat, ut fideles pariter spiritu orent & mente; & qui sic, ut passim solent, orant, parum se oratione ædificant, & alios nequaquam suo sermone ædificare valent.
units.tr: The greater part of men, when they now pray, I know not whether by the Spirit, yet they do not pray with the mind: for they pray in a tongue which they do not understand. Yet Paul especially proves that the faithful should pray alike in spirit and in mind; and those who pray as they commonly do everywhere edify themselves little by their prayer, and are by no means able to edify others by their speech.

units.la: 1515. Valentini in Hispaniâ.
units.tr: 1515. Valencia in Spain.

units.la: Quadraginta aut circiter abhinc annis (inquit Frid. Furius in Bononiâ Anno 1555. edito) sacra Scriptura Valentinis literis impressa fuit: quam populo interdixit Inquisitorum, quos vocant, Societas & Ordo hoc nomine: quòd Judæi aliquot, qui de 120. millibus ex Hispaniâ exulorum superierant, dicerent, se intelligere ipsos ritus, cæremonias & sacrificandi genus ab ipsis Bibliis desumere. Itaque ita veritum est eam legi; ut iis qui originem nullam à Judæis haberent, legi liceret, aliis non item. Idem in universâ Hispaniâ cautum est: habebant enim fere reliquæ Hispaniæ nationes etiam Biblia, in suam quæque linguam versa. Hactenus Frid. Furius Valentinus. At alii ex Pontificiis multi reperiuntur; qui Ferdinandi & Elizabethæ Hispaniæ Regis ac Reginæ, edictum magnopere laudant, quo sub gravissimis pœnis prohibuerunt: Ne quis sacras literas in linguam vulgarem transferret, aut ab aliis translatas quoquo pacto retineret. (Alphonsus de Castro de Hæresib. lib. 1. cap. 13. Claud. Coussford in Confutat. error. Valdensf. cap. 23. Hardingus artic. 15. sect. 13. & Jac. Ledesima cap. 18.) Sed quantopere ab antiquo Justiniani Imp. decreto (quod supra in Hebræorum sententiis produximus) distet, consideret æquus Lector. Sed & his temporibus Michael Adam Judæus conversus Biblia vertit in linguam Germanicam, & in usum
units.tr: About forty years ago (says Frid. Furius, in the edition published at Bologna in 1555), the Holy Scripture was printed at Valencia in the vernacular. The Society and Order of the so-called Inquisitors forbade it to the people, on this ground: that some Jews, of the one hundred and twenty thousand exiles from Spain who had survived, said that they understood the rites, ceremonies and manner of sacrifice to be drawn from the Bible itself. So they were so afraid of it being read that it was made lawful to read it only for those who had no origin from the Jews, and not for others. The same caution was taken throughout the whole of Spain, for almost all the other nations of Spain also had Bibles, each translated into its own language. So far Frid. Furius of Valencia. But many others among the Papists are to be found who greatly praise the edict of Ferdinand and Elizabeth, King and Queen of Spain, by which they forbade under the most severe penalties: that anyone should translate the holy letters into the vernacular, or keep, in any way, translations made by others. (Alphonsus de Castro, De haeresibus, bk. 1, ch. 13; Claudius Coussford, in Confutatio errorum Valdensium, ch. 23; Harding, article 15, sect. 13; and Jacob Ledesima, ch. 18.) But let the fair reader consider how far this is from the ancient decree of the Emperor Justinian, which I cited above among the opinions of the Hebrews. And in these times too, Michael Adam, a Jew who had converted, translated the Bibles into German and, for use,

units.la: {f} Illyricus in Catal. Test. Verit. ex relatione Nicolai Midleri. Hebraeorum characteribus Hebraicis expressit ( Sixtus Senensis lib. 4. Biblioth. & Eisengrenius in Catalogo Test. Verit.) Liber Precationum Anniversariarum secundum usum Hebraeorum in Germaniâ, Germanicè, sed literis Hebraicis, habetur in Bibliothecâ Bodleianâ.
units.tr: {f} Illyricus, in his Catalogue of Witnesses of the Truth, on the report of Nicolas Midler, expressed them in Hebrew characters (Sixtus of Siena, bk. 4 of the Bibliotheca, and Eisengrenius, in the Catalogue of Witnesses of the Truth). A book of Yearly Prayers, according to the custom of the Hebrews in Germany, in German but in Hebrew letters, is held in the Bodleian Library.

units.la: 1515. Erasmus Roterodamus
units.tr: 1515. Erasmus Roterodamus

units.la: In enarratione I. Psalmi (tomo 5. Operum, pag. 153.) Legant & idiotæ legem Domini quacunque linguâ, legant & Scythæ; meditentur in eâ pro suâ virili: scrutentur pro suo quisque captu; de hac inter se confabulentur, de hac colloquantur, &c. At nunc sunt, qui summopere cauendum putant, ne quid vulgus attingat de sacris literis in popularem versus linguam: clamant eos nihil intelligere, prolabi in hæreses. Quasi verò ea sit doctrina Christi, ut non nisi à paucis Theologis possit intelligi. Immò ut ipsi Christo nihil fuit communius, ita doctrinâ illius nihil popularius. Legat arator; erit quo pascatur: legat eruditissimus; erit quod discat, &c. Verum enimvero vereor, ne isti qui velint populum nihil attingere, non tam periculo commoveantur illorum quàm sui respectu; videlicet ut ab ipsis solis velut ab oraculis petantur omnia. Quid hàc de re scriptum est? Hoc scriptum est. Quem habet sensum, quod scriptum est? Sic intellige, sic senti, sic loquere. Atqui isthuc est bubalum esse non hominem. Fortassis movet & hoc nonnullos, quoniam animadvertunt divinas Scripturas parum quadrare ad vitam suam: malunt eas antiquari, aut certè nescíri, ne quid hinc jaciatur in os. Et ad humanas traditiunculas populum avocant; quas ipsi ad suam commoditatem probè commenti sunt. Hæc ante exortum Lutheri Erasmus. Et quidem Lovanienses Theologi in expurgatione Operum ejus à Belgicis Censoribus comprobatâ locum hunc intactum reliquerunt. Sed Hispani Censores, oculatiores paulò, in Indice librorum expurgatorum Gasparis Quirogæ Cardinalis & Toletani Archiepiscopi jussu edito, eum integrum delendum censuerunt.
units.tr: In his exposition of Psalm 1 (Works, vol. 5, p. 153), he writes: Let the unlearned also read the law of the Lord in whatever language they have, let the Scythians read it too; let them meditate on it to the best of their power; let each search it according to his capacity; let them talk about it among themselves and discuss it together, and so on. But there are now those who think great care must be taken that the common people should not touch the Holy Scriptures translated into the vernacular: they cry out that the people understand nothing and will fall into heresies. As if the teaching of Christ were such that it could be understood only by a few theologians! On the contrary, just as nothing was more common to Christ himself, so nothing is more popular than his teaching. Let the ploughman read it; there will be something to feed him. Let the most learned read it; there will be something for him to learn, and so on. But I fear that those who want the people to touch nothing are moved less by concern for the danger to them than by concern for themselves, namely that everything should be sought from them alone, as from oracles. What has been written on this matter? This has been written. What meaning has what is written? Understand it thus, feel it thus, speak thus. Yet that is to be a beast, not a man. Perhaps this too troubles some, since they notice that the divine Scriptures do not fit well with their way of life; they prefer that the Scriptures be made obsolete, or at least unknown, so that nothing may be thrown in their face. And they call the people away to human little traditions, which they themselves have cleverly devised for their own convenience. Erasmus said this before Luther arose. Indeed the Louvain theologians, in the expurgated edition of his Works approved by the Belgian censors, left this passage untouched. But the Spanish censors, a little sharper-sighted, in the Index of Expurgated Books published by order of Gaspar de Quiroga, Cardinal and Archbishop of Toledo, judged that it must be deleted entirely.

units.la: Idem in Præfatione ad Lectorem, Paraphrasi in Matthæum præfixâ. Cur indecorum videtur, si quisquam sonet Evangelium eâ linguâ, quâ natus est, & quam intelligit: Gallus Gallicâ, Britannus Britannicâ, Germanus Germanicâ, Indus Indicâ? Mihi magis indecorum vel ridiculum potius
units.tr: The same in the Preface to the Reader, prefixed to his Paraphrase on Matthew: Why does it seem unseemly, if anyone should sound the Gospel in the language in which he was born and which he understands: the Frenchman in French, the Briton in British, the German in German, the Indian in Indian? To me it seems more unseemly, or rather ridiculous,

units.la: {e} In Indice expurgat. excud. Antverp. 1571. {h} Excud. Madriti 1584. videtur; quòd idiotæ & mulierculæ, psittaci exemplo, psalmos suos & precationem Dominicam Latinè murmurant; quùm ipsæ, quod sonant, non intelligunt. Ego cum D. Hieronymo sentiens, citius gratulor gloriæ crucis, magnificumque cumprimis ac triumphale dixerim; si linguis omnibus ab omni hominum genere celebretur. Si stivam tenens arator aliquid suâ linguâ decantat è Psalmis mysticis. Si textor assidens telæ, nonnihil ex Evangelio modulans, sileatur laborem. Hinc nauclerus affixus clavo cantillet aliquid. Denique ad colum sedenti matronæ sodalis aut cognata hinc recitet aliquid. Nec hunc locum attingunt Lovanienses; sed Inquisitores Hispani totam Præfationem deleri jubent.
units.tr: {e} In the Index expurgatorius, printed at Antwerp 1571. {h} Printed at Madrid 1584. that the unlearned and simple women should mumble their psalms and the Lord's Prayer in Latin like parrots, since they do not understand what they are saying. I, agreeing with St Jerome, would rather congratulate the glory of the cross and call it a most magnificent and above all triumphal thing, if it were celebrated in all languages by every kind of person. If the ploughman, holding the plough, sings something from the mystical Psalms in his own tongue, let his labour be relieved. If the weaver, sitting at his loom, hums something from the Gospel, let him be left to his work. Then let the sailor fixed to the tiller sing something. Finally, let a companion or a kinswoman recite something to the matron sitting at her distaff. The Louvain theologians do not touch this passage; but the Spanish Inquisitors order the whole Preface to be deleted.

units.la: Hanc sententiam etiam tuetur Erasmus adversùs Nicolaum Ecmondanum [in epistolâ ad Nicolaum Everardum, quæ habetur lib. 21. Epistolarum ejusdem.] adversùs Natalem Beddam [tomo 9. Operum, pag. 377, 378, 455, 456.] adversùs Petrum Sutorem [ibid. pag. 628, 629, 630, 652.] adversùs Theologos Parisienses [ibid. pag. 703, &c. 729. &c.] adversùs Albertum Pium [ibid. pag. 914, 945.]
units.tr: Erasmus also defends this view against Nicolaus Ecmondanus [in his letter to Nicolaus Everardus, which is found in book 21 of his Letters], against Natalis Beda [vol. 9 of his Works, pp. 377, 378, 455, 456], against Petrus Sutor [ibid., pp. 628, 629, 630, 652], against the Parisian theologians [ibid., pp. 703 ff., 729 ff.], and against Albertus Pius [ibid., pp. 914, 945].

units.la: Idem Annotat. in 1 Corinth. XIV. Hàc in re mirum est, quomodo mutata est Ecclesiæ consuetudo. In templis enim multi clarâ voce sonant eas preces, etiamsi nihil intelligant.
units.tr: The same, in his Annotations on 1 Corinthians 14: In this matter it is remarkable how the custom of the Church has changed. For in the churches many people chant those prayers in a loud voice, even though they understand nothing.

units.la: 1523. Adrianus VI. Trajectensis, Pontifex Romanus.
units.tr: 1523. Adrian VI, Bishop of Utrecht, Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Equidem uti neminem [ad Scripturarum studium] arctari intendo; ita multo minùs omnes excusare possim; cùm certum sit unumquemque ad tantam divinæ legis arctari notitiam, quanta possit actus suos pro qualitate personæ citra peccatum mortale dirigere. Et de Pastoribus quidem, quos Dominus in Ecclesiam suam vocavit ad statum oculi, quorum est aliorum conscientiis & saluti consulere, non video quî sine damnabili culpâ, omissâ divinæ legis notitiâ, aliis intendant. Sed ita etiam unicuique laico peccatum, nisi invicem sibi in his quæ ad communem vitæ usum pertinent, operam fideliter dederint. Viderint ergo etiam laici; ne apud districtum judicem censeantur oculos à proposito seu statuto declinare in terram; dum pro temporalium facultatum & honorum quæstu, divinis neglectis, humanis legibus ardentius invigilant, studiaque divina quàm humana remissius attendunt; plus corporis quàm animæ pabulo, profanis quàm Sacris Scripturis plùs intendant. Non, inquam, videant, quomodo Deum salutaris ejusdem Scripturæ inspiratorem super omnia diligant. Citatur ab Eipensaco commen. in Tit. cap. 2. p. 254, 255.
units.tr: I do not intend to confine anyone to the study of Scripture, and so I can much less excuse everyone. For it is certain that each person must have as much knowledge of the divine law as enables him to direct his actions, according to the kind of person he is, without mortal sin. As for the ministers whom the Lord has called into his Church to a position of watchfulness, whose duty is to care for the consciences and salvation of others, I do not see how they can attend to others without blameworthy fault if they neglect knowledge of the divine law. But in the same way, it is a sin for every layperson not to devote faithful effort to one another in the matters that pertain to ordinary life. Let the laity also take care, lest they be judged by the strict judge to have turned their eyes away from their purpose or rule to the earth, while, in pursuit of temporal wealth and honours, they neglect divine things and watch more eagerly over human laws, and attend more carelessly to divine studies than to human ones; while they devote more attention to the food of the body than of the soul, and to profane writings than to the Holy Scriptures. They should not, I say, fail to see how they ought to love above all else God, the inspirer of that saving Scripture. Cited from Eipensacus, commentary on Titus, ch. 2, pp. 254, 255.

units.la: 1530. Beatus Rhenanus
units.tr: 1530. Beatus Rhenanus

units.la: Libro 2. Rerum Germanicarum. Perpetua laus Francorum veterum est, qui sacros libros in suam, b. e. Germanicam linguam vertendos curârint: quod nuper à Theologis quibusdam improbatum scimus. Hæc ille: Novatrice aurâ afflatus; ut veteratoriâ aurâ afflatus pronunçiat Gretserus in Appendice secundâ ad librum 2. Bellarmini de Verbo Dei col. 1065. (vid. & col. 840.)
units.tr: In Book 2 of Rerum Germanicarum: It is the lasting praise of the ancient Franks that they took care to have the sacred books translated into their own, that is, the German, language; which, as we know, was recently disapproved by certain theologians. So he writes, inspired by a novel breeze; as Gretser, in the second Appendix to Bellarmine's second book On the Word of God, col. 1065 (see also col. 840), says that he was inspired by an old-fashioned, crafty breeze.

units.la: 1526. Johannes Aventinus
units.tr: 1526. Johannes Aventinus

units.la: Annalium Boiorum lib. 4. de sui temporis Sacerdotibus & Monachis ita scribit. Inter se mendacii silentium velut orgia quædam sanciunt; quibus cæteris veluti pueris ac infantibus more suo fabulis inludant. Quamobrem vel pro concione indignantur, irascuntur, insaniunt; si quis prosanus sacras literas, mandata Christi comitum, ejus doctrinam legerit. Timent talpæ, ne eorum cæcitas deprehendatur, & avaritia tenebræque luce appareant.
units.tr: In book 4 of his Annals of the Bavarians, he writes thus about the priests and monks of his own time: Among themselves they keep a silence about lies, as if it were some kind of secret rite, and with it they mock everyone else, like children and infants, with their fables, as is their custom. Therefore, if anyone reads the sacred letters, the commands and the doctrine of Christ's companions, they grow indignant, angry and frenzied, even in the sermon. The moles fear that their blindness will be detected, and their greed and darkness will appear in the light.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Contraria Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ praxis & sententia, & sæva Orthodoxorum S. Scripturam legentium persecutio, sæculo postremo.
units.tr: The contrary practice and opinion of the Papal Church, and the savage persecution of the Orthodox who read Holy Scripture in the last century.

units.la: 1506. Amershamenses in Angliâ.
units.tr: 1506. The Amersham people in England.

units.la: EX his 30. quòd contra superstitionem & idololatriam loquerentur, & sacras Scripturas audire & legere desiderarent; sub Henrico Smithæo Lincolniensi Episcopo, stigmata ferro candente dextris maxillis inusta pertulerunt; quemadmodum ex relatione illorum, qui tum adfuerunt, prodit Joannes Foxus a.
units.tr: Of these, thirty, because they spoke against superstition and idolatry and wanted to hear and read Holy Scripture, were branded on the right cheek with a red-hot iron under Henry Smyth, Bishop of Lincoln. John Foxe reports this from the account of those who were present at the time a.

units.la: 1511. Londinenses.
units.tr: 1511. The Londoners.

units.la: Thomas Austius cum Joannâ uxore, Thomas Graunt, Joannes Garterus, Christophorus Ravius cum sorore Dionysiâ, Thomas Vincentius, Ludovicus Johannes cum Joannâ uxore, ad Ricardum Fitz James Londinensem Episcopum delati sunt; cùm aliis de causis, tum quòd libros quosdam fidei Romanæ Ecclesiæ repugnantes legerint: inter quos fuerunt IV. Evangelistæ, liber X. mandatorum Dei omnipotentis, Apocalypsis S. Johannis, Pauli & Jacobi Epistolæ b. Eodem anno ab eodem Episcopo condemnatus & combustus in Foro fabrili fuit die XVIII. Octobr. Jacobus Brewster; cui inter alia objectum est, quòd libellum quendam Scripturæ, antiquâ manu exaratum & præ vetustate ferè detritum, habuerit. [Ex Registro Rich. Fitz James c.]
units.tr: Thomas Austin with his wife Joan, Thomas Graunt, John Garter, Christopher Ravis with his sister Dionysia, Thomas Vincent, and Ludovic John with his wife Joan, were denounced to Richard Fitz James, Bishop of London. This was partly for other reasons, but also because they had read certain books opposed to the faith of the Roman Church. Among these were the four Evangelists, the tenth book of the commandments of Almighty God, the Apocalypse of St John, and the Epistles of Paul and James b. In the same year, Jacob Brewster was condemned by the same Bishop and burned in the Smithfield market on 18 October. Among other charges, it was objected to him that he had possessed a little book of Scripture, written in an ancient hand and almost worn away with age. [From the Register of Richard Fitz James c.]

units.la: a Pag. 710. b Fox, pag. 735. c Fox, pag. 748.
units.tr: a Page 710. b Foxe, page 735. c Foxe, page 748.

units.la: 1514. Richardus Hunnus.
units.tr: 1514. Richard Hunne.

units.la: Huic coram Londinensi Episcopo objectum est, quòd libros lege prohibitos & damnatos secum retinuerit: nempe Apocalypsin, Epistolas & Evangelia in linguâ Anglicanâ, &c. Post mortem etiam ejus ex Prologo ipsius in Biblia sua Anglicana articuli isti excerpti sunt, & Episcopi Londinensis Richardi Fitz James jussu ad Crucem Paulinam pro concione populo publicè recitati; 1. Quòd pauperes & idiotæ veritatem sanctarum Scripturarum magis habeant; quàm mille Præla-ti, Monachi, aut Clerici Scholastici. 2. Defendit translationem S. Scripturæ in linguam Anglicanam; quod matris nostræ sanctæ Ecclesiæ legibus est prohibitum. [Ex Registro Londinensi Richardi Fitz Jamesd] Observetur hîc Romanæ Ecclesiæ sententia.
units.tr: Before the Bishop of London he was charged with keeping books forbidden and condemned by law, namely the Apocalypse, the Epistles and the Gospels in the English tongue, etc. After his death, too, these articles were extracted from his preface to his English Bible, and at the command of Richard Fitz James, Bishop of London, they were publicly read to the people at St Paul's Cross in a sermon: 1. That poor men and laymen have a better grasp of the truth of the holy Scriptures than a thousand prelates, monks or scholastic clerics. 2. He defends the translation of Holy Scripture into the English tongue, which is forbidden by the laws of our mother, the holy Church. [From the London Register of Richard Fitz James d.] Let the judgment of the Roman Church be noted here.

units.la: 1518, 1520. Londinenses.
units.tr: 1518, 1520. The Londoners.

units.la: Richardus Butler, Johannes Samme, Gulielmus King, Robertus Durdant, & Henricus Woolman, ad tribunal Richardi Fitz James Londinensis Episcopi accusati sunt; quòd libros quosdam hæreticos Anglicanâ linguâ scriptos perlegissent: inter quos etiam Evangelium Jesu Christi à quatuor Evangelistis conscriptum, horrendâ blasphemiâ numerârunt Pontificii. Sic enim Episcopi Cancellarius & Vicarius generalis, Thomas Benet Legum Doctor, Richardo Butler articulum 8. objecit in hanc sententiam. Item objicimus tibi (inquit) quòd cùm aliàs sæpe, tum abhinc circiter triennium, nocte quadam in ædibus Roberti Durdant de Tver Court prope S'anes, erroneè & damnabiliter legisti in magno libro hæreseos ejusdem Roberti Durdant, totâ illâ nocte, capitula quædam Evangelistarum in linguâ Anglicanâ, continentia in se diversas erroneas & damnabiles opiniones & conclusiones hæreticas, in præsentia dicti Roberti Durdant, Johannis Butler, Roberti Carder, Jenkini Butler, Wilhelmi King, & diversorum aliorum; qui hæreses suspecti habebantur; & tum præsentes prædictas tuas erroneas lectiuras & opiniones audiebant. [Ex Registro Rich. Fitz. Jamese] Vid. infra in Anno 1521.
units.tr: Richard Butler, John Samme, William King, Robert Durdant and Henry Woolman were accused before the court of Richard Fitz James, Bishop of London, because they had read certain heretical books written in English. Among these the Papists even count the Gospel of Jesus Christ written by the four Evangelists, as a dreadful blasphemy. Thomas Benet, Doctor of Laws, the Bishop's Chancellor and Vicar General, put article 8 to Richard Butler in these words: "Likewise we object to you," he says, "that although on other occasions often, so also about three years ago, one night in the house of Robert Durdant of Tver Court near St Anne's, you wrongly and damnably read, in a great heretical book of the same Robert Durdant, the whole night through, certain chapters of the Evangelists in English, containing various erroneous and damnable opinions and heretical conclusions, in the presence of the said Robert Durdant, John Butler, Robert Carder, Jenkin Butler, William King, and various others who were held suspect as heretics; and they, being present, heard your said erroneous readings and opinions." [From the Register of Richard Fitz James e.] See below under the year 1521.

units.la: {d} Fox, pag 737. {e} Iox, pag. 735. Anno 1520. alii etiam, numero 35. objurare coacti sunt, cùm aliis de causis, tum etiam quòd libros Scripturæ in lingua Anglicanâ habuerint; inter quos speciatim nominantur isti: Liber IV. Evangelistarum; Liber Epistolarum Pauli & Petri; Epistola S. Jacobi; Liber Apocalypseos, & de Antichristo, &c. [Ex eodem Registro f.]
units.tr: d Foxe, page 737. e Foxe, page 735. In the year 1520 others also, thirty-five in number, were compelled to abjure, partly for other reasons, but also because they had books of Scripture in English. Among these the following are specially named: the Book of the Four Evangelists; the Book of the Epistles of Paul and Peter; the Epistle of St James; the Book of the Apocalypse, and "On Antichrist", etc. [From the same Register f.]

units.la: 1520. Johannes Hacker, & Alicia Doly.
units.tr: 1520. John Hacker and Alice Doly.

units.la: Coram Doctore Londono Aliciæ ab ancillâ suâ Elizabethâ Wighthill objectum est, de Hackero (qui Londini in Colmani platea aquator fuit) illam aliquando dixisse; quòd Evangeliorum & omnium aliorum, quæ ad divina officia pertinebant, peritissimus fuerit; eademque simul & orationem Dominicam Anglicè declarare non minùs expeditè potuerit atque Sacerdotum quivis. Objectum est etiam, librum quendam eandem habuisse duodecim Fidei articulos continentem; & alium quem maximi æstimabat, & in conclavi vel arculâ cum aliis semper asservabat. [Ex Registro Lincoln. g]
units.tr: Before Doctor London, Alice's maidservant Elizabeth Wighthill objected against Hacker (who was a water-carrier in Colman Street in London) that Alice had once said of him that he was most skilled in the Gospels and all the other books pertaining to the divine services, and that he could explain the Lord's Prayer in English as readily as any priest. It was also objected that he had a book containing the twelve articles of the faith, and another which he valued most highly and always kept with the others in his closet or chest. [From the Register of Lincoln g.]

units.la: 1521. Lincolnienses & Londinenses.
units.tr: 1521. The Lincolnians and Londoners.

units.la: h Hoc anno in Diœcesi Lincolniensi mota est persecutio à Joanne Longland Episcopo; ex cujus Registro quorundam nomina proponentur; qui ob studium legis divinæ ab Antichristi satellite vexati sunt; ut ex unius anni historiâ conjectura fiat, quantopere in Christi servos ante nostra tempora grassata sit Pontificiorum tyrannis; utcunque homines impudentes clamitent, ante exortum Lutherum nulla Ecclesiæ nostræ extitisse vestigia. Certè, si in uno Orbis angulo, sub densissimis Papatùs tenebris, tot reperti sunt, qui humanis commentis facessere jussis, ex divinorum oraculorum fontibus (quantumvis fremententibus Episcopis) purioris religionis dogmata haurire sategerunt; quot extitisse credimus, non dico in Anglià, sed in universo terrarum orbe, qui non flexerunt genua Baali? Sed ecce specimen religionis Papisticæ!
units.tr: h In this year a persecution was stirred up in the diocese of Lincoln by John Longland, Bishop. From his Register the names of some will be set out, who were harassed by this satellite of Antichrist for their zeal for the divine law. From the history of this one year one may guess how greatly the tyranny of the Papists raged against the servants of Christ before our time, however shamelessly men cry out that before Luther arose there were no traces of our Church. Certainly, if in one corner of the world, under the thickest darkness of the Papacy, so many were found who, bidding farewell to human inventions, strove to draw from the fountains of the divine oracles the doctrines of a purer religion (however the bishops raged), how many do we believe there were, I do not say in England but in the whole world, who did not bend the knee to Baal? But behold a specimen of the Papist religion!

units.la: {f} Fox, pag. 745. {g} Fox, pag. 897. {h} Fox, pag. 751, &c. Robertus & Richardus Bartlet fratres, seipsos accusare coacti sunt; quòd Robertus quidem legerit, Richardus ab eo didicerit, Epistolam Jacobi hoc modo incipientem: James the servant of God to the twelve kindes, &c. Jacobus Dei servus, duodecim tribubus, &c.
units.tr: f Foxe, page 745. g Foxe, page 897. h Foxe, page 751, etc. Robert and Richard Bartlet, brothers, were compelled to accuse themselves: Robert had read, and Richard had learned from him, the Epistle of James beginning in this way: "James the servant of God to the twelve kindes", etc. James, servant of God, to the twelve tribes, etc.

units.la: Agnes istorum soror, uxor Johannis Wellis, à fratribus suis detecta est; à Roberto quidem quòd Epistolam Jacobi ab ipso, à Richardo verò quòd eandem à Thurstano Littlepage Anglicè didicisset. Indeque ex articulis Agneti propositis decimus in Registro notatus est hujusmodi: Utrùm Thurstanus Littlepage eam unquam docuerit Epistolam S. Jacobi, vel Epistolas S. Pauli Anglicè, & utrùm eandem S. Jacobi Epistolam Thurstano, præsente fratre suo Ricardo Bartlet, aliquoties repetiverit? Item 11us & 15us. Utrùm fratres, Richardus & Robertus, Epistolam S. Jacobi eam unquam docuerint; & si docuerint, quoties, & quo in loco?
units.tr: Their sister Agnes, wife of John Wellis, was detected by her brothers: by Robert, because he had read her the Epistle of James, and by Richard, because she had learned the same epistle in English from Thurstan Littlepage. Hence the tenth of the articles put to Agnes is noted in the Register in this form: "Whether Thurstan Littlepage ever taught her the Epistle of St James, or the Epistles of St Paul, in English, and whether she repeated the same Epistle of St James to Thurstan, in the presence of her brother Richard Bartlet, several times?" Likewise the eleventh and fifteenth: "Whether the brothers, Richard and Robert, ever taught her that Epistle of St James; and if they taught it, how often, and in what place?"

units.la: Thomas Chase à Jacobo Mordeno delatus, quòd bis auditus fuisset Epistolam S. Jacobi recitare, ita incipientem: 1 <bl>James the</bl> <bl>servant of God, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve kindes</bl>, &c. Item hæc verba (Luc. I. 5.) 2 <bl>It was by the</bl> <bl>dayes of Herod King of Jews, that there was a Priest, Zacharye by name, and he came of the sort of Abias, and his</bl> <bl>wife of the daughters of Aaron. Both they were just before</bl> <bl>God, going in all the commandments</bl>, &c.
units.tr: Thomas Chase, reported by James Mordeno for having been heard twice reciting the Epistle of St James, beginning thus: "James the servant of God, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve kindreds," etc. Likewise these words (Luc. I. 5.): "It was in the days of Herod King of Jewry, that there was a Priest, Zacharye by name, and he came of the course of Abias, and his wife of the daughters of Aaron. And they were both just before God, going in all the commandments," etc.

units.la: 1 Jacobus Dei & Domini nostri Jesu Christi servus, duodecim tribubus.
units.tr: James, servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes.

units.la: 2 Fuit in diebus Herodis Regis Judææ, sacerdos quidam nomine Zacharias, de vice Abia; & uxor illius de filiabus Aaron, & nomen ejus Elisabeth. Erant autem justi ambo ante Deum, incedentes in omnibus mandatis, &c.
units.tr: In the days of Herod, King of Judea, there was a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments, etc.

units.la: 3 Vos estis sal terræ. Quod si sal evanuerit, in quo salietur? ad nihilum valet ultra. Non potest civitas abscondi supra montem posita. Neque accendite lucernam, & ponite eam sub modio, sed super candelabrum, ut luceat omnibus, qui in domo sunt. Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus; ut videant opera vestra bona, & glorificent patrem, qui in cælis est. Iota unum, aut unus apex non præteriit a lege, donec omnia fiant. shine your light before men, as they may see your workes, and glorifie the father that is in heaven. No tittle nor letter of the law shall pass over, till all things be done. Item quod hanc lectionem eundem docuerit (ex Matth. V. 1.) 4 Jesus seeing his people: as he went up to a hill, was set; and his disciples came to him: he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying: Blessed be the poore men in spirite; for the kingdome of heaven is theirs. Blessed be mild men: for they shall welde the earth. Quinquies ad Agneten accesslit Mordenus ut priorem, bis ut alteram, discerct lectionem: & utramque ipsa Agnes recitare jussa est coram sex Episcopis; qui severe eidem interdixerunt, ne ullos omnino in posterum, ac liberos suos praesertim, lectiones istas edoceret. [Ex Registr. Longland, fol. 11.]
units.tr: 3 You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savour, wherewith shall it be salted? It is thenceforth good for nothing but to be cast out and trodden under foot of men. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. One iota or one tittle shall not pass from the law until all things be fulfilled. Likewise, that he taught this lesson (from Matt. 5.1): 4 Jesus, seeing his people, went up into a hill, and when he was set, his disciples came unto him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: Blessed be the poor in spirit; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed be the meek; for they shall inherit the earth. Mordenus came to Agnes five times, to teach her the former lesson, and twice the latter; and Agnes herself was ordered to recite both in the presence of six bishops, who strictly forbade her ever again, and especially her children, to teach those lessons to anyone at all. [From the Register of Longland, fol. 11.]

units.la: Henricus Miller & Joannes Phips, à Thomâ Holmes detecti, ut Scripturarum periti.
units.tr: Henry Miller and John Phips, detected by Thomas Holmes as skilled in the Scriptures.

units.la: Joannes Butler faber lignarius, Richardus Butler, Wilhelmus King de Uxbridge, quòd in aedibus Durdanti de Ivencourt totâ nocte Scripturæ codicem legissent. Item Durdantus senex, quòd inter prandendum (puero, qui astiterat, abscedere jussło) liberis suis eorumque uxoribus loca quaedam ex Epistolis Paulinis & Evangeliis recitâssent. Item Jo. Butler à proprio fratre accusatus est; quod librum quendam Scripturæ ipsi legisset, & ut eidem auscultaret, persuasisset.
units.tr: John Butler, carpenter, Richard Butler, and William King of Uxbridge, because they had read a book of the Scriptures all night in the house of Durdant de Ivencourt. Likewise old Durdant, because at dinner (having ordered a boy who was standing by to leave) he had recited certain passages from the Pauline Epistles and the Gospels to his children and their wives. Likewise John Butler was accused by his own brother, because he had read to him a certain book of Scripture and persuaded him to listen.

units.la: Durdantus prope Stanes, Durdantus senex, Isabella T. Hardingi uxor, Hartop de Windsor, Joanna Barret uxor Joannis Barret Londinensis, Henricus Miller, Stilmanus sartor, accusati omnes, quòd ad nuptias filiæ Durdanti convenientes in horreo, Epistolam quandam D. Pauli audivissent: cujus lectionem cùm reliqui, tum praecipuè Durdantus, approbârint & commendârint.
units.tr: Durdant near Staines, old Durdant, Isabella, wife of T. Hardinge, Hartop of Windsor, Joan Barret, wife of John Barret of London, Henry Miller, and Stilman the tailor, were all accused because, gathering in the barn at the wedding of Durdant's daughter, they had heard a certain Epistle of St Paul read; the others, and especially Durdant, had approved and commended the reading.

units.la: Johannes Barret aurifaber Londinensis; quòd domi suæ, uxore & ancillâ praesentibus, Epistolam S. Jacobi (quam cum aliis multis tenebat memoriter) recitâsset. Item Joanna uxor, quòd Joanni Scrivener Evangelium secundum Matthæum & Marcum mutuò commodâsset, quem librum ipse Episcopo Smitho tradidit. Item
units.tr: John Barret, goldsmith of London, because in his house, with his wife and maidservant present, he had recited the Epistle of St James (which he held by heart along with many others). Likewise his wife Joan, because she had lent John Scrivener the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, which book he himself handed to Bishop Smith. Likewise

units.la: 4 Videns autem Jesus turbas suas, ascendit in montem; & cum sedisset, accesserunt ad eum discipuli ejus; & aperiens os suum, docebat eos, dicens: Beati pauperes spiritu; quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Beati mites; quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram. Johannes Newnan, quòd adsuisset, cùm in ædibus Johannis Barret legerentur Scripturæ.
units.tr: 4 And Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up into a mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. John Newnan, because he was present when the Scriptures were read in the house of John Barret.

units.la: Wilus quidam delatus, quòd Johannem & Wilhelmum Wood Evangelium Matthæi post Magnam abjurationem docuisset: quos etiam pater Robertus senex (Buckinghamiæ postea combustus) D. Pauli Epistolas docuerat.
units.tr: A certain Wilus was denounced, because after the Great Abjuration he had taught John and William Wood the Gospel of Matthew; old Father Robert (afterwards burned at Buckingham) had also taught them the Epistles of St Paul.

units.la: Johannes Tracher de Chesham, quòd Aliciam Browne (quæ eum detexit) hanc Christi sententiam ex Evangelio docuisset: Beati qui verbum Dei audiunt & custodiunt illud. Item quòd eandem octo Beatitudines linguâ Anglicanâ docuit.
units.tr: John Tracher of Chesham, because he had taught Alice Browne (who detected him) this saying of Christ from the Gospel: Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it. Likewise, because he taught the same eight Beatitudes in English.

units.la: Thomas Geffrey sartor Ipswichensis, quòd legisset & docuisset Johannem Butler (qui eum detegere juramento coactus est) Acta Apostolorum: quódque Scripturæ librum (quem accusatus Episcopo Londinensi tradidit) in linguâ Anglicanâ habuisset.
units.tr: Thomas Geffrey, tailor of Ipswich, because he had read the Acts of the Apostles and taught them to John Butler (who was compelled by oath to inform on him); and because he had a copy of Scripture in English, which he handed to the Bishop of London when he was accused.

units.la: Radulphus Carpenter, quòd libros quosdam Apocalypseos in Anglicanâ linguâ habuisset, &c.
units.tr: Ralph Carpenter, because he had certain books of the Apocalypse in English, etc.

units.la: Johannes Butler tres fratres suos, unâ cum matre Richardi Ashforde, detexit; quòd Cheshami in ædibus Ashfordi duabus horis librum Actorum Apostolicorum Anglicè legissent.
units.tr: John Butler informed on his three brothers, together with the mother of Richard Ashford; because at Chesham, in Ashford's house, they had read the Acts of the Apostles in English for two hours.

units.la: Johannes Mordenus, cum fratre Richardo Ashford, accusatus; quòd domi suæ librum Evangelia & alia nonnulla capitula Anglicè translata continentem habuisset; in quo libro ipse ter vel quater, semel verò Ashfordus frater legerit.
units.tr: John Mordenus, accused together with his brother Richard Ashford, because in his house he had a book containing the Gospels and some other chapters translated into English; he had read in that book three or four times, and his brother Ashford once.

units.la: Geldenerus senior, cum duabus filiabus: quòd R. Benet Epistolam D. Jacobi Anglicè legentem audivissent.
units.tr: Geldener senior, with his two daughters, because they had heard R. Benet reading the Epistle of St James in English.

units.la: A Johanne Grosar quæsitum est, num Evangeliorum librum linguâ Vernaculâ habuisset; qui confessus est se ejusmodi librum à Tho. Tykill sacerdote missatico accepisse, eundemque Thomæ Spensero (qui cum uxore librum illum legere solebat) & postea Joanni Knight commodatum esse, qui librum Vicario de Rikemansworth demum tradiderit.
units.tr: John Grosar was asked whether he had a book of the Gospels in the vernacular. He confessed that he had received such a book from Thomas Tykill, a travelling priest, and had lent it to Thomas Spenser (who used to read that book with his wife), and afterwards to John Knight, who finally handed it to the vicar of Rickmansworth.

units.la: Johannes Hill juramento coactus est detegere Joannem Gun de Chelsham, quòd ipsum ante abjurationem suam in Epistolâ D. Jacobi instituisset.
units.tr: John Hill, compelled by oath to inform on John Gun of Chelsham, because before his abjuration he had instructed him in the Epistle of St James.

units.la: Robertus Pope juramento coactus est detegere, 1. Thomam Africum & uxorem ejus; quòd cum ipso post magnam abjurationem in oppido Amershamensi tactam, in Evangelio S. Matthæi contulissent. 2. Thomam Scrivener; quòd ab eo librum Epistolarum in linguâ lingua Vernacula habuisset. 3. Benedictum Warde de Bekencsfeilde, quòd ab eo librum X. Mandatorum accepisset, quódque Evangelia Matthæi & Marci habuisset. 4. Tho. Man cum uxore, quòd cum ipso sæpius in libris Scripturæ contulissent. 5. Richardum Colyns, quòd librum Lucæ & alium Pauli, necnon Glossam Apocalypseos habuisset. 6. Thomam Colyns Richardi patrem, quòd librum Pauli & minorum Epistolarum habuisset. 7. Edwardum Pope suum ipsius patrem, quòd Evangelium Matthæi lectum audivisset, & de eodem cum filio suo (Roberto hoc) contulisset. 8. Wilhelmum Halydaie de Eastenred, quòd Acta Apostolorum Anglicè versa ab ipso (quùm Rogerus Dodde caperetur) ad eum allata custodivisset. 9. Thomam Philippe & Laurentium Tayler, quòd in ædibus Richardi Colyns ex libro Anglicano Epistolam ad Romanos & primum caput Evangelii secundum Lucam legissent. 10. Uxores Johannis Harrys & Richardi Colyns, quòd in ædibus Johannis Harrisi de Apocalypsi & Actis Apostolorum essent collocutæ: ipsum quoque Johannem, quod de septem macilentis & septem pinguibus vaccis loqui esset auditus.
units.tr: Robert Pope, compelled by oath to inform on: (1) Thomas Africus and his wife, because after the great abjuration taken in the town of Amersham they had compared the Gospel of St Matthew with him; (2) Thomas Scrivener, because he had had a book of Epistles in the vernacular from him; (3) Benedict Warde of Bekencsfeilde, because he had received from him a book of the Ten Commandments, and because he had the Gospels of Matthew and Mark; (4) Thomas Man with his wife, because they had often compared the books of Scripture with him; (5) Richard Colyns, because he had the book of Luke and another of Paul, and also a gloss on the Apocalypse; (6) Thomas Colyns, Richard's father, because he had a book of Paul and of the minor Epistles; (7) Edward Pope, his own father, because he had heard the Gospel of Matthew read and had compared it with his son Robert; (8) William Halydaie of Eastenred, because he had kept the Acts of the Apostles translated into English, which had been brought to him by Roger Dodde when Dodde was arrested; (9) Thomas Philippe and Laurence Tayler, because in the house of Richard Colyns they had read from an English book the Epistle to the Romans and the first chapter of the Gospel according to Luke; (10) the wives of John Harrys and Richard Colyns, because in the house of John Harris they had talked about the Apocalypse and the Acts of the Apostles; also John himself, because he was heard speaking of the seven lean and seven fat kine.

units.la: Robertus Colins juramento coactus est detegere, 1. Richardum Colins, quòd legisset ipsi X. Mandata, deinde Epistolam Jacobi, & aliam quandam minorem Petri docuisset, & demum Evangelium D. Joannis Anglicè ipsi per se legendum tradidisset. Eidemque objectum est, quòd cum alios libros Anglicanos, tum Evangelium Johannis, Epistolas D. Pauli, Jacobi & Petri, expositionem Apocalypseos, librum Solomonis, &c. habuisset. 2. Johannem Harris, quòd cum ipso de primo capite Evangelii Johannis, & alio Matthæi, in quo de octo Beatitudinibus agebatur, contulisset. 3. Ro. & W. Lyvord, Bruges & uxorem Johannam, Harris & uxorem, Richardum Colins; quòd in Brugesii ædibus librum expositionem Apocalypseos continentem simul legissent, & de apertione libri septem sigillis obsignati, &c. communicâssent: 4. Stacyum laterarium Londinensem, quòd librum Apocalypseos habuisset.
units.tr: Robert Colins, compelled by oath to inform on: (1) Richard Colins, because he had read the Ten Commandments to him, then taught him the Epistle of James and another short Epistle of Peter, and finally handed him the Gospel of John in English to read on his own. It was also objected to him that he had other English books, namely the Gospel of John, the Epistles of Paul, James and Peter, an exposition of the Apocalypse, the book of Solomon, etc.; (2) John Harris, because he had compared with him the first chapter of John's Gospel and another of Matthew, in which the eight Beatitudes were discussed; (3) Ro. and W. Lyvord, Bruges and his wife Joan, Harris and his wife, and Richard Colins, because in Bruges's house they had read together a book containing an exposition of the Apocalypse, and had shared their thoughts on the opening of the book sealed with seven seals, etc.; (4) Stacy, a London bricklayer, because he had had a book of the Apocalypse.

units.la: 5. Tho. Philips & Laurentium Wharsar, quòd Epistolam D. Petri Anglicè in ædibus Roberti Colins legissent.
units.tr: (5) Thomas Philips and Laurence Wharsar, because they had read the Epistle of St Peter in English in the house of Robert Colins.

units.la: 1 Genes. XLI.

Johannes Colins de Burforde sequentes Episcopo detulit: 1. Rob. Colins de Asthall, quòd legisset ipsi in spisso quodam Scripturæ Vernaculæ volumine. 2. Johannem Edmunds, quòd legisset ipsi X. mandata, docuissetque Johannem Baptistam dixisse, venturum post se alium, cujus non esset dignus qui solveret corrigiam calceamentorum. 3. Johannem Hacker Londinensem, quòd Burfordam librum, in quo de X. plagis Pharaonis agebatur, secum attulisset.
units.tr: John Colins of Burford reported the following to the bishop: (1) Robert Colins of Asthall, because he had read to him from a thick volume of Scripture in the vernacular; (2) John Edmunds, because he had read him the Ten Commandments and had taught that John the Baptist said another would come after him, whose shoe-thong he was not worthy to loose; (3) John Hacker of London, because he had brought to Burford a book in which the ten plagues of Pharaoh were described.

units.la: Rogerus Dods de Burforde juramento coactus est detegere, 1. Johannem Drury Vicarium Windrishensem in Comitatu Wigorniensi, quòd Alphabetum ipsum docuisset; ut Apocalypsin intelligeret, ex quâ omnem mundi falsitatem omnemque veritatem illum percepturum asseret at. 2. Henricum Miller, quòd ostendisset illi Historiam mulieris in Apocalypsi bestiæ coccineæ insidentis. 3. Johannem Fippe de Hichenden, quòd Anglicè Evangelium quoddam ipsi legisset. 4. Johannem Ledilsdall de Hungerforde, quòd Burfordiæ in ædibus Roberti Burges, unà cum Colins, Lyvordo, Thomâ Hall & aliis Biblia legisset. 5. Rob. & Jo. Collins cum uxoribus, quòd Biblia à Stacio 20. solidis emissent. 6. Joh. Hacker, Joh. Brabant, cum uxore, filiis & nuribus, & Reginaldum Brabant de Stanlake, quòd Stanlaki in ædibus Jo. Brabant librum quendam Scripturæ Anglicè legissent.
units.tr: Roger Dods of Burford, compelled by oath, disclosed: (1) John Drury, vicar of Windrish in the county of Worcester, that he had taught him the alphabet so that he might understand the Apocalypse, from which he said he would learn all the falsehood of the world and all the truth; (2) Henry Miller, that he had shown him the history of the woman sitting on the scarlet beast in the Apocalypse; (3) John Fippe of Hichenden, that he had read to him a certain Gospel in English; (4) John Ledilsdall of Hungerford, that at Burford, in the house of Robert Burges, together with Collins, Lyvord, Thomas Hall and others, he had read the Bibles; (5) Robert and John Collins with their wives, that they had bought Bibles from Stacy for 20 shillings; (6) John Hacker, John Brabant with his wife, sons and daughters-in-law, and Reginald Brabant of Stanlake, that at Stanlake, in the house of John Brabant, they had read a certain book of Scripture in English.

units.la: Johannes Edmunds de Burforde detexit, 1. Aliciam uxorem Richardi Colins, quæ cùm multum Scripturarum teneret memoriter, ad conventus Burfordiæ factos accersi solebat, ut X. Mandatorum declarationem cum Epistolis Petri & Jacobi recitaret.
units.tr: John Edmunds of Burford disclosed: (1) Alice, wife of Richard Collins, who, since she held much of Scripture in memory, was accustomed to be summoned to the meetings held at Burford, to recite the exposition of the Ten Commandments together with the Epistles of Peter and James.

units.la: 2. Johannam Richardi Colins & Aliciæ filiam, quòd cum patre & matre X. mandata, VII. peccata mortalia, VII. Opera misericordiæ, V. sensus corporales & spirituales, VIII. beatitudines, & V. Cadiæ, V. sensus corporales & spirituales, VIII. beatitudines, & V. Capita Epistolæ D. Jacobi didicisset. 3. Agnetem Edmunds, suam ipsius filiam, quòd domum Richardi Colins eam ipse adduxisset, ut in lege Domini ibidem institueretur: ubi etiam X. mandata, V. sensus, & VII. peccata mortalia didicerat.
units.tr: (2) Joan, daughter of Richard Collins and Alice, that with her father and mother she had learned the Ten Commandments, the seven deadly sins, the seven works of mercy, the five bodily and spiritual senses, the eight beatitudes, and the five chapters of the Epistle of St James. (3) Agnes Edmunds, his own daughter, whom he himself had brought to the house of Richard Collins so that she might be instructed there in the law of the Lord; there too she had learned the Ten Commandments, the five senses and the seven deadly sins.

units.la: Johannes Brabant Johannem Hacker nominavit, quòd sacram Scripturam in ædibus paternis legisset; Patrem item suum Johannem Brabant ac matrem, quòd adfuissent, quùm Hackerus ista negm legerit. Ubi notanda examinationis forma ab Episcopo Johanni Brabant
units.tr: John Brabant named John Hacker, that he had read Holy Scripture in his father's house; likewise his father, John Brabant, and his mother, that they had been present when Hacker read those things. Here the form of examination used by the Bishop with John Brabant is to be noted:

units.la: {k} Apoc. XVII. Brabant proposita ; An fc. unquam audivit Johannem Hacker legentem sacram Scripturam contra determinationem Ecclesiæ. [Ex Registro Jo. Longland, Lincoln. sol. 85.]
units.tr: {k} Apoc. XVII. Question put to John Brabant: whether he had ever heard John Hacker reading Holy Scripture against the determination of the Church. [From the Register of John Longland, Lincoln, fol. 85.]

units.la: Johanna Steventon detexit Aliciam Colins, quòd Alicia docuisset eam X. Mandata, & primum Caput Evangelii secundùm Johannem ; Item Johannem Harris, quòd docuisset eam primum capitulum Petri.
units.tr: Joan Steventon disclosed that Alice Collins had taught her the Ten Commandments and the first chapter of the Gospel according to John; likewise that John Harris had taught her the first chapter of Peter.

units.la: Johannes Hacker detexit, 1. Th. Vincentium Londinensem, quòd dedisset Hackero librum S. Matthæi Anglicè scriptum. 2. Richardum Colins, quòd accepisset ab Hackero librum Anglicum de X. Mandatis. 3. Wilhelmum Gunne, quòd accepisset ab eodem, librum X. Plagarum, quibus afflictus est Pharao. 4. Johannem Heron, quòd Evangeliorum expositionem vernaculam pulchrè descriptam haberet. [Ex Regiftro Longlandi Lincolniensis.]
units.tr: John Hacker disclosed: (1) Thomas Vincent of London, that he had given Hacker a book of St Matthew written in English; (2) Richard Collins, that he had received from Hacker an English book on the Ten Commandments; (3) William Gunne, that he had received from the same a book of the ten plagues with which Pharaoh was afflicted; (4) John Heron, that he possessed a fine copy of a vernacular exposition of the Gospels. [From the Register of Longland, Bishop of Lincoln.]

units.la: 1523. Johannes Higges.
units.tr: 1523. John Higges.

units.la: Huic inter alios articulos sub Cuthberto Tunstallo Londinensi Episcopo objectum est; quod librum IV. Evangelistarum in linguâ Anglicanâ haberet, frequenterque legeret. Verum cessò hic in rebus Anglicanis ulterius progredi; tùm quòd propiùs nostra tempora attingant, cum quòd eas in Actis & Monumentis Eccles. Hist. Angl. diligenter persecutus sit Jo. Foxus. Illud tantùm monendum, Scripturarum in linguam Anglicanam Versiones, quarum hic & in superioribus frequens facta est mentio, prioribus Seculis omnes prodiisse. Nondum enim Guilhelmus Tindallus, sanctissimus Dei Martyr (qui primus nostris temporibus optimo successu negotium hoc tentavit) Translationem suam aggressus est. Ad alias verò nationes quod attinet; memorabilis extat Historia Librarii ob Biblia Avenione vendita exusti apud Joannem Crispinum in Act. Martyrum lib. 3. sol. 97. b. & incolarum Merindolii, ibid. sol. 112. & Richardi Feuri, ibid. sol. 264.
units.tr: Among other articles, this was brought against him under Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of London: that he had a book of the four Evangelists in the English tongue and read it frequently. But I will stop here and not proceed further in English affairs, both because they come closer to our own times and because John Foxe has diligently followed them in his Acts and Monuments of the English Church. It is only to be noted that the versions of Scripture into English, of which frequent mention has been made here and above, all appeared in earlier centuries; for William Tyndale, most holy martyr of God (who was the first in our times to attempt this work with great success), had not yet undertaken his translation. As for other nations, there is a memorable account of the bookseller who was burnt for selling Bibles at Avignon, in John Crispin's Acts of the Martyrs, book 3, p. 97b; of the inhabitants of Mérindol, ibid. p. 112; and of Richard Feur, ibid. p. 264.

units.la: m Fox. pag. 735.
units.tr: m Fox. p. 735.

units.la: n De quo vid. Fox. pag. 983, 928, 929, 930, 931. & Matt. Parker. Hist. Archiep. Cantuar.
units.tr: n On this see Foxe, pp. 983, 928, 929, 930, 931, and Matthew Parker, History of the Archbishops of Canterbury.

units.la: Anno 1526.
units.tr: In the year 1526.

units.la: Cuthberti Tunstalli Episcopi Londinensis, postea Dunelmensis, prohibitio Anglicanæ Translationis Novi Testamenti Latinè habetur in 1a editione Act. & Monument. Jo. Foxi, pag. 449.
units.tr: The prohibition by Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of London, later of Durham, of an English translation of the New Testament is given in Latin in the first edition of Foxe's Acts and Monuments, p. 449.

units.la: Anno 1559.
units.tr: In the year 1559.

units.la: In Catalogo librorum prohibitorum, Pauli IV. jussu confecto, & Romæ anno 1559. ex decreto S. Romanæ & Universalis Inquisitionis edito, ita sancitum legimus. Biblia omnia vulgari idiomate sc. Germanico, Hispanico, Italico, Anglico sive Flandrico, &c. conscripta, nullatenus vel imprimi vel legi vel teneri possint absque licentia Sacri Officii S. Romanæ Inquisitionis. Item, Novi Testamenti libri vulgari idiomate conscripti sine licentia in Scriptis habita ab Officio S. Romanæ & Universalis Inquisitionis nullatenus vel imprimi vel teneri possint.
units.tr: In the Catalogue of prohibited books, drawn up by order of Paul IV and published at Rome in 1559 by decree of the Holy Roman and Universal Inquisition, we read the following decree: All Bibles written in the vernacular, namely in German, Spanish, Italian, English or Flemish, and so forth, may in no way be printed, read or kept without the licence of the Holy Office of the Roman Inquisition. Likewise: The books of the New Testament written in the vernacular may in no way be printed or kept without a licence in writing obtained from the Office of the Holy Roman and Universal Inquisition.

units.la: Anno 1564.
units.tr: Year 1564.

units.la: Postea in 4a Regula per Patres à Tridentina Synodo delectos confecta, & anno 1564. in Indice librorum prohibitorum à Pio IV. Pontifice edita in hunc modum conclusum est. Cum experimento manifestum fit, si sacra Biblia vulgari lingua passim sine discrimine permittantur; plus inde, ob hominum temeritatem, detrimenti quàm utilitatis oriri: hàc in parte judicio Episcopi aut Inquisitoris stetur, ut cum consilio Parochi vel Confessarii, Bibliorum à Catholicis auctoribus versorum lectionem in vulgari linguâ eis concedere possint; quos intellexerint ex hujusmodi lectione non damnum, sed fidei atque pietatis augmentum capere posse: quam facultatem in scriptis habeant. Qui autem absque tali facultate ea legere seu habere præsumpserint; nisi prius Bibliis ordinario redditis, peccatorum absolutionem percipere non possint. Bibliopolæ vero, qui prædictam facultatem non habenti Biblia idiomate vulgari conscripta vendiderint vel aliis quovis modo concesserint, librorum pretium in usus pios ab Episcopo convertendum amittant, aliisque pœnis pro delicti qualitate ejusdem Episcopi arbitrio subjaceant. Regulares vero nonnulli facultate à Prælatis suis habitâ ea legere aut emere possint. Sed istam Regulam restringendam esse monuit postea Gregorius Capuccinus (unus ex Deputatis Patribus pro revisione librorum in Civitate Neapolitana) in Enchiridio Ecclesiastico ° edito Venet. an. 1533. Quantum (ait) ad 4m. Regulam, inquam permitti Sacra Biblia vulgaria; nihilominus à R. Theologis fide digniss fuit determinatum quòd, in posterum non concedantur: sed cùm conditionibus positis in dictâ 4a. Regulâ possunt concedi Evangelia & Epistolæ vulgares, cùm quotidie in Missâ audiantur. A Gregorio etiam XIII. restrictam esse illam facultatem Rainoldus p notat ex Septimo Decretalium lib. 5. tit. 4. cap. 6. Biblia tamen in Polonicam linguam per Jacobum Viecam Jesuitam mandante Gregorio XIII Pontifice Maximo & approbante Clemente VIII. translata esse notat Gretserus in Tractatu de Novis Translationibus col. 939. Vid. Poslevinum in Jacobo Viecâ; & nota necessitatem quâ impulsi sunt transferre Scripturas & Officia. Habetur quidem in Septimo Decretalium edit. Francofurt. an. 1590. pag. 542.
