Bulla illa à Rainoldo citata: sed Gregorii XIII. nomen ibi per errorem pro Pio IV. est positum; cujus hæc est Constitutio in Bullario Petri Matthæi pag. 464, 465. ad verbum.
units.tr: Afterwards, in the Fourth Rule drawn up by the Fathers chosen by the Council of Trent, and published in the Index of prohibited books by Pope Pius IV in 1564, it was concluded in this manner: Since experience shows clearly that if the Holy Bibles are allowed indiscriminately in the vernacular, more harm than good arises from them, owing to the rashness of men, in this matter it shall rest with the judgment of the Bishop or the Inquisitor, so that, with the advice of the parish priest or confessor, they may grant to those whom they judge can gain from such reading not harm but an increase of faith and piety, the reading of the Bibles in the vernacular translated by Catholic authors; and they shall have this permission in writing. But those who presume to read or possess them without such permission cannot receive absolution of their sins unless they first surrender the Bibles to the ordinary. Booksellers, moreover, who sell or otherwise supply Bibles written in the vernacular to someone without this permission, shall forfeit the price of the books, to be applied to pious uses by the Bishop, and shall be liable to other penalties, at the discretion of the same Bishop, according to the nature of the offence. Some regulars, however, may read or buy them with permission obtained from their prelates. But Gregory the Capuchin (one of the Fathers deputed to revise books in the city of Naples) later warned that this Rule was to be restricted, in his Enchiridion Ecclesiasticum published at Venice in 1533: As to the 4th Rule, I say, the vernacular Holy Bibles are permitted; nevertheless, it has been determined by reliable learned theologians that they are not to be granted henceforth; but the vernacular Gospels and Epistles may be granted under the conditions laid down in the said 4th Rule, since they are heard every day in the Mass. That this permission was also restricted by Gregory XIII, Rainoldusp notes, from the Seventh Book of the Decretals, book 5, title 4, chapter 6. Gretser, in his Treatise on the New Translations, col. 939, notes that the Bibles were translated into Polish by the Jesuit Jacob Vieca, at the command of Pope Gregory XIII and with the approval of Clement VIII. See Possevinus on Jacob Vieca; and note the necessity which impelled them to translate the Scriptures and the Offices. That bull cited by Rainoldus is indeed found in the Seventh [Book of the Decretals], Frankfurt edition of 1590, p. 542; but the name of Gregory XIII is put there by mistake in place of Pius IV. Its actual text, word for word, is in Petrus Matthaeus's Bullarium, pp. 464, 465.

units.la: Anno 1595.
units.tr: Year 1595.

units.la: Itaque Clemens Papa VIII. cùm Indicem librorum prohibitorum denuo recognitum Anno 1595. edi jussisset; ne quis per novam illam editionem, Regulæ illius 4. authoritatem denuò etiam renovatam existimaret, sequentem Observationem circa 4am Regulam addi curavit. Animadvertendum est circa suprascriptam 4am Regulam felicis recordationis Pii Papæ IV. nullam per hanc impressionem vel editionem de novo tribui facultatem Episcopis vel Inquisitoribus aut Regularium Superioribus concedendi licentiam emendi, legendi aut retinendi Biblia vulgari linguâ edita: cùm hactenus mandato & usu Sanctæ Romanæ & universalis Inquisitionis subiata eis fuerit facultas concedendi hujusmodi licentias legendi aut retinendi Biblia vulgaria, aut alias S. Scripturæ tam Novi quàm Veteris Testamenti partes quavis vulgari linguâ editas, ac insuper Summaria & Compendia etiam historica eorundem Bibliorum, seu librorum S. Scripturæ, quocunque vulgari idiomate conscripta: quod quidem inviolatè servandum est.
units.tr: Therefore Pope Clement VIII, when he ordered the Index of prohibited books, newly revised, to be published in 1595, lest anyone should think that the authority of that 4th Rule had been renewed by this new edition, took care to add the following observation on the 4th Rule: It must be noted, with regard to the 4th Rule above written of Pope Pius IV of happy memory, that by this printing or edition no new faculty is granted to Bishops, Inquisitors or Superiors of Regulars to grant licence to buy, read or keep Bibles published in the vernacular. For hitherto, by the command and practice of the Holy Roman and Universal Inquisition, they have been deprived of the power of granting such licences to read or keep the vernacular Bibles, or any other parts of Holy Scripture, of the New as well as the Old Testament, published in any vernacular language, and moreover summaries and compendia, even historical ones, of these same Bibles or books of Holy Scripture, written in any vernacular idiom. This must indeed be observed inviolably.

units.la: ° Fol. 218. b. ᵖ In Thesibus, pag. 145.
units.tr: ° Fol. 218 b. ᵖ In Theses, p. 145.

units.la: Anno 1602.
units.tr: The year 1602.

units.la: Hinc Joannes Azorius Hispanus Jesuita q: Quæres, An Bibliorum partes, nimirum libri, aut librorum capita, in vulgares linguas translata permittantur? Respondeo, primo aspectu in prædictâ quartâ Regulâ solùm prohiberi, ne sacra Biblia vulgari linguâ passim sine discrimine permittantur legi, emi, retineri aut vendi. In Hispaniâ tamen in Indice librorum Prohibitorum ibi edito auctoritate Generalis in illis provinciis Inquisitoris, Regula Sexta sic habet: Prohibentur Biblia vulgari linguâ cum omnibus suis partibus: ac si dicat, Biblia & eorum partes. Et in Indice recenti edito jussu S. D. N. Clementis VIII. in Observatione circa quartam prædictam Regulam Indicis editi jussu Pii IV. ita habetur: [cùm] sublata eis fuerit (sc. Episcopis, Inquisitoribus, & Regularium Superioribus) facultas concedendi licentiam legendi vel retinendi Biblia vulgaria, aut alias S. Scripturæ tam Novi quam Veteris Testamenti partes quavis vulgari linguâ editas. Quæres insuper an permittantur conscripti vulgari linguâ Precationum Horariarum libelli, in quibus continentur Psalmi & Cantica ex Bibliis excerpta? In Indice Hispaniensi ac Regulâ sextâ omnes hujusmodi linguâ Vernaculâ conscripti libelli prohibentur. Et in Indice novissimè edito jussu S. D. N. Clementis VIII. in Observatione circa quartam Regulam, prohibentur S. Scripturæ partes tam Novi quàm Veteris Testamenti quavis vulgari linguâ editæ; ac insuper Summaria & Compendia etiam historica eorundem Bibliorum seu librorum Sacræ Scripturæ quocunque vulgari idiomate conscripta; quod quidem inviolatè præcipitur servandum.
units.tr: Hence Juan Azor, the Spanish Jesuit, asks: Are parts of the Bible, that is, whole books or chapters of books, permitted to be translated into the vernacular languages? I answer: at first sight the fourth Rule above forbids only that the Holy Bibles in the vernacular be read, bought, kept or sold indiscriminately. In Spain, however, the Index of Prohibited Books published there by the authority of the Inquisitor General in those provinces has a Sixth Rule which reads: the Bibles are prohibited in the vernacular together with all their parts, as if to say, the Bibles and their parts. And in the recent Index published by order of our Lord Pope Clement VIII, the observation on the fourth Rule of the Index published by order of Pius IV reads: [when] the power of granting licence to read or keep vernacular Bibles, or other parts of Holy Scripture of either the New or the Old Testament published in any vernacular language, has been taken away from the bishops, inquisitors and superiors of the religious orders. Further, you will ask whether small books of the Hours written in the vernacular, containing Psalms and canticles taken from the Bibles, are permitted? In the Spanish Index and in the Sixth Rule, all such small books written in the vernacular are prohibited. And in the Index recently published by order of our Lord Pope Clement VIII, in the observation on the fourth Rule, parts of Holy Scripture of either the New or the Old Testament published in any vernacular language are prohibited, and in addition summaries and compendia, even historical ones, of these same Bibles or books of Holy Scripture written in any vernacular idiom; which is indeed commanded to be observed without exception.

units.la: His addam Pontificiorum quorundam Theologorum de Scripturis & Sacris Vernaculis sententias. Prædictus itaque Azorius eodem loco hæc habet. Quarto quæritur, An expediat & deceat sacra volumina in maternas, & vernaculas linguas converti? Respondeo, Minimè, quia detrimentum inde paceretur fidelium concordiæ. Deinde variæ hæresium & errorum causæ nascerentur. Præterea magna insciliæ & ignorantiæ causa in Republicâ Christianâ sequeretur. Ex varietate etiam, incertitudine & multitudine Versionum contentiones innumeræ, dissidia, ac infinita propemodum alia incommoda & mala provenirent. Atque iterum, Quicquid Lutherani & Calvinistæ sibi velint & obstrepant; error est intolerabilis asse-
units.tr: I shall add the opinions of certain Papist theologians on Scripture and the sacred books in the vernacular. Thus the aforementioned Azor says in the same place: Fourthly, it is asked whether it is expedient and fitting for the sacred volumes to be turned into the mother tongues and vernacular languages? I answer: by no means, because from this a loss would follow for the harmony of the faithful. Then various causes of heresies and errors would arise. Besides, great ignorance and unlearnedness would follow in the Christian commonwealth. From the variety, uncertainty and multitude of versions, innumerable quarrels, dissensions, and almost infinite other inconveniences and evils would also arise. And again, whatever the Lutherans and Calvinists may wish and clamour, it is an intolerable error to assert

units.la: ¶ Institut. Moral. lib. 8. cap. 26. rere publicas Ecclesiæ ad Deum precationes vulgari idiomate cantari, recitari & fundi debere: & neminem fidelium earum fructûs posse esse participem, nisi intelligat idioma quo recitantur. Mos enim generalis Ecclesiæ habet, ut non nisi certis quibusdam linguis Hebraicâ nimirum, Syriacâ, Græcâ & Latinâ, celebrentur: qui mos plurimis abhinc annis in Ecclesiam inductus & nunc retinetur & servatur. Quæres, an expediat prædicta publica Officia vulgari linguâ celebrari? Respondeo, Nequaquam: quia multa inde incommoda nascerentur; ut paulò antè vidimus. Porrò non idem juris est de privatis precationibus, quas quivis fundit ad Deum, nec de iis quæ ad Catechismum spectant; quale est Apostolorum Symbolum, Salutatio Angelica, & cætera Christianæ fidei rudimenta. Hæc enim licèt Latinè sæpe tradantur, materna tamen linguâ proponi & addisci solent; quia publica Ecclesiæ officia minimè censentur. Hæc Azorius.
units.tr: ¶ Institutes of Moral Theology, book 8, chapter 26. that the public prayers of the Church to God ought to be sung, recited and poured out in the vernacular idiom; and that none of the faithful can share in their fruits unless he understands the idiom in which they are recited. For the general custom of the Church holds that they are celebrated only in certain languages, namely Hebrew, Syriac, Greek and Latin; a custom introduced into the Church many years ago, and now retained and observed. You will ask whether it is expedient for the aforesaid public offices to be celebrated in the vernacular? I answer: by no means, because many inconveniences would arise from it, as we saw a little earlier. Moreover, the law is not the same for private prayers, which anyone pours out to God, nor for those which pertain to the catechism, such as the Apostles' Creed, the Angelic Salutation, and the other rudiments of the Christian faith. For although these are often taught in Latin, they are customarily presented and learned in the mother tongue, since they are not regarded as public offices of the Church. Thus Azor.

units.la: Joannes Molanus in Theologiæ Practicæ compendio Tractat. 3. cap. 27. Conclus. 2. sect. 16. Negamus à vulgo Christianorum requiri studium Scripturarum; immò salubriter dicimus eos à lectione Scripturarum arceri; sufficereque eis, ut ex præscripto Pastorum & Doctorum Ecclesiæ vitæ cursum moderentur.
units.tr: John Molanus, in the Compendium of Practical Theology, tract. 3, chap. 27, conclusion 2, section 16: We deny that the common people of Christians are required to study the Scriptures; indeed we say wholesomely that they are kept away from reading the Scriptures, and that it is enough for them to guide the course of their lives by the prescription of the ministers and teachers of the Church.

units.la: Jacobus Ledesima de divinis Scripturis quavis linguâ non legendis, cap. 2. Pro fide Catholicâ scopus hic præcipuus nostræ disputationis erit; ut ostendamus divinas Scripturas non esse quàvis passim vulgari linguâ vertendas, nec omnibus sine discrimine communicandas.
units.tr: Jacob Ledesma, On the divine Scriptures not to be read in any language, chap. 2: For the Catholic faith the chief aim of our disputation will be to show that the divine Scriptures are not to be translated everywhere into the vernacular, nor communicated to all without distinction.

units.la: Concilium Mediolanense III. (Caroli Borromæi) ita statuit: Libri de officio & precibus horariis Beatæ Mariæ Virginis vulgariter, vel Italicè, vel Gallicè, vel Hispanicè, vel Germanicè, vel partim Latino, partim vulgari sermone expressi, venales ne proponantur neque vendantur. Siqui verò eos adhuc habent; ad sacræ Inquisitionis Officium statim deferre compellantur; ut edita à Pio V. Constitutione sancitum est (præfix. Officio 3. Mariæ.)
units.tr: The Third Council of Milan (of Charles Borromeo) decreed as follows: Books of the office and the hour prayers of the Blessed Virgin Mary, expressed in the vernacular, whether in Italian, French, Spanish or German, or partly in Latin and partly in the vernacular, shall not be put forward or sold for sale. If anyone still has them, he is to be compelled to hand them over at once to the Office of the sacred Inquisition; as was sanctioned by the Constitution issued by Pius V (prefixed to the Office of Mary, 3).

units.la: In Clementin. de Celebrat. Missarum lib. 3. cap. 1. Gravi. gloss. ver. Fructum. Et arguitur (inquit) ex hoc, quod satis est labiis servire in divinis Horis, licèt cor divertat ad alia. Romani tamen Correctores iusmodi antidotum apponunt ad marginem. Priusquam descendas in hanc Glossæ sententiam; consule Theologos, & præsertim B. Thomam lib. 4. Sent. dist. 15. qu. 4. art. 1. & ibidem Paludanum dist. 15. qu. 5. & Gabrielem in Canonem Missæ lect. 62.
units.tr: In the Clementines, on the celebration of Masses, book 3, chapter 1, Gravi, gloss on the word Fructum. And it is argued (he says) from this, that it is enough to serve with the lips in the divine Hours, even though the heart wanders to other things. The Roman Correctors, however, put an antidote of this kind in the margin. Before you descend to this opinion of the gloss, consult the theologians, and especially St Thomas, book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 15, question 4, article 1, and there Paludanus, distinction 15, question 5, and Gabriel on the Canon of the Mass, lecture 62.

units.la: {r} Tomo ult. Concil. edit. Venet. pag. 588. Anglo-Rhemenses in 1 Cor. XIV. Populus Christianus antiquae suae consuetudini parere debet, & Latinis precibus uti potius quàm vulgatis. Contra Erasmus in 1 Cor. XIV. Hæc in re mirum est, quomodo mutata est Ecclesiæ consuetudo.
units.tr: {r} In the last volume of the Council, Venice edition, page 588. The Anglo-Rhemists on 1 Corinthians 14: The Christian people ought to obey their ancient custom, and to use Latin prayers rather than those in the vernacular. Against this, Erasmus on 1 Corinthians 14: In this matter it is remarkable how the custom of the Church has been changed.

units.la: Tho. Bosius in Præfatione libri de Italiæ statu. Nos contendimus ex antiquo tempore adversus Hæreticos mysteria nostra non esse vulgaribus linguis explicanda, sed Latinæ linguæ omnino relinquenda.
units.tr: Thomas Bozio, in the Preface to his book on the state of Italy: We contend that from ancient times, against the heretics, our mysteries are not to be explained in the vernacular languages, but must be left entirely to the Latin language.

units.la: Petrus Licetius scripsit Dialogum de sacris utriusque Testamenti libris in vulgare idioma, sive (uti ille vocat) Eloquium minimè vertendis, rudique plebi haudquaquam invulgandis [Possevinus.] Idem argumentum tractárunt Hosius Cardinalis Varmiensis in Dialogo De sacro vernaculè legendo: Jesuitæ authores Coloniensis Censuræ in Præfationem Monhemii; Joannes Hesselsii Oratione de divinorum Officiorum in linguâ Latinâ celebratione; Hardingus articulo 3. & 15. contra Juellum; Sanderus in declamatione de linguis divinorum Officiorum [In Vitâ quidem ejus legimus scripsisse cum de divinis Officiis non celebrandis in linguâ vulgari librum 1. sed nondum editum: ejus sententiam videre licet in lib. de Visib. Monarch. pag. 597. & præfat. in Petram Ecclesiæ, & lib. de Imag.] Robertus Bellarminus in Prælectionibus Romæ habitis Anno 1576. editis Ingolstadii Anno 1587. quem secutus est in Controversiarum Epitome MS. Personius: Costerus in Enchiridio: Rhemenses in Præfatione Novi Testamenti, & in 1 Corinth. XIV. Tho. Stapletonus in Relectione Principiorum Doctrinalium editâ Anno 1596. & in Antidotis 1 Corinth. XIV. à pag. 718. ad 734. Fr. Agricola de Verbo Dei: Reginaldus & Giffordus in Calvino-Turcismo lib. 4. cap. 7. Staphylus in Apologiâ: Alphonsus Salmeron in 1 Corinth. [Tom. 14. à pag. 255. ad 273.] Martinus Perefius de Traditionibus, sol. 41. b. 44. a.
units.tr: Pietro Licet wrote a Dialogue on the sacred books of both Testaments, that they should not be translated into the vernacular idiom, or (as he calls it) the eloquence, and by no means made common to the rude populace [Possevinus]. The same subject was treated by Cardinal Hosius, Bishop of Warmia, in his Dialogue on reading the sacred books in the vernacular; by the Jesuit authors of the Cologne Censure on the Preface of Monheim; by John Hesselsius in his Oration on the celebration of the divine Offices in the Latin language; by Harding in articles 3 and 15 against Jewel; by Sanders in his declamation on the languages of the divine Offices [we read in his Life that he wrote a first book on not celebrating the divine Offices in the vernacular, but it was not yet published; his opinion can be seen in the book On the Visible Monarchy, page 597, and in the preface to Petra Ecclesiae, and in the book On Images]; Robert Bellarmine in his lectures given at Rome in 1576, published at Ingolstadt in 1587, whom Personius followed in his manuscript Epitome of Controversies; Costerus in his Enchiridion; the Rhemists in the Preface to the New Testament and on 1 Corinthians 14; Thomas Stapleton in his Reading of the Doctrinal Principles, published in 1596, and in the Antidotes on 1 Corinthians 14, from page 718 to 734; Fr. Agricola, On the Word of God; Reginald and Gifford in Calvino-Turcismus, book 4, chapter 7; Staphylus in his Apology; Alphonsus Salmeron on 1 Corinthians [vol. 14, pages 255 to 273]; Martin Perez, On Traditions, folios 41b and 44a.

units.la: Nullus ex Catholicis est, qui non existimet, absolutè & simpliciter longè magis è re Christianâ fore, si abstineremus à Versionibus vernaculis: ait Jac. Gretserus in Examine 2. Disputat. Pappicæ, col. 2009.
units.tr: There is no Catholic who does not think, absolutely and simply, that it would be far more to the advantage of the Christian religion if we abstained from vernacular versions: says Jacob Gretser in the Examination of the second Disputation of the Papist, column 2009.

units.la: CAPUT VII. DECRETA ECCLESIASTICA.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. ECCLESIASTICAL DECREES.

units.la: SECT. I. Ex Conciliorum Sententiis.
units.tr: SECT. I. From the Sentences of the Councils.

units.la: Anno 325.
units.tr: Year 325.

units.la: IN Concilio Nicæno sancitum est, Ne quis Christianus sacris Bibliorum voluminibus careret; quemadmodum contra Beddam & Sutorem asserit Erasmus (tom. 9. Operum, pag. 378. 456. 652.) & Cornelius Agrippa de Vanitate Scient. cap. 100.
units.tr: IN the Council of Nicaea it was decreed that no Christian should be without the sacred volumes of the Bible, as Erasmus asserts against Bedda and Sutor (vol. 9 of his Works, pp. 378, 456, 652), and Cornelius Agrippa in De vanitate scientiarum, ch. 100.

units.la: Anno 341.
units.tr: Year 341.

units.la: Concilium Antiochenum, can. 2. (1) Statuitur, ut quicunque non communicantes nec orationem facientes, Scripturas tantum divinas in Ecclesiâ audire voluerint, abjiciantur: a Sicut etiam refert Fulgentius Ferrandus in Canonum Breviario §. 168. Idem ipsum decretum habetur in Capitulis Græcarum Synodorum à Martino Bracarensi Episcopo collectis, can. 83. & in Canone 10. (qui dicuntur) Apostolorum, his verbis: Πάντας τοὺς εισιόντας πρὸς τὴν γεγραμμένων ἀκούοντας, μὴ παεμένοντας τῇ προσευχῇ ἐν τῇ ἀχρὶ μεταλήψει, ὡς ἀταξίας ἐμποιοῦντας τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ἀφορίζεσθαι h. e. (ut ad verbum vertit Dionysius, seu quisquis erat Author versionis illius veteris, quæ in Isidori collectione Conciliorum habetur) Omnes fideles, qui ingrediuntur Ecclesiam, & Scripturas audiunt, non autem perseverant
units.tr: The Council of Antioch, canon 2: (1) It is laid down that whoever, not communicating and not joining in the prayers, wish only to hear the divine Scriptures in the Church, are to be cast out: a As Fulgentius Ferrandus also reports, in his Breviary of Canons §168. The same decree is found in the chapters of the Greek synods collected by Martin, bishop of Braga, canon 83, and in Canon 10 of the so-called Apostles, in these words: [Πάντας τοὺς εισιόντας πρὸς τὴν γεγραμμένων ἀκούοντας, μὴ παεμένοντας τῇ προσευχῇ ἐν τῇ ἀχρὶ μεταλήψει, ὡς ἀταξίας ἐμποιοῦντας τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ἀφορίζεσθαι]; that is (as Dionysius, or whoever was the author of that old version found in Isidore's collection of councils, renders it word for word) All the faithful who enter the Church and hear the Scriptures, but do not persevere

units.la: a Confer. Cæsarium Homil. 5. de divin. myster. & homil. 12. in Biblioth. Patr.
units.tr: a Compare Caesarius, Homily 5 on the divine mysteries, and Homily 12, in the Bibliotheca Patrum.

units.la: (1) Πάντας τοὺς εισιόντας πρὸς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐν τῇ ἱερῶν χαρῶν ἀκούοντας, μὴ κοινωνοῦντας ἀ' ἐοχῆς ἅμα τῷ λαῷ, τύτας ἀποκλήτους γινέσθαι ἐκκλησίας. perseverant in oratione, nec sanctam communionem percipiunt, velut inquietudines Ecclesiae commoventes, convenit communione privari. Gratianus vero hunc Canonem Decreto suo inferens (de Consecrat. dist. 1. cap. Omnes fideles) ita refert: Omnes fideles, qui conveniunt in solennitatibus sacris ad Ecclesiam, & Scripturas Apostolorum & Evangelium audiant. Sed utcunque sit, ex Canonibus istis satis apparet, fideles Laicos (de quibus Canones isti agunt, ut recte notatum est in Cresconii Breviario Canonum §. 12.) prisces illis temporibus Ecclesias veluti Auditoria quaedam frequentasse; uti ex sacris Scripturis publice praelectis Dei voluntatem possent intelligere. b Verum cum illi ad precum & sacrae Coenae communionem insuper admitterentur; etiam Catechumeni & Energumeni, & qui poenitentiam agebant, Psalmodiam & divinam sanctarum Scripturarum lectionem audiebant: ut est apud Dionysium de Ecclesiast. Hierarch. cap. 3. in Θεωρία τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς συνάξεως μυστικῆς, pag. 16. vel 25. edit. Latin. ἐ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπ' αὐτῆς (ait ille pag. 28, 29.) ἵνα τινὲς ἰσχὺ μεταλαβεῖν, ἡ δ' ἀξίως λογίων ὑπηρετικῆς δεῖ τὰ κρείττω διδασκαλίας i. e. Neque enim fas eis est alterius cujuscunque sacrae rei esse participes, quam eloquiorum Dei, quorum magisterio possunt ad meliorem converti frugem. Atque hinc in Vetere Ecclesia fuit illa poenitentium classis, qui in Concilii Nicaeni I. Canone 11. & 14. ἀκροώμενοι, h. e. Audientes c (ut etiam eos Tertullianus in lib. de Poenit. cap. 6. & 7. & Cyprianus lib. 3. epist. 17. & 22. vocant) appellantur: cujus etiam consuetudinis in 12. ejusdem Concilii, itemque 4, 6, & 9. Ancyrani Concilii Canone mentionem factam legimus. Dicebatur enim ἀκροώμενος, cum quis ad Ecclesiae fores stans divinas Scripturas audiebat; ut ad tertiam Orationem Gregorii Nazienzeni adversus Julianum notat Elias Cretensis. Unde Gregorius Neocaesariensis in epistola Canonica de iis qui in Barbarorum incursione peccaverunt, can. 11. (3) Auditionem inquit esse intra portam, in loco, quem νάρθηκα (i.e. ferulam) vocant; ubi oporteat eum qui peccavit, stare post Catechumenos: & ubi Scripturas & Doctrinam audierit, inde egredi; ut qui indignus habeatur, qui precationi interfit.
units.tr: (1) [Πάντας τοὺς εισιόντας πρὸς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐν τῇ ἱερῶν χαρῶν ἀκούοντας, μὴ κοινωνοῦντας ἀ' ἐοχῆς ἅμα τῷ λαῷ, τύτας ἀποκλήτους γινέσθαι ἐκκλησίας]; they persevere in prayer, but do not receive the holy communion, stirring up the disorder of the Church; it is fitting that they be deprived of communion. Gratian, however, inserting this canon in his Decretum (De consecratione, dist. 1, ch. Omnes fideles), gives it thus: All the faithful who gather at the sacred solemnities in the Church should hear the Scriptures of the Apostles and the Gospel. But however that may be, it is sufficiently clear from these canons that the lay faithful (with whom these canons deal, as rightly noted in the Breviarium Canonum of Cresconius, §12) in those early times frequented the churches as a kind of lecture halls, so that they might understand the will of God from the Holy Scriptures read publicly. b But since they were also admitted to prayer and to the communion of the holy Supper, the catechumens and energumens, and those who were doing penance, were also listening to the psalmody and the divine reading of the holy Scriptures, as is found in Dionysius, On Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, ch. 3, in the Theoria of the ecclesiastical mystical assembly, p. 16 or 25 of the Latin edition. He says (pp. 28, 29): [ἐ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπ' αὐτῆς ἵνα τινὲς ἰσχὺ μεταλαβεῖν, ἡ δ' ἀξίως λογίων ὑπηρετικῆς δεῖ τὰ κρείττω διδασκαλίας]; that is, For it is not lawful for them to share in any other holy thing than the oracles of God, by whose teaching they may be turned to better fruit. Hence in the ancient Church there was that class of penitents who, in canons 11 and 14 of the First Council of Nicaea, are called [ἀκροώμενοι], that is, Hearers (as Tertullian, in De paenitentia, chs. 6 and 7, and Cyprian, book 3, letters 17 and 22, also call them). We read of this custom also being mentioned in canon 12 of the same council, and likewise in canons 4, 6 and 9 of the Council of Ancyra. For a person was called [ἀκροώμενος] when he stood at the doors of the church and heard the divine Scriptures; as Elias of Crete notes on the third oration of Gregory Nazianzen against Julian. Hence Gregory of Neocaesarea, in his canonical letter concerning those who sinned during the barbarian invasion, canon 11 (3), says: He says that the hearing is within the door, in the place which they call the narthex (that is, the ferula), where the one who has sinned ought to stand behind the catechumens; and when he has heard the Scriptures and the teaching, he should go out from there, as one considered unworthy to take part in prayer.

units.la: b Vid. Concil. Carthag. IV. can. 84. c Vid. Theoriani colloquium cum Armeno, p. 153.
units.tr: b See the Council of Carthage IV, canon 84. c See the colloquy of Theorianus with the Armenian, p. 153.

units.la: (2) Ubi ἀκροάσεω exponitur ἡ ἀκοὴ τῶν ἀκούων χαρῶν. (3) Ἡ ἀκρόασις ἐστὶν ἡ πύλη ἐν τῷ νάρθηκι, ὅπου ἑστὼς καὶ ἡ ἀμαρτωλὸς ... ἡ ἀκοὴ ... ἐκβαλλέσθω, ᾗ μὴ ἀξιούσθω προσ-ευχῆς.
units.tr: (2) Where ἀκροάσεως is explained as [ἡ ἀκοὴ τῶν ἀκούων χαρῶν]. (3) [Ἡ ἀκρόασις ἐστὶν ἡ πύλη ἐν τῷ νάρθηκι, ὅπου ἑστὼς καὶ ἡ ἀμαρτωλὸς ... ἡ ἀκοὴ ... ἐκβαλλέσθω, ᾗ μὴ ἀξιούσθω προσ-ευχῆς.]

units.la: Anno 381.
units.tr: Year 381.

units.la: In Canone 7. Concilii Constantinopolitani I. ubi de iis qui in Ecclesiam recipiendi sunt, agitur, ista legimus: (4) Atque ibi catechizamus sive instituimus, & erudimus eos, damusque operam ut longiore tempore maneant ac versentur in Ecclesiâ, diligenterque & attentè audiant Scripturas: tunc tandem eos baptizamus. [Ex Synodicarum Constitutionum libello, Tom. 1. Concil. edit. Colon. 1551. pag. 552. Laur. Sifano interprete.]
units.tr: In canon 7 of the First Council of Constantinople, where it is treated of those who are to be received into the Church, we read the following: (4) And there we catechize, or instruct and train them, and we take care that they remain and dwell in the Church for a longer time, and that they listen diligently and attentively to the Scriptures; only then do we baptize them. [From the little book of Synodical Constitutions, vol. 1 of the Cologne edition of the Councils, 1551, p. 552, translated by Laurentius Surius.]

units.la: Anno 393.
units.tr: In the year 393.

units.la: In Concilio Hipponensi de Lectoribus statutum est, cap. 20. Ut usque ad annos pubertatis legant; ut verò ante 25 annos non ordinentur Clerici, nisi primùm divinis Scripturis instructi, vel ab infantiâ eruditi, propter fidei professionem vel assertionem. cap. 2. tom. 1. Concil. edit. Venet. an. 1551. p. 434.
units.tr: In the Council of Hippo it was decreed concerning Readers, canon 20: "That they read until the years of puberty; but that clerics are not to be ordained before the age of 25, unless first instructed in the divine Scriptures, or educated from infancy, for the sake of their profession or defence of the faith." Canon 2, vol. 1 of the Council, Venice edition, 1551, p. 434.

units.la: Anno 398.
units.tr: In the year 398.

units.la: In Concilio Carthaginensi 4. cap. 84. Statutum est, ut Episcopus nullum prohibeat ingredi Ecclesiam, & audire verbum Dei, sive Gentilem, sive Haereticum, sive Judaeum, usque ad missam Catechumenorum.
units.tr: In the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 84: "It is decreed that a bishop shall not forbid anyone to enter the Church and hear the word of God, whether a Gentile, a heretic, or a Jew, up to the Mass of the Catechumens."

units.la: Anno 507.
units.tr: In the year 507.

units.la: In Valentino Hispaniae Concilio (5) congregati Patres: Antiquos (inquiunt cap. 1.) Canones relegentes, inter cetera hoc esse censuimus observandum: ut sacrosancta Evangelia ante munerum illationem in Missâ Catechumenorum, in ordine lectionum post Apostolum legantur; quatenus salutaria praecepta Domini nostri Jesu Christi, vel sermones sacerdotis, non solum fideles, sed etiam Catechumeni ac Poenitentes, & omnes qui è diverso sunt, audire licitum habeant. Sic enim Pontificum praedicatione audità nonnullos attractos ad fidem evidenter scimus. [tom.2. Concil. edit. Nicolini, pag. 538.]
units.tr: The Fathers assembled at the Council of Valencia in Spain, reviewing the ancient canons, said (canon 1): "We have judged that the following among other things should be observed: that the most holy Gospels be read, in the order of the lessons after the Apostle, in the Mass of the Catechumens, before the offering of the gifts; so that the saving precepts of our Lord Jesus Christ, or the sermons of the priest, may be heard lawfully not only by the faithful, but also by catechumens, penitents, and all who are outside. For we know clearly that, by hearing the preaching of the bishops, some have been drawn to the faith." Vol. 2 of the Council, Nicolini edition, p. 538.

units.la: In (6) Actione 1. Synodi Constantinopolitanæ sub Mennâ celebratæ contra Anthimum ita legimus: (7) Magnâ autem horâ ex utraque parte consistentibus, & psallentibus hanc Psalmodiam Cantores supervenientes converterunt se dicere Trisagium. Et cùm ipsi incepissent, totus populus quievit, & audiebat astantis auribus Trisagium. Et post lectionem sancti Evangelii ex more sacrâ Missâ finitâ (Catechumenorum sc. sic Baronius) & januis clausis, ac sanctâ lectione juxta consuetudinem lectâ, tempore diptychorum cucurrit omnis multitudo cum magno silentio circum circa altare, & audiebant. (tom. 2. Concil. edit. Nicolin. p. 601.)
units.tr: In the first Action of the Constantinopolitan Synod held under Menas against Anthimus we read as follows: "While both sides stood for a long time and sang this psalmody, the cantors who came up began to say the Trisagion. And when they had begun, the whole people became quiet and listened to the Trisagion standing by. And after the reading of the holy Gospel, the sacred Mass of the Catechumens (so Baronius) being finished, and the doors closed, and the holy lesson read according to custom, at the time of the diptychs the whole crowd ran with great silence around the altar, and they listened." Vol. 2 of the Council, Nicolini edition, p. 601.

units.la: Concilium Toletanum 4. can. 24. Ignorantia mater cunctorum errorum maximè in sacerdotibus Dei vitanda est, qui dicendi officium in populis susceperant. Sacerdotes enim legere sanctas Scripturas frequenter admonet Paulus, &c. [Quam sententiam etiam retulit Burchardus in Decret. lib. 1. cap. 100. Ivo par. 5. cap. 202. & Gratianus in Decret. par. 1. Distinct. 38. §. Ignorantia mater.] Hîc observa. 1. Ignorantiam matrem esse cunctorum errorum. 2. Corrigendam esse sacrarum Scripturarum lectione. 3. Vitandam etiam esse à laicis, licèt maximè à sacerdotibus. Contra verò Pontificii crassam illam in vulgo ignorantiam, implicitæ fidei nomine defendunt, eamque ut pietatis & devotionis matrem commendant; populumque à Scripturarum in linguâ vernaculâ lectione, veluti errorum atque hæresium parente, homines impii abigunt.
units.tr: Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 24: "Ignorance, the mother of all errors, is to be avoided above all in the priests of God, who have taken up the office of teaching the people. For Paul often admonishes priests to read the holy Scriptures," etc. [This sentence is also cited by Burchard, Decretum, book 1, chapter 100; Ivo, part 5, chapter 202; and Gratian, Decretum, part 1, distinction 38, §. "Ignorantia mater."] Observe here: (1) ignorance is the mother of all errors; (2) it is to be corrected by the reading of the holy Scriptures; (3) it is to be avoided also by the laity, though especially by the priests. The Papists, on the other hand, defend that gross ignorance among the common people under the name of implicit faith, and commend it as the mother of piety and devotion; and they drive people away from reading the Scriptures in the vernacular, as though it were the parent of errors and heresies, wicked men that they are.

units.la: Θείας λειτουργίας ἐπιπλεούσης, ἡ δὲ Συρῶν κλεισθεισῶν, ἡ τὰ ἁγία μυστήρια ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ λεχθῆναι, τοῦ χαροῦ δὲ ἀπὸ ἠχούντων μὴ πολλῆς ἡσυχίας συνέσχεμον ἀπὸ τὸ πάνδος ᾠκλο τῷ συναχθείς, ἡ ἠκοῦντο. Tunc vox magna omnes de populo tanquam uno ore clamarunt: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel; quia visitavit, &c. Ad multas autem horas illis ex utraque parte cantantibus, &c. Sic habet antiqua versio, Graeco magis consona, in edit. G. L. Paris. 1618.
units.tr: [Θείας λειτουργίας ἐπιπλεούσης, ἡ δὲ Συρῶν κλεισθεισῶν, ἡ τὰ ἁγία μυστήρια ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ λεχθῆναι, τοῦ χαροῦ δὲ ἀπὸ ἠχούντων μὴ πολλῆς ἡσυχίας συνέσχεμον ἀπὸ τὸ πάνδος ᾠκλο τῷ συναχθείς, ἡ ἠκοῦντο.] Then a great voice, all the people as with one mouth cried out: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; because he has visited," etc. For many hours, while they sang from both sides, and so on. This is how the old version reads, more in agreement with the Greek, in the Greek-Latin Paris edition of 1618.

units.la: Synodus Constantinopolitana in Trullo (quæ Quinisexta seu Πενθέκτη dicitur) Canone 66. ita statuit: (8) A sancta Christi Dei nostri resurrectionis die usque ad novum Dominicum tota Septimana in Ecclesiis vacare fideles jugiter oportet psalmis & hymnis & spiritualibus Canticis, in Christo gaudentes, festumque celebrantes, & divinarum Scripturarum lectioni mentem adhibentes, & sanctis mysteriis jucundè & lautè fruentes. Sic enim cum Christo exaltabimur, & una resurgemus, (tom. 3. Concil. p. 403.). Ibid. Can. 75. (9) Eos qui in Ecclesiis ad psallendum accedunt, volumus nec inordinatis vociferationibus uti, & naturam ad clamorem urgere; nec aliquid eorum, quæ Ecclesia non conveniunt & apta non sunt, adscisçere; sed cum magna attentione & compunctione psalmodias Deo, qui est occultorum inspector, offerre. [Refertur iste Canon à Photio in Nomocanonem, tit. 3. cap. 2.]
units.tr: The Synod of Constantinople in Trullo (called the Quinisext, or [Πενθέκτη]) decreed in canon 66: "From the holy day of the resurrection of Christ our God until the next Sunday, the faithful must continually stay in the churches for the whole week, occupied with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, rejoicing in Christ and celebrating the feast, applying their minds to the reading of the divine Scriptures, and enjoying the holy mysteries with delight and abundance. For thus we shall be exalted with Christ and rise together with him." Vol. 3 of the Council, p. 403. Also canon 75: "We wish that those who come into the churches to sing psalms should not use disorderly shouting, nor urge nature to clamour, nor adopt anything that does not befit the Church and is not fitting; but that they offer psalmody to God, who is the inspector of hidden things, with great attention and compunction." This canon is cited by Photius in the Nomocanon, title 3, chapter 2.

units.la: In Anglicana Synodo, quæ anno 33. Æthelbaldi Regis Merciorum coacta est (ut refert Wilhelmus Malmesburiensis, lib. 1. de gestis Pontif. Angl. p. 112. editionis Savilianæ) decretum est ;d Ut per monasteria lectio sacrarum scripturarum frequentetur. Et ut Presbyteri Dominicam Orationem & Symbolum Anglicè discant & doceant. At hodie (ut conquestus est Trithemius, lib. 2. epist. 1. ad Jacobum fratrem suum) studium Scripturarum à multis claustralibus omnium pene Regularium contemnitur, & in paucis vigere monasteriis videtur. Immò & Regularibus interdictum est (in Indice librorum prohibit. edit. à Pio IV. Reg. 4.) ne Biblia vel à Catholicis authoribus versa legant, nisi facultatem à Prælatis suis habuerint. Quàm verò religiosè alterum illud præceptum de Oratione Dominicâ & Symbolo Anglicè docendis
units.tr: In the English synod that was held in the 33rd year of Æthelbald, king of the Mercians (as William of Malmesbury reports, book 1, On the Deeds of the Bishops of England, p. 112 of the Savile edition), it was decreed: That the reading of the holy Scriptures be made frequent throughout the monasteries. And that presbyters should learn and teach the Lord's Prayer and the Creed in English. But today (as Trithemius complains, book 2, letter 1, to his brother James) the study of the Scriptures is despised by many of the cloistered men of almost all the religious orders, and seems to flourish in few monasteries. Indeed, the regular clergy have been forbidden (in the Index of prohibited books published under Pius IV, rule 4) to read the Bibles, even those translated by Catholic authors, unless they have permission from their prelates. How scrupulously that other precept, about teaching the Lord's Prayer and the Creed in English, was observed by the English presbyters,

units.la: (9) Τὰς ὅτι τῶν ψαλμῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀναγινώσκειν, &c. ἀλλὰ μὴ πολλῆς φωνῆς ... (Greek note, illegible in part) docendis servaverint Presbyteri Anglicani, vel illud Richardi FitzJames Londinensis Episcopi factum ostendit ; qui Joannem Coletum (nisi Gulielmus Warhamus Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis opem ei tulisset) eo nomine hæreseos reum peregisset, quòd Orationem Dominicam in linguam Anglicanam transtulisset: (quemadmodum refert contra Tho. Morum, Gulielmus Tindallus c) nec non Coventriensis Episcopi (qui eo tempore, anno sc. 1519. erat Galfridus Blitheus) qui è dioecesi suâ sex viros unà cum viduâ igni adjudicavit; quòd liberos & domesticos suos Orationem Dominicam, Symbolum Apostolicum, & Decalogum linguâ Anglicanâ docuissent: quemadmodum ex testimonio eorum, qui tum præsentes adsuerant, refert Jo. Foxus: f Quâ de re vid. Sutlivium in responsione ad postremam partem libri R. Personii de 3. conclusionibus, p. 62, 63. Similiter Norvicensis Episcopus anno 1507. apud Balæum (qui tunc aderat) præfat. in tract. Joh. Lamberti de Sacramento altaris: Pari modo anno 1521. coram Jo. Longlando Lincolniensi Episcopo Joannes Mordenus & uxor ejus à Jacobo Mordeno nepote accusati sunt, quòd domi suæ, eo præsente, Decalogum Anglicè recitassent (Fox, p. 752. ex Registro Longlandi Lincoln. sol. 15.) Alicia Atkins ab eodem Jacobo Mordeno accusata, quòd ab ipsâ Orationem Dominicam, Salutationem Angelicam, & Symbolum Apostolicum linguâ vernacula didicisset g Jacobum verò illum propria soror juramento accusare coaëta est; quòd eam Orationem Dominicam, Symbolum, & Salutationem Angelicam Anglicè docuisset. h Sed & Wilhelmus Littlepage juramento coaëtus accusavit Thurstanum Littlepage; à quo Orationem Dominicam & Salutationem Angelicam; & Joannem Frier, à quo Decalogum linguâ vernaculâ didicisset (Symbolum enim ab aviâ didicerat) atque etiam fratrem suum Jo. Littlepage, quòd ab Aliciâ uxore Thurstani Littlepage Decalogum Anglicè didicisset. (Ibid. apud Fox, p. 755. quem etiam vide p. 610. 713. & supra in anno 1485.) Atque hæc fuit miseranda illa servitus, quâ à Clero Papistico populus Anglicanus detentus est: priusquam ab Henrico VIII. (abdicatâ Romani Pontificis tyrannide) anno 1536. Regiâ auctoritate injunctum est: ut omnes ab infantiâ Orationem Dominicam, Articulos fidei, & Decalogum linguâ maternâ ediscerent. Sed & quingentis ante Henricum annis Canutus i rerum summam in Angliâ
units.tr: (9) [Τὰς ὅτι τῶν ψαλμῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀναγινώσκειν, &c. ἀλλὰ μὴ πολλῆς φωνῆς ...] That the psalms are read in the church, etc., but not with loud voice ... (the rest of the Greek is illegible in part) is shown by the deed of Richard FitzJames, bishop of London, who would have prosecuted John Colet for heresy on this account, because he had translated the Lord's Prayer into English, had not William Warham, archbishop of Canterbury, come to his aid (as William Tyndale reports in his work against Thomas More, book 3, chapter 15); and likewise by that of the bishop of Coventry and Lichfield (who at that time, in 1519, was Geoffrey Blythe), who condemned six men, together with a widow, to the fire from his diocese, because they had taught their children and household the Lord's Prayer, the Apostles' Creed, and the Decalogue in English, as John Foxe reports from the testimony of those who were present at the time. On this matter see Sutcliffe in his reply to the last part of Robert Persons' book on the three conclusions, pp. 62, 63. Similarly, in 1507 the bishop of Norwich (as Bale, who was present, reports in the preface to John Lambert's treatise on the sacrament of the altar); in the same way, in 1521, before John Longland, bishop of Lincoln, John Morden and his wife were accused by their nephew James Morden, because they had recited the Decalogue in English in their home in his presence (Foxe, p. 752, from the register of Longland of Lincoln, fol. 15). Alice Atkins, accused by the same James Morden, because she had learned from him the Lord's Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, and the Apostles' Creed in the vernacular. Indeed James himself was compelled by oath to accuse his own sister, because she had taught him the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, and the Angelic Salutation in English. Also William Littlepage, compelled by oath, accused Thurstan Littlepage, from whom he had learned the Lord's Prayer and the Angelic Salutation, and John Frier, from whom he had learned the Decalogue in the vernacular (for he had learned the Creed from his grandmother), and even his brother John Littlepage, because he had learned the Decalogue in English from Alice, the wife of Thurstan Littlepage (ibid., in Foxe, p. 755, which see also at pp. 610, 713, and above under the year 1485). Such was that wretched servitude in which the English people were held by the Papist clergy, before, in 1536, by royal authority (the tyranny of the Roman Pontiff having been abjured), Henry VIII ordered that everyone from infancy should learn the Lord's Prayer, the articles of faith, and the Decalogue in their mother tongue. But also five hundred years before Henry, Canute, holding the supreme power in England,

Lambardo edita. obtinens lege latâ cavit, ut unusquisque Christianus operam daret, ut Orationem saltem Dominicam & Articulos fidei intelligeret: quandoquidem per primum illud Deum invocent Christiani, per alterum rectam fidem profiteantur. Sed & Carolus Magnus in constitutionibus factis anno regni sui undecimo ex Concilii consensu statuit, ut Episcopi diligenter discutiant per suas Parochias. Anno 779. Presbyterorum fidem, &c. ut Missarum preces bene intelligant, & ut Psalmi digne secundum divisiones versuum modulentur; & Dominicam Orationem ipsi intelligant, & omnibus praedicent intelligendam, ut unusquisque sciat quid petat à Deo: & ut Gloria Patri, cum omni honore apud omnes cantetur; & ipse sacerdos cum sanctis Angelis & populo Dei communi voce Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, decantet [pag. 251. editionis quae prodiit Moguntiae anno 1602. cum Epistolis Hincmari: Habetur etiam in Legum ab Ansegiso collectarum libro 1. capitulo 70.]

Also Charles the Great, in the constitutions made in the eleventh year of his reign with the consent of the Council, decreed that the bishops should carefully examine through their parishes the faith of the presbyters, etc. In 779: that they understand well the prayers of the Masses, and that the Psalms be sung properly according to the divisions of the verses; and that they themselves understand the Lord's Prayer, and preach to all that it is to be understood, so that each may know what he asks of God; and that the Gloria Patri be sung with all honour by all; and that the priest himself, with the holy Angels and the people of God, sing in a common voice Holy, Holy, Holy. Quoniam dum Psalmos canimus, Deo in haec verba promittimus, In Justificationibus tuis meditabor, non oblivisear eloquiorum tuorum: Omnes quidem Christianos hoc servare salutare esset, eos autem praecipuè qui sacerdotalem dignitatem obtinent (ut sc. (10) in omni divina Scriptura versentur, & populum doceant, quemadmodum paulò post sequitur.)
units.tr: [Greek text of canon 2, illegible.] For while we sing the Psalms, we promise God in these words: "I will meditate on your statutes; I will not forget your words." It would be good for all Christians to observe this, but especially for those who hold the priestly dignity (namely, that they should be occupied with all divine Scripture and teach the people), as follows a little later.

units.la: Rhemensis Synodi (Caroli M. jussu anno 813. habitae) capitulum 1. est de fidei ratione; ut unusquisque juxta intellectum suae capacitatis Domino largiente discerec & intelligeret, atque operibus pleniter observaret. 2. Ut Orationem, quam Dominus noster Jesus Christus discipulos suos orare docuit, verbis discerent, & sensum bene intelligerent:
units.tr: The Synod of Reims (held by order of Charlemagne in 813), chapter 1, concerns the grounds of faith: that each person, according to the understanding of his capacity, with the Lord granting it, should learn and understand, and fully observe it in his works. 2. That they should learn the Prayer which our Lord Jesus Christ taught his disciples to pray, in its words, and understand its meaning well.

(10) [Greek note, illegible, ~20 letters] quia illam ignorare nulli Christiano licet. Sic libro 5. Legum Franc. à Benedicto Levitâ collect. capitulo 103. statutum est, ut omnes qui Christiano nomine censentur, Orationem Dominicam & Symbolum memoriter teneant & intelligant. Et libro 6. cap. 163. ut fideles Orationem Dominicam discant & intelligant, & suis sacerdotibus eam verbo ex verbo reddant, & aliis fidelibus, qui eam nesciant, doceant. Et in Capitulo 7. eorum (11) quæ falsò tribuuntur Synodo VI. Constantinopolitanæ (& in Anselmi Lucensis Collectione Decretorum habentur, ut annotatum est à Romanis correctoribus ad Gratiani Decretum dist. 16. cap. 10.) Commonendi sunt fideles omnes à minimo usque ad maximum, ut Orationem Dominicam & Symbolum discant; & dicendum est eis, quòd his duabus sententiis omne fidei Christianæ fundamentum incumbit. Et nisi quis has duas sententias & memoriter tenuerit & ex toto corde crediderit, & in oratione sapissimè frequentaverit, Catholicus esse non poterit, (tom. 3. Concil. edit. Nicolin. p. 388.) Capitulum istud est (12) cap. 23. Epistolæ Theodulphi Aurelianensis Episcopi. Et in Germaniâ quidem ad nostra usque tempora Orationem Dominicam, Angelicam Salutationem, Apostolorum Symbolum, & Decalogi præcepta sic in linguâ vernaculâ fuisse retenta, ut in animos hominum unà cum materno lacte instillarentur, ex capite 25. Synodi Dioecesanæ Augustensis (anno 1548. celebratæ) colligitur, ubi etiam plebanis Ecclesiarum parochialium præcipitur, ut singulis diebus Dominicis, finità concione, omnia vernaculo sermone distinctè ac tractatim ita prælegant; ut populus legentem repetitione subsequi, ea discere, & memoriæ mandare possit (tom. 5. Concil. p. 308.) Cum Gallis verò haud multò melius actum esse quàm cum Anglis, vel illud Cabilonensis Episcopi factum ostendit (à Crispino m commemoratum) qui Merindolii pueris grandiusculis simul & parvulis ad se vocari jussis, pecuniam singulis largitus, blandè præcepit, ut Orationem Dominicam cum Symbolo Apostolorum Latino idiomate ediscerent. Plerisque autem eorum excipientibus se Latinè quidem nôsse Pater Noster & Credo, non posse tamen reddere rationem eorum quæ recitarent, nisi suo, i.e. Gallico idiomate; respondit egregius Episcopus, non requiri tantam in ipsis scientiam, satis esse
units.tr: (10) [Greek note, illegible] because no Christian is permitted to be ignorant of it. So in book 5 of the Frankish laws collected by Benedict the Levite, chapter 103, it has been enacted that all who are counted by the Christian name should hold the Lord's Prayer and the Creed by heart and understand them. And in book 6, chapter 163, that the faithful should learn the Lord's Prayer and understand it, and should recite it word for word to their priests, and teach it to other faithful who do not know it. And in chapter 7 of those (11) things which are falsely attributed to the Sixth Council of Constantinople (and are found in Anselm of Lucca's collection of decrees, as the Roman correctors noted on Gratian's Decretum, dist. 16, chap. 10): All the faithful, from the least to the greatest, are to be reminded to learn the Lord's Prayer and the Creed; and they must be told that the whole foundation of the Christian faith rests on these two sayings. Unless someone has both held these two sayings by memory and believed them with his whole heart, and has frequently practised them in prayer, he cannot be a Catholic. (vol. 3 of the Councils, Nicolini edition, p. 388.) This chapter is (12) chapter 23 of the letter of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans. And in Germany, indeed, down to our own times, the Lord's Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, the Apostles' Creed and the precepts of the Decalogue have been retained in the vernacular in such a way that they were instilled into people's minds along with their mother's milk. This is gathered from chapter 25 of the diocesan synod of Augsburg (celebrated in 1548), where the parish priests of the parochial churches are also commanded that on every Lord's Day, when the sermon is finished, they should read out everything in the vernacular distinctly and piece by piece, so that the people, repeating after the reader, may be able to learn these things and commit them to memory (vol. 5 of the Councils, p. 308.) As for the French, that they fared not much better than the English is shown by that deed of the bishop of Chalon (recorded by Crispin), who, having had the boys of Mérindol, both somewhat older and younger, called to him and given each of them money, kindly ordered them to learn the Lord's Prayer with the Apostles' Creed in Latin. units.la: Aquisgranense Concilium ( Ludovici I. Imp. jussu habitum ) capite 3. Lectoris Officium proponens ex Isidoro de Ecclesiast. Officiis lib. 2. cap. 11. Sic expeditus (inquit) vim pronuntiationis tenebit ; ut ad intellectum omnium mentes sensusque promoveat, discernendo genera pronuntiationis, atque exprimendo omnium sententiarum proprios effectus. Et post. Auribus & cordi consulere debet Lector, non oculis : ne potius ex seipso eos spectatores magis quàm auditores faciat. Et cap. 132. Psallentium in Ecclesia Domino mens concordare debet cum voce ; ut impleatur illud Apostoli, Psallam spiritu, Psallam & mente. Et cap. 133. Tales ad legendum, cantandum & psallendum in Ecclesia constituantur, qui non superbè sed humiliter debitas Domino laudes persolvant ; & suavitate lectionis ac melodia & doctos demulceant & minùs doctos erudiant, plúsque velint in lectione vel cantu populi ædificationem, quàm popularem vanissimam adulationem. Qui vero hæc docte peragere nequeunt, erudiantur prius à Magistris, & instructi hæc adimplere studeant, ut audientes ædificent. Hinc probabiliter colligitur sacra hoc tempore ita esse peracta, ut à populo aliquo modo intelligi possent : cum quibus conferantur leges illæ (Caroli M. ut videtur) à Benedicto Levitâ collectæ, libro 6. Capitularium : quarum una, cap. 173. ita habet. Placuit ut fideles silentium in Ecclesiâ teneant, & devotè verbum Dei audiant. Altera, cap. 192. Admoneant Presbyteri plebem, ut in Ecclesiâ verbositate non præsumant ; sed cum fletu & cum compunctione cordis Dei implorent auxilium tam pro se, quàm & pro proximis suis. Et quando Presbyter celebrat Missam, corda illorum semper ad cœlestia attendant. Et quando sancta lectiones vel Evangelia recitata fuerint, cum silentio & devotâ mente pariter audiant, sicut Deus dixit per Moysen, Audi Israel & tace. Et cap. 43. Concilii Moguntiaci anno 813. Caroli M. jussu celebrati, quod ita habet : Nullus Presbyter, ut nobis videtur, solus Missam cantare valet rectè. Quomodo enim
units.tr: The Council of Aachen (held by order of the Emperor Louis I), in chapter 3, setting out the office of the reader, drawing on Isidore, On the Ecclesiastical Offices, book 2, chapter 11. Thus equipped, he says, the reader shall hold the force of pronunciation, so as to advance the minds and understanding of all towards comprehension, by distinguishing the kinds of pronunciation and by expressing the proper effects of all sentences. And afterwards: The reader ought to consult the ears and the heart, not the eyes, lest he make them spectators rather than hearers by himself. And chapter 132: In the church the mind ought to agree with the voice when psalms are sung to the Lord, so that that saying of the Apostle may be fulfilled: I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind. And chapter 133: Let such persons be appointed to read, sing and chant in the church, as will render due praises to the Lord not proudly but humbly; and who by the sweetness of reading and melody may both delight the learned and instruct the less learned, and who would rather seek in the reading or singing the edification of the people than the most vain popular flattery. Those who cannot perform these things skilfully should first be taught by masters, and, being instructed, should strive to fulfil them, so that they may edify those who hear. From this it is probably gathered that the sacred offices were at this time performed in such a way that they could be understood by the people in some measure. With these may be compared those laws (of Charlemagne, as it seems) collected by Benedict the Levite, in book 6 of the Capitularies, one of which, chapter 173, reads thus: It is agreed that the faithful keep silence in the church and hear the word of God devoutly. Another, chapter 192: Let the presbyters admonish the people not to presume to wordiness in the church, but with weeping and compunction of heart to implore God's help both for themselves and for their neighbours. And when the presbyter celebrates Mass, let them always attend with their hearts to heavenly things. And when the holy lessons or Gospels have been read, let them listen with silence and a devout mind, just as God said through Moses: Hear, Israel, and be silent. And chapter 43 of the Council of Mainz, celebrated in 813 by order of Charlemagne, which reads thus: No presbyter, as it seems to us, can rightly sing Mass alone. For how

(Habetur etiam in Legibus à Benedicto Levitâ collectis, lib. 5. capit. 93.) Si populus sacerdotem non intellexisset, perinde esset, utrum solus haec verba pronuntiâsset sacerdos, an praesente populo. Ideo enim sacerdos ante orationem praefatione praemissâ parat fratrum mentes dicendo [sursum corda] ut dum respondet plebs [Habemus ad Dominum] admoneatur nihil se aliud quam Dominum cogitare debere, ut est in Decreto de Consecrat. units.tr: ¹ 1 Cor. XIV. will he say "The Lord be with you" or admonish them to have "Lift up your hearts," and many other things like these, when no one else is with him? (It is also found in the laws collected by Benedict the Levite, book 5, chapter 93.) If the people did not understand the priest, it would make no difference whether the priest pronounced these words alone or with the people present. For this reason the priest, before the prayer, sets the minds of the brothers in order by a preface, saying [Lift up your hearts], so that when the people answer [We have them unto the Lord], they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing but the Lord, as is found in the Decretum, De Consecratione, dist. 1, chap. Quando autem. [From Cyprian, On the Lord's Prayer, concerning which see above under the year 250.]

units.la: Concilium Lateranense sub Innocentio III. cap. 9. ita statuit: Quoniam in plerisque partibus infra eandem civitatem atque diaecesin permixti sunt (13) populi diversarum linguarum, habentes sub unâ fide varios ritus & mores: districtè praecipimus, ut Pontifices hujusmodi civitatum sive (14) diaecesium provideant viros idoneos, qui secundùm diversitates ritVum & linguarum divina illis officia celebrent, & ecclesiastica sacramenta ministrent, instruendo eos verbo pariter & exemplo. [Translatum est etiam hoc Decretum à Gregorio IX. in primum librum Decretal. tit. 31. de offic. judicis ordinarii, cap. 14. Quoniam plerisque].
units.tr: The Lateran Council under Innocent III, canon 9, decreed thus: Since in many regions, within the same city and diocese, peoples of diverse languages are intermingled, having under one faith various rites and customs, we strictly command that the bishops of such cities or dioceses provide suitable men who may celebrate the divine offices for them according to the diversities of rites and languages, and administer the ecclesiastical sacraments to them, instructing them by word as well as by example. [This decree was also taken over by Gregory IX into the first book of the Decretals, title 31, on the office of the ordinary judge, chapter 14, Quoniam plerisque.]

units.la: IN Authenticis Collat. 9. tit. 20. Novell. Constitut. 137. Justiniani Imp. Sanctio (Antonio Contio interprete) in hæc verba habetur. Jubemus omnes Episcopos & Presbyteros (15) non in secreto, sed cum eâ voce, quæ à fidelissimo populo exaudiatur, divinam oblationem & precationem, quæ fit in sancto baptismate, facere; ut inde audientium animi in majorem devotionem, & Dei laudationem & benedictionem efferantur. Sic enim & divinus Apostolus docet, dicens in priore ad Corinthios Epistolâ: Cæterùm (inquit °) si solùm benedicis spiritu; is qui idiotæ locum implet, quomodo tuæ gratiarum actioni subjiciet Deo sanctum illud Amen: Siquidem quid dicas non novit: tu autem pulchrè gratias agis, sed alius non ædificatur. Et rursus in eâ quæ est ad Romanos, sic dicit ᵖ Corde quidem creditur ad justitiam; ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. (16) Idcirco igitur convenit, ut ea precatio, quæ in sanctâ allatione dicitur; & alia orationes cum voce à sanctissimis Episcopis & Presbyteris proferantur Domino nostro Jesu Christo Deo nostro cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto: sciturisreligiosissimis sacerdotibus, quod si quid horum contempserint, & horrendo Dei & Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi judicio rationem reddituri sunt, & nos ista cognoscentes non relinquemus quieta & inulta. ᵃ [Hactenus Justinianus, p. 346. editionis Dionysii Gothofredi, quæ prodiit Lugduni, an. 1585. Est in Novellis Constitutio 123. A Photio in Nomocanone, tit. 3. cap. 1. Et à Balsamone ejus scholiaste citatur nomine 17. Constitutionis primi tituli Novellarum.] Vid. Fox. p. 1922.
units.tr: In the Authenticae, Collatio 9, tit. 20, Novella Constitutio 137 of the Emperor Justinian (in the translation of Antonius Contius), the sanction is found in these words: We command all bishops and presbyters to perform the divine oblation and the prayer which is made at holy baptism not in secret, but with such a voice as can be heard by the most faithful people, so that the minds of the hearers may be raised to greater devotion and to the praise and blessing of God. For the divine Apostle also teaches this, saying in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: "Otherwise, if you bless only in the Spirit, how will he who fills the place of the layman say the holy 'Amen' at your thanksgiving to God, since he does not know what you are saying? For you give thanks well, but the other is not edified." And again in the Epistle to the Romans he says: "With the heart man believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Therefore it is fitting that the prayer which is said at the holy oblation, and the other prayers, be pronounced aloud by the most holy bishops and presbyters to our Lord Jesus Christ, our God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit; the most religious priests should know that if they despise any of these things, they will render an account at the dreadful judgement of God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and we, knowing these things, will not leave them quiet and unpunished. [Thus far Justinian, p. 346 of the edition of Dionysius Gothofredus, published at Lyons in 1585. It is Novella Constitutio 123. It is cited by Photius in the Nomocanon, tit. 3, cap. 1, and by his scholiast Balsamon as the 17th Constitution of the first title of the Novellae.] See Fox, p. 1922.

Statuit igitur Imperator, ut in Synagogis illorum sacri libri (17) in omni linguâ, quam locus accommodatiorem & magis familiarem redderet, auditoribus legerentur; quo magis per ipsorum lectionem intelligentibus tota dictorum series ordine manifesta sit, secundumque ea & vitam & studia sua instituant. Qui verò hoc prohibuerint, castigari jubet corporalibus poenis & facultatum privatione; (18) ut vel inviti (inquit) consentiant nobis, meliora & Deo amabiliora (seu magis accepta) volentibus ac jubentibus. Monet insuper eos (19) qui aut per istam aut per illam linguam (i.e. vel Hebraicam vel maternam) sacros libros audiunt, non solùm considerare literas, sed rebus refici, & divinum veraciter intellectum accipere; quo magis & quod praestantius est addiscant, & aliquando decipi, atque ab eo, quod omnium praestantissimum est (vel opportunissimum, καιρότατον) nempe in Deum fiduciâ, aberrare desinant: (20) Propterea enim (inquit) omnem ipsis linguam ad sacrorum librorum lectionem aperuimus; ut omnes de caetero eorum scientiam amplectentes, ad meliora perdiscenda reddantur aptiores, cùm in confesso sit multò paratiorem ad meliora discernenda & capessenda esse eum, qui sacrorum librorum lectione innutritus, non longè à correctione, & ut ad bonam frugem perducatur, dissidet: quàm qui nihil horum intelligit, sed ex solo religionis nomine dependet, eique tanquam sacra adharet anchora, &
units.tr: Ibid., tit. 28, Novella Constitutio 146: Justinian wishes the holy books to be read in any language whatever, rebuking the cunning of the Jews, who, so that they might more easily deceive those ignorant of the Hebrew language, admitted no language but Hebrew (as Jacobus Cujacius observes in his commentary on this Constitution). From this it came about that their teachers, to the great loss of the simpler people whom they wished to, poured out their errors upon them (as Baronius himself acknowledges, year 552, §1). The Emperor therefore ordains that in their synagogues the holy books be read to the hearers in every language which the place makes more suitable and more familiar, so that by their reading the whole sequence of the said matters may be made plain in order to those who understand, and that they may shape their life and their studies accordingly. Those who forbid this he orders to be punished with bodily penalties and the loss of property, so that they may agree with us (he says) even against their will, we who wish and command better things, more acceptable and more pleasing to God. He further warns those who hear the holy books either in this language or in that (that is, either in Hebrew or in their mother tongue), not only to look at the letters, but to be refreshed by the things, and to receive the divine meaning truly; so that they may learn more, and what is more excellent, and may at last cease to be deceived and to go astray from that which is the most excellent of all (or the most opportune, καιρότατον), namely trust in God: For this reason (he says) we have opened to them every language for the reading of the holy books, so that all of them, embracing this knowledge from now on, may be made more fit to learn better things, since it is agreed that he is much more ready to discern and to grasp better things who, nourished by the reading of the holy books, is not far from correction and does not dissent from being brought to good fruit, than he who understands none of these things, but depends only on the name of religion, and clings to it as to a sacred anchor, and

Καὶ πρὸς, ἀλλὰ ἐν ἰλλυρίδων φωνῆς, ἢ ἢ ἢ πάσῃ τύχῃ (τ' Ἰταλίας ταύτης φωνῇ) ἢ ἢ ἢ ἄλλων ἁπλῶς, τῆς τόποις τυμπεταβαλλομένης ἡ γλώσσης, ἢ ἡ δὲ αὐτῶν ἀναβιώσεως, ἵ' ᾧ ἐπὶ τὰ ἀσφάλεια τῆς συνιέναι ἅπαντα ἱερὰς.] I command that every language whatever be used, so that the place may make it simpler or more understandable to the hearers; and in the language of the Illyrians, or of any other people in the places where the language is changed, for the sake of their life, so that all the holy things may be understood with certainty.

units.la: (20) Διὰ τοῦτο ἢ δὲ ἡ πᾶσαν αὐτοῖς φωνὴν ἀνοίξαμεν πρὸς τὸ τῆς ἱερῶν βίβλων ἀνάγνωσιν, ὥστε πάντας ἐρεξῆς ἡ αὐτῶν λαμ- πρότερας εἶναι, ἐμμαθέσιμους πρὸς τὰ χαλλίω γνῶσιν, &c. scientiam Dei putat in sola secta appellatione versari (col. 356, 357. editionis Gothofredi: col. 509. edit. quae prodiit Lugduni 1585. sol. cum glossis.) Ibidem (21) Ipsas ergo sacras voces legant, libros ipsos evolventes (ἀναγινώσκοντες) neque celantes ea quae in iis prolata sunt, extrinsecus assumant sine scriptis traditas vocum inanitates, ab ipsis ad perditionem simpliciorum excogitatas.
units.tr: (20) [Διὰ τοῦτο ἢ δὲ ἡ πᾶσαν αὐτοῖς φωνὴν ἀνοίξαμεν πρὸς τὸ τῆς ἱερῶν βίβλων ἀνάγνωσιν, ὥστε πάντας ἐρεξῆς ἡ αὐτῶν λαμ- πρότερας εἶναι, ἐμμαθέσιμους πρὸς τὰ χαλλίω γνῶσιν, &c.] For this reason we have opened to them every language for the reading of the holy books, so that all of them, in order, may be more ... and capable of learning better things, etc. He thinks the knowledge of God consists in the mere name of the sect (col. 356, 357 of the edition of Gothofredus; col. 509 of the edition published at Lyons in 1585, with glosses). In the same place (21) Let them therefore read the holy words themselves, unrolling the books themselves, and not concealing what is set forth in them; let them take from outside the empty sounds of words handed down without writings, which were devised by them for the ruin of the simpler people.

units.la: (21) Καὶ αὐτὰς Ν̄ τὰς ἱερὰς γραφὰς ἀναγινώσκοντες, τὰς βίβλους αὐτὰς ἀναπτύσσοντες, ἀλλὰ μὴ κατακρύπτοντες μηδὲ τὰ ἐν αὐτὰς σημεῖα. Nonnulli quidem Codices pro ἀναγινώσκοντες habent ἀναγινώσκοντες; adeoque Holoander, aliique interpretes Latini locum sic verterunt, codices ipsos respuentes; quae si verior lectio sit, pro αὐτὰς legendum est ταύτας, & sententia ad Ἰουδαίων Judaeorum, seu fabulas Misnicas & Talmudicas, quas Justinianus in periodo immediatè praecedenti Legi interdixerat, referenda: quod Antonius etiam Contius agnoscit, appositâ hac ad locum notâ. 'Ἀναγινώσκοντες. Sensus, si Judaïs est animus sacras Scripturas legendi; sacros Codices evolvant, non eos in quibus mera tantùm fabulae continentur.
units.tr: (21) [Καὶ αὐτὰς Ν̄ τὰς ἱερὰς γραφὰς ἀναγινώσκοντες, τὰς βίβλους αὐτὰς ἀναπτύσσοντες, ἀλλὰ μὴ κατακρύπτοντες μηδὲ τὰ ἐν αὐτὰς σημεῖα.] And reading the holy Scriptures themselves, unrolling the very books, and not hiding the signs in them. Some codices have ἀναγινώσκοντες instead of ἀναγινώσκοντες; and so Holoander and other Latin translators rendered the passage as rejecting the codices themselves. If that is the truer reading, then instead of αὐτὰς one must read ταύτας, and the sense refers to the fables of the Jews, the Misnic and Talmudic ones, which Justinian had forbidden in the period immediately preceding the law; Antonius Contius also acknowledges this, adding this note to the passage. Ἀναγινώσκοντες. The sense is: if the Jews have the intention of reading the sacred Scriptures, let them unroll the holy codices, not those in which mere fables are contained.
