units.la: Ex Jure Canonico, sententiisque Romanorum Pontificum.
units.tr: From the Canon Law and the sentences of the Roman Pontiffs.

units.la: IN 1. parte Decreti, Distinct. 38. cap. 9. [Ex Hieronymo ad Eustochium in proœmio Comment. in Esaiam] Si juxta Apostolum Paulum * Christus Dei virtus est & Dei sapientia; & qui nescit Scripturas, nescit Dei virtutem ejusque sapientiam: Scripturarum ignorantia Christi est ignorantia.
units.tr: In the first part of the Decretum, Distinction 38, chapter 9 [from Jerome to Eustochium, in the preface to his Commentary on Isaiah]: If, according to the Apostle Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, then whoever does not know the Scriptures does not know the power of God and his wisdom. Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

units.la: Ibid. cap. 10. [Ex Gregorio in Pastorali, par. 1. cap. 1.] Qui ea, quæ Dei sunt, nesciunt, à Deo nesciuntur; Paulo attestante, qui ait: Si quis ignorat, ignorabitur. [Vid. plura ex Gregorio Papâ supra ad an. 595.]
units.tr: Ibid., chapter 10 [from Gregory, in the Pastoral Rule, part 1, chapter 1]: Those who do not know the things that are of God are not known by God; as Paul bears witness, who says: "If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored." [See more from Pope Gregory above, under the year 595.]

units.la: Ibid. cap. 8. [Ex Zephyrini Papæ fictâ Epistolâ 1. ad Episcopos Siciliæ] Sicut stellas cæli non extinguit nox, sic mentes fidelium firmamento inhærentes sanctæ Scripturæ non obscurat mundana iniquitas. Ubi Glossa: Firmamento, i. e. meditationi & lectioni. (Hug.) Mundana] Unde dicitur: Ama scientiam Scripturarum, & carnis vitia non amabis. De Consecr. Dist. 5. Nunquam. (Hug. & Lan.) Sententia hæc in commentitiam Zephyrini Epistolam translata est ex libro Sententiarum ex Operibus Augustini a Prospero excerptarum sentent. 120.
units.tr: Ibid., chapter 8 [from the spurious first Epistle of Pope Zephyrinus to the bishops of Sicily]: Just as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not obscure the Holy Scripture of the faithful, who cling to the firmament. Where the Gloss says: Firmament, that is, meditation and reading. (Hug.) Worldly: Hence it is said: Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. De Consecratione, Distinction 5, "Nunquam." (Hug. & Lan.) This sentence was carried over into the fictitious Epistle of Zephyrinus from the Book of Sentences, excerpted by Prosper from the works of Augustine, sentence 120.

units.la: In 3. parte Decreti, de Consecrat. Distinct. 1. cap. 68. [Ex Anastasio primo Romano Episcopo ad Episcopos Germaniæ ac Burgundiæ, epist. 1. cap. 1.] Apostolicâ authoritate mandamus, dum sancta Evangelia in Ecclesia recitantur, ut sacerdotes & cæteri omnes præsentes, non sedentes, sed venerabiliter curvi, in conspectu Evangelii stantes Dominica verba intentè audiant, & fideliter adorent. Ibid. cap. 70. Vid. supra in Cypriano ad an. 250.
units.tr: In the third part of the Decretum, De Consecratione, Distinction 1, chapter 68 [from Anastasius, the first Roman bishop, to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy, Epistle 1, chapter 1]: By apostolic authority we command that, while the holy Gospels are read in the Church, the priests and all others present, not sitting but bowing reverently, stand before the Gospel and listen attentively to the words of the Lord and adore them faithfully. Ibid., chapter 70. See above under Cyprian, year 250.

units.la: Ibid. Distinct. 5. cap. 24. Non mediocriter. [Ex Hieronymo, ut dicitur.] Nunquid verborum multitudine flecti Deus ut homo potest? Non enim verbis tantum, sed corde orandus est Deus. Melior est quinque Psalmorum decantatio cum cordis puritate &
units.tr: Ibid., Distinction 5, chapter 24. Not moderately. [From Jerome, as it is said.] Can God be moved by a multitude of words, as a man can? For God is to be prayed to not only with words but with the heart. Better is the chanting of five Psalms with purity of heart and

units.la: * 1 Cor 1. serenitate & spiritali hilaritate, quàm totius Psalterii modulatio cum anxietate cordis & tristitia. [Habentur hæc fere, & in hanc sententiam plura in Regulâ Monachorum ex Hieronymi & aliorum scriptis à Lupo de Oliveto collecta, & Martini V. Romani Pontificis authoritate confirmata, tom. 4. Operum Hieronymi edit. Basil. 9. verò edit. Mariani Victorii.]
units.tr: * 1 Cor 1. serenity and spiritual cheerfulness than the recitation of the whole Psalter with anxiety of heart and sadness. [These things are found almost word for word, and more to this effect, in the Rule of the Monks, collected by Lupus de Oliveto from the writings of Jerome and others, and confirmed by the authority of Pope Martin V; in volume 4 of the works of Jerome, Basel edition; in the ninth volume, the edition of Marianus Victorius.]

units.la: Part. 1. Distinct. 27. cap. 1. Cleros. [Ex Isidoro, lib.7. Etymolog. cap. 12.] Lectores à legendo, Psalmista à Psalmis canendis vocati. Illi enim prædicant populis quid sequantur; isti canunt, ut excitent ad compunctionem animos audientium. Prædicant] i. e. legunt, recitando, non autem prædicando; quia illud est officium sacerdotum, 16. qu. 1. Adjicimus. (Glossa.)
units.tr: Part 1, Distinction 27, chapter 1. Clerks. [From Isidore, Etymologies, book 7, chapter 12.] Readers are so called from reading, psalmists from chanting psalms. For the former proclaim to the peoples what they are to follow; the latter sing so as to stir the hearts of the hearers to compunction. "Proclaim", that is, they read by reciting, not by preaching, because preaching is the office of priests, 16 qu. 1, "Adjicimus." (Gloss.)

units.la: Distinct. 38. cap. 12. Sedulò monendi. [Ex Augustino de catechizandis rudib. cap. 9.] in publicâ Ecclesiæ Liturgiâ illud corrigendum esse dicitur: Quod antistites & ministri cum barbarismis & solœcismis Deum invocent; vel eadem verba, quæ pronunciant, non intelligant, perturbatéque distinguant. Et ratio additur; ut populus ad id, quod plané intelligit, dicat Amen.
units.tr: Distinction 38, chapter 12. Diligently admonished. [From Augustine, On Catechizing the Uninstructed, chapter 9.] In the public liturgy of the Church it is said that this must be corrected: that the bishops and ministers invoke God with barbarisms and solecisms, or do not understand the very words they pronounce, and divide them in a confused way. And the reason is added: so that the people may say Amen to what they plainly understand.

units.la: Distinct. 92. cap. 1. [Ex Hieronymo, lib. 3. Comment. ad cap. 5. Epist. ad Ephef.] Cantantes & psallentes in cordibus vestris Domino.] Audiant hæc adolescentuli; audiant ii, quibus psallendi in ecclesia officium est: Deo non voce sed corde cantandum: Nec in tragœdorum morem guttur & fauces dulci medicamine linienda sunt, ut in Ecclesia Theatrales moduli audiantur & cantica; sed in timore, in opere, in scientiâ Scripturarum.
units.tr: Distinction 92, chapter 1. [From Jerome, book 3, Commentary on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians.] "Singing and psalming in your hearts to the Lord." Let the young hear this; let those hear it whose office it is to sing in the church: God is to be sung to not with the voice but with the heart. Nor should the throat and jaws be smeared with sweet ointment in the manner of tragic actors, so that theatrical tunes and songs are heard in the Church; but in fear, in work, and in the knowledge of the Scriptures.

units.la: Lib. 1. Decretal. tit. 31. de offic. judicis ordinarii, cap. Quoniam est cap. 9. Lateranensis Concilii (de quo supra) De Leone 1. supra ad an. 450. Nicolao I. an 860. Joanne VIII. an. 880. Innocentio III. an. 1200. & 1215.
units.tr: Book 1 of the Decretals, title 31, On the Office of the Ordinary Judge, chapter Quoniam, is chapter 9 of the Lateran Council (mentioned above). On Leo I, see above under 450; on Nicholas I, 860; on John VIII, 880; on Innocent III, 1200 and 1215.

units.la: In ordine Romano, de Officiis divinis (quem à Gelasio Papâ collectum constantior opinio est; si credimus r Baronio; s Bellarmino licèt author floruisse videatur post annum 700. Benedictio Lectorum ita proponitur. Domine sancte, pater omnipotens, æterne Deus, benedicere dignare hos famulos tuos in officium Lectorum; ut assiduitate lectionum sint apti pronuntiare verba vitæ, & mentis ac vocis distinctione populo monstrare intelligibilia: Et in utroque sanctæ Ecclesiæ
units.tr: In the Roman Ordo, On the Divine Offices (which the more constant opinion holds was collected by Pope Gelasius; if we believe Baronius, though Bellarmine thinks the author seems to have flourished after the year 700), the blessing of Readers is set out thus: Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, deign to bless these your servants for the office of Readers, so that by the constancy of their readings they may be fit to pronounce the words of life, and by the distinctness of mind and voice may show intelligible things to the people; and in both may they sound forth, according to their measure, the grace of the holy Church

units.la: r An. 692. sect. 44. s Lib. 2. de Missa, cap. 14. gratiam pro suis modulis spirituali devotione resonent (in Liturgicis Romæ excus. 1591. sol. pag. 64.) Sed & in Pontificali Romano impresso Lugduni, & postea Clementis VIII. jussu restituto, & Romæ, anno 1595. edito, Pontifex Lectores à se ordinandos ita admonere jubetur. Studete verba Dei, videlicet lectiones sacras distincte & aperte ad intelligentiam & edificationem fidelium absque omni mendacio falsitatis proferre; ne veritas divinarum lectionum incuriâ vestrâ ad instructionem audientium corrumpatur. Quod autem ore legitis, corde credatis, atque opere compleatis; quatenus auditores vestros verbo pariter & exemplo vestro docere possitis. Ideoque dum legitis, in alto loco Ecclesiæ stetis, ut ab omnibus audiamini & videamini, &c. (pag. 22.)
units.tr: r An. 692, sect. 44. s Book 2, On the Mass, chapter 14. with spiritual devotion (in the liturgical books printed at Rome, 1591, p. 64). But also in the Roman Pontifical printed at Lyons, and afterwards restored by order of Clement VIII and published at Rome in 1595, the Pontiff is directed to admonish the Readers he ordains thus: Take care to pronounce the words of God, that is, the sacred lectures, distinctly and openly, for the understanding and edification of the faithful, and without any lie of falsehood; lest through your carelessness the truth of the divine lessons be corrupted to the instruction of the hearers. What you read with your mouth, believe in your heart, and carry out in your deeds, so that you may teach your hearers equally by word and by your example. And therefore, while you read, you stand in a high place in the Church, so that you may be heard and seen by all, etc. (p. 22.)

units.la: Canon Apost. 85. Ἔσω πᾶσιν ὑμῖν ἀναγινωσκέσθω... Greek text. Sint autem vobis omnibus Clericis & Laicis venerabiles & sancti libri, Veteris quidem Testamenti Moysis, quinque, Genesis, Exodus, &c. Nostra verò, hoc est, Novi Testamenti, Evangelia quatuor, &c. In quem Canonem ita scribit Jo. Zonaras (22) Quùm venerabiles Apostoli præscripsissent, quomodo fideles Christi oportet vivere; tandem subjunxerunt etiam quos libros decet ipsos legere.
units.tr: Apostolic Canon 85. [Ἔσω πᾶσιν ὑμῖν ἀναγινωσκέσθω...] But let the venerable and holy books be yours, both for clerics and for laymen: of the Old Testament, the five books of Moses, Genesis, Exodus, etc.; but ours, that is, of the New Testament, the four Gospels, etc. On this canon John Zonaras writes thus: When the venerable Apostles had prescribed how the faithful ought to live, they finally added also which books they ought themselves to read.

units.la: In Clementis Romani (quæ dicuntur) Apostolicis constitutionibus, lib. 1. cap. 4. (23) Scripturas sanctas assiduâ memoriâ meditare. Scriptum est enim: In lege ejus meditaberis die ac nocte, deambulans in agro, & domi sedens, cubans & experrectus, ut in omnibus sis intelligens. Et cap. 5. (24) Intus sedens, lege Legem, libros de Regibus, Prophetas, cane Psalmos David, percurre diligenter Evangelium, in quo sunt haec consummata. (tom. 1. Concil. edit. Nicolin. pag. 64.
units.tr: In the so-called Apostolic Constitutions of Clement of Rome, book 1, chapter 4: Meditate on the holy Scriptures with constant memory. For it is written: "In his law you shall meditate day and night, walking in the field and sitting at home, lying down and rising, so that you may be intelligent in all things." And chapter 5: Sitting within, read the Law, the Books of Kings, the Prophets; sing the Psalms of David; read the Gospel carefully through, in which these things are brought to completion. (vol. 1 of the Councils, Nicolini edition, p. 64.)

units.la: Lib. 3. cap. 6. Ubi de corruptis viduarum moribus agitur, ita legimus (25) Non enim ad Ecclesiam, quæ est communis omnium requies, Dominicâ die adeunt; ut faciunt, qui vigilantes sunt, &c. Immo
units.tr: Book 3, chapter 6, where the corrupt morals of widows are discussed. There we read thus: For they do not come to the Church, which is the common rest of all, on the Lord's day, as those who are watchful do, etc. Rather

units.la: (22) Διατρίβοντες οἱ σπουδαῖοι ἀπόστολοι πῶς χρὴ τὸν πιστὸν βίον, ἐπάγειν πλάττειν ἢ τίνα δὲ αὐτὸς ἀναγινώσκειν βιβλία.
units.tr: (22) [Διατρίβοντες οἱ σπουδαῖοι ἀπόστολοι πῶς χρὴ τὸν πιστὸν βίον, ἐπάγειν πλάττειν ἢ τίνα δὲ αὐτὸς ἀναγινώσκειν βιβλία.] The diligent apostles, dwelling on how the faithful life ought to be, went on to shape it and to say what books he himself ought to read.

units.la: (23) Τὰ τῆς Χριστοῦ λόγια ἐναπομνημονεύομεν διανυκτὸς μελέτα, λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφή, ὅτι ἐν τῷ νόμῳ αὐτοῦ μελετήσεις ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός, &c.
units.tr: (23) [Τὰ τῆς Χριστοῦ λόγια ἐναπομνημονεύομεν διανυκτὸς μελέτα, λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφή, ὅτι ἐν τῷ νόμῳ αὐτοῦ μελετήσεις ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός, &c.] We keep the sayings of Christ in memory by meditating through the night; for the Scripture says: in his law you shall meditate day and night, etc.

units.la: (24) Καθεζόμενος ἔνδον, ἀναγινώσκε τὸν νόμον, τὰς βασιλείας, τοὺς ψαλμούς, &c.
units.tr: (24) [Καθεζόμενος ἔνδον, ἀναγινώσκε τὸν νόμον, τὰς βασιλείας, τοὺς ψαλμούς, &c.] Sitting within, read the Law, the Kings, the Psalms, etc.

units.la: (25) Οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τὸ κοινὸν τῆς συναγωγῆς ἀνάπαυσιν ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ, ὡς οἱ ἐγρηγορότες, &c. ὑμεῖς δὲ... ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ λόγῳ, &c. nec sinunt alios vigilantes ac sobrios esse in Domino, sed potius sic eos praparant, ut tales exeant, quales ingrediuntur, vacui scilicet; idque quia non audiunt ista vel eos qui docent, vel eos qui verbum Dei legunt. Hujusmodi sunt, de quibus ait Propheta: Auditu audietis, & non intelligetis; & videntes videbitis, & non scietis: incrassatum est enim cor populi hujus, (pag. 92.)
units.tr: (25) [Οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τὸ κοινὸν τῆς συναγωγῆς ἀνάπαυσιν ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ, ὡς οἱ ἐγρηγορότες, &c. ὑμεῖς δὲ... ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ λόγῳ, &c.] They do not come to the common assembly for rest on the Lord's day, as the watchful do, etc.; but you... in the word of the Lord, etc. Nor do they allow others to be watchful and sober in the Lord; rather they so prepare them that they go out such as they came in, that is, empty, and this because they do not hear these things, or those who teach, or those who read the word of God. Such are those of whom the Prophet says: By hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive: for the heart of this people has grown fat (p. 92.)

units.la: Lib. 4. Constitut. Apostol. cap 10. (26) Docete filias vestros a pueritia literas sacras, & vestras & divinas; omnemque divinam Scripturam eis tradite. Si haec a Clemente Romano profecta sunt temporibus Apostolorum, & Divi ipsius Petri Successore (ut hunc ipsum locum citans audacter pronuntiat Possevinusv) mirum qua fronte legem Apostolicam vel saltem Pontificiam Romanenses nostri repudiare audent.
units.tr: Book 4 of the Apostolic Constitutions, chapter 10 (26): "Teach your daughters the sacred letters from childhood, both yours and the divine ones; hand over to them all divine Scripture." If these words came from Clement of Rome in the time of the Apostles, and the successor of the blessed Peter himself (as Possevinus, citing this very passage, boldly declares), it is remarkable with what face our Romanists dare to reject the Apostolic law, or at least the papal one.

units.la: * Isai. 6. v Biblioth. select. lib. 4. cap. 6.
units.tr: * Isa. 6. v Bibliotheca selecta, book 4, chapter 6.

units.la: (26) Ἐνδιδάσκωσι τὸ ὑμῶν τὰ τέκνα ἀπὸ βρέφους διδάσκοντες ... αἱ τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, υἱοῖς ἡμῶν τὴν θεῖαν, τὸν λόγον κυρίου, ... ἀπὸ βρέφους διδάσκοντες, πᾶσαν γραφὴν θείαν παραδιδόντες.
units.tr: (26) "Let them teach your children from infancy the sacred letters, ... teaching them from infancy the divine word of the Lord, ... handing on to them all divine Scripture." [Ἐνδιδάσκωσι τὸ ὑμῶν τὰ τέκνα ἀπὸ βρέφους διδάσκοντες ... αἱ τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, υἱοῖς ἡμῶν τὴν θεῖαν, τὸν λόγον κυρίου, ... ἀπὸ βρέφους διδάσκοντες, πᾶσαν γραφὴν θείαν παραδιδόντες.]

units.la: CAPUT VIII. PRAXIS ECCLESIÆ.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. THE PRACTICE OF THE CHURCH.

units.la: SECT. I. Scripturæ passim in linguis vulgaribus extabant.
units.tr: SECT. I. Scriptures were everywhere extant in the vernacular languages.

units.la: CHaldaicæ versiones à Jonathane filio Uzzielis, Onkelo proselyto, Aquila proselyto, R. Joseph. Cæco, &c. elaboratæ sunt. Vid. Eliam in præfatione Methurgeman, & in Tischbi, radice ⊏ıø, & quæ supra à nobis in Hebræorum sententiis, notata sunt. Apud Græcos variæ interpretationes (Sciendum est, inquit Moses Barcepha, a Vetus Testamentum pluribus tralationibus ex Hebræa in Græcam linguam esse transpositum) LXX. interpretum, Aquilæ, Theodotionis, Symmachi, Quintæ etiam & Sextæ editionis, extiterunt; quas omnes in Octaplis suis conjunxit Origenes; & ex iis etiam unam editionem confecit, notis quibusdam ita distinctam, ut quid esset in Hebræo, quid non, quomodo à LXX. aliæ interpretationes variarent, statim appareret. (Vid. Eusebium, lib. 6. hist. cap. 13. Athanasium in Synopsi, & Epiphanium in lib. de mensuris & ponderibus, atque Isidorum, lib. 6. Orig. cap. 4.) Sed & Lucianus Martyr, cùm in prædictas editiones & scripturas Hebraicas incidisset, ac sedulò inspexisset verba quædam scripturæ veritati defesse, quædam verò irrepsisse superflua; libros sacros ex Hebraico sermone magno labore restituit. (Athanasius in Synopsi, & Suidas in voce Λουκιανός.) Accessit demum Hesychius, qui Interpretationem LXX. à se emendatam Ægyptiis tradidit. Unde Hieronymus præfat. in lib. Paralipomenon (quam etiam inseruit Apologiæ adversus Rufinum) Alexandria, inquit, & Ægyptus in LXX. suis Hesychium laudat authorem, Constantinopolis usque ad Antiochiam Luciani Martyris exemplaria probat:
units.tr: Chaldaic versions were produced by Jonathan son of Uzziel, Onkelos the proselyte, Aquila the proselyte, R. Joseph the Blind, and others. See Elias in the preface to Methurgeman, and in Tischbi, under the root ⊏ıø, and what we have noted above among the opinions of the Hebrews. Among the Greeks there were various translations. "It must be known," says Moses Barcepha, "that the Old Testament was rendered from Hebrew into Greek in several translations." There were those of the Seventy interpreters, of Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus, and also the fifth and sixth editions. Origen brought all of these together in his Octapla, and from them he also made one edition, marked with certain signs so that it would be immediately clear what was in the Hebrew and what was not, and how the other translations differed from the Septuagint. (See Eusebius, Church History, book 6, ch. 13; Athanasius in the Synopsis; Epiphanius in his book on weights and measures; and Isidore, Origines, book 6, ch. 4.) But Lucian the Martyr too, when he had come upon the aforesaid editions and the Hebrew Scriptures, and had carefully examined them, found that some words had fallen away from the truth of Scripture and that some superfluous things had crept in; with great labour he restored the sacred books from the Hebrew language. (Athanasius in the Synopsis, and Suidas s.v. Lucian.) Finally Hesychius came, who handed on to the Egyptians the Septuagint as he had corrected it. Hence Jerome in the preface to Paralipomenon (which he also included in his Apology against Rufinus): "Alexandria and Egypt," he says, "commend Hesychius as the author of their Septuagint; Constantinople as far as Antioch approves the copies of Lucian the Martyr."

units.la: a De Paradiso, part. 1. cap. 28. media inter has provincias Palaestinos codices legunt, quos ab Origene elaboratos Eusebius & Pamphilus vulgaverunt: totusque orbis hac inter se trifariâ varietate compugnat. Psalterium quoque & Prophetas, quos Hieronymus de Hebraeo in Latinum vertit, Sophronius de Latino in Graecum vertit; quemadmodum in Catalogo suo testatur Hieronymus. Quam quidem Graecam translationem, ut ex collectaneis Procopii in Octateuchum apparet, multi Graeci expositores, citato etiam Hieronymi nomine, commentariis illustrarunt.
units.tr: (a De Paradiso, part. 1, ch. 28.) "Midway between these regions they read Palestinian codices, which Eusebius and Pamphilus published, prepared by Origen; and the whole world is at odds over this threefold variety." Jerome also testifies, in his Catalogue, that the Psalter and the Prophets, which he translated from Hebrew into Latin, were translated from Latin into Greek by Sophronius. Many Greek expositors illustrated this Greek translation with commentaries, as appears from the collections of Procopius on the Octateuch, even citing Jerome's name.

units.la: Caeterum quàm latè usus linguae Graecae olim patebat, omnes nôrunt. Unicum tamen Hieronymum testem dabo: qui proœmio, lib. 2. Commentar. in Epist. ad Galat. ait, Galatas, excepto sermone Graeco, quo omnis Oriens loquitur, propriam linguam, eandem penè habere quam Treviros.
units.tr: Moreover, everyone knows how widely the use of the Greek language once extended. I will give one witness only, Jerome, who in the preface to book 2 of his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians says that the Galatians, apart from Greek, which the whole East speaks, have a native tongue almost the same as that of the Treveri.

units.la: De Latinis ita Augustinus de Doctrinâ Christianâ, lib. 2. cap. 11. Qui Scripturas ex Hebraeâ linguâ in Graecam linguam verterunt, numerari possunt: Latini autem nullo modo. Ut enim cuique primis fidei temporibus in manus venit Codex Graecus, & aliquantulum facultatis sibi utriusque linguae habere videbatur, ausus est interpretari. Quamvis non defuerit temporibus nostris (inquit idem lib. 18. de civitate Dei, cap. 43.) Presbyter Hieronymus, homo doctissimus, & omnium trium linguarum peritus; qui non ex Graeco sed ex Hebraeo in Latinum eloquium easdem Scripturas converterit.
units.tr: Augustine speaks thus of the Latins in On Christian Doctrine, book 2, ch. 11: "Those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek can be counted; but Latins cannot be counted at all. For as soon as anyone in the earliest times of the faith came upon a Greek codex and seemed to have some ability in both languages, he ventured to translate." Yet, as the same Augustine says in The City of God, book 18, ch. 43, in our own times there was "the presbyter Jerome, a most learned man and skilled in all three languages, who translated the same Scriptures into Latin not from Greek but from Hebrew."

units.la: Innumeris verò ferè gentibus unica versio Latina Scripturarum notitiam tunc temporis praebere poterat. Incredibile enim linguae Latinae amplitudinem obtinuisse demonstrat P. Merula in Cosmographh. pag. 796, 797. qui eam Africae etiam partem, quam incolebant Romani (pariter ac eam Italiae partem, quam incolebant Graeci) bilinguem fuisse ostendit, ibid. pag. 791, 792. Sanè Afros Latinè locutos confirmat Apuleius in Floridis. Ipsa etiam Britannia victricis Romae linguam accepit. Si quis sit (inquit Camdenus, pag. 83. edit. 1607.) qui non credat Britannos linguam Latinam provincialem usurpâsse; ne ille noverit, quantopere Romani laborârint, ut Provinciae loquerentur Latinè; nec viderit, quanta vis Latinarum dictionum in Britannicam linguam irrepserit; ut Taciti authoritatem non urgeam, qui scribit Britannos Domitiani tempore Latinae linguae eloquentiam concupisse.
units.tr: Indeed, for countless peoples at that time a single Latin version could provide knowledge of the Scriptures. For P. Merula, in his Cosmography, pp. 796–797, shows that the Latin language had gained an incredible breadth; and he shows, ibid., pp. 791–792, that the part of Africa inhabited by the Romans was bilingual, just as the part of Italy inhabited by the Greeks was. Apuleius in the Florida certainly confirms that Africans spoke Latin. Britain itself received the language of victorious Rome. "If anyone," says Camden (p. 83, ed. 1607), "does not believe that the Britons used the Latin of the province, let him learn how greatly the Romans laboured to make the provinces speak Latin, and let him see how great a force of Latin words crept into the British language; not to press the authority of Tacitus, who writes that in Domitian's time the Britons desired the eloquence of the Latin language."

units.la: {b} In Sophronio. {c} Vid. Sixtum Senens. Biblioth. Sanct. in Procopio & Sophron. {d} Vid. de Vulg. Latin. pulchram sententiam Jac. Gretseri in Defens. Eccliarum, col. 779. concupisse. * Hæc Camdenus. Hinc Gildas de Saxonicis navibus, ut linguâ ejus exprimitur, Cyulis, nostrâ, longis navibus. De Hispanis Strabo, lib. 3. Turdetani, maximè qui ad Batim sunt, plane Romanos mores assumpserunt, ne sermonis quidem vernaculi memores; ac plerique facti sunt Latini, & colonos acceperunt Romanos; parumque abest, quin omnino Romani facti sint. Et qui hanc formam sequuntur Hispani, Stolati seu Togati appellantur; in quibus sunt Celtiberi, quondam omnium maximè feri inhumanique habiti. Hæc ille, [ubi observare licet Romanæ linguæ, sed paulatim depravatæ, in Hispaniâ primordium.]
units.tr: {b} On Sophronius. {c} See Sixtus of Siena, Bibliotheca Sancta, on Procopius and Sophronius. {d} On the Vulgate, see the fine opinion of Jacob Gretser in his Defence of the Churches, col. 779. "Desired." * Thus Camden. Hence Gildas, on the Saxon ships, which in their language are called Cyulis, and in ours long ships. Strabo, book 3, on the Spaniards: "The Turdetani, especially those near the Baetis, have quite adopted Roman customs, not even remembering their native speech; and most of them have become Latins, and have received Roman colonists; and it is hardly short of their becoming wholly Roman. The Spaniards who follow this way of life are called Stolati or Togati; among them are the Celtiberians, once considered the fiercest and most inhuman of all." Thus he. [Here one may observe the beginning, in Spain, of the Roman language, though gradually corrupted.]

units.la: Sed & Scripturas per varias interpretum linguas longè latéque diffusas innotuisse gentibus ad salutem testatur Augustinus, lib. 2. de Doctr. Christ. cap. 5. quem suo loco citavimus. Et Hieronymus in præfatione in 4 Evangelia ad Damasum, Scripturam multarum gentium linguis ante Luciani & Hesychii tempora translatam esse confirmat. Unde Augustinus Epist. 48. ad Vincentium (pag. 76. b. edit. Paris. 1586. Neque enim, inquit, sic potuit integritas atque notitia literarum unius quamlibet illustris Episcopi custodiri; quemadmodum Scriptura Canonica tot linguarum literis & ordine & successione celebrationis ecclesiastica custoditur. Hoc ipsum ex testimonio Eutebii, quod supra an. 335. Chrysostomi (in Johan. Homil. 1.) quod an. 390. & Theodoreti, quod an. 450. reposuimus: ita manifestè liquet; ut mira sit Roberti Bellarmini vel inscitia vel impudentia; qui nullum antiquum authorem meminisse alicujus alterius translationis, quam Græcæ & Latinæ, satis confidenter pronunciat.
units.tr: But Augustine also testifies, in On Christian Doctrine, book 2, ch. 5, which we cited in its place, that the Scriptures, translated into the languages of various interpreters, became known to many peoples far and wide for their salvation. And Jerome, in his preface to the four Gospels addressed to Damasus, confirms that Scripture had been translated into the languages of many peoples before the times of Lucian and Hesychius. Hence Augustine, in Epistle 48 to Vincentius (p. 76b, ed. Paris 1586): "For the integrity and knowledge of the letters of any one illustrious bishop could not be kept in such a way, as the Canonical Scripture is kept in the letters of so many languages, and by the order and succession of ecclesiastical celebration." This very point is clear from the testimony of Eusebius, which we placed above under the year 335, of Chrysostom (on John, Homily 1), which we placed under 390, and of Theodoret, which we placed under 450. So clearly is it evident that the ignorance or the impudence of Robert Bellarmine is remarkable, who confidently declares that no ancient author recalls any translation other than the Greek and the Latin.

units.la: De translatione in usum Gothorum factâ supra dictum est an. 370. in Ulphilâ: cujus exemplar MS. idque vetustissimum Gothicis literis majoribus scriptum in aliqua Germaniæ Bibliothecâ delitescere dicitur; quemadmodum refert Bonaventura Vulcanius præfatione in Commentarium de literis & linguâ Getarum. Huc referantur, quæ habet Suffridus Petrus præfatione in Scriptorum Frisiæ Decades. Et nobis etiam, inquit, hic (Coloniæ) coram testatus est Clariss. V.J.C. Matalius Metellus Sequanus, ad suas manus aliquando pervenisse Novum Testamentum linguâ Gothicâ, characteribus Græcis, scriptum. Et Stephanus Vinandus Pighius Scholasticus Sanctensis, literis ad me datis
units.tr: Concerning the translation made for the use of the Goths, it was said above under the year 370, in the entry on Ulfilas. His manuscript, very ancient and written in large Gothic letters, is said to lie hidden in some German library, as Bonaventura Vulcanius reports in the preface to his commentary on the letters and language of the Getae. To this may be referred what Suffridus Petri says in the preface to his Decades of Frisian writers: "And here at Cologne," he says, "the most distinguished jurist Matalius Metellus of Sequania testified in my presence that a New Testament written in the Gothic language, with Greek characters, had once come into his hands." And Stephanus Vinandus Pighius, scholastic of Sankt-..., wrote to me in a letter

units.la: Lib. 2. de verbo Dei, cap. 14. prid. Id. Maii anno 1588. scripsit à se Dominum Joachimum Hopperum mutuo habuisse vetustissima linguæ Germanicæ, quam ille Frisicam appellabat, Orationem Dominicam ex ejus linguæ Novi Testamenti libro quodam descriptam, characteribus antiquissimis Græcis. Hactenus Suffridus. Et extabat sanè in Bibliothecâ D. Hermanni Comitis de Newenar liber vetustissimus aureis argenteisque characteribus in papyro exaratus, continens universum Novum Testamentum linguâ antiquâ Frisonum; ut nobilis ille Philippus Marnixius Dominus Sanct-Aldegundius literis suis Sibrandum Lubbertum docuit. Ex hoc libro idem Aldegundius dicit se habere descriptam Orationem Dominicam Frisico vel Saxonico antiquo charactere, qui non multum à Muscovitico charactere differre, & ad Græcum accedere, videtur. Ejus initium est: Atta unsar thu in himina; waikmi namo thien, &c. Eadem ipsa {g}Oratio Dominica (cum quibusdam {h}ex Evangelio secundum Marcum) descripta est à Joanne Goropio Becano, lib. 7. Originum Antverpianarum, ex schedis Antonii Morilloni, qui Antonio Perrenoto Cardinali Granvellano fuit ab Epistolis Latinis, & à Bibliothecâ : quo in munere successit eidem Stephanus Vinandus Pighius , qui, ut supra dictum (ex eodem Codice proculdubio), Orationem Dominicam descriptam Joachimo Hoppero dedit; quam ille, ut & Philippus Marnixius (eadem enim oratio est ab eo descripta ex Bibliothecâ Hermanni Comitis de Newenar) vetustissimâ linguâ Germanicâ vel Frisicâ exaratam putavit; quanquam ea Gothica doctissimi cujusque apud Colonienses judicio habebatur, ut in loco proximè citato confirmat Goropius: unde etiam à Goldasto citatur nomine Gothici Evangeliorum Interpretis. Estque ille ipse argenteus Codex, vetere Gothorum linguâ & literis scriptus; ex quo tum Orationem Dominicam descripsit, tum alia nonnulla Marci & Lucæ citavit Antonius Morillonus, vel quicunque author fuit Commentarioli de linguâ Gothicâ à Bonav. Vulcanio editi (pag. 1, 10, 31, 32, 48, &c.) Oratio enim Dominica, pag. 32. convenit tam cum eâ quam habet Goropius, tam cum illâ quam habet Philippus Marnixius ex Novo Testamento aureis argenteisque characteribus in papyro exarato ex bibliothecâ Hermanni Comitis
units.tr: in book 2 of De verbo Dei, ch. 14, on the day before the Ides of May 1588, that he had written that Lord Joachim Hopper had borrowed from him a very ancient text in the German language, which Pighius called Frisian: the Lord's Prayer copied from a certain book of the New Testament in that language, in very ancient Greek characters. Thus far Suffridus. And indeed there was in the library of Lord Hermann, Count of Newenar, a most ancient book written on papyrus in gold and silver letters, containing the whole New Testament in the old language of the Frisians; as the noble Philip Marnix, Lord of Sint-Aldegonde, taught Sibrandus Lubbertus in his letters. From this book the same Aldegonde says he has a copy of the Lord's Prayer in ancient Frisian or Saxon characters, which seem not much to differ from Muscovite characters and to approach Greek. Its beginning is: "Atta unsar thu in himina; waikmi namo thien, &c." The same Lord's Prayer (with some passages from the Gospel according to Mark) was copied by John Goropius Becanus, in book 7 of his Antwerp Origins, from the papers of Antonius Morillonus, who was Latin secretary and librarian to Cardinal Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle; Stephanus Vinandus Pighius succeeded him in that office, and, as said above (doubtless from the same codex), gave the copied Lord's Prayer to Joachim Hopper. Hopper, like Philip Marnix (for that prayer was copied by him from the library of Count Hermann of Newenar), thought it was written in a very old German or Frisian language; yet it was held by the soundest judgement of the learned at Cologne to be Gothic, as Goropius confirms in the passage cited just above, whence Goldast also cites him under the name of Gothic interpreter of the Gospels. And that is the same silver codex, written in the old language and letters of the Goths, from which Antonius Morillonus (or whoever was the author of the little commentary on the Gothic language edited by Bonaventura Vulcanius, pp. 1, 10, 31, 32, 48, etc.) copied the Lord's Prayer and cited other passages of Mark and Luke. For the Lord's Prayer on p. 32 agrees both with the version Goropius has and with the one Philip Marnix has from the New Testament written on papyrus in gold and silver letters, from the library of Count Hermann.

units.la: {f} Lubbert. de princip. Christian. dogmat. lib. 3. cap. 7. {g} Goropius pag. 740. {h} Gorop. p. 750. {i} Gorop. pag. 739. {k} Pighius præfat. ad Lectorem in Annales Magistrat. Roman. {l} Scrip. Parænet. part. 1. pag. 232. de Newenar. Neque aliud videtur fuisse Novum illud Testamentum, lingua Gothica, characteribus Græcis, scriptum; quod ad manus suas aliquando pervenisse testatus est Matalius Metellus Sequanus. Characteres enim illi ad Græcos (vel potius Illyricos) proximè accedere videntur. Porrò Antonium Morillonum ista descripsisse ex antiquissimo codice Monasterii Werdeni in regione Bergensi, quatuor plus minus milliaribus à Colonia distantis testatur Goropius. Similiter Arnoldus Mercator ait extare in Bibliothecâ Abbatiæ Werdinensis Codicem antiquissimum, ante mille plus minus annos in pergameno aureis & argenteis literis perscriptum, continentem quatuor Evangelistarum opus, sed (quod dolendum est) lacerum, diruptum, & nullo ordine ignorantiâ compactoris colligatum. Ex eo magnam partem sexti Capitis Matthæi (sc. Orationem Dominicam cum præcedentibus & proximè subsequentibus) & initium Evangelii secundum Marcum (eandem habens inscriptionem cum eâ, quam ex schedis Authoris Commentarii de linguâ Gothica descripsit Bonav. Vulcanius, pag. 66.) delineavit Arnoldus operâ & adminiculo D. Henrici Duden pro tempore Abbatis: nam plura communicare vetabat obscuritas literarum jam vetustate evanescentium. Ea verò cum Alphabeto, & lectionis explicatione (quæ aliquando diversa est ab eâ, quæ in Commentariolo de linguâ Gothicâ posita est; licet characteres Gothici iidem prorsus sint; quippe sine omni controversiâ ex eodem exemplari descripti) ex Arnoldi schedis descripta in magno Inscriptionum Opere (pag. 146, 147, 148.) reposuit Janus Gruterus.
units.tr: {f} Lubbert, De principiis christianae dogmatis, lib. 3, cap. 7. {g} Goropius, p. 740. {h} Goropius, p. 750. {i} Goropius, p. 739. {k} Pighius, praefatio ad Lectorem in Annales Magistratuum Romanorum. {l} Scripta Parænetica, pars 1, p. 232, de Newenar. Nor does that New Testament, written in the Gothic language with Greek characters, appear to have been anything else. Matalius Metellus of Sequania testified that it once came into his hands. Those characters seem to lie close to the Greek, or rather to the Illyrian. Goropius further testifies that Antonius Morillonus copied these texts from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Werden in the region of Berg, about four miles from Cologne. Similarly, Arnoldus Mercator says that there is in the library of the Abbey of Werden a very ancient codex, written on parchment in gold and silver letters more than a thousand years ago, containing the four Gospels. Sadly, it is torn and ruined, and through the ignorance of the binder it has been bound with no order at all. From it Arnoldus, with the work and help of Dr Henricus Duden, then Abbot, drew out a large part of the sixth chapter of Matthew (namely the Lord's Prayer with the verses immediately before and after) and the beginning of the Gospel according to Mark, which bears the same inscription as the one Bonaventura Vulcanius copied from the papers of the author of the Commentary on the Gothic language (p. 66). The obscurity of the letters, already fading with age, prevented him from communicating more. These texts, together with the alphabet and an explanation of the reading (which sometimes differs from the one given in the short Commentary on the Gothic language, although the Gothic characters are exactly the same, since they were without doubt copied from the same exemplar), were taken from Arnoldus's papers and placed by Janus Gruterus in his great work of Inscriptions (pp. 146, 147, 148).

units.la: In linguâ Syriacâ, Armenicâ, & Æthiopicâ cùm Veteris tum Novi Testamenti Versiones integras reperiri testatur Guido Fabricius in Dedicatione Testamenti Syriaci interlineari (anno 1584. Parisiis editi) ad Henricum III. Gallorum Regem. Syriam editionem Veteris Testamenti Eusebius Emesenus & alii Græci Patres unà cum ceteris Græcis & Latinis editionibus sæpe ediderunt: inquit Sixtus Senensis . Et Veteris quidem Testamenti Translationem Syriacam tempore Thaddæi Apostoli, & Abgari Syrorum regis, factam fuisse, ex Prologo quodam Psalterio Syriaco præmisso tradit Georgius Amira in Præludio de Chaldaicæ linguæ utilitate, Grammaticæ suæ
units.tr: Guido Fabricius, in the dedication to Henry III, King of the French, of the interlinear Syriac New Testament published at Paris in 1584, testifies that complete versions of both the Old and New Testaments are found in the Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopic languages. The Syriac edition of the Old Testament was often published by Eusebius of Emesa and other Greek Fathers, together with the other Greek and Latin editions, says Sixtus of Siena. That the Syriac translation of the Old Testament was made in the time of the Apostle Thaddaeus and Abgar, king of the Syrians, is handed down by George Amira in his Prelude on the usefulness of the Chaldee language, prefixed to his Grammar, from a certain Prologue placed before a Syriac Psalter.

units.la: m Orig. Antverp. lib. 7. pag. 739. n Biblioth. Sanct. lib. 4. voc. Eusceb. Emef. & Syra editio. Syriacæ præfixo. Et Syriacæ quidem editionis meminit Eusebius Emesenus in Catenâ Græcâ in Genesin, Basilius Magnus in hexaemeron, homil. 2. Ambrosius, lib. 5. hexaemer. cap. 8. Augustinus de Civitate Dei, lib. 15. cap. 13. Theodoretus in Jonæ 3. caput, Polychronius in Danielis 3. caput (in Catenâ Græcâ, teste Ant. Caraffâ) Moses Barcepha in Commentar. de Paradiso, par. 1. cap. 28, &c (Vid. annum 370 in Ephræm Syro, 390. in Jo. Chrysostomo, homil. 1. in Johannem; 616. in Syris) Hieronymus Epist. 27. in Epitaphio Paulæ Syricorum Psalmorum meminit. Novi Testamenti libros à Marco Evangelistâ translatos in linguam Syram ex avitâ traditione affirmant Syri; quemadmodum ab iis accepit Gulielmus Postellus, qui etiam secum ab Oriente Novi Testamenti exemplar Syrum, jam ab anno 1500. regni Alexandri (circa annum Christi 1190.) manu descriptum attulit (Guido Fabricius præfat in Novum Testamentum Syriac. tom. 5. Biblior. Reg. Quin & omnes (inquit Robertus Personius°) Ecclesiæ Asiaticæ & Africanæ usque ad hunc diem, etiam ipsi Abyssini, qui Presbytero Johanni subsunt, (licet alterius linguæ sint) hoc Testamento Syriacè utuntur, ut à S. Marco conversō. Porrò annis abhinc 50. Antiochenus Patriarcha, quum in suis Ecclesiis non Latino, sed qui illic intelligitur, Syriaco sermone utatur; & necessariis ad ministerium quasi instrumentis, h. e. libris, destitueretur; misit quendam ordinis Ecclesiastici hominem, Mosen Mardenum, qui vel Romæ vel Venetiis Novum Testamentum Syriacè imprimendum curaret. Sed cùm id esset frustra; iter ad Ferdinandum Cæsarem dirigens, incidit in virum doctissimum Albertum Widmanstadium Austriæ Orientalis per id tempus Cancellarium; cujus operâ effectum est, ut sumptus Cæsare subministrante Novum Testamentum linguâ & characteribus Syris, anno 1555. Viennæ pulcherrimè excusum prodierit. (Alb. Widmanstad.& Imman.Tremell. præfat. in Testam.Syriac.) Illud verò Opus Ferdinandus Cæsar Episcopo Ephesino dono misisse dicitur, ut suis Diœcesanis & vicinis Episcopis communicaret. Quod ejus factum ihiquissimo animo tulisse Papam, & corruptorem quendam, Lucretium nomine, subornâsse affirmant. (Johan. Wolfius Lection. Memorabil. Centenario 16. anno 1564.) Vid. Gretserum de hoc, ex Paulo Vergerio. Utrumque verò Testamentum affirmat Georgius Amira
units.tr: m Origen, Antwerp, lib. 7, p. 739. n Bibliotheca Sancta, lib. 4, s.v. Eusebius of Emesa, and the Syriac edition prefixed to the Syriac. Mention of the Syriac edition is made by Eusebius of Emesa in the Greek Catena on Genesis; by Basil the Great in the Hexaemeron, homily 2; by Ambrose, Hexaemeron book 5, ch. 8; by Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 15, ch. 13; by Theodoret on the third chapter of Jonah; by Polychronius on the third chapter of Daniel (in the Greek Catena, according to Antonius Caraffa); and by Moses Bar-Cepha in his Commentary on Paradise, part 1, ch. 28, etc. (See the year 370 for Ephraem the Syrian, 390 for John Chrysostom, homily 1 on John, and 616 for the Syrians.) Jerome, in Epistle 27, the Epitaph of Paula, mentions the Syriac Psalms. The Syrians affirm from ancient tradition that the books of the New Testament were translated into Syriac by the Evangelist Mark. William Postel received this from them, and he also brought with him from the East a Syriac New Testament copy, written by hand already in the year 1500 of the reign of Alexander (about AD 1190). (Guido Fabricius, preface to the Syriac New Testament, vol. 5 of the Biblia Regia.) Indeed, all (says Robertus Personius) the churches of Asia and Africa, down to this day, even the Abyssinians themselves who are subject to Prester John, although they speak another language, use this Testament in Syriac, as translated by St Mark. Moreover, some fifty years ago the Patriarch of Antioch, since in his churches the Syriac language, which is understood there, is used rather than Latin, and since he lacked the books needed for the ministry as its instruments, sent a man of ecclesiastical order, Moses Mardenus, to arrange for the New Testament to be printed in Syriac either at Rome or at Venice. But when this proved fruitless, Mardenus directed his journey to the Emperor Ferdinand and fell in with the most learned Albert Widmanstadt, at that time Chancellor of Eastern Austria. Through his work it was brought about that, with the Emperor supplying the cost, the New Testament came out in the Syriac language and characters, splendidly printed at Vienna in 1555. (Albert Widmanstadt and Immanuel Tremellius, preface to the Syriac Testament.) It is said that Emperor Ferdinand sent that work as a gift to the Bishop of Ephesus, so that he might share it with his diocesans and neighbouring bishops. They affirm that the Pope took this very ill, and suborned a certain corrupter named Lucretius. (John Wolf, Lectiones Memorabiles, century 16, year 1564.) See Gretser on this, from Paul Vergerius. Both Testaments are affirmed by George Amira...

units.la: ° Epitome Controverf. de verbo Dei, qu. 3. cap. de edit. Syriacâ. Syrus (loco citato) ab Apostolorum temporibus hucusque magno omnium Orientis populorum, qui Chaldaicâ sive Syriacâ utuntur linguâ, studio retentum, & semper summâ in veneratione & authoritate esse habitum, & demum publicè in omnibus eorum Ecclesiis, antiquissimis constitutis in Syriâ, Mesopotamiâ, Chaldæâ, Ægypto, & denique in universi Orientis partibus dispersis ac disseminatis lectum esse ac legi. Sed de versionibus Syriacis satis. Id tantùm addam, quod habet Moses Barcephas, Vetus Testamentum Syriacè redditum esse unâ quidem Interpretatione ex ipso Hebræo, alterâ verò ex Græco. Vid. Pet. Galesinium de Bibliis Græcis, pag. 53, & Josephus Scaligerum Canon. Isagog. lib. 3. pag. 264. quodque Jacobus Navarchus Hondischotanus de Ecclesiarum Asiaticarum praxi refert. Omnes (inquit) Ecclesiæ Asiæ Syriacâ linguâ, ut nostra Latinâ, utuntur.
units.tr: ° Epitome of Controversies on the Word of God, question 3, ch. on the Syriac edition. The Syrian (in the place cited) says that from the times of the Apostles until now it has been kept with great zeal by all the peoples of the East who use the Chaldee or Syriac language, that it has always been held in highest reverence and authority, and that at last it has been publicly read in all their churches, the most ancient of which were founded in Syria, Mesopotamia, Chaldea, Egypt, and finally throughout the scattered parts of the whole East. But enough on the Syriac versions. I will add only what Moses Bar-Cepha says, that the Old Testament was rendered into Syriac in two translations, one indeed from the Hebrew itself and the other from the Greek. See Peter Galesinius, On the Greek Bibles, p. 53, and Joseph Scaliger, Canon Isagogicus, lib. 3, p. 264; and what James Navarchus of Hondschoote reports of the practice of the Asian churches: All (he says) the churches of Asia use the Syriac language, as ours use Latin.

units.la: Utriusque Testamenti in linguam Armenicam extat Translatio (Psalterium in linguâ & characteribus Armenicis MS. habetur Cantabrigiæ in Bibliothecâ S. Benedicti) qua nunc Armeni utuntur; Chrysostomi, ut ipsi credunt, industriâ & sollicitudine edita. Meminit hujus Translationis Georgius Patriarcha Alexandrinus in vitâ Chrysostomi, referens eum, cùm in Cucusum Armeniæ oppidum exularet, incolas ejus regionis ad Christum perduxisse; ac subinde curâsse ut Psalmi Davidis unà cum sanctis Evangeliis atque aliis veteris Instrumenti historiis Armenicè verterentur, quò facilius divinæ Scripturæ cognitionem gentes provinciæ illius obtinerent. (Sixtus Senensis, lib. 4. Biblioth. Sanct. in Johan. Chrysost.) Vid. supra an. 400. in Scythis, & 450. in Theodoreto, atque Angelum Roccham in Biblioth. Vatican. pag. 157. Petrus Victor Cajetanus ait se cum Thomâ Angelo Armeno Psalmis Armenicis diligenter incubuisse; quos Thomas ille constanti famâ apud Armenos à D. Johanne Chrysostomo Armenicâ linguâ editos perhiberi asserit. Quin & Armenam versionem à S. Joanne Chrysostomo ei nationi præstitam esse prodit Pet. Galesinius. Quò verò res clarius pateat, integrum Georgii Alexandrini locum apponam. Sic igitur ille de rebus Chrysostomi apud Cucusum agens.
units.tr: A translation of both Testaments into the Armenian language exists. A Psalter in the Armenian language and characters is found in manuscript at Cambridge, in the library of St Benedict. This is the translation the Armenians now use, made, as they believe, by the diligence and care of Chrysostom. George, Patriarch of Alexandria, mentions this translation in the Life of Chrysostom, reporting that when Chrysostom was in exile at Cucusus, a town of Armenia, he led the people of that region to Christ, and afterwards took care that the Psalms of David, together with the holy Gospels and other histories of the Old Instrument, should be turned into Armenian, so that the peoples of that province might more easily gain knowledge of divine Scripture. (Sixtus of Siena, Bibliotheca Sancta, lib. 4, on John Chrysostom.) See above at the year 400 among the Scythians, and at 450 in Theodoret, and Angelus Rocca, Bibliotheca Vaticana, p. 157. Peter Victor Cajetan says that he applied himself diligently to the Armenian Psalms together with Thomas Angelus, an Armenian; Thomas asserts that, by the constant report among the Armenians, these were published in the Armenian language by St John Chrysostom. Indeed, Peter Galesinius also reports that the Armenian version was given to that nation by St John Chrysostom. But so that the matter may appear more clearly, I shall set out the whole passage of George of Alexandria, who, speaking thus of Chrysostom's activity at Cucusus:

units.la: a De Paradiso, part. 1. cap. 28. b Epist. Asiatic. c Paradigm. ling. Armen. pag. 73. d De Bibliis Græcis, pag. 8. e De vitâ Chrysost. §. 59. tom. 8. edit. Savil. 1612. pag. 236. Ἐχειροτόνησε δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐπὶ ἐπισκόπους, καὶ πάσῃ ἀρετῇ ἀρχιερέων καὶ διακόνων ὡς τὸ ἱππι- κὸν, πῶς ὄχλοις εἰς λειτουργίαν ἐκκλησίας, καὶ θυσίας ἱερὰν καὶ ἀναίμακτον. Ἠμερ- ώσατο αὐτοῖς, καὶ κανόνας ψαλμῳδίας, ἐνδιδοὺς αὐτοῖς καὶ τὴν θείαν μυσταγωγίαν. Ἴνα γὰρ χρὴ χειν Θεοῦ πρὸς ὅς αὐτῶν ὑπεσημαίνει τὴν ἰλλυρίδα γλῶσσαν, καὶ παραξιλάσιν αὐτοῦ μεταφράσαι τῷ νόμῳ διαθήκῃ καὶ τὸ ψαλτήριον τῇ ἰδίᾳ αὐτῶν διαλέκτῳ, ὅπως γνῶσιν λόγιον ἡ θείας χάριτος. Παρέλαβε δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐκμανθάνειν τὸ ψαλτήριον ἵνα ἐν τῇ ἀμάρτων αὐτοῦ ἀδῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, εἰπὼν ὡς χρὴ μιᾷ καὶ τῷ παλαιῷ διαθήκῃ ἐρμηνεῦσαι ἔχειν ὑμῖν. Ordinavit illis septem Episcopos, Presbyterorum vero ac Diaconorum ingentem numerum; tot scilicet quot sufficerent populo ad ecclesiastica officia peragenda & sacrosanctum incruentumque sacrificium obeundum. Tradidit illis insuper & Psalmodia regulas, data etiam mystagogia divina. Invenit enim largiente Deo quosdam ex eis Graece scientes; quos Novum Testamentum & Psalterium in vernaculam ipsorum linguam convertere effecit; uti notitiam S.Scriptura obtinerent: Illis etiam mandavit Psalterium edisseere; ut ex Canticis illius in Ecclesiis cantarent: Subjiciens, illorum officii esse, ut saltem partem Veteris Testamenti in vernaculam linguam transferrent.
units.tr: a On Paradise, part 1, ch. 28. b Asiatic letter. c Paradigm of the Armenian language, p. 73. d On the Greek Bibles, p. 8. e On the Life of Chrysostom, §59, vol. 8, Savile edition, 1612, p. 236. He ordained for them seven bishops, and a great number of presbyters and deacons, as many as were sufficient for the people to carry out the ecclesiastical offices and the holy and unbloody sacrifice. He also gave them rules for psalmody, and imparted to them the divine mystagogy. For, since it was necessary for them to have the word of God, and he had found some of them who knew Greek, he had the New Testament and the Psalter turned into their own language, so that they might gain knowledge of the divine grace. He also charged them to learn the Psalter by heart, that they might sing its songs in the churches, saying that it was their duty to translate at least part of the Old Testament into their vernacular language. [Ἐχειροτόνησε δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐπισκόπους ἑπτά, καὶ πρεσβυτέρων καὶ διακόνων πλῆθος ὡς ἂν ἀρκέσαι τῷ λαῷ εἰς τὴν λειτουργίαν τῆς ἐκκλησίας καὶ θυσίαν ἱερὰν καὶ ἀναίμακτον. Ἐδωκε δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ κανόνας ψαλμῳδίας, ἐνδοὺς αὐτοῖς καὶ τὴν θείαν μυσταγωγίαν. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἔδει αὐτοὺς ἔχειν τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ, εὗρε τινας ἐξ αὐτῶν Ἑλληνίζοντας, καὶ ἐποίησε τὸν Νόμον καὶ τὴν Καινὴν Διαθήκην καὶ τὸ ψαλτήριον μεταφράσαι εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν διάλεκτον, ὅπως γνῶσιν λάβωσι τῆς θείας χάριτος. Παρήγγειλε δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ μανθάνειν τὸ ψαλτήριον, ἵνα ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ἄδωσι τὰς ᾠδὰς αὐτοῦ, λέγων ὅτι χρὴ καὶ μέρος τι τῆς Παλαιᾶς Διαθήκης εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν γλῶσσαν ἑρμηνεῦσαι.]

units.la: Hinc manifeste patet, quàm parum fidei mercatur Græculi cujusdam Relatio de origine errorum Armeniacorum; quam in MS. quodam Codice Bibliothecæ Bavaricæ se repetisse prodit, atque exinde ista citat Gretserus in Defensione, cap. 15. lib. 2. Bellarmini, col. 881. Βασιλεὺς Ῥωμαίων Θεοδόσιος, καὶ Περσῶν Βραμσάπος, μὴ εὐεξηγούμεναι τῶν ἐν Ἀρμενίᾳ λαλεῖν Ῥωμαϊκὴ ἢ γράμματα εἰδέναι, ἀνάγκη τινὲς ἀπὸ τῆς διατάξεως τῆς μεγάλης Γενηρεῖα, καὶ μεταφράσαι ἑαυτοῖς ἑρμηνεῖαι ψαλμῳδίαν καὶ γράμματα καὶ μελῳδίας. ὅπως μαθὼν Θεοδόσιος ὁ βασιλεὺς, ἐγερθὴν Ἀρμενίοις διὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῆς ἁγίας Γενηρείας παραδόσεων. Imperante Theodosio, & regnante apud Persas Bramsapo, cum nulli in Armenia reperirentur, qui Romanam (ita Graecam linguam vocat Author, ut notat Gretserus, quia Imperatores Constantinopolitani nominabant se Romanos Imperatores, quibus ipsa Constantinopolis erat Nova Roma) linguam perspectam haberent; extiterunt nonnulli, qui contra formam à magno Gregorio (Armeniæ Episcopo) prescriptam, sibimetipsis Armeniacâ linguâ Psalmos & literas & cantiones transtulerunt. Quod audiens Theodosius Imperator, valde succensuit Armenis; eò quòd traditionem à Sancto Gregorio acceptam violássent. Narrat deinde Author, quomodo quidam ex Armenis ad Theodosium profecti ejusdem animum mitigare studuerint; & inter cætera etiam hoc promiserint, se nunquam amplius ab Ecclesiâ Catholicâ & Apostolicâ secessionem facturos; semperque Romanam, h. e. Græcam linguam retenturos, διὰ τὸ τὸν ταύτην, ἡγὴν πρὸ ἡμῶν Ῥωμαίων μελῳδίαν ἀγγελικὴν ὡς ἀχρίτον, διὰ τὸ μὴ ἀνάξιος τῶν ἡμετέρων παχύτητα αὐτῶν εἶναι ταύτῃ: Quod hæc, h. e. Romana seu Græca melodia sit angelica & cœlestis; quam rusticitate nostrâ nequaquam assequi aut æquare liceat. Addit Gretserus: En quanti referre arbitrati sunt Græci, ut divina officia Græcâ linguâ celebrarentur! Et tamen schismaticus Balsamo (vid. supra an. 1194.) omnibus nationibus sacra vernaculè peragendi largam potestatem facit. Hactenus Gretserus: Quasi verò minor esset Balsamonis Patriarchæ, quàm alterius nescio cujus Græculi authoritas. Sed consule de Armeniis graviores utriusque Authores supra commemoratos, anno 450. in Theodoreto, & 490. in Sabâ. Nihil etiam tale de Armenis in Nicone & Euthymio legimus, neque in Actis Gregorii Armeni apud Metaphrastem: immo contrarium potiùs, ut ostenditur pag. 9.
units.tr: Hence it is plain how little credit deserves the account of a certain little Greek on the origin of the Armenian errors. He professes to have copied it from a manuscript codex of the Bavarian Library, and Gretser cites it from there in his Defence of Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 15, col. 881. [Βασιλεὺς Ῥωμαίων Θεοδόσιος, καὶ Περσῶν Βραμσάπος ...] In the reign of the Emperor Theodosius and of Bramsapo among the Persians, when no one in Armenia could be found who spoke or knew the Roman language (the author so calls Greek, as Gretser notes, because the Constantinopolitan emperors called themselves Roman emperors, and Constantinople itself was the New Rome), some men arose who, contrary to the form prescribed by the great Gregory, Bishop of Armenia, translated the Psalms, the letters and the chants into their own Armenian tongue by themselves. When the Emperor Theodosius heard this, he was greatly angered with the Armenians, because they had violated the tradition received from Saint Gregory. The author then relates how some of the Armenians went to Theodosius and tried to soothe his temper, and among other things promised that they would never again secede from the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and that they would always keep the Roman, that is the Greek, language, because this Roman or Greek melody is angelic [ἀγγελικὴν] and heavenly, and it is not possible for our rusticity to reach or equal it. Gretser adds: See how much the Greeks thought it mattered that the divine offices be celebrated in the Greek language! And yet the schismatic Balsamon (see above, year 1194) gives all nations a wide power of performing the sacred rites in their own vernaculars. So far Gretser. As if the authority of the Patriarch Balsamon were less than that of some Greek whom I do not know! But consult the weightier authors of both sides on the Armenians, mentioned above: under the year 450 in Theodoret, and under 490 in Sabas. We read nothing of the kind about the Armenians in Nicon or Euthymius, nor in the Acts of Gregory the Armenian in Metaphrastes; rather the contrary, as is shown on page 9.

units.la: Apostolorum temporibus sacrum Prophetiarum contextum idiomate Æthiopico in manibus Eunuchi Reginæ Candacis conscriptum extitisse pronuntiat Petrus Victor Cajetanus . Et nostris quidem temporibus Johannes Potken, præpositus Ecclesiæ S. Georgii Coloniensis, Psalterium linguâ Æthiopicâ (quam ille Chaldaicam falsò putavit, sicut ostendunt Munsterus , Postellus , & Theseus Ambrosius , excudendum anno 1518. curavit: Quo nunc utuntur Monachi Æthiopes, qui se Indos appellant; ipsumque in templo, quod Romæ habent, publicè decantant, (ut refert Sixtus Senensis .) Hinc Paulus Jovius , Abissinæ linguæ, inquit, Chaldaicis elementis scripta sacros libros Romæ impressos videmus; quos Abissini religionis causâ ab Hierosolymis Romam venientes, pro insigni miraculo in patriam deferre solent. Petrus etiam Æthiops Monachus, an. 1548. idiomate Æthiopico imprimendum curavit Testamentum Novum (cum Epistolâ Pauli ad Hebræos tantùm) & Missale cum benedictione incensi, ceræ, &c. Sed pessimâ fide Æthiopum libros traductos esse & mendosissimè affirmat Josephus Scaliger : Malam, inquit, fidem interpretum agnoscas in Epistolis Pauli; in quibus vix tria commata continua reperias, in quibus aut verba aut mens Apostoli reddita sint. Evangeliorum & Psalmorum translationes habent omnes varias lectiones, quæ ultimis temporibus in textum sacræ Scripturæ irrepserunt. Quod quidem pate-
units.tr: Petrus Victor Cajetanus asserts that in the times of the Apostles the sacred text of the Prophecies existed, written in the Ethiopic language, in the hands of the eunuch of Queen Candace. In our own times Johannes Potken, provost of the Church of Saint George at Cologne, had the Psalter printed in 1518 in the Ethiopic language, which he falsely thought was Chaldean, as Münster, Postel and Theseus Ambrosius show. The Ethiopian monks, who call themselves Indians, now use it and publicly chant it in the church they have at Rome, as Sixtus of Siena reports. Hence Paulus Jovius: We see the sacred books of the Abyssinian language, written in Chaldean letters, printed at Rome; the Abyssinians, coming to Rome from Jerusalem for religious reasons, are accustomed to carry them home as a remarkable wonder. Also Peter the Ethiopian, a monk, had the New Testament (with only the Epistle to the Hebrews) and the Missal, with the blessing of incense, wax, etc., printed in the Ethiopic language in 1548. But Joseph Scaliger affirms that the books of the Ethiopians were translated with very bad faith and most corruptly: You may recognise the bad faith of the translators in the Epistles of Paul, in which you will scarcely find three continuous verses in which either the words or the meaning of the Apostle are rendered. The translations of the Gospels and Psalms have all the variant readings which in recent times have crept into the text of Holy Scripture. This indeed

units.la: v Paradigm. ling. Æthiop. x Grammat. Chaldaic. y Alphabet. 12. linguar. z Introduct. in lingu. Chaldaic. sol. 13, 14. a Biblioth. Sanct. lib. 4. b Hist. lib. 18. pag. 218. c Lib. 7. de Emendat. temp. in Computo Æthiop. facit nuperam eorum tam translationem sacrorum librorum quàm profes-sionem Christianismi. Acta sanè Apostolorum, quæ Romæ edita sunt, ex vulgari Italico conversa esse, tametsi is, qui edidit, non testatus esset, tamen ex innumeris locis id & puero colligere haud difficile fuerit. (Hactenus Scaliger.) Chrysostomus tamen homil. 1. in Evang. Johan. indicat Æthiopas, sicut & Persas, Indos ac Ægyptios, libros sacros suâ linguâ jam tum habuisse.
units.tr: v Paradigm. ling. Æthiop. x Grammat. Chaldaic. y Alphabet. 12. linguar. z Introduct. in lingu. Chaldaic. sol. 13, 14. a Biblioth. Sanct. lib. 4. b Hist. lib. 18. pag. 218. c Lib. 7. de Emendat. temp. in Computo Æthiop. shows the recent translation of the sacred books, as well as their profession of Christianity. Indeed, that the Acts of the Apostles, published at Rome, were translated from the common Italian, although the editor did not attest it, may easily be gathered even by a boy from countless passages. (So far Scaliger.) Yet Chrysostom, in Homily 1 on the Gospel of John, indicates that the Ethiopians, like the Persians, Indians and Egyptians, already had the sacred books in their own language.

units.la: Psalterium Ægyptiacum in lucem se editurum promisit Scaliger. (Si Sibrando Lubberto credimus.) P. Victor Cajetanus d asserit sibi præ manibus esse exemplar Ægyptiacum manuscriptum, continens B. Pauli Epistolas, quod Clemens VIII. Papa Ebroicensi Episcopo commodavit. Ibidemque ait, se cum Thoma suo Armeno, Arabico Novo Testamento & Persico quotidie operam dare, Quatuor Evangelistas Romæ linguâ Persicâ excudendos fuisse testatur Possevinus e. Albertus Widmanstadius in Præfatione Novi Testamenti Syriaci ad Ferdinandum Cæsarem; & post eum Guido Fabricius in Præfatione Testamenti Syriaci ad Henricum III. Francorum Regem, meminit Arabicæ versionis librorum veteris Testamenti Sahadiæ Gaonis, itemque Persicæ Jacobi Tarvasi Pavonis. Et quidem apud Franciscum Raphelengium, Hebraicæ linguæ Lugduni Batavorum Professorem, extat R. Saadiæ Quadrilingue Pentateuchum; in quo est Persica interpretatio, sed Hebraicis characteribus conscripta; unde initium Geneseos transscripsit Bon. Vulcanius in Specimine linguæ Persicæ (ad calcem Commentarioli de literis & linguâ Getarum, pag. 87.) Denique Persicam editionem Pentateuchi excusam fuisse in Urbe Constantinopolitanâ, unà cum Arabicâ, characteribus Hebraicis, fidem facit Drusius de Tetragrammato, cap. 15.
units.tr: Scaliger promised to publish an Egyptian Psalter (if we believe Sibrandus Lubbertus). Father Victor Cajetanus asserts that he has before him a manuscript Egyptian copy containing the Epistles of blessed Paul, which Pope Clement VIII lent to the Bishop of Évreux. In the same place he says that he daily works with his Armenian Thomas on the Arabic New Testament and the Persian. Possevinus testifies that the Four Evangelists were to be printed at Rome in the Persian language. Albert Widmanstadt, in the Preface to the Syriac New Testament addressed to Emperor Ferdinand, and after him Guy Fabricius, in the Preface to the Syriac Testament addressed to Henry III, King of the French, mention an Arabic version of the books of the Old Testament by Saadiah Gaon, and likewise a Persian one by Jacob Tarvasus Pavo. Indeed, at Franciscus Raphelengius's, professor of Hebrew at Leiden, there exists a Quadrilingual Pentateuch of R. Saadiah, in which there is a Persian translation written in Hebrew characters; from it Bonaventura Vulcanius transcribed the beginning of Genesis in his Specimen of the Persian language (at the end of his little commentary on the letters and language of the Getae, p. 87). Finally, Drusius, On the Tetragrammaton, chapter 15, assures us that a Persian edition of the Pentateuch was printed in Constantinople, together with an Arabic one, in Hebrew characters.

units.la: Arabica versio libri Geneseos cum Commentariis eâdem linguâ scriptis manuscripta apud me extat: Sed quam aliam esse à R. Saadiæ Paraphrasi tum ex Commentariis apparet, quos abhomine Christiano scriptos esse constat; tum ex ipsâ Versione, quæ non Hebraicam veritatem, sed Græcam interpretationem tum alibitum Geneseos 5. & 11. sequitur. (Vid. supra in anno 740.) Psalterium Arabicum in Octaplo suo edidit Augustinus Justinianus Nebiensis Episcopus ex editione, quam Syram vocat; alterius etiam Arabicæ, quam Ægyptiam appellat, subinde mentionem faciens,
units.tr: I have by me a manuscript Arabic version of the book of Genesis, with commentaries written in the same language. But that it is other than the Paraphrase of R. Saadiah appears both from the commentaries, which are known to have been written by a Christian, and from the version itself, which follows not the Hebrew truth but the Greek interpretation, at Genesis 5 and 11 (see above, under the year 740). Augustinus Justinianus, Bishop of Nebbio, published the Arabic Psalter in his Octapla, from the edition which he calls Syriac, and from time to time he also mentions another Arabic one, which he calls Egyptian,

units.la: d Paradigm. lingu. Armen. pag. 73.
units.tr: d Paradigm. lingu. Armen. p. 73.

units.la: e Biblioth. select. lib. 9. cap. 8. (ut in Psal. 81, 84, & 116. juxta Hebræos) sicut & Theseus Ambrosius in suâ Introductione. Sunt etiam penes me duo MSS. exemplaria alterius versionis Arabicæ Psalterii: Secundùm quam Psalmum 50. anno 1595. edidit Fr. Raphelengius in specimine characterum Arabicorum officinæ Plantinianæ. Evangelia IV. Arabica Romæ ex magni Hetruriæ Ducis typographiâ elegantissimis typis excusa prodierunt. Acto rum etiam Apostolorum, & Epistolarum Pauli editio parabatur. (Possevinus, lib. 9. Biblioth. select. cap. 8.) Acta Apostolorum & Epistolas duas ad Corinthios ex Arabico transtulit Fr. Junius. Epistolam ad Galatas Arabicè edidit Ruthgerus Spey Bopardianus. Ex Psalterio, Evangelio Matthæi, Actis Apostolorum, Epistolis Pauli, Petri, Jacobi, Joannis & Judæ, itemque Geneseos 18. prioribus capitibus Arabicis Lexicon collectum est Wittebergæ, anno 1585. (cujus meminit Christoph. Hammer. in Epist. de Elianis Bibliis, pag. 74.) In Evangelia tres diversos Paraphrastas Arabas se habere testatur Josephus Scaliger . Augustinus Justinianus Nebiensis Episcopus universum Vetus Testamentum linguâ Hebræâ, Latinâ, Græcâ, Arabicâ & Chaldæâ editurus erat; & Novum quidem Testamentum absolutum fuisse, Vetus autem brevi futurum paratum affirmat ipse in Epist. ad Bendinellum de Saulis Cardinal. Ex quo opere præter Psalterium, quod typis excusum extat, in universa IV. Evangelia Octaplum, ipsa Authoris manu, atramento minioque descriptum se vidisse ait Sixtus Senensis . Romæ etiam in Collegio Maronitarum Vetus Testamentum Arabicum ex Oriente advectum conservari testatur Georgius Amira . Psalterium Syriacum, interpretatione Arabicâ (vulgari sc.) singulis verbis Syriacis inter binas lineas interjectâ, penès se fuisse indicat Josephus Scaliger . Arabicam verò linguam in universâ penè Asiâ & Africâ usurpari nos docet Jacobus Navarchus Hondischotanus . Arabica Rabbi Sahadiæ Haggaon translatio (inquit Rob. Wakseldus in disputat. de fratris uxore non ducendâ, præhixa Syntagmati de Hebræorum Codicum incorruptione) in Africa ubique legitur; eamque Hebræorum peritissimi sequuntur ac allegant tanquam authenticam, utpote ab homine literarum & traditionum atque rerum
units.tr: e Biblioth. select. lib. 9. cap. 8. (as in Psalms 81, 84 and 116, according to the Hebrews), and likewise Theseus Ambrosius in his Introduction. I also have two manuscript copies of another Arabic version of the Psalter. According to it Fr. Raphelengius published Psalm 50 in 1595, in a specimen of Arabic characters from the Plantin press. Four Arabic Gospels were issued at Rome, printed in very elegant type from the press of the Grand Duke of Tuscany. An edition of the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of Paul was also being prepared. (Possevinus, lib. 9 Biblioth. select., cap. 8.) Fr. Junius translated the Acts of the Apostles and two Epistles to the Corinthians from the Arabic. Ruthgerus Spey of Bopard edited the Epistle to the Galatians in Arabic. From the Psalter, the Gospel of Matthew, the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles of Paul, Peter, James, John and Jude, and also the first eighteen chapters of Genesis in Arabic, a Lexicon was compiled at Wittenberg in 1585 (which Christoph Hammer mentions in his letter On the Elian Bibles, p. 74). Joseph Scaliger testifies that for the Gospels there are three different Arab paraphrasts. Augustinus Justinianus, Bishop of Nebbio, was going to publish the whole Old Testament in Hebrew, Latin, Greek, Arabic and Chaldean; he himself affirms in his letter to Bendinelli on Cardinal Sauli that the New Testament was finished, and that the Old Testament would soon be ready. Besides the Psalter, which is extant in print, Sixtus of Siena says that he saw from this work the Octapla of all four Gospels, written out in the author's own hand with ink and red lead. Georgius Amira testifies that an Arabic Old Testament brought from the East is kept at Rome in the College of the Maronites. Joseph Scaliger indicates that he possessed a Syriac Psalter with an Arabic (that is, vernacular) interpretation placed between the lines beside each Syriac word. Jacob Navarchus of Hondschoote teaches us that the Arabic language is used in almost all of Asia and Africa. The Arabic translation of Rabbi Saadiah Haggaon (says Robert Wakeley in his dispute On Not Taking a Brother's Wife, prefixed to the Syntagma on the incorruption of the Hebrew codices) is read everywhere in Africa; and the most skilled of the Hebrews follow and cite it as authentic, as coming from a man of letters and of traditions and of things

units.la: f De emendat. temp. lib. 4. p. 225. edit. ult. g Apud Gesnerum, tom. 1. Biblioth. in Augustino Justiniano. h Biblioth. Sanct. lib. 4. i Prælud. de linguæ Chald. antiquitate, præfix G. ammaucæ suæ. k Canon. Isagog. lib. 3. pag. 264. l Epist. Asiatic. Hebraicarum peritissimo profectam. Sed de versionibus in linguâ Arabicâ editis (quæ quàm late pateat, Postellum consulce in Introduct. 12. linguar. & Præfat. in Grammat. Arabic. & Waserum de nummis) plus satis. Vid. supra ad an. 740. 936. 1040. & 1179.
units.tr: f On the Emendation of Time, book 4, p. 225, last edition. g In Gesner, vol. 1 of the Bibliotheca, under Augustinus Justinianus. h Bibliotheca Sanctorum, book 4. i Prelude on the antiquity of the Chaldean language, prefixed to his grammar. k Canon, Isagoge, book 3, p. 264. l Asiatic letter, sent by a most skilled Hebrew scholar. But concerning the versions published in the Arabic language (how widely these extend, consult Postel in the Introduction to the twelve languages and in the Preface to his Arabic Grammar, and Waserus on coins), there is more than enough. See above under the years 740, 936, 1040 and 1179.

units.la: Transtulit Hieronymus, ut ipsemet in epistola ad Sophronium testatur, universum totius Scripturæ Corpus in Dalmaticam linguam, ad utilitatem nationis suæ gentium; quæ usque in hanc diem hujus translationis lectione summâ cum veneratione utuntur (Sixtus Senensis, lib. 4. Biblioth. Sanct. in Hieronymo.) Vid. Bibliandrum de ratione communi omnium linguarum, p. 15. & Angelum à Roccha in Append. Biblioth. Vatic. pag. 337, 339. præcipuè Dubravium, lib. 1. Histor. Bohem. pag. 4. Illyricam versionem olim edidisse traditur, ille summâ eruditione & sanctitate celeberrimus Ecclesiæ Doctor Hieronymus; inquit P. Galesinius de Bibliis Græcis, p. 8. Ita Erasmus in Apologiâ adversus Sutorem, tom. 9. Operum, pag. 630. & Hosius in Dialogo de sacro vernaculè legendo, constare dicunt Dalmaticâ linguâ sacros libros Hieronymum vertisse. Et Alphonsus de Castro, lib. 1. hæres. cap. 15. Fatemur (inquit) olim sacros libros in linguam vulgarem fuisse translatos, Beatumque Hieronymum in linguam Dalmaticam eos vertisse [Quanquam in illâ ad Sophronium Epistolâ, quæ est 134. per linguæ suæ homines Latinos potiùs intelligere videatur, quàm Dalmatas; ut in procem. lib. 3. in Hier. & in 6. & 10. Zachar. &c.] Receptæ tamen opinioni favet Josephus Scaliger in literis anno 1599. scriptis ad Paulum Merulam; ubi in linguâ Sclavonicâ duplicem haberi sacrorum librorum Translationem scribit, Rutenicam recentiorem, & Hieronymianam vetustiorem.
units.tr: Jerome translated, as he himself testifies in his letter to Sophronius, the whole body of Scripture into the Dalmatian language, for the benefit of the nation of his own people; and to this day they use the reading of this translation with the greatest veneration (Sixtus of Siena, book 4 of the Bibliotheca Sanctorum, under Jerome). See Bibliander, On the Common Reason of All Languages, p. 15, and Angelus a Rocca in the Appendix to the Vatican Library, pp. 337, 339, and especially Dubravius, book 1 of the Bohemian History, p. 4. It is said that the Illyrian version was once published by that most celebrated Doctor of the Church, Jerome, of the greatest learning and holiness, says P. Galesinius, On the Greek Bibles, p. 8. So Erasmus in his Apology against Sutor, vol. 9 of his Works, p. 630, and Hosius in his Dialogue on reading Scripture in the vernacular, say that it is established that Jerome translated the sacred books into the Dalmatian language. And Alphonsus de Castro, book 1 Against Heresies, ch. 15: We admit (he says) that the sacred books were once translated into the vulgar tongue, and that Blessed Jerome translated them into the Dalmatian language. [Although in that letter to Sophronius, which is letter 134, he seems rather to mean by "his own tongue" the Latin people and not the Dalmatians; as in the preface to book 3 on Hieronymus, and on Zechariah chapters 6 and 10, etc.] Nevertheless Josephus Scaliger, in a letter written in 1599 to Paulus Merula, favours the accepted opinion, where he writes that in the Slavonic language there are two translations of the sacred books: a more recent Ruthenian one and an older Hieronymian one.

units.la: Methodius vel Cyrillus in Sclavorum sermonem divina eloquia translulit (ut supra anno 860. ostensum est) Russi suâ linguâ habent Psalterium Davidis (quod apud Ostrocenses impressum est) Novum Testamentum (Acta Apostolorum, Pauli Epistolas omnes) ut est in Narratione de Religione eorum ad Dav. Chytræum anno 1581. scriptâ pag. 236. Theologiæ Moscoviticæ, an. 1582. editæ. Biblia Rutenica sive Moscovitica apud Eliam Hutterum se vidisse affirmat Adam Bohoriz (in Epistolâ de Bibliis Elianis, pag. 46.) & Biblia apud eundem tum Moscovitica tum Croatica linguâ extitisse apparet
units.tr: Methodius or Cyril translated the divine oracles into the Slavonic speech (as was shown above under the year 860). The Russians have the Psalter of David in their own language (printed at Ostrog), the New Testament (the Acts of the Apostles and all the Epistles of Paul), as is stated in the Account of their religion written to David Chytraeus in 1581, p. 236, of the Muscovite Theology published in 1582. Adam Bohoriz affirms that he saw a Russian or Muscovite Bible at Elias Hutter's (in his letter on the Bibles of Elias, p. 46), and it appears that there were Bibles in both Muscovite and Croatian at the same place.

units.la: Apud Merulam Cosmograph. par. 2. lib. 1. cap. 8.

units.la: Vid.
