Quàm latè verò pateat Sclavonica vel Illyrica lingua, consule Sigismundum liberum Baronem in Heberstein, initio Commentariorum rerum Moscoviticarum; Martinum Cromerum in Poloniae libro priore (tom. 1. Corporis Polonicae Historiae à Pistorio editae, pag. 85.) Matthium Michovium de Sarmatiâ, lib. 1. cap. 13. (ibid. pag. 134.) Hosium in Dialogo de sacro vernaculè legendo, Paulum Merulam in Cosmographiâ suâ, part. 2. pag. 271. praecipuè verò Angelum Roccham in Appendice Biblioth. Vatic. pag. 338.
units.tr: See Angelus a Rocca, loc. cit., from the specimen of the Polyglot Work (prefixed to vol. 1 of the Quadrilingual Bibles), and as several Psalms are found in a certain Euchologion, which is in my possession in manuscript (in Serbian or Illyrian letters). How widely the Slavonic or Illyrian language extends, consult Sigismund, Baron von Herberstein, at the beginning of his Commentaries on Muscovite affairs; Martin Cromer in the first book of his Poland (vol. 1 of the Corpus of Polish History edited by Pistorius, p. 85); Matthias Michovius, On Sarmatia, book 1, ch. 13 (ibid., p. 134); Hosius in his Dialogue on reading Scripture in the vernacular; Paulus Merula in his Cosmography, part 2, p. 271; and especially Angelus a Rocca in the Appendix to the Vatican Library, p. 338.

units.la: De Germanicis & Francicis versionibus jam ante dictum est, an. 807. 820. 850. 870. 1200. 1250. 1370. Germanicas Bibliorum versiones antiquiores Luthero agnoscit Gretserus in Defensione capitis 15. libri 2. Bellarmini de Verbo Dei, col. 806. Item col. 18. repetit Germanicâ linguâ extitisse integra Biblia aliquot ante annis quàm Lutherus nasceretur. Et col. 545. aliquot ante Lutherum natum annis Biblia in Germanicam linguam translata, typis etiam excusa fuisse. Francica Evangeliorum versio, quam habuit Beatus Rhenanus, à nostris nullo pacto intelligitur, [ut notat Pantaleon Theveninus ad cap. 1. Grammaticae Latino-Francicae] Harmoniae Evangelicae à Tatiano concinnatae vetustissimam interpretationem Teutonicam apud se extare affirmat Bonav. Vulcanius in Specimine veteris linguae Teutonicae (ad Calcem Commentarioli de literis & linguâ Getarum, pag. 54.) Ex vetere etiam Germanicâ Psalmorum versione versiculum proponit Elias Hutterus in Specimine Operis Polyglotti (praefixo tom. 1. Bibliorum Quadrilinguium) sicut etiam ex Hibernicâ [de quâ vid. supra an. 1358.] De Saxonicis & Anglicis versionibus vid. supra an. 670. 706. 730. bis 890. 930. 990. 1170. 1380. 1396. 1407. 1416. 1485. 1506. 1511. 1514. 1518. 1520. 1521. 1523. De Italicis, an. 1290. De Hispanicis an. 1425. 1440. 1450. 1515. Psalterium Scoticum & Gallicum Cantabrigiae in Bibliothecâ Collegii S. Benedicti, & partem Bibliorum Gallicorum (à Tobia) MS. in privatâ Bibliothecâ Gualteri Copi (jam distractâ) haberi notat Th. James in posteriore parte Eclogae suae pag. 60. His addere licet, quae Joannes Trevisa sacerdos in Dialogo praefixo Polychronico Ranulphi Cestrensis scribit Anglicè, Nosti etiam ubi loci Apocalypsis parietibus ac laqueari cujusdam Capella Latinè simul ac Gallicè inscribitur. Erasmus in Apologiis contra Beddam, Sutorem, & Parisienses, asserit; si quae constitutio prodita sit, prohibens ne laici libros sacros legant, non esse comprobatam usu publico. Jam olim enim à multis seculis haberi sacros libros in linguas vulgares diversarum gentium translatos, connivente ad id Ecclesiâ, & à populo palàm legi. Hinc Fridericus Furius in Bononiâ suo (pag. iii.) de Bibliis in vulgi linguam convertendis, ex communi omnium ferè Christianorum opinione argumentum deducit. Nam cùm jamdiu (inquit) haec agitari coepta sit opinio, fuerintque multi qui verti debere negarent; tacitus tamen Christianorum consensus approbavit, verti debere hoc ipso, quod sine discrimine ferè ubique jam versi ad promiscuam plebis utilitatem libri & imprimantur & vendantur & legantur. Habet enim Italia providens jam in suam linguam versos libros sacros, Gallia pia etiam in suam, Germania inferior etiam in suam. De Germaniâ superiori & Britanniâ, & Daniâ, & Poloniâ nihil dico: Quoniam & pueri sciunt, multis abhinc retro annis in suas quamque linguas scripturas sacras convertisse. Concludit demum semper habitos esse libros sacros in linguam vulgarem versos, & in Hispaniâ, & Galliâ, & Germaniâ, & Italiâ, & Britanniâ, & universâ Europâ; idque cùm ipsimet Pontifices & certò scirent, & suis oculis inspicerent. Quae opinio (inquit) i. e. ea quae affirmat libros sacros verti oportere, tantùm abest, ut successu temporis evanuerit; ut quotidie vehementius & certius multò confirmetur. Indies enim videas & plures vernaculos factos de Latinis libros imprimi & vendi & legi, & à pluribus etiam expeti, quàm fuerint & patrum & nostrâ memoriâ unquam. Hactenus Fridericus Furius, homo etiam Pontificius. Sic igitur hâc in re praxin Ecclesiae, & veteris Catholicae, & recentioris Pontificiae, vidimus. Unde falsum esse perspicitur, quod Rob. Bellarminus negat nostros editionem vernaculam Scripturarum, nisi à paucis annis factam, proferre posse. Desinat ergo mirari P. Victor Cajetanus, quid nostris in mentem venerit (quos Ecclesiae perturbatores appellat Apostata) quòd velint sacras Scripturas vulgari idiomate in omnium manus exponi. Siquidem mendacium impudentissimum, quod tenebrionem istum effutire non puduit, nullam unquam fuisse gentem, quae sacra sua cum vulgo haberet communia. Audiat Sixtum Senensem,
units.tr: German and French versions have already been mentioned above, under the years 807, 820, 850, 870, 1200, 1250 and 1370. Gretser acknowledges that the German versions of the Bible are older than Luther, in his Defence of ch. 15 of book 2 of Bellarmine, On the Word of God, col. 806. Likewise, at col. 18, he repeats that the whole Bible existed in German some years before Luther was born, and at col. 545 that Bibles translated into German, and even printed, existed some years before Luther's birth. The French version of the Gospels which Beatus Rhenanus had is by no means understood by our people [as Pantaleon Theveninus notes on ch. 1 of his Latin-French Grammar]. Bonaventura Vulcanius, in his Specimen of the Old Teutonic Language (at the end of his little commentary on the letters and language of the Getae, p. 54), affirms that he has the very ancient German translation of the Harmony of the Gospels composed by Tatian. Elias Hutter, in the Specimen of the Polyglot Work (prefixed to vol. 1 of the Quadrilingual Bibles), offers a verse from an old German version of the Psalms, as he does from the Irish [on which see above, under 1358]. On the Saxon and English versions see above, under the years 670, 706, 730, 890 (twice), 930, 990, 1170, 1380, 1396, 1407, 1416, 1485, 1506, 1511, 1514, 1518, 1520, 1521, 1523. On the Italian, see 1290; on the Spanish, 1425, 1440, 1450, 1515. Thomas James, in the latter part of his Eclogue, p. 60, notes that a Scottish and a French Psalter are held in the library of St Benedict's College at Cambridge, and part of a French Bible (from Tobias) in manuscript in the private library of Walter Cope (now dispersed). To these may be added what the priest John Trevisa writes in English in the dialogue prefixed to Ranulph of Chester's Polychronicon: You also know where, in the walls and ceiling of a certain chapel, the Apocalypse is inscribed in Latin and in French at once. Erasmus, in his Apologies against Beda, Sutor and the Parisians, asserts that if any decree has been issued forbidding laymen to read the sacred books, it has not been confirmed by public use. For for many centuries the sacred books have been held translated into the vulgar tongues of various nations, with the Church conniving at this, and read openly by the people. Hence Friedrich Furius, in his book from Bologna (p. iii), on translating the Bible into the speech of the common people, draws his argument from the general opinion of almost all Christians. For although this opinion (he says) has been debated for a long time, and there have been many who denied that the books ought to be translated, yet the silent consent of Christians has approved it, by the very fact that books translated almost everywhere without distinction are now printed, sold and read for the shared benefit of the people. For Italy already has the sacred books translated into its own tongue, pious France into its own, and lower Germany into its own. About upper Germany, Britain, Denmark and Poland I say nothing, since even boys know that many years ago they turned the Scriptures into their own languages. Finally he concludes that sacred books translated into the vulgar tongue have always been held in Spain, France, Germany, Italy, Britain and all of Europe, and this both the Pontiffs themselves knew for certain and saw with their own eyes. This opinion (he says), that is, the one affirming that the sacred books ought to be translated, is so far from having faded with time that it is daily confirmed more vehemently and more certainly. For every day you may see more books translated from Latin into the vernacular printed, sold, read, and sought by more people than were ever known in the memory of the Fathers or of ours. So far Furius, himself a Papist. Thus we have seen the practice of the Church in this matter, both of the ancient Catholic Church and of the more recent Papists. From this it is clear that what Robert Bellarmine denies is false: that ours can produce a vernacular edition of Scripture made only a few years ago. Let P. Victor Cajetan therefore cease to wonder what has come into the minds of our people (whom the apostate calls disturbers of the Church), that they want the Holy Scriptures set out in the common idiom in everyone's hands. For that most shameless lie, which that dark fellow was not ashamed to babble, that there never was any nation that held its sacred books in common with the people, is refuted. Let him hear Sixtus of Siena.

units.la: ° Tom. 9. Operum, pag. 377. 629. & 703. · P De Sacram. in genere lib. 2. cap. 31. q In Paradigm. ling. Armen. p. 59. Senensem, lib. 6. Biblioth. Sanct. Annot. 152. Fatemur nos (inquit ille) quondam sacros libros vulgari idiomate redditos magna Christiane fidei propagatione. At nunc id ipsum fieri non omnino expedit; quando certissimo experimento cognovimus plurimam simplicium turbam ex hac occasione in detestabiles & irremeabiles errores corruisse. Ecce habemus confitentes reos; Ecclesiam Romanam a veteris Catholicae consuetudine recessisse; quippe jam experimento sapientiorem factam. Ita & Azorius Jesuita de Hieronymi & Chrysostomi aetate agens, Nos libenter (inquit) fatemur tunc temporis Laicos in scripturarum lectione fuisse versatos; quia sacra eloquia erant Graeco vel Latino sermone conscripta; quem sermonem vulgus quoque callebat. Nunc vero plebs fere rudis est, & imperita Latini sermonis. At Laici, qui Graece vel Latine noverunt, Scripturas jure optimo legitant. Hactenus Azorius; qui quidem Bellarmino maxime adversatur: iste enim statum quaestionis in eo situm dicit, Utrum legendae sint Scripturae, non, Utrum Translationes.
units.tr: ° Tom. 9. Operum, pag. 377. 629. & 703. · P De Sacram. in genere lib. 2. cap. 31. q In Paradigm. ling. Armen. p. 59. Senensem, lib. 6. Biblioth. Sanct. Annot. 152. We admit, he says, that the sacred books were once rendered into the vernacular, to the great spread of the Christian faith. But now this very thing is not at all advisable, since we have learned by most certain experience that a great crowd of simple people has fallen, on this occasion, into detestable and irreversible errors. Here we have men confessing their guilt: the Roman Church has departed from the old Catholic custom, having now become wiser by experience. So too Azorius the Jesuit, speaking of the age of Jerome and Chrysostom: We gladly admit, he says, that at that time the laity were conversant with reading the Scriptures, because the holy oracles were written in Greek or Latin, a language which the common people also understood. But now the plebs is almost uneducated and unskilled in Latin. Yet laymen who know Greek or Latin read the Scriptures with the best right. Thus far Azorius; who indeed is strongly opposed to Bellarmine, for Bellarmine says the state of the question lies in this: whether the Scriptures are to be read, not whether translations are.

units.la: In vetere Ecclesiâ nulli hominum generi Scripturarum lectione interdictum est.
units.tr: In the early Church no class of people was forbidden the reading of Scripture.

units.la: DE Imperatoribus ac Regibus Christianis illud in præcedentibus declaratum est, quibus addere licet Theodosii senioris conjugem Placillam Augustam (quæ divinas leges eum sæpius admonebat, seipsam tamen priùs erudiens perfecte, uti habet Historia Miscella ?) Leonem Philosophum Imp. studiosum Scripturarum; uti constat ex Homiliis ejus à Jac. Gretsero editis: Bathildim uxorem Clodovæi Francorum Regis, quæ (facta monialis) divinam lectionem sæpius frequentabat; ut estn Vitâ ejus ab æquali ejus scriptâ: & Dagobertum Francorum Regem; qui voluit, ut S. Amandus filium Sigebertum recèns natum enutriret, atque lege imbueret divinâ, ut in vitâ Sigeberti Author est Sigebertus Gemblacensis v. Sed & in Ethnicis & hæreticis Imperatoribus studium illud comprobatum est. (1) Non dubito (inquit Athenagoras in Apologiâ pro Christianis ad Imperatores Antoninum & Commodum) quin vos doctissimi & sapientissimi principes, historias & Scripta Moisis, Esaiæ, Hieremiæ, & reliquorum aliquâ ex parte cognoveritis. Et paulò post: (2) Sed vobis relinquo, qui libros novistis, studiosiùs in illorum Prophetias inquirere ac perpendere. Nec minùs in Constantio Imperatore Ariano illud celebravit Athanasius (initio suæ ad eundem Apologiæ) quod (3) Verborum B. Pauli dilgens fuisset auscultator.
units.tr: What has been declared in the preceding pages about Christian emperors and kings may be confirmed by adding the empress Placilla, wife of the elder Theodosius, who, as the Historia Miscella has it, often admonished him in divine laws while herself being perfectly instructed first; the emperor Leo the Philosopher, a devoted student of the Scriptures, as is clear from his Homilies edited by Jacob Gretser; Bathildis, wife of Clovis, king of the Franks, who, after becoming a nun, frequently read the divine lessons, as her Life written by a contemporary says; and Dagobert, king of the Franks, who wished that St Amandus should bring up his newly born son Sigebert and imbue him with divine law, as Sigebert of Gembloux, the author of the Life of Sigebert, relates. But this zeal has also been approved in pagan and heretical emperors. (1) "I do not doubt," says Athenagoras in his Apology for the Christians addressed to the emperors Antoninus and Commodus, "that you, most learned and wisest princes, have to some extent come to know the histories and writings of Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest." And a little later: (2) "But I leave it to you, who know the books, to inquire into and weigh their prophecies more diligently." Athanasius likewise praised the Arian emperor Constantius for this, saying (at the beginning of his Apology addressed to him) that he had been (3) "a diligent listener to the words of the blessed Paul."

units.la: (1) Νομίζω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἐκ ἀπόντος γεγονέναι ἐπὶ τῆς Μωϊσέως ἐπὶ τῆς Ησαΐου καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν προφητῶν. (2) Καταλείπω δὲ ὑμῖν, ἐπ' αὐτῶν τῆς βιβλίων γραμμάτων, ἀκριβέστερον τὰς ἐκδοτιν ἐξετάσαι σπουδῆς. (3) Τῶν ἁγίων ἡμῶν Παύλου φιλήκοον. ait Simplicianus, sanctam Scripturam, omnesque Christianas literas investigabat studiosissimè & perscrutabatur; & dicebat Simpliciano, non palam, sed secretiùs & familariùs: Noveris me jam esse Christianum. Sed ubi mihi (inquit Augustinus, cap. 5.) homo tuus Simplicianus de Victorino ista narravit; exarsi ad imitandum. Ad hoc enim & ille narraverat. Posteaquam verò & illud addidit, quòd Imperatoris Juliani temporibus lege datâ prohibiti sunt Christiani docere literaturam & oratoriam; quam legem ille amplexus, loquacem scholam deserere maluit quàm verbum tuum, quo linguas infantium facis disertas; non mihi fortior quàm felicior visus est, quia invenit occasionem vacandi tibi. Et cap. 6. de seipso & Politiano (quem ut praeclarè in Palatio militantem commendat) loquens: Consedimus, inquit, ut colloqueremur; & fortè supra mensam lusoriam, quae ante nos erat, attendit codicem, tulit, aperuit, invenit Apostolum Paulum, inopinatè sanè; putaverat enim aliquid de libris, quorum professio me conterebat. Tum verò arridens meque intuens, gratulatoriè miratus est, quòd eas & solas pra oculis meis literas repentè comperisset. Christianus quippe & fidelis erat, & saepe tibi Deo nostro prosternebatur in Ecclesiâ crebris & diuturnis orationibus. Cui ego cùm indicassem illis me scripturis curam maximam impendere, ortus est sermo ipso narrante de Antonio, &c. Hactenus Augustinus, qui etiam cap. 12. indicat se post hunc sermonem cum Alypio in hortulum concessisse; ubi cum codicem Apostoli aperuisset, & legisset illud, Rom. XIII. Non in comessationibus & ebrietatibus, &c. Statim, inquit, cum sine hujusce sententiae quasi luce securitatis infusâ cordi meo, omnes dubitationis tenebrae dissugerunt. Haec Augustinus de conversione suâ, (à Manichaeorum haeresi ad fidem orthodoxam) historiam narrans.
units.tr: (1) "For I think you were present in spirit at the time of Moses, Isaiah and the other prophets" [Νομίζω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἐκ ἀπόντος γεγονέναι ἐπὶ τῆς Μωϊσέως ἐπὶ τῆς Ησαΐου καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν προφητῶν]. (2) "But I leave it to you, who have the books themselves, to examine their teaching with more exact zeal" [Καταλείπω δὲ ὑμῖν, ἐπ' αὐτῶν τῆς βιβλίων γραμμάτων, ἀκριβέστερον τὰς ἐκδοτιν ἐξετάσαι σπουδῆς]. (3) "a listener to our holy Paul" [Τῶν ἁγίων ἡμῶν Παύλου φιλήκοον]. Simplicianus says that Victorinus investigated and studied the holy Scripture and all Christian writings most eagerly, and said to Simplicianus, not openly but more privately and familiarly: "Know that I am now a Christian." But when your man Simplicianus told me these things about Victorinus, says Augustine in chapter 5, I was fired with a desire to imitate him. For he had told me this too. But when he added that under the emperor Julian a law had been issued forbidding Christians to teach literature and rhetoric, and that Victorinus embraced this law and preferred to give up his talkative school rather than your Word, by which you make the tongues of infants eloquent, he seemed to me not braver but happier, because he had found an opportunity to be free for you. And in chapter 6, speaking of himself and of Ponticianus (whom he commends as a man serving brilliantly at court): We sat down to talk, he says, and by chance he noticed on the game table which lay before us a book; he took it up, opened it and found the Apostle Paul, quite unexpectedly, for he had supposed it would be one of the books whose profession was my trade. Then, smiling and looking at me, he was astonished with pleasure that he had suddenly found that book and nothing else in front of my eyes. For he was a Christian and a believer, who often prostrated himself before you, our God, in the Church with frequent and long prayers. When I had told him that I was giving the greatest care to those Scriptures, a conversation arose, he himself telling of Antony, and so on. So far Augustine, who in chapter 12 also says that after this conversation he withdrew with Alypius into the little garden, where, having opened the book of the Apostle and read that passage of Romans 13, "Not in revelling and drunkenness, etc.," immediately, he says, as if a light of certainty had been poured into my heart, all the shadows of doubt fled away. Augustine tells these things as the history of his conversion from the heresy of the Manichees to the orthodox faith.

units.la: De Catechumenis idem constat, ex sententiis Conciliorum antè prolatis. Unde rectè Erasmus in Apologiâ adversus Sutoris debacchationes: Sit populus eo loco doctis, quo olim erant Catechumeni Christianis. Illis ante baptismum enarrabantur historiae veteris Instrumenti, & ad sacram lectionem admittebantur, quae tum intelligebatur à promiscuâ plebe. Et Augustinus docet cum nullis Catechumenis minus fuisse negotii, quàm cum eruditis, qui sacros libros priùs evolverant. Ita concionator populum habebit certè magis docilem; si fuerit utcunque lectione sacrorum voluminum praparatus.
units.tr: That the same held for catechumens is clear from the decisions of the councils cited above. Hence Erasmus rightly says in his Apology against the ravings of Sutor: "Let the people be in the place of the learned, where catechumens once stood among Christians. Before baptism they were told the histories of the Old Testament, and were admitted to the sacred reading, which was then understood by the common folk. And Augustine teaches that he had no less trouble with any catechumens than with the learned who had first thoroughly read the sacred books. So the preacher will certainly have a more teachable people, if it has been prepared in some measure by reading the sacred volumes."

units.la: De fœminis tam nuptis quàm virginibus, cùm ex iis quæ in superioribus prolata, tum ex iis quæ proferenda sunt, id ipsum confirmatur. In Actis S. Cæciliæ Virginis (quæ anno 230. Martyrium passa est) apud Sym. Metaphrasten Novemb. 22. istiusmodi verba reperiuntur. Abscondsum Christi Evangelium semper circumferebat in pectore; & nec noctu nec interdiu intermittebat divina legere eloquia. Eusebius de Alexandrinis mulieribus à Maximino (anno 307.) vexatis agens: Atque ex mulieribus (inquit) (4) non minus ipsis viris à doctrinâ divini Verbi animatis reboratisque, pars eadem cum viris certamina subeuntes æqua virtutis præmia reportârunt.
units.tr: The same is confirmed both for married women and for virgins, from what has been brought forward above and from what is yet to be brought forward. In the Acts of St Cecilia, the virgin who suffered martyrdom in the year 230, in Symeon Metaphrastes, under November 22, such words are found: "She always carried the hidden Gospel of Christ in her breast, and neither by night nor by day did she cease to read the divine oracles." Eusebius, speaking of the Alexandrian women harassed by Maximinus in the year 307, says: "And of the women, not less than the men, who were inspired and strengthened by the teaching of the divine Word, some, undergoing contests together with the men, won equal rewards of courage."

units.la: Gregorius Nazianzenus orat. 25. in laudem Gorgoniæ, sororem suam (quæ nupta erat) ita commendat. Quanam ea, quæ Dei sunt, melius novit, tum ex divinis oraculis, tum suopte ingenii acumine? Item, Prudenti Psalmodia intentione, vel divinorum oraculorum lectione & explicatione, quis vel virorum vel mulierum est, qui eam à se superatam gloriari queat? Hieronymum non virgines modò & viduas, sed etiam matronas rei domesticæ curâ implicitas, ad sacræ Scripturæ studium inflammâsse, Epistolæ ad illas scriptæ luculenter testantur. Vid. supra an. 390. in Hieronymo. In Marcellæ Epitaphio (Epist. 16. ad Principiam virginem) ita studium nobilis illius viduæ describit. Divinarum scripturarum ardor erat incredibilis, semperque cantabat: In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi. Et quia (inquit ibid. Hieronymus) alicujus tunc nominis esse existimabar super studio scripturarum; nunquam convenit, quin de scripturis aliquid interrogaret; nec statim acquiesceret, sed moveret è contrario quæstiones, non ut contenderet, sed ut quærendo disceret earum solutiones, quas opponi posse intelligebat, &c. Ita quicquid in nobis longo fuit studio congregatum, & meditatione diuturnâ quasi in naturam versum; hoc illa libavit, didicit atque possedit; ita ut post profectionem nostram si in aliquo testimonio Scripturarum esset orta contentio, ad illam judicem pergeretur. Hæc de Marcellâ Hieronymus, qui plura de eâdem habet Præfatione in lib. 1. Comment. in Ep. ad Galatas. Similiter etiam & Fabiolæ studium in Epitaphio ejus (Epist. 30. ad Oceanum) miratur. Jesu bone (inquit) quo illa fer-
units.tr: Gregory of Nazianzus, in Oration 25 in praise of Gorgonia, commends his sister (who was married) in this way: "Who knows better the things of God, both from the divine oracles and from the keenness of her own wit?" Likewise: "With prudent attention to the psalmody, or to the reading and explanation of the divine oracles, who among men or women could boast of having surpassed her?" That Jerome inflamed not only virgins and widows, but also matrons burdened with household cares, to the study of holy Scripture, his letters written to them clearly show. See above under the year 390 on Jerome. In the Epitaph of Marcella (Letter 16, to the virgin Principia) he describes the zeal of that noble widow in this way: "Her ardour for the divine Scriptures was incredible, and she was always singing: 'I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you.' And because (Jerome says in the same place) I was thought to have some reputation for my study of the Scriptures, she never met me without asking me something about the Scriptures; nor did she, once answered, rest content, but on the contrary raised questions, not to argue, but to learn by asking the solutions to the objections she understood might be raised, etc. So whatever had been gathered in us by long study, and had become, as it were, second nature through long meditation, she drew off, learned and possessed; so that after my departure, if any dispute arose over some testimony of the Scriptures, they went to her as judge." Jerome says these things about Marcella, and he has more about her in the preface to his first book of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. In the same way he also admires the zeal of Fabiola in her Epitaph (Letter 30, to Oceanus). "Good Jesus," he says, "with what passion she was intent on the divine volumes, and desired, as it were, to satisfy a certain hunger, she ran through the Prophets, the Gospels and the Psalms, both proposing questions and storing away the answers in the little chest of her heart."

units.la: (4) Οὐχ ἥλιον ἀνδρῶν ἀλλὰ τῆς θεῖας λόγου διδασκαλίας ἱππευομένων. vore, quo studio intenta erat divinis voluminibus & veluti quandam famem satiare desiderans, per Prophetas, Evangelia, Psalmosque currebat; quaestiones & proponens & solutas recondens in scriniolo pectoris sui.
units.tr: Not only men but women too, nourished by the teaching of the divine Word [Οὐχ ἥλιον ἀνδρῶν ἀλλὰ τῆς θεῖας λόγου διδασκαλίας ἱππευομένων]. ...vore, with which she was intent on the divine volumes, and ran through the Prophets, Gospels and Psalms, as if desiring to satisfy a certain hunger; storing up her questions and their answers in the little chest of her heart.

units.la: Idem in Epitaphio Paulae (Epist. 27. ad Eustochium) Nec licebat (inquit) cuiquam sororum ignorare Psalmos, & non de Scripturis sanctis quotidie aliquid discere. Addit ibidem, Paulam scripturas sanctas tenuisse memoriter. Denique (inquit) compulit me; ut Vetus & Novum Instrumentum cum filia, me differente, perlegeret. Filiam vero habuit Paula Eustochium, cui testimonium perhibet Hieronymus y, quod diebus ac noctibus in Dei lege meditaretur: & Blesillam, de cujus obitu agens Hieronymus z: Vacillabant (inquit) agrotatione gressus; & pallentem ac trementem faciem vix collum tenue sustinebat; & tamen aut Prophetam aut Evangelium semper in manibus tenebat. Epist. 10. ad Furiam, de sorore ejus ita scribit. Si videres sororem tuam, & illud sacri oris eloquium coram audire te contingeret. Cerneres in parvulo corpusculo ingentes animos. Audires totam Veteris & Novi Testamenti supellectilem ex illius corde fervere. Epist. 140. ad Principiam, cum obtrectatoribus respondisset; qui quod ad mulieres solebat scribere, eum criminabantur: Hac & istiusmodi (inquit) ςμνσνον filia, perstrinxi breviter; ut nec te puduisset sexus tui, nec viros nomen suum erigeret; in quorum condemnationem feminarum in scripturis sanctis vita laudatur. Et paulo post: Habes ibi in studio Scripturarum & in sanctimonia mentis & corporis Marcellam & Asellam; quarum altera te per prata virentia & varios divinorum voluminum flores ducat ad eum, qui dicit in Cantico, Ego flos campi, & lilium convallium; altera ipsa flos Domini tecum mereatur audire; Ut lilium in medio spinarum, sic proxima mea in medio filiarum. Certe quaestiones e Scripturis Hieronymo explicandas ex ultimis Galliarum finibus Hedibiam & Algasiam a, Suniam vero & Fretelam b ex Getarum & Germaniae oris, misisse constat. Unde de his Hieronymus c: Quis hoc crederet, ut barbara Getarum lingua Hebraicam quaereret veritatem; & dormitantibus, immo contemnentibus Graecis, ipsa Germania Spiritus Sancti eloquia scrutaretur? Denique ex Commentariis (qui Hieronymo tribuuntur) in Psalm. 133. con-
units.tr: Jerome says the same in the Epitaph of Paula (Letter 27, to Eustochium): "Nor was it permitted for any of the sisters not to know the Psalms, and not to learn something from the holy Scriptures every day." He adds in the same place that Paula had the holy Scriptures by heart. "Finally," he says, "she made me, though I was reluctant, read through the Old and New Testaments with her daughter." Paula's daughter Eustochium, to whom Jerome bears witness that she meditated day and night on the law of God, was indeed one such; and of Blesilla, whose death Jerome describes: "Her steps faltered from illness, and her pale and trembling face could scarcely bear up her slender neck; yet she always held either the Prophet or the Gospel in her hands." In Letter 10 to Furia he writes thus of her sister: "If you could see your sister, and if it were your lot to hear that sacred utterance from her own lips, you would perceive great spirits in a little body. You would hear the whole stock of the Old and New Testaments boiling in her heart." In Letter 140 to Principia, after he had answered his detractors, who accused him of writing to women: "These and similar things, my daughter, I have touched on briefly, so that you would not be ashamed of your sex, nor men be elated by their name; for in their condemnation the life of women is praised in the holy Scriptures." And a little later: "You have there, in the study of the Scriptures and in the holiness of mind and body, Marcella and Asella; one of whom may lead you through green meadows and the various flowers of the divine volumes to him who says in the Song, 'I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys'; the other, the flower of the Lord herself, may deserve to hear with you: 'As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.'" Certainly it is known that Hedibia and Algasia from the farthest parts of Gaul, and Sunia and Fretela from the shores of the Goths and Germany, sent questions to be explained by Jerome. Hence Jerome says of them: "Who would believe it, that in the barbarous tongue of the Goths they should seek Hebrew truth, and that while the Greeks slept, or rather scorned, Germany itself should search the words of the Holy Spirit?" Finally, from the Commentaries (which are attributed to Jerome) on Psalm 133, it appears that the custom had by then grown strong that not only monks and men, but even little women, among themselves...

units.la: y Procem. lib. 1. Commentr. in Esai. z Epist. 25. ad Paulam. a Ex Epist. 150, 151. b Ex Epist. 135. c ibid. suetudinem tunc temporis invaluisse apparet, ut non monachi solùm & viri, sed etiam mulierculæ hoc inter se haberent certamen, ut plures ediscerent Scripturas; & in eo se putarent esse meliores, si plures edidicissent. Unde sicut suo tempore Paulam celebravit Hieronymusd, quòd Scripturas sanctas tenuisset memoriter; ita etiam (circa an. 500.) Fuscinam sororem suam hoc nomine commendat Alcimus Avitus, in libro de consolatoriâ castitatis laude ita canens.
units.tr: y Procem. lib. 1. Commentar. in Esai. z Epist. 25. ad Paulam. a Ex Epist. 150, 151. b Ex Epist. 135. c ibid. It appears that by that time the custom had taken hold that not only monks and men, but even little women, competed with one another to learn more Scriptures, and thought themselves the better for having learned more. Hence, just as Jerome in his own time praised Paula because she had kept the holy Scriptures in her memory, so too (around the year 500) Alcimus Avitus commends his sister Fuscina by this same title, singing thus in his book on the praise of consoling chastity.

units.la: Præterea verò quis vito ex hoste rebellesAtque resultantes victrici in corpore motusArtibus allidas, Christoque in cote retundas; Divino eloquio, Scripturâque indice nosti. Nam quicquid sacra divina volumina legisAut sensu aut verbo monstrant, quod prædicat illeAntiquus mundi repetens exordia vates, Sive ille historias texit, seu forte figuras; Quidque etiam ille Nave Mosi successor Iesus, Succiduoque simul quod quisque in tempore JudexGesserit; ut digitos soror isthæc omnia dudumDocta tenes, &c. Tota Instrumenti Veteris tibi pagina nota est. Dehinc quicquid prisca succedens gratia legiIntonat, atque Novi miracula Testamenti.
units.tr: Moreover, who among you, sister, does not know how you crush the rebellious movements that rise up against victory in the body, and grind them down on the whetstone of Christ? You know it by the divine word and the index of Scripture. For whatever the sacred divine volumes teach, in sense or in word, which that ancient prophet proclaims, retracing the beginnings of the world, whether he wove histories or perhaps figures; and whatever Jesus, the successor of Moses in the ministry of Nave, and the judge who in his time did what each one did, you have long known all these things with your fingers, sister, learned in them, etc. The whole page of the Old Instrument is known to you. Then whatever grace of old, following on, has read, and the wonders of the New Testament, it thunders forth.

units.la: Syncleticam Diaconissam, qui illius temporibus vixit, Cœlius Sedulius ita commendat in Epistolâ ad Macedonium (quæ est Operis Paschalis Præfatio) Scripturas Ecclesiastici dogmatis ita sitiens epotavit; ut nisi secus licentia defuisset, potuisset docere, quàm membris fœminei corporis animus sit virilis. Ea verò plenitudinem cœlestium nosse desiderabat Scripturarum: quemadmodum confirmat Eustathius, qui Basilii Hexaemeron Latinè à se versum eidem dicavit. Vid. Præfationem Fausti ad Reginam in libro de fide contra Arianos. Elsledam nobilem Abbatissam (circa an. 684.) laudat Beda c, quòd in sanctis Scripturis erudita fuerit. Eirenen etiam filiam Chaiani regis Cazarorum, quam Christianam factam Leo Isaurus anno 16. Imperii sui (circa annum Domini 732.) filio suo Constantino matrimonio
units.tr: Caelius Sedulius thus commends the deaconess Syncletica, who lived in their times, in his letter to Macedonius, which is the preface to his Paschal Work: she so thirstily drank in the Scriptures of ecclesiastical doctrine that, had the licence not been lacking, she could have taught how a woman's mind can be manly in a female body. Indeed, she longed to know the fullness of the heavenly Scriptures, as Eustathius confirms, who dedicated to her his Latin version of Basil's Hexaemeron. See Faustus's preface to the Queen in his book on the faith against the Arians. Bede praises the noble abbess Elfled (about the year 684) because she was learned in the holy Scriptures. Theophanes commends Irene, daughter of Chaianus, king of the Khazars, whom Leo the Isaurian made a Christian and married to his son Constantine in the sixteenth year of his reign (about the year of the Lord 732), on this ground: that after she had learned the sacred letters, she became famous by devoting herself to piety.

units.la: {d} Epist. 27. {c} In vitâ Cuthberti, cap. 24. sociavit, hoc argumento commendat Theophanes (eumque secutus Anastasius Bibliothecarius & Landulphus Sagax , quòd cùm sacras literas didicissêt, pietati operam dans claruerit. Addam Chrysostomi verba, Si tela in virginum domibus pertexitur; & primus, & medius, & novissimus est David. O rem inauditam! Multi qui literarum experimenta minùs sumpserunt, neque ipsis edocti principiis, totum Davidem in pectore conservant. Neque in urbibus solùm atque Ecclesiis sic per omne tempus, per omnem aetatem fulget; sed in foro medio, atque in ipsâ solitudine, & inhabitabili terrâ, certatim Deo sacras stationes excitat. Sed & ante haec tempora nullum decretum receptum esse, ne in Ecclesiâ quidem Pontificiâ, quo Laici arcerentur à legendis sacris libris, eo argumento confirmat Erasmus ; quod Beghinae dicant preces suas & Psalterium linguâ vulgari, Deoque dicatae Virgines (sic enim Nonnas Papisticas appellat) etiam canticum amatorium legant canantque publicitùs in templis suis.
units.tr: {d} Letter 27. {c} In the Life of Cuthbert, ch. 24. Anastasius the Librarian and Landulphus Sagax follow him in this. I will add the words of Chrysostom: If the loom is worked in the houses of virgins, the first, the middle and the last is David. O unheard-of thing! Many who have had little experience of letters, and have not been taught the first principles, keep the whole of David in their breast. He shines thus not only in cities and churches, at all times and in every age, but in the middle of the forum, in solitude itself and in an uninhabitable land, he eagerly stirs up sacred gatherings for God. But that before these times no decree had been accepted, not even in the Papist Church, by which laymen were debarred from reading the sacred books, Erasmus confirms by this argument: that the Beguines say their prayers and the Psalter in the vernacular tongue, and the virgins dedicated to God (for so he calls the Papist nuns) even read the love songs and sing them publicly in their churches.

units.la: Denique ut ab omnibus legerentur sacrae Scripturae, voluisse Patres, patet ex gravissimis, quibus Christianorum hominum ignorantiam subinde notârunt, censuris. Sic enim Clemens Alexandrinus in Protreptico ad Graecos (edit. Latin. Florent. an. 1551. Lapidibus est insensibilior homo, qui est tinctus ignorantiâ. Ibid. Ducamur ergo poenitentiâ; & ex ignoratione traducamur ad scientiam, ex imprudentiâ ad prudentiam, &c. Ibid. Nisi Verbum (forte Filium intelligit) cognovissemus, & eo illuminati essemus; nihil differremus ab avibus quae pascuntur; ut qui pinguefiamus in tenebris, & morte nutriamur. Capiamus lucem, ut Deum capiamus, &c. Ibid. Philosophi ignorantiam insaniae genus describentes, nihil aliud quàm multos fatentur insanire. Idem, Paedagog. lib. 1. cap. 6. Tenebrae sunt ignoratio, per quam in peccata incidimus circa veritatem hallucinantes. Idem, Paedagog. lib. 3. (5) Enutriamini in sermonibus fidei: ait suis pueris Paedagogus, sc. 1 Tim. 4. Id. Stromat. lib. 1 Firmum (conscientiae) fundamentum est recta vita, cum eâ, quae convenit, doctrinâ. Chrysostomus in Serm. de vitando Scandalo, tom. 5. edit. Basil. an. 1558. col. 791. & 792. d. egregiè hâc de re disserit: & lib. 6. de Sacer-
units.tr: Finally, that the sacred Scriptures were meant to be read by all is clear from the very grave censures with which the Fathers from time to time noted the ignorance of Christian people. Thus Clement of Alexandria, in his Exhortation to the Greeks (Latin edition, Florence, 1551): A man who is steeped in ignorance is more insensible than stones. Ibid.: Let us therefore be led by repentance, and be brought over from ignorance to knowledge, from folly to prudence, etc. Ibid.: Unless we had known the Word (he perhaps means the Son) and been enlightened by him, we would differ in nothing from the birds that are fed, so that we grow fat in the darkness and are nourished for death. Let us take the light, so that we may take hold of God, etc. Ibid.: Philosophers, describing ignorance as a kind of madness, admit nothing else than that many men are mad. The same, in the Paedagogus, book 1, ch. 6: Darkness is ignorance, through which we fall into sins, wandering about in error concerning the truth. The same, Paedagogus, book 3 (5): Be nourished in the words of the faith, the Paedagogue says to his boys, see 1 Tim. 4. The same, Stromateis, book 1: The firm foundation of conscience is a upright life together with the teaching that suits it. Chrysostom discusses this matter at length in his sermon On Avoiding Scandal, vol. 5, Basel edition of 1558, cols. 791 and 792 d, and in book 6 On the Priesthood.

units.la: (5) 'Ερπίφει πῆς λόγοις ἕ πίστεως. dotio hæc habet (6) Unde & Episcopum necesse est in singulos (ut sic dicam) dies sementem facere; ut ipsa saltem assuetudine doctrinæ sermonem auditorum animi retinere possint. Idem ad populum Antiochen. Homil. 24. Nec solis hoc (sc. Petre pasce oves) dictum est sacerdotibus, i. e. ut ego accipio, Episcopis) sed unicuique nostrûm (Presbyterorum, qualis tunc erat Chrysostomus) cui vel pusillus creditus est grex. PseudoClemens Epist. 3. (tom. I. Concil.) Grande malum est, ut diximus, ignorantia. Tertullianus de præscriptione adversus Hæreticos, istiusmodi Objectionem ab Hæreticis factam profert. Novissimè ignorare melius est, ne quod non debeas noris. Fides (inquit) tua te salvam fecit, non exercitatio Scripturarum. Ibid. Nihil scire, omnia scire est. Haud dissimilem Objectionem adducit Augustinus, contra Epist. Manichæi, quam vocant Fundamenti. Turbam non intelligendi vivacitas, sed credendi simplicitas tutissimam facit. Idem Confession. lib. 13. cap. 22. hæc habet: Et sacramenta & voces mysticas, ubi intenta sit ignorantia mater ignorationis in timore occultorum signorum. Marcus Eremita, de his qui putant ex operibus se justificari, cap. 97. Πάντων δὲ κακῶν ... Omnium malorum dux est ignorantia: secunda post hanc est incredulitas. Concilium Aurelianense, can. 33. Episcopus, si infirmitate non fuerit impeditus, Ecclesiæ, cui proximus fuerit die Dominico, deesse non debet. Concilium Moguntiacum, can. 25. Numquam deesse dominicis diebus aut festivitatibus, qui verbum Dei prædicet, & juxta quod intelligere vulgus possit. Concilium Lateranense sub Innocentio III. can. 10. Præcipimus tam in Cathedralibus quàm in aliis Conventualibus Ecclesiis viros idoneos ordinari; quos Episcopi possint coadjutores & cooperarios habere, &c. Verba Concilii Toletani IV. can. 24. Turonensis III. can. 17. Moguntiaci & Rhemensis, supra adduximus, pag. 46. 87. 88. Vid. Fulgentium, ad Gallam, epist. 2. cap. 21.
units.tr: (5) [nourished] in the words of faith [ἐντρεφόμενος τοῖς λόγοις τῆς πίστεως]. ...the same work contains this (6): Hence it is necessary for the bishop to sow the seed, as it were, every single day, so that at least by the very habit of teaching the hearers' minds may retain the sermon. The same, to the people of Antioch, Homily 24: This (namely, "Peter, feed my sheep") was said not only to the priests, that is, as I understand it, to the bishops, but to each one of us (of the presbyters, such as Chrysostom then was) to whom even a small flock has been entrusted. Pseudo-Clement, Letter 3 (vol. 1 of the Councils): Ignorance is, as we have said, a great evil. Tertullian, in his book On Prescription against Heretics, brings forward an objection of this kind made by the heretics: Lastly, it is better to be ignorant, lest you know what you ought not to know. Your faith (they say) has saved you, not the practice of the Scriptures. Ibid.: To know nothing is to know all. Augustine, against the letter of the Manichaean which they call the Foundation, brings forward an objection not very different: It is not the liveliness of understanding but the simplicity of belief that makes the crowd most secure. The same, Confessions, book 13, chap. 22, has this: And the sacraments and mystical words, where ignorance, the mother of ignorance, is intent upon fear of hidden signs. Mark the Hermit, on those who think they are justified by works, chap. 97: Of all evils the leader is ignorance; second after it is unbelief. The Council of Orléans, canon 33: A bishop, unless he is prevented by infirmity, ought not to be absent from the congregation nearest to him on the Lord's day. The Council of Mainz, canon 25: There should never be lacking, on the Lord's days or festivals, someone who preaches the word of God, and in a way the common people can understand. The Lateran Council under Innocent III, canon 10: We order that suitable men be ordained not only in cathedral but also in other conventual churches, whom the bishops may have as helpers and co-workers, etc. The words of the Council of Toledo IV, canon 24, Tours III, canon 17, and of Mainz and Reims, we have cited above, pp. 46, 87, 88. See Fulgentius, to Galla, letter 2, chap. 21.

units.la: SECT. III. Biblia in Ecclesiis passim habebantur.
units.tr: SECT. III. The Bible was commonly kept in the churches.

units.la: ID vel Constantini cura in Constantinopolitanâ Ecclesiâ testatur (supra anno 330.) idque in duplicem finem, 1. Ut quisque privatim ad libros illic asservatos posset recurrere; quemadmodum ex versibus illis colligitur, quos Secretario sacrorum librorum in Nolanâ Basilicâ inscripsit Paulinus .
units.tr: This is attested by the care Constantine took for the church at Constantinople (see above, year 330), and it served two purposes. (1) So that anyone could privately have recourse to the books kept there, as is gathered from the verses Paulinus inscribed to the secretary of the sacred books in the basilica at Nola:

units.la: Si quem sancta tenet meditandi in lege voluntas ;Hic poterit residens sacris intendere libris.
units.tr: If holy desire to meditate on the law holds anyone, he may sit down here and attend to the sacred books.

units.la: 2. Ut publicè toto populo audiente recitarentur; quod quidem institutum ab ipsis Apostolis non injuriâ repetit Origenes . Ita refert Chrysostomus librum Geneseos semel quotannis lectum fuisse per Ecclesias; ex Evangeliis verò, quemadmodum & ex Epistolis Pauli, bis hebdomadatim lectiones propositas; sed præ cæteris utriusque Instrumenti scripturis librum David sic adamatum fuisse omnibus Christianis; ut in Ecclesiis & extra Ecclesias primus & medius & novissimus fuerit David. Epistolæ Apostolicæ (inquit Augustinus ) non tantùm illis scriptæ sunt; qui tempore illo, quo scribebantur, audiebant, sed etiam nobis. Non enim ob aliud in Ecclesiâ recitantur. Neque fuisset necessarium (ut rectè Origenes ) legi hæc in Ecclesiâ, nisi ex his ædificatio aliqua audientibus præberetur. Certè ex veterum homiliis constat, hunc in Ecclesiâ servatum esse ordinem; ut lectio sacra Scripturæ linguâ popularì à Lectoribus recitaretur; deinde suisior eorum, quæ prælecta fuerant, explicatio ab Episcopis vel Presbyteris subjungeretur. Hinc illa apud eos solennia: Audistis hodie dicentem Dominum Jesum Simoni, Duc in altum, &c. (Ambrosius de Virginibus, lib. 3. versus finem) Audistis filii librum legi Job, qui solenni munere est decursus & tempore. Matutinis horis lectum est, ut meministis,
units.tr: (2) So that they might be read publicly, with the whole people listening. Origen rightly traces this practice back to the Apostles themselves. Chrysostom reports that the book of Genesis was read once a year in the churches, and that lessons from the Gospels, as also from the Epistles of Paul, were appointed to be read twice a week. Above all the other Scriptures of both Testaments, the book of David was so beloved by all Christians that in the churches and outside the churches David was first, middle and last. The Apostolic Epistles (says Augustine) were written not only for those who heard them at the time they were written, but also for us. For they are read in the Church for no other reason. Nor would it have been necessary (as Origen rightly says) for these to be read in the Church, unless some building up were given to the hearers from them. It is certain from the old homilies that this order was observed in the Church: first the sacred lesson of Scripture was read by the readers in the vernacular, then a plain explanation of what had been read was added by the bishops or presbyters. Hence those solemn words among them: You heard today the Lord Jesus saying to Simon, "Put out into the deep," etc. (Ambrose, On Virgins, book 3, near the end). You heard, sons, the book of Job read, which is run through at a solemn office and time. It was read in the morning hours, as you remember,

units.la: p Vid. etiam tom. 9. Bibliotb. Patrum, col. 1433. B. q Epist. 12. ad Severam. r Initio Homil. 15. in Josuam. s Homil. 6. de Poenitentiâ. t Contra Cresconium, lib. 1. cap. 9. v In Levitic. Homil. 5. meministis, fratres, quod summo animi dolore respondemus: Deus, venerunt gentes in hæreditatem tuam. (Idem lib. 5. epist. 33.) Audistis hodie in lectione desursâ, quid legio dixerit; Quid mihi & tibi est, Jesu fili David? (Idem de Helia & Jejunio, cap. 20.) Hodierno etiam die ad ipsam rem pertinet capitulum, quod modo cum legeretur, audivimus. (Augustinus de verbis Domini secundum Matth. serm. 15.) Lectiones sanctæ propositæ sunt, & quas audiamus; & de quibus aliquid sermonis adjuvante Domino proferamus. In lectione Apostolicâ gratiæ aguntur Deo de fide gentium; utique ideo, quia ipse fecit. In Psalmo diximus; Deus virtutum converte nos, & ostende faciem tuam & salvi erimus. In Evangelio ad Cænam vocati sumus, &c. (Idem de verbis Domini secundum Lucam, Serm. 33.) Apostolum audivimus, Psalmum audivimus, Evangelium audivimus. Consonant omnes divinæ lectiones, ut spem non in nobis, sed in Domino collocemus. (Idem de verbis Apostoli, Serm. 7.) De divinis lectionibus, quod Dominus admonere dignatus, intentis audite fratres, illo dante, me ministrante. Primam lectionem audivimus Apostoli: Fidelis sermo, & omni acceptatione dignus, &c. Hoc de Apostolicâ lectione percepimus. Deinde cantavimus Psalmum, exhortantes nos invicem, una voce, uno corde dicentes: Venite adoremus, & prosternamur ei, &c. Post hæc Evangelica lectio decem leprosos mundatos nobis ostendit, &c. Has tres lectiones, quantum pro tempore possumus, pertractemus, &c. Memento quid ultima Evangelica lectio resonet, quomodo Jesus Dominus laudat gratias agentem, &c. (Ibid. serm. 10.) Timere debeo, ne contingat mihi, quod contigit Apostolo Paulo; quod modo cum legeretur, si intenti fuistis lectioni, audivistis: Ergo inimicus factus sum vobis, vera prædicans. (Idem in libro L. Homiliarum, homil. 49. à Bedâ etiam inseritur habetur initio enarrationis 1 Corinth. VII.) Audivimus Apostolicum lectionem: & forte aliquem moveat, quod ibi scriptum est: Secundum justitiam, quæ ex lege est, qui fuerim sine querelâ, &c. (De Tempore, serm. 49.) Volueram aliquando, ut per singulos annos secundum omnes Evangelistas etiam passio legeretur: factum est; non audierunt homines, quod consueverunt, & perturbati sunt. Qui autem amat literas Dei, & non semper vult esse idiota, omnia novit, & omnia diligenter inquirit. Sed sicut cuique à Deo parata est mensura fidei, sic quisque proficit. Nunc attendamus, quod hodie, cum legeretur, audivimus, &c. (Serm. 144. de Tempore) Lectiones divinorum eloquiorum, cum recitarentur, audivimus. Ea nobis est materies loquendi propositá; proposita ; inde sapere debemus, inde seminare quod sapimus, &c. Lectio prima Prophetica quid nobis commendaverit, me commemorante recolite. (Serm. 236. de Tempore) Lectiones sanctas plures, cùm recitarentur, audivimus, & de his nos oportet dicere, quod Dominus fuerit donare dignatus. Sed lectionem omnis auditor, quod recentius lectum est, magis meminit, & ut inde aliquid à tractatore verbi dicatur expectat. Cùm ergo in ultimum sit sanctum Evangelium recitatum; non dubita expectare charitatem vestram, ut de istâ vineâ & de conductis, & de mercede denarii aliquid audiatis. (Serm. 237. de Tempore) Audivistis vocem Apostoli, cœlestis tubæ, spiritualis lyræ, &c. (Chrysostomus Homil. 1. ad populum Antiochenum, in illud Apostoli, Vino modico utere, &c.) Vid. Leonem I. supra an. 450. Cæsarius Arelatensis, homil. 8. In lectione Apostolicâ, quæ nobis paulò ante recitata est, fratres charissimi, audivimus, &c. sic homil. 19. 22. Chrysostomus in Matth. 23. homil. 73. circa sin. (7) Literas forte nescis, & scripturam perlegere non potes, ut inde priscorum virtutes virorum perdiscas: culpa quidem etiam hæc est, cùm ecclesia semper tibi pateat, non venire ad degustanda hæc fluenta. Ita Sozomenus Gallum & Julianum refert libros Ecclesiasticos ac divinos in Ecclesia populo perlegisse. Vid. Maximum Taurinensem supra anno 440. Populum intellexisse lectiones, vid. testimonium Augustini de Jonæ cucurbitâ (sol. 22. b.) & locum, lib. 1. de Prædest. Sanctorum, cap. 14. Non debuit repudiari sententia libri Sapientiæ, qui meruit, &c. ab omnibus Christianis Episcopis usque ad extremos Laicos, Fideles, Catechumenos, Pænitentes, cum veneratione divinæ authoritatis audiri.
units.tr: p See also vol. 9 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, col. 1433 B. q Letter 12 to Severa. r At the beginning of Homily 15 on Joshua. s Homily 6 on Repentance. t Against Cresconius, book 1, chapter 9. v On Leviticus, Homily 5. remember, brothers, that with the greatest grief of soul we answer: "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance." (The same, book 5, letter 33.) You heard today in the lesson from above what the legion said: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of David?" (The same, On Elijah and Fasting, chapter 20.) Today also the passage that we just heard read bears on the matter itself. (Augustine, On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew, sermon 15.) The holy lessons have been set before us, which we hear, and on which, with the help of the Lord, we bring forward some discourse. In the Apostolic lesson thanks are given to God for the faith of the Gentiles, surely because he himself made it so. We said in the Psalm: "God of hosts, turn us again, and show us your face, and we shall be saved." In the Gospel we were called to the supper, etc. (The same, On the Words of the Lord according to Luke, sermon 33.) We heard the Apostle, we heard the Psalm, we heard the Gospel. All the divine lessons agree, so that we place our hope not in ourselves but in the Lord. (The same, On the Words of the Apostle, sermon 7.) Concerning the divine lessons, listen attentively, brothers, since the Lord has deigned to admonish us, he giving, I ministering. We heard the first lesson from the Apostle: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation," etc. This we have received from the Apostolic lesson. Then we sang the Psalm, exhorting one another with one voice, with one heart, saying: "Come, let us worship and fall down before him," etc. After this the Gospel lesson showed us the ten lepers cleansed, etc. As far as time allows, let us go through these three lessons, etc. Remember what the last Gospel lesson sounds, how the Lord Jesus praises the one who gives thanks, etc. (Ibid., sermon 10.) I ought to fear that what happened to the Apostle Paul may happen to me, which, as it was read just now, you heard if you were attentive to the lesson: "So have I become your enemy, because I tell you the truth." (The same, in book 50 of the Homilies, homily 49; also inserted by Bede at the beginning of the exposition of 1 Corinthians 7.) We heard the Apostolic lesson, and perhaps someone is troubled by what is written there: "According to the righteousness which is of the law, I was blameless," etc. (On the Time, sermon 49.) I once wished that the Passion should be read every year according to all the Evangelists as well. It was done; the people did not hear what they were used to, and were disturbed. But he who loves the letters of God, and does not always want to be unlearned, knows all things and inquires diligently into all things. But as the measure of faith is given to each by God, so each makes progress. Now let us attend to what we heard read today, etc. (Sermon 144, On the Time.) We heard the lessons of the divine utterances as they were read. This is set before us as the matter for our speaking; from it we ought to grow wise, from it to sow what we know, etc. Call to mind, as I recall it, what the first prophetic lesson has commended to us. (Sermon 236, On the Time.) We heard many holy lessons as they were read, and we ought to speak of them in the way that the Lord has deigned to give. But every hearer more readily remembers what was read most recently, and expects that some discourse on it be given by the one who handles the Word. Since, then, the holy Gospel has been read to its end, do not hesitate, dear hearers, to expect to hear something about that vineyard, and about the workers hired, and about the reward of the penny. (Sermon 237, On the Time.) You have heard the voice of the Apostle, the heavenly trumpet, the spiritual lyre, etc. (Chrysostom, Homily 1 to the people of Antioch, on the words of the Apostle, "Use a little wine," etc.) See Leo I, under the year 450. Caesarius of Arles, homily 8: In the Apostolic lesson, which was read to us a little while ago, dearest brothers, we heard, etc.; so also homilies 19 and 22. Chrysostom on Matthew 23, homily 73, near the end.

units.la: In Ecclesiâ Primitivâ commune officium vulgari linguâ celebratum fuit.
units.tr: In the primitive Church the common office was celebrated in the vernacular language.

units.la: ID fatentur Nicolaus Lyranus , & Thomas Aquinas , ipse etiam Hardingus , Tum (inquit) preces linguâ popPulari & usitatâ vulgo hominum fiebant, ut eâ melius instituerentur. Et tamen Ambrosius Catharinus , Doctrina (inquit) Lutheri, quae linguam cognitam in precibus exigit, Diaboli calliditatem sapit: Cum tamen idem ipse, In initio (inquit) Evangelii forsan aliter observabatur. Hoc verò in Ecclesiâ Catholicâ usque ad natum Antichristum obtinuisse, Liturgiae tum suscepta ratio satis indicat. Neque enim tunc temporis ab Episcopo aut Presbyteris tantum, sed totius Ecclesiae conjunctis operis administrata sunt sacra publica. In Liturgiis, quae Jacobi, Clementis , Basilii, & Chrysostomi nominibus feruntur, Diaconis praescribitur, ut populum hisce verbis compellent; Oremus, Attendamus; populo etiam, ut ad ministri precationem aliquando responderet Amen; aliquando Dominus misereatur nostri; aliquando, Et cum spiritu tuo; aliquando, Habemus ad Dominum, &c. (quas quidem responsiones recto tempore proferre non potuissent; si preces linguâ non intellectâ fuissent habitae.) Idque ipsum ex indubitatis Patrum monumentis manifesto constat. Cum populus semel audivit, εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, statim omnes respondent, Amen; inquit Chrysostomus . Idem de Romanâ Ecclesiâ testatur Hieronymus , ad similitudinem caelestis tonitrui, Amen reboare. (1) Quin in precationibus quoque (inquit Chrysostomus ) illud quispiam conspexerit, popua In 1 Cor. XIV. b Contra Juellum, artic. 3. sect 28. c Apud. Sixt. Senens. d Annot. adv. Cajetan. p. 88. e Lib. 8. Constitut. Apostol. cap. 11 & 12. edit. Turriani. f In 1 Cor. XIV. g Praefat. lib. 2. in Epist. ad Galat. h Homil. 18. in 2 Cor. cap. VIII. (1) Καὶ ἐν τῇ ἐυχαῖς ᾗ πολὺ ἡ λέγειν ἴδοι ... νεωτερικὰ ... ἐπὶ ... ἔτι ... lum permultum erogare. Etenim pro arreptitiis (seu energumenis) & pro iis, qui in pænitentia sunt, communia & à sacerdote & ab ipsis vota fiunt; atque omnes unam eandemque precem concipiunt, precem inquam illam misericordia plenam. Rursus quùm eos, qui sacrosanctæ mensæ participes esse nequeunt, à sacris septis arcemus; incunda est altera oratio; in qua omnes peræquè humi jacemus, omnes peræquè consurgimus. Ad hæc, quùm pax danda vicissimque accipienda est; omnes æque nos osculamur. Jam in tremendis quoque mysteriis, ut sacerdos pro plebe, ita plebs pro sacerdote vota facit. Hæc enim verba [Et cum spiritu tuo] nihil aliud, quam hoc, significant. Rursus ea oratio, quâ Deo gratia agitur, utrisque communis est. Neque enim ipse solus gratias agit, sed etiam plebs universa. Nam quùm prius illorum vocem sumpsit, atque illi assenserunt; Id digne ac juste fieri: tum demum gratiarum actionem auspicatur. Quid autem est, quamobrem tibi mirum videatur, si cum sacerdote plebs interdum loquatur; quùm etiam cum ipsis Cherubim ac supernis virtutibus sacrosanctos illos hymnos communiter in cælum mittat. Hæc Chrysostomus. Paria Basilius, Quod si mare bonum est apud Deum, si pulchrum, si laudabile; quonam pacto non pulchrius est hoc talis Ecclesiæ Concilium, in qua (2) permixtus sonitus resultat. Confer sententiam Ambrosii Hexaemer. lib. 3. cap. 5. supra anno 377. Vide & Ausonium, vel Paulinum potius, tom. 3. Biblioth. Patr. col. 398. Cyrillum Hierosolym. Catechesi Mystagogica 5. tom. 2. Biblioth. Patr. col. 204, 205, 207. Sic vero Clemens Alexandrinus, Est ergo (3) quod hic est apud nos altare; terrestris congregatio eorum, qui sunt dedicati orationibus; qui veluti unam vocem habent communem & unam mentem. Chrysostomus illam sententiam ex veteri Liturgia repetit: Οremus omnes communiter. Similiter Augustinus, de orationibus Ecclesiæ agens, sacerdotem Dei ait exhortari populum Dei orare pro incredulis; ut eos Deus convertat ad fidem; & pro Catechumenis, ut eis desiderium regenerationis inspiret; & pro fidelibus, ut in eo quod esse cœperunt, ejus munere perseverent. Unde ibidem Vitalem ita interrogat. Nunquid ubi audieris sacerdotem Dei ad ejus altare populum
units.tr: Nicholas of Lyra, Thomas Aquinas, and Harding himself all admit this. Harding says: "Then (he says) the prayers were made in the popular language, in common use among the people, so that they might be better instructed by it." Yet Ambrosius Catharinus says: "The doctrine of Luther, which requires that the language be understood in prayers, savours of the Devil's cunning." But the same Catharinus also says: "At the beginning of the Gospel it was perhaps observed otherwise." That this practice held in the Catholic Church until the birth of Antichrist, the form of the liturgy as it then was sufficiently shows. For at that time the public sacred rites were administered not by the bishop or the presbyters alone, but by the joint work of the whole Church. In the liturgies that go under the names of James, Clement, Basil and Chrysostom, the deacons are instructed to address the people with these words: "Let us pray; Let us attend." The people too are bidden to answer the minister's prayer sometimes with "Amen," sometimes with "The Lord have mercy on us," sometimes with "And with thy spirit," and sometimes with "We lift them up to the Lord," etc. (They could not have given these responses at the right time if the prayers had been offered in a language they did not understand.) This very thing is plainly established by the undoubted monuments of the Fathers. "When the people have once heard 'world without end,' all at once they answer 'Amen'," says Chrysostom. Jerome testifies the same of the Roman Church: "Amen resounds like a heavenly thunderclap." "Moreover," says Chrysostom, "in the prayers too one may see the people contribute a great deal. For common vows are made both by the priest and by the people for the possessed (or energumens) and for those who are in repentance; and all conceive one and the same prayer, I mean that prayer full of mercy. Again, when we keep from the holy enclosures those who cannot be partakers of the sacred table, the other prayer is said together, in which we all equally lie prostrate on the ground and all equally rise. Besides, when peace is to be given and in turn received, we all alike kiss one another. Now in the tremendous mysteries too, as the priest makes vows for the people, so the people make them for the priest. For these words [And with thy spirit] mean nothing other than this. Again, that prayer by which thanks are given to God is common to both. For he does not give thanks alone, but the whole people too. For when he has first taken up their voice, and they have assented, saying: It is fitting and right, then at last he begins the thanksgiving. Why then should it seem strange to you if the people sometimes speak with the priest, since they too send up those sacred hymns to heaven together with the Cherubim and the heavenly powers?" Thus Chrysostom. Basil says similar things: "If the sea is good in God's sight, if it is beautiful and praiseworthy, how much more beautiful is this assembly of such a Church, in which a mingled sound resounds." (2) Compare the opinion of Ambrose, Hexaemeron book 3, ch. 5; see also above, the year 377. See too Ausonius, or rather Paulinus, vol. 3 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, col. 398; Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catechesis 5, vol. 2 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, cols. 204, 205, 207. Clement of Alexandria says: "There is therefore here among us an altar: an earthly congregation of those who are dedicated to prayers, who as it were have one common voice and one mind." (3) Chrysostom repeats that sentiment from the ancient liturgy: "Let us all pray together." Likewise Augustine, speaking of the prayers of the Church, says that God's priest exhorts God's people to pray for unbelievers, that God may convert them to the faith; and for catechumens, that he may inspire in them the desire for regeneration; and for the faithful, that they may persevere by God's gift in what they have begun. Hence in the same place he asks Vitalis thus: "When you hear God's priest at his altar exhorting the people to pray to God, or himself praying aloud that he may bring the unbelieving nations to his faith, will you not answer Amen?" The same, Epistle 119, ch. 18: "When, moreover, is there no time when the brothers are gathered in the Church for singing holy things, except when something is read or discussed, or the antiphons are chanted aloud, or a common prayer is announced by the voice of the deacon?" The same, On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 23: "Or who dares, when the priest, calling on the Lord over the faithful, says: 'Lord, grant them to persevere to the end,' to rebuke him, not with loud voice, but at least in thought? Ought he not rather to answer to such a blessing with a believing heart and a confessing mouth?" And ch. 22: "Would that the slow of heart and the weak, who cannot, or not yet, understand the Scriptures or their expositions, might hear or not hear our disputations on this question in such a way that they would rather look at their prayers, which the Church has always had and will have from its beginnings until this age ends, etc." Note that the slow and the weak were able to understand the prayers of the Church. Hilary on Psalm 65: "Let anyone standing outside the Church hear the voice of the praying people; let him observe the solemn sound of the hymns; and among the offices of the divine sacraments let him receive the devout response of confession. Every adversity must necessarily be terrified and wage war against the Devil, and death must be overcome by faith in the resurrection, by the jubilation of our exultant voice, as has been said. Let him know that this is pleasing to God, that this is a testimony of our hope: that our public and victorious voices of exultation resound." The Prophet is not negligent of this, mentioning elsewhere: "I went round and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation." And lest we think the teaching and observance of this jubilation to be trifling, he testifies elsewhere: "Blessed is the people that knows jubilation." The Council of Braga I (about the year 572), ch. 21: "It is resolved that bishops and presbyters should not greet the people in different ways, but in one manner, saying: 'The Lord be with you,' as is read in the book of Ruth; and that the people should answer: 'And with your spirit,' as handed down by the Apostles themselves, which all the East retains, and not as the Priscillianist perversity has altered it." Caesarius of Arles, homily 33: "I rejoice, dearest brothers, and give thanks to God, because I see you faithfully running to hear the divine lessons. But if you wish to bring your progress and our joy to completion, you ought to assemble earlier, etc. So I ask you both to come earlier, and when you have come, to strive rather to pray or sing psalms than to occupy yourselves with idle or worldly tales. For he who comes to the churches and wishes to chatter would have been better off not coming; because while he occupies himself with unfruitful tales, he neither sings psalms himself nor allows others to sing psalms or hear the divine lessons." And homily 34: "I ask and admonish you, dearest brothers, that whenever prayer is offered beside the altar by the clergy, or prayer is announced by the deacon crying aloud, you should faithfully bow not only your hearts but also your bodies. For while I frequently and diligently attend, as is fitting, when the deacon cries 'Let us bend our knees,' I see the greater part of the people standing upright like columns; which is by no means lawful or expedient for Christians while prayer is said in church. For the deacon cries out not for our sake but for yours. And therefore, because that voice is addressed especially to you, and most of all to the negligent, it is right that it be faithfully fulfilled by us, etc." And after this: "When you come to church, do only what is expedient to do in church, that is, either pray or sing psalms: so that by praying you may receive forgiveness of sins, and by singing you may attain spiritual joy. He who occupies himself in church with foolish and unfitting tales is known to offer poison and a sword to other men, while he himself neither hears the word of God nor allows others to hear it." Ibid.: "Since [the Devil] cannot drive us bodily from the assembly of the Church, he strives to occupy us within the Church itself with fruitless talk, so that through vain and empty, and perhaps even biting, conversations and filthy thoughts he may take from us the fruit of the divine lesson or the remedy of prayer; so that we seem to stand in the Church only in body, while in heart or thought we withdraw far from the sight of the divine majesty." Thus far Caesarius.
