units.la: (3) Τὸ ἀληθινὸν δὲ ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἀνακ- ἡ μία γραμμή. hortantem ad Deum orandum, vel ipsum clara voce orantem, ut incredulas gentes ad fidem suam venire compellat; non respondebis Amen? Idem Epist. 119. cap. 18. Quando autem non est tempus, cum in Ecclesia fratres congregantur sancta canendis; nisi cum legitur, aut disputatur, aut Antiphites clara voce deprecantur, aut communis oratio voce Diaconi indicitur? Idem de bono Persever. cap. 23. Aut quis sacerdotem super fideles Dominum invocantem, si quando dixit; Da illis Domine perseverare utique in finem: non solutā voce ausus est, sed saltem cogitatione reprehendere, ac non potius super ejus talem benedictionem & corde credente, & ore confitente respondaet? Ut cap.22. Atque utinam tardi corde & infirmi, qui non possunt, nec nondum possunt, scripturas vel earum expositiones intelligere; sic audirent, vel non audirent in hac quaestione disputationes nostras; ut magis intuerentur orationes suas, quas semper habuit & habebit Ecclesia ab exordiis suis, donec finiatur hoc saeculum, &c. Nota tardos & infirmos preces Ecclesiae intelligere potuisse. Hilarius in Psalm 65. Audiat orantis populi, consistens quis extra Ecclesiam, vocem; speculet celebres hymnorum sonitus; & inter divinorum quoque sacramentorum officia, responsionem devota confessionis accipiat. Necesse est terreri omnem adversitatem, & bellari adversus Diabolum, vincique resurrectionis fide mortem tali exultantis vocis nostrae (ut dictum est) jubilo. Sciat hoc Deo placitum esse, hoc spei nostrae testimonium, publicas victricesque exultationis nostrae voces personare. Quarum Propheta non negligens est, loco altero memorans Circuivi & immolavi in Tabernaculo ejus hostiam jubilationis. Et ne tinnem hujus jubilationis doctrinam atque observantiam crederemus, alibi protestatur. Beatus populus, qui scit jubilationem. Concilium Bracarense I. (circa an. 572.) cap. 21. Placuit, ut non aliter Episcopi, & aliter Presbyteri populum, sed uno modo salutent, dicentes; Dominus sit vobiscum; sicut in libro Ruth legitur: Et ut respondeatur a populo: Et cum spiritu tuo; sicut & ab ipsis Apostolis traditum omnis retinet Oriens: & non sicut Priscilliana pravitas permutavit. Caesarius Arelatensis, homil. 33. Gaudeo, fratres dilectissimi, & Deo gratias ago; quia vos ad audiendas lectiones divinas video fideliter currere; sed si & profectum vestrum & gaudium nostrum complere ad integrum vultis; maturius convenire debetis, &c. Ideo rogo vos, ut & maturiùs veniatis, & cùm veneritis, magis orare vel psallere, quàm otiosis vos vel secularibus studeatis fabulis occupare. Qui enim ad Ecclesias veniens verbosare voluerit, melius illi fuerat non venisse; quia dum se infructuosis fabulis occupat; nec ipse psallit, nec alios psallere aut lectiones divinas audire permittit. Et homil. 34. Rogo vos & admoneo, fratres charissimi, ut quotiescunque juxta altarium à Clericis oratur, aut oratio Diacono clamante indicitur; non solùm corda, sed etiam corpora fideliter inclinetis. Nam dum frequenter, sicut oportet, & diligenter intendo Diacono clamante. Flectamus genua, maximam partem populi velut columnas erectos stare conspicio; quod Christianis, dum in Ecclesiâ oratur, omnino nec licet nec expedit. Non enim propter nos, sed propter vos Diaconus clamat. Et ideo quia ad vos specialiter vox illa, vel maximè ad negligentes dirigitur, justum est ut à nobis fideliter impleatur, &c. Et post: Venientes ad Ecclesiam, hoc solum, quod in Ecclesiâ expedit fieri, agite; id est, aut orate, aut psallite; ut orando, peccatorum veniam accipere; & psallendo, ad spiritualem possitis laetitiam pervenire. Qui in Ecclesiâ ineptis & incongruis fabulis occupatur, quasi venenum & gladium reliquis hominibus ingerere vel prabere cognoscitur; dum verbum Dei nec ipse audit, nec alios audire permittit. Ibid. Quia [Diabolus] nos non potest corporaliter de Ecclesiae conventu repellere; in ipsâ Ecclesiâ infructuosis nos studet sermonibus occupare; ut nobis per inanes & vacuas, & forte etiam mordaces collocutiones ac sordidas cogitationes, divinae lectionis fructum, vel orationis remedium possit auferre; ut corpore tantùm videamur in Ecclesiâ stare, & corde vel cogitatione longè à conspectu divinae majestatis abscedere. Haetenus Caesarius.
units.tr: (3) The true [Τὸ ἀληθινὸν δὲ ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἀνακ- ἡ μία γραμμή.] Exhorting someone to pray to God, or praying aloud himself, so that he compels unbelieving nations to come to his faith: "Will you not answer Amen?" The same author, Epistle 119, chapter 18: "But when there is no time, when the brethren gather together in the Church to sing holy things, except when something is read or discussed, or when the antiphons are chanted with a loud voice, or when a common prayer is announced by the voice of the deacon?" The same author, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 23: "Or who would dare, when the priest calls upon the Lord over the faithful and says, 'Lord, grant them to persevere to the end,' to censure him in thought, if not aloud, and not rather respond to his blessing with a believing heart and a confessing mouth?" As in chapter 22: "And would that the slow of heart and the weak, who cannot yet understand the Scriptures or their explanations, would hear or not hear our disputations on this question in such a way that they might rather attend to their own prayers, which the Church has always had from its beginnings and will have until this age ends, etc." Note that the slow and weak were able to understand the prayers of the Church. Hilary on Psalm 65: "Let anyone standing outside the Church hear the voice of the praying people; let him listen for the sound of the celebrated hymns, and among the rites of the divine sacraments let him receive the devout response of confession. Every adversity must be terrified, and the devil must be warred against and conquered by faith in the resurrection, by the jubilation of our voice (as has been said) in such exultation. Let him know that it is pleasing to God, a testimony of our hope, that our public and victorious shouts of exultation resound." The Prophet is not negligent of these, mentioning in another place: "I went round and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation." And lest we believe this doctrine and practice of jubilation to be trivial, he testifies elsewhere: "Blessed is the people who know jubilation." The First Council of Braga (about the year 572), chapter 21: "It has pleased [the council] that bishops and presbyters should not greet the people in different ways, but in one manner, saying, 'The Lord be with you,' as is read in the book of Ruth, and that the people respond, 'And with your spirit,' as the whole East keeps, handed down by the Apostles themselves, and not as the Priscillianist heresy has changed it." Caesarius of Arles, Homily 33: "I rejoice, dearest brethren, and give thanks to God, because I see you running faithfully to hear the divine readings; but if you wish to complete fully both your progress and our joy, you ought to come together earlier, etc. So I ask you both to come earlier, and when you have come, to be more eager to pray or sing than to occupy yourselves with idle or worldly tales. For whoever comes to the churches and wishes to chatter would have been better off not coming; for while he occupies himself with fruitless stories, he neither sings nor permits others to sing or hear the divine readings." And Homily 34: "I ask and admonish you, dearest brethren, that whenever prayer is offered by the clergy near the altar, or a prayer is announced by the deacon crying out, you bow not only your hearts but also your bodies faithfully. For while I often and diligently watch, as is proper, when the deacon cries out, 'Let us bend the knee,' I see that the greater part of the people stand upright like pillars; which is not at all lawful or expedient for Christians while prayer is being offered in the Church. For the deacon does not cry out for our sake, but for yours. And since that voice is addressed especially to you, and most of all to the negligent, it is right that it be faithfully fulfilled by us, etc." And afterwards: "When you come to the Church, do only what is fitting to do in the Church; that is, either pray or sing, so that by praying you may receive forgiveness of sins, and by singing you may attain spiritual joy. Whoever occupies himself with foolish and unseemly tales in the Church is known to offer or present to the rest of men something like poison and a sword, since he neither hears the word of God himself nor permits others to hear it." Ibid.: "Since [the devil] cannot drive us bodily from the assembly of the Church, he strives to occupy us inside the Church itself with fruitless talk, so that through empty and idle, and perhaps even biting, conversations and foul thoughts he may take from us the fruit of the divine reading or the remedy of prayer; so that we seem to stand in the Church only in body, while in heart or thought we withdraw far from the sight of the divine majesty." Thus far Caesarius.

units.la: Huc etiam referantur alia Patrum testimonia, quae significant hymnos in Ecclesiâ non à Clero solo (ut nunc fit in Papatu) sed ab universâ Plebe simul decantatos; quod necessario arguit vernaculâ & non ignotâ populo linguâ illud factum. Dionysius in Ecclesiasticâ Hierarchiâ, cap. 3. §. 2. (ἐν μυσταγωγίᾳ συνάξεως) Pontifex, inquit ἀπάρχεται ἡ ἱερὰς τῶν ψαλμῶν μελῳδίας, συνάδουσι αὐτῷ ἡ ψαλμικὴ (seu ψαλμῳδικὴ) ἱεροψαλτίας ἀπέρασις ἡ ἐκκλησιαστικὴ διακονία. Psalmorum incipit melos, concinentibus secum sacra carmina omnibus Ecclesiastici ordinis gradibus. Et paulo post. οἱ δὲ ἡ λειτουργικὴς διακονίας ἵκανοὶ συνάπτουσι τῶν ἱερέων ὅτι τῷ Θεῷ ἀσάσσειν σεπτίζωσι ἡ ἱερὰν ἀρχὴν, ἡ τὸ ἡ εὐλογίας ποιεῖσθαι, συλλογισθεῖσα ὑπὸ πάντων τὰ ἡ ἐκκλησίας ταπεινωσίᾳ ἡ καθολικῆς ὑπνολογίας. h. e. Qui verò ipsius ordinis praecipui sunt, unà cum sacerdotibus sanctum panem & calicem sacrosanctis altaribus imponunt ; cum ante praecesserit ab omni Ecclesia plenitudine (non Clero tantum, ut interpres Latinus male vertit) universalis laus atque confessio. Sic etiam §. 3. (in Θεωρία) mentio fit καθολικῆς ὁμολογίας, quam ita appellatam notat ibi Maximus, ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ πάντων ἀδομένῳ, ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ καθολικῆς χάριτος γρωμένῳ, sive quòd ab universis cantaretur, seu quòd gratiam universalem postularet, Plinius Secundus q Christianos refert statato die convenire solitos, carmenque Christo quasi Deo dicere secum invicem. Ephraem de Vitâ Spiritali, r cap. 16. Si in domo Domini ad divinum spiritalemque cultum constiteris ; in Psalmodiis te alacrem promptumque præbeto. Si autem tacueris ; tacebo & ego, tacebit & proximus ; unde necessariò cantum cessare necesse sit. Sed hoc quaeso absit, &c. Gregorius Nazianzenus in funebri Oratione Basilii refert, Valentem Imperatorem in Ecclesiam ingressum, in quâ Basilius prædicabat, psalmodiâ fuisse quasi tonitru perculsum & obstupefactum. Τῷ ἀκολῳ ἐκπληξάντι τῇ ψαλμῳδίᾳ ταπεινοῦσι. Victor, lib. 2. de Persecut. Vandalic. Jam (inquit) ob celebritatem festivitatis (Epiphaniorum) hymni nocturni per totam Ecclesiam (de Fausti Basilicâ in Urbe Carthaginiensi loquitur) canente populo concrepabant. Chrysostomus t: Quondam (inquit) (3) psallebant in unum omnes ; facimus & nos. Idem ibid. (4) Et ubi omnes succinuerunt, velut uno ex ore vox defertur. Idem in Epist. ad Ephes. Serm. 3. (5) Ita tu quoque advenisti, hymnum cecinisti cum omnibus reliquis ; ex eorum te numero esse, qui digni sunt, hoc ipso confessus es, quòd non abscessisti. Et in Epist. ad Hebraeos, hom. 4. (6) Quid enim (sibi volunt) Hymni? nonne ut Deum glorificemus & ut gratiam agamus ; quoniam jam coronavit discedentem, quoniam à laboribus liberavit, de servitute ducens, apud se habens? Nonne propter hoc psalmi & hymni? nonne propter hoc psalmodia? omnia ista gaudentium sunt.
units.tr: Other testimonies of the Fathers belong here too. They show that hymns in the Church were sung not by the clergy alone (as now happens in the Papacy) but by the whole common people together. This necessarily proves that the thing was done in a vernacular language that the people knew. Dionysius, in the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 3, §2 (in the account of the mystical assembly), says: "The high priest begins the sacred melody of the psalms, and all the grades of the ecclesiastical order sing sacred songs along with him" [ἀπάρχεται ἡ ἱερὰς τῶν ψαλμῶν μελῳδίας, συνάδουσι αὐτῷ ἡ ψαλμικὴ ἱεροψαλτίας ἀπέρασις ἡ ἐκκλησιαστικὴ διακονία]. And a little later: "Those of the liturgical ministry who are fit place the holy bread and cup upon the sacred altars with the priests, when the universal praise and confession has first been offered by the whole fullness of the Church, not by the clergy alone, as the Latin translator wrongly renders it." Likewise in §3 (in the Theory) he mentions the "universal confession," which Maximus explains as so called "either because it is sung by all, or because it asks for universal grace" [ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ πάντων ἀδομένῳ, ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ καθολικῆς χάριτος γρωμένῳ]. Pliny the Younger reports that Christians were accustomed to meet on a fixed day and to sing a hymn to Christ as to a god, in turn among themselves (Letters, book 10, to Trajan). Ephraem, in On the Spiritual Life, chapter 16: "If you stand in the house of the Lord for divine and spiritual worship, show yourself eager and ready in the psalmody. But if you keep silent, I too will be silent, and the neighbour too will be silent, so that the singing must of necessity cease. But God forbid this..." Gregory Nazianzen, in his funeral oration for Basil, relates that the Emperor Valens, when he entered the church where Basil was preaching, was struck and stunned as by thunder by the psalmody [τῷ ἀκολῳ ἐκπληξάντι τῇ ψαλμῳδίᾳ ταπεινοῦσι]. Victor, in book 2 of On the Vandal Persecution, says: "Now, because of the solemnity of the feast" (of the Epiphany; he is speaking of the basilica of Faustus in the city of Carthage) "the night hymns resounded through the whole church, with the people singing." Chrysostom: "Once upon a time all sang psalms together; we do so too." The same, in the same place: "And when all have joined in the refrain, the voice is carried as if from one mouth." The same, in his third sermon on the Epistle to the Ephesians: "So you too came, and sang the hymn with all the others; by the very fact that you did not leave, you confessed that you are among those who are worthy." And in his fourth homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews: "For what do hymns mean? Surely that we may glorify God and give thanks, since he has already crowned the one departing, since he has freed him from labours, leading him out of servitude and keeping him with himself. Is it not for this reason that there are psalms and hymns? Is it not for this reason that there is psalmody? All these things belong to those who rejoice."

units.la: (3) Τπίλαον κοινῆ, τῶν πάντων ἡ ῥῶν. (4) Καὶ πάντες ὑμνῶσιν, ὡς ἐξ ἑνὸς φωνῇ χέει. (5) Τὸν ὕμνον ἕως μὴ πάντων. (6) Τί ἡ ᾄδειν; οἱ ὕμνοι; ὑμεῖς ἡ δόξα δοξάζομεν ἡ εὐχαριστοῦμεν; ἡ δὲ τῶν ὑμνοι; ἡ δὲ τῶν ψαλμῳδίαι; ταῦτα πάντα χαίρουσιν ὄντα. rialibus coacti ad Ecclesiam accesserunt: Quorum (inquit) si videas in Christi pace laetitias, frequentias, alacritates, & ad hymnos audiendos & canendos, & ad verbum Dei percipiendum celebres hilaresque conventus, &c. diceres nimiae fuisse credulitatis; si isti in aeternum perdendi & sempiternis ignibus cruciandi relinquerentur. Idem de Verbis Apostoli, serm. 10. Cantavimus (inquit) psalmum, exhortantes nos invicem, una voce, uno corde dicentes: Venite, adoremus, & prosternamur ei, &c. Idem Retract. lib. 2. cap. 1. Inter haec Hilarius quidam vir tribunitius laicus, Catholicus, nescio unde adversus Dei ministros, ut fieri assolet, irritatus, morem, qui tunc esse apud Carthaginem experat, ut hymni ad altare dicerentur ex Psalmorum libro, &c. maledicta reprehensione ubicunque poterat lacerabat, asserens fieri non oportere. Huic respondi jubentibus fratribus. Idem Confession. lib. 10. cap. 33. Tamen cum mihi accidit, ut me amplius cantus, quam res quae canitur, moveat; poenaliter me peccare confiteor, & tunc mallem non audire cantantem. Hieronymus in epist. ad Lucinium: Sonabant Psalmi, & aurata templorum reboans in sublimi quatiebat Allelnia. Basilius in Psal. CXIV. hom. 28. Ut vero ne diutius vos detinentes tristitiam vobis inferamus; ubi pauca ex psalmo, quem vos cantantes deprehendimus, dissimulerimus, &c. Ambrosius in Orat. ad populum de Auxentio: Hymnorum meorum carminibus populum deceptum volunt. Plane nec hoc abnuo. Grande carmen istud est, & quo nihil potentius. Quid enim potentius, quam confessio Trinitatis, quae quotidie totius populi ore celebratur? Certatim omnes student fidem fateri: patrem & Filium & Sp. Sanctum norunt versibus praedicare. Hi nimirum erant hymni; de quibus ita Augustinus, lib. 9. Confess. cap. 6. & 7. Quantum flevi in hymnis & canticis tuis, suave sonantis Ecclesiae tuae vocibus commotus acriter! Voces illae influebant auribus meis, & eliquabatur veritas tua in cor meum; & exaestuabant affectus pietatis, & currebant lachrymae, & bene mihi erat cum eis. Non longe coeperat Ecclesia Mediolanensis genus hoc consolationis & exhortationis celebrare, magno studio fratrum concinentium vocibus & cordibus. Nimirum annus erat, aut non multo amplius, cum Justini Valentiniani regis pueri mater hominem suum Ambrosium persequeretur haeresis suae causa, quae fuerat seduita ab Arianis. Excubabat pia plebs in Ecclesia, mori parata cum Episcopo suo, servo tuo. Tunc hymni & psalmi ut canerentur secundum morem Orientalium partium, ne populus moeroris studio contabesceret, institutum est, & ex illo in hodiernum retentum, multis jam ac pene omnibus gregibus tuis & per cetera orbis imitantibus. Hæc ibi. Hinc Concilium Laodicenum edixit, cap. 59. {7} Quod non oportet ab idiotis (i. e. privatis) Psalmos compositos & vulgares in Ecclesiis dicere. Similiter Concilium Braccarense I.° cap. 60. cujus etiam cap. 30. est hujusmodi. Placuit ut extra Psalmos Canonicarum Scripturarum Novi & Veteris Testamenti nihil poeticè compositum in Ecclesiâ psallatur; sicut & sancti præcipiunt Canones. Socrates, lib. 7. Hist. Eccles. cap. 22. {8} Imperator vero medius inter eos, hymnos ordiebatur, ac veste privatâ ingrediebatur. Sozomenus, lib. 8. cap. 8. Ariani extra urbem Constantinopolitanam in publicis porticibus congregati, {9} & per cætus divisi, per vices & modum alternandi in respondendi psallebant,&c. Joannes veritus, ne de suis aliqui per ista seducerentur, populum suum {10} ad parem psallendi modum instituit. Ibid. cap. 18. Populus {11} psalmos canens ad præsens negotium compositos, obviam ei progressi, ad Ecclesiam eum deduxerunt. Theodoritus {x} (aut potiùs apud eum Athanasius) de Flaviano & Diodoro refert, quòd licet sacerdotii ministrationem nondum fuissent consecuti, sed annumerari laicis; Tamen noctu & interdiu ad pietatis studium omnes sedulò excitarunt. {12} Hi primi (inquit) psallentium choro in duas partes divisò, hymnos Davidicos alternis canendos tradiderunt. Quæ res primùm Antiochiæ incæpta, ubique pervasit, & ad ultimas orbis terræ oras pervagata est. Hi etiam rerum divinarum studiosis ad martyrum monumenta in unam congregatis, totam noctem unâ cum illis Deum hymnis celebrando contriverunt. Hæc ibi: Bellarminus {y} quidem ait, quòd initio, quia Christiani erant pauci, omnes simul psallebant in Ecclesiâ, & respondebant in divinis officiis: at postea crescente populo, divisa sunt magis officia; & solis Clericis relictum est, ut communes {x} Hist. Eccles. lib. 2. cap. 24. {y} De Verbo Dei, lib. 2. cap. 16. {7} Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ἰδιωτικὸς ψαλμοὺς λέγειν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ. {8} Βασιλεὺς δὲ μέσος ὑμνῶν ἐξήρχετο τῆς ᾠδῆς. {9} Εἰς σύνταγμα μεριζόμενοι, καὶ ἀντιφώνων τρόπῳ ἐψάλλον. {10} Ἐπὶ τοῦ λαοῦ τὸν ψαλμῳδίας συνήγειρε. {11} Ἐν ψαλμῳδίαις ὡς τὸ συμβὰν πεπληρωμένας. {12} Ὅτι ἀνθρώπων διχῇ διελόντες τοῦ ψαλλόντων χόρους, ἐν διαδοχῇ ἀδὴν ἐδίδαξαν μελῳδίαν, ἐν τῷ ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ πρῶτον ἀρξάμενον, κἀντεῦθεν διέσπαρται, καὶ κατέλαβε τὴν οἰκουμένην τὰ πέρατα. Preces & laudes in Ecclesiâ peragant. Verùm idem etiam postea longo tempore servatum esse, tam in Oriente quàm in Occidente, paulò ante in hoc capite confirmavit ipse Bellarminus, tum ex Liturgiâ Chrysostomi, ubi apertissimè distinguuntur, quæ Sacerdos, quæ Diaconus, quæ populus in divinis Officiis canebant; item ex Cypriano, serm. de Oratione Dominicâ, ubi dicit, plebem respondere, Habemus ad Dominum; denique ex Hieronymi Præfat. lib. 2. in Epist. ad Galat. qui scribit, in Ecclesiis Urbis Romæ quasi cœleste tonitru audiri populum reboantem Amen.
units.tr: (3) They sing together, with the voice of all [Ψάλλουσι κοινῇ, τῶν πάντων ἡ φωνή]. (4) And all sing hymns, as if the voice poured forth from one mouth [καὶ πάντες ὑμνῶσιν, ὡς ἐξ ἑνὸς φωνῇ χέει]. (5) The hymn is sung by all [τὸν ὕμνον ἕως μὴ πάντων]. (6) What do hymns mean? Do we not glorify God and give thanks through them? What are the psalms and psalmody for? All these things belong to those who rejoice [τί ἡ ᾄδειν; οἱ ὕμνοι; ... ταῦτα πάντα χαίρουσιν ὄντα]. decrees, came to the church: "If you see among them joy, crowds and eagerness in Christ's peace, and lively, cheerful gatherings both for hearing and singing hymns and for receiving the word of God, you would say it was excessive credulity if these people were left to perish for ever and to be tormented in everlasting fires." Augustine, in his sermon On the Words of the Apostle, 10: "We sang a psalm, exhorting one another with one voice, with one heart, saying: Come, let us worship and bow down before him," etc. Augustine, Retractations, book 2, chapter 1: "Meanwhile a certain Hilarius, a lay tribune and Catholic, I know not why, was provoked against the ministers of God, as is often the case, and he tore apart with abusive censure wherever he could the custom, which at that time was in Carthage, that hymns from the Book of Psalms should be sung at the altar, and he asserted that this should not be done. I answered him at the bidding of the brethren." Augustine, Confessions, book 10, chapter 33: "Yet when it happens that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I sin grievously, and then I would rather not hear the singer." Jerome, in his letter to Lucinius: "The Psalms resounded, and the golden Alleluia echoed and shook the lofty temples." Basil, on Psalm 114, homily 28: "So that we do not detain you longer and bring sadness upon you, we have passed over a few things from the psalm which we found you singing, etc." Ambrose, in his address to the people concerning Auxentius: "They want the people deceived by the songs of my hymns. Certainly I do not deny this. That song is great, and nothing is more powerful. For what is more powerful than the confession of the Trinity, which is celebrated daily from the mouth of the whole people? All eagerly strive to confess the faith; they know how to proclaim in verses the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit." These, no doubt, were the hymns of which Augustine speaks thus in Confessions, book 9, chapters 6 and 7: "How much I wept at your hymns and canticles, deeply moved by the voices of your Church sounding sweetly! Those voices flowed into my ears, and your truth melted into my heart; the emotions of piety surged, tears ran, and it was well with me among them." Not long before, the Church of Milan had begun to celebrate this kind of consolation and exhortation, with the eager zeal of the brethren singing with voices and hearts. It was in fact a year, or not much more, when the mother of the boy-king Valentinian Justinus was persecuting her servant Ambrose on account of her heresy, which had been seduced by the Arians. The pious people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their bishop, your servant. Then it was ordained that hymns and psalms be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, so that the people might not waste away in grief, and from that time it has been kept to the present day, now imitated by many, indeed almost all, of your flocks throughout the rest of the world. Thus far Augustine. Hence the Council of Laodicea decreed, canon 59: "It is not fitting to say in the churches psalms composed by private persons (i.e. laymen) and in common use." Similarly the First Council of Braga, canon 60, and canon 30 of the same council is of this kind: "It has been decided that in the Church nothing composed in verse be sung in psalmody, except the psalms of the canonical Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, as the holy canons also prescribe." Socrates, book 7 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22: "The emperor, in the midst of them, led the hymns and entered in private dress." Sozomen, book 8, chapter 8: the Arians, gathered outside the city of Constantinople "in the public colonnades," "divided into groups, sang psalms in turn, in the manner of alternate responses." John, fearing that some of his people might be seduced by these things, trained his people "to the same manner of singing psalms." The same, chapter 18: "The people, singing psalms composed for the present occasion, went out to meet him and escorted him to the church." Theodoret (or rather, Athanasius, as cited by him) reports of Flavian and Diodore that although they had not yet obtained the ministry of the priesthood but were counted among the laity, "nevertheless by night and by day they all zealously stirred up the pursuit of piety. These men (he says) were the first to divide the choir of singers into two parts and to hand down hymns of David to be sung in alternation. This practice, begun first at Antioch, spread everywhere and reached to the farthest ends of the earth. These men also, gathering together those devoted to divine things at the monuments of the martyrs, spent the whole night praising God with hymns together with them." Thus far. Bellarmine indeed says that at first, because the Christians were few, all sang together in the Church and answered in the divine offices, but afterwards, as the people grew, the offices were divided more, and it was left to the clergy alone to offer prayers and praises in the Church. But Bellarmine himself, a little earlier in this chapter, confirmed that the same practice was kept for a long time afterwards, both in East and West, from the Liturgy of Chrysostom, where it is most clearly distinguished what the priest, what the deacon, and what the people sang in the divine offices; likewise from Cyprian's sermon on the Lord's Prayer, where he says that the people respond, "We have lifted them up to the Lord"; and finally from the preface of Jerome to book 2 of his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, where he writes that in the churches of the city of Rome the people's "Amen" was heard resounding like heavenly thunder.

units.la: SYri & Ægyptii non solùm suâ veteri sed & Arabicâ linguâ, quam vulgarem vocant, sacra celebrant, teste Josepho Scaligero ; qui Coptitas hodie & Ægyptios vetustissimos Christianos linguâ priscâ Ægyptiacâ sacros utriusque Testamenti libros conscriptos habere, & sacra itidem in templis obire, alibi confirmat. Apud Ægyptum & Alexandrum Arabicâ in sacris & divinis officiis hodie linguâ utiChristianos ipse fatetur Jacobus Ledelina . Per totam Syriam & circa Hierosolymam (inquit Barthol. Georgievez de Turcarum moribus, in fine, pag. 178. edit. Lugduni 1553.) Græci non utuntur linguâ Græcâ; sed transtulerunt totam Sacram Scripturam in Arabicum idioma; neque literis, quibus Græci olim utebantur; sed Arabicis characteribus utuntur, etiam Missam Arabico sermone celebrant, & omnia divina officia decantant. In Oppido Tauro Templum est Caloicrorum Maronitarum (ita Bellonius, lib. 2. Observat. cap. 67.) quorum sacra adiimus, partim Arabicâ, partim Armeniacâ, partim Græcâ linguâ decantata. Omnes quinetiam Asiæ Ecclesias Syriacâ linguâ in sacris uti, ex Epistolâ Asiaticâ Jacobi Navarchi Hondischotani supra confirmavimus. Syriacâ linguâ Asiaticos omnes Christianos uti, cùm inter se, tum verò
units.tr: The Syrians and Egyptians celebrate their sacred rites not only in their ancient language but also in Arabic, which they call the vulgar tongue, as Joseph Scaliger testifies. He also affirms elsewhere that the Copts, the most ancient Egyptian Christians, have the sacred books of both Testaments written in the old Egyptian language and likewise perform the rites in their churches. That Christians in Egypt and Alexandria today use Arabic in sacred and divine services is confessed by Jacob Ledelina himself. "Throughout all Syria and around Jerusalem," writes Bartholomew Georgievitz, in On the Customs of the Turks, at the end, p. 178, Lyon edition of 1553, "the Greeks do not use the Greek language. They have translated the whole of Holy Scripture into the Arabic idiom, and they do not use the letters the Greeks once used but Arabic characters. They also celebrate the Mass in the Arabic language and chant all the divine offices. In the town of Tauros there is a temple of the Maronite Caloicri," so Belon, book 2 of his Observations, ch. 67, "whose rites we attended, sung partly in Arabic, partly in Armenian, and partly in Greek." Moreover, we have already shown, from the Asian letter of Jacob Navarchus of Hondischoten, that all the churches of Asia use the Syriac language in worship. That all Asian Christians use the Syriac language, both among themselves and especially in their sacred rites, is affirmed by

units.la: a De Emendat. temp. lib. 7. pag. 674. novæ editionis. b Lib. 2. pag. 185. c Cap. 33. sect. 5. Vid. Pollevin. tom. 2. Apparat. sacr. in Maronitis, pag. 397. præcipuè in suis sacris, affirmat. P. Victor Cajetanus in Paradigmate linguæ Syriacæ. Certè Asiaticos Christianos vetere Syrorum linguâ partim vulgò, partim in sacris tantùm usos, ante eum prodidit Albertus Widmanstadius . Nempe in sacris (alioqui vulgaris sermo Arabicus est) eâ utuntur quamplurimi Christiani, qui in totâ Syriâ habitant, sed præcipuè circa montem Libanum ad quatuor millia hominum, qui vulgò Christiani de Zamâ dicuntur; ut est apud Gulielmum Postellum (qui in has partes iter suscepit) in Introductione 12. linguarum: quod non solùm in Syriâ fieri, sed etiam in Mesopotamiâ, Chaldæâ, Ægypto, & denique in universi Orientis partibus dispersis ac disseminatis, testis est Georgius Amyra Syrus Edenien-sis è Libano (in Præludi. de Chaldaicæ linguæ utilitate, præfix. Grammaticæ suæ Syriacæ.) Narrat etiam Theseus Ambrosius , Syris, qui ad Concilium Lateranense sub Leone X. convenerant, libertatem sacra in Urbe Romanâ celebrandi priùs concessam non fuisse, quàm quo ritu quibusque verbis illa peragerent, clarè intellectum fuisset. Itaque Elia Chaldæo seu Syro subdiacono verba Chaldaicè, Syriacè & Arabicè (quòd sc. Syriacum omne vulgus eâ linguâ passim utatur; inquit Theseus Ambrosius) recitante, Josephum Gallum Hebræum Doctorem eadem materno atque etiam Latino retulisse sermone. Extat etiam Basilii Anaphora, ex vetustissimo codice Syriaco traducta per Andr. Masium; necnon Severi Alexandrini Patriarchæ de ritibus Baptismi & sacræ Synaxis apud Syros Christianos receptis liber, à Guidone Fabricio ex Syriaco Codice translatus. Nuper quoque Augustæ Vindelicorum, an. 1604. prodiit Liturgia Sanctorum Patrum à Victorino Scialach ex Arabico conversa. Ægyptii enim Christiani (qui hodie Kopti dicuntur) vetustissimâ Ægyptiacâ linguâ in sacris utuntur: quâ tres Liturgias conscriptas, Gregorii, Cyrilli, & Ignatii, cum interpretatione Arabicâ penès se haberi prodit Vir Clarissimus Josephus Scaliger (eas sc. ipsas, quas à Victorio Scialach Maronitâ conversas diximus) à quo etiam accepit Bonav. Vulcanius , Nubianos inferioris Ægypti partibus conterminos sub Patriarchâ Alexandrino sacra linguâ Elkupti celebrâsse. Nestorianos linguâ Chaldaicâ in sacris officius celebrandis & in scripturis suis uti;
units.tr: (a) On the Emendation of Times, book 7, p. 674, new edition. (b) Book 2, p. 185. (c) Ch. 33, sect. 5. See Pollevin, vol. 2 of the Apparatus sacer, on the Maronites, p. 397. Father Victor Cajetan, in his Paradigm of the Syriac Language. Certainly, Albert Widmanstadt had earlier reported that Asian Christians used the old Syriac language, partly in common speech and partly only in their sacred rites. For the sacred rites are performed in that language (otherwise the common speech is Arabic) by very many Christians who live throughout Syria, but especially around Mount Lebanon, some four thousand people, commonly called "Christians of Zama." So Guillaume Postel, who undertook a journey to those parts, reports in his Introduction to Twelve Languages. Georgius Amyra, a Syrian of Edessa from Lebanon, testifies that this happens not only in Syria but also in Mesopotamia, Chaldaea, Egypt, and finally in the scattered and dispersed parts of the whole East (in the Preliminary Discourse on the usefulness of the Chaldaic language, prefixed to his Syriac grammar). Thesevs Ambrosius also relates that the Syrians who had gathered at the Lateran Council under Leo X were not granted freedom to celebrate the sacred rite in the city of Rome until it had been made clear what rite they used and in what words they performed it. Therefore, when Elias, a Chaldaean or Syrian subdeacon, recited the words in Chaldaic, Syriac and Arabic (since, says Thesevs Ambrosius, all the Syrian common people use that language everywhere), Joseph Gallus, a Hebrew teacher, rendered them in his own native language and also in Latin. There also exists the Anaphora of Basil, translated by Andreas Masius from a very ancient Syriac codex; and likewise a book by Severus, Patriarch of Alexandria, on the rites of Baptism and of the sacred Synaxis received among Syrian Christians, translated from a Syriac codex by Guido Fabricius. Recently too, at Augsburg in 1604, the Liturgy of the Holy Fathers appeared, translated from Arabic by Victorinus Scialach. The Egyptian Christians (today called Copts) use their most ancient Egyptian language in worship. Joseph Scaliger, a most distinguished man, reports that three liturgies written in it, those of Gregory, Cyril and Ignatius, are in his possession with an Arabic interpretation (the very ones that we said were translated by Victorius Scialach, a Maronite). From him Bonaventura Vulcanius also learned that the Nubians, neighbours of Lower Egypt, celebrated their sacred rites under the Patriarch of Alexandria in the sacred language, Elkupti. Nestorians use the Chaldaic language in celebrating their services and in their writings;

(g) On the Emendation of Times, book 7, p. 66, new edition. See Gretser, on the Jesuit Bellarmine, pp. 879, 880, 892. The same writer reports of the Armenians (i) that, though they generally know several languages, they use the Armenian language in the divine office, the Mass, prayers and ceremonies, and it is understood by all, men and women alike, of that country. He also reports that the Maronites use their genuine Syriac language in performing sacred rites.

units.la: Meridionales Indos rem divinam suâ linguâ facere agnoscit Eckius l, idemque confirmat Erasmus m. Hi nimirum Indi Æthiopes sunt, quos Abassinos vocant; ex quibus aliquos Romæ se convenisse narrat Joannes Potken (Præfatione in Æthiopicum Psalterium à se editum) à quibus non sine difficultate didicerit, ipsos in eorum sacris Chaldæis literis uti. Id etiam præterire nolo (inquit ibid. Jo. Potken) quòd hâc tempestate viginti populi vel circa Æthiopiam, quæ sub Ægypto est, & alia loca Australia, præsertim ad Nilum & Gion flumina, & inter illa, ac citra & ultra Æquinoctialem circulum sub Zodiaco incolentes, & totidem maternis seu vulgaribus inter se differentibus linguis utentes, omnes in eorum sacris hac Chaldaea (licet enim Jo. Potken perperam existimavit esse hanc linguam, ut supra attigimus) utuntur linguâ, & à tempore nascentis fidei Christianæ (sicut ipsi, qui ex eis nos peregrinationis & devotionis causâ accedunt, affirmant) usi fuerunt, &c. Hæc ille. De iisdem Thevetus n hæc habet. Complures illorum Episcopos vidi; eorumque Missam audivi, quam linguâ celebrant Abyssinâ; quæ accedit multùm ad Arabicam, etiam in characteribus. Paulo aliter Alvaresius o: Omnes eorum libri, quorum sanè numerus est permagnus, membranis conscripti sunt; neque enim papyrum habent; & scriptura eorundem in linguâ Tygicâ exaratur, quæ est Abyssina. Propiùs Joanni Potken accedit Nunnesius p, haud dissimili quippe errore abreptus: Quicquid (inquit) habent sacrarum literarum qui à D. Thomæ tempore Christiani, & Zgcotorani, ac qui Æthiopum Regi subjecti sunt, quicquid precum horariarum, quicquid traditionum, sola Chaldaicâ linguâ scriptum habent, nec fidem ullam adhibent Scripturis, nisi eo idiomate citentur. Josephus Scaliger q, horum Christianorum Æthiopum Ecclesias quasdam in Italiâ fuisse memoriâ nostra; esse & Hierosolymis, Alexandriæ, & Cairi, commemorat. Addit etiam eâ linguâ solâ, quam liberam vocant ipsi,
units.tr: Eck acknowledges that the Indians of the south perform their divine service in their own language, and Erasmus confirms the same. These Indians are of course Ethiopians, whom they call Abyssinians. John Potken (in the preface to his edition of the Ethiopic Psalter) relates that some of them had met in Rome, and from them he learned, not without difficulty, that they use Chaldaic letters in their sacred rites. "I do not wish to pass over this either," says John Potken in the same place, "that at this time there are twenty peoples, or thereabouts, around Ethiopia, which lies under Egypt, and other southern places, especially along the rivers Nile and Gihon, and among those and on both sides of the equinoctial circle under the zodiac, who inhabit these places and use as many mother or vernacular languages, differing from one another, all of whom use this Chaldaic language in their sacred rites (for although John Potken wrongly thought this was the language, as we touched on above), and have used it from the time of the rise of the Christian faith, as they themselves, who come to us from among them for the sake of pilgrimage and devotion, affirm, etc." So he writes. Thevet has this to say about the same people: "I have seen many of their bishops, and I have heard their Mass, which they celebrate in the Abyssinian language, which comes very close to Arabic, even in its letters." Alvarez writes somewhat differently: "All their books, which are indeed very numerous, are written on parchment, for they have no papyrus; and their writing is in the Tigrinya language, which is Abyssinian." Nuñez comes closer to John Potken, though led astray by a not dissimilar error: "Whatever sacred writings they have, those who have been Christians since the time of St Thomas, and the Zgcotorani, and those who are subject to the King of the Ethiopians, whatever hours of prayer, whatever traditions they have, they have written only in the Chaldaic language, and they give no credence to the Scriptures unless they are cited in that idiom." Joseph Scaliger records that some churches of these Ethiopian Christians existed in Italy within our memory, and that there are also some at Jerusalem, Alexandria and Cairo. He adds that they use only that language, which they themselves call "free," for learned purposes, for writing histories and for celebrating sacred rites; a language which differs from true Ethiopic only as Italian and Illyrian, or German and Hungarian, differ. In the year 1548 Peter the Ethiopian had the New Testament printed in this language, with a Missal added, including the blessing of incense, wax, etc. He also had translated into Latin from this language the Method of Baptizing, the prayers and blessings for a woman in childbirth, the prayers which the Ethiopians use in the sacraments of Baptism and Confirmation, and the Mass which they commonly use, which is also called the Universal Canon [Louvain edition, 1550, 4to, and vol. 6 of the Bibliotheca Patrum]. See Francisco Alvarez, Description of Ethiopia, ch. 11 (where he teaches that the Ethiopians use this language in their sacred rites), and Bernard Breydenbach in his Itinerary.

Vid. ipsum pag. 637, 638, 639. novæ editionis. doctos uti, historias scribi, sacra celebrari; quae quidem à verâ Æthiopicâ tantùm discrepet, quantum Italica & Illyrica, Germanica & Hungarica. Hâc linguâ anno 1548. Novum Testamentum imprimi curavit Petrus Æthiops, adjecto Missali, cum benedictione incensi, ceræ, &c. Latinè etiam ex hâc linguâ vertenda curavit, Modum baptizandi, preces & benedictiones puerperæ, Orationes quibus utuntur Æthiopes in Sacramento Baptismi & Confirmationis; Missam, quâ communiter utuntur, quæ etiam Canon Universalis appellatur, [edit. Lovanii 1550. 4. & tom. 6. Biblioth. Patrum.] Vide Francisci Alvarez descript. Æthiop. cap. 11. (ubi hâc linguâ Æthiopas in sacris uti docet) & Benardum Breitembachium in suo Itinerario.
units.tr: q Scaliger, de emendatione temporum, lib. 7. See the same work, pp. 637, 638, 639, of the new edition. learned men use it, histories are written in it, and sacred rites are celebrated in it. This language differs from true Ethiopic as much as Italian and Illyrian, or German and Hungarian, differ from one another. In this language, in 1548, Peter the Ethiopian had the New Testament printed, with a Missal added, including the blessing of incense, wax, etc. He also had translated into Latin from this language the Manner of Baptizing, the prayers and blessings for a woman in childbirth, the prayers the Ethiopians use in the Sacrament of Baptism and Confirmation, and the Mass which they commonly use, also called the Universal Canon [edition Louvain 1550, 4to, and vol. 6 of the Bibliotheca Patrum]. See Francisco Alvarez, Description of Ethiopia, ch. 11 (where he teaches that the Ethiopians use this language in their worship), and Bernard Breitenbach in his Itinerary.

units.la: Moscovitas, Armenios, & Æthiopas (quibus Presbyter Joannes dominatur) preces publicas vernaculo semper sermone celebrâsse ipse fatetur Hardingus . De Ruthenis & Armenis illud confirmat Jacobus Ledesma . Speciatim verò de Armenis Bellonius : Omnes (inquit) qui Missam audiunt, sacerdoti respondent Armeniacâ linguâ. Item, Armenorum sacerdos Evangelium legente, qui intersunt omnes intelligunt quod ipsis prælegitur. Nam Armeniaca lingua veterem elocutionem ferè retinet. Pari modo B. Idenbachius, Habent (inquit) Armeni proprium idioma, & proprias literas; quibus tam Laici quàm Clerici in communi sermone & in divinis etiam officiis utuntur. Postellus vero Armenicam linguam esse ait in usu sacrorum Armenis non tantùm in utràque Armenia, ut vulgò putant, sed ubicunque Mahamedes audit ur; cùm lingua vulgaris omnino Turcica sit. Ita refert P. Victor Cajetanus duplicem esse hujus populi linguam, primamque atque excellentiorem esse Craper, i.e. linguam Latinam vel literariam, quâ utuntur in Ecclesiâ. Nihilominus Jacobus de Vitriaco diserte asserit Armenos in vulgari sermone divinas Scripturas pronuntiare; ita ut sacerdotes & Clerici eorum à laicis in Ecclesiis intelligantur: quemadmodum de Græcis affirmat (an autem vere, multùm dubito: vid. contra Crucii Turco-Græciam, qui Græcos Constantinopolitanos hodiernos linguâ puriore Græcâ, vulgo ignotâ, concionari; satis esse putantes, si duo trelve intelligant, refert )
units.tr: Hardingus himself admits that the Muscovites, the Armenians and the Ethiopians (over whom Prester John rules) have always conducted their public prayers in the vernacular. Jacobus Ledesma confirms this for the Ruthenians and the Armenians. Of the Armenians in particular, Bellonius writes: All who attend the Mass (he says) answer the priest in the Armenian language. Again: When the Armenian priest reads the Gospel, all who are present understand what is read to them, for the Armenian language still largely keeps its ancient idiom. Likewise B. Idenbachius: The Armenians (he says) have their own language and their own letters, which both the laity and the clergy use in ordinary speech and also in the divine services. Postellus, however, says that the Armenian language is used in the sacred rites by the Armenians not only in the two Armenias, as is commonly thought, but wherever the Mahometans reach, since the ordinary language there is entirely Turkish. P. Victor Cajetanus likewise reports that this people has a twofold language, and that the first and more excellent is the Craper, that is, the Latin or literary language, which they use in the Church. Nevertheless, Jacobus de Vitriaco plainly asserts that the Armenians read the divine Scriptures in the vulgar tongue, so that their priests and clergy are understood by the laity in the churches, just as he affirms of the Greeks. (Whether this is true I greatly doubt; see against it Crucius's Turco-Graecia, which reports that the Greeks of present-day Constantinople preach in a purer Greek that is unknown to the common people, thinking it enough if two or three understand.)

units.la: r Artic. 3. sect. 38. s Cap. 33. sect. 4. 6. t Observat. lib. 3. cap. 12. v In Introduct. 12. linguarum. x In Paradigm. ling. Armen. y Hist. Oriental. lib. 1. cap 79. z Cap. 75. a Pag. 157. & 205. eos Græcâ linguâ in vulgari & in scripturis ita uti, ut sacerdotes suos in Ecclesiis & in literali sermone, qui idem est cum vulgari, intelligant. In Ecclesiis Rutenorum linguâ Serviorum, quæ est Sclavonica, divina celebrant, legunt, & cantant: in Ecclesiis Armenorum sermone Armeno , ut est apud Matthiam Michovium Armenos nempe intelligit, oppida quædam Russiæ Podoliæque incolentes ; qui suis ibi ritibus suáque linguâ in sacris utuntur; quemadmodum testatur Martinus Cromerus . Cæterùm apud Russos (seu Moschos) totum sacrum seu Missa gentili ac vernaculo sermone peragi solet. Epistola præterea & Evangelium pro tempore, quò magis à populo percipiantur, extra chorum populo astanti clarâ voce recitantur; inquit Sigismundus ab Heberstain in rerum Moscoviticarum Commentariis . Verba etiam consecrationis linguâ Ruthenicâ sacerdos proloquitur; nempe, Hoc est corpus; &, Hic est sanguis Domini Jesu Christi; quem Judæi innocentem morte multârunt; ut est in Narratione de Russorum religione ad Davidem Chytræum anno 1581. scriptâ . In Moscoviâ sacra vulgari linguâ peraguntur; inquit Philippus Pernesten Cæsaris legatus in Relatione de statu regni Moscoviæ anno 1579. Tom. 1. Thesauri Politici edit. Francofurt. 1610. pag. 336. Quin & precationes linguâ Moscovitica & Finlandica habentur in Archivis Bodleianæ Bibliothecæ. Addam quæ Thevetus de iisdem habet. Moscovitis (inquit) pauci sunt prædicatores, contentis quippe illis lectionibus solis, quas sacerdotes ipsis prælegunt, singulis diebus Dominicis. Isti enim populo legunt Evangelia & Epistolas Apostolorum, & Doctorum libros in linguâ ab iis intellecta. Vid. supra ad annum 86o.
units.tr: r Art. 3, sect. 38. s Chap. 33, sect. 4, 6. t Observ. lib. 3, cap. 12. v In Introduct. 12 linguarum. x In Paradigm. ling. Armen. y Hist. Oriental. lib. 1, cap. 79. z Chap. 75. a Pp. 157 and 205. They use Greek in the vernacular and in the Scriptures so that their priests are understood in the churches and in the literal speech, which is the same as the vulgar tongue. In the churches of the Ruthenians they celebrate, read and sing the divine offices in the Slavonic language, which is that of the Serbs. In the churches of the Armenians they use the Armenian language, as Matthias Michovius reports; it is understood by the Armenians who live in certain towns of Russia and Podolia, who use their own rites and language in worship, as Martinus Cromerus attests. Moreover, among the Russians (or Muscovites) the whole sacred service, that is the Mass, is usually performed in the native and vernacular tongue. Besides, the Epistle and the Gospel for the day are read aloud outside the choir to the standing people, so that they may be better understood by the people, says Sigismund von Herberstein in his Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs. The priest also pronounces the words of consecration in the Russian language: namely, This is the body, and This is the blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, whom the Jews put to death though he was innocent; as stated in the account of the Russian religion written to David Chytraeus in 1581. In Muscovy the sacred rites are performed in the vulgar tongue, says Philip Pernesten, the Emperor's envoy, in his report on the state of the kingdom of Muscovy in 1579 (Vol. 1 of the Thesaurus Politicus, Frankfurt edition 1610, p. 336). Indeed, prayers in Muscovite and Finnish are also held in the archives of the Bodleian Library. I will add what Thevet has about the same people: The Muscovites (he says) have few preachers, since they are content with those readings alone which the priests read to them on each Lord's Day. For these read to the people the Gospels and the Epistles of the Apostles, and the books of the Teachers, in a language they understand. See above, under the year 860.

units.la: Tzervianos seu Posnanianos in Priscâ suâ linguâ omnia vulgaria & sacrificium ipsum habere perhibet Postellus . Gotbi (inquit Scaliger ) sacra Græco ritu celebrant linguâ veteri Gothicâ; in usu autem quotidiano magnâ ex parte Teutonissant. Dalmatico idiomate Hieronymus Vetus ac Novum Testamentum cum sacrificio & precationibus traduêta reliquit. Ita Theodorus Bibliander de ratione communi
units.tr: Postellus reports that the Tservians, or Posnanians, have all the vulgar services and the sacrifice itself in their ancient language. The Goths (says Scaliger) celebrate their sacred rites in the Greek manner in the ancient Gothic language, though in daily use they largely speak German. In the Dalmatian idiom Jerome left a translation of the Old and New Testaments, together with the sacrifice and prayers. So Theodor Bibliander, in his general account of the languages of all peoples.

units.la: b De Sarmat. Europ. lib. 2. cap. 1. c Descript. Polon. lib. 1. d Sub titulo de Decimis. e Pag. 239. Theologiæ Moscovit. f Cosmograph. lib. 19. cap. 12. g Introduct. 12. linguar. h In literis anno 1590. scriptis ad P. Merulam, apud eund. Cosmograph. par. 2. lib. 1. cap. 8. communi omnium linguarum, pag. 15. Habet gens Dalmatica (inquit Marianus Victorius) & Missam & alias divinas preces Illyricâ conscriptas linguâ; sedisque Apostolicæ authoritate (quam à Paulo II. habuerunt) publicè illis ubique utuntur. Eas autem à D. Hieronymo accepisse persuasissimi ita sunt; ut captis potiùs armis omnes disperire malint, quàm eas relinquere. Hæc Victorius in Indice sex posteriorum Tomorum Hieronymi (verbo Illyricum) quæ etiam ab Angelo Roccha translata sunt in Bibliothecam suam Vaticanam ; qui addit insuper se vidisse codicem horarium ceterasque divinas preces Illyricâ conscriptas linguâ ab omnibus Dalmatis intellectâ. Idem tamen in Appendice præter vulgarem Illyricam linguam, extare alteram notat, huic valdè assimilem & ferè eandem; quæ à rudioribus absque regulis non rectè intelligitur, nec rectè pronuntiatur. In hanc linguam (inquit) à S. Hieronymo Scripturam sacram Sclavonicis literis & à S. Cyrillo Servianis characteribus translatam fuisse, credendum est. Id quod etiam de Missali, de Codice horario, deque aliis Sclavorum libris dicendum putat Antonius Bonfinius ; qui de Ludovico I. rege, Caroli filio, agens ita scribit: In Sclavonicâ, & in eâ quidem regione, quam Lipnam nunc appellant, cùm multos depravatis opinionibus esse intellexisset, quibus sacerdotes ex Divi quondam Hieronymi institutione sacra ministrabant, ad veram sapientiam reduxit. Verùm hi nunc in pristinum errorem recidisse dicuntur. Hæc Bonfinius. Vid. supra an. 860. Joannes Bapt. Palat. civis Romanus de ratione scribendi, de Illyricis sive Sclavis ita loquitur. Sciendum est, quod vulgaris illorum sermo idem ille est, quo continuè utuntur in officiis divinis; & universus populus intelligit, haud secus atque nos intelligimus vulgarem sermonem nostrum. Rei totius veritatem agnoscit Azorius Jesuita hisce verbis. Objiciunt Protestantes, quòd Jacobus Apostolus Chaldaicè aut Syriacè apud Judæos Liturgiam composuit; quâ nunc quoque fortasse utuntur Æthiopes, Maronitæ, Armeni: Basilius & Chrysostomus Græcè pro Græcis: Hieronymus perhibetur Dalmaticâ linguâ Liturgiam composuisse. CONCEDO: sed id factum est, quia illi extorserunt, &c. Quod verò Costerus habet
units.tr: b On the Sarmatians of Europe, lib. 2, cap. 1. c Description of Poland, lib. 1. d Under the title On Tithes. e P. 239, Theology of Muscovy. f Cosmography, lib. 19, cap. 12. g Introduction to the Languages, 12. h In a letter of 1590 written to P. Merula, cited in the same author's Cosmography, part 2, lib. 1, cap. 8, on the common [history] of all languages, p. 15. The Dalmatian people (says Marianus Victorius) have both the Mass and other divine prayers written in the Illyrian language; and by the authority of the Apostolic See (which they had from Paul II) they use them publicly everywhere. They are so firmly persuaded that these were received from St Jerome that they would rather perish, taking up arms, than give them up. Thus Victorius in the index to the last six volumes of Jerome (under the word Illyricum). These things were also translated by Angelo Roccha into his Vatican Library, and he adds that he himself saw a breviary and other divine prayers written in the Illyrian language and understood by all the Dalmatians. Yet the same author notes in his Appendix that, besides the vulgar Illyrian tongue, there exists another, very close to it and nearly the same, which is not rightly understood or rightly pronounced by the less educated without rules. It is to be believed that the holy Scripture was translated into this language by St Jerome in Slavonic letters, and by St Cyril in Serbian characters. Antonius Bonfinius thinks the same should be said of the Missal, of the breviary and of the other books of the Slavs. Speaking of King Louis I, son of Charles, he writes thus: When he had learned that in the Slavonic region, which they now call Lipna, many people were held in corrupt opinions, by which the priests administered the sacred offices according to the institution of the late St Jerome, he brought them back to true wisdom. But these are now said to have fallen back into their former error. So Bonfinius. See above, under the year 860. Giovanni Battista Palatino, a Roman citizen, in his work on the manner of writing, speaks thus of the Illyrians or Slavs: It must be known that their vulgar speech is the same that they continually use in the divine offices, and the whole people understands it just as we understand our own vernacular. The Jesuit Azorius acknowledges the truth of the whole matter in these words: The Protestants object that the Apostle James composed a Liturgy in Chaldean or Syriac among the Jews, which perhaps the Ethiopians, Maronites and Armenians still use; that Basil and Chrysostom composed theirs in Greek for the Greeks; that Jerome is said to have composed a Liturgy in the Dalmatian language. I GRANT IT: but this was done because they were compelled, etc. As to what Costerus holds,

It is most false, as is clear from the start of the fourth section, that the divine services were performed in the regions of Greece, Chaldea and Rome not in the vulgar idiom of the peoples but in common languages. Moreover, the Illyrian Breviary (with a calendar prefixed) was published in octavo at Venice in Illyrian type; concerning these see Gesner's Pandects of Grammar. I saw it at Oxford in the Bodleian Library.

units.la: SAcræ Scripturæ volumina flammis tradere flagitiosissimorum Ecclesiæ hostium semper habita est consuetudo. Id quod ab impio Jehoiakimo factum legimus, Jerem. XXXVI. 23. ab Antiocho Epimane 1 Mac. I. 59. (Vid. & 1 Mac. III. 48.) Diocletiano, apud Eusebium lib. 8. hist.Eccl. cap. 2. & Augustinum in Breviculo collationis 3. diei cum Donatistis, cap. 13. & 15. (unde patet, in ista persecutione non quoslibet infimos, sed etiam patresfamilias, cum persecutoribus respondissent se Scripturas non tradituros, crudelissimis mortibus occisos, ex literis Secundi Tigisitani.) à Donatistis, in Collatione Carthaginensi 3. §. 302. Tom. 7. Operum Augustini, & in Breviculo Collationis diei 3. cap. 11. à Georgio Cappadoce (quem isti in Divum transformarunt) quum per Arianos persecutio fieret, apud Athanasium in Epist. ad Orthodoxos, tom. 1. Oper. pag. 729. edit. Commelinianæ. Hinc Augustinus Epist. 68. ad Januarium (sol. 210.) de Fœlice. Cui divinarum Scripturarum productio atque exustio videretur objecta. Et Hieronymus lib. 2. Commentar. in Zachar. cap. 8. In tantam rabiem persecutorum ferilas excitata est; ut etiam conciliabula nostra destruerent, divinos libros ignibus traderent. Diocletiani certè temporibus persecutione sæviente, Saturninus Martyr Proconsuli roganti, Habes Scripturam aliquam in domo tua? respondit, Habeo, sed in corde meo. O martyrem Apostoli 2 memorem! (inquit Auctor Actorum illius apud Surium, tom 1. die 2 Febr. quem Donatistam fuisse apparet) qui legem Domini conscriptam habuit non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei vivi; non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carnalibus. O martyrem legis sacræ idoneum diligentemque custodem; qui Traditorum facinus perhorrescens, Scripturas Dominicas b ne peraret, inter secreta sui pectoris collocavit. Hic ipse status nostrorum sub Pontificiis & In-
units.tr: It has always been the custom of the most wicked enemies of the Church to hand the volumes of Sacred Scripture over to the flames. We read that this was done by the impious Jehoiakim (Jer. 36:23), by Antiochus Epiphanes (1 Macc. 1:59; see also 1 Macc. 3:48), and by Diocletian, as Eusebius reports (Ecclesiastical History 8.2), and Augustine in the Breviculus of the third day's Collation with the Donatists, chapters 13 and 15. From the latter it is clear that in that persecution not only the lowliest people but even heads of families, who answered the persecutors that they would not hand over the Scriptures, were put to death by the cruellest means, according to the letter of Secundus of Tigisis. The Donatists did the same, in the Carthaginian Collation 3, §302, vol. 7 of Augustine's works, and in the Breviculus of the Collation of the third day, chapter 11. George of Cappadocia (whom they turned into a saint) did it too, when a persecution was carried on by the Arians, according to Athanasius in the Epistle to the Orthodox, vol. 1, p. 729, Commelin edition. Hence Augustine, Epistle 68 to Januarius (al. 210), concerning Felix, to whom the production and burning of the divine Scriptures seemed to be imputed. And Jerome, book 2 of the Commentary on Zechariah, chapter 8: Such a frenzy of persecutors was stirred up that they even destroyed our meeting-houses and handed the divine books over to the fires. Certainly in the times of Diocletian, while the persecution raged, Saturninus the martyr, when the proconsul asked him, Do you have any Scripture in your house?, replied: I have, but in my heart. O martyr mindful of the Apostle! (says the author of his Acts in Surius, vol. 1, 2 February, who was evidently a Donatist) who had the law of the Lord written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone but on the fleshly tablets of the heart. O martyr, a fit and diligent guardian of the sacred law, who, shuddering at the crime of the traitors, so that he would not lose the Lord's Scriptures, placed them among the secret places of his breast. This very condition of ours under the Papists and Inquisitors.

units.la: 2 2 Cor. III. b Confer Antonium Benbellonum, pag. 76. quisitoribus. Ibid. Fœlix Martyr; Collectam (inquit) religiosissimè celebravimus; ad scripturas Dominicas legendas in Dominicum convenimus semper. Item in Actis Euplii Martyris Diocletiano VIII. Maximiano VII. Coss. (anno Domini 303.) pridie Idus Augusti; cùm Euplius ab exploratoribus inventus legere Evangelia, cum libro perductus esset ad Calvisianum Consularem; unus ex amicis Calvisiani, nomine Maximus, dixit: Non decet tales chartas eum tenere contra regalem præceptionem. Calvisianus dixit ad Euplium positum in tormentis: Quare apud te habuisti, & non tradidisti has lectiones, quas Imperatores vetuerunt? Respondit Euplius: Quia Christianus sum, & tradere non licebat; magisque expedit mori quàm tradere. In his vita æterna est; qui tradit, vitam æternam perdit; ut eam non perdam, vitam meam do. Calvisianus interlocutus dixit: Euplius, qui secundùm edictum principum non tradidit Scripturas, sed legit populo, torqueatur. Tunc appensum est ad collum ejus Evangelium, cum quo apprehensus fuerat, &c. (Baronius anno 303.) Inter Libros improbatæ lectionis (quorum meminit Domitius Ulpianus JC. Ethnicus lib. 10. Digestor. tit. 2. Famil. herciscunda, lib. 4.) Propheticos etiam numeratos fuisse vult Baronius : quos ex Senatusconsulto vetitos, & magnis pœnis eorum lectionem interdictam fuisse author est Justinus Martyr: quos etiam sub magicis libris comprehensos, (Christianos enim ab Ethnicis Magos existimatos ex Arnobio notat Baronius ) à Paulo JC. verisimile est, cum lib. 5. recept. sentent. tit. 23. ait: Libros magicæ artis apud se neminem habere licet; & si penes quoscunque reperti sint, bonis ademptis, ambustisque his publice, in insulam deportantur; humiliores capite puniuntur. Quod etiam spectare videtur Diocletiani edictum, quod in fragmentis libri 7. Codicis Hermogeniani (alias Gregoriani) superesse, sub tit. de Maleficis & Manichæis (in Legum Judaic. & Romanar. collatione, tit. 15.) Jubemus namque auctores quidem ad principes, unà cum abominandis scripturis eorum, severiori pœna subjici; ita ut flammeis ignibus exurantur. (Vid. Baronium, an. 287. §.4. & Ant. Benbellonum, p. 68.)
units.tr: 2 Cor. 3. b See Antonio Benbellonus, p. 76. Ibid. Felix the martyr: We celebrated the collection most devoutly, he says; we have always come together on the Lord's day to read the Lord's Scriptures. Likewise in the Acts of Euplius the martyr, in the consulship of Diocletian (for the 8th time) and Maximian (for the 7th) (year of the Lord 303), the day before the Ides of August: when Euplius, found reading the Gospels by the spies, had been brought with the book before the consular Calvisianus, one of Calvisianus's friends, named Maximus, said: It is not fitting for such papers to be held by him against the royal command. Calvisianus said to Euplius, who had been placed in torments: Why did you have these readings with you and not hand them over, which the emperors have forbidden? Euplius replied: Because I am a Christian, and it was not permitted to hand them over; and it is better to die than to hand them over. In these is eternal life; whoever hands them over loses eternal life. So that I do not lose it, I give my life. Calvisianus interposed and said: Euplius, who did not hand over the Scriptures according to the emperors' edict but read them to the people, shall be tortured. Then the Gospel with which he had been seized was hung around his neck, etc. (Baronius, year 303.) Among the books of disapproved reading (of which Domitius Ulpian, the pagan jurist, speaks in Digest 10, tit. 2, Family Erciscunda, book 4), Baronius thinks the prophetic books were also counted. Justin Martyr is the authority that these were forbidden by senatorial decree and that their reading was prohibited under heavy penalties. It is likely that they were also included among the magical books by Paulus the jurist, when in Sentences 5, tit. 23, he says: No one is permitted to keep books of magical art; and if they are found with anyone, his goods are confiscated, the books are publicly burned, and he is deported to an island; the humbler sort are punished with death. (Christians were thought by the pagans to be magi, as Baronius notes from Arnobius.) This also seems to pertain to the edict of Diocletian, which survives in fragments of book 7 of the Hermogenian (otherwise Gregorian) Code, under the title On Malefactors and Manichaeans (in the Collatio of Jewish and Roman Laws, tit. 15): We order that the authors themselves, together with their abominable writings, be subjected to a more severe punishment, so that they are burned in flaming fires. (See Baronius, year 287, §4, and Antonio Benbellonus, p. 68.)

units.la: c An. 225. sect. 3. d An. 302. sect. 20. extiterit, qualis Antiochi temporibus describitur, 1 Mac. I. 60. Ubicunque inveniebatur apud aliquem liber Fœderis, aut si quis acquiescebat legi; edicto Regis afficiebatur morte. Neque verò illo colore turpitudinem suam celare poterunt Pseudo-Catholici, quòd cum iis solummodò libris ita actum fuerit; qui ab hæreticis (sic enim Orthodoxos appellant Hæretici perditissimi) fuissent versi. Nam à veteribus certè Catholicis (quorum se successores magno cum supercilio jactant) manifestum est hîc eos degenerâsse: à quibus Judæus Aquila, Symmachus & Theodotion Judaizantes hæretici (quos malâ fide vertisse Testamentum in odium Christianorum affirmat Epitome Parsoniana c) longè aliter f sunt accepti. Quamvis enim multa mysteria Salvatoris (Hieronymo teste) subdolâ interpretatione celavissent, nonnulla etiam ad hæreses suas stabiliendas, Judaicam puta & Hebioniticam, studiosè pervertissent g; nunquam tamen Catholici Scripturas ab iis versas flammis objecerunt h: Sed curiosè potiùs legerunt & explanârunt, & per Origenis laborem Ecclesiis dedicârunt. Quid quòd in omnis generis Biblia, in quibus vel leviores lapsus occurrant, hoc modo procedunt Censores Pontificii. Sic enim Gregorius Capuccinus (unus ex Deputatis Patribus pro revisione librorum in Civitate Neapolitanâ) Biblia (inquit i) quæ deficiunt in textu, juxta Concil. Trident. Sess. 4. in decret. de usu sacrorum librorum, semper comburo; & facio experimentum in 3 cap. Genesis, ubi invenio; In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane, donec revertaris in terram; & non dicit, In sudore vultûs tui vesceris pane tuo, donec, &c. Ego sine remissione, tanquam textum suspectum, non transeo ad ipsam censurando, sed igniendo. Hæc severus ille Censor, quem non k Aristarchum sed Phalarin Grammaticum habemus, qui non notam apponat ad malum versum, sed totum opus ferro & igne persequatur.
units.tr: c Year 225, sect. 3. d Year 302, sect. 20. existed, just as it is described in the time of Antiochus, 1 Macc. 1:60: Wherever a book of the covenant was found with anyone, or if anyone assented to the law, he was put to death by the king's edict. Nor will the Pseudo-Catholics be able to hide their shame behind the excuse that only those books were treated in this way which had been translated by heretics (for so the most depraved heretics call the Orthodox). For it is certain that the ancient Catholics, whose successors they proudly boast of being, behaved very differently here. Those ancient Catholics, to be sure, accepted quite differently the translations of the Jewish Judaizing heretics Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, whom the Epitome of Parsons c) claims translated the Testament in bad faith out of hatred for Christians. Although these men, as Jerome testifies, had cunningly concealed many mysteries of the Saviour f, and had eagerly distorted some passages to establish their own heresies, Judaic and Ebionite, g Catholics never threw the Scriptures translated by them into the flames h. Instead they read and explained them carefully, and through the labour of Origen they dedicated them to the Churches. What then of the fact that Papist censors proceed in this way against Bibles of every kind, even those containing only slight slips? Gregory the Capuchin (one of the Deputed Fathers for the revision of books in the city of Naples) says: I always burn the Bibles which are lacking in the text, according to the Council of Trent, Session 4, in the decree on the use of the sacred books i (he says); and I make the experiment on the third chapter of Genesis, where I find: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the earth," and it does not say, "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until, etc." I do not pass over this suspect text without remission, judging it not by correcting but by burning. So that severe Censor, whom we have not as an Aristarchus but as the grammarian Phalaris, who does not place a mark against a bad verse but pursues the whole work with sword and fire.

units.la: Operâ & instinctu malorum Dæmonum, mortis supplicium adversus librorum Hystapsis aut Sibyllæ, aut Prophetarum lectores à Gentilibus constitutum esse, conquestus est olim Justinus Martyr l: ut per timorem ab illis homines (quò minus scripta ea legentes rerum bonarum notitiam perciperent, sed in servitute eorum retinentur)
units.tr: Justin Martyr once complained that, by the work and instigation of evil demons, the penalty of death had been established by the Gentiles against readers of the books of Hystaspes, or of the Sibyl, or of the Prophets, so that men were frightened off by fear, lest by reading those writings they should come to know good things, but be kept in servitude to them l.

Augustum certè, cùm effet Pontifex, noluisse Sibyllina à vulgo legi testantur Tacitus ac Suetonius . An eâdem jam operâ & instinctu malorum dæmonum, Christiano populo Propheticorum librorum lectione à Romanis præsulibus interdictum sit: judicent alii. Illud quidem negari non potest, à sacrilegii hujus Patronis hoc ipso argumento interdictum illud defendi; quòd antiqui illi Romani Sibyllina carmina legendi facultatem certis tantùm Magistratibus, viris prudentissimis, concessissent. Ut ab eodem prorsus spiritu & hos & illos actos esse appareat. (13) Ast vero nos (inquit Christianorum nomine adversus gentes Justinus) absque timore non tantum hujusmodi scripta legimus; verum etiam vobis ad inspiciendum, quae in eis traduntur, offerimus, grata acceptaque omnibus fore scientes. Vid. supra an. 200. Tertulliani Apologet. cap. 31. Huc etiam referatur, quod Melchior Canus , & Jac. Ledesima proserunt ex Valerio Maximo , de Tarquinio Rege; qui M. Tullium Duumvirum, quòd librum secreta civilium sacrorum continentem, custodiæ suæ commissum Petronio Sabino describendum dedisset, culeo insutum in mare abjici jussit. In Sibyllinorum enim librorum custodiâ non bonâ fide rem gerere M. Attilium (sic enim appellat) visum, prodit Dionysius Halicarnasseus, lib. 4. Antiquit. Roman.
units.tr: c On the Word of God, question 3, chapter on the Greek edition. f Jerome, in the Apology against Rufinus, and the Preface to Job. g Epiphanius, On Weights and Measures. Athanasius, in the Synopsis. Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 24. h Jerome, loc. cit. i Ecclesiastical Enchiridion, p. 166. k Cicero, against Piso. l Second Apology for the Christians, p. 64, Sylburg edition. were deterred. Tacitus and Suetonius attest that Augustus, while he was Pontifex, did not want the Sibylline books to be read by the common people. Let others judge whether, by the same work and instigation of evil demons, the reading of the prophetic books was forbidden to the Christian people by the Roman prelates. This much at least cannot be denied: the patrons of this sacrilege defend that prohibition by this very argument, that the ancient Romans had granted the right to read the Sibylline verses only to certain magistrates, men of the greatest prudence. So it appears that both these and those were moved by the same spirit. But we (says Justin, in the name of the Christians, against the Gentiles) not only read such writings without fear, but also offer them to you to inspect what is handed down in them, knowing that they will be pleasing and acceptable to all. See above, year 200, Tertullian's Apologeticus, chapter 31. To this also should be referred what Melchior Cano and Jacob Ledesma put forward from Valerius Maximus about King Tarquin, who, because the duumvir M. Tullius had given a book containing the secrets of the civil rites, entrusted to his custody, to Petronius Sabinus to copy, ordered him to be sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus reports that M. Attilius (for so he calls him) seemed to have acted in bad faith in guarding the Sibylline books, in book 4 of the Roman Antiquities.

units.la: Sanctiora sacrorum [gentilium] tantùm initiati sciebant, ut est apud Senecam, lib. 15. Epistolar. Multa enim (inquit Varro ) sunt vera; quae non modò vulgo scire non est utile, sed etiam tametsi falsa sint, aliter populum existimare expedit. Et ideò Graeci μυστήρια taciturnitate parietibusque clauserunt. Ita Ægyptios sacerdotes, quæ in arcanis condita habebant, ut veritas ignota esset, ad multos manare noluisse, authores sunt Diodorus Siculus ac Lucianus pœnâ iis adjectâ, qui ea in vulgus proderent. Similiter Ægyptios
units.tr: Only the initiated knew the more sacred things of the [pagan] rites, as Seneca says in Epistle 15. For, as Varro puts it, "there are many things that are true, which it is not only useless for the common people to know, but even if they are false, it is expedient for the people to think otherwise." And so the Greeks shut up their mysteries [μυστήρια] with silence and walls. Diodorus Siculus and Lucian are authorities that the Egyptian priests kept what they held hidden in secret, so that the truth remained unknown, and did not want it to spread among many, with a penalty attached for anyone who published it to the crowd. Similarly the Egyptians
