Sulpicium Juris consl. Si quid fuerit apud majores nostros in Juris studio admirationis, id enuntiatis vestris mysteriis totum. contemptum est & abjectum. Posset agi lege, neene, pauci quondam sciebant. Fastos enim vulgò non habebant. In magnâ erant potentiâ, qui consulebantur; à quibus etiam, dies, tanquam à Chaldais, petebantur. Inventus est scriba quidam, Cn. Flavius, qui cornicum oculos confixerit, & ab ipsis Jurisconsultis eorum sapientiam compilarit. De eodem Flavio Livius, lib. 9. sub finem. Anno U. C. 550. Jus repositum in penetralibus Pontificum evulgavit, fastosque circa forum in alto proposuit; ut quando lege agi posset, sciretur. Vid. eâ de re Plinium, lib. 33. cap.1. Aulum Gellium, lib. 6. cap. 9. Pomponium de Origine Juris, & Ciceronem ad Atticum, lib.6. epist. 1. Denique ex Canonibus etiam Apostolorum testimonium proferre poterat Ledesima. De Constitutionibus enim à se editis decernit Pseudo-Clemens, ὃς ἀ ἢ ἀμιντἰ-ῶν ἀὶ πόντων διὰ τὸ ἐν αἰτ̃αῖς μυστικῷ, quòd non oporteat eas publicare omnibus, ob quædam arcana, quæ in se continent: Nisi quòd hoc ad octo libros specialiter accommodatum (quorum arcana inter apocrypha referri non magnopere dolendum) libros sacræ Scripturæ ibidem recensitos omnibus publicandos esse non obscurè significet. Sic etiam Bellarminus a silentium in Traditionibus requirit; non in Scripturis, quæ toti mundo leguntur. Quid autem de fidis istis silentiis Christiana Ecclesia olim judicaverit, illa Lactantii reprehensio satis indicat, quam lib. 5. Institut. cap. 20. legimus. Hinc fida silentia (inquit) sacris instituta sunt ab hominibus callidis; ut nesciat populus quid colat. Tantum abest, ut cum Jesuitis Ethnicorum exemplar Ecclesiæ imitandum commendaverit. Vide hàc de re Melchiorem Canum, lib. 3. cap. 3. sol. 57. & qui eum χ̃ τ̃ ν̃ῶν sequitur, Jacobum Ledesimam, cap. 22. à pag.178. præcipuè verò Barnab. Brissonium de Formulis, lib. 1.
units.tr: (13) Apology, Apology 2 for the Christians. Clement of Alexandria affirms that they did not entrust their mysteries to just anyone, nor pass on knowledge of divine things to the profane, but only to those destined to attain the kingdom; and that from among the priests, only those were chosen who had been judged most approved in upbringing, learning and birth. Lest we be ignorant of the masters from whom the Papists drew this practice, James Ledesma insists on it diligently in On the Divine Scriptures Not to Be Read in Any Language, ch. 22, where he cites Plato, who, writing to Dionysius about certain sacred mysteries, advises him to tear up the letter at once, lest it fall into the hands of the unworthy crowd. He could also have added from the Orphic Sacred Rites (which Henri Estienne published among the Greek poets, vol. 2, p. 481, and which are cited by the Jewish Peripatetic Aristobulus in his work addressed to Ptolemy Philometor, in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 13, ch. 7, p. 388, Greek edition; by Justin Martyr in the Exhortation to the Greeks, p. 12, and in On the Monarchy of God, p. 81, ed. Sylburg; by Tatian in his Oration against the Greeks; by Clement of Alexandria in the Protrepticus, p. 21, ed. Sylburg; by Theodoret in Sermon 1, On Curing the Diseases of the Greeks, pp. 15 and 19, ed. Sylburg; where also the testimonies of Pindar and Plato cited by Cano and Ledesma are found. It appears from Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 3, ch. 5, near the end, that Porphyry used the same poem) I will speak holy things to the worthy: keep the profane far away [Ἀπὸ ξουμα δὲ ἱερὰ ἀπὸ ἔξω, ἐάσαι... ἐκ βιβλίου]; or the verses of Horace, book 3, ode 1: I hate the uninitiated crowd and keep it at a distance, which Sozomen notes is the indication in the hymn of Epiphanius, concerning the rites of Bacchus. On the rites of Ceres, which were celebrated with nothing more solemnly than silence, see Justin, History, book 5, at the very beginning, and Theodoret, Sermon 1, On Curing the Diseases of the Greeks. Hence the Romans regarded it as a grave crime to publish sacred secrets to the crowd. Valerius Maximus, book 2, ch. 1: The civil law, hidden for many ages among the sacred rites and ceremonies of the immortal gods, and known only to the Pontiffs, was published by Gnaeus Flavius, born of a freedman father and a scribe, when he was made curule aedile to the enormous indignation of the nobility, and he displayed the calendar almost throughout the whole forum. Cicero, in his speech For Murena, to Servius Sulpicius, the jurist: If there was anything of admiration in the study of law among our ancestors, it has all been held in contempt and cast aside by your revelations of mysteries. Once, few knew whether a case could be brought under the law. For they did not commonly have the calendar. Those who were consulted were very powerful, and days were sought from them as from the Chaldeans. A certain scribe, Gnaeus Flavius, was found, who pierced the eyes of the crows and plundered their wisdom from the jurists themselves. Livy speaks of the same Flavius, book 9, near the end, in the year of the city 550: He published the law stored in the inner shrines of the Pontiffs, and displayed the calendar high up around the forum, so that it might be known when a case could be brought under the law. On this matter see Pliny, book 33, ch. 1; Aulus Gellius, book 6, ch. 9; Pomponius, On the Origin of Law; and Cicero to Atticus, book 6, letter 1. Finally, Ledesma could have cited the testimony of the Canons of the Apostles as well. For Pseudo-Clement decrees concerning the constitutions edited by himself that they ought not to be published to all, because of certain secrets they contain. Except that this is specially fitted to the eight books (whose secrets, being counted among the apocrypha, are no great loss), and it clearly signifies that the books of Holy Scripture recounted there ought to be published to all. So also Bellarmine demands silence about Traditions, not about Scriptures, which are read throughout the whole world. What the Christian Church once judged about these trusted silences is sufficiently indicated by Lactantius's rebuke, which we read in Institutes, book 5, ch. 20. Hence (he says) trusted silences were established for sacred rites by crafty men, so that the people might not know what it worships. So far was he from commending the practice of the pagans to the Church as something to be imitated, as the Jesuits do. On this matter see Melchior Cano, book 3, ch. 3, sol. 57; and Jacob Ledesma, who follows him, ch. 22, from p. 178; and above all Barnabas Brisson, On Formulas, book 1.

units.la: Verùm enimverò nequaquam primi fuerunt Pontificii, qui hàc in re Ethnicorum callidam superstitionem imitati sunt. Majores ipsorum, veteres Hæretici (hàc de causâ non minus quàm Gentiles, ab hominibus Catholicis notati) viam hanc illis jamdudum demonstrarunt. Illi, cùm ex Scripturis arguerentur, in accusationem conversi sunt ipsarum Scripturarum, quasi varìè essent dicta, & quasi non posset ex his inveniri veritas ab his, qui nesciant Traditionem. Non enim per literas traditam illam, sed per vivam vocem; ob quam causam & Paulum dixisse b. Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, Sapientiam autem non mundi hujus. Irenæus, lib. 3. cap. 2. qui ibidem cap. 3. & 15. hanc
units.tr: Yet the Papists were by no means the first to imitate the crafty superstition of the pagans in this matter. Their forebears, the ancient heretics (noted for this reason by Catholic men no less than the Gentiles), showed them this road long ago. When they were refuted from Scripture, they turned to accuse Scripture itself, as if its statements were variously expressed, and as if the truth could not be found in it by those who do not know the Tradition. For that Tradition was handed down not by letters but by the living voice; for this reason Paul also said b "We speak wisdom among the perfect, but not the wisdom of this world." Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 2, who in the same place, at ch. 3 and 15, shows that he does not approve this view.

units.la: {a} Lib. 4. de Verbo Dei, cap. 8. {b} 1 Cor. II. 6. sententiam sibi non probari innuit. Doctrina Apostolorum (inquit.cap. 15.) manifesta est & firma, & nihil subtrahens, neque alia quidem in abscondito, alia vero in manifesto docentium. Hæretici non omnia volebant Apostolos omnibus revelâsse; quædam enim palam & universis, quædam secretò & paucis demandâsse: quia & hoc verbo usus est Paulus ad Timotheum: O Timothee, depositum custodi: & rursum, Bonum depositum custodi. [Tertullianus de Præscript. adv. Hæreticos, cap. 25. quam dementiam, sic enim cap. 28. appellat, cap. 26. solidè refutat, concludens capitis 27. initio, incredibile esse, Apostolos non omnem ordinem regulæ omnibus simpliciter, & plenè (al. plane) omnibus edidisse.] Hæc eadem Pontificiorum nostri temporis vox est, Scripturam gladium esse Delphicum, Lesbiam regulam, nasum cereum, tantis obscuritatibus involutam, ut nec à vulgo Christianorum legi tutum sit, nec sine traditionis adminiculo controversias fidei possit componere. Neque illud etiam prætereunt, mysteria quædam, præsertim sacra, clam populo rudi habere voluisse Apostolos, perfectis & majoribus seorsim communicanda: ideoque Paulum dixisse, 1 Cor. II. Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos: & 2 Tim. I. 14. Bonum depositum custodi. His enim ipsis firmamentis hâc in causâ utitur Melchior Canus c; & eum secutus Jacobus Ledesima d. Fr. etiam Agricola e prius illud testimonium 1 Cor. II. in præsenti quæstione usurpat; Tho Stapletonus f, & alii: Ut veterum hæreticorum (quos Scripturarum lucifugas non infscitè appellavit Tertullianus g) germanos filios possis agnoscere. Sed istos occultarum Traditionum patronos suis fruì somniis sinamus; nos Catholicæ Ecclesiæ traditiones quas ex ipsâ Scripturâ omnibus qui velint hauriendas proponit amplectamur; quas veteribus illis Hæreticis suas Ἀπόστολοι jactitantibus opponit Irenæus. h Traditionem (inquit) Apostolorum in toto mundo manifestatam, in Ecclesia adest perspicere omnibus, qui vera velint audire. Et post, Hunc patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi ab ecclesiis annuntiari, ex ipsâ Scripturâ, qui velint, discere possunt, & Apostolicam Ecclesiæ traditionem intelligere. Pessimè itaque Joannes à Sancto Andrea, Præfat. in Liturgias Sanctorum Patrum ad Cardinalem Lotharingum. Quanquam si veteres illi (inquit) audiendi sunt; profanum ab iis sacris longè vulgus arcendum est; quæ alioqui ita recondenda sunt, ut tum demum, si quædam procella emergat vehementior,
units.tr: {a} Book 4, On the Word of God, ch. 8. {b} 1 Cor. 2:6. He says (ch. 15): The teaching of the Apostles is clear and firm, and withholds nothing, nor teaches one thing in secret and another in public. The heretics did not want the Apostles to have revealed everything to everyone; they said some things were entrusted openly and to all, and others secretly and to a few. For Paul also used this word to Timothy: O Timothy, guard the deposit; and again, Guard the good deposit. [Tertullian, in On the Prescription against Heretics, ch. 25, refutes this madness solidly (for so he calls it in ch. 28), in ch. 26, concluding at the beginning of ch. 27 that it is incredible that the Apostles did not publish the whole order of the rule to all simply and fully (other editions read plainly).] This same voice is that of the Papists of our time: Scripture is a Delphic sword, a Lesbian rule, a leaden nose, so involved in such obscurities that it is not safe to be read even by the common Christians, nor can it settle controversies of faith without the help of Tradition. Nor do they pass over the fact that the Apostles wished to keep certain mysteries, especially sacred ones, hidden from the untrained people, to be shared separately with the perfect and mature; and therefore that Paul said, 1 Cor. 2: We speak wisdom among the perfect; and 2 Tim. 1:14: Guard the good deposit. For Melchior Cano uses these very supports in this cause, and Jacob Ledesma follows him. Francis Agricola also used the former testimony, 1 Cor. 2, in the present question; Thomas Stapleton, and others, so that you may recognise the true sons of the ancient heretics, whom Tertullian not unhappily called enemies of the light of Scripture. But let us allow these defenders of hidden Traditions to enjoy their own dreams; let us embrace the traditions of the Catholic Church, which it sets forth to be drawn from Scripture itself by all who wish, and which Irenaeus opposes to those ancient heretics who boasted of their own Apostolic traditions. The Tradition of the Apostles (he says) made manifest in the whole world is present in the Church for all to see who wish to hear the truth. And afterwards: That this Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is announced by the churches, all who wish can learn from Scripture itself, and understand the Apostolic tradition of the Church. Therefore John of St Andrew very badly, in his preface to the Liturgies of the holy Fathers, addressed to the Cardinal of Lorraine: Although, if those ancient writers (he says) are to be heard, the profane crowd must be kept far away from those sacred things; which otherwise are to be hidden in such a way that only if some more violent storm should arise

units.la: {c} Loc. Theolog lib. 3. cap. 3. {d} De Divinis Script. quavis linguâ non legendis, cap. 22. §. 28. {e} De Verbo Dei, c. 12. {f} Antidot. in 1 Cor. II, 6. {g} De Resurrect. carnis, cap. 47. {h} Lib. 3 cap. 3. vehementior, deprimantur; & tanquam Cynosura dux, navigationisque magistra, inter tempestates effulgeant. Quod enim publicatur, labefactatur. Haec ille, Horatium potius quam veteres Patres secutus. Etsi enim (ut optime veteris Ecclesiae mentem aperuit Augustinus i) Catechumenis fidelium sacramenta non produntur; non ideo fit, quod ea ferre non possunt, sed ut ab eis tanto ardentius concupiscantur, quanto eis honorabilius occultantur.
units.tr: {c} Loc. Theolog. lib. 3, cap. 3. {d} De Divinis Script. quavis linguâ non legendis, cap. 22, §. 28. {e} De Verbo Dei, c. 12. {f} Antidot. in 1 Cor. II, 6. {g} De Resurrect. carnis, cap. 47. {h} Lib. 3, cap. 3. Let it be brought down by a more violent storm, and then let it shine out among the tempests like the Cynosure, the guide and mistress of navigation. For what is made public is weakened. So he wrote, following Horace rather than the ancient Fathers. For although (as Augustine has very well revealed the mind of the ancient Church) the sacraments of the faithful are not disclosed to catechumens, this is not because they cannot bear them, but so that they may desire them all the more eagerly the more honourably they are kept hidden from them.

units.la: Carpocratiani Jesum dicebant in mysterio discipulis suis & Apostolis seorsim locutum; & illos expostulasse, ut dignis & assentientibus seorsim haec traderent: per fidem enim & charitatem salvari: quemadmodum habet Irenaeus, lib. 1. adverf. Haeref. cap. 24. & ex eo Theodoritus, lib. 1. Haeretic. Fabular. Atque hinc illos dicere solitos refert Epiphanius k, τὰς ἀξίους ταῦτα κατακτᾶσθαι δυνάμεις. Dignis haec recensere dignamur.
units.tr: The Carpocratians said that Jesus had spoken in mystery apart to his disciples and Apostles, and had asked them to hand these things on separately to those who were worthy and who assented: for they are saved through faith and charity, as Irenaeus has it in Book 1 of Against Heresies, ch. 24, and Theodoret after him in Book 1 of Heretical Fables. Hence, Epiphanius reports, they were accustomed to say that only the worthy acquire these powers. We deign to recount these things to the worthy.

units.la: Basilidiani dicebant mysteria sua esse ineffabilia, neque multos ea scire posse, sed unum a mille, & duos a myriadibus: (ut est apud Irenaeum, lib. 1. adverf. haeref. cap. 23. & Theodoritum, lib. 1. haeretic. fabular.) neque oportere omnino ipsorum mysteria effari, sed in abscondito continere per silentium (ut addit ibidem Irenaeus) similiter de Basilide Epiphanius l, Jubet (inquit) solum de Patre & suo mysterio nemini revelare, sed silentio in seipsis continere: Uni vero de mille revelare, & duobus de decem millibus. Hinc infamae illae Agyrtae voces ab eodem commemoratae. Ἡμεῖς ἱζῶμεν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, οἱ δ᾽ ἄλλοι κύνες ἢ κύνες. ἡ δὲ τοῦτο εἶπεν, μὴ βάλητε τοῖς μαργαρίταις ὑμῶν ἐμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων, μηδὲ δότε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσίν. Nos homines sumus; caeteri omnes canes sunt & sues. Nolite igitur margaritas projicere porcis, aut dare sanctum canibus. Ita nimirum Pontificii persuasum nobis esse volunt, sacrarum literarum oracula, religionisque Christianae mysteria omnia passim vulgo tradere, nihil aliud esse, quam adversus Christi legem sanctum dare canibus, & inter porcos spargere margaritas. Vid. Canum, lib. 3. locor. Theologic. cap. 3. fundam. 4: Harding. artic. 15. §. 7. & art. 16. §. 4. Basilidis etiam sectatores, ad imperitorum & mulierculorum animos concitandos, peregrina quaedam nomina, quasi de Hebraicis fontibus hausta, usurpare consueverunt; barbaro simplices quosque terrentes sono; ut quod non intelligunt, plus mirentur. (Hieronymus epist. 29. ad Theodorum, quae Epitaphium Lucinii Boetici inscribitur.) Barbara hujusmodi nomina in mun-
units.tr: The Basilidians said that their mysteries were unspeakable, and that not many could know them, but one in a thousand, and two in ten thousand (as found in Irenaeus, Book 1 of Against Heresies, ch. 23, and Theodoret, Book 1 of Heretical Fables), and that their mysteries ought not to be uttered at all, but kept hidden in silence (as Irenaeus adds in the same place). Epiphanius likewise says of Basilides: He commands that the things about the Father and his mystery be revealed to no one, but kept in silence within oneself; and to one in a thousand, and to two in ten thousand, only. Hence come those infamous words of the charlatans, recorded by the same writer: We are men; all others are dogs or pigs. Do not therefore cast your pearls before swine, nor give what is holy to dogs. Thus, of course, the Papists wish us to be persuaded that to deliver the oracles of the sacred letters and all the mysteries of the Christian religion everywhere to the common people is nothing other than, contrary to Christ's law, to give what is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls among swine. See Canus, Book 3 of Theological Places, ch. 3, fundament 4; Harding, article 15, §7, and article 16, §4. The followers of Basilides also used to employ certain foreign names, as if drawn from Hebrew sources, to stir up the minds of the unlearned and silly women, terrifying each simple person with barbarous sound, so that they may marvel the more at what they do not understand (Jerome, letter 29 to Theodorus, which is entitled the Epitaph of Lucinius Boeticus). Barbarous names of this kind in the world

units.la: ¹ Tract. 56. in John. ᵏ Lib. 1. Panarii, haeref. 27. ˡ Panar, lib. 1, haeref. 24. dum invexisse Nicolaum Antiochenum refert Damascenus . Atque ita de Nicolaitis refert Augustinus , nescio quae barbara principum nomina miscere eos disputationibus suis, quibus terreant auditores, quae prudentibus risum potius faciunt quam timorem. Verbis illis abuti solet immundissima haeresis (inquit Hieronymus ) apud simplices quosque atque deceptos; ut terrorem faciat novitate sermonum, &c. Ita nimirum Principem quendam Caulaucac habuerunt (quemadmodum & Basilidiani eorum soboles ex vocibus Hebraicis Esai. XXVIII. 10. קו קו) appellatione sumpta; ςαπαπλάζων φιλοπμίμανοι ταύ ἀπείρες διὰ ὁ ἕυ ὀνομάτων ὀπαλύξεως, ἡ ... βαρβαρικῶν, in vanas imaginationes impellere conantes imperitos per nominum terriculamenta & confictam barbari nominis appellationem. [Epiphanius in Panar. lib. 1. haeref. 25. Νικολαΐτων.] Similiter & Heracleonitas invocationes suas Hebraicis verbis dicere solitos notat Augustinus, ad Quodvultdeum, haeref. 16.
units.tr: ¹ Tract. 56 on John. ᵏ Book 1 of the Panarion, heresy 27. ˡ Panarion, Book 1, heresy 24. Damascene reports that Nicolaus of Antioch introduced barbarous names into the world. And Augustine reports of the Nicolaitans that they mix into their disputations certain barbarous names of princes, with which they frighten their hearers, names which rather make the wise laugh than fear. The most filthy heresy is accustomed to abuse these words (Jerome says) among each simple and deceived person, so as to cause terror by the novelty of its words, etc. Thus, of course, they had a certain prince named Caulaucac (just as the Basilidians, their offspring, took the name from the Hebrew words of Isaiah 28:10, kav kav). The Greek words, roughly, say that they seek to drive the ignorant into vain imaginations through the terrifying effect of names and of a barbarous-sounding appellation [Epiphanius, Panarion, Book 1, heresy 25, Nicolaitans]. Augustine, in his letter to Quodvultdeus on heresies, likewise notes that the Heracleonites were accustomed to pronounce their invocations in Hebrew words.

units.la: Marci (haeretici Valentiniani) discipulos sacris suis obscura nomina indidisse testatur Arnobius; quibus efficerent, ut sacratiora augustioraque haberentur, οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ ... ὀνομάτων, &c. Quidam enim ex ipsis sponsale quoddam cubiculum adaptantes, & quasi mysticum (munus sc.) conficiunt cum quibusdam profanis dictionibus, iis qui sacrantur (i. e. initiantur) &c. Alii autem & Hebraica nomina superfantur; ut stupori sint, vel perterreant eos, qui sacrantur, &c. (Irenaeus, lib. 1. cap. 18. & eum secutus Eusebius, lib. 4. hist. cap. 10. Epiphanius, lib. 1. Panar. haeref. 34. pag. 114. edit. Graec. Μαρκοσίων. Theodoritus, lib. 1. haeretic. fabular. Nicetas Choniates, lib. 4. Thesauri Orthodoxae fidei haeref. 6. ubi Hebraica haec nomina a Marci sectatoribus usurpari monet, quo majorem ei, qui baptizatur, stuporem injiciant) Similiter Pontificii obscuris & populo ignotis verbis in sua Liturgia, ac in Sacramentis etiam (ut Epphata in Baptismo) utuntur; sacra sua lingua vulgo ignota & barbara celebranda esse defendentes; ut gravior & magis reverenda eorum majestas videatur [Bellarminus, lib. 2. de Verbo Dei, cap. 15. §. 34.]
units.tr: Arnobius testifies that the disciples of Marcus (the Valentinian heretic) gave obscure names to their sacred rites, by which they might make them seem holier and more majestic: For some of them, fitting a kind of bridal chamber, and making as it were a mystic gift, with certain profane words, to those who are consecrated (that is, initiated), etc. Others also heap up Hebrew names, so that they may astonish or terrify those who are consecrated, etc. (Irenaeus, Book 1, ch. 18, and Eusebius after him, Book 4 of the History, ch. 10; Epiphanius, Book 1 of the Panarion, heresy 34, p. 114 of the Greek edition, Marcosians; Theodoret, Book 1 of Heretical Fables; Nicetas Choniates, Book 4 of the Treasury of Orthodox Faith, heresy 6, where he warns that these Hebrew names were used by the followers of Marcus, so as to strike greater astonishment into the one being baptized.) In the same way the Papists use obscure words unknown to the people in their Liturgy, and also in the sacraments (such as Ephphatha in Baptism), defending that their sacred language, generally unknown and barbarous, ought to be used in worship, so that their majesty may seem more weighty and more reverend [Bellarmine, Book 2 on the Word of God, ch. 15, §34].

units.la: Messaliani haeretici, ita lingua Syra appellati a שמיא. Graece vero Εὐχῖται hoc est, Precatores dicti sunt. (inquit Theodoritus ) οἱ πεοσεύχεσθαι, ἐμὲν μὲν ... εὐχῆ ...
units.tr: The heretics called Messalians, from the Syriac word for prayer, were called in Greek Euchites, that is, Precatores (says Theodoret), those who pray [οἱ προσεύχεσθαι ... εὐχῆ ...].

units.la: m Lib. de Haeref. o De Haeresibus ad Quodvultdeum §.5. o Lib.9.Comment.in Esai. c.XXVIII.
units.tr: m Book on Heresies. o On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus, §5. o Book 9, Commentary on Isaiah, ch. 28.

units.la: p Lib. 4. haeretic. fabular. ἰχθλακότης ἂ ὑμίεχς τὸ ἀεὶ ἱσον καδάδ<ον. h. e. Decepti homines longè miserrimi, nullum opus aggrediuntur (Spirituales enim seipsos vocant) sed orationi istique vacantes maximam diei partem dormiunt. [Viva effigies Monachorum & aliorum ex Pontificiis, qui Spirituales se vocant.] καθ' ἱζπὶ- chorum & aliorum ex Pontificiis, qui Spirituales se vocant.] καθ' ἱζπι- ἐαν ἢ χρ ἐ ἑω (ait de iisdem Epiphanius) μὴ πολλῆς λυχναψίας ἢ φάτων συναθροι- ζομενοι, ὅπι πλὺ ἐ χαπαλεσμένα τινα ἐπὶ τῆς παρ' αὐτοῖς αοπαίων, ἢ ἐυφημίας τινας ἀδῶν ὠ'πομένοι, ὡς χαπαλεσμάτων ἢ ἐυφημῶν ὥσπερ ἐξιλεύμενοι, ἐαν τῶ ἀπαο- ἐις ἢ ἀπὸ ποιμένοι, ὡς χαπαλεσμάτων ἢ ἐυφημῶν ὥσπερ ἀπὸ ἐξιλεύμενοι, ἐαν τῶ ἀπα- ὠκὶ.
units.tr: p Book 4, Heretical Fables. Deceived men, most wretched, undertake no work (for they call themselves Spiritual) but, given over to prayer, sleep for the greater part of the day. [A living likeness of the monks and others among the Papists who call themselves Spiritual.] Epiphanius says of the same people: [Greek, garbled in the scan: they gather at evening and in the morning with many lamps and lights, and for a long time through their teachers they read certain lessons and sing certain praises to God, as if by such readings and praises they appease God, and so deceive themselves. Being blind in ignorance, he brings about all these things by the opinion of seductive estimation.]

units.la: h. e. Ad vesperam & mane multis lucernis ac luminibus incensis congregantur; & diu per longum tempus lectiones quasdam per doctos suos, & laudes quasdam in Deum facientes, velut per lectiones ac laudes Deum placantes, seipsos decipiunt. Caeterum ignorantia caeca existens, omnia haec per opinionis existimationem seductis illis efficit.
units.tr: That is: At evening and in the morning they gather with many lamps and lights lit; and for a long time, through their teachers, they read certain lessons and sing certain praises to God, as if by lessons and praises placating God, deceiving themselves. Moreover, existing in blind ignorance, he brings about all these things in those who have been seduced, by the estimation of opinion.

units.la: Psalliani sive Euchitae (inquit Erasmus) auxerunt haereticorum catalogum: qui in otio degentes incredibilem psalmorum vim mirâ linguae volubilitate absolvebant. Haec Erasmus, addens paulo post. Fortassis & hi displicent Domino, qui hoc ipsum putant eximiam quandam esse pietatem, ore quamplurimum Psalmorum recitare, quùm nec adsit intellectus, nec pius affectus.
units.tr: The Psalliani, or Euchites (says Erasmus), have added to the catalogue of heretics: they, living in idleness, used to get through an incredible quantity of psalms with a remarkable fluency of tongue. So Erasmus, adding a little later: Perhaps these also displease the Lord, who think it an extraordinary piety to recite very many Psalms with the mouth, when neither understanding is present nor a devout feeling.

units.la: Ossenorum & Helcesaitarum Pseudo-Propheta Elxai (ut est apud Epiphanium) dicebat.(19) Nemo quaerat interpretationem; sed solùm in oratione haec dicat: Quae quidem ex Hebraicâ linguâ transtulit; & vel ex hac parte deprehendimus, nihili esse istius hominis commenta. Ita enim orare jubet. Abar, Anid, Moib, Nochile, Daasim, Ane, Daasim, Nochile, Moib, Anid, Abar, Selam; Quae hunc sensum continent, Transeat abjectio à patribus meis propagata, &c.
units.tr: The pseudo-prophet Elxai, of the Ossenes and Helcesaites, said (as Epiphanius reports): Let no one seek an interpretation; but let him say only these words in prayer (which he translated from the Hebrew language, and by this very point we perceive that the inventions of this man are worth nothing). For he orders them to pray thus: Abar, Anid, Moib, Nochile, Daasim, Ane, Daasim, Nochile, Moib, Anid, Abar, Selam; which contain this sense: Let the rejection handed down by my fathers pass away, etc.

units.la: Theodoti vel Gnostici alicujus videtur illa quaestio, quae habetur in Clementis Alexandrini Eclogis, πόπεον χεῖον ἀναξίω δῦναι, ἢ ἀξίω μὴ πε- φαδῦναι, &c. (Vid. locum.) Conjuguntur enim cum Excerptis ex Theodoto: quem Theodotum coriarium haeresiarcham accipio; cujus sectatorum mores à Pontificiis haud multùm alienos ita depingit antiquus ille author, qui librum contra Artemonis haeresim scripsit. (20) Sa-
units.tr: The question found in Clement of Alexandria's Eclogae, πόπεον χεῖον ἀναξίω δῦναι, ἢ ἀξίω μὴ πε- φαδῦναι, &c. (see the passage), seems to belong to Theodotus or some other Gnostic. It is joined with the Excerpts from Theodotus, whom I take to be Theodotus the tanner, the heresiarch. The ancient author who wrote against the heresy of Artemon paints the morals of his followers, which differ little from those of the Papists. (20) Sa-

units.la: (19) Mndsis ζηπίζη ἐ ἐμιυνείαν, ἀλλ' ἢ μόνον ἐν τῇ εὐχῇ τάδε λέγετο. ἢ αὐτὰ ἐδὲν ἀπὸ ἐβεχίνης διαλεξία μυπνέσησε, &c.; (20) Ἑεχαῖς μὴ Ἰσαι ἐρύθεως ἡδάνω γήκαν, πίστως ἢ ἐχαία κανόνα ἰνπίηεν. Χειτὸν ἢ ἰγροίηεαν, ἐ τί ἀὶ δεῖαι λῖσαι ἡ- φαί, ζητεῖτες, ἀλλ' ὁσον χῆμα συλλο- γισμῶ, &c. cras audacter depravárunt Scripturas; veteris fidei Canonem abrogárunt; Christum ignorárunt; neque quid sacræ & divinæ literæ de illo dicant, conquisiverunt; sed quænam syllogismi figura ad suam impietatem confirmandam reperiretur, studiosè indagárunt. Quòd si quisquam forte illis aliquod divini eloquii testimonium proferat; quærunt utrùm conjunctam aut disjunctam syllogismi figuram possit efficere. Relictis verò & depositis sacrarum literarum studiis omni curâ & cogitatione in Geometriam incumbunt: tanquam ex terrâ editi, de terrâ loquuntur: & Christum, qui sit de cælo venturus, penitus ignorant, &c. Porrò ipsius Clementis quænam fuerit hâc in re sententia, verba ibidem statim subsequentia (ejusdem etiam nomine à Damasceno, lib. 2. parall. cap. 19. citata) apertè restantur: ὡς ἡ θάλασσα ἀπὸ πάντων, &c. Quemadmodum mare omnibus patet, atque alius natat, alius negotiatur, alius piscatur: & rursus, quemadmodum terra communis est omnibus; atque alius iter facit, alius arat, alius ædificat; (21) eodem modo dum sacra Scriptura legitur, alius in fide, alius in moribus juvatur, aliis per literarum agnitionem superstitio eximitur; pugil denique, ubi Olympicum curriculum agnoverit, doctrinæ beneficio ad certamen se comparat, & pugnat, & palmam adipiscitur, clusis nimirum & fractis adversariis, iisque qui veræ scientiæ viam exagitant. Hæc ille.
units.tr: (19) They used no interpretation, but only these words were said in prayer; and they themselves understood nothing of the meaning of the words, &c. (20) Those who are wise in their own eyes and do not accept the rule of faith, nor seek to understand what the divine letters say about Christ, but only the form of a syllogism [σχῆμα συλλογισμῶν], &c. They boldly corrupted the Scriptures, abrogated the canon of the old faith, and ignored Christ. They have not sought what the sacred and divine letters say about him, but have eagerly searched for what form of syllogism could be found to confirm their impiety. If anyone brings them some testimony of the divine word, they ask whether a conjunctive or disjunctive syllogism can be made of it. Having left and laid aside the study of the sacred letters, they devote all their care and thought to geometry; like men born from the earth, they speak of the earth, and they utterly ignore Christ, who is to come from heaven, &c. Moreover, what Clement himself thought on this matter is plainly stated in the words that follow immediately there (and that Damascene also cites under his name, book 2 Parallels, chap. 19): ὡς ἡ θάλασσα ἀπὸ πάντων, &c. As the sea is open to all, and one man swims, another trades, another fishes; and again, as the earth is common to all, and one man travels, another ploughs, another builds; (21) so, while the holy Scripture is read, one is helped in faith, another in morals, and for others superstition is removed through knowledge of the letters. Finally, the athlete, when he has recognised the Olympic course, through the benefit of teaching prepares himself for the contest, fights, and wins the palm, namely by crushing and breaking his opponents, and those who harass the way of true knowledge. So far he.

units.la: Gnosimachi omni Christianorum cognitioni ac scientiæ ita adversantur; at vanum & minùs necessarium laborem esse dicant eorum, qui sacris in scripturis scientiam ullam aut cognitionem investigant: cùm præsertim à Christianis Deus præter bona opera nihil requirat; ut sit satius, si quis simpliciùs ambulet, nec curiosiùs quicquam perscrutetur. Jo. Damascenus in lib. de Hæresibus: & Nicetas lib. 4. Thesaur. Orthodox. hæref. 39. qui in hæreseos illius confutationem subjicit. Si ex erroneæ traditionis vestræ regulâ, lectione sacrarum Scripturarum contenti, nullâ scientiæ & cognitionis habitâ ratione, vitam nostram instituissemus; quid tandem, quæso, utilitatis ex illis reportassemus? aut quonam modo, quod credimus, id oratione scisscitantibus explicare potuissemus?
units.tr: The Gnosimachi oppose all Christian knowledge and learning in this way, and they say that the labour of those who seek any knowledge or understanding in the holy Scriptures is vain and less necessary; especially since God requires nothing of Christians beyond good works, so that it is better for a man to walk more simply and not to inquire into anything too curiously. John Damascene in his book On Heresies; and Nicetas, book 4 of the Thesaurus of Orthodox Heresies, 39, who adds this as a refutation of that heresy. If we had lived our lives according to the rule of your erroneous tradition, content with reading the holy Scriptures and taking no account of knowledge and learning, what, I ask you, would we have gained from them? Or how could we have explained to those who ask us what we believe, by speech?

Commelin. pag. 248.] (22) Omne sacrarum literarum studium supervacaneum esse; tum quòd propria cuique fides sufficiat, tum quòd inquisitio obscuriores nobis res ipsas reddit. [Vid. supra an. 360.] Item, (23) Sacrarum Scripturarum oracula auribus quidem audienda; ita tamen ut verborum sensus non perpendatur, nec dictorum consequentia spectetur, nec ad finem quo edita sunt scopum attendatur. [Vid.pag.259.& an.360.] An verò illa accusatio, pag. 260. quæ Ϯ τὰς λέξεις attingit, Pontificiorum hæresin non jugulet, penès ipsos judicium esto.
units.tr: (21) For just as joy in reading... the letter alpha benefits... from knowledge, one benefits for faith, another for conduct; ... and knowledge is proportion, &c. [Commelin edition, p. 248.] (22) All study of the sacred letters is superfluous, both because each person's own faith is sufficient, and because inquiry makes the matters themselves more obscure for us. [See above, at the year 360.] Likewise, (23) The oracles of the sacred Scriptures are to be heard with the ears, but in such a way that the sense of the words is not weighed, nor the consequence of what is said considered, nor attention paid to the purpose for which they were given. [See p. 259 and the year 360.] Whether that accusation on p. 260, which touches on the words, does not destroy the heresy of the Papists, let them judge for themselves.

units.la: In Judæis etiam illud perstringit Hieronymus y, quòd ambulaverint in tenebris, ita scripturas sanctas, quasi cæci palpantes parietem; verba tantùm in eis & folia, non sensum fructumque quærentes, qui tenetur in litteris: absque sensu & intelligentiâ scripturarum, tantùm verba meditantes, quæ decantant memoriter. Addit ibidem Hieronymus, solam verborum meditationem, simplicitatem esse absque prudentiâ, quæ vicina stultitiæ est. Certè illorum Rabbinos circa annum Domini 552. sacrorum librorum in linguâ populo intellectâ recitationem prohibere conatos, constat ex Justiniani Imp. Novell. Constitut. 146. [In Authenticis, collat. 9. tit. 28. Vid. supra in sententiis Hebræorum circa sin. & Imperatorum, ex Jure Civili.] Qui conatus, licèt eo tempore Justiniani Imp. authoritate repressus fuerit, prævaluit tandem: atque etiam Romanæ Synagogæ Rabbinis (ne negari posset cum Ecclesiæ hostibus hic conspirare iltos) luculentum argumentum præbuit ejusdem moris in Christianâ Ecclesiâ retinendi. Sic enim horum exemplum præscribit nobis, Romanensium Coryphæus, Rob. Bellarminus z: Usque ad hanc diem in Synagogis Judæi Scripturas Hebraicè legunt; cùm nulli nationi hoc tempore lingua Hebraica sit vulgaris. Quasi verò Judæorum & Antichristianorum conjuratio adversùs Dominum & Ecclesiam ejus maximo nobis esse deberet argumento ad socia arma cum illis conjungenda. A Judæis interim, quorum adhuc cordibus hæret velamen cæcitatis, Biblia sancta perlegi ferè ab incunabulis, fatetur Possevinus a. Quidni igitur hic eos sequatur Bellarminus, qui in sacris peragendis sequendos sibi proponit. Cæterùm de Hebræorum traditione de initio Geneseos non legendo
units.tr: Jerome also censures this among the Jews: that they walked in darkness, groping at the wall like the blind, seeking in the Scriptures only the words and the leaves, not the sense and the fruit that is held in the letters; meditating only on words without sense and understanding of the Scriptures, which they chant from memory. y Jerome adds there that meditation on words alone is simplicity without prudence, which is close to foolishness. It is certain, from Justinian Emperor's Novel 146 [in the Authenticum, collation 9, title 28; see above under the opinions of the Hebrews concerning sin and the emperors, from the Civil Law], that around the year of the Lord 552 the rabbis tried to forbid the reading of the sacred books in a language the people understood. Although this attempt was checked at that time by the authority of Emperor Justinian, it finally prevailed; and it has also given the rabbis of the Roman Synagogue (lest it be denied that they conspire with the enemies of the Church in this) a striking argument for keeping the same custom in the Christian Church. For the Roman champion Robert Bellarmine holds up their example to us: To this day the Jews read the Scriptures in Hebrew in their synagogues, although at this time Hebrew is the vernacular of no nation. z As if the conspiracy of Jews and Antichristians against the Lord and his Church should be our greatest reason to join arms with them! Meanwhile Possevinus a admits that the Jews, whose hearts still hold the veil of blindness, have read the holy Bibles almost from the cradle. Why then should Bellarmine not follow them here, he who proposes to follow them in performing sacred rites? Moreover, concerning the Hebrew tradition that the beginning of Genesis is not to be read

units.tr: (22) We overstate the experience of understanding that we have from the holy Scriptures. (23) For the purpose of things not revealed... concerning reading by the young, see Mercer on Genesis, sol. 4b, and Capito on the Hexaemeron, sol. 6, 7, 8; and Origen (or whoever the author was) in the prologue to the Homily on the Song of Songs, near the beginning (among the works of Jerome), where we clearly understand that the rest of Scripture is permitted even to boys.

units.la: Turcæ similiter (quos Bellarminum prætermisisse non oportuit, à Reginaldo & Giffordo b Turcopapistis hac in causa nequaquam prætermissos) eandem insistunt viam. Ita enim de sacerdotibus eorum (Papisticis simillimis) scribunt Bartholomæus Gyorgievitz c & Antonius Geuffræus d [lib. 2. de Turc. relig. & cæremoniis.] Non magna in ipsis doctrina requiritur. Satis erit, si Alcoranum & Mussaphum noverint legere. Illi autem, qui etiam interpretari secundum textum noverint, peritissimi habentur: quoniam non vulgari lingua Turcicâ, sed Arabicâ à Mehemmeto sunt tradita: quòd nefas esse putant, si vulgari linguâ interpretata describerentur. [Christophorus Richerius, de Turcarum moribus, lib. 2. Arabicas (inquit) voces Turci à pueris edisce re solent, cùm primùm suâ religione imbuuntur. Legem enim Arabicè conscriptam habent, & in omnibus publicis privatisque rebus Arabicis literis utuntur.] Solent enim Turcæ, ut refert Gerlachius c, ab incunabulis pueros docere Alcoranum legere, crebrâque iteratione memoriæ ipsorum imprimere; quod credunt lectionem ejus, etiam non intellecti, infinita præmia in altero sæculo habituram esse. De Turcarum ignorantiâ (quam evidens argumentum esse ait infidelitatis hujus sectæ) ita scribit Septemcastrensis, de moribus Turcorum, cap. 21. Licèt maxima sint astutia ad omne opus malum perficiendum; & in rebus naturalibus magnam & quasi supernaturalem habeant practicam & experientiam: tamen in his quæ ad salutem pertinent, & ad res spirituales cognoscendas, tam stolidi, tamque inepti sunt; ut videantur ad modum bestiarum usu rationis carere, & quasi saxa induratæ, nihil spiritualis intelligentiæ posse capere. Addit ibidem, eos de cæremoniis legis suæ & institutis nullam scire dare rationem. Sacerdotes verò quicquid dicunt, quidve præcipiunt, ita velle ab omnibus observari, quasi præceptum Dei; ut nemo audeat vel in minimo contradictionem vel resistentiam facere. Denique Turcæ linguâ Arabicâ, quam pauci inter illos intelligunt, preces fundunt, & multiplici in precibus utuntur battologiâ. [Sutlivius in Turcopapismo, lib. 2. cap. 9.]
units.tr: The Turks likewise follow the same path (and Bellarmine should not have been passed over, since Reginald and Gifford b did not pass over the Turkish Papists in this matter). For they write this about their priests, who are very like the Papists, Bartholomew Gyorgievitz c and Antonius Geuffræus d [book 2, On Turkish Religion and Ceremonies]: Not much learning is required of them. It is enough if they know how to read the Koran and the Mussaphum. Those who also know how to interpret the text according to the original are held to be most skilled, since the Koran was delivered by Muhammad not in the common Turkish tongue but in Arabic, and they think it wrong for it to be written out translated into the common tongue. [Christophorus Richerius, On the Manners of the Turks, book 2: Turks, he says, are accustomed to learn Arabic words from boyhood, as soon as they are imbued with their religion. For they have the law written in Arabic, and in all public and private affairs they use Arabic letters.] For the Turks, as Gerlachius c reports, are accustomed from the cradle to teach their boys to read the Koran and to impress it on their memory by constant repetition, because they believe that reading it, even without understanding, will bring infinite rewards in the next age. On the ignorance of the Turks, which he calls clear evidence of the unbelief of this sect, Septemcastrensis writes in On the Manners of the Turks, chap. 21: Although they are very cunning in carrying out any evil deed, and have a great, almost supernatural, practical experience in natural matters, yet in those things that pertain to salvation and to knowing spiritual things, they are so dull and inept that they seem to lack the use of reason like beasts, and, hardened like stones, they can grasp nothing of spiritual understanding. He adds there that they can give no account of the ceremonies and institutions of their law. The priests, whatever they say or command, want it observed by all as though it were the command of God, so that no one dares to make the slightest objection or resistance. Finally, the Turks pour out their prayers in the Arabic language, which few of them understand, and in their prayers they use much babbling repetition. [Sutlivius, Turkish Papism, book 2, chap. 9.]

units.tr: b Calvinus, Turcica, bk. 4, ch. 7, pp. 766, 778. c In Historia Saracenica cum Alcorano, printed 1580, p. 183. d Part 1 of the Aula Turcica, 1577, Basel edition, p. 44. e In Martin Crusius, Turco-Graecia, bk. 7, p. 502. Bellonius asserts that Turkish priests need only know how to read the Koran and translate it word for word into Turkish. Elsewhere, however, he says that the Koran was first written in Arabic and afterwards turned into the Turkish language.

units.la: Pharisæi accuratiorem cæteris hominibus legis notitiam sibi arrogabant, quemadmodum confirmat Josephus . Atque hinc est quòd plebi ita superbè insultaverint, Joan. VII. 49. Turba hæc, quæ non novit legem, execrabilis est. Ipsi nimirum cæci, cæcorum duces esse voluerunt (Mat.XV.14.) Ipsique Legis interpretes professi, cognitionis clavem sustulerunt: ipsi non introiverunt; & eos, qui introibant, prohibuerunt (Matth. XXIII. 13. Luc. XI. 52.) Claves scientiæ apud illos sunt, qui libros Prophetarum & legis habeant in manibus, ait Origenes . Et Author Operis Imperfecti in Matthæum (quod Chrysostomo tribuitur.) Regnum (inquit ) cælorum dicuntur Scripturæ; quia in illis infertum est regnum cælorum. Janua eorum, intellectus earum. Vel regnum est beatitudo cælestis: janua autem ejus est Scriptura, per quam introitur ad eam. Clavicularii autem sunt sacerdotes, quibus creditum est verbum docendi & interpretandi Scripturas. Clavis autem est verbum scientiæ Scripturarum, per quam aperitur hominibus janua veritatis: Adapertio autem est interpretatio vera. Vide quia non dixit [hîc Christus:] Væ vobis, qui non aperitis regnum cælorum, sed qui clauditis. Ergo non sunt scriptura clausæ, sed obscura quidem, ut cum labore inveniantur; non autem clausæ, ut nullo modo inveniantur. Neque enim abscondita est (ut paulò pòst addit Author) in scripturis veritas, sed obscura; non ut non inveniant eam, qui quærunt eam, sed ut non inveniant eam, qui quærere eam nolunt: ut ad illorum quidem gloriam pertineat, qui inveniunt eam; quia desideraverunt eam, & quæsierunt, & invenerunt; ad illorum autem condemnationem, qui non inveniunt eam; quia nec desideraverunt eam, nec quæsierunt, nec invenerunt. Nec potest eis esse excusatio condemnationis ignorantia veritatis; quibus erat inveniendi facultas, si fuisset quarendi voluntas. Nam si veritas salus & vita est cognoscentium se; magis debet quæri quàm quærere. Hoc deinde ad sui temporis Hæreticos, Arianos (unde intelligitur hanc partem Operis a nobis citati ab homine Ariano nequaquam profectam) ita Author accommodat. Sic & modò hæretici sacerdotes claudunt januam veritatis. Sciunt enim quoniam si
units.tr: The Pharisees claimed for themselves a more exact knowledge of the Law than other men, as Josephus confirms. Hence they spoke so arrogantly to the common people: "This crowd, which does not know the Law, is accursed" (John 7:49). They themselves, of course, wanted to be "blind guides of the blind" (Matt. 15:14). And as self-professed interpreters of the Law, "they have taken away the key of knowledge; they did not enter in themselves, and they hindered those who were entering" (Matt. 23:13; Luke 11:52). "The keys of knowledge are with those who hold the books of the Prophets and the Law in their hands," says Origen. The author of the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew (which is attributed to Chrysostom) says: "The Scriptures are called the kingdom of heaven, because the kingdom of heaven is contained in them. Their gate is their understanding. Or the kingdom is heavenly blessedness, and its gate is Scripture, through which one enters into it. The keepers of the keys are the priests, to whom the word of teaching and interpreting the Scriptures has been entrusted. The key is the word of the knowledge of the Scriptures, by which the gate of truth is opened to men; the opening is the true interpretation. See that he did not say [here Christ says]: 'Woe to you who do not open the kingdom of heaven, but who shut it.' Therefore the Scriptures are not closed, but obscure, so that they are found with labour; yet not closed, so that they can in no way be found. For the truth is not hidden in the Scriptures (as the author adds a little later), but obscure: not so that those who seek it do not find it, but so that those who are unwilling to seek it do not find it. It turns to the glory of those who find it, because they desired it, sought it and found it; but to the condemnation of those who do not find it, because they neither desired it, nor sought it, nor found it. Nor can ignorance of the truth be an excuse for condemnation to those who had the ability to find it, had they had the will to seek it. For if truth is the salvation and life of those who know themselves, it ought rather to be sought than to seek." The author then applies this to the heretics of his own time, the Arians (whence it is clear that this part of the work that we cite was by no means written by an Arian): "So also now the heretical priests shut the gate of truth. For they know that if the truth were made manifest, the Church of theirs must be abandoned, and they themselves would come down from priestly dignity to popular humility. Therefore, when they read in their people something such as 'He who sent me is greater than I,' they shut the gate of truth by a perverse interpretation, saying that the Son is less than the Father; whereas it is said to be less according to the dispensation of the flesh. Nor do they themselves enter into the truth of Scripture, on account of their avarice; nor do they permit others to enter, on account of their ignorance. Will the ignorant people then be excusable? Far from it. For if you were going to buy clothes, you would go round one merchant and another, etc." See the passage: "And if you wished to enter into the truth of the Scriptures" (for so I read in the manuscript codex of our library) "(1) you would not ask only by prayers, you would not seek only in the Scriptures, you would not knock only by good works, you would not question the priests, now these, now those [you would not investigate] who are the true keepers of the keys of the Scriptures, and who are the false." But these things are not done, because the word of God is not believed; because its promise of blessedness is not desired, nor is the threat of its judgment feared. And we see that this lazy negligence is still commended to the people by the Papist teachers as especially wholesome; they, following the footsteps of their forefathers (the Pharisees and Arians), want to be the leaders of others (themselves for the most part most blind), and taking away the key of knowledge from the people, they keep them from reading the Scriptures; they order them to look for the truth from themselves alone; they sternly forbid them to inquire into their doctrines; as if they alone seemed to be wise among all men.

units.la: {f} Observat. lib.3. cap 30. {g} Lib 2.cap.32. {h} Antiq. Judaic. lib.17.cap.3. & de bello Judaico, lib. 1. cap. 4 {i} Lib. 4. περὶ ἀρχῶν. {k} Homil. 44. manifestata fuerit veritas, eorum Ecclesia est relinquenda; & ipsi de sacerdotali dignitate ad humilitatem venient popularem. Ideo quando legunt in populo suo aliquid tale, Qui me misit, major me est; perversa interpretatione claudunt januam veritatis, dicentes, Filium minorem Patre; cum secundum dispensationem carnis dicatur minor. Et nec ipsi intrant in veritatem scripturae, propter avaritiam; neque alios intrare permittunt, propter ignorantiam. Quid ergo ignorans populus excusabilis erit? Absit. Si enim vestimenta empturus, gyras unum negotiatorem & alterum, &c. Vide locum: Et si velles scripturarum ingredi veritatem (sic enim lego in Codice MS. Bibliothecae nostrae) (1) non peteres orationibus, non quaereres in scripturis, non pulsares bonis operibus, non interrogares sacerdotes, nunc ipsos, nunc illos [non investigares] qui veri sint Clavicularii Scripturarum, qui falsi. Sed ista non fiunt, quia verbum Dei non creditur: quia nec promissio beatitudinis ejus desideratur, nec judicium comminationis ejus timetur. Et istam sane supinam negligentiam a Pontificiis Doctoribus ut maxime salutarem populo commendari etiamnum cernimus; qui patrum suorum (Pharisaeorum & Arianorum) insistentes vestigiis, caeterorum duces esse volunt (ipsi plerunque caecissimi) clavemque scientiae populo auferentes, a Scripturarum lectione arcent; ab ipsis solis veritatem ut expectent, mandant; in eorum dogmata ne inquirant, severe interdicunt; quasi ipsi soli omnium hominum sapere videantur.
units.tr: {f} Observat. lib.3. cap 30. {g} Lib 2.cap.32. {h} Antiq. Judaic. lib.17.cap.3. & de bello Judaico, lib. 1. cap. 4 {i} Lib. 4. On Principles [περὶ ἀρχῶν]. {k} Homil. 44. Their Church is to be abandoned once the truth has been made plain, and they themselves will come down from their priestly dignity to the humility of the people. So when they read to their people something like "He who sent me is greater than I," they shut the door of truth by a perverse interpretation, saying that the Son is less than the Father, when it is said that he is less according to the dispensation of the flesh. Nor do they themselves enter into the truth of Scripture, because of their greed, and they do not allow others to enter, because of their ignorance. Will the ignorant people then be excused? Far from it. For if you were about to buy clothes, you would go round one merchant and then another, etc. See the passage: And if you wished to enter into the truth of the Scriptures (for so I read it in a manuscript codex of our library) (1) you would not seek it by prayers, you would not inquire in the Scriptures, you would not knock with good works, you would not question the priests, not now these, now those, [you would not investigate] who are the true keepers of the keys of the Scriptures and who are the false. But these things are not done, because the word of God is not believed, because its promise of blessedness is not desired, and its threatened judgment is not feared. And we see that this lazy negligence is still commended by the Papist teachers as most wholesome for the people; they, following the footsteps of their fathers (the Pharisees and Arians), want to be leaders of the rest (though they are themselves for the most part most blind), and, taking the key of knowledge away from the people, they keep them from reading the Scriptures; they command them to look to these men alone for the truth; they severely forbid them to inquire into their doctrines; as if they alone seemed to be wise among all men.

units.la: Priusquam a Pharisaeis discedamus, illud etiam attexendum duximus, quod ad Matth. XXIII. 5. (ubi in illis notat Dominus, quod Phylacteria sua dilatent) observat praediatus Author ¹ Operis imperfecti. puto (inquit) quod illorum tunc Scribarum & Pharisaeorum exemplo, & nunc multi aliqua nomina Hebraica Angelorum confingunt, & scribunt, & alligant sibi; quae non intelligentibus linguam Hebraicam metuenda videntur. Sic ergo & isti vani sunt, sicut illi fuerunt: quoniam persona illorum de mundo recesserunt, non mores. De hominibus itaque nostri temporis exponentes, de illis videmur exponere. Ergo sacerdotes ex eo, quod ab hominibus volunt videri justi, phylacteria alligant circa collum, quidam vero partem aliquam Evangelii scriptam. Dic sacerdos insipiens: Nonne quotidie Evangelium in Ecclesia legitur, & auditur ab hominibus? Cui ergo in auribus posita Evangelia nihil prosunt; quomodo eum poterunt circa collum suspensa salvare? Deinde ubi est virtus Evangelii, in figuris lite-
units.tr: Before we leave the Pharisees, we have thought it right to add this also, which the aforementioned author of the Opus imperfectum observes on Matthew 23:5 (where the Lord notes that they enlarge their phylacteries): "I think," he says, "that after the example of those scribes and Pharisees, many now also invent Hebrew names of angels, write them, and bind them on themselves, which seem fearful to those who do not understand the Hebrew language." So these men are vain just as those were, since the persons of those men have departed from the world, but not their manners. Therefore, in speaking of the men of our time, we seem to be speaking of those. So the priests, because they wish to be seen as righteous by men, bind phylacteries about the neck, and some bind a part of the Gospel written out. Say, foolish priest: is not the Gospel read and heard by men every day in the Church? To whom then do the Gospels placed in their ears do no good; how will they be able to save him when hung about the neck? Then, where is the power of the Gospel, in rare figures of speech, or in the sense of the meaning? If in the signs, then you hang it well about the neck; if in the meaning, then it profits more when placed in the heart than when hung about the neck. Thus he.

units.la: (1) Nunc pro non ubivis habent editiones impressae. rarum, an in intellectu sensuum? Si in signis, bene circa collum suspendis: si in intellectu, ergo melius in corde posita prosunt, quàm circa collum suspensa. Hæc ille.
units.tr: (1) Now the printed editions have "rarum" (rare) where others read "not everywhere." Is it rare, or is it in the sense of the meaning? If it refers to the signs, you are right to hang them around the neck. If it refers to the meaning, then the things placed in the heart profit more than those hung around the neck. So he says.

units.la: Donatistis hæreticis olim impegit D. Augustinus , quòd timerent ne sæculi Reges sacrorum codicum eloquia nôssent. Sed vultis (inquit) nolitis, Ecclesiam intrant & lectionibus aurem admovent. (Espensæus Episcopus, lib. de sex Tract. pag. 98.) Donatistæ sanè, licet ipsorum majores sanctos codices flammis tradiderunt (ut apparet ex Augustino, lib. 1. contra literas Petiliani, cap. 27.) hoc tamen crimen Catholicis objicere nunquam desierunt. Adversus hos ita scribit Augustinus in libro de unitate Ecclesiæ, cap. 3. Sunt certè libri Dominici, quorum authoritati utrique consentimus: ibi quæramus Ecclesiam, ibi discutiamus causam nostram. Hic forte dicturi sunt: Quid quaeris in libris, quos ignibus tradidisti? Ad hoc respondeo. Quid times, ne legantur isti libri; si eos ab ignibus custodisti? Eos certè ille tradidisse credatur, qui eis lectis non consentire convincitur. Hæc Augustinus; eodemque modo & nos Donatistas nostrorum temporum provocare possumus. Nec minus justè illos premere possumus eâ accusatione, quâ olim Donatistas Optatus Milevitanus. Illud prætermittere nequeo (inquit ille ) quod nec Deo est placitum, nec à vestris cultoribus excusari, nec ab aliquo homine defendi potest. Per judicia sæcularia & leges publicas, divina legis instrumenta executione officiorum à plurimis eripienda esse dixistis; volentes soli habere, quod pax in communione possederat. [Ita videlicet Romana Ecclesia omnes ab ipsius communione alienos Scripturarum possessione prorsus privandos esse vult, testibus Rhemensibus in præfat. §. 13.] Huc etiam illud Augustini (epist. 119. ad Januarium, cap. 18.) de hymnis & psalmis canendis, referri potest. De hac (inquit) re tam utili ad movendum pie animum,& accendendum divinæ lectionis, dilectionis substituerunt contra omnium exemplarium fidem Lovanienses Assertum, varia consuetudo est; & pleraque in Africa Ecclesiæ membra pigriora sunt; ita ut Donatistæ nos (sicut Papistæ nos) reprehendant, quòd sobriè psalmus in Ecclesiâ divina cantica Prophetarum; cùm ipsi ebrietates suas ad Canticum psalmorum humano ingenio compositorum, quasi tubas exhortationis inflamment. Quando autem non est tempus, cùm in Ecclesiâ fratres congregantur, sancta cantandi; nisi cùm legitur, aut disputatur, aut Antistites clarâ voce precantur, aut communis oratio voce Diaconi indicitur? Vid. Augustini, lib. 2. contra Petiliani literas, cap. 92. Lib. 6. Aliis vero particulis temporum quid melius à congregatis Christianis fiat, quid utilius, quid sanctius, omnino non video.
units.tr: St Augustine once charged the Donatists, who were heretics, with fearing that the kings of this world might come to know the words of the sacred books. "But whether you wish it or not," he says, "they enter the Church and bring their ears to the readings." (Espencaeus, bishop, in his book on the six tracts, p. 98.) The Donatists, indeed, though their forebears gave the holy codices to the flames (as appears from Augustine, book 1 against the letters of Petilianus, chapter 27), never ceased to bring this charge against the Catholics. Against them Augustine writes thus in his book on the unity of the Church, chapter 3: "Surely there are the books of the Lord, to whose authority we both assent. Let us seek the Church there; let us examine our cause there. Perhaps they will say here: 'Why do you look in books which you handed over to the fires?' To this I answer: why do you fear that these books be read, if you have kept them safe from the fires? Surely he is to be believed to have handed them over who is shown to have not agreed with them when they were read." So Augustine; and in the same way we can challenge the Donatists of our own time. Nor can we press them less justly with the accusation by which Optatus of Milevis once charged the Donatists. "I cannot pass over this (he says), which is neither pleasing to God, nor can be excused by your devotees, nor defended by any man. You have said that the instruments of the divine law should be snatched from most people by secular judgments and public laws and the execution of offices, wishing alone to have what peace had held in common." [So, evidently, the Roman Church wishes that all who are alien to its communion be wholly deprived of possession of the Scriptures; the Rhemists witness to this in their preface, §13.] To this too may be referred Augustine's words (letter 119 to Januarius, chapter 18) about singing hymns and psalms. "On this matter, so useful for stirring the heart to piety and kindling the love of divine reading, there is a varied custom; and many members of the Church in Africa are rather sluggish. So the Donatists reproach us (as the Papists reproach us) for singing soberly the psalms and the divine canticles of the Prophets, while they inflame their drunken revelries with songs of psalms composed by human wit, as if they were trumpets of exhortation. But when is there no time for holy singing, when the brothers are gathered together in the Church, except when there is reading, or disputation, or the bishops pray with a clear voice, or the common prayer is announced by the voice of the deacon?" See Augustine, book 2 against the letters of Petilianus, chapter 92; book 6. "As for the other periods of time, I altogether fail to see what could be done better, more usefully, or more holily by Christians gathered together."

units.la: Pelagio quidem objicit Hieronymus , quod scripserit scientiam legis etiam feminas habere debere; cum Apostolus doceat esse tacendum mulieribus in Ecclesia; &, si quid ignorant, domi viros suos debere consulere. Nec sufficit tibi (inquit ibid. Hieronymus) dedisse agmini tuo scientiam scripturarum, nisi earum voce & canticis delectaris. Jungis enim & ponis in titulo, quòd & faemina deo psallere debeant. Quis enim ignorat, psallendum esse faeminis in cubiculis suis, & absque virorum frequentia & congregatione turbarum? Verum tu donas, quod non licet; ut quod verecundè facere debeant, & absque ullo arbitro, magistri authoritate proclament. Haec Hieronymus, à δημάρχης, ἀλλ' ἀγνοίας (ut loquitur Basilius ) differens. Cantum fortasse in faeminis non alium reprehendit, quàm qualem intelligit Concilium Laodicenum, cap. 15. decernens: (1) Quòd non oportet amplius praeter eos, qui regulares Cantores existunt, qui & de codice canunt, alios in pulpitum ascendere & in Ecclesiâ psallere. Augustinus sanè Victorianae villae Dominam cum ancillis suis & quibusdam Sanctimonialibus ad vespertinos hymnos & orationes ex more venisse atque hymnos cantâsse innuit; quod in aliis quoque factitatum (quaecunque fuerit loci, ubi commoratus est Hieronymus, consuetudo) ex iis quae in superioribus prolata sunt, apparet. Rem confirmat Ambrosius, Hexaemer. lib. 3. cap. 5. Responsoriis (inquit) psalmorum, cantu virorum, mulierum, virginum, parvulorum consonus undarum fragor resultat: Ecclesiam mari assimilans. Augustinus etiam epist. 109 ad faeminas scriptâ (ex quâ fecerunt Regulam 3. Monachorum in fine tom.1.) rem extra dubium ponit. Psalmis (inquit) & hymnis cùm oratis Deum; hoc versetur in corde, quod profertur in voce, (al. ore) & nolite cantare nisi quod legistis esse cantandum; quod autem non ita scriptum est ut cantetur, non cantetur. Studium verò Scripturarum in faeminis quis magis quàm ipsemet Hieronymus commendavit? Hieronymus studium sacrarum literarum etiam in faeminis commendat, ait Erasmus. Vid. epistolam ejus 140. ad Principiam virginem (Explanatio est Psalmi 44.) ubi se ac muliebrem sexum à calumniis hàc in re defendit. Sanè Pelagius (vel quisquis fuerit epistolae ad Demetriadem Author Pelagianus, quae Augustino & Hieronymo perperam ascripta est) primam Vir-
units.tr: Jerome objects to Pelagius that he wrote that women too ought to have knowledge of the law, although the Apostle teaches that women must keep silent in the Church, and that if they are ignorant of anything they should ask their husbands at home. Jerome goes on (he says in the same place): It is not enough for you to have given your troop knowledge of the Scriptures, unless you also take delight in their voice and songs. For you join and place in your title that women ought to sing psalms to God. For who does not know that women should sing psalms in their own chambers, without a crowd of men and a gathering of people? But you grant what is not permitted, so that what they ought to do modestly, and without any witness, they proclaim with the authority of a teacher. Thus Jerome, differing [not from malice but from ignorance, ἀλλ' ἀγνοίας] (as Basil puts it). Perhaps he found fault only with that kind of singing by women which the Council of Laodicea, canon 15, has in mind, when it decrees: (1) that it is not fitting for anyone to go up into the pulpit and sing in the Church, besides those who are the regular cantors, who sing from the book. Augustine plainly indicates that the lady of the Victorian estate came with her maidservants and some nuns to the evening hymns and prayers, as was the custom, and sang hymns there; and that this was also practised elsewhere (whatever the custom of the place where Jerome lived), as appears from what has been set out above. Ambrose confirms the matter in Hexaemeron, book 3, chapter 5: With the responses of the psalms, the sound of the waves resounds in harmony with the singing of men, women, virgins and little children, comparing the Church to the sea. Augustine too, in letter 109 written to women (from which they made the Third Rule of the Monks at the end of volume 1), puts the matter beyond doubt: When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is uttered with the voice be in the heart as well (other reading: mouth), and do not sing except what you have read is to be sung; what is not written to be sung, let it not be sung. But who has commended the study of the Scriptures even in women more than Jerome himself? Jerome commends the study of the sacred letters even in women, says Erasmus. See his letter 140 to the virgin Principia (it is an explanation of Psalm 44), where he defends himself and the female sex against slanders on this point. Indeed Pelagius (or whoever was the Pelagian author of the letter to Demetrias, which was wrongly ascribed to Augustine and Jerome) urges that the first care and chief study of a virgin ought to be this: to know the will of her Lord, and what pleases him or displeases him, and to inquire diligently; so that, according to the Apostle (Rom. 12), she may render a reasonable service to God, and may order the whole course of her life by his judgment. For it is impossible (he says) for anyone to please him whose wishes he does not know; and it may happen that one offends even with the desire to obey, if he has not learned beforehand how he ought to obey. Hence, in the same place, he addresses the virgin Demetrias thus: Although you ought to dedicate the whole time of your life to the divine work, and it is fitting that no hour should be empty of spiritual progress, since you must meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, yet there ought to be some fixed and appointed number of hours, by which you may devote yourself more fully to God. [See above, at the year 390, at the end of the appendix of testimonies of Jerome.] And afterwards: For this reason above all the study of the holy Scriptures is to be cherished by you: the soul is to be enlightened by the divine words, and by the shining of God's word the darkness of the devil is to be driven away. For that spirit flees quickly from the soul which the divine word enlightens, a soul which is always occupied with heavenly thoughts, in which the word of God is constantly present, and whose power the wicked spirit cannot bear. But the Catholic teachers who sent an antidote against the poisons of that Pelagian letter, Augustine and Alypius indeed to Demetrias' mother Juliana, and Jerome and Prosper to Demetrias herself, warned that there was no danger in these admonitions. Rather, Prosper approves the devotion of the pious virgin in this, that, signifying that he wishes to pass over testimonies from the pages of both the New and the Old Testament, he immediately adds the reason: especially since my discourse is to your holiness, to whom all the things we have mentioned will present themselves, either to your memory or to your reading. More plainly, and more fully than Pelagius himself, Jerome himself urges Demetrias to the study of the Scriptures (as was shown above at the year 390, from his letter 8 to Demetrias), where, among other things, he advises her to fast in such a way that she does nothing less in reading, in psalms, or in vigils. He adds, however, in the same place (which will perhaps help to clarify the earlier passage against the Pelagians): I have known, in both sexes, that through excessive abstinence the sanity of the mind has been troubled in some people, especially in those who lived in damp and cold cells, so that they did not know what they were doing, or where they were turning, what they ought to say or what to keep silent. Certainly, if those who are untaught in secular letters read something from the treatises of eloquent men, they learn only verbosity, without knowledge of the Scriptures; and, according to the old saying, since they do not know how to speak, they cannot keep silent. units.la: (1) Πλὴν ἡ γυναικῶν ψαλτῶν ἡ ἐπὶ ἡ ἐμβῶνα ἀναβαινόντων ἐκ ἀπὸ ἐκκλησίας ψάλλοντων. ginis curam primumque studium esse debere monet, scire voluntatem Domini sui, & quid ei placeat, quidve displiceat, diligenter inquirere; ut secundum Apostolum (Rom. XII.) rationabile Deo reddat obsequium, totumque vitæ suæ cursum ex ejus possit ordinare sententiâ. Impossibile est enim(inquit) ei quenquam placere, cui quid placeat ignorat: fierique potest, ut etiam obsequendi voto offendat, qui quomodo obsequi debeat, antea non didicit. Hinc ibidem Demetriadem virginem ita affatur. Quanquam omne vitæ tuæ tempus divino debeas operi consecrare; & nullam prorsus horam spirituali profectu vacuam esse conveniat; cùm tibi in lege Domini die ac nocte meditandum sit h: debet tamen aliquis esse determinatus & constitutus horarum numerus, quo plenius Deo vaces. [Vid. supra an. 390. in sine Appendicis testimoniorum Hieronymi.] Et postea, Propter quod maximè sanctarum tibi scripturarum studium diligendum est, illuminanda divinis eloquiis anima, & corruscante Dei verbo Diaboli repellenda sunt tenebræ. Citò enim fugit ille ab eâ animâ, quam sermo divinus illuminat, quæ cœlestibus semper cogitationibus occupatur, in qua assiduum est Dei verbum, cujus vim nequam spiritus non potest ferre. At verò qui adversus Pelagianæ illius Epistolæ venena antidotum transmiserunt Catholici Doctores, Augustinusi quidem & Alipius ad Julianam Demetriadis matrem, Hieronymus k verò, & Prosper l ad ipsam Demetriadem, nihil his admonitionibus subesse periculi monuerunt. Immò potiùs Prosper piæ virginis studium in eo comprobat, quòd testimoniis ex paginis & Novi & Veteris Testamenti se supersedere velle significans, rationem hujusmodi mox attexat. Præsertim cùm mihi sermo esset ad sanctimoniam tuam; cui ex formulâ eorum, quæ commemoravimus, omnia se aut recordanti offerent aut legenti. Planiùs verò (& plenìus quam ipse Pelagius) Demetriadem ad Scripturarum studium incitat ipse Hieronymus (ut supra ad an. 390. ex Epistolâ ejus 8. ad Demetriadem ostensum est) ubi inter alia sic eam jejunare debere monet; ut nec in lectione, nec in psalmis, nec in vigiliis, soli o quid minus faceret. Addit tamen ibidem (quod fortasse ad superioris loci contra Pelagianos illustrationem faciet.) Novi ego in utroque sexu, per nimiam abstinentiam, cerebri sanitatem quibusdam fuisse vexatam; præcipuéque in his, qui in humectis & frigidis habitavere cellulis: ita ut nescirent quid agerent, quòve se verterent, quid loqui, quid tacere deberent. Certè si rudes secularium literarum, de tractatibus hominum disertorum quippiam legerint; verbofitatem solam discunt, absque notitiâ Scripturarum; & juxta vetus elogium, cùm loqui nesciant, tacere non possunt.
