units.la: {h} P. al. I. {i} August. epist. 143. {k} Epist. 8. ad Demetriadem. {l} Inter Ambrosii epistolas, lib. 10. epist. 84. fœminis docentibus scripturas loquatur Hieronymus, lib 1. contra Pelagianos ; textus ab eo citatus ex 1 Tim. II. ad rem non facit,) Docentque scripturas, quas non intelligunt: & cùm aliis persuaserint, eruditorum sibi assumunt supercilium, prius imperitorum magistri, quàm doctorum discipuli. Bonum est igitur obedire majoribus, parere perfectis; & post regulas scripturarum, vita sua tramitem ab aliis discere: nec præceptore uti pessimo, sc. præsumptione suâ. De talibus fœminis & Apostolus loquitur m: Quæ circumferuntur omni vento doctrinæ ; semper discentes, & nunquam ad scientiam veritatis pervenientes. Hactenus Hieronymus. Augustinus & Alipius (in Epistola ad Julianum) virus illud Pelagianæ doctrinæ admissum patefacit; Deum, præter quòd nobis revelat scientiam, nihil ultra nos adjuvare, ut ea quæ facienda discendo novimus, etiam diligendo faciamus. Hoc pestiferum dogma latiùs explicat Augustinus(epist. 107.ad Vitalem) Deum sc. per legem suam, per scripturas suas, operari ut velimus, quas vel legimus vel audimus; sed eis consentire vel non consentire ita nostrum esse, ut si velimus fiat; si autem nolimus, nihil in nobis operationem Dei valere faciamus. Hæc est illa (inquit ibi Augustinus) Pelagianorum mala, malè diffamata, meritoque reprobata, & ab ipso etiam Pelagio timente damnari in Orientalium Episcoporum judico damnata, sententia: quâ dicunt gratiam Dei ad singulos actus dari, sed in libero arbitrio esse, vel in lege atque doctrinâ. Hinc commotus Hieronymus, lib. 1. adv. Pelagianos ita scripsit. Dicis, sine peccato esse non posse, nisi qui scientiam legis habuerit: per quod magnam partem Christianorum excludis à justitiâ; & qui prædicator es impeccantiæ, omnes propè peccatores esse pronuntias. Quotus enim quisque Christianorum habet legis scientiam; quàm in multis doctoribus Ecclesiæ aut raro aut difficulter invenias. Verùm quid de hujusmodi Doctoribus (quibus Romana Ecclesia referta est) sentiat ipse Hieronymus, ex Commentariis ejus in I. cap. Epist. ad Titum intelligere licet. Hic locus (inquit) adversùs eos facit, qui inertia se & otio & somno dantes, (Pontificiorum ad exemplum) putant peccatum esse, si Scripturas legerint; & eos qui in lege Domini meditantur die ac nocte, quasi garrulos inutilesque contemnunt; non animadvertentes Apostolum, post catalogum conversationis Episcopi, etiam doctrinam similiter præcepisse. Denique ex testimoniis supra ex Hieronymo (an. 390.) prolatis apparet, illum non minùs à populo Christiano Scripturarum studium requirere quàm Pelagium (aut certè Pelagianum Authorem Annotationum in Paulinas Epistolas, quæ D. Hieronymo olim ascriptæ sunt) qui in illa Apostoli verba Coloss. 3. [Verbum Christi habitet in vobis abundanter.] ita annotat. Hic ostenditur verbum Christi non sufficienter sed abundanter etiam
units.tr: {h} P. (others read I.) {i} Augustine, letter 143. {k} Letter 8 to Demetrias. {l} Among Ambrose's letters, book 10, letter 84; the text quoted by him from 1 Timothy 2 does not bear on the point. Jerome speaks of women teaching the Scriptures, book 1 against the Pelagians. They teach the Scriptures, which they do not understand; and when they have persuaded others, they take to themselves the haughtiness of the learned, being masters of the unlearned before they are disciples of the learned. It is good, therefore, to obey the elders and to submit to the perfect, and after the rules of the Scriptures to learn the path of one's life from others, and not to use the worst teacher, namely one's own presumption. The Apostle also speaks of such women: who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth. So far Jerome. Augustine and Alypius (in the letter to Julian) reveal that poison of Pelagian doctrine: God, besides revealing knowledge to us, helps us in nothing further, so that we may also do with love the things we have learned to do. Augustine explains this pestilent dogma more widely (letter 107, to Vitalis): that God operates through his law and his Scriptures, so that we may will, whichever we read or hear; but whether we consent to them or do not consent is so much ours that, if we will, it happens; but if we are unwilling, we make God's operation count for nothing in us. This is (says Augustine there) that evil of the Pelagians, ill-reputed and justly condemned, and condemned by the judgment of the Eastern bishops, the opinion which even Pelagius himself, fearing, condemned: by which they say that the grace of God is given for each individual act, but that it lies in free will, or in the law and the teaching. Moved by this, Jerome wrote in book 1 against the Pelagians thus: You say that no one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law: by which you exclude a great part of Christians from righteousness; and you, who are a preacher of sinlessness, pronounce almost all men to be sinners. For how few Christians have knowledge of the law; in how many teachers of the Church you will find it rarely or with difficulty. But what Jerome himself thinks of teachers of this kind (with whom the Roman Church is crammed) may be understood from his Commentaries on the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus. This passage (he says) is against those who, giving themselves to idleness, leisure and sleep (following the example of the Papists), think it a sin if they read the Scriptures, and who scorn those who meditate in the law of the Lord day and night as chatterers and useless men; not noticing that the Apostle, after the list of the bishop's conduct, has likewise commanded teaching. Finally, from the testimonies of Jerome cited above (at the year 390) it appears that he required the study of the Scriptures from the Christian people no less than Pelagius did (or at any rate the Pelagian author of the Annotations on the Pauline Epistles, which were formerly ascribed to St Jerome), who, on those words of Paul in Colossians 3, [Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly], annotates thus: Here it is shown that the word of Christ is to dwell not merely sufficiently but abundantly.

units.la: 2 Tim. III. Laicos habere debere,& docere se invicem vel monere.Videant potius Pontificii, annon ipsi in Pelagianorum castra concedant; qui exaggerare solent,ut olim Julianus, hæreticus Pelagianus (quod ex libro illius 3. contra Augustinum scripto repetit ipse Augustinus lib. 5. contra Julianum, cap. 5.) quam sit difficilis, paucisque conveniens eruditis, sanctarum cognitio literarum. Verba ejus paulò explicatius repræsentat Beda, lib. 1. Expositionis in Cantica Cantic.non procul ab initio. Julianus Pelagianus (inquit) in libro de Amore docet clausa legis sacramenta solos intueri posse eos ; quos oculatos & eruditio reddidisset & pietas: oblitus gratia Dei, quae etiam illiteratis & idiotis scripturarum arcana revelavit.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 3. Laymen ought to have the Scriptures and to teach or admonish one another. The Papists should rather consider whether they themselves are not conceding ground to the Pelagians, who, as Julian the Pelagian heretic once did, tend to exaggerate how difficult the knowledge of the sacred letters is and how suited only to a few learned men. (Augustine himself repeats this from the third book of Julian's writing against him, in Augustine's fifth book against Julian, ch. 5.) Bede sets out Julian's words somewhat more fully in the first book of his Exposition of the Song of Songs, not far from the beginning: "Julian the Pelagian," he says, "teaches in his book on Love that only those whom learning and piety have made keen-sighted can see the closed mysteries of the law, forgetting the grace of God, which has also revealed the secrets of the Scriptures to the unlettered and the simple."

units.la: Celsus etiam, Epicuræus Philosophus, Christianorum acerrimus hostis, in Romanensibus nostris jam revixit; adversus quem ita pugnat Origenes. (2)Ideo prophetiarum auctores scriptis eas tradiderunt asservandas posteris ; ut lectores admirarentur tanquam divina oracula, & proficerent non tantùm ex admonitionibus reprehensionibusque ; verum etiam ex praedictionibus ; & ex eorum eventu agnoscentes divinum spiritum fatidicum, juxta pietatis doctrinam se exercerent obediendo legi ac prophetis. Certè ipsi prophetæ, quicquid erat opus mox ab auditoribus intelligi, & quicquid ad corrigendos mores faciebat, absque ullis involucris proposuerunt eis ita ut Deus voluit. Quicquid autem arcanum erat, & dispiciendum amplius, ut vulgari captu sublimius, id figuris obscurioribus convelaverunt, aenigmatis, allegoriis, paræmiis ac parabolis ; ut non ab ignavis inveniretur & segnibus, sed à virtutis ac veritatis studiosis perscrutatoribus ; & inventum juxta divinam doctrinam in usum proprium verteretur. At praeclarus hic Celsus, velut iræ impotens, quòd propheticas voces intelligere non valeat, convitiis eas impetit, dicens ostentari jactarique obscura quaedam ac fanatica, eóque intellecta sapienti nemini ; sed stultis & praestigiatoribus occasionem usurpandi ea in quamlibet sententiam. (3) Mihi videtur versutè dixisse, volens quantum in se esset, arcere lectores à diligentius discutiendis & examinandis prophetarum sensibus. Hactenus Origenes contra Celsum,lib.7.non minùs (si non multò etiam magis) Pontificios quàm illum feriens.
units.tr: Celsus too, the Epicurean philosopher, the most bitter enemy of the Christians, has now revived among our Romanists; Origen fights against him thus: "Therefore the authors of the prophecies committed them in writing to be preserved for posterity, so that readers might admire them as divine oracles, and profit not only from admonitions and rebukes but also from the predictions, and, recognising from their fulfilment the divine prophetic Spirit, might exercise themselves in obedience to the law and the prophets, according to the teaching of piety." Certainly the prophets themselves set out, without any wrappings, whatever needed to be understood at once by their hearers and whatever served to correct morals, as God willed. But whatever was hidden and required further searching, being too lofty for common understanding, they veiled in more obscure figures, riddles, allegories, proverbs and parables, so that it would not be found by the idle and sluggish, but by those who searched diligently after virtue and truth; and what was found was to be turned to its own use according to the divine teaching. But this distinguished Celsus, as though powerless in his anger because he cannot understand the prophetic voices, attacks them with insults, saying that certain obscure and fanatical things are displayed and boasted of, and so understood by no wise man, but offer an opportunity to fools and charlatans to apply them to whatever opinion they like. (3) It seems to me he has spoken cunningly, wishing, as far as he could, to keep readers from discussing and examining the senses of the prophets with more care." Thus Origen against Celsus, book 7, striking the Papists no less (if not much more) than him.

units.la: (2) Διὸ ἡ οἱ κατ' αὐτὸ ἀποχαλύμμενοι τὰς σεφοπετείας ὠπῶν ἰφύλαξαν ἵνα ἡ οἱ μὲ-τυγνίσεσι ἀναγνώσκοντες θαυμάζωσιν ὡς λόγος Θεοῦ, ἡ ὀφελέμενοι ... τὸν χῆ λόγον ἰσόσβειαν ἀκούοντες διατηλῶσι πεισόμενοι τῷ ῥόμῳ ἡ τῆς σεφεύσεως... ἡ ἀπὸ τὴν ἴδιον ἰσπαργώσιον. ἡ ἡ μυσικώτερα ἡν ἡ ἱποθεικώτερα, &c.
units.tr: (2) "Therefore the authors of the prophecies committed them in writing to be preserved for posterity, so that readers might admire them as the word of God, and profit ... hearing the word ... they might proceed, bound to the rule of the ... and from their own ... more mystical or more hidden, etc." [Διὸ ἡ οἱ κατ' αὐτὸ ἀποχαλύμμενοι τὰς σεφοπετείας ὠπῶν ἰφύλαξαν ἵνα ἡ οἱ μὲ-τυγνίσεσι ἀναγνώσκοντες θαυμάζωσιν ὡς λόγος Θεοῦ, ἡ ὀφελέμενοι ... τὸν χῆ λόγον ἰσόσβειαν ἀκούοντες διατηλῶσι πεισόμενοι τῷ ῥόμῳ ἡ τῆς σεφεύσεως... ἡ ἀπὸ τὴν ἴδιον ἰσπαργώσιον. ἡ ἡ μυσικώτερα ἡν ἡ ἱποθεικώτερα, &c.]

units.la: (3) Καὶ πανύεγως μοι ἐδὲξε ταῦτ' εἰρηκέναι, κωλύειν, τὸ ὅπερ ἐφ' ἑαυτῷ, βιλόμενοις πὼ ἐναγχόμενοις τῆς σεφεύσεως βασιλεῖαν ἡ ἐξεπάζειν ἀυτῶν τ̄ γῆν. Julianus Apostata, cùm ex piis & religiosis parentibus esset ortus (4) ab ineunte ætate, ut ritus Ecclesiæ postulat, initiatus, sacras literas didicit, & in iisdem ab Episcopis & aliis viris ecclesiasticis educatus fuit; ut est apud Sozomenum . Ita S. Pigmenium Presbyterum illum à pueritia sacris literis erudivisse in Martyrologiis Bedæ, Usuardi, Adonis, & Galesinii legimus. Postmodum verò Christianæ fidei defensor, hoc objecit Christianis, quod nobis hodie Pontificii. Ex omnibus vestris eleemosynis pueros, & ut in scripturis exercerentur, operam dedistis, etiamsi videantur magis ad servilitatem nati. Contra quem Cyrillus, lib. 7. (idemque pro nobis contra Romanenses) Pueri etiam (inquit) in sacris enutriti literis, statim fiunt religiosissimi, etiamsi minus eloquentes. Dicis illos minimè differre à servis, quia non sunt tam disserti. Fortassis ob hoc solum censet admirationem contingere, contempsâ omni aliâ virtute, propter quam Deo quis familiaris fit, & ad summam pervenit nobilitatem. Hactenus Cyrillus. Idem Julianus in libro, quem inscripsit Cynisinum, dum docere instituit, quatenus fabulæ sacræ sint effingendæ, ait, Veritatem in ejusmodi rebus occultandam esse, hisque utitur verbis. Natura aves in abstruso latere; occultaque Deorum essentia non patitur se planis & apertis verbis impuris hominum auribus inculcari. Videtur Imperator (inquit Socrates, lib. 3. histor. Eccles. cap. 19. vel 23. ut in Græco est, ubi locus ille Juliani citatus est) eam de sacris divinisque scripturis habere opinionem; quòd illarum sermones mystici sint, quódque arcanam quandam intelligentiam complectantur: sed ægrè propterea fert, quòd non omnes eandem de illis opinionem concipiunt; inque eos Christianos insultat, qui simpliciter eorum oracula accipiunt. (5) At verò neque vulgi simplicitatem tantopere insectari debuisset, neque illius (sc. vulgi) gratiâ in sacras literas tantâ insulentiâ invehi; neque propterea eos odisse, atque adeo sensus sententiasque præclaras in illis comprehensas detestari; quod non omnes eas pro ejus arbitrio intelligant. Hæc contra Julianum Socrates. Sanè Melchior Canus , & eum secutus Jacobus Ledesma , religionis arcana occultanda esse confirmant præclaro hoc ex Porphyrio (sic namque Juliani sententiam n Hist. Eccles. lib. 5. cap. 2. o Ad IV. Cal. April. p Lib. 3 cap. 3. q Cap. 22. (4) Greek text: Ἐκ τῶν ἰμυήσεων ... &c. (5) — Οὐκ ἴδιν ἡ πολλὴ ... &c. uterque Porphyrio errore ascribit, satis profecto idoneo ejusmodi religionis Magistro) producto testimonio. Amat natura celari; nec divina mysteria Deus patitur in aures vulgi introire pollutas.
units.tr: (3) "And it seemed to me that he spoke very properly, forbidding, as far as he could, those who wish to enter the kingdom of the Scriptures or to explore their land." Julian the Apostate, though born of pious and religious parents, (4) was initiated from early childhood, as the rite of the Church requires, learned the sacred letters, and was educated in them by bishops and other churchmen, as is found in Sozomen. Likewise we read in the Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado and Galesinius that the priest Pigmenius was taught the sacred letters from boyhood. Afterwards, however, as a defender of the Christian faith, he objected to the Christians what the Papists object to us today: "Out of all your alms you have taken care that boys should be educated and exercised in the Scriptures, even though they seem born rather for servitude." Against him Cyril, in book 7 (and on our side against the Romanists too), says: "Boys brought up in the sacred letters, he says, at once become most devout, even if less eloquent. You say they differ little from slaves because they are not so eloquent. Perhaps for this reason alone he thinks they become objects of admiration, while every other virtue is despised, through which someone becomes familiar with God and attains the highest nobility." Thus Cyril. Julian too, in the book he entitled Cynisinum, while setting out how sacred fables ought to be fashioned, says: "The truth must be hidden in matters of this kind," and uses these words: "Nature wills birds to lie hidden in what is obscure; and the hidden essence of the gods does not allow itself to be impressed on impure human ears in plain and open words." "The Emperor," says Socrates (book 3 of the Ecclesiastical History, ch. 19 or 23, as it is in the Greek, where that passage of Julian is cited), "seems to hold this opinion of the sacred and divine Scriptures: that their words are mystical and embrace some hidden understanding; but he is grieved that not all conceive the same opinion of them, and he insults those Christians who receive their oracles simply." (5) "But he ought neither to have railed so much against the simplicity of the common people, nor to have attacked the sacred letters with such arrogance on their account, nor on that account to have hated them and so detested the noble senses and opinions contained in them, merely because not all understand them according to his judgement." Thus Socrates against Julian. Certainly Melchior Canus, and Jacobus Ledesma following him, confirm that the mysteries of religion must be kept hidden, citing this excellent saying from Porphyry (for both ascribe Julian's opinion to Porphyry by mistake, a teacher of such religion who is certainly suitable enough): "Nature loves to be concealed; and God does not allow the divine mysteries to enter the defiled ears of the common crowd." [(5) Οὐκ ἴδιν ἡ πολλὴ ... &c.]

units.la: Pythagoræ quoque & sectatoris ejus Lysidis authoritate sententiam suam confirmant Canus & Ledesima: quasi digitum intendentes ad fontes, unde interdictum illud, ne Laici scripturas attingerent, emanavit. De Pythagoricis ita scribit Jamblichus de vita Pythagoræ, cap. 32. Quae praecipua imprimis & continentissima (αὐτοπαθήματα) doctrinarum in eâ sectâ sunt firmamenta, inter se arcana omnes semper servabant cum exactâ εχεμυθία, seu loquendi erga externos eosque qui ab ipsorum vita instituto alieni essent, continentiâ; quae ἀπόῤῥητα enunciari fas non est, sine ullo scripto posteris successoribusque in memoria conservantes; quae simul cum Deorum mysteria tradebant. Quamobrem nihil eorum, quae alicujus momenti essent, egrediebatur. Jam quae longo temporis spatio tum docebantur, tum discendo percipiebantur, intra privatos tantum parietes cognoscebantur. Cum externis vero, & (ut sic dicam) profanis si quando usus ferret congrediendum esse; nequaquam sua sacra enunciabant, sed per symbola & arcanas tesseras obscurè latentesque sibi mutuò sensa mentis velut aenigmatibus significabant. Porrò extat Lysidis Pythagorici epistola, quâ Hipparchum objurgat, quòd Philosophiæ mysteria cum prophanis & indoctis communicâsset. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἡ (inquit Lysis) ...
units.tr: Canus and Ledesma also support their view by the authority of Pythagoras and his follower Lysis, as though pointing the finger at the sources from which the prohibition that laymen should not touch the Scriptures flowed. Jamblichus writes thus of the Pythagoreans in his Life of Pythagoras, ch. 32: "The chief and most restrained of their doctrinal foundations, which belong to that sect, all of them always kept among themselves with strict silence, that is, with restraint in speaking before outsiders and those who were foreign to their way of life; and they did not think it lawful to utter these unspeakable things, but preserved them in memory for posterity and successors without any writing, handing them down together with the mysteries of the gods." For this reason none of what was of any importance went beyond them. "And what was taught over a long span of time, and learned by those who studied, was known only within private walls. When they were obliged to meet outsiders, and (so to speak) profane people, they did not at all declare their sacred things, but by symbols and secret tokens they signified to one another their thoughts, obscurely and covertly, as if by riddles." Moreover there is extant a letter of Lysis the Pythagorean, in which he rebukes Hipparchus because he had shared the mysteries of philosophy with the profane and the unlearned. "But, for indeed ... (says Lysis) ..." [Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἡ ...]

units.la: Multi vero dicunt, publicè ne etiam Philosophari: id quod facere Pythagoras aversatus est: qui cùm Damoni filiæ commentarios sua commendaret, jussit ne cui extra domum eas traderet. Illa verò cùm multis pecuniis vendere hujusmodi libros posset, noluit: sed inopiam patrisque mandata auro pretiosiora censuit. Aiunt autem eandem moriturum Bistulia suæ filiæ hoc idem præceptum dedisse. At nos cùm sumus viri, non re Ʒè nos erga illum gerimus; sed conventorum sumus transgressores. Et alibi in eadem Epistolâ: Ὄντως χαῖρε ... (inquit Lysis) ...
units.tr: Many, however, say that they did not philosophise even in public; and Pythagoras avoided doing this. When he commended his commentaries to the daughter of Damo, he ordered her not to give them to anyone outside the house. Although she could have sold such books for much money, she refused, and judged her father's poverty and his command more precious than gold. They say moreover that Bistulia, when dying, gave the same precept to his own daughter. But we, since we are men, do not so treat him in deed, but are transgressors of the agreements. And elsewhere in the same letter: "Truly, farewell ... (says Lysis) ..." [Ὄντως χαῖρε ... ]

units.la: ¹ In Appendice Diog. Laertii. ² Vid. Diog. Laertium ab Henrico Stephano editum p. 594. & 875 & Jamblichum de vita Pythagoræ, c. 17. ³ Vid. Jamblichum, loc. cit. Pium (vel possibile) est, inquit, ne quoque divinorum & gravissimorum ejus praeceptorum esse memorem: neque sapientiae bona iis facere communia, qui ne per somnium quidem animos habent a sordibus repurgatos. Siquidem fas non est quibusvis offerre, quae tantis laboribus comparata sunt: non magis, quam duarum Eleusiniarum Dearum (Cereris & Proserpinae) mysteria profanis exponere. Simuliter namque injusti ac impii sunt utrique, qui talia designant. Hactenus Lysis. Dicebant Pythagorici alii non esse omnibus pandenda omnia: ut ex Aristoxeno in 10. refert Laertius; quod Casaubonus (in notis) ex Proclo de iis maxime exponit, quae ad Deos pertinent. Huc illud referatur ex Cicerone: Nec tu me celas, ut Pythagoras solebat alienos: nec consulto dicis occulte, tanquam Heraclitus. Collationis hujus apodosin ex Tho. Moresino accipe: Sic Papa custos unicus, ut ait, praeceptorum & scriniorum Dei, & interpres, qui omnia jura in pectoris scrinio habeat; & in quo est omnis sufficientia, licet ignaro & insufficiente, extra familiam & fani sui limites, i.e. rasura stigmata, tam legem, quam lectionem & interpretationem legis divinae egredi non permittit; anathemate laicos feriens qui conantur, Biblia aut legere aut penes se habere, (in his etiam longe durior Pythagoricis) satis esse dicens, si laici crederent ut filia mater Ecclesia, etsi penitus ignorent, quid Ecclesia sentiat.
units.tr: ¹ In the Appendix to Diogenes Laertius. ² See Diogenes Laertius, as edited by Henricus Stephanus, pp. 594 and 875, and Iamblichus, On the Life of Pythagoras, c. 17. ³ See Iamblichus, loc. cit. "It is pious (or possible)," he says, "not even to be mindful of his divine and most weighty precepts, nor to share the goods of wisdom with those who do not have minds cleansed of filth, not even in a dream. For it is not right to offer to just anyone what has been acquired with such great labours, any more than it is right to expose the mysteries of the two Eleusinian goddesses, Ceres and Proserpina, to the profane. For those who designate such things are equally unjust and impious." Thus far Lysis. Other Pythagoreans said that "not everything is to be disclosed to everyone," as Laertius reports from Aristoxenus in book 10. Casaubon, in his notes, explains this chiefly from Proclus, with reference to matters that concern the gods. To this may be referred what Cicero says: "You do not hide from me, as Pythagoras used to do with outsiders, nor do you speak obscurely on purpose, like Heraclitus." Take the conclusion of this comparison from Thomas Moresinus: "Thus the Pope, the sole guardian, as he says, of God's precepts and archives, and interpreter, who has all law in the chest of his breast, and in whom all sufficiency lies, though ignorant and insufficient, does not permit anyone to go beyond the household and the limits of his temple, that is, by the erasure of the stigmata, either to pass beyond the law or to read and interpret the divine law. He strikes with anathema the laymen who attempt either to read the Bibles or to keep them in their possession" (in this he is even far harsher than the Pythagoreans), saying that it is enough if laymen believe, as a daughter believes her mother, the Church, even if they are utterly ignorant of what the Church thinks.

units.la: Ad Eleusinia sacra quod attinet (quibus Christiana Ecclesia, si Cilnum & Ledesimam audiat, similia est habitura) abi Aristophane in Nebulis, i.e. non dicenda sacra appellantur. Hinc si quando convenissent inter se aliqui secreto de re quapiam arcana tractantes; paroemiam hanc usurpari solitam refert Duris (apud Zenodotum in Proverbiorum Collectione) Aἰνεῖ τὰ Ἐλευσίνια, supple ταῦτα ἀπὸ, hic. Attici Eleusinia inter se. Pausanias in Atticis de rebus Eleusiniis agens, Ἃ δ' ἔστι ἐν ... ἱερὰ ... σιγᾶν, inquit: h. e. At quae intra sacrum panicem servantur, scribere somnio prohibemur. Iis enim, qui initiati non fuerint, non tantum eorum aspectu interdictum est; verum etiam ne percontari quidem aut audire fas quicquam est. Hinc & illud Catulli: Pars obscura cavis celebrabant orgia cistis, Orgia, quae frustra cupiunt audire profani. Et Juvenalis Talia secreta coluerunt orgia tedae Sat VI. 2. Cecropiam solitis Baptae lassare Cotyton. (Proserpinam)
units.tr: As for the Eleusinian rites (to which the Christian Church, if it listens to Cilnus and Ledesima, would have a similar status), in Aristophanes' Clouds they are called rites that are not to be spoken of, that is, non dicenda sacra. Hence, if at any time some men met in secret and discussed some hidden matter, Duris (in Zenodotus's collection of proverbs) reports that the proverb commonly used was "Aἰνεῖ τὰ Ἐλευσίνια" [supply "these things from" here], "the Athenians speak of the Eleusinian things among themselves." Pausanias, in his Attica, speaking of the Eleusinian matters, says: "But the things that are kept within the sacred enclosure ... [Ἃ δ' ἔστι ἐν ... ἱερὰ ... σιγᾶν], we are forbidden to write about in a dream. For it is forbidden not only to look upon them for those who have not been initiated, but it is not even right to ask about or hear anything." Hence also that line of Catullus: "A hidden part celebrated the orgies in hollow chests, orgies which the profane vainly desire to hear." And Juvenal: "Such secret rites did the torch-bearing women keep, the Baptae weary Cecropian Cotyto (Proserpina) with their usual rites."

units.la: ¹ Lib. 8 p. 577. ² De Natura Deorum, l. 1. ³ Lib. de depravatae religionis origine & incremento.
units.tr: ¹ Book 8, p. 577. ² On the Nature of the Gods, book 1. ³ On the origin and growth of a depraved religion.

units.la: Unde Horatius in Epodis Caniniam sagam sibi minitantem inducit, quòd sacra Cotyttia ipsi commissa videns divulgaverit. Inultus ut tu veriferis Cotyttia Vulgata, sacrum liberi Cupidinis. Alcibiades, ut tradit Plutarchus, accusatus fuit, quòd sacra Cereris enunciâsset. Unde Clemens Alexandrinus in Protreptico (p. 4. edit. Sylburg.) τι δ' εἰ οι καταλέιψομ τὰ μυστήρια; ἐκ ἐξοφχόμενοι μὲν, ὥσπερ Ἀλκιβιάδην λέγειν, ἀπορμισθῶν ἢ τῶ μέλλα ἀπὸ ... ἀπὸ ἀληθείας λόγῳ, ἢ γνωσίας ἢ ἱεροφυμένην αὐτῶν, &c. Quid si tibi recensem mysteria? Non propalabo quidem, ut aiunt olim Alcibiadem; sed per verbum veritatis, praestigias, quae in eis latent, rectè aperiam. Et post z, cùm ex Orpheo τὰ πρὸς τὰ Ἀθηναῖων μυστήρια repetìsset, & Eleusiniorum sacrorum symbola commemoraísset; ita concludit. Ἀξιά μὲν ἐν ὑπνῷ τὰ πολλὰ ... μυστικά ... Nocte certè ac tenebris ista mysteria digna sunt, & magnanimo illo, immò verò levissimo Erectthidarum populo. Inter Ethnicorum Idololatrarum superstitiones, Sapient. XIV. 23. κρύφια μυστήρια, i. e. occulta mysteria (obscura sacrificia reddit vetus Interpres) recensentur. De mysteriis Eleusiniis plura vide in Commentar. Lud. Vivis ad Augustin. de Civit. Dei, lib. 7. cap. 20. & Barnab. Brisson. lib. 1. de Formulis, pag. 1. Casaubonum contra Baronium, p. 549, 550, 555. sin. & Diogenem Laertium, lib. 2. p. 154. in Aristippo. Illa tantùm Epilogi loco attexere libet, quae Macrobius habet (ut antea Lysis) in Somnio Scipionis, lib. 1. cap. 2. quare Philosophi fabulis uti soleant; editìserens. Quia (inquit) sciunt inimicam esse naturae apertam nudamque expositionem sui: quae sicut vulgaribus hominum sensibus intellectum sui vario rerum tegmine operimentoque subtraxit; ita à prudentibus arcana sua voluit per fabulosa tractari. Sic ipsa mysteria figurarum cuniculis operiuntur; ne vel hac adeptis nuda rerum talium se natura praebeat: sed summatibus tantùm viris sapientiâ interprete veri arcani conscïis, contenti sint reliqui ad venerationem figuris defendentibus à vilitate secretum. Numenio denique inter Philosophos occultorum curiosiori offensam numinum, quòd Eleusinia sacra interpretando vulgaverit, somnia prodiderunt visas sibi ipsas Eleusinias Deas habitu meretricio ante apertum lupanar ludere prostantes, admirantique & causas non convenientis numinibus turpitudinis consulenti respondisse iratas, ab ipsa se adyto pudicitiae suae vi abstractas & passim adeuntibus prostitutas. Hactenus Macrobius.
units.tr: Hence Horace, in the Epodes, introduces the witch Canidia threatening him, because, having seen the Cotyttian rites entrusted to her, he had divulged them: "Unavenged, since you have made known the Cotyttian rites to the truth-bearing ..., the sacred rites of free Cupid." Alcibiades, as Plutarch relates, was accused because he had revealed the rites of Ceres. Hence Clement of Alexandria in the Protrepticus (p. 4, ed. Sylburg): "What if I should reveal the mysteries to you? I will not indeed disclose them, as they say Alcibiades once did; but by the word of truth I will rightly expose the tricks that lie hidden in them [τι δ' εἰ ... ἀπὸ ἀληθείας λόγῳ, ...]." And afterwards, when he had repeated from Orpheus the things concerning the Athenian mysteries and had recited the symbols of the Eleusinian rites, he concludes thus: "Worthy of the night ... mystical ... Surely these mysteries are worthy of night and darkness, and of that magnanimous, or rather very frivolous, people of the Erechthidae." Among the superstitions of the pagan idolaters, the secret mysteries (the old translator renders them "obscure sacrifices") are enumerated in Wisdom 14:23 [κρύφια μυστήρια]. For more on the Eleusinian mysteries see the commentary of Ludovicus Vives on Augustine, On the City of God, book 7, chapter 20; Barnabas Brisson, On Formulas, book 1, p. 1; Casaubon against Baronius, pp. 549, 550, 555; and Diogenes Laertius, book 2, p. 154, in the life of Aristippus. As a kind of epilogue I think it fitting to add what Macrobius says (as Lysis did before) in the Dream of Scipio, book 1, chapter 2, explaining why philosophers are accustomed to use fables: "Because (he says) they know that an open and naked exposition of its nature is hostile to it. Nature, which has withdrawn the understanding of itself from common human senses by a varied covering of things, so wise men have wished its secrets to be treated through fables. Thus the mysteries themselves are concealed under coverings of figures, lest nature, even to those who have attained these things, show herself naked; but only to the foremost men, with wisdom as their interpreter, who are aware of the true secret, while the rest are content to revere the figures that defend the secret from vulgarity." Finally, among the philosophers, Numenius: the curious, who by interpreting the Eleusinian rites had divulged them, gave offence to the gods. Dreams reported that the Eleusinian goddesses themselves seemed to them to play in the guise of harlots before an open brothel, and when he, marvelling, asked the reason for such shamefulness unsuited to the gods, they answered that they were angry, dragged away from the inner sanctuary by the violence of their chastity and offered to whoever came by as prostitutes. Thus far Macrobius.

units.la: Julius Firmicus, non ille Christianus, qui de errore profanarum Religionum scripsit, sed alter Astrologus, in totius Operis sui perora-
units.tr: Julius Firmicus, not that Christian who wrote on the error of profane religions, but the other, an astrologer, in the peroration of his whole work,

units.la: ᵃ P.-g. 6. tione Mavortium Lollianum Proconsulem sic alloquitur. Tu vero praecedenti admonitione conventus, ac religiosa jusjurandi auctoritate commonitus, hos libros paro animo puraque mente custodi; ne imperitis & sacrilegis auribus scientia istius Operis intimetur. Celari enim & abscondi pluribus tegumentis natura divinitatis ab initio voluit; ne omnibus facilis esset accessu, neve cunctis patefacta majestatis sua origine pandceretur. Hoc etiam nos in his libris facere convenit; ut scilicet eorum lectio religiosis tantum pateat, profanis autem & sacrilegis denegetur; ne veterum occultanda commenta nefariis quodammodo editionibus polluamus. Haec ille lib. 8. cap. 33. [prorsus ut Julianus.]
units.tr: ᵃ P.-g. 6. addresses the proconsul Mavortius Lollianus thus: "But you, admonished by the earlier warning of the assembly and reminded by the religious authority of your oath, guard these books with a prepared spirit and a pure mind, lest the knowledge of this work be disclosed to unskilled and sacrilegious ears. For nature, from the beginning, wished the divinity to be concealed and hidden by many coverings, so that it would not be easily accessible to all, nor be laid open to everyone, its majesty's origin revealed. We ought also to do this in these books: namely, that their reading be open only to the religious, but denied to the profane and sacrilegious, lest we pollute the ancient secrets, as it were, by impious publication." Thus he, book 8, chapter 33 [exactly as Julianus].

units.la: Porphyrio (in Epistola ad Anebonem Aegyptium sacerdotem) quaerente, cur sacerdotes utantur nominibus quibusdam nihil significantibus; Jamblichus a respondet (1) omnia ejusmodi nomina significare aliquid apud Deos, quamvis in quibusdam significatio nobis sit ignota, &c. Cum autem quaereretur, cur nam inter nomina divinorum barbara caeteris anteponeret? causam assignat Jamblichus, (2) quia sacrarum gentium, velut Aegyptiorum Assyriorumque, totum Dii sermonem approbaverunt, tanquam sacris maxime congruentem: quia antiquior primusque extitit modus iste loquendi: quia denique qui prima nomina divinitus acceperunt, ita nobis servanda perpetuo tradiderunt; nosque ita ipsam traditionis regulam rite deinceps conservare debemus. Excipiente vero Porphyrio b, illum qui vocem audit nominum divinorum, ad significata respicere; ideoque sufficere notionem ipsam eandem ubique manentem, qualiscunque sit dictio; respondet Jamblichus (3) hunc in modum. Non est tale, quale tu putas: si enim nomina ex hominum pacto conventuque posita essent; nihil interesset alia pro aliis commutare. Sin autem natura rerum accommodata fuerint; quae huic maxime congruunt, haec & diis maxime sunt amica. Ex his perspicue patet sacrarum gentium vocem rationaliter caeteris esse praepositam: Neque enim prorsus eandem mentem servant nomina in aliam linguam interpretata:
units.tr: Porphyry, in his letter to Anebo the Egyptian priest, asking why priests use certain names that signify nothing, Iamblichus answers: (1) "all such names signify something among the gods, although for some the meaning is unknown to us, etc." When it was asked why he preferred barbarian names above the rest, Iamblichus gives the reason: (2) "because the gods have approved the entire language of the sacred nations, such as the Egyptians and Assyrians, as most fitting to sacred things; because this mode of speaking is older and was the first; because those who first received names from the divinity handed them down to us to be kept forever; and so we ought properly to preserve the very rule of that tradition thereafter." Porphyry objecting that the one who hears the names of the gods looks to the things signified, and that therefore the same notion remaining everywhere suffices, whatever the expression, Iamblichus replies (3) in this manner: "It is not as you think. For if names had been established by human agreement and convention, it would make no difference to exchange one for another. But if they have been fitted to the nature of things, those that agree most with it are also most dear to the gods. From these things it is plainly evident that the speech of the sacred nations is rationally preferred to the rest; for names translated into another language do not keep altogether the same meaning:"

units.la: a De mysterio Aegypt. §. 7. cap. 4. b Cap. 5.
units.tr: a On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, §. 7, ch. 4. b Ch. 5.

units.la: (1) ἡμῖν μὲν ἀγνοεῖα, τοῖς μὲν τοῖς ... πάντα σημαντικά ἐστιν ἢ κ᾿ ... (2) Διὰ τί γὰρ τὰς ἱερὰς ἔθνων ... ἈΙγυπτίων ... (3) Εἰ δὲ γὰρ ἦν κ᾿ ... ῥήματα, ἐὰν διάφορα τὰ ἑτέρων ... μεταλαμβάνων. Εἰ δ᾿ ἡ τῆς φύσεως συνάψει ... ὅπως, τὰ μᾶλλον αὐτῇ ... ἔπεσεν. (Greek notes, partly illegible.) terpretata: sed sunt gentibus singulis propria quaedam, quae gentibus aliis per vocem significari non possint. Accedit ad haec, quòd si significationum proprietates per aliam linguam interpretari possumus; non tamen eandem conservant permutata potentiam. (4) Habent insuper nomina barbara nullam emphasin, i. e. insinuationis demonstrationisque efficaciam, habent & concisam brevitatem; minimum verò ambiguitatis, & varietatis, multitudinisque verborum: propter haec omnia superis maximè congruunt. Depone igitur suspiciones a veritate cadentes; quibus suspicaris Ægyptiam ibi conferre linguam aut axat, ubi Ægyptius est, vel usus Ægyptiâ linguâ, qui tunc invocatur. Potius autem existimato, quoniam primi omnium Ægyptii praesentiam participationemque Deorum sortiti sunt; ideò Deos invocantem potissimùm approbare, quando Ægyptio ritu vocantur. Neque vero dicendum est barbara haec obscuraque divinorum nomina esse quaedam praestigiatorum fascinatorumque machinamenta. Quo enim pacto quae maximè conjuncta sunt diis, nosque etiam conjungunt, & quasi aequales cum superis habent, phantastica figmenta erunt; (5) sine quibus nullum in sacris opus efficitur! &c. Quemadmodum veritatem consecuti sunt primi, qui leges nobis de religionis sanctimoniâ tradiderunt, sic perseveramus in eis: siquid enim aliud in sacris legibus atque ritibus Deo placet; firmitas ipsa maximè Deo placet, & praecipuè congruit. Oportet igitur ritus adorationis antiquos tanquam sacros conservare semper intactos; neque demere quicquam, neque aliunde quid addere. Fermè namque & hâc causâ nuper exstitit, ut omnia & numina & vota debilitata jam sint; propterea quòd propter ipsam praevaricationem & innovandi cupiditatem permutata sunt semper, & permutari non desinunt. Graeci namque naturâ rerum novarum studiosi sunt, ac praecipites usquequaque feruntur, instar navis saburrâ carentis, nullam habentes stabilitatem; novaeque inventionis elocutionem transformare solent. (6) Barbari verò sicut moribus graves firmique sunt; sic & in eisdem sermonibus firmiter perseverant: ob quam sanè stabilitatem & ipsi Diis sunt amici, & orationes offerunt illis acceptas; quas nulli ullâ unquam ratione fas est permutare. Hactenus Jamblichus, ejusmodi proterens argumenta, qualia pro Latinâ suâ Liturgiâ adversùs
units.tr: (1) For us it is unknown, but for them... all things are significant, or... (2) For why do the sacred names of the nations... of the Egyptians... (3) For even if there were... words, if the words of others differ... exchanging. But if they were joined to the nature of things... how, those that agree most with it... fell. [Greek fragments, partly illegible.] Translated from the Latin: ...but they are peculiar to individual nations, and cannot be expressed through a word to other nations. Moreover, even if we can translate the properties of meanings into another language, the altered words do not keep the same power. (4) Foreign names have, besides, no emphasis, that is, no efficacy of insinuation or demonstration; they have also a concise brevity, but very little ambiguity, variety, or multiplicity of words. For all these reasons they agree most with the gods above. Therefore put aside the suspicions that fall from the truth, by which you suspect that the Egyptian language is brought in there, or the usage of the Egyptian language, which is then invoked, where the Egyptian is present. Rather, consider that since the Egyptians first of all obtained the presence and participation of the gods, therefore the gods above chiefly approve of one who invokes them when they are called in the Egyptian manner. Nor must it be said that these barbarous and obscure divine names are certain contrivances of magicians and enchanters. For in what way would the things that are most closely joined to the gods, and that also join us, and have something like equality with the gods above, be phantasms and fictions; (5) without which no work in sacred rites is accomplished! etc. Just as the first men, who handed down to us the laws of the sanctity of religion, attained the truth, so we persevere in them: for if anything else in sacred laws and rites pleases God, firmness itself pleases God most, and agrees especially. It is therefore fitting always to keep the ancient rites of worship as sacred and untouched; neither to remove anything nor to add anything from elsewhere. For almost for this reason, not long ago, all the divinities and vows have been weakened, because through this very prevarication and desire for innovation they have been always changed, and do not cease to be changed. For the Greeks, by nature, are eager for new things, and are carried headlong everywhere, like a ship without ballast, having no stability; and they are accustomed to alter the expression of every new invention. (6) Barbarians, however, are as grave and firm in their customs as they are; so also they persevere firmly in the same speech; and by this very steadfastness they are friends of the gods themselves, and offer prayers acceptable to them, which it is never lawful for anyone to change by any reason. So far Iamblichus, pressing arguments of this kind, such as those used against the Latin liturgy of

units.la: (4) Ἔχει δὲ καὶ τὰ ἰδέσεχα ὀνόματα πάλαι μὲν ἐμφασιν, πάλιν δὲ συντομίαν, &c.
units.tr: (4) It has, moreover, the sacred names, formerly emphasis, and again brevity, etc. [Ἔχει δὲ καὶ τὰ ἱερὰ ὀνόματα πάλαι μὲν ἔμφασιν, πάλιν δὲ συντομίαν, κτλ.]

units.la: (5) Ὧν χρεὶς ὑδὲν ἱερᾶς ἐργον γίνεται.
units.tr: (5) Of these, nothing of the sacred work is accomplished. [Ὧν χωρὶς οὐδὲν ἱερὸν ἔργον γίνεται.]

units.la: (6) Βάρβαροι δὲ μόνιμοι τῆς ἡθῶν ὄντες, ἀνδρῶν ἀκινήτων ἐστιν, καὶ τοῦ λόγου ἀυτῆς ἐνδιστῆσθαι. nos usurpat Jacobus Ledesima. [Nempe Romanenses Sacerdotes Ægyptios secuti suis mysteriis extraneas adhibent voces, gravi impositâ pœnâ, si secus quis fecerit, aut enodare alio idiomate mysteria attendat Missæ: ut quæ enucleata Diis grata non sint futura; sed quæ vilescere apud plebem sint incæptura, continuò detectis involucris, & vanitatis tacitæ latebrâ. Tho. Morefinus.]
units.tr: (6) But barbarians, being steadfast in their customs, are men immovable, and cling to their speech. [Βάρβαροι δὲ μόνιμοι τῶν ἠθῶν ὄντες, ἀνδρῶν ἀκινήτων ἐστιν, καὶ τοῦ λόγου αὐτῆς ἐνδιατρίβειν.] Jacobus Ledesima also uses this. [Namely: the Roman priests, following the Egyptians, use foreign words in their mysteries, with a heavy penalty imposed if anyone does otherwise, or who attempts to explain the mysteries of the Mass in another idiom; since things made plain would not be pleasing to the gods, but would begin to become cheap among the common people, once the veils were uncovered and the hidden corner of empty vanity exposed. Thomas Morefinus.]

units.la: Ethnicus Sacerdos sacrificaturus, versus, meditato & solemni precationis carmine, verbis priscis ex annalium vetustate erutis numina & Deos precatus, vota effundebat; quam precationem plerunque tergeminabat. [Alexander ab Alexandro, lib. 4. Genial. Dier. cap. 17. & Lilius Giraldus in Histor. Deorum, Syntagm. 17.] Hinc duos ritus mutuati sunt Pontificii. I. Priscum idioma mutare cum intelligibili apud eos non licet. Latinum enim non intellectum cum vulgari quod intelligitur, commutare, à temporibus Caroli Magni hucusque piaculum semper fuit habitum. II. Precum illa reiteratio & παπλολογία, (de cujus origine supra ad an. 1080. dictum est.) retenta est: eòque evasit res (inquit Tho. Morefinus) ut dicerent, quicunque dixerit tot Pater Noster, cum totidem Ave, & uno vel pluribus Credo, coram hujus vel illius dei imagine, singulis diebus statis vel interceptis; habebit Indulgentiarum millia, vel centena millia annorum, &c. Sed cùm non quàm multa, sed quantâ cum fide preces fiant, κατὰ δύναμιν ille spectare solet; omnibus in universum in omni vitâ cum Christo semper orandum erit, ita quidem ut preces ponderentur non numerentur. Athenodorusque Philosophus multùm eos damnari debere aiebat, qui longis orationibus Deum fatigarent Morefinus.) Ethnicorum praxin Romanæ consentaneam fuisse agnoscit Alphonsus Salmeron. Omnis (inquit) religio externa, etiam in Idololatriâ, minimè propriâ & vulgari linguâ utebatur in sacris, sed alienâ & externâ. Sic Babylonii, Romani, Græci. Igitur nostri Germani non debent exigere ab Ecclesiâ jus sacra celebrandi in linguâ vulgari.
units.tr: An ethnic priest, about to sacrifice, used to pour out his prayers and vows, invoking the divinities and gods with a meditated and solemn chant, in ancient words dug up from the antiquity of the annals; and he would usually repeat this prayer three times. [Alexander ab Alexandro, book 4, Genial Days, ch. 17, and Lilius Giraldus in the History of the Gods, Syntagma 17.] Hence the Papists borrowed two rites. I. It is not permitted to change the ancient language for one that is understood; for to exchange an unintelligible Latin for the vernacular that is understood has always been regarded as a sacrilege, from the times of Charlemagne until now. II. The repetition of prayers and the [παπλολογία] (about whose origin it was said above under the year 1080) has been retained, and the matter has come to this (says Thomas Morefinus), that they say: whoever says so many Our Fathers, with as many Hail Marys, and one or several Creeds, before the image of this or that god, on set or chosen days, will have thousands or hundreds of thousands of years of indulgences, etc. But since it is not how many prayers are made, but with how great faith, that he usually regards according to his power, it will be necessary for all, in general, to pray always throughout their whole life with Christ, so that prayers are weighed, not counted. And the philosopher Athenodorus used to say that those who weary God with long prayers ought to be condemned much (Morefinus). Alphonsus Salmeron acknowledges that the practice of the ethnics was consistent with the Roman one. Every external religion (he says), even in idolatry, used in its rites not the proper and vernacular language, but a foreign and external one. So the Babylonians, Romans, and Greeks did. Therefore our Germans ought not to demand from the Church the right to celebrate sacred rites in the vernacular.

units.la: Denique ut recentiorum Hæreticorum cum Ecclesiâ Romanâ concordiam demonstrem: fuit illa blasphema insani Swenckfeldii vox; f Scripturam mortuam esse literam, necnon g incertam & flexibilem doctrinam, quæ se in varios sensus trahi pateretur. Unde illa hæretica fanaticorum hominum nata est conclusio; h Scripturas, quarum tot
units.tr: Finally, to show the agreement of the more recent heretics with the Roman Church: that was the blasphemous saying of the mad Schwenckfeld: f Scripture is a dead letter, and g an uncertain and pliable doctrine, which allows itself to be drawn into various senses. Whence that heretical conclusion of fanatical men was born: h Scriptures, of which we now see not only different but even contrary interpretations brought forward, we shall order to be removed. It is not necessary to be learned in the Law or in Scripture, but to be taught by God, etc.

units.la: c In 1 Cor. XVI. f Lib. de sacrâ Scriptură. g Lib. de Evangelio. jam, non diversas modo, verùm & contrarias, interpretationes adferri videmus, facessere jubebimus. Non oportet Legis aut Scripturæ esse peritum, sed à Deo doctum, &c. Quid verò Pontificii? Ecclesiam Dei clamant esse vivum pectus Christi, Scripturam autem quasi mortuum atramentum; ideoque majorem esse fidem habendam viventi Ecclesiæ, quàm per se velut mortuis codicibus; potiùs consultis, mandatis, institutis, præceptis atque exemplis, quàm literarum monumentis, quàm scriptionibus, quàm chartulis, quàm macrocollis, quàm membranulis standum esse. Sic Ludovicus Canonicus Lateranensis in Oratione ad Concilium Tridentinum, Dilingæ anno 1563. impressâ. Scripturas ¹ esse velut nasum cereum; qui se horsum, illorsum & in quam volueris partem, trahi, retrahi, fingique facilè permittit; & tanquam plumbeam quandam Lesbiæ ædificationis regulam, quam non sit difficile accommodare ad quidvis volueris. Atque hinc populum Christianum à Scripturarum cognitione (quas ignotæ linguæ velamine abscondunt) abducunt; fidemque implicitam Laicis sufficere persuadent. Addunt ᵏ, Evangelicam legem, testante Ezechiele Prophetâ, non scriptam, sed inditam esse cordibus, Spiritu Sancto interiùs docente adeòque. Ecclesiæ suæ Prælatis, imprimis Romano Pontifici (qui omnia jura in pectoris sui scrinio conclusa habet) licèt indoctis & sacrarum literarum ignaris, propter cathedræ dignitatem Spiritus Sancti afflatum (uti Swenkfeldiani) velut hæreditarium faciunt.
units.tr: c On 1 Cor. 16. f Book on Sacred Scripture. g Book on the Gospel. Already, we see not only different but contrary interpretations brought forward; we shall order them to be removed. It is not necessary to be learned in the Law or Scripture, but to be taught by God, etc. But what do the Papists say? They cry out that the Church of God is the living breast of Christ, but Scripture is as it were dead ink; therefore greater faith must be given to the living Church than to the books, as if they were dead in themselves; one should rather stand by counsels, commandments, institutions, precepts and examples than by the monuments of letters, by writings, by little papers, by parchments, by membranes. So Ludovicus, canon of the Lateran, in his Oration to the Council of Trent, printed at Dillingen in the year 1563. He says that Scriptures are ¹ like a wax nose, which easily allows itself to be drawn this way and that, pulled back, and shaped into whatever part you wish; and like a certain leaden rule of Lesbian building, which it is not difficult to adapt to whatever you wish. And from this they lead the Christian people away from the knowledge of the Scriptures (which they hide under the veil of an unknown tongue), and they persuade the laity that implicit faith is enough. They add that the Evangelical law, as the prophet Ezekiel testifies, is not written but placed in the hearts, the Holy Spirit teaching inwardly; and so they make it, like the Spirit-breathing of the Swenkfeldians, a hereditary possession for the prelates of their Church, above all for the Roman Pontiff (who keeps all rights shut up in the chest of his breast), even if they are unlearned and ignorant of the sacred letters, on account of the dignity of the chair.

units.la: ¹ Apud Hofium de expresso Dei verbo, & lib. 1. contra Brentii. Prolegom. pag. 438. ¹ Pighius Hierarch. lib. 3. cap. 4. Censur. Coloniensi. ᵏ Petrus Soto contra Brentium, & Hosius, lib. 3. Prolegom. Brentii, pag. 559, 560. Vid. Kemnitii Examen, ex Andradio & Lindano.
units.tr: ¹ At Hosius, On the Expressed Word of God, and book 1 against Brenz; Prolegomena, p. 438. ¹ Pighius, Hierarchy, book 3, ch. 4; Censure of Cologne. ᵏ Peter Soto against Brenz, and Hosius, book 3, Prolegomena to Brenz, pp. 559, 560. See Kemnitz's Examen, drawn from Andradius and Lindanus.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Adversariorum Testimonia.
units.tr: Testimonies of the Adversaries.

units.la: GEorgius Cassander in Defensione libelli contra Calvinum. Optandum videtur; ut juxta Apostolicum mandatum, & priscum Ecclesiae morem in lingua vulgari preces peragerentur. Priscum autem esse hunc Ecclesiae morem pluribus testimoniis confirmat idem in Liturgicis suis, cap. de lingua qua lectiones & preces in divinis officiis & celebratione mysteriorum concipiuntur.
units.tr: Georgius Cassander, in his Defence of the booklet against Calvin: It seems desirable that, according to the apostolic command and the ancient custom of the Church, prayers be offered in the vernacular tongue. He confirms by several testimonies that this custom is ancient, in the same author's Liturgies, in the chapter on the language in which the lessons and prayers in the divine offices and the celebration of the mysteries are framed.

units.la: Aquinas Comment. in 1 Cor. XIV. Quantum ad fructum devotionis, privatur is, qui non in speciali intelligit ea quae orat. Rhemenses tamen in 1 Cor. XIV. preces ignotas ad aedificationem non minus, ad devotionem saepe magis valere, quam cognitas, asserunt. Addit tque Costerus Jesuita, Ad consolationem plurimum adjuvare.
units.tr: Aquinas, Commentary on 1 Corinthians XIV: As far as the fruit of devotion goes, he is deprived who does not understand in particular what he prays. The Rheims translators, however, on 1 Corinthians XIV, assert that unknown prayers are no less useful for edification, and often more effective for devotion, than known ones. The Jesuit Costerus adds that they greatly help consolation.

units.la: Cajetanus Comment. in 1 Cor. XIV. Melius est orare in mente distincte intelligente ea, quae orat, quam confuse.
units.tr: Cajetan, Commentary on 1 Corinthians XIV: It is better to pray in the mind, distinctly understanding what one prays, than confusedly.

units.la: Joannes Cuspinianus in Austria sua (in vita 6. Marchionis) Hodie psallitur in Caenobiis; psallitur & cantatur sine intellectu, sine eruditione, sine (quod pejus est) mente.
units.tr: Johannes Cuspinianus, in his Austria (in the life of the sixth Margrave): Today they chant in the monasteries; they chant and sing without understanding, without learning, and (what is worse) without mind.

units.la: Lindanus Panopl. lib. 4. cap. 78. Quis hujus aetatis musicam cum illa prisca componat? Quae nunc cantantur omnia, non tam ad populi intelligentiam erudiendam; quod priscos ubique spectasse indubitatum est. Unde Erasmus de Amab. Concord. Eccl. Posset illud modulata Musica genus citra pietatis jacturam omitti, si placet: curandum est, ut illa Musica sit templo Dei necessaria, &c. Vid. eund. in 1 Cor. XIV. De origine ejus vid. Bellarm. de bonis Operibus, cap. 17.
units.tr: Lindanus, Panoplia, book 4, chapter 78: Who in this age could compose music like that ancient music? Everything that is now sung is not aimed so much at instructing the understanding of the people, which it is beyond doubt the ancients everywhere had in view. Hence Erasmus, on the Amiable Concord of the Church: That kind of modulated music could be dropped without loss to piety, if one pleases: care must be taken that such music is necessary to the temple of God, etc. See the same author on 1 Corinthians XIV. On its origin, see Bellarmine, On Good Works, chapter 17.

units.la: Agrippa de Vanit. Scient. cap. 18. Hodie cum Missa ipsius Canone obscaena cantiuncula pares vices habent. De his quoque Lindanus conqueritur Panopl. lib. 4. cap. 78. Vid. Espenseum Comment. in 1 Tim. digress. 1. pag. 225.

units.la: Dionysii nomine circumferuntur libri quidam de Hierarchiâ cœlesti, & Ecclesiasticâ, de divinis Nominibus, de mysticâ Theologiâ, atque Epistolæ undecim: Quæ quidem Opera Dionysio Areopagitæ Pauli discipulo à nonnullis magni nominis hominibus attribuuntur; & nominatim à Michaele Syngelo in Dionysii Encomio, Suidâ in Lexico, Adone, Gregorio Turonensi, Dionysio Carthusiano, Ambrosio Camaldulensi, Marsilio Ficino, Pachimere, Joanne Novio in Apologia, &c. Non defuerunt contra, Viri doctissimi, qui certissimas protulerunt demonstrationes, quibus non esse hunc verum Dionysium appareat. Eas nos ordine hic subjiciemus; Præmissis quatuor illis Argumentis olim contra Dionysium adhibitis; quæ ex Theodoro Presbytero in Bibliothecâ suâ recenset Photius Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha.
units.tr: Under the name of Dionysius there circulate certain books, On the Celestial Hierarchy, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, On the Divine Names, On the Mystical Theology, and eleven Epistles. These works are ascribed to Dionysius the Areopagite, the disciple of Paul, by some men of great name, and in particular by Michael Syncellus in his Encomium of Dionysius, by Suidas in his Lexicon, by Ado, Gregory of Tours, Denys the Carthusian, Ambrose Camaldolese, Marsilio Ficino, Pachymeres, John Nobilis in his Apology, and others. On the other side there have not been lacking very learned men who have produced the most certain demonstrations that this is not the true Dionysius. I shall set these out in order here, first premising the four arguments once brought against Dionysius, which Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, records in his Bibliotheca from Theodore the Presbyter.

units.la: I. Ἐι δι γνωσία, πῶς ἐκ ἰμνήσιτai τῆς ἐν αὐτῆ ρητῶν ἐ, ἡ χρήσιν τινες τῆς μετα-φυσικῆς πεπίσμ. Nullus admodum Antiquus Author horum librorum meminit: quod satis arguit libros istos non ejus Antiquitatis fuisse, ac seculi, cujus Dionysius Areopagita fuit. Multa in illis occurrunt, quæ contra veteres hæreticos faciant, præsertim Arianos; quæ certè Patres Nicæni non omisissent, si tales libri extitissent, & illorum Author fidem aliquam habuissset. Atque inde Constantinum Philosophum, (qui Romam sub Adriano juniori Papâ venit) dicere solitum refert Anastasius (in Epist. ad Carolum:) quòd si Sanctos priores, qui hæreticos vix, & quodammodo cum fuste decollaverunt, Dionysium contigisset habere, cum acuto illos gladio proculdubio trucidâssent. At contrà, excipit Duræus, cum aliis non-nullis
units.tr: I. If indeed it is knowledge, how is it that none of the sayings in it is mentioned, or that certain people make use of the metaphysical [...] [Εἰ δὲ γνῶσις, πῶς ἐκ ἱμνήσιται τῆς ἐν αὐτῇ ῥητῶν, ἢ χρῆσιν τινὲς τῆς μεταφυσικῆς πεπίστ...]. Hardly any ancient author mentions these books at all, which sufficiently shows that these books did not belong to the antiquity and the age of which Dionysius the Areopagite was a part. Many things occur in them that would tell against the ancient heretics, especially the Arians, and the Fathers of Nicaea would certainly not have passed these over had such books existed and had their author enjoyed any credit. Hence Anastasius reports (in his Letter to Charles) that Constantine the Philosopher, who came to Rome under Pope Adrian the Younger, used to say: if the earlier saints, who all but beheaded the heretics with a club, had possessed Dionysius, they would undoubtedly have slaughtered them with a sharp sword. But on the contrary, Duraeus objects, along with some others,

Humfredum contra rationem quintam, pag. 514. Rainoldum collat. cum Hart. cap. 8. Divif. 2. pag. 417. Mornæum de Missa, lib. 1. cap. 2. Hospinianum de Origine Monachatus, pag. 111. Martyrem loc. commun. de Missâ n. 9. 892. p & 80, 81. Lubbertum de principiis Christianorum Dogmatum, lib. 7. cap. 10. pag. 665. Scultetum Medullæ Patrum lib. 11. cap. 9. pag. 383. nullis Papatûs propugnatoribus; Dionysium citatum esse ab Origene in Joannem homiliâ primâ, (quæ secunda est inter homil. in varios locos Novi Testamenti)& Gregorio Nazianzeno, 38.Orat. εἰς τὰ γενέθλια, Origenem verò Erasmus disertè negat ex hoc Dionysio aliquid citare: Sic enim scribit in Annot. in Act. XVII. Deinde mirum, si tam Priscus Author fuit, & tam multa scripsit, à nemine Veterum seu Græcorum, seu Latinorum fuisse citatum; non ab Origene, non à Chrysostomo; ne ab Hieronymo quidem, qui nihil intentatum reliquit. Et homiliam istam Origenis non esse evidenter comprobat Sixtus Senensis, tum ex Manichæorum, tum ex Arianorum nominibus in eâ commemoratis, quæ multò post Origenem exorta sunt. Et ex Prologo Maximi apparet, à veteribus Dionysio huic objectum esse; quod illius Eusebius & Origenes non meminere. Nazianzenus Authorem quendam laudat, quem minimè nominat: Budæi solummodo conjectura est (in Commentariis linguæ Græcæ) Dionysium intelligi; eáque non ita probabilis. Nicetas in commentario in Gregor. Nazianzenum, Athanasium intelligendum monet: idque multò rectiùs, ut apparet ex Orat. Nazianzeni in laudem Athanasii, collata cum iis, quæ idem Athanasius scripsit in tractat. de ocmmuni essentiâ Patris, Filii, & S. S. & de humanâ naturâ suscepta. Nazianzeni verba ex orat. in nativitat. Christi sunt hujusmodi: Οὐτω μὲν ἐν τῷ ἁγίᾳ τῆς ἁγίων, ἃ ἐν τῆς σεσεμνῶν, ἡ ἀδελφή, ἐν ἀγαθῷ ἐστὶν ἀναζωῆς εἰς μίαν συνήθειαν νεωτέρα, ἡ σύνταξις. quæ ita paraphrastice exponit Nicetas; Sic (inquit) se habet sancta Trinitas; (quam ego Sancta Sanctorum voco, ut omnem sanctitatem in se complectentem;) quæ quidem & à Seraphim contegitur, ac tribus sanctitatibus, atque unâ dominatione celebratur. Nam juxta magnum Athanasium, Eximia hæc Animalia eò quòd ter dictionem hanc SANCTUS proferunt, tres personas absolutè ostendunt; rursus eò quod semel dunt axat nomen hoc DOMINUS clamant, Essentiam unam declarant. Hæc ille. Citatur etiam Dionysius in quæstionibus ad Antiochum, quæ Athanasii nomine circumferuntur: Sed eas Athanasii non esse, vel inde manifestum est, quòd ab earum Authore ipse Athanasius citetur; (quæst. 33.) & ab eo etiam diversa Sententia proferatur. Quin & eas Sixtus Senensis quarto bibliothecæ Sanctæ, eo etiam argumento b Vid. pag. 880, & 1123. c Pag. 617. d Pag. 992. Athanasii non esse concludit, quòd in quæst. 4. Mystica Theologia Dionysii allegetur, quam Athanasii seculo ignotam opinatur. Videmus igitur Duræi exceptiones nullius esse momenti: quod ipsi Papistæ non obscurè etiam significant cùm; alias rationes, quibus vim hujus Argumenti eludant, subinde excogitant. Objiciunt enim; Ambrosius Camaldulensis, &c. nec Origenem, nec Ambrosium memorâsse; quia nec iste Ambrosius, nec Origenes, nec Eusebius omnium Ecclesiasticorum libros viderit, ac noverit: Nec Hieronymus, nec Augustinus, nec Ambrosius allegant propter difficultatem, & quia fuerunt absconditi ab Hæreticis. Ita hæc simplex responsio est ingenua confessio, & concors nobiscum consensio; causas etiam reddens cur non legerint. Bellarminus etiam (de Monachis, lib. 2. cap. 5.) non modò nullum temporibus Apostolicis vicinum Authorem proferre, aut nominare potuit, qui horum librorum meminit; sed ingenuè etiam fatetur Ambrosio, Chrysostomo, Augustino, Hieronymo, aliisque Gregorio Romano antiquioribus Patribus incognitos fuisse, quantum ex eorum operibus colligi potest. Quod etiam confirmat Anastasius Bibliothecarius in Epistolâ ad Carolum Regem: Notandum est (inquit) quòd licet tanta gloria, tanta scientia, sive Antiquitatis ipse S. Dionysius fuerit, nunquam tamen aliqua Opuscula eum edidisse, nisi fallor, quæcunque Orthodoxorum Scripta traditio prodit, priusquam Romani Pontifices, Gregorius, Martinus, & Agatho dictorum ejus in conscriptis suis mentionem fecerint. Unde ego veram esse Græcorum opinionem conjicio, perhibentium libros ejus à prioribus Hæreticis occultatos, donec longo post tempore ex opusculis ejus solus Codex, qui nunc habetur, est Romæ repertus; cæterisque non inventis, in Græciam asportatus. Hæc Anastasius. Hinc igitur manifestum est verum quod asserit P. Martyr, p. 892. (in loco de Missâ) Gregorium Romanum (qui sexcentis post Christum elapsis Annis Pontificis R. locum, & nomen in Ecclesia obtinuit) primum omnium Scriptorum Dionysii mentionem fecisse; & evincit, eos antiquissimis temporibus inauditos fuisse, nec esse Areopagitæ. Quod autem Bellarminus ut necessarium nobis objicit, ab hæreticis suppressos fuisse; Conjectura tantum est, & quidem levis admodum; quandoquidem nullo modo fit verisimile ab ipsius Dionysii ad Gregorii usque tempora latere aut supprimi potuisse: cùm Episcopi scripta sua apud Ecclesias reponere
units.tr: ¹ See Illyricus, Centuria I, book 2, p. 625, On the Lies of the Papists, p. 38, and on the Mass against Faber of Augsburg; Whitaker, On Scripture, question 6, chapter 12, p. 432; Humfrey, against the fifth argument, p. 514; Reynolds, collated with Hart, chapter 8, division 2, p. 417; Mornay, On the Mass, book 1, chapter 2; Hospinian, On the Origin of Monasticism, p. 111; Martyr, Common Places, on the Mass, n. 9, 892, and pp. 80, 81; Lubbertus, On the Principles of Christian Doctrines, book 7, chapter 10, p. 665; Sculteti, Marrow of the Fathers, book 11, chapter 9, p. 383; none of them defenders of the papacy. Dionysius is cited by Origen in his first Homily on John (which is the second among the Homilies on Various Passages of the New Testament), and by Gregory Nazianzen in Oration 38, On the Birthday [εἰς τὰ γενέθλια]. Erasmus, however, flatly denies that Origen quotes anything from this Dionysius; for he writes thus in his Annotations on Acts 17: Again, it is strange, if he was so ancient an author and wrote so much, that he was cited by none of the ancients, whether Greek or Latin: not by Origen, not by Chrysostom, not even by Jerome, who left nothing untried. And that Origen's homily is not genuine is clearly proved by Sixtus of Siena, both from the names of the Manichaeans and of the Arians mentioned in it, which arose long after Origen. And from the Prologue of Maximus it appears that this Dionysius was objected to by the ancients, since Eusebius and Origen did not mention him. Nazianzen praises a certain author whom he does not name; Budaeus alone conjectures (in his Commentaries on the Greek language) that Dionysius is meant, and that conjecture is not very probable. Nicetas, in his commentary on Gregory Nazianzen, warns that Athanasius is meant, and this much more correctly, as appears from Nazianzen's oration in praise of Athanasius, compared with what Athanasius himself wrote in his treatise on the common essence of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and on the human nature assumed. The words of Nazianzen, from his oration on the Nativity of Christ, are of this kind: [Οὕτω μὲν ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις τῶν ἁγίων... ἀναζωῆς εἰς μίαν συνήθειαν νεωτέρα, ἡ σύνταξις.] Nicetas paraphrases them thus: So (he says) stands the Holy Trinity, which I call the Holy of Holies, as embracing all holiness in itself; which indeed is also covered by the Seraphim, and celebrated with three holinesses and one dominion. For according to the great Athanasius, these wondrous living creatures, because they utter this word HOLY three times, show forth three persons absolutely; and again, because they cry this name LORD only once, they declare one essence. So far Nicetas. Dionysius is also cited in the Questions to Antiochus, which circulate under the name of Athanasius; but that these are not Athanasius's is clear from this alone, that their author is himself cited by Athanasius (question 33), and that a view contrary to his is put forward in them. Indeed Sixtus of Siena, in the fourth book of his Bibliotheca Sancta, concludes on this very ground that they are not Athanasius's, namely that in question 4 the Mystical Theology of Dionysius is cited, which he thinks was unknown in Athanasius's age. We see, then, that Duraeus's exceptions are of no weight, as the Papists themselves do not obscurely indicate, when they from time to time devise other reasons by which they try to evade the force of this argument. For they object that Ambrose Camaldolese, etc., neither Origen nor Ambrose mentioned them, because neither that Ambrose, nor Origen, nor Eusebius had seen and known all the books of the Churchmen. Nor do Jerome, Augustine, or Ambrose cite them, on account of their difficulty, and because they were hidden by the heretics. Thus this simple answer is an ingenuous confession and a harmonious agreement with us, giving also the reasons why they did not read them. Bellarmine too (On the Monks, book 2, chapter 5) not only was unable to produce or name any author near the Apostolic times who mentions these books, but also frankly admits that they were unknown to Ambrose, Chrysostom, Augustine, Jerome, and other Fathers older than Gregory of Rome, so far as can be gathered from their works. Anastasius the Librarian also confirms this in his Letter to King Charles: It must be noted (he says) that although St. Dionysius himself was of such great glory, such great learning, and of such great antiquity, nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, he never published any little works, as far as any tradition of orthodox writings hands down, before the Roman Pontiffs Gregory, Martin, and Agatho made mention of his writings in their own works. Whence I conjecture that the opinion of the Greeks is true, who say that his books were hidden by the earlier heretics, until, after a long time, only one codex, the one that is now held, was found at Rome among his little works; and the others not being found, it was carried off into Greece. So Anastasius. Hence it is clear that what Peter Martyr asserts (p. 892, in the place on the Mass) is true, namely that Gregory of Rome, who obtained the place and the name of Roman Pontiff in the Church some six hundred years after Christ, was the first of all writers to mention the works of Dionysius; and it proves that they were unheard of in the most ancient times and are not the work of the Areopagite. As for what Bellarmine objects to us as necessary, that they were suppressed by the heretics, this is only a conjecture, and indeed a very slight one; since it is in no way likely that they could have lain hidden or been suppressed from the time of Dionysius himself to the time of Gregory, when bishops were accustomed to deposit their writings in the churches,

units.la: * Bell. de Monachis, pag. 142. soliti essent: Neque credibile est Hæreticos potuisse omnia Exemplaria ad se undiquaque corradere. (Cujus rei nemini unquam quidem Gregorius, aut Agatho suspicionem dederunt.) Vel si corrasissent, eò quod ejusmodi essent genuina Dionysii scripta, quibus ipsorum hæreses oppugnarentur (neque enim alia excogitari potest causa) videtur certè aut in æternum suppressuros, aut saltem egregiè interpolatos fuisse emissuros. Cur enim Dionysio Areopagitæ [inter hæreticos (forte Severianos) solummodo latitanti] non obtingeret, quod Dionysio Corinthio [publicè profstanti] usu venit; sicut ipse (apud. Eusteb. lib. 4. cap. 23.) conqueritur: Fratribus ut scriberem rogantibus, scripsi Epistolas; sed illas ministri Diaboli zizaniis, alia eximentes, alia verò adjicientes, repleverunt; quibus Va in extremum judicium est repositum.] Sanè si ita se res haberet, ac Papistæ nobis conantur persuadere; non immerito potuisset opinari Erasmus, cum eruditissimis Græcis, qui Vallæ fuerunt temporibus, ex Apollinaris hæretici Officinâ ista prodiisse. Nec defuerunt etiam antiquitus, qui hæresis libros hosce insimulabant; ut apparet ex f Maximi Prologo in Dionysium circa med. Quid quòd ipse Gregorius s (cujus Authoritas fundamentum Bellarmini est, quo Dionysium hunc Apostolicum esse evincat) non indicat fuisse illum Dionysium Areopagitam? ut Valla, & Erasmus monuerunt. h Citatur quidem à Gregorio in homiliâ de centum Ovibus (hom. 34. in Evangelia) sed ita, ut Cardinalis Cajetanus (in Act. XVII.) eo Argumento moveatur de libris Dionysii dubitare; quod Gregorius (in homiliâ 33. de 10. drachmis) non audeat asserere Authorem horum librorum fuisse Dionysium Areopagitam: Sed dicat; Fertur Dionysius Areopagita, (Antiquus, videlicet, & Venerabilis Pater,) dicere; quod ex minorum Angelorum agminibus foras ad explendum ministerium vel visibiliter, vel invisibiliter mittuntur, &c. At verò, si credidisset Gregorius, Hierarchiam illam, quæ nuper ex tenebris emerserat, à Dionysio Pauli discipulo fuisse editam; illam proculdubio per omnia sequeretur. At illud non facit; sed ipsos quidem Angelorum ordines aliter describit, quàm iste Dionysius. Posteriorum verò Scriptorum, qui à Papistis objiciuntur, Authoritas non est tanta, ut ra-
units.tr: (Bellarmine, On the Monks, p. 142). Nor is it credible that the heretics could have gathered in all the copies from every quarter (of which matter neither Gregory nor Agatho ever gave anyone the least suspicion). Or even if they had gathered them in, because such were the genuine writings of Dionysius, by which their heresies were assailed (for no other cause can be devised), they would surely seem either to have suppressed them forever, or at least to have published them thoroughly interpolated. For why should it not happen to the Areopagite Dionysius [lurking only among the heretics, perhaps the Severians], what happened to Dionysius of Corinth [who openly professed the faith]; as he himself complains (in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 23): When the brethren asked me to write, I wrote letters; but these the ministers of the Devil, removing some things and adding others to them, filled with tares; for which there is reserved a woe at the last judgment. Certainly, if things were as the Papists try to persuade us, Erasmus could not unreasonably have suspected, with the most learned Greeks of Valla's time, that these works came out of the workshop of the heretic Apollinaris. Nor were there lacking in antiquity those who accused these books of heresy, as appears from the Prologue of Maximus on Dionysius, near the middle. What is more, Gregory himself (on whose authority Bellarmine rests his claim that this Dionysius is the Apostolic one) does not indicate that it was that Dionysius the Areopagite? As Valla and Erasmus pointed out. Gregory does indeed cite him in his homily on the hundred sheep (Homily 34 on the Gospels), but in such a way that Cardinal Cajetan (on Acts 17) is moved by this argument to doubt the books of Dionysius; because Gregory (in his homily 33, on the ten drachmas) does not dare to assert that the author of these books was Dionysius the Areopagite, but says: It is said that Dionysius the Areopagite (an ancient and venerable Father, that is) says that from the troops of the lesser angels they are sent forth, either visibly or invisibly, to carry out their ministry, etc. But if Gregory had believed that that Hierarchy, which had recently emerged from darkness, was published by Dionysius the disciple of Paul, he would undoubtedly have followed it in all things. But he does not do so; rather he describes the orders of the angels differently from that Dionysius. As for the authority of the later writers, whom the Papists object, it is not so great that the arguments brought against them should be
