XII. 53.) scilicet, ut Lucas probat in Actis Apostolicis, qui de libris nihil dixit :- Tantummodo enim loquitur de Dionysii mentis illustratione per Pauli prædicationem, & de Conversione à Dialecticiæ tendiculis, & Gentilium erroribus.
units.tr: {f} Rather, it is by John of Scythopolis; see those sentences in Anastasius's Hodegos, pages 241, 339 and 341. {g} No one before Gregory the Great mentions the books of Dionysius. {h} See Junius against Bellarmine, On Monks, chapters 5, 18 and 21, pages 223 and 224. ...to be a match for the arguments brought against them. Such are the Sixth Synod (the third, namely the Constantinopolitan, held more than 680 years after the birth of Christ); the Seventh, chapter 2 (that profane synod, namely the Second Nicene, gathered about 800 years after Christ to establish the worship of images); and the Eighth (namely the Fourth Constantinopolitan, held 870 years after Christ); Martin I in the Roman Council; Agatho in his letter to the Sixth Synod, chapter 2; his letter to the Emperor Constantine IV and Tiberius Augustus; Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, to Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople, Act II of the Sixth Synod; Pope Nicholas I in his letter to the Emperor Michael; Maximus, who wrote annotations on Dionysius (in which he also cites the scholia on the same by Dionysius, Archbishop of Alexandria); Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, book 1, chapter 12, and book 2, chapter 18; Nicephorus, book 2, chapter 2; Euthymius in the Panoplia, part 1, title 2, sermon 57; Anastasius the Librarian in his letter to Charles the Bald; Hilduin in his letter to Louis the Pious, and so on. Alan Copus also, in Dialogue 2, proves that all the books of Dionysius are genuine, on the testimony of Theophylact (on Luke 12:53). Namely, as Luke proves in the Acts of the Apostles, who said nothing about books: for he speaks only of the enlightening of Dionysius's mind through Paul's preaching, and of his conversion from the snares of dialectic and the errors of the Gentiles.

units.la: II. Alterum Argumentum à Theodoro adductum etiam in Pro- logo Joannis Sycopolitæ (qui alias Maximo tribuitur) superiori affine est;
units.tr: II. A second argument, adduced by Theodore, which is also akin to the former, appears in the Prologue of John of Scythopolis (who is otherwise attributed to Maximus).

units.la: Ἐν Ἐυσεβίῳ ὁ Παμφίλου ἀναγραφὴ πεποίηται τῆς συγγραφέων τῶν μαρτυρίων πᾶσιν ἱκανῶς βιβλίων, ἱστορίαν ταύτης μνήμην ἐποίησατο. Eusebius Scriptores Antiquos diligenter persequitur, & quos libros, aut Epistolas singuli ediderint, nominatim indicat; Dionysius etiam Corinthiorum Episcopus (qui sub Commodo circa annum Dom. 185. vixit) de Dionysio Areopagitâ.
units.tr: In Eusebius, the catalogue of the writers of the martyrdoms made by Pamphilus, of the books sufficiently known to all, he made mention of this history. [Ἐν Ἐυσεβίῳ ὁ Παμφίλου ἀναγραφὴ πεποίηται τῆς συγγραφέων τῶν μαρτυρίων πᾶσιν ἱκανῶς βιβλίων, ἱστορίαν ταύτης μνήμην ἐποίησατο.] Eusebius diligently follows up the ancient writers and names individually which books or letters each one published; Dionysius also, bishop of Corinth (who lived under Commodus, around the year of the Lord 185), (speaks) of Dionysius the Areopagite.

units.la: ¹ In Libris Brevi. rio, cap. 10. Vol. 2. Concil. Venet. edit. pag. 780. citatur Dionysius Areopagita Corinthiorum Episcopus ; sed illud Areopagita redundat. * Videlicet τῆς μεγάλης Διονυσίου τῆς Αλεξανδρείας ἐπισκόπου, τῆς ἀπὸ ῥυπαρῶν. Scholia in B Dionysium sibi cognominem. Sed (ut Sculletus recte observat) dubium quis, & cujus ætatis Dionysius iste Scholiastes fuerit. De veteri sane illo nihil tale commemorat Eusebius, aut Hieronymus : (quorum temporibus Dionysii Areopagitæ nihil existisse certum est :) Et de illo eam notavit Basilii Magni censura in Epist. 41. ad Maximum Philosoph. pag. 802. Nos istius Viri omnia non amplectimur. Sunt quæ proprias damnamus ;. Habent enim quandam femina impietatis. Eadem ipsa verba habet Anastasius Sinaita in Hodegos pag. 340, ex cuius fide hoc citatum à Maximo, ait Fr. Turrianus, & eum secutus Baronius. ¹ Pag. 420. scribens, quomodo à Paulo primum ad fidem conversus, deinde Atheniensium Episcopus factus est, declaravit: neuter tamen horum librorum meminit. Hieronymus etiam & Sophronius in Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Catalogo, & Gennadius de viris illustribus, Scriptorum praecipuorum, qui per 500 à Christo annos in Ecclesiâ claruerunt, Catalogum pertexentes, Dionysii Areopagitae non meminerunt. At quis putet eos, qui veterum libros ita studiosè collegerunt, ut ne Epistolam quidem ab Eximio aliquo, & Pio Viro scriptam praeterierint, libros à Pauli discipulo, de rebus tam mirificis conscriptos, fuisse omissuros? Hoc Argumentum non Vallam & Erasmum solùm, sed etiam Cardinalem Cajetanum movit; ut de libris hisce dubitarent: quòd vix credibile putarent, Eusebium, & Hieronymum, cùm de libris Dionysii Episcopi Corinthiorum multam mentionem faciant, tacituros fuisse de Dionysio Pauli discipulo, si tantum Voluminum numerum reliquisset. At Bellarminus (de Monachis, lib. 2. cap. 5.) nobis persuadere vult, Argumentum hoc sibi maximè favere. Nam cùm Hieronymus, & Seculi Superioris Patres non citent haec Opera; Signum est (inquit) Authorem hunc non extitisse ipsorum tempore (sanè!) Ex Gregorio autem constat eum non esse illis posteriorem; idcoque sequitur necessariò esse longè antiquiorem. Quinam verò hoc ex Gregorio colligitur? Gregorius sc. Dionysium citans, vocat antiquum & venerabilem Patrem: non autem vocaret Antiquum hominem, suo seculo proximum. Mirum Jesuitae acumen! At ostendat (1.) Necesse esse, nullos esse Antiquos & Venerabiles Patres appellandos, nisi qui ante Annos ducentos vixerint; tot enim anni inter Hieronymum & Gregorium magnum intercesserunt. (2) Gregorium appellasse Authorem librorum, qui ex haereticorum latibulis (ut vult Bellarm.) nuper lucem aspexerant, antiquum, & venerabilem Patrem; aliter, quàm ex eorum Hypothesi, qui illum veluti Dionysium Areopagitam Pauli discipulum, Ecclesiae obtruserunt. Sed ea de re satis in Superioris Arg. tractatione dictum est.
units.tr: ¹ In the Breviary, chapter 10, vol. 2 of the Venice Council edition, page 780, Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Corinth, is cited; but the word Areopagite is superfluous. * Namely, the scholia of the great Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, [τῆς μεγάλης Διονυσίου τῆς Αλεξανδρείας ἐπισκόπου, τῆς ἀπὸ ῥυπαρῶν], on Dionysius his namesake. But (as Scultetus rightly observes) it is doubtful who this Dionysius the Scholiast was, or of what age. Certainly Eusebius and Jerome record nothing of that kind about the ancient man (in whose times it is certain that nothing of Dionysius the Areopagite existed), and Basil the Great's censure of him in Epistle 41 to Maximus the Philosopher, page 802, noted it: "We do not embrace all of that man's works. Some we condemn outright, for they have a certain female impiety." Anastasius Sinaita has the same words in the Hodegos, page 340; on whose authority, says Fr. Turrianus, this was cited by Maximus, and Baronius followed him. ¹ Writing on page 420 how he was first converted to the faith by Paul and then made bishop of the Athenians, he declared it; yet neither of these books is mentioned. Jerome and Sophronius in their Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, and Gennadius in On Illustrious Men, when they weave a catalogue of the chief writers who flourished in the Church during the five hundred years after Christ, make no mention of Dionysius the Areopagite. But who would think that men who gathered the books of the ancients so diligently that they did not pass over even a letter written by some eminent and pious man, would have omitted books by Paul's disciple, written on such wondrous matters? This argument moved not only Valla and Erasmus but also Cardinal Cajetan to doubt these books, since they thought it hardly credible that Eusebius and Jerome, while making much mention of the books of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, would have been silent about Dionysius, Paul's disciple, had he left so great a number of volumes. But Bellarmine (On Monks, book 2, chapter 5) wants to persuade us that this argument especially favours him. For since Jerome and the Fathers of the previous century do not cite these works, "it is a sign," he says, "that this author did not exist in their time" (certainly!). "But from Gregory it is established that he is not later than they are; therefore it necessarily follows that he is much older." But how is this gathered from Gregory? "Gregory, namely in citing Dionysius, calls him an ancient and venerable Father; he would not call an ancient man, close to his own century, that." Wonderful Jesuit acumen! But let him show (1) that it is necessary that no one be called an "ancient and venerable Father" unless he lived two hundred years earlier (for so many years lay between Jerome and Gregory the Great); and (2) that Gregory called the author of books which had only recently come to light from the hiding-places of heretics (as Bellarmine would have it) an ancient and venerable Father, otherwise than on the hypothesis of those who forced him on the Church as Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's disciple. But on this matter enough has been said in the treatment of the previous argument.

units.la: III. Πὼς οὖν ἐχ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἢ διὰ μακρῷ τῶν χρόνων ἀξιόσιτων παρὰ ...
units.tr: III. How then, in the Church, or through the long passage of time, were these books regarded as trustworthy by [Πὼς οὖν ἐχ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἢ διὰ μακρῷ τῶν χρόνων ἀξιόσιτων παρὰ ...]

units.la: In libris hisce de multis
units.tr: In these books he treats of many things

units.la: Greek text in smaller type, partially illegible at this resolution. multis agitur, quæ in primâ illâ Apostolorum ætate, & aliquandiu post nondum fuerunt in usu; sed aliquot demùm seculis post instituta, atque recepta. In lib. de Ecclesiastica Hierarchiâ multa scribit de Templis, de Altaribus, de Locis Sacris, de Choro, de Catechumenis extra fores Templi statuendis. Atqui temporibus Apostolorum (quibus vixit Dionysius) & 100 annis postea, non habuerunt Christiani tam solennia templorum ædificia; Sed initio in domibus conveniebant eâ simplicitate, quam Lucas testatur adhibitam Act. 1. 13. & 12. 12. & 20. 8. Coacti enim sunt in locis abditis atque occultis convenire propter tyrannos, atque ibi preces & conciones habere. Dionysius autem ille Suppositititius in Epistolâ ad Demophilum, ostendit suo tempore solennia fuisse templa, Judaico similia, quæ haberent ἅγια ἁγίων, & adyta eâ sanctificatione à reliquo templo distincta, ut in illa ne Monachis quidem (nedum Laicis) liceret ingredi. Deinde in Ecclesiastica Hierarchiâ plurimorum meminit Ordinum, ut Pontificum, Præsulum, Sacerdotum, Monachorum, &c. quorum nomina temporibus Apostolicis ignota erant. Monachos, ut medium quendam ordinem inter Clericos & Laicos facit, & multis Ceremoniis consecratos meminit; cum ne Monachi quidem ulli usque Constantini Magni fere tempora, spatio trecentorum prope Annorum à Christi natali in rerum Naturâ prorsus fuerint. Et quidem Papistæ dant (quod etiam Hieronymus in Epist. Pauli, & Epist. ad Eustochium; & Ruffinus, lib. 1. histor. cap. 8. confirmant) Paulum & Antonium fuisse primos Monachorum Parentes; qui post Dionysium Areopagitam Seculis aliquot floruerunt. Tonsuram verò eorum, cujus Dionysius ille meminit, probari non potest, vix sexcentis post Christum Annis introductam fuisse; nisi quòd generaliter Patres monuerint eos, qui ad Clerum pertinebant, ne vanos illos homines imitarentur, qui Capillis longis gloriabantur. Ut hinc evidentissimè appareat, paulo ante Gregorium primum hos libros Dionysii nomine fuisse editos. Præterea SuscEptorum in Baptismo meminit; quorum ne minimum quidem Vestigium, multis post Dionysium lustris, ex ullo Veterum Scriptorum seu Græcorum, seu Latinorum ostendi potest; licet evidentissimè ceremonias omnes in Baptismo usitatas describant. Denique multas Ceremonias novas, Paulino seculo incognitas, & inaniffimas speculationes ingerit: Mihi, autem, inquit Erasmus, non videtur priscis illis temporibus tantum fuisse Christianarum Ceremoniarum, quantum ille describit, numerum.
units.tr: Greek text in smaller type, partially illegible at this resolution. Many things are discussed that were not yet in use in that first age of the Apostles, nor for some time after; they were instituted and received only some centuries later. In the book On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy he writes much about temples, altars, sacred places, the choir, and the catechumens who are to be stationed outside the doors of the temple. Yet in the times of the Apostles (in whose time Dionysius lived) and for about a hundred years afterwards, Christians did not have such solemn church buildings. At first they met in private houses, with the simplicity that Luke attests in Acts 1:13, 12:12 and 20:8. For they were forced to gather in hidden and secret places because of the tyrants, and there to offer prayers and hold sermons. That spurious Dionysius, however, in his letter to Demophilus, shows that in his own time there were solemn temples, similar to the Jewish ones, which had a holy of holies and inner sanctuaries set apart from the rest of the temple by such consecration that not even monks, let alone laymen, might enter them. Further, in On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy he mentions many orders: pontiffs, prelates, priests, monks, and so on, whose names were unknown in apostolic times. He makes monks a kind of middle order between clergy and laity, and speaks of them as consecrated with many ceremonies; yet there were no monks at all until about the time of Constantine the Great, that is, for nearly three hundred years after the birth of Christ. Indeed, the Papists grant (as Jerome confirms in his Life of Paul and in the letter to Eustochium, and Rufinus in book 1 of his History, chapter 8) that Paul and Anthony were the first fathers of the monks, who flourished some centuries after Dionysius the Areopagite. The tonsure of which that Dionysius speaks cannot be shown to have been introduced until barely six hundred years after Christ, unless it be that the Fathers in general warned those who belonged to the clergy not to imitate those vain men who gloried in long hair. From this it appears most clearly that these books were published under the name of Dionysius only shortly before Gregory the Great. Moreover, he mentions the sponsors at baptism, yet not the slightest trace of them can be shown in any writer of the ancients, Greek or Latin, for many decades after Dionysius, although these books describe all the ceremonies used in baptism most clearly. Lastly, he introduces many new ceremonies, unknown in the Pauline age, and most empty speculations. "To me," says Erasmus, "it does not seem that in those early times there were as many Christian ceremonies as he describes."

units.la: IV. ᾿Πῶς μέντοι ἡ τῆς Σοφίας Ἰγνατίου ἐπιστολὴ ἡ πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἐστιν; Ὁ δὲ ἅγιος Διονύσιος τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐπήκοος γέγονε. Ἰγνάτιος δὲ ἐπὶ Ῥαίαν ἡ διὰ μαρτυρίας ἀληθῶς ἀμφότερα· ὃς γὰρ ἐκ Βεαχὴ ἡ πολλῆς τούτῳ ἐπιστολῶν, ἧς ἡ βίβλος μνημονεύει, χάρις.
units.tr: IV. How then is the Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans? Indeed, the holy Dionysius became a hearer of the apostles [Ὁ δὲ ἅγιος Διονύσιος τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐπήκοος γέγονε]. Ignatius, however, going to Rome, truly bore witness to both, for he was a man of many letters, which the book mentions, a grace.

units.la: In libro de divinis Nominibus, cap. 4. citat ex Ignatii Epistolâ ad Romanos suavissimam illam sententiam, ᾿Ο ἐμὸς ἔρως ἐσταύρωται. Jam verò Ignatius hanc Epistolam misit ad Romanos, cùm in Itinere esset Romam prosecturus ad certam mortem, imperante Trajano, (ut Eusebius, in Chronico testis est, & in Hist. Eccles. lib. 3. cap. 36. & Hieronymus in Catalogo) circa annum illius nonum, ut refert Michael Syngelus in Dionysii Encomio. At Dionysius Areopagita occisus est sub Domitiano, priusquam Trajanus ad Imperium perveniret; ut testantur Methodius in Martyrio Dionysii Areopag. Symeon Metaphrastes in illius vitâ: Hilduinus in vitâ ejusdem. Nicephorus, lib. 2. Ecclesiast. Hist. Historia Lombardica, & Jo. Trithemius. Quomodo verò potuit ex Ignatio citare, quod Ignatius tum nondum scripserat? Michael Syngelus in Dionysii Encomio, & eum secutus Suidas, sub Trajano etiam Dionysium passum volunt: Sed cùm profiteatur Syngelus se colligere hoc ex citatione sententiæ Ignatianæ; nihil hac in re, contra Historiæ consensum valebit illius Authoritas. At verò necesse est, ut liber hic de divinis Nominibus scriptus fuerit ante Trajani tempora; si, ut fingitur, ad Timotheum Episcopum Ephesi scriptus fuerit: Timotheum enim sub Domitiano Martyrium perpessum refert Cedrenus. Et quo tempore Ignatius scripsit, mortuum esse Timotheum, apparet ex ejusdem Ignatii Epistolâ ad Ephesios; ubi Onesimus ipsorum Episcopus memoratur, qui Timotheo successit. Aut igitur Dionysius noster Ignatii sententiam illam non citavit, (quam in libro illius hodie legimus) aut ad Timotheum jam vitâ functum librum suum conscripsit. Atque hoc etiam
units.tr: In the book de divinis Nominibus, chapter 4, Dionysius quotes from Ignatius's Epistle to the Romans that most lovely saying: "My love has been crucified" [Ὁ ἐμὸς ἔρως ἐσταύρωται]. Now Ignatius sent this Epistle to the Romans while he was on his journey to Rome, about to go there to certain death under the emperor Trajan, as Eusebius bears witness in his Chronicle and in the Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 36, and Jerome in his Catalogue, around the ninth year of Trajan's reign, as Michael Syncellus reports in his Encomium of Dionysius. But Dionysius the Areopagite was put to death under Domitian, before Trajan came to the empire; as Methodius in his Martyrdom of Dionysius the Areopagite, Symeon Metaphrastes in his Life of him, Hilduin in his Life of him, Nicephorus in book 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, the Lombard History, and John Trithemius testify. How then could he quote from Ignatius what Ignatius had not yet written? Michael Syncellus in his Encomium of Dionysius, and Suidas following him, want Dionysius to have suffered also under Trajan; but since Syncellus professes that he infers this from the quotation of the Ignatian saying, his authority will count for nothing in this matter against the consensus of history. Indeed, it is necessary that this book de divinis Nominibus was written before the time of Trajan, if, as is pretended, it was written to Timothy, bishop of Ephesus; for Cedrenus reports that Timothy suffered martyrdom under Domitian. And that Timothy was dead by the time Ignatius wrote appears from Ignatius's own Epistle to the Ephesians, where Onesimus, their bishop, who succeeded Timothy, is mentioned. Therefore either our Dionysius did not quote that saying of Ignatius (which we read today in his book), or he wrote his book to Timothy after Timothy had already died. And this also

units.la: a Anno Dom. 532. inter Catholicos & Severianos iussu Imperatoris habita est Collatio. In ea cum hereticì Dionysii Areopag. scripta inter alia commemorarent; Catholici de falsitate Authoris excellent: quod illa neque Cyrillus, neque Athanasius agnoverit. (Petavius in Chronolog. lib. 13. sin. pag. 844.) Vide egregium locum apud Baronium, an. 512, 537, 538, 539. & Tom. 2. Conciliorum, pag. 599. edit. postremæ Binii, & nota ex Apolinaristarum officinâ ista primum prodiisse, & à Severianis primùm allegata, à Catholicis rejecta fuisse. ○ Jo. Cyparissiot. Decad. 2. cap. 2. Dionysius in Epist. ad Titum, &c. Alter verò Dionysius hæc ediflerens ait, eos qui apertam theologiam, & velis nudam audierunt, typos cogitatione sua formare, qui ad intelligentiam Auditores adjuvent. etiam antiquitus objectum esse, ut librum hunc Dionysii non esse probaretur, testatur Maximus in Scholiis ad hunc locum: Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ (inquit) τινὲς οἱονῇ διαλέγεσθαι ἐυρέσεως τὸ πεῖρᾶν εὑρεσεως, ὡς μὰ ἐν τῇ Ἀδε Διονυσίῳ ἑαυτὸν Ἰησοῦς λέγων μετεγέγραπται ἀπὸ τῶ, &c. Nec ipse Maximus aliter hunc nodum potuit solvere, quàm ut diceret, vel citationem illam à studioso aliquo in Margine annotatam, irrepsisse in textum; vel usitatum hoc fuisse Ignatio Apothegma, & saepius ab eo scriptum; cujus rei argumentum (admodum frigidum) affert, quod Dionysius non dicat, ῥωμαῖοι (sc. Romanis, sed simpliciter) Ῥωμαίοις ἡ ἐπ Ἰγνατίῳ. Vide Papir. Masson. in Annal. Franc. p. 70,71. infra à nobis exscript. p. 167, 168. & Vedelium in Notis ad Ignatii epistolas (E. 2. 4.) pag. 126. ad. 130. quaeque apud eosdem pro Hypothesi; & Franciscum Combefis notis in Andream Hierosolym. pag. 359,360. Sunt & alia certissima Argumenta hinc petita, ab Illyrico prolata, quae evidenter evincunt Dionysium istum suppositititium esse. Citat in suâ Hierarchia Joannis Evangelium, & Apocalypsim; idque ita, tanquam ea scripta jamdiu fuissent pars sacrae Scripturae: At contrà, si credimus historicis, utrumque Joannes paulò ante mortem suam scripsit; defuncto jam Dionysio ante 14. annos, aut circiter. Inter Epistolas istius Dionysii est una ad Polycarpum scripta; quae cum ita alloquitur tanquam jam Doctorem, & Episcopum, & ἱερομάρτυρα salutat. Jam testantur Scriptores Dionysium esse passum in Gallis, Anno Dom. 96. & Polycarpum 168, vel 166. suae verò aetatis 86. Unde liquidò apparet, Polycarpum tempore passionis Dionysii adhuc impuberem fuisse.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 532, by order of the emperor, a conference was held between the Catholics and the Severians. When, in it, the Severians cited among other things the writings of the heretic Dionysius the Areopagite, the Catholics objected to the falsity of the author, because neither Cyril nor Athanasius had acknowledged them (Petavius, Chronology, book 13, near the end, page 844). See the excellent passage in Baronius, years 512, 537, 538, 539, and volume 2 of the Councils, page 599, in the latest edition of Binius, and note that these writings first came out of the workshop of the Apollinarists, were first cited by the Severians, and were rejected by the Catholics. John Cyparissiotes, Decad 2, chapter 2: Dionysius, in the Epistle to Titus, etc. The other Dionysius, explaining these things, says that those who have heard theology openly and bare of veils form types in their thought which help the hearers to understand. That this book of Dionysius was objected to even in antiquity, so that it would not be proved to be Dionysius's, is attested by Maximus in his Scholia on this passage: "And here (he says) some seem to speak of an invention, to try an invention, as if in the Acts Jesus calling himself..." Nor could Maximus himself solve this knot in any other way than by saying either that a quotation noted in the margin by some studious reader had crept into the text, or that this saying was a customary remark of Ignatius, often written by him. As proof of this (quite a cold one) he offers the fact that Dionysius does not say "to the Romans" simply, but "to the Romans, the epistle of Ignatius" (To the Romans, the Epistle of Ignatius). See Papirius Masson, Annals of the Franks, pages 70–71, which we have copied out below at pages 167–168, and Vedelius in his Notes on the Epistles of Ignatius (E. 2. 4.), pages 126–130, and the things they offer in favour of this hypothesis, and Francis Combefis, notes on Andrew of Jerusalem, pages 359–360. There are also other most certain arguments drawn from this, put forward by Illyricus, which clearly prove that this Dionysius is spurious. In his Hierarchy he cites the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse, and does so as if those writings had long been part of Holy Scripture; whereas, if we believe the historians, both were written by John shortly before his death, and Dionysius had been dead for about fourteen years already. Among the Epistles of this Dionysius there is one written to Polycarp, which addresses him as already a teacher and bishop, and greets him as a "holy martyr" [ἱερομάρτυρα]. Now the writers testify that Dionysius suffered in Gaul in the year of the Lord 96, and Polycarp in 168 or 166, in the eighty-sixth year of his age. From which it is clearly evident that Polycarp was still a boy at the time of Dionysius's suffering.

units.la: V. Dionysius ad Timotheum scribens de divinis Nominibus, cap. 3. affirmat, se cum Timotheo & multis fratribus Mariae Virginis demortuum Corpus conspexisse: Unde etiam hoc à Nicephoro citatur, lib. 2. histor. Eccles. cap. 22. & Damasceno de dormitione Deiparae. Si hoc audivisset, & credidisset Epiphanius; in haeres. Antidicomar. non dixisset ignorare se, mortuane esset Maria, an non. Et Commentitiam omnino fabulam esse, temporis ratio demonstrat . Jesuitae Rhemenses in Chronologicâ tabulâ in Act. Apost. fatentur, Anno Christi 51. Dionysium à Paulo conversum
units.tr: V. Dionysius, writing to Timothy in de divinis Nominibus, chapter 3, affirms that he, together with Timothy and many brothers, saw the dead body of the Virgin Mary. Hence it is also quoted by Nicephorus, book 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22, and by Damascene in his work on the Dormition of the Mother of God. If Epiphanius had heard this and believed it, he would not, in his Antidicomarianites, have said that he did not know whether Mary had died or not. And the reasoning from time shows that the story is wholly fabricated. The Jesuits of Reims, in their chronological table on the Acts of the Apostles, admit that in the year of Christ 51 Dionysius was converted by Paul.

units.la: p Basilius in lib. de Spiritu S. cap. 29. citat Alexandrini Dionysii secundam ad sibi cognominem epistolam. fuisse. Ita 17. Anno post Christi Ascensum, Dionysius adhuc Senator Atheniensis fuerit. Quod etiam ex tempore, quo Paulus ascendit cum Barnaba ad Hierosolymitanam Synodum (Act. XV. 4. Gal. II. 1.) collato cum Itineribus, quae postea suscepisse dicitur per Derben, Lystram, Phrygiam, Galatiam, Mysiam, Macedoniam, priusquam Athenas veniens Dionysium convertit (Act. XVI. 1. & XVII 34.) apparet; & à Laur. Codomano, lib. 4. Chronolog. cap. 31. amplius confirmatur. Inquiramus jam quo tempore mortua est Maria. Melito de transitu Mariae, assumptam illam asserit anno altero post Christi Ascensionem; quem idcirco Beda reprehendit. Nihilominus Elizabethae moniali hoc ab ipsā Mariā revelatur: ut scribit Antonin. hist. part. 1. tit. 6. cap. 3. & Vincentius Speculi hist. lib. 7. cap. 80. & à calculo illo parum recedit Marianus Scotus in Chronico. Nicephorus, lib. 2. hist. Ecclesiast. cap. 3. Mariam scribit cùm Christum peperit, 15. annorum fuisse: Annos autem 59. vixisse; quod etiam Euodii testimonium confirmat. Ita Anno Christi 44. fuerit mortua. Eusebius in Chronico refert, nonnullos habere, revelatum sibi fuisse, Mariam assumptam Anno Christi 48. Atque ita defendunt Papistae (ut legimus in novo Sacerdotali, part. 1. pag. 156.) Mariam concepisse 14 anno aetatis suae, peperisse 15. mortuam esse 63. Et Rhemenses (annot. in Act. I. 14.) assumptam Virginem fuisse narrant 48 anno Christi, 15 Anno post illius Ascensionem. Vel Rhemensibus igitur testibus (qui omnium longissimè Mariae vitam extendunt) Maria ante mortua est, quàm Dionysius ad fidem Christianam à Paulo conversus fuit; ideoque cum fratribus, Mariae ex hac vitā decedenti non adfuit. Quò magis miranda est eorum tum insciitia, tum impudentia; qui non solùm assumptionem corporis Mariae astruere conantur ex Dionysii Areopagitae Epistolâ ad Timotheum, quae nulla habetur; (legerunt sc. hâc de re Dionysium scripsisse ad Timotheum, atque inde novam Epistolam commenti sunt; cùm in libro de divinis Nominibus ad Timotheum scripto illud tantùm reperiatur:) Sed etiam de suo illi affingunt, XII. Apostolos à se invicem in varias Mundi partes distractos miraculosè convenisse, praeter Thomam, qui triduo demum post Virginis mortem affuit, &c. De hâc fabellâ ne verbum quidem in Dionysio reperitur. Nominatim quidem narrat Jacobum fratrem Domini, & Petrum adfuisse; quod aequaquam verisimile est de duobus Apostolis tantùm notaturum fuisse, si omnes adfuissent. Nec ullo modo defendi poterit Jacobum fratrem Domini Mariæ sepulturam celebrâsse; siquidem Anno 3. vel (ut alii volunt) 10. post Christi Ascensionem, regnante Claudio, interfectus est; quod & Genebrardus ait in Chronologiâ suâ, & Eusebius in Chronico.
units.tr: Basil, in his book on the Holy Spirit, chapter 29, cites the second epistle of Dionysius of Alexandria to his namesake. So in the seventeenth year after Christ's ascension, Dionysius would still have been an Athenian senator. This also appears from the time when Paul went up with Barnabas to the Synod at Jerusalem (Acts 15:4; Gal. 2:1), compared with the journeys which he is said afterwards to have undertaken through Derbe, Lystra, Phrygia, Galatia, Mysia and Macedonia, before coming to Athens and converting Dionysius (Acts 16:1; 17:34); and it is further confirmed by Laurentius Codomanus, book 4 of his Chronology, chapter 31. Let us now inquire at what time Mary died. Melito, in his work on the Passing of Mary, asserts that she was taken up in the second year after Christ's ascension, which is why Bede rebukes him. Nevertheless, this was revealed to the nun Elizabeth by Mary herself, as Antoninus writes in his History, part 1, title 6, chapter 3, and Vincent in his Speculum Historiale, book 7, chapter 80; and Marianus Scotus in his Chronicle departs little from that reckoning. Nicephorus, book 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 3, writes that Mary was fifteen years old when she bore Christ, and that she lived fifty-nine years; which the testimony of Euodius also confirms. So she would have died in the year of Christ 44. Eusebius in his Chronicle reports that some held it had been revealed to them that Mary was taken up in the year of Christ 48. And so the Papists defend it (as we read in the New Priest's Book, part 1, page 156): that Mary conceived in the fourteenth year of her age, bore a child at fifteen, and died at sixty-three. And the Reims writers (notes on Acts 1:14) say the Virgin was taken up in the year of Christ 48, fifteen years after his ascension. So, on the testimony of the Reims writers themselves, who extend Mary's life longest of all, Mary died before Dionysius was converted to the Christian faith by Paul; and therefore he was not present with the brothers at her departure from this life. All the more amazing is the ignorance and the impudence of these men, who not only try to establish the bodily assumption of Mary from the Epistle of Dionysius the Areopagite to Timothy, which does not exist (they seem to have read that Dionysius wrote about this matter to Timothy, and from that invented a new Epistle, whereas in the book de divinis Nominibus, written to Timothy, only that is found); but they also add of their own that the twelve Apostles, scattered from one another into various parts of the world, miraculously came together, except Thomas, who arrived only three days after the Virgin's death, etc. Not so much as a word of this fable is found in Dionysius. He indeed names James the brother of the Lord and Peter as present, which is by no means probable, since he would hardly have singled out only two Apostles if all had been present. Nor can it in any way be defended that James the brother of the Lord celebrated Mary's burial, since he was put to death in the year 3 after Christ's ascension, or (as others want) 10, under the reign of Claudius; as Genebrardus says in his Chronology, and Eusebius in his Chronicle.

units.la: VI. Solent Apostoli, & Prophetæ plurimum inculcare suam immediatam Vocationem; ut suam doctrinam apud Auditores confirment. Optimo ergò jure, necessitatéque id ipsâ postulante, Deóque præcipiente, Apostolorum discipuli ipsorum Authoritatem in docendo citare debebant, ac testari, se hæc aut illa coràm à seleêto Christi Organo Paulo audisse, eóque auditores debere illis plenâ fide assentiri. At Dionysius Pauli Præceptoris, & aliorum Apostolorum aut nunquam, aut rarò meminit; alios interim Doctores multos, & Hierotheum Præceptorem subinde inducit. Alicubi ait; Eucharistia est juxta inclytum Præceptorem nostrum πλεῖστ' πλεῖστ' non Paulum, sed Hierotheum Præceptorem intelligens, ut annotat Scholiastes. Mox de Chrismate; Atque ideo Præceptores nostri istud quasi æquale sacro Synaxeos mysterio conjunxêre. Post de Monachis; Sancti nostri Patres (inter quos sanè Paulus non fuit) divinis eos appellarunt nominibus, partim Therapeutas, partim Monachos. Nec, si Dionysius iste discendi cupidus fuit, necesse habuit sese in Disciplinam Hierotheo (homini obscuro, in Ecclesiâ planè ignoto) dedere; cum per integrum biennium Paulum quasi domi habere potuerit. Ille enim mox post Areopagitæ conversionem, Corinthi diu, & Ephesi diutiùs docuit; quæ loca facilè Athenis adiri possunt. Quis verò, quando, ubi fuit Gentium iste Hierotheus?
units.tr: VI. Apostles and prophets very often insist on their immediate calling, so that they may confirm their teaching among their hearers. Accordingly, the disciples of the Apostles rightly, and indeed of necessity, since the situation demanded it and God commanded it, ought to cite their masters' authority in teaching and testify that they heard this or that from Paul, the chosen organ of Christ, so that the hearers should give full assent to them. But Dionysius rarely if ever mentions Paul, his teacher, or the other Apostles. Meanwhile he brings forward many other teachers, and his teacher Hierotheus from time to time. Somewhere he says: The Eucharist is, according to our famous teacher, very much [πλεῖστα], understanding by teacher not Paul but Hierotheus, as the scholiast notes. Soon after, about the chrism: And so our teachers joined this, as if equal, to the sacred mystery of the Synaxis. Afterwards, about the monks: Our holy Fathers (among whom Paul certainly was not) called them by divine names, some Therapeutae, some Monks. Nor, if this Dionysius was eager to learn, was he obliged to give himself up as a disciple to Hierotheus (an obscure man, quite unknown in the Church), since for a whole two years he could have had Paul, as it were, at home. For Paul, immediately after the conversion of the Areopagite, taught for a long time at Corinth and for longer at Ephesus, places that can easily be reached from Athens. But who, when, and where was this Hierotheus, a Gentile?

units.la: VII. Ecclesiasticæ Hierarchiæ, cap. 7. de infantum baptismo verba faciens; hæc de re (inquit) ea dicimus, quæ divini nostri Præceptores ᾿ες ἐκ ἀρχαίας παραδόσεως (veteri edocti traditione) ad nos pertulerunt. Quibus verbis homo incautus, se Apostolorum discipulum minime fuisse prodidit: quippe quum, non veteri traditione, sed ab ipso Christo Apostoli doctrinam baptismi acceperint. Neque enim si eodem cum Apostolis tempore vixit Dionysius; eorum traditionem Antiquam appellare potuit: & si potuisset, illud quidem dicere non potuit, Apostolos edoctos fuisse veteri traditione Apostolorum. Et cùm (& hîc, & in Hierarchia initio) suos præceptores (plurali numero) istam doctrinam ab Apostolis accepisse dicit ; satis ostendit, per plures sibi invicem succeedentes præceptores, eam doctrinam ab Apostolis ad se pervenisse. Si fuit Pauli discipulus ; qui ante eum scriberent libros, habere multos Majores non potuit ; imo si Bessarioni (lib. 2. cap. 3. defensionis Platonis) credimus, Dionysius hic neminem ante se habuit divinarum rerum Scriptorem, præter Apostolum Paulum, & Hierotheum Athenarum Pontificem. Unde ergo Dionysio nostro tot Scriptores, Duces, Doctores, Pontifices, Præceptores, Patres? Eritne cuiquam credibile, ista tam multa sine verbo, traditione quâdam evulgâsse? aut istos eum tanquam ignobiles, & Anonymos producere noluisse?
units.tr: VII. In the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 7, speaking of the baptism of infants, he says: We say these things on this matter, which our divine teachers have handed down to us, taught by ancient tradition [ἐκ ἀρχαίας παραδόσεως]. By these words the incautious man revealed that he was by no means a disciple of the Apostles. For the Apostles received the doctrine of baptism not from an ancient tradition but from Christ himself. Nor, even if Dionysius lived at the same time as the Apostles, could he call their tradition ancient; and even if he could, he could not say that the Apostles had been taught by the ancient tradition of the Apostles. And since he says (here, and at the beginning of the Hierarchy) that his teachers, in the plural, received this doctrine from the Apostles, he sufficiently shows that this doctrine reached him from the Apostles through several teachers succeeding one another. If he was a disciple of Paul, he could not have had many predecessors who wrote books; indeed, if we believe Bessarion (book 2, chapter 3, of the Defence of Plato), this Dionysius had no writer on divine matters before him except the Apostle Paul and Hierotheus, bishop of Athens. Where then did our Dionysius get so many writers, leaders, teachers, bishops, instructors, and Fathers? Will anyone believe that he published so many things without a word, by some tradition? Or that he did not wish to bring forward these men, as obscure and anonymous?

units.la: VIII. In Hierarchia Ecclesiastica, Timotheum vocat filium (quod idem est usu Scripturæ, & Ecclesiæ, ac discipulus) eúmque docet multa mysteria ; cùm tamen fuerit Timotheus in Evangelio frater major, à Paulo ad fidem ante Areopagitam conversus, Paulóque adhuc vivo celebris doctor, ac Episcopus ; denique Dionysio authoritate, gravitate, eruditione, omníque dignitate par (si non superior.) Timotheus diutissimè, & familiarissimè cum Paulo Apostolo vixit, ab eóque plenè eruditus est : familiaris etiam fuisse scribitur Johanni Apostolo, qui diutiùs Dionysio vixit, & plerunque Ephesi, & in Asiâ Minori fuit, ubi & Timotheus egit. Quomodo ergò iste Dionysius ausus fuisset docere Timotheum, tantos Præceptores habentem; ut ille potius hunc Dionysium docere potuerit, quàm ab eo doceri: Et non potiùs millies repetendo petiisset, ut sibi Timotheus vel de hâc re, vel de aliâ suam, aut Pauli, Joannisve Sententiam præscriberet? IX. Dictio, & forma Orationis non est simplex, & sincera ; sed arguta nimis, & inflata, obscura, affectata, & parum apostolica. Et ille tumidus, horridus, obscurus, improprius, & intricatus Stylus nequaquam tempore Apostolorum Athenis fuit usitatus; sed 300 demum postea annis in Græciâ, & etiam Romæ cœpit esse in usu. Epistola ad Lectorem in Dionysii Carthusiani Commentar. super Dionysium Areopagit. dicit, hunc Dionysium, quisquis fuit, esse asperiorem, multis mendis antèa scatuisse, vix intelligibilem, nonnullis etiam Theologis facessere negotium. Ignorâsse illum linguam Hebraicam liquet ex hís verbis (in Ecclesiast. Hierarch.) de interpretatione Seraphim; Si, ut aiunt, qui Hebraicam linguam callent, &c.
units.tr: VIII. In the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy he calls Timothy son (which in the usage of Scripture and the Church means the same as disciple), and teaches him many mysteries; yet Timothy was, in the Gospel, an older brother, converted to the faith by Paul before the Areopagite, a celebrated teacher and bishop while Paul was still alive, and in authority, weight, learning, and every dignity the equal (if not the superior) of Dionysius. Timothy lived for a very long time and very intimately with the Apostle Paul, and was fully taught by him. He is also written to have been a close friend of the Apostle John, who lived longer than Dionysius and was for the most part at Ephesus and in Asia Minor, where Timothy also worked. How then would this Dionysius have dared to teach Timothy, who had such great teachers, so that he could teach this Dionysius rather than be taught by him? And would he not rather have asked a thousand times, by repeated requests, that Timothy prescribe for him his own opinion, or that of Paul or John, on this matter or another? IX. The diction and form of his speech are not simple and sincere, but too subtle and bombastic, obscure, affected, and little apostolic. And that turgid, rough, obscure, improper, and intricate style was certainly not in use at Athens in the time of the Apostles; it began to be in use in Greece, and also at Rome, only about 300 years later. The letter to the reader in the Carthusian's commentary on Dionysius the Areopagite says that this Dionysius, whoever he was, is harsher, once full of many faults, scarcely intelligible, and giving trouble even to some theologians. That he did not know Hebrew is clear from these words (in the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy) about the interpretation of the Seraphim: If, as those who know the Hebrew language say, &c.

units.la: X. Nec illa Pauli discipulo conveniunt, dubitare de suâ doctrinâ, & ignorare utrum à vero recesserit. Si hæc (inquit in Epilogo de divinis Nominibus) vel minùs recte, aut minus sufficienter se habent, & ab ipsa veritate vel omnino vel ex parte deficimus: erit profectò humanitatis tuæ corrigere non sponte ignorantem. In primo etiam cap. Ecclesiastica Hierarchiæ præcipit Timotheo, ut non omnibus revelet sua scripta. Non sunt igitur Apostolica.
units.tr: X. Nor do these things suit a disciple of Paul: to doubt his own doctrine and not know whether he has departed from the truth. If these things (he says in the epilogue on the divine Names) are less correct or less adequate, and we fall away from the truth itself wholly or in part, it will surely be the part of your humanity to correct one who does not knowingly err. Also, in the first chapter of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy he instructs Timothy not to reveal his writings to everyone. They are therefore not Apostolic.

units.la: XI. Nullum ex Apostolis, aut eorum discipulis videmus tam de industriâ tulisse (forte lusisse) in tradendâ Ecclesiæ doctrinæ subtilibus, imo intricatis, ac præter Authorem ipsum, vix alii cuiquam explicabilibus speculationibus, & argutiis. At nihil minùs certè convenit isti ætati, cui Dionysius tribuitur; ut in quâ homines rudes rerum, de Christo, de Regno Dei, de Justitiâ, & Salute æternâ, singulari simplicitate, & perspicuitate, non subtilitatum involucris, doceri necesse fuit. Quod quidem judicium, ut minimè dubium, aut fallax, etiam de reliquis libris Apocryphis Ecclesia perpetuò pronunciavit: quod videlicet Stylus eorum & dicendi forma ab elocutione Apostolicâ procul absit. Scribendi verò genus, quo Dionysius iste utitur, præsertim de divinis Nominibus, & Hierarchia cælesti, inanis Philosophiæ potiùs doctrinam continet, quam Christianilini puram doctrinam, ac ædificatione prorsus caret. In Mystica etiam Theologia Platonizat plus quàm Christianizat. Effundit ænigmata, (ait de illo Marsilius Ficinus) concinit Dithyrambos.
units.tr: XI. We see that none of the Apostles, or their disciples, deliberately wrote (perhaps played) in teaching the doctrine of the Church with subtle, indeed intricate, speculations and subtleties, which could hardly be explained by anyone except the author himself. Yet nothing is less suited to that age, to which Dionysius is attributed, than this, since in that age rude men needed to be taught about Christ, the Kingdom of God, righteousness, and eternal salvation with a singular simplicity and clarity, not wrapped in layers of subtleties. This judgment, which is not doubtful or deceptive, the Church has always pronounced also about the remaining Apocryphal books: namely, that their style and manner of expression are far from apostolic eloquence. The kind of writing that this Dionysius uses, especially in On the Divine Names and the Celestial Hierarchy, contains the doctrine of empty philosophy rather than the pure doctrine of the Christian religion, and is wholly lacking in edification. In the Mystical Theology too he Platonizes more than he Christianizes. He pours out enigmas (Marsilio Ficino says of him), he sings dithyrambs.

units.la: XII. In libris de cælesti Hierarchiâ divinam sanè rem tractat, ipsum ordinem cœlestis Reipublicæ; Argumentum & difficultatis, & audaciæ plenissimum. Paulus Apostolus (qui in tertium Cœlum raptus est) 2 Cor. XII. 4. ista, & hujusmodi reliqua omnino ἄρρητα esse dicit; præterea, ait nefas esse homini, ea loqui. Unde ergo aut ausus est Dionysius ista enunciare, si sciret; aut scire potuit? Unde tandem tam mirificam scientiam adeptus est? Num ex revelatione? Unde constat? Cur non Apostolis ista potiùs revelata sunt; si modò nostrâ interesset ea scire? Si non interfuit; cur hæc mysteria Dionysius evulgavit? Paulo sc. sapientior fuit: Ita ut de hujusmodi hominibus Nazianzenus pronunciat, 34. Orat. (quae secunda est de Theolog.) Quin & Paulo, inquit, praestabiliorem esse te demus; ut Angelorum vel Archangelorum ordinem cognitionemque teneas. Irenaeus, lib. 2. cap 54. praeclaram sententiam habet contra istos Hierarchiarum Scriptores; Nihil sanum dicunt, (inquit) delirant; non oportet iis credere, & Mosen, ac Prophetas relinquere. Dicant nobis, quae sit invisibilium natura; Enarrent numerum Angelorum, & ordinem Archangelorum; demonstrent Thronorum Sacramenta; & doceant diversitates dominationum, Principatuum, Potestatum, atque Virtutum: Sed non habent dicere. Augustinus etiam in Enchirid. ad Laurent. cap. 58. affirmat se nescire ordines Angelorum, & eorum differentias, qui Throni, quae Dominationes, qui Principatus, quae Virtutes. Dicant (inquit) qui possunt; si modo probare possunt, quod dicunt. At haec omnia, & alia etiam multa Dionysius superstitiose, & curiose de Angelis explicat: sed nihil probat; nec rationem, nec authoritatem affert. In Antiqua vero Ecclesia vidimus tale argumentum fuisse Arcanum, & ignotum, & inauditum, necdum a quoquam pertractatum. Praeterea Gregorius Magnus aliter Angelorum ordines describit, quam iste Dionysius; similiter Bernardus etiam: ut Eckius fatetur, in Homil. 4. de Fest. Michaelis. At si tanta fides hujus Dionysii, tantaque authoritas hujus libri, illi nunquam aliter de rebus hisce scripsissent; cum in eo inventarium quoddam haberent totius Caeli supellectilis, & Angelicorum subselliorum.
units.tr: XII. In the books On the Celestial Hierarchy he certainly treats divine matters, namely the very order of the heavenly commonwealth: a subject full both of difficulty and of audacity. The Apostle Paul (who was caught up into the third heaven), 2 Cor. 12:4, says that these and all similar things are unspeakable [ἄρρητα]; moreover, he says it is unlawful for a man to speak of them. Then how did Dionysius dare to set these things forth, if he knew them, or how could he know them? How at last did he obtain such wonderful knowledge? By revelation? How is that known? Why were these things not revealed rather to the Apostles, if it were in fact of interest to us to know them? If it was not of interest, why did Dionysius publish these mysteries? Was he, I ask, wiser than Paul? So Nazianzen, in Oration 34 (the second on Theology), pronounces of men of this kind: Indeed we grant that you are better even than Paul, he says, so that you hold the order and knowledge of the Angels or Archangels. Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 54, has a splendid sentence against these writers of hierarchies: They say nothing sound, he says, they rave; one ought not to believe them, and leave Moses and the Prophets. Let them tell us what is the nature of the invisible things; let them recount the number of the Angels and the order of the Archangels; let them show the sacraments of the Thrones; and let them teach the differences of the Dominions, Principalities, Powers, and Virtues. But they cannot say. Augustine too, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 58, affirms that he does not know the orders of the Angels and their differences: which are the Thrones, which the Dominations, which the Principalities, which the Virtues. Let those (he says) who can say, if only they can prove what they say. Yet all these things, and many others, Dionysius explains about the Angels superstitiously and curiously, but proves nothing; he brings neither reason nor authority. In the ancient Church we have seen that such a subject was secret, unknown, unheard of, and not yet treated by anyone. Moreover, Gregory the Great describes the orders of the Angels differently from this Dionysius; Bernard also does so, as Eck admits, in Homily 4 on the Feast of Michael. But if this Dionysius had such great authority, and this book such weight, they would never have written otherwise about these matters, since in it they would have had a kind of inventory of the whole heavenly furniture and the Angelic seats.

units.la: XIII. In septima Epistola, quae est ad Polycarpum, scribit se fuisse in Aegypto; cum esset celebris illa Solis eclipsis per totum Orbem terrarum, eo tempore, quo Dominus noster Jesus Christus mortem in Cruce obiit.
units.tr: XIII. In the seventh Epistle, which is addressed to Polycarp, he writes that he was in Egypt when that famous eclipse of the sun occurred over the whole world, at the time when our Lord Jesus Christ died on the Cross.

units.la: At Origenes, tractat. 35. in Matthaeum, ait tenebras illas, quarum mentio fit, Matth. XXVII. 45. in Judaica tantum {1} terra fuisse. Origenes igitur aut libros Dionysii non vidit; aut non tantum illis detulit, quantum Papistae tribui volunt. Quin & Laur. Valla (in Act. XVII.) deridet eorum ineptiam, qui, quasi non fuerit in vicinis civitatibus illa Eclipsis,
units.tr: But Origen, in tractate 35 on Matthew, says that the darkness mentioned at Matthew 27:45 was confined to the Jewish land alone. Origen therefore either did not see the books of Dionysius, or did not attribute to them as much weight as the Papists wish. Indeed Laurentius Valla (on Acts 17) also mocks the folly of those who, as if that eclipse had not been seen in the neighbouring cities, {1}

units.la: {1} Julius Africanus, cujus χρονογραφίαι & familiaris, toto mundo factas per ... tenebras. (In Georgii Cedreni Chronico, pag. 155. & Graecis Collectaneis Eusebianis Scaligeri, pag. 63.) quam volunt fuisse Athenis, faciunt Dionysium de eâ scribentem literas ad alium. Maximus in Scholiis, pag. 319. ait Julium Africanum, & Eusebium in Chronographiis suis meminisse hujus Eclipseos: quorum alter (Eusebius) cùm testem advocet ejus rei Phlegontem: Alter (Africanus) apud Georgium Syncellum in Græcis Eusebianis Scaligeri, pag. 63. neuter tamen Dionysium commemorat; qui testis tamen omnium maximè opportunus fuisset, utpote αὐτόπτης, si tum uspiam extitisset.
units.tr: {1} Julius Africanus, whose chronography is also familiar, mentions the darkness that came over the whole world. (In George Cedrenus's Chronicle, p. 155, and in Scaliger's Greek collections from Eusebius, p. 63.) They claim it was seen at Athens, and they make Dionysius describe it in a letter to someone else. Maximus, in his Scholia, p. 319, says that Julius Africanus and Eusebius in his Chronographies both mention this eclipse. Eusebius calls on Phlegon as a witness to the matter. Africanus, as reported by George Syncellus in Scaliger's Greek Eusebius, p. 63, does not mention it. Neither of them, however, mentions Dionysius, although he would have been the most fitting witness of all, as an eyewitness [αὐτόπτης], if he had been anywhere at that time.

units.la: XIV. In libro de divinis Nominibus citat Clementem Philosophum, dicentem, Quòd exemplaria rerum principalia, aut ideæ, seu causæ formales sint relativa. Pachymeres ait, Interpretes quosdam Clementem Romanum hic intellexisse. At nullus fuit alius Clemens Philosophus, quàm Alexandrinus, qui ducentis post Christum annis vixit. Videmus etiam omnino quòd, locus ille citatus in fine 8. lib. Stromatum est; ubi Clemens dicit, causas, præsertim formalem, esse relativam. Vide Matthæi Galeni Areopagitica, sol. 12, 52, 53, 54. & 91. b. XV. Hincmarus Rhemensis Episcopus, & Johannes Scotus in Epistolis ad Carolum, affirmant Dionysium, qui in Galliam missus est ad prædicandum Evangelium, fuisse Dionysium Areopagitam. Nec fortè ratio ex computo temporis contradicit, sicut aliqui objicere voluerunt; inquit Author Lombardicæ Historiæ. At Galli, inter quos Apostolatu suo functos dicitur, ita negligenter Apostoli sui scripta conservârunt; ut ad annum usque Domini 825. iisdem caruerint. Anno enim 10. Ludovici Pii, Galliarum Regis, Caroli magni F. (inter cætera munera) delati sunt ei à legatis Michaëlis Imperatoris Constantinopolitani libri Dionysii de cœlesti Hierarchiâ; qui ut summo gaudio sunt excepti; ita homines cæci, surdi, infirmi, plus minus novendecim, eâ nocte in illâ Ecclesiâ sunt curati; Ut Jacobus de Voragine in legendâ aureâ, & Antoninus, part. 2. tit. 16. cap. 2. authores sunt. Ea verò tum temporis fuit Gallorum inscitia; ut ne verba quidem Dionysii possent intelligere, priusquam Johannes Scotus (qui ex Hibernia in Gallias concesserat) in Latinam linguam traduxisset. Eundem Scotum, quemadmodum & Anastasium Bibliothecarium, Joan. Saracenum, & alios, argumentis, quae nonnulli contra Dionysii libros produxerant, satisfecisse, refert Sixtus Senensis lib. 2. Bibliothecae sanctae; qui licet eo loco libros Dionysii tanquam veros ac proprios illius foetus agnoscat; tamen lib. 4. (ut antea diximus) Quaestiones ex Veteri & Novo Testamento Athanasii non esse eo argumento confirmat; quod in illis Theologia Mystica Dionysii allegetur, Athanasii seculo, ut arbitratur, ignota. Ex his omnibus duo ista colligimus, 1. Novis, & vix credendis miraculis, atque mendaciis huic Dionysio autoritatem Pontificios conciliare. 2. Nonnullos & ante nostra tempora fuisse, qui de libris Dionysii dubitarent: Id quod ex IV. illis primis objectionibus, quas ex Theodori Presbyteri disputationibus adduximus, evidenter apparet: de quibus quid Photius senserit, non obscure illa sua censura significavit: τινὲς τίνα ἐχεις ἀποείας ἐκαλδον ἐπιγράφονται, βασανοῖ (τὴν ἐπ' αὐτῷ) γνώσιν τῶ τῆς μεγάλης Διονυσίου τῶν βίβλων. Maximus etiam (vel potius Joannes Sycopolita) in prologo testatur fuisse, qui negarent libros hos fuisse Dionysii Areopagitae; ἀλλὰ τινὲς τῶν μεταγενεστέρων. Theodorus Gaza, in praefat. in Problemata Alexandri Aphrodisaei ad Nicolaum V. statim ab initio, libros de Hierarchia non esse Dionysii Atheniensis Viri doctissimi significat. Idem facit Laurentius Valla in Annot. in Act. XVII. addito etiam, quosdam suae aetatis eruditissimos Graecos collegisse, authorem horum librorum fuisse Apollinarem. Item Johannes Coletus, concedente ipsomet Hardingo in Replica adv. Juel. sol. 44. Erasmus Roterod. & in Annotationibus suis in Acta, & contra censuras Parisiensium; & Thomas de Vio Cajetanus Cardinalis S. Christi in Comment. Actuum Apostolicorum, & tertii libri Regum. Inprimis vero memorabile est, quod refert Erasmus sua memoria de Guilhelmo Grocino Anglo, viro (ut ait) incomparabili, Ecclesiasticarum constitutionum observan-
units.tr: XIV. In the book de divinis Nominibus, he cites Clement the Philosopher as saying that the principal exemplars of things, or ideas, or formal causes, are relative. Pachymeres says that some interpreters have understood this to mean Clement of Rome. But there was no other Clement the Philosopher than the Alexandrian, who lived about two hundred years after Christ. We also see clearly that the passage cited comes at the end of Book 8 of the Stromata, where Clement says that causes, especially the formal cause, are relative. See Matthaeus Galenus, Areopagitica, pp. 12, 52, 53, 54, and 91 b. XV. Hincmar, bishop of Reims, and John Scotus, in their letters to Charles, affirm that Dionysius, who was sent into Gaul to preach the Gospel, was Dionysius the Areopagite. Nor does the reckoning of time perhaps contradict this, as some have wished to object, says the author of the Lombard History. But the Gauls, among whom he is said to have exercised his apostolate, so carelessly preserved the writings of their apostle that they lacked them until the year of the Lord 825. For in the tenth year of Louis the Pious, King of the Gauls, son of Charlemagne, among other gifts, the books of Dionysius On the Celestial Hierarchy were brought to him by envoys of the Emperor Michael of Constantinople. They were received with the greatest joy, and that same night about nineteen men who were blind, deaf, or sick were cured in that church, as Jacobus de Voragine in the Golden Legend and Antoninus, part 2, title 16, chapter 2, record. Such was the ignorance of the Gauls at that time that they could not even understand the words of Dionysius until John Scotus (who had come into Gaul from Ireland) translated them into Latin. The same Scotus, as also Anastasius the librarian, John Saracenus, and others, answered the arguments which some had brought against the books of Dionysius, says Sixtus of Siena in book 2 of the Bibliotheca sancta. Although in that place he acknowledges the books of Dionysius as true and genuine works of his, yet in book 4 (as we said before) he argues that the Questions on the Old and New Testament are not by Athanasius, on this ground: that they cite the Mystical Theology of Dionysius, which was, as he thinks, unknown in Athanasius's age. From all this we gather two things: (1) the Papists lend this Dionysius authority by new and scarcely credible miracles and lies; (2) even before our own time there were some who doubted the books of Dionysius. This clearly appears from those first four objections which we brought forward from the disputations of Theodore the Presbyter. What Photius thought of them he indicated not obscurely in his censure: some who bear the title [τινὲς ... ἐπιγράφονται], test the knowledge (concerning them) of the books of the great Dionysius [βασανοῖ ... τῶν βίβλων]. Maximus too (or rather John of Scythopolis) testifies in his prologue that there were some who denied that these books were by Dionysius the Areopagite: but some of the later writers [ἀλλὰ τινὲς τῶν μεταγενεστέρων]. Theodore Gaza, in the preface to his edition of the Problems of Alexander of Aphrodisias addressed to Nicholas V, states at the very beginning that the books On the Hierarchy are not by Dionysius the Athenian, a most learned man. Lorenzo Valla does the same in his annotations on Acts 17, adding that some very learned Greeks of his own age had concluded that the author of these books was Apollinaris. So too John Colet, with Harding himself conceding it in his Replica against Jewel, p. 44. So too Erasmus of Rotterdam, both in his annotations on Acts and against the censure of the Parisians; and Thomas de Vio Cajetan, cardinal, in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles and on the third book of Kings. Most memorable of all is what Erasmus reports from his own memory about William Grocyn, an Englishman, a man (as he says) incomparable, most observant of ecclesiastical constitutions, almost to superstition, thoroughly learned in scholastic theology, of acute judgement by nature, and finally thoroughly versed in every branch of learning.

units.la: {c} Ita Possevinus (in Photio, pag. 91.) Opera B. Dionysii at Pseudepigrapha videntur ab to notari. {v} Plurimam utique Laurentii, sed multo magis Erasmi judicio tribuendum puto: Inquit hac in causa Rossensis contra Velenum, pag. 1357. Opinatur tamen Erasmus in principio methodi perveniendi ad veram Theologiam (Tom. 5. operum ipsius, pag. 2.) Dionysium hunc Augustino anciquiorem, Et ante Augustinum (inquit) opinor, Dionysius quidem de div. nominibus. tissimo pene usque ad superstitionem, scholastica Theologia ad unguem docto, natura etiam acerrimi judicii, demum in omni disciplinarum genere exactè versato. Circa initium regni Henrici VIII. auspicaturus Londini in Ædę Paulinâ, magnâ celebritate, Enarrationem cœlestis Hierarchiæ, meditatâ præfatione multum asseveravit, hoc opus esse Dionysii Areopagitæ; vehementer destomachans in eorum impudentiam, qui dissentirent. Verùm ubi jam aliquot hebdomadas esset professus; atque, ut fit, propiùs, ac familiariùs introspexisset Autoris ingenium; priusquam Operis dimidium confecisset, non dubitavit apud eosdem auditores priorem sententiam; ingenuè profitens, sibi, verso calculo, nequaquam videri id opus esse Dionysii Areopagitæ. Hæc annotâsse necessarium fuit, ut occurreretur tum Bellarmino, qui nullo modo verisimile putat, tot Patres non potuisse videre id, quod nunc Valla & Erasmus vidisse se dicunt (neque enim recens fuit hæc controversia, & à paucis agitata;) tum etiam Parisiensibus Theologis, qui (censurâ suâ in Epist. præposita Erasmi Paraphrasi in 1 Epist. ad Corinth.) aiunt neminem hâc de re dubitare præter ineruditos, temerarios, & novitatum studiosos: (cùm viri doctissimi,& Papisticarum superstitionum tenacissimi libros hosce ἀναπέμπτος arguant.) Nostros igitur insimulare non possunt Pontificii; quòd Dionysii libros ideo tantùm commentitios esse clament, quia contra ipsos testimonium dicant. Ceremonias enim plurimas habet Dionysius, quibus Romanenses non utuntur (ut Exempli gratiâ, cap. 3. Hierarch. Eccles. quod ait, solitos fuisse Cadaver salutare, & oleo perfundere:) & in rebus, quæ substantiæ sunt, nostras partes tuetur. Hierarchia enim Ecclesiastica, cap. 3. in Actione Cœnæ sacræ, quam ἱερουργίαν συμβολικὴν nominat, Communionem publicam proponit, non privatam; eamque non dimidiatam, sed integram; & theatricis gesticulationibus liberam: Scripturæ item lectionem factam esse vernaculè, ac preces similiter publicas eodem in loco commemorat; ut alia omittamus. Nos quidem Bellarmino non inviti concedimus, libros hosce nec ˣ Ex Marchai Galeni Areopagiticis intelligere licet; alios Pontificios de libris hisce dubitasse. ʸ Ad hoc vide responsionem Fr. (ubi à Pauli tamen discipulo hæc profecta, pro certo affirmare non audet.) recentes esse, nec contemnendos: sed nunquam protulerunt Pontificii argumentum, quo à Dionysio Pauli discipulo scriptos fuisse persuaderent. Multa quidem Patrum nomina allegant , quæ Dionysium antiquum quidem, non autem Apostolicum evincunt. At urgent , apparere illud exipsis libris; in quibus multorum meminit, & nonnullorum dicta proponit, qui temporibus illis floruerunt; quorum & Actuum liber, & Epistolæ Pauli meminerunt. Quibus, cum Erasino contra Parisiensium censuram, respondemus: Eum, qui hos libros scripsit, id studio curâsse , ut ab illo magno Dionysio scripti viderentur. Nec id videri potest absurdum; quum illo seculo ejusmodi libris falso celebrium virorum titulo commendatis undique scaterent omnia. Tum enim (inquit Erasinus) piis etiam viris persuasum erat, Deo gratum esse, si tali fuco populus ad aviditatem legendi provocaretur. Vid. Delrii disquisit. Magic. lib. 6. pag. 519, 520. & Stephanum de Sampayo (T.11.6.11.) sol.26, &c. & Calvinum in Act. XVII. v. ult. Hamelman de traditionibus, pag. 731, 732, 743. Chemnitium, part. 1. loc. theolog. sol. 2. Guilh. Eisengreyn Centenario 1. Hist. Ecclesiasticæ. Matthæum Galenum in Areopagiticis; ubi Dionysii scripta à nostrorum objectionibus vindicare conatur (teste Baronio in Martyrolog. Roman. Oct.9. pag. 456, & 458. vide eund. in Annalibus ad an. 109.) Et Godefridum Tilmannum in Apologia, quam præfixit Pachymeræ Paraphrasi in Dionysium à se Latinè conversæ (de quâ T. 1.7.6. p 640.) & Michael. Syngelum in Censur. de hoc lib., pag. 104. Magdeburgenses Centur.4.cap.10. col.1129. de Dionysii scripto ita statuunt: Probabilibus ducti rationibus, maximè quæ ex statu, formâ, gubernatione, ritibus Ecclesiæ, quos in Hierarchiis liber ille, Dionysii Areopagitæ inscriptus nomine, depingit; & judicamus, & pronunciare non dubitamus, ad hoc Quartum Seculum id genus scripti pertinere, à quocunque tandem Authore consarcinatum. Hæc illi. Ego potiùs ad Quintum Seculum retulerim. * Vid. pag. 161. in Joanne Scythopolitâ. Sed si Apollinarius Hæreticus Author sit (ut Græci sentiunt apud Laurentium Vallam in Act. XVII.) tum rectè sentiunt Magdeburgenses. Fertur Dionysii ad Apostolum Paulum Epistola; sed non est ejus; ut ipsamet Epistola clamat. In Jacobi de Vora-
units.tr: {c} Thus Possevinus (in Photius, p. 91): the works of the blessed Dionysius are seen to be noted by this as pseudepigrapha. {v} Indeed I think this should be attributed mostly to the judgement of Laurentius, but much more to that of Erasmus. Rossaeus says so on this matter against Velenus, p. 1357. Yet Erasmus, at the beginning of his Method of Arriving at True Theology (Vol. 5 of his works, p. 2), thinks this Dionysius is older than Augustine: "And before Augustine, I think, there was Dionysius, On the Divine Names, most observant almost to superstition, thoroughly learned in scholastic theology to the very nail, of an acute judgement by nature, and finally thoroughly versed in every kind of discipline." When he was about to begin, at the start of the reign of Henry VIII, in St Paul's in London, with great crowds, a commentary on the Celestial Hierarchy, he asserted strongly in a carefully prepared preface that this work was by Dionysius the Areopagite, and he vehemently railed against the impudence of those who disagreed. But when he had lectured for some weeks and, as happens, had looked more closely and familiarly into the author's genius, before he had finished half the work he did not hesitate, before the same audience, to change his former opinion, frankly declaring that, on reflection, the work did not seem to him to be by Dionysius the Areopagite at all. It was necessary to note these things so that a reply could be made both to Bellarmine, who thinks it in no way likely that so many Fathers could not have seen what Valla and Erasmus now say they have seen (for this controversy is not recent, nor has it been debated by only a few), and to the Parisian theologians, who (in their censure prefixed to Erasmus's paraphrase on 1 Corinthians) say that no one doubts this matter except the unlearned, the rash, and those who are eager for novelties, although the most learned men, and the most tenacious defenders of Papist superstitions, refute these books. The Papists therefore cannot accuse us of crying that these books are spurious only because they bear witness against them. For Dionysius has many ceremonies which the Romanists do not use (for example, in chapter 3 of Hierarch. Eccles., where he says that they were accustomed to kiss the corpse and anoint it with oil), and in matters of substance he defends our side. For in the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 3, in the action of the Lord's Supper, which he calls the symbolic sacred rite [ἱερουργίαν συμβολικὴν], he sets forth a public communion, not a private one, and that not halved but whole, and free of theatrical gestures. He likewise records that the reading of Scripture was done in the vernacular, and that prayers were similarly public in the same place, to say nothing of other things. We indeed concede to Bellarmine, not unwillingly, that these books are not ancient but recent, and yet not to be despised. {x} From Matthaeus Galenus's Areopagitica it may be understood that other Papists also doubted these books. {y} On this see Fr. Junius's reply against Bellarmine, de Monachis, pp. 222, 223. {z} The writings of Dionysius are cited by the author of the Quaestiones ad Antiochum (vol. 2 of Athanasius, Greek-Latin, p. 277), by Jobius or Jovius the monk (in Photius's Bibliotheca, p. 312, Greek edition), and by Ephraem of Antioch (ibid., p. 40), in the times of Justinian (ibid., p. 406). {a} On the Eucharist, book 2, chapter 4; On Grace and Free Will, book 5, chapter 25; On the Word of God, book 4, chapter 7 (where, however, he does not dare to affirm for certain that these things came from a disciple of Paul). But the Papists have never produced an argument by which they could persuade us that they were written by Dionysius, a disciple of Paul. They do indeed cite many names of the Fathers, which show Dionysius to be ancient, but not Apostolic. But they press that it appears from the books themselves, in which he mentions many people and records the sayings of some who flourished in those times, whom the book of Acts and the Epistles of Paul also mention. To these, together with Erasmus against the censure of the Parisians, we reply: the man who wrote these books took pains to ensure that they would seem to be by that great Dionysius. Nor can this seem absurd, since in that century all things were teeming with such books, falsely commended under the title of famous men. For then (says Erasmus) it was thought by even pious men that it was pleasing to God if the people were roused to eagerness for reading by such a deception. See Delrio, Disquisitiones magicae, book 6, pp. 519, 520; Stephanus de Sampayo, sol. 26, etc.; Calvin on Acts 17, last verse; Hamelmann, On Traditions, pp. 731, 732, 743; Chemnitz, part 1, Loci theologici, sol. 2; Wilhelm Eisengrein, Centenary 1 of Church History; Matthaeus Galenus in the Areopagitica, where he tries to defend the writings of Dionysius against the objections of our side (as reported by Baronius in the Roman Martyrology, October 9, pp. 456, 458; see the same in his Annals for the year 109); Godfrey Tilmann in the apology which he prefixed to his Latin version of Pachymeres's paraphrase on Dionysius (on which see vol. 1, p. 640); and Michael Syngelus in Censura on this book, p. 104. The Magdeburg Centuriators, Century 4, chapter 10, col. 1129, judge the writing of Dionysius as follows: Led by probable reasons, especially those drawn from the state, form, government, and rites of the Church, which that book inscribed with the name of Dionysius the Areopagite depicts in its Hierarchies, we judge, and do not hesitate to pronounce, that this kind of writing belongs to the fourth century, whoever at last was its compiler. So they. I would rather assign it to the fifth century. {*} See p. 161 on John of Scythopolis. But if Apollinaris the heretic is the author (as the Greeks think, according to Laurentius Valla on Acts 17), then the Magdeburg Centuriators are right. An Epistle of Dionysius to the Apostle Paul is reported, but it is not his, as the Epistle itself proclaims. In the Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine, many passages are cited from this Epistle in the Life of Peter (chapter 84), and...
