Many things are cited from this Epistle in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend, in the Life of Peter (chap. 84) and the Life of Paul (chap. 85). Godefridus Tilemannus, a Carthusian, published with his Latin version of the Epistles of Dionysius the Paraphrase of George Pachymeres as a companion volume.

units.la: * In loco stellulâ notato (uti & supra §. 4.) Cl. Usserius Lectorem ad Bibliothecam suam Theologicam remittere videtur. Operis legendi copia olim mihi data fuit, impræsentiarum verò denegatur. Locum interim ejusdem egregium de Joannis Scythopolitani & Dionysii Alexandrini in Areopagitam Scholiis; quem antea in usum Cl. V. Gulielmi Cave Historiæ suæ Literariæ inserendum descripsi, hic loci exhibere non inconsultum duximus: id solum præfati Illustrissimum Primatem in Opere præaicto Apollinarem Haereticum Authorem fuisse scriptorum Areopagita suppositorum probare imprimis conari.
units.tr: At the place marked with a little star (as also above, §4), the Most Learned Ussher seems to refer the reader to his Theological Library. I was once given the opportunity of reading that work, but at present it is refused me. Meanwhile, I have thought it not inappropriate to set out here the excellent passage of the same work on the Scholia of John of Scythopolis and Dionysius of Alexandria on the Areopagite, which I had previously copied for insertion into the Literary History of the Most Learned Gulielmus Cave. In it the aforesaid most illustrious Primate, in the work mentioned above, chiefly sought to prove that Apollinaris the heretic was the author of the writings falsely ascribed to the Areopagite.

units.la: Joannes Scythopolitanus scripsit in Dionysium Areopagitam Scholia pariter ac Maximus. Verùm in libris Dionysii ab anno 1562. inclusivè editis simul confusa sunt Joannis & Maximi Scholia: quæ non in antiquioribus solùm quæ Cyparissioti tempore ferebantur, editionibus fuerunt distincta: Sed etiam in utroque, quo usus est ipse Morellius, Codice: In quorum altero ad marginem appositæ sunt (Joannis Scythopolitani) sine nomine Scholia: in altero verò seorsim (post absolutum textum integrum Dionysii) Maximi nomine insignita Scholia, eò breviora, quòd ab amplioribus Joannis, cum quibus ea conjunxit Morellius, separata fuerant. Porrò vulgata illa Scythopolitani Scholia eadem illa ipsa sunt, quæ Dionysio Alexandrino ab aliis sunt attributa; quod ex sententiâ à Cyparissioto ex Dionysii Scholiis citatâ patet; quæ in Scholiis istis totidem verbis reperitur. Istam verò sententiam Scythopolitani, non Maximi esse, liquet ex Latinâ Versione Scholiorum Scythopolitani à Roberto Episcopo Lincolniensi factâ, & in Bibliothecâ Collegii Corporis Christi apud Oxonienses MS. asservatâ; in quâ reperitur.
units.tr: John of Scythopolis wrote Scholia on Dionysius the Areopagite, as did Maximus. But in the editions of the books of Dionysius published from 1562 onwards, the Scholia of John and of Maximus have been confused together. They were distinguished not only in the older editions that were in circulation in the time of Cyparissiotes, but also in both manuscripts which Morellius himself used. In one of these, Scholia of John of Scythopolis were placed in the margin without any name; in the other, separately (after the complete text of Dionysius), Scholia bearing the name of Maximus were given. These were shorter, because they had been separated from the longer Scholia of John, with which Morellius joined them. Moreover, those commonly printed Scholia of Scythopolis are the very same ones that others have attributed to Dionysius of Alexandria. This is clear from an opinion cited by Cyparissiotes from the Scholia of Dionysius, which is found word for word in these Scholia. That this opinion belongs to Scythopolis and not to Maximus is clear from the Latin version of the Scholia of Scythopolis made by Robert, Bishop of Lincoln, which is preserved in manuscript in the library of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and in which the opinion is found.

units.la: Ejusdem de Epistolâ ad Laodicenses Disserta- tiuncula.
units.tr: A short dissertation on the same author's Letter to the Laodiceans.

units.la: TErtullianus contra Marcionem, lib. 5. cap. 11. Praterea hîc & de aliâ Epistolâ; quam nos ad Ephesios praescriptam habemus, Haretici verò ad Laodicenos. Et cap. 17. cui vetus Inscriptio haec attexebatur (teste Pamelio) De Epistolâ ad Laodicenos sive ad Ephesios; Ecclesia quidem (inquit Tertullianus) veritate Epistolam illam ad Ephesios habemus emissam, non ad Laodicenos. Sed Marcion ei titulum aliquando interpolare gestiit; quasi & in isto diligentissimus Interpolator. Nihil autem de Titulis interest; cum ad omnes Apostolos scripserit, dum ad quosdam. Hactenus Tertullianus.
units.tr: Tertullian, against Marcion, book 5, ch. 11: Moreover, here also we have the other letter, which we hold to be addressed to the Ephesians, but the heretics to the Laodiceans. And ch. 17, to which this old inscription was attached (according to Pamelius): Concerning the letter to the Laodiceans or to the Ephesians. The Church indeed (says Tertullian) holds that letter to have been sent to the Ephesians in truth, not to the Laodiceans. But Marcion was eager at some time to tamper with its title, as though he were a most diligent interpolator in this matter too. Nothing, however, turns on the titles, since he wrote to all while addressing certain ones in particular. Thus far Tertullian.

units.la: Epiphanius, Haeref. 42. pag. 142. lin. 2. a Marcione locum hunc productum notat ex Epistolâ ad Laodicenos. Εἰς Κύριον, μία πίστις, ἐν βάπτισμα, εἷς Θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ πάντων, ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων καὶ διὰ πάντων, καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν, quod habetur in quarto Capite ad Ephesios, pag. 163. lin. 4. Ἀποσταλῇ δὲ (inquit de Marcione) ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ Ἀποστολικῇ ψαλμῳδίᾳ, καὶ ἐν ψαλμῷ ψαλμῷ πρὸς Λαοδικείας εἰς, Κύριον, μία πίστις, &c. συναδύνατος μὲν τῇ πρὸς Ἐφεσίους. ὁ Μαρκίων ἐν ταύτης τῆς ὅλης μαρτυρείας ἀπὸ τῆς λεγομένης πρὸς Λαοδικέας συνάψεως καὶ τῆς μαρτυρείας. Et paulò post, p. 164. lin. 16. Οὐ γὰρ ἰδοὺ ἐξ ἐπιστολῆς Μαρκίωνι ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς Ἐφεσίους ταύτην τὴν μαρτυρείαν λέγειν, ἀλλὰ τῆς πρὸς Λαοδικέας, τῆς μὲν ἔσω ἐν τῷ Ἀποστόλῳ. Ubi nota, inter Epistolas Paulinas à Marcione receptas septimo loco collocatam esse Epistolam ad Ephesios; quae apud nos ordine est quinta; secundùm Epiphanium (pag. 138, 141, 162.) Unde illa ab eo citata Testimonia eadem habentur in nostrâ ad Ephesios Epistola: quae eadem Marcioni Epistola fuit ad Laodicenos, secundùm Tertullianum (ubi supra.) Praeter hanc tamen ad Ephesios Epistolam, putat Epiphanius recepta etiam esse à Marcione Epistolae ad Laodicenses Fragmenta. Ἐχει ἡ ἐκ τῆς πρὸς Λαοδικέας μίαν, inquit, pag. 138. lin. 21. E quibus tamen unicum illud à se productum reperit. Jacobus Pamelius, Annot. 259. in lib. 5. Tertulliani adv. Marcionem. Fortassis (inquit) occasionem dedit Marcioni hujus Tituli huic Epistolæ imponendi; quòd legisset, Col. 4. Salutate fratres, qui sunt Laodiceæ. Et cùm lecta fuerit apud vos Epistola hæc: facite ut & in Laodicensium Ecclesiâ legatur. Legatur vobis & ea, quæ est Laodicensium. Quæ autem Marcionem moverint, ista fuisse videntur.
units.tr: Epiphanius, Haer. 42, p. 142, line 2, notes that Marcion cited this passage from the Letter to the Laodiceans: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in you all" [Εἷς Κύριος, μία πίστις, ἓν βάπτισμα, εἷς Θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ πάντων, ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων καὶ διὰ πάντων, καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν], which is found in chapter 4 of Ephesians, p. 163, line 4. Epiphanius says of Marcion that it was placed in his own apostolic collection, and in psalm after psalm to Laodicea, "One Lord, one faith," and so on, which is not consistent with the letter to the Ephesians. Marcion, in the whole of this testimony, took it from the so-called letter to the Laodiceans and its connection with the testimony. And a little later, p. 164, line 16: "For Marcion does not say that this testimony comes from the letter to the Ephesians, but from the one to the Laodiceans, the inner one in the Apostle." Here note that among the Pauline letters received by Marcion, the Letter to the Ephesians stood in seventh place, whereas in our order it is fifth, according to Epiphanius (pp. 138, 141, 162). Hence the testimonies he cites are found in our Letter to the Ephesians, which, according to Tertullian (see above), was Marcion's Letter to the Laodiceans. Epiphanius nevertheless thinks that Marcion also received fragments of a Letter to the Laodiceans besides this letter to the Ephesians: "He has one from the letter to the Laodiceans," he says, p. 138, line 21. Of these, however, he found only the single passage that he cites. Jacobus Pamelius, Annot. 259 on book 5 of Tertullian against Marcion: Perhaps (he says) the occasion for Marcion's attaching this title to this letter was that he had read Col. 4: "Salute the brothers who are in Laodicea." And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans. Let that also be read to you which is from the Laodiceans. These, it seems, were the things that moved Marcion.

units.la: I. Supracitata Apostoli sententia ex Col. IV. collata cum his duabus rationibus: (1.) Quòd Epistola ad Colossenses ejusdem sit argumenti cum eâ, quæ scripta est ad Ephesios (quod etiam notat Chrysostomus initio Homil. X. in Coloss. IV.) nec quicquam differat ab eâ, nisi quòd in hâc sit aperta significatio Judaicarum Ceremoniarum, ad Ephesios verò tenuis earum mentio: quod ad finem Explicationis Epistolæ ad Colossenses notat Adamus Sasbout. Cùm igitur eædem res eodem fere modo & ordine in utrâque Epistolâ tractarentur; ut altera videri posset Explicatio alterius: (Est enim Epistola ad Colossenses quasi Epitome Epistolæ ad Ephesios; ut Epistola ad Ephesios Epistolæ ad Romanos;) jure mandare videatur Apostolus; ut utraque Epistola ab utrisque legeretur. (2.) Quòd utraque Epistola eodem tempore scripta videatur; & per eundem nuncium Tychicum quemadmodum ad VI. Caput Epistolæ ad Ephesios notat Hieronymus ex Collatione Coloss. IV. 7, 8. cum Ephes. VI. 21, 22. Ex quâ etiam colligit Adamus Sasbout Epistolam ad Colossenses planè eodem tempore, loco & impetu scriptam esse; quo scripta est illa ad Ephesios: ut in quâ succurrerent Paulo eadem verba ex propinquâ cogitatione de præcedente Epistolâ. Contra tamen Baronius, anno 59. §. 19. collat. cum anno 60. §. 9. Confer & Theodoreti Argumentum in Epistolam ad Ephesios, Erasmus (qui multa habet de supposititiâ ad Laodicenses Epistola) initio Annot. in cap. I. ad Ephes. Certè (inquit) stylus tantum dissonat à cæteris Pauli Epistolis; ut alterius videri possit: nisi pectus atque indoles Paulinæ mentis hanc prorsus illi vindicaret. At tamen stylus planè convenit cum Epistolâ ad Colossenses.
units.tr: I. The saying of the Apostle quoted above from Col. 4, taken together with these two reasons: (1) because the Letter to the Colossians deals with the same subject as the one written to the Ephesians (which Chrysostom also notes at the beginning of his tenth homily on Col. 4), and differs from it in nothing except that the former openly refers to the Jewish ceremonies, whereas the latter mentions them only slightly, as Adam Sasbout notes at the end of his explanation of the Letter to the Colossians. Since therefore the same matters were treated in nearly the same way and order in both letters, so that one could seem to be an explanation of the other (for the Letter to the Colossians is like an epitome of the Letter to the Ephesians, as the Letter to the Ephesians is of the Letter to the Romans), the Apostle seems rightly to have commanded that each letter be read by both churches. (2) Because both letters seem to have been written at the same time and sent by the same messenger, Tychicus, as Jerome notes on chapter 6 of Ephesians, comparing Col. 4:7, 8 with Eph. 6:21, 22. From this too Adam Sasbout gathers that the Letter to the Colossians was written at exactly the same time, place and impulse as the one to the Ephesians, so that the same words came to Paul from a close thought about the preceding letter. Against this, however, Baronius, year 59, §19, compared with year 60, §9. Compare also Theodoret's argument on the Letter to the Ephesians, and Erasmus (who has much to say about the spurious Letter to the Laodiceans), at the start of his notes on Eph. 1: Certainly (he says) the style alone differs from the other Pauline letters, so that it could seem to be by another author, unless the heart and character of the Pauline mind claimed it entirely for him. Yet the style agrees completely with the Letter to the Colossians.

units.la: II. In utriusque Epistolæ Argumento, quod extat apud Oecumenium (vide & Theophylactum) ita scriptum est tam de Epistolâ ad Ephesios, quam de illâ quæ est ad Colossenses. Ταῦτα δὲ ἀπὸ Ῥώμης, ὅτι μὲ ἐναρξάμενοι αὐτῶν, ἀλλὰ ὁ ἐν ἐνῶν. Et de Epistola ad Colossenses confirmat id Joannes Chrysostomus, Hom. 1. in eam Epistolam (reclamante tamen Theodorito, & ex eo Baronio, anno 60. §. 14.) De Epistolâ verò ad Ephesios id collegisse videantur ex Ephes. I. 15. & III. 2, 4. Certum verò est Paulum antea Ephesios vidisse; quippe apud quos biennio commoratus sit; & ad vincula proficiscens, solenni modo benedixit, Act. XX.
units.tr: II. The Argument to both letters, which is found in Oecumenius (see also Theophylact), is written thus, both of the Letter to the Ephesians and of the one to the Colossians: "These were written from Rome" [Ταῦτα δὲ ἀπὸ Ῥώμης]. John Chrysostom confirms this for the Letter to the Colossians in his first homily on it (though Theodoret objects, and following him Baronius, year 60, §14). For the Letter to the Ephesians they seem to have inferred it from Eph. 1:15 and 3:2, 4. It is certain, however, that Paul had seen the Ephesians before, since he stayed among them for two years, and, setting out for his chains, he blessed them in solemn manner, Acts 20.

units.la: III. In antiquis Exemplaribus, illud ἐν Ἐφέσῳ (cap. I. ver. 1.) defuisse apparet ex illis Basilii verbis circa med. lib. 2. adv. Eunomium. Τοῖς Ἐφεσίοις ἀποστόλων, ὡς γινώσκειν ἀναμίνησις τῷ ἀγίῳ δὲ ἐπιγράφονος, ἵνα αὐτὸν ἐδιδάσκωσι (i. e. per excellentiam) ἀπόμαζον, ἀπὸν. Τοῖς ἁγίοις, τοῖς οὖσιν, καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Οὕτω γὰρ ἡ οἱ ἐκ ἡμῶν ἐδιδάσκοντο, ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς ἀπὸ ἀπὸ ἐν χάριτι εὐχόμεθα. (Sic enim citat Candarius in Scholiis ad Ephes. I.) vel (ut est in Græcâ Basilii Editione, pag. 668. lin. 13.) ἐν τοῖς ταλαιοῖς ἐν ἀντιχάρῳ εὐχόμεθα. Hinc Hieronymus in Comment. ad Ephes. I. Quidam (ait) curiosius, quàm necesse est, putant ex eo quòd Moysi dictum sit (Exod. 3.) Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me; etiam eos qui in Epheso sunt sancti & fideles, Essentiæ vocabulo nuncupatos. Alii verò simpliciter, non ad eos qui sunt, sed qui Ephesi sancti & fideles sint, scriptum arbitrantur. Theodorus Beza in fine Notarum in Epistolam ad Ephesios suspicatur verba illa [ἐν Ἐφέσῳ] ideò sublata; quod non tam ad Ephesios ipsos proprie missa fuerit Epistola, quàm Ephesum, ut ad cæteras Asiaticas Ecclesias transmitteretur.
units.tr: III. In the old copies the phrase "in Ephesus" (ch. 1, ver. 1) seems to have been missing, judging from those words of Basil about the middle of book 2 against Eunomius: "To the Ephesians, the apostle..., to the saints who are also faithful in Christ Jesus" [Τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ]. For thus those who ... we pray in the ancient copies. (So Candarius cites it in his scholia on Eph. 1.) Or, as it is in the Greek edition of Basil, p. 668, line 13, the ancient copies read it thus. Hence Jerome, on Eph. 1: Some (he says) think, more curiously than necessary, that because the words were spoken to Moses (Exod. 3), "Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me," so also those who are holy and faithful in Ephesus are named by the word of Essence. Others, however, think it was written simply not to those who are, but to those who are holy and faithful at Ephesus. Theodore Beza, at the end of his Notes on the Letter to the Ephesians, suspects that the words [ἐν Ἐφέσῳ] were therefore removed, because the letter was sent not so much to the Ephesians themselves properly as to Ephesus, so that it might be passed on to the other Asian churches.

units.la: De Epistola ad Laodicenses plura habet Jacobus Pamelius, Annot. 239. in lib. 5. Tertulliani adversus Marcionem. Bellarminus in Recognitione Controversiarum suarum. Pontificii in Colloquio Ratisbonensi. Baronius anno 60. §. 12, 13, 14. (quem etiam vide de Epistolâ ad Ephesios, anno 59. §. 19, 20, 21.) Sixtus Senensis, Biblioth. Sanct. lib. 2. in Paulo. Commentatores in postremum Caput Epistolæ ad Colossenses. Zegerus tum in Epanorthote (ubi ait, non sibi probabile judicari Marcionis judicium) tum in Scholiis. Salmeron, pag. 357. lin. 8. & Beza (ubi uterque ait; Male ab Epiphanio citari eam, quæ extat, supposititiam Epistolam: cum in ea citata ab Epiphanio sententia non reperiatur, sed in Epistolâ ad Ephesios) Ambrosius Catharinus, Cajetanus, Claudius Guilliaudus, Joannes Gagneus, Erasmus. Quibus adde etiam Theodoritum, Oecumenium, & Chrysostomum.
units.tr: On the Letter to the Laodiceans more is found in Jacobus Pamelius, Annot. 239 on book 5 of Tertullian against Marcion; in Bellarmine's Recognition of his Controversies; among the Papists in the Colloquy of Regensburg; in Baronius, year 60, §§12–14 (see also on Ephesians, year 59, §§19–21); in Sixtus of Siena, Bibliotheca Sancta, book 2, on Paul; in the commentators on the last chapter of the Letter to the Colossians; in Zegerus, both in his Epanorthotes (where he says that Marcion's judgment does not seem probable to him) and in his Scholia; in Salmeron, p. 357, line 8; and in Beza (where both say that Epiphanius wrongly cites that letter which survives as spurious, since the sentence he cites is not found in it but in the Letter to the Ephesians). Add also Ambrosius Catharinus, Cajetan, Claude Guillaud, John Gagney and Erasmus. To these add also Theodoret, Oecumenius and Chrysostom.

units.la: AUCTARIUM Historiæ Dogmaticæ JACOBI USSERII ARMACHANI DE Scripturis & Sacris Vernaculis. CAPUT I.
units.tr: AUCTARIUM of the Dogmatic History of James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, concerning the Scriptures and the Vernacular Sacred Books. CHAPTER I.

units.la: IN disponendis Authorum Judæorum, quos citat ætatibus Illustrissimus Primas, calculum communiorem sequitur. An verior sit ista, parùm constat nisi ex ipsorum Authoritate Judæorum; quibus fabulas fabulis nectere, & temporum seriem immanibus parachronismis perturbare solenne est. Veri sanè haud absimilis est ista Judæorum traditio quoad ætatem primorum Doctorum, quæque haud adeò facilè confutari queat; dignis tamen fide testibus caret, & pro arbitrio confiçta videtur. Neque desunt Eruditi, qui Onkelon, Jonathanem, & hujusmodi alios Doctores longè inferioris ætatis, quàm quæ à Judæis ponitur, esse contendunt; atque eorum Paraphrases multis post Christum seculis confectas autumant. Mihi potior videtur sententia Paraphrases ipsas revera antiquas esse; verùm Authorum nomina iis pro lubitu appositisse Judæos. Utut sit, & in his & in aliorum Rabbinorum, (quos testes adhibet Cl. Usserius) Historiâ texendâ non parùm discrepant ipsi Judæi, quique Judæos sequuntur, Christiani. Plures Onkelon æquè ac Jonathanem Christi tempora præcessisse, saltem illi coævos fuisse, volunt: Alii, quorum sententiam refert Usserius, illum Titi Imperatoris nepotem faciunt (ea est enim Judæorum mendacum ambitio; ut ferè omnes Rabbinos suos Romanis Imperatoribus consanguineos fuisse jactitent) Quidam illum Magni Gamalielis familiarem ponunt, cujus proinde exequias superstes curaverit. Nonnulli denique eundem cum R. Akila (qui sub Antonino Imp. floruisse noscitur) alii eundem cum Aquilâ Pontico (qui claruit circa annum 130.) fuisse asserunt. Nec minor equidem Authorum dissensio de Jonathane; quem pars Scriptorum potior Onkeli condiscipulum fuisse tradunt: aliqui tamen integras tres ætates illis interponunt; adeò ut Hillel præceptor fuerit Jonathanis & Joannis ben Zaccai, Joannes iste præceptor R. Eleazaris & R. Josuæ, quibus discipulus fuisse dicitur Onkelos. Recepta est opinio Jonathanem triginta ante Christum natum annis Paraphrasin suam elucubrâsse; cùm tamen nonnulli eundem cum Theodotione (qui vixit anno Christi 180.) fuisse ponant. Longum esset, si varias Scriptorum de reliquis, qui à Cl. Usserio laudantur, Doctoribus Hebræis sententias in medium proferrem. Id solum admonandum duxi, illorum testimonia ex Pirke Aboth ferè omnia produci, adeóque incertæ admodùm fidei esse. Liber enim iste, quamvis non contemnendæ sit ætatis, ab audaculo tamen quodam Judæo est compositus; qui sententias Veterum Doctorum traditione perpetuâ conservatas scripto consignare præ se ferens, Lectoribus fucum facere meritò censeri posset. Novimus enim quàm fluxæ fidei sit traditio; quæ cum ubique anceps & lubrica sit, apud Judæos planè adulterina est & commentitia. Majoris forsitan momenti sunt testimonia, quæ ex Talmude Judaico adducta sunt, licèt ipsa etiam sint meritò suspecta. Neque enim ante annum Christi 505. finitum esse Talmud constat; ante centum plùs minùs annos à Rau Ascè, Scholæ (uti fertur) Babylonicæ Rectore, inchoatum. Hucusque autem sententias Doctorum incorruptâ traditione transmissas fuisse parùm credibile est. Denique quod Quartum Esdræ librum ab Usserio citatum spectat; ille à fallario quodam Judæo longè post Christi tempora confictus videtur. Neque tamen inutilia sunt prorsus, de quibus suspicionem movimus, testimonia. Saltem enim recentiorum Judæorum hâc de re sententiam declarant, quidque isti majores suos sensisse existimarunt, notum faciunt: Argumentum sanè adversus adversùs Traditionis patronos, quales sunt Pontificii, non infirmum. Valeant itaque, quantùm valere possunt.
units.tr: In arranging the dates of the Jewish authors whom the most illustrious Primate cites, he follows the more common reckoning. Whether it is the truer one is hardly clear except from the authority of the Jews themselves, among whom it is customary to tie fables to fables and to disturb the sequence of times with monstrous anachronisms. Indeed this Jewish tradition about the age of the first teachers is not very unlike the truth, and it cannot easily be refuted; yet it lacks trustworthy witnesses and seems to have been invented at will. Nor are there lacking learned men who contend that Onkelos, Jonathan and other teachers of much later date than the Jews assign are to be placed, and who maintain that their Paraphrases were composed many centuries after Christ. To me the opinion seems more probable: the Paraphrases are really ancient, but the Jews attached the names of authors to them at their pleasure. However that may be, in weaving their history from these and from the other rabbis (whom the learned Ussher cites as witnesses), the Jews themselves, and the Christians who follow the Jews, differ not a little. Many hold that Onkelos, like Jonathan, preceded the times of Christ, or at least was his contemporary. Others, whose opinion Ussher reports, make him a grandson of the Emperor Titus (for such is the vanity of Jewish liars, that nearly all their rabbis boast of being related to Roman emperors). Some place him as a close companion of Rabban Gamaliel, whose funeral he therefore survived and arranged. Some finally assert that he is the same as R. Akiba (who is known to have flourished under the Emperor Antoninus), and others that he is the same as Aquila of Pontus (who flourished about the year 130). Indeed the disagreement of authors about Jonathan is no less. The greater part of the writers say he was a fellow-pupil of Onkelos; yet some insert three whole generations between them, so that Hillel was the teacher of Jonathan and of Johanan ben Zakkai, Johanan was the teacher of R. Eleazar and R. Joshua, and Onkelos is said to have been a pupil of these. The accepted opinion is that Jonathan composed his Paraphrase thirty years before Christ's birth; yet some hold him to be the same as Theodotion (who lived in the year 180 of Christ). It would be long to set out the varied opinions of the writers concerning the other Hebrew teachers cited by the learned Ussher. I have thought only this should be noted: almost all their testimonies are drawn from the Pirke Aboth, and are therefore of very doubtful trustworthiness. For that book, although not of contemptible antiquity, was composed by a certain bold Jew who, pretending to commit to writing the opinions of the ancient teachers preserved by unbroken tradition, could justly be thought to deceive his readers. For we know how unstable the faith in tradition is; while it is everywhere uncertain and slippery, among the Jews it is altogether spurious and fabricated. Perhaps the testimonies drawn from the Jewish Talmud are of greater weight, although these too are rightly suspect. For it is established that the Talmud was not finished before the year 505 of Christ, and was begun about a hundred years earlier by Rav Ashi, head (as it is said) of the Babylonian school. Now it is hardly credible that the opinions of the teachers were handed down to that time without corruption. Finally, as regards the Fourth Book of Esdras cited by Ussher, it seems to have been fabricated by some deceitful Jew long after the time of Christ. Nevertheless, the testimonies about which we have raised suspicion are not entirely useless. For at least they declare the opinion of the more recent Jews on this matter, and make known what they thought their forebears had held. This is certainly no weak argument against the defenders of tradition, such as the Papists. Let them therefore keep whatever value they can have.

units.la: Certiora sunt, quæ ex Josepho & Philone proferuntur. Summam isti in rebus Judaicis explicandis diligentiam præstitere; quæque probè, si unquam alii, nôrunt suæ gentis instituta, pari gravitate retulerunt. Plura Josephi testimonia dedit Arnachanus; unicum tamen compendio refert; quod cùm maximè insigne sit, pleniùs subjiciendum duximus.
units.tr: More certain are the things brought forth from Josephus and Philo. These men showed the greatest diligence in explaining Jewish matters, and, as well as anyone ever has, they knew the institutions of their own nation and related them with equal seriousness. Arnachanus (Ussher) gave several testimonies from Josephus; yet he reports only one in summary. Since it is especially notable, we have thought it should be set out more fully.

units.la: Lib. 2. contra Apionem. Moses, ne ignorantiam, velut aliquam deprecandæ pænæ speciem relinqueret, (1) longè pulcherrimum nobis maximèque necessarium disciplinæ genus legem ipsam esse voluit; nec satis id futurum putavit, ut semel, iterum, aut sæpius eam audiissemus, nisi hebdomadis quoque singulis, ab alio quolibet opere feriatos omnes, ad illam dum recitaretur audiendam, animoque penitus informandam convenire juberet.
units.tr: Book 2, Against Apion. Moses, lest he leave ignorance as a kind of excuse for escaping punishment, wished the law itself to be the most beautiful and most necessary kind of instruction for us; and he did not think it enough that we should hear it once, twice, or more often, unless he also ordered everyone, released from every other work, to assemble every seventh day to hear it read and to be thoroughly instructed in mind.

units.la: Idem, seu quisquis fuerit Author orationis Panegyricæ in Maccabæos Fratres elegantissimæ, certè Judæus, illos à patre in divinæ legis scientiâ diligenter institutos refert. Sic enim Juvenes patrem laudant. (2) Ille nos docuit superstes adhuc, Legem & Prophetas. Abelem à Caine occisum pralegit nobis, Isaacum victimæ loco sacrificatum, Josephum carceri inclusum. Narravit nobis zelotem Phinean. Edocuit nos res gestas Ananiæ, Azariæ & Misaelis, in ignem conjectorum. Laudavit & Danielem in specu leonum, quem beatum prædicavit. Nobis in memoriam revocavit Isaiæ Scripturam, dicentem, &c.
units.tr: The same author, or whoever he was, of the most elegant panegyric on the Maccabean brothers, who was certainly a Jew, relates that they were carefully instructed by their father in knowledge of the divine law. For thus the young men praise their father: (2) While still alive he taught us the Law and the Prophets. He read to us of Abel slain by Cain, of Isaac offered as a victim, of Joseph shut up in prison. He told us of the zealot Phinehas. He taught us the deeds of Ananias, Azarias and Misael, cast into the fire. He also praised Daniel in the den of lions, whom he proclaimed blessed. He brought to our memory the Scripture of Isaiah, saying, etc.

units.la: Ex Philonis lib. 1. de Judæorum ab Ægypto egressu egregium haberi testimonium in Eusebio, lib. 8. Præpar. Evang. cap. 7.
units.tr: From the first book of Philo's On the Exodus of the Jews from Egypt, an excellent testimony is found in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica, book 8, chapter 7.

units.la: (1) Καλλιστον ... ἀναγκαιοτατον ... (Eusebii præparatio, lib. 8. cap. 7.)
units.tr: (1) Most beautiful ... most necessary ... [Καλλιστον ... ἀναγκαιοτατον ...] (Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica, book 8, chapter 7.)

units.la: (2) Os ἰδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς ... ὁ νόμον ... sin. monet Reverendissimus Primas. Locus est istiusmodi. (3) Hoc in magni cujusdam & eximii operis loco ponendum Legislator putavit; ut non caeteris modo rebus tam intermittendis quàm gerendis idonei, sed etiam ut patriarum legum & consuetudinum gnari peritique forent. Quid igitur septimis illis diebus instituit? Eos nimirum eundem in locum unà convenire voluit; ut silentio summâque cum modestia confidentes, legum recitationi aures accommodent, itaque nihil ipsos omnino fugiat. Atque hunc illi conveniendi simul confidendique morem sic perpetuò retinent, ut multitudo quidem universa sileat; nisi cùm ea quae leguntur, faustis ac laetis acclamationibus prosequuntur: è Sacerdotibus autem vel Senioribus aliqui, sacras Leges palàm recitans, omnes sigillatim exponat; donec altà jam vesperà discedant universi, tum divinorum mandatorum instructi cognitione, tum etiam admodum pietate aucti. Nunquid hoc quovis studii genere magis tibi necessarium videtur? Eninverò causae nihil est, quamobrem istos legum Ennarratores de rebus agendis consulant; (seu potiùs, Necesse igitur non habent, ut Mystas de rebus agendis consultum veniant,) quorum ut responsis careant; nihil tamen, vel apud se unquàm, earum ignoratione perperam molientur. Quemcunque enim ipsorum appellaveris (melius, compellaveris) ac de patriis institutis percontatus eris; cùm respondere per se commodè ac facile poterit; & ejusmodi sanè videbitur, quis seu vir uxorem, seu liberos pater, seu famulos dominus, legum notione informare queat.
units.tr: (2) [Who taught us ... the law ...] The Most Reverend Primate notes this, and the passage is of this kind. (3) The Lawgiver thought this should be placed in the course of a great and excellent work: that men should be fit not only for the other matters, to be left off as well as undertaken, but also should be learned and skilled in the laws and customs of their country. What, then, did he establish on those seven days? He wished, of course, that they should come together at the same place; so that, keeping silence and with the greatest modesty, they might give their ears to the recitation of the laws, and so nothing at all might escape them. And they keep this custom of coming together and listening in such a way that the whole multitude is silent, except when they accompany what is read with favourable and joyful acclamations; and one of the priests or elders, reading the sacred laws openly, explains them all one by one, until at last, when evening is far advanced, all depart, instructed in the knowledge of the divine commandments and also greatly increased in piety. Does anything seem more necessary to you than this kind of study? Indeed there is no reason why they should consult these expounders of the laws about the business of life (or rather, they have no need that initiates should come for consultation about affairs), and although they lack their answers, they nevertheless never act wrongly through ignorance of them. For whomever of them you address (or rather, accost) and ask about the ancestral customs, he will be able to answer readily and easily for himself; and it will certainly appear that whoever is a husband, a father with children, or a master with servants, can be informed by knowledge of the laws.

units.la: Apponi etiam meretur locus Philonis in libro de Agricultura, quo necessitatem intellectus in precibus adhibendi asserit. Sic igitur ille libro dicto, paulò ante med. Duo chori, ille quidem virorum, iste verò mulierum, ex adverso invicem stantes, alternam Deo harmoniam modulenter. (4) Virorum equidem chorum ducet Moses, i. e. intellectus perfectus; mulierum Maria, i. e. sensus purificatus.
units.tr: The passage of Philo in the book On Husbandry should also be added, where he asserts the necessity of using the understanding in prayers. Thus he says in the book mentioned, a little before the middle: Two choirs, the one of men, the other of women, standing opposite each other, sing in alternation a harmony to God. Moses will lead the choir of men, that is, the perfect understanding; Mary that of women, that is, the purified sense.

units.la: (3) Πεῖς ἔργα μεγάλα ἢ δαιμασιῶν πυ... μᾶλλον ἀναξηρία αὐτῆς; — ὅτι ἐκ αὐτῆν κινεῖς, ἢ οὐ τῶν πατέρων διατωδάτη, ... (illegible Greek; transcription uncertain)
units.tr: (3) [Πεῖς ἔργα μεγάλα ἢ δαιμασιῶν πυ... μᾶλλον ἀναξηρία αὐτῆς; — ὅτι ἐκ αὐτῆν κινεῖς, ἢ οὐ τῶν πατέρων διατωδάτη, ...] (The Greek is too garbled in the transcription to be translated reliably.)

units.la: (4) Χρίσοι ἢ ὁ μὲ τῆς ἀνδρῶν χορῷ ἡγεμόνις Μωσῆς, τῷ πελεία. ὁ ἢ τῆς γυναικῶν Μαρίαν, αἰσθήσει καθαρθεῖσαι. (Greek; transcription uncertain) Justum enim est intelligibiliter & sensibiliter Deo hymnos dici, gratiarum actionem imperturbatè fieri, & utrumque instrumentum concinnè pulsari, tàm Intellectum quàm Sensum, in solius Dei Servatoris laudem & gloriam.
units.tr: Moses led the men's choir with the lyre [Χρίσοι ... πελεία], and Miriam led the women's, purified by the sound [ὁ ἢ τῆς γυναικῶν Μαρίαν, αἰσθήσει καθαρθεῖσαι]. For it is right that hymns be sung to God both intelligently and audibly, that thanksgiving be offered without distraction, and that both instruments be struck in harmony, the mind as well as the voice, for the praise and glory of God alone, the Saviour.

units.la: Philoni & Josepho Eusebium adjiciam, quo nemo è Christianis antiquis Judæorum disciplinam melius novit. Is libro Præparationum Evangelicarum duodecimo omnia in civitate bene instituta à Platone requisita inter Judæos reperiri probans; istud etiam, quod Plato in primis flagitat, illis non deesse asserit, quòd pueri patriis legibus & disciplinâ diligenter instruantur. Sæpius id disciplinæ genus à Judæis maximopere excoli affirmat, præsertim verò, cap. 17. ubi hæc habet: (5) Quem sanè morem Juniores omnes pietatis ac religionis præceptis informandi, etiam olim Hebræi tenuerunt, & hucusque tanquam patrium aliquod institutum Judæa natio summâ diligentiâ studioque conservat.
units.tr: I will add Eusebius to Philo and Josephus, since no one among the ancient Christians knew the discipline of the Jews better. In the twelfth book of his Preparation for the Gospel, he shows that everything Plato requires of a well-ordered state is found among the Jews. He also asserts that what Plato above all demands, that children be carefully instructed in the laws and discipline of their country, was not lacking among them. He often affirms that the Jews cultivated this kind of discipline with the greatest zeal, and especially in chapter 17, where he says: Indeed, all the young were formed in the precepts of piety and religion by this custom, which the Hebrews of old also kept, and to this day the Jewish nation preserves it with the greatest diligence and care, as a kind of ancestral institution.

units.la: Consuetudinem istam Judæos sequentibus etiam seculis constanter retinuisse, Theodoreti & Maimonidis autoritas confirmat. Ille igitur postquam linguam Hebraicam Judæis vernaculam esse jamdiu desiisse præfatus esset, adeò ut cunčti linguis cujusque gentis, in quâ versabantur, uterentur: hæc habet. Judæorum igitur liberi Hebraicam linguam nequaquam à primâ nativitate usurpant, linguam autem illis, apud quos nati sunt, propriam. (6) Dein adolescentes facti literarum Hebraicarum characteres erudiuntur. Literarum scientiam nacti, harum ope S. Scripturam, quæ Hebraicâ linguâ exarata est, addiscunt. Maimonides (7) autem, cui soli inter Rabbinos, sanum fuisse cerebrum videtur; morem apud Judæos à Patribus receptum & religiosè observatum fuisse tradit; ut quilibet Judæus unicum saltem eumque integrum S. Scripturæ Codicem manu propriâ describere teneretur; etiamsi plures aliunde Codices possideret vel ære emptos, vel donatos, vel hæreditate transmissos.
units.tr: That the Jews who followed them retained this custom constantly in later centuries is confirmed by the authority of Theodoret and Maimonides. Theodoret, after remarking that Hebrew had long ceased to be the vernacular language of the Jews, so that they all used the language of whatever nation they lived among, says this: Therefore Jewish children by no means use the Hebrew language from their first birth, but the language proper to those among whom they are born. (6) Then, when they have grown into young people, they are taught the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Having gained knowledge of the letters, by their means they learn the Holy Scripture, which is written in the Hebrew language. Maimonides (7), who alone among the rabbis seems to have had a sound mind, relates that it was a custom among the Jews, received from the fathers and religiously observed, that every Jew was bound to copy out with his own hand at least one complete copy of Holy Scripture, even if he possessed several other copies, whether bought, given, or inherited.

units.la: (5) Ὁ δὲ ἡ αρέσκει ... &c.
units.tr: But he, ... &c. [Ὁ δὲ ἡ αρέσκει ... &c.]

units.la: (6) Μεγάλα γινόμενα διδάσκει ...
units.tr: Great things becoming ... he teaches ... [Μεγάλα γινόμενα διδάσκει ...]

units.la: (7) Locus non occurrit. Vide tamen Morè Nevochim, lib. 3. cap. 56.
units.tr: (7) The passage does not occur. See however the Guide of the Perplexed, part 3, chapter 56.

units.la: Quæst. 60. in Genesin.
units.tr: Question 60 on Genesis.

units.la: Verùm enimvero non melius dignosci queat Ecclesiae Judaicae sententia de Scripturis vernaculâ linguâ legendis, quàm ex innumeris ferè, quae à Judaeis adornatae sunt, Scripturarum Versionibus. Voluit Deus, ut populus legem sibi divinitus datam jugi memoriâ tenerent & excolerent. Id Mosi, id Prophetis omnibus in mandatis dederat; ut populum ad assiduum legis studium excitarent. Patribus familias sub gravi poenâ injunctum est, ut filios eam edocerent: Sacerdotibus jussum, ut eam populo statis temporibus solenniter praelegerent; Regibus, ut exemplar ejus sibi compararent, quod assiduâ lectione & meditatione tererent; omni denique hominum ordini, ut eam jugi studio sibi familiarem facerent. Quoties itaque lingua Judaeis, seu captivitate, seu peregrino incolatu, mutata est; toties iis necesse fuit S. Scripturam in linguas sibi vernaculas convertere; & toties sanè eam ab illis revera conversam repetimus.
units.tr: Indeed, the opinion of the Jewish Church about reading Scripture in the vernacular cannot be better discerned than from the almost countless versions of the Scriptures that the Jews have produced. God willed that the people should keep and cherish the law given to them by divine revelation in constant remembrance. This Moses and all the Prophets had commanded, that they should stir the people to a constant study of the law. Heads of families were charged under severe penalty to teach it to their sons; priests were ordered to read it aloud to the people solemnly at fixed times; kings were to procure a copy for themselves, to wear out by constant reading and meditation; and finally every order of men was to make it familiar to themselves by unceasing application. Therefore, whenever the language of the Jews was changed, whether by captivity or by living as strangers abroad, it was necessary for them to turn Holy Scripture into their own vernacular; and so often, certainly, we find that they really did translate it.

units.la: Primam itaque mutationem passa est Judaeorum lingua in captivitate Babylonicâ. Ex diuturno enim inter Chaldaeos incolatu & commercio factum est; ut linguae patriae usum paulatim remitterent, & Chaldaicè loqui inciperent. Vel si qui forsan Hebraicae linguae notitiam retinerent (quod quidem ut sedulo facerent, legis divinae studium impulit) legendi tamen scribendive Hebraicè peritia apud omnes ferè exolevit, utpote diversis characteribus apud Chaldaeos receptis jamdiu assuefactos. Veteres enim Hebraeorum characteres, quibus ante captivitatem Babylonicam utebantur, alios fuisse ab illis, quibus hodie utimur, & Samaritanis communes, apud omnes Eruditos in confesso jam est. Quò melius igitur S. Scriptura populo innotesceret, Prophetae illius temporis, qui extra Judaeam scripserunt, Chaldaicè etiam scribendum putarunt. Hinc maxima Danielis libri pars Chaldaicâ linguâ exarata est, hinc & Ezrae libri pars potior Chaldaicè conscripta, post reditum à captivitate quidem, ante immutatos tamen characteres antiquos. Post reductos enim à captivitate Judaeos, Ezras, quem divino motum afflatu omnes nôrunt, ut ignorantiae popularium, qui linguam pariter ac characterem Hebraicum Chaldaico commutârunt, saltem ex parte subveniret, & legis scientiam faciliorem redderet; sacram Scripturam Chaldaicis literis exarandam curavit, depositis antiquioribus Hebraicae linguae characteribus, qui populi notitiam jamdiu effugerant; & exinde Samaritanis, à quibus semper retenti fuerant, proprii esse coeperunt. Addunt Judaei & è Patribus nonnulli, id communi Sacerdotum ac Seniorum decreto factum.
units.tr: The first change in the Jewish language came during the Babylonian captivity. From a long residence and dealings among the Chaldeans it came about that they gradually lost the use of their native tongue and began to speak Chaldean. Even if some retained a knowledge of Hebrew (which the zeal for the divine law indeed urged them to do diligently), the skill of reading and writing Hebrew nearly died out among almost everyone, since they had long been accustomed to the different letters current among the Chaldeans. That the ancient Hebrew characters, which they used before the Babylonian captivity, were different from those we use today, and were the same as those of the Samaritans, is now admitted by all the learned. So that Scripture might be better known to the people, the prophets of that time who wrote outside Judea thought they should also write in Chaldean. Hence the greater part of the book of Daniel is written in the Chaldean language, and hence most of the book of Ezra is also written in Chaldean, after the return from captivity, but before the ancient characters were changed. For after the Jews were brought back from captivity, Ezra, whom everyone knows was moved by divine inspiration, arranged for Holy Scripture to be written in Chaldean letters, to help at least in part the ignorance of the common people, who had replaced the Hebrew language and script with Chaldean, and to make the knowledge of the law easier. He set aside the older Hebrew characters, which had long escaped the people's knowledge; and from then on they began to belong to the Samaritans, by whom they had always been kept. The Jews and some of the Fathers add that this was done by the common decree of the priests and elders.

units.la: Nugas igitur agit nuperus Bibliothecæ Rabbinicæ conditor Pontificius; Julius Bartoloccius de Celleno, Hebraicæ linguæ apud Romam Professor; qui ut impio Ecclesiæ Romanæ decreto de Scripturis vernaculè non legendis autoritatem ex Judaicæ Ecclesiæ exemplo conciliaret, S. Scripturæ lectionem plebi Judaicæ olim interdictam fuisse affirmare non veretur . Id montstri ut credibile efficiat, miram planè de punctis Hebraicis hypothesin proponit; ea nempe à primâ linguæ Hebraicæ origine in usu fuisse, & Moisis ævo probè nota; S. Scripturæ autem codices sine iis consultò exaratos fuisse: ut propterea nonnisi à peritioribus doctioribusque legi atque addisci possent; neve quis idiota sine Magistro & Directore legem pervolvere & disciplinam patriam scire valeret; adeóque ad Sacerdotes scisciturus confugere cogeretur. Puncta interim in Scripturis profanis & civilibus passim usurpata fuisse "Neque enim "erat conveniens (inquit) ut sacra Dei lex communis & vulgaris "efficeretur; ne sacra Legis mysteria ab imperito vulgo contaminarentur sinistrâ & falsâ interpretatione. Evidenter itaque patet "S. Scripturæ mysteria plebi propalata non fuisse in Veteri Lege, "neque authenticum S. Scripturæ Codicem vulgari linguâ in manus "vulgi traditum esse antiquitus. Hinc usus in Ecclesiâ Catholicâ "semper fuit, ut nullâ aliâ linguâ essent authentica sacra volumina "nisi linguis illis, quæ à summis Pontificibus, Conciliis, &c. approbatæ fuerunt. Ea sunt Hebræa, Græca & Latina, quas Dominus "titulo suæ Crucis honoravit, ac quibus ipsi libri ab Auctoribus suis "initio scripti fuerunt. Apage nugas nugerrimas, nec farfari folio dignas. Tantam quidem punctorum Hebraicorum antiquitatem; ne hodiernorum Rabbinorum, qui plus solito iracundi esse solent, inimicitias provocem impræsentiarum negare nolim. Id tantum dixerim, omnia Authori nostro, quæ ponit, incredibilia, tutò concedi posse; frivolum tamen & inane esse commentum. Neque enim populum à Scripturæ scientiâ removebit punctorum defectus in linguâ vernacula; qualem tunc fuisse Hebræum in confesso est. Puncta in plurimis Orientalibus linguis deesse notum est, neque in communi etiam usu adhiberi; & sanè bardus omnium stultissimus sit necesse erit, qui maternæ linguæ, solis consonantibus descriptæ, vocales proprias ap-
units.tr: So the recent founder of the Rabbinical Library, the Papist Giulio Bartolocci of Celleno, professor of Hebrew at Rome, talks nonsense. In order to lend authority, from the example of the Jewish Church, to the impious decree of the Roman Church against reading Scripture in the vernacular, he does not hesitate to assert that the reading of Scripture was once forbidden to the Jewish people. To make this monstrous claim seem credible, he proposes a remarkably odd hypothesis about the Hebrew points: that they were in use from the very origin of the Hebrew language and well known in the time of Moses, but that the codices of Scripture were deliberately written without them, so that they could be read and learned only by the more skilled and learned, and so that no ignorant person could go through the law and know the national discipline without a teacher and guide, and would thus be forced to resort to the priests for answers. Meanwhile, he says, the points were used everywhere in profane and civil writings. "For it was not fitting," he says, "that the sacred law of God should become common and vulgar, lest the mysteries of the sacred Law be defiled by the ignorant crowd through a perverse and false interpretation. It is therefore clearly evident that the mysteries of Scripture were not made known to the people in the Old Law, nor was the authentic codex of Scripture handed over in the vernacular into the hands of the people in ancient times. Hence it has always been the custom in the Catholic Church that the sacred volumes should be authentic in no other languages than those approved by the supreme Pontiffs, Councils, etc. These are Hebrew, Greek and Latin, which the Lord honoured with the title of his Cross, and in which the books were first written by their authors." Away with these most trifling trifles, not worthy even of a leaf of farfarum! Indeed, I am not willing to deny so great an antiquity of the Hebrew points, lest I provoke at present the enmity of the modern rabbis, who are wont to be more irritable than usual. I will only say this: all the things our author puts forward may safely be granted as incredible; yet it is a frivolous and empty invention. For the lack of points in the vernacular language will not remove the people from knowledge of Scripture; that the Hebrew of the time was of that kind is admitted. It is well known that points are lacking in most Oriental languages, and are not even used in common practice; and surely the greatest dolt would have to be one who did not know how to supply the proper vowels for his mother tongue, written only with consonants.

units.la: a Biblioth. Rabbin. pars 1. Romæ, 1675. £ p. 143. b P. 160, 161. ponere non noverit. Omnimodam interim sacri, & prophani sive communis, characteris apud Judæos distinctionem invictè refutavit Eruditissimus Waltonus in Prolegomenis ad Biblia Polyglotta Londinensia, cap. 3. §. 34, &c. Vereor adhuc ne versioni etiam Latinæ, quam authenticam declarárunt boni Patres Tridentini, dicam ineluctabilem intulerit plùs æquo diligens Bartoloccius; dum nullas in Scripturâ sacrâ linguas adhiberi velit; nisi quibus Authores ejus initio usi sunt. Quis enim unquam de S. Scripturæ libro Latinè primùm conscripto inaudiverit! Verùm aliter Judæis antiquis visum esse, sanctissimorum Prophetarum Danielis & Ezræ Exemplis probatum dedimus, qui Chaldaicè populo Chaldaicè loquenti scripserunt; præsertim autem Ezræ, qui S. Scripturam Chaldaicis characteribus in usum vulgi describi fecit; quòd nec ipse Bartoloccius diffitetur, qui puncta sacris Codicibus ab Esdrâ primum apposita fuisse docet, non illis quidem, qui in Arcâ sacrâ asservabantur, id nefas enim fuisse somniat, sed illis, qui communiter & à vulgaribus hominibus attrectabantur, & in locis privatis legebantur.
units.tr: a Bibliotheca Rabbinica, part 1, Rome, 1675, p. 143. b P. 160, 161. ... to supply. Meanwhile, the most learned Walton, in the Prolegomena to the London Polyglot Bible, chapter 3, §34 and following, has invincibly refuted the complete distinction among the Jews between sacred and profane or common script. I still fear that Bartolocci, being more careful than is right, has brought in an unavoidable consequence even for the Latin version, which the good Fathers of Trent declared authentic; since he wishes no languages to be used in Holy Scripture except those in which its authors first wrote. For who has ever heard of a book of Holy Scripture first written in Latin! But we have shown by the examples of the most holy prophets Daniel and Ezra that it seemed otherwise to the ancient Jews, since they wrote in Chaldean for a people who spoke Chaldean; especially Ezra, who had Holy Scripture written in Chaldean characters for the use of the common people. Bartolocci himself does not deny this, since he teaches that the points were first added to the sacred codices by Ezra, not indeed to those kept in the sacred Ark (for he dreams that this would have been sacrilege), but to those that were commonly handled by ordinary people and read in private places.

units.la: Neque verò officio & commissæ sibi animarum curæ satis fecisse rata est Ecclesia Judaica; nisi sacram Scripturam tam linguâ quàm literis Chaldaicis populo donaret. Ab Ezræ enim temporibus invaluit consuetudo, ut in Synagogis in singulis Sabbatis in lectione Parasciæ seu portionis S. Scripturæ, priùs legeretur versiculus Hebraicè, deinde idem repeteretur vernaculè, i. e. Chaldaicè (teste Eliâ Levitâ Præsat. in Methurgeman.) Nec absimile veri est morem istum etiam ante reditum, populo in captivitate adhuc posito, coepisse. Utut quandocunque coeperit, in omnibus postea Judæorum Synagogis obtinuisse constat. Id ex traditione desumptum testantur Rabbini; id narrant Scriptores Judæi melioris notæ, id Patres Christiani produnt; id plura Novi Testamenti loca non obscurè innuunt; id denique constans perque tot ætates continuata Judæorum praxis confirmat. Isti enim ubique terrarum S. Scripturæ periochas primò Hebraicè legunt (id enim religioni habent) dein easdem linguâ quàdam communi ab omnibus intellectâ ordine reddunt. Sunt qui Hellenistas Judæos, missō penitus textu Hebræo, Græcam solummodò LXX. Versionem in Synagogis suis legisse volunt. Verùm id
units.tr: The Jewish Church did not think it had fulfilled its duty and the care of souls entrusted to it unless it gave Holy Scripture to the people in the Chaldee language as well as in Chaldee script. From the time of Ezra it became the custom in the synagogues, on every Sabbath during the reading of the parashah, or portion of Scripture, first to read a verse in Hebrew and then to repeat the same verse in the vernacular, that is, in Chaldee (on the testimony of Elias the Levite, in the preface to the Methurgeman). It is not unlikely that this custom began even before the return, while the people were still in captivity. Whenever it began, it is agreed that it was afterwards established in all the synagogues of the Jews. The rabbis testify that this practice derives from tradition; the more reputable Jewish writers relate it; the Christian Fathers report it; several passages of the New Testament clearly hint at it; and the constant practice of the Jews, continued through so many ages, confirms it. For they everywhere read the passages of Holy Scripture first in Hebrew (for they regard this as a religious duty), and then render them in order into a common language understood by all. Some hold that the Hellenist Jews, with the Hebrew text entirely set aside, read in their synagogues only the Greek version of the Seventy. But this is not very certain.

units.la: {c} In Addend. pag. 741. parùm certum. Textum autem Hebræum Doctores & Sacerdotes Judæos populo inter legendum interpretari solitos, ipsa Philonis verba ex Eusebio nuper adducta docent; qui lectionem S. Scripturæ in Synagogis factam referens, inquit: E sacerdotibus autem vel Senioribus aliquis, sacras Leges palàm recitans, omnes sigillatim exponit, ἀναγινώσκει τὰς ἱερὰς γραμμὰς αὐτῆς, ἐξ ἀπὸ ἑκάστου ἑρμηνεύει.
units.tr: {c} In the Addenda, p. 741. The Hebrew text, however, was customarily explained to the people by the Jewish teachers and priests as it was read; the very words of Philo, cited lately from Eusebius, show this. Describing the reading of Scripture in the synagogues, he says: And one of the priests or elders, reading aloud the sacred laws, explains them all one by one [ἀναγινώσκει τὰς ἱερὰς γραμμὰς αὐτῆς, ἐξ ἀπὸ ἑκάστου ἑρμηνεύει].

units.la: Ex more isthoc apud Judæos recepto factum est; ut plures S. Scripturæ Versiones Chaldaicæ procuderentur, & scriptis commissæ evulgarentur. Integrum enim publico Lectori fuit interpretationem legis seu ex tempore fusam seu ex scripto recitatam in Synagogis dare. Atque adeò scriptam extitisse Pentateuchi Versionem Chaldaicam & in usu Judæis fuisse etiam ante reditum à captivitate Babylonicâ non immeritò conjicit ipse Bartoloccius; cùm in ipsâ captivitate Babylonicâ populus Hebraeus Chaldaicè loqui didicerit, relictâ lingua Hebraâ & in Chaldaam commutatâ, in quam & Pentateuchus Hebraicus translatus est, in linguam sc. vernaculam & ab omnibus intellectam. Versiones istæ à Judæis dictæ sunt Targumim seu Paraphrases, quæ tamen plerunque Translationes sunt satis justæ; plurimæque hodienum extant in omnes S. Scripturæ libros, exceptis Danielc, & Ezrâ; qui cùm Chaldaicè ferè scripti sint, Chaldaicâ interpretatione non egebant. Inter has binæ antiquitatis speciem præ se non vanam ferunt, una in Pentateuchum, quæ Onkeli dicitur, altera in Prophetas omnes, quæ Jonathani Ben Uzzielis ascribitur. Utraque circa Christi tempora confecta censetur. Certè antiquas admodum esse & longè ante Talmudem factas, insignis linguæ Chaldaicæ puritas, quâ Talmudem longè superant, demonstrat. Habetur utraque in Editione Bibliorum Venetâ Danielis Bombergi secundâ & tertiâ, in editione Antverpiensi Ariæ Montani, Parisianâ Michaelis de Jay anno 1645. & Londinensi Waltoni 1657. Recentius est Targum Pentateuchi Hierosolymitanum; quod ab incerto Authore compositum est dialecto eâdem quâ & Talmud, sc. Syro-Hierosolymitanâ, quâ post excidium Templi usi sunt Judæi. Eodem tempore, quo & Talmud scriptum fuisse vult Elias in Methutgeman sc. trecentis post excidium Templi annis: Buxtorfius & Waltonus paulò post Talmud (quod in illo citatur) sc. quingentis post Christum natum annis.
units.tr: From this custom, received among the Jews, it came about that many Chaldee versions of Scripture were produced and, once committed to writing, were made public. For it was open to the public reader to give in the synagogues an interpretation of the law, either improvised or read from a written text. Hence Bartoloccius himself rightly conjectures that a written Chaldee version of the Pentateuch existed and was in use among the Jews even before the return from the Babylonian captivity: since in the Babylonian captivity itself the Hebrew people learned to speak Chaldee, the Hebrew language having been abandoned and changed into Chaldee, into which the Hebrew Pentateuch was also translated, namely into the vernacular language, understood by all. These versions the Jews call Targumim, or Paraphrases, though for the most part they are fairly faithful translations. Most of them survive today, covering all the books of Scripture except Daniel and Ezra, which, being written almost entirely in Chaldee, did not need a Chaldee interpretation. Among these, two bear a not empty appearance of antiquity: one on the Pentateuch, called Onkelos, and another on all the Prophets, ascribed to Jonathan Ben Uzziel. Both are thought to have been composed around the time of Christ. That they are very ancient, and were written long before the Talmud, the remarkable purity of their Chaldee, by which they far surpass the Talmud, clearly shows. Both are found in the second and third Venetian Bible of Daniel Bomberg, in the Antwerp edition of Arias Montanus, in the Paris edition of Michael de Jay of 1645, and in the London edition of Walton of 1657. More recent is the Jerusalem Targum on the Pentateuch, composed by an unknown author in the same dialect as the Talmud, namely Syro-Jerusalemite, which the Jews used after the destruction of the Temple. Elias, in the Methurgeman, holds that it was written at the same time as the Talmud, that is, three hundred years after the destruction of the Temple; Buxtorf and Walton, a little after the Talmud (which is cited in it), that is, about five hundred years after the birth of Christ.

units.la: Pag. 406. Extat in Tomo 4. Bibliorum Polyglottorum Londinensium. Paulò inferioris aetatis esse videtur Targum in Hagiographa, quod R. Josè seu Josepho Cæco inscribitur. De Authore tamen haud adeò constat. Linguâ Syro-Hierosolymitanâ utitur; & à Sixto Senensi circa annum Christi 400. à Buxtorfio circa annum 600. confectum putatur. Reperitur in editionibus omnibus Bibliorum supra memoratis. Porrò Jonathan Ben Uzzielis dicitur scripsisse etiam Targum in Hagiographa, quod interiit; & aliud in Pentateuchum, quod sub illius nomine prodiit à Judaeis editum Hanoviae 1591. & à Manasse Ben Israel 1640. & in Bibliis Londinensis Tom. 4. Verum istud Jonathani neutiquam deberi censent Criticorum pars potior. Alia praterea innumera fuerunt Targumim (R. Akilas enim scripsit Targum in Prophetas & Hagiographa, ut alios taceam) ex quibus quaedam penitus interierunt, aliquorum fragmenta supersunt, nonnulla MSS. delitescunt. Prodiit nuper in Germania typis excusa Paraphrasis Chaldaica in primum librum Paralipomenon. Parem in secundum etiam se aliquando edituros spondent Typographi. Illae enim in prioribus Paraphrasibus deerant. Antiquiores enim Judaei libros Paralipomenon, eò quod in libris Regum fere toti contineantur, Chaldaicè interpretari insuper habuerunt.
units.tr: Page 406. It is found in volume 4 of the London Polyglot Bible. The Targum on the Hagiographa, which is inscribed as that of Rabbi Jose, or Joseph the Blind, seems to be of somewhat later date. Yet about its author there is not much certainty. It uses the Syro-Jerusalemite language, and it is thought by Sixtus of Siena to have been produced around the year 400 after Christ, and by Buxtorf around the year 600. It is found in all the editions of the Bible mentioned above. Furthermore, Jonathan Ben Uzziel is said to have also written a Targum on the Hagiographa, which has perished; and another on the Pentateuch, which appeared under his name, published by the Jews at Hanau in 1591, and by Manasseh Ben Israel in 1640, and in volume 4 of the London Bible. But most critics hold that this one is in no way due to Jonathan. Besides these there were countless other Targumim (for Rabbi Akiba wrote a Targum on the Prophets and the Hagiographa, not to mention others). Some of them have been utterly lost, fragments of some survive, and some lie hidden in manuscripts. Recently there appeared, printed in Germany, a Chaldee paraphrase on the first book of Chronicles. The printers promise that they will one day publish a similar one on the second. For these were lacking in the earlier Paraphrases; the older Jews had thought it unnecessary to render the books of Chronicles into Chaldee, since they are for the most part contained in the books of Kings.

units.la: Hactenus de Versionibus Judaeorum Chaldaicis. Post fundatum Macedonum imperium, in omnibus fere Orientis regionibus Graeca lingua communis esse coepit; & Judaeis, qui relictâ patriâ, in universis regni Macedonici civitatibus magno numero confederant, vernacula est facta. In horum igitur usum evulgata fuit Versio illa celeberrima, quae οἱ ο′ audit. An Ptolomaeo Philadelpho procurante & sumptus suppeditante facta fuerit ista Versio, parum ad rem nostram spectat; cùm id satis constet, à quocunque demum facta fuerit, in usum Judaeorum factam fuisse, & à Judaeis maximâ veneratione susceptam, in Synagogis praelectam, & divino afflatu consectam credi. Ipse Rex Ptolomaeus (modò is illius adornandae Author fuerit) se id operis in Judaeorum ubique terrarum habitantium utilitatem aggredi profitetur. Sic enim ille in Epistola ad Eleazarum Pontificem apud Aristeam c & Eusebium f. Βουλόμενον δ' ἡμῶν χαρίζεσθαι τῶν τῆς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ Ἰουδαίων ἐν τῇ πατρίδι, ἐκκομίσασθαι δ' νόμον ἀμφὶ μεταφρμωῒ δῶναι χρῆμα πεπαν ἰλλιπνωῖς ἐπ ἡμῖ μὲ ὑμῖν λεγομένων ἱερωτῶν χαμάπᾶν.
units.tr: So much for the Chaldee versions of the Jews. After the founding of the Macedonian empire, Greek began to be the common language in almost all the regions of the East, and it became the vernacular of the Jews, who, having left their homeland, had settled in large numbers in the cities of the Macedonian kingdom. It was therefore for their use that that most famous version, called the Seventy, was published. Whether it was made at the instigation and expense of Ptolemy Philadelphus is of little concern to our purpose; for it is sufficiently established that, by whomever it was made, it was made for the use of the Jews, was received by them with the greatest veneration, was read in the synagogues, and is believed to have been produced under divine inspiration. King Ptolemy himself (if he was indeed the author of its preparation) professes that he undertakes this work for the benefit of the Jews living everywhere in the world. For he says so in his letter to Eleazar the High Priest, preserved by Aristeas and Eusebius: [Βουλόμενον δ᾽ ἡμῶν χαρίζεσθαι τῶν τῆς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ Ἰουδαίων ἐν τῇ πατρίδι, ἐκκομίσασθαι δὲ νόμον ἀμφὶ μεταφρμωῒ δῶναι χρῆμα πεπαν ἰλλιπνωῖς ἐπ ἡμῖ μὲ ὑμῖν λεγομένων ἱερωτῶν χαμάπᾶν] — the Greek is corrupt here.

units.la: Cùm cupiamus gratificari omnibus Judæis in orbe terrarum, illis etiam qui sunt in posterum futuri ; constituimus Legem vestram ex Hebraica lingua interpretatione traducere in Græcam. Et egregiam quidem consilii sui rationem exhibet in Epistola ad Eleazarum & Synedrium Judaicum secunda, apud Epiphanium Θεσαυροὶ κεκρυμμένοι ἡ μηνὸς ἰζοσεκκακέμενοι τῆς ἀφελείας· — ἀλλ᾽ ἡ μὲ ἐνναμίνουν ἀναγκάσαι χρήματα τῶτον, ὡς ἔσῖν ὄφελος ἡμῶν χρείαν. Occulti thesauri & obsignati fontis quanam esse potest utilitas? — Nam cùm scriptas in his (libris S. Scripturæ) literas legere nequeamus; nulli esse nobis usui & emolumento possunt. Et sanè Ptolomæi Philadelphi studio adornatam esse LXX. versionem vix dubitandum censeo. Non illubens equidem concedo Aristeæ Historiam ab Impostore quodam Judæo longè post Philadelphi tempora confictam esse; ante Philonis tamen & Josephi tempora, à quibus laudatur, emissam constat. Forsitan nec melioris census, antiquior tamen, est Aristobuli liber de rebus Judaicis, Ptolomæo Philometori nuncupatus; qui apud Josephum, Clementem Alex. & Eusebium passim citatur, eandemque historiam narrat. Tanto quidem rerum apparatu, tam magnificis cæremoniis procuratam esse à Philadelphio τὴν Versionem, fabulam sapit Judaicam. Incredibile tamen prorsus videtur, aut Pseudo-Aristobulum & PseudoAristean id Historiæ comminisci ausos esse; aut Philonem, qui Alexandriæ versatus est, & Josephum, qui in Græcorum usum scripserit, utrumque notæ gravitatis Scriptorem, eandem scriptis suis divulgare voluisse; nisi id inter Græcos etiam, præsertim Alexandrinos, traditione constaret, ejusmodi Translationem procurante Philadelpho olim factam fuisse; licèt temporis distantia, & Historicorum silentium Aristeæ fabulandi ansam dedisset. Certè Justinus Martyr , testis oculatus, id se Alexandriæ positum ex constanti incolarum traditione didicisse diserte affirmat. Porrò etiam ante celebrem istam LXX. Translationem, extitisse Versionem S. Scripturæ Græcam prodit Aristobulus, & ex eo Clemens Alexandrinus , Justinus Martyr , Eusebius , Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, aliique.
units.tr: Since we desire to do a favour to all the Jews in the world, including those who are yet to be born, we have resolved to translate your Law from the Hebrew language into Greek. And he sets out an excellent rationale for his plan in the second letter to Eleazar and the Jewish Sanhedrin, preserved by Epiphanius: [Θησαυροὶ κεκρυμμένοι καὶ πηγὴ σεσφραγισμένη τίνα τὴν ὠφέλειαν ἔχειν δύναται; — ἀλλὰ ἡμῖν ἐννοήσαντι ἀναγκαῖον ἦν τοῦτο ποιῆσαι, ὡς ἔστιν ὄφελος ἡμῖν χρεία] — Hidden treasures and a sealed fountain, what use can they have? — For since we cannot read the letters written in these books of Scripture, they can be of no use or profit to us. And indeed I hardly doubt that the Septuagint version was undertaken through the zeal of Ptolemy Philadelphus. I readily concede that the history of Aristeas was fabricated by some Jewish impostor long after the time of Philadelphus; yet it is certain that it was published before the times of Philo and Josephus, by whom it is praised. Perhaps the book of Aristobulus on Jewish affairs, dedicated to Ptolemy Philometor, is of no better repute but is nonetheless older; it is cited throughout by Josephus, Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius, and it relates the same story. That the translation was carried out by Philadelphus with such an apparatus of affairs and such magnificent ceremonies smacks of Jewish fable. Yet it seems quite incredible that either the pseudo-Aristobulus or the pseudo-Aristeas dared to invent this history, or that Philo, who lived at Alexandria, and Josephus, who wrote for the Greeks, both writers of serious authority, wished to spread the same story in their writings, unless it had been a matter of common knowledge among the Greeks, especially the Alexandrians, through tradition, that such a translation had once been made under the patronage of Philadelphus; even though the lapse of time and the silence of the historians gave Aristeas occasion to embellish. Certainly Justin Martyr, an eyewitness, expressly affirms that he learned at Alexandria, from the constant tradition of the inhabitants, that this had happened. Moreover, Aristobulus reports that a Greek version of Holy Scripture existed even before this famous translation of the Seventy, and following him Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, Eusebius, Chrysostom, Theodoret and others (say so).

units.la: Nec tamen LXX. Interpretum diligentia, aliorum Judæorum conatibus viam præclusit. Id semper apud Judæos licuit legis scientiam eâ, quâ quisque meliùs poterat, methodo promovere. Hinc plures S. Scripturæ Translationes Græcæ; præsertim post Christum natum, cùm Versio LXX. apud Judæos, seu odio Christianorum, seu studio partium, quibus minùs favere deprehensa est, invisa esse cœpit. Aliam itaque Translationem, ex Hebræo factam, molitus est Aquila Ponticus, Proselytus Judæus, circa annum 130. secundam Theodotion, Apostata Judæus, circa an. 180. tertiam Symmachus circa an. 200. His adde tres Anonymas, quæ in Origenis Octaplo locum habuerunt: quarum una à Studioso quodam Hierosolymitano in doliis Hierichunte reperta est imperante Caracalla; alia Nicopoli ad Actium à quodam Origenis discipulo inventa sub Alexandro Severo; tertia, quæ Psalmos solummodo complexa est, unà cùm Codice Hierichuntino in lucem eruta. De his ita Hieronymus Quinta autem & Sexta & Septima Editio, licet quibus censeantur auctoribus, ignoretur; tamen ita probabilem sui diversitatem tenent, ut authoritatem sine nominibus meruerint. Singulas à Judæis profectas esse minimè dubitari potest; cùm eâ semper veneratione Versionem LXX. Christiani sint secuti; ut aliam Versionem Græcam procudere tantùm non nefas duxerint.
units.tr: Yet the diligence of the Seventy translators did not block the efforts of other Jews. Among the Jews it has always been permitted for each person to advance the knowledge of the Law by whatever method he could manage best. Hence there were several Greek translations of Scripture, especially after the birth of Christ, when the Septuagint, whether from hatred of the Christians or from partisan zeal, was found to favour them less, began to be disliked among the Jews. So Aquila of Pontus, a Jewish proselyte, undertook another translation, made from the Hebrew, around the year 130; the second was by Theodotion, a Jewish apostate, around the year 180; the third by Symmachus around the year 200. To these add three anonymous versions, which had a place in Origen's Octapla: one of which was found in jars at Jericho by a certain Jerusalem student under the emperor Caracalla; another was discovered at Nicopolis near Actium by a certain disciple of Origen under Alexander Severus; a third, which embraced only the Psalms, was brought to light together with the Jericho codex. Of these Jerome says: "The Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Editions, although the authors to whom they are ascribed are unknown, nevertheless hold such a probable variety of their own that they have earned authority without names." That each of these came from Jews cannot be doubted, since Christians have always followed the Septuagint with such reverence that they regarded it as almost sinful to produce another Greek version.

units.la: Postquam Saracenorum armis Religio Mahumetana longè latéque per orbem diffusa esset; lingua Arabica præ aliis invaluit. Circa annum igitur 900. Rabbi Saadias Gaon, Scholæ Judaicæ apud Babylonem Rector, universum Vetus Testamentum ex Hebraico fonte Arabicè convertit, literis tamen Hebraicis; quas diuturnus usus Judæis maximè familiares reddiderat. Prodiit duntaxat Pentateuchum ejus, à Judæis editum in Bibliis suis Constantinopolitanis 1551. sol. Integram se habuisse testatur Erpenius Versionem; quam & editurum se promisit. Nonnullos S. Scripturæ libros ex eâdem Versione penes Cl. Pocockium MSS. extare Waltonus monuit. Alia Pentateuchi Versio Arabica à Judæis Mauris olim facta, cha-
units.tr: After the religion of Mohammed had spread widely across the world by the arms of the Saracens, the Arabic language prevailed over the others. So around the year 900 Rabbi Saadia Gaon, head of the Jewish school at Babylon, translated the whole Old Testament from the Hebrew source into Arabic, but in Hebrew letters, which long use had made especially familiar to the Jews. Only his Pentateuch was published, by the Jews in their Constantinople Bible of 1551. Erpenius testifies that he had a complete version, which he also promised to publish. Waltonus noted that some books of Scripture from the same version exist in manuscript with the distinguished Pococke. Another Arabic version of the Pentateuch, made long ago by Moorish Jews, with characters likewise Hebrew,

Longum esset enumerare omnes, quæ à Judæis elucubratæ sunt, Versiones Scripturæ vernaculas. Paucis abhinc seculis, Jacobus Tusiensis, quem Tawosum & Tusium appellant, Pentateuchum ex Hebraica in Persicam linguam transtulit. Translatio à Judæis Constantinopolitanis excusa est characteribus Hebraicis in Bibliis suis 1551. Habetur & in Appendice ad Tom. 4. Bibliorum Londinensium characteribus Persicis. Judæi Caraitæ S. Scripturam Græca vulgari reddiderunt, & Constantinopoli imprimendam curárunt. Hispanicam Versionem confecit Abraham Usque, Judæus Lusitanus. Excusa est ita à Judæis Ferrariæ 1553. Mitto Translationes Scripturæ Germanicas, Italicas, Gallicas, &c. quæ à Judæis adornatæ in lucem prodierunt.
units.tr: ᵠ Prolegomena to the Polyglot Bible: in Arabic letters, was published by Erpenius at Leiden in 1622, from the library of Joseph Scaliger. It would be long to list all the vernacular versions of Scripture that the Jews have produced. A few centuries ago Jacob of Tus, whom they call Tawosus and Tusius, translated the Pentateuch from the Hebrew into the Persian language. That translation was printed by the Constantinopolitan Jews in Hebrew characters in their Bible of 1551; it is also found in the appendix to the fourth volume of the London Bible, in Persian characters. The Karaite Jews rendered Scripture into the common Greek and had it printed at Constantinople. The Spanish version was made by Abraham Usque, a Portuguese Jew; it was printed by the Jews at Ferrara in 1553. I pass over the German, Italian, French and other translations of Scripture which the Jews prepared and brought out.

units.la: Ne verò Judæos ab Ezræ temporibus in vertendis & evulgandis S. Scripturæ libris à primæva disciplina recessisse arbitremur; ipsi etiam Samaritani, quibus alibi Judæis adversari & obtrectare religio erat, eandem inierunt viam. Hi quidem antiquos characteres Hebraicos tenaciter retinebant; vulgarem tamen linguæ usum, immixtis Cuthæis aliarumque nationum colluvie, paulatim amiterunt. Pentateuchum igitur (id solum enim agnoverunt) ex Hebraica veteri dialecto, seu Hebræo-Samaritana in vernaculam linguam seu Chaldæo-Samaritanam transtulerunt. Versio ista circa Ezræ tempora ab eruditissimo Morino facta censetur. Certè ante Christum factam esse constat. Illam unà cum textu HebræoSamaritano Europæ primus intulit Reverendissimus Armachanus; edidit autem Morinus in Bibliis Parisiensibus 1645. Waltonus in Bibliis Londinensibus 1657. Porrò habuerunt Samaritani, æque ac Judæi, suam Pentateuchi Translationem Græcam, neque minus forsitan vetustam. Illam sæpe memorant Græci Patres antiquiores, præsertim verò Eusebius in Chronico; ubi Patriarcharum Antediluvianorum annos supputans, calculum quendam exhibet. Denique, ut ne his longius immorer, post Mahometis tempora, Samaritani illi, quibus Arabica fuit vernacula,
units.tr: But lest we think that the Jews, from the time of Ezra onward, departed from the primitive discipline in translating and publishing the books of Scripture, the Samaritans themselves, who elsewhere had a religious habit of opposing and disparaging the Jews, followed the same path. They stubbornly retained the ancient Hebrew characters; yet, through the mixing of Cuthaeans and a jumble of other nations, they gradually lost the common use of the language. So they translated the Pentateuch (for they acknowledged only this) from the old Hebrew dialect, that is the Hebrew-Samaritan, into the vernacular language, that is the Chaldee-Samaritan. This version is thought to have been made around the time of Ezra by the very learned Morinus. Certainly it is established that it was made before Christ. The most reverend Archbishop of Armagh was the first to bring it into Europe together with the Hebrew-Samaritan text; Morinus published it in the Paris Bible of 1645, and Walton in the London Bible of 1657. Moreover, the Samaritans, as well as the Jews, had their own Greek translation of the Pentateuch, perhaps no less ancient. The earlier Greek Fathers often mention it, especially Eusebius in his Chronicle, where, reckoning the years of the Antediluvian Patriarchs, he gives a certain calculation. Finally, not to linger longer on these matters: after the time of Mohammed, those Samaritans for whom Arabic was the vernacular

This existed in manuscript in the possession of Ussher, according to Walton, to whom Ussher had communicated it. A double copy of the same is said to be held in the Royal Library of France.

units.la: In disponendâ Authoris istius ætate communem Eruditorum, parùm tamen certum calculum sequor. Id solum apertè liquet, illum Origene (à quo citatur Homil. 15. in Josue) priorem, Christo posteriorem esse. Christianum enim fuisse mihi compertum est; utut nonnulli Judæum fuisse, & Hebraicè scripsisse velint: & Cl. Cave de sectâ ejus haud ita liquidò constare asserat. Sectam quidem Judaicam præ se fert Impostor; ut exinde Judæis fucum piâ fraude faciat, & sub venerandis Patriarcharum nominibus venditet prophetias, quæ Jesum Christum tantùm non digito monstrarent.
units.tr: In fixing the date of this author I follow the opinion common among the learned, though without a very certain reckoning. This alone is clear: he is earlier than Origen (from whom he is cited, Homily 15 on Joshua) and later than Christ. For I have found that he was a Christian, although some want him to have been a Jew who wrote in Hebrew; and the learned Cave asserts that his sect is not very clearly established. The impostor does indeed display a Jewish sect, so that by a pious fraud he may deceive the Jews and, under the venerable names of the Patriarchs, put forward prophecies which all but point to Jesus Christ with a finger.

(4) Honorate Judam & Levi; quoniam ex ipsis vobis orietur Agnus Dei, gratiâ salvans omnes Gentes & Israel. Deiparam enim Matrem ex tribu Levi ortam esse recepta erat apud plerosque Veteres sententia.
