Testimonium est ejusmodi. d Et nunc filii, mando vobis, ut timeatis Dominum Deum vestrum ex toto corde, & ambuletis in simplicitate secundùm omnem legem ipsius. Docete autem filios vestros literas: ut habeant intellectum in omni vitâ eorum, legentes indesinenter Legem Dei. Quoniam omnis qui cognoscit legem Dei, honorabitur; & non erit peregrinus, quocunque vadat. Græca nondum impressa sunt. Reperiuntur autem MSS. penès Illustrissimum Primatem, & clementissimum Patronum meum, Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem; ex cujus Codice locum Græcè apponam. Καὶ ῥυῶ, τέκνα μου, ἐπιτέλλομαι ὑμῖν φοβεῖσθαι Κύριον τὸν Θεὸν ἡμῶν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, καὶ πορεύεσθε ἐπ' ἁπλότητι καρδίας καὶ πάντα τὸν νόμον αὐτοῦ. Διδάσκετε δὲ ὑμεῖς τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν γεάμματα, ἵνα ἔχωσι σύνεσιν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ ζωῇ αὐτῶν, ἀναγινώσκοντες ἀδιαλείπτως τὸν νόμον τοῦ Θεοῦ· ὅτι πᾶς ὁς γνώσεταί νόμον Θεοῦ, τιμηθήσεται, ᾧ ἂν ἔσται ξένος, ὅπου ἀπάγει.
units.tr: But the deceit shows through everywhere, betrayed by plain indications. Whoever reads the book through will gladly come round to my view. Meanwhile I will set out two passages, which will settle the matter well enough and more than enough. So this Planus, in chapter 10, speaking of the future Messiah, says: "(3) Through water God will save Israel and all the nations, hidden in a man." The same author, in chapter 11, says: "(4) Honour Judah and Levi, for from them shall arise for you the Lamb of God, saving all the Gentiles and Israel by grace." For it was the received opinion among many of the Ancients that the Mother of God was born of the tribe of Levi. Many more passages of this kind may be noted near the end of the work, which clearly prove that he was a Christian. We have therefore not without reason admitted him among the Christian witnesses. The testimony is of this kind: "And now, my sons, I charge you to fear the Lord your God with your whole heart, and to walk in simplicity according to all his law. Teach your sons letters, so that they may have understanding in all their life, reading the Law of God unceasingly. For everyone who knows the Law of God will be honoured, and he will not be a stranger wherever he goes." The Greek has not yet been printed. It is found, however, in manuscripts in the possession of the most illustrious Primate, my most gracious Patron, the Archbishop of Canterbury; I will set out the Greek from his codex. [Καὶ νῦν, τέκνα μου, ἐπιτέλλομαι ὑμῖν φοβεῖσθαι Κύριον τὸν Θεὸν ἡμῶν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, καὶ πορεύεσθε ἐπ' ἁπλότητι καρδίας καὶ πάντα τὸν νόμον αὐτοῦ. Διδάσκετε δὲ ὑμεῖς τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν γράμματα, ἵνα ἔχωσι σύνεσιν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ ζωῇ αὐτῶν, ἀναγινώσκοντες ἀδιαλείπτως τὸν νόμον τοῦ Θεοῦ· ὅτι πᾶς ὁ γνωσόμενος νόμον Θεοῦ, τιμηθήσεται, ᾧ ἂν ἔσται ξένος, ὅπου ἀπέρχεται.]

units.la: Stromat. lib. 7. Est ergo quod est hic apud nos altare, (5) terrestris congregatio eorum, qui sunt dedicati orationibus, qui veluti unam vocem habent communem & unam mentem.
units.tr: In his Stromateis, book 7: "There is therefore here among us an altar, (5) the earthly assembly of those who are dedicated to prayers, who have, as it were, one common voice and one mind."

units.la: b In Orthodoxogr. Basil. Tom. 2. p. 887. c Pag. 891. d Cap. 3. post med. p. 870.
units.tr: b In Orthodoxographa, Basil, vol. 2, p. 887. c p. 891. d Chapter 3, after the middle, p. 870.

units.la: (3) Δι' ὕδατος ἔτι σώσει τὸ Ἰσραὴλ ἐν πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ὁ Θεὸς εἰς ἄνδρα ὑποχωρεῖ. (4) πρῶτη ἡ Ἰούδα καὶ ἡ Λευΐ, ὅτι ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἀνατελεῖ ὑμῖν ὁ ἀμνὸς τῷ Θεῷ, χάρειν. (5) Τὸ ἀδροτσμα τῆς ἡ εὐχαῖς ἀναπεμπόμεναι, μίαν ἔχειν φωνὴν τῶν κοινὴν ἐν μίαν γνώμην.
units.tr: (3) Through water God will again save Israel and all the nations, withdrawing into a man. (4) First Judah and Levi, for from him the Lamb of God will rise up for you, bringing grace. (5) Having offered up prayers of the sacrifice, to have one common voice and one mind.

units.la: Ibid. Oportet ergo Deo offerre sacrificia, non sumptuosa ac splendida, sed qua sunt pia & ei accepta; & suffitum illum in lege compositum, qui constat ex multis linguis & vocibus in oratione.
units.tr: Ibid. "It is therefore necessary to offer God sacrifices, not sumptuous and splendid ones, but such as are pious and acceptable to him; and that incense prescribed in the law, which consists of many tongues and voices in prayer."

units.la: Ibid. pag. 758. Hæreticos Gnosticos fusè insequitur; qui plusquam vulgaris scientiæ opinione inflati, Scripturas utpote omnibus notas & infimis etiam Christianis communes insuper habuerunt. Inter alia hæc habet: Cùm viderent ergo sibi imminere periculum, non de uno dogmate sed de conservandâ hæresi; non veritatem invenire (nam cùm ea, quæ sunt in medio posita & in promptu apud nos, legerunt, tanquam vilia ea contempserunt) sed quod est commune in fide, superare contendentes, excessernt à veritate. Nam cùm Ecclesiastica cognitionis non didicerint mysteria, neque veritatis perceperint magnitudinem; ut qui in perscrutando rerum profundo fuerint socordes, & superficie tenus legerint; Scripturas valere jusserunt. Inani ergo sapientiæ opinione elati perpetuò litigant, &c.
units.tr: Ibid. p. 758. He pursues the Gnostic heretics at length, who, puffed up with an opinion of knowledge beyond the ordinary, regarded the Scriptures as things known to all and common even to the lowliest Christians. Among other things he says: "When they saw danger hanging over them, not over one doctrine but over the preservation of their heresy, they did not seek to find the truth (for when they read what lies in the midst and is ready to hand among us, they despised it as cheap), but, striving to surpass what is common in faith, they departed from the truth. For since they have not learned the mysteries of ecclesiastical knowledge, nor grasped the greatness of the truth, being slack in searching the depths of things and reading only on the surface, they bade the Scriptures farewell. Therefore, elated by a vain opinion of wisdom, they quarrel perpetually, etc."

units.la: Lib. 6. post med. Auferunt veram Domini doctrinam, qui non pro dignitate Dei & Domini Scripturas differunt & tradunt. Depositum enim quod Deo redditur, est divina traditionis intelligentia & exercitatio conveniens doctrinæ Domini per Apostolos ejus data.
units.tr: Book 6, after the middle: "They take away the true doctrine of the Lord, who do not expound and hand down the Scriptures in a manner worthy of God and the Lord. For the deposit that is returned to God is the understanding of divine tradition and the fitting practice of the teaching of the Lord given through his Apostles."

units.la: Ibid. Annon enim qua Herma quoque in visione apparuit potestas in typo Ecclesiæ, dedit librum legendum, quem voluit annunciari electis? Eum autem (inquit) transcripsit ad literam, cum non inveniret quomodo finiret syllabas. Significabat utique literam esse omnibus claram, si in nudâ lectione accipiatur; & hanc esse fidem quæ locum obtinet elementorum.
units.tr: Ibid. "Did not also the power which appeared to Hermas in a vision, in the figure of the Church, give a book to be read, which it wished to be announced to the elect? And he (it says) copied it letter by letter, since he could not find how to end the syllables. It signified, surely, that the letter is clear to all if it is taken in a plain reading, and that this is the faith which holds the place of the elements."

units.la: Ibid. Non est ergo versandum in dictione, sed in iis quæ significantur. Nam corvi quoque voces imitantur humanas, cùm ejus rei quam dicunt nullam habeant notitiam. Intelligens autem apprehensio fidem proximè consequitur.
units.tr: Ibid. "One must not therefore dwell on the word, but on what is signified. For ravens too imitate human voices, though they have no knowledge of the thing they say. Intelligent apprehension, however, closely follows faith."

units.tr: (6) "Speaking in many tongues or in voice, in a fitting and orderly prayer."

units.tr: 240. Origen Adamantius

units.la: Homil. 27. in Numer. “ Ita ergo & in cibis rationalibus, divinorum dico voluminum, non continuò aut culpanda aut refutanda “ est Scriptura, quæ difficilior aut obscurior ad intelligendum videtur; vel ea continere, quibus sive incipiens & parvulus, sive “ infirmior & minùs ad intelligenda omnia validus, uti non potest; nec conferri sibi ex iis utilitatis aliquid existimat aut salutis. Sed consiederare debet; quia sicut serpens & ovis & homo, &c. competentem unicuique eorum capiant cibum; ita & hæc omnia quæ verba Dei sunt, & in quibus diversus pro captu animarum cibus est, unusquisque prout sanum se & validum sentit, assumat. Quamvis etsi diligentius requiramus, verbi causâ, in Evangelii lectione, vel Apostolicâ Doctrinâ, in quibus delectari videris, & in quibus tibi aptissimum & suavissimum deputas cibum; quanta sunt, quæ te latent, si discutias & perscruteris mandata Domini? Quòd si ea, quæ obscura videntur & difficilia, refugienda sunt protinus & vitanda; invenies etiam in illis, in quibus valdè confidis, tam multa obscura & difficilia; ut si hanc sententiam teneas, sic tibi etiam inde recedendum. Sunt tamen plurima in illis, quæ apertius & simplicius dicta sunt, quàm ut parvi sensus ædificent auditorem.
units.tr: Homily 27 on Numbers. "So also with rational food, I mean the food of the divine volumes, Scripture should not be condemned or rejected outright because it seems more difficult or obscure to understand, or because it contains things which a beginner or a little child, or one who is weaker and not strong enough to understand everything, cannot make use of, and thinks no benefit or salvation can come to him from them. Rather, he ought to consider that just as the serpent, the sheep and the man, etc., take the food suited to each of them, so too all these things which are the words of God, and in which there is varied food according to the capacity of souls, each person should take as he feels himself sound and strong. Yet if we examine more carefully, for example in the reading of the Gospel or the Apostolic teaching, in which you seem to delight and which you judge to be the most fitting and sweetest food for you, how many things lie hidden from you, if you investigate and search the commandments of the Lord? But if those things which seem obscure and difficult must at once be shunned and avoided, you will find in those things in which you place great trust so many obscure and difficult matters that, if you held to this opinion, you would have to withdraw from them too. There are, however, very many things in them which are said more openly and simply, so that they may edify even the hearer of little understanding."

units.la: Homil. 20. in Josue (11) “ Summa utilitas ab ejusmodi lectione “ ad eos pervenit, qui veram [Scripturæ Sententiam] intelligere possunt, &c. Sed quoniam difficile est invenire, qui tantam capiat “ utilitatem; adhortari volumus audientes, ne animum inter legendum despondeant. Quodnam igitur solatium sit, ne succumbat, “ qui ei lectioni interest, dicendum. Quemadmodum igitur carmina vim quandam habent insitam; utque imprudens aliquid à “ carmine accipit, qui incantatur: Ea nimirum est natura sonorum “ carminis. Sic velim existimes omni carmine potentiorem esse “ significationem nominum divinæ Scripturæ. Sunt enim in nobis
units.tr: Homily 20 on Joshua. "The greatest benefit from such reading comes to those who are able to understand the true sense of Scripture, etc. But since it is difficult to find those who derive so great a benefit, we wish to exhort our hearers not to lose heart while reading. What consolation there is, so that the one who attends this reading does not give way, must now be said. Just as songs have a certain power inherent in them, and the man who is charmed by a song receives something even without understanding it, so is the nature of the sounds of a song. So I would have you think that the meaning of the names in divine Scripture is more powerful than any song. For there are within us"

units.la: (11) Ἡ μὲν ἀρχὴ ἀφέλεια ἀπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης ἀναγνώσεως, τῆς ξυναμένων νοῆσαι. — ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἡ λύπη ... βουλόμεθα παρακαλεῖν ... ἀκούοντας μὴ ἐκλυθῆναι· δεῖ δ᾽ ἡ ἀναγ-
units.tr: (11) The beginning is benefit from such reading, for those who are able to understand… since the sorrow… we wish to exhort… the hearers not to be discouraged; one must read… [Ἡ μὲν ἀρχὴ ἀφέλεια ἀπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης ἀναγνώσεως, τῆς ξυναμένων νοῆσαι. — ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἡ λύπη ... βουλόμεθα παρακαλεῖν ... ἀκούοντας μὴ ἐκλυθῆναι· δεῖ δ᾽ ἡ ἀναγ-]

units.la: ὡς ἀναγνωσκομένης, ἀφελῆ δ᾽ ἡ χάρις ἱκανῶς ἔτι πρᾶξαι. plurimæ facultates, quæ veluti sortitione animas nostras & corpora possident; quæ si sanctæ sint, lectione Scripturæ juvantur, & validores fiunt, &c.
units.tr: …as it is read, but grace is still able to bring benefit enough to act. [ὡς ἀναγνωσκομένης, ἀφελῆ δ᾽ ἡ χάρις ἱκανῶς ἔτι πρᾶξαι.] Several faculties, which as if by allotment possess our souls and bodies; if these are holy, they are helped by the reading of Scripture and become stronger, etc.

units.la: Homil. 18. in Jerem. (12) "Unusquisque pro facultate suâ intelligit quæ scripta sunt; unus quidem magis superficialiter, utpote quasi ad fontis scatebram sensum eorum accipiens; alius verò profundius, quasi è puteo educens: & possunt ambo capere utilitatem; quandoquidem unum idemque uni quidem fons est, alteri verò puteus. Testatur hoc Evangelium, quando agit de Samaritanâ. Ibi enim idem & fons & puteus nuncupatur; & vicissim aliquando dicitur fons, & aliquando puteus. Consideret hoc qui potest; ut sciat unum idemque naturâ, persunctorio quidem fontem, profundiori autem puteum existere.
units.tr: Homily 18 on Jeremiah. (12) "Each one understands what is written according to his own capacity: one more superficially, as if drawing their meaning from the bubbling of a spring; another more deeply, as if drawing it up from a well. Both can receive benefit, since the one same thing is a spring to one and a well to another. This the Gospel bears witness to when it speaks of the Samaritan woman, for there the same thing is called both a spring and a well, and at other times is called now a spring, now a well. Let him who can consider this, so that he may know that one and the same thing exists by nature as a spring for the one who draws near on the surface, and as a well for the one who goes deeper."

units.la: Homil. de Engastrimythâ. Ex initio patet Lectiones diurnas S. Scripturæ in Ecclesiâ antiquâ admodum prolixas fuisse. Illâ enim die, quâ Homiliam istam habuit Origenes, Capita XXV, XXVI, XXVII, XXVIII. è primo Samuelis libro prælecta sunt. Lectione finitâ, assurrexit Origenes, & præcipua Lectionis argumenta summatim recensens, quodnam potius ex iis explicari vellet, Episcopum rogavit: cumque ille Engastrimythæ Historiam explicari jussisset, Homiliam istam extempore effudit.
units.tr: Homily on the Pythoness. From the beginning it is clear that the daily lessons of Holy Scripture in the ancient Church were quite long. On that day, when Origen gave this homily, chapters 25, 26, 27 and 28 of the first book of Samuel were read aloud. When the reading was finished, Origen rose, briefly ran over the main points of the reading, and asked the bishop which of them he wished to have explained; and when the bishop told him to explain the story of the Pythoness, he poured forth this homily extempore.

units.la: 250. S. Gregorius, Neocæsariensis Episcopus,
units.tr: 250. Saint Gregory, Bishop of Neocaesarea

units.la: Serm. 2. de Annuntiat. (13) B. Virginis (modò Gregorii sit) "Quando porrò Evangelium legitur, vel Apostolicum; non libro attendas aut Lectori, sed Deo è Cœlis loquenti. Liber siquidem est id, quod cernitur; at Christus est id, de quo disseritur. Evangelizat igitur nobis celeberrimam Salvatoris Oeconomiam: Evangelizat nobis, &c. Sermonem istum post Concilii Ephesini tempora scriptum censeo.
units.tr: Sermon 2 on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin (if it is indeed by Gregory). "When the Gospel or the Apostolic writing is read, do not attend to the book or the reader, but to God speaking from heaven. For what is seen is a book, but Christ is the one of whom it treats. Thus it announces to us the most celebrated economy of the Saviour: it announces to us, etc." I think this sermon was written after the time of the Council of Ephesus.

units.la: (13) "Ὅταν δὲ ἀναγινώσκῃ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, ἢ ἀποστολικόν, μὴ ὡς ἀρχῆς τῇ βίβλῳ ἀλλὰ τῷ ἀναγινώσκοντι, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐκ οὐρανῶν λέγοντι Θεῷ." (Greek footnote, right column)
units.tr: (13) [Ὅταν δὲ ἀναγινώσκῃ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, ἢ ἀποστολικόν, μὴ ὡς ἀρχῆς τῇ βίβλῳ ἀλλὰ τῷ ἀναγινώσκοντι, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐκ οὐρανῶν λέγοντι Θεῷ.] "When he reads the Gospel or the Apostolic writing, not attending to the book as its ruler but to the reader, but to God speaking from heaven."

units.la: 335. Eusebius, Cesariensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 335. Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea.

units.la: In citandis Praeparationum Evangelicarum libris Cl. Armachanus secutus est Georgii Trapezuntii Versionem Latinam; quae cum non tam Versio sit, quam Compendium quoddam, elegans quidem, sed parum fidele; eadem testimonia ex fideliori Francisci Vigeri Versione reponere necesse erit.
units.tr: In citing the books of the Praeparatio Evangelica, the illustrious Archbishop of Armagh followed George of Trebizond's Latin version. Since that is less a translation than a certain compendium, elegant but not very faithful, the same testimonies must be set out again from the more faithful version of Francesco Vigeri.

units.la: Lib. 8. cap. 1. "Nam cum felix illud tempus instaret, quo salutaris hujus Servatoris nostri doctrinae lux, sub Romanis Imperatoribus in cunctos sese homines longe latéque diffunderet; adeoque (14) praecipua tum quaedam ratio postularet, ut quae de ipso extarent oracula, necnon Hebraeorum illorum vita, ac religiosae disciplinae leges, quos longe Deus ipse carissimos habuisset, cum tot ea seculorum intervallo Patrii sermonis integumentis clausae latuissent; caeteris tandem aliquando nationibus, quae postmodum in cognitionis divinae communionem vocandae erant, omnibus paterent. Deus ille tantorum bonorum auctor, singulari egit providentia; ut quae de venturo paulo post generis humani Servatore, eodemque sanctioris erga unum praepotentem Deum religionis omnibus sub sole gentibus Doctore futuro, praedicta jam olim essent; ea demum accurata explicatione patefacta, & publicis in Bibliothecis collocata, cunctorum in lucem venirent; immissa hac Ptolomaeo Regi mente divinitus; nimirum ut quaedam quasi penus esset, unde illa postmodum in populorum omnium usum fructumque promerentur.
units.tr: Book 8, chapter 1. "For when that happy time was drawing near, in which the light of the saving teaching of our Saviour was to spread far and wide among all men under the Roman emperors, there was at that time a special reason why the oracles concerning him, and likewise the life of those Hebrews and the laws of their religious discipline, which God himself had held most dear, should be made known to all nations, which were afterwards to be called into fellowship with the knowledge of God, since for so many ages they had lain hidden, enclosed in the wrappings of their native tongue. God, the author of such great goods, acted with a singular providence, so that what had been foretold long before, concerning the Saviour of the human race soon to come, and concerning the one who would teach all the nations under the sun a more holy religion toward the one almighty God, might at last be laid open by exact explanation, placed in public libraries, and brought to light for all. This was put into the mind of King Ptolemy by God, so that there might be, as it were, a storehouse from which those things might afterwards be drawn for the use and profit of all peoples."

units.la: Lib. 12. cap. 1. "Verum igitur omnino fuit Hebraeorum Scripturam tanto ante [Platonem] praecipere, uti divinarum literarum "intelligentiam ac disquisitionem fides antecedat; ut dum ait:
units.tr: Book 12, chapter 1. "Indeed it was entirely right that the Hebrew Scripture should so long before [Plato] prescribe that faith should go before the understanding and investigation of divine letters; so that, as it says:

units.la: (14) Λόγος ἡ ἐχ ἡ τυχὼν ἀρὶ, τὰς ἀπὸ ἐπὶ ἀφρητικὰς, τοῦτο βίον, &c. τὰ ... ἐπὶ ἀφρῶν ... Θεὸς τὰς ... ἐπιγλυφῶν ...
units.tr: "Word ... not ... the ... this life, etc. ... the ... of the ... God ... the ... engraved ...

units.la: ἐπ' ἀρχῆς μετακλησίας, Σημεῖον ἡ βιβλιοθήκης ἀναπαύσεως ... Πτολεμαίῳ τῷ βασιλεῖ ... ἐπιτ ... μετηλάψεως. Nisi ᵃ crediderit͞is, non intelligetis. Itemque, ᶦ Credidi, propter quod locutus sum. (15) “ Quo quidem nos etiam consilio, quos- “ novissimè rerum in nostrarum communionem admisimus [Cate- “ chumenos] iis tanquam rudioribus adhuc & inchoatis, animoque “ propemodum infantibus, divinæ Scripturæ lectionem simpliciùs “ ita tradimus; ut eos simul ad fidem iis quæ proponantur tanquam “ Dei verbis habendam adhortemur. At quorum jam robustior mentis “ habitus, & cana quædam intelligentiæ vis fuerit, iis verò penetrare “ altiùs verborumque sententiam explorare concedimus. Atque hos “ Hebræi Deuterotas, quasi Scripturarum Interpretes atque Explana- “ tores, vocare solebant.
units.tr: "... from the beginning, the ... library ... of rest ... to King Ptolemy ... change. Unless you believe, you will not understand. Likewise, 'I believed, therefore I spoke.' "For which purpose we also, when we have admitted to our communion those most recently come to us, the catechumens, hand down the reading of divine Scripture to them rather simply, as to those still rude and only beginning, and almost infants in mind, so that we at the same time exhort them to hold what is proposed to them as the words of God. But to those whose mental disposition is now stronger and who have a certain grey vigour of understanding, we allow to penetrate more deeply and to examine the sense of the words. And these the Hebrews used to call Deuterotai, as interpreters and expounders of the Scriptures."

units.la: His unicum addam ex eodem Opere locum, brevem quidem, sed eximium. Sic igitur, lib. 12. cap. 20. Eusebius. (16) “ Ergo- “ jure sanè ac merito Pueri quoque nostri divinorum Prophetarum “ odas, hymnosque de Deo scriptos terere sæpiùs ac repetere con- “ suescunt.
units.tr: I will add to these one more passage from the same work, brief but excellent. Thus Eusebius, book 12, chapter 20. "Therefore it is truly right and proper that even our children are accustomed to sing and repeat often the odes and hymns about God written by the divine Prophets."

units.la: Idem libro de Martyribus Palæstinis, cap. 1. Procopium primum è Palæstinis in Persecutione decimâ martyrium obiisse refert. Acta hujusce Martyrii ex antiquissimo Codice edidit Henricus Valesius, not. in Euseb. pag. 154. Inibi leguntur ista. “ In verbis di- “ vinis ei tantùm studium erat. Illa verò quæ extrinsecus sunt, “ mediocriter attigerat. Igitur genere quidem Æliensis, conversa- “ tione autem vel habitatione Scythopolitanus erat. Ibi Ecclesiæ “ tria ministeria præbebat: unum in legendi officio, alterum in Syri- “ interpretatione sermonis, & tertium adversus Dæmones manûs “ impositione consummans. Hinc luculenter patet, in Ecclesiâ antiquâ, ubi Versiones S. Scripturæ vernaculæ deerant, Interpretem adhiberi solitum, qui Lectiones in coetu publico factas in plebis usum vernaculè exponeret: ipso etiam fatente Valesio, qui in Annotat. pag. 155. hæc habet. “ Ex Actis illis discimus Procopium habitâsse
units.tr: In the same work, On the Palestinian Martyrs, chapter 1, he relates that Procopius was the first from Palestine to die a martyr in the tenth persecution. The Acts of this martyrdom were published from a very ancient codex by Henry Valesius, in his notes on Eusebius, page 154. There the following is read. "He was devoted only to the divine words. Those things which lie outside them he had touched only moderately. So he was by birth from Aelia, but by manner of life or residence a Scythopolitan. There he performed three ministries for the Church: one in the office of reading, another in translating the speech into Syriac, and a third, completing the rite, the laying on of hands against demons. From this it is clearly evident that in the ancient Church, where vernacular versions of Holy Scripture were lacking, an interpreter was customarily employed, who would expound in the vernacular, for the use of the people, the lessons read in the public assembly. Valesius himself admits this, who in his Annotations, page 155, has the following. 'From those Acts we learn that Procopius lived

units.la: Epist. ad Marcellinum de Interpretat. Psalmorum. Qui igitur non ad istum modum legunt sacras Odas (nimirum ut mentem excolant, & passiones illius sedent,) non prudenter psallunt, sed seipsos oblectant, habituri reprehensionem. (17) Qui autem secundùm prædictam rationem concinunt, ut melodia verborum ex numeris vocum cum spiritus harmonià congruat; isti psallunt & lingua & mente; nec seipsos solùm, verum etiam alios, qui audire volunt, magnificè adjuvant. Ibid. (19) Arbitror autem in Scripturis hujus libri omnem vitam humanam, tum animæ affectiones, tum mentis conceptiones, suo modo ac magnitudine definitas contineri, nihilque ultra hæc in rebus humanis reperiri posse. Si enim pœnitentia aut confessionis usus requiratur; aut tentatio, aut tribulatio apprehenderit te, &c. omnium istarum rerum institutionem in Psalmis habes. Ibid. Siquidem Deus injunxit Mosi scribere Canticum magnum (19) & id populum docere, unà cum duce constituto. Jubet item scribere Deuteronomium, & in manibus gestare,
units.tr: Letter to Marcellinus on the Interpretation of the Psalms. Those, therefore, who do not read the sacred Odes in this manner (namely, to cultivate the mind and calm its passions) do not psalm wisely, but amuse themselves, and will incur reproof. But those who sing in the way described above, so that the melody of the words agrees with the rhythm of the voice and the harmony of the spirit, these psalm with both tongue and mind, and greatly help not only themselves but also others who wish to hear. Ibid. For I think that in the Scriptures of this book the whole of human life is contained, both the affections of the soul and the conceptions of the mind, defined in their own way and measure, and that nothing beyond these can be found in human affairs. For if repentance or the practice of confession is required, or if temptation or tribulation seizes you, etc., you have the instruction for all these things in the Psalms. Ibid. For God enjoined Moses to write a great Song and to teach it to the people, together with the leader appointed. He likewise bids him write Deuteronomy and carry it in his hands,

units.la: (18) Ἡγοῦμαι γὰρ ἐν τούτοις τοῖς λόγοις τὴν βίβλον τὴν πᾶσαν βίον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, &c. μερισμοὺς καὶ σειρὰς, ἢ μᾶλλον τούτων πλείονα ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὑρίσκεσθαι. εἴτε γὰρ μετανοίας ἢ ἐξομολογήσεως χρεία, &c. Ἴχι τούτων τῶν διδασκαλιῶν ἐν τοῖς θείοις ψαλμοῖς.
units.tr: For I think that in these words the whole book contains the life of men, etc., with its divisions and series, or rather that more of these are found among men. For whether there is need of repentance or of confession, etc., you have instruction in these matters in the divine Psalms.

units.la: (19) Καὶ διδάξαι ὁ λαὸς, ἡ ἐ κατεσταμένον ἀρχηγὸν, καὶ ἱ χρῆσθαι τὸ Δευτερονόμιον, ἴχει ἢ μὴ ἐπιστῆσαι, ἢ μελετᾶν τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ ῥήματα, ὡς ἀρχόντων, &c. gestare,& perpetuò ejus verba meditata habere; cùm ea sufficiant ad virtutis admonitionem, & opitulationem illis, qui se probè in iis exercuerint, &c.
units.tr: And that the people should be taught, with a leader appointed, and that they should use Deuteronomy, having it on hand, or not stop attending to it, or meditate on the words in it as of rulers, etc. carry it, and constantly keep its words meditated upon; since they suffice for admonition to virtue and for help to those who have exercised themselves well in them, etc.

"Cum enim non omnes possunt Scripturas legere; & alios quidem insicitia, alios verò occupatio quaedam impedit à cognitione; ne ob insicitiam animam perdas, in paucis versibus universam fidei doctrinam comprehendimus; quod in ipsâ lectione meminisse vos volo, & apud vos ipsos studiosè recolere, &c. "(*) Excerpe autem tempore opportuno ex sacris Scripturis, quae est insita illis, probationem.
units.tr: Catechesis 5 on Illumination: "Since not all can read the Scriptures, and some are hindered from knowledge by lack of learning and others by some occupation, so that you do not lose your soul through ignorance, we sum up the whole doctrine of faith in a few verses. I want you to remember this in your own reading and to recall it diligently among yourselves, etc." (*) Pick out in due time from the sacred Scriptures the proof that is implanted in them.

units.la: Catech. Mystag. 5. (20) Postea (in sacrâ Synaxi) clamat sacerdos, Sursum corda. Vos deinde respondetis, Habemus ad Dominum, assentientes et profitendo. Nullus autem sic consistat, ut ore quidem dicat, Habemus ad Dominum, mente verò circa vita hujus curas vagetur. Dicit deinde Sacerdos, Gratias agamus Domino. Ad hac vos subjicitis, Dignum & justum est. Sacerdos autem postea dicit, Sancta Sanctis. Vos deinde respondetis, Unus Sanctus, unus Dominus Jesus Christus.
units.tr: Catechesis 5 on the Mysteries (20) Afterwards, in the holy Synaxis, the priest cries, Lift up your hearts. You then answer, We have them lifted up to the Lord, assenting and professing it. Let no one stand there saying with the mouth, We have them lifted up to the Lord, while in his mind he wanders among the cares of this life. Then the priest says, Let us give thanks to the Lord. To this you add, It is meet and right. Then the priest says, The holy things are for the holy. You then answer, One is holy, one is the Lord, Jesus Christ.

"Psallentem cogitare oportet, quæ in Cantico proferuntur; non enim in collisione ac carminis modulatione versandum est iis, qui proficere student; sed intelligentiâ percipere "quæ canuntur, opus est. Nam eos qui non ita psallunt, sed tantùm sonitum vocis emittunt, rejicit Deus dicens, Discede à me; "sonum viarum tuarum & psalmum organorum tuorum non audiam.
units.tr: On Psalm 46.7, in the Golden Catena on the Psalms translated into Latin by Daniel Barbaro: "The one who sings the psalm ought to think about what is sung in the Canticle. For those who strive to make progress must not be occupied with the clash and the tune of the song, but it is necessary to grasp with understanding what is sung. For God rejects those who do not sing in this way but only utter a sound with the voice, saying, 'Depart from me; I will not hear the sound of your ways and the psalm of your instruments.'"

units.la: Inter S. Maximi Capita Theologica, seu Sermones per Excerpta, Serm. 17. ʰ sententia ista ex Didymo citata reperitur. (23) "Legendæ sunt divinæ Scripturæ. Uti enim vini potus dolorem sedat, "& cor ex tristitiâ in lætitiam transfert; sic spiritale vinum gaudio "perfundit animum.
units.tr: In the Theological Chapters of St Maximus, or Sermons in Excerpts, Sermon 17, this sentence cited from Didymus is found: (23) "The divine Scriptures are to be read. For just as the drinking of wine calms pain and turns the heart from sadness to joy, so spiritual wine fills the soul with gladness."

units.la: Integrum describat Chrysostomum oportet; qui cuncta ejus testimonia de Scripturis vernaculè legendis congesserit. Plurima dedit Armachanus Latinè, quibus nos Græca è regione apposuimus, nisi in pauculis quibusdam, quæ nonnisi Latinè adhuc prodierunt. Verbi gratiâ, Expositio in Psalmum 90. & Homilia in Esai. 62. neque in Savilianâ neque in Morelliana editione reperiuntur. Utraque autem habetur Latinè in Editione Parisiensi 1556. Tom. I. illa pag. 861. ista pag. 1248. Idem & de aliis dicendum. Post plenam Reve-
units.tr: One ought to describe Chrysostom in full, since he gathered together all his testimonies on reading Scripture in the vernacular. The Armagh archbishop gave most of them in Latin, and we have set the Greek beside them, except for a few that have so far appeared only in Latin. For example, the Exposition on Psalm 90 and the Homily on Isaiah 62 are found neither in the Savile edition nor in the Morell edition. Both, however, are given in Latin in the Paris edition of 1556, vol. 1: the former on p. 861, the latter on p. 1248. The same should be said of others. After the full harvest of that most distinguished Primate, it would be a vain labour to glean further; but I should think it unfair to pass over entirely the homily in which Chrysostom deliberately treats this subject.

units.la: Homil. de utilitate Lectionis Scripturæ, Edit. Morell. Tom. V. pag. 582. (24) "Est enim spirituale pratum, ac deliciarum paradisus, sacrarum lectio Scripturarum. ——— Hunc Paradisum Deus "non uno circumscriptum loco posuit; sed ubique terrarum expandit, "& in fines orbis terrarum extendit. Atque ut intelligas in universum "orbem terrarum expansas esse Scripturas; audi prophetam dicentem. In omnes terras exivit sonus eorum, & in fines orbis terræ verba eorum. Sive ad Indos te conferas, quos Oriens primos Sol respicit, (25) sive ad Oceanum te conferas. * [Sive ad Britannicas insulas iter facias.] Sive in Euxinum Pontum naviges, "sive ad Australes partes abeas; omnes ubique audies de iis, quæ in "Scriptura sunt, Philosophantes; aliâ quidem voce, sed non aliâ "fide, ac linguâ quidem diversâ, sed mente consona. ——— Habet & fontem hic Paradisus." ——— Fons iste in singulas fidelium mentes dividitur, & non minuitur; dividitur & non consumitur; dispertitur & minor non fit; apud omnes integer & in singulis integer. ——— In hoc igitur Paradiso versemur; assideamus fonti; ——— in lectione Scripturæ istius permaneamus. "——— Lectio Scripturæ colloquium est cum Deo. ——— Lectioni ergo simus intenti, non duas tantum has horas, (non enim ad securitatem sufficit hæc auditio nuda) sed perpetuò quisque domum reversus libros sacros in manus sumat, & eorum quæ dicta sunt sensus percurrat; siquidem perpetuam & sufficientem utilitatem percipere cupiat ex Scripturâ. ——— Is qui Scripturas sacras
units.tr: Homily on the usefulness of reading Scripture, Morell edition, Vol. V, p. 582. (24) "For the reading of the sacred Scriptures is a spiritual meadow and a paradise of delights. God did not place this Paradise in one confined spot, but spread it everywhere on earth and extended it to the ends of the world. And that you may understand that the Scriptures have been spread over the whole world, hear the prophet saying: Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Whether you betake yourself to the Indians, whom the rising sun sees first, (25) or go to the Ocean, * [or make your way to the British isles]. Whether you sail into the Euxine Sea, or go to the southern parts, you will hear everywhere people discoursing about the things that are in Scripture, in a different voice, but not a different faith; in a language indeed diverse, but in a mind in harmony. ——— This Paradise has a fountain too." ——— This fountain is divided among the minds of the faithful and is not diminished; it is divided and not used up; it is distributed and does not become smaller; with all it is whole, and in each it is whole. ——— Therefore let us dwell in this Paradise; let us sit beside the fountain; ——— let us remain in the reading of that Scripture. "——— Reading Scripture is a conversation with God. ——— Let us then be intent on reading, not for these two hours only (for this bare hearing is not enough for security), but let each one, on returning home, always take the sacred books into his hands and run over the sense of what has been said, if indeed he wishes to receive a lasting and sufficient profit from Scripture. ——— He who [reads] the holy Scriptures"

[the Greek continues in the lower columns as printed]. He who reads assiduously and sits beside their streams draws off benefit, though he has no one to interpret; by frequent reading he draws off great benefit, as if from roots. [The Greek reads "much benefit"; Fronto Ducaeus rendered it more loosely.]

units.la: Unicam addam sententiam de precibus linguâ à precantibus intellectâ faciendis, ex Expositione in Psalmum XLI. desumptam. Quotidie Deum interpellemus per Psalmos & Orationes. (26) Ne autem verba solum offeramus; sed ipsam etiam sciamus vim dictionum.
units.tr: I will add one sentence on making prayers in a language understood by those who pray, taken from the Exposition on Psalm 41: "Let us entreat God every day through the Psalms and prayers. But lest we offer only words, let us also know the force of the expressions."

(27)puros verò in animum inferamus sanctorum "Prophetarum sermones, ac per Mosen accepta decreta, in ænigmaticam traducentes veritatem, & inprimis Evangelicam salutaremque doctrinam, Apostolicos libros; non ut quibusdam mos est, ad contemplationem indecoram eorum, quæ scripta sunt, sententiam detorquentes, nec à recto sensu impiè trahentes; verùm quâ se viâ contemplatiorum explicat scopus, eandem nos ipsi quoque strenuè insistamus.
units.tr: Homily for Easter 16: "Let us therefore abstain from such food [from Jewish fables]. (27) Rather, let us bring into our minds the pure sayings of the holy Prophets and the decrees received through Moses, turning them into enigmatic truth, and above all the Evangelical and saving teaching, the Apostolic books. Let us not, as some are wont, twist the sense of what has been written into an unseemly contemplation, nor wrench it impiously from the right meaning; rather, let us strenuously follow that path by which the aim of the contemplation unfolds."

(30) Cui quidem rei "nihil æquiparandum fuerit inculpatam vitam laudantibus, optimis, "præstantissimisque actionibus vacare volentibus, & mentem divino "lumine repletam habentibus: Propterea quòd oporteat in iis quæ "de Deo scripta sunt, indesinenter sese oblectare, ac veluti lucernam "quandam S. Scripturam sibi statuere, juxta Psalmistam clamantem & "dicentem; Lucerna pedibus meis, &c.
units.tr: (29) It would not be able to lead to eternal life by any other means, unless (etc.) [Οὐχ ἑτέρας ἀν ἰσχύσαι τ αἰωνίας ζωῆς ἐγκλεῖς πρὸς, ἀναρρίψασα λόγων, εἰ μὴ, &c.], that is, unless they search out Christ. Likewise (30) nothing is to be set beside this for those who praise a blameless life, who wish to devote themselves to the best and most excellent actions, and who have a mind filled with divine light: because they ought to delight without ceasing in what has been written concerning God, and to set up Holy Scripture for themselves as a certain lamp, according to the Psalmist crying out and saying: "Your word is a lamp to my feet," etc.

For the Word of God is food sufficient for the life of the soul."

units.tr: On Colossians 3:16, "Singing in your hearts to God": "For, he says, you shall meditate on them sitting, and rising, and lying down, and walking on the way. The divine Apostle also prescribes this: that we should always carry the teaching of the Lord about in our minds, praise him, and sanctify each moment with spiritual songs. But the words 'in your hearts' stand for 'not with the mouth only'."

units.la: Orat. 16. in Davidem. "Animae pabulum, veritatis est cognitio, creatoris intelligentia, divinarum rerum narratione repleri. Ac circa ejusmodi alimoniam otium impendere Dominus homines docebat, &c. Per commodè partitur alimentum Conditor, dum utrumque nutrit [Corpus & Animam] Corpori quidem res cognatas, quibus alii consuevit, Animae verò commentarios ingenio ejus congruentes. Eam enim ob rem literarum monumenta, Sanctorum vitas complexa, notitiam ad posteros transmittunt, quo ad imitationem impellantur; utque nondum natis thesaurus paretur, Virtutis promptuarium ad vitae rationes perutile objiciunt."
units.tr: Oration 16, on David: "The food of the soul is the knowledge of the truth, the understanding of the Creator, being filled with the narration of divine things. The Lord taught men to devote their leisure to such nourishment, etc. The Creator divides the nourishment conveniently, feeding both [the body and the soul]: to the body, things akin to it, with which it is accustomed; to the soul, commentaries suited to its nature. For this reason the monuments of letters, embracing the lives of the saints, transmit knowledge to posterity so that they may be moved to imitation; and so that a treasure may be prepared even for those not yet born, they set before them a storehouse of virtue, most useful for the conduct of life."

units.la: In Psal. XLVI. 7. in Catenâ Aur. in Psal. L. à Daniele Barbaro Latinè versâ. "Ter Deo psallendum merito praecepit; ut linguâ & mente & spiritu psallamus. Psallere verò sapienter ideo jubet, ne carminibus & numeris vacantes, vim eorum, quae canimus, ignoremus, neque aes sonans aut cymbalum tinniens efficiamur; sed scientes Regem omnis terrae, hoc est, totius humanitatis Deum esse, membra illi omnia tum corporis tum animi subjiciamus."
units.tr: On Psalm 46.7, in the Catena Aurea on Psalm 50, translated into Latin by Daniele Barbaro: "God rightly commands us to sing to him three times, so that we may sing with tongue, mind and spirit. He bids us sing wisely so that we do not, occupied with the verses and the rhythms, ignore the meaning of what we sing, and so become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. Rather, knowing that the King of all the earth, that is, God of all humanity, we should subject all our members, both of body and of soul, to him."

units.la: Præfat. ad Libros Testimon. adv. Judæos. Plus roboris tibi dabitur, & magis ac magis intellectus cordis operabitur, scrutanti Scripturas veteres ac novas plenius, & universa librorum spiritalium volumina perlegenti. Vox Spiritalium redundare videtur. Libros enim potius Canonicos Cyprianus innuit: atque adeo vox ista in Codice MS. vetusto Bibliothecæ Archiepiscopalis Lambethanæ non invenitur.
units.tr: From the Preface to the Books of Testimonies against the Jews: More strength will be given to you, and the understanding of the heart will work more and more in you, as you search the ancient and new Scriptures more fully and read through all the volumes of the spiritual books. The word spiritalium seems to be superfluous. For Cyprian is referring rather to the canonical books, and so this word is not found in the old manuscript in the Archiepiscopal Library at Lambeth.

units.la: De Habitu Virg. Scripturis sanctis nos instrui Dominus voluit & moneri.
units.tr: From On the Dress of Virgins: The Lord willed that we be instructed and admonished by the holy Scriptures.

units.la: De Spectaculis §. 11. Habet Christianus spectacula meliora, si velit. Scripturis, inquam, sacris incumbat Christianus fidelis; ibi inveniet condigna fidei spectacula. Quàm hoc decorum spectaculum, fratres? quàm jucundum? quàm necessarium? intueri semper spem suam, & oculos aperire ad salutem suam. Hunc librum Cypriano abjudicant Critici recentiores; neque adeo tamen Cypriano indignus est; & ante Constantini tempora scriptum esse constat. Author, quisquis demum fuerit, argumenta ex Tertulliano emendicâsse videtur.
units.tr: From On the Spectacles, §11: The Christian has better spectacles, if he wishes. I say that the faithful Christian should devote himself to the holy Scriptures; there he will find spectacles worthy of faith. How becoming this spectacle is, brethren! How pleasing! How necessary! To always gaze upon one's hope, and to open one's eyes to one's salvation. Recent critics deny this book to Cyprian; yet it is not unworthy of him, and it is agreed that it was written before the time of Constantine. Its author, whoever he was, seems to have borrowed his arguments from Tertullian.

units.la: De Disciplinâ & Bono Pudicitiæ, in sin. Ego pauca dictavi. Vos Scripturas aspicite, exempla vobis de ipsis præceptis hujus rei majora conquirite. Liber Cypriano receptâ apud eruditos sententiâ abjudicatur. Antiquus tamen est; quemque Erasmus Cornelio Papæ deberi conjicit. Certè Authorem fuisse Episcopum ex initio ejus patet.
units.tr: From On the Discipline and Good of Chastity, near the end: I have dictated a few things. Look to the Scriptures yourselves, and seek out for yourselves examples greater than the precepts themselves concerning this matter. This book is denied to Cyprian by the prevailing opinion of learned men. Nevertheless it is ancient; Erasmus conjectures that it is owed to Pope Cornelius. Certainly its author was a bishop, as is clear from its beginning.

units.la: Confessio S. Cypriani (quæ tametsi genuina non sit, Authoris est admodum vetusti) publicam Christianorum Liturgiam sic describit, prope sin. Aliâ autem die ivimus in sanctam Ecclesiam Dei; & vidi exlestem chorum super terram Hymnum referentem Deo cum multâ glorificatione. Audivi autem ibi laudem per singulos versus omnium vocem consonantem; ut putarem omnium esse unam vocem, tanquam vocem Angelorum.
units.tr: The Confession of St. Cyprian (which, although not genuine, is the work of a very ancient author) describes the public liturgy of the Christians thus, near the end: On another day we went into the holy Church of God; and I saw a heavenly choir upon the earth singing a hymn to God with much glorification. I heard praise there, the voice of all sounding together verse by verse, so that I thought the voice of all was one, like the voice of angels.

units.la: Lib. 5. cap. 20. Quomodo enim Deus praestabit precanti, quicquid oraverit; cum ad precandum neque ex animo, neque observanter accedat? Isti autem cum ad sacrificandum veniunt, nihil intimum, nihil proprium diis suis offerunt, non integritatem mentis, non reverentiam, non timorem. Peractis itaque sacrificiis inanibus, omnem religionem in templo, & cum templo, sicut invenerant, relinquunt; nihilque secum exeâ neque afferunt neque referunt. Inde est, quod ejusmodi religiones neque bonos facere possunt, neque firmos atque immutabiles. Traducuntur itaque ab his homines facile; quia nihil ibi ad vitam, nihil ad sapientiam, nihil ad fidem discitur. Quae est enim superstitio illorum deorum? quae vis? quae disciplina? quae origo? quae ratio? quod fundamentum? quae substantia? quo tendis? aut quid pollicetur? ut ab homine possit fideliter servari, fortiterque defendi? In quâ nihil aliud video, quàm ritum ad solos digitos pertinentem?
units.tr: From Book 5, chapter 20: For how will God grant to one who prays whatever he has asked, when he approaches to pray neither from the heart nor with due observance? But those men, when they come to sacrifice, offer nothing inward, nothing of their own to their gods: neither integrity of mind, nor reverence, nor fear. Therefore, once the empty sacrifices are finished, they leave all their religion in the temple, and with the temple, just as they found it; and they bring away nothing with them and carry nothing back. Hence such religions can make men neither good nor firm and unchangeable. Men are therefore easily led astray by them, because nothing is learned there for life, nothing for wisdom, nothing for faith. For what is the superstition of those gods? What is its power? What its discipline? What its origin? What its reasoning? What its foundation? What its substance? Where does it lead? Or what does it promise, that it can be faithfully kept and bravely defended by a man? In it I see nothing other than a ritual concerned only with the fingers?

units.la: Lib. 1. ad Parmenian. Nam fermè ante annos LX. & quod excurrit, per totam Africam persecutionis devagata est tempestas. Quid commemorem Laicos, qui tunc in Ecclesiâ nullâ fuerant dignitate suffulti? Quid ministros plurimos? Quid Diaconos in tertio? Quid Presbyteros in secundo sacerdotio constitutos? Ipsi apices & principes omnium aliqui Episcopi illis temporibus, ut damno aeternae vitae, istius incertae lucis moras brevissimas compararent, Instrumenta divinae legis impiè tradiderunt. Penès Laicos igitur erant Instrumenta divinae legis.
units.tr: From Book 1, against Parmenian: For about sixty years, and a little more, the storm of persecution has raged through all Africa. Why should I mention the laymen, who at that time had no office of dignity in the Church? Why the many ministers? Why the deacons of the third rank? Why the elders established in the second priesthood? The very leaders and princes of all, some bishops at that time, impiously handed over the instruments of the divine law, so that they might exchange eternal life for the briefest delay in this uncertain light. Therefore the instruments of the divine law were in the hands of the laymen.

units.tr: Commentary on Ephesians 5:19, "Singing in your hearts to the Lord": The Holy Spirit loves a reasonable way; for if we live well, we shall be filled with it, as he says, to confess and extol the gift of God with a varied sound of voice, so that praise is sung to God in every tongue.

units.la: Epist. 103. ad Paulinum. Sola Scripturarum ars est, quam sibi omnes passim vindicant. Scribimus indocti doctique poemata passim. Hanc garrula anus, hanc delirus senex, hanc sophista verbosus, hanc universi præsumunt, lacerant, docent antequam discant. [Hic quidem reprehendit Hieronymus petulantiam illorum, qui S. Scripturæ expositionem illotis manibus aggredi auderent; omnibus interim Scripturam olim in usu familiari fuisse fidem facit. Quin ipse Scripturæ lectionem indoctis adeo non interdicit; ut illorum gratia simplici sermone conscriptam esse prodat.] Oro te, frater carissime, inter hæc vivere, ista meditari, nihil aliud nôsse, nihil quærere. Nonne tibi videtur jam hic in terris regni cælestis habitaculum? Nolo offendaris in Scripturis sanctis simplicitate & quasi utilitate verborum; quæ vel vitio Interpretum vel de industria sic prolata sunt, ut rusticam concionem facilius instruerent; & in unâ eademque sententia aliter doctus, aliter audiret indoctus.
units.tr: Epist. 103 to Paulinus. Scripture alone is an art which everyone everywhere claims for himself. Learned and unlearned alike write verses everywhere. This art is presumed upon by all: the chattering old woman, the doting old man, the verbose sophist; they tear it apart and teach before they have learned. [Here Jerome indeed rebukes the presumption of those who dared to take up the exposition of Holy Scripture with unwashed hands. Meanwhile he shows that Scripture was once in familiar use among everyone. Indeed he does not forbid the unlearned to read Scripture at all; rather he declares that it was written in simple language for their sake.] I beg you, dearest brother, to live among these things, to meditate on them, to know nothing else and seek nothing else. Does it not seem to you that here on earth is already the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom? I do not want you to be offended by the simplicity, and as it were the plainness, of words in the holy Scriptures. Whether through the fault of translators or deliberately, they have been set forth in such a way that they might more easily instruct a rustic congregation, and in one and the same sentence the learned man hears one thing, the unlearned another.

units.la: Præfat. in 4 Evang. ad Damasum. Præterminitto eos codices, quos à Luciano & Hesychio nuncupatos paucorum hominum asserit perversa contentio: quibus utique nec in toto Veteri Instrumento post Septuaginta Interpretes emendare quid licuit, nec in Novo profuit emendásse: cùm multarum gentium linguis Scriptura ante translata doceat falsa esse, quæ addita sunt.
units.tr: Preface to the Four Gospels, to Damasus. I pass over those manuscripts which a stubborn contention of a few men claims were named after Lucian and Hesychius. With them, after the Seventy translators, nothing could be emended in the whole Old Testament, and in the New it was of no use to have emended anything, since Scripture translated earlier into the languages of many nations shows that the things added are false.

units.la: Comm. in Psal. XLVI. 7. (quod inter Opera ejus habetur) Psallite sapienter.] Ut quæ canitis per literam, intelligatis spiritualiter dicta.
units.tr: Comm. on Ps. 46.7 (which is found among his works). Sing wisely. [Psallite sapienter.] So that you may understand spiritually the things you sing according to the letter.

units.la: Author Epistolæ ad Amicum de Scientiâ divinæ legis, inter Hieronymi Opera, Tom. 9. Edit. Mariani Victorii, p. 38.
units.tr: Author of the Letter to a Friend on the Knowledge of the Divine Law, among the Works of Jerome, Vol. 9, ed. Marianus Victorius, p. 38.

units.la: Hoc plane præmoneo; ne Domini verba despicias, quæ pio affectu tibi nunc Ecclesiæ parvulo, ad confovendam infantiæ novitatem porrigo. Rudis igitur & in Christianæ doctrinæ studio tyro fuit, cui hæc scripta sunt. Hunc tamen ad Scripturæ studium Author Epistolæ multis hortatur. Rogo ut ad institutionis plenitudinem, verbum Domini, hoc est Evangelium, diligentius legas; ex quo scientiam ampliorem ejus quàm credidisti lucis accipias, ut possis in omnibus nôsse quid facturus sis. Nam sine divinæ legis & disciplinæ cælestis scientiâ difficile esse quenquam posse salvari, non menis, sed divinus sermo probabit. Ait Esaias Propheta, &c. Scripta est itaque hæc Epistola, uti ex fine patet, antequam Monachorum nomen viris devotis in turbâ etiam commorantibus imponi desiisset, viz. ante annum 600.
units.tr: This I plainly forewarn you: do not despise the words of the Lord, which I now offer to you, a little one of the Church, with loving affection, to nourish the novice's infancy. The one to whom these writings are addressed was therefore untrained and a beginner in the study of Christian doctrine. Yet the author of the letter urges him to the study of Scripture in many ways. I ask that you read the word of the Lord, that is the Gospel, more diligently for the fullness of instruction, so that from it you may receive a knowledge of its light greater than you believed, and so be able to know in all things what you are to do. For that without the knowledge of the divine law and heavenly discipline it is difficult for anyone to be saved, not men's reasoning but the divine word will prove. Isaiah the prophet says, etc. This letter was therefore written, as is clear from its end, before the name of monks had ceased to be given to devout men who even dwelt in the crowd, namely before the year 600.

units.la: 420. Augustinus, Episcopus Hipponensis,
units.tr: 420. Augustine, Bishop of Hippo,

units.la: Ennarrat. in Psal. XLVI. Psallite intelligenter.] Docet nos & admonet nos, ut psallamus intelligenter; non quaeramus sonum auris, sed lumen cordis. Psallite, inquit, intelligenter.
units.tr: Enarrations on Psalm 46. "Sing wisely." He teaches us and admonishes us to sing wisely, not to seek the sound of the ear but the light of the heart. "Sing," he says, "wisely."

units.la: In Psal. CV. Et interfecta est terra in sanguinibus.] Putaremus autem hic scriptoris errorem esse; atque eum diceremus pro eo quod est infecta, fecisse interfecta: nisi haberemus beneficium Dei, qui Scripturas suas in multis linguis esse voluit, atque ita esse scriptum.
units.tr: On Psalm 105. "And the land was defiled with blood." We would think this an error of the writer, and we would say that he wrote "defiled" (interfecta) for "stained" (infecta). But we have the benefit of God, who willed that his Scriptures should exist in many languages, and that it should be written thus.

units.la: Epist. 107. Exerce [tu qui pro infidelibus orandum non esse dicis.] contra Orationes Ecclesiae Disputationes tuas; & quando audis sacerdotem Dei ad altare exhortantem populum Dei, orare pro incredulis, ut eos Deus convertat ad fidem; & pro catechumenis, ut eis desiderium regenerationis inspiret; & pro fidelibus, ut in eo quod esse coeperunt, ejus munere perseverent; subsanna pias voces, & dic te non facere quod hortatur, id est, Deum pro infidelibus, ut eos fideles faciat, non rogare.
units.tr: Epistle 107. "Exercise [you who say that one must not pray for unbelievers]." Exercise your disputations against the prayers of the Church. When you hear the priest of God at the altar exhorting the people of God to pray for unbelievers, that God may convert them to the faith; and for catechumens, that he may breathe into them the desire for regeneration; and for the faithful, that they may persevere by his gift in what they have begun, scoff at these pious words and say that you do not do what he urges, namely, that you do not ask God to make unbelievers faithful.

units.la: De Magistro, cap. 7. Primo omnium recordor, aliquandiu nos quaesisse, quam ob causam loquamur; inventumque esse, docendi commemorandi gratia nos loqui; quandoquidem nec cum interrogamus, aliud agimus; quam ut ille qui rogatur, discat quid velimus audire. In orando Deo, quem doceri aut commoneri existimare non possumus, id verba valeant; ut vel nos ipsos commonefaciamus, vel alii commoneantur; doceanturve per nos.
units.tr: On the Teacher, chapter 7. First of all I recall that for a while we asked why we speak, and it was found that we speak for the sake of teaching and reminding; since, when we ask a question, we do nothing else than that the one who is asked may learn what we wish to hear. In praying to God, whom we cannot think to be taught or reminded, let words serve only this purpose: that we may remind ourselves, or that others may be reminded, or be taught through us.

units.la: 430. Joannes Cassianus, Presbyter Massiliensis,
units.tr: 430. John Cassian, Presbyter of Marseilles,

units.la: De Instit. Coenob. lib. 2. cap. 5. Monachorum Aegyptiorum mores & instituta referens, eos formam vivendi a Marco Apostolo accepisse & inviolatam tenuisse scribit. Eo fervore Scripturarum divinarum lectionibus, orationique, & operi manuum diebus ac noctibus incubabant; ut nec escarum quidem appetitus vel memoria interpellaret. Et mox, Quotidianos orationum ritus volentibus celebrare, unus in medio Psalmos Domino cantaturus exurgit. Cumque sedentibus cunctis (ut moris est nunc usque in Aegypti partibus) & in psallentis verba omni cordis intentione defixis, undecim Psalmos orationum interjectione distinctos contiguis versibus parili pronuntiatione cantasset, duodecimum sub Alleluia responsione consummat.
units.tr: De Instit. Coenob. book 2, chapter 5. Describing the customs and institutions of the Egyptian monks, he writes that they received their way of life from the Apostle Mark and kept it unbroken. With such zeal they devoted themselves day and night to the reading of the divine Scriptures, to prayer, and to manual labour, that not even the desire for food or the thought of it disturbed them. And soon after: When those who wish to observe the daily rites of prayer have assembled, one man rises in the midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. While all sit (as the custom still is in the regions of Egypt), and fix their whole heart's attention on the words of the one singing, he sings eleven Psalms, divided by interposed prayers, in continuous verses and with even delivery, and then concludes the twelfth with the response Alleluia.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 7 De eorundem precibus publicis. Antequam flectant genua, paulisper orant; & stantes in supplicatione majorem temporis partem expendunt. Itaque post hac puncto brevissimo procidentes humi, velut adorantes tantum divinam clementiam, summâ velocitate consurgunt; ac rursus erecti, expansis manibus eodem modo quo prius stantes oraverant, suis precibus intentius immorantur.
units.tr: Book 2, chapter 7, on the public prayers of the same monks. Before they bend their knees, they pray for a little while, and they spend most of the time in supplication while standing. Then, after a very brief moment, they fall prostrate on the ground, as if only adoring the divine mercy, and rise again with great speed; and once upright again, with hands outstretched, they remain longer in their prayers, standing as they did before.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 10. Credunt iidem Diabolum cogitationibus seu diversis humoribus excitatis, abducere mentem nostram à supplicationis intentione festinare. Quamobrem utilius censent breves quidem orationes, sed creberrimas, fieri.
units.tr: Book 2, chapter 10. The same monks believe that the Devil, by stirring up thoughts or various humours, draws our mind away and hurries it from the intent of supplication. For this reason they think it more useful to make prayers that are brief but very frequent.

units.la: Lib. 2. cap. 12. Hunc sanè canonicum duodenarium Psalmorum numerum tali corporis quiete relevant; ut has easdem Congregationum solennitates ex more celebrantes, absque eo qui dicturus in medium Psalmos surrexerit, cuncti sedilibus humillimis insidentes, ad vocem Psallentis omni cordis intentione dependeant. Monachos hosce Ægyptios cum indoctissimis juxta indoctos fuisse constat; Scripturas tamen assiduè terebant, Psalmos attentè audiebant, & ex psallentis ore omni cordis intentione pendebant. Scriptura igitur & Officia divina apud illos linguâ vernacula habebantur. Aliter frustra attenti, frustra verborum intellectum sectati erant; quod de illis refert Cassianus, lib.2. cap.11. Non enim multitudine versuum, sed mentis intelligentiâ delectantur; Illud totâ virtute sectantes; Psallam spiritu, Psallam & mente.
units.tr: Book 2, chapter 12. Indeed, they lighten this canonical number of twelve Psalms by such a rest of the body that, celebrating these same solemnities of the congregation as is customary, all sit on the lowest seats, and, apart from the one who has risen to sing the Psalms in the midst, they all hang upon the voice of the singer with their whole heart's attention. It is well known that these Egyptian monks were, among the unlearned, the most unlearned; yet they constantly wore out the Scriptures, listened attentively to the Psalms, and hung upon the mouth of the singer with their whole heart's attention. The Scripture and the divine offices were therefore held among them in the vernacular tongue. Otherwise they would have listened in vain and pursued the sense of the words in vain. Cassian reports this of them in book 2, chapter 11: For they delight not in the multitude of verses, but in understanding of the mind; pursuing this with all their strength: I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind.

units.la: Collat. 9. cap. 34. Satis verò constat, illum trina orationis numerum, qui solet in congregationibus fratrum ad concludendam synaxin celebrari, cum qui intento animo non supplicat, observare non posse.
units.tr: Collation 9, chapter 34. It is quite clear, however, that a person who does not pray with an attentive mind cannot observe that threefold number of prayers which is customarily said in the assemblies of the brothers to close the synaxis.

units.la: Collat. 10. cap. 13. Mens mobilis semper ac vaga in tempore quoque synaxeos velut ebria per diversa distrahitur, nullum Officium competenter exolvens. Verbi gratiâ, dum orat, Psalmum aut aliquam recolit lectionem; dum cantat, aliud quid meditatur, quàm textus ipsius continet Psalmi: cùm lectionem recitat, faciendum aliquid volvit factumve reminiscitur. Atque in hunc modum nihil disciplinatè nec opportunè recipitur vel dimittitur.
units.tr: Collation 10, chapter 13. A mind that is always restless and wandering, even at the time of the synaxis, is drawn away to various things as if drunk, and fulfils no office properly. For example, while it prays, it recalls a Psalm or some reading; while it sings, it meditates on something other than what the text of the Psalm contains; when it recites the lesson, it turns over something to be done or recalls something already done. In this way nothing is received or dismissed in an orderly and fitting manner.

units.la: 520. S. Cæsarius, Arelatensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 520. St Caesarius, Bishop of Arles.

units.la: In Vitâ a ejus à Cypriano discipulo conscriptâ, cap. 8. Voluit verò, atque etiam compulit Laicos & populares homines, Psalmos & Hymnos
units.tr: In his Life, written by his disciple Cyprian, chapter 8. He wished, and indeed compelled, the laymen and common people to sing the Psalms and Hymns

units.la: a Apud Surium, Augusti XXVII. pag. 947. promere, altâque & modulatâ voce, instar Clericorum ; alios Græcè, alios Latinè, Prosas & Antiphonas decantare ; ne illis spatium suppeteret ad fabulas in Ecclesiâ effutiendas. Hinc patet plebem olim in Ecclesiâ Gallicanâ Psalmos Hymnosque unà cum Clero decantare consuevisse ; Officiaque divina diversis linguis pro auditorum intellectu celebrata fuisse ; saltem Arelate, in quâ, utpote Galliarum Præfecti sede, multi Græci, qui Latinè nesciebant, commorati fuisse videntur.
units.tr: a In Surius, August 27, p. 947. aloud and with a high, modulated voice, like the clergy; some in Greek, others in Latin, to chant the proses and antiphons, so that they would have no time left for idle talk in the Church. From this it is clear that in the Gallican Church of old the people were accustomed to sing Psalms and Hymns together with the clergy, and that the divine offices were celebrated in different languages according to the understanding of the hearers; at least at Arles, where, as the seat of the Prefect of the Gauls, many Greeks who did not know Latin seem to have lived.

units.la: 550. Aurelius Cassiodorus.
units.tr: 550. Aurelius Cassiodorus.

units.la: Annot. in Psal. XLIV. Circumamicta varietate.] Perscrutemur, cur Ecclesia Dei de vestis varietate laudetur ; cui totum simplex convenit atque unum. Sed hic varietatem aut linguas multiplices significat ; quia omnis gens secundùm suam Patriam in Ecclesiâ psallit auctori ; aut virtutum pulcherrimam diversitatem.
units.tr: Notes on Psalm 44. "Clothed about with variety." Let us examine why the Church of God is praised for the variety of her garment, when everything simple and one belongs to her. Here, however, it signifies either the manifold tongues, since every nation sings to the Author in the Church according to its own country, or the most beautiful diversity of virtues.

units.la: 550. Facundus, Episcopus Hermianensis,
units.tr: 550. Facundus, Bishop of Hermiane,

units.la: Pro defens. trium Capit. lib. 12. cap. 1. Nam si obstinatus ille dicendus, qui non cedit Ecclesiæ constitutis earundem Scripturarum authoritate firmatis ; quanto deterioris obstinationis dicendus est ; qui ipsis divinis Scripturis dedignans acquiescere, inviolabili earum plenitudini aut abrogat veritatem, aut aliquid deesse putat, quod propriâ debeat adinventione supplere. Et mox, Postquam multos in fide imperfectos esse dixerat, qui omnes fidei argutias non capiunt, nec in omnibus recte sentiunt, nec tamen Hæretici sunt dicendi ; quia dociles sunt, & perfectiorem scientiam à doctis recipere semper parati, addit: Imperfectus iste profectò nihil sui cordis adinventione confictum, propriâ quâdam authoritate docere præsumit, sicut quidam Hæretici ; neque talia docentes sequitur : sed authoritati divinarum literarum innititur ; atque ubi earum intelligentiam non fuerit assecutus (in multis siquidem pro illarum magnâ profunditate humanus caligat aspectus) cognoscens quid inde statuerit universalis Ecclesia, errori suo piâ cordis humilitate renuntiat. Verùm enimverò si Christiano imperfecto fides è Scripturis haurienda fuerit ; si ad Ecclesiam recurrendum, quoties earum sensum minùs assecuti fuerint ; certè Scripturæ imperfectis etiam & indoctis patebant, neque illis ex imperitiâ factum esse præjudicium credebatur.
units.tr: In defence of the Three Chapters, book 12, chapter 1. For if he must be called obstinate who does not yield to the decrees of the Church, which are confirmed by the authority of these same Scriptures, how much more obstinate must he be called who, disdaining to submit to the divine Scriptures themselves, either denies the truth of their inviolable fullness or thinks that something is lacking, which he ought to supply by his own invention. And soon after, having said that many are imperfect in the faith, who do not grasp all the subtleties of faith and do not think rightly on everything, yet are not to be called heretics because they are teachable and always ready to receive fuller knowledge from the learned, he adds: Such an imperfect man, certainly, does not presume to teach, with some authority of his own, anything invented from the fabrication of his own heart, as certain heretics do, nor does he follow those who teach such things; but he relies on the authority of the divine letters, and where he has not attained their understanding (for in many things human sight is dimmed by the great depth of those letters), knowing what the universal Church has decided on the matter, he renounces his error with pious humility of heart. But truly, if faith for an imperfect Christian is to be drawn from the Scriptures, and if recourse must be had to the Church whenever they have not grasped their sense, then certainly the Scriptures were open even to the imperfect and the unlearned, and it was not believed that any prejudice arose for them from their inexperience.

units.la: 560. S. Germanus, Parisiensis Episcopus.
units.tr: 560. S. Germanus, Parisian Bishop.

units.la: Quali studio plebs atque Clerus Parisiensis psalmodiam in Ecclesiâ sub Germano Episcopo communi voce frequentârint, Venantius Fortunatus nos docet hisce versibus d. Flagranti studio populum domus irrigat omnis: [omnem.] Certatimque monent, quis prior ire valet, &c. Pontificis monitis Clerus, Plebs psallit, & Infans: Unde labore brevi fruge replendus erit. Sub Duce Germano fœlix exercitus hic est.
units.tr: Venantius Fortunatus shows us with what eagerness the people and clergy of Paris sang psalms together in the church under Bishop Germanus, in these verses: "With ardent zeal the whole household fills the people with song. They urge one another eagerly, to see who can go first, etc. At the bishop's bidding the clergy, the people and even the infants sing psalms; so that the harvest is ready to be gathered after a short labour. Under the leadership of Germanus this is a happy army."

units.la: 595. Gregorius I. Romanus Episcopus,
units.tr: 595. Gregory I, Bishop of Rome,

units.la: Homil. 15 in Ezech. In Scripturis invenimus prædicamenta operis & exempla virtutis: ibi jubetur, quid agere etiam corporaliter debemus; ibi hoc quod ad operandum præcipitur, in sanctorum virorum ac fortium actione monstratur, &c. Studete, quaso, fratres charissimi, Dei verba meditari; nolite despicere scripta nostri Conditoris, quæ ad nos missa sunt. Multum valde est, quod per ea animus refricatur ad calorem, ne iniquitatis suæ frigore torpescat. Cùm illâ precedentes justos fortiter egisse cognoscimus; & ipsi ad fortitudinem bonæ operationis accingimur; sanctorum exemplorum flammâ animus legentis accenditur. Videt quæ fortia ab eis facta sunt; & valdè indignatur sibi, quia talia non imitatur. Unde rectè sponsæ voce ad sponsam dicitur. Sicut turris David collum tuum, &c. Mille clypei pendent ex eâ, omnis armatura fortium. In collo etenim guttur, in gutture vox est. Quid ergo per collum sanctæ Ecclesiæ nisi sacra ejus eloquia designantur? In quâ dum mille clypei dependere memorantur; per hunc perfectum numerum numerus universus ostenditur, quia universa nostra munitio in sacro eloquio continetur. Ibi quippe sunt præcepta Dei, ibi exempla justorum, &c.
units.tr: Homil. 15 in Ezech. In the Scriptures we find precepts of works and examples of virtue. There we are commanded what we ought to do even in bodily terms; there what is commanded for us to do is shown in the actions of holy men and brave warriors, etc. I beg you, dearest brothers, study to meditate on the words of God; do not despise the writings of our Creator, which have been sent to us. It is of great value that through them the mind is rekindled to warmth, lest it grow numb with the cold of its own wickedness. When we learn that the just who went before us acted bravely, we too are girded for the strength of good works, and the mind of the reader is set on fire by the flame of holy examples. It sees what brave deeds were done by them, and it is greatly indignant with itself because it does not imitate such things. Therefore it is rightly said by the bride to the bride: "Thy neck is like the tower of David, builded for an armoury; a thousand bucklers hang upon it, all shields of mighty men." For the neck is the throat, and in the throat is the voice. What, then, is signified by the neck of the holy Church but her holy utterances? In that a thousand bucklers are said to hang from it, the whole number is shown by this perfect number, because our whole defence is contained in the holy word. For there are the precepts of God, there the examples of the just, etc.

units.la: d Poemat. lib. 2. c Cant. IV.
units.tr: d Poemat. lib. 2. c Cant. IV.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: FRustra à nobis quærunt Pontificii tempus & Authorem introductæ in sacris obeundis ignotæ linguæ. Sensim id atque incuriâ factum; prout lingua, quâ Officia Ecclesiastica condita erant, paulatim desiit esse vernacula. Citiùs id in nonnullis, tardiùs in aliis regionibus evenit: & nullibi unico seculo, neque forsan pluribus, inchoatum simul ac finitum fuit: adeò ut certam quandam mutationis factæ epocham exigere absurdum sit. Id solum dixerimus, linguam Latinam in illis Occidentis partibus, quibus in usu communi fuerat, vernaculam esse desiisse inter finem sexti & initium decimi seculi: Plura de mutatione in Galliis factâ observavit Reverendissimus Primas; quibus nos quædam adnotabimus. Linguam Latinam Galliæ olim vulgarem fuisse, in confesso est. Postquam autem Franci, Burgundiones, aliæque gentes, ♣ Germaniâ profecti, Galliam insederant; immensam vocum peregrinarum vim induxerunt; quibus adeò contaminarunt linguam pristinam, ut quamvis à linguâ Germanicâ recederent, & ad Romanam propiùs accederent, ab utraque tamen diversam efformarent linguam; quæ Rustica Romana vulgò appellabatur. Cl. Usserius quidem dubitat, annon eadem fuerit lingua Gallorum & Germanorum, Caroli M. tempore communis: & communem fuisse strenuè contendit Vitus Amerbachius ab Usserio citatus, cap. 5. ad annum 807. & Beatus Rhenanus, Rerum German. lib. 2. pag. 106. Verùm rem extra controversiam ponet Concordatio Ludovici & Caroli fratrum in Conventu Argentoratensi anno 842. facta; quæ habetur inter Capitularia Caroli Calvi, Tit. 8. & apud Nithardum lib. 3. Convenerant Argentinam Galli & Germani; illi Carolum, illi Ludovicum secuti, ad pacem inter fratres sanciendam. Pax cosit: & sacramenta quæ subiter notata sunt Lodhunvicus Romanâ, Karolus verò Theudisca lingua juraverunt; ac sic ante Sacramenta circumfusam plebem alter Theudisca, alter Romana linguâ alloquuti sunt: Dein Allocutio utriusque ad populum facta sequitur; cui subjiciuntur Sacramenta à Fratribus & à populo utrinque præstita. Sacramentum Lodhunvici, linguâ Romanâ.
units.tr: The Papists ask us in vain for the time and the author of the introduction of an unknown language into the performance of sacred rites. It happened gradually and without anyone taking notice, as the language in which the ecclesiastical offices had been composed slowly ceased to be the vernacular. It happened sooner in some regions and later in others, and nowhere was the change begun and finished at once within a single century, or perhaps even within several. So it would be absurd to demand some fixed epoch for the change. We may say only this: in those parts of the West where Latin had been in common use, it ceased to be the vernacular somewhere between the end of the sixth and the beginning of the tenth century. The most reverend Primate has noted some of the changes made in Gaul, and I shall add a few remarks of my own. That Latin was once the common tongue of Gaul is beyond dispute. But after the Franks, Burgundians and other peoples, coming from Germany, settled in Gaul, they introduced a huge number of foreign words, and so corrupted the older language that, although it moved away from German and drew nearer to Latin, it nevertheless formed a language different from both, which was commonly called Rustic Roman. The learned Ussher indeed doubts whether the language of the Gauls and Germans was the same in the time of Charlemagne, but Vitus Amerbach, cited by Ussher (chap. 5, at the year 807), and Beatus Rhenanus (Rerum German. book 2, p. 106) vigorously maintain that it was common. The matter, however, is placed beyond controversy by the agreement made between the brothers Louis and Charles at the assembly of Strasbourg in the year 842, which is found among the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 8, and in Nithard, book 3. The Gauls and Germans had gathered at Strasbourg, the former following Charles and the latter Louis, to confirm the peace between the brothers. The peace was made; and the oaths, which were noted down at once, Louis swore in the Romance tongue and Charles in the Teutonic tongue; and thus, before the oaths, the one addressed the surrounding people in the Teutonic language and the other in the Romance language. Then follows an address by each to the people, and after it the oaths sworn on both sides by the brothers and by the people. The oath of Louis, in the Romance language.

units.la: Pro Deo amur, & pro Christian poblo, & nostm commun salvamen
units.tr: For the love of God, and for the Christian people, and for our common salvation.

units.la: a Capitular. à Baluzio edita, Tom. 2. p. 39. b Inter Scriptores Corp. Pithæi, p. 353. dist di 1 in avant, in quant Deus savir & podir me dunat ; si salvarai 2 io cist meon fradre Karlo, & in adjudha & in cadhuna cosa 3 si com per dreit son 4 fradre salvar dist, 5 in o quid il mi altre si fazet. Et ab Ludher nul plaid nunquam prindrai, qui meon vol 6 cist meon fradre Karle in damno sit.
