units.la: Hinc patet toto cœlo distâsse linguas Gallicam & Germanicam tempore Conventûs istius habiti, nonnisi annis 28. post Caroli M. obitum. Quin & Rusticam Romanam Gallis tunc vulgarem fuisse exinde constat; quodque notari imprimis meretur, eam à Latinâ haud adeò discrepâsse; quin populus Officia divina Latinè celebrata adhibitâ aliquali industriâ intelligere posset. Neque enim preces publicas in plebis usum vernaculè converti & recitari Ecclesiæ Antistites curabant; sive id incuriâ factum, seu quod magis crediderim, ex nimio Sedis Romanæ cultu: cui in sacris dissentire Carolini Principes piaculum duxerunt, aut saltem ducere præ se tulerunt. Hinc exterminatus ab illis ex Ecclesiâ Gallicanâ antiquus Cantus, & Liturgia; & Romanus Ordo ac Psalmodia introducta. Factum id à Carolo Magno Cl. Armachanus probare contendit: neque id dissimulem quidem, rem ab illo promotam maximè & consummatam. Pipinum interim Regem id primùm molitum esse, Carolus ipse testis est. Ita enim in Constitutione c de emendatione librorum Ecclesiasticorum, præfatur. Accensi Pippini genitoris nostri exemplis, qui totas Galliarum Ecclesias Romanæ traditionis suo studio cantibus decoravit. Item alibi, d Monachi cantum Romanum plenitèr & ordinabiliter per nocturnale vel graduale officium peragant, secundum quod genitor noster Pipinus Rex decretavit, ut fieret, quando Gallicanum cantum tulit, ob unanimitatem Apostolicæ sedis, & sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ pacificam concordiam. En causam introducti in Ecclesiam Gallicanam cantus Romani. Nec dissimilis linguæ Romanæ in sacris retinendæ prætextus.
units.tr: From this it is plain that the languages of Gaul and Germany, at the time of that assembly, were worlds apart, and this was only twenty-eight years after the death of Charlemagne. It is also clear that Rustic Roman was then the common speech of the Gauls; and what deserves special notice is that it did not differ greatly from Latin, so that the people could, with some effort, understand divine offices celebrated in Latin. The bishops did not take care to have public prayers translated into the vernacular and recited for the people, whether this was through carelessness or, as I rather believe, through excessive devotion to the Roman See, in matters of worship with which the Carolingian princes thought it sinful to disagree, or at least professed that they thought so. Hence the ancient chant and liturgy were driven out of the Gallican Church, and the Roman order and psalmody were introduced. The most learned Archbishop of Armagh contends that this was done by Charlemagne; I do not deny that it was mainly promoted and completed by him, but Charlemagne himself bears witness that King Pepin first undertook it. For in his Constitution on the emendation of ecclesiastical books he says: Inspired by the examples of our father Pepin, who adorned all the churches of Gaul with chants of Roman tradition by his zeal. Likewise elsewhere: Let the monks perform the Roman chant fully and in an orderly way, through the nocturnal or gradual office, as our father King Pepin decreed when he set aside the Gallican chant, for the unity of the Apostolic See and the peaceful concord of the Church of God. Here is the cause of the introduction of Roman chant into the Gallican Church, and it is no different a pretext for retaining the Roman language in worship.

units.la: Procul autem abfuit ab istius ævi simplicitate; ut Ecclesiæ Rectores Scripturam aut Liturgiam à populi notitia consultò occultari vellent. Pluribus modis plebis instructioni cautum est. Primùm enim tanta assinitas inter linguam Latinam & Rusticam Romanam, tempore saltem Caroli M. intercessit; ut populus Missam Latinam, præsertim toties recitatam, haud ægrè intelligeret, Scripturam etiam penitus non ignoraret. Præterquam enim, quòd Lectores jubeantur S. Scripturam clarè & distinctè legere, ita ut à plebe intelligi possint (1), prout ex variis Conciliorum hujusce temporis decretis adnotavit Illustrissimus Armachanus, cap. 7. constat plebem in Liturgiâ sacrâ crebris responsoriis partes suas obiisse, & communes cum Sacerdote preces obtulisse. Id autem fieri nequaquam poterat; nisi intellectæ essent populo preces & responsoria. Sic enim in capitularibus à Benedicto Levita collectis habetur; Laicus non debet in Ecclesiâ lectionem recitare, nec Alleluia dicere, sed psalmum tantùm aut responsoria sine Alleluia. Et iterum, Gloria Patri & Filio & Sp. S. cum omni honore apud omnes canatur; & ipse Sacerdos cum sanctis Angelis & populis Dei cum unâ voce, Sanctus, Sanctus, cantet. Deinde cum in tantùm mutata fuerit lingua, ut Latina apud plebem penitus exolescere coeperit; duplex remedium adhibitum fuit: alterum ut Scriptura Sacra & Officia divina populo in Ecclesiâ coadunatâ linguâ vernaculâ à sacerdotibus exponerentur; aliud ut populus elementis Latinis imbueretur. Prius præceptum reperitur inter Capitularia prædicta, lib.6. cap. 376. Episcop idiligenter per suas parochias discutiant Presbyteros; ut Missarum preces bene intelligant, & ut Psalmi digne secundùm divisiones versuum modulentur; & Dominicam Orationem ipsi intelligant & omnibus prædicent intelligendam; ut quisque sciat quid petat à Deo. Quin & Episcopus cùm Diœcesin suam pro more visitaret, petere tenebatur ab omni Presbytero; Si Epistolam & Evangelium bene legere posset, atque saltem ad literam ejus sensum manifestare. Prout legitur in Inquisitione solenni, quæ apud Reginonem extat. In nulla autem re magis enituit Ecclesiæ studium; ut Plebs sacram Liturgiam & Oracula calleret, quàm in infinitis ferè, quæ edidit, decretis de Scholis passim fundandis, in quibus pueri cujuscunque sortis, linguâ Latinâ gratis instituerentur. Id Ecclesia canonibus, id Imperatores edictis strenuè procurabant. Scholæ illæ in Monasteriis
units.tr: Yet this was far from the simplicity of that age, so that the rulers of the Church deliberately wished to hide Scripture or the liturgy from the knowledge of the people. The instruction of the people was provided for in several ways. First, there was such close kinship between the Latin language and Rustic Roman, at least in the time of Charlemagne, that the people could readily understand the Latin Mass, especially since it was recited so often, and they were not wholly ignorant of Scripture. For besides the fact that readers are ordered to read Holy Scripture clearly and distinctly, so that it can be understood by the people (1), as the most illustrious Archbishop of Armagh has noted from various decrees of the councils of this period (chap. 7), it is established that the people played their parts in the sacred liturgy through frequent responses, and offered prayers together with the priest. This could by no means have happened unless the prayers and responses were understood by the people. For so it is found in the capitularies collected by Benedict the Deacon: A layman must not recite the lesson in church, nor say the Alleluia, but only the psalm or the responses without the Alleluia. And again: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, is to be sung with all honour by everyone; and the priest himself, with the holy Angels and the people of God, is to sing with one voice, Holy, Holy, Holy. Then, since the language had changed so much that Latin began to die out completely among the people, a twofold remedy was applied: one, that Holy Scripture and the divine offices should be expounded by the priests to the people gathered in the church in the vernacular language; the other, that the people should be taught the rudiments of Latin. The first precept is found among the aforementioned Capitularies, book 6, chap. 376: Let the bishops carefully examine the priests throughout their parishes, so that they understand the prayers of the Mass, and so that the Psalms are sung properly according to the divisions of the verses, and that they themselves understand the Lord's Prayer and proclaim it to all so that it may be understood, that each may know what he asks of God. Indeed, when the bishop visited his diocese in the customary way, he was bound to ask every priest: Whether he could read the Epistle and the Gospel well, and at least make their sense plain to the letter. So it is read in the solemn inquiry which is found in Regino. But the Church's zeal shone out most of all in the almost countless decrees she issued for founding schools everywhere, in which children of every rank were taught Latin free of charge, so that the people might know the sacred liturgy and the oracles. The Church pressed this through canons, and the emperors through edicts. Those schools were first established in the monasteries…

units.la: (1) Inter Capitula Caroli M. in Theodonis villâ anno 805. edita, primum est, Lectores in Ecclesiâ distinctè legantur. primùm instituta sunt: quâ de re extat Epistola Caroli M. ad Baugulfum Abbatem Fuldensem, quâ illum obnixè rogat, ut Scholam in Monasterio suo aperiret. Postea verò cùm ad conservandam S. Scripturae & Missae publicae intelligentiam id necessarium deprehenderetur; singulis Presbyteris injunctum est, ut Scolas vicatim instituerent, & Pueros omnes suae Parochiae linguam Latinam gratis edocerent. Refert Monachus Engolismensis, qui scripsit Vitam ejus, Carolum M. in eam maximè curam incubuisse, post tertium iter Romanum, cùm Grammaticos ab Urbe secum adduxisset anno 787. Hinc in Capitulari Aquisgranensi anno 789. evulgato jussum est ut Presbyteri pueros sibi locient; Et ut Scolae legentium puerorum fiant, Psalmos, notas, cantum, compotum, Grammaticam per singula Monasteria vel Episcopia discant, sed & libros catholicos bene emendatos habeant; quia sape dum bene aliquid Deum rogare cupiunt, per inemendatos libros male rogant. Et in Capitulari Theodulphi Episcopi Aurelianensis anno 797. lato, caput 20. sic habet; Presbyteri per villas & vicos scolas habeant; & si quilibet fidelium suos parvulos ad discendas literas eis commendare vult, eos suscipere & docere non renuant, sed cum summâ caritate eos doceant, &c. Nihil ab eis pretii pro hac re exigant, neque aliquid ab eis accipiant. Neve id Scripturae discendae gratiâ factum dubitemus; idem mandatum iisdem verbis renovatur in Concilio Valentino III. anno 855. Canone 18. addità ratione istâ; Quia ex hujus studii longâ intermissione, pleraque Ecclesiarum Dei loca & ignorantia fidei & totius scientiae inopia invasit. Sic & in Capitulari interrogationis de iis, quae Karolus M. pro communi omnium utilitate interrogandā constituit, in Theodonis villâ anno 811. Articulus tertius est hujusmodi; Interrogare volumus ipsos Ecclesiasticos; ut qui Scripturas sanctas non solùm ipsi discere, sed etiam alios docere debent. Caroli decretum à Concilio Cabilonensi II. an. 813. confirmatum est hisce verbis; Oportet etiam, ut sicut Dominus Imperator Carolus praecepit, Episcopi scolas constituant, in quibus & literaria scientia disciplina, & S. Scripturae documenta discantur. Canonem istum renovárunt Patres Concilii Parisiensis anno 829. Inter Capitula Hincmari Archiepiscopi Rhemensis cautum est, ut inquiratur in omni Parochia; Si Sacerdos habeat Clericum, qui possit tenere scolam, aut legere
units.tr: (1) Among the chapters of Charles the Great issued in Theodo's villa in the year 805, the first is: Let readers be read distinctly in the church. The schools were first established for this purpose. There survives a letter of Charles the Great to Baugulf, Abbot of Fulda, in which he earnestly asks him to open a school in his monastery. Later, when it was judged necessary for preserving the understanding of Holy Scripture and of the public Mass, each presbyter was ordered to set up schools village by village and to teach all the boys of his parish the Latin language free of charge. The monk of Angoulême who wrote his life reports that Charles the Great devoted himself especially to this care after his third journey to Rome, when he had brought grammarians with him from the city in the year 787. Hence, in the Capitulary of Aachen published in the year 789, it was commanded that the presbyters should hire teachers for themselves: And that schools of boys who are reading be established, that they learn the Psalms, the musical notation, singing, computation and grammar in every monastery or bishopric, and also that they have good, carefully corrected catholic books; because often, while they wish to pray to God well, they pray badly through uncorrected books. And in the Capitulary of Theodulf, Bishop of Orléans, issued in the year 797, chapter 20 reads thus: Presbyters shall keep schools in the villages and hamlets; and if any of the faithful wish to entrust their little children to them for learning letters, let them not refuse to receive and teach them, but teach them with the greatest kindness, etc. Let them demand no payment from them for this, nor accept anything from them. Lest we doubt that this was done for the sake of learning Scripture, the same command is renewed in the same words at the Council of Valence III in the year 855, canon 18, with this reason added: Because through the long neglect of this study, most places of the churches of God have been overrun by ignorance of the faith and a lack of all learning. Likewise in the Capitulary of questions concerning those things which Charles the Great established to be asked for the common benefit of all, issued in Theodo's villa in the year 811, the third article is of this kind: We wish to question the ecclesiastics themselves, since they must not only learn the holy Scriptures themselves, but also teach others. The decree of Charles was confirmed by the Council of Chalon II in the year 813 in these words: It is also fitting, as the lord Emperor Charles has commanded, that bishops establish schools in which both literary learning and discipline and the teachings of Holy Scripture are learned. The Fathers of the Council of Paris in the year 829 renewed this canon. Denique cùm neque frequens scholarum multitudo, nec assidua Presbyterorum interpretatio, crassam S.Scripturæ ignorantiam laicorum mentibus eximere potuerint; Concilium apud Saponarias anno 859. habitum, collapsum divinæ legis studium deflet, idque iterum instaurari vehementer suadet, Canone 10z. qui ascribi huic loco imprimis meretur; Statuimus, ut Scolæ sanctarum Scripturarum, & humanæ quoque literaturæ; unde annis præcedentibus, per religiosorum Imperatorum studium magna illuminatio Ecclesiæ & eruditionis utilitas processit; deprecandi sunt pii Principes nostri, & omnes Fratres & Coepiscopi nostri instantissimè commonendi; ut ubicunque omnipotens Deus idoneos ad docendum, id est, fideliter & veraciter intelligentes, donare dignatur; constituantur undique Scolæ publicæ: scilicet ut utriusque eruditionis, & divinæ sc. & humanæ, in Ecclesiâ Dei fructus valeat accrescere; quia, quod nimis dolendum est, & perniciosum maximè; divinæ Scripturæ vera & fidelis intelligentia jam ita dilabitur; ut vix ejus extrema vestigia reperiantur. Et idcirco ingenti curâ & studio remedium procurandum est.

Nor should books be lacking for those who read: in the Capitularies collected by Benedict the Deacon it was commanded that the true canonical books be kept in the churches. Finally, since neither the frequent multitude of schools nor the constant interpretation of the presbyters could free the minds of the laity from their gross ignorance of Holy Scripture, the Council held at Saponières in the year 859 laments the collapsed study of divine law and strongly urges that it be restored again, in canon 102, which deserves to be quoted especially here: We decree that schools of holy Scriptures, and also of human literature, from which in preceding years, through the zeal of religious emperors, great enlightenment of the Church and benefit of learning has come forth, must be requested of our pious princes; and that all our brothers and fellow bishops be most urgently admonished, that wherever almighty God deigns to grant men fit for teaching, that is, those who understand faithfully and truly, public schools be established everywhere; so that the fruit of both kinds of learning, divine and human, may grow in the Church of God; because, what is to be lamented very much and is most harmful, the true and faithful understanding of divine Scripture is now so far fallen away that scarcely any last traces of it can be found. Therefore a remedy must be procured with great care and zeal.

De die autem accinge rursum ad opus tuum pro viribus tuis peragendum. Non mediocriter solet illustrare & colligere mentem lectio. units.tr: Scala Paradisi, step 27, ch. 2, nos. 38, 39. (1) Devote yourself to prayers and meditations for the most part at night, and to psalmody only a little. By day, gird yourself again to carry out your work with all your strength. Reading is wont to illuminate and gather the mind considerably. For these are the words of the Holy Spirit, and they wholly guide and govern the readers. Let your reading, while you work, be suited to the activity.

units.la: Grad. 28. num. 5,&c. Fusè disputat orationi mente necessario attendendum esse; ita ut inter precandum (2) mens in iis tantùm hæreat, quæ meditanda & tractanda proposuit, &c. Magnus ille magna & perfecta orationis cultor, Volo (inquit) quinque verba sensu meo loqui; & qua sequuntur.

He argues at length that the mind must necessarily attend to prayer, so that while praying (2) the mind should cling only to those things which it has proposed to meditate on and handle, and so on. units.tr: That this Chronicle was written under the reign of Heraclius is plain from the clearest indications in its later part. That the author was an Alexandrian by birth is fairly clearly gathered from p. 366. On p. 213 words of this kind are read: "David wished to compose and sing four psalms concerning matters pertaining to the Lord alone; (3) but all the others he meant to set forth for all, for the salutary instruction of other men, whether of matters or of histories. Wherefore he wished to publish those [precepts] set to melody and arranged in rhythms, so that they would be easy to grasp and easily retained in memory by all, because of

units.la: (3) Κοινωφελῆ διδασκαλίαν τῆς πάσαν ἐπαπολυμένην. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἱμνικῶς, καὶ μὴ ῥυθμῷ πεζὰ ἐξέπεμψεν, ἵνα εὐπρόσεκτα καὶ εὐμνημόνευτα τοῖς πᾶσιν ὡς πρὸς τὰ χαρᾶς. Καὶ τοῦτο εὔδηλον ὡς ἐν πᾶσιν ἡδονῇ καὶ ἐνλλογὴ... (Greek note, partly illegible) eorum suavitatem comprehenderentur. Id quod minimè est obscurum; cùm per totum terrarum orbem in omnibus templis Davidis odaria decantentur, atque etiam in omnium ferè ore parvorum juxta ac magnorum circumferantur ac celebrentur quotidie, menteque assiduè ac memoriâ revolvantur, & plùs quàm aliorum Prophetarum scripta ac monumenta recolantur. Sic locum frigidè satis vertit Matthæus Raderus Jesuita, vir quidem non indoctus, in hac tamen Versione conficiendâ parùm fidelis aut accuratus. Unicum inauditæ ofcitantiæ exemplum proferam, p. 563. Juxta Versionem Latinam pura puta hæresis docetur, nempe falsum esse justos Cœlum assecuturos propter Christi in Terris actam vitam; adeòque Raderus, Lectori timens, consultum duxit cautelam margini apponere, & durius esse dictum clamare. Verùm enimverò si Græca consulas; nihil durum, nihil non orthodoxum reperies.
units.tr: (3) A teaching useful to all, for everyone. Therefore he sent them forth in hymn form and not in prose rhythm, so that they would be attentively heard and easily remembered by all, for joy. And this is clear: in all pleasure ... (Greek note, partly illegible) ... that their sweetness might be grasped. This is by no means obscure, since throughout the whole world David's odes are sung in all churches, and are carried on the lips of nearly everyone, small and great alike, and are celebrated daily, and are constantly turned over in mind and memory, and are recalled more than the writings and records of the other Prophets. Matthew Raderus the Jesuit translated the passage rather coldly. He was indeed no unlearned man, but in making this version he was not very faithful or accurate. I will give one example of unheard-of drowsiness, p. 563. According to the Latin version, sheer heresy is taught, namely that it is false that the righteous will attain heaven because of the life Christ lived on earth. Raderus, fearing for the reader, thought it wise to add a caution in the margin and to say that the statement was harsher than it should be. But indeed, if you consult the Greek, you will find nothing harsh and nothing unorthodox.

units.tr: Mystagogy (or Exposition of the Church's Liturgy), ch. 8. (4) "The Master used to say that the divine readings of the most sacred books hint at (declare) the divine and blessed wills of holy God. From them we receive instructions and precepts for our conduct, each according to his capacity and the power that is in him; and we learn the laws of divine and blessed contests. By the rule of these, contending lawfully, we obtain crowns worthy of Christ's kingdom, crowns of victory."

units.la: τῶν ἀναλόγως ἴσως δι' ἡμῖν λαμβάνοντες, ἡ τοῦ θείου ἢ μαρτυρίων ἀγώνων νόμως ματαιό-ζομεν, καὶ ἐς τοῦμων ἀλλήλαις ἀγῶνες, &c. Junius Cedmono tribuit. Exemplar ejus MS. penès Armachanum fuerat. Id enim Somnero Dictionarium Saxonicum molienti commodavit; uti Somnerus in Praefatione gratus agnoscit. Quin & Junius in Praefatione exemplar suum Armachano acceptum refert. De Cedmono ista habet Joannes Tinmuthensis in Historiâ Aureâ MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, lib. 20. cap. 7. Cedmon fecit mira poemata quasi per omnes sacrae Scripturae Historias. ―― Divinitus edoctus in linguâ Patriâ facere carmina compunctiva; cui nullus alius in hujusmodi potuit aequiparari.
units.tr: Junius attributes it to Caedmon. His manuscript copy was in the possession of the Archbishop of Armagh, for he lent it to Somner while he was preparing his Saxon Dictionary, as Somner gratefully acknowledges in his Preface. Junius too, in his Preface, mentions that he received his copy from the Archbishop of Armagh. About Caedmon, John of Tynemouth says in his Historia Aurea, a manuscript in the Lambeth Library, book 20, ch. 7: "Caedmon made wonderful poems covering nearly all the histories of Holy Scripture ... divinely taught in his native tongue to make songs that pierce the heart; no one else could be compared with him in this kind."

units.la: Lib de Virginitate (inter Orthodoxographa Basil. 1569. Tom. V. pag. 1677.) laudat Virgines sacras ad quas scribit; quòd in earum Epistolâ ad se scriptâ, melliflua divinarum studia Scripturarum sagacissimâ sermonum serie patefecerunt. Et postea eaedem praedicat, quòd per ampla Scripturarum stadia decurrentes, sagacissimam animorum industriam, & vivacis ingenii qualitatem assiduâ lectionis instantiâ exercere noscantur. Hinc clarè patet Versionem S. Scripturae Anglicam Aldhelmi aevo extitisse. Aliter impossibile fuisset foeminis Scripturae studium excolere: cum Latinae linguae notitia adeò rara apud Anglos illâ aetate fuerit, ut paucissimi etiam è Clero eam vel summis labiis degustârint. Primus certè Anglorum Aldhelmus Latinè scripsit, Latinis literis Romae & in Galliis imbutus. Quin & ipsum Versionem Scripturae Anglicam fieri curâsse veri non est absimile. Ut Balei enim testimonium de Psalterio ab illo Saxonicè seu Anglicè converso taceam: extat etiamnum Epistola ejus ad Ehfridum, quâ illum multis obsecrat, ut divina eloquia in communem omnium usum vernaculâ linguâ explicaret. Illam ex vetustissimo exemplari (quod ante Normannorum adventum exaratum, primò Monasterii Abendoniensis, dein viri doctissimi Thomae Allen, Oxoniensis, fuerat) descripsit Cl. Usserius, & cum tribus aliis ejusdem exemplaribus in Bibliothecis Regiâ, Cottoniana, & D. Willelmi Howard de Naworth, accuratè contulit; adjectis etiam Glossis, quae in Codice Abendoniensi, singulis lineis interjectae erant. Apographum inter laceras quasdam Reverendissimi Primatis schedas inveni, quod tamen dolendum erat, in fine mutilatum. Quae deerant igitur Epistolae ex Codice Abendoniensi supplevi & Cottoniano contuli; illamque, utpote hactenus ineditam, integram subjeci.
units.tr: In his book On Virginity (among the Orthodoxographa, Basel 1569, vol. V, p. 1677) he praises the holy virgins to whom he writes, because in their letter to him they set forth the sweet studies of the divine Scriptures in a most shrewd sequence of words. Later he commends the same women, saying that running through the broad racecourses of the Scriptures, they are known to exercise the most keen diligence of their minds and the quality of a lively wit by constant application to reading. From this it is clearly evident that an English version of Holy Scripture existed in Aldhelm's age. Otherwise it would have been impossible for women to cultivate the study of Scripture, since knowledge of Latin was then so rare among the English that very few, even of the clergy, had tasted it, even on the lips. Aldhelm was certainly the first of the English to write in Latin, having been trained in Latin letters at Rome and in Gaul. Nor is it unlikely that he himself arranged for an English version of Scripture to be made. To say nothing of Bale's testimony about the Psalter turned by him into Saxon or English, there still exists his letter to Ehfrid, in which he earnestly begs him to expound the divine oracles in the vernacular for the common use of all. Mr Ussher, the distinguished scholar, copied it from a very ancient exemplar (written before the coming of the Normans, first belonging to the monastery of Abingdon, then to the most learned Thomas Allen of Oxford), and carefully collated it with three other copies of the same in the Royal Library, the Cottonian Library, and that of Mr William Howard of Naworth. He also added the glosses which were written between the lines of the Abingdon codex. I found a copy among some torn papers of the most reverend Primate, which, it must be regretted, was mutilated at the end. I therefore supplied what was missing from the Abingdon codex, collated it with the Cottonian, and, since it has hitherto been unpublished, I have set it out entire.

units.la: Primitus pantorum procerum praetorumque pio potissimum paternoque praesertim privilegio panegyricum poemataque passim prosatori sub polo promulgantes stridulo vocum symphoniâ; ac melodiae cantilenaeque carmina modulaturi hymnizemus: praecipuè quia tandem almae editum puerperae sobolem ob inextricabile fogus Protoplastorum piaculum priscorumque chirographum [peccaminum, MS.Cot.& Reg.]obliteraturum terris tantundem destinare dignatus est: luridum qui linguis celydrum trisulcis rancida virulentaque vomentem per aevum venena torrenda tetrae tortionis in tartara trusit. Et ubi pridem eadem nefandae nutricis ermula cerbulusque crudâ fanis colebantur stoliditate in profanis; versâ vice discipulorum gurgitia, immo almae oraminum aedes architecti ingenio faebrè conduntur. Fateor sodalitatis fraternae cliens, altique municipatûs municeps; postquam vestram repedantem isthuc ambrosiam ex Iberniae drumosis circionis insulae climatibus; ubi ter bino circiter annorum circulo uber sophiae fugens metabatur; Territorii marginem Britannici sospitem applicuisse rumigerulis referentibus comperimus: Illico, ut flammiger flagransque flagitabat amor, ineffabiles altithrono grates pansis in edito utrinque volis tripudiantes obtulimus. Potissimum quod te exulem almus arbiter priscam paterna visitantem clientelam rura caerula ponti trans glaucia inormesque dodrantium glareas atque spumiferas lymphae obstirpationes circili carenâ procellosum sulcante salum reducere ovante novarco dignatus est: ut ubi dudum incunabulis tyrocini editus rudibus adulto tenus pubertatis aevo adoleveras; nunc
units.tr: First, we who sing hymns, modulating poems and songs of melody and cadence, make panegyrics and poems everywhere, with a shrill harmony of voices, chiefly because the kindly Father of all, the most loving and especially paternal, has deigned at last to send down to the earth, under the sky, the offspring born of the fostering Mother, to wipe out the dreadful sin of the first parents and the ancient bond of sins; he who thrust into the hellish pits of cruel torment the livid one who vomited through his three-forked tongues the rancid and venomous poisons to be burned for ever. And where once the wild beasts of the foul nurse were worshipped in profane temples with crude stupidity, now, in turn, the whirlpools of the disciples, or rather the sacred halls of prayers, are built with the skill of the craftsman. I confess that I am a client of the brotherly fellowship and a citizen of the high municipality; since we have learned from the travellers' reports that your ambrosia has returned safely from the wooded climes of the island of Ireland, where for about three times twelve years you sought and found the rich fount of wisdom, and have reached the border of the British territory: at once, as the fiery love flamed and demanded, we offered our inexpressible thanks to the High Throne, with wings spread wide in exultation upon the height. Especially because the kindly Judge deigned to bring you back, an exile visiting your ancestral clientage over the blue fields of the sea and the grey pebbles of the waves, ploughing the stormy waters with a ship without a keel, with exultant new helmsmanship; so that, where you were once born in the cradle of learning and grew up, rude, to the age of adult youth; now, supported in abundance by heavenly help, returning from your sojourn in a foreign land, having obtained the summons of a teacher, you discharge your office, relying on the lot assigned to you.

units.la: Illud æquè altnitati Beatitudinis vestræ ex penetrabilibus præcordii nequaquam promsisse dissimulo propalare ad agmentum mystisque ut reor tripudii; immo ad doxam onomatis cyrii magnopere inolevisse; quod præconio ultra modum rumoris Scottico in solo degentium, quorum contubernio parumper fretus es, centonitruali quodam boatu, fragore nimbosò emergenti, auditus nostri quatiuntur: & per tot tantaque telluris stadia lectionis opinio pagus provinciisque devulgata crebrescit. Siquidem tam creber meatus est isthinc illincque , navigero æquoreas fretantium calle gurgites; velut quædam contribula apium germanitas nectar fabrè conficientium. Nam quemadmodum alternantes reciprocâ facessante noctis nebulâ mellifluum examen emergente axe tenus æthere Titanæ glescentium culmina tiliacum florulenta, ad crates graciles farcinatam flauci bajulans gestamina asportat. Eodem modo, ni fallor, lurconum conglobatio lectorum tunningtac fpiñ, ac residua sagax discipulorum caterva florigeris agiographæ ex arbis non solùm artes grammaticas atque geometricas, bisternasque omissas Physicæ artis mechinas; quinimo allegoricæ potiora ac tropologicæ disputationis bipertita bis oracula æthralibus opacorum mellita in ænigmatibus problematum siticulosè sumentes carpunt; & in alveariis sophiæ jugi meditatione, idem tenus servanda condentes abundant: è quorum catalogo tuam proficisci solertiam prædâ onustâ atque torrente sacro sanctè propinatum redundantemque excellens fama procrebuit .
units.tr: Likewise I do not hide, from the innermost depths of my heart, that the report of your Blessedness has by no means failed to reach the company, or, as I think, the dance of the initiates; rather, the fame of your name has greatly grown in glory. This report, beyond the measure of rumour, has struck our hearing with a certain thunderous roar and a storm-cloud crash, from those dwelling in the Scottish soil, among whom you dwelt for a little while; and through so many and so great stretches of land the opinion of your reading has spread abroad and grows, from village to province. For there is so frequent a coming and going from here to there, the waves of the sea being crossed by ship-bearing paths of sailors, like a kindred band of bees making nectar skilfully. For just as, when the night-mist recedes and then alternates in turn, the honey-sweet swarm rises up, reaching the flowery summits of the Titanian heights as far as the sky, and carries to its slender wicker cells the burdens of golden honey; in the same way, unless I am mistaken, the crowd of greedy readers and the remaining wise band of disciples, gathering the flowering grammatical and geometrical arts from the sacred fields of the divine books, and also the mechanisms of physics that have been left aside, and the chief oracles of the allegorical and tropological disputation, twice divided, taking in the honeyed mysteries of the hidden things in riddles and problems with thirsty mouths, and pouring them into the hives of wisdom by continual meditation, abound; and from the catalogue of these your skill has come forth, and excellent fame has grown up, that the sacred things have been drunk, and the overflowing stream poured out to the holy, laden with spoil.

units.la: Quamobrem tuum effabilem discipulatum ceu cernuus singulatim arcuatis poplitibus subnixisque precibus effl agito; ut obliteratâ nequaquam memoriâ excedat, quod pacificus coelitus ambrosiâ praeditus, subrogatus genitore jure haereditario, bis quaternis temporum lustris Israelitici Plebis imperii sceptro fungens, almo auctus spiramine, prompsit dicens: Bibe aquam de cisternâ tuâ, & fluenta putei tui; deriventur fontes tui foràs, & in plateis aquas divide; solus habeto eas; ne sint alieni participes tui. Quapropter his sacris imbutus sagminibus, jugi conamine orthographiae aperito gurgitem; & sitientia rigito arva mentium; quatenus germen aethralis extaseos vivis foecundisque in horthodoxorum satoris sudore sulcis satum, nullo torridae obstaculo siccitatis obtinente pullulans glescat; & ubertim spissa Dei suffragio seges demum maturescat. Nam idcirco supplex tam obnixè haec cernitur oramen suggessisse; quòd nonnulli supernâ noscuntur sophâ praediti, & archanâ luce inormiter ferti. Attamen quod gratuitâ coelitus munificentiâ Deique dapsili dedicatione receptantes proprio facessante meritorum quaestu adepti sunt: Nequaquam gazophylacio scientiae serrato plenè promulgantes, sed particulatim lurconibus largientes. Nam cata Evangelicum experimentum auctoritatis nequaquam flagrans lichinus clanculae fuscata tetrâ occulitur latebrâ urnae; qui candelabri summitate cunctis limpido lumine lucere decuit. Necnon frustra talenti foenora subterraneis clanculantur obstructa sablonibus; quae trapezitarum numerosis monetae oportuissent nummismatibus profligari; ne forte ut iners adepto segnitia torpens mancipium talento supremo ergastulorum in squalores trusus praecipitaretur: sed potius evax eugeque ingressuro tripudium à profatore
units.tr: Therefore I beseech your admirable discipleship, bending my knees and suppliant in prayer, one by one, that it may never escape the memory, obliterated by no means, what the peaceful one, endowed with ambrosia from heaven, appointed by his father by hereditary right, wielding the sceptre of the empire of the Israelite people for twice four lustres, enriched with the holy breath, uttered, saying: Drink water out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well; let thy fountains be dispersed abroad, and rivers of waters in the streets; let them be only thine own, and not strangers' with thee. Wherefore, being imbued with these holy mysteries, open the stream with continual labour in the orthography; and water the thirsty fields of minds; so that the seed of heavenly ecstasy, sown in the furrows of the orthodox sower's sweat, living and fruitful, may sprout and grow, no obstacle of parched dryness holding it back; and that, with God's favour, a thick harvest may at last ripen abundantly. For this reason the supplicant is seen to have pressed this entreaty so earnestly; because some are known to be endowed with heavenly wisdom and are carried wildly by secret light. Yet, what they have received and obtained by the gratuitous bounty of heaven and the lavish gift of God, with their own merits as the gain, they do not by any means fully publish from the treasury of learning that has been locked, but give out in portions to gluttons. For just as the Gospel experience of authority, a flaming lamp, is hidden in a dim hiding place under a jar; yet it ought to shine with clear light for all from the top of the lampstand. Likewise, the interest of the talent is vainly concealed under sand buried underground, when it ought to have been spent in the countless coins of the money-changers; lest, like a sluggish servant torpid from idleness, having received the talent, he should be cast into the squalor of the dungeons and thrown out; but rather, for the one about to enter the joy of the good and faithful, there should be joy from the speaker.

Scriptura aquam de cisterna sua bibere, id est, proprium sablum de scientia sua elicere; & post derivare foràs, i.e. aliis talentum scientiae suae participare, & post participationem habere eas solus, id est, non insanem gloriam ex iis quaerere. units.tr: v "So affable", Cot. w That is, Solomon. x "heavenly", Cot. This reading is also noted in the margin of the Regius manuscript. a That is, honoured. b That is, appointed. c That is, by the father David. d "Israelite", Cot. e That is, kingdom. f That is, holy. g That is, spirit. Proverbs 5. Other writers of a later age also interpret this passage about spreading knowledge of the Scriptures in much the same way. Thus Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his Exposition of Isaiah, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, on chapter 2, verse 3, and on Proverbs, says: "Drink water from your own cistern, and have it to yourself alone." First, one ought rather to drink water from one's own cistern in Holy Scripture, that is, to draw out one's own proper sap from one's knowledge; and afterwards to pour it out abroad, that is, to share with others the talent of one's knowledge, and after sharing it, to have the waters to oneself, that is, not to seek empty glory from them. Peter Comestor too, in Sermon 19, on the Ascension of the Lord, manuscript in the same place: "Give us this day our daily bread." For Holy Scripture is the bread by which the soul is fed, once the truth is known. It is necessary to put the Lord's talent out at interest. Your fountains must be poured out abroad. h "recovered", Cot. i That is, brought up. k "sagninta", from sanciendo, that is, confirming, Gl. m "watered", Cot. n "of the orthodox", Cot. o "gleaming". p "this", Cot. q "wisdom", Cot. r "and", Cot. s "filled", Cot. t "dedication", Cot. and Reg. v "unlocked", Cot. w "full", Reg. x "poet". z "lamp", Cot. b "secretly", Cot. c "dark", Cot. d That is, are hidden. e Alternative reading: "hidden". f "money" in Cot. g from interposed, Cot. and Alan. h "supreme", Cot. i "may be thrown headlong", Cot. l "entering" or "about to enter", Cot. m That is, from the father, J.V.; "may be earned" by him. Hence the Psalmist, the poet, expiating this guilt of his own sin, begins with a sacred presage and says: "I have not hidden thy righteousness," and so on.

units.la: Sed haec miserrimus homuncio dictando volvens scrupulo ancipiti extimplo quatiens angebar. Quur, inquam, Hibernia, quà catervatim isthinc lectitantes classibus advecti confluunt, ineffabili quodam privilegio efferatur; ac si isthic foecundo Britanniae in cespite dedasculi Argivi Romanive Quirites repperire minimè queant: qui coelestis tetrica enodantes Bibliothecae problesmata, sciolis referare se sciscitantibus valeant. Quamvis enim praedictum Hiberniae rus discentium opulans vernansque, ut ita dixerim, pascuosâ numerositate Lectorum; quemadmodum poli cardines astriferis micantium ornentur vibraminibus siderum: at tamen climatis Britannia occidui in extremo fermè orbis margine sita, verbi gratiâ, ceu Solis flammigeri & luculento Lunae specimine potiatus, id est, Theodoro infulâ Pontificatus fungenti, ab ipso tyrocinio rudimentorum in flore Philosophiae artis adulto; necnon & ejusdem sodalitatis cliente Hadriano duntaxat urbanitate enucleatâ ineffabiliter praedito; & audacter in propatulo contestans pellaci falsitatis tribulo neglecto aequâ veritatis censurâ trutinante discernam: etiamsi beatae memoriae Theodorus summi sacerdotii gubernacula regens, Hibernensium globo discipulorum, ceu aper truculentus molossorum cataltâ ringente vallatus stipetur; limato perniciter grammatico dente jactură dispendii carens rebelles phalanges discutit, autpote belliger in meditullio campi arcister legionum phalangibus septus aemulorum spissis mox nervosis tenso lacertorum vocis arcu spiculisque ex pharetrâ exemptis, hoc est, Chronographiae opacis acutisque sillogismis turma supercilii typho turgens, amissâ ancilium testudine terga dantes, latebras antrorum atras triumphante victore praeproperè petunt. Neu tamen haec Philosophando, Scoticos sciolos, quorum gemmato tua sagacitas dogmatum favo aliquantisper abusa est,
units.tr: But while I turned these things over in dictating, I was tormented by a double doubt at once. Why, I ask, is Ireland, where scholars come flocking from here in fleets to read, exalted with some unspeakable privilege, as if among the fruitful turf of Britain there could be found no Argive or Roman Quirites who could unravel the knotty problems of the heavenly Library and answer the questions of the half-learned? For although that Irish country, flourishing and green with its pasture-like crowd of readers, as I may say, is adorned as the poles of heaven are adorned by the twinkling of the stars; nevertheless Britain, lying on the western edge of the world at the far margin of the climate, enjoys, as it were, the fiery Sun and a bright example of the Moon, that is, Theodore, who holds the office of Pontiff, from the very apprenticeship of his rudiments grown to maturity in the flower of the philosophical art; and likewise Hadrian, his companion in the same fellowship, endowed beyond words with polish and urbanity alone; and I will boldly declare in the open, neglecting the deceitful thorn of falsehood, weighing with equal judgement the discernment of truth. Even though Theodore, of blessed memory, governing the helm of the highest priesthood, is surrounded and crowded by a throng of Irish disciples, like a fierce boar surrounded by a pack of mastiffs, whose grammatical tooth, sharpened swiftly, shakes off the rebel ranks without loss; or, like a warrior archer in the middle of the field, surrounded by the phalanxes of legions, with the dense, sinewy arms of his voice bending the bow and his arrows drawn from the quiver, that is, with the dark and sharp syllogisms of chronology, the proud troop, swollen with conceit, having lost the tortoise-shell of its shields, turns its back and in triumph the victor hastens to the black caves. Yet, lest these things seem to be said in a philosophical spirit, the Scottish smatterers, whose honeyed dogmas your sagacity has to some extent abused,

Si verò {i}quippiam inscitiâ suppeditante garrula frontosè convincitur pagina {j}promtisse: ut Versidicus ait:
units.tr: {i} That is, multitude. A multitude of soldiers is either a legion or a disorderly crowd, Gl. {l} That is, of the unskilled. {m} "of the voice", Cot. {n} That is, brief or temporal Scripture, Gl. {o} "wrongly", Cot. {p} That is, of the saints, this shield, Gl. {q} "quickly", Cot. {a} I think I am to be disparaged by no one; for while I was striving to weave the praise of our people in a kindly way, I was not mocking their disparagement with ridiculous laughter, nor was I scoffing at your people, but rather, in the manner of a jester and a buffoon, I was joking with a fraternal irony under the pretext of affection, by the rash wit of those who speak. But if, by the chattering of ignorance, any statement is found in my page to be rashly brought forward, as the versifier says:

units.la: Digna fiat fante glingio gurgo {k}fugax fambulo.
units.tr: Let it be made worthy of the stammering tongue of a fleeting, babbling gurgo, a fugitive fambulo.

units.la: {l}Neu timeat Scriptor terrentis ludicra linguæ.
units.tr: And let not the writer fear the playful tongue that terrifies.

units.la: Sic semper cupiunt Scriptorum carpere cartas:
units.tr: Thus always the writers of books desire to pick at the pages of others,

units.la: Ut caper hirsutus rodet cum dente racemos.
units.tr: As a shaggy goat gnaws the grape-clusters with its tooth.

units.la: Nec tamen emendant titubantis gramma Poetæ.
units.tr: Yet they do not correct the grammar of a stumbling poet.

units.la: {m}Arbiter æternus tibi jam miserescat in ævum,
units.tr: May the eternal Judge now have mercy on you for ever,

units.la: Fulgens divitiis, semper & ore clarus.
units.tr: shining in riches and always famous in speech.

units.la: Hastenus Aldhelmi Epistola. Heahfridum (quem etiam Ehfridum, Eadfridum, Ecgfridum, Ecgbertum vocant) Aldhelmo morem gessisse patet ex Gulielmi Butleri testimonio; quod à Baleo {n}mutuatus Cl Usserius supra reposuit, cap. 5. ad an. 710. Addit Baleus Bedam Egberto sive Ecgsrido Lindisfarnensi Episcopo missâ Epistolâ objurgatoriâ muneris Pastoralis incuriam increpuisse, & de Sacrâ Scripturâ in linguam Saxonicam vertendâ submonuisse. Errâsse quidem Baleum, quamque Ecgberto Eboracensi Archiepiscopo nuncupavit Beda, Lindisfarnensi Episcopo cognomini inscripsisse Epistolam, libenter crederem. Healhfridum autem nostrum, ad quem scripsit Aldhelmus, sedem postea Lindisfarnensem tenuisse parùm dubito. Et nomen enim & tempus & eruditio apprimè conveniunt. Quodque de nostro indicat Aldhelmi Epistola de Lindisfarnensi narrat Beda {o}, illum pluribus annis in Hiberniâ sacrarum literarum studio operam dedisse, & in Scripturis doctissimum fuisse. Verum ut ad librum eius de Virginitate redeam; habetur inibi paulò post initium locus non contemnendus,
units.tr: Thus far the Epistle of Aldhelm. That Heahfrith (whom they also call Ehfrith, Eadfrith, Ecgfrith, Ecgberht) obeyed Aldhelm is clear from the testimony of William Butler, which the most illustrious Ussher borrowed from Bale and placed above, chapter 5, under the year 710. Bale adds that Bede, in a letter of rebuke sent to Ecgberht or Ecgfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne, reproached him for neglect of his pastoral duty and urged him to translate Holy Scripture into the Saxon tongue. I would gladly believe that Bale was mistaken, and that Bede addressed the letter to Ecgberht, Archbishop of York, whom he named, rather than to the Bishop of Lindisfarne of the same name. But I hardly doubt that our Healfrith, to whom Aldhelm wrote, later held the see of Lindisfarne. For name, time and learning agree very well. And what Aldhelm's letter indicates about our man, Bede relates about the Lindisfarne man: that he had devoted many years in Ireland to the study of sacred letters, and was most learned in the Scriptures. But to return to Aldhelm's book on Virginity: a not unimportant passage appears in it shortly after the beginning,

units.la: {a} i.e. Reprehendere. {b} non horum, Cot. {c} rumigerari, Cot. {d} Jocista dicitur, qui in verbis jocatur, Gl. {e} vel scurrique, Gl. Dicax, qui verbum bene loquitur. {f} i.e. loquacitate. {g} fraterna, Cot. {h} i.e. calumniabitur. {i} quempiam inscitia movéat suppeditantem, Cot. {j} prorumpente, Cot. {k} Gl Fugax Gurgo est (id est, Cot.) Virgo imperante novercâ de matrimonio exposita, inter feras enutrita, ferarum consuetudinibus assuescens. Quæ alio nomine Jucurna. Fante glingio, i.e. rogante fratre, vel alio quolibet amico, ut digna fieret illi fugax gurgo fambulo, i.e. reverentione & sine laboris, (vel sine laborum, Cot.) {l} Heu, Cot. {m} Binos hosce versus addit Codex Corronianus, in Abendoniensi desideratos.
units.tr: {a} That is, to reprehend. {b} "not of these", Cot. {c} "to be jested at", Cot. {d} A jester is one who jokes in words, Gl. {e} or buffoon, Gl. A witty person is one who speaks well. {f} That is, with loquacity. {g} "fraternal", Cot. {h} That is, he will slander. {i} "someone may be moved by ignorance supplying", Cot. {j} "bursting forth", Cot. {k} Gl. Fugax Gurgo is a maiden exposed by a stepmother's command to marriage, reared among wild beasts and accustomed to the habits of wild beasts; she is also called Jucurna. Fante glingio, that is, at the request of a brother or some other friend, so that the fugitive gurgo might be made worthy of the fambulo, that is, with reverence and without labour (or "without labours", Cot.). {l} "Alas", Cot. {m} The Corronian Codex adds these two verses, which are missing from the Abingdon copy.

units.la: {n} Cent. 2 cap. 4. {o} Hist. Eccl. Angl. lib. 5. cap. 4. 10. nisi quòd in exemplaribus vulgatis miserè depravetur. Illum igitur ex venerandæ vetustatis Codice MS. Bibliotli. Lambethanæ, Saxonicis literis pulcherrimè exarato, emendatum dabo. Nam quemadmodum ex amena riâ (Codex Lamb. examen arta) fenestrarum foramina & angusta alvearii vestibula catervatim per turmas egressus (egressum, Cod. Lamb. amœna arborum (arvorum, Lamb.) prata populatur: eodem modo vestrum, ni fallor, memoriale mentis ingenium per florulenta Scripturarum arva late vagans, bibulâ curiositate decurrit; nunc divina prisco rum Prophetarum Oracula, certis astipulationibus jamdudum Salvatoris adventum vaticinantia enixiùs investigando, nunc antiquarum arcana legum ab illo (Mose) mirabiliter digesta, &c. sollicitâ intentione scrutando: Nunc quadrifariam (quadrifaria Lamb.) Evangelica relationis dicta solerter indagando.
units.tr: {n} Century 2, chapter 4. {o} Ecclesiastical History of England, book 5, chapter 4 and 10, except that in the printed copies it is wretchedly corrupted. I shall therefore give it emended from the venerable and ancient manuscript in the Lambeth Library, most beautifully written in Saxon letters. For just as the swarms, through the narrow openings of the windows and the small doorways of the beehive, pour out in troops and plunder the pleasant meadows of trees (Lambeth codex: examen arta; egressum, Cod. Lamb.; amoena arborum, Lamb. arvorum), in the same way, I think, your memorial mind, wandering widely through the flowery fields of the Scriptures, runs about with thirsty curiosity: now searching eagerly into the divine oracles of the ancient Prophets, which long ago foretold the coming of the Saviour by certain agreements, now carefully examining the secrets of the ancient laws marvellously set in order by him (Moses), and so on: now diligently inquiring into the sayings of the Evangelical account in fourfold form.

units.la: Locum ex Aldhelmi cujusdam Abbatis Epistolâ, jussu S. Bonifacii Archiepiscopi Moguntini conscriptâ, ab Ill. Primate indicatum, nos supra exhibuimus, cap. 5. ad an. 700. Aldhelmum istum Serarius in Notis a eundem fuisse asserit cum Aldhelmo Episcopo Schirburnensi; errore quidem manifesto. Noster enim Aldhelmus anno 709. obiit, quatuordecim sc. annis antequam Bonifacius dignitatem Episcopalem obtinuit. Id quod etiam ex præcedentibus Bonifacii Epistolis Serarius observare potuerat; in quibus b Aldhelmi Episcopi & Scriptoris, utpote jampridem defuncti, memoria celebratur.
units.tr: I have already set out, in chapter 5 under the year 700, the passage from the letter of a certain Abbot Aldhelm, written at the command of St Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz, which the Most Illustrious Primate pointed out. Serarius, in his Notes, asserts that this Aldhelm was the same man as Aldhelm, Bishop of Sherborne. That is clearly an error. Our Aldhelm died in 709, fourteen years before Boniface obtained episcopal dignity. Serarius could have observed this from Boniface's earlier letters, in which the memory of Aldhelm, bishop and writer, long since dead, is celebrated.

units.la: 730. Beda Venerabilis.
units.tr: 730. Bede the Venerable.

units.la: Extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Bedæ Expositio Geneseos, ad Accam, libris III. In eâ explicantur 21. priora Geneseos Capita. Expositio Capitis primi duntaxat habetur inter Opera Bedæ, Tom. IV. titulo Commentarii in Hexaemeron. Reliqua nondum prodierunt. Inibi lib. 2. ad cap. 11. de confusione linguarum agens, hæc habet: "Mirâ immutatione dexterœ excelsi factum est; ut sicut hic (in "ædificatione turris Babel) linguis ob superbiam divisis, gentes sunt "ab invicem toto orbe dispersæ; ita illic (in Ecclesiâ) ob meritum "humilitatis adunatâ diversitate linguarum, collecti ex omni nation "tione, quæ sub Cœlo est, populi, unâ ac non dispari confessione "ac fide laudes & magnalia Dei resonarent. Meritòque hæc civitas,
units.tr: There survives in manuscript in the Lambeth Library Bede's Exposition of Genesis, addressed to Acca, in three books. It explains the first twenty-one chapters of Genesis. The exposition of the first chapter alone is found among the works of Bede, vol. IV, under the title Commentary on the Hexaemeron. The rest has not yet been published. In book 2, on chapter 11, where he treats of the confusion of tongues, he has the following: "By a wonderful reversal of the right hand of the Most High it came about that, just as there (at the building of the tower of Babel) the tongues were divided on account of pride and the nations were scattered from one another across the whole earth, so here (in the Church), on account of the merit of humility, a diversity of tongues being gathered together, peoples called from every nation under heaven might with one and the same confession and faith resound the praises and great works of God. And rightly this city,

units.la: {a} Pag. 303. {b} Epist. 4. “in quâ linguæ divisæ, ac gentes sunt disperse: Babylon, i.e. confusio. “illa dicitur Jerusalem, i. e. visio pacis; in quâ adunatis in Dei laudem “loquelis, universarum gentium est facta concordia.
units.tr: {a} Page 303. {b} Letter 4. "in which the tongues were divided and the nations scattered: Babylon, that is, confusion. That city is called Jerusalem, that is, vision of peace, in which, with speech united in the praise of God, there has been made a concord of all nations."

units.la: Lib. 3. in cap. 18. “Tulit quoque Abraham butirum & lac & vitulum, & posuit coram eis.] Per lac primordia & velut elementa “legis Mosaicæ, per butirum Evangelicæ perfectio doctrinæ; per “lac simplicitas literæ in Scripturis; per butirum virtus sensûs myshtici, qui de literâ generari solet, exprimitur. Vel certè lac initium fidei, butirum perfectionem operis, quæ ex fide creatur, insinuat. Quæ cuncta Abraham posuit coram viris quos susceperat; “ut significaret filios promissionis epulas spirituales Domino semper “oblaturos, panes videlicet lectionum sacrarum, vitulum dominicæ “incarnationis, lac fidei sive Historicæ perfectionis, butirum sensuum, “sive operum bonorum.
units.tr: Book 3, on chapter 18: "Abraham also took butter and milk and the calf, and set them before them." [Gen. 18:8] "By the milk and, as it were, the elements of the Mosaic law are signified; by the butter, the perfection of the Gospel teaching; by the milk, the simplicity of the letter of Scripture; by the butter, the power of the mystical sense, which is usually generated from the letter. Or certainly the milk indicates the beginning of faith, the butter the perfection of the work which is created from faith. Abraham set all these before the men whom he had received, so that he might signify that the sons of promise would always offer spiritual feasts to the Lord: the loaves, namely, of sacred readings; the calf, of the Lord's incarnation; the milk, of faith or of historical perfection; the butter, of the senses or of good works."

units.la: Expofit. super Canticum Abacuc Prophetæ, MS. ibid. post med. “Adaperient ora sua, sicut pauper edens in occulto.] Sicut enim “pauper aliquandiu jejunus permanens, si forte alicubi cibos invenerit, his se confestim in occulto reficere satagit; neque eos in “publicum vult proferre, ne forte diripiantur ab alio, & ipse fame “percat. Sic nimirum, sic populi gentium oblato sibi per Apo“ stolos panc verbi, à quo diutius jejuni duraverant, mox aperuerunt “ora cordis sui, & hunc omni aviditate gustare cœperunt; tantò “amplius audiendis sive legendis Scripturis operam dantes; quantò “se meminerunt diutius miserrimo genere paupertatis, supervacuis “immò etiam noxiis aures atque animum mancipâsse doctrinis.
units.tr: Exposition on the Canticle of the prophet Habakkuk, MS. ibid., after the middle: "They shall open their mouths as the poor man eating in secret." [Hab. 3:14] "For just as a poor man, remaining fasting for a long time, if he happens upon food somewhere, takes care at once to refresh himself with it in secret, and does not want to bring it out into the open, lest it be snatched away by another and he himself perish of hunger; so, in truth, so the peoples of the Gentiles, once the morsel of the word had been offered to them through the Apostles, by which they had long remained fasting, at once opened the mouths of their hearts and began to taste it with all eagerness; the more eagerly they applied themselves to hearing or reading the Scriptures, the more they remembered having long given their ears and minds over to superfluous, indeed even harmful, doctrines, in the most wretched kind of poverty."

units.la: Ibid. paulò ante sin. “Defecerunt ab esca oves, & non erant in præsepio boves.] Oves & Boves (1) typicè erant in eadem plebe “(Judæorum) Oves videlicet in eis, qui vocem summi Pastoris humiliter audiebant; Boves verò in illis, qui jugum legis (2) gnaviter “portantes, ad faciendos bonorum operum fructus corda audientium “sedulò docendo & castigando, quasi terram Domini arando, para“ bant. Hisque spiritualiter viventibus spirituales faciebant escas “campi divinarum Scripturarum latissimi; quorum pabulo delectabatur ille; qui ut jumentum factus erat apud Dominum, & semper “illi adhærebat dicens; Dominus regit me, & nihil mihi deerit:
units.tr: Ibid., a little earlier, near the foot of the page: "The sheep failed from the food, and there were no oxen in the stall." [Hab. 3:17] "The sheep and the oxen were typically in the same people (of the Jews): the sheep, namely, those who humbly heard the voice of the chief Shepherd; the oxen, however, those who, diligently bearing the yoke of the law (2), by teaching and rebuking, prepared the hearts of their hearers to bring forth the fruits of good works, as if ploughing the Lord's land. And for those living spiritually they provided spiritual food from the very broad field of the divine Scriptures, by whose pasture he was delighted who, made like a beast of burden before the Lord, always clung to him, saying: The Lord rules me, and nothing shall be lacking to me." [Ps. 23:1]

units.la: (1) Typi erant in eadem plebe. Sic legit Codex alter MS. (2) Graviter, Cod. alter. in loco pascuæ ibi me collocavit. — “ Campi non faciunt escas; “ cùm Plebs eadem apertis divinorum apicum paginis pascua veritatis “ invenire rectè intelligendo non valet.
units.tr: (1) Typi erant in eadem plebe. So reads the other manuscript. (2) Graviter, the other manuscript. In loco pascuae ibi me collocavit. "The fields do not make food, since the same people, with the pages of the divine letters opened, cannot rightly understand and find the pastures of truth."

units.la: Lib de Templo Solomonis, cap 20. “ In quo nimirum Spiritu “ clamamus Abba Pater. Abba videlicet, qui ex Hebræis venimus “ ad fidem ; Pater, qui ex Gentibus; variis quidem linguis pro diver- “ sitate nationum, sed unum eundemque Patrem Deum propter unius “ donum Spiritûs invocantes.
units.tr: From the book on the Temple of Solomon, chapter 20: "In that Spirit we cry, Abba, Father: Abba, indeed, those of us who have come to faith from the Hebrews; Father, those from the Gentiles; invoking, indeed, in various tongues according to the diversity of nations, but one and the same Father God, on account of the one gift of the one Spirit."

units.la: Epistolâ ad Egbertum Archiepiscopum Eboracensem, pag. 65. “ In quâ prædicatione [Presbyterorum vicatim] populis exhibendâ “ hoc præ cæteris omni instantiâ procurandum arbitror; ut fidem “ Catholicam, quæ Apostolorum Symbolo continetur, & Dominicam “ Orationem, quam sancti Evangelii nos Scriptura edocet, omnium “ qui ad tuum regimen pertinent, memoriæ radicitus infigere cures. “ Et quidem omnes, qui Latinam linguam lectionis usu didicerunt, “ etiam hæc optime didicisse certissimum est: sed idiotas, hoc est, “ eos qui propriæ tantùm linguæ notitiam habent, hæc ipsâ suâ linguâ “ dicere ac sedulò decantare facito, &c. Propter quod & ipse multis “ sæpe Sacerdotibus idiotis hæc utraque, & Symbolum videlicet & Ora- “ tionem Dominicam in linguam Anglorum translatam obtuli.
units.tr: From the letter to Egbert, Archbishop of York, p. 65: "In which preaching [of the elders, village by village] to be delivered to the people, I think that above all things this should be secured with every urgency: that you take care to fix deeply in the memory of all who belong to your rule the Catholic faith, which is contained in the Apostles' Creed, and the Lord's Prayer, which the Scripture of the holy Gospel teaches us. And indeed it is most certain that all who have learned the Latin tongue by the practice of reading have learned these also very well; but the unlearned, that is, those who know only their own language, you should make them say these things in their own tongue and diligently sing them, etc. On account of which I myself have often offered to many unlearned priests both of these, namely the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, translated into the English tongue."

units.la: 750. Chrodogangus, Episcopus Metensis.
units.tr: 750. Chrodogang, Bishop of Metz.

units.la: Romanæ Ecclesiæ cantum Gallicanæ à Pipino & Carolo M. introductum fuisse, Cl. Armachanus, cap. 4. Nosque in Auctuario, cap. 4. pluribus observavimus. Romanum cantum primùm in Metensi Ecclesiâ receptum, dein ad cæteras Galliæ Ecclesias derivatum fuisse omnes illius temporis Historici tradunt. Illum itaque Metensi Ecclesiæ à Chrodogando invectum fuisse tantùm non constat. Sedem enim Metensem ab anno 742. ad 766. tenuit, vir præclarus apud suos famæ, apud Franciæ Reges potentiæ; quique Romam sæpius profectus, immensum Romanorum rituum studium conceperat. Quantum igitur Cantores Romani illo seculo auditorum institutioni studebant, ex Chrodogandi Regulâ, quam Diœcesèos suæ Clericis anno 757. præscripsit, optimè dijudicari queat. Inibi enim de Cantorum Officio agens, hæc habet: a “ Sonum etiam
units.tr: That the Gallican Church received the chant of the Roman Church, introduced by Pepin and Charlemagne, the learned Archbishop of Armagh shows in chapter 4, and we have noted this at greater length in the Auctuarium, chapter 4. All the historians of that period report that the Roman chant was first received in the Church of Metz and then spread from there to the other churches of Gaul. It is not clearly established, however, that Chrodogang introduced it into the Church of Metz. He held the see of Metz from 742 to 766, a man of distinguished reputation among his own people and of power at the court of the Kings of France, who had often gone to Rome and had conceived an immense zeal for Roman rites. How much the Roman singers of that age cared for the instruction of their hearers can be well judged from Chrodogang's Rule, which he prescribed for the clergy of his diocese in 757. There, treating of the office of the singers, he says: a "Let them also pronounce the sound of the vowels well and elegantly.

units.la: a Cap. 50, 51. vocalium literarum bene & ornatè proferant. Hi verò qui hujus artis minùs capaces sunt, donec erudiantur, melius convenit, ut tileant, quàm cantare volendo quod nesciunt, aliorum voces dissonare compellant. Psalmi namque in Ecclesiâ non cursim aut in excelsis atque inordinatis seu intemperatis vocibus, sed plane & lucidè cum compunctione cordis recitentur; ut & recitantium mens illorum dulcedine pascatur, & audientium aures illorum pronuntiatione demulceantur, &c. Plùs velint in lectione & cantu populi ædificationem, quàm popularem vanissimam adulationem.
units.tr: a Chapters 50, 51. Those who are less capable of this art should, until they are taught, be better advised to keep silent rather than, by wishing to sing what they do not know, force the voices of others out of tune. For the Psalms in the Church are not to be recited hastily, or in high, disordered or immoderate voices, but plainly and clearly, with compunction of heart, so that the mind of those who recite is fed by their sweetness, and the ears of those who hear are soothed by their delivery, etc. In reading and singing they should seek the edification of the people rather than the most empty popular flattery.

units.la: 800. Ordo Romanus.
units.tr: 800. The Roman Order.

units.la: Quænam fuerit Ecclesiæ Romanæ consuetudo ac judicium à Gregorii M. tempore usque ad Caroli M. ætatem, luculenter nos docet Ordo Romanus; qui ritus & cæremonias istius Ecclesiæ ab illo saltem tempore usurpatas tradit. Hunc à Gregorio M. primitus compositum esse tantùm non constat. Ab illo omnia pene Ecclesiastica Officia habemus, inquit Ivo Carnotensis (quo non alius res Liturgicas Ecclesiæ antiquæ melius novit) in libro de Ecclesiasticis Officiis MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, cap. 33. Ecclesiæ autem Romanæ ritus Galli haud aliunde nôrunt quàm ex Ordine Romano; qui Galliæ sub Carolo M. invectus, deinceps in pretio esse cœpit. Hujus rei indicia sunt manifesta libri de Ecclesiasticis Officiis editi ab Alcuino, Rabano, Amalario, Walafrido, Ivone, aliisque conscripti; qui quicquid de rebus Romanis habent, ex Ordine Romano hauserunt. Plurimæ ejus Editiones olim exiterunt, à sequentibus seculis pro lubitu concinnatæ: Illam autem, quæ in omnium jam manibus impressa habetur, præclaras Caroli ætate additiones & interpolationes accepisse constat. Plurimi id ab Alcuino factum esse suspicati sunt, non levibus sanè conjecturis ducti. Lucem forsan dabit ampliorem locus, qui in Ivonis libro MS. (de quo nuper mentionem injeci) prope finem reperitur. "Fecit Albinus, Magister Karoli, in Ecclesiâ non contemnendum opus. Nam Gregorianas Orationes in libro Sacramentorum collegisse asseritur, paucis aliis adjectis, quas tamen sub obelo notandas esse judicavit. Deinde alias Orationes sive Præfationes, etsi non Gregorianas, Ecclesiasticæ tamen celebritati idoneas, collegit." Librum quidem immutavit & auxit Alcuinus, vel quispiam alius coætaneus; neque tamen Romanæ disciplinæ notitiam minus certam exinde reddiderunt. Præterquam enim quòd eadem disciplina, quæ in Ecclesiâ Romanâ obtinuit, Gallicanæ à Carolo M. inducta fuerit; adeòque ut Ordo Romanus Gallorum usibus commodè inserviret, non tam immutandus fuit, quàm variis ritibus & formulis, quæ post Gregorii tempora apud Romanos in usu esse cœperant, augendus: ut id, inquam, taceam: Scriptores de rebus Ecclesiasticis supra memorati, quorum Opuscula totidem ferè sunt Ordinis Romani Expositiones, ejusmodi ritus Romæ usurpatos esse fidem faciunt; præsertim verò Amalarius, qui Romam profectus fuerat, & cum Clero Romano diu versatus. Horum itaque Expositiones haud tam Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ quàm Romanæ statum spectant, cujus disciplinam & cæremonias, in Ordine suo positas, explicandas suscipiunt, earumque rationes & significationem exhibent.
units.tr: The Ordo Romanus clearly teaches us what the custom and judgment of the Roman Church were from the time of Gregory the Great to the age of Charlemagne; it sets out the rites and ceremonies of that Church, at least as they were practised from that time. That Gregory the Great first composed it is not clearly established. "From him we have almost all the offices of the Church," says Ivo of Chartres (than whom no one knew the liturgical matters of the ancient Church better) in his manuscript book On the Ecclesiastical Offices, in the Lambeth Library, chapter 33. The Gauls, however, know the rites of the Roman Church only from the Ordo Romanus, which was brought into Gaul under Charlemagne and then began to be held in high esteem. The clear evidence of this is the books On the Ecclesiastical Offices published by Alcuin, Rabanus, Amalarius, Walafrid and Ivo, and others, who wrote on the subject; whatever they have about Roman matters they drew from the Ordo Romanus. Many editions of it existed in earlier times, variously put together by later centuries; but the edition that is now in everyone's hands is known to have received notable additions and interpolations in the age of Charlemagne. Many have suspected that Alcuin did this, and not without slight conjectures. A passage near the end of Ivo's manuscript book (which I mentioned a little while ago) may perhaps give more light: "Albinus, the teacher of Charles, produced a work of no small value in the Church. For he is said to have collected the Gregorian prayers in the Book of Sacraments, adding a few others, which he nevertheless judged should be marked with an obelus. Then he collected other prayers or prefaces, if not Gregorian, yet suitable for the solemnity of the Church." Alcuin, or some other contemporary, indeed altered and enlarged the book, yet they did not make knowledge of the Roman discipline any less certain by this. For apart from the fact that the same discipline that prevailed in the Roman Church was introduced into Gaul by Charlemagne, so that the Ordo Romanus might serve the use of the Gauls conveniently, it needed not so much to be altered as to be enlarged with various rites and formulas which had begun to be in use among the Romans after the time of Gregory; to pass over this, I say, the writers on ecclesiastical matters mentioned above, whose little works are almost all expositions of the Ordo Romanus, make it plain that rites of this kind were used at Rome; especially Amalarius, who had gone to Rome and had long associated with the Roman clergy. Their expositions therefore look less to the state of the Gallican Church than of the Roman, whose discipline and ceremonies, set out in its Order, they undertake to explain, and whose reasons and meaning they present.

units.la: His positis, disciplinam in Ordine Romano institutam dispiciamus. Primò itaque Lectiones S. Scripturæ, quæ frequentes admodum erant præ hodiernis, ad instructionem populi solummodo collimârunt, & ab illo probè intellectæ sunt. Id evincit Formula Benedictionis Lectorum, quæ in Ordine Romano a extat, & à Cl. Armachano supra est adducta b. Hoc orat Episcopus super eos quos Lectores ordinat (inquit c Gulielmus Malmsburiensis in Abbreviatione Amalarii librorum de Officiis Eccles. MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ) ut assiduitate lectionum sint apti pronuntiare verba vitæ, & vocis distinctione populo monstrare intelligibilia. Paria habet Amalarius, lib. 2. cap. 8. qui lectionem ad doctrinam pertinere sæpius confirmat d. Hinc similitudinem inter Lectores Christianos & Judaicos intercessisse volunt. Lectores fuisse in vetere lege, qui librum Hesdræ legit, intelligit. Is quippe legit super gradum ligneum stans, distincte & aperte. Sic Gulielmus Malmsburiensis in Abbreviatione c suâ MS. Ille igitur nos docebit, qualiter legere debeamus, inquit Amalarius f. § Lectio enim Legis & Prophetarum frequentabatur à populo antiquo. Lector legem Domini debet tradere auditoribus, quasi incipientibus in Scholâ Domini exerceri, &c. In lectione pascitur auditor, quasi quodammodo bos. Hinc crebræ, quæ in Ordine Romano observari possunt, Diaconi ad populum Allocutiones ante inchoatas lectiones. State cum silentio audientes intentè ; vel, State cum disciplinâ & silentio, audientes intentè: Eandem disciplinæ rationem docent plures aliæ inter adhibitæ legendum cæremoniæ. Alcuinus, vel quisquis Author est libri de Divinis Officiis, de Diacono Evangelium lecturo hæc habet. "Salutat populum, dicens, Dominus vobiscum. Quatenus corda illorum Deus à mundanis cogitationibus emundet, & ad suscipienda verba salutifera aperire dignetur. Ad cujus salutationem populus crucem in frontibus ponit; ut à malis cogitationibus corda sua emundet, ut ad intelligenda verba salutis pura permaneant. Perlecto Evangelio, iterum se signo crucis populus munire festinat; ut quod ex divinis eloquiis ad salutem percepit, signatum sigillo crucis atque munitum permaneat; ne à mentibus eorum diabolica fraude evacuari valeat. Post recitatum Evangelium, iterum Sacerdos populum salutat, orans in cordibus eorum verba salutis, quæ perceperunt à Domino, confirmari: & invitat illum secum pariter ad Orationem dicens, Oremus." Pari de causâ libri, ex quo lectio desumpta est, titulus à Lectore prænuntiabatur; ut attentio excitaretur, & memoria adjuvetur. Ita enim Amalarius: Lectionem è gradu solemus proferre; ut omnis populus eam audiat. Prænuntiato libri titulo, Auctor ad memoriam reducitur, ut si forte aliquis eorum qui congregantur ex universis locis, propter raritatem lectionis, incognitam habet historiam; audiat auctorem, qui forte non est incognitus, & ex ejus auctoritate firmius infigantur verba lectionis in corde. Id enim ab Auditoribus postulabant; ut verba Evangelica lectionis frequenti meditatione revolverent. Ipse cantus usu suo non caruit, ad instructionem populi compositus; Ut qui ad legem audiendam obsurduerant, illo cantu excitarentur. Uti habet Malmsburiensis, Amalario consonus. Hinc à totâ simul plebe, pariter ac Sacerdotibus, Hymnus decantari solebat. "Nam & optimus & salubberrimus (inquit Amalarius) in sanctâ Ecclesiâ mos inolevit, ut "Hymnus ipsius (de Christo nato) quotidie cum psalmodiâ vespertinæ laudis ab omnibus canatur; quatenus ex hoc animos fidelium
units.tr: Having laid this down, let us look at the discipline instituted in the Ordo Romanus. First, then, the readings of Holy Scripture, which were very frequent compared with today's, aimed solely at the instruction of the people, and were properly understood by them. The formula of blessing for readers, which is found in the Ordo Romanus a and was cited above by the learned Archbishop of Armagh b, proves this. "The bishop prays this over those whom he ordains as readers," says William of Malmesbury c in his manuscript abridgement of Amalarius's books On the Offices of the Church, in the Lambeth Library, "that by their constant readings they may be fit to pronounce the words of life and, by the distinct voice, make intelligible things plain to the people." Amalarius has the same, book 2, chapter 8, where he often affirms that reading pertains to teaching d. Hence some hold that there was a likeness between Christian and Jewish readers. "There were readers in the old law; he who reads the book of Hesdras understands it. For he reads standing upon a wooden platform, distinctly and openly." So William of Malmesbury in his manuscript abridgement c. "He therefore will teach us how we ought to read," says Amalarius f. § For the reading of the Law and the Prophets was frequent among the ancient people. The reader ought to hand on the law of the Lord to the hearers, as beginners who are to be trained in the School of the Lord, etc. The hearer is fed in the reading, as it were like an ox. Hence the frequent addresses of the deacon to the people before the readings begin, which can be observed in the Ordo Romanus: Stand in silence, listening attentively; or, Stand with discipline and silence, listening attentively. Several other ceremonies used before reading teach the same reason for discipline. Alcuin, or whoever is the author of the book on the Divine Offices, says this of the deacon who is about to read the Gospel: "He greets the people, saying, The Lord be with you, so that God may cleanse their hearts from worldly thoughts and deign to open them to receive the words of salvation. At this greeting the people place the cross on their foreheads, so that they may cleanse their hearts from evil thoughts and remain pure for understanding the words of salvation. When the Gospel has been read, the people hasten again to fortify themselves with the sign of the cross, so that what they have received from the divine utterances for salvation may remain sealed and fortified by the seal of the cross, and not be able to be emptied from their minds by the devilish fraud. After the Gospel has been recited, the priest again greets the people, praying that the words of salvation which they have received from the Lord may be confirmed in their hearts; and he invites them to pray with him, saying, Let us pray." For the same reason the title of the book from which the reading was taken was announced by the reader beforehand, so that attention might be aroused and memory helped. For so Amalarius: We are accustomed to read the lesson from the step, so that the whole people may hear it. With the title of the book announced beforehand, the author is brought back to memory, so that if by chance any of those who gather from all places, because the reading is rare, does not know the story, he may hear the author, who perhaps is not unknown, and by his authority the words of the reading may be fixed more firmly in the heart. For they demanded this of the hearers, that they should turn over the words of the Gospel reading by frequent meditation. The chant itself, composed for the instruction of the people, did not lack its use; so that those who had grown deaf to hearing the law might be roused by that chant. So William of Malmesbury, agreeing with Amalarius. Hence a hymn was customarily sung by the whole people together with the priests. "For (says Amalarius) a very good and most salutary custom has grown up in holy Church, that the hymn of the birth of Christ be sung every day by all with the evening psalmody of praise, so that from this the minds of the faithful..."
