Lib. 4. cap. 7. “frequentior Dominicæ Incarnationis memoria ad affectum devo-” “tionis accendat.” Item plures alios Hymnos à populo simul ac Sacerdotibus decantari solitos recenset. Haud dissimilia habet Ivo Carnotensis in libro MS. de Ecclesiasticis Officiis: “Sergius “Papa (inquit) in ordine 82. constituit, ut in tempore confractionis “Dominici Corporis Agnus Dei à Clero & Populo decantetur; “videlicet ut ille nobis propitietur; cujus Corpus ibi confringi “videmus & credimus.” Infinitus essem, si omnia congererem argumenta, quæ preces à populo intellectas fuisse suadent. Hoc crebræ Diaconi attentionem imperantis Allocutiones; hoc innumeræ populi Responsiones evincunt. Hinc Ivo Carnotensis in libro MS. supra citato: “Sacerdos versus ad populum dicit, Dominus “vobiscum. Resp. Et cum Spiritu tuo. Notandum ex his “verbis semper debere esse plures respondentes & unum salutan-” “tem, &c. Sancti quoque Patres in Aurelianensi Concilio, cap. 3, “constituerunt; ut ad salutationes Sacerdotis non solum Clerici & “Deo dicati, sed & omnis Plebs consonâ voce respondeant. In “omni enim legitimâ Oratione respondent fideles,” inquit Alcuinus : qui rem alibi fuse persequitur. Post oblationem “convertit se Sacerdos ad populum, poscens; ut jungant preces suas “precibus ejus, & mereatur exaudiri pro salute illorum, &c. “Acclinans ergo se populus orare debet ita. Sit Dominus in “corde tuo & in ore tuo, &c. Vel hoc dicant omnes: Exaudiat te “Dominus in die tribulationis. Protegat te nomen Dei Jacob. usque “pingue fiat. Hucusque præfatio, i. e. præloquutio & allocutio populi. “Hinc sequitur exhortatio,” Sursum corda; “Hortatur enim “Sacerdos populum, tanquam dicat. Jam Apostolicis & Evangelicis præceptis sufficienter instructi & confirmati, corda vestra “à terrenis curis sursum ad Dominum dirigite. Respondet populus, “Habemus ad Dominum,&c.”. Quinimo postquam superstitione pravâ, Eucharistia non tam communio Corporis Christi, quàm juge sacrificium Patri quotidie offerendum haberi cœpit; & Sacerdotes Canonem Missæ seù preces consecratorias tacitè obmurmurârunt; alias tamen preces distinctè & apertè pronuntiârunt, ut à populo
units.tr: {h} Pag. 39, 40, 41, &c. {i} Cap 40. pag. 280. Lib. 4. cap. 3. Amalar. lib. 4. cap. 7. Lib. 2. cap. 9. Lib. 3. cap. 11. Lib. 4. cap. 7. "a more frequent remembrance of the Lord's Incarnation kindles the feeling of devotion." He likewise lists several other hymns which were customarily sung by the people together with the priests. Ivo of Chartres in his manuscript book on the ecclesiastical offices says something not unlike this: "Pope Sergius (he says) ordained in his eighty-second decree that at the time of the breaking of the Lord's Body the Agnus Dei should be sung by the clergy and the people, namely so that he who is shown and believed to have his Body broken there might be merciful to us." I would be endless if I gathered together all the arguments that show the prayers were understood by the people. The frequent exhortations of the deacon calling for attention, and the countless responses of the people, prove this. Hence Ivo of Chartres, in the manuscript book cited above: "The priest turns to the people and says, The Lord be with you. Response: And with your spirit. It should be noted from these words that there should always be several responding and one greeting, etc." The holy Fathers also decreed at the Council of Orléans, chapter 3, that in response to the priest's greetings not only the clergy and those dedicated to God, but the whole common people should answer with one voice. "For in every lawful prayer the faithful respond," says Alcuin, who pursues this point at length elsewhere. After the offering the priest turns to the people, asking that they join their prayers to his, and that he may deserve to be heard for their salvation, etc. "So the people, bowing themselves, ought to pray thus: May the Lord be in your heart and in your mouth, etc. Or let all say this: May the Lord hear you in the day of trouble. May the name of the God of Jacob protect you, down to be made fat." Thus far the preface, that is, the people's address and greeting. Then follows the exhortation, "Lift up your hearts." "For the priest urges the people, as if to say: Now that you have been sufficiently instructed and confirmed by the precepts of the Apostles and the Gospels, direct your hearts upward from earthly cares to the Lord. The people answer, We have them toward the Lord, etc." Indeed, after a depraved superstition had begun to hold that the Eucharist was not so much the communion of Christ's Body as a continual sacrifice to be offered daily to the Father, and the priests murmured the Canon of the Mass, or the consecratory prayers, in silence, they nonetheless pronounced other prayers distinctly and openly, so that they could be understood by the people.

units.la: {q} Lib 3. cap. 21. {r} Cap. 25. {s} Cap. 10. {t} De divinis Offic. cap. 40. pag. 290. {u} Pag. 281. intelligi possent. Testis est Amalarius ; cujus hæc sunt verba : "Sacerdos clamat ad populum ; ut quod ipse jam habet, habeat "& ille, hoc est, Sursum Cor : ac deinde ut gratias agat Deo pro "serenitate mentis. Igitur hoc necessariò extollitur voce, quod "omnibus licet simul agere, i. e. gratias referre Deo, hoc accla"matur. Quod ad solum Sacerdotem pertinet, i. e. immolatio "panis & vini, secretò agitur." Adeò necessariam fuisse inter precandum mentis attentionem Amalarius credidit ; ut in exponendis Missæ orationibus insignem illum protulerit Cypriani locum (ex Exposit. in Orat. Domin. §. 22.) quem illustrissimus Primas supra citatum exhibuit, cap. 3.
units.tr: {q} Lib 3. cap. 21. {r} Cap. 25. {s} Cap. 10. {t} De divinis Offic. cap. 40. pag. 290. {u} Pag. 281. Amalarius is a witness; his words are these: "The priest calls out to the people, so that he who already has it may have it too, that is, 'Lift up your hearts,' and then that they may give thanks to God for the calm of their minds. Therefore that which is common to all, namely giving thanks to God, is necessarily raised aloud and proclaimed, since everyone may do it together. What belongs to the priest alone, namely the offering of the bread and wine, is done in secret." Amalarius so firmly believed that attentiveness of mind was necessary in prayer that, in explaining the prayers of the Mass, he brought forward that notable passage of Cyprian (from the Exposition of the Lord's Prayer, §22), which the most illustrious Primate cited above, in chapter 3, has set out.

units.la: Restat Ecclesiæ Romanæ consuetudo notatu cumprimis digna. In Ecclesiâ Antiquâ stata fuisse sacrum Baptismum atque Ordines conferendi tempora omnibus notum est. Illud semel, Sabbato sc. Sancto, isti quater, in quaternis sc. anni tempestatibus, in anno conferebantur : Saltem post Simplicium Papam, Omnes enim Apostolicos à Beato Petro usque ad Simplicium Papam Ordinationes tantum in Jejunio Decembris celebrasse adnotavit Ivo Carnotensis in libro de Eccles. Offic. MS. Ingens igitur Candidatorum numerus sacramentum Baptismatis, atque Ordines simul susceperunt ; qui Lectionibus divinis, Catechizationibus, aliisque mediis Ecclesiasticis priùs instruendi erant. Postquam autem divisâ bifariam Imperii sede, & apud Constantinopolin pariter ac Romam positâ, diuturnum inter Græcos & Latinos in utrâque urbe commercium intercesserat ; multi è Græcis in urbe Româ continuò versati sunt, qui tamen Latinè nesciebant ; multique è Latinis Constantinopoli, qui Græcè. His itaque sive ad Baptismum sive ad Ordines suscipiendos in urbe alienâ accedentibus ; necesse erat, ut Lectiones sacræ, Catechismi, & id genus alia, utrâvis linguâ proponerentur ; ut ab advenis pariter ac inquilinis intelligi possint. Idque factum quidem tam in Urbe Româ quàm Constantinopoli reperimus. Sic enim vetustus Ordo Officiorum Romanus, (vulgato multò brevior & simplicior, quique quasi Epitome videtur antiqui Ordinis, nondum à Gallis interpolati.) MS. in Bibliothecâ Archiepiscopali Lambe-
units.tr: It remains to consider a custom of the Roman Church which is especially worthy of notice. It is well known that in the ancient Church fixed times were set for conferring holy Baptism and Orders. Baptism was conferred once, namely on Holy Saturday; Orders were conferred four times a year, namely in the four seasons of the year. At least this was so until Pope Simplicius; for Ivo of Chartres, in his manuscript book on ecclesiastical offices, noted that all the Apostolic ordinations from blessed Peter down to Pope Simplicius were celebrated only in the December fast. A huge number of candidates therefore received the sacrament of Baptism and Orders at the same time; they had first to be instructed by the divine readings, catechizings and other ecclesiastical means. But after the seat of the Empire was divided in two, and placed at Constantinople as well as at Rome, a long-standing traffic arose between Greeks and Latins in both cities. Many Greeks lived continually in the city of Rome, yet did not know Latin; and many Latins at Constantinople did not know Greek. When such people came to receive either Baptism or Orders in a foreign city, it was necessary that the sacred readings, the catechism and the like be set forth in either language, so that they could be understood alike by the newcomers and by the residents. And we find that this was indeed done both in the city of Rome and at Constantinople. For thus the ancient Roman Order of Offices (much shorter and simpler than the printed one, and which seems to be an epitome of the old Order, not yet interpolated by the French), a manuscript in the Archbishop's library at Lambeth,

units.la: {a} Lib. 3. cap. 20. {b} Lib. 3. cap. 19. {c} Cap. 36. thană. Sabbato (in primâ è quatuor solennibus septimanis ordinationi sacris) ad S. Petrum fit statio in XII. Lectionibus. Ideo autem vocantur XII. Lectiones; quia VI. Lectiones, quarum sexta est Epistola, leguntur Graece & Latinè. Et iterum; Sabbato Sancto mane reddunt pueri [ Baptizandi ] Symbolum, & Catechizantur ab Episcopo vel Presbyteris. (Scrutinium id appellatur) Congregantur eâ die in Basilica Constantiniana, vestitur altare, imponuntur reliquiae. Horâ decimâ ascendit Subdiaconus in ambonem, & legit Graece Lectionem, In Principio; andemque legit alter Latinè. Item Pontifex dicit Orationem, praecipiente Diacono ut flectantur genua; similiterque ad omnes. Secunda Lectio est, Factum est in vigiliâ matutinâ; Quâ Graece & Latinè dicta, sequitur Canticum Graece & Latinè cantandum. Cantemus Domino, Eodem cantante Latinè qui Latinè legit, similiterque qui Graecè. Sicque per omnes Lectiones & Cantica. Et paulò post; Sabbato Pentecostes eodem modo leguntur Lectiones Graecè & Latinè, sicut in Pascha. Ivo Carnotensis in libro de Offic. Eccles. MS. In omni Jejunio (Ordinationem praecedente) Sabbatum, quamvis sex tantùm Lectiones habeat, dicitur tamen XII. habere Lectiones; eò quòd antiquitus Ecclesiasticae Lectiones bis legebantur, Graecè videlicet & Latinè. Amalarius: Sex Lectiones ab antiquis Romanis Graecè & Latinè legebantur (qui mos apud Constantinopolin hodieque servatur) ni fallor, duas ob causas. Una, quia aderant Graeci, quibus ignota erat lingua Latina; aderant & Latini, quibus incognita erat Graeca. Altera causa propter unanimitatem utriusque populi. Idem habent Pseudo-Alcuinus & Gulielmus Malmsburiensis ; quorum ille post annum 1000. iste post annum 1100 scripsit. Uterque autem eandem consuetudinem suo etiam tempore apud Constantinopolin obtinuisse produnt. In XII. Lectionibus consecrationem sacrorum Ordinum celebratam esse totidem verbis docet Amalarius: Leguntur autem Lectiones (inquit ex illo Malmsburiensis ) ut habeat ordinandus notitiam legis & Prophetiae. Ut in istis Lectionibus imbuantur Ordinandi ad exempla sanctorum Patrum . Sic Alcuinus . Eadem fuit & in baptismo repetitae lectionis ratio; sc. ad instruendos Baptismi candidatos: Propter instructionem Catechumenorum, inquit Amalarius: cujus verba compendio reddit {d} Post init. {e} Post. med. {f} Cap. 36. {g} Lib. 2. cap. 1. {h} De Offic. divin. cap. 29. pag. 265. {i} Abbreviat. Amalar. MS. cap. 15. {k} Loc. cit. {l} Lib. 1. cap. 19.
units.tr: {a} Lib. 3. cap. 20. {b} Lib. 3. cap. 19. {c} Cap. 36. On the Sabbath (in the first of the four solemn weeks set aside for ordinations) there is a station at St Peter's for the twelve Lessons. These are called the twelve Lessons because six Lessons are read, of which the sixth is an Epistle, in Greek and in Latin. And again: On Holy Saturday in the morning the boys [to be baptized] return the Creed, and are catechized by the Bishop or the elders. (This is called the scrutiny.) They gather that day in the Constantinian basilica; the altar is dressed, the relics are placed. At the tenth hour the subdeacon goes up to the pulpit and reads the Lesson in Greek, In the beginning; and then another reads it in Latin. Likewise the Pontiff says the prayer, the deacon directing that the knees be bent; and similarly for all. The second Lesson is, It came to pass in the morning watch; when this has been said in Greek and in Latin, a Canticle follows, to be sung in Greek and in Latin, Let us sing to the Lord; while the one who reads in Latin sings in Latin, and likewise the one who reads in Greek sings in Greek. And so through all the Lessons and Canticles. And a little after: On the Sabbath of Pentecost the Lessons are read in the same way, in Greek and in Latin, as at Easter. Ivo of Chartres in his manuscript book on the ecclesiastical offices: In every fast (preceding an ordination) the Sabbath, although it has only six Lessons, is nonetheless said to have twelve Lessons; because in ancient times the ecclesiastical Lessons were read twice, namely in Greek and in Latin. Amalarius: Six Lessons were read by the ancient Romans in Greek and in Latin (a custom still kept today at Constantinople), unless I am mistaken, for two reasons. One, because Greeks were present, to whom the Latin tongue was unknown; and Latins were present, to whom Greek was unknown. The other reason was for the unity of both peoples. Pseudo-Alcuin and William of Malmesbury say the same; the former wrote after the year 1000, the latter after the year 1100. Each of them reports that this same custom also prevailed at Constantinople in his own time. Amalarius teaches in so many words that the consecration of the holy Orders was celebrated in the twelve Lessons: The Lessons are read (says William of Malmesbury, following him) so that the one to be ordained may have knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, so that the candidates may be formed in these Lessons after the examples of the holy Fathers. So Alcuin. The same reason applied to the repeated reading at Baptism, namely to instruct the candidates for Baptism: For the instruction of the catechumens, says Amalarius, whose words he renders in brief.

units.la: Malmsburiensis : "Quatuor modis intelligitur sacra Scriptura; per Historiam, per Allegoriam, per Tropologiam, per Anagogen. Isti modi Scripturarum in Lectionibus & Canticis illius diei praefcruntur; ut intelligant plenè Catechumeni ad quid vocantur." Et alibi: " Quarta feria quartæ quadragesimalis hebdomadæ vocatur in Apertione aurium; quia more antiquo tangebantur illà die nares & aures Catechumenorum; & tradebatur eis Symbolum, quod redderent Sabbato Paschæ: & fiebat Scrutinium; i. e. scrutabantur Presbyteri, quid crederent; & docebant eos, quomodo vivere & quid credere deberent. Ideo illà die sunt duæ lectiones & duo responsoria. In priore lectione de fide & baptismo agitur. Nec minus in Responsorio vocantur ad fidem. Secunda lectio de moribus agit. Item Responsorium de fide. Versus de virtutibus morum; quas baptizandi per Deum habituri sunt. Ratio ergo quare duæ lectiones leguntur, est, quia audiant baptizandi non solum quid credere debeant, sed etiam quemadmodum se ab hoc seculo perverso eripiant." Omnia quippe propter fidem & mores, quibus instruendi erant Catechumeni, ut Amalarii verbis utar, fiebant. Extat Scrutinii forma in vulgato Ordine Romano ; in quo quidem Catechumeni Latini Symbolum Latinè, Græci Græcè reddunt. Denique quo magis instructioni Catechumenorum consuleretur: In Sabbato Sancto XII. Lectiones juxta Romanum Ordinem legenda erant absque titulis ante baptismum, teste Ivone Carnotensi, in libro de Eccles. Offic. MS. Cujus disciplinæ rationem ex Amalario reddit Malmsburiensis his verbis: Lectiones autem ideo sine nominibus librorum, de quibus sumptæ sunt, proferuntur; quia frustra Catechumenis profertur Auctor incognitus; quibus firmissima auctoritas potest vilescere per ignorantiam. Eadem fusius docet Amalarius, lib. 1. cap. 21.
units.tr: Malmsburiensis: "Holy Scripture is understood in four ways: historically, allegorically, tropologically, and anagogically. These modes of Scripture are set before the candidates in the readings and canticles of that day, so that the catechumens may fully understand to what they are being called." And elsewhere: "The Wednesday of the fourth week of Lent is called the Opening of Ears, because in the old custom the nostrils and ears of the catechumens were touched on that day. The Creed was handed to them, to be recited back on Easter Saturday, and the Scrutiny took place; that is, the elders examined what they believed and taught them how they ought to live and what they ought to believe. Therefore on that day there are two lessons and two responsories. In the first lesson, the subject is faith and baptism; likewise the responsory calls them to faith. The second lesson deals with morals; likewise the responsory concerns faith, and the verse concerns the virtues of conduct which those to be baptized are to receive from God. The reason, then, why two lessons are read is that those to be baptized may hear not only what they ought to believe but also how they may rescue themselves from this perverse age." Indeed, all these things were done for the sake of faith and morals, in which the catechumens were to be instructed, to use the words of Amalarius. The form of the Scrutiny is found in the published Roman Order, in which the Latin catechumens recite the Creed in Latin and the Greek catechumens in Greek. Finally, so that the instruction of the catechumens might be better provided for: On Holy Saturday, twelve lessons were to be read according to the Roman Order before baptism, without the titles, as Ivo of Chartres attests in his book on the ecclesiastical office (manuscript). Malmsburiensis gives the reason for this practice from Amalarius in these words: The lessons are therefore delivered without the names of the books from which they are taken, because an unknown author is read to the catechumens in vain; the most firm authority can become worthless to them through ignorance. Amalarius teaches the same more fully in book 1, chapter 21.

units.la: Immo verò in Ecclesiis Romanâ & Constantinopolitanâ S. Scripturæ Lectiones utrâvis linguâ recitatæ fuisse videntur, non solùm in Sabbato Sancto & Jejuniis quatuor, sed & in omnibus celebrioribus Festivitatibus. Certè id Nicolaus I. Papa Constantinopoli factum esse diserte affirmat; "quùm linguæ Latinæ laudes deprædicans adversùs Michaelem Imp. CP. qui illam Barbaram appellárat,
units.tr: Indeed, in the Roman and Constantinopolitan Churches the lessons of Holy Scripture seem to have been recited in either language, not only on Holy Saturday and the four fasts, but also at all the more solemn festivals. Certainly Pope Nicholas I plainly affirms that this was done at Constantinople, when, praising the Latin tongue against Michael, Emperor of Constantinople, who had called it barbarous,

units.la: Pag. 42. Cap. 61. Concil. Tom. VIII. p. 298. infit: "Ecce quotidie, immo vero in praecipuis Festivitatibus, inter "Graecam linguam, veluti quiddam pretiosum, hanc quam Barbaram "& Scythicam linguam appellatis, miscetis. Istius enim dictione "linguae Constantinopolitana Ecclesia lectionem Apostolicam & E"vangelicam in stationibus fertur primitus recitare: Sicque demum "Graeco sermone propter Graecos utique ipsas lectiones pronuntiare.". Eandem disciplinam apud Romanos vicissim obtinuisse haud dubium est; cum neutiquam credibile fit, Graecos lectiones Latinè Romanorum advenarum gratiâ recitare voluisse; nisi Romani etiam easdem Graecè in Graecorum gratiam pariter recitâssent. Rem confirmat Durandus. ° In Missâ (inquit) Romani Pontificis, in praecipuis solemnitatibus legitur Evangelium & Epistola, non solum in Latino, verùm etiam in Graeco. Constat interim Paschalem I. sub initium Seculi noni, S. Praxedis Coenobium Romae posuisse; In quo & sanctam Graecorum Congregationem aggregans; quae diu noctuque Graeca modulationis Psalmodiae laudes omnipotenti Deo Sanctisque illius ibidem quiescentibus sedulò persolveret, introduxit. Anastasius Bibliothecarius, in Vitâ ejus.
units.tr: (page 42, chapter 61; Councils, vol. 8, p. 298) he begins: "Behold, every day, indeed on the chief festivals, you mix this language, which you call barbarous and Scythian, with the Greek, as if it were something precious. For in this language the Church of Constantinople is said first to recite the Apostolic and Gospel lesson in the stations, and only then to pronounce the same lessons in Greek, for the sake of the Greeks." It is beyond doubt that the same practice prevailed among the Romans in turn; for it is by no means credible that the Greeks wished to read the lessons in Latin for the sake of the Roman newcomers, unless the Romans had also read the same lessons in Greek for the sake of the Greeks. Durandus confirms the point: In the Mass of the Roman Pontiff, on the principal solemnities, the Gospel and the Epistle are read, not only in Latin but also in Greek. It is established, meanwhile, that Paschal I, at the beginning of the ninth century, founded the monastery of St Praxedes at Rome: In which, gathering also a holy congregation of Greeks, which day and night diligently rendered to almighty God and to his saints resting there the praises of Psalmody in Greek melody, he introduced. Anastasius the Librarian, in his Life.

units.la: 807. Carolus Magnus Imp.
units.tr: 807. Charles the Great, Emperor

units.la: Incredibile, quod in totâ Carolinâ Familiâ enituit, Scripturarum studium, Historici coætanei passim depraedicant. De Caroli M. & Ludovici filii studio, Reverend. Usserius plurima congessit testimonia: quibus addere nobis liceat, Carolum consuetis Scripturae lectionibus, quae inter sacra recitabantur, nequaquam contentum fuisse, sed lectoribus certam Scripturae portionem inter Officia divina legendam pro lubitu mandâsse; Lectores, quoscunque vellet, quosque magis sonoros noverat, evocare; & Lectiones quotidianas pro arbitrio producere vel contrahere solitum. Id enim testatur Monachus Sangallensis, qui Vitam ejus scripsit: q Digito autem vel baculo protento, vel ex latere suo ad procul sedentes (Clericos) aliquo directo, demonstravit, quem legere oporteret vel voluisset. Finem verò lectionis sono gutturis designavit.
units.tr: The incredible zeal for the Scriptures that shone forth in the whole Carolingian family is praised on every side by contemporary historians. Reverend Ussher has gathered very many testimonies about the study of Charles the Great and his son Louis; to these we may add that Charles was by no means content with the customary readings of Scripture that were recited during the sacred offices, but at his pleasure assigned to the readers a fixed portion of Scripture to be read during the divine offices. He was accustomed to summon whichever readers he wished, especially those whose voices he knew to be most sonorous, and to extend or shorten the daily lessons at his discretion. The monk of St Gall who wrote his Life attests this: With a finger or a staff held out, or by some sign to the (clerics) sitting far off from his side, he showed whom he wished or ought to read. He indicated the end of the reading by a sound of the throat.

units.la: ° Rational. divin. Offic. lib. 4. cap. 1. p Cap. 5. ad an. 809, 820. q Lib. 2. cap. 10. navit. Ipse lectionem S. Scripturæ in Epistolâ ad Leonem III. Papam impensè laudat, "Lectionis (inquit) sacra cognitio, imbecillis baculum, nervosis arma ministrat; hostium subdolas fortiter premit insidias; & victoribus æternas fœliciter promittit coronas, &c." Quinimo idem studium sequior etiam è Carolinâ familiâ sexus excoluit. Sic enim Gisla, Caroli filia, & Rectruda, Moniales, ad Alcuinum scribunt, in Epistolâ Commentario ejus in Joannem præfixâ: "Postquam, venerande Magister, aliquid de melliflua S. Scripturæ cognitione, vestrâ lagacitate exponente, haustimus; ardebat nobis, ut fatemur, de die in diem desiderium hujus sacratissimæ lectionis. In quâ Purificatio est animæ, solatium mortalitatis nostræ, & spes perpetuæ beatitudinis. In quâ beatus vir, juxta Psalmistam, quotidianâ seipsum exercet meditatione, intelligens omnibus mundi divitiis hujus esse agnitionem præferendam." Neque à Proavorum studio Caroli etiam nepotes deflexisse, satis arguit liber, ineptus quidem, vetustus tamen, qui in Bibliothecâ Lambethianâ MS. extat, continens Cænam quandam, æmulatione Cænæ Pseudo-Cyprianicæ compositam; nisi quòd ex solis Personis in Veteri Testamento memoratis constet. Mauri cujusdam Auctoris nomen præ se fert (nolim credere Rabanum operam tam inutiliter posuisse) & Lothario Regi nuncupatur. In Epistolâ autem nuncupatoriâ Maurus hortatur Lotharium, quùm Cœnam suam legere voluerit, ad Veteris Testamenti paginas recurrere, quare singula singulis sunt imputata.
units.tr: (Durandus, Rational. divin. Offic. lib. 4, cap. 1; p. chap. 5, under the year 809, 820; q lib. 2, cap. 10.) Himself, in his letter to Pope Leo III, greatly commends the reading of Holy Scripture: "The knowledge of the sacred reading (he says) furnishes a staff to the weak and arms to the strong; it bravely presses down the crafty snares of enemies, and happily promises eternal crowns to the victors, etc." Indeed, the later men of the Carolingian family also cultivated this same zeal, of both sexes. For Gisla, daughter of Charles, and Rectrudis, nuns, write to Alcuin in the letter prefixed to his Commentary on John: "After, venerable Master, we have drunk in something of the honeyed knowledge of Holy Scripture, as expounded by your acuteness, a desire for this most sacred reading burned in us, as we confess, from day to day. In it is the purification of the soul, the solace of our mortality, and the hope of perpetual blessedness. In it, as the Psalmist says, the blessed man exercises himself by daily meditation, understanding that this knowledge is to be preferred to all the riches of the world." That the grandsons of Charles also did not turn aside from the zeal of their forefathers is sufficiently shown by a book, indeed foolish but old, which exists in manuscript in the Lambeth Library, containing a certain Supper, composed in emulation of the Pseudo-Cyprianic Supper; except that it consists solely of persons mentioned in the Old Testament. It bears the name of a certain author Maurus (I would not believe that Rabanus wasted his labour so uselessly) and is dedicated to King Lothair. In the dedicatory letter, Maurus urges Lothair, when he wishes to read his Supper, to return to the pages of the Old Testament, where each item is assigned to each.

units.tr: 830. Amalarius, chorepiscopus of Metz:

units.la: De Ecclesiast. Offic. lib. 4. cap. 2. "Psalmi pertinent ad opera, lectio ad doctrinam. Quâ de re, ut opinor, mos inolevit; ut per Monasteria Deo devota legatur Lectio in Capitulo; quatenus hi, qui diebus ac noctibus occupati sunt in servitio Domini, non sint sine lectione. Avidi sunt cœlestis pabuli; non se possunt continere, quin omni horâ, quantumcunque sit, manducent de cibo Scripturarum."
units.tr: From De Ecclesiasticis Officiis, bk. 4, ch. 2: "The Psalms belong to the work, the reading to the teaching. For this reason, as I think, the custom has grown up that in monasteries devoted to God a lesson is read in chapter, so that those who are busy day and night in the service of the Lord may not be without reading. They are eager for heavenly food; they cannot refrain from eating of the food of the Scriptures every hour, however long it lasts."

units.la: Concil. Tom. VII. pag. 1199. Lib. 2. cap. 2. "Vel certè ut propter simpliciores manifestius, quod volumus, eloquamur, Psalmus ad corpus, Canticum refertur ad mentem. Et canere igitur & psallere & laudare Deum magis animo quàm voce debemus.
units.tr: Councils, vol. 7, p. 1199, bk. 2, ch. 2: "Or certainly, so that we may speak more plainly to the simpler folk what we mean, the Psalm is referred to the body, the Canticle to the mind. And so we ought to sing, chant and praise God more with the mind than with the voice."

units.la: 840. Paschasius Radbertus
units.tr: 840. Paschasius Radbertus

units.la: In Threnos, lib. 4. pag. 1491. "Necessarii sunt Doctores; ut infirmi quique cùm petierint valentiores Scripturae sacrae sententias exponendas comminui, valeant aperire, & in singulis necessaria apponere. Sed luget Propheta; quando qui exponere debet, inveniri non valet. Est etiam Scriptura sacra potus lactis; de quo propheta dicit: Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas, &c. Ex quo liquidò patet, cum dicit, venite ad aquas, quia Scriptura sancta verus est potus; cum dicit, comedite, verus est cibus. Cùm autem dicit, vinum & lac; nutrimentum infantiae, & ebrietas Spiritûs S. designatur; ut per lac teneritudo nostra nutriatur, per vinum vero corda inebrientur. Quod si omnino aperta mandata Dei in Scripturis sanctis non essent; per semetipsam veritas non clamaret: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, & bibat.
units.tr: In Lamentations, bk. 4, p. 1491: "Teachers are necessary, so that whenever weaker people ask for the meanings of the sayings of Holy Scripture to be explained more fully, they may be able to open them up and set out what is needed in each case. But the Prophet laments, since the one who ought to expound cannot be found. Holy Scripture is also a drink of milk, of which the prophet says: Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters, etc. From this it is clear that when he says come to the waters, Holy Scripture is the true drink; when he says eat, it is the true food. When he says wine and milk, the nourishment of infancy and the intoxication of the Holy Spirit are meant: so that through the milk our tenderness may be nourished, and through the wine our hearts may be made drunk. And if the plain commands of God were not in the Holy Scriptures at all, Truth itself would not cry out: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink."

units.la: Epist. ad Frudegardum, pag. 1633. "Sacerdos orat ut [Panis & Vinum] fiat Corpus & Sanguis Jesu Christi. Quâ prece expletâ, consonâ voce omnes Amen dicimus: sicque omnis Ecclesia in omni gente & linguâ orat & confitetur, quòd hoc fit quod orat."
units.tr: From the letter to Frudegard, p. 1633: "The priest prays that [bread and wine] be made the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ. When this prayer is finished, we all say Amen with one voice; and so the whole Church in every nation and tongue prays and confesses that what it prays for is being done."

Horum decimum sextum est hujusmodi: "Ante Missam completam ne exeant, & verbum Dei intentè audiant [Omnes fideles.] De Oratione Dominicâ & Symbolo; ut memoriter omnes teneant, & Gloria Patri, ac Sanctus, atque Credulitas [i.e. Symbolum] & Kyrie eleison, à cunctis reverenter canatur. Psalmi
units.tr: He gave these 140 chapters to his presbyters, gathered in synod in 858. The sixteenth of them is of this kind: "Before the Mass is finished, let them not go out, but let them listen attentively to the word of God. [All the faithful.] Let the Lord's Prayer and the Creed be held in memory by all, and let the Gloria Patri, the Sanctus, the Credo [i.e. Symbolum] and the Kyrie eleison be sung reverently by everyone. The psalms

units.la: b Capitular. à Baluzio edit. Tom. I. pag. 1289. & Concil. Tom. VIII. pag. 629. “ similiter distinctè à Clericis. Et ut secreta Presbyteri non “ inchoent, antequam Sanctus finiatur, sed cum populo Sanctus “ cantent.
units.tr: b Capitularies, edited by Baluze, vol. 1, p. 1289, and Councils, vol. 8, p. 629. "likewise be sung distinctly by the clergy. And let the priests not begin the secret prayers until the Sanctus is finished, but sing the Sanctus together with the people."

units.tr: 860. Nicholas I, Roman Pope

units.la: Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum, cap. 11. “ Sanè scien- “ dum est, quoniam idcirco in diebus Festis ab opere mundano “ cessandum est; ut liberius ad Ecclesiam ire, Psalmis & Hymnis “ & Canticis spiritualibus insistere, Orationi vacare, Oblationes “ offerre, memoriis Sanctorum communicare, ad imitationem “ eorum assurgere, eloquiis divinis intendere, eleemosynas indi- “ gentibus valeat ministrare Christianus.
units.tr: From the Responses to the Consultations of the Bulgarians, ch. 11: "Surely it must be known that on feast days a Christian must therefore cease from worldly work, so that he may more freely go to the church, devote himself to psalms, hymns and spiritual canticles, give himself to prayer, offer oblations, share in the commemorations of the saints, rise up in imitation of them, attend to the divine words, and be able to give alms to the needy."

units.la: 870. Otfridus, aliique Interpretes Germanici.
units.tr: 870. Otfrid, and other German interpreters.

units.la: De Otfridi Versione Evangeliorum Germanicâ Cl. Usserius plurima congessit, Tritbemii & Illyrici ductum secutus; adeóque communes cum illis errores iniit. Principio itaque Otfridi Opus non tam Versio est quàm Harmonia seu Diatessaron Evangeliorum rythmo Germanico Veteri concinnatum; & in libros quinque (non quatuor, quod vult Trithemius) distributum. Ipsi Operi titulus fuit: Volumen Evangeliorum: neutiquam vero: Gratia Dei Theotiscè: Prout Trithemius, & à Trithemio deceptus Illyricus, crassè hallucinati existimarunt; argumento erroris exinde sumpto; quòd in Operis titulo vetusto Otfridus dicatur id Domini gratiâ Theotiscè confecisse. Denique Otfridus ipse Monachus Coenobii Wizanburgensis in Alsatiâ fuit, non S. Galli; quod in exemplaris excusi titulo ab Illyrico positum habetur: Munchu S. Gallen. Qui Opus enim istud Basileæ 1571. 8vo. excudendum curavit sub emendito Achillis Gassari nomine, non alius erat quàm Flaccius Illyricus; qui quidem
units.tr: Clarus Usserius has gathered a great deal concerning Otfrid's German version of the Gospels, following the lead of Trithemius and Illyricus, and so has fallen into the same errors as they. To begin with, Otfrid's work is not so much a version as a harmony, or Diatessaron, of the Gospels, composed in old German rhythm and divided into five books (not four, as Trithemius maintains). The work bore the title Volumen Evangeliorum, and by no means Gratia Dei Theotiscè ("the grace of God in German"), as Trithemius and Illyricus, deceived by him, grossly imagined; they took as the basis of their error the fact that in an old title of the work Otfrid is said to have produced it by the grace of the Lord in German. Finally, Otfrid himself was a monk of the monastery of Weissenburg in Alsace, not of St Gall, as the title of the printed copy put out by Illyricus has it: Munchu S. Gallen. For the man who had this work printed at Basel in 1571, 8vo, under the false name of Achilles Gasser, was none other than Flacius Illyricus, who indeed

units.la: * Concil. Tom. VIII. pag. 522. quidem Codice usus est mendoso admodum & hiulco. Lacunas supplevit ex Codice MS. optimæ notæ (qui ipsius Otfridi ætate scriptus, in Bibliotheca Cæsarea Vindobonensi nunc asservatur) Lambecius in eruditissimo Opere Commentariorum de Bibliotheca Vindob. lib. 2. pag. 420. Versionem suam Otfridus nuncupavit non solùm Liutberto Archiepiscopo Moguntino (ad quem extat Præfatio Latina) verùm etiam Solomoni ejus decessori (qui obiit anno 873.) & Ludovico Franciæ Orientalis Regi; ad quos totidem Præfationes rythmicæ linguâ Germanicâ reperiuntur, & in Editione Basileensi, & apud Lambecium loc. cit. Porrò scripsit Otfridus Oratione solutâ Versionem Psalterii Paraphrasticam; cujus exemplar MS. ipsi Authori coævum in Bibliothecâ Vindobonensi habetur, teste Lambecio ; qui Psalmum primum & Orationem Dominicam exinde dedit . Ad finem enim Codicis ab eodem versa inveniuntur Cantica S. Scripturæ omnia, Symbola Apostolorum & Athanasii, & Oratio Dominica. Cæterùm Versio Evangeliorum rythmica, quam Waldoni Episcopo Frisingensi Cl. Armachanus, Beati Rhenani auctoritate ductus, ad annum 890. ascripsit: non alia est, quàm Otfridi Harmonia; quam Waldo Sigefridi Presbyteri manu describi fecit; quod ex Præfationis initio patet. Tetrastichon enim illud, quod illustrissimus Primas ex Rhenano repræsentavit, Otfridi Volumen Evangeliorum inchoat.
units.tr: * *Councils, vol. 8, p. 522.* used a copy that was very corrupt and full of gaps. He supplied the missing parts from a manuscript of the highest quality (written in Otfrid's own lifetime, and now kept in the Imperial Library at Vienna), Lambecius doing so in his most learned work, *Commentaries on the Library at Vienna*, bk. 2, p. 420. Otfrid dedicated his version not only to Archbishop Liutbert of Mainz (to whom a Latin preface survives), but also to Solomon, his predecessor (who died in 873), and to Louis, king of East Francia. To each of these there are rhythmic prefaces in German, found both in the Basel edition and in Lambecius, loc. cit. Moreover, Otfrid wrote in prose a paraphrastic version of the Psalter. A manuscript of it, written in the author's own time, is held in the Vienna library, as Lambecius attests; he published from it the first Psalm and the Lord's Prayer. At the end of the same codex, translated by the same author, are found all the canticles of Holy Scripture, the Creeds of the Apostles and of Athanasius, and the Lord's Prayer. But the rhythmic version of the Gospels, which the most illustrious Armagh scholar, relying on the authority of Beatus Rhenanus, ascribed to Bishop Waldo of Freising around the year 890, is nothing other than Otfrid's *Harmony*. Waldo had it copied by the hand of the priest Sigifrid, as is clear from the beginning of the preface. For that tetrastich which the most illustrious Primate has quoted from Rhenanus begins Otfrid's *Volumen Evangeliorum*.

units.la: Willerami, Monachi Fuldensis, Paraphrasin Germanicam in Canticum Canticorum à Paulo Merulâ editam fuisse ex Goldastii fide Armachanus refert . Willeramus equidem geminam Cantici Canticorum Paraphrasin concinnavit; alteram Latinam rythmo Heroico, alteram Germanicam prosaicam. Utramque evulgavit Paulus Merula Lugduni Bat. 1598. 8vo. verùm ex Codice mendosissimo & miserè interpolato. Genuini Operis exemplar extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Cæsareâ, ipsius Willerami ætate scriptum; cujus amplum satis Specimen Lambecius exhibuit, Comment. lib. 2. pag. 765.
units.tr: Armagh reports, on the authority of Goldast, that a German paraphrase of the Song of Songs by Willeram, a monk of Fulda, was published by Paul Merula. Willeram did indeed compose a twofold paraphrase of the Song of Songs: one in Latin in heroic verse, the other in German prose. Paul Merula published both at Leiden in 1598, 8vo, but from a most corrupt and wretchedly interpolated codex. A genuine copy of the work survives in manuscript in the Imperial Library, written in Willeram's own lifetime. Lambecius gave a fairly full specimen of it, Commentaries, bk. 2, p. 765.

Lambecius Manuscripta asservari memorat. 1. Integram S. Scripturæ Versionem, Wenceslai Imperatoris jussu paulò ante annum 1400. factam & elegantissimè descriptam.
units.tr: Bk. 2, pp. 459, 749. b P. 461. c At the year 1070. Several other vernacular versions of Scripture were prepared by the Germans before the time of Luther. For the learned Lambecius records that manuscripts are kept in the Imperial Library at Vienna. 1. A complete version of Holy Scripture, made by command of the Emperor Wenceslas shortly before the year 1400, and very elegantly copied.

units.la: 2. Aliam ejusdem Translationem , à Joanne Liechstensternio Monachiensi confectam sumptibus Nobilis Viri Matthiæ Eberleri, & Basileæ, anno 1464. absolutam. 3. Alias binas Psalterii Versiones; quarum ultima auspicio ac sumptibus Frederici V. Imp. anno 1477. scripta est. 4. Epistolas Dominicales & Festivales totius anni, lingua Germanicâ, magnâque ex parte rythmicâ, anno 1210. conscriptas. 5. Explicationem Evangeliorum antiquam Germanicam. Quinimo typis excusa prodierunt Biblia Germanica, armis Austriacæ Domûs gentilitiis in fronte ornata, loco atque anno innominato: Norimbergæ etiam anno 1483. vol. 2. sol. & Lubeca 1494. sol. Denique habetur MS. in Bibliothecâ Norfolciana Versio Germanica Missalis, ante trecentos plus minus annos conscripta.
units.tr: 2. Another translation of the same, made by John Liechtenstern of Munich, at the expense of the noble man Matthias Eberler, and completed at Basel in 1464. 3. Two other versions of the Psalter, the latter of which was written at the instigation and expense of Emperor Frederick V in 1477. 4. Sunday and festival epistles for the whole year, in German, and for the most part in rhyme, written in 1210. 5. An ancient German explanation of the Gospels. Indeed, German Bibles were also printed, bearing on the title page the heraldic arms of the Austrian house, without place or year: at Nuremberg, also in 1483, in two volumes folio, and at Lübeck in 1494, folio. Finally, there is a manuscript in the Norfolk Library, a German version of the Missal, written some three hundred years ago more or less.

units.la: His omnibus antiquior, atque ipsius adeò Otfridi præceptor, Rabanus Maurus ad vulgarem S. Scripturæ cognitionem populares suis haud parum contulit. Scripsit enim Glossarium LatinoTheotiscum in tota Biblia Sacra Veteris & Novi Testamenti: quod Gentilibus indoctioribus S. Scripturæ studium aggressuris adjumento esset. Extat etiamnum ejus Exemplar MS. Autori coævum, in Bibliotheca Cæsareâ; teste Cl. Lambecio, lib. 2. pag. 416.
units.tr: Older than all these, and indeed the teacher of Otfrid himself, Rabanus Maurus contributed no little to the popular knowledge of Holy Scripture for the common people. For he wrote a Latin-German glossary on the whole of the Holy Bible, Old and New Testaments, which would be an aid to the less learned laity who were taking up the study of Scripture. His manuscript copy, written in the author's own time, still survives in the Imperial Library, as the learned Lambecius attests, bk. 2, p. 416.

units.la: 870. Methodius & Cyrillus.
units.tr: 870. Methodius and Cyril.

units.la: Quæ de Methodio & Cyrillo referunt Historici ab Illustrissimo Primate laudati, parum accurata sunt. Id quidem constat hosce Slavis à se converlis S. Scripturam & Liturgiam lingua vernacula tradidisse; Latinis autem ritibus vel Liturgiæ authoritatem abrogásse, purum putum commentum videtur, nulli fundamento nixum. Methodius & Cyrillus enim illos, inter quos versati sunt, Slavos primi omnium ad fidem Christianam convertebant; adeoque qualemcunque Liturgiam primi omnium induxerunt. Sic enim Annales MSS. Andreæ Danduli, Ducis Veneti, à Lucio k citati testantur. "Anno 874. "Constantinus Natione Thessalonicus (cui Papa, Cyrillus, "nomen imposuit) vir Catholicus, divinisque Scripturis eruditus, & in variis idiomatibus peritus, Regem Bulgarorum "cum gente suâ ad fidem convertit, &c. Hujus autem B. Cyrilli prædicatione Sveropolis Rex Dalmatiæ cum toto suo "populo fidem catholicam suscepit, &c. Hic Beatus Cyrillus "pene omnium Slavorum dictus est Apostolus, quia hos ad "fidem reduxit, & divinum Officium in linguâ Slavonica iis "transtulit." Dandulum autem hæc eadem mutuatum esse affirmat Lucius ab Historiâ Presbyteri Diocleatis; quam Regum Dalmatiæ nomine Mauro Orbinus in Opere suo nuncupato (Il Regno delli Slavi, Regnum Slavorum) inclusam vulgavit, anno 1601. Paria cum Dandulo & Diocleate refert Constantinus Porphyrogennetus 1 in Vitâ Basilii Macedonis. Porrò Versionem & Liturgiam Cyrilli hodienum extare veri non est absimile: Amplissimam enim librorum Slavicorum copiam in Catalogo Bibliothecæ Seguierianæ videre est. Extat etiam MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Codex linguâ & litteris Slavinicis (quales à Cyrillo inventæ dicuntur) pulcherrimè exaratus. Illum animadverti continere Acta Apostolorum (quibus titulus est, Deanja Apostolesca) & alia quædam, forsitan Epistolas Pauli, Canonicas, & Apocalypsin, cum Liturgiâ ad finem addita. An Versio Cyrillo debeatur, necne, non habeo quod affirmem; cum linguam minimè intelligam. Missale autem Romanum editum est Urbani VIII. Pontificis jussu, linguâ & literis Sclavonicis, Romæ 1631. 4°.
units.tr: The Historians whom the most illustrious Primate praises have reported things about Methodius and Cyrillus with little accuracy. It is certainly established that these men handed down Scripture and the Liturgy in the vernacular to the Slavs they had converted. But the claim that they abolished the authority of the Latin rites or of the Liturgy seems a pure invention, resting on no foundation. Methodius and Cyrillus were the first of all to convert the Slavs among whom they worked to the Christian faith, and so they were the first to introduce some kind of Liturgy. The unpublished Annals of Andrea Dandulo, Doge of Venice, cited by Lucius k, bear witness to this: "In the year 874, Constantine, a Thessalonian by birth (whom Pope Cyrillus named), a Catholic man, learned in the divine Scriptures and skilled in various languages, converted the King of the Bulgarians with his people to the faith, etc. Through the preaching of this Blessed Cyrillus, Sveropolis, King of Dalmatia, with his whole people, received the Catholic faith, etc. This Blessed Cyrillus was called the Apostle of almost all the Slavs, because he brought them back to the faith and translated the divine Office for them into the Slavonic tongue." Lucius affirms that Dandulo borrowed these same things from the History of the Presbyter of Diocleas, which Mauro Orbini published in 1601 in his work (Il Regno delli Slavi, Regnum Slavorum), included under the name of the Kings of Dalmatia. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in his Life of Basil the Macedonian, reports things like Dandulo and Diocleas. Moreover, it is not unlikely that the version and Liturgy of Cyrillus still exist today: a very large number of Slavonic books may be seen in the Catalogue of the Seguier Library. There is also in the Lambeth Library a manuscript codex, most beautifully written in the Slavonic language and letters (such as are said to have been invented by Cyrillus). I have observed that it contains the Acts of the Apostles (entitled Deanja Apostolesca) and certain other things, perhaps the Epistles of Paul, the Catholic Epistles and the Apocalypse, with a Liturgy added at the end. Whether the version is owed to Cyrillus or not, I have no grounds to affirm, since I do not understand the language at all. The Roman Missal, however, was published in the Slavonic language and letters by order of Pope Urban VIII, at Rome, in 1631, in quarto.

units.la: 880. Joannes VIII. Papa.
units.tr: 880. Pope John VIII.

units.la: Invitus admodum Joannes licentiam sacra vulgari linguâ celebrandi Slavis dedit; veritus scilicet, ne si prætractè renueret illi Patriarchæ CP. ditioni, Bulgarorum exemplo, sese submitterent. A Græcis Sacerdotibus conversi fuerant; adeóque Patriarchatui CP. jure subjiciendi erant. Verùm Joannes Methodium astu quodam Romam anno præcedente accersiverat: specie quidem, ut doctrinæ suæ, quam nonnulli minùs orthodoxam esse apud Papam criminati erant, rationem redderet; revera autem ut Ecclesiam à se recens fundatam Romano Patriarchatui subjiceret. Methodium igitur tanquam obsidem quendam Slavis charissimum, honoribus & amicitiâ cumulatum, Romæ detinuit; & ut Slavos insigni quodam beneficio Romanæ sedi devinciret, vernaculâ Liturgiâ uti illis concessit. In hunc finem collimâsse Papam, liquet ex ipsâ, quâ licentiam concedit, Epistolâ; cujus pars longè potior Romanæ Sedis majestati & prærogativis ampliandis insumitur, variisque argumentis texendis, quibus Slavi in ditionem ejus transire inducantur. Hinc Sfentopulcro crasse adulatur; & nihil petitum negare ausus, se petitioni ejus de sacris Slavicè celebrandis annuisse in fine Epistolæ scribit. Ipse autem Papa, antequam ejusmodi ratio intercederet, Liturgiam vernaculè celebrari adeo non probavit; ut in Epistolâ ad Methodium anno 879. datâ, ipsum eo nomine criminaretur: "Audimus etiam, inquit, quòd Missam cantes in Barbarâ, hoc est, "in Slavinâ linguâ; unde jam litteris nostris per Paulum Episcopum Anconitanum tibi directis prohibuimus, ne in eâ "linguâ sacra Missarum solennia celebrares, sed vel in Latinâ "vel in Græcâ linguâ; sicut Ecclesia Dei toto terrarum orbe "diffusa & in omnibus gentibus dilatata cantat. Prædicare verò
units.tr: John was most unwilling to grant the Slavs permission to celebrate sacred rites in the vernacular tongue, fearing, of course, that if he obstinately refused, they would submit to the rule of the Patriarch of Constantinople, as the Bulgarians had done. They had been converted by Greek priests, and so they were liable to be subjected by right to the Patriarchate of Constantinople. But John had summoned Methodius to Rome the year before by a certain trick: ostensibly so that he might give an account of his teaching, which some had accused of being less than orthodox in the Pope's eyes, but in reality so that he might subject to the Roman Patriarchate the Church he had recently founded. Accordingly, he kept Methodius at Rome, as a kind of hostage most dear to the Slavs, loaded with honours and friendship; and in order to bind the Slavs to the Roman See by a notable favour, he allowed them to use a vernacular Liturgy. That the Pope aimed at this end is clear from the letter in which he grants the permission: the greater part of it is devoted to exalting the majesty and prerogatives of the Roman See and to weaving various arguments by which the Slavs might be induced to pass under his authority. Hence he flatters Svatopluk grossly, and, not daring to refuse any request, he writes at the end of the letter that he has assented to Svatopluk's petition that the sacred rites be celebrated in Slavonic. But the Pope himself, before any such consideration intervened, so far disapproved of the Liturgy being celebrated in the vernacular that in a letter to Methodius, dated 879, he accused him on this very account: "We have heard, he says, that you sing Mass in the barbarous tongue, that is, in the Slavonic language; for which reason we have already, by our letter sent to you through Paul, Bishop of Ancona, forbidden you to celebrate the solemn rites of the Masses in that language, but in Latin or in Greek, as the Church of God, spread throughout the whole world and extended among all nations, sings. Moreover, you may preach or give a sermon to the people; since the Psalmist

units.la: 890. Alfredus, Rex Angliæ.
units.tr: Alfred, King of England.

units.la: Prodiit Versio Saxonica Psalterii una cum textu Latino interlineari, à Joanne Spelmanno Henrici filio edita Londini 1640. 4to. Ista ab Alfredo confecta, saltem inchoata, censetur. Alia autem Psalterii Versio interlinearis Saxonica habetur in Bibliotheca Archiepiscopali Lambethanâ; quæ Alfredo parum recentior videtur. In fine enim Codicis reperitur Litania vetus Latina, in quâ Dunstanus & Odilo recentiores sunt inter Sanctos qui invocantur; adeoque paulò post initium seculi undecimi conscripta censeri potest. Psalterium multo veriustiore manu, quàm Litania exaratur. Libro præfixitur prolixum Psalmorum Encomium literis Saxonicis, ex Augustino desumptum; quod incipit: Canticum Psalmorum animas decorat, invitat Angelos in adjutorium, effugat Dæmonas, expellit tenebras, efficit sanctitatem. Succedit Oratio præfatoria Interpretis ad Deum; in quâ oratur, ut isti Psalmi omnibus proficiant ad salutem & remedium animarum, & ad veram pænitentiam faciendam. Psalterium sequuntur preces nonnullæ Saxonico-Latinæ; dein Cantica omnia S. Scripturæ, Te Deum, Oratio Dominica, Symbola Apostolorum & Athanasii Latinè, cum Versione Saxonicâ interlineari. Plures aliæ Psalterii Versiones Saxonicæ olim videntur factæ. Spelmannus enim Editioni suæ in margine apposuit Lectiones Codicum M. S. quatuor adeo variantes; ut totidem diversæ Translationes facilè videantur.
units.tr: The Saxon version of the Psalter appeared with the Latin text interlinear, edited by John Spelman, son of Henry, London, 1640, in quarto. This version is regarded as the work of Alfred, at least as a beginning. Another interlinear Saxon version of the Psalter is held in the Archbishop's Library at Lambeth; it seems somewhat later than Alfred. At the end of this manuscript there is an old Latin litany, in which Dunstan and Odilo are among the more recent saints invoked, so it may be thought to have been written shortly after the beginning of the eleventh century. The Psalter is written in a much more accurate hand than the litany. Before the book there is a long Saxon encomium on the Psalms, taken from Augustine, which begins: The singing of the Psalms adorns souls, invites angels to help, puts demons to flight, drives away darkness, and produces holiness. Next comes the translator's prefatory prayer to God, in which he asks that these Psalms may profit everyone for salvation and as a remedy for souls, and for making true repentance. The Psalter is followed by some Saxon-Latin prayers, then all the canticles of Holy Scripture, the Te Deum, the Lord's Prayer, and the Apostles' Creed and the Athanasian Creed in Latin, with an interlinear Saxon version. Several other Saxon versions of the Psalter seem to have been made in former times, for Spelman placed in the margin of his edition readings from four manuscripts that differ so much that they can easily be seen as four different translations.

units.la: Versionem librorum Ecclesiasticorum è linguâ Latinâ in Saxonicam se tam in Cleri quàm in Plebis gratiam suscepisse. Alfredus confirmat in Præfatione ad Gregorii Pastorale à se versum.
units.tr: That he undertook the translation of the ecclesiastical books from Latin into Saxon for the benefit of the clergy as much as of the people, Alfred affirms in the preface to his translation of Gregory's Pastoral Care.

units.la: (Hympnarium Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ admodum copiosum, Cantica S. Scripturæ & Orationes Ecclesiasticas in fine habens, extat unâ cum Versione Saxonicâ interlineari in Bibliotheca Cottoniana .) Certè quicquid sibi blandiantur Pontifícii, Versiones S. Scripturæ & Liturgiæ vernaculæ non minus Clero quàm Plebi plerunque sunt necessariæ. Plebem à Clero solo divinæ legis scientiam haurire Pontificii volunt; populum ab ore Sacerdotis orantis cæcâ fide pendere jubent. Sed quid si Sacerdos ipse neque S. Scripturam neque Liturgiam linguâ alienâ obsignatam intelligat. Tunc certè, si unquam aliàs, cæcus cæcum ducet. Fuit tamen aliquando; cùm ne centesima Cleri pars Latinè calleret; quin & hodie potior Cleri Catholici toto orbe terrarum divisi pars ultra linguam vernaculam non sapit; forsan & pars Cleri Romani non contemnenda Latinè non novit. Id sanè olim contigisse, testis fide dignus est Rex Alfredus, qui in Præfatione modò memoratâ hæc habet: "Adeo funditus concidit apud gentem Anglicanam [Doctrina] ut paucissimi fuerint cis Humbrum [Sacerdotes] qui vel preces suas communes in sermone Anglico intelligere potuerant, vel scriptum aliquod è Latino in Anglicum transferre. Tam sanè pauci fuerunt; ut ne unum quidem recordari possim ex australi parte Thamesis tum cùm ego regnare occœperam. Literarum quidem studium Rex eruditissimus tam exemplo quàm liberalitate præclarè restituit: crassa tamen adhuc ignorantia apud plerosque Sacerdotes mansit. Gulielmi enim Normanni tempore, Clerici quoque & Ordinati adeo literaturâ carebant; ut cæteris esset stupori, qui Grammaticam didicisset: inquit Matthæus Paris . Sub initium seculi decim tertii Giraldus Cambrensis, Episcopus Menevensis, in Gemmâ suâ Ecclesiasticâ, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, prolixè deflet spissam ignorantiam Cleri Anglicani; qui tamen (præfescinè dixerim) tunc etiam nullius Ecclesiæ Clero doctrinâ cessit. Nimium esset singula ejus verba describere. Unicum tamen locum, qui
units.tr: (The Church of England's very full hymnal, which has the canticles of Holy Scripture and the ecclesiastical prayers at the end, survives together with an interlinear Saxon version in the Cotton Library.) Whatever the Papists may flatter themselves with, vernacular versions of Holy Scripture and of the liturgy are generally no less necessary for the clergy than for the people. The Papists want the people to draw their knowledge of divine law from the clergy alone, and they command the people to hang blindly on the lips of the priest who prays. But what if the priest himself understands neither Holy Scripture nor the liturgy, sealed in a foreign tongue? Then certainly, if ever, the blind will lead the blind. Yet there was a time when not one hundredth part of the clergy knew Latin; indeed, even today the greater part of the Catholic clergy, scattered over the whole world, knows nothing beyond its vernacular tongue, and perhaps a not inconsiderable part of the Roman clergy does not know Latin. That this happened once is attested by King Alfred, a trustworthy witness, who in the preface just mentioned says this: "So utterly has doctrine collapsed among the English people that there were very few priests on this side of the Humber who could understand their common prayers in English, or translate any writing from Latin into English. Indeed there were so few that I cannot recall even one south of the Thames when I began to reign. The most learned King has splendidly restored the study of letters, both by example and by generosity; nevertheless gross ignorance has remained among most priests. For in the time of William the Norman, clerics and ordained men were so lacking in learning that anyone who had learnt grammar was a wonder to the rest," says Matthew Paris. At the beginning of the thirteenth century Giraldus Cambrensis, bishop of St David's, in his manuscript Gemma Ecclesiastica in the Lambeth Library, laments at length the thick ignorance of the English clergy; yet (I might almost say beforehand) at that time they also yielded to the clergy of no church in learning. units.la: * Sub effigie Julii, A 6. P Vide testimonium insigne ex Elfrici Grammatica, infra. q In Gulielmo Conqu. paulò post init. r D.st. 2. cap. 36, 37. festivam quidem, pudendam tamen, Sacerdotum insciitiam indicat, apponam: Qualiter autem Evangelia, sacramque Scripturam hodie Presbyteri Parochianis suis exponant, per exempla quædam ostendemus. Exemplum de Presbytero, qui sermonem faciens ad populum de S. Barnabâ inter cætera dixit; Bonus vir & sanctus erat, sed tamen latro fuerat: auctoritatem sumens de Evangelio hoc, &c. Erat autem Barrabas latro: Item Exemplum de Sacerdote; qui sermonem faciens de muliere Cananæa dixit eam partim canem esse, partim mulierem. Item Exemplum de Presbytero; qui Festum Simonis, & Judæ denuncians, dixit, alterum bonum virum & sanctum fuisse, alterum verò proditorem Christi; nec ei honorem aliquem, vel diei propter ipsum, sed propter socium ejus, deferendum. Item, &c. Deinde capite sequenti subdit: Non solum autem in minoribus Sacerdotibus, sed & in majoribus, Abbatibus sc. Prioribus, magnis Ecclesiarum Decanis, Episcopis & Archiepiscopis tales interdum defectus invenies. Neve posterioris ævi Clerum decessores scientiâ superâsse existimemus; non minimum fuit Scholasticis Theologis argumentum, quare Opus Operatum Missæ etiam sine intellectu vel devotione prodesse determinarent; nimirum quia multi sint Clerici parum literati, qui ea, quæ proferunt, minimè intelligunt; & tamen debitum solvunt. Sic enim Scholæ sententiam exprimit Gabriel Biel. 900. Regino, Abbas Prumiensis, De Disciplin. Eccles. lib. 2. pag. 215. Inter Interrogationes à quovis Episcopo singulis Parochiis seu Villis in Visitatione suæ Diœcesis proponendas, octogesima octava est istiusmodi: Si aliquis in Ecclesiam intrans, fabulis vacare consuevit, & non diligenter auscultat divina eloquia? Et si antequam Missa finiatur, de Ecclesiâ exit? s Cap. 35. t Expos. in Can. Missæ, lect. 62. 1000. Effricus
units.tr: * Under the figure of Julius, A 6. P See the notable testimony from the Grammar of Aelfric, below. q In William the Conqueror, shortly after the beginning. r Dist. 2, chs. 36, 37. How priests today expound the Gospels and holy Scripture to their parishioners, we will show by certain examples. An example of a priest who, preaching to the people about St Barnabas, said among other things: "He was a good and holy man, but he had been a robber," taking his authority from this Gospel, etc. Barabbas was a robber. Likewise an example of a priest, who, preaching about the Canaanite woman, said that she was partly a dog and partly a woman. Likewise an example of a priest, who, announcing the feast of Simon and Judas, said that the one was a good and holy man, but the other a traitor to Christ; and that no honour should be paid to him either on the day, but to his companion, etc. Then in the following chapter he adds: Not only among the lesser priests, but also among the greater, abbots, that is, priors, great deans of churches, bishops and archbishops, you will sometimes find such defects. And lest we think that the clergy of a later age surpassed their predecessors in learning: the Scholastic theologians had no small argument for determining why the work done (opus operatum) of the Mass benefits even without understanding or devotion; namely, because there are many clerics with little learning, who do not understand at all what they utter, and yet pay their due. For this is how the school expresses its opinion, as Gabriel Biel puts it. 900. Regino, Abbot of Prüm, On Church Discipline, bk. 2, p. 215. Among the questions to be put by any bishop to each parish or village in the visitation of his diocese, the eighty-eighth is of this kind: If anyone, entering the church, is accustomed to idle over stories and does not diligently listen to the divine words? And if he leaves the church before the Mass is finished? s Ch. 35. t Exposition of the Canon of the Mass, lect. 62. 1000. Elfric
