Presbyter etiam, seu Missalis sacerdos in diebus Solis & Missalibus Evangelii ejus intellectum populo dicet Anglicè: & ipsorum etiam Orationem Dominicam & Symbolum, toties quoties eos poterit instruendos adhibere: & ut Symbolum fidei memoriter discant [curabit] Christianamque suam teneant confessionem, monente hoc Domino, unà & Prophetâ inquiente: Canes muti non possunt latrare, &c. Rev. Armachanus eadem habet verba usque ad ȝeleaȝan ex Epistolis Elfrici Anglosaxonicis citata. Postea eadem in libro Canonum ejus à Fulcone citato haberi prodit; quæque immediatè sequuntur, ex Epistola ejus de Clericis adducit; nescius tria hæc, Epistolam ad Clericos, Epistolam Anglosaxonicam, & Canonum librum, unum idemque esse Opus. Locum proinde integrum restituere ac repræsentare non inconsultum duxi.
units.tr: Letter on the Clergy, ch. 23: "The mass-priest must explain the Gospel to the English people on Sundays and on mass-days, in plain English, and likewise the Lord's Prayer and the Creed, as often as he can gather them to be taught; and he shall see that they learn the Creed by heart and hold to their Christian confession, as the Lord warns, and the Prophet says: Dumb dogs cannot bark, etc." (Old English original, transliterated: "Maesse-preost sceal reccan on rumran dagum ... ond on maessedagum ... on Englisc ... ond swa eac Pater noster ond Creda, ... ond hi cunnon gelaeran, ... ond heora cristendom gehealdan, ... swa swa se Drihten cwaeth ..."). The Most Reverend Armachanus has the same words, up to gelaeran, taken from Ælfric's Anglo-Saxon letters. Afterwards he shows that the same material is found in the book of Canons cited by Fulcone, and he gives from the letter On the Clergy what immediately follows. He did not realise that these three, the Letter to the Clergy, the Anglo-Saxon Letter, and the Book of Canons, are one and the same work. I have therefore thought it not out of place to restore and set out the passage in full.

units.la: Idem Grammaticam, & Dictionarium Latino-Saxonicum composuit. Utrumque à Somnero editum est ad calcem Dictionarii sui Saxonici, Oxon. 1659. sol. In præfatione secundâ ad Grammaticam dicit Ælfricus, se opus istud suscepisse ad promovendum rerum divinarum studium, præsertim in pueris: ac postea subdit. Ιηuþoŋþι ȝoþer þeopum. ȝ mýnꝛtep mannum ȝeopne, &c. Sedulo cavendum est igitur Dei servis, & viris Ecclesiasticis, ne in diebus nostris sacra deferveat aut deficiat eruditio; quemadmodum per paucos aliquot jampridem annos in Angliâ contigit; ita ut Anglicorum sacerdotum nullus, donec Dunstanus Archiepiscopus & Æthelwaldus Episcopus in Monasteriis doctrinam resuscitâssent, Epistolam Latinè scribere, aut Latine scriptam interpretari posset. Hoc loco notare liceat errorem viri doctissimi, Gulielmi Cave ; qui in Elfrici scriptis recensendis, Grammaticam ejus, & Excerpta ex Frisiano distinguens, illam prodiisse, isthæc MSS. delitescere, affirmat: cùm tamen unicum opus fuisse ex prologo apertè constet. Quin & postea Ope-
units.tr: The same man also composed a Grammar and a Latin-Saxon Dictionary. Both were published by Somner at the end of his Saxon Dictionary, Oxford, 1659, folio. In the second preface to the Grammar, Ælfric says that he undertook the work to promote the study of divine things, especially among boys; and afterwards he adds (in Old English, transliterated: "ond manna gehwylc ... gehyrne"): Therefore the servants of God and churchmen must take care that sacred learning does not boil over or fail in our days, as it has for a few years past in England. So it happened that none of the English priests could write a letter in Latin, or translate a Latin letter, until Dunstan the Archbishop and Æthelwold the Bishop revived teaching in the monasteries. Here I may point out the error of the most learned William Cave, who, in reviewing Ælfric's writings, distinguishes the Grammar from the Excerpts from Friesian, and affirms that the former was published while the latter lie hidden in manuscript, although the preface makes it plain that there was one work only. Moreover, in a later place he counts Ælfric's Latin-Saxon Dictionary among the manuscript works, though it was published by Somner together with the Grammar.

units.la: Concil. Angl. Tom. 1. p. 578. Supra, cap. 5. ad An. 1000. Hist. Liter. p. 590. Pag. 571. ribus Manuscriptis annumerat illius Dictionarium Latino-Saxonicum; quod unà cum Grammaticâ à Somnero evulgatum est.
units.tr: Council of England, vol. 1, p. 578. Above, ch. 5, at the year 1000. Literary History, p. 590. Page 571.

units.la: Porrò Eltricus noster ab Episcopis rogatus in usum Ecclesiae patriae, quamplurimas Homilias Saxonicè partim convertit, partim confecit. Illae inter Sacerdotes passim distributae, populo diebus Dominicis aut Festis publicè legi mandabantur: Exstant etiamnum plurimae illarum Collectiones MSS. praesertim in Bibliothecâ publicâ Academiae Cantabrigiensis. Ex his Abrahamus Whelocus in notis suis ad Bedae Historiam Ecclesiasticam plurima Excerpta Latinè & Saxonicè dedit de Scripturarum lectione. Nimirum ex Homilia in Dominicam primam in Adventu (quae 39. est in Collectione Sermonum LXXXVIII. quibus titulus est, Liber Catholicorum Sermonum Anglicè in Ecclesiâ per annum recitandorum.) pe rceolon habban, &c. Debemus nos spirituale convivium habere: habeat quisque vestrum in ore doctrinam salubrem; in manu quoque Psalterium. Ex Homiliâ de Assumptione Virginis Mariae (quae 73. est itidem) Gip pe mape recgab, &c. Si plura de hoc festo die diceremus, quàm in sanctis legimus bibliis, quae Dei instinctu institua sunt; tum haereticis similes futuri sumus, qui suo proprio instinctu aut somniis multa scripsere mendacia, &c. Sufficit fidelibus legere & discere quod verum est; & perpauci sunt, qui possunt tota biblia sacra, quae vel ore Dei, vel Spiritus instinctu edita sunt, perfectè perscrutari. Projiciat quisque haeretica mendacia, quae incautos in perniciem ducunt; & legat sive Adtonsus [Clericus] sive Laicus, vel auscultet sacram doctrinam, quae nos ad caelestè regnum dirigit, si illam audire velimus. Ex Homiliâ de Scripturarum lectione, (quae in aliâ Collectione Homiliarum & Tractatum LI. loco 42. habetur) Deo naeping haligna geppita, &c. Lectio sacrarum Scripturarum est aeternae felicitatis in sanctis Scripturis intelligentio; quibus homo seipsum possit contemplari: qualiscunque enim in singulis contemplator fuerit, talis omnino sacrarum Scripturarum lectio erit. Illa animam purgat lectoris. Illa metum inferni supplicii in mentem adducit. Illa quoque cor ipsius ad supernum gaudium allevat. Quicunque cum Deo unà esse voluerit, saepius debet orare, & saepius sacras Scripturas legere. Quando enim oramus, alloquimur Deum; & quando sacra Biblia legimus, tunc Deus nos alloquitur. Sacrorum Bibliorum lectio duplicem frugem affert lectoribus. Prima est, quòd mentis intellectum duceat, ut fiat sapientiâ
units.tr: Furthermore, our Ælfric, asked by the bishops to serve the Church of his country, translated and composed a great many homilies in Anglo-Saxon. These were distributed among the priests, and they were ordered to be read publicly to the people on Sundays or feast days. Many collections of them in manuscript still survive, especially in the public library of the University of Cambridge. From these, Abraham Whelock, in his notes to Bede's Ecclesiastical History, gave many extracts, in Latin and Saxon, on the reading of the Scriptures. Namely, from the Homily on the First Sunday in Advent (which is number 39 in the collection of eighty-eight sermons entitled The Book of Catholic Sermons to be recited in English in the Church through the year): "We ought to have a spiritual feast; let each of you have wholesome teaching in his mouth, and the Psalter in his hand." From the Homily on the Assumption of the Virgin Mary (which is likewise number 73): "If we said more about this feast day than we read in the holy books, which were written by the instinct of God, we would be like the heretics, who through their own instinct or dreams have written many lies, etc. It is enough for the faithful to read and learn what is true; and there are very few who can thoroughly search through the whole holy Bible, which was given either by the mouth of God or by the inspiration of the Spirit. Let each man cast away the heretical lies, which lead the unwary to destruction; and let him read, whether he is clergy or layman, or listen to the sacred teaching which guides us to the heavenly kingdom, if we wish to hear it." From the Homily on the Reading of the Scriptures (which is found in another collection of homilies and treatises, number 51, at place 42): "The reading of the holy Scriptures is the understanding, in the holy Scriptures, of eternal happiness; in them a man can contemplate himself. For whatever kind of contemplator each one is, such will his reading of the holy Scriptures be. It cleanses the reader's soul. It brings to mind the fear of the punishment of hell. It also lifts his heart to heavenly joy. Whoever wishes to be with God must pray often and read the holy Scriptures often. For when we pray, we speak to God; and when we read the holy Bible, then God speaks to us. The reading of the holy Bible brings a twofold fruit to its readers. The first is that it leads the understanding of the mind, so that it becomes wiser;

units.la: {f} Rectiùs forsan verba ista sic reddi possunt. Lectio SS. Scripturarum est cognitio aeterna felicitatis. In SS Scripturis homo potest seipsum contemplari, tanquam in quodam speculo, quamdiu vixerit: Quinimo lectio SS. Scripturarum purificat animam, &c. fagacior; altera, ut illam ab hujus mundi nugis ad amorem Dei perducat. Sacrorum Bibliorum lectio opus valdè honorificum existit, multúmque animæ purgandæ conducit. Quemadmodum corpus cibis naturalibus nutritur; sic etiam homo sublimior, h. e. anima, divinis nutritur colloquiis; sicut Psalmista ait: Colloquia tua oris mei palato mellè aut savo dulciora sunt. Perquam fœlix illè est, qui sacras legit Scripturas; si verbum in opus convertat. Revera omnes Scripturæ sacræ in nostram salutem scriptæ sunt, & per illas possumus nosse veritatem. Sæpius cæspitat cæcus quàm videns; sic etiam qui nescit Dei præcepta: Sæpius offendunt, quicunque illa nesciunt, quàm qui sciunt. Quemadmodum & cæcus absque ductore; sic etiam homo quivis absque doctore perquam difficulter in rectâ viâ præceptorum Dei procedet.
units.tr: {f} Perhaps these words can be rendered more correctly thus: The reading of the Holy Scriptures is the knowledge of eternal happiness. In the Holy Scriptures a man can contemplate himself, as in a kind of mirror, as long as he lives. Indeed the reading of the Holy Scriptures purifies the soul, etc. the other, that it leads the mind from the trifles of this world to the love of God. The reading of the holy Bible is a most honourable work, and it greatly helps to cleanse the soul. As the body is nourished by natural foods, so also the higher man, that is, the soul, is nourished by divine conversations; as the Psalmist says: Your words are sweeter to my mouth than honey or the honeycomb. Very happy is he who reads the holy Scriptures, if he turns the word into deed. Indeed all the holy Scriptures were written for our salvation, and through them we can know the truth. The blind man stumbles more often than the one who sees; so too whoever does not know God's commandments: those who do not know them offend more often than those who know them. Just as the blind man without a guide, so too any man without a teacher will very hardly walk in the right path of God's commandments.

units.la: Porrò scripsit Elfricus lingua Saxonicâ ad Sigwerdum virum nobilem Compendium quoddam Veteris & Novi Testamenti: quod ab Illustri viro, Gulielmo L' Isle editum est Londini 1638. 4°. In eo S. Scripturæ studium sæpiùs commendat; & pag. 40. omnibus Christianis necessarium esse docet. Hu mæg se man pel papan, se his mob apenc spam ealluw pirum bocum, &c. Quomodo illi bene esse potest? qui ab his libris cor avertit, & præstrato animo vitam potiùs pro effræni suâ libidine ducere cupit; ita ut Christi præcepta nesciat. Quòd si ab his libris imbui & doceri renuas; illic tandem, ubi nolis, inter horrenda tormenta disces scire, quem Deum atque cujus mandata insuper habuisti. Plures etiam S. Scripturæ libros à se lingua Vernaculâ redditos inibi commemorat, pag. 11. integrum Pentateuchum, & librum Josuæ. pag. 12. librum Judith. pag. 15. partem librorum Regum. pag. 22. libros Hester, & Judith. pag. 23. libros Maccabæorum. Versioni Geneseos præmisit insignem Præfationem; quâ objectioni vulgari adversus Scripturarum translationem, à pravo imperitorum intellectu ductæ, satisfacit. Extat ea in binis Codicibus MSS. Cantabrigiensibus (altero Bibliothecæ Publicæ, Collegii Corporis Christi altero) & in unico Bibliothecæ Publicæ Oxoniensis. Illam itaque, utpote nondum editam, integram subjecimus; addità & Latinè redditâ Versione viri doctissimi & literarum Saxonicarum peritissimi, Georgii Hickes, S. T. D. Decani Wigorniensis; quam pro summâ humanitate suâ in gratiam meam consecit Anglicé.
units.tr: Moreover, Ælfric wrote in the Saxon tongue, for the noble man Sigwerd, a certain Compendium of the Old and New Testaments, which was published by the illustrious William L'Isle at London in 1638, quarto. In it he often commends the study of Holy Scripture, and on page 40 he teaches that it is necessary for all Christians. (Old English, transliterated: "Hu maeg se man wel wesan, se his mod apenc fram ealle thisum bocum," etc.) How can it be well with that man who turns his heart from these books, and prefers to lead his life in a dulled mind for the sake of his unbridled lust, so that he does not know the precepts of Christ? But if you refuse to be imbued and taught from these books, you will at last learn, where you would not wish to, amid dreadful torments, what God you have despised, and whose commandments you have set at nothing. He also mentions there several books of Holy Scripture which he rendered into the vernacular: on page 11 the whole Pentateuch and the book of Joshua; on page 12 the book of Judith; on page 15 part of the books of Kings; on page 22 the books of Esther and Judith; on page 23 the books of the Maccabees. He prefixed to his version of Genesis a notable Preface, in which he answers the common objection against translating the Scriptures, an objection drawn from the perverse understanding of the unlearned. This is found in two manuscript codices at Cambridge (one in the Public Library, the other in Corpus Christi College) and in one in the Public Library at Oxford. Since it has not yet been published, I have therefore set down the whole of it, and added a Latin version by the most learned man and most skilled in Saxon letters, George Hickes, S.T.D., Dean of Worcester, who, out of his great kindness, made an English version of it for my benefit.

units.la: Incipit PRÆFATIO
units.tr: Beginning of the Preface

units.la: Englisc.
units.tr: English.

units.la: Ðis ic Munuc GRETÆðelpæno ealdopman eadmodlice þe bæde me leoþ þ ic rceolde þe aþenban oþ leðen on englirc þa boc generir þa þuhte me heþig time þe to tiðienne þæf. ȝ þu cpæðe þa þ ic ne þoþfte na manu aþenban þæþe bec. buton to Irƨace Abrahamer runa ropðam þe rum oðep man þe hæfde aþenð rnam ırıaace þ boc oðe enðe. nu ðinc ðme leoþ þ þ þeonc ir rpiðe pleoluc me oððe æniȝum men to unðepbeȝinnenne ropðam þe ic ono næþe ȝip rum ðyriȝ man þar boc þæt ðe næðan ȝehyŋð þ he pille penan þ he mote lybban nu on þæpe. ᶜ rpa rpa þa ealðan pæðepar leoporðon þā on þæpe tiðe ꝅp þan þe reo ealðe æ ȝe-rett pæpe. oðþe rpa rpa men leoporðon unðep moýrer æ.
units.tr: Here I, the monk Ælfric, humbly greet Ealdorman Æthelweard, who asked me to turn the book of Genesis from Latin into English for him. It seemed to me a heavy task to undertake, and you said I should not translate the whole book, only as far as Isaac, son of Abraham, since someone else had already translated the rest, from Isaac to the end. It seems to me, however, that this undertaking is very dangerous, either for me or for any other man, because I fear that if a foolish man reads this book, or hears it read, he will think that he must now live under the new law in the same way the patriarchs lived before the Old Law was given, or as men lived under the law of Moses.

units.la: Ðpilon ic pirte þ rum mærre pneort re þe min magirtep pær on þam timan hæfðe þa boc generir. ȝ he cuðe be ðæle lyðen unðeprtanðan. þa cpæð he be þam heah pæðepe ıa-cobe þ he hæfde reoþen þir tra ȝef-
units.tr: I have learned that a certain great scholar, who was my teacher at that time, had the book of Genesis and knew how to understand it. He spoke about the holy patriarch Jacob, saying that he had had four wives, …

units.la: ¹ Æthelwoldum forsan, postea Episcopum W[?]
units.tr: ¹ Perhaps Æthelwold, afterwards Bishop of W[?]

units.la: ² Forte nipan.
units.tr: ² Perhaps "nipan" (new) should be read.

units.la: Incipit PRÆFATIO Saxonica.
units.tr: Beginning of the Old English Preface.

units.la: ELfricus Monachus Æthelwerdo Comiti salutem humiliter precatur. Mihimet olim mandâsti, Domine, ut librum Geneseos ex Latino in Anglicum sermonem tibi converterem. Difficile mihi videbatur petitioni tuæ satisfacere. Dixisti itaque mihi non opus esse ampliorem libri partem convertere, quàm quæ ad Isaacum Abrahami filium pertingit: quandoquidem alius quidam reliquam libri partem ab Isaaco ad finem usque tibi convertisset. Videtur autem mihi, Domine, opus istud suscepta periculosum valdè, sive mihi, sive alii cuicunque viro: quoniam verendum est; ne si vir insipiens librum istum perlegat, aut perlectum audiat, existimet sibi nunc sub nova Lege vivendum esse eodem modo, ac Patriarchæ ante Veterem Legem datam vixerunt, aut homines etiam sub Lege Mosaicâ vixere.
units.tr: Ælfric the monk humbly greets Æthelweard the Count. Lord, you once asked me to turn the book of Genesis from Latin into English. It seemed hard to me to satisfy your request. So you told me that I need not translate more of the book than what reaches as far as Isaac, son of Abraham, since some other man had already translated the rest of the book from Isaac to the end. It seems to me, Lord, that this undertaking is very dangerous, both for me and for any other man, since it must be feared that if a foolish man reads this book, or hears it read, he will think that he must now live under the new Law in the same way the Patriarchs lived before the Old Law was given, or as men lived under the Mosaic Law.

units.la: Novi quondam Presbyterum ; qui mihi præceptor fuit. Ille tunc temporis librum Geneseos habuit; & Latina pauxillùm scivit. Dixit itaque de Patriarchâ Jacobo, istum quatuor uxores habuisse; duas scipurtna ʒ heopa tpa þinena ful roð he ꝛæðe. ac he nýrt ne ic na ʒit hu micel to ðal ꝛ betpeohx þæpe ealðan æ ʒ þæpe nipan.
units.tr: Once I knew a priest who was my teacher. At that time he had the book of Genesis, and he knew a little Latin. So he said of the patriarch Jacob that he had four wives: two sisters and their two handmaids, as he read it. But he did not know, and I do not yet know, how great the difference is between the old law and the new.

units.la: On anginne þirepe poþulðe nam þe bnoðep hýr rpurtep to pipe. ʒ hpilon eac þe pæðep týmðe be hiꝑ aʒenne ðehtep. ʒ manega hærþon ma pipa to polcep eacan. ʒ man ne mihte þa æt rnuman pipian butan on hiꝑ riblinꝗum.
units.tr: In the beginning of the world a man took his sister as his wife, and sometimes a father had children by his own daughter; and many men had several wives at once, to increase the people. A man could not then take a wife except from among his own kin.

units.la: Gýꝑ hpa pýlle nu rpa lýbban æptep cniꝑtep to-cýme rpa rpa men leoporðon æn moýrep æ. oððe unðep moýrep æ. ne biþ þe man na cniꝑten ne he pupðe pupðe pýpðe ne býð þ him ænig cniꝑten man miðeþe.
units.tr: Whoever now wishes to live as men lived before the law of Moses, or under the law of Moses, let him know that then he is no Christian, and no Christian man should keep company with him.

units.la: þa ungelæ peðan pneortar ʒiꝑ hi hpæt litlep unðeꝑrtanðaþ of þam lýðen bocum. þonne þincþ him rona þ hi magon mæpe lapeopaꝛ heon ac hi ne cunnon rpa þeah þ ʒartlice andʒit þæp-to. ʒ hu reo ealðe æ þer ʒetacnunʒ topeaꝛnðna pinʒi. oððe hu reo niþe ʒecýðnir æpt cniꝑtep meinnip-cniꝑþe þær ʒepilleðnýr ealna þæna þinʒa þe reo ealðe ʒecýðnir ʒetacnoðe topeanðe be cniꝑte. ʒ be hýꝑ ʒecopenum.
units.tr: Then unlearned priests, if they understand a little of the old books, at once think that they can be great teachers. But they do not understand truly, nor how the old law signified and prefigured things to come, or how the new law of Christ's birth is the fulfilment of all those things which the old law signified and prefigured concerning Christ and his chosen ones.

units.la: Hi cpeðaþ eac oꝑt be paul hpi hine motan habban riꝑ. rpa rpa petpur þe
units.tr: They also say, moreover, about Paul, that he might have a wife, as Peter …

units.la: ᵃ Typus, sive umbra. ᵇ Presbyteros intelligit [illegible, ~10 letters] farius.
units.tr: ᵃ Type, or shadow. ᵇ He means the elders … [illegible] …

units.la: ᶜ I Cor. IX. s. licet sorores, & earundem ancillas. Et verissimè quidem dixit. Id autem non novit, neque ipsemet ego quidem adhuc, quanta sit differentia inter Veterem & Novam Legem.
units.tr: ᶜ 1 Cor. 9: "have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife …" And indeed he spoke most truly. But they do not know, nor do I myself yet know, how great the difference is between the Old and the New Law.

units.la: In principio Orbis Conditi frater sororem suam sibi uxorem duxit; & aliquoties pater ex propriâ filiâ liberos suscepit; & multi plures simul habebant uxores in propagationem humani generis; & sub initio vir uxorem ducere nisi ex cognatione suâ non potuit.
units.tr: At the beginning of the created world a brother took his sister to be his wife; and more than once a father had children by his own daughter; and many men at once had several wives, for the propagation of the human race; and at the beginning a man could take a wife only from his own kin.

units.la: Si quis hodie post Christi adventum vitam eodem modo instituere velit; ac homines ante Legem Mosaicam aut sub Lege Mosaicâ instituerunt; ille Christianus non est; neque est nec esse potest dignus, quocum Christianus aliquis cibum sumat.
units.tr: If anyone today, after the coming of Christ, wishes to order his life in the same way that men lived before the Mosaic Law or under the Mosaic Law, he is not a Christian, nor is he, or can he be, worthy that any Christian should eat with him.

units.la: Presbyteri indocti, si vel paululum quid ex Latinis libris sciant; statim opinantur se eximios esse praeceptores. Mysticum tamen illorum sensum neutiquam sciunt; & quomodo vetus Lex significatio erat rerum futurarum; quódque Novum Testamentum post Christi Incarnationem impletio esset omnium, quae Vetus Testamentum de Christo venturo, & de Electis ejus praefigurabat..
units.tr: Unlearned priests, if they know even a little from Latin books, at once think themselves outstanding teachers. Yet they by no means know the mystical meaning of those books, nor how the Old Law was a sign of things to come, and how the New Testament, after the Incarnation of Christ, is the fulfilment of all that the Old Testament foreshadowed concerning the coming Christ and his Elect.

units.la: Isti saepe dicunt, licuisse illi uxorem duxisse; pari
units.tr: They often say that it was permitted for him to have taken a wife; likewise

units.la: git conjugatos; quorum acerrimus fuit adversarius apostol
units.tr: …they were married; of whom the most fierce adversary was the apostle …

units.la: aportol hæfde. ⁊ hi nellaþ gehinan ne pitan þ þe eaðiga petpur leopeðe æpten moises æ. oþ þæt cnipt þe on þam timan to mannum com. ⁊ begin to bodienne hiʒ halige godspel ⁊ ge- ceaʒ petpum æpeʒt hin to ʒeʒepan.
units.tr: and they will neither know nor learn that the blessed Peter lived under the law of Moses until the time when Christ came among men and began to preach his holy gospel, and Peter was the first to follow him.

units.la: þa popleʒ petpur þæn pihte hiʒ pip ⁊ ealle þa tpelf aportolaʒ þa þe pip hæfdon. penlæton æʒðep ge pip ge æhta. ⁊ polgodon cnipter lane. to þæpe nipan æ. ⁊ clænijfe þe he pilf þa apæpþe.
units.tr: Then Peter at once left his wife, and all the twelve apostles who had wives; they abandoned both wives and property, and followed the teaching of Christ according to the new law and the purity he taught.

units.la: Pneortar pinðon geferte to lapeopum þam læpeðum polce. nu gebap- noðe him þ hiʒ cupon þa ealdan æ gaptlice unðenptanðan. ⁊ hpæt cnipt pilf tæhte ⁊ hiʒ aportolaʒ on þæpe nipan gecýðnipre þ hiʒ mihtoñ þim polce pel pirrian to goðer geleapan. ⁊ pel biʒnian to gebuum peopcum.
units.tr: Teachers were sent to the unlearned people. It is now evident that they understand the old law poorly, and what Christ taught and his apostles in the new law, so that they might lead the people well to the true faith and instruct them well in good works.

units.la: þe recgaþ eac popan to þ þeo boc ir rpiðe beop gaptlice to unðenptanðenne. ⁊ þe ne pnitaþ na mape buton þanaceðan genecebnipre. þonne þincþ þam ungelæpeðum þ eall þ anðgit beo belocen on þæpe anpealðan genecebniþre. ac hit ýr rpiðe þeop þam.
units.tr: They also say that this book is very hard to understand, and they reflect on it only superficially; so it seems to the unlearned that all its meaning is shut up in the single literal sense, but for them it is very deep.

units.la: Seo boc ir gehaten generir. þ ýr gecýnð boc popðam þe heo ýr sýp- niert boca. ⁊ rþpiċ þ be ælcum gecinðe. ac heo ne rþpiċ na be þæpa eʒla ʒercea penipre. Heo ongin þur. In principio creavit Deus cœlum & terram. þ ýr on engliʒe. on anginne jure, ac Petrus Apostolus duxerit. Audire autem nolunt neque scire, Beatum Petrum Apostolum secundùm Legem Mosaicam vitam duxisse usque ad tempus, quo Christus ad homines advenit; & sanctum suum Evangelium prædicare incipiens, Petrum omnium primum sibi comitem adjunxit.
units.tr: This book is called Genesis, because it is the source of all books, and it speaks of all things; but it does not speak of the number of the angels' … It begins: In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram, which in English is: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." Hearing this, they do not want to hear or know that the blessed Apostle Peter lived according to the Mosaic Law until the time when Christ came to men; and, beginning to preach his holy Gospel, he first of all joined Peter as his companion.

units.la: Tunc Petrus uxorem suam statim deseruit; omnesque pariter Apostoli, quibus uxores fuerunt, & uxores & facultates suas deseruerunt; & Christi doctrinam secuti sunt, secundùm Novam Legem & puritatem, quam ipse præceperat.
units.tr: Then Peter at once abandoned his wife; and all the apostles alike, who had wives, abandoned both their wives and their possessions, and followed the doctrine of Christ, according to the New Law and the purity that he had prescribed.

units.la: Sacerdotes Laicis præceptores dantur. Oportuit igitur, ut Veterem Legem mysticè intelligant; quidque Christus, quidque Apostoli ejus in Novo Testamento docuerint: ut plebem ad fidem Dei probè dirigerent; & ad bona opera bonis exemplis [præirent.]
units.tr: Priests are given to the laity as teachers. It was fitting, therefore, that they should understand the Old Law mystically, and what Christ and his apostles taught in the New Testament, so that they might properly direct the people to the faith of God and lead them by good examples to good works.

units.la: Præfamur etiam hunc librum valde profundum esse in intellectu mystico: & non amplius quàm nudam ejus narrationem scribimus. Indocti itaque existimeni, totum illum [mysticum] sensum in simplici narratione obseratum teneri; & ab ipsis procul removeri.
units.tr: We also state beforehand that this book is very profound in its mystical meaning, and that we write no more than its bare narrative. Therefore let the unlearned think that the whole mystical sense is kept hidden within the simple narrative and is far removed from them.

units.la: Liber iste vocatur Genesis, id est, liber Generum; quoniam primus est liber; & de quocunque [rerum] genere verba facit. Nil autem habet de Creatione Angelorum. Sic incipit: In principio creavit Deus cælum & terram: id est, Anglicé.
units.tr: This book is called Genesis, that is, the book of Generations, since it is the first book and treats of every kind of thing. It says nothing about the creation of the angels. It begins thus: In the beginning God created heaven and earth: that is, in English:

units.tr: God created heaven and earth. It is commonly said that God Almighty thought in the beginning, when he wished to create, but in a spiritual understanding. That beginning is what he spoke of when he said to the Jews, "I am the beginning, who also speak to you." Through this beginning God thought heaven and earth, because he created all creatures through the Son, who is born of the Father, the wisdom of the wise Father from the beginning of the world.

units.tr: Again it is written in the first verse of this book: And the Spirit of God moved upon the waters. That is in English: "And God's Spirit moved over the waters." God's Spirit is the Holy Spirit, through whom the Father quickened all the creatures that he created through the Son. The Holy Spirit moves the human heart and grants us remission of sins, first through water in Baptism and afterwards through repentance. Then, too, the Holy Spirit moves the penitent heart, so that it may be unsettled and quickened, and it is then renewed through repentance. Whoever rejects the remission given by the Holy Spirit, his sin will be unforgivable for ever.

units.tr: Again the Holy Spirit has here been reported in this book, where God said, concerning the making of man, to our likeness. In what he said, "Let us make," the Trinity is indicated; in what he said, "to our likeness," the true Unity is declared. He did not say "to our likenesses" in the plural, but in the singular; and afterwards the three came to Abraham, and he spoke to them all as to one. Again the three angels came.

units.la: {1} Joan. VIII.
units.tr: {1} John 8.

units.la: {2} Gen. I. on anginne gerceop god heofenan ꝥ eopsan. Ita enim sese res habuit. Deus omnipotens in principio operatus est ; quùm creationem voluit ; sed sensu mystico. Principium illud est Christus ; uti ipse Judæis dixit k. Principium, qui & loquor vobis. Per hoc Principium Deus cœlum & terram creavit ; quia omnes creaturas creavit per Filium ; qui Sapientia fuit à Sapienti Patre genitus ab omni ævo.
units.tr: {2} Gen. 1. "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." For so the matter stood. Almighty God worked in the beginning when he willed creation, but in a mystical sense. That beginning is Christ, as he himself said to the Jews: The beginning, who also speak to you. Through this Beginning God created heaven and earth, because he created all creatures through the Son, who was begotten of the Father, the Wisdom, from all eternity.

units.la: Rursum habetur in primo libri commate : Et Spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas ; id est, Anglicé. ꝥ gober gart pær gerepnoþ opep pætepu. Spiritus Dei est Spiritus Sanctus ; per quem Pater vivificavit omnes creaturas quas per Filium creavit. Et Spiritus Sanctus per cor humanum movet ; & remissionem peccatorum nobis donat, primùm per aquam in Baptismo, & postea per pœnitentiam. Et si quis remissionem à Spiritu Sancto datam aspernetur ; tunc peccatum ejus erit irremissibile in æternum.
units.tr: Again it is found in the first verse of the book: And the Spirit of God moved upon the waters; that is, in English: "And God's Spirit moved over the waters." The Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit, through whom the Father quickened all the creatures that he created through the Son. The Holy Spirit also moves the human heart, and grants us remission of sins, first through water in Baptism and afterwards through repentance. And if anyone should despise the remission given by the Holy Spirit, then his sin will be unforgivable for ever.

units.la: Sacrosancta Trinitas sæpe in hoc libro revelatur ; ut in illis verbis, quæ Deus locutus est : 1 Faciamus hominem secundùm similitudinem nostram. In eo quod dicit Faciamus, Trinitas designatur ; in eo quod dicit secundùm similitudinem nostram, vera Unitas declaratur. Non dicit pluraliter secundùm similitudines nostras ; sed in singulari to abnahame ꝥ he ꝥpnæc to him eallon þnian rþa rþa to anum.
units.tr: The most holy Trinity is often revealed in this book, as in those words which God spoke: Let us make man according to our likeness. In what he says, Let us make, the Trinity is designated; in what he says, according to our likeness, the true Unity is declared. He does not say in the plural according to our likenesses, but in the singular, and he spoke to Abraham as to one, though all three were with him.

Man offpnoþe eac fela cinna
units.tr: How Abel called his blood to God, except as every man's evil deeds accuse him before God, without words. Through this little matter one can understand how the book is in a spiritual sense, though it appears in easy words. Again, Joseph, who was sold into the land of Egypt and saved the people from great hunger, had the meaning of Christ, who was sold for us to death and saved us from the eternal hunger of hell. The great tabernacle which Moses made in the wilderness with wonderful craft, as God himself had prescribed to him, had the meaning of the Church, which he himself established through his apostles with many adornments and fitting rites. The people brought gold and silver and precious stones and various kinds of costly things, and purple and scarlet, and fine linen and goats' hair, and many kinds of wood. Some also brought rams' skins dyed red, as God had commanded. The gold signified our faith, and the purple signified the holy lives of the saints which we ought to have for God's service. The scarlet signified the fire of love in other men, which the grace of God kindles in men's hearts. The linen signified the pure and innocent lives of men who keep their chastity. One also offered many kinds

units.tr: {b} Gen. 4. in number, according to our likeness. Afterwards, three angels came to Abraham, and he spoke to all three together, as to a single man.

units.la: Quomodo clamavit n sanguis Abel ad Deum; nisi ut uniuscujusque hominis peccata illum coram Deo accusant, sc. sine verbo? Ex paucis hisce exemplis animadvertere quis poteft, quàm profundus sit iste liber in mystico sensu; quamvis verbis minimè obscuris conscribatur. Postea Josephus, qui in Ægyptum venditus est, & à gravi fame populum liberavit; significavit Christum, qui pro nobis venditus est in mortem, & ab æternâ inferni fame nos liberavit. Eximium illud Tabernaculum, quod miro artificio Moses in deserto fabricatus est, prout Deus ipse illi præscripsit, significavit Dei Ecclesiam; quam ipsemet per Apostolos suos instituit variis ornamentis & decoris ritibus. Populus aurum & argentum & pretiosos lapides & diversa magnalium genera ad opus istud [conficiendum] obtulit. Nonnulli etiam pilos caprarum obtulerunt; prout Deus præceperat. Aurum fidem nostram designavit & veneration em, quam Deo offerre debemus. Argentum verbum Dei figuravit & pias instructiones, quas habere debemus ad [perficiendum] Dei opus. Pretiosi lapides multionf zobe to lace binnan ham zetxlde be ham yr rpde menizpealo zetacnunz. ȝ pæɼ bebodon ƿ re tæzel rceolde beon zehal æfne on ham nÿtene æt pæne orfpunge. fon pæpe zetac-nunze ƿ zoo pile ƿ pæ rimle pel don oð ende upeɼ liper. þonne biȝ re tæzel zeorffnoð on upum peopcum.•
units.tr: How did the blood of Abel cry out to God, except that the sins of each man accuse him before God, namely without a word? From these few examples one can see how profound this book is in its mystical sense, although it is written in words by no means obscure. Afterwards Joseph, who was sold into Egypt and freed the people from grievous famine, signified Christ, who was sold for us into death and freed us from the eternal famine of hell. That remarkable tabernacle, which Moses made in the desert with wonderful skill, as God himself prescribed to him, signified God's Church, which he himself instituted through his apostles with various ornaments and becoming rites. The people offered gold and silver and precious stones and various kinds of precious things to complete that work. Some also offered goats' hair, as God had commanded. The gold signified our faith and the veneration which we ought to offer to God. The silver signified the word of God and the pious instructions which we ought to have to complete the work of God. Many precious stones [were brought] for the breastplate within the tabernacle, which signified many kinds of virtue; and it was commanded that the cord should be kept whole and unbroken to the end of the work. That signified that God's commandments ought to be kept whole and constantly in our hearts until the end of life; then the cord is loosened in us.

units.la: Nu ir reo soneræde boc on manegum stopum spiðe ◦ næpolice gefett. ȝ þeah spiðe seoplice on þam ȝarzlicum anbyzte. ȝ heo ir spa ȝeendebyndra spa spa god silf hi ȝebihte þam pnitesne moise ȝ þe ne bunnon na mape appitan on englirc þonne ƿ liben hæfþ ne þa enðebypðnirre apentan buton þam anum þæt ƿ leben ȝ ƿ englirc nabbaþ ne ane piɼan on þæpe ɼpnæce ȝanbunȝe. æfne re þe apent. oþþe re þe tæcþ of lebene on englirc æfne he rceal geɼaðian hit ɼpa ƿ þæt englirc hæbbe hiɼ agene piɼan eller. hit biþ ɼpiðe ȝebpolþum to nædenne þam þe þæɼ lebenep piɼan ne can.•
units.tr: Now the Holy Scripture is in many places very obscure and not easily understood, and yet very plain in its literal sense. It is so profound that God himself, when he taught Moses, gave him no more to understand than he could grasp, and those who translate it into English are not able to render its meaning except by using the English words which it has. Whoever explains it, or whoever teaches it in English, must add in the English the sense of the words, so that the English may have its own meaning. It is very difficult to do this for one who does not know the meaning of the words.

units.la: Ir eac to pitanne ƿ rume ȝebpolmen pæþon þe polþon apunpan þa ealban æ. ȝ rume polþon habban þa ȝ apinpan þa nipam ɼpa ɼpa þa iudeiscan boþ. ac cpiɼt ɼylf ȝ hiɼ apoɼtolaɼ uɼ plicem servorum Dei pulchritudinem designârunt. Pili caprini rigidam hominum de peccatis dolentium poenitentiam denotârunt. Plurima quinetiam animalium genera Deo in Tabernaculo sacrificabant: cujus instituti ratio est multiplex. Et praeceptum est ut cauda bestiae in oblatione semper esset integra; ut significaretur Deum velle, ut ad extremum usque vitae terminum bene faceremus; quippe cùm cauda in operibus nostris offertur.
units.tr: It must also be asked: some men of old, indeed many, dissolved the ancient law, and some held that the rites were to be dissolved as the Jews do. But Christ himself and his apostles, "by the pure beauty of God's servants," designated the old law, and the goats' hair signified the stern repentance of men grieving over their sins. Moreover, they sacrificed many kinds of animals to God in the Tabernacle, and the reason for this institution is manifold. It was also commanded that the tail of the beast in the offering always be kept whole, to signify that God wills us to do good right up to the final end of our life, since the tail is offered in our works.

units.la: Liber praedictus in multis locis clarissimè conscribitur; valdè profundus tamen est in mystico sensu. Et ita quidem conditur; prout Deus ipse Mosi scriptori ejus dictavit. Neque audemus amplius quid scribere Anglicè, quàm in Latino habetur; neque ordinem immutare, nisi in hoc duntaxat; quùm Latinus & Anglicus sermo eandem loquendi formam non observent. Qui interpretatur aut docet Latina Anglicè [reddere] eam semper methodum observare debet; ut Anglicus sermo suum idioma teneat. Aliter lectio in plurimos errores inducet illos; qui idioma Latinum non intelligunt.
units.tr: The aforesaid book is written very clearly in many places, yet it is very deep in its mystical sense. It was composed just as God himself dictated it to Moses his scribe. Nor do we dare to write anything more in English than is found in the Latin, nor to change the order, except in this one respect: since Latin and English do not observe the same form of speech. Whoever translates or teaches the Latin in English [render] ought always to keep to this method, so that the English keeps its own idiom. Otherwise the reading will lead into many errors those who do not understand the Latin idiom.

units.la: Sciendum autem est, nonnullos fuisse Haereticos; qui Veterem Legem rejiciebant. Iltam aliqui retineri, & Novam rejici, voluerunt: quod Judaei faciunt. Chri-
units.tr: It should be noted that there were some heretics who rejected the Old Law. Some wished to retain it and reject the New, which the Jews do.

units.la: : Forsan neapolice legendum, id est, brevissimè tæhton æʒþer to healdenne þa ealdan ʒartlice. ʒ þa nipan ʃoplice nuð ʃeopʃcum.
units.tr: Perhaps it should be read as Neapolitan, that is, very briefly: they taught both to hold the old law duly and to keep the new law truly.

units.la: Gos ʒerceop ur tpa eazan ʒ tpa eapan, tpa norþpiplu. ʒ ʒ pelepar. tpahanda ʒ tpeʒen pet. ʒ he ꝑolde eac habban tpa ʒecyðniʒʒa on þirrepe ꝓopulo ʒe-ꝛet. þa ealdan. ʒ þa nipan. ꝓopþam þe he ꝺeþ ʃ ʃa hine ʃyʃlne ʒeʃypðꝺ. ʒ he næʒne ꝑæbbonan næʃ. ne nan man ne ꝑeanʃ hini cpeðan to hpi ꝺert þu ʃpa. ꝑerceolon apendan upne pillan to hiʃ ʒerꝑetniʃʃum ʒ þe ne magon ʒebi-ʒean hiʃ ʒeretniʃʃa to upum luʃtum.
units.tr: God made us two eyes and two ears, two nostrils, two lips, two hands and two feet; and he also wished to have two testaments in this world, the old and the new, because he works for the sake of his own honour and does not take counsel with anyone, nor will anyone say to him, "Why do you do so?" We ought to shape our wills to his precepts, and never to bend his precepts to our lusts. For they are not able to bring his teaching to our desires.

units.la: Ic cpeðe nu þ ic ne ꝺeapp ne ic nelle nane boc æʃtep ðirrepe oʃ leꝺene on enʒliʃc apendan. ʒ ic bidde þe leoʃ ealꝺonmon þ þu me þæʃ na lenʒ ne bidde. þe læʃ þe ic beo þe unʒehiʃʃum oꝺꝺe leaʃ ʒiʃ ic ꝺo. Gos þe riʒ milde ꝺ on ecniʃʃe. Ic bidde nu on ʒoꝺeʃ naman ʒiʃ hpa þaʃ boc appiꝛan pylle. þ he hiʒ ʒepihte pel be þæpe biʃrne. ꝓopꝺan þe ic ꝑ nah ʒepeolꝺ þeah þe hiʒ hpa to roʒe bpinʒe þuph leaʃe ppiꝛepaʃ. ʒ hiꝛ biʃ ꝑonne hiʃ pleoh na min. Mycel ʒiʃel beꝺ ʃe unʃpiꝛepe ʒiʃ he nele hiʃ ꝑoh ʒepihꝛan.
units.tr: I say now that I dare not and will not translate any book from this Latin into English after this. And I ask you, dear sirs, all of you, that you not ask me this any longer, lest I be disobedient to you, or else I do it and then do wrong. May God always have mercy on you. I now bid in God's name whoever wishes to write this book to write it well, for I do not own it, though someone for love of reward may have it written; then it will not be his own. Great blame is on the unfaithful scribe, who will not write it faithfully.

units.la: Præfationi in Codicibus Cantabrigiensium Lectionem; quæ ex Sermo-nibus tegra est desumpta, paucis immutati-
units.tr: The Preface in the Cambridge codices is followed by the reading, which is taken entire from the Sermons, with few changes.

units.la: ᵖ Forte na. stus autem ipse ejusque Apostoli, Veterem Legem in mysterio, & Novam in veritate cum [bonis] operibus observare nos docuerunt.
units.tr: Perhaps no. But he himself and his apostles taught us to observe the Old Law in mystery and the New in truth, with [good] works.

units.la: Deus nobis creavit duos oculos, & duas aures, & duos nares, & duo labia, & duas manus, & duos pedes: & duo etiam Testamenta, Vetus sc. & Novum, in orbe stabiliri voluit; quoniam operatur honoris sui gratia; & consiliarium sibi non adhibet; neque aliquis ei dicet: Cur ita facis? Voluntates nostras praeceptis ejus conformare debemus; neutiquam vero praecepta ejus ad libidines nostras inflectere.
units.tr: God made for us two eyes, and two ears, and two nostrils, and two lips, and two hands, and two feet; and he also willed that two Testaments, the Old and the New, be established in the world, since he works for the sake of his own honour, and does not take counsel with anyone, nor will anyone say to him, "Why do you act so?" We ought to conform our wills to his precepts, and by no means bend his precepts to our lusts.

units.la: Dico amplius, me neque audere neque velle alium aliquem post hunc librum ex Latino Anglicè convertere. Teque, dilecte Comes, obsecro; nequid à me posthac efflagites: ne aut tibi inobediens fiam [si renuam] aut mendax, si faciam. Deus tui semper misereatur. Si quis istum librum exscribere velit; istum per Dei nomen obteftor, ut illum juxta autographum diligenter corrigat. Nolem enim, ut per errata scriptionis aliquem in errorem ducat. Quod si contigerit; discrimen non meum erit, sed illius. Librarius negligens multum affert damni; si errata sua nolit corrigere.
units.tr: I say further that I neither dare nor wish to translate any other book from Latin into English after this one. And I beg you, dear Earl, that you ask nothing more of me after this, lest I become disobedient to you if I refuse, or a liar if I comply. May God always have mercy on you. If anyone wishes to copy this book, I call upon him by the name of God to correct it diligently according to the autograph. For I would not have anyone led into error by the mistakes of copying. If it happens, the blame will not be mine but his. A careless scribe causes much loss if he is unwilling to correct his own errors.

units.la: gienfibus succedit Exhortatio ad Scribas ne Augustini 112. de Tempore inscriptus; atque incipit. Deo paetnng haligna. Illam supra habes ex Versione Wheloci; qui ex Homilia quadam Elfrici descriptam Latino-Saxonicè dedit in Notis ad Bedæ Historiam Ecclesiasticam, pag 173. nisi quòd penultimam sententiam (vir tamen, si quis alius, Saxonicè peritissimus) aliud agens, in Versione suâ mutilaverit. Illam itaque restitutam damus. Oncep ꝥꝛꝓuꝑnæꝰ þe blinda þonne þe lociense' þꝛa eac þe þe nat ꝓoser bebofa. cꝛtep ꝛyngaꝰ ꝛꝓa ꝛꝓa he hit nat. þonne ꝺo þe þe hit pat. Sæpius impingit cæcus quàm videns: sic etiam qui nescit Dei præcepta, sæpius peccat, eò quòd ea nesciat, quàm ille qui ea scit.
units.tr: The sermons are followed by the Exhortation to Scribes, entitled "Augustine's 112th, On Time," and it begins: "Deo gratias..." You have the first part above, from Wheloc's version, who from a certain homily of Ælfric gave a copy in Latin and Old English in his notes to Bede's Ecclesiastical History, p. 173; except that he, though he was very skilled in Old English, in his version, while attending to something else, mutilated the penultimate sentence. We therefore give it restored: "Often the blind man stumbles more than the one who sees; so too he who does not know God's commandments often sins more than he who knows them." Often the blind man stumbles more than the one who sees; so too he who does not know God's precepts sins more often, because he does not know them, than he who knows them.

units.la: Notandum est, quod supra in Præfatione dicit Elfricus, se istam solummodo Genesis partem transtulisse, quæ ab initio libri ad Isaacum pertingit. Utrque enim Codex Cantabrigiensis eam solummodo partem continet, in Capite XXIV. terminatus. Codex autem Oxoniensis integrum ferè absolvit Heptateuchum; minimè tamen accurata Versio censenda est. Neque ipsimet Interpretes ejusmodi Versionem in animo habuisse, sed utiliora atque insigniora duntaxat loca selegisse videntur. In Codice enim Oxoniensi, ut hiatum lacerati voluminis taceam; in libro Genesi, decimi Capitis nonnisi duo priora atque ultimum commata exprimuntur. Vicesimi secundi à versu vicesimo ad finem usque Capitis omittuntur. Vicesimi tertii brevis, satis accurata tamen, Epitome habetur. Vicesimi sexti duo solummodo posteriora commata repræsentantur. Tricesimi sexti nonnisi 6us 7us & 8us versus. Dein ad finem usque libri omnia satis fideliter redduntur. Exodus in quarto versu Tricesimi quinti Capitis terminatur. Leviticus ea duntaxat habet, quæ Legem Moralem spectant: Ceremonialia ferè omittuntur. Plura habent libri Numerorum, Deuteronomii, & Josuæ, minimè tamen omnia. Judicum liber in ultimo decimi sexti Capitis commate finitur. Ista mihi datis literis retulit, qui Codicem consuluit, vir Saxonicæ literaturæ scientissimus, D. Edmundus Gibson, Oxoniensis. Hactenus de Elfrici Versionibus.
units.tr: It should be noted that Ælfric, in the preface above, says that he translated only that part of Genesis which runs from the beginning of the book to Isaac. For both Cambridge codices contain only that part, ending at chapter XXIV. The Oxford codex, however, nearly completes the whole Heptateuch; yet it is not to be judged a very accurate version. Nor do the translators themselves seem to have intended such a version, but to have selected only the more useful and notable passages. In the Oxford codex, to pass over the gap in the damaged volume: in the book of Genesis, of the tenth chapter only the first two verses and the last are expressed. From verse twenty of the twenty-second chapter to the end of the chapter, things are omitted. Of the twenty-third there is a brief, yet fairly accurate, epitome. Of the twenty-sixth only the last two verses are represented. Of the thirty-sixth only verses 6, 7 and 8. Then, to the end of the book, everything is rendered fairly faithfully. Exodus ends at the fourth verse of the thirty-fifth chapter. Leviticus has only those things which concern the Moral Law; the Ceremonial matters are for the most part omitted. Numbers, Deuteronomy and Joshua have more, but not all. The book of Judges ends at the last verse of the sixteenth chapter. These things were reported to me in a letter by the man who consulted the codex, a most learned man in Old English literature, Mr Edmund Gibson of Oxford. So far concerning Ælfric's versions.

units.la: Cæterùm ea fuit olim Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ cura in promovendâ plebis sibi commissæ instructione; ut quoties lingua popularis insignem mutationem passa est; toties recenti versione adornatâ Elementa fidei in vulgus edenda duxerit. Indicio est Codex MS. Anglo-saxonicus Homiliarum & Tractatuum variorum, in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ asservatus; qui præter Homilias XIV. & Tractatus ac Orationes diversas, continet Orationem Dominicam, & Symbolum Apostolorum, cum Expositionibus satis prolixis. Utitur autem linguâ, quæ à Saxonicâ veteri haud parum distat, & ad hodiernam Anglicam propiùs accedit; dit; eâ sc. quâ usi sunt Anglo-Saxones, postquam ex diuturno cum Normannis convictu antiqua dialectus exolescere coepisset. Non statim enim ab adventu Normannorum lingua Saxonica exolevit; quae per multos adhuc annos non solùm apud vulgus, sed & in publicis etiam scriptis usurpata fuit. Testimonio sit Charta Originalis (inter Archiva Bibliothecae Lambethanae) Henrici I. Regis, Willelmo Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi sedis suae fundos ac possessiones confirmans, post sexaginta circiter à Conquestu annos. Scribitur autem linguâ tam Latinâ quàm Saxonicâ, à veteri quidem Saxonicâ paululum diversâ, quae tamen & Grammaticam & characteres Saxonicos retinet.
units.tr: Moreover, it was once the care of the English Church, in promoting the instruction of the people committed to her, that whenever the vernacular tongue underwent a notable change, she thought fit to prepare a fresh version and to publish the elements of the faith among the common people. Evidence is the manuscript Anglo-Saxon codex of Homilies and various Tracts, kept in the Lambeth Library, which, besides fourteen Homilies and various Tracts and Prayers, contains the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed, with fairly lengthy explanations. It uses a language which differs not a little from the old Saxon and comes closer to modern English, namely that which the Anglo-Saxons used after the old dialect had begun to fall into disuse through long intercourse with the Normans. For the Saxon language did not fall out of use straight away at the arrival of the Normans; it was used for many years still, not only among the common people but also in public writings. Witness is an original charter (among the archives of the Lambeth Library) of King Henry I, confirming to William, Archbishop of Canterbury, the estates and possessions of his see, about sixty years after the Conquest. It is written, however, in both Latin and Saxon, in a Saxon somewhat different from the old, which nevertheless retains both the grammar and the Saxon characters.

units.la: 1000. Author Libri de duplici Martyrio ad Fortunatum.
units.tr: 1000. Author of the book On the Double Martyrdom, addressed to Fortunatus.

units.la: Inter Cypriani Opera, Append. 2. pag. 45. edit. Oxon. Tutissimum cordis munimentum est sobrietas cum instanti oratione, jugique Scripturarum meditatione. Omnis enim Scriptura divinitus inspirata utilis est, &c. Ex hac igitur colligendae sunt sententiae; quas ad manum & velut in procinctu habeas; ut his protinus Serpentem caput erigentem dejicias. Nullus est enim animorum morbus, cui non praesens remedium divina Scriptura suppeditaret. Hinc comparanda sunt exempla piorum, sed praecipuè Christi, quibus se quisque vel animet vel consoletur. Videtur iste Tractatus saltem post annum millesimum scriptus; postquam Turci, (de quibus inibi mentio fit) Occidentalibus Christianis innotuerunt.
units.tr: In Cyprian's Works, Appendix 2, p. 45, Oxford edition: Sobriety together with constant prayer and unceasing meditation on the Scriptures is the safest protection for the heart. For all Scripture, inspired by God, is useful, etc. From this, therefore, sentences should be gathered, which you may have at hand and as it were ready for battle, so that you may at once strike down the serpent as it raises its head. For there is no disease of the soul for which divine Scripture does not supply a ready remedy. Hence the examples of the pious, and above all of Christ, should be gathered, by which each may either encourage or comfort himself. This treatise seems to have been written at least after the year 1000, since the Turks (of whom it makes mention there) had become known to Western Christians.

units.la: Huic adjiciam locum ex libro de XII. Abusionibus saeculi, ibid. p. 47. cap. 5. Pudica foemina bonis semper moribus delectatur & consentit; & assiduis Scripturarum meditationibus & eloquiis animam vegetat. Citatur iste liber ab Hincmaro Epist. ad Carolum III. Imp. Tom. 2. Opp. pag. 186.
units.tr: To this I will add a passage from the book On the Twelve Abuses of the Age, ibid., p. 47, chap. 5: A modest woman always delights in and consents to good morals, and invigorates her soul by constant meditation on the Scriptures and by their words. This book is cited by Hincmar in his letter to the Emperor Charles III, Vol. 2 of his Works, p. 186.

units.la: 1020. Canutus, Angliae & Daniae Rex.
units.tr: 1020. Canute, King of England and Denmark.

units.la: Isto, ut videtur, aevo Scriptura Sacra in linguam etiam Danicam conversa est. Extat enim in Bibliothecâ Cottoniana (sub effigie Caligulae, A. 7.) liber MS. sermone Danico pulcherrimè conscriptus, & picturis elegantissimis ornatus; qui fuit quondam Canuti Regis. Titulum praefert recentiore manu additum: Evangelia IV. sermone Danico. Verùm mihimet Codicem inspicienti compertum est, non tam Quatuor Evangelia, quàm Harmoniam Evangeliorum IV. in eo continueri; tineri; qualis ab Ammonio, & Tatiano, Græcè, à Victore Capuano Latinè est concinnata. Latinæ itaque Harmoniæ Versio videtur, minimè tamen χτ̄ τοῦας facta. Ex gr. Jesu, aut Christi nomen vix ullibi habet; pro eo Godes barn, Dei Filium, sæpiùs reponens. Characteri Saxonico propè accedit; quin & innumera vocabula Saxonicæ linguæ habet communia. Præfigitur præfatio hujus initium expressi.
units.tr: In this age, it seems, the Holy Scripture was also turned into the Danish language. For there exists in the Cotton Library (under the press mark Caligula A. 7) a manuscript book written most beautifully in the Danish tongue and adorned with most elegant pictures, which once belonged to King Canute. It bears a title added in a more recent hand: The four Gospels in the Danish language. But when I examined the codex myself, I found that it contains not so much the four Gospels as a Harmony of the four Gospels, such as was composed in Greek by Ammonius and Tatian, and in Latin by Victor of Capua. It seems therefore to be a version of the Latin Harmony, though not rendered word for word. For example, it hardly ever has the name Jesus or Christ; in its place it often substitutes Godes barn, the Son of God. It comes close to the Saxon character, and indeed has countless words in common with the Saxon language. A preface stands at the head of it; I have set out the beginning of it.

units.la: Incipit Quatuor-Evangelium MANEC AWARON theliairomod gespon thatsia bigunnun uuord godef reckean thaz giruni thaz thi riceo Crist undar mancunnea maritha gifrumida miduuordun endimid uuercun. Historia Vocationis Petri & Andreæ hisce verbis narratur; quibus te- xtum Vulgarem è regione appositi; quo major illis lux affulgeret.
units.tr: Here begin the Four Gospels: "Many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the words by which the kingdom of Christ among mankind has been brought to pass, in word and in deed." The calling of Peter and Andrew is related in these words, with the common text placed opposite, so that more light may shine upon them.

units.la: Gieng im thuo bienef uuateref strode thar thie habda iordan aneban galileo land enna seo giuuarahtan thar hie sittean fand Andreafe endi Petrufe bithem aha stromę bethia thia gibruoder thar fia anbred uuatar suithuo niudlico netti theni dun. ficodun im anthem fluode thar fea thar fritha barn godef, &c. Ambulans autem Jesus juxta mare Galileæ, vidit duos fratres, Simonem qui vocatur Petrus, & Andream fratrem ejus, mittentes rete in mare: erant enim Piscatores. Et ait illis: Venite post me; & faciam vos fieri piscatores hominum. At illi continuò relictis retibus, secuti sunt eum. Vulgatæ Versioni consentit Victoris sive Ammonii Harmonia; nisi quòd vocem Jesus omittat.
units.tr: As he went on, by the wide shore where the Jordan flows past the land of Galilee, he found there Andrew and Peter, brothers, who were casting their nets into the water, the sea of the living people. They were fishermen in the sea, the sons of the Lord, etc. Now as Jesus walked by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them, Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men. Immediately they left their nets and followed him. The Harmony of Victor or Ammonius agrees with the Vulgate version, except that it omits the word Jesus.

units.la: 1030. Herlevinus, Abbas Beccensis.
units.tr: 1030. Herlevinus, Abbot of Bec.

units.la: Vitam ejus scripsit Gilbertus Crispinus, Abbas Westmonasteriensis, qui Cœnobii Beccensis Monachus fuerat. Inibi de Herlevino ista refert. Semper inquibat: Homo literarum & mandatorum Dei nescius, quid præstat? &c. Laicos quâ instantiâ, ut ad discendum Psalmos intenderent, agebat? Quibus modis ut quod inchoaverant, amando tenerent, instabat? Tantùm abfuit, ut viri sancti illius temporis Laicis Scripturæ lectionem interdicerent; ut illam omnibus potiùs sedulò commendarent; cùm tamen è Laicis, qui Latinè nôrit, monstro esset. Quin
units.tr: His life was written by Gilbert Crispin, Abbot of Westminster, who had been a monk of the monastery of Bec. There he reports the following about Herlevinus: He always used to say: "What use is a man who knows nothing of letters and the commandments of God?" etc. With what urgency did he urge the laity to apply themselves to learning the Psalms? By what means did he press them to hold fast, by loving, to what they had begun? So far was it from the case that the holy men of that time forbade the laity to read Scripture, that they rather earnestly commended it to all; although among the laity a man who knew Latin was a marvel. Indeed

units.la: 9 In Append. ad Lanfranci Opp. Parif. 1648. pag. 38. & praecipuum erat sanctitatis argumentum etiam in Foeminis, divinas Scripturas lectitare. Sic enim Petrus Damiani, Cardinalis Romanus, Agnetem Imperatricem in Epistola ad ipsam collaudat.{r} In orationibus & Psalmodiae sedulâ modulatione perfistis, &c. Hinc est, quòd à me requisisti; utrùm licer[illegible, ~3 letters]omini, inter ipsum debiti naturalis egerium, aliquid ruminare Psalmos.
units.tr: 9 In the Appendix to Lanfranc's Works, Paris 1648, p. 38. It was also a principal mark of holiness, even in women, to read the divine Scriptures. For thus Peter Damian, Roman Cardinal, praises the Empress Agnes in his letter to her: You persist in prayers and in the diligent chanting of the Psalms, etc. Hence it is that you have asked me whether, between the natural discharge of a due need, it is lawful [illegible] to ruminate on some Psalms.{r}

units.la: Laicos, quos tantâ instantiâ ad discendum Psalmos Herlevinus hortabatur, Latinam linguam calluisse minimè credibile est. Sacram quidem Scripturam Caroli M. ævo Gallicè conversam esse Cl. Armachanus supra{f} demonstravit. Verùm adeò mutata est sæculis intermediis Gallica dialectus; ut Translatio ante annos ducentos facta Normannis Herlevini æqualibus parùm inserviret. Alia igitur Gallica Scripturæ Versio sub istius tempora adornata videtur. Sanè extat MS. in Collegio SS. Trinitatis apud Cantabrigiam Psalterium ingenti volumine pulcherrimè descriptum & picturis elegantissimis ornatum ab Eadwino Monacho Anglo, sæculo, prout conjici queat, undecimo. In eo præter Versiones plures Latinas, & Anglosaxonicam Alfredi, habetur Versio Gallica, eâ videlicet linguâ, quæ Normannis illo tempore vulgaris erat. Extat & in Bibliothecâ Cottonianâ{t} MS. Psalterium GallicoLatinum: quod in Angliâ conscriptum est (Calendarium enim præfixum Anglicos ferè Sanctos exhibet) scriptum autem saltem ante finem sæculi duodecimi. Thomæ enim Cantuariensis Calendarium non meminit. Incipit, Bakun chi ne alat el cunseil des feluns; & en la veie des pecheurs ne stout; & en la chaere de pestilence ne sist.
units.tr: It is by no means credible that the laity whom Herlevinus urged so eagerly to learn the Psalms had mastered the Latin tongue. That the Holy Scripture was translated into French in the age of Charles the Great has been demonstrated by the learned Archbishop of Armagh above.{f} But the French dialect changed so much in the intervening centuries that a translation made two hundred years earlier would scarcely have served the Normans of Herlevinus's contemporaries. Another French version of Scripture therefore seems to have been prepared about this time. Indeed there exists a manuscript in the College of the Holy Trinity at Cambridge, a Psalter of great size, most beautifully written and adorned with most elegant pictures, by Eadwine, an English monk, probably of the eleventh century. In it, besides several Latin versions and the Anglo-Saxon version of Alfred, there is a French version, in that language which was then common among the Normans. There is also in the Cotton Library{t} a manuscript Psalter in French and Latin, written in England (for the calendar prefixed exhibits almost only English saints), but written at least before the end of the twelfth century, since it does not mention Thomas of Canterbury in its calendar. It begins: Blessed is he who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.

units.la: 1040. Theophanes Cerameus, Archiepiscopus Tauromenitanus,
units.tr: 1040. Theophanes Cerameus, Archbishop of Taormina,

units.la: Homil. in Dormitione B. Virginis, propè sin. p. 417. [?]Ἀλλὰ σπουδάζωμεν ἐν ἡμῖν ἕκαστος ὑποδέξασθαι τὸν δεσπότην ἐν ἑαυτῷ διὰ νοερᾶς ἐννοίας καὶ ἀγαθῆς ἀγωγῆς, καὶ ὡς Μαρία τοῖς ἀχράντοις ποσὶν αὐτοῦ προσπίπτωμεν. [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀλλὰ τὰς θείας βίβλους, αἳ τὸ γάλα τῆς διδασκαλίας δαψιλῶς ἐκχέουσιν. Studeat unusquisque nostrum in seipsum recipere Dominum per contemplationem [& actionem:] ac Mariæ modo ad purissimos ipsius pedes assidui. Per pedes porrò possunt intelligi Libri divinitus inspirati; qui lac abundè profundunt.
units.tr: Homil. in Dormitione B. Virginis, propè sin. p. 417. "But let each of us be eager to receive the Lord within himself, through a thoughtful contemplation and a good way of life, and like Mary fall at his spotless feet. [illegible, about 12 letters] but the divine books, which pour out the milk of teaching abundantly." [Ἀλλὰ σπουδάζωμεν ἐν ἡμῖν ἕκαστος ὑποδέξασθαι τὸν δεσπότην ἐν ἑαυτῷ διὰ νοερᾶς ἐννοίας καὶ ἀγαθῆς ἀγωγῆς, καὶ ὡς Μαρία τοῖς ἀχράντοις ποσὶν αὐτοῦ προσπίπτωμεν. [illegible] ἀλλὰ τὰς θείας βίβλους, αἳ τὸ γάλα τῆς διδασκαλίας δαψιλῶς ἐκχέουσιν.] Each of us should take care to receive the Lord into himself through contemplation [and action] and, like Mary, to be constantly at his most pure feet. The feet, moreover, can be understood as the books inspired by God, which pour out milk abundantly.

units.la: {r} Apud Baron. ad An 1052. num. 96.
units.tr: Cited in Baronius, at the year 1052, no. 96.

units.la: {f} Cap. 5. ad An. 807.
units.tr: Chapter 5, at the year 807.

units.la: {t} Sub effigie Neronis.
units.tr: Under the effigy of Nero.

units.la: 1040. Berengarius, Archidiaconus Andegavensis,
units.tr: 1040. Berengarius, Archdeacon of Angers,

units.la: Expofit. super Apocalypsin, MS. in Bibliothecà Lambethanà, in cap. 1. Multi namque sunt, qui mandata Dei aut audiunt aut legunt: sed nihil eos juvat; quia cùm corpore præsentes sint, mente absentes sunt.
units.tr: Exposition on the Apocalypse, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, on chap. 1. For there are many who either hear or read the commandments of God, but it does them no good, because although they are present in body, they are absent in mind.

units.la: Ibid. Visione 1a. prope sin. in Apoc. III. 18. Eme à me aurum probatum, ignitum.] Per aurum sapientia intelligitur; sicut scriptum est: Thesaurus desiderabilis requiescit in ore sapientis. Quod probatum dicitur; quia probatos & perfectos reddit omnes, quos possidet. Ignitum verò ideo dicitur; quia eorum mentes, in quibus habitat, in amorem Dei atque proximi accendit. Et quia vera sapientia ex divinis Scripturis accrescit, Psalmista manifestat, cum dicit: Eloquia Domini eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum, probatum terrà, purgatum septuplùm. Eloquia Domini eloquia casta sunt; quia castas mentes à vitiis reddunt. Sed cùm nihil purgari possit, nisi quod sordidum est; quærendum nobis est, quomodo eloquia Domini purgari dicuntur; in quibus nihil sordidum esse potest. Eloquia ergo Domini sicut argentum igne examinata dicuntur: quia mentes fidelium aliquando igne pœnitentiæ, aliquando igne caritatis, ab omnibus sordibus vitiorum examinant. Quod autem ait probatum terræ, in Hebræo habet, se paratum à terrà. Quod etiam septuplùm purgatum dicitur, propter septem purgationes, quas divina Scriptura in se continet, septem videlicet virtutes, quibus omnia vitia purgantur, &c. Ecce sto ad ostium, & pulso.] Pulsat Dominus ad hostium nostrum; cùm per Scripturam divinam cotidie nos ammonet; ut vitia relinquentes, ad bona opera agenda convertamur. Vocem ejus audimus, & januam aperimus; cùm mandata ejus totà mentis intentione suscipimus.
units.tr: Ibid., Vision 1, near the beginning, on Apoc. III. 18: "Buy of me gold tried in the fire." By gold wisdom is understood, as it is written: "A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise." It is said to be tried because it makes perfect and proven all those whom it possesses. It is said to be fiery because it kindles the minds in which it dwells to love of God and of neighbour. And since true wisdom grows from the divine Scriptures, the Psalmist makes this plain when he says: "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in the fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold." The words of the Lord are pure words, because they make chaste minds free from vices. But since nothing can be purged except what is foul, we must ask how the words of the Lord are said to be purged, when nothing in them can be foul. The words of the Lord are therefore said to be like silver examined in the fire, because they test the minds of the faithful from all the filth of vices, sometimes by the fire of repentance, sometimes by the fire of charity. As for the phrase "proved in the earth," the Hebrew has "prepared itself from the earth." It is also said to be purged sevenfold, on account of the seven purgings which the divine Scripture contains in itself, namely the seven virtues by which all vices are purged, etc. "Behold, I stand at the door and knock." The Lord knocks at our door whenever He admonishes us daily through the divine Scripture, that, leaving our vices, we turn to doing good works. We hear His voice and open the door, when we receive His commandments with the whole intention of our mind.

units.la: Ibid. in Præfatione. Sicut terræ sterili amplius proficit aspersio stercoris, quàm alicujus metalli pretiosi: ita & indoctis hominibus plus proficit divina Scriptura mediocriter prolata, quàm si Philosophico aut Poetico sermone proferatur. Sciantque Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum sacramenta doctrinæ suæ non primò Philosophis, sed Piscatoribus tradidisse; ut per Piscatores veniret ad Philosophos.
units.tr: Ibid., in the Preface: As a sterile land profits more from the spreading of dung than from any precious metal, so divine Scripture, though plainly set forth, profits unlearned men more than if it were delivered in philosophical or poetic speech. Let them know that our Lord Jesus Christ delivered the sacraments of His teaching not first to the philosophers, but to the fishermen, so that through the fishermen it might come to the philosophers.

units.la: Expositio ista Ambrosio supposita, inter Opera illius excusa reperitur, demptis Præfatione & Introductione; quæ in excusis frustra quæruntur. Ambrosio autem illam minimè deberi nullus non novit. Restat igitur, ut de Authore genuino nonnulla dispiciamus. Duplex ejus exemplar MS. in Bibliothecà Lambethanà habetur; alterum vetustius (quòd quidem Berengarii ætate haud multò inferius videtur) in principio mutilum, titulo & præfatione caret: alterum recentius Beringuedis cujusdam nomen inscriptum præ se fert. Aliud exemplar vidi MS. in Bibliothecâ Collegii Gonvilii & Caii apud Cantabrigienses, Berengario inscriptum. De eo certior à me factus, uti & de Codicibus Lambethanis ab amico quodam doctissimo, Vir Cl. Guilielmus Cave, librum Berengario abjudicandum, Beringuedi tribuendum conjecit u. Vereor autem ne infelici conjecturâ. Plurimi quidem Codices MSS. à Jamesio x memorati, Beringuedis nomen præferunt. Id tamen aut ignorantiâ aut fraude Monachorum librariorum, quibus invisum erat Berengarii nomen, factum videtur. Neque enim Scriptor ullus Beringuedem memoravit; aut de istiusmodi Scriptore vel inaudivit. Pitsæus equidem illum in Appendicem suam rejecit; nihil aliud autem de illo dicendum habuit, quàm se nomen ejus in fronte Expositionis in Apocalypsin reperisse. Neque certius aliquid novit Bostonus Burienfis; qui in Catalogo suo Scriptorum Eccles. (cujus exemplar MS. imperfectum penès Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem manet) Berengaudi quidem Opera, & in his Expositionem Apocalypseos, enumerat; quod tamen Bostono solenne est, è solâ fide titulorum, quos Codicibus MSS. affixos deprehenderat. Quin & inter ipsos Codices de nomine nequaquam convenit. Alii Beringuedim, alii Berengwiddin, alii denique Berengaudum vocant. Verùm enimvero ut quod sentio, dicam: inficeti quidam tenebriones, quibus aut Berengarii nomen, abbreviatè scriptum, ignotum erat; aut ob dogma de Eucharistiâ invisum: Auctoris nomen sibi pro lubitu cudendum aut immutandum susceperunt. En præclarum igitur commentum, quod in fronte recentioris Codicis Lambethani comparet. Quisquis auctoris nomen scire desideras, literas Expositionum in Capitibus septem Visionum primas attende. Numerus quatuor vocalium quæ desunt, si Græca posueris est 81. Literæ Expositionum septem primæ hæ sunt B. R. N. G. V. D. S. Verò vocales secundùm præfixum numerum quæ desunt, hæ videntur. Præfationi succedit Carmen, quod incipit. Hunc qui composuit librum, plerique vocatum Dant Berengaudum; verumque velut reor, aiunt.
units.tr: This exposition, ascribed to Ambrose, is found printed among his works, except that the Preface and Introduction are omitted; these are sought in vain in the printed editions. Yet no one is unaware that it is not rightly owed to Ambrose. It remains, therefore, that we examine something about its genuine author. There are two manuscript copies of it in the Lambeth Library: one, the older (which seems not much later than the age of Berengarius), is mutilated at the beginning and lacks the title and preface; the other, more recent, bears the name of a certain Beringuedis. I have seen another manuscript copy in the library of Gonville and Caius College at Cambridge, inscribed with the name of Berengarius. Being informed of this, and of the Lambeth codices, by a certain very learned friend, the distinguished Mr. William Cave conjectured that the book should be taken from Berengarius and assigned to Beringuedis, though I fear his conjecture may be unlucky. Indeed, most of the manuscript codices recorded by James bear the name Beringuedis. Yet this seems to have come about either through the ignorance or the fraud of the monk-scribes, to whom the name of Berengarius was hateful. For no writer has mentioned any Beringuedis, nor has he heard of any such author. Pits indeed threw him out into his Appendix, but had nothing else to say of him except that he had found his name at the head of the Exposition on the Apocalypse. Nor does Boston of Bury know anything more certain, who in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers (an imperfect manuscript copy of which remains with the Archbishop of Canterbury) lists the works of Berengaudus, including an Exposition of the Apocalypse; but this is characteristic of Boston, who relied solely on the authority of the titles he had found attached to manuscript codices. Indeed, the codices themselves by no means agree about the name. Some call him Beringuedis, others Berengwiddin, others finally Berengaudus. But to say what I think: certain stupid rogues, to whom either the name of Berengarius, written in abbreviated form, was unknown, or who hated him on account of his doctrine of the Eucharist, took upon themselves to fashion or alter the author's name at their pleasure. Here, then, is the splendid contrivance that appears at the head of the more recent Lambeth codex. Whoever you are who desire to know the author's name, attend to the first letters of the Expositions in the chapters of the seven Visions. The number of the four vowels that are missing, if you put them in Greek, is 81. The first seven letters of the Expositions are these: B, R, N, G, V, D, S. The vowels, according to the number prefixed, which are missing, appear to be these. The Preface is followed by a poem, which begins: "He who composed this book, most call him Dant Berengaudus; and this, as I think, is true."

units.la: Ipsi igitur, qui calculum tam præclarè subduxerunt nebulones, de commenti sui veritate subdubitarunt. Neque Berengarium enim neque Berengaudum de istiusmodi artificio somniasse arguit error ejus manifestus. Inter consonas enim antepenultima, inter vocales ultima, otiosæ sunt. Incredibile autem est, Authorem si istiusmodi quid in animo habuisset, artificium quod nomini suo adamussim congrueret, excogitare non potuisse. Be-
units.tr: Those very rogues, then, who worked out this calculation so neatly, had their own doubts about the truth of their contrivance. For their obvious error proves that neither Berengarius nor Berengaudus dreamed of such a device. Among the consonants the antepenultimate, and among the vowels the last, are superfluous. Moreover, it is hard to believe that the author, if he had had any such thing in mind, could not have devised a device fitting his name exactly. Be-

units.la: u Hist. Liter. p 602. x Eclog. Oxon-Cant. rengario igitur potiùs, quam Berengaudo isti fictitio, Opus est relinquendum. Rem extra omne dubium ponet Johannes Subprior, qui prolixum in Apocalypsim conscripsit Commentarium, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ asservatum. In prologo enim Expositores Apocalypseos recensens, post Jeronymum, Augustinum, Primasium, Victorinum & Bedam memoratos, hæc habet : Nostri quoque temporis Magister Berengarius, & Robertus Prior; qui quanto sunt tempore posteriores, tantò sunt per experientiam & manifestationem ipsius prophetiæ ad exponendum certiores; totum librum ex ordine pleniter exposuerunt; & Expositiones suas ex locis sanctarum Scripturarum fortiter munierunt. Ex horum pariter ac priorum Expositionibus Commentarium suum Johannes conflavit, paucis de suo additis. In eo igitur reperiuntur continua ferè & ampla Berengarii Excerpta; quæ in Codicibus nostris MSS. totidem verbis comparent. Atque has quidem Berengarii vindicias me egisse, Eruditos, spero, non pigebit.
units.tr: u Hist. Liter. p. 602. x Eclogue Oxon.-Cant. Berengarius, then, rather than that fictitious Berengaudus, is to be retained as the author. The matter will be placed beyond all doubt by John, sub-prior, who wrote a lengthy Commentary on the Apocalypse, preserved in the Lambeth Library. For in the prologue, reviewing the expositors of the Apocalypse, after Jerome, Augustine, Primasius, Victorinus and Bede, he has this: Our own age also had Master Berengarius and Robert the Prior; who, being later in time, are all the more certain in expounding the prophecy through experience and the manifestation of the prophecy itself; they have expounded the whole book in order, and have strongly fortified their expositions from passages of holy Scripture. From the expositions of these men and of the earlier writers alike, John put together his own commentary, with few additions of his own. In it, therefore, are found almost continuous and extensive excerpts from Berengarius, which appear word for word in our manuscript codices. And I hope that learned readers will not regret that I have pleaded this claim on behalf of Berengarius.

units.la: 1070. Lanfrancus, Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis,
units.tr: 1070. Lanfrancus, Archbishop of Canterbury,

units.la: Comm. in 1 Cor. XIV. pag. 74, 75. Qui enim loquitur linguâ.] sc. auditoribus incognitâ. [Non hominibus loquitur.] Simplex bonum. Ipse enim solus intelligit. [sed Deo. Nemo enim audit.] i. e. intelligit, &c. Et ideo] quia quærenda sunt dona quæ prosunt. [qui loquitur linguâ, oret ut interpretetur. Nam si orem] loquar [linguâ; spiritus meus] vox mea [orat.] id est, ego nulli prosum. [mens autem mea sine fructu est.] i. e. sine compunctione; quia non intelligo, quæ linguâ loquor. [Quid ergo est?] Quandoquidem non prosum loquens linguam non interpretans: esse debet, quod sequitur, sc. [Orabo spiritu:] i. e. voce. [Orabo & mente.] ut interpretari sciam, &c. Sic Glossa. Commentarius autem in illud [Quid ergo?] sic docet. Esse debet, si bene. Si vox loquens incognitâ linguâ benedicat Deum vel cibum vel aliquid hujusmodi; Auditor idiota, i. e. audiens & non intelligens, nescit quando debeat respondere Amen, aut Deo gratias; nec est qui suppleat locum responsionis ejus, i. e. qui vice illius respondeat; cùm omnes ignorent verba loquentis.
