units.tr: Comm. in 1 Cor. XIV. pp. 74, 75. "For he that speaketh in a tongue" (that is, in a tongue unknown to the hearers). "Speaketh not unto men": simple good. "For no man understandeth him, but God." That is, no one understands him, etc. "Therefore" because the gifts that profit are to be sought. "Let him that speaketh in a tongue pray that he may interpret." "For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit" (my voice) "prayeth." That is, I profit no one. "But my understanding is unfruitful": that is, without compunction, because I do not understand what I say in the tongue. "What is it then?" Since I profit nothing when I speak in a tongue I do not interpret, what follows must be the case: "I will pray with the spirit," that is, with the voice. "I will pray with the understanding," so that I may know how to interpret, etc. So the Gloss. The Commentary, however, on the words "What is it then?" teaches thus: It must be, if it is well done. If a voice speaking in an unknown tongue blesses God, or the food, or something of the kind, the hearer who is untaught, that is, one who hears and does not understand, does not know when he ought to answer "Amen" or "Thanks be to God"; nor is there anyone to supply the place of his response, that is, to answer in his stead, since all are ignorant of the words of the speaker.

units.la: 1080. S. Wulstanus, Episcopus Wigorniensis.
units.tr: 1080. S. Wulstan, Bishop of Worcester.

units.la: Frequentibus Conciliorum decretis cautum est; ut SS. Scripturæ non solùm in Ecclesiis, Monasteriis, & Scholis, verùm etiam in conviviis virorum Ecclesiasticorum prælegerentur. [Vid. infra, cap. 7.] Cùm verò vero fieri non potuit; quin convivarum pars maxima Scripturas Latino sermone praelectas minus intelligerent; mos fuit Episcopis, qui salutem animarum magis curae habuerunt, Lectiones convivis suis indoctioribus vernaculo sermone interpretari. Exemplo sit Wulstanus, Episcopus Wigorniensis, quo non alius inter Antistites Anglicanos majorem sanctitatis famam obtinuit. De eo ista habet Joannes Vicarius de Tynmouth; qui Historiam Aureram tribus praegrandibus voluminibus circa An. 1360. conscripsit, MS. in Bibliotheca Lambethana asservatam, lib. 21. cap. 106. Legebantur ad mensam ejus libri aedificationi accommodi; cunctis interim summum praestantibus silentium. Jam vero quiete epulis data, exponebat lectionem patria lingua; ut caelestem impertiret alimoniam, quibus ministraverat corporalem. Eadem verba paulum immutata in Wulstani Vita refert Capgravius, sol. 333. Legend. Nov. qui integrum fere Opus suum ex Tynmuthensis Historia Aurea descripsit. Paria de Roberto Betune, Herefordensi Episcopo, (qui in Concilio Remensi Anno 1148. XVI. Cal. Maii, non sine sanctitatis opinione obiit) narrat Willelmus Prior Lanthoniensis, discipulus ejus ac familiaris; qui Vitam illius non inelegantler conscripsit libris duobus ad Henricum Episcopum Wintoniensem, Stephani Regis fratrem (MS. in Bibliotheca Lambethana) Lectionem Scripturarum ad mensam audire consueverat; de quibus inter epulandum aut cum literatis breviter & modestissime conferebat; aut illiteratis assidentibus aliquid aedificatorium utiliter exponebat. lib. 2. cap. 15.
units.tr: By frequent decrees of councils it was provided that the holy Scriptures should be read aloud not only in churches, monasteries and schools, but also at the tables of ecclesiastical men. [See below, chapter 7.] But since this could not truly be done without the greater part of the diners understanding less the Scriptures read in Latin, it was the custom for bishops, who cared more for the salvation of souls, to explain the readings to their less learned guests in the vernacular. Let Wulstan, Bishop of Worcester, serve as an example; no other among the English prelates gained a greater reputation for holiness. John of Tynemouth, who composed the Historia Aurea in three very large volumes around the year 1360, a manuscript kept in the Lambeth Library, says this about him, book 21, chapter 106: Books suited to edification were read at his table, while all gave the highest attention in silence. But when the meal was over and rest allowed, he would expound the reading in the native tongue, so that he might impart heavenly nourishment to those to whom he had supplied bodily food. Capgrave, in his Life of Wulstan, p. 333 of the Legenda Novella, who copied nearly his whole work from Tynemouth's Historia Aurea, reports the same words, slightly changed. William, Prior of Llanthony, a disciple and intimate of Robert de Bethune, Bishop of Hereford (who died in 1148 at the Council of Reims, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, with a reputation for holiness), tells similar things about him. William wrote his Life elegantly in two books addressed to Henry, Bishop of Winchester, brother of King Stephen (manuscript in the Lambeth Library): He had been accustomed to hear the reading of the Scriptures at table; and of these, while eating, he would briefly and most modestly discuss them with the learned, or, for those unlearned who sat beside him, he would usefully expound something edifying. Book 2, chapter 15.

units.la: 1090. Ivo, Episcopus Carnotensis,
units.tr: 1090. Ivo, Bishop of Chartres,

units.la: Lib. de Ecclesiasticis Officiis, MS. in Bibliotheca Lambethana. Cap. 19. Hunc autem Hymnum (Sanctus) & ipse Sacerdos cum aliis necessario debet dicere: ne seipsum sua prece videatur privasse; qui & suas & aliorum voces angelicis laudibus admitti deprecatus est in praefatione. Cap. 12. Nimiam precum multitudinem, quae in quibubam Ecclesiis obtinere coeperat, reprehendit; eo quod populi attentionem inducto taedio dissiparet. Cap. 26. Orationem, quam inclinati dicimus, antequam communicemus, non ex ordine, sed ex Religiosorum traditione habemus: sc. Domine Jesu Christe, qui ex voluntate Patris. Item & illud. Corpus & sanguis Domini nostri Jesu Christi: quod dicimus, cum aliis Eucharistiam distribuimus. Sunt & aliae multae orationes; quas quidam ad pacem & communionem privatim frequentant. Sed diligentiores
units.tr: Book on the Ecclesiastical Offices, manuscript in the Lambeth Library. Chapter 19: This hymn (the Sanctus) both the priest himself must say with the others, lest he seem to have excluded himself by his own prayer; he who asked in the preface that both his voice and the voices of others be admitted to the angelic praises. Chapter 12: He reproves the excessive multitude of prayers, which had begun to prevail in certain churches, because it scatters the attention of the people through the tedium it induces. Chapter 26: The prayer which we say bowing, before we communicate, we have not from the order, but from the tradition of the religious: namely, "Lord Jesus Christ, who by the will of the Father." Likewise also that: "The body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ," which we say when we distribute the Eucharist to others. There are also many other prayers, which some privately use frequently for peace and communion. But more careful

units.la: {y} In Micrologo est cap. 11. Ibid. cap. 4. Ibid. cap. 18. antiquarum Traditionum observatores nos in hujusmodi privatis orationibus brevitati studere docuerunt, potiusque publicis precibus in Officio Missæ occupare voluerunt. Nam ut B. Innocentius Papa scribens S. Augustino & Aurelio Episcopis, asserit: Nos plùs communibus & publicis, quàm singularibus & privatis orationibus, proficere poterimus.
units.tr: {y} In the Micrologus, chapter 11. Ibid. chapter 4. Ibid. chapter 18. observers of the ancient traditions have taught us to aim at brevity in such private prayers, and have wished us rather to occupy ourselves with public prayers in the Office of the Mass. For Pope Innocent the Blessed, writing to Augustine and Aurelius, the bishops, asserts: "We shall be able to profit more by common and public prayers than by singular and private ones."

units.la: Ex Codice isto MS. Ivonem Micrologi auctorem esse (quod quidem hactenus Eruditos latuit) deprehendi. Codex enim ipse præclaræ vetustatis est, Ivone haud multò inferior; adeoque nihil non fidei meretur. In fronte autem istiusmodi titulum præfert, Liber Ivonis, Carnotensis Episcopi, de Ecclesiasticis Officiis. Constat Capitulis LXXI. Ex his octo priora (quæ De Nocturnis Vigiliis, De matutinis Laudibus, De Primâ, De Tertiâ, De Sextâ, De Nonâ, De Vespertinâ Synaxi, & De Completorio, inscribuntur) nondum, quod scio, prodierunt. Sequentia Capitula LXII. Micrologum constituunt. Ultimum (quod de Missæ singularumque ejus partium Authoribus agit) Micrologo deest.
units.tr: From this manuscript I have discovered that Ivo is the author of the Micrologus (which has hitherto escaped the notice of the learned). For the codex itself is of remarkable antiquity, not much later than Ivo, and so deserves all credence. It bears on its front a title of this kind: Book of Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, on the Ecclesiastical Offices. It consists of seventy-one chapters. Of these, the first eight (headed On the Night Vigils, On the Morning Praises, On Prime, On Terce, On Sext, On None, On the Evening Synaxis, and On Compline) have not, as far as I know, yet been published. The following sixty-two chapters constitute the Micrologus. The last (which treats of the authors of the Mass and of its individual parts) is missing from the Micrologus.

units.la: 1100. Richardus de Dumellis, Abbas Pratellinus.
units.tr: 1100. Richard de Dumellis, Abbot of Pratellum.

units.la: Extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ fusissimus in priora XXVIII. Geneseos Capita Commentarius; cujus Prologus sic incipit. Anselmo Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ Archiepiscopo, quondam Dominicæ crucis Servus, & Minister Cœnobii Pratellini, &c. Inibi Author omnia ferè ad Scripturam, importunè etiam aliquoties, solet trahere; atque illi mysticè accommodare res maximè communes, puta Cœlum, Solem, Aquas, Paradisum, &c. Sic enim lib. 1. ad illud [Producat terra herbam virentem.] Postquam utilitatem Scripturæ latè prædicâsset, ait: Quid est herba virens aliud quàm sensus literæ simplicis? quæ rudi populo, jumentis videlicet summi Regis, pabulum salutiferum suministrat. Scriptum est enim: Qui dat jumentis escam ipsorum. Ecce virens herba, unde parvulorum intellectus educatur. [Et Stellas] Quid sunt aliud stellæ in firmamento positæ, quàm electorum animæ, quæ S. Scripturis invigilant? Et Lib. 2. ad illud: [Crescite, & multiplicamini, & replete aquas maris.] Et bene aquæ reptile producere dicuntur; quia S. Scriptura parvulos sensu quasi vivido calore fovet, membra illorum informat; quousque provectus eorundem intelligentiam superiorem mysticarum locutionum pernice cursu adire valeat. — Crescit liquidem creatura rationalis in sui crea-
units.tr: There is a very extensive manuscript commentary on the first twenty-eight chapters of Genesis in the Lambeth Library, whose prologue begins: To Anselm, Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, once a servant of the Lord's cross, and minister of the monastery of Pratellum, etc. There the author usually draws almost everything into Scripture, sometimes even unreasonably, and applies to it, in a mystical way, things that are most common: heaven, the sun, the waters, paradise, and so on. Thus in book 1, on the words [Let the earth bring forth grass], after praising at length the usefulness of Scripture, he says: What is the green grass but the sense of the plain letter? It supplies a wholesome pasture to the untrained people, that is, to the beasts of the great King. For it is written: He gives to the beasts their food. Behold the green grass, by which the understanding of little ones is nourished. [And the stars.] What else are the stars set in the firmament but the souls of the elect, who keep watch over the holy Scriptures? And in book 2, on the words: [Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea.] And it is rightly said that the waters bring forth creeping things, because holy Scripture cherishes little ones with a sense of living warmth, as it were, and forms their limbs, until those who have advanced can swiftly reach the higher understanding of the mystical sayings. — For the rational creature grows in the devotion of its Crea-

units.la: {b} Monasterium id Normanniæ est, in Diœcesi Lexoviensi, circa Annum 1057. fundatum. toris devotione; multiplicatur bonorum operum consummatione; replet aquas maris, per investigationem legis mysticae. Cum enim pauci profunditatem sanctarum Scripturarum intelligunt; quasi pauca reptilia aquae producunt. At ubi vero ad solidum cibum capiendum idonei facti fuerint, & interiora mysteriorum, prout intelligunt, aliis revelaverint; crescere quidem & multiplicare & aquas maris implere videntur. Igitur aquae maris replentur; cum tripartitus sensus sacrae legis simplicibus etiam panditur. Quid sunt pascua nisi S. Scripturae, quae mundis animalibus alimoniam praestat? Inde fortitudinem interiori homini suministrat, &c. De Paradiso. Quis est Paradisus ille, quem Dominus plantavit, & in quo hominem ipse posuit, nisi sancta Ecclesia, vel sacra Scriptura, ubi omnes species deliciarum inveniuntur, & ubi Lignum Vitae, Lignum quoque Scientiae boni & mali plantantur? Lib. 3. Dominum autem in Paradiso deambulare, est per diversa loca sacrarum Scripturarum, quae quotidie in Ecclesia lectitantur, salutem animarum quaerere, & multifariam cunctos deviantes exhortatione ad viam veritatis reducere.
units.tr: {b} This monastery in Normandy, in the diocese of Lisieux, was founded about the year 1057. tor; it is multiplied by the completion of good works; it fills the waters of the sea through the investigation of the mystical law. For when few understand the depth of the holy Scriptures, they bring forth, as it were, a few creeping things of the waters. But when they have become fit to take solid food, and have revealed the inner meanings of the mysteries to others, as far as they understand them, then they seem indeed to grow, to multiply, and to fill the waters of the sea. Therefore the waters of the sea are filled when the threefold sense of the sacred law is also opened to the simple. What are pastures but the holy Scriptures, which furnish nourishment to clean animals? From them they supply strength to the inner man, etc. On Paradise. What is that Paradise which the Lord planted, and in which he placed man, if not the holy Church, or the sacred Scripture, where all kinds of delights are found, and where the Tree of Life and the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil are planted? Book 3: The Lord walking in Paradise means seeking the salvation of souls through the various places of the sacred Scriptures, which are read daily in the Church, and bringing back all who go astray, in many ways, by exhortation, to the way of truth.

units.la: Ibid. Quid igitur accipitur convenientius per Cherubin , qui plenitudo scientiae interpretantur, quam sacra Scriptura; per quam nobis onus nostrarum miseriarum; & iter, quo redimimur ad patriam, satis abunde quoque declaratur? In ea nimirum promissiones gloriae caelestis describuntur; rursus in eadem minae terroresque gehennalis incendii continentur; quae, ni fallor, nomine flammei gladii praefigurantur, &c. Visne redire ad Paradisum? Volo, inquis. Adito, inquam, Cherubim; hoc est, scrutare profunda mysteria sacrarum Scripturarum; quarum eruditione habes redire ad Paradisum; quem perdideras per primi parentis appetitum illecebrosum. Alioquin clauditur tibi via Paradisi; nisi tui cordis aurem consilio sacrae Scripturae summiseris. Lib. 5. Miram profunditatem divinarum Scripturarum, quae cuncta sacramenta Catholicae religionis continent, deprædicat. Lib. 9. Vertitur autem iste fons [Vitae] in puteum juxta capacitatem legentium. Quippe sermo divinus minimis & magnis sese capabilem reddit; & omnibus omnia factus condescendit. Benedictus Dominus Deus; qui parvulis hauritorio carentibus, Scripturam suam juxta morem fontis in superficie terrae manantem ad potandum propinat; caeteris vero jam sensus exercitatos habentibus atque valentibus potum trahere de profunditate sacri eloquii, puteum Viventis & Videntis me praeparat effodiendo. Lib. 10. Remissum atque sensim evanescens in Ecclesia S. Scripturae studium deflet. Appropinquante jam termino mundi labentis, & refri-
units.tr: Ibid. What, then, is more fitting to be understood by the Cherubim, which are interpreted as the fullness of knowledge, than the sacred Scripture? Through it the burden of our miseries, and the way by which we are redeemed to our homeland, are also made abundantly clear. In it, no doubt, the promises of heavenly glory are described; again, in the same book, threats and terrors of the fire of hell are contained, which, unless I am mistaken, are prefigured by the name of the flaming sword, etc. Do you wish to return to Paradise? I do, you say. Then approach the Cherubim, I say; that is, search out the deep mysteries of the sacred Scriptures; by whose learning you may return to Paradise, which you had lost through the enticing desire of the first parent. Otherwise the way to Paradise is closed to you, unless you have submitted the ear of your heart to the counsel of the sacred Scripture. Book 5: he proclaims the wonderful depth of the divine Scriptures, which contain all the sacraments of the Catholic religion. Book 9: But this fountain [of life] is turned into a well, according to the capacity of its readers. For the divine word makes itself capable of the least and the greatest, and, becoming all things to all, it condescends. Blessed be the Lord God, who, for the little ones who lack a bucket, offers his Scripture to drink, flowing on the surface of the earth in the manner of a spring; but for others who now have trained senses and are able to draw drink from the depth of the holy utterance, he prepares a well of the Living and Seeing One by digging. Book 10: He laments that the study of the holy Scriptures has grown lax and gradually fades away in the Church. As the end of the falling world draws near, and the love of many grows cold,

units.la: {b} Gen. III. {c} Gen. XVI. 14. gescente caritate quamplurium, rigor quidem Christianæ religionis oppidò frigescit; & opera sacræ lectionis, quam constat esse fomitem animi ad superna gaudia tendentis, fermè redacta est in nihilum. Lib. 11. De Versione LXX. Ptolomæo Rege procurante factâ locutus, infit. Nam Sacramenta realiter illarum literarum sapientibus & insipientibus patuerunt. Et post pauca subdit: [Vir pius] ne quando deficiat, fortitudinem sacræ lectionis oppositam sibi conspicit. Est autem sermo dominicus mirabile speculum unicuique, qui jam arcem sanctitatis ascendit, vel ascendere molitur. Denique Patresfamilias omnes, etiam Plebeios, ut conjuges atque liberos suos S. Scripturæ cognitione pro facultate suâ imbuant, hortatur, Lib. 15. Qui sunt illi, qui remanent ad sarcinas compede copulationis uxoriæ devincti? nisi quidam Christianæ plebis, quibus committitur sarcina custodiendæ legis, forma videlicet simplicis eruditionis, per quam procurat familiam suam. Non enim est parvæ laudis, hominem habere conjugem suis imperiis parentem, & filios habere subditos disciplinæ spirituali. Qui cùm profunda mysteria sacrarum Scripturarum ob tarditatem ingenii nequeunt penetrare; circa simplicem intellectum historiæ jubentur degere. Codex quidem Lambethanus nullius Authoris nomen præfert. Ab Abbate tamen quodam Pratellino conscriptum fuisse opus, ex ipso Epistolæ Nuncupatoriæ initio constat. Richardum Abbatem suisse docet Codex MS. in Monasterio Pratellino asservatus; è quo descriptam Præfatoriam ad Anselmum Epistolam Gerberonius evulgavit in nuperâ Operum Anselmi editione, pag. 451. Richardum denique istum de Dumellis cognomen traxisse indicant Fratres Sammarthani, Tom. 4. pag. 756.
units.tr: {b} Gen. III. {c} Gen. XVI. 14. the rigour of the Christian religion grows very cold; and the work of sacred reading, which is certainly a spur to the soul striving toward heavenly joys, has almost been reduced to nothing. Book 11, on the Septuagint version, made at the instigation of King Ptolemy, he says: For the sacraments of those letters were laid open in reality to the wise and the foolish. And a little later he adds: [The godly man] sees that the strength of sacred reading is set against him, lest he ever fail. Indeed, the Lord's word is a wonderful mirror for everyone who has already climbed, or is striving to climb, the citadel of holiness. Finally, he urges all heads of families, even the common people, to imbue their wives and children with knowledge of holy Scripture, as far as each is able. Book 15: Who are those who remain behind for the burdens, bound by the fetters of marriage? Are they not some of the Christian common people, to whom is entrusted the burden of keeping the law, namely the form of simple learning, by which they care for their household? For it is no small praise for a man to have a wife who obeys his commands and sons who are subject to spiritual discipline. Since they cannot penetrate the deep mysteries of the sacred Scriptures on account of the slowness of their wit, they are commanded to dwell on the simple understanding of the history. The Lambeth codex, indeed, bears the name of no author. But that the work was written by a certain abbot, Pratellinus, is clear from the beginning of the dedicatory epistle itself. That the abbot was named Richard is shown by a manuscript codex kept in the monastery of Pratellum, from which Gerberon published the prefatory epistle to Anselm in his recent edition of Anselm's works, p. 451. Finally, that this Richard took the surname de Dumellis is indicated by the Fathers of St Maur (Sammarthani), vol. 4, p. 756.

units.la: 1100. Hildebertus, Episcopus Cenomannensis.
units.tr: 1100. Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans.

units.la: Habentur MSS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Sermones ejus LXXIX. (quorum duo solummodo, viz. 1us & 78us, evulgati sunt) Codice admodum vetusto, quique (prout ex Epistolâ brevi ad calcem addità videri posset) ab ipso Hildeberto ad Decanum Salesbirien-sem dono missus est.
units.tr: There are manuscripts of his sermons in the Lambeth Library, seventy-nine in number (of which only two, namely the 1st and the 78th, have been published). The codex is very old and, as a short letter added at the end might suggest, was sent by Hildebert himself as a gift to the Dean of Salisbury.

units.la: Serm. 6. de Purificat. S. Mariæ Virginis. Fugiamus ergo ad Scripturam; quoties sentimus temptationem ejus (Diaboli) callidam. Si ait nobis; Exerce adulterium; parata est Scriptura, quæ docet, Non moechaberis. Si dicit; Furtum exerce; Scriptura se objicit, quæ prohibet, Ne furtum facias. Cùm jubet irasci; Scriptura minatur; Qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit judicio. Cùm mendacium persuadet, Scriptura pœnam nunciat; nunciat ; Perdes omnes, qui loquuntur mendacium. Juxta hujusmodi fluenta sedeat fidelis anima; & notet adventum insidiantis inimici.
units.tr: Sermon 6, on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Let us therefore flee to Scripture whenever we feel the cunning temptation of the devil. If he says to us, "Commit adultery," Scripture is at hand, which teaches, "Thou shalt not commit adultery." If he says, "Steal," Scripture sets itself against him, forbidding, "Thou shalt not steal." When he bids us be angry, Scripture threatens, "Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment." When he persuades us to lie, Scripture announces punishment, announcing: "Thou shalt destroy all who speak lies." Let the faithful soul sit beside such streams, and let it mark the coming of the lurking enemy.

units.la: Serm. 8. in initio Jejunii Quadragef. Ultiones, fratres Karissimi, Veteris Testamenti ad correctionem hominum illius temporis factae sunt ; sed ad nostram informationem sunt scriptae.
units.tr: Sermon 8, at the beginning of Lent. The punishments of the Old Testament, dearly beloved brothers, were inflicted to correct the men of that time; but they were written down for our instruction.

units.la: Serm. 9. In Quadragesimâ. Ideo, fratres Karissimi, proponuntur ista antiquorum Patrum (V. Testamenti) ut nostra vita in aliquo informetur exemplis eorum.
units.tr: Sermon 9, in Lent. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, these examples of the ancient Fathers (of the Old Testament) are set before us, so that our life may be shaped in some measure by their examples.

units.la: Serm. 20. In Coenâ Domini. Satis novit caritas vestra, dilectissimi fratres, quòd tota perfectio nostrae aedificationis ex Evangelio accipitur. Cujus verba, quia à summo Magistro nobis data sunt, pretiosiora sunt. Ea satis nos hortantur, vos cotidie aedificant; & ea modò vobis repraesentamus ; non quia non bene intelligatis, sed ut intellecta ad memoriam reducatis.
units.tr: Sermon 20, at the Lord's Supper. Your charity, most beloved brothers, knows well that the whole perfection of our edification is derived from the Gospel. Its words, since they were given to us by the highest Teacher, are most precious. They exhort us enough, and they build you up daily; and we now set them before you, not because you do not understand them well, but so that what you understand may be brought back to memory.

units.la: Serm. 27, in Pentecoste. Sancti viri secus fluenta divinae Scripturae, quibus eorum corda rigantur, inhabitant ; ut earum munimento ab incursu diaboli evadant.
units.tr: Sermon 27, at Pentecost. The holy men dwell beside the streams of divine Scripture, by which their hearts are watered, so that by its defence they may escape the assault of the devil.

units.la: Serm. 32. de Ecclesiâ. Non in solo pane vivet homo, sed in omni verbo Dei. Ideo ad hostium tabernaculi erat posita mensa Propositionis ; super quam erant duodecim panes. Quia ingredientibus Ecclesiam necessaria est esca doctrinae, & mensa divinarum Scripturarum ; in quibus sententiae duodecim Apostolorum continentur ; qui per duodecim panes significantur.
units.tr: Sermon 32, on the Church. "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." Therefore the table of the showbread was placed at the door of the tabernacle, with the twelve loaves upon it. For those who enter the Church need the food of doctrine and the table of the divine Scriptures, in which the sayings of the twelve Apostles are contained, which are signified by the twelve loaves.

units.la: Serm. 38. de Lectoribus. Debet etiam [Lector] lectiones in choro legere, & cibum animae hominibus dare legendo. Ipse ergo doctrinâ & libris debet esse imbutus, sensuumque ac verborum scientiâ perornatus; ut distinctè & aperte sonans cordia audientium possit instruere. Et tam clara debet esse vox Lectoris ; ut quamvis longè positorum audientium aures adimpleat.
units.tr: Sermon 38, on Readers. [The reader] ought also to read the lessons in the choir, and by reading to give food to men's souls. He himself therefore must be steeped in learning and in books, and adorned with knowledge of the meaning and the words, so that by speaking distinctly and clearly he can instruct the hearts of his hearers. And the voice of the reader must be so clear that it fills the ears even of hearers placed far away.

units.la: Serm. 44. ad Sacerdotes. Quid firmamentum, nisi Scriptura? super quam fundata est Ecclesia. Quid luminaria firmamenti, nisi Pastores Ecclesiae, qui eam illuminant, eam exponendo aliis?
units.tr: Sermon 44, to the Priests. What is the firmament, if not Scripture? On it the Church is founded. What are the lights of the firmament, if not the ministers of the Church, who illuminate it by expounding it to others?

units.la: Serm 46. ad Sacerdotes. Manna ergo significat panem verbi Evangelii, &c. Dat itaque Dominus Populo suo in cibum utrumque Testamentum, &c. Pascite gregem vobis commissum [isto manna] Nolite legem Dei abscondere, quasi in crastino reservare; ne fiat vobis vermis, ne sit causa damnationis.
units.tr: Sermon 46, to the Priests. Manna therefore signifies the bread of the word of the Gospel, etc. The Lord therefore gives to his people both Testaments as food, etc. Feed the flock committed to you [this manna]. Do not hide the law of God, as if keeping it until tomorrow; lest it breed worms for you, lest it become a cause of condemnation.

units.la: Serm. 61. ad Populum. Fratres Karissimi, ideo leguntur Scripturae, & traditae sunt memoriae; ut videntes peccata antecessorum, audientes à Deo super eos infusa, eisdem divitiis occupati, similes poenas pertimescamus. Serm. 74. Ecce cibus Ecclesiæ paratus! Ideo apposita erat mensa juxta ostium Tabernaculi; cui duodecim panes supponebantur. Tabernaculum Ecclefiam fidelium Dei, quæ in mundo est, significat. Mensa autem in Templo juxta ostium Tabernaculi posita, Scriptura divina intelligitur; quæ per fidem intrantibus Ecclesiam pro eorum capacitate ministratur. Sequitur: Quæ ædificata est propugnaculis. Propugnacula sunt divinarum Scripturarum sacramenta; de quibus scientiæ veluti jacula procedunt, quibus adversariæ partes repelluntur. Gladio enim, quod est verbum Dei, debet unusquisque fidelium fe tueri. Cum enim dixerit hostis: Exerce adulterium; respondeas è contrario; Non, quia scriptum est: Non mœchaberis. Cùm instigaverit: Exerce furtum: tu respondeas è contra: Non, quia scriptum est: Non furtum facies, &c. His igitur armis instruit nos Dominus; ut quoties insistunt tentationes, quæramus à divinis sententiis defensiones.— singulis vitiis opponendo finguias Scripturarum auctoritates. Hac armaturâ muniti, erunt fortes; & in die malo resistere poterunt.
units.tr: Sermon 61, to the People. Dearly beloved brothers, the Scriptures are therefore read and handed down to memory, so that, seeing the sins of our predecessors and hearing the punishments poured out upon them by God, we may fear similar penalties, lest we be overtaken by the same riches. Sermon 74. Behold, the food of the Church is prepared! Therefore the table was set beside the door of the tabernacle, and twelve loaves were laid upon it. The tabernacle signifies the Church of the faithful of God, which is in the world. The table placed in the Temple beside the door of the tabernacle is understood as the divine Scripture, which is ministered by faith to those entering the Church according to their capacity. It follows: "which is built with bulwarks." The bulwarks are the sacraments of the divine Scriptures, from which the points of knowledge go forth like darts, by which the adversaries are driven back. For each of the faithful ought to defend himself with the sword, which is the word of God. For when the enemy says, "Commit adultery," answer him on the contrary: "No, for it is written, 'Thou shalt not commit adultery.'" When he urges, "Steal," answer him on the contrary: "No, for it is written, 'Thou shalt not steal,' etc." The Lord therefore arms us with these weapons, so that whenever temptations press upon us, we may seek defences from the divine sayings… by opposing to each vice the authority of the Scriptures. Fortified with this armour, they will be strong, and will be able to stand in the evil day.

units.la: Serm. 79. (seu potiùs Epistola ad quandam Reclusam) Scio, carissima mea, scio quia Solomonem legisti dicentem: Qui timet Deum, faciet bona. Et in Psalmo; Initium sapientiæ timor Domini. Item legeras apud Apostolum, &c. Reclusa ista nuperrimè à seculo, in quo solutissimè vixit, discesserat.
units.tr: Sermon 79 (or rather, a letter to a certain Recluse). I know, my dearest, I know that you have read Solomon saying, "He who fears God will do good." And in the Psalm: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." Likewise you had read in the Apostle, etc. This recluse had very recently withdrawn from the world, in which she had lived most loosely.

units.la: 1120. Petrus Abælardus
units.tr: 1120. Peter Abelard

units.la: Ad Heloissam conjugem Epist. 8. quæ Institutio seu Regula est Sanctimonialium, quibus Heloissa præfuit. Speculum animæ Scripturam sacram constat esse; in quam quilibet legendo vivens, intelligendo proficiens, morum suorum pulchritudinem cognoscit, vel deformitatem deprehendit; at illam videlicet augere, hanc studeat removere, &c. Qui autem Scripturam conspicit, quam non intelligit, quasi cæcus ante oculos tenet; in quo qualis sit cognoscere non valet; nec doctrinam quærit in Scripturâ; ad quam ipsa tantummodo facta est; & tanquam asinus applicetur ad lyram, sic otiosus sedet ad Scripturam: & quasi panem appositum habet, quo jejunus non reficitur; dum Verbum Dei nec se per intelligentiam penetrante, nec alio ei docendo frangente, inutiliter cibum habet, qui ei nullatenus prodest. Unde & Apostolus generaliter ad Scripturarum studium nos exhortans, Quæcunque, inquit, scripta sunt, &c. [Rom. XV.] Et alibi Implemini Spiritu S. &c. [Ephes. V.] Sibi quippe vel secum loquitur, qui
units.tr: To Heloissa his wife, Epist. 8, which is the Rule or Institute of the nuns over whom Heloissa presided. It is agreed that Holy Scripture is a mirror of the soul; whoever reads it while living, and advances by understanding it, recognises the beauty of his own character or detects its deformity; and he should strive to increase the one and to remove the other, and so on. But whoever looks at Scripture without understanding it holds it before his eyes like a blind man; he cannot know what kind of person he is in it, and he does not seek teaching from Scripture, for which alone she has been made; and like an ass applied to a lyre, he sits idle before Scripture. He has bread set before him, but he is not refreshed by it, since he is hungry; the Word of God does not penetrate him through understanding, and no one breaks it open for him by teaching, so he has food that does him no good at all. Hence the Apostle, exhorting us in general to the study of the Scriptures, says: Whatever things were written, etc. [Rom. XV.] And elsewhere: Be filled with the Holy Spirit, etc. [Eph. V.] For he who speaks, speaks to himself or with himself, who

units.la: ç Cantic. IV. {f Pag. 188, &c. quod profert, intelligit; vel de intelligentia verborum suorum fructum facit. Idem ad Timotheum. Dum venio, attende lectioni, &c. [1 Tim. IV.] Et iterum. Tu verò permane in iis, &c. [2 Tim. III.] Qui etiam ad intelligentiam Scripturæ Corinthios admonens; ut quæ videlicet alii de Scripturâ loquuntur, exponere valeant: Sectamini, inquit, charitatem, &c. [1 Cor. XIV.] Loqui lingua dicitur, qui ore tantùm verba format, non intelligentia exponendo ministrat. Prophetat verò sive interpretatur; qui more Prophetarum, qui Videntes dicuntur, i. e. Intelligentes, ea quæ dicit intelligit, ut ipsa exponere possit. Orat ille spiritu sive psallit, qui solo prolationis flatu verba format, non mentis intelligentiam accommodat. Cùm verò spiritus noster orat, i. e. nostræ prolationis flatus solummodò verba format; nec quod ore profertur, corde concipitur; mens nostra sine fructu est; quem in oratione videlicet habere debet; ut ipsa scilicet ex intelligentiâ verborum in Deum compungatur atque accendatur. Unde hanc in verbis perfectionem nos admonet habere; ut non more plurimorum verba tantùm sciamus proferre, verùm etiam intelligentiæ sensum in iis habere; atque aliter nos orare vel psallere infructuosè protestatur. Quem & Beatus sequens Benedictus: Sic stemus, inquit, ad psallendum; ut mens nostra concordet voci nostræ. Hoc & Psalmista præcipiens ait: Psallite sapienter; ut videlicet verborum prolationi sapor & condimentum intelligentiæ non deest; & cum ipso veraciter Domino dicere valeamus: Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua! Et alibi. Non in tibiis viri beneplacitum erit ei. Tibia quippe sonitum emittit ad delectationem voluptatis, non ad intelligentiam mentis. Unde bene in tibiis cantare, nec in hoc Deo placere, dicuntur; qui melodiâ sui cantûs sic oblectantur; ut nullâ hinc edificentur intelligentiâ. Quâ enim ratione, inquit Apostolus, cùm benedictiones in Ecclesiâ fiunt, respondebitur Amen? si quod oratur in illâ benedictione, non intelligitur: Utrum videlicet bonum sit, quod oratio postulat, aut non? Sic enim sæpe multos idiotas & literarum sensum ignorantes videmus in Ecclesiâ per errorem nonnulla sibi nociva quàm utilia precari, &c. Cui etiam periculo Apostolus providens ait: Caeterum si benedixeris spiritu, id est, prolationis tantùm flatu verba benedictionis formaveris, non sensu mentem audientis instruxeris; Quis supplet locum idiotæ, id est, quis de assistentibus, quorum est respondere, id aget respondendo, quod idiota non valet, immo nec debet. Quomodo dicet Amen? cùm videlicet nesciat utrùm in maledictionem potiùs quàm benedictionem inducas. Denique qui Scripturæ non habent intelligentiam, quomodo sermonis ædificationem sibi ministrabunt; aut etiam regulam exponere vel intelligere, aut vitiosè prolata corrigere valebunt? Unde non mediocriter miramur, quæ inimici suggestio in Monasteriis hoc egit; ut nulla ibi de intelligendis Scripturis sint studia; sed de cantu tantùm vel de verbis solummodò formandis, non intelligendis, habeatur disciplina: quasi ovium balatus plus utilitatis habeat quàm pastus. Cibus quippe est animæ, & spiritualis refectio ipsi divina intelligentia Scripturæ, &c. Pluribus pergit Abælardus S. Scripturæ studium commendare & Monialibus suadere. m His monitis se suasque Moniales animum sedulò adhibuisse, & Scripturæ lectioni diligenter incubuisse, Abælardum certiorem reddit Heloïssa in Epistolâ problematibus ad ipsum propositis præmissâ.
units.tr: Cant. IV. understands what he utters, or makes the fruit of the understanding of his own words. The same to Timothy: While I come, give attention to reading, etc. [1 Tim. IV.] And again: But you continue in those things, etc. [2 Tim. III.] Admonishing the Corinthians also to understand Scripture, so that they may be able to explain what others say about Scripture: Follow after charity, he says, etc. [1 Cor. XIV.] He is said to speak with the tongue who only forms words with the mouth and does not serve by explaining their meaning. But he prophesies, or interprets, who, after the manner of the Prophets, who are called Seers, that is, Understanding Ones, understands what he says, so that he can explain it himself. He prays in the Spirit, or sings psalms, who only forms words with the breath of utterance and does not apply the understanding of the mind. When our spirit prays, that is, when the breath of our utterance merely forms words, and what is spoken with the mouth is not conceived in the heart, our mind is without fruit, which it ought to have in prayer, namely that through understanding the words it may be pricked and kindled toward God. Hence he admonishes us to have this perfection in words: that, not after the manner of most people, we should know how not only to utter words but also to have the sense of understanding in them; and he declares that otherwise we pray or sing psalms to no profit. The blessed Benedict, following him, says: Let us so stand to sing, that our mind may agree with our voice. The Psalmist also, commanding this, says: Sing wisely [Ps. 47], so that the utterance of words may not lack the savour and seasoning of understanding, and so that we may truly be able to say with the Lord himself: How sweet are your words to my throat! And elsewhere: His pleasure will not be in the pipes of a man. For the pipe sends out a sound for the delight of pleasure, not for the understanding of the mind. Hence they are rightly said to sing in pipes, and not to please God in this, who are so delighted by the melody of their singing that they are edified by no understanding from it. For, the Apostle says, on what ground, when blessings are made in the Church, will the Amen be answered, if what is prayed in that blessing is not understood, whether it is good or not what the prayer asks? For we often see many laymen and those ignorant of the sense of the letter in the Church, through error, praying for things that are harmful to them rather than useful, etc. Foreseeing this danger too, the Apostle says: But if you bless in the Spirit, that is, if you merely form the words of blessing with the breath of utterance, and do not instruct the mind of the hearer by sense, who will fill the place of the layman? That is, who among those present, whose duty it is to respond, will do by answering what the layman cannot do, nor indeed ought to do? How will he say Amen, since he does not know whether you are leading him toward a curse rather than a blessing? Finally, those who do not have understanding of the Scriptures, how will they gain edification from the sermon, or be able to explain or understand the rule, or correct what has been uttered wrongly? Hence we wonder not a little what suggestion of the enemy has brought it about in the monasteries that there is no study of understanding the Scriptures there, but that discipline is kept only in singing or merely in forming words, not in understanding them; as if the bleating of sheep had more usefulness than their pasture. For the food of the soul, and its spiritual refreshment, is the divine understanding of Scripture, etc. Abelard goes on at length to commend the study of Holy Scripture and to persuade the nuns to it. Heloissa, in the letter prefixed to the questions she put to him, assures Abelard that she and her nuns have applied their minds carefully to these admonitions and have diligently devoted themselves to reading Scripture.

units.la: 1120. Hugo de Folieto, Monachus Corbeiensis,
units.tr: 1120. Hugo de Folieto, monk of Corbie,

units.la: Scripsit Opus prolixum de Claustris & Claustralibus, libris V. Extat id MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Hugoni nostro inscriptum. Prodiit sæpius inter Hugonis de S. Victore Opera, omisso autem libro quinto; qui De Duabus Rotis (viz. Rotâ veræ Religionis, & Rotâ Simulationis) titulum habet. Lib. 2. cap. 11. Congruum mihi fore videtur; ut qui in Ecclesiâ ante conspectum Dei convenimus, ibi deteriores non simus. Sunt enim quidam, qui mente vagi, Psalmodiæ verba proferunt, sed psalmodiæ sensum non attendunt. Unde Beatus Gregorius: Vox, inquit, psalmodiæ, cùm per intentionem cordis agitur; per hoc omnipotenti Deo ad cor iter paratur, &c.
units.tr: He wrote a long work, On Cloisters and Those Who Live in Them, in five books. It survives in manuscript in the Lambeth Library, inscribed to our Hugo. It has often been printed among the works of Hugo of Saint Victor, but with the fifth book omitted; that book has the title On the Two Wheels (namely, The Wheel of True Religion and The Wheel of Pretence). Book 2, chapter 11: It seems fitting to me that we who gather in the church before the sight of God should not be worse there. For there are some who, wandering in mind, utter the words of the psalmody but do not attend to the meaning of the psalmody. Whence Blessed Gregory: "The voice of psalmody, when it is carried on with the intention of the heart, by this a way is prepared to almighty God in the heart," etc.

units.la: Lib. 3. cap. 9. In hoc refectorio [animæ] tres ponuntur mensæ; i. e. tres intellectus divinæ Scripturæ, videlicet, historialis, mysticus, & moralis. Prima mensa simplicibus, secunda Doctoribus, tertia communis est utrisque, &c. Cæterùm in disponendâ Hugonis ætate secuti sumus calculum Viri Cl. Thomæ Jamesii in Catalogo Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ. De eodem ista notavit Joannes Tinmuthensis in Historiâ Aureâ MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ. Hujus Hugonis (Victorini) libros supra memoravi. Erat autem liber Hugonis de Claustro Animæ, nomine quidem Hugonis de Folieto intitulatus; qui & ipse S. Petri Corbeiensis fuisse dicitur Canonicus; sed quo tempore, ignoramus, lib. 22. cap. 44.
units.tr: Book 3, chapter 9: In this refectory [of the soul] three tables are set; that is, three understandings of divine Scripture, namely the historical, the mystical, and the moral. The first table is for the simple, the second for the teachers, the third is common to both, etc. Moreover, in fixing Hugo's date I have followed the reckoning of the learned Thomas James in his manuscript Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers in the Lambeth Library. John of Tynemouth noted the same things about him in his manuscript Historia Aurea in the Lambeth Library. I have already mentioned the books of this Hugo (of Saint Victor). But there was a book of Hugo's, On the Cloister of the Soul, indeed entitled under the name of Hugo of Folieto; he too is said to have been a canon of Saint Peter's at Corbie, but at what time we do not know, book 22, chapter 44.

units.la: m Pag. 385.
units.tr: m Page 385.

units.la: 1140. Robertus Pullenus, Cardinalis Romanus.
units.tr: 1140. Robert Pullen, Roman Cardinal.

units.la: Inter Sermones ejus MSS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ. Serm. 1. ‘ Est autem cellarium, ubi quæque optima, quæ nascuntur in agro vel ‘ in orto, reconduntur; cellarium Domini est divina Scriptura. Ibi enim ‘ quicquid natum est in orto virtutum, ad opus nostrum inveniemus ‘ repositum. Si morum doctrinam, si allegoriarum intelligentiam, ‘ si historiarum veritatem requirimus, totum ibi reperiemus. Ille ergo, ‘ quem in orto redolentia virtutum delectabat, fructum eorum in cel- ‘ lario percipiat. —Domini Cellarium, i. e. divinarum Scripturarum ‘ studium, omnem tuam cognitionem, id est, quæ te angit, curiositatem exterminabit.
units.tr: "There is a storehouse where all the best things that grow in the field or the garden are laid up. The Lord's storehouse is divine Scripture. For there we shall find stored up, for our use, whatever has grown in the garden of virtues. If we seek the teaching of morals, the understanding of allegories, or the truth of history, we shall find it all there. Let him who was delighted by the fragrance of the virtues in the garden receive their fruit in the storehouse. The Lord's storehouse, that is, the study of divine Scriptures, will drive out all that curiosity of yours, that is, the kind of knowing that torments you."

units.la: Serm. 6. ‘ Quilibet Christianus scire debet Dominum. Sed quo- ‘ modo sciunt illi Dominum qui nec Catholicæ fidei veritatem, nec ‘ Doctores audiunt, nec Scripturas scrutantur; de quibus fidei veritas, ‘ ut piscis de aquâ, multo labore & studio eruitur.
units.tr: "Every Christian ought to know the Lord. But how do they know the Lord who hear neither the truth of the Catholic faith nor the teachers, and who do not search the Scriptures? From these the truth of faith is drawn out, as a fish is drawn out of water, only with great labour and study."

units.la: Serm. 7. ‘ Quòd autem Manna defecerit [Judæis] postquam come- ‘ derunt de fructibus terræ; significat Scripturas, quæ nostra refectio ‘ sunt in viâ, cessaturas, postquam erimus in patriâ.
units.tr: "That the manna failed (for the Jews) after they ate of the fruits of the land signifies that the Scriptures, which are our refreshment on the way, will cease once we are in our homeland."

units.la: Serm. 14. Sequitur : Singuli tenentes gladios in manibus, & docti ad bella. ] ‘ Per gladium Evangelium accipimus, &c. Sed quid prodest habere gladium, nisi teneatur in manibus ? Sunt enim, qui habent divinas Scripturas in Manticâ. Philosophis dictum est; Libros ferre manu, non sensum corde nec ore. Verbum inane parùm ‘ proficit, immo nihil. Oportet autem scientiam Scripturarum habere in cordis memoriâ. —Hæc (V. & N. Testamenta) sunt duo Cherubin, quæ sese respiciunt. Interpretatur autem Cherubin plenitudo: sc. quia etsi aliqua habeatur scientia alibi, in his duobus tamen non alibi plena & perfecta.
units.tr: "It follows: Each holding a sword in his hands, and skilled in war. By the sword we understand the Gospel, and so on. But what good is it to have a sword unless it is held in the hands? For there are those who keep the divine Scriptures in a wallet. It was said of philosophers: To carry books in the hand, but not their sense in the heart or on the lips. An empty word profits little, or rather nothing. One must, however, have knowledge of the Scriptures in the memory of the heart. These (Old and New Testaments) are the two Cherubim, which look at each other. Now Cherubin is interpreted as fullness, namely because, even if some knowledge is had elsewhere, it is not full and perfect anywhere else but in these two."

units.la: 1150. Anonymus, Clericus Rothomagensis,
units.tr: 1150. Anonymous, a Clerk of Rouen,

units.la: Apologetic. pro Sacerdotum conjugio. ‘ Quòd Deus hoc (Cœlibatum Cleri) ‘ instituerit; nec in Veteri Testamento, nec in Evangelio, nec in Apostolorum Epistolis scriptum reperitur; in quibus ‘ quicquid Deus hominibus præcepit, insertum describitur. Quodque ‘ de Scripturis non habet authoritatem, eâdem facilitate contemnitur, ‘ quâ dicitur.’ Tractatum istum MS. vidi inter alios ejusdem generis Tractatus in Codice satis vetusto in Bibliothecâ Collegii Corporis Christi
units.tr: An apology for the marriage of priests. "That God instituted this (the celibacy of the clergy) is not found written either in the Old Testament, or in the Gospel, or in the Epistles of the Apostles; in which whatever God commanded men is set down as inserted. And what does not have authority from the Scriptures is despised with the same ease with which it is asserted." I saw this treatise in manuscript, among other treatises of the same kind, in a fairly old codex in the library of Corpus Christi College

units.la: Testimonium de sufficientiâ S. Scripturæ. apud Cantabrigienses, Clas. O. numb. 230. Illum autem postea deprehendi evulgatum fuisse à Josepho Hallo, ° Episcopo demum Norvicensi, qui seculo duodecimo eum scriptum fuisse non malè conjecit.
units.tr: Testimony on the sufficiency of Holy Scripture. at Cambridge, Class O, number 230. I later discovered that it had been published by Joseph Hall, at last bishop of Norwich, who rightly conjectured that it had been written in the twelfth century.

units.la: 1150. Ailredus, Abbas Rievallensis.
units.tr: 1150. Ailred, Abbot of Rievaulx.

units.la: In vetusto Codice MS. Bibliothecæ Lambethanæ intermiscentur Sermones S. Bernardi & Ailredi. Illi XXXVIII. debentur, literis A. C. vel B. A. C. notati; isti XXXII. literis A. R. insigniti. Sermones quidem Ailredi quamplurimi prodierunt inter opuscula ejus Duaci 1631. & in Bibliothecâ Patrum novissimâ, Tom. 23. Verum inter istos Sermones à nobis citati non reperiuntur. Nescio annon inter Sermones XXV. novos, qui in Nuperâ Cisterciensium Bibliothecâ evulgati sunt Tom. 5. pag. 162.
units.tr: An old manuscript in the Lambeth Library mixes together sermons of St Bernard and Ailred. Thirty-eight of them are attributed to Bernard and marked with the letters A.C. or B.A.C.; thirty-two are marked with the letters A.R. Many sermons of Ailred have been published among his opuscula at Douai in 1631, and in the newest Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 23. But the sermons cited by us are not found among those. I do not know whether they are among the twenty-five new sermons published in the recent Cistercian Bibliotheca, vol. 5, p. 162.

units.la: Serm. in Festo S. Benedicti, in illud [Os justi meditabitur scientiam] circa med. Fœlix justus, cujus os sapientiam meditatur; qui cum sancto Isaac egreditur in agrum ad meditandum. Ager iste, ut mihi videtur, sacra Scriptura est; ager utique festivus, plenus omni benedictione. Ecce, inquit, odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni, cui benedixit Dominus. In agro isto odor mirræ & thuris & universi pulveris pigmentarii. Vere, fratres, non est virtus, non est sensus, non est sapientia, cujus odor non fragret in agro isto.
units.tr: Sermon on the Feast of St Benedict, on the words [The mouth of the just shall meditate wisdom], about the middle. A happy man, whose mouth meditates wisdom, who with holy Isaac goes out into the field to meditate. That field, as it seems to me, is Holy Scripture: a field, to be sure, flourishing and full of every blessing. Behold, he says, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed. In that field there is the fragrance of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer. Truly, brethren, there is no virtue, no understanding, no wisdom, whose fragrance does not breathe from that field.

units.la: Serm. in Synodo, de Aaron & filiis ejus. Habes forte, O sacerdos, maculam in oculis; nescis quomodo doceas, quomodo moneas, quomodo corripias, quomodo punias. Ligas non alligANDA; non solvenda solvis. Sequeris sensum tuum; sequeris stomachum tuum. O quomodo te ingeris ad alios docendos; cùm ipse errabundus per avia quæque incedas? Vade ergo ad aquam Syloe, & lava. Nam sermo Domini utique lavat, sicut habes in Evangelio. Et vos mundi estis propter sermonem, quem locutus sum vobis. Ubi est quaeso sacerdos; qui quotiens populus legem quærit ab eo; ad instar Moysi ingreditur tabernaculum; ut inter duo Cherubim, utriusque sc. Testamenti scientiam, divinam consulat voluntatem? Non sic, non sic multi hujus nostri temporis sacerdotes; in quorum manibus sæpius inveniuntur calices fœcundi, quàm divinæ auctoritatis libri; à quibus sæpiùs denarii numerantur, quàm Scripturæ perscrutantur; magis negotiis sæcularibus implicati, quàm sacris libris legendis occupati. Fœlix, fœlix ille sacerdos, qui in omnibus, in quibus caligat oculus interior;
units.tr: Sermon at a Synod, on Aaron and his sons. Perhaps you have a speck in your eyes, O priest; you do not know how to teach, how to admonish, how to rebuke, how to punish. You bind what should not be bound; you loose what should not be loosed. You follow your own sense; you follow your own anger. O how you thrust yourself forward to teach others, when you yourself wander through every byway? Go therefore to the pool of Siloam, and wash. For the word of the Lord certainly cleanses, as you have in the Gospel: And you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. Where, I ask, is the priest who, whenever the people seek the law from him, goes into the tabernacle like Moses, so that between the two Cherubim he may consult the divine will by the knowledge of both Testaments? Not so, not so do many priests of our time, in whose hands cups of wine are found more often than books of divine authority; by whom coins are counted more often than the Scriptures are searched; more entangled in secular business than occupied in reading the holy books. Happy, happy is that priest, who in all things in which the inner eye is dim,

units.la: ° Lib. vernac. de Honore Cleri Conjugati, ad finem. in omnibus, de quibus consulitur; in omnibus, quae agenda vel docenda incumbunt; vadit ad aquas Syloe, & divinum consulit oraculum.
units.tr: ° From the vernacular book On the Honour of the Married Clergy, at the end. In all things about which he is consulted; in all things which must be done or taught; he goes to the waters of Siloam and consults the divine oracle.

units.la: 1150. Hildebrandus Junior
units.tr: 1150. Hildebrand the Younger

units.la: Expofit. in Evang. S. Matthæi, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, S. Scripturæ ubertatem atque plenitudinem, omnibus ex æquo Christianis paratam, sæpius deprædicat. Hinc illam comparat cum Fermento, cujus admixtione integra farinæ massa animatur; cum Margaritâ, pro cujus acquisitione omnia sunt vendenda: cum Vineâ in quam Dominus omnes confertim servos ad operandum immisit: cum Talento , quod Dominus peregrè profecturus universis servis negotiandum concredidit: Denique cum Prandio, ad quod Dominus omnia hominum genera invitari voluit. Sic enim scribit, lib. 8. homil. 64. in illud Matthæi cap. 22. Dicite invitatis, quòd prandium meum paravi.]
units.tr: Exposition of the Gospel of St Matthew, MS. in the Lambeth Library. It often proclaims the abundance and fullness of Scripture, offered equally to all Christians. Hence he compares it with leaven, by whose admixture the whole mass of flour is quickened; with the pearl, for whose acquisition everything must be sold; with the vineyard into which the Lord sent all his servants together to work; with the talent, which the Lord, about to set out on a journey, entrusted to all the servants to trade with; and finally with the feast, to which the Lord wished every kind of person to be invited. For thus he writes, book 8, homily 64, on the words of Matthew chapter 22: Tell those who are invited that I have prepared my dinner.

units.la: Prandium est doctrina justitiæ, & verba cœlestium mysteriorum de Dei Filio. Ex omni igitur lege, & ex omnibus Prophetis & Scripturis, mensam S. Scripturæ ordinavit: in quâ mensâ doctrina omnis justitiæ & diversorum mysteriorum; quia diversi cibi sunt. Magnitudo igitur & abundantia divinorum mysteriorum, quinimo cibi animarum, in mensâ sanctæ Scripturæ inveniuntur. Expositionem istam Hildebrando Cardinali, qui postea Gregorius VII. fuit, deberi credidit Vir Doctissimus, P. Allixius; qui ex eâ descriptum de Eucharistiâ fragmentum edidit in Præsat. ad Joannem Pasisiensem. pag. 7. Verùm longè à Gregorii VII. genio ac sententia abludit istius libri Author. Ille Hæreticos & Ecclesiæ Romanæ adversarios ferro flammâque excindendos clamavit, & exemplo præivit: Clavium potestatem Petro à Christo datam super omne fas nefasque extulit; Ecclesiam super Petrum fundatam esse constanter docuit; & Ordinem Monasticum, cui impensè favit, summo sibi studio addictum habuit. Iste è contra Hæreticos morte nequaquam mulandos esset contendit: de clavium potestate haud minùs sobriè sentit quàm Reformatorum quivis; omnibusque ex æquo Apostolis datam fuisse docet: Ecclesiam non super Petrum, sed super ipsum solummodo Christum, ædificatam esse asserit: & Monachorum ordinem Pharisæis semel atque iterum comparans; eorum tonsuram, vestes religiosas & vigilias vellicat. His adde Gregorium VII. preces linguâ populo ignotâ factas maximè comprobâsse. Nostèr autem Hildebrandus ejus-modi
units.tr: The feast is the teaching of righteousness, and the words of the heavenly mysteries concerning the Son of God. From all the law, therefore, and from all the Prophets and Scriptures, he has set up the table of Holy Scripture; on this table is the teaching of all righteousness and of diverse mysteries, because the foods are diverse. The greatness and abundance of the divine mysteries, indeed the food of souls, are therefore found on the table of holy Scripture. This exposition, the learned man P. Allix believed, is to be attributed to Hildebrand the Cardinal, who was afterwards Gregory VII; from it he published a fragment on the Eucharist in the Preface to John of Pasis, p. 7. But the author of this book differs far from the character and opinion of Gregory VII. Gregory cried out that heretics and adversaries of the Roman Church must be cut down with sword and fire, and he led the way by example; he raised the power of the keys given to Peter by Christ above all right and wrong; he steadfastly taught that the Church was founded upon Peter; and he held the Monastic Order, to which he was very devoted, closely bound to himself with the greatest zeal. This man, on the contrary, maintained that heretics ought by no means to be punished with death; he judges the power of the keys no less soberly than any of the Reformed; and he teaches that it was given equally to all the Apostles. He asserts that the Church was built not upon Peter, but upon Christ alone; and, comparing the order of monks once and again to the Pharisees, he taunts their tonsure, religious garments and vigils. To these add that Gregory VII greatly approved prayers made in a language unknown to the people. But our Hildebrand does not obscurely disapprove of prayer of that kind, on the words of Matthew 23: straining out the gnat and swallowing the camel.

units.la: {p} Matth. XIII. {q} Ibid. {r} Matth. XX. {s} Matth. XXV. {t} Lib, 6. homil. 42. {u} Lib. 6. homil. 50. {x} Ibid. {y} Lib. 9. homil. 69. modi orationem non obscurè improbat ; ad illud Matth. XXIII. Excolantes culicem, camelum autem glutientes.] Væ nobis, ad quos vitia Pharisæorum pervenerunt. Quia in tonsurâ, & veste religionis, & oratione labiorum, & jejuniis & vigiliis quibusdam nos quasi bonos ostendimus. Et cùm talia facimus ; quid aliud quàm vilia olera decimamus ; & relinquamus dilectionem Dei & proximi, justitiam, & fidem, & simplicitatem, & humanitatem, puram in Spiritu Sancto orationem, & alia virtutum germina ? Demum, quod rem extra omne dubium ponit, noster Bernardum citavit, Gregorio VII. inferiorem. Ecclesiasticorum enim vitia infectatus, ista subinfert : Lege librum Domini Bernardi Clarævallensis Abbatis de Consideratione valde bonum ; quem scripsit Eugenio Papæ ; ibi plenius invenies descriptos errores malorum Prælatorum. Hildebrandus itaque Junior quidam hujus Expositionis Author fuit. Istum circa Sæculi duodecimi medium collocavimus, tum quòd certior calculus desit ; tum quòd & Codicis MS. ætas, & loquendi de Bernardo modus, illi ætati optimè conveniant.
units.tr: {p} Matt. XIII. {q} Ibid. {r} Matt. XX. {s} Matt. XXV. {t} Book 6, homily 42. {u} Book 6, homily 50. {x} Ibid. {y} Book 9, homily 69. Woe to us, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have come. For in the tonsure, and the garment of religion, and the prayer of the lips, and certain fasts and vigils, we show ourselves as if we were good. And when we do such things, what else do we do than tithe worthless herbs; and leave aside the love of God and neighbour, justice, and faith, and simplicity, and humanity, prayer pure in the Holy Spirit, and the other seeds of the virtues? Finally, what places the matter beyond all doubt, our author cited Bernard, who was inferior to Gregory VII. For, inveighing against the vices of churchmen, he adds this: Read the book of the Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, On Consideration, which is very good; which he wrote to Pope Eugenius; there you will find the errors of bad prelates described more fully. Hildebrand the Younger, therefore, was a certain author of this Exposition. We have placed him about the middle of the twelfth century, both because a more certain calculation is lacking, and because both the age of the manuscript and the manner of speaking about Bernard agree very well with that age.

units.la: 1160. Arnoldus, Abbas Carnotensis,
units.tr: 1160. Arnoldus, Abbot of Chartres,

units.la: De Operibus sex dierum, pag. 66. &c. Quarta verò dies (Hexaemeri, in quâ Deus creavit Solem, &c.) est Ecclesiastica doctrina & Scriptura sancta divinitus inspirata ; in quâ certas fidei regulas invenimus ; ut non quisque suo sensu, sed veritatis æternæ auctoritate firmetur, &c. Quarta, per verbum Dei ex testimonio Scripturarum mentis illuminatio, &c. Oportet hominem & ipsas spirituales intelligentias, quæ ex Scripturis nascuntur, diligenter attendere ; quomodo ipsa veritas quasi Sol illuminet animam ; ipsa verò anima quasi Luna irradiet noctem, id est, corporales sensus, &c. Nihil est ad hominis perfecti nem, quod non hæc duo doceant Testamenta, &c. Dividit hæc Scriptura inter diem & noctem, separans à sinceritate doctrinæ Catholicæ hæreticorum inquinamenta, & à moribus sanctorum eradicans, quæcunque non competunt honestati. Lux ista veritatem separat à mendacio, &c. Verbum Dei, lux æterna, omnia per Scripturam sanctam intimat & comprehendit.
units.tr: On the Works of the Six Days, p. 66, etc. The fourth day (of the Hexaemeron, in which God created the sun, etc.) is ecclesiastical teaching and holy Scripture divinely inspired, in which we find certain rules of faith, so that each person is confirmed not by his own sense but by the authority of eternal truth, etc. The fourth is the illumination of the mind through the Word of God, from the testimony of the Scriptures, etc. A man must carefully attend to those spiritual understandings which arise from the Scriptures: how truth itself illumines the soul as the sun does, and how the soul itself shines on the night as the moon does, that is, on the bodily senses, etc. Nothing is needed for human perfection that these two Testaments do not teach, etc. This Scripture divides between day and night, separating from the purity of Catholic doctrine the defilements of heretics, and uprooting from the morals of the saints whatever does not befit honesty. That light separates truth from falsehood, etc. The Word of God, the eternal light, makes known and comprehends everything through holy Scripture.

units.la: 1160. Laurentius, Dunelmensis Præcentor, & postea Abbas Westmonasterienis,
units.tr: 1160. Laurentius, Precentor of Durham, and afterwards Abbot of Westminster,

units.la: In Hypognostico Veteris & Novi Testamenti, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, Lib. 4.
units.tr: In the Hypognosticon of the Old and New Testament, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, Book 4.

units.la: Lib. 8. homil. 62.
units.tr: Book 8, homily 62.

units.la: De rebus dubiis verba faciens. Consule Scripturas de talibus obsecro sacras: Omne quod est homini scire necesse, docent. Non opus est sciri, quicquid nequit hic reperiri. Ergo sperne vagum, Lector amice, Magum.
units.tr: Speaking about doubtful matters: "I beg you, consult the sacred Scriptures about such things; they teach everything that it is necessary for a man to know. It is not necessary to know whatever cannot be found here. Therefore, friendly reader, spurn the wandering magician."

units.la: Lib. 5. de Excellentiâ Psalmorum. Adde quòd Ecclesiæ mysteria quælibet unus, Quælibet & Christi continet ille liber. Ille docet quæcunque decet; sed & aspera planat: Curat fracta, fugat noxia, lapsa levat. Hostibus ille liber gravis incantatio; claudis Pes, cæcis oculus, magna medela reis. Summis ille liber confœderat ima; Deumque Inducens homini, hunc ducit in usque Deum.
units.tr: Book 5, On the Excellence of the Psalms. Add that whichever one book contains the mysteries of the Church, that book contains whatever mysteries of Christ there are. That book teaches whatever is fitting, and it also smooths out what is rough; it heals the broken, drives away harmful things, and raises up the fallen. That book is a heavy incantation against enemies; it is a foot for the lame, an eye for the blind, a great remedy for the guilty. That book unites the lowest with the highest, and, leading God down to man, it leads man up to God.

units.la: 1170. Clemens, Presbyter & Prior Lanthoniensis.
units.tr: 1170. Clement, Presbyter and Prior of Llanthony,

units.la: Extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ amplissimus ejus Commentarius in septem Canonicas Epistolas. Codex ipsâ Authoris ætate nequaquam inferior videtur.
units.tr: There is extant in manuscript in the Lambeth Library his very full commentary on the seven Catholic Epistles. The codex does not seem at all inferior in age to the author himself.

units.la: In 1 Petr. IV. 11. Si quis loquatur; quasi sermones Dei loquatur.] Timens scilicet ne præter voluntatem Dei, vel præter quod in Scripturis sanctis evidenter præcipitur, vel dicat aliquid vel imperet; & inveniatur tanquam falsus testis Dei, aut sacrilegus, introducens aliquid alienum à doctrinâ Domini; vel certè subrelinquens & praeteriens aliquid eorum quæ Deo placita sunt: cùm ipse manifestissimè prædicatoribus veritatis de his quos imbuerent, præciperet, dicens; docentes eos servare omnia quæcunque mandavi vobis. Et ea enim quæ ipse mandavit, non alia, Jesus non ex parte, sed omnia, suis auditoribus servanda tradere jubet.
units.tr: On 1 Peter 4:11, "If anyone speaks, as if he speaks the words of God." Fearing, that is, lest he say or command anything beyond the will of God, or beyond what is clearly commanded in the holy Scriptures, and be found as a false or sacrilegious witness of God, introducing something foreign to the teaching of the Lord; or else lest he leave out and pass over something of those things that are pleasing to God, since the Lord himself, most plainly commanding the preachers of the truth concerning those whom they were to instruct, said: "teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." For Jesus orders that those things which he himself commanded should be handed down to his hearers to be observed, not in part, but all of them.

units.la: 1 Petr. V. 14. Gratia vobis omnibus, qui estis in Christo Jesu.] Consultò cùm diceret, Gratia vobis, addidit; Omnibus qui estis in Christo Jesu: ut ea quæ paucis Ecclesiis, id est, Ponti, Galatiæ, Cappadociæ, Asiæ & Bithyniæ, scripsit; cunctis per orbem Christi Ecclesiis se scribere designet. Sic & Johannes in Apocalypsi, cùm septem Asiæ Ecclesias fingil-
units.tr: On 1 Peter 5:14, "Grace be with you all who are in Christ Jesus." Deliberately, when he had said "Grace be with you," he added: "all who are in Christ Jesus," so that he might indicate that what he wrote to a few churches, namely those of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, he was writing to all the churches of Christ throughout the world. So also John in the Apocalypse, when he addressed the seven churches of Asia, as was fitting, one by one,

units.la: {2} Quadcunque Cod. MS. alter. latim, prout competebat, admoneret; adjunxit, per singula ita concludens: Qui habet aures, audiat, quid Spiritus dicat Ecclesiis: aperte insinuans, quòd cuncta quæ unicuilibet Ecclesiæ scripsit, omnibus qui auditum salubrem haberent, universis fidelium scriberet Ecclesiis.
units.tr: {2} Whatever, as another manuscript has it. Concluded each address in this way: "He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches," clearly implying that what he wrote to any single church he was writing to all the churches of the faithful, to all who would have a healthy hearing.

units.la: 2 Petr. I. 19. Lucernæ signatur nomine sacræ lumen Scripturæ. Nunc ergo lucerna super caput Ecclesiæ splendet. Quia sacra eloquia tenebras nostræ mentis irradiant; ut in hoc caliginoso vitæ præsentis loco, dum verborum Dei lucem percipimus, quæ sint agenda videamus. Verba ista citavit ex Gregorio M. lib. 19. Moralium in Job.
units.tr: On 2 Peter 1:19, The light of the sacred Scripture is signified by the name lamp. Now, therefore, the lamp shines above the head of the Church, because the sacred words illumine the darkness of our mind, so that in this misty place of the present life, while we receive the light of God's words, we may see what is to be done. He quoted these words from Gregory the Great, Book 19 of the Moralia on Job.

units.la: 1170. Petrus Comestor
units.tr: 1170. Peter Comestor

units.la: Tractat. brev. de Pœnitentiâ, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, cap. 16. Oratio talis debet esse; ut sonus vocis non dissonet à devotione cordis. Orationem enim ad Deum non faciunt, ut ait Gregorius, verba, sed vota; id est, non solùm verba, sed etiam vota.
units.tr: Tractatus brevis de Poenitentia, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, chapter 16. Prayer ought to be such that the sound of the voice does not disagree with the devotion of the heart. For, as Gregory says, it is not words that make prayer to God, but desires; that is, not words alone, but desires as well.

units.la: Extat MS. in eâdem Bibliothecâ Sermonum ejusdem Volumen pulcherrimum. Ex his Sermo 14us, qui est 1us in Cœnâ Domini, ista habet. [Dicit anima Christiani ad Deum] Velle mihi adjacet: perficere autem non invenio. Doce ignorantiam meam; adjuva impossibilitatem; quia sicut sine te nihil scio, ita sine te nil possum facere. Dicet ei profectò Spiritus Sanctus: Scrutare Scripturas; quas per me scripsit Filius; quia ego sum lingua calami scribæ velociter scribentis: & invenies plenè domûs tuæ dispositionem. Legat itaque Scripturas animus noster; & inveniet quod quærebat.
units.tr: In the same library there is also a most beautiful manuscript volume of his Sermons. From these, Sermon 14, which is the first on the Lord's Supper, contains the following. [The soul of the Christian says to God] The will lies ready in me, but I do not find the power to carry it out. Teach my ignorance; help my inability, for as without you I know nothing, so without you I can do nothing. The Holy Spirit will certainly say to him: Search the Scriptures, which the Son has written through me, for I am the tongue of the pen of a scribe writing swiftly; and you will fully find the arrangement of your house. Let our mind therefore read the Scriptures, and it will find what it was seeking.

units.la: Serm. 33. qui est 5us in Synodo. Si senserit in me [Christus] pueritiam fatuitatis, qui debeo psallere sapienter; scilicet, ut intelligam quæ dicam: quare non me maledicet cum pueris clamantibus ad Helisæum. Ascende, calve; Ascende, calve?
units.tr: Sermon 33, which is the fifth in the Synod. If Christ perceives in me the childishness of folly, when I ought to sing wisely, that is, so that I understand what I say; why would he not curse me, as he did the boys shouting at Elisha? Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead?

units.la: 1185. Baldewinus, Cantuarienfis Archiepiscopus, & Bar- tholomæus, Exonienfis Episcopus.
units.tr: 1185. Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Bartholomew, Bishop of Exeter.

units.la: Horum Provinciale MS. habetur in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ; dignissimum profectò, quod lucem aliquando videat.
units.tr: A manuscript Provinciale of these men is held in the Lambeth Library. It is certainly most worthy of coming to light at some time.

units.la: Cap. 2. De Fide: Quicunque Deo & Sacerdoti suam cbtu'erit pœnitentiam, primùm diligenter de fide Catholicâ inquiratur, ut vel minus instituatur & confirmetur; vel si Catholicè credit, id sollempnibus verbis Symboli memxriter memoriter ore confiteatur.——Catholica verò fides est, quæ Symbolo Catholico continetur : Quo tanquam fidei signaculo unusquisque fidelium se munire debet. Unde Augustinus ; Accipite regulam fidei ; quod Symbolum dicitur ; & cùm acceperitis, in corde scribite, & cotidie dicite apud vos, antequam dormiatis, antequam procedatis, symbolo vestro vos munite. Unde ex Concilio Gangrensi. Symbolum, quod est signaculum fidei, & orationem dominicam discere semper ammoneant sacerdotes populum Christianum ; volumusque ut disciplinam condignam habeant, qui hoc discere negligunt, sive in jejunio, sive in aliquâ castigatione. Præterea dignum est, ut filios suos donent ad Scolas, sive ad Monasteria, sive foràs Presbyteris ; ut fidem Catholicam recte discant & orationem Dominicam, ut domi alios edocere valeant. Qui autem aliter non potuerit, in suâ hoc discat linguâ. [Quæ de examine Pœnitentium ad Confessionem accedentium in hujusce fragmenti principio leguntur ; in plurimis etiam aliorum Episcoporum Constitutionibus reperiuntur. Siquidem inter Constitutiones Gulielmi Blesensis, Episcopi Wigorniensis, anno undecimo Pontificatûs sui, viz. Christi 1229. promulgatas, (MSS. in Bibl. Lambeth.) octava hisce verbis concipitur. Statuimus, ut Sacerdos ante Confessionem Laici Pœnitentis instruat eum de fide secundùm formam & ordinem contentum in Symbolo Apostolorum sub linguâ ei notâ.]
units.tr: Chapter 2, On Faith: Whoever has made his repentance to God and to the priest, first let him be carefully examined about the Catholic faith, so that he may either be instructed and confirmed, or, if he believes in the Catholic manner, confess it orally and from memory in the solemn words of the Creed.——The Catholic faith, however, is that which is contained in the Catholic Creed, and with this as the seal of faith every one of the faithful ought to fortify himself. Hence Augustine: Receive the rule of faith, which is called the Creed; and when you have received it, write it in your heart, and say it daily among yourselves, before you sleep and before you go out, fortify yourselves with your Creed. Hence from the Council of Gangra: Let the priests always admonish the Christian people to learn the Creed, which is the seal of faith, and the Lord's Prayer; and we wish that those who neglect to learn this be subjected to fitting discipline, whether by fasting or by some other punishment. Moreover, it is fitting that they give their sons to schools, whether to monasteries or to elders elsewhere, so that they may learn the Catholic faith and the Lord's Prayer rightly, and be able to teach others at home. But whoever cannot do otherwise, let him learn this in his own tongue. [What is read about the examination of penitents who approach confession, at the beginning of this fragment, is found in very many other bishops' constitutions as well. Indeed, among the constitutions of William of Blois, Bishop of Worcester, promulgated in the eleventh year of his pontificate, namely in the year of Christ 1229 (manuscripts in the Lambeth Library), the eighth reads in these words: We decree that the priest, before the confession of a lay penitent, instruct him about the faith according to the form and order contained in the Apostles' Creed, in a tongue known to him.]

units.la: Cap. 13. de Oratione.
units.tr: Chapter 13, On Prayer.

units.la: Debet verò, qui orat, quantùm potest, diligenter attendere, ut non aliquando mens distrahatur à linguâ, & dicatur ei à Domino: Homo iste labiis me honorat ; cor autem ejus longè est à me. Magna siquidem est præsumptio, ut servus dicat ad Dominum : Fiant aures tuæ intendentes in vocem deprecationis meæ: cùm ipsius servi cor non intendat ad Dominum,&c. Omnium autem orationum excellentissimam & efficacissimam, si de puro procedat affectu, Orationem credimus esse Dominicam ; cujus non solùm sensum, sed & verba, & petitionum numerum & formam ex ipsius institutione Salvatoris suscepimus. Hanc, sicut & Symbolum fidei, scire & memoriter Deo reddere, omnibus indicendum est Christianis. Unde ex Concilio Cabilonensi: Jubendum est, ut Oratio Dominica, in quâ omnia necessaria humanæ vitæ comprehenduntur, & Symbolum Apostolorum, in quo fides Catholica ex integro comprehenditur, ab omnibus discatur, tam Latinè quàm Barbaricè ; ut quod ore profitentur, corde credatur & intelligatur. Tractat. Moral. Baldwini de utilitate & virtute Sermonis Dei vivi, in Hebr. IV. 12. MS. ibid. cap. 1. Quòd auditus pro intellectu accipiendus {a} Canon est 45. Concilii Moguntini anno 813. habiti. Canones Gangrenses nil ejusmodi habent. fit, idem Apostolus ostendit; ubi dicit: Qui loquitur linguis, non hominibus loquitur sed Deo. Nemo enim audit. h. e. nemo intelligit. Nam qui linguâ loquitur peregrinâ non intelligentibus eam; quasi barbarus est illis; & non œdificat non intelligentes. Ergo intellectus necessarius est.
units.tr: He who prays ought, as far as he can, to attend carefully, lest at some time the mind be drawn away from the tongue, and the Lord say to him: This people honours me with its lips, but its heart is far from me. For it is great presumption for a servant to say to the Lord: Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication, when the servant's own heart is not attentive to the Lord, etc. Of all prayers, we believe the Lord's Prayer to be the most excellent and most effective, if it proceeds from a pure affection; we have received from the Saviour's own institution not only its sense but also its words, and the number and form of its petitions. This, like the Creed of faith, all Christians are to know and to recite from memory to God. Hence from the Council of Chalon: It is to be commanded that the Lord's Prayer, in which all things necessary for human life are comprehended, and the Apostles' Creed, in which the Catholic faith is comprehended in full, be learned by all, in Latin as well as in the vernacular, so that what they profess with the mouth may be believed and understood in the heart. Baldwin's moral treatise on the usefulness and power of the living Word of God, on Hebrews 4:12, manuscript in the same place, chapter 1: That hearing must be taken according to understanding, {a} is the canon 45 of the Council of Mainz held in 813. The Canons of Gangra have nothing of this kind. the same Apostle shows, where he says: He who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men but to God; for no one hears, that is, no one understands. For he who speaks in a foreign tongue to those who do not understand it is a barbarian to them, and does not edify those who do not understand. Therefore understanding is necessary.
