units.la: His subjungam præclarum ejusdem testimonium de plenitudine ac sufficientiâ S. Scripturæ, exemplo Illustrissimi Armachani; qui multa ejusmodi testimonia passim dedit. Baldwinus itaque in Sermone in die omnium Sanctorum, MS. ibid. sic scribit. cap. 4. De Deo quidem falsa opinio periculosissimè admittitur. Nam quæ Dei sunt occulta & arcana, ex incerto humanæ opinionis ventilare non licet, nec aliud de Deo credere, quàm ipse dignatus est de se revelare. Ipse enim sibi testis est; & secretorum suorum conscios eatenus habere voluit, quatenus fidei conscientia sese extendit; quæ de testimoniis Scripturarum affruitur, & earum ratione subnixa immobiliter statuitur & stabilitur. Scriptura enim sancta divinitus inspirata est. In eâ præscripta est nobis forma fidei. Quicquid ultra quæritur, non invenitur. Omnis humana adinventio, quæ pietati fidei formæque præscriptæ obviat, præsumptionis spiritus deputanda est.
units.tr: I shall add to these his excellent testimony on the fullness and sufficiency of Holy Scripture, following the example of the most illustrious Archbishop of Armagh, who gave many testimonies of this kind here and there. Baldwin, then, in a sermon on All Saints' Day, manuscript in the same place, writes thus, chapter 4: A false opinion about God is admitted most dangerously. For it is not permitted to bring into the open, from the uncertain opinion of man, the things of God that are hidden and secret, nor to believe anything about God other than what he has deigned to reveal of himself. For he is a witness to himself, and he has wished to have the knowers of his secrets only so far as the conscience of faith extends, which is supported by the testimonies of the Scriptures and, being grounded on their reasoning, is established and made firm immovably. For holy Scripture has been inspired by God. In it the form of faith has been prescribed for us. Whatever is sought beyond it is not found. Every human invention that opposes piety, faith and the prescribed form must be counted as the spirit of presumption.

units.la: 1200. Innocentius III. Papa Romanus.
units.tr: 1200. Innocent III, Roman Pope.

units.la: De Officio Missæ, lib. 2. cap. 61. Monet autem Sacerdos, ut Sursum corda habeamus ad Dominum, secundum exhortationem Apostoli dicentis: Quæ sursum sunt, quærite. Nam ubi est thesaurus tuus, ibi erit & cor tuum. Multi quippe, dum ore loquuntur cœlestia, corde meditantur terrena. Quibus Dominus improperat per Prophetam: Populus hic labiis me honorat; cor autem eorum longè est à me. In quâlibet igitur oratione peccatum, sed in istâ periculum, cor habere divisum ab ore, vel os habere divisum à corde. Nam qui semetipsum non audit, nec Deus illum exaudit. Chorus igitur respondens profitetur se Sacerdotis monita suscepisse cum ait: Habemus ad Dominum. Sacerdos autem, postquam attentos reddidit & devotos, hortatur ut gratias agamus Domino Deo nostro, &c. Parilem sententiam Idem habet in Sermone 2°. in Concilio Lateranensi habito. d Sed qui semetipsum non audit; quomodo Deus illum exaudiet? Qui taliter orat, non inclinat Deum ad indulgentiam; sed provocat illum ad iracundiam.
units.tr: From his book On the Office of the Mass, bk. 2, ch. 61. The priest then admonishes us to lift up our hearts to the Lord, according to the exhortation of the Apostle who says: Seek the things that are above. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Indeed, many, while they speak heavenly things with their mouth, meditate on earthly things in their heart. Of these the Lord complains through the Prophet: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In any prayer, therefore, the sin lies in having the heart divided from the mouth, or the mouth divided from the heart; but in this prayer the danger is greater. For he who does not hear himself, God does not hear either. The choir, answering, professes that it has received the priest's admonition when it says: We have them lifted up to the Lord. The priest then, after he has made them attentive and devout, urges us to give thanks to the Lord our God, etc. He has a similar judgement in his second Sermon, delivered at the Council of the Lateran: d But he who does not hear himself, how will God hear him? He who prays in this way does not incline God to forgiveness, but provokes him to anger.

units.la: b 1 Cor XIV. c Divisum utrobique legit Codex MS. Lambethanus. d Concil. Tom. XI. pag. 137. Innocentius author Canonum Concilii Lateranensis anno 1215. habiti vulgò habetur. Ex illis praeclarum testimonium protulit Illustrissimus Primas cap. 5. sect. 1. Eorundem Codex MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ reperitur; qui à vulgatâ editione parum discrepat, nisi in divisione capitum. Ipsi Concilio parum aetate cedit. Ut vana sit illorum suspicio; qui Canones hosce recentiorum Pontificiorum fraude suppositos arbitrantur.
units.tr: b 1 Cor. XIV. c The Lambeth manuscript codex reads "divisum" in both places. d Council, vol. XI, p. 137. Innocent is commonly held to be the author of the canons of the Council of the Lateran held in 1215. The most illustrious Primate has brought forward an excellent testimony from these in ch. 5, sect. 1. A manuscript codex of the same canons is found in the Lambeth Library, and it differs little from the printed edition, except in the division of the chapters. It is also only a little younger than the Council itself. So vain is the suspicion of those who think these canons were forged by recent Papists.

units.la: 1200. Joannes Subprior.
units.tr: 1200. John, Subprior.

units.la: Hujus Commentarium in Apocalypsin MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ asservari supra memoravimus. Quo tempore Author vixerit, haud satis constat. Nullus enim è Scriptoribus nostris illius meminerunt. Eum igitur ad annum 1200. reposuimus, neque vanâ forsitan conjecturâ. Certè non multò inferior fuit; ipse enim Codex ante annos circiter quingentos videtur scriptus: nec multò superior. Roberti Prioris enim Expositionem Apocalypseos in prologo laudat. Hunc autem Robertum suspicarer fuisse, aut Robertum Canutum, Priorem Canonicorum Regularium Oxoniensium ad Fanum S. Fridesswidae, aut Robertum Scribam, Priorem Bridlintonensem; quorum uterque, teste Baleo, Expositionem in Apocalypsin scripsit, & sub Henrico II. Rege floruit circa an. 1170. & 1180.
units.tr: We have mentioned above that his Commentary on the Apocalypse, in manuscript, is preserved in the Lambeth Library. The time when the author lived is not sufficiently clear, for none of our writers mentions him. We have therefore placed him at about the year 1200, and perhaps not on mere vain conjecture. He was certainly not much later, for the codex itself appears to have been written about five hundred years ago; nor was he much earlier, since in his prologue he praises the Exposition of the Apocalypse by Prior Robert. I suspect this Robert was either Robert Canutus, Prior of the Regular Canons of Oxford at the church of St Frideswide, or Robert the Scribe, Prior of Bridlington. According to Bale, each of them wrote an Exposition of the Apocalypse, and both flourished under King Henry II, about the years 1170 and 1180.

units.la: In cap. 1. tit. 8. Beatus, qui legit & audit verba Prophetiae hujus.] Quid est quòd secundùm quosdam singulariter legit, audiunt autem & servant pluraliter dicitur? Quia unus est, qui legit in Ecclesiâ, & docendo exponit, multi qui audiunt. Omnes doctores & auditores, Christi imitatores, verba prophetiae hujus pariter observant. Principium ergo libri, ut Hieronymus ait, beatitudinem legenti, audienti, & servanti promittit; ut lectioni studens, exinde opera discat, & quae percipit custodiat, & qui audiunt imitentur; & utique servando quae vel legunt vel audiunt, coronam mereantur & accipiant aeternam.
units.tr: On ch. 1, verse 8: Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this prophecy. Why does it say, according to some, that he reads in the singular, but that they hear and keep in the plural? Because there is one who reads in the Church and explains by teaching, and there are many who hear. All teachers and hearers, imitators of Christ, observe equally the words of this prophecy. The beginning of the book, therefore, as Jerome says, promises blessedness to the reader, the hearer and the keeper, so that, studying the reading, one may learn the works from it, guard what one perceives, and those who hear may imitate; and surely by keeping what they read or hear, they may merit and receive the eternal crown.

units.la: Tit. 48. Datae sunt linguae [ Apostolis ] in revelationem Scripturarum, ad praedicandum omnibus gentibus.
units.tr: Verse 48. Tongues were given [to the Apostles] for the revelation of the Scriptures, to preach to all nations.

units.la: Visio. 7. cap. 12. Qui lumen fidei & caritatis, & intelligentiam Scripturarum cordis aure percepit, ad hoc alios convocet.
units.tr: Vision 7, ch. 12. He who has perceived with the ear of the heart the light of faith and of love, and the understanding of the Scriptures, should call others to the same.

units.la: {a} Ad an. 1040. {f} De Scriptor. Angl. cent. 3. cap. 4. 11.
units.tr: {a} At the year 1040. {f} On the English Writers, cent. 3, ch. 4, 11.

units.la: 1200. Anonymus Author Libri de Admonitione profectus animæ.
units.tr: 1200. The anonymous author of the book On the Admonition of the Soul's Progress.

units.la: Extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Liber Anonymus de Admonitione profectus Animæ, ad Mulierem quandam Deo devotam scriptus. Codex ante quingentos circiter annos exaratus videtur. Capite autem antepenultimo ista habet. Non est in his diu morandum; quia transmitto caritatem tuam ad latissimum campum divinarum Scripturarum; ut quod tibi hic deesse cernis, ibi solerter perquiras. Quapropter oro dilectionem tuam; ut studium semper in te crescat legendi. Nullus enim potest perfectè Dei nosse præcepta, nisi qui legendi continuum habet studium. Quia quantò quisque in divinis Scripturis assiduus fuerit; tantò ex eis majorem intelligentiam capiet. Sicut terra, quæ quantò magis excolitur, tantò amplius fructificat. Nam quamvis homo tardum sensum habeat; aliquid tamen discere poterit ex Scripturarum mysteriis; si assiduitatem habuerit legendi. Sicut scriptum est in Evangelio. ᵋ Qui enim habet, dabitur ei; & qui non habet, etiam hoc quod videtur habere, auferetur ab eo. Id est: Qui habet studium legendi, dabitur illi etiam intelligendi facultas; & qui non habet studium legendi, etiam quod videtur habere, id est, quod naturaliter bonum intelligit, propter ejus ignaviam auferetur ob eo. Et sicut ille, qui tardus est ad intelligendum, pro suâ intentione recipiet gloriam; ita ille, qui talentum sibi datum negligit, condemnabitur. Quapropter admoneo caritatem tuam, ut studium habeas legendi; quia omnis profectus ex lectione procedit. Quæ enim nescimus, ex lectione discimus. Dicit enim Isidorus; quòd orationibus mundamur, lectionibus instruimur, &c.
units.tr: There is a manuscript in the Lambeth Library, an anonymous book On the Admonition of the Soul's Progress, written to a certain woman devoted to God. The codex appears to have been written about five hundred years ago. Near the end, in the second-to-last chapter, it reads as follows: We should not linger long over these things, because I send your charity to the wide field of the divine Scriptures, so that you may diligently seek there what you see is lacking here. Therefore I beg your love that your zeal for reading may always grow. For no one can know the precepts of God perfectly unless he has a continual zeal for reading. For the more assiduous anyone is in the divine Scriptures, the greater the understanding he will gain from them, just as the land, the more it is cultivated, the more abundantly it bears fruit. For although a man may have a slow mind, he will still be able to learn something from the mysteries of the Scriptures, if he has persistence in reading. As it is written in the Gospel: For whoever has, to him shall be given; and whoever has not, even what he seems to have shall be taken away from him. That is: whoever has zeal for reading will be given also the power of understanding; and whoever has no zeal for reading will lose, on account of his sloth, even what he seems to have, that is, what he naturally understands as good. And just as he who is slow to understand will receive glory in proportion to his effort, so he who neglects the talent given to him will be condemned. Therefore I admonish your charity to have zeal for reading, because all progress comes from reading. For what we do not know, we learn from reading. For Isidore says that we are cleansed by prayers, and instructed by reading, etc.

units.la: 1200. Petrus, Cantor Parisiensis, & postea Episcopus.
units.tr: 1200. Peter, Cantor of Paris, and afterwards Bishop.

units.la: Illum ad annum 1215. refert Jamesius in Catalogo MS. Scriptorum Eccles. ad an. 1199. Sedem Parisiensem obtinuit anno 1208. juxta Sammarthanos, Gall. Sacr. Tom. 1. p. 441. Joannes de Mimallis, Tornacensis, qui Annales ab orbe condito ad annum 1512. contexuit; plura de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis notatu digna passim habet; de Petro autem ista solummodò: An. 1199. Petrus, Cantor Parisiensis, & postea Episcopus, scripsit Grammaticam Theologorum, & alia. Extant hi Annales MSS. inter scrinia Lambethana.
units.tr: Jamesius, in his Catalogue of manuscript ecclesiastical writers, refers him to the year 1215, under the year 1199. According to the Sammarthani (Gallia Christiana, vol. 1, p. 441), he obtained the see of Paris in 1208. John of Mimallis of Tournai, who compiled Annals from the creation of the world to the year 1512, has many notable things about ecclesiastical writers scattered throughout, but about Peter he says only this: In the year 1199 Peter, Cantor of Paris, and afterwards Bishop, wrote the Grammar of the Theologians, and other things. These Annals are extant in manuscript among the Lambeth archives.

units.la: ᵋ Matth. XXV.
units.tr: Matth. XXV.

units.la: Habetur vero in Bibliotheca eâdem Petri Cantoris liber MS. cui titulus, Verbum Abbreviatum. Est autem Summa quaedam Theologiae, constans Capitibus CII. seu totidem titulis de Virtutibus & Vitiis.
units.tr: There is also in the same library a manuscript book by Peter the Cantor entitled Verbum Abbreviatum. It is a certain Summa of theology, consisting of 102 chapters, or as many titles, on the virtues and vices.

units.la: In Prologo. Verbum abbreviatum facit Dominus super terram. Si enim Verbum de Patris sinu nobis missum, immo si Filius Dei incircumscriptibilis, quem totus non capit orbis, brevitate uteri virginalis voluit circumscribi; quanto magis verbum sacrae paginae, quod nobis in arram & pignus suae dilectionis reliquit, voluit abbreviari; in quo vias & semitas ejus deprehenderemus; in quo cursus nostri viam breviter & succincte ad aeternam beatitudinem legeremus expressam? Superfluitas verborum, immo infinitas, est in aliis Scripturis, respectu sacrae Scripturae; quam respuit illa, &c. Ubi vehementer suadet, missis aliis libris, soli Scripturae studio ab omnibus incumbendum.
units.tr: In the Prologue: The Lord makes the Word abbreviated upon the earth. For if the Word sent to us from the bosom of the Father, indeed if the Son of God, unbounded, whom the whole world cannot contain, willed to be confined within the narrowness of the virginal womb; how much more did he will that the word of Sacred Scripture, which he left us as a pledge and earnest of his love, be abbreviated; in which we might discover his ways and paths; in which we might read set out briefly and succinctly the way of our course to eternal blessedness? There is superfluity, indeed infinity, of words in other writings, in comparison with Sacred Scripture, which that one rejects, &c. There he strongly urges that, other books set aside, everyone should devote himself to the study of Scripture alone.

units.la: Cap. 56. Contra caeremoniarum & traditionum Ecclesiasticarum multitudinem acerrimè disputans, omnes ad S. Scripturae normam contrahi & reformari hortatur. Nunc multitudine novarum traditionum revocare videmus jugum & onus ipsorum; quod neque nos neque patres nostri portare potuerunt: quae saepe dant materiam & occasionem delinquendi,&c. Antonius autem Heremita, quibusdam Religiosis quaerentibus ab eo regulam & formam religiosè vivendi, tradidit eis codicem Evangelii.
units.tr: Chapter 56. Disputing most sharply against the multitude of ceremonies and ecclesiastical traditions, he exhorts that all be brought together and reformed to the rule of Holy Scripture. Now we see, by the multitude of new traditions, the yoke and burden of them recalled, which neither we nor our fathers could bear; which often give matter and occasion for sinning, &c. Antony the Hermit, when certain religious asked him for a rule and form of living religiously, handed them a codex of the Gospel.

units.la: Cap. 57. Contra mollientes arcum Sacrae Scripturae [per traditiones superadditas] In casibus & humanis negotiis sequenda sunt exempla prudentium. In via verò fidei, vitae & morum imitanda & attendenda est potius regula & forma vivendi & credendi sufficienter praescripta à Domino [sc. in S. Scriptura] quia verba ejus Spiritus & vita sunt.
units.tr: Chapter 57. Against those who soften the bow of Holy Scripture [by traditions added on top]. In cases and human affairs the examples of the prudent are to be followed. But in the way of faith, of life and of morals, the rule and form of living and believing, sufficiently prescribed by the Lord [namely in Holy Scripture], is rather to be imitated and attended to, because his words are spirit and life.

units.la: Porrò S. Scripturae plenitudinem innumeris in locis asserit; adeò ut in unico Novi Testamenti libro omnia fidei necessaria contineri doceat; sensumque ejus ita planum ac facilem esse; ut glossarum multitudine obscuretur potius quam illustretur. Sic enim cap. 2. Cùm Dominus ante offensam idololatriae Judaico populo tantùm Decalogum commisisset sufficientem ad salutem; post illam multiplices contulit caeremonias, quibus meritis eorum exigentibus onerati sunt & afflicti. Eorum exemplo nos vereri debemus; quia cùm Dominus tantummodo textum Matthaei Ecclesiae primitivae commisisset, omnia necessaria salutis continentem; meritis nostris, utputa vanis exercitationibus, inquisitionibus superfluis, & peccatis aliis, glossarum multitudine, lectionum superfluitate, & prolixitate onerati sumus; in quibus est tantum labor & afflictio spiritus, &c. Non ideo data est nobis Sacra Scriptura; ut in eâ superflua & vana quaeramus; sed fidem & doctrinam nam morum & consilia & responsiones ad infinita negotia in Ecclesiâ emergentia. Et cap. 57. Maximè autem nobis [Christianis] obiici potest; cùm dicamus omnia esse in luce & aperta in doctrinâ Christi; cur sic à spiritu vivificante & literâ Evangelicâ planâ recessimus, exponendo & allegorizando, magis quàm Judæi à literâ occidente. Et mox de Glossatoribus & Commentatoribus. Qui utinam non Sacræ Scripturæ dominarentur; sed permitterent eam liberè currere in gravitate & maturitate suâ. Caput sequens contra Pigros inscripsit; idque sic inchoat. Enervantibus arcum S. Scripturæ peccatorumque pessimis ponderatoribus adjuncta est & collatanea Pigritia; ob quam non lectitant, non perscrutantur S. Scripturam. Denique attentionem in oratione necessario adhibendam flagitat, & opinionem sensim in Scholis invalescentem de Opere operato precum Ecclesiasticarum pluribus oppugnat cap. 56. Hilariter psallentem & orantem diligit Deus, non ex tristitiâ vel necessitate. Absit igitur ex præcepto multiplicare matutinos psalmos & preces: nisi affuerit devotio, &c. Et cap. 85. Propter igitur orationis fastidium, periculosæ sunt Traditiones datæ de multitudine Horarum vel Psalmorum decantandorum.
units.tr: Moreover, he asserts the fullness of Holy Scripture in countless places, so much so that he teaches that all things necessary for faith are contained in the single book of the New Testament, and that its sense is so plain and easy that it is obscured rather than illuminated by the multitude of glosses. Thus in chapter 2: when the Lord, before the offence of idolatry, had committed to the Jewish people only the Decalogue, sufficient for salvation, after that offence he bestowed manifold ceremonies, by which they were burdened and afflicted, as their merits demanded. We ought to fear by their example; because when the Lord had committed to the early Church only the text of Matthew, containing all things necessary for salvation, by our merits (namely vain exercises, superfluous inquiries and other sins) we have been burdened with a multitude of glosses, a superfluity of readings and prolixity, in which there is only labour and affliction of spirit, &c. Holy Scripture was not given to us so that we should seek superfluous and vain things in it, but faith and doctrine, and also counsels and answers to the infinite affairs that arise in the Church. And in chapter 57: Moreover, it can be objected especially to us [Christians]: since we say that all things are in light and open in the teaching of Christ, why have we so departed from the life-giving Spirit and the plain letter of the Gospel, by expounding and allegorizing, more than the Jews from the killing letter? And soon after, about the glossators and commentators: would that they did not lord it over Sacred Scripture, but allowed it to run freely in its gravity and maturity. The following chapter he entitled Against the Lazy, and it begins thus: To those who weaken the bow of Holy Scripture, and to the worst weighers of sins, sloth is joined and allied; on account of it they do not read, do not search through Holy Scripture. Finally, he urges that the attention necessary in prayer be applied, and in chapter 56 he attacks at length the opinion, gradually gaining strength in the schools, about the efficacy of ecclesiastical prayers by the mere performance of the work. God loves one who prays and sings psalms cheerfully, not from sadness or necessity. Let it be far, therefore, that by precept the morning psalms and prayers be multiplied, unless devotion is present, &c. And in chapter 85: therefore, on account of weariness of prayer, the traditions given concerning the multitude of Hours or of psalms to be sung are dangerous.

units.la: 1210. Stephanus Langton, Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis,
units.tr: 1210. Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury,

units.la: Expositio in Esaiam, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, in illud cap. LV. Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas. Scripturæ scilicet, sive doctrinæ. Notandum quod dicitur sitit. Qui enim non sitit, non curat aquam. Et qui non habetis argentum] id est, qui non appetitis terrenas divitias. Talis erat Petrus, qui ait: Argentum & aurum non est mihi &c. Tales appetunt has aquas. Alii verò fastidiunt. Unde sic legitur in Judicum [libro:] Qui curvatis genibus biberunt, repulsi sunt à bello Domini. Properate.] Quidam enim tardè veniunt ad aquas Scripturæ. Sed in Exodo legitur, quòd manna colligebatur in principio diei. In robore enim juventutis debes colligere manna Scripturæ, non in vespere senectutis, ne liquescat. Unde in Ecclesiastico: Ne tardes converti ad Dominum &c. Vinum & lac] Alicubi est Sacra Scriptura vinum, alicubi est lac: vinum quoad majores, lac quoad minores.
units.tr: Commentary on Isaiah, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, on chapter 55, "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters." That is, to the waters of Scripture, or of doctrine. It should be noted that it says "thirsteth", for one who is not thirsty does not care for water. "And ye that have no money" means: those who do not desire earthly riches. Peter was such a man, who said, "Silver and gold have I none," etc. Such people desire these waters; others, however, despise them. Hence it is written in Judges, "Those who drank kneeling down were rejected from the Lord's battle." "Make haste": for some come slowly to the waters of Scripture. But in Exodus we read that the manna was gathered at the beginning of the day. For in the strength of youth you ought to gather the manna of Scripture, not in the evening of old age, lest it melt away. Hence in Ecclesiasticus: "Delay not to turn to the Lord," etc. "Wine and milk": in some places Holy Scripture is wine, in others it is milk: wine for the greater, milk for the lesser.

units.la: Carm. de Contemptu Mundi, MS. ibid. propè sin. de S. Scripturâ loquens.
units.tr: Poem On the Contempt of the World, manuscript in the same place, near the end, speaking of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Omne quod ostendo, potes hicque videre legendo. Indice Scripturâ, poteris cognoscere plura. Vitam quærenti dat iter sacra lectio menti.
units.tr: Whatever I set out, you may see by reading it. With Scripture as your index, you will be able to know more. Sacred reading gives the seeker of life a road for the mind.

units.la: 1220. Jacobus de Vitriaco, Cardinalis Romanus,
units.tr: 1220. Jacques de Vitry, Roman Cardinal,

units.la: Hist. Oriental. lib. 1. cap. 74. Græci qui eâdem linguâ in vulgari & in Scripturis utuntur, sacerdotes suos in Ecclesiâ & in literali sermone, qui idem est cum vulgari, intelligunt. Cap. 77. Maronitæ utuntur [ in sacris ] Chaldæâ literâ & vulgari idiomate Saraceno. Cap. 78. Armeni habent proprium idioma, & proprias literas, & in vulgari sermone divinas Scripturas pronuntiant, ita quod sacerdotes & Clerici eorum à Laicis in Ecclesiis intelliguntur: sicut dictum est de Græcis.
units.tr: Hist. Oriental. lib. 1. cap. 74. The Greeks, who use the same language in the vernacular and in the Scriptures, understand their priests in the Church and in the literal speech, which is the same as the vernacular. Cap. 77. The Maronites use [in their sacred rites] the Chaldean letters and the vernacular Saracen idiom. Cap. 78. The Armenians have their own idiom and their own letters, and they recite the divine Scriptures in the vernacular speech, so that their priests and clergy are understood by the laity in the churches, as was said of the Greeks.

units.la: 1220. Alexander Neckam, Abbas Exoniensis.
units.tr: 1220. Alexander Neckam, Abbot of Exeter.

units.la: Exposit. in Cantica Canticorum, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, Lib. 1. cap. 1. In principio creavit Deus Cœlum & Terram.] ‘ Domi‘ne, puteus S. Scripturæ altus est: da mihi hauritorium humilitatis, ‘ quod dependens a ligno soliditatis fidei, demittatur cum fune discretionis perseverantis; ut sic aquas refrigerium præstantes contra intentiva mœrorum hauriam. Ad has aquas salutares venite passibus fidei ‘ omnes sitientes justitiam, doctrinam Salvatoris, laudem Matris salutis. Et etiam vos, qui simplices & idiotæ videmini, qui non habetis ‘ argentum intentis eloquentiæ; præparate vobis, emite diligentiâ & ‘ devotione; comedite delectando in veris præconiis illius; quæ mater ‘ est veritatis. Venite, emite: reputabitur enim vobis pro emptione; ‘ quod tamen gratis accipietis. Emite absque argento, & etiam absque ‘ ullâ commutatione terrenâ vinum, hoc est, jocundam dulcedinem sacri eloquii, & lac, h. e. simplicium doctrinam. Sacra enim Scri‘ ptura cibus est & potus. Cibus in occultis, potus in apertis; cibus ‘ recreationis, potus delectationis.
units.tr: Exposition on the Song of Songs, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, Book 1, chapter 1. "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." "Lord, the well of Holy Scripture is deep. Give me a bucket of humility, which, hanging from the wood of the firmness of faith, may be let down on the rope of persevering discernment, so that I may draw up, against the anxious thoughts of sorrows, waters that bring refreshment. Come to these saving waters with the steps of faith, all you who thirst for righteousness, for the teaching of the Saviour, for the praise of the Mother of salvation. And you too, who seem simple and untutored, who do not have silver of eloquence in your purses: prepare for yourselves, buy with diligence and devotion, eat with delight in her true praises, who is the mother of truth. Come, buy; for it will be reckoned to you as a purchase, though you shall receive it freely. Buy without silver, and without any earthly exchange, wine, that is, the joyful sweetness of the sacred word, and milk, that is, the teaching suited to simple folk. For Holy Scripture is food and drink: food in its hidden meanings, drink in its plain sense; food for refreshment, drink for delight."

units.la: Lib. 4. cap. 19. ‘ Sacra namque Scriptura & puteus est & fons. ‘ Puteus est propter mysteriorum profunditatem, fons est propter ha‘ bundantiam indeficientem. Dives est sapientiæ vena; nec aquarum ‘ copia fons destitui potest, jugi scaturigine defluens. Fons ortorum est ‘ sacra Scriptura, qui spirituales animarum ortos amantium fideliter irrigat. Hi orti læta proferunt virtutum germina, quæ aquis gratiæ sa‘ ‘ luberrimis irrorantur.Hæ sunt aquæ, quas Dominus in Isaiâ promittit ‘ populo suo, dicens : Ponam in deserto viam, & in sicco flumina, &c.
units.tr: Book 4, chapter 19. "For Holy Scripture is both a well and a spring. It is a well because of the depth of its mysteries; it is a spring because of its unfailing abundance. The vein of wisdom is rich, and no abundance of waters can be lacking to a spring that flows from a constant gushing. Holy Scripture is the fountain of gardens, which faithfully waters the spiritual gardens of loving souls. These gardens put forth the joyful shoots of virtues, which are watered by the most abundant waters of grace. These are the waters which the Lord promises to his people through Isaiah, saying: I will make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert, and so on."

units.la: Lib. 5. cap. 11. ‘ Sententiæ item sacræ Scripturæ non immerito mi‘ tes dicuntur. Sicut enim nux cibum, lac lumen ministrat; ita sacra ‘ Scriptura nunc cibus est, nunc potus; nunc lucis exhibet solatium ‘ expellendo tenebras ignorantiæ. Orti prædicti humile est ostium ; ‘ nec erectæ cervici patebit ingressus ipsius. Humilitas introducit in‘ trare volentes; cujus fidus comes est amor honestus. O pudor, O de‘ decus! multi dedignantur intrare in ortum istum; in quem Sapientia ‘ patris intrare dignata est,&c.Descendit enim in ortum sacrae Scripturae ‘ Christus, cùm per sanctos Expositores cœlestem paginam elucidavit, ‘ &c. Quotidie etiam tam in legentibus quàm in exponentibus de‘ scendit Christus in sacram Scripturam; & videt poma convallium; ‘ dum ipsos intelligere facit fructus & utilitatem incarnationis ipsius. ‘ Inspicit autem an floruerunt vineæ; cùm transitus in sacrâ Scripturâ ‘ pertinentes ad virtutem sacramentorum Ecclesiæ nos videre & intelli‘ gere facit, &c.
units.tr: Book 5, chapter 11. "Likewise, the sayings of Holy Scripture are not undeservedly called gentle. For as the nut supplies food, and milk supplies light, so Holy Scripture is now food, now drink; now it offers the comfort of light, driving away the darkness of ignorance. The door of the aforesaid garden is low; nor will entrance be open to a stiff neck. Humility introduces those who wish to enter, and honest love is its faithful companion. Oh shame, oh disgrace! Many disdain to enter that garden, into which the Wisdom of the Father has deigned to enter, and so on. For Christ descends into the garden of Holy Scripture when he makes the heavenly page plain through the holy expositors, and so on. Daily, both in those who read and in those who expound, Christ descends into Holy Scripture, and he looks upon the fruits of the valleys, while he makes them understand the fruit and profit of his incarnation. He inspects whether the vines have flourished, when he makes us see and understand the passages in Holy Scripture that pertain to the power of the sacraments of the Church, and so on."

units.la: Lib. 6. cap. 5. ‘ Fœlice fœlicior est, qui etiam ætatis primitias Deo ‘ offerens, lectione sacræ Scripturæ se diutius informavit, sub Hely sa‘ cerdote, spiritualibus utilitatis exercitiis cum Samuele [innutritus.] ‘ Fœlix est, qui in agro divinæ lectionis spicas collegit remanentes, se‘ quutus melliorum vestigia; & ne ad momentum quidem revertitur ‘ erroris pristini. Audi lector consilium Booz alloquentis Ruth. Audi filia, ne vadas in alterum agrum ad colligendum, nec recedas ab hoc loco; sed jungere puellis meis, & ubi messuerunt, sequere. Attende, ‘ lector, quòd monet ne vadas in alterum agrum quàm in agrum sacræ ‘ Scripturæ. Fertilis est ager iste, suis contentus deliciis.
units.tr: Book 6, chapter 5. "Happier still is he who, offering the first fruits of his age to God, has formed himself for a long time by reading Holy Scripture, nourished under the priest Eli, with Samuel, in the spiritual exercises of profit. Happy is he who, in the field of divine reading, has gathered the ears left behind, following the footsteps of the better sort; and he does not turn back, even for a moment, to his former error. Hear, reader, the counsel of Boaz addressing Ruth: Hearken, my daughter, go not to glean in another field, nor depart from this place; but join my maidens, and follow where they have reaped. Note, reader, that he warns you not to go into another field than the field of Holy Scripture. Fertile is that field, content with its own delights."

units.la: Lib. 6. cap. 6. ‘ Si autem tibi, cùm adhuc mammotrectus sis, ‘ nondum corrigendus est crater vino subtilis intelligentiæ coronatus ; ‘ si nondum idoneus es esui panis tritici confirmantis cor hominis : ecce ‘ admovet ori tuo ubera sua cœlestis Scriptura, mater, nutrix, gerula. ‘ Ubera fuge fœcunditatis uberrimæ. Lac tibi non ætate novum non ‘ frigore deerit. Lactei fontes sunt, vena divite lac incessanter fun‘ dentes. Sugi desiderant lactis ubera; ut amplior sit ubertatis gloria.
units.tr: Book 6, chapter 6. "But if, while you are still being handled at the breast, the cup crowned with the wine of subtle understanding is not yet to be given you; if you are not yet fit to eat the bread of wheat which strengthens the heart of man: behold, heavenly Scripture, mother, nurse, and bearer, brings its breasts to your mouth. Shun the breasts of most abundant fruitfulness. Milk will not be lacking to you, new in age and not in cold. They are springs of milk, a rich vein pouring out milk without ceasing. Infants long to suck the breasts of milk, so that the glory of their abundance may be greater."

units.la: 1229. Concilium Tolosanum.
units.tr: 1229. Council of Toulouse.

units.la: Decretum Concilii Tolosani, à Cl. Armachano supra memorati, his verbis continetur, cap. 14. Prohibemus etiam, ne libros Veteris Testamenti aut Novi Laici permittantur habere; nisi forte Psalterium vel Breviarium pro divinis officiis, aut horas B. Mariae, aliquis ex devotione habere velit. Sed ne praemissos libros habeant in vulgari translatos, arctissimè inhibemus. Conciliarem quidem autoritatem præ se ferunt Canones Tolosani. Verùm si quis Præfationem attentè legat; privata fuisse Romani, Cardinalis S. Angeli, Apostolicæ sedis Legati, & apud Tolosanos Inquisitoris, edicta facilè animadvertet. Sic enim præfatur. Licèt à diversis Apostolicæ sedis Legatis diversa emanaverint instituta contra Hæreticos, &c. nos tamen [post illos] ordinandum duximus & statuendum de Consilio Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum, & Prælatorum, & Baronum, & Militum; quæ ad purgationem hæreticæ pravitatis, &c. novimus expedire. Propriâ igitur autoritate Legatus Canones istos edidit; & Concilium, quod vocant, Tolosanum nil aliud erat quàm Conventus quorundam Præsulum simul & Laicorum; quos Legatus sibi satellites asciverat.
units.tr: The decree of the Council of Toulouse, cited by the most distinguished Archbishop of Armagh above, is contained in these words, chapter 14: We also forbid that laymen be permitted to have the books of the Old or New Testament; unless perhaps someone, out of devotion, wishes to have the Psalter, or the Breviary for the divine offices, or the Hours of the Blessed Mary. But we most strictly forbid that they have the aforesaid books translated into the vernacular. The Canons of Toulouse certainly bear the appearance of conciliar authority. But if anyone reads the Preface carefully, he will readily see that these were the private edicts of the Roman Cardinal of St Angelo, Legate of the Apostolic See, and Inquisitor among the Toulousans. For it begins thus: Although various decrees have gone out against the heretics from various Legates of the Apostolic See, etc., we have nevertheless [after them] judged it right to ordain and decree, with the counsel of archbishops, bishops, prelates, barons and soldiers, those things which we know to be expedient for the purging of heretical depravity, etc. Therefore the Legate issued these canons on his own authority, and the so-called Council of Toulouse was nothing other than a gathering of certain prelates together with laymen, whom the Legate had taken on as his attendants.

units.la: 1230. Gregorius IX. Papa Romanus,
units.tr: 1230. Gregory IX, Roman Pope,

units.la: Epist 6. ad Germanum, Patriarcham CP. Cùm juxta testimonium veritatis, cessatio fit errorum ignorantia Scripturarum; cunctis expedit illas legere vel audire; quia quæ in eis inspiratio divina reposuit pro doctrinâ sequentium, ad cautelam trahere voluit modernorum.
units.tr: Epistle 6, to Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople. Since, according to the testimony of truth, error ceases through ignorance of the Scriptures, it is good for all to read or hear them, because the things which divine inspiration has set down in them, for the teaching of those who follow, it wished to draw for the caution of those of our own time.

units.la: 1240. Robertus Grosthead, Episcopus Lincolniensis,
units.tr: 1240. Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln,

units.la: Tract. de Curâ Pastorali, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, paulò post init. Postquam dixisset sacerdotes verbum Dei, quod est pabulum animæ, gregi suo assiduè prædicare debere; subdit. Si aliquis dicat, quòd nescit; proprium remedium est, quòd resignet Beneficium suum. Tamen melius remedium dicam. Potest enim quilibet Persona vel Sacerdos repetere in septimanâ nudum textum Evangelii diei dominicæ; ut ita sciat saltem li-
units.tr: In his Tract on Pastoral Care (MS. in the Lambeth Library, shortly after the beginning). After saying that priests ought to preach constantly to their flock the word of God, which is the food of the soul, he adds: "If anyone says that he does not know how, the proper remedy is that he resign his benefice. Yet I will tell a better remedy. For any Person or Priest can repeat in the week the bare text of the Gospel for the Lord's day, so that he may at least know the gross story to tell his subjects.

units.la: Cap. 5. ad An. 1229. Concil. Tom. XI. pag. 430. Concil. Tom. XI. pag. 322. storiam grossam subditis suis referre. Et hoc dico, si Latinum intelligat; & si faciat singulis septimanis, in veritate bene proficiet, &c. Si verò non intelligit Latinum; saltem potest adire vicinum aliquem intelligentem, qui caritativè ei exponet; & sic ulterius gregem suum doceat; & in uno anno potest sic repetere Epistolas Festorum, & in secundo Vitas Sanctorum, & deinde subditis referre. Priora hujus loci verba ab Authore Fragmenti Wigorniensis adducta supra k habes, verùm ex Anglico à me conversa. Codex enim MS. Lincolniensis ad manum non erat. Scripsit ille duplicem hujus argumenti Tractatum; alterum modò citatum qui incipit, Scriptum est de Levitis; cujus exemplar vidi etiam Cantabrigiæ in Bibliothecâ Collegii D. Joannis; alterum, qui incipit, Moyses, qui, tradente Domino. Iste inter Epistolas Lincolniensis MSS. haberi solet: Seorsim tamen positum vidi in Collegio S. Trinitatis apud Cantabrigienses.
units.tr: Chapter 5, for the year 1229. Councils, Vol. XI, p. 430. Councils, Vol. XI, p. 322. And I say this if he understands Latin; and if he does this every week, he will truly profit well, etc. But if he does not understand Latin, he can at least go to some neighbour who understands it, who will explain it to him charitably; and so he may teach his flock further; and in one year he can repeat in this way the Epistles for the feast days, and in the second year the Lives of the Saints, and then report them to his subjects. You have the earlier words of this passage, quoted above at k by the author of the Worcester Fragment, but I translated them myself from the English, since the Lincoln manuscript was not at hand. That author wrote two treatises on this subject: one, just cited, which begins "Scriptum est de Levitis", a copy of which I also saw at Cambridge in the library of St John's College; and the other, which begins "Moyses, qui, tradente Domino". The latter is usually found among the Letters in the Lincoln manuscripts; I have seen it, however, by itself in Trinity College at Cambridge.

units.la: Serm. ad Clerum, in Psal. CXXXII. 9. (in Appendice ad Fascic. Rerum expetend. Londini 1689. pag. 303.) ‘Pro libro vitæ, quem ‘hic aperte non possumus legere, sicut Angeli legunt, datur nobis liber duorum Testamentorum; in quo debemus assiduè legere, & quæ ‘illustrant mentis nostræ contemplationem, & quæ nostram regant ‘actionem. Ab hujus libri lectione & speculi inspectione nihil nos ‘avellat, nisi proximorum vel nostri justa necessitas vel pia utilitas: ‘recolentes illud quod in typum nostrì dictum est Ezechieli l, & Joanni ‘in Apocalypsi m; scilicet ut comederent volumen vel librum sibi ostensum. Quid est autem librum edere, nisi illum avidè legere, lectumque intelligere. Namque ipsa scientia est sicut cibus animæ, &c. Prudentiam generet Scripturarum frequens immò assidua inspectio, &c.
units.tr: From the Sermon to the Clergy, on Psalm 132.9 (in the Appendix to the Fasciculus Rerum Expetendarum, London 1689, p. 303): "In place of the book of life, which we cannot here read openly, as the Angels read, we are given the book of the two Testaments; in which we ought to read constantly, both what illuminates the contemplation of our mind and what governs our action. Nothing should draw us away from the reading of this book and the inspection of this mirror, except the just necessity or pious usefulness of our neighbours or ourselves; recalling what was said as a figure of us to Ezekiel l and to John in the Apocalypse m, namely that they should eat the scroll or book shown to them. What is it to eat a book, except to read it eagerly and, having read it, to understand it? For knowledge itself is like food for the soul, etc. Frequent, or rather constant, inspection of the Scriptures generates prudence, etc."

units.la: Constitut. Eccles. (ibid. pag. 410.) ‘Provideant etiam attentius Ecclesiarum Rectores & Sacerdotes Parochiales, ut pueri Parochiarum ‘suarum diligenter doceantur & sciant Orationem Dominicam & Symbolum, & Salutationem B. Virginis, & crucis signaculo se recte ‘consignare. Et quia, ut audimus, etiam quidam adulti hæc ignorant; ‘præcipimus, ut cùm Laici ad confessionem accedunt, diligenter examinentur, utrùm scierint prædicta; & secundùm quod expedit, in ‘eis à Sacerdotibus instruantur.' Superiùs præceperat; ut Presbyteri Parochianos suos Decalogum edocerent.
units.tr: From the Constitutions of the Church (ibid., p. 410): "Let the rectors of the churches and the parish priests take more careful heed that the children of their parishes are diligently taught and know the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, and the Salutation of the Blessed Virgin, and to sign themselves rightly with the sign of the cross. And because, as we hear, even some adults are ignorant of these things, we command that when laymen approach confession they be carefully examined as to whether they know the aforesaid, and, as is expedient, be instructed in them by the priests." Earlier he had ordered that the elders teach their parishioners the Decalogue.

units.la: Tractat. de Oculo Morali, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, Cap. 44. Sacra Scriptura est tanquam Spiritûs S. apotheca; in quâ invenitur efficax
units.tr: From the Tract on the Moral Eye (MS. in the Lambeth Library, ch. 44): "Holy Scripture is like the storehouse of the Holy Spirit, in which is found an effective ointment against every wound, a wholesome antidote against disease, a saving remedy against pain.

units.la: {k} Cap. 5. ad An. 1410. {l} III. 1. {m} X. 9. contra omne vulnus unguentum, salubre contra morbum antidotum, salutiferum contra dolorem remedium. Et sic dicit Chrysostomus. In Scriptura sacra invenit ignorans quid discat, contumax quid timeat, laborans praemia, pusillanimis solatia. Ecce quanta est in Scriptura sacra soliditas? & quam elongata est ab ea vanitas? Et ideo Sapiens invitans nos ad studium divinae sapientiae, dicit Proverb. XXII. Ecce descripsi eam tripliciter in cogitationibus & scientia; ut ostenderem tibi firmitatem, & eloquia veritatis. Et ideo ad hanc tanquam ad objectum firmum & solidum debemus dirigere rationis oculum. Unde dicitur Petr. I. Habemus firmiorem Propheticum sermonem, &c.
units.tr: {k} Chapter 5, for the year 1410. {l} III. 1. {m} X. 9. And so Chrysostom says: in Holy Scripture the ignorant find what they should learn, the obstinate what they should fear, the labouring their rewards, the faint-hearted their consolations. Behold how great is the solidity of Holy Scripture, and how far from it is vanity! And therefore the Wise Man, inviting us to the study of divine wisdom, says in Proverbs 22: Behold, I have described it threefold in thoughts and knowledge, that I might show you firmness and the words of truth. And so to this, as to a firm and solid object, we ought to direct the eye of reason. Whence it is said in Pet. I: "We have a more sure prophetic word," etc.

units.la: Sententiam istam Lincolniensis adducit Praefationis in Versionem Scripturae Anglicanam Author n, de quo plura infra ad Ann. 1290: Deus voluit, ut plures Interpretes S. Scripturam transferrent, & diversae Translationes in Ecclesia essent; idcirco ut quod unus obscurius dixerat, alter manifestius redderet.
units.tr: The author of the Preface to the English version of Scripture, whom more will be said below at 1290, cites this opinion of the Lincoln bishop: "God willed that many interpreters should translate Holy Scripture, and that there should be various translations in the Church, so that what one had said more obscurely, another might render more plainly." n

units.la: 1250. Thomas Aquinas.
units.tr: 1250. Thomas Aquinas.

units.la: Summ. par. I. qu. I. art. 9. Convenit etiam sacrae Scripturae, quae communiter omnibus proponitur; ut spiritualia sub similitudinibus corporalium proponantur; ut saltem vel sic rudes eam capiant, qui ad intelligibilia secundum se capienda non sunt idonei.
units.tr: Summ. par. I. qu. I. art. 9. It also belongs to Holy Scripture, which is commonly set before everyone, that spiritual things are presented under likenesses of bodily things, so that at least in this way the unlearned may grasp it, since they are not fit to grasp intelligible things as they are in themselves.

units.la: 2. 2. qu.83. art. 12. Utrum oratio debeat esse vocalis? Duplex est oratio, communis & singularis. Communis quidem oratio est, quae per ministros Ecclesiae in persona totius fidelis populi Deo offertur. Et ideo oportet quod talis oratio innotescat toti populo, pro quo profertur; quod non posset fieri, nisi esset vocalis. Et ideo rationabiliter institutum est; ut Ministri Ecclesiae hujusmodi orationes alta voce pronuntient, ut ad omnium notitiam possint pervenire.
units.tr: 2. 2. qu. 83. art. 12. Whether prayer ought to be vocal? Prayer is of two kinds, common and private. Common prayer is that which is offered to God through the ministers of the Church in the person of the whole body of the faithful. Therefore such prayer must be made known to the whole people for whom it is offered, which could not happen unless it were vocal. And so it was reasonably instituted that the ministers of the Church should pronounce such prayers in a loud voice, so that they may come to the knowledge of all.

units.la: Comment. in I Cor. XIV. Idiota] scilicet non habens nisi linguam maternam. Nonne dicent quod insanitis?] Objectio. Idem est loqui linguis, & loqui literaliter, quantum ad idiotas. Cum ergo omnes loquantur literaliter in Ecclesia, quia omnia dicuntur in Latino; videtur quod similiter fit insania. Dicendum est ad hoc, quod ideo erat insania in Primitiva Ecclesia, quia erant rudes in ritu Ecclesiastico. Unde nesciebant, quae fiebant ibi nisi exponeretur eis. Modo vero omnes sunt instructi. Unde licet in Latino omnia dicantur; sciunt tamen illud quod fit in Ecclesia. Ita {a} Prope sin. quidem concedit Thomas linguâ alienâ orare vel prædicare, juxta Apostoli & Ecclesiæ Primitivæ sententiam, insaniæ indicium fuisse: quod nobis nequaquam concedent hodierni Pontificii. Quod de majori autem hodiernæ quàm primitivæ plebis scientiâ adducit; vereor ne è contra plebs Christiana olim res divinas melius nôrit, quàm etiam Clerus Romanus hodie. Utut sit, Apostoli argumentum non minùs in Romanenses recurret; quicquid enim sit de fidelium cœtu sacris jamdiu assueto; certè infideles in Ecclesiam intrantes populum linguâ alienâ orantem insanire dicent.
units.tr: Comment. in I Cor. XIV. "Idiota" [that is, one who has nothing but his mother tongue]. "Will they not say that you are mad?" Objection: "To speak in tongues and to speak literally are the same, as far as the unlearned are concerned. Since therefore everyone speaks literally in the Church, because everything is said in Latin, it seems that the same madness arises. To this it must be replied that it was madness in the primitive Church because the people were ignorant of the ecclesiastical rite, so they did not know what was done there unless it was explained to them. But now all are instructed. Hence, although everything is said in Latin, they nevertheless know what is done in the Church." Thus {a} near the end, Thomas concedes that to pray or preach in a foreign tongue, according to the opinion of the Apostle and the primitive Church, was a sign of madness; which the modern Papists will by no means concede to us. As to what he adduces about the greater knowledge of the people today than in the primitive Church, I fear that, on the contrary, the Christian people of old understood sacred things better than even the Roman clergy do today. However that may be, the Apostle's argument will recur no less against the Romanists; for whatever may be said of a congregation long accustomed to sacred rites, unbelievers entering the Church will certainly say that a people praying in a foreign tongue is mad.

units.la: 1255. Thomas Cantipratensis, Episcopus Lusentinus.
units.tr: 1255. Thomas Cantipratensis, Bishop of Lusentinus.

units.la: Memorabil. lib. 1. cap. 23. num. 3. Rem suo tempore factam narrat, de piâ quâdam Reclusâ in Brabantiæ partibus, viri pauperrimi filiâ; quæ cum puella nondum septennis miro interiùs fervore spiritûs traheretur, rogavit Patrem cum lachrymis ut sibi Psalterium compararet. Cui Pater: Unde, inquit, filia, Psalterium comparabo, qui vix tibi quotidie Panem lucrari sufficio? [B. Virgo igitur, puellæ miserta, ei in somnis apparuit, & Psalterium in manus tradidit. Puella rem patri narrat, ille filiam irridet] & consolans eam, Vade, inquit, tantùm diebus Dominicis & Festivis ad magistram, quæ filias divitum psalterium docet; & primò discas legere; & posteà B. Maria tibi psalterium forsitan procurabit. Mira res, quòd ubi puella simpliciter accepit, & ad magistram, quæ divitum filias docebat, venit; Psalterium inspexit & legit.
units.tr: Memorabil. lib. 1. cap. 23. num. 3. He relates a thing that happened in his time, concerning a pious recluse in the region of Brabant, the daughter of a very poor man: "who, while still a girl not yet seven, was drawn inwardly by a wonderful fervour of spirit, and tearfully asked her father to get her a Psalter. The father said: 'Daughter, where shall I get a Psalter, when I can barely earn enough bread for you each day?'" [Therefore the Blessed Virgin, taking pity on the girl, appeared to her in a dream and placed a Psalter in her hands. The girl told her father, and he laughed at her.] "And consoling her, he said: 'Go only on Sundays and feast days to the mistress who teaches the daughters of the rich to read the Psalter; and first learn to read; afterwards the Blessed Mary will perhaps provide you with a Psalter.' A remarkable thing: when the girl simply accepted this and went to the mistress who taught the daughters of the rich, she looked into the Psalter and read it."

units.la: 1260. Humbertus de Romanis, Dominicanorum Præpositus Generalis.
units.tr: 1260. Humbert of Romans, Master General of the Dominicans.

units.la: Exposit. in Regulam S. Augustini, cap. 63. Psalmis & hymnis tum oratis; dum hoc versetur in corde, quod profertur in ore.
units.tr: Exposit. in Regulam S. Augustini, cap. 63. "With psalms and hymns then said, while that which is uttered in the mouth is turned over in the heart."

units.la: Cap. 65. Porrò multùm debent omnes, & maximè Religiosi, dare operam; ut in orando versetur in corde, quod profertur in ore: alias oratio esset simiatica. Simia enim interdum labia movet ad modum orantis, licèt nesciat quid dicat. Unde dicitur: Populus hic labiis me honorat. Item in docendo, in disputando, in fabricandis, & in omni actione etiam corporali, fatuus reputatur, qui non cogitat in eo quod facit; secundùm Glossam dicentem super illud: Psallite sapienter: Nemo sapienter agit quod non intelligit; quantò magis in orando? Et in illud; Os sapientium in corde ipsorum : quod ideo dicitur, quia quae dicunt, versantur in corde ipsorum. Iterum cum quis loquitur proximo suo, cogitat in eo quod dicit; & tanto magis, quanto major est, cui loquatur. Cum ergo orando loquimini Deo summo; quantum cogitare debet quilibet in oratione suâ? &c. Iterum, oratio cibus est cordis. Sicut ergo amittit dulcedinem boni morsélli, qui non masticat eum: sic dulcedinem spiritualem orationum, qui non committit dentibus intelligentiae orationem. Nam cibus in ore, psalmus in corde sapit. Non negligat anima illum terere dentibus intelligentiae; ne si forte integrum glutiat, frustretur sapore palatum dulciore super mel & favum: Iterum in oratione petimus, ut Deus nobis intendat, juxta illud: Intende mihi, & exaudi me. Quomodo autem est probabile, quod hoc faciat; si nos nobis non intendimus? Nam quomodo mihi intendet, qui mihi non intendo? Item quod magis efficax est in oratione, est ex parte cordis, &c.
units.tr: Cap. 65. Moreover, all owe much, and especially religious, to take care that in praying, what is uttered in the mouth be turned over in the heart; otherwise the prayer would be apelike. For an ape sometimes moves its lips in the manner of one praying, though it does not know what it says. Hence it is said: "This people honours me with their lips." Likewise in teaching, in disputing, in building, and in every action, even a bodily one, he is reckoned foolish who does not think about what he does; according to the Gloss on the words "Sing wisely": no one acts wisely in what he does not understand; how much more in praying? And on the words "The mouth of the wise is in their heart," which is said because what they say is turned over in their heart. Again, when someone speaks to his neighbour, he thinks about what he says, and the more so the greater the person to whom he speaks. Since, then, in praying you speak to the most high God, how much ought each one to think in his prayer? etc. Again, prayer is the food of the heart. As he loses the sweetness of a good morsel who does not chew it, so he loses the spiritual sweetness of prayers who does not bring the prayer to the teeth of understanding. For food tastes in the mouth, a psalm in the heart. The soul should not neglect to grind it with the teeth of understanding, lest, if it perhaps swallows it whole, the palate is cheated of a sweeter taste than honey and the honeycomb. Again, in prayer we ask that God attend to us, according to the words: "Attend to me and hear me." But how is it probable that he will do this, if we do not attend to ourselves? For how will he attend to me, if I do not attend to myself? Again, what is more effective in prayer is on the part of the heart, etc.

units.la: Cap. 150. S. Scripturae studium operosè commendans, inter alia haec habet: Interdum verò propter desperationem proficiendi [Scripturae lectio rejicitur.] Sunt enim quidam, qui Scripturas non intelligentes, nec de intelligendi possibilitate confidentes, refugiunt lectionem; quamvis innumerabiles matronae & mulieres Deo devotae non dimittunt propter hoc legere Psalterium cotidie, quia non intelligunt, ut debent. Sed non est propter hoc dimittendum. Credendum est enim, quod verba sacra, etsi non intelligantur à legente; habent tamen virtutem contra spirituales nequitias; sicut verba incantantis contra serpentem, quamvis non intelligantur ab ipso incantatore. Liber iste Humberti typis aliquoties excusus prodiit. Verùm cum exemplar impressum ad manum non esset; loca ista ex Codice MS. Bibliothecae Lambethanae descripsi.
units.tr: Cap. 150. Earnestly commending the study of Holy Scripture, among other things he says this: "Sometimes indeed, on account of despair of making progress, [the reading of Scripture is rejected]. For there are some who, not understanding the Scriptures, and not confident of being able to understand them, shun reading; although countless matrons and women devoted to God do not on this account give up reading the Psalter every day, though they do not understand it as they ought. But it should not be abandoned for this reason. For it must be believed that the sacred words, even if they are not understood by the reader, nevertheless have power against spiritual wickednesses; as the words of an enchanter against a serpent, although they are not understood by the enchanter himself." This book of Humbert has been printed several times. But since a printed copy was not at hand, I copied these passages from the manuscript codex in the Lambeth Library.

units.la: 1280. Rogerus Bacon.
units.tr: 1280. Roger Bacon.

units.la: Habetur MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Epistola ejus de laude sacrae Scripturae ad Clementem IV. Papam; justi voluminis molem exaequans. In illâ portentosum quidem & impossibile commentum, de Scripturae scientiâ apud omnes fideles propagandâ, Pontifici proponit; quod tamen sententiam illius de necessariâ Scripturae cognitione luculenter declarat. Nimium esset omnia, quae huc spectant, ipsius verba describere; commenti igitur rationem duntaxat summatim repraesentabo.
units.tr: His Epistle on the praise of Holy Scripture, addressed to Pope Clement IV and equal in bulk to a large volume, survives in manuscript in the Lambeth Library. In it he proposes to the Pope a portentous and impossible scheme: the spread of knowledge of Scripture among all the faithful. Yet the scheme clearly sets out his view of the necessity of knowing Scripture. It would be too long to copy out all his words on these matters, so I will give only a summary of the scheme.

units.la: Primùm igitur ponit, omnia ad credendum necessaria, omnia scitu digna, in S. Scripturâ contineri, fidei quidem articulos & absolutè necessaria, literaliter; scientias autem humanas & minùs necessaria, autem mysticè & spiritualiter. Sic enim cap. 28. inquit: Dein aggressus sum sum partem secundam (majoris cujusdam Operis, ejusdem cum Epistolâ argumenti ad quod passim Lectorem remittit) in quâ ostendo, quod una sola est sapientia perfecta ab uno Deo data uni generi humano propter unum finem, scilicet vitam æternam: quæ in sacris literis tota continctur; per Jus tamen Canonicum & Philosophiam explicanda. Sub Philosophiâ comprehendo Jus civile. Dein cap. 30. docet utrumque etiam Jus in S. Scripturâ comprehendi. Et sic terminatur pars secunda, in quâ principale propositum est ostendere, quod tota sapientia concluditur in sacrâ Scripturâ; per jus tamen & Philosophiam explicanda: ut sicut in pugno colligitur, quod latius in palmâ explicatur; sic tota sapientia utilis homini continetur in sacris literis, licèt non tota explicetur; sed ejus explicatio est Jus Canonicum & Philosophia. Nam utrumque jacet in visceribus sacræ Scripturæ, & de his exivit; & super hoc fundantur omnia, quæ utiliter dicuntur in Jure Canonico & Philosophia; & hoc per probabiles considerationes ostendo; quas hîc non expono. Nonnullas tamen rationes adjungit; & post multa subdit: Secunda causa quare docui sapientiam totam comprehendi in lege Dei utriusque Testamenti, est summè notanda, quia nihil in Ecclesiâ Dei plus debet considerari. Quia si fiant, quæ narro; tunc totum studium rectificabitur per seipsum; & tota Ecclesia regetur sicut in temporibus Sanctorum; & fiet pax universalis tam apud Ecclesiastica negotia, quàm apud regimen Principum & Laicorum. Et nisi per vestram hæc fiant sapientiam; non credo quòd unquam fient. Et tamen Prophetatum est à multis temporibus; quòd per unum Papam debent fieri quæ narrabo. Et debet ille esse istis temporibus; sicut inferiùs explicabo magis. Et quod volo dicere, est quòd regimen Ecclesiæ, sicut per legem Dei regebatur antiquitus apud Hebræos, sic debet esse nunc apud Christianos. Et sicut in primitivâ Ecclesiâ, regebatur per eam, sic nunc habet regi. Et si tota sapientia est ibi principaliter contenta & fontaliter; tunc principaliter ad minus debet per illam regi. Sed nunc non est ita, &c.
units.tr: First, then, he holds that everything necessary for belief and everything worth knowing is contained in Holy Scripture: the articles of faith and what is absolutely necessary literally, but human sciences and less necessary matters mystically and spiritually. For in chapter 28 he says: Next I have begun the second part (of a certain larger work, on the same subject as the Epistle, to which he refers the reader in many places) in which I show that there is one perfect wisdom, given by one God to the one human race for one end, namely eternal life; which is wholly contained in the sacred letters, yet is to be explained through the Canon Law and Philosophy. Under Philosophy I include the civil law. Then in chapter 30 he teaches that both laws too are contained in Holy Scripture. And so the second part ends, whose chief purpose is to show that all wisdom is comprised in Holy Scripture, yet is to be explained through law and Philosophy: just as what is gathered in the fist is unfolded in the palm, so all the wisdom useful to man is contained in the sacred letters, although it is not all unfolded; its explanation is the Canon Law and Philosophy. For both lie in the bowels of Holy Scripture and have come forth from it, and everything that is usefully said in the Canon Law and Philosophy is founded upon this; and I show this by probable considerations, which I do not set out here. He adds several arguments, and after much more he continues: The second reason why I have taught that all wisdom is comprised in the law of God of both Testaments is most worthy of note, because nothing in the Church of God ought to be considered more. For if the things I describe come about, then the whole course of study will be set right of its own accord, and the whole Church will be governed as in the times of the Saints, and there will be universal peace, both in ecclesiastical affairs and in the government of princes and laymen. And unless these things are brought about through your wisdom, I do not believe they will ever come about. Yet it has been prophesied for many ages that the things I shall relate are to be done through one Pope. And he ought to be in these times, as I shall explain more fully below. What I wish to say is that the government of the Church, as it was once governed among the Hebrews by the law of God, so ought it now to be among Christians. And as in the primitive Church it was governed by that law, so now it ought to be governed by it. And if all wisdom is contained there chiefly and as its fountain, then at least chiefly it ought to be governed by it. But now it is not so, etc.

units.la: Proximo loco ostendit omnia reipublicæ Christianæ mala ac pestes à Scripturæ ignorantiâ provenire. Populum quidem fidem & officii sui rationem parùm scire, mores corruptissimos passim inolescere, fœdissimos errores atque hæreses enasci: ista autem omnia, aliaque, si quæ sint ejusmodi, mala, exinde oriri; quòd populus Scripturas nesciat, immò quod magis dolendum est, à presulibus Ecclesiæ in ignorantiam datâ operâ deducatur. Sic enim cap. 27. ait. Causa namque quare fideles non convertuntur ad fidem, est quia Principes & Prælati eorum tenent eos in errore, & sic est in omni statu. Scilicet, infinitus est defectus in eis qui præsunt nunc temporis studio & vitâ: & ideo est quòd subjecta multitudo errat in infinitis. Apprimè igitur necessarium esse concludit, ut omnes Christiani sacras Scripturas, fidei suæ fontem & regulam, perfectè sciant & perscrutentur.
units.tr: In the next place he shows that all the evils and plagues of the Christian commonwealth arise from ignorance of Scripture: that the people scarcely know the faith or the reason of their duty, that the most corrupt morals grow everywhere, and that the foulest errors and heresies spring up; and that all these evils, and any others of this kind, arise from this, that the people do not know the Scriptures, or, what is more lamentable, are deliberately led into ignorance by the prelates of the Church. For in chapter 27 he says: The reason why the faithful are not converted to the faith is that their princes and prelates keep them in error, and it is so in every rank. Indeed, there is endless failing in those who now preside, in their study and their way of life; and so it is that the subject multitude errs in countless ways. He therefore concludes that it is most necessary for all Christians to know thoroughly and to search out the holy Scriptures, the fountain and rule of their faith.

units.la: Neque tamen satis esse ut simplicem Scripturæ sensum sciant, nisi & fontes Hebraicos & Græcos consulent. Quicunque enim sacram Scripturam accuratè scire velit, necessarium est ut linguarum Originalium notitiam sibi comparet; tum quòd multa sint in S. Scripturâ, quæ in aliam conversa linguam, vim &·affectum amittunt; tum quòd multa perperam transferantur. Ipse enim Hieronymus in Versione conficiendâ infinitis in locis turpiter hallucinatus est; aliique Interpretes magis adhuc lapsi sunt. His adde, Codices Latinos turpissimè depravatos esse librariorum & sciolorum vitio; maximè à viginti retro annis, in quo pessimus inter Minores, & Scolares, potissimum verò Prædicatores mos inolevit, quòd quilibet corrigat pro suâ voluntate, & quilibet mutat quod non intelligit; quod non licet facere in libris Poetarum. Ista fusè docet cap. 31.
units.tr: Yet it is not enough for them to know the plain sense of Scripture unless they also consult the Hebrew and Greek sources. For whoever wishes to know Holy Scripture accurately must acquire knowledge of the original languages, both because there are many things in Scripture which lose their force and feeling when turned into another language, and because many things are translated wrongly. Jerome himself, in making his version, went badly astray in countless places, and other translators have slipped even more. Add to this that the Latin manuscripts have been shamefully corrupted by the fault of copyists and half-learned men, above all in the last twenty years, in which the worst custom has taken hold among the Minorites and Scholars, and above all among the Preachers, that anyone corrects as he likes, and anyone changes what he does not understand; which is not allowed in the books of the Poets. He teaches these things at length in chapter 31.

units.la: Res quidem incredibilis, ut singuli Christiani totidem linguarum notitiam sibi comparare possint; res tamen, si Baconum audias, factu perquam facilis. His enim præmissis, commenti sui rationem explicat. Nimirum sibi visus est invenisse Grammaticam quandam Universalem; cujus ope quilibet intra paucos dies linguas Hebræam, Græcam, Latinam, & Arabicam addiscere queat; licèt de Arabicâ, utpote minus necessariâ, minus laboret. Ut unicum enim duntaxat locum attingam; sic homo ventosus de artificio suo gloriatur: cap. 25. Sed certum est mihi, quòd infra tres dies ego quemcunque diligentem & confidentem docerem, Hebræum ut sciret legere, & intelligere quicquid Sancti dicunt & sapientes antiqui in expositione sacri textûs, & quicquid pertinet ad illius textûs correctionem & expositionem; si vellet se excitare secundùm doctrinam datam. Et per tres dies sciret de Græco iterum; ut non solum sciret legere & intelligere quicquid pertinet ad Theologiam, sed ad Philosophiam, & ad Linguam Latinam. Nam consideret vestra sapientia, quòd in linguarum cognitione sunt tria: scilicet ut homo sciat legere & intelligere ea, quæ Latini tractant in expositione Theologiæ & Philosophiæ & linguæ Latinæ. Et hoc est facile, ut dixi, dummodo composuissem primò quoddam scriptum sub compendio de potestate Scientiarum & Linguarum.
units.tr: It is indeed an incredible thing that individual Christians could acquire knowledge of so many languages; yet, if you listen to Bacon, it is quite easy to do. Having laid down these premises, he explains his scheme. He evidently thought he had discovered a certain Universal Grammar, by whose help anyone could learn the Hebrew, Greek, Latin and Arabic languages within a few days, although he takes less trouble over Arabic, as being less necessary. To mention only one passage: so does this windy man boast of his craft, in chapter 25: But I am certain that within three days I could teach any diligent and confident person to read Hebrew, and to understand whatever the Saints and the ancient wise men say in the exposition of the sacred text, and whatever pertains to the correction and exposition of that text, if he were willing to rouse himself according to the teaching given. And in three days he would know Greek in the same way, so that he could not only read and understand whatever pertains to Theology, but also to Philosophy and to the Latin language. For let your wisdom consider that there are three things in the knowledge of languages: namely, that a man should know how to read and understand those things which the Latins treat in the exposition of Theology, Philosophy and the Latin language. And this is easy, as I have said, provided I had first composed a certain writing in brief on the power of the Sciences and Languages.

units.la: Linguarum igitur cognitionis obtinendæ facilitate demonstratâ, unica restabat objectio; ne vulgares Christiani, linguarum licèt scientiâ præditi,
units.tr: With the ease of acquiring knowledge of languages thus demonstrated, one objection remained: that ordinary Christians, even if endowed with knowledge of languages,

units.la: ¿ Cap. 31. in init. præditi, verum Scripturæ sensum minus rectè assequantur. Id autem minimè verendum esse Rogerus clamat. Quia si sciat legere, poterit intelligere. Nam autores exponunt omnia, & dant intellectum. Quò tutior tamen Lectoribus Scripturæ ingressus pateat; se Opus quoddam manuductorium seu Præliminare editurum spondet. Quamvis enim Scriptura legentibus sit intellectu facilis: non tamen nego, inquit, quin verò scriptum Philosophiæ de quibusdam communibus debet fieri, quæ non possunt poni in explicatione Scripturæ; sed tamen illa debent anteponi, ut totum fiat volumen. Et satis modicum erit præ librorum Philosophiæ & Theologiæ numero; immo nihil revera his comparatum. Et sic omnis superfluitas infinita, quæ nunc est, resecabitur; & omnis falsitas tolletur, & omnis vanitas excludetur; & omnia necessaria sapientiæ divinæ & humanæ, quorum infinita quasi nunc desunt, addentur; & redigetur studium sapientiæ ad statum debitum, scilicet istius temporis possibilitatem.
units.tr: Chapter 31, at the beginning: endowed with it, yet might not grasp the true sense of Scripture. Roger cries out that this is by no means to be feared. For if he can read, he will be able to understand. For the authors expound everything and give the meaning. Yet so that the approach to Scripture may lie open more safely to its readers, he promises to publish a certain guiding or Preliminary work. For although Scripture is easy for readers to understand, nevertheless, he says, I do not deny that a philosophical writing must be made on certain common matters, which cannot be set down in the explanation of Scripture; but these ought to be placed first, so that the whole becomes a volume. And it will be quite a small thing compared with the number of books of Philosophy and Theology; indeed, in truth, nothing compared with them. And so all the endless superfluity that now exists will be cut away, and every falsehood will be removed, and every vanity excluded; and all the things necessary for divine and human wisdom, of which an endless number now seem to be lacking, will be added; and the study of wisdom will be restored to its due state, namely the possibility of this time.

units.la: Tot & tam præclara itaque beneficia, ex universali S. Scripturæ linguarumque cognitione proventura, ne Ecclesiæ invideat, Papam multis orat. Id frequentibus vaticiniis confirmatum, id summis omnium votis expetitum; ut tandem aliquando Pontificis Romani operâ Ecclesia reformetur & Scripturæ studium restituatur. Neque enim multa annorum lustra requiri, ut res ab ipso excogitata inchoetur simul & absolvatur. Quin & unus, qui vidit hæc per revelationem, dixit & dicit, quòd ipse videbit hæc magnifica fieri temporibus suis. Et certè infra annum unum possent fieri; si Deo placuerit, & summo Pontifici; & infra minus. Unde temporibus nostris possent fieri. Et Deus confirmet vitam vestram; ut hæc per vos fiant. Enixè igitur postulat, ut Pontisex artificium suum autoritate Apostolicâ confirmet, & Ecclesiæ universæ excolendum commendet; salvâ tamen omnibus illo utendi libertate. Sic enim præfatur, cap. 22. Nec est intentio mea suscitare vestram Clementiam; ut per violentiam corrigatur multitudo, nec capita multitudinis. Neque ego contendam cum eis; sed ago ad hæc propter causas prædictas. Et si vestræ sapientiæ placeat; quod dicetur; primò possunt sapientes recipere exemplar; dein paulatim quicunque velit; ut nullus togatur. Et tamen scio, quòd omnes vellent accipere.
units.tr: So he earnestly begs the Pope not to begrudge the Church such great and splendid benefits, which are to come from a universal knowledge of Holy Scripture and of languages. This has been confirmed by frequent prophecies and is sought with the highest wishes of all, so that at last the Church may be reformed and the study of Scripture restored through the work of the Roman Pontiff. For many lustra are not needed for a thing devised by him to be begun and completed at once. Indeed, one who has seen these things through revelation has said and still says that he himself will see these magnificent things come about in his own times. And certainly they could be done within one year, if it pleases God and the Supreme Pontiff, and in less time. Hence they could be done in our times. And may God confirm your life, so that these things may be done through you. He therefore asks insistently that the Pontiff confirm his invention by apostolic authority and commend it to be cultivated by the whole Church, yet with freedom for everyone to use it. For he says this in the preface, chapter 22: Nor is it my intention to stir up your Clemency, that the multitude, or the heads of the multitude, be corrected by violence. Nor will I contend with them; but I act in these matters for the reasons stated above. And if it pleases your wisdom, what is said will be done: first the wise may receive the model; then gradually whoever wishes, so that no one is compelled. And yet I know that all would want to accept it.

units.la: Ultimo loco innumera beneficia ex hoc artificio Ecclesiæ proventura prædicat. Horum præcipua sunt, quòd Officium divinum ab omnibus fidelibus intelligeretur: quòd legis divinæ scientia, latiùs diffusa, haud ita facilè corrumpi posset: quod Christiani sacris oraculis instructi, futu-
units.tr: Lastly he proclaims countless benefits that will come to the Church from this invention. The chief of these are: that the divine office would be understood by all the faithful; that knowledge of the divine law, spread more widely, could not so easily be corrupted; and that Christians, instructed by the sacred oracles, would be better able to resist the dangers of the future Antichrist

units.la: p Cap. 25. q Cap. 30. r Cap. 30. s Cap. 32. ris Antichristi periculis fortius resistere valerent; quoque fidei normam & vitae documenta e puro & incorrupto fonte haurirent. His adde conversionem infidelium & schismaticorum, ac reprobationem eorum, qui converti non possunt: ubivis manifesta est utilitas linguarum, ubivis necessaria Scripturae scientia.
units.tr: p Cap. 25. q Cap. 30. r Cap. 30. s Cap. 32. and that they would draw the rule of faith and the teaching of life from a pure and uncorrupted source. To these add the conversion of unbelievers and schismatics, and the reprobation of those who cannot be converted: everywhere the usefulness of languages is evident, everywhere the knowledge of Scripture is necessary.

units.la: 1290. Anglicanus Interpres.
units.tr: 1290. The English Translator.

units.la: Facta ante Wiclefum creditur Anglica totius Scripturae Versio, quam Cl. Usserius Jamesii auctoritate ductus ad Annum 1290. refert. Idem Praesationem docti imprimis viri in Vetus Testamentum Anglice ante Annos 300. conscriptam ex Joanne Caio saepius citavit . Praefationem vidi MS. in Bibliotheca publica Academiae Cantabrigiensis, nulli Authori inscriptam. Prodiit autem typis excusa sub Wiclefi nomine Londini 1550. 12°. Eandem esse, quam Caius citavit, indicio est utrumque testimonium a Caio laudatum, & in Praefatione prope finem repertum. Author vero passim dicit se totam Scripturam Anglice transtulisse: adeo ut pronum sit credere Typographos Londinenses in apponendo Wiclefi nomine hallucinatos esse. Rem confirmat impotens animi iracundia; qua Praefationis Author Academicos Oxonienses insequitur; quum e contra Wiclefus Academiae alumnus & magistratus fuerit, maximoque semper honore ab Academicis affectus. Praefatio est admodum prolixa; & de autoritate atque usu singulorum S. Scripturae librorum agit. Canonem Veteris Testamenti juxta Hebraeos dispositum, rejectis Apocryphis: & Scripturae studium omnibus Christianis, tam viris quam foeminis, tam doctis quam indoctis, excolendum ubivis docet; & Cleri repugnantiam dolet. Sic enim cap. 13. Sed proh dolor! Pessima quae unquam in Christiano Clero audita est, abominatio nunc in Anglia proposita est a mundanis Clericis & larvatis Religiosis. Idque in prima nostrae gentis Academia, (ut multi fide digni dolentes narrant) horribile istud & diabolicum scelus moliuntur Christi adversarii & Christianorum parricidae; ut nullus Theologiam aut S. Scripturam discat; nisi Cursum suum (quod vocant) in Artibus peregerit; id est, Artium Magisterium obtinuerit, & per duos exinde annos Regens fuerit. Hinc novem aut decem anni absolvendi sunt post Grammaticae studium recte finitum, antequam edisci anda sit S. Scriptura; quamvis etiam sagax adsit ingenium, & jedula diligentia, & ingens Scripturas discendi cupido. Istud procul dubio Diaboli commentum videtur, scilicet ut pauci admodum aut fere nulli Dei legem discerent & intelligerent. Postea quatuor abominationes in Clero passim obtinere deflet, sc. Impietatem, Sodomiam, Simoniam, & quartam, quam his verbis depingit. Quarta autem Abominatio est quod nunc moliuntur propositum interdicendi Christianis, immo etiam Sacerdotibus & Curatis legis divinae studium; antequam novem aut decem annos Artium studio insumpserint, &c. Capite ultimo Versionis suae rationem reddit, & Apologiam texit. Summa argumenti huc redit.
