Cum Christus Evangelium suum in omni mundo praedicandum esse edixerit; & Scripturae populorum esse a Psalmista dicantur; & ob instructionem populi primitus conscriptae sint: Ob has aliasque rationes, pro salute omnium in hoc regno Electorum, simplex homo Bibliam ex Latino in Anglicum sermonem transtulit. Quamobrem se juncta cum plurimis amicis operâ varios Codices congessisse dicit; lectiones optimas selegisse, & in versione secutum esse; Patrum expositiones, & eruditorum (praesertim Lyrani) glossas adhibuisse; & in vertendo non tam verba quam sensum spectasse: Demum illos refutare nititur, qui versionem vernaculam temeritatis arguebant. Delirare illos dicit: cum versiones innumerae Latinae, & Graeca LXX. fuerint olim evulgatae; dum Graeca & Latina vulgares erant linguae: Nec minus vere & eleganter sacra eloquia in Anglicam linguam converti modo posse, quam in Latinam olim potuisse: Bedam potiorem Bibliae partem Saxonice transtulisse, ut & Alfredum Regem priorem Psalmorum partem. Gallos, Belgas, & Britonas S. Scripturam lingua materna conversam legere; pari igitur jure ab Anglis etiam Biblia vernaculo sermone legenda esse. Haec aliaque argumenta profert Versionis Author; de cujus nomine atque aetate certius aliquid est disquirendum.
units.tr: The English version of the whole of Scripture is believed to have been made before Wiclef, and the distinguished Ussher, led by the authority of James, dates it to 1290. The same learned man often cited from John Caius a preface to the Old Testament in English, written more than 300 years ago. I have seen this preface in manuscript in the public library of the University of Cambridge; it is inscribed to no author. It was published in print under Wiclef's name at London in 1550, in 12°. That it is the same preface that Caius cited is shown by both testimonies that Caius quoted, which are found near the end of the preface. The author, however, says throughout that he has translated the whole of Scripture into English, so that it is easy to believe the London printers were mistaken in putting Wiclef's name on it. The point is confirmed by the impotent anger with which the author of the preface attacks the Oxford academics, although Wiclef was a student and teacher of that university and was always held in the highest honour by its academics. The preface is quite long and deals with the authority and use of each book of Holy Scripture. It sets out the Old Testament canon arranged according to the Hebrews, with the Apocrypha rejected, and teaches that the study of Scripture should be cultivated everywhere by all Christians, women as well as men, learned as well as unlearned; and it laments the opposition of the clergy. For he says in chapter 13: But alas! The worst thing ever heard of among the Christian clergy is now being put forward in England, an abomination by worldly clergy and masked religious. And in the first academy of our nation (as many trustworthy men sadly report) the enemies of Christ and murderers of Christians are devising this horrible and diabolical crime: that no one should learn theology or Holy Scripture unless he has completed his course in the arts, as they call it, that is, has obtained the degree of Master of Arts and then been a regent for two years. From this it follows that nine or ten years must be spent after a properly finished study of grammar, before Holy Scripture can be learned, even if one has a keen mind, diligent application and a great desire to study the Scriptures. Without doubt this seems a contrivance of the devil, namely that very few or almost none would learn and understand the law of God. Afterwards he laments that four abominations are found everywhere among the clergy, namely impiety, sodomy, simony, and a fourth, which he describes in these words: The fourth abomination is that they are now plotting to forbid Christians, indeed even priests and parish clergy, the study of the divine law until they have spent nine or ten years on the study of the arts, etc. In the last chapter he gives the reason for his version and weaves an apology. The sum of the argument comes to this. Since Christ commanded that his Gospel be preached in the whole world, and since the Scriptures are said by the Psalmist to belong to the peoples, and were originally written for the instruction of the people: For these and other reasons, for the salvation of all the elect in this kingdom, a plain man has translated the Bible from Latin into the English tongue. Therefore he says that he has gathered various manuscripts with the help of many friends, selected the best readings and followed them in the translation, consulted the expositions of the Fathers and the glosses of learned men (especially Lyra), and in translating he looked not so much at the words as at the sense. Finally he tries to refute those who charged the vernacular version with rashness. He says they are raving, since innumerable Latin versions and the Greek Septuagint were once published when Greek and Latin were the common languages; and that sacred writings can now be translated into English no less truly and elegantly than they once could be into Latin. He notes that Bede translated the greater part of the Bible into Saxon, and likewise King Alfred the first part of the Psalms. The French, the Belgians and the Britons read Holy Scripture translated into their mother tongue; by the same right, therefore, the English too should read the Bible in their own language. The author of the version offers these and other arguments; but something more certain must be sought about his name and age.

units.la: Inprimis itaque id constat, eidem Authori deberi istam Praefationem, ac Versionem integram S. Scripturae Anglicam, quae in Bibliothecis nostratibus Wicleso inscripta passim extat. Quaecunque enim de Translatione sua praefatur ille, huic Versioni adamussim conveniunt. Ex. gr. Cap. 1. Dicit Praefationis Author, se nonnisi primum Esdrae librum atque illum Neemiae transtulisse, tertium autem & quartum Esdrae libros praetermisisse. Cap. 15. Plura locorum S. Scripturae difficilium dat specimina; disputatque quomodo converti debeant, & quomodo a se conversa fuerint, indicat. Isthaec omnia dictae Versioni exactissime concordant. Denique; Cap. 17. Se Prophetas omnes Glossis nonnullibi illustrasse fidem facit. Et sane in Codice Lambethano Glossae in Prophetas, in nullum autem alium S. Scripturae librum, comparent. Illas in aliis Codicibus me vidisse non memini. Versionem istam Codices omnes quos vidi (& sanè quamplurimos vidi u) Wiclefo unà voce tribuunt. Wiclefum quidem S. Scripturam Anglicè convertisse extra dubium est. Ut Balei etenim auctoritatem taceam; id confirmat Joannes Hussus; cujus testimonium Cl. Usserius supra x adduxit. Quæ autem apud nos vulgò extant Biblia MSS. Anglica, Wiclefo minimè deberi censeo. Neque ut aliter sentiam, unanimes Codicum MSS. Inscriptiones movent. Cunctæ enim recenter sunt additæ, ab incautis puto Lectoribus, qui Anonymâ Versione repertâ, cùm inter Interpretes antiquos Anglicanos Wiclefi nomen sit longè celeberrimum, illud apposuerunt. Ex adverso autem præstò sunt rationes fortissimæ. Primò enim eundem fuisse Versionis istius ac Præfationis supradictæ Authorem, neque tamen Præfationem Wiclefo deberi, supra ostensum est. Dein aliâ prorsus Versione utitur Wiclefus in Commentario suo vernaculo in Psalmos; quod MS. extat in Bibliothecis Lambethanâ & Norfolciana. Postremò ab indubiâ Wiclefi Translatione ista est diversissima. Me quidem integram Wiclefi Versionem nunquam vidisse fateor. Vidi tamen partem ejus non contemnendam in Bibliothecâ Norfolciana, Cod. MS. 254. 4°. sc. Quatuor Evangeliorum Harmoniam, Septem Epistolas Canonicas; & Lectiones Dominicales ac Festivales totius anni è S. Scripturâ depromptas. Codicem istum Wiclefo deberi probat tum Balei auctoritas y scribentis illum Harmoniam Clementis Lanthonien-sis vernaculo sermone reddidisse, tum Præfatio præmissa; de quâ plura vide infra in Wiclefo. Quæ in istoc autem Codice habentur Versiones, à vulgatis Codicibus MSS. sunt planè diversissimæ; quantùm tamen ex sedulâ dialecti collatione conjectari poteram, eâdem prorsus ætate confectæ. Siquis indicium petat, cujus ope utriusque Authorem agnoscat; sciat Wiclefo solenne esse in Interpretatione suâ S. Scripturæ voces difficiliores additis Synonymis dilucidioribus explicare. Seu specimen utriusque malis; locum illum Lucæ II. Et reclinavit eum in præsepio; quia non erat ei locus in diversorio. Wiclefus sic reddit: And puttide him in a Cratche; for place was not to him in the comyn stable. Alter Interpres sic: And leide him in a Cratche; for there was no place to him in no chaumbre.
units.tr: First of all, it is established that this preface and the whole English version of Holy Scripture, which is found in our libraries everywhere inscribed with Wiclef's name, are owed to the same author. For whatever that man says about his translation in the preface fits this version exactly. For example, in chapter 1 the author of the preface says that he translated only the first book of Esdras and that of Nehemiah, but omitted the third and fourth books of Esdras. In chapter 15 he gives several specimens of difficult passages of Scripture, and explains how they ought to be translated and how he has translated them. All these things agree exactly with the said version. Finally, in chapter 17 he makes it clear that he has illustrated all the Prophets with glosses in some places. And indeed in the Lambeth manuscript glosses appear on the Prophets, but on no other book of Scripture. I do not remember seeing these glosses in other manuscripts. All the manuscripts of this version that I have seen (and I have seen very many) ascribe it to Wiclef with one voice. That Wiclef translated Scripture into English is beyond doubt; to say nothing of the authority of Bale, John Huss confirms it, and the distinguished Ussher cited his testimony above. But I do not think the English manuscript Bibles commonly found among us are owed to Wiclef at all. Nor do the unanimous inscriptions of the manuscripts move me to think otherwise. For all of them were added recently, I suppose by careless readers who, having found an anonymous version, put Wiclef's name on it, since among the old English translators the name of Wiclef is by far the most famous. On the other side, however, there are very strong reasons. First, that the author of this version and of the aforesaid preface was the same person has been shown above, and yet the preface is not owed to Wiclef. Then, Wiclef uses an entirely different version in his vernacular commentary on the Psalms, which survives in manuscript in the Lambeth and Norfolk libraries. Lastly, this translation is very different from the undoubted translation of Wiclef. I confess that I have never seen Wiclef's complete version. I have, however, seen a considerable part of it in the Norfolk library, manuscript 254, in 4°: namely a harmony of the four Gospels, the seven Catholic Epistles, and the Sunday and festival lessons of the whole year taken from Scripture. That this manuscript is owed to Wiclef is proved both by the authority of Bale, who writes that he rendered the harmony of Clement of Llanthony into the vernacular, and by the preface prefixed to it, concerning which see more below under Wiclef. The versions in this manuscript are entirely different from those in the common manuscripts, though, as far as I could conjecture from a careful comparison of the dialect, made in exactly the same age. If anyone asks for a sign by which he may recognise the author of each, let him know that it is Wiclef's habit in his translation of Scripture to explain more difficult words by adding clearer synonyms. Or if you prefer a specimen of each, take that passage of Luke 2: And he laid him in a manger, because there was no room for him in the inn. Wiclef renders it thus: And puttide him in a Cratche; for place was not to him in the comyn stable. The other translator thus: And leide him in a Cratche; for there was no place to him in no chaumbre.

units.la: Rejecto itaque Wiclefo, restat ut alium Authorem quæramus. Duo solummodò, quod sciam, mediâ ætate fuerunt Interpretes S. Scripturæ Anglicani; Wiclefus & Joannes Trevisa, de quo plura ad Annum
units.tr: Having therefore set aside Wycliffe, we must look for another author. So far as I know, there were only two English translators of Holy Scripture in the Middle Ages: Wycliffe and John Trevisa, of whom more under the year 1387.

units.la: u Vid. infra ad An. 1380. x Pag. 162. y Cent. 6. cap. 1.
units.tr: u See below under the year 1380. x Page 162. y Century 6, chapter 1.

units.la: 1387. Huic itaque dictam Versionem libenter ascriberem. Optimè certè illius ætas Versioni convenit. Quùm in Præfatione enim Ricardi Armachani Summa adversus Armenos citetur; illam post medium Seculum XIV. scribi necesse est.
units.tr: I would gladly ascribe the said Version to him, since his age certainly suits the Version well. For since the Preface of Richard of Armagh's Summa against the Armenians is cited in it, it must have been written after the middle of the fourteenth century.

units.la: Obstat equidem, quod de Versione Anglicâ centum saltem annis ante Wiclefum atque adeò Trevisam coætaneum factâ Cl. Usserius ex Jamesio supra adduxit. Et sanè, quod neutiquam dissimulare vellem, in ipsâmet Versione nonnulla reperiuntur, quæ Seculum Trevisâ anterius primâ fronte demonstrare possent. In Codice enim Lambethano, Glossa ad Cap. XI. Danielis hæc habet: Ab isto tempore (pollutione Templi Hierosolymitani ab Antiocho Epiphane factâ) ad nos effluxerunt plusquam mille quadringenti anni. Secundùm istum quidem calculum, cùm Antiochus Hierosolymam expugnaverit anno ante Christum (juxta Eusebium) 171. Versio facta erit circa annum post Christum 1229. Verùm & Interpretem in calculis subducendis, & Jamesium in ætate illius ponendâ, errâsse manifestè patet. Interpres enim in Præfatione Lyranum sæpiùs, Armachanum semel citat; eundemque fuisse Præfationis nostræ ac Versionis Jamesianæ Authorem, constat ex testimonio de libris Scripturæ Canonicis; quod ex sui Interpretis Præfatione Jamesius ibidem protulit, in nostrâ Præfatione statim post principium totidem verbis repertum. Pari modo supra lapsus est Usserius; quùm Anglicanum Interpretem Jamesianum ad An. 1290. Præfationis autem à Caio citatæ Authorem ad Annum 1360. retulerit. Neque enim alius fuit Interpres ille à dictæ Præfationis Authore; uti supra ostensum est.
units.tr: It is true that there is an objection in the matter of the English Version said by James to have been made at least a hundred years before Wycliffe, and so before Trevisa, which Usher adduced from James. And indeed, which I would by no means wish to conceal, some things are found in the Version itself which at first sight might point to a century earlier than Trevisa. For in the Lambeth manuscript the gloss on Daniel chapter 11 reads: From that time (the pollution of the Temple of Jerusalem made by Antiochus Epiphanes) more than fourteen hundred years have flowed down to us. By this reckoning, since Antiochus took Jerusalem in the year 171 before Christ (according to Eusebius), the Version would have been made about the year 1229 after Christ. But that the translator erred in his calculations, and James in placing his age, is clearly evident. For the translator cites Lyra often in the Preface and Armachanus once; and that he was the author both of our Preface and of James's Version is established by the testimony about the canonical books of Scripture, which James cited from the Preface of his translator in that place, and which is found word for word in our Preface immediately after its beginning. In the same way Usher went astray above, when he referred James's English translator to the year 1290, but the author of the Preface cited by Caius to the year 1360. For that translator was not other than the author of the said Preface, as has been shown above.

units.la: 1340. Richardus Hampole.
units.tr: 1340. Richard Hampole.

units.la: De emendatione Peccatoris, cap 9. Si cupis ad amorem Dei pervenire, & succendi desiderio cælestium gaudiorum, & induci ad contemptum terrenorum; non sis negligens ad meditandum & legendum sacram Scripturam; & maximè in his locis, ubi mores instituit, & insidias diaboli cavere docet; ubi loquitur de amore Dei, & de contemplativâ vitâ. Difficiliores verò sententiæ disputantibus & ingeniosis viris longo tempore in sanctâ doctrinâ exercitatis relinquantur.
units.tr: On the Amendment of the Sinner, chapter 9. If you desire to come to the love of God, and to be kindled with longing for heavenly joys, and to be led to despise earthly things, do not be negligent in meditating upon and reading Holy Scripture; and especially in those places where it sets out morals and teaches us to beware the snares of the devil; where it speaks of the love of God and of the contemplative life. But the more difficult sayings should be left to those disputing and to men of talent who have long been trained in holy teaching.

units.la: Cæterùm quod habet Jo. Foxus à Cl. Usserio supra citatus, Richardum nempe nostrum ad versum illum Davidis [Ne auferas ab ore meo verbum
units.tr: Moreover, what John Foxe, cited above by Usher, reports, namely that our Richard set forth his judgment on the necessity of vernacular Scriptures in his comment on that verse of David [Take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth

units.la: {z} Cap. 12. {a} Pag. 155. {b} Pag. 155, 157. {c} Cap. 5. ad An. 1401. verbum veritatis usquequaque.] judicium suum de necessitate Scripturarum Vernacularum propositsse; id in Commentario illius in Psalmos, quod hodie vulgatum extat, nequaquam comparet. Sin Foxus Hampolum id in Versione sua Psalterii Anglicana, quam memorat, fecisse voluerit; me nunquam aliàs de eâ inaudivisse fateor. Res tamen veri haud absimilis est. Plures enim Tractatus Vernaculos in populi usum Hampolum elucubrasse constat. Ex his nonnulli in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ hodienum asservantur. Immo verò tandem comperi Versionem Psalmorum Anglicam ab Hampolo evulgatam fuisse, ex testimonio Authoris Speculi B. Virginis (de quo infra) qui in Prologo sic scribit. Paucos admodum Psalmos translatos dedi; ideò quòd vobis praestò sint ex Richardi Hampoli Versione, aut ex Bibliis Anglicis; modò licentiam eorum legendorum habeatis.
units.tr: {z} Chapter 12. {a} Page 155. {b} Pages 155, 157. {c} Chapter 5, under the year 1401. Psalm 119:43 — "take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth" — does not appear at all in his commentary on the Psalms which is printed today. But if Foxe wished to say that Hampole did this in his English version of the Psalter, which he mentions, I confess I have never heard of it before. The thing is not entirely unlikely, however. It is established that Hampole composed several vernacular treatises for the use of the people, and some of these are still preserved today in the Lambeth Library. Indeed I have at last discovered that an English version of the Psalms was published by Hampole, on the testimony of the author of the Mirror of the Blessed Virgin (of whom more below), who writes thus in the Prologue: I have given only a very few Psalms translated; because they are at hand for you from Richard Hampole's Version, or from the English Bible; provided you have permission to read them.

units.la: 1350. Nicolaus Cabasilas, Archiepiscopus Thessalonicensis.
units.tr: 1350. Nicholas Cabasilas, Archbishop of Thessalonica.

units.la: Expos. Liturg. cap. 21. Sacerdos cùm hoc exclamavit, & Doxologiam adjecit; cantandi hymni Trisagii sacro populo hoc veluti signum proponit; & cum ipsi ut mos est Doxologiæ Amen subjecerint, hymnum incipiunt. Post hymnum autem, Sacerdos jubet omnes non socorditer & negligenter stare, sed ea quæ fiunt & canuntur attendere. Πεθχωμεν enim, quo vocabulo utuntur, idem est, quod, Mentem adhibeamus, &c. Quia autem cum convenientibus cogitationibus necesse est stare & mysterii esse participes, & sacrarum ejus auditionum & contemplationum; nisi eis frustra sumus interfuturi & tempus consumpturi: hoc autem non est facile: propterea opus est quidem ipsos à nobis ipsis excitari & esse sobrios; opus est autem externâ admonitione; ut nostram mentem ab oblivione assiduè surreptam & ad vanas curas attractam possimus recipere. Hoc etiam sibi vult Canticum, quod canitur, dum pretiosa dona ad altare offeruntur, &c. Vult nos esse certamini intentos; qui ad Deum & divina mysteria accedimus; & non socorditer, sed cum studio & diligentiâ omnique reverentiâ in eis versari; sive videre, sive dicere, sive audire aliquid ex sacris oportebit. — τὰ ὑμνε ἀπέρχονται· μὴ ὃ τ' ὑμνον δ ἱερὺς κελεύει πάντας μὴ ῥαθύμως ἐν ἀμελῶς, ἀλλὰ τοῖς τελεσμένοις ἐν ἀδωσίνοις περιστῆναι τ' τὸν· τὸ γὰρ περιφαν μένῳ, τοῦτο δύνατα, &c. Ἐπεὶ δ μὴ τῆ περιστάντων λογισμῷ ἀναγκαῖον ἐστάναι, ἐν μετέχειν τ' τελετῆς ἐν τῷ ἱερῶν αὐτῆς ἀκουσμάτων ἐν θεαμάτων, &c. ἀτι ὁρᾶν, εἴτε λέγειν, εἴτε ἐν ἀκοέων τι δείσει ἱερῶν.
units.tr: Exposition of the Liturgy, chapter 21. When the priest has cried out this and added the Doxology, he sets before the holy people the singing of the Trisagion hymn as a kind of signal; and when they have added the Amen to the Doxology, as is the custom, they begin the hymn. After the hymn, the priest bids everyone not to stand carelessly and negligently, but to attend to what is being done and sung. For the word they use, pthechōmen, means the same as, let us give heed with our mind, etc. Since it is necessary to stand with gathered thoughts, and to be partakers of the mystery and of its sacred hearings and contemplations, otherwise we shall be present in vain and waste the time; but this is not easy; therefore we need to be roused by ourselves and to be sober; but we also need external admonition, so that we may recover our mind, which is constantly stolen away by forgetfulness and drawn to vain cares. This is also the meaning of the Canticle which is sung while the precious gifts are offered at the altar, etc. It wishes us to be intent on the struggle, we who draw near to God and to the divine mysteries; and to be occupied with them not carelessly, but with zeal and diligence and all reverence; whether it be necessary to see, or to speak, or to hear anything of the sacred things. — [ta hymna aperchontai; mē ho tōn hymnōn hieros keleuei pantas mē rhathymōs, all' … ] [the hymn goes on; the holy one bids all not to stand carelessly and negligently, but to stand around the things being performed with attention; for that which is around …]. [Epei de mē tē peristantōn logismō anankaion estanai, en metechein tēs telethēs en tōn hierōn autēs akousmatōn en theamatōn, etc. … idein, eite legein, eite akouein ti dei hierōn.] [Since it is necessary to stand with the thought of those standing around, and to partake of the rite in its sacred hearings and sights, etc. … to see, or to speak, or to hear something of the sacred things.]

units.la: Cap. 22. Sed quid sibi vult hic sacrarum literarum lectio. Si vis quidem usum scire; dictum est. (supra dixerat, divinorum eloquiorum auditionem esse magnum bonum, μέγα τι ἀγαθὸν. Ἐστιν ἡ τῶν Θεῶν λόγιων ἀκοῆς.) ἅνεπάσυς.) Nos enim praeparant & praepurgant ante magnam mysteriorum sanctificationem. παρακαλίσων γὶ ήμας ἱ περικαθαίρωμεν πεὶ τὶ μεγάλα τὰς μυστείων ᴍγιασμί.
units.tr: Chap. 22. But what is the point of reading the sacred letters here? If you want to know its use, it has been stated. (Above he had said that hearing the divine oracles is a great good, μέγα τι ἀγαθόν. It is the hearing of the words of the gods [Ἐστιν ἡ τῶν Θεῶν λόγιων ἀκοῆς].) [ἅνεπάσυς.] For they prepare us and purify us before the great sanctification of the mysteries. They exhort us to purify ourselves before the great sanctification of the mysteries [παρακαλίσων γὶ ήμας ἱ περικαθαίρωμεν πεὶ τὶ μεγάλα τὰς μυστείων ᴍγιασμί].

units.la: 1357. Richardus Radulphi, Archiepiscopus Armachanus.
units.tr: 1357. Richard FitzRalph, Archbishop of Armagh.

units.la: Summa adv. errores Armen. lib. 9. cap. 1. Quaeritur, nunquid aliqua certa verborum Forma sit necessaria ad consecrationem corporis & sanguinis Christi, & quae est illa? Richardus. Non intelligo, quid Formam verborum certam appellant. Aut enim illud appellant certae linguae verba certa; & non est dubium quod dicunt. Nemo enim Christianus dubitat, quin ita vere consecratur in una lingua, sicut in alia; quoniam sic fecerunt Apostoli & sic tradiderunt facere. Matthaeus enim scripsit Evangelium in Hebraico, Johannes in Graeco, Marcus in Italico. Et Paulus Epistolam ad Romanos [Corinthios proculdubio legendum, & ita quidem legit Codex MS. Bibliothecae Lambethanae,] ubi de ista consecratione fit mentio, etiam scripsit in Graeco; & singuli in illis linguis, in quibus scripserunt, non dubium consecrare docuerunt: unde constat in singulis consecrationem posse fieri. Immo videtur, quod linguae omnes ob hoc erant datae Apostolis, sicut legitur Actuum secundo: ut modum consecrationis hujus Sacramenti, sicut & alia salutis documenta, singulis nationibus singularum linguarum crederent exercenda.
units.tr: Summa against the errors of the Armenians, book 9, chapter 1. It is asked whether any fixed form of words is necessary for the consecration of the body and blood of Christ, and what that form is? Richard: I do not understand what they mean by a fixed form of words. If they mean fixed words of a particular language, there is no doubt about what they say. No Christian doubts that the consecration is equally valid in one language as in another, since the Apostles did so and handed down that it should be done so. For Matthew wrote the Gospel in Hebrew, John in Greek, Mark in Italian. And Paul wrote the Epistle to the Romans [undoubtedly to be read as Corinthians, and so indeed reads the manuscript codex of the Lambeth Library], where mention is made of this consecration, also in Greek; and each of them, in the languages in which they wrote, taught without doubt that consecration should be performed, so it is plain that consecration can be done in each. Indeed it seems that all tongues were given to the Apostles for this reason, as we read in Acts 2: that they should entrust the manner of consecrating this sacrament, like the other tokens of salvation, to the nations of each language to be practised.

units.la: Locum e Defensorio Curatorum ejus Cl. Usserius supra f leviter memoravit. Illum igitur integrum subjiciendum duxi. Extat itaque MS. in Bibliotheca Lambethana istius Defensorium Curatorum, seu Propositio facta in Consistorio Avenione coram Papa & Cardinalibus contra Fratres Mendicantes, Anno 1357. die 8. Novembris. Inibi paulo ante medium haec leguntur. Item est aliud dampnum tam grave, quod cedit ad consumptionem & evacuationem doctrinae in Saecularibus cujuslibet Facultatis; scilicet quod isti Ordines Mendicantium propter infinita lucra, quae mediantibus praedictis privilegiis de Confessionibus & Sepulturis & aliis acquirunt; tantum multiplicati sunt in Conventibus & personis Conventuum; quod non reperitur in Studiis Communibus de Facultate Artium, S. Theologiae, & Juris Canonici, nisi raro, aliquis utilis multum liber venalis. Scilicet omnes emuntur a Fratribus; ita ut in singulis Conventibus sit una grandis ac nobilis Libraria: & ut singuli Fratres habentes statum
units.tr: Cl. Usher above lightly mentioned a passage from the Defensorium Curatorum of this author (f). I therefore thought it right to subjoin the whole of it. There is therefore a manuscript of this Defensorium Curatorum in the Lambeth Library, or Proposition made in Consistory at Avignon before the Pope and Cardinals against the Friars Mendicant, in the year 1357, on 8 November. In it, a little before the middle, these things are read: Likewise there is another loss so grave that it leads to the consumption and emptying of learning among the secular clergy of every faculty: namely, that these orders of Mendicants, through the infinite gains which they acquire by the aforesaid privileges concerning confessions, burials and other matters, have so multiplied in their convents and in the number of their members, that in the common studies of the faculties of Arts, of Sacred Theology and of Canon Law, one scarcely finds any useful and very cheap book for sale, unless rarely. All are bought up by the Friars, so that in each convent there is one large and noble library; and so that individual friars, holding a status

units.la: e Prodiit Opus istud typis semel excusum. Verum exemplar impressum ad manum non est. f Cap. 5. ad An. 1358. in studiis, quales sunt modò innumeri; nobilem etiam habeant librariam. Unde ego de mihi subjectis Rectoribus tres aut quatuor misi ad Studium; & dictum est mihi, quòd quia nec Bibliam eis utilem, nec alios libros Theologiæ venales eis congruos ibi poterant reperire; ad suam propriam sunt reversi, aut unus saltem eorum jam rediit. Tractatus iste à Joanne Trevisa sub finem ejusdem Seculi Anglicè conversus est. Versio habetur MS. in Amplissimâ Bibliothecâ Reverendi Viri, Thomæ Tenison, Theologi nostrâtis. Cæterùm Fraterculos S. Scripturæ Codices incarcerandi potiùs quàm lectitandi animo undique conquisivisse, res à Melchiore Adamo in Vitâ Lutheri narrata innuit: Lutherum nempe, utcunque avidum librorum helluonem, & sacræ lectionis imprimis cupientissimum, nunquam Scripturæ Codicem nancisci potuisse; donec forte fortunâ exemplar quoddam in obscuro Bibliothecæ Cœnobii sui angulo, tineis & blattis semesum, invenit.
units.tr: e This work was printed once. However, a printed copy is not at hand. f Chapter 5, under the year 1358. in the schools, which are now countless; they also have a noble library. Hence I sent three or four of the Rectors subject to me to the school; and I was told that, since they could find there neither a Bible useful to them nor other books of Theology for sale suitable to them, they have returned to their own homes, or at least one of them has already returned. This treatise was translated into English by John Trevisa towards the end of the same century. The version is held in manuscript in the very ample library of the Reverend Thomas Tenison, our theologian. Moreover, that the little friars gathered up copies of Holy Scripture from every quarter with the intention of locking them up rather than reading them is suggested by a matter related by Melchior Adam in the Life of Luther: namely, that Luther, however much a greedy devourer of books and most eager above all for sacred reading, could never get hold of a copy of Scripture, until by chance he found a certain copy, half eaten by moths and worms, in an obscure corner of the library of his monastery.

units.la: 1360. Bartholomæus de Glanvillâ, Anglicus dictus.
units.tr: 1360. Bartholomew de Glanville, the Englishman, so called.

units.la: Ad calcem librorum ejus de Proprietatibus Rerum in Codice MS. Lambethano, reperiuntur tres Sermones; primus in illud, Psal. XIX. 8. Præceptum Domini lucidum, illuminans oculos. Reliqui in illud, Job XXXVIII. 37. Concentum cœli quis dormire faciet? In singulis Encomium S. Scripturæ contexuit; unicum id argumentum tractans. In ultimo autem Cœlum per S. Scripturam allegoricè interpretatus; eam omnes scientias, omnia ad fidem necessaria continere, doctis etiam indoctisque pariter patere, fusissimè docet. Omnes humili sermone invitat; ne ipso superbo eloquio non audeat accedere mens tardiuscula & inerudita, quasi pauper ad divitem. Et ex hoc liquet mirabile in hac Scriptura; quòd sermo eius etiam est manifestus (eloquentem antea dixerat) ut parva nutriantur, & magna oblectentur ingenia; secundum Augustinum: manifestus & aperta continens; ut amicus familiaris ad cor loquitur doctorum & indoctorum. —Sola sapientiam veram & completam notitiam tradit; quâ perveniatur ad vitam æternam, &c.
units.tr: In the manuscript codex of his books On the Properties of Things in the Lambeth Library, there are three sermons at the end; the first on Psalm 19:8, The commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes. The others on Job 38:37, Who can make the concord of heaven sleep? In each he has woven an encomium of Scripture, treating this single theme. In the last, interpreting heaven allegorically through Scripture, he teaches at great length that Scripture contains all sciences and all things necessary for faith, and is equally open to the learned and the unlearned. He invites all with a humble style; lest a mind somewhat slow and unlearned should not dare to approach it through a proud eloquence, like a poor man to a rich one. And from this it is clear that there is a wonderful thing in this Scripture: that its speech is also plain (he had said earlier, eloquent) so that small minds are nourished and great minds delighted; according to Augustine: plain, and containing open things; so that it speaks to the heart of the learned and the unlearned as a familiar friend. —It alone delivers true wisdom and complete knowledge, by which one attains eternal life, etc.

units.la: 1360. Joannes Thoresbeius, Archiepiscopus Eboracensis.
units.tr: 1360. John Thoresby, Archbishop of York.

units.la: Extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Pastorale ejus, seu Injunctiones Clericis Provinciæ Eboracensis datæ, Anglicè. Inibi Oratio Dominica, Symbolum Apostolicum, & Decalogus linguâ vernaculâ traduntur, & Expositione luculentâ illustrantur. Firmiter autem injungit git Archiepiscopus, ut singuli Christiani ista omnia memoriter discant; & an recte didicerint, à Sacerdotibus suis crebrò interrogentur. Never, inquit, aliquis ignorantiam & imperitiam discendi prætendat; Pater noster Archiepiscopus constituit & præcepit, ut singula populo publicè enarrentur lingua Anglicana. In Explicatione Symboli hæc habet: Fides nostra nos docet, Deum instituisse integrum Symbolum, & jussisse ut homines id ediscerent atque intelligerent & alios docerent. Siquè Præsules in hoc muneri suo desint; Christus edixit ipsos etiam lapides exclamaturos; voluitque ut Seculares viri [Domini] ob Præsulum defectum seu negligentiam, legem Dei linguâ Vernaculâ discant & edoceant. Iterum in Expositione quarti præcepti Decalogi: Populus diebus Dominicis res divinas solummodò curent. Tunc Officio divino cum reverentiâ & devotione attendas; & Orationem Dominicam, Symbolum, Salutationem Angelicam, devotâ mente recites; aliasque etiam pias Orationes, si possis. Quinetiam legem divinam maternâ linguâ prædicatam audito. Id enim tibi utilius est, quàm multas audire Missas.
units.tr: His Pastoral, or Injunctions given to the clergy of the Province of York, in English, is extant in manuscript in the Lambeth Library. There the Lord's Prayer, the Apostles' Creed and the Decalogue are handed down in the vernacular and illustrated with a clear exposition. The Archbishop firmly enjoins that all Christians learn all these things by heart, and that their priests frequently question them whether they have learned them correctly. Never, he says, let anyone plead ignorance and inexperience in learning; our Archbishop, Father, has decreed and commanded that each thing be publicly explained to the people in the English tongue. In his exposition of the Creed he has this: Our faith teaches us that God instituted the whole Creed, and commanded that men should learn it by heart, understand it and teach others. If the prelates are lacking in this duty, Christ has declared that even the stones will cry out; and He willed that laymen, because of the defect or negligence of the prelates, should learn and teach the law of God in the vernacular tongue. Again, in the exposition of the fourth commandment of the Decalogue: Let the people attend only to divine things on the Lord's Days. Then attend to the divine Office with reverence and devotion; and recite with a devout mind the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, the Angelic Salutation, and other pious prayers too, if you can. Moreover, hear the divine law preached in your mother tongue. For this is more useful to you than to hear many Masses.

units.la: Iterum in Expos. sexti Mandati. Quinetiam improbi Præsules & Curati hominum tam animas quàm corpora interficiunt, verbum Dei subtrahendo, & bonæ vitæ exemplum denegando. Nullus enim fidem aliasque virtutes spiritualiter vivens exercere potest, nisi Dei verbum audiendo & observando. Atque adeò illi sub pœnâ damnationis tenentur docere istud Dei verbum, quod humanæ animæ cibus est. Illos increpare præsules & sacerdotes videtur; qui vulgarem sacræ Scripturæ lectionem plebi suæ interdixerunt. Factum id primùm in Angliâ à quibusdam Prælatis circa illud tempus non malè censeri queat. Idque factum Thoresbio culpare integrum fuit. Nondum enim latum erat Concilii Oxoniensis decretum de Scripturis vernaculè non legendis. Id in animo autem habuisse Thoresbeium, nullus facilè dubitabit; qui integrum Pastorale perlegerit, noveritque quantâ mordacitate, quali sincerè religionis zelo ille Præsulum & Fraterculorum sui temporis vitia, errores & præstigias ubivis insectetur.
units.tr: Again, in the exposition of the sixth commandment: Moreover, wicked prelates and parish priests destroy the souls as well as the bodies of men, by withholding the Word of God and by denying the example of a good life. For no one living spiritually can exercise faith and other virtues unless he hears and observes the word of God. And so they are bound, under pain of damnation, to teach that word of God, which is the food of the human soul. He seems to rebuke those prelates and priests who forbade the common reading of Holy Scripture to their people. It can fairly be judged that this was first done in England by certain prelates around that time. And it was entirely fitting for Thoresby to blame it. For the decree of the Council of Oxford on not reading Scripture in the vernacular had not yet been issued. That Thoresby had this in mind, no one will easily doubt, who reads through the whole Pastoral and knows with what biting wit, and with what sincere zeal for religion, he attacks everywhere the vices, errors and deceits of the prelates and friars of his time.

units.la: Thoresbeio in hac sententiâ præivit Robertus Pullanus, Cardinalis; cujus insigne testimonium antea omissum, hic loci apponam. Sic igitur ille in Sermone 16. MS. Sunt nonnulli omnium, quos terra sustinet, miserrimi; qui nec boni in se aliquid habent; & cum in aliis audierint vel viderint, non diligunt, sed invident: Et eos quos ad divinam lectionem vel prædicationem proficisci cognoverint, à bono proposito virulentis diffuasionibus, quantum in ipsis est, revocant.
units.tr: Robert Pullan, the Cardinal, went before Thoresby in this opinion; I will set here his notable testimony, which was previously omitted. Thus he speaks in his Sermon 16 (manuscript): There are some of all those whom the earth bears who are most wretched; who have nothing good in themselves; and when they hear or see good in others, they do not love it, but envy it. And those whom they know to be setting out for divine reading or preaching, they turn away from their good purpose, as far as in them lies, with virulent dissuasions.

units.la: 1361. Simon Langham, Episcopus Eliensis, postea Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis.
units.tr: 1361. Simon Langham, Bishop of Ely, afterwards Archbishop of Canterbury.

units.la: Sermo ejus in Synodo factus habetur MS. penès me, ex Bibliothecâ Collegii D. Petri apud Cantabrigienses descriptus. In illo sequentia reperiuntur. ‘Quia sine Decalogi observatione salus animarum non consistit; exhortamur in Domino firmiter injungentes, ut unusquisque pastor animarum & quilibet sacerdos parochiarum sciat Decalogum, i. e. decem mandata legis Mosaicæ; eademque suo populo subjecto frequenter prædicet & exponat, &c. Et hi, qui sunt Sacerdotes, maximè sciant quæ exiguntur ad veræ Confessionis & Pœnitentiæ Sacramentum, formamque baptizandi; & doceant frequenter laicos in idiomate communi, &c. In Ecclesiâ quoque divinum Officium integrè fiat & devotè; ut videlicet lectiones, hymni, Psalmi, & alia quæ in Dei laudem recitantur in Ecclesiâ, integram habeant verborum prolationem, mentisque ad sensus verborum devotam attentionem: ne, quod absit, pro hostiâ vivâ & integrâ offeratur hostia mutilata vel mortua, &c. Provideant etiam attentius Ecclesiarum Rectores & Sacerdotes parochiales; ut pueri parochiarum suarum diligenter doceantur & sciant Orationem Dominicam & Symbolum & Salutationem B. Virginis, & crucis signaculo se rectè consignare. Et quia, ut audivimus, etiam quidam adulti hæc ignorant; præcipimus ut cùm laici ad confessionem accedunt, diligenter examinentur, utrùm scierint prædicta; & si quid expedit, in eis à sacerdotibus instruantur.
units.tr: His sermon delivered in the Synod is found in a manuscript in my possession, copied from the library of St Peter's College at Cambridge. In it the following passages occur. 'Since the salvation of souls does not stand without the observance of the Decalogue, we earnestly exhort and enjoin in the Lord that every minister of souls and every parish priest should know the Decalogue, that is, the ten commandments of the Mosaic law, and should often preach and expound the same to the people committed to him, etc. And those who are priests should especially know what is required for the sacrament of true Confession and Repentance, and the form of baptizing; and they should frequently teach the laity in the common language, etc. In the church also let the divine Office be performed whole and devoutly; so that the lessons, hymns, Psalms and the other things recited in the church to the praise of God are pronounced in full, and that the mind gives devout attention to the sense of the words; lest, which God forbid, a mutilated or dead victim be offered in place of a living and whole victim, etc. Let the rectors of the churches and the parish priests also take more careful thought that the boys of their parishes be diligently taught and know the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, and the Salutation of the Blessed Virgin, and that they rightly sign themselves with the sign of the cross. And because, as we have heard, some adults also are ignorant of these things, we command that when the laity come to confession they be carefully examined as to whether they know the aforesaid things; and if anything is needed, they should be instructed in it by the priests.'

units.la: 1380. Joannes Wiclefus.
units.tr: 1380. John Wycliffe.

units.la: In Ostiolo, seu Tractatu adversus Transubstantiationem vernaculo, Norimbergæ Anno 1546. excuso, pag. 4. ‘Paulus Apostolus ubique ostendit omnes pœnitentiam agere debere. Præ aliis autem pœnitere debet Clerus; utpote qui Deo semper adversatus est & in Veteri & in Novâ Lege, Prophetas Dei verbum annunciantes interficiendo. Illi olim quidem, ut probè nostis, neque ipsi Dei filio pepercerunt; cùm Sæcularis Judex illum liberare voluisset; & pari modo insecuti sunt Apostolos & Martyres, qui verbum divinum illis verè annunciarunt. Hodiè verò læresin esse clamant S. Scripturas Anglicè prædicare; adeóque etiam condemnant Spiritum S. qui linguas Christi Apostolis, uti scriptum est, donavit; ut in omnibus dialectis totius orbis à Deo constitutis, verbum divinum praedicarent. Quinetiam Spiritus S. super Gentiles descendit, quemadmodum super Apostolos in Hierosolymis descenderat. Sin vero Christus pro infinitâ suî misericordiâ Spiritum S. Gentilibus immiserit, atque illos sanctissimi sui verbi participes fecerit; quamobrem à Nobis in hac gente positis, qui Christiani sumus, auferatur? Videte annon idem sit Christi verba haereticos incusare ac Christum ipsum Haereticum efficere. Si mea enim verba sint mendacia; tunc ego, qui verba loquor, mendax sum. Si mea igitur verba sint Haeretica; ego etiam qui verba loquor, Haereticus ero. Idem igitur est Dei verbum in quacunque linguâ, ac Deum ipsum verbi authorem, haereseos damnare. Is enim ejusque verbum, unum idemque sunt; & separari non possunt. Et si verbum ejus sit vita mundi; sicut scriptum est: Non in solo pane vivet homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit ex ore Dei; & omne Dei verbum sit vita animae humanae; quod ait D. Joannes; quomodo, per Deum, ausus est Antichristus id à nobis Christianis auferre, & efficere, ut populus fame pereat aut in haeresin incidat.
units.tr: In his little book, or treatise against Transubstantiation, in the vernacular, printed at Nuremberg in the year 1546, page 4: "Paul the Apostle everywhere shows that all men ought to do penance. But above others the clergy ought to repent; as those who have always opposed God, both in the Old and in the New Law, by killing the prophets who announced God's word. Indeed they, as you well know, did not spare even the Son of God himself, when the secular judge wished to free him; and in like manner they pursued the Apostles and the martyrs, who truly announced the divine word to them. But today they cry out that it is heresy to preach the Holy Scriptures in English; and so they also condemn the Holy Spirit, who gave the tongues to Christ's Apostles, as it is written, so that they might preach the divine word in all the languages of the whole world established by God. Moreover, the Holy Spirit descended upon the Gentiles just as he had descended upon the Apostles in Jerusalem. But if Christ, in his infinite mercy, has bestowed the Holy Spirit upon the Gentiles and made them partakers of his most holy word, why should it be taken away from us, who are Christians, placed in this nation? See whether it is not the same thing to condemn Christ's words as heretical and to make Christ himself a heretic. For if my words are lies, then I, who speak the words, am a liar. If therefore my words are heretical, then I too, who speak the words, will be a heretic. Therefore to condemn God's word in any language is the same as to condemn God himself, the author of the word. For he and his word are one and the same, and cannot be separated. And if his word is the life of the world, as it is written: 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God'; and if every word of God is the life of the human soul, as St John says; then, by God, how has Antichrist dared to take it away from us Christians, and bring it about that the people perish by famine or fall into heresy."

units.la: In Prologo in Expos. Orationis Domin. Anglicè MS. penes Cl. Tenisonum. Quùm Oratio Dominica optima sit omnium orationum; (cùm illâ enim omnes aliæ concludi debent, modò Deo gratæ sint) verba ejus ab omnibus sunt memoriter tenenda, & intellectus verborum investigandus. Cúmque Dei veritas non magis in unâ quàm alterâ linguâ sit posita; quicunque autem melius vivit & melius docet; Deo melius placet, cujuscunque demum sit linguæ; ista igitur oratio Anglicè enarrata tam indoctam plebem aedificare queat, quam doctos Latiné. Porrò cùm Evangelium sit Christi, idque Christus populo praedicari jusserit; ut omnes illud ediscerent, scirent, & juxta ejus praecepta viverent; quare nobis non licet linguâ Anglicanâ conscribere Evangelium, aliaque opuscula Evangelium explicantia ad Christianorum aedificationem & animae humanae utilitatem; prout à Concionatore plebi verè praedicantur. Quòd si enim conscribendum non esset; eâdem ratione neque praedicandum esset. Procul absit à Christianis ista haeresis & blasphemia. A Diabolo enim proficiscitur; uti Christus ait, Diabolus est mendaciorum parens. Sic & secta Pharisaica à Deo execrata est; quæ, ut Pauli verbis utar, Jesum non amat, & Evangelium populo praedicari prohibet. Si quis enim artem aliquam humano generi necessariam calleat; aliosque doctrinae suae capaces docere nolit; illis ignorantiae causa est. Similiter dicendum est de Evangelii versione in linguam vernaculam, in vulgi usum & scientiam. Quis Christum minus amat, quis à Deo execratur; nisi qui istiusmodi versionem impedit? Ipse enim Satan est Christi adversarius. Impia autem ista secta otiosum dormire Evangelium cupit; & licet Christi nomen praeferat, parum tamen de illo praedicat. Sic fecerunt olim Mahometes & Sergius Monachus; cum legem ex arbitrio confictam evulgarunt, nonnihil tamen de Evangelio ad carnalem intelligentiam deflexum immiscentes; quorum fraude factum est, ut Gentiles sint hodienum à fide alieni. Similiter prava ista gens integram Evangelii veritatem non praedicat. Vitam enim praeceptis ejus contrariam ducunt; Christusque filios suos ex operibus judicium ferre jubet. In exponendo autem primo Orationis articulo, haec habet: Pater Noster, qui es in coelis: Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Et ita quidem Christus Apostolos integram istam orationem docuit. Scitote autem, quod nec Latine nec Gallice; sed lingua illis vulgari & usitata. Istam enim melius norunt. Ecce regulam omnibus Christianis, cujuscunque sint linguae, positam: nimirum gratum esse Deo sacrificium, scire Orationem Dominicam, Evangelium, aliasque S. Scripturae partes animae saluti necessarias; & juxta illa vitam instituere; sive illis explicentur Latine, sive Anglice, sive Gallice, sive Belgice, sive quavis alia lingua, quam populus intelligit. Clero itaque laetandum esset, si populus legem divinam sciret; & laborandum omnibus, quibuscunque possent, mediis, ut populum sibi commissum veritatem scire efficerent.
units.tr: In the Prologue to his exposition of the Lord's Prayer, in English, manuscript in the possession of the distinguished Tenison: "Since the Lord's Prayer is the best of all prayers (for all others must be concluded with it, provided they are pleasing to God), its words must be held in memory by all, and the meaning of the words must be sought out. And since the truth of God is no more placed in one language than in another; and since whoever lives better and teaches better pleases God better, whatever language he speaks; this prayer, explained in English, can edify the unlearned people as much as the learned are edified in Latin. Furthermore, since the Gospel belongs to Christ, and Christ commanded it to be preached to the people, so that all might learn it, know it, and live according to his precepts; why should we not be allowed to write the Gospel in the English tongue, and other little works explaining the Gospel, for the edification of Christians and the profit of the human soul, just as they are truly preached to the people by the preacher? For if it were not to be written down, by the same reasoning it would not be to be preached. Far be such a heresy and blasphemy from Christians. For it proceeds from the Devil; as Christ says, the Devil is the father of lies. So too the Pharisaical sect has been cursed by God, which, to use Paul's words, does not love Jesus, and forbids the Gospel to be preached to the people. For if someone knows some art necessary to the human race, and is unwilling to teach others capable of his teaching, he is the cause of their ignorance. The same must be said of the translation of the Gospel into the vernacular tongue, for the use and knowledge of the common people. Who loves Christ less, who is more cursed by God, than the one who hinders such a translation? For he is Satan himself, Christ's adversary. This impious sect wishes the Gospel to lie idle and asleep; and although it bears the name of Christ, it preaches little of him. So once did Mahomet and the monk Sergius, when they spread a law invented at their own pleasure, mixing in some things from the Gospel bent to a carnal understanding; by whose deceit it has come about that the Gentiles to this day are alien from the faith. In like manner this perverse people does not preach the whole truth of the Gospel. For they regard their life as contrary to his precepts; and Christ bids his sons to judge by works. In expounding the first article of the Prayer, he has this: 'Our Father, who art in heaven: hallowed be thy name.' And indeed Christ taught the Apostles this whole prayer in that way. Note, however, that it was not in Latin nor in French, but in their own common and familiar tongue; for they knew that best. Here is a rule laid down for all Christians, of whatever language they may be: namely, that it is pleasing to God that people should know the Lord's Prayer, the Gospel, and other parts of Scripture necessary for the salvation of the soul, and should order their lives according to them; whether these are explained in Latin, in English, in French, in Dutch, or in any other language which the people understand. Therefore it would be a joy to the clergy if the people knew the divine law; and everyone should labour, by whatever means they can, to make the people committed to them know the truth."

units.la: Comment. in Psalmos, quod prolixum admodum scripsit lingua vernacula, MS. in Bibliotheca Lambethana. In Psalm. XLVII. Magnatum Laicorum officium explicans, ista monet: Sepositio autem humano consilio, Legem Dei legant; ejusque studio sedulo incumbant; eamque intelligant; atque inibi optima regiminis praecepta invenient.
units.tr: His commentary on the Psalms, which he wrote at great length in the vernacular, manuscript in the Lambeth Library. On Psalm 47, explaining the duty of lay magnates, he advises as follows: "Setting aside human counsel, let them read the Law of God and apply themselves diligently to its study; and let them understand it; and there they will find the best precepts of government."

units.la: In Psal. LVIII. Christus jubet, ut nullus articulis fidei addere aut detrahere praesumat; neque eam aliter formula concipere, quam Scripturae textus docet. Aliter errore tenemur.
units.tr: On Psalm 58: Christ commands that no one presume to add to or take away from the articles of faith, nor to frame them in any form other than the text of Scripture teaches. Otherwise we are held in error.

units.la: In Psal. LXXIV. Olim in Ecclesia praeceptum fuit, antequam avaritia radices egerat; ut postquam Evangelium Latine lectum fuerat, plebi lingua vernacula interpretaretur.
units.tr: On Psalm 74: "Long ago it was commanded in the Church, before avarice had taken root, that after the Gospel had been read in Latin, it should be interpreted to the people in the vernacular tongue."

units.la: Extat MS. in Lambethana aliisque plurimis Angliae Bibliothecis, Vernaculum Wiclefi Manuale; cui titulus est Pauper Rusticus. Continet autem complures Tractatus pios, & in his Decalogi Expositionem; in cujus Epilogo haec leguntur. Ista sunt Dei Mandata decem; ex quorum normâ omnes tam viros quàm foeminas vitam suam dirigere oportet; si modò salutem consequi velint. Atque adeò Christus omnibus in aeternam utiam vitam intrare volentibus præcipit, ut ista mandata observent. Eadem etiam Dei mandata cunctì liberos & servos suos docere debent. Propterea enim Deus generale universo suo populo præceptum dedit ; ut singuli filiis suis annunciarent ; quemodo Deus populum suum Ægypto eduxerit. Fritque, inquit Deus, quasi signaculum in manibus tuis, & memoriale ante oculos tuos ; & lex Domini semper erit in ore tuo, &c.
units.tr: There exists, in manuscript in the Lambeth Library and in very many other libraries of England, a vernacular manual of Wycliffe, entitled "The Poor Rustic." It contains several devout treatises, and among them an exposition of the Decalogue; in whose epilogue the following is read: "These are the ten commandments of God; by whose rule all men and women alike ought to direct their lives, if indeed they wish to obtain salvation. And so Christ commands all who wish to enter eternal life to keep these commandments. All these commandments of God ought also to be taught by everyone to their children and servants. For God gave a general precept to his whole people for this reason: that each should announce to his sons how God led his people out of Egypt. 'And it shall be,' says God, 'as a sign upon your hands, and a memorial before your eyes; and the law of the Lord shall always be in your mouth,' etc."

units.la: Lib. de Quæstionibus variis contra Clerum, in illud 1 Cor. III. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, &c. Anglicè, MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, cap. 3. Evangelium Joannis refert Pontifices & Pharisæos de Christo dixisse: Si illum sinamus; omnes in illum credent; & Romani venient, nostramque gentem & regionem auferent. Christum enim veriti sunt; ne si verba ejus in vulgus propalarentur, Romani venirent, & Pontifices simul ac Pharisæos male perderent. Similiter præsules & Pharisæi juncto hodie consilio dicunt: Occultemus legem Dei; ne Seculares Proceres veniant, & Baronias nostras reditusque auferant. Ab illo die, dicit Evangelium, Christum interficere quæsiverunt. Ita nunc hi majori etiam scelere occidunt illos, qui veritatem Evangelii Christi docent; atque adeò Christum in populi sui animabus efficaci fide vivere non sinunt. Fides enim oritur solummodo ex scientia legis; quam à populo tam nefariè abscondunt. Atque hoc modo Christum interficere crudelius longè est, quàm proprium ipsius corpus interfecisse. Exinde enim maximum humano generi evenit bonum, salus nempe electorum ad salutem. Ex alio autem Christum occidendi modo, sc. ex occultatione legis divinæ, nulla utilitas provenit. Adversatur enim Christi voluntati, & Diabolo gratissimus est, & animarum jacturæ causa. S. Paulus igitur ait: Si opertum est Evangelium nostrum; his qui pereunt est opertum; in quibus Deus hujus mundi excæcavit mentes infidelium. Quicunque autem cogitat malitiam, quam Pontifices & Scribæ & Clerici contra Christum in terris positum demonstrârunt; ejusdem generis malitiam in nostratibus Episcopis & Religiosis renovatam inveniet.
units.tr: From the book of Various Questions against the Clergy, on the text of 1 Corinthians 3: "Other foundation can no man lay, etc." In English, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, chapter 3: "The Gospel of John reports that the chief priests and Pharisees said of Christ: If we let him alone, all men will believe on him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation. For they feared Christ, lest if his words were spread abroad among the people, the Romans would come and utterly destroy the chief priests together with the Pharisees. Likewise the prelates and Pharisees, with counsel joined today, say: Let us hide the law of God, lest the secular lords come and take away our baronies and revenues. From that day, says the Gospel, they sought to kill Christ. So now these, with even greater wickedness, kill those who teach the truth of Christ's Gospel; and thus they do not allow Christ to live by effective faith in the souls of his people. For faith arises only from knowledge of the law, which they so wickedly hide from the people. And in this way to kill Christ is far more cruel than to have killed his very body. For from the latter the greatest good has come to the human race, namely the salvation of the elect unto salvation. But from the other way of killing Christ, namely by concealing the divine law, no benefit comes. For it is opposed to Christ's will, is most pleasing to the Devil, and is the cause of the loss of souls. St Paul therefore says: If our Gospel is hidden, it is hidden to those who perish; in whom God has blinded the minds of unbelievers. And whoever considers the malice which the chief priests and scribes and clergy showed against Christ on earth, will find the same kind of malice renewed in our own bishops and religious."

units.la: De Versione S.Scripturæ à Wiclefo factâ ista dudum adnotavi Anglicam totius S.Scripturæ versionem ex vulgatâ Hieronymi versione concinnavit, An. 1383. prout Codex MS. in Collegio Emanuelis Cantab. asservatus in fronte ascriptum habet. Habetur etenim MS. ista Versio in Bibliothecâ dicti Collegii pulcherrimè exarata; uti & in Bibliothecâ Cottoniana sub effigie Claudii, E.2. & in Bibliothecâ Regiâ Westmonasterienfi, ut & in Lambethanâ, & Collegii Sionensis Londinatis. Porrò extat in Bibliothecâ publicâ Academiæ Cantab.
units.tr: Concerning the version of Holy Scripture made by Wiclef, I have noted the following for some time: the English version of the whole of Holy Scripture was compiled from Jerome's Vulgate translation in 1383, as a manuscript kept in Emmanuel College, Cambridge, has written at its front. This version is indeed found there, beautifully written out, in the library of that college; and also in the Cotton Library under the bust of Claudius, E.2, and in the Royal Library at Westminster, as well as in Lambeth Library and the library of Sion College, London. Moreover, it exists in the public library of the University of Cambridge.

units.la: {a} Matth. XIX. {b} Exod. XIV. {c} 2 Cor. IV. {d} Append. ad Hist. Literar. pag. 53. Versio Novi Testamenti, eodem autore; cui praefigitur prolixa admodum introductio de auctoritate atque usu S. Scripturae. His adde exemplar omnium pulcherrimum in Bibliotheca Norfolciana, 2. vol. sol. & bina ejusdem Versionis Novi Testamenti exemplaria MSS. Introductione tamen destituta, reperiri in Bibliotheca Lambethana. Horum alterum Epistolam ad Laodicenses exhibet. Istius versioni praeponitur praefatio; in cujus fine haec nota legitur: Isthaec Epistola in vulgatis Latinis codicibus non comparet; adeoque nuper admodum in linguam Anglicam conversa est. Hinc patet aut antiquiorem fuisse quandam S. Scripturae Translationem Anglicam, aut duplicem fuisse Translationis Wiclevianae editionem. Suaviter autem illi somniant, qui Versionem a Wiclefo ex Hebraeis Graecisque fontibus adornatam fuisse arbitrantur. Quisquis Versionem inspexerit, ex vulgata Translatione Latina factam fuisse facile reperiet. De Wiclefi autem Translatione vide quae supra annotata sunt ad Annum 1290.
units.tr: {a} Matth. XIX. {b} Exod. XIV. {c} 2 Cor. IV. {d} Append. ad Hist. Literar. pag. 53. A version of the New Testament, by the same author, to which a very lengthy introduction on the authority and use of Holy Scripture is prefixed. To these add the most beautiful copy in the Norfolk Library, in two folio volumes, and two manuscript copies of the same version of the New Testament, lacking the introduction, are found in Lambeth Library. One of these contains the Epistle to the Laodiceans. A preface is prefixed to its version, at the end of which this note is read: This Epistle does not appear in the printed Latin codices, and so was only very recently turned into English. From this it is clear that either there was some older English translation of Holy Scripture, or the Wiclifite translation had two editions. But those dream pleasantly who think that the version was made by Wiclef from the Hebrew and Greek sources. Whoever inspects the version will easily find that it was made from the Latin Vulgate translation. On Wiclef's translation, see what has been noted above at the year 1290.

units.la: Porro extat MS. in Bibliotheca Collegii Emanuelis Cantab. Anglica totius fere Missae Translatio, una cum Decalogo, aliisque quibusdam ad pietatem spectantibus. Mihi cursim eam perlustranti Wiclesum Authorem habuisse visa est. Certe eadem conscripta est manu, qua Versio totius Scripturae ibidem asservata: Ista enim Wiclefum Authorem prae se ferebat. De hac autem re vide certiora supra ad Annum 1290.
units.tr: Moreover, there exists a manuscript in the library of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, containing an English translation of almost the whole Mass, together with the Decalogue and certain other things pertaining to piety. When I glanced through it cursorily, it seemed to me to have Wiclef as its author. Certainly it is written in the same hand as the version of the whole of Scripture kept there, for that one bore Wiclef's name as its author. On this matter, see the more certain facts above at the year 1290.

units.la: Caeterum, quod Cl. Armachanus habet k de Versione librorum XII. Clementis Lanthoniensis de Concordia Evangelistarum; sc. in ejus Praesatione Wiclefum Scripturarum Vernacularum prohibitionem Antichristianam esse confirmasse: aliquando sum veritus, ne id ab aliis minus fide dignis acceperit. Extat enim MS. penes amicum quendam ista Versio; in qua quidem nil ejusmodi reperitur. Tandem vero Exemplar ejus MS. in Bibliotheca Norfolciana inveni; in quo post Praefationem brevem de Authore Operis & instituti sui ratione atque utilitate, succedit prolixior de Scripturis Vernaculae legendis. Nimium esset illam integram describere: pauca tamen dabo.
units.tr: Furthermore, as to what the learned Archbishop of Armagh says, in his k, concerning the version of the twelve books of Clement of Lanthony on the Concord of the Evangelists, namely that in its preface Wiclef confirmed the prohibition of vernacular Scriptures to be antichristian: I have sometimes feared that he had taken this from others less worthy of trust. For a copy of that version is in the possession of a certain friend, and in it nothing of this kind is found. At last, however, I found its manuscript in the Norfolk Library, in which, after a brief preface on the author of the work and the purpose and usefulness of his undertaking, there follows a longer discussion on the reading of Scripture in the vernacular. It would be too much to describe the whole of it; I will give a few points, however.

units.la: Sub incunabulis sanctae Ecclesiae prohibitum erat, ne quis lingua peregrina loqueretur, nisi auditoribus lingua Vernacula oratio ejus manifestaretur. Atque hinc optima consuetudo in nonnullis Ecclesiis inolevit; ut postquam Evangelium in Ecclesia juxta literam praelectum esset, Auditoribus lingua sua vulgari statim pronunciaretur & explica-
units.tr: In the infancy of the holy Church it was forbidden for anyone to speak in a foreign tongue unless his speech were made clear to the hearers in their own vernacular language. And from this an excellent custom grew up in some churches: after the Gospel had been read aloud in the church according to the letter, it was at once proclaimed and explained to the hearers in their common tongue.

units.la: {k} Cap. ç. ad An. 1380. retur. Quid nobis itaque nostris diebus agendum est; quùm pauci aut nulli, iis quæ legunt, intendant; vel quæ lecta audiunt, intelligant? Nunc igitur impletum videtur, quod olim erat dictum. Erit sacerdos sicut unus è populo. ——Christiani homines multam operam S. Scripturæ & præsertim quatuor Evangeliorum in linguâ suâ Vernaculâ lectioni diu noctuque impendere debent. ——Proh Deus; si quis Dei timor, quâ fronte impediuntur Laici illiterati; quò minùs Evangelium sciant & custodiant; & de eo in mansuetudine & charitate palàm loquantur, ad eradicanda vitia & plantandas virtutes in Christianorum animis? Avari autem Sacerdotes mundiales contra objiciunt, Laicos citò errare posse; adeóque illis de Christianâ fide disputandum non esse. Helas, Helas! quænam ista crudelitas, integram regionem aliquam cibo corporeo privare, eò quòd stulti nonnulli illo in gulam, suique & aliorum damnum abutantur; quamvis alii eundem sobriè sumant? Æquè adversùs Scripturam Latinè conscriptam errare potest superbus mundialis Sacerdos, ac simplex Laicus adversùs Evangelium Anglicè conscriptum. ——Sine scientiâ atque observatione illius nullus ab inferni pœnis liberari queat. Indocti itaque viri illam ediscere deberent à Deo principaliter, & piè vivendo, & sedulum studium impendendo; & ubi obscurior fuerit, veram ejus sententiam à Clericis doctioribus sciscitando. ——Quænam itthæc ratio? Siquidem puer Scholæ traditus in lectione suâ primo die erraverit, idcirco nunquam permittere, ut pueri literas ediscant? Quis unquam ista ratione doctus evaserit? Quilibet Christianus in suscipiendâ primùm fidei professione, sese S. Scripturæ in disciplinam tradit; idque in se recipit, ut illam totâ vitâ pro viribus suis discat & doceat; aliter inferni pœnas passurus, cœli gaudia amissurus. Quisnam igitur, quæso, Antichristus, si quæ Christianorum cura, illiteratis inhibere ausit ediscere lectionem suam, à Deo tam firmiter præscriptam? Quam quidem quilibet sectari debet; ut salvari possit. ——Sacerdotes autem mundani clamant, Sacram Scripturam Anglicè perlectam, dissidium Christianæ Reipublicæ inducere, Subditosque ad arma contra Principes cienda incitare; adeóque Laicis permittendam non esse. Helas! quomodo apertiùs calumniari possunt Dei auctoritatem & pacem, & sanctam ejus legem, docentem mansuetudinem, patientiam & charitatem? ——Sic & mendaces Judæi, nempe Primores Sacerdotum, Scribæ & Pharisæi, Christum dissentionem in populo concitasse exclamârunt. Jesu Christe, qui ad confirmandam Legem tuam & redimendas Christianorum animas, mortem obiisti; Antichristi christi & mundialium Sacerdotum blasphemias repelle; desque ut sanctum tuum Evangelium à simplicibus tuis fratribus sciatur & observetur; illosque adaugeas in fide, spe & charitate, in mansuetudine & patientiâ; ut pro te ac tuâ lege mortem læti patiantur. Amen.
units.tr: {k} Chap. ç. at the year 1380. What, then, ought we to do in our own days, when few or none attend to what they read, or understand what they hear read? Now therefore it seems fulfilled what was said of old: The priest shall be as one of the people. ——Christian men ought to devote much effort, day and night, to the reading of Holy Scripture, and especially of the four Gospels, in their own vernacular tongue. ——O God! If there is any fear of God, with what face are unlettered laymen hindered from knowing and keeping the Gospel, and from speaking of it openly, in gentleness and charity, to root out vices and plant virtues in the souls of Christians? But greedy worldly priests object that laymen may quickly err, and that therefore they should not be disputed with about the Christian faith. Alas, alas! What cruelty is this, to deprive a whole region of bodily food because some fools abuse it to their gluttony and to their own and others' harm, though others take the same soberly? A proud worldly priest can err just as much against Scripture written in Latin as a simple layman can against the Gospel written in English. ——Without knowledge and observance of it, no one can be freed from the pains of hell. Unlearned men therefore ought to learn it by heart, chiefly from God, by living piously and devoting diligent study to it; and where it is more obscure, by asking the true sense of it from the more learned clergy. ——What kind of reasoning is this? If a boy handed over to school has erred in his reading on the first day, is it therefore never to be allowed that boys learn their letters? Who ever became learned by such a method? Every Christian, on first making his profession of faith, gives himself over to Scripture as his discipline, and undertakes to learn and teach it throughout his life as far as his powers allow; otherwise he will suffer the pains of hell and lose the joys of heaven. What Antichrist, then, I ask, dares to forbid the unlettered, under the pretext of Christian care, to learn their lesson, which God has so firmly prescribed? A lesson which everyone ought to follow, so that he may be saved. ——But worldly priests cry out that Holy Scripture read in English introduces discord into the Christian commonwealth and incites subjects to take up arms against princes; and therefore it is not to be permitted to laymen. Alas! How more openly could they slander the authority of God, and his peace, and his holy law, which teaches gentleness, patience and charity? ——So too the lying Jews, namely the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees, cried out that Christ had stirred up dissension among the people. Jesus Christ, who underwent death to confirm your Law and to redeem the souls of Christians, repel the blasphemies of the Antichrists and of worldly priests; and grant that your holy Gospel may be known and observed by your simple brothers, and increase them in faith, hope and charity, in gentleness and patience, so that they may joyfully suffer death for you and your law. Amen.

units.la: 1387. Joannes Trevisa, Sacerdos Cornubiensis.
units.tr: 1387. John Trevisa, Priest of Cornwall.

units.la: In Dialogo inter Patronum & Clericum præfixo Versioni suæ Anglicæ Polychronici Ranulphi Higdeni à Caxtono excusæ Londini 1482. de utilitate Translationum, præsertim verò S. Scripturæ, multis agit. Pauca quædam describam. Sacra quidem Scriptura Latinè etiam tradita (Græcas Versiones LXX. Aquilæ, Symmachi, &c. magnoperè ab Ecclesiâ collaudatas esse prius dixerat) & bona est & pulchra. Sermonem tamen S. Scripturæ Latinè recitare hominibus Anglicam solummodo linguam & non Latinam intelligentibus insanum esset; cùm auditores nihil proficerent; nisi verò sensus Latini sermonis Anglicè illis exponeretur. Anglicè autem exponi non potest nisi per Translationem è Latino in sermonem Anglicum. Oportet igitur habere Anglicam Translationem. Porrò ut res memoriâ diutius conserventur, & ab oblivione vindicentur; Præstat istam Translationem fieri & literis mandari, quàm ore tenus recitari & non conscribi. Rex Alfredus magnam Psalterii partem è Latino Anglicè transtulit: & Wyrefrithum Episcopum Wigornien-sem S. Gregorii Dialogos è Latino in Saxonicum sermonem convertere effecit: Cedno-mus etiam Whitbeiensis à Spiritu S. afflatus egregia Poemata Anglicè concinnavit de omnibus ferè S. Scripturæ historiis. Vir quoque sanctus Beda S. Joannis Evangelium è Latino in Anglicum transtulit. Nósti quinetiam ubi Apocalypsis parietibus & laqueari Capellæ cujusdam inscribitur tum Latinè tum Gallicè. (1) Evangelium enim & Prophetiæ & recta fides S. Ecclesiæ, illis qui Latinè nesciunt, Anglicè necessariò est docenda & prædicanda. Evangelium igitur & Prophetiæ & recta fides S. Ecclesiæ illis Anglicè sunt explicanda. Id autem non fit nisi per Anglicam Translationem. Istiusmodi enim Anglica explicatio, ipsissima est Translatio: & talis explicatio bona est & utilis; ergo Anglica Translatio bona est & utilis.
units.tr: In the Dialogue between Patron and Clerk, prefixed to his English version of Ranulph Higden's Polychronicon, printed by Caxton at London in 1482, he discusses at length the usefulness of translations, especially of Holy Scripture. I will set out a few points. Holy Scripture, indeed, even when delivered in Latin (he had earlier said that the Greek versions of the Seventy, Aquila, Symmachus and others were highly praised by the Church) is good and beautiful. Yet to recite the words of Holy Scripture in Latin to people who understand only English and not Latin would be foolish, since the hearers would gain nothing unless the sense of the Latin were explained to them in English. But it cannot be explained in English except through a translation from Latin into English. It is necessary, therefore, to have an English translation. Moreover, so that things may be kept longer in memory and rescued from oblivion, it is better that this translation be made and committed to writing than recited by word of mouth and not written down. King Alfred translated a large part of the Psalter from Latin into English, and caused Wulfric (Wyrefrith), Bishop of Worcester, to turn the Dialogues of St Gregory from Latin into the Saxon tongue. Cædmon of Whitby, inspired by the Holy Spirit, also composed excellent English poems on almost all the histories of Holy Scripture. The holy Bede too translated the Gospel of John from Latin into English. Moreover you know where the Apocalypse is inscribed on the walls and ceiling of a certain chapel, both in Latin and in French. (1) For the Gospel, the Prophecies and the sound faith of the holy Church must necessarily be taught and preached in English to those who do not know Latin. Therefore the Gospel, the Prophecies and the sound faith of the holy Church must be explained to them in English. But this is not done except through an English translation. For such an English explanation is itself a translation, and such an explanation is good and useful; therefore an English translation is good and useful.

units.la: (1) Extat etiamnum MS in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ Apocalypsos Versio & Expositio vetus Gallica, picturis miniatis & deauratis elegantissimè exornata. Trevisæ ætatem Cl. Usserius à Caxtono deceptus malè posuit. Quæ enim ex fine Translationis Polychronici citat, à Caxtono fœdè corrupta sunt. Namque is Versionem passim emendare & pro lubitu mutare in se recepit; quod in Præfatione editionis suæ fatetur. Cùm itaque Historia Polychronici Anno 1357. desierit; ille Versionem isto anno finitam esse, aut imprudens credidit, aut forsan etiam sciens substituit. Propius ad veritatem accedunt bini Codices MSS. ab Usserio memorati, alter D. Forsteri, alter Cottonianus;. quorum ille notat Versionem finitam esse die Jovis, Aprilis octavo, Anno 1387. decimo Richardi II. iste autem die Jovis, Aprilis decimo octavo, Anno 1387. duodecimo Richardi II. Uterque verò lapsus est. Neque enim (in priore calculo,) Aprilis octavus dies Anni 1387. in diem Jovis incidit sed in diem Lunæ; nec (in posteriore,) Annus 1387. incidit in duodecimum Richardi II. annum, sed in vicesimum. Utrique igitur scrupulo fœliciter satisfacit, & finitæ Versionis tempus rectè definit Codex MS. qui in instructissimâ Cl. Tenisoni Bibliothecâ habetur; his verbis. Ista Translatio finita est die Jovis, decimo octavo Aprilis die, Anno Domini 1387. decimo Richardi II. post Conquestum anno, anno autem tricesimo quinto ætatis Patroni mei Domini Thomæ Baronis de Berkeley, qui me Translationem istam aggredi fecit. Crassius adhuc hallucinatur Seldenus (in fine præfat. ad X. Scriptores Angl.) qui Trevisam Higdeni Polychronicon convertisse, & ad initia Edwardi I. annum sc. 1460. continuâsse dicit. Qui Versionem enim Polychronici primus edidit Caxtonus, Continuationem ejus ab Anno 1357. ad 1460. non à Trevisâ, sed à semetipso conscriptam fuisse disertis verbis affirmat.
units.tr: (1) There still exists in the Lambeth Library a manuscript old French version and exposition of the Apocalypse, most elegantly adorned with painted and gilded miniatures. Usher, misled by Caxton, wrongly placed it in Trevisa's time. For the passages Usher cites from the end of the translation of the Polychronicon have been foully corrupted by Caxton. He undertook to correct the version throughout and change it at his pleasure, as he admits in the preface to his edition. Since the history in the Polychronicon ends in the year 1357, Caxton either carelessly believed, or perhaps knowingly supplied, that the version was finished in that year. Two manuscript copies mentioned by Usher come nearer the truth, one belonging to Mr Forster, the other the Cottonian copy. The former notes that the version was finished on Thursday, 8 April, in the tenth year of Richard II, 1387; the latter on Thursday, 18 April, in the twelfth year of Richard II, 1387. Yet both have slipped. For in the former reckoning, 8 April 1387 did not fall on a Thursday but on a Monday; and in the latter, 1387 did not fall in the twelfth year of Richard II but in the twentieth. The manuscript held in the very well-furnished library of the distinguished Mr Tenison resolves both difficulties happily and correctly fixes the date of the finished version, in these words: This translation was finished on Thursday, 18 April, in the year of the Lord 1387, in the tenth year of Richard II after the Conquest, and in the thirty-fifth year of the age of my patron, Lord Thomas, Baron of Berkeley, who caused me to undertake this translation. Selden (at the end of the preface to the Ten English Writers) is still more grossly mistaken, saying that Trevisa translated Higden's Polychronicon and continued it down to the beginning of Edward I's reign, that is to 1460. For he expressly affirms that Caxton, who first printed the version of the Polychronicon, wrote the continuation from 1357 to 1460 himself, not Trevisa.

units.la: 1420. Nicolaus de Clamengiis.
units.tr: 1420. Nicholas de Clamengis.

units.la: De corrupto Ecclesiæ statu, cap. 16. De literis verò & doctrinâ quid loqui attinet? cùm omnes fere Presbyteros sine aliquo captu aut rerum aut vocabulorum morose syllabatimque vix legere videamus. Quem ergo fructum, quam exauditionem ex suis orationibus sive sibi sive aliis impetrabunt; quibus barbarum est quod orant?
