units.tr: On the corrupt state of the Church, ch. 16. But what need is there to speak of learning and doctrine? When we see almost all the presbyters scarcely able to read, and then only haltingly and syllable by syllable, without any grasp either of the things or of the words. What fruit, what answer to their prayers will they obtain, for themselves or for others, when what they pray is barbarous to them?

units.la: 1420. Simeon, Archiepiscopus Thessalonicensis.
units.tr: 1420. Simeon, Archbishop of Thessalonica.

units.la: Sub medium praecedentis saeculi Barlaamus nova dogmata commentus, maximas inter Graecos turbas excitavit. Errores ejus sigillatim explicat & refutat Simeon Thessalonicensis, in Opere pererudito de fide, ritibus & mysteriis Ecclesiasticis; quod multum diuque desideratum, integrum demum prodiit Graece excusum Jassii in Moldavia 1683. sol. Inter alios errores, Barlaamus circa preces Ecclesiasticas insigniter deliravit. Nam τὸ νοερὰν προσευχὴν ἀπορρίπτει. Orationem intellectualem, seu à precantibus intellectam improbavit. Illum igitur his verbis Simeon oppugnat: Οὗτος ὁ δύσφρων Βαρλαὰμ ἡ πλάσσε ... τῆς ἱερᾶς προσευχῆς ἐξλασφήμησε τε καὶ συνέγραψε, &c. Sceleratus ille Barlaam multa etiam adversus sanctam orationem divinamque gratiam & cognitionem blasphemè effutivit & conscripsit; non intelligens illud Apostoli; Indefinenter orate, neque quidem prae mentis tumore & superbia intelligere valens. Quin nec illud intellexit: Orabo spiritu, orabo & mente. Neque istud, Cantantes & psallentes in cordibus vestris Domino. Et quòd Emisit Deus Spiritum Filii sui, gratiam videlicet, in corda nostra, clamantem, Abba Pater. Et, In Ecclesia malim quinque verba ex intelligentia mea loqui, quam decem millia verborum lingua. Hactenus Simeon: qui quidem istum Barlaami errorem dilucidè nequaquam explicat. Verùm ex Refutatione constat Barlaamum preces lingua à precantibus non intellectâ admitti voluisse, Simeonem improbàsse. Videtur Barlaamus errore Mysticis Theologiae Naturalis Doctoribus familiari, Orationum efficaciam non in orantis devotione sed in mystica verborum intelligentia posuisse; adeoque preces efficacissimis, quamvis ignotis nullumque sensum praebentibus, vocibus concipiendas esse docuisse. Sic olim docuerant, ab Illustrissimo Armachano o supra memorati, Philosophi & Haeretici; qui Theologiae Mysticae studium prae aliis coluerunt. Barlaamum autem Simeon eo nomine fusè insequitur; quòd futilibus Graecorum Philosophorum ineptiis & subtilitatibus perdite deditus fuerit; omnemque Theologiam in profundâ rerum naturalium & Astrologiae cognitione sitam esse contenderit. Dogma istud Barlaamo & priscis Haereticis commune suscipere & tueri Pontificii non erubescunt; qui quoties precum populo ignotarum futilitas objicitur; vocum Latinarum, Graecarum, vel Hebraicarum, prae aliis efficaciam allegant.
units.tr: Towards the middle of the previous century Barlaam devised new doctrines and caused the greatest disturbances among the Greeks. Simeon of Thessalonica explains and refutes his errors one by one in his very learned work On faith, rites and ecclesiastical mysteries, which, though long and much desired, was at last published complete in Greek at Jassy in Moldavia in 1683, in folio. Among other errors, Barlaam raved notably about ecclesiastical prayers. For he rejected τὸ νοερὰν προσευχὴν (intellectual prayer). He disapproved of intellectual prayer, that is, prayer understood by those who pray. Simeon assails him in these words: [Οὗτος ὁ δύσφρων Βαρλαὰμ ... τῆς ἱερᾶς προσευχῆς ἐξλασφήμησε τε καὶ συνέγραψε], etc. That wicked Barlaam has blasphemed and written much against holy prayer and divine grace and knowledge, not understanding that saying of the Apostle, "Pray without ceasing", being unable to understand it for the swelling and pride of his mind. Nor did he understand this: "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind" (1 Cor. 14), nor this: "Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord" (Eph. 5), nor that God sent forth the Spirit of his Son, that is grace, into our hearts, crying, "Abba, Father" (Gal. 4). And: "In the Church I would rather speak five words with my understanding than ten thousand words in a tongue" (1 Cor. 14). So far Simeon, who certainly does not explain Barlaam's error clearly. But from the refutation it is evident that Barlaam wished prayer in a tongue not understood by those who pray to be admitted, while Simeon disapproved. Barlaam seems, by an error familiar to the mystical doctors of natural theology, to have placed the efficacy of prayers not in the devotion of the one praying but in the mystical understanding of words; and so he taught that prayers should be conceived in the most efficacious words, even though they are unknown and give no sense. The philosophers and heretics mentioned above, who cultivated the study of mystical theology before others, taught this in former times, as the most illustrious Archbishop of Armagh (o) has shown. Simeon pursues Barlaam at length on this account: that he was wholly given over to the trifling absurdities and subtleties of the Greek philosophers, and maintained that all theology consists in a profound knowledge of natural things and of astrology. The Papists are not ashamed to adopt and defend this doctrine, shared by Barlaam and the ancient heretics; whenever the triviality of prayers unknown to the people is objected to them, they cite the efficacy of Latin, Greek or Hebrew words above all others.

units.la: n Cap. 31. pag. 51. o Cap. 9. Mitto recentiores causæ Pontificiæ Advocatos. * Vetus is prætextus. Sic enim Glossa MS. in S. Pauli Epistolas, in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, ante ducentos saltem annos conscripta, ad illud 1 Cor. XIV. Quomodo dicet Amen super tuam benedictionem; cùm quid dicis nescit?] Quomodo igitur, dicis secundùm Apostolum, cùm mysterium Missæ celebras, vel Sermonem facis, vel Sermonem populo dicis; quomodo respondebit verbum confirmatorium, cùm non intelligat? Huic objectioni respondet Adimantius; non parum utilitatis animæ confertur; cùm lectio licèt obserata Dei sermonis ad aures nostras illabitur. Si enim per Gentilium Carmina sopiuntur serpentes; multò magis per virtutem Dei sermonis Dæmones expelluntur: Origenis locus à nobis supra adductus est, cap. 2. ad An. 240. Eundem pro suâ causâ allegat Bellarminus ; qui cum Anonymo Glossæ Authore consentiens, Adimantii verba de lectione S. Scripturæ ne minimum quidem intellectâ dici vult. Fraude manifestâ. Neque enim aliud Origenes docet, quàm Scripturæ lectionem multùm prodesse; quamvis omnia illius loca & sententiæ à legentibus plenè non intelligantur. Hinc illum maximè deprædicat, qui verum Scripturæ sensum accuratè novit. Quùm tamen is rarò inveniatur; non statim rejiciendam esse lectionem dicit illis, quibus ad difficiliores Scripturæ sententias hæret aqua.
units.tr: n Chap. 31, p. 51. o Chap. 9. I pass over the more recent advocates of the Papal cause. * This is an old pretext. For the manuscript gloss on the Pauline Epistles in the Lambeth Library, written at least two hundred years ago, on the words of 1 Cor. 14, "How shall he who occupies the place of the unlearned say Amen at your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you say?", reads: How then, as the Apostle says, when you celebrate the mystery of the Mass, or preach a sermon, or speak to the people, how will he who does not understand answer with the word of assent? Adimantus answers this objection: it confers no little benefit on the soul, since the reading of God's word, though unsealed, slips into our ears. For if serpents are charmed by the songs of the Gentiles, much more are demons driven out by the power of God's word. The passage of Origen which we cited above, ch. 2, at the year 240, is the same. Bellarmine too cites it for his cause; and agreeing with the anonymous author of the Gloss, he wishes Adimantus's words about the reading of Holy Scripture to be taken as referring to a reading not understood at all. This is manifest deceit. For Origen teaches nothing other than that the reading of Scripture is very profitable, even though not all its passages and sentences are fully understood by the readers. Hence he greatly praises the one who knows the true sense of Scripture accurately; but since such a person is rarely found, he says that reading should not be rejected at once by those who stick fast at the more difficult sentences of Scripture.

units.la: Preces Græcorum publicas Simeonis ætate à populo intellectas fuisse patet ex innumeris, quæ à populo faciendæ erant, Responsionibus, quæque unà cum sacerdote recitandæ, Orationibus atque Hymnis. Pauca hujusce rei testimonia describam. In Synaxi igitur Symbolum Apostolorum [Greek] ab omnibus recitatum fuisse dicit . Dein Oratio pro omnibus tam vivis quàm defunctis, communi fit voce & supplicatione; Sacerdote quidem præeunte, omnibus autem unà orantibus ([Greek]), Pro religiosis Imperatoribus, pro Orthodoxis Episcopis, &c. Mox Omnes simul Trisagium & Orationem Dominicam cantant. ([Greek]) Iste etiam Hymnus, Gloria tibi in excelsis, &c. junctà ab omnibus voce decantatur ([Greek]) Iterum populus recitat orationem istam. Domine, Miserere, &c. ([Greek]) Denique Sacerdos surgens unà cum plebe ([Greek]) gratias agens dicit: Tuum est enim miserèri & salvare, &c. Et in ritibus nuptiarum celebrandis Omnes simul ([Greek]) Orationem Dominicam recitant.
units.tr: The public Greek prayers were understood by the people in Simeon's time, as is clear from the countless responses the people were to make along with the priest, and from the orations and hymns they recited together with him. I will set out a few testimonies. In the Synaxis, then, he says that the Apostles' Creed [Σύμβολον τῶν Ἀποστόλων] was recited by everyone. Next, the prayer for all, both living and dead, is offered with one common voice and supplication, the priest leading and all praying together, for the pious emperors, for the Orthodox bishops, etc. Soon everyone sings the Trisagion and the Lord's Prayer together. This hymn too, Glory to you in the highest, etc., is sung by all with one voice. Again the people recite that prayer, Lord, have mercy, etc. Finally the priest, rising with the people, gives thanks and says: For yours is the power of mercy and of salvation, etc. And in the rites for celebrating marriage everyone together recites the Lord's Prayer.

units.la: Istam enim ʸ, aliasque Ecclesiæ Orationes ac Hymnos quilibet Orthodoxus Christianus sine omni exceptione tenetur scire. Χρὴ εἰδέναι, δίχα προφάσεως πάσης, τὴν ἐκ δωρὸς φρονῆσαι πάντα Χεμαζων. Lectiones autem in Synaxi recitatæ ad plebis instructionem unicè spectant. ᶻ Ideo enim divini Sermones præcipiuntur; ne brutorum ad instar ventris solius curam agamus (ἀλλ' ὡς λογικοὶ μὴ σαρκὸς, τὸ μὲν σάρκα σηείζομεν τοῖς ἰδιομένοις, τὴν ψυχὴν δ' τοῖς λεγομένοις) sed, utpote qui animâ pariter ac corpore constamus, corpus quidem eduliis, animam autem lectionibus confirmemus. Dein surgentes, suffultâ oratione, (δεξολογοῦμεν ἅπαντες) omnes simul Doxologiam recitamus, &c.
units.tr: For every Orthodox Christian without exception is bound to know this prayer, and the other prayers and hymns of the Church. It is necessary to know, without any excuse, the things that are sung [Χρὴ εἰδέναι, δίχα προφάσεως πάσης]. The readings recited in the Synaxis look solely to the instruction of the people. For this is why the divine sermons are prescribed, so that we do not, like brute beasts, care only for the belly (but, as rational beings and not merely flesh, we nourish the body with what is eaten and the soul with what is read), but, since we consist of soul as well as body, let us strengthen the body with food and the soul with readings. Then, rising, with our prayer supported, we all together recite the Doxology, etc.

units.la: * Populus igitur Simeonis ætate sacras Liturgiæ preces probè intellexit; utque intelligeret quidem, Simeon necessarium duxit. Hinc defervescentem populi sui Thessalonicensis in orando feruorem deflet; acriterque illis increpat, qui neque rei necessitate nec repetitis Sacerdotis adhortationibus moti, Responsiones in cœtu Ecclesiastico aut insuper haberent, aut ocitanter darent. Sic enim populum affatur ª. Τὸ Ἀρχιερέως τὸ Ἐιρήνη πᾶσι, λεγόμενα, &c. Episcopo, Pax vobis omnibus, dicente; & Diacono antea, Attendamus, clamante; nullius ad hoc mentem adhibet neque audire cupit; neque respondet, [Et cum Spiritu tuo] Et alibi, Ecclesia, inquit ᵇ, fideles sæpe inter sacra consulto admonet, ut attenti sint. [Dicamus omnes,] inquit (hanc vel illam orationem sive hymnum) Εἰπωμεν πάντες, φησὶν, ἐκ δὲ ἐλῆς τῆς διανοίας ἀπωμεν) & ex toto corde nostro dicamus.] Illud enim [Dicamus omnes] & quæ sequuntur, nobis excitandis & docendis inserviunt; sicut & illud [Sapientia] & [Attendamus, Πεῤῥάμεν] & istud [Sapientiâ recti Σοφίᾳ ἐρθοί] quasi diceretur, In intelligentiâ erecti state omnes. Nunc verò, Proh dolor, Fratres (ἃ νῦν μεν, ἐδὲ τῆς λεγομένων ἀιδανόμεθα, &c.) non intelligimus, neque quæ in Ecclesiâ dicta sunt persentimus, sed ex consuetudine labiis solummodo loquimur, de devotione cordis adhibendâ minus solliciti, &c. Aliquando neque respondemus quidem [Miserere] neque ad Responsionis sensum attendimus. Pluribus argumentum istud tractat cap. 231, 232.
units.tr: So the people in Simeon's time understood the sacred prayers of the Liturgy well; and Simeon thought it necessary that they should understand them. Hence he laments the cooling zeal of his Thessalonian people in prayer, and sharply rebukes those who, moved neither by the need of the matter nor by the priest's repeated exhortations, either ignored the responses in the ecclesiastical assembly or gave them carelessly. For he addresses the people thus: when the Bishop says, Peace be with you all, and the Deacon earlier cries, Let us attend, he pays no heed to this and does not wish to hear; he does not respond [And with your spirit]. And elsewhere he says: the Church often advises the faithful during the sacred rites, deliberately, that they be attentive. [Let us all say] he says (this or that prayer or hymn; let us all say it, he says, with our whole mind) and let us say it with our whole heart. For that [Let us all say] and what follows serve to rouse and teach us; so also [Wisdom] and [Let us attend, Πρόσχωμεν] and [Stand upright in wisdom, Σοφίᾳ ὀρθοί], as if it were said: Stand all upright in understanding. But now, alas, brethren (what we now sing of what is said...) we do not understand, nor do we perceive what has been said in the Church, but from habit we only move our lips, less concerned to bring devotion of the heart. Sometimes we neither respond [Lord, have mercy] nor attend to the sense of the response. He treats this matter at greater length in chapters 231 and 232.

units.tr: I am not in the habit of favouring the undertakings of the mystical theologians. Yet since I have called on so many witnesses from every class of writers, I would certainly not wish

units.la: ʸ Cap. 320. ᶻ Cap. 358. ª Cap. 231. ᵇ Cap. 322. 226, 227. Mysticos sese ultro ingerentes repellere. Hujusce commatis Theologis praeire solent Carthusiani; & inter Carthusianos enituit Gualterus Hilton; quo non alius sublimius deliravit. Quod tamen in laudem ejus haud parum cedit; celeberrimum illud Opus de imitatione Christi non minus aequo jure sibi forsan vendicare queat, quam Thomas Kempensis, aut quivis alius. Extant enim in Bibliotheca Lambethana bini Codices MSS. & alii plures; qui tres priores Operis istius libros complectuntur, titulo Musicae Ecclesiasticae. Codicum alter Hiltoni nomen praefert; illumque ejusmodi Opus conscripsisse Balcus confirmat. Scripsit idem Scalam Perfectionis, seu de Vita Contemplativa libros duos, sermone Anglico, ad Mulierem quandam Deo devotam. Asservatur Opus MS. in Bibliotheca Lambethana. In eo multa agit Hiltonus de unione animae cum Deo, de igne amoris divini, & de lumine coelitus dato, aliisque Mysticorum Scriptorum Locis Communibus. Ponit autem omnibus Electis, licet indoctissimis, possibile esse hunc perfectionis statum assequi: a nullo autem obtineri posse sine diligenti Scripturarum studio & lectione: adeoque Christum singulis animabus (quamvis literarum penitus ignaris) seipsum sincere amantibus Scripturarum intelligentiam coelitus dare; quin & potissimam contemplationis & consolationis ejus, quam in perfectis Ascetis haberi jactitat, partem ex Scripturarum lectione & meditatione exoriri. Nimium esset omnia, quae huc faciunt, describere. Unicum tamen locum dabo ex lib. 2. cap. 43. Qualis sit Jesus in essentia sua, nulla, dum in terris manet, anima pervidere potest: per effectus tamen operationum ejus, gratiae lumine adjuta videre potest. Verbi gratia. Potestas ejus in creando omnes ex nihilo creaturas patet; Sapientia ejus in ordinata earundem dispositione; bonitas ejus in salute illis data; misericordia ejus in remissione peccatorum; sanctitas ejus in gratiae donis; justitia ejus in severa peccati punitione; veritas ejus in certa bonorum operum remuneratione. Atque isthaec omnia in Sacra Scriptura declarantur; eaque & omnia huc spectantia anima in S. Scriptura clare videt. Illud itaque pro certo habeas, desiderabiles ejusmodi notitias in Sacra Scriptura aut alia quavis per gratiam condita, vere esse dulcissimas Epistolas sive nuncios inter animam amantem & Jesum amatum: Jeu, ut verius dicam, inter Jesum verum Amatorem & animas ab illo amatas. Summa etenim amore prosequitur omnes Electos suos, vitae corporeae coeno hic incarceratos: & quamvis absens sit illis, in sinu Patris supra occultatus, beatissimae Deitatis deliciis cumulatus; illorum tamen reminiscitur; & per desideratissimam spiritualem sui praesentiam frequentissime invisit; missis S. Scripturae literis consolatur; anxietatem & dolorem, suspiciones & timores ex animis eorundem depellit; gaudiumque & fiduciam donans, illos omnibus suis promissis fideliter inniti & voluntatis suae completionem patienter expectare facit. Ita enim S. Paulus, Rom. XV. Quaecunque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt; ut per consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus. Atque hoc aliud est Contemplationis opus, Jesum sc. in Scripturis secundum spiritualis oculi manifestationem contemplari, &c.
units.tr: ʸ Ch. 320. ᶻ Ch. 358. ª Ch. 231. ᵇ Ch. 322, 226, 227. to repel the mystics who thrust themselves forward unasked. The Carthusians are usually the leaders of this kind of theology, and among the Carthusians Walter Hilton shone brightest; no one raved more loftily than he. Yet this brings him no small credit: his famous work On the Imitation of Christ may perhaps claim for him as good a right as it does for Thomas à Kempis or anyone else. For in the Lambeth Library there are two manuscript codices, and several others, which contain the first three books of that work under the title Music of the Church. One of these codices bears Hilton's name, and Bale confirms that he wrote such a work. The same man also wrote The Ladder of Perfection, or two books on the contemplative life, in English, addressed to a certain woman devoted to God. The manuscript work is kept in the Lambeth Library. In it Hilton treats at length of the union of the soul with God, of the fire of divine love, of the light given from heaven, and of other common topics of the mystical writers. He holds that this state of perfection is attainable by all the Elect, however unlearned, but that it cannot be reached without diligent study and reading of the Scriptures; and so Christ gives the understanding of the Scriptures from heaven to every soul that sincerely loves him, even one wholly ignorant of letters. Indeed, he boasts that the chief part of that contemplation and consolation which he claims the perfect ascetics possess arises from reading and meditating on the Scriptures. It would take too long to describe everything that bears on this. I will give one passage only, from book 2, chapter 43. What Jesus is in his essence, no soul can see while it remains on earth; yet through the effects of his operations, aided by the light of grace, it can see him. For example: his power in creating all creatures out of nothing is evident; his wisdom in the ordered arrangement of them; his goodness in the salvation given to them; his mercy in the forgiveness of sins; his holiness in the gifts of grace; his justice in the severe punishment of sin; his truth in the sure reward of good works. All these things are declared in Holy Scripture, and the soul clearly sees in Holy Scripture both these and everything that pertains to them. Be assured, therefore, that such desirable knowledge, whether found in Holy Scripture or in any other thing made by grace, is truly the sweetest letters or messages between the loving soul and the beloved Jesus; or, to speak more truly, between Jesus the true Lover and the souls loved by him. For he pursues all his Elect with the greatest love, though they are shut up here in the mire of bodily life; and although he is absent from them, hidden in the bosom of the Father and laden with the delights of the most blessed Deity, yet he remembers them, visits them very often by his most desired spiritual presence, comforts them by sending the letters of Holy Scripture, drives anxiety and sorrow, suspicion and fear from their minds, and, bestowing joy and trust, makes them rely faithfully on all his promises and patiently await the fulfilment of his will. For so St Paul says, Rom. XV. Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. And this is another work of contemplation, namely to contemplate Jesus in the Scriptures, according to the revelation of the spiritual eye, etc.

units.la: 1440. Marcus Eugenicus, Archiepiscopus Ephesinus.
units.tr: 1440. Mark Eugenicus, Archbishop of Ephesus.

units.la: Paria Simeoni docet, alterum Ecclesiae Graecae isthoc saeculo ornamentum, & invictissimus in Concilio Florentino Pugil, Marcus Ephesinus; cujus Expositio τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς ἀπολυσίας ad calcem Simeonis Operum evulgata est. Nimium esset innumeras fere, quas à populo inter sacra faciendas esse docet, Responsiones recensere; singulaque quae ad nostram causam spectant, loca describere. Quae de Psalmorum autem lectione habet, notatu non indigna sunt. Post decantatum Alleluia, Psalterii portionem quandam praelegimus; isti etiam Doxologias, & Troparia, quae ϰαθίσματα dicuntur, frequenter interjicientes. Si rationem istiusmodi Psalmorum lectionis quaeras; non alia erit (2) praeter summam illorum utilitatem & divinae voluptatis quam praebent ubertatem; quodque omnino oportet, integrum Davidis Psalterium singulis septimanis percurri, semel aut etiam bis perlectum.
units.tr: Simeon teaches similar things, as does Mark of Ephesus, the other ornament of the Greek Church in this age and the most unconquered champion at the Council of Florence; his exposition of the ecclesiastical dismissal was published at the end of Simeon's works. It would take too long to list the almost countless responses which he says must be made by the people during the sacred rites, and to describe each passage that bears on our cause. But what he says about the reading of the Psalms is worth noting. After the Alleluia has been sung, we read a certain portion of the Psalter, the people also frequently interjecting doxologies and troparia, which are called kathismata. If you ask the reason for this kind of reading of the Psalms, it will be none other than (2) their great usefulness and the abundance of divine delight they offer; and it is absolutely necessary that the whole Psalter of David be run through every week, read once or even twice.

units.la: 1450. Reginaldus Peacock, Episcopus Cicestrensis.
units.tr: 1450. Reginald Pecock, Bishop of Chichester.

units.la: Cl. Usserius nos plura de isthoc sciturus ad Stoum, Chronici de Rebus Angliae Vernaculi Authorem, remittit. Et refert quidem Stows Peacocum in vertendis Anglicè S. Scripturae libris multis annis insudâsse; eoque inter alia nomine ab invidis Episcopis damnatum esse. Mihi tamen res parùm comperta, immò error manifestus, videtur. Neque enim Peacocus, cui in omnibus sui scriptis, singulos quos ediderat, quosque edendos meditabatur, libros recensere solenne est, ejusmodi Versionem ullibi memoravit; nec in ipsis quidem de Fide libris, quos paulò ante
units.tr: The learned Ussher sends us to Stow, the author of the Chronicle of the Affairs of England, to learn more about this. And it is true that Stow reports that Peacock toiled for many years at translating the books of Holy Scripture into English, and that for this, among other things, he was condemned by hostile bishops. To me, however, the matter seems little established, indeed a manifest error. For Peacock, who in all his writings regularly reviewed the individual books he had published and those he was planning to publish, never mentions such a version anywhere; nor does he mention it in the books On Faith that he had written shortly before

units.la: (2) Τὰ πλουσιως εἰς αὐτὸν ἐν ἀνθρώπων θείας | πληρώσεως ... ψαλτήριον, ἅπαξ ἢ ἐν διὰ ... (Greek note, partly illegible) obitum conscripsit, & in quibus amplum Scriptorum suorum indiculum exhibuit. Nec id etiam in Articulis Peacoco objectis, qui hodienum extant , comparet; cùm tamen credi nequeat, si Scripturam Anglicè transtulerit, adversarios missum facere voluisse istiusmodi crimen, quod à Concilio Oxoniensi sub initium hujusce Sæculi damnatum fuerat. Utut verò Peacocus Scripturæ versionem nequaquam concinnavit (quæ post tot Versiones jamdiu evulgatas inutilis fuisset) vertendam tamen censuit; ejusque lectionem omnibus ex æquo Christianis patere docuit.
units.tr: (2) The things ... richly ... fulfilment of divine ... the Psalter, once or twice ... (Greek, partly illegible) his death, and in which he set out a full list of his writings. Nor does it appear among the articles objected to Peacock, which survive to this day; yet it cannot be believed that, if he had translated Scripture into English, he would have wished to pass over in silence his adversaries' charge of such a crime, which had been condemned by the Council of Oxford at the beginning of this century. However, although Peacock by no means produced a version of Scripture (which, after so many versions long since published, would have been useless), he nevertheless held that it ought to be translated, and he taught that its reading lay open equally to all Christians.

units.la: De Fide lib. 2. (quem Londini Anno 1688. imprimendum curavi) cap. 2. pag. 14, 15. Scriptura tamen data & relicta à Deo, & Apostolis, & Apostolorum discipulis fidem Christianam satis superque fundare potest in omni Clerico & Laico, qui quod in Novo Testamento legit, intelligere queat, quamvis eandem fidem à Generali Concilio aut collectâ Clericorum multitudine non edisceat, &c. Sique scire velis, quamnam Scripturam intelligam; certè est Scriptura Veteris & Novi Testamenti, &c. Præcipitur Deuteronomii capite undecimo, ut patresfamiliæ totusque populus Dei leges & beneficia Scripturæ consignata habeant. Illic enim mandatur, ut leges istas & beneficia ante oculos assiduè habeant. Plura de hoc argumento videre potes in libro de Doctrinâ in linguâ vernaculâ, &c. Non igitur necessarium erat, ut ad diversas regiones diversas Scripturas isto sensu darent (nempe ut singuli Apostoli totidem Evangelia conscriberent eo sc. animo, ut) ut res diversas traderent: quamvis fieri bene potuit ut una eademque res diversis linguis scriberetur, aut in diversas scripta transferretur.
units.tr: From On Faith, book 2 (which I had printed in London in the year 1688), chapter 2, pages 14 and 15: Scripture, however, given and left by God, by the Apostles, and by the disciples of the Apostles, can lay a sufficient and more than sufficient foundation for the Christian faith in every cleric and layman who can understand what he reads in the New Testament, even though he does not learn that same faith from a General Council or from a gathered multitude of clerics, etc. And if you wish to know which Scripture I mean, it is certainly the Scripture of the Old and New Testament, etc. In the eleventh chapter of Deuteronomy it is commanded that the heads of families and the whole people of God have the laws and benefits set down in Scripture. For there it is ordered that they keep those laws and benefits constantly before their eyes. You may see more on this subject in the book On the Teaching in the Vernacular Tongue, etc. It was therefore not necessary that the apostles give different Scriptures to different regions in this sense (namely, that each apostle write as many gospels, with the intention that) they hand down different things; although it could well happen that one and the same thing was written in different languages, or was transferred into different writings.

units.la: Cap. 4. pag. 30. Certè enim fieri potest, ut simplex aliquis bonus, siquidem famam & vulgi opinionem spectes, verum sensum cujusdam Scripturæ loci, aut veritatem cujusdam articuli rectius intelligere, indicare & definire queat, ob diuturnum sc. Scripturæ studium & meditationem; quàm illustre quoddam Generale Concilium.
units.tr: Indeed it can happen that some simple good person, if you consider reputation and popular opinion, can better understand, point out and define the true sense of some passage of Scripture, or the truth of some article, because of his long study and meditation on Scripture, than some famous General Council.

units.la: In Repressore nimiæ Cleri reprehensionis, Anglicè, MS. in Bibliothecâ publicâ Academiæ Cantabrigiensis. Par. 1. cap. 16. Lex igitur divina prohibet, ne quilibet Christianus credat aut arbitretur id salubre esse institutum, fidem & opinionem suam clam tenere, neque in examen quodcunque deduci permittere. Certè si quis velit permittere fidem & opiniones suas in lucem produci, & argumentorum ignè tentari; falsas hæreses & adulterinum aurum jactitare meritò existimandus est. Et ejusmodi qui-
units.tr: In The Repressor of Over-Much Blaming of the Clergy, in English, a manuscript in the public library of the University of Cambridge, part 1, chapter 16: Divine law therefore forbids any Christian to believe or think it a wholesome institution to keep his faith and opinion secret, or not to allow them to be brought under examination of any kind. Certainly, if anyone is unwilling to allow his faith and opinions to be brought into the light and tested by the fire of arguments, he is rightly judged to be boasting of false heresies and counterfeit gold. And that this kind of institution is opposed to reason is clear from this. It is like the law of Mahomet and the Saracens on that article in which especially…

units.la: {e} Apud Fevi Hist Eccl. Lat. Bapt. 1563; par 1. pag 129. & in Registro Caroli Booth, Episcopi Herefordensis, MS. dem institutum rationi adversari hinc evidenter patet. Simile est enim legi Mahometis & Saracenorum in eo articulo; in quo præsertim lex illorum rationi repugnat. Lex etenim Mahometica sub gravi acerrimarum pœnarum comminatione vetat; ne quis postquam admissam semel ejusce legis credulitatem, disputare aut argumentari cum ullo alio de quavis illius legis conclusione aut articulo audeat. Ob hoc impium & execrabile præceptum, levius sectæ populus ita vinculis obstrictus tenetur; ut multo plures ad fidem veram converti possent, si tam infausta lex non obstitisset. Et si Christiani se vinculis ullis constringant; quo minus de quovis fidei Christianæ articulo liberè cum aliis disputare & argumentari queant; uti de quibusdam narratum audivi; certè illi maximum legi Christianæ tam naturæ quàm fidei opprobrium faciunt: quasi verò Christiana lex tam infirma esset, spuria, & erroneas; ut grave examen nequaquam ferre posset. Contra Innocentium IV. Papa in Epist. 11. Firmiter inhibemus, ne cuiquam personæ Laicæ liceat publicè vel privatim de fide Catholicâ disputare. Qui verò contra fecerit, excommunicationis laqueo innodetur.
units.tr: {e} From Fevus's Ecclesiastical History of the Latin Baptists, 1563, part 1, p. 129, and from the Register of Carolus Booth, Bishop of Hereford, MS. That this institution is contrary to reason is clearly evident from this. For it is like the law of Mahomet and the Saracens on that article, in which their law is especially opposed to reason. Mahomet's law, under the heavy threat of most severe punishments, forbids anyone, once he has admitted belief in that law, to dispute or argue with anyone else about any conclusion or article of that law. Because of this impious and detestable precept, the people of that sect are held so bound by chains, though lightly, that many more could be converted to the true faith if this unhappy law did not stand in the way. And if Christians should bind themselves with any chains so that they cannot freely dispute and argue with others about any article of the Christian faith, as I have heard reported of some, they certainly bring the greatest reproach upon the Christian law, both natural and of faith, as if the Christian law were so weak, spurious and erroneous that it could by no means bear a serious examination. Against Innocent IV, in Epistle 11: We firmly forbid that any lay person be permitted, publicly or privately, to dispute about the Catholic faith. Whoever acts against this shall be bound with the noose of excommunication.

units.la: Part 2. cap. 5. Abusum rei non tollere usum ejus licitum disputans, adeoque nec imagines Ecclesiis eliminandas ob frequentes ex illis oriundos abusus; hæc habet. Sic autem res se habet, ut mala quæ ab imaginibus in Ecclesiis positis & retentis proveniunt, non sint majora malis, quæ ex licitis artificiis & mercaturâ per accidens oriuntur; nec majora malis, quæ exinde eveniunt, quòd Laici sacram Scripturam linguâ vernaculâ uturpent; nec majora malis, quæ exinde nascuntur, quòd sacerdotes sint & concionatores. Quapropter argumentum istud imaginum usum necessariò abolendum esse non evincit; nisi etiam pariter evinceret illicitum esse usum omnium artificiorum, & usum sacræ Scripturæ inter Laicos; immò etiam nisi evinceret Sacerdotes & Prædicatores in Ecclesiâ esse non debere.
units.tr: Part 2, ch. 5, arguing that the abuse of a thing does not remove its lawful use, and so images should not be removed from the churches on account of the frequent abuses arising from them. He says this: The matter stands thus: the evils that come from images placed and kept in churches are no greater than the evils that arise by accident from lawful crafts and trade; nor greater than the evils that follow from laymen defiling Holy Scripture in the vernacular; nor greater than the evils that arise from there being priests and preachers. Therefore this argument does not prove that the use of images must necessarily be abolished, unless it likewise proved that the use of all crafts is unlawful, and the use of Holy Scripture among the laity; indeed, unless it proved that priests and preachers ought not to be in the Church.

units.la: Part. 2. cap. 20. Postquam imaginum usum asseruisset; monet omnes, ne istiusmodi signis visibilibus nimis inhæreant; quin potiùs ut omnes qui legere queant, ad unicum sacræ Scripturæ studium se conferant; qui que legere non possint, alios legentes aut exponentes audiant. Hujus enim studium omnibus externis Cæremoniis & subtilibus humano ingenio excogitatis longè præstare; id solum veram scientiam & salutarem consolationem gignere. Rem pluribus persequitur. Lucum itaque prolixiorem describere insuper habui.
units.tr: Part 2, ch. 20. Having asserted the use of images, he warns everyone not to cling too closely to such visible signs, but rather that all who can read should devote themselves solely to the study of Holy Scripture, and those who cannot read should listen to others who read or expound it. For the study of this, he says, far surpasses all external ceremonies and subtle devices thought out by human ingenuity; it alone produces true knowledge and saving consolation. He pursues the matter at greater length. I have therefore thought it unnecessary to describe the passage more fully.

units.la: In Pauperis Speculo, MS. Anglicè (Codicem ab opifice quodam Nor-
units.tr: In the Pauper's Mirror, a manuscript in English (a copy that I bought from a certain craftsman of Norwich, and have deposited in the library of Cl. Tenison),

units.la: * Concil Tom. 11. pag. 617. vicensi redemptum in Cl. Tenisoni Bibliothecam consignavi) indoctæ plebi rudimenta fidei enucleare & præcepta vitæ infimæ etiam Christianorum sorti convenientia tradere in se recipit. Cap. 7. discipulum ita instruit. Gratias Deo agere debemus ob institutum suum sapientissimum; quo voluit, ut sacra Scriptura tam Veteris quàm Novi Testamenti nos instruat & memoriam confirmet, & sanctissimam nostram fidem nobis perfectissimè & devotissimè suppeditet.
units.tr: * Concil. vol. 11, p. 617. he undertakes to explain the rudiments of the faith to the untaught common people and to hand down precepts of life suited even to the humblest lot of Christians. In ch. 7 he instructs the pupil thus: We ought to give thanks to God for his most wise institution, by which he willed that holy Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, should instruct us, confirm our memory, and supply us with our most holy faith most perfectly and most devoutly.

units.la: Ad finem hujus Speculi adjiciuntur Consilia quædam ad institutionem humanam, ex Sanctorum Patrum, præsertim verò Isidori, scriptis congesta: Paulò ante med. istud Consilium legitur. Plurimam ad legendum operam dato. Vide ut Scripturæ meditationi insistas. In lege Dei assiduus esto. Frequens cum divinis codicibus commercium habeto; legens diligenter quæ tibi sint agenda & tenenda. Lectio ostendit quid timere debeas. Lectio monstrat quò vadis. Lecti ne scientia & intellectus augentur. Multùm legendo proficies; si juxta ea, quæ legis, facias.
units.tr: At the end of this Mirror are added certain Counsels for human instruction, gathered from the writings of the holy Fathers, especially Isidore. A little before the middle of these, this counsel is read: Give most of your effort to reading. See that you keep to the meditation of Scripture. Be constant in the law of God. Keep frequent company with the divine books, reading diligently what must be done and kept by you. Reading shows you what you ought to fear. Reading shows where you are going. By reading, knowledge and understanding are increased. You will make great progress by reading, if you act according to what you read.

units.la: 1470. Speculi B. Virginis Interpres Anglicanus.
units.tr: 1470. The English Interpreter of the Speculum of the Blessed Virgin.

units.la: Integrum B. Virginis Officium, quod à S. Brigitta concinnatum, Moniahibus sui Ordinis in usu publico fuit; Anglicè ab Anonymo quodam conversum, Londini prodiit ante Annum 1500. sol. ex Caxtoni, ut videtur, prælo editum. Versionem suam Interpres nuncupavit Monialibus Sionensibus; quas in priore Prologo sic alfatur. Quandoquidem multæ è vobis, quamvis publica B. Virginis Officia cantare & in choro legere queatis; sensum tamen eorum minùs intelligatis; ideirco ad unicam Domini nostri Jesu Christi & Matris eius clementissimæ gloriam, vestrumque omnium spiritualem consolationem & utilitatem, Legendam vestram totumque Officium in Anglicam linguam converti; ut ex intellectu ejus percipiatis, quàm pulchra sanctaque gloriosæ Virginis præconizatio inibi continetur; & majori cum devotione & intellectu id cantetis, legatis, & ad cultum ejus recitetis. Succedit Tractatus de Officio Divino, & alter de Lectione: in cujus fine sacras Virgines consilio monet; ut Officium suum in Conventu vernaculâ linguâ legant; primam duntaxat singularum Lectionum, Hymnorum, vel Orationum vocem aut sententiam Latinè recitantes; ac demum subdit. Quoniam autem sub anathematis pœnâ prohibetur [sc. in Concilio Oxoniensi, Anno 1407] ne quis aliquem S. Scripturæ textum Anglicè transferat, sine Episcopi Diœcesani permissione; in multis autem vestri Officii Lectis S. Scripturæ textus reperiantur; ideirco ab Episcopo rogavi & impetravi licentiam illiusmodi locorum Anglicè convertendorum ad spiri-
units.tr: The complete Office of the Blessed Virgin, composed by St Bridget for the use of the nuns of her Order, was translated into English by some anonymous person and was published at London before the year 1500, apparently from Caxton's press. The translator dedicated his version to the nuns of Syon, whom he addresses in the earlier Prologue as follows: Since many of you, although you are able to sing the public Offices of the Blessed Virgin and read them in choir, nevertheless understand their sense less well, therefore, to the sole glory of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his most merciful Mother, and for the spiritual consolation and benefit of you all, I have translated your Legend and the whole Office into the English tongue, so that from understanding it you may perceive how beautiful and holy is the praise of the glorious Virgin contained therein, and may sing, read and recite it to her honour with greater devotion and understanding. There follows a treatise on the Divine Office, and another on the Reading. At its end he advises the holy Virgins that they should read their Office in the vernacular tongue in the convent, only reciting in Latin the first word or sense of each individual Lesson, Hymn or Prayer. Finally he adds: Since, however, under penalty of anathema it is forbidden [namely by the Council of Oxford, in the year 1407] that anyone translate any text of Holy Scripture into English without the permission of the diocesan Bishop; and since many passages of Holy Scripture are found in many of the Lessons of your Office; therefore I have asked and obtained from the Bishop a licence to translate such passages into English, for your spiritual

units.la: spiraspiritualem vestram consolationem & utilitatem. Cæterum Operi suo Interpres titulum dedit: Speculum B. Virginis.
units.tr: your spiritual consolation and profit. The translator gave his work the title: The Mirror of the Blessed Virgin.

units.la: 1480. Gabriel Biel
units.tr: 1480. Gabriel Biel

units.la: De Canone Missæ, lect. 62. Rationabiliter statuit Ecclesia, ut Ministri Ecclesiæ orationes etiam alta voce pronuncient; ut ad notitiam omnium pervenire, &c. Nam cantus in laudem Dei factus cum intellectu & advertentia eorum quæ cantantur, animos cantantium exhilarat simul & audientium, &c. Magis verborum laudis divinæ intelligentiam tollunt; dum propter nimiam artificiosam vocum fractionem, non verba, sed tantùm cantantium sonus percipitur. Quod utique reprehensione dignum non dubitatur, &c. Et licet sufficit oratio mentalis quoad Deum; utilis tamen est vocalis propter plures causas, &c. Secunda [causa] est mentis illuminatio. Verbis enim instruitur intellectus ad discernendum petenda; propter quod Dominus Apostolis quemadmodum orarent discerent petentibus orationem vocalem tradidit; quam cùm proferrent vocaliter, intellectus ad ea quæ petenda sunt a Deo, illuminaretur. Tertia est, facilior recordatio rerum tempore orandi, &c. Oratio non solùm voce fieri debet. Probatur; quia oratio vocalis ordinatur ad mentalem; non è converso. Unde Isidorus. Oratio cordis est, non labiorum. Neque enim verba deprecantis Deus attendit solùm, sed orantis cor aspicit. Unde melius est cum silentio orare corde sine sono vocis, quàm solis verbis sine intuitu mentis, &c. Nihil est solâ voce canere sine cordis intentione. Sed sicut ait Apostolus: Cantantes in cordibus vestris; hoc est, non solùm voce sed & corde psallentes. Item sicut supra patet: Oratio est ascensus in Deum; ille autem fieri non potest per voces, nisi conjunctæ sint menti.
units.tr: On the Canon of the Mass, lecture 62. The Church has reasonably ordained that the ministers of the Church pronounce the prayers even with a loud voice, so that they may come to the knowledge of all, etc. For singing in praise of God, when it is done with understanding and attention to what is sung, gladdens the minds both of those who sing and of those who hear, etc. Rather, they take away the understanding of the words of divine praise, since because of the excessive artificial breaking up of the notes, the words are not perceived, but only the sound of the singers. This is undoubtedly deserving of reproof, etc. And although mental prayer is sufficient as regards God, vocal prayer is nevertheless useful for several reasons, etc. The second [reason] is the illumination of the mind. For the understanding is instructed by words to discern what is to be asked; for which reason the Lord, when the Apostles asked him how they should pray, taught them a vocal prayer, which, when they uttered it aloud, would illuminate the understanding as to what is to be asked of God. The third is the easier recollection of things at the time of prayer, etc. Prayer ought not to be made by the voice alone. This is proved, because vocal prayer is ordered to mental prayer, not the reverse. Hence Isidore: Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips. For God does not attend only to the words of the one who entreats, but looks upon the heart of the one who prays. Hence it is better to pray in silence with the heart, without sound of voice, than with words alone without attention of the mind, etc. There is nothing in singing with the voice alone without intention of the heart. But as the Apostle says: Singing in your hearts; that is, psalming not only with the voice but also with the heart. Likewise, as is clear above: Prayer is an ascent to God; but this cannot be done through voices, unless they are joined to the mind.

units.la: 1485. Laurentius Gulielmus de Savonâ, S. T. D. Ordinis Minorum,
units.tr: 1485. Laurentius Gulielmus de Savona, S.T.D., of the Order of Minors,

units.la: Scripsit Librum, cui titulus, Triumphus Amoris Domini Nostri Jesu Christi. Extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, cum Epistolâ Prætatoriâ valdè prolixâ, ad Wilhelmum de Waynflete, Episcopum Wintoniensem, Londini in Conventu Minorum Anno 1485. scriptâ. Inibi isthæc habentur. Quotiescunque à verâ semitâ propter imbecillitatem nostram, carnisque blanditias, dæmonum insuper jugiter nos impugnantium astutias, declinasse contigerit; per sacrarum literarum præclara documenta ad rectitudinem verae viae reducimur. Quippe quoniam Sacra Scriptura sit speculum lucidissimum, sinceraeque & integerrimae veritatis ostensivum; quo Deum vivum & verum nosque metipsos luculentissime contemplemur & cognoscamus; quantum ad veram salutem consequendam opportunum esse videtur: modo lippis oculis aut animo malignan i ad hoc Speculum divino munere praeparatum non accedatur. Quoniam scriptum sit: In malevolam animam non introibit sapientia; neque habitabit in corde subdito peccatis. Haec est igitur Paradisus deliciarum.
units.tr: He wrote a book entitled The Triumph of the Love of Our Lord Jesus Christ. A manuscript survives in the Lambeth Library, with a very lengthy prefatory letter addressed to William of Waynflete, Bishop of Winchester, written at London in the convent of the Minors in the year 1485. In it the following is found: As often as, because of our weakness and the allurements of the flesh, and moreover the cunning of the demons who constantly assail us, we happen to have turned aside from the true path, we are led back to the right way of true life by the excellent teachings of the sacred letters. Since Holy Scripture is a most clear mirror, showing forth the sincere and most unblemished truth, in which we may contemplate and know most fully the living and true God and ourselves, it seems very useful for attaining true salvation; provided that one does not approach this Mirror, prepared by divine bounty, with bleary eyes or with a malicious mind. For it is written: Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins. This, therefore, is the Paradise of delights.

units.la: 1510. Thomas Cajetanus, Cardinalis Romanus.
units.tr: 1510. Thomas Cajetan, Roman Cardinal.

units.la: In 1 Cor. XIV. Et affert haec [Apostolus] ut intelligamus, quod esse barbarum est esse relativum, & nullum hominem esse absolute barbarum: quoniam in omni genere sunt homines communicantes in idiomate: ac per hoc inter se nullus est barbarus. Hinc enim properat ad deducendum inconveniens, dicendo [Si ergo nescicro, ero cui loquar] hoc est, loquenti. [barbarus] ego audiens & non intelligens significatum vocis, ero barbarus loquenti; & e converso, &c. Benedicere spiritu, est laudare Deum lingua aliena ex dono spiritus. [Quis supplet locum idiotae?] Idiota Graeca dictio est & illiteratum significat, &c. Ex hac Pauli doctrina habetur; quod melius ad aedificationem Ecclesiae est orationes publicas, quae audiente populo dicuntur, dici lingua communi Clericis & Populo, quam dici Latine.
units.tr: On 1 Cor. XIV. And [the Apostle] brings this forward so that we may understand that to be a barbarian is relative, and that no man is a barbarian absolutely: since in every kind there are men who share a language, and therefore none of them is a barbarian to another. For he hastens from this to draw out the absurdity, saying: [If therefore I know not the meaning of the voice], that is, of the one speaking: [I shall be a barbarian to the one speaking to me], I, hearing and not understanding the meaning of the voice, shall be a barbarian to the speaker; and conversely, etc. To bless in the Spirit is to praise God in a foreign tongue by the gift of the Spirit. [Who fills the place of the unlearned?] Idiota is a Greek word [ἰδιώτης] and means one unlearned, etc. From this teaching of Paul it follows that it is better for the edification of the Church that public prayers, which are said while the people listen, be said in a common language by clergy and people, than be said in Latin.

units.la: Volo quinque verba in sensu meo loqui, &c.] Unde discere debemus eligibilius esse, ut in Ecclesia dicantur divina [horae scilicet Canonicae & Missae] intelligibiliter sine melodia musica; quam sic, ut non intelligi possint.
units.tr: [I had rather speak five words with my understanding, etc.] Whence we ought to learn that it is more desirable that the divine offices [namely the canonical hours and the Mass] be said in the Church intelligibly and without musical melody, than in such a way that they cannot be understood.

units.la: Comment. in Aquinat. 2. 2. qu. 83. Art. 12. Propter quod dicentes privatas missas ita submisse de industria, ut intelligi ab Auditoribus nequeant, a ratione devii videntur & inexcusabiles; nisi forte per accidens, coram aliis non celebrent.
units.tr: Commentary on Aquinas, 2.2, q. 83, art. 12. Wherefore those who say private Masses so softly and on purpose that they cannot be understood by the hearers seem to be led astray from reason and inexcusable; unless perhaps they celebrate them accidentally, in the presence of no others.

units.la: Quodlibet. 7. qu. 6. art. 14. Sacra Scriptura ad hoc divinitus est ordinata; ut per eam nobis veritas manifestetur necessaria ad salutem.
units.tr: Quodlibet 7, q. 6, art. 14. Holy Scripture has been divinely ordained for this: that through it the truth necessary for salvation may be made manifest to us.

units.la: 1520. Joannes, Episcopus Chemnicensis.
units.tr: 1520. Joannes, Bishop of Chemnitz.

units.la: Onus Ecclesiae, cap. 23. Concitato & praerupto oris motu Clerici orantes feruntur cum confusa labiorum festinatione & titubatione; ac magis murmurare quam orare videntur; ut nec ipsi quid orant, intelligant; nec astantes audiant: ac proinde Deus eos non exaudiat.
units.tr: Onus Ecclesiae, chap. 23. Clergy praying with a hurried and abrupt movement of the mouth are carried along with a confused rush of the lips and stammering; and they seem to murmur rather than to pray, so that neither they themselves understand what they are praying, nor do those standing by hear; and therefore God does not hear them.

units.la: 1520. Polydorus Virgilius.
units.tr: 1520. Polydorus Virgilius.

units.la: Lib. 6. cap. 2. Sed hodie longè minus è republicâ nostrâ esse videtur [Cantorum ordo ] quando Cantores nostri ita in templis constrepunt, ut nihil præter vocem audiatur ; & qui intersunt (intersunt autem quotquot civitas capit) ejusmodi clamorum concentu, quo eorum aures maximè calent, contenti, de vi verborum minimè curant. Unde eò ventum est ; ut apud vulgus omnis divini cultûs ratio in istis Cantoribus sita esse videatur, &c. Quare dubio procul ex religionis usu foret, aut ejusmodi graculos è templis ejicere, vel omnino ita eos instituere, ut canentes more potiùs legentium quàm instrepentium hymnos recitarent: quod Divum Athanasium Alexandrinum Episcopum olim in Diœcesi suâ fecisse Augustinus attestatur atque magnopere laudat.
units.tr: Book 6, chap. 2. But today it seems far less in the interest of our commonwealth [the order of singers] when our singers so clamour in the churches that nothing is heard but the voice; and those who are present (and present are as many as the city holds) are content with the harmony of such shouting, by which their ears are most excited, and care very little for the force of the words. Whence it has come about that among the common people the whole manner of divine worship seems to lie in these singers, etc. Therefore, without doubt, it would be to the advantage of religious practice either to drive such chattering jackdaws out of the churches or to train them altogether so that, singing, they would recite the hymns in the manner of readers rather than of noisy shouters; which Augustine attests that Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, once did in his diocese, and greatly praises.

units.la: {b} Confess. lib. 10.
units.tr: {b} Confessions, book 10.

units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: PErfecutionis à Pontificiis in Anglià sæculo postremo adversùs S. Scripturam commotæ historiam Reverendissimus Armachanus diligentissimè contexuit. Unicum ego ejusdem insaniæ Papalis addam testimonium; quod Illustrissimi Primatis notitiam fugit. Extat MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ (&, ni fallor, à Cl. Spelmanno editum est Tomo Conciliorum Anglicorum secundo) Instrumentum super Decreto & ordinatione Domini Henrici VIII. Regis Angliæ quoad reprobationem & condemnationem Novi Testamenti, ac aliorum librorum in vulgari linguâ impressorum, hæreticam pravitatem ac damnatam Lutherianam hæresin continentium. Anglicè. Ipsum est (quod vocant) Originale Instrumentum, à Gulielmo Warhamo, Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi confectum, & Notariorum publicorum subscriptionibus confirmatum Anno 1530. In Præfatione Archiepiscopus Henrici Regis consilium explicat, Regem nimirum indies serpenti hæresis veneno obicem ponendi animo, plures Præsules, Doctores, & Theologos ab utrâvis Academiâ delegatos coegisse; ut Libros quosdam vernaculos nuper in Angliam invectos examinent & censurâ notent. Illos post maturum examen infinitos ferè errores, hæreses & blasphemias adinvenisse & excerptos exhibuisse. Dein sequuntur ista excerpta; ex quibus quatuor solummodò selegi, quæ hic loci repræsentarem.
units.tr: Persecution stirred up by the Papists in England in the last century against Holy Scripture has been set out in full detail by the most reverend Archbishop of Armagh. I will add one single piece of evidence of that Papal madness, which escaped the notice of the most illustrious Primate. There is a manuscript in the Lambeth Library (and, unless I am mistaken, it was published by the learned Spelman in the second volume of his Councils of England), entitled Instrument concerning the decree and ordinance of Lord Henry VIII, King of England, on the rejection and condemnation of the New Testament and of other books printed in the vernacular, containing heretical depravity and the condemned Lutheran heresy. In English. It is the original instrument, as they call it, drawn up by William Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury, and confirmed by the signatures of public notaries in the year 1530. In the preface the Archbishop explains the King's purpose: the King, intent on placing an obstacle to the poison of the serpent of heresy, had gathered several prelates, doctors and theologians sent from either university, so that they might examine certain vernacular books lately brought into England and mark them with censure. After a careful examination they had found almost countless errors, heresies and blasphemies in them, and had presented extracts. Then follow those extracts, of which I have selected only four to set before the reader here.

units.la: Errores & Hæreses contentæ in libro, cui titulus est, Summa Scripturæ.
units.tr: Errors and heresies contained in the book titled The Sum of Scripture.

units.la: Num. 4. Suscepto-res & Suscep-trices tenentur, quantùm possunt, curare, ut infantes (pro quibus in Baptismo spoponderunt) ad scholam mittantur; ut Evangelium & Epistolas D. Pauli intelligant.
units.tr: No. 4. Godparents are bound, as far as they can, to see to it that the infants (for whom they stood surety at baptism) are sent to school, so that they may understand the Gospel and the Epistles of St Paul.

units.la: Num. 5. Omnes ex æquo tenemur scire Evangelium & Epistolas D. Pauli.
units.tr: No. 5. We are all equally bound to know the Gospel and the Epistles of St Paul.

units.la: Num. 66. Homines curare debent; ut liberi sui Ecclesias adeant concliones audiendi gratiâ.
units.tr: No. 66. People ought to take care that their children go to the churches to hear sermons.

units.la: Num. 83. Evangelium omnibus personis & hominum ordinibus, Magnatibus, Principibus, Pontifici & Imperatori, scribitur.
units.tr: No. 83. The Gospel is written for all persons and all orders of men, for great lords, for princes, for the Pope and for the Emperor.

units.la: Post errores sigillatim notatos succedit Interdictum Regis: quod sic incipit: Quos quidem omnes enormes errores & pestiferas hæreses; quùm contagiosæ sint & damnabiles, una cum omnibus libris illas continentibus, cum Translatione etiam Scripturæ à Gulielmo Tindallo corruptæ (1) tam Veteris quàm Novi Testamenti, & omnes alios libros lingua vernacula ejusmodi errores continentes; Regia Majestas ex consilio & assensu Antistitum, Doctorum, & utriusque Academiæ, determinat penitus repellendos, rejiciendos, & subditorum omnium manibus excutiendos esse. Quo facilius autem Decretum Regium populo innotesceat; Monitorii cujusdam formula præscribitur, plebi à singulis Sacerdotibus è suggesto legenda. In eâ quisque libros prædictos & in his Anglicam Novi Testamenti Versionem, Curatis suis tradere sub gravi pœnâ jubetur. Neve quis Scripturæ lectionem sibi interdictam queratur; narratur Regem habito Episcoporum, virorumque doctorum conventu, in medium consuluisse, An S. Scripturæ lectionem vernaculam populo permittere expediret? Post gravem autem & solennem disceptationem concordi suffragio definitum esse: Quòd editio Sacræ Scripturæ linguâ vernaculâ Christianis non sit necessaria: quódque Regia Majestas & Episcopi vulgarem S. Scripturæ linguâ Anglicâ evulgatæ usum populo interdicentes, rectè facerent.
units.tr: After the errors noted one by one comes the King's proclamation, which begins thus: All of which enormous errors and pestilential heresies, since they are contagious and damnable, together with all the books containing them, along with the translation of Scripture corrupted by William Tyndale (1) of both the Old and New Testament, and all other books in the vernacular containing such errors, His Royal Majesty, by the counsel and assent of the bishops, doctors and of both universities, determines must be utterly repelled, rejected, and cast out of the hands of all his subjects. In order that the royal decree might become more readily known to the people, a form of admonition is prescribed, to be read from the pulpit by each priest to the common people. In it everyone is ordered, under heavy penalty, to hand over the aforesaid books, and among them the English version of the New Testament, to their curates. And lest anyone complain that the reading of Scripture has been forbidden to him, it is related that the King, having gathered a meeting of bishops and learned men, put to them the question whether it was expedient to allow the common people to read Holy Scripture in the vernacular. After a grave and solemn debate, it was determined by unanimous vote: That an edition of Holy Scripture in the vernacular is not necessary for Christians; and that His Royal Majesty and the bishops rightly forbid the common people the use of the vernacular English Scripture that has been published.

units.la: Parile edictum paulò ante ediderant Ferdinandus & Isabella Hispaniæ Reges. Id Alfonsus à Castro laudare neutiquam veretur. Quapropter laudandum, inquit , merito venit Edictum Illustrissimorum Catholicorumque Hispaniæ Regum, Ferdinandi videlicet ejusque conjugis Helisabetæ; quo sub gravissimis pœnis prohibuerunt, ne quis sacras literas in linguam vulgarem transferret, aut ab alio translatas quoquam pacto retineret. Timuerunt namque prudenter plebi suæ, quam regendam susceperant; ne ulla occasio illi daretur errandi: nec tamen gratis & sine causâ timuerunt: quoniam longâ experientiâ compertum fuerat plures hac occasione hæreses fuisse olim suscitatas.
units.tr: Ferdinand and Isabella, Kings of Spain, had published a similar edict a little earlier. Alfonso de Castro by no means hesitates to praise it. Wherefore, he says, the Edict of the most illustrious and Catholic Kings of Spain, namely Ferdinand and his consort Elizabeth, deserves praise; by which, under the most severe penalties, they forbade anyone to translate the sacred letters into the vulgar tongue, or to keep a translation made by another in any way. For they wisely feared for their people, whom they had undertaken to rule, lest any occasion be given them for error; nor did they fear without reason or cause, since by long experience it had been ascertained that many heresies had formerly been stirred up on this very occasion.

units.la: Istam quidem interdictæ Scripturæ rationem Pontificii Scriptores comminisci solent. Nec mirum quidem, Os deforme fucum quærit. Veram autem rationem Paulus Vergerius exhibet in commentitio Patrum Bononiensium Consilio de Romanâ Ecclesiâ stabiliendâ ad Julium III. Papam. Postquam enim illi monuissent, ut summopere curaret, ut quàm minima Scripturæ Portio linguâ vernaculâ prælegeretur; saltem ut illa pars sufficeret, quæ in Missâ recitari solet; ista subdunt. Hic ille est liber, qui præter cæteros hasce nobis tempestates ac turbines concitavit;
units.tr: The Papist writers are wont to invent this reason for forbidding Scripture. Nor is it any wonder, for a deformed face seeks a mask. The true reason, however, is set out by Paul Vergerius in the spurious Counsel of the Bolognese Fathers on the Establishing of the Roman Church, addressed to Pope Julius III. For after they had advised him to take great care that as little as possible of Scripture be read aloud in the vernacular, or at least only that part which is customarily recited in the Mass, they add these words: This is the book which, above all others, has stirred up these storms and whirlwinds among us.

units.la: * Adv. Hæret. lib. 1. cap. 13.
units.tr: * Against Heresies, book 1, chapter 13.

units.la: (1) Inanis is prætextus. Tindallus enim Scripturam satis fideliter transtulit. quibus prope abrepti sumus. Et sanè si quis illum diligenter expendat; deinde quæ in nostris fieri Ecclesiis consueverunt, singula ordine contemplatur; videbit plurimùm inter se dissidere, & hanc doctrinam nostram ab illâ prorsus diversam esse, ac sæpe contrariam etiam. Quod simulatque homines intelligunt, à docto sciɛet aliquo Adversariorum nostrorum simulati; non ante clamandi in nos finem faciunt, donec re tandem pervulgatâ nos invisos omnibus reddiderint.
units.tr: (1) This is a empty pretext. For Tyndale translated Scripture quite faithfully. by which we have been nearly carried away. And indeed, if anyone weighs it carefully, and then examines one by one what is customarily done in our churches, he will see that they differ greatly from one another, and that our doctrine is entirely different from that one, and often even contrary to it. As soon as men understand this, having been deceived by some learned one of our adversaries pretending to be a friend, they do not cease crying out against us until, the matter at last made public, they have made us hateful to everyone.

units.la: Atque utinam istam solummodo Sacræ Scripturæ Pontificii injuriam fecissent. Inhibitam illius lectionem vidimus, excussa fidelium manibus unica fidei instrumenta, obsignatos vitæ fontes, sacræ lectionis studiosos seu anathemate percussos seu vivicomburio extinctos: spes tamen restabat, non eousque impietatis deventum iri; ut sacris Codicibus corruptrices inferre manus auderent. Tam immane facinus aggredi si non divini nominis reverentia, saltem infamiæ timor inhiberet. Neque enim sperare possent ejusmodi fraudem latere posse. Eò tamen improbum causæ desperatæ studium Adversarios impulit; ut nec Legi Divinæ pepercerint; ut sacrosanctos Codices interpolare fœdissimisque additamentis viciare ausi sint. Satius erat profectò vernaculam S. Scripturæ lectionem in æternum fidelibus interdixisse; satius nunquam in vulgares linguas transfudisse; quàm inaudito sæculis flagitio ipsammet Scripturam mutilare. Jam quidem id, quod antea non licuit, jactitare possunt Pontificii, se in nonnullis saltem regionibus Sacrorum Codicum lectionem omnibus passim perhibere. Jam verò & nos vicissim, quod antea haud ita licuit, vitiatæ ac corruptæ Scripturæ crimen eidem intentare possumus. Siquidem unius sceleris infamiam alio longè atrociori redimunt; idque Orbi Christiano liquidò demonstrant; Pontificios aut nullam aut nonnisi corruptam Scripturam plebi permissuros. Rem, satis scio, factam denegabunt viri perfrictæ frontis, qui se unicos fidei monumentorumque ejus conservatores perhibent; & expurgata ab Indicibus suis Expurgatoriis SS. Patrum Scripta, rem toti orbi notissimam, inficiari non erubescunt: forsitan nec credent posteri; nisi suis etiam temporibus (quod minimè futurum non vanis auguriis ducti speramus) qui veritati solitis artibus adversentur, exstiterint Pontificii. Rem tamen nostro Sæculo heu nimium compertam loquor; cujus eximium aliquod monumentum in illhoc Opere in æternùm Pontificii nominis opprobrium exstare volo.
units.tr: And would that the Papists had done this injury to Holy Scripture alone. We have seen its reading forbidden, the sole instruments of faith struck from the hands of the faithful, the fountains of life sealed up, the students of the sacred reading either struck with anathema or extinguished by burning alive. Still there remained the hope that they would not sink so far into impiety as to dare to lay corrupting hands upon the sacred Codices. Had not reverence for the divine name restrained them from undertaking so monstrous a crime, at least the fear of infamy would have done so; for they could not hope that such a fraud would remain hidden. Yet the shameless zeal of desperate cause drove the adversaries to this point: they did not spare the Divine Law either, but dared to interpolate the most sacred Codices and to defile them with most foul additions. It would surely have been better to have forbidden the reading of Holy Scripture in the vernacular for ever, and better never to have poured it into the common tongues, than by an unheard-of crime of the ages to mutilate Scripture itself. Now indeed the Papists can boast of what was not allowed before, that in some regions at least they make the reading of the Sacred Codices available to all everywhere. And now we in turn can bring against them the charge of Scripture being spoiled and corrupted, which before we could not so freely do. For they buy off the infamy of one crime with another far more atrocious; and this they clearly demonstrate to the Christian world, that the Papists will either permit no Scripture to the people or only a corrupted one. I know well that men of brazen face will deny the deed, men who call themselves the sole keepers of the faith and its monuments, and who are not ashamed to deny what is known to the whole world, that the writings of the holy Fathers have been purged by their Expurgatory Indexes. Perhaps posterity will not believe it either, unless in their own times (as we, led by no vain omens, hope will not fail to happen) there should arise Papists who oppose the truth by their accustomed arts. Yet I speak of a matter, alas, all too well known to our age; and I wish some outstanding monument of it to stand in this work, to the eternal reproach of the Papist name.

units.la: Prodierunt plures à triginta annis in Galliâ S. Scripturæ Versiones Vernaculæ à Theologis Pontificiis elucubratæ. Vix ullam ex his sinceraм atque fraudis immunem reperies. Præ cæteris autem sceleri palmam.
units.tr: For more than thirty years there have appeared in France several vernacular versions of Holy Scripture, elaborated by Papist theologians. You will scarcely find any one of them sincere and free of fraud. Above all others, however, the palm for wickedness has been carried off

units.la: main tulit nupera Novi Testamenti Versio, à Theologis Lovanienfibus confecta, & Burdegalis excusa Anno MDCLXXXXVI. in 4°. ab Archiepiscopi Burdegalensis Typographo, præmissa etiam solenni Theologorum Præli Curatorum licentia. Exinde nonnulla selegi gravioris corruptelæ specimina, quæ Lectori exhiberem; addita Translatione eorundem Latinâ; ne cum hodiernæ dialecti, quæ indies mutatur, interitu, fraudis etiam memoria depereat.
units.tr: by the recent version of the New Testament, prepared by the theologians of Louvain and printed at Bordeaux in the year 1686 in quarto, by the printer of the Archbishop of Bordeaux, also with the solemn licence of the theologians and curates prefixed. From it I have selected several specimens of more serious corruption, which I might set before the reader, with a Latin translation of the same added, so that the memory of the fraud may not perish along with the passing of the present dialect, which changes daily.

units.la: Par. I. pag. 364. Act. XIII. 2.
units.tr: Part I, p. 364. Acts 13:2.

units.la: Or Comme ils offroient au Seigneur le Sacrifice de la Messe.
units.tr: Now, as they were offering to the Lord the Sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: Par. II. pag. 53.
units.tr: Part II, p. 53.

units.la: 1 Cor. III. 15. Mais is sera sauvé quant à luy, ainsi toutefois comme par le seu du Purgatoire.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 3:15. But he himself will be saved, yet so as through the fire of Purgatory.

units.la: Pag. 70.
1 Cor. XI. 10. Partant la femme à cause des Anges, qui la voyent, doit avoir sur la tête un enseigne qu' elle est sous puissance.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11:10. Therefore the woman, because of the angels who see her, ought to have upon her head a sign that she is under authority.

units.la: Pag. 72.
1 Cor. XI. 26, 27. C' est pourquoy quiconque mangera ce pain de vie. —Car toutes les fois que vous mangerez ce pain vivant.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11:26, 27. Therefore whoever shall eat this bread of life. For as often as you eat this living bread.

units.la: Coloss. II. 18. Que personne ne vous seduisie à son plaisir sous pretexte d' humilité, & de Religion donnée à Moise par des Anges. Offerentibus autem illis Domino Sacrificium Missæ. Ministrantibus autem illis Domino. Sic Versio Vulgata; ex quâ Versionem suam Gallicam expressisse præ se ferunt Lovanienses.
units.tr: Col. 2:18. Let no one seduce you at his pleasure, under the pretext of humility and of a religion given to Moses by angels. Offering to the Lord the Sacrifice of the Mass. Ministering to the Lord. So reads the Vulgate version, from which the Louvain writers claim to have expressed their French version.

units.la: Ipse autem salvus erit; sic tamen quasi per ignem Purgatorii. Deest vox ultima in Vers. Vulgat.
units.tr: But he himself will be saved, yet so as through the fire of Purgatory. The last word is missing in the Vulgate version.

units.la: Ideo debet mulier subjectionis insigne habere supra caput suum, propter Angelos, qui eam vident. Vers. Vulgat. velamen habere supra caput suum, & propter Angelos.
units.tr: Therefore a woman ought to have a sign of subjection upon her head, because of the angels who see her. The Vulgate version has: to have a veil upon her head, and because of the angels.

units.la: Itaque quicunque manducaverit panem hunc vitæ. — Quotiescunque enim manducabitis panem hunc viventem. Deest ubique vox ultima in Vers. Vulgat.
units.tr: Therefore whoever shall eat this bread of life. For as often as you shall eat this living bread. The last word is missing everywhere in the Vulgate version.

units.la: Nemo vos seducat pro arbitrio suo, prætextu humilitatis & Religionis Mosi ab Angelis datæ; rebus quæ non vidit sese immiscens; temerès'ingerant es chofes, qu' il n' a point vùës, eftant temerairement enflé du fang de fa chair.
units.tr: Let no one seduce you at his own will, under the pretext of humility and of the religion of Moses given by angels, intruding into things he has not seen, rashly puffed up by the blood of his flesh.

units.la: 1 Tim. IV. 1. Or l' Efprit dit clairement, qu' es derniers temps quelques uns fe fepareront de la Foy Romaine. inflatus à sanguine carnis suæ. Vers' Vulgat. Nemo vos seducat volens, in humilitate & religione Angelorum, quæ non vidit ambulans; frustra inflatus sensu carnis suæ.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 4:1. Now the Spirit says clearly that in the latter times some will separate from the Roman Faith. Let no one seduce you of his own will, in humility and the religion of angels, which he has not seen when walking; vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh. The Vulgate version reads thus.

units.la: Spiritus autem manifestè dicit, quia in novissimis temporibus discedent quidam à Fide Romanâ. Deest vox ultima in Vers. Vulgat.
units.tr: Now the Spirit says clearly that in the last times some will depart from the Roman Faith. The last word is missing in the Vulgate version.
