units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: NON solùm clarissimi Ecclesiæ Doctores S. Scripturæ studium omnibus patere voluerunt; sed & Conciliorum, Pontificum atque Principum decreta idem confirmârunt. Testimonia Cl. Armachanus capite 7. affatim profert. His breve quoddam Spicilegium nobis addere licebit. Quantum igitur plebi olim interesse credebatur, ut preces publicas intelligeret; frequentes Diaconi admonitiones, Sacerdotis allocutiones, & omnium fidelium Responsiones demonstrant. Plenæ his sunt omnes antiquorum Liturgiæ, plena Scriptorum Liturgicorum monumenta. Exemplo sint Constitutiones Apostolicæ; quæ disciplinam Orientalis Ecclesiæ primævis sæculis receptam optimè demonstrant. Inibi præcipitur, {a} ut ante singulas Sacerdotis petitiones; Diaconus clamaret: ἐκτενῶς πάντες δεηθῶμεν. Intentè omnes precemur. ἐπὶ ἑκάστῳ ὧν τόπων, ὧν ὁ διάκονος προσφωνεῖ, λεγέτω ὁ λαὸς, κύριε ἐλέησον, ἡ περὶ πάντων τῶν πνευμάτων σου. In singulis horum, quæ Diaconus dicit, respondeat populus, Kyrie eleison; & ante omnes respondeant pueri. Et cap. 11. Λεγέτω ὁ διάκονος, προσευχώμεθα· ἡ ἀσπαζέσθω ὁ ἐπίσκοπος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, ἡ λεγέτω, ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ θεοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν· ἡ ὁ λαὸς ἀποκρινέσθω, καὶ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματός σου. Dicat Diaconus: Attendamus. Et salutet Episcopus Ecclesiam & dicat: Pax Dei cum omnibus vobis. Et respondeat Populus: Et cum spiritu tuo. Cap. 12. Episcopus dicit: Gratia Dei, &c. sit cum omnibus vobis. Et omnes unâ voce respondeant (πάντες συμφώνως λεγέτωσαν) Et cum spiritu tuo. Ac rursus Episcopus: Sursum mentem. Respondeant omnes: Habemus ad Dominum. Et Episcopus: Gratias agamus Domino. Et Omnes: Dignum & justum est.
units.tr: The most distinguished Doctors of the Church did not only wish the study of Holy Scripture to be open to all; the decrees of Councils, Popes and princes have confirmed the same. The illustrious Archbishop of Armagh brings forward plenty of testimonies in his seventh chapter, and I may add a short gleaning of my own. As much as it was once thought to matter to the common people that they understand the public prayers, the frequent admonitions of the deacon, the addresses of the priest and the responses of all the faithful show. All the ancient liturgies are full of this, and the liturgical records of the writers are full of it. Let the Apostolic Constitutions serve as an example, which very clearly demonstrate the discipline received in the Eastern Church in the earliest centuries. There it is ordered that before each of the priest's petitions the deacon should cry out: "Let us all pray earnestly" [ἐκτενῶς πάντες δεηθῶμεν], "Let us all pray with attention." For each of the things the deacon announces, let the people reply: "Lord, have mercy" [κύριε ἐλέησον], "concerning all your spirits." To each of these things the deacon says, the people should answer "Kyrie eleison," and the boys should answer before all the others. And in chapter 11: "Let the deacon say, Let us pray; and let the bishop greet the Church and say, The peace of God be with all of you; and let the people answer, And with your spirit" [Λεγέτω ὁ διάκονος, προσευχώμεθα· ἡ ἀσπαζέσθω ὁ ἐπίσκοπος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, ἡ λεγέτω, ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ θεοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν· ἡ ὁ λαὸς ἀποκρινέσθω, καὶ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματός σου]. In chapter 12: the bishop says, "The grace of God, etc., be with all of you," and all should answer with one voice [πάντες συμφώνως λεγέτωσαν], "And with your spirit." Again the bishop says, "Lift up your hearts," and all should answer, "We have them towards the Lord." And the bishop says, "Let us give thanks to the Lord," and all say, "It is meet and right."

units.la: Eandem populi attentionem in lectionibus sacris audiendis Patres exegerunt. Sic enim Anastasius I. Papa in Epistolâ Decretali ad Germaniæ & Burgundiæ Episcopus. {b} Dum sancta Evangelia in Ecclesiâ recitantur; Sacerdotes & cæteri omnes præsentes, non sedentes sed venerabiliter curvi, in conspectu sancti Evangelii stantes, Dominica verba intentè audiant, & fideliter adorent. Nullum S. Scripturæ lectione defraudatum, non solùm è perfectioribus & in fide confirmatis, sed neque è rudibus & imperfectis, voluerunt. Ita Canon 18. Concilii Arausicani I.
units.tr: The Fathers demanded the same attention of the people in hearing the sacred readings. Thus Pope Anastasius I, in his decretal letter to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy: "While the holy Gospels are read in the Church, let the priests and all the others present, not sitting but standing reverently bowed in the sight of the holy Gospel, listen attentively to the words of the Lord and adore them faithfully." They wished that no one, not only of the more advanced and those confirmed in the faith, but also of the simple and unskilled, should be deprived of the reading of Holy Scripture. So too canon 18 of the First Council of Arausio.

units.la: {a} Lib. 8. cap. 6.
units.tr: {a} Lib. 8. cap. 6.

units.la: {b} Concil. Tom. II. pag. 1192. Anno 441. celebrati. Evangelia deinceps placuit Catechumenis legi apud omnes provinciarum nostrarum Ecclesias. Neque in Ecclesia solùm, sed & in conviviis virorum Ecclesiasticorum, idiotas lectione divinâ ædificari præceperunt. Id mandat Concilium Rhemense II. Anno 813. habitum, Can. 17. d Ut Episcopi, & Abbates, pauperes & indigentes secum ad mensam habeant; & lectio divina ibi personet; & sumant cibum cum benedictione & laude Domini. Idem habet Herardus, Archiepiscopus Turonensis, capit. 108.
units.tr: {b} Council, Vol. II, p. 1192, held in the year 441: It has been decided that from now on the Gospels be read to the catechumens in all the churches of our provinces. They ordered that the unlearned be edified by the divine reading not only in church but also at the tables of churchmen. The Council of Reims II, held in the year 813, canon 17, commands the same: d That bishops and abbots have the poor and needy at their table with them, and that the divine reading resound there, and that they take their food with a blessing and praise of the Lord. Herard, Archbishop of Tours, chapter 108, has the same.

units.la: Postquam autem exolevit apud Occidentales vulgaris linguæ Latinæ usus: quantâ sollicitudine curarunt Ecclesiæ Antiliites; ne Scripturæ rerumque divinarum notitia apud vulgum Christianum interiret? Concilium Anglicum Clovesshoviæ sub Cuthberto Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi Anno 747. habitum, præcepit Canone 10. e Ut Presbyteri Symbolum fidei, ac Dominicam Orationem, sed & sacrosancta quoque verba, quæ in Missæ celebratione & officio Baptismi solenniter dicuntur, interpretari atque exponere posse propriâ linguâ qui nesciant, discant. [Anglicè discant & doceant. Sic Gulielmus Malmsburiensis Canonem refert f.] Et Canone 7. g Episcopi, Abbates atque Abbatissæ [in quorum familiis omnes Nobilium pueri, aliique innumeri, tunc temporis, educari solebant.] studeant & diligenti curâ provideant; ut per familias suas lectionis studium indesinenter in plurimorum pectoribus versetur, & ad lucrum animarum laudemque Regis æterni multorum vocibus innotescat. Nam dictu dolendum est, quod his temporibus perpauci inveniantur, qui ex intimo corde sacræ scientiæ rapiantur amore, & vix aliquid elaborare in discendo voluerint: quin potiùs à juvenile ætate vanitatibus diversis & inanis gloriæ cupiditatibus occupantur; atque præsentis vitæ instabilitatem, plusquam sacrarum Scripturarum assiduitatem, vagabundâ mente sequuntur. Proinde coherceantur & exerceantur in Scholis pueri ad dilectionem sacræ scientiæ; ut per hoc bene eruditi sint. Inter Capitula Saxonica incertæ ætatis, vicesimum est hujusmodi. h [Saxon text, illegible, ~60 letters] Presbyteri per villas & vicos scholas habeant: & si quislibet fidelium suos parvulos ad discendas literas eis commendare vult; eos suscipere & docere non renuant; sed cum summâ charitate eos doceant. Cùm ergo eos docent; nihil ab eis pretii pro hâc re exigent, nec aliquid ab eis accipient. Rationem hujus disciplinæ reddit Capitulum præcedens (quod ex Capitularibus Carolinis c Concil. Tom. III. pag. 1450. d Concil. Tom. VII. pag. 1256. e Concil. Anglic. Tom. I. pag. 248. f De gestis Pontif. Angl. lib. 1. g Concil. Angl. Tom. I. p. 247. h Ibid. p. 595. desumptum est ꝑ pɪtcoblıce peah eall halguge ppitu mid birenum, &c. Omnium sacrarum Scripturarum paginæ instrumentis bonorum operum refertæ sunt: & per sanctarum Scripturarum Campos possunt inveniri arma, quibus vitia comprimantur, & virtutes nutriantur.
units.tr: But after the common use of the Latin language had died out among the Western peoples, with how much care did the churchmen of those times take steps so that knowledge of Scripture and of divine things would not perish among the Christian common people? The English Council held at Clovesho under Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury, in the year 747, ordered in canon 10: e That priests should learn, and be able to interpret and explain in their own tongue, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, and also those most holy words that are solemnly said in the celebration of the Mass and in the office of baptism, for those who do not know them. [In English: let them learn and teach. Thus William of Malmesbury quotes the canon, f.] And in canon 7: g Bishops, abbots and abbesses [in whose households the sons of all the nobles, and countless others, were then usually brought up] should take care and diligently provide that the study of reading be constantly kept alive in the hearts of many in their households, and that it become known, by the voices of many, for the gain of souls and the praise of the eternal King. For it is to be lamented that in these times very few are found who are carried off by a love of sacred learning from the depths of their heart, and who are willing to labour at all in learning. Rather, from their youth they are occupied with various vanities and desires for empty glory, and with a wandering mind they follow the instability of the present life more than the constant reading of the holy Scriptures. Therefore let boys be restrained and trained in the schools to love sacred learning, so that they may be well taught through it. Among the Saxon chapters of uncertain date, the twentieth is of this kind. h [Saxon text, illegible, about 60 letters] Let the priests have schools in the villages and towns; and if any of the faithful wishes to entrust his little children to them to learn letters, they should not refuse to receive and teach them, but should teach them with the greatest charity. When they teach them, they shall demand no payment from them for this, nor accept anything from them. The reason for this discipline is given by the preceding chapter, which is taken from the Carolingian capitularies c Council, Vol. III, p. 1450. d Council, Vol. VII, p. 1256. e English Council, Vol. I, p. 248. f On the Acts of the English Pontiffs, bk. 1. g English Council, Vol. I, p. 247. h Ibid., p. 595: [thæt pitcoblice peah eall halguge pitu mid birenum, etc.] The pages of all the sacred Scriptures are filled with the tools of good works, and through the fields of the holy Scriptures can be found the weapons by which vices are checked and virtues nourished.

units.la: Ita quidem integram Sacræ Scripturæ lectionem vel auditum omnibus Christianis expedire Veteres crediderunt: Symbolum verò (Scripturæ compendium quoddam) & Orationem Dominicam ut omnes perfectè scirent, penitus necessarium duxerunt. Id quod hæreticæ pravitatis indicium ferro flammâque puniendum Pontificii olim k judicârunt. Sic enim Concilium Moguntinum, Anno 813. Canone 45. statuit. l Symbolum, quod est signaculum fidei, & Orationem Dominicam, discere semper admoneant Sacerdotes populum Christianum. Volumusque ut disciplinam condignam habeant; qui hæc discere negligunt; sive in jejunio, sive in aliâ castigatione emendentur. Propterea dignum est, ut filios suos donent ad scholam, sive ad Monasteria, sive foràs Presbyteris; ut fidem Catholicam rectè discant & Orationem Dominicam; ut domi alios edocere valeant. Et qui aliter non potuerit, vel in suâ linguâ hoc discat. Pastorale quoddam Latinum, vetustum admodum MS. vidi in Collegio Corporis Christi Cantab. quod in Conciliis Anglicis m Saxonico-Latinum reperitur. Canon ejus 22us sic habet. n Commonendi sunt fideles; ut generaliter omnes à minimo usque ad maximum, Orationem Dominicam & Symbolum discant. Et dicendum est eis, quòd in his duabus sententiis omne fidei Christianæ fundamentum incumbit. Et nisi quis has duas sententias memoriter tenuerit, & ex toto corde crediderit, & in oratione sæpissimè frequentaverit, Catholicus esse non poterit. Constitutum namque est, ut nullus chrismetur; neque baptizetur, neque è lavacro fontis alium suscipiat, neque coram Episcopo ad confirmandum quemlibet teneat; nisi Symbolum & Orationem Dominicam memoriter tenuerit; exceptis iis, quos ad loquendum ætas minimè perduxit.
units.tr: Thus the Ancients believed that the entire reading or hearing of Holy Scripture was useful for all Christians; but they judged it absolutely necessary that everyone know perfectly the Creed (a kind of summary of Scripture) and the Lord's Prayer. The Papists once judged that failure to do so was a sign of heretical depravity, to be punished with fire and sword. For the Council of Mainz, in the year 813, canon 45, decreed thus: Let the priests always admonish the Christian people to learn the Creed, which is the seal of faith, and the Lord's Prayer. And we wish that those who neglect to learn these be disciplined appropriately, whether by fasting or by some other chastisement. Therefore it is fitting that they give their sons to school, whether to monasteries or to the priests outside, so that they may rightly learn the Catholic faith and the Lord's Prayer, and be able to teach others at home. And whoever cannot do this otherwise, let him learn it in his own language. I have seen in the College of Corpus Christi, Cambridge, a very old Latin pastoral manuscript, which is found in the English Councils in a Saxon-Latin version. Its 22nd canon reads thus: The faithful are to be admonished that all, generally, from the least to the greatest, learn the Lord's Prayer and the Creed. And they must be told that the whole foundation of the Christian faith rests on these two sentences. Unless someone has held these two sentences in memory, and believed them with his whole heart, and very often repeated them in prayer, he cannot be Catholic. For it is decreed that no one is to be anointed with chrism, nor baptized, nor receive another from the font of baptism, nor stand before a bishop as sponsor for anyone's confirmation, unless he has held the Creed and the Lord's Prayer in memory; excepting those whom age has not yet brought to the power of speech.

units.la: Denique si expressum Concilii Decretum, preces alienâ linguâ factas damnans, requiratur; neque id etiam deerit. Qui preces enim alienâ linguâ peroratas tuebantur, isto imprimis argumento usi
units.tr: Finally, if an express decree of the Council condemning prayers made in a foreign tongue is required, this too will not be lacking. For those who defended prayers spoken in a foreign language used, and still use, chiefly this argument:

units.la: i Ibid. pag. 595. k Vid. supra, cap. 7. l Concil. Tom. VII. pag. 1351. m Tom. I pag. 584. n Vid: Theodulphi Aureliancnsis Capit. 22. Concil. Tom. VI pag. 1206. sunt, & adhuc utuntur: Nimirum tres solummodo linguas, Hebræam, Græcam, & Latinam, sacras esse, & divinis laudibus in Ecclesiâ resonandis idoneas; has solas dignas fuisse habitas, quæ Christi cruci inscriberentur; reliquas omnes barbaras ab Apostolo appellari, divinis officiis celebrandis minùs aptas natas, & ex usu Ecclesiastico eliminandas. E contra autem Concilium Francofordiense, Anno 794. coactum (quod ab Occidentalibus Generale habitum est) Canone 52. decernit. Ut nullus credat, quòd nonnisi in tribus linguis Deus orandus sit; quia in omni linguâ Deus adoratur, & homo exauditur, si justa petierit.
units.tr: {i} Ibid., p. 595. {k} See above, chapter 7. {l} Council, vol. VII, p. 1351. {m} Vol. I, p. 584. {n} See Theodulf of Orléans, Capitulary 22, Council, vol. VI, p. 1206. That there are only three sacred languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin, fit to resound divine praises in the Church; that these alone were judged worthy to be inscribed on Christ's cross; that all the others are called barbarous by the Apostle, born less suited to the celebration of divine offices, and to be removed from ecclesiastical use. On the other hand, the Council of Frankfurt, assembled in the year 794 (which was held as a General Council by the Western churches), decrees in canon 52: "That no one believe that God can be prayed to only in three languages; for God is adored in every language, and a man is heard if he asks what is right."

units.la: MULTA de Versionibus S. Scripturæ in linguas Orientales Illustrissimus Primas congessit. Cùm plures autem ex iis Versiones abhinc prodierint, aliæ in notitiam devenerint; pauca addere non abs re erit. De Versionibus Judæorum supra egimus cap. I. A Christianis Orientalibus factæ sunt Translationes Syriacæ, Armenicæ, Æthiopicæ, Copt icæ, Arabicæ, & Persicæ.
units.tr: MANY things about the versions of Holy Scripture into the Eastern languages have been gathered by the most illustrious Primate. Since several more of these versions have since appeared and have come to notice, it will not be out of place to add a few. We have already dealt with the versions of the Jews in chapter I. The Christians of the East made the Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, Coptic, Arabic and Persian translations.

units.la: Duplex exstat Versio S. Scripturæ in linguam Syriacam sive Chaldæam [unica enim est lingua, diversis tamen characteribus exarata.] Altera ex Hebræo facta, quæ Simplex & Antiqua vocatur; altera ex Græco, recentior. Antiquâ solummodò in divinis Officiis hodie utuntur Maronitæ. Factam esse à Thaddæo aliisque Apostolis tempore Abgari Regis ex Syriacis Scriptoribus ostendit Abraham Ecchellensis . Eandem tamen, saltem ex parte, conditam esse tempore Solomonis in gratiam Hirami Regis Tyri, reliquam curâ Thaddæi cæterorumque Apostolorum tempore Abgari Regis, plerique è Syris contendunt . Apud alios tamen Syros constans viget Traditio à D. Marco factam esse. Utut id certum est temporibus Apostolorum factam fuisse; antequam Canon N. Testamenti communi Ecclesiarum consensu confirmatus esset. Unde fit, quòd Epistolæ 2a. Petri, 2a. & 3a. Joannis, illa Judæ, & Apocalypsis in eâ omittantur. Prodiit Novum Testamentum istius Versionis à Widmanstadio editum (de quâ editione vide Cl. Usserium cap. 8. sect. 1.) & in Editione Bibliorum Antverpiensi Ariæ Montani. Utrumque Testamentum, aliquoties mutilum, in Bibliis Parisiensibus Michaelis Jaii, integrum in Londinensibus Polyglottis Waltoni. Versio Syriaca è Græco facta, nondum integra prodiit. Apocalypsin tamen edidit Ludovicus de Dieu: Epistolas Canonicas Cl. Pocockius; qui Evangelia MSS. penès se habet. Quod ætatem ejus spectat: extitit exemplar ejus MS. penès Andream Masium ante Annos mille exaratum: aliud in Bibliothecâ Florentinâ, Evangelia continens; quod Anno 925. scriptum est. Quin & Ephræmio Edesseno antiquior est, ab illo passim usurpata; Siquidem Gerardus Vossius Opera ejus fideliter transtulerit: judice Richardo Simonio . Sacra autem
units.tr: There is a twofold version of Holy Scripture into the Syriac or Chaldee language [for it is one language, though written in different characters]. One was made from the Hebrew and is called the Simple and Ancient version; the other, more recent, was made from the Greek. Today the Maronites use only the ancient version in their divine offices. Abraham Ecchellensis shows from Syriac writers that it was made by Thaddaeus and other apostles in the time of King Abgarus. Most Syrians, however, contend that it was drawn up, at least in part, in the time of Solomon for the sake of Hiram king of Tyre, and that the rest was completed under Thaddaeus and the other apostles in the time of King Abgarus. Among other Syrians, however, the firm tradition holds that it was made by St Mark. Whatever the truth, it is certain that it was made in apostolic times, before the canon of the New Testament was confirmed by the common consent of the Churches. Hence it is that the Second Epistle of Peter, the Second and Third of John, the Epistle of Jude and the Apocalypse are omitted from it. The New Testament of this version was published by Widmanstadt (on that edition see the learned Usher, chapter 8, section 1), and in the Antwerp edition of the Bible of Arias Montanus. Both Testaments, though at times mutilated, appear in the Paris Bible of Michael Jay, and the whole in the London Polyglot of Walton. The Syriac version made from the Greek has not yet appeared in full. Ludovicus de Dieu, however, published the Apocalypse, and the learned Pococke the Catholic Epistles; he has the Gospels in manuscript. As to its age: a manuscript copy of it, written more than a thousand years ago, was in the possession of Andreas Masius; another, containing the Gospels, is in the Florentine library and was written in 925. Indeed it is older than Ephraem of Edessa, who frequently used it; for Gerard Vossius faithfully translated his works, according to the judgement of Richard Simon. The Syriac language is used in sacred worship by the following, as reported by Walton from various writers:

units.tr: {a} In the notes on Hebedjesu. {b} Walton, Prolegomena to the Polyglot Bible, chapter 13. {c} Critical History, book 2, chapter 15.

units.la: 1. Maronitæ in monte Libano, Patriarchæ in eodem monte vel Tripoli sedem obtinenti subjecti. 2. Nestoriani, Patriarchæ in Urbe Muzal sedenti subditi. 3. Jacobitæ, quorum Patriarcha sedem habet in Caramit Mesopotamiæ metropoli. Ipsorum Liturgiam habemus ex Syriaco in Latinum conversam operâ Andreæ Masii, quæ in Bibliothecâ Patrum sub nomine Anaphoræ Basilii reperitur. 4. Copti seu Coptitæ, quotcunque religionem Jacobitarum sectantur. Isti post lectum Evangelium lingua Syriaca, legunt idem Arabicâ; quæ iis jam vernacula est. Patriarchæ Alexandrino subjecti sunt; & Liturgiâ utuntur Severi Patriarchæ Alexandrini [rectius Antiocheni, juxta Simonium ; neque enim Patriarcha Alexandrinus istius nominis fuit.] Latinè isthæc versa est à Fabricio Boderiano. 5. Indi, sive S. Thomæ Christiani. Habetur eorum Liturgia ex Syriaco Latinè versa in Bibliothecâ Patrum. 6. Christiani qui Insulam Zocotoram extra sinum Arabicum inhabitant, & Patriarchæ in urbe Mozal sedenti subsunt.
units.tr: (1) The Maronites on Mount Lebanon, subject to the patriarch who holds his see on the same mount or at Tripoli. (2) The Nestorians, subject to the patriarch who sits in the city of Mosul. (3) The Jacobites, whose patriarch has his seat at Karamit, the metropolis of Mesopotamia. We have their liturgy translated from Syriac into Latin by the labour of Andreas Masius, which is found in the Bibliotheca Patrum under the name of the Anaphora of Basil. (4) The Copts, or Coptites, as many as follow the religion of the Jacobites. After the Gospel has been read in Syriac, they read the same in Arabic, which is now their vernacular. They are subject to the Alexandrian patriarch, and use the liturgy of Severus, patriarch of Alexandria [more correctly of Antioch, according to Simon; for there was no Alexandrian patriarch of that name]. This was translated into Latin by Fabricius Boderianus. (5) The Indians, or Christians of St Thomas. Their liturgy, translated from Syriac into Latin, is in the Bibliotheca Patrum. (6) The Christians who inhabit the island of Socotra, outside the Arabian Gulf, and are subject to the patriarch who sits in the city of Mosul.

units.la: Armeniaca Versio à Chrysostomo confecta existimatur, saltem à quibusdam doctis Chrysostomi tempore. Hos vetusta traditio Moscn Grammaticum & Davidem Philosophum fuisse perhibet. Quamvis Armenorum plurimi Translationem suam Gregorio primo Patriarchæ acceptam referant. Evangelia quatuor extiterunt Armenicè penès Waltonum . Anno demum 1662. Jacobus Caractri, Patriarcha Armenorum, Ufcanem Episcopum Vufchuavanchæ in Europam misit, qui Biblia Armenicis typis imprimi curaret. Is itaque utrumque Testamentum in 4°. & Novum Testamentum in 8°. excudi fecit Amstelodami 1664.
units.tr: The Armenian version is thought to have been made by Chrysostom, or at least by some learned men in Chrysostom's time. Ancient tradition reports that Moses the Grammarian and David the Philosopher were its authors, although most Armenians refer their translation to Gregory, the first patriarch. Four Gospels in Armenian exist in the possession of Walton. Finally, in 1662, Jacob Caractri, patriarch of the Armenians, sent Bishop Ufcanes of Vufchuavancha into Europe, to see to the printing of the Armenian Bible. He therefore had both Testaments printed in quarto, and the New Testament in octavo, at Amsterdam in 1664.

units.la: Apud Æthiopas constans est traditio Versionem S. Scripturæ vernaculam extitisse à primis Conversionis temporibus; sive illa Apostolorum seu Constantini Imp. ævo contigerit. Translatio Æthiopica totius Veteris Testamenti MS. penès Gaulminum fuit. Psalterium, Canticum Canticorum, aliaque Cantica Ecclesiastica à Potkenio edita sunt Romæ 1513. Colon. 1518. Novum Testamentum (demptis Epistolis Catholicis) à Petro Æthiope evulgatum est Romæ 1548. unà cum Missali Æthiopico [cujus Versio Latina in Bibliothecâ Patrum invenitur] Epistolæ Catholicæ ab eodem, Romæ 1551. Omnia demum prius impressa, cæta sunt simul in Bibliis Polyglottis Londinensibus.
units.tr: Among the Ethiopians there is a firm tradition that a vernacular version of Holy Scripture existed from the first times of their conversion, whether that occurred in the age of the apostles or of the emperor Constantine. The Ethiopic translation of the whole Old Testament was in manuscript in the possession of Gaulmin. The Psalter, the Song of Songs and other ecclesiastical canticles were published by Potken at Rome in 1513 and at Cologne in 1518. The New Testament (without the Catholic Epistles) was published by Peter the Ethiopian at Rome in 1548, together with an Ethiopic Missal [whose Latin version is found in the Bibliotheca Patrum]. The Catholic Epistles, by the same editor, appeared at Rome in 1551. Finally, all the works previously printed were brought together in the London Polyglot Bibles.

units.la: Prolegom. cap. 13. sect. 17. L. 2. c. 24. Prolegom. cap. 5. Ludolphus Hist. Æthiop. l. 3. c. 4.
units.tr: Prolegomena, chapter 13, section 17. Book 2, chapter 24. Prolegomena, chapter 5. Ludolf, History of Ethiopia, book 3, chapter 4.

units.la: Coptica sive Ægyptiaca Versio facta est circa tempus Concilii Nicæni, censente Kirchero ᵉ. In Bibliothecâ enim Collegii Maronitarum se Copticum Martyrologium vidisse dicit ante Annos circiter 1300. scriptum; in quo repperit præcipuum fuisse veterum Monachorum Ægyptiorum studium, S. Scripturam ex Hebraico, Chaldæo, & Græco, in usum Populi Græcè non intelligentis, transferre. Vidit ipse in Bibliothecâ Vaticanâ plurimos libros MSS. linguâ Coptica exaratos; puta, Pentateuchum tribus Tomis; Evangelia IV. seorsim; S. Pauli Epistolas, & tres Canonicas Epistolas, & Acta Apostolorum, in alio volumine. Apocalypsin seorsim, uti & Psalterium; Liturgiam S. Marci, cum aliis precibus quotidianis; Liturgiam S. Gregorii, cum precibus S. Cyrilli; Liturgiam S. Basilii, aliaque Ritualia & Missalia. Item Ordinale Copticum Latine translulit & excudi curavit, à Morino recusum, lib de Ordinat. sacris, pag. 504. Denique in Bibliothecâ Segvierii Galliæ Cancellarii ʰ extabat MS. Consecratio Patriarchæ Copticè, & Arabicè, & Plures S. Scripturæ Translationes, ac Orationes, utrâque linguâ. Vetustus Evangeliorum Codex Copticus penès Isaacum Vossium nuper fuit.
units.tr: The Coptic or Egyptian version was made about the time of the Council of Nicaea, according to Kircher ᵉ. For in the library of the Maronite college he says he saw a Coptic martyrology, written about 1300 years ago, in which he found that the chief zeal of the ancient Egyptian monks was to translate Holy Scripture from the Hebrew, Chaldee and Greek for the use of the people who did not understand Greek. He himself saw in the Vatican library very many manuscript books written in the Coptic language, namely: the Pentateuch in three volumes; the four Gospels separately; the Epistles of St Paul, and the three Catholic Epistles, and the Acts of the Apostles, in another volume; the Apocalypse separately, as also the Psalter; the Liturgy of St Mark, with other daily prayers; the Liturgy of St Gregory, with the prayers of St Cyril; the Liturgy of St Basil, and other Rituals and Missals. He also translated the Coptic Ordinal into Latin and had it printed; it was reprinted by Morinus, in his book on sacred ordinations, page 504. Finally, in the library of Séguier, Chancellor of France ʰ, there existed a manuscript Consecration of a Patriarch in Coptic and Arabic, and several translations of Holy Scripture and prayers in both languages. Not long ago the ancient Coptic codex of the Gospels was in the possession of Isaac Vossius.

units.la: Arabicæ Versiones complures reperiuntur ⁱ. Veteris Testamenti duplex est; Antiochena, & Alexandrina. Utraque usus est Augustinus Justinianus, Episcopus Nebiensis; & utramque in Bibliothecis Vaticanâ & Medicæâ haberi Cornelius à Lapide fidem facit Comm. in Prophet. Min. in Argumento, pag. 5. Ex Antiochenâ Nebiensis Psalmos edidit, unà cùm Versionibus ejusdem Chaldæâ, Græcâ, & Latinâ, & textu Hebræo, Genuæ 1516. Alexandrina omnes S. Scripturæ libros complectitur; & in his Pentateuchum & Joshuam ex Hebræo, Job ex Syriaco, reliquos ex Græco 5. conversos. Ferè eadem est cum illâ Saadiæ (de quâ supra, cap. I.) adeò ut aut revera non differant, aut unus Interpres alium descripserit. Facta est post Alcoranum conditum; quodque verisimile est, circa Saadiæ tempora, viz. circa Annum 900. Exemplar ejus ante Annum 300. scriptum nactus Gabriel Sionita edidit in Bibliis Parisiensibus, dein Waltonus in Londinensibus. Novi Testamenti Variæ sunt versiones, Evangeliorum sc. tres. Prima Romæ prodiit typis Medicæis, sol. incertæ ætatis, docti tamen Interpretis. Secunda unà cum reliquis Novi Testamenti libris, Erpenio curante, Lugduni Bat. 1616. 4°. & in Bibliis Parisiensibus ac Londinensibus.
units.tr: Several Arabic versions are found ⁱ. The Old Testament exists in two forms: the Antiochene and the Alexandrine. Augustinus Justinianus, bishop of Nebbio, used both, and Cornelius à Lapide assures us that both are held in the Vatican and Medici libraries (Commentary on the Minor Prophets, in the Argument, page 5). From the Antiochene version Justinianus published the Psalms, together with the Syriac, Greek and Latin versions of the same and the Hebrew text, at Genoa in 1516. The Alexandrine version embraces all the books of Holy Scripture; in it the Pentateuch and Joshua were translated from the Hebrew, Job from the Syriac, and the rest from the Greek by five translators. It is almost the same as that of Saadiah (of whom we spoke above, chapter 1), so that either they do not really differ, or one translator copied the other. It was made after the Qur'an was composed, and probably around the time of Saadiah, that is, around the year 900. Gabriel Sionita, having obtained a copy written less than 300 years earlier, published it in the Paris Bible, and then Walton in the London Bible. There are various versions of the New Testament, namely three of the Gospels. The first appeared at Rome from the Medici press, a folio of uncertain age but by a learned translator. The second, together with the other books of the New Testament, was published under the care of Erpenius at Leiden in 1616, in quarto, and is in the Paris and London Bibles.

units.la: ᵉ Prodrom. Copt. cap. 8. ʰ Catal. MSS. pag. 31. ⁱ Walton. Prolegom. cap. 14. Priori non multùm absimilis est; atque ex Syriaco, prout videtur, facta. Authorem habet Nefiulaman F. Azalkefati. Utraque Versio est longè antiquissima, & ante hæresin Arii à Waltono elucubrata censetur: Propterea quòd desit insignis ille locus 1 Joan. V. 7. & Doxologia Orationis Dominicæ. Simonio autem multò recentiores videntur. Tertia Evangeliorum Versio MS. penès Waltonum fuit, admodùm antiqua.
units.tr: {e} Prodromus to the Coptic, chapter 8. {h} Catalogue of Manuscripts, page 31. {i} Walton, Prolegomena, chapter 14. The first is not much unlike the former, and was made, as it seems, from the Syriac. Its author is given as Nefiulaman F. Azalkefati. Both versions are very ancient, and are thought by Walton to have been composed before the heresy of Arius; because that famous passage 1 John 5:7 and the doxology of the Lord's Prayer are missing. To Simon, however, they seem much more recent. A third version of the Gospels, in manuscript and very ancient, was in the possession of Walton.

units.la: Versiones Evangeliorum Persicæ binæ extant, una ab Abrahamo Wheloco Cantabrigiæ evulgata; altera (quæ ex Syriaco facta est) à Waltono, Tomo 5. Bibliorum Londinensium, ex Codice Anno 1341. in Urbe Cassâ conscripto. Versiones istæ recentioris ævi sunt. Fuit olim quidem Translatio Persica Theodoreti tempore. Hodiernæ autem post mutatam linguam, & Mahometis longè tempora, confectæ sunt.
units.tr: There are two Persian versions of the Gospels: one, published at Cambridge by Abraham Wheelock, and another, made from the Syriac, which Walton published in volume 5 of the London Polyglot Bible from a manuscript written in the city of Cassa in the year 1341. These versions belong to a more recent age. There was indeed a Persian translation in Theodoret's time, but the present ones were made after the language had changed and long after Mahomet.

units.la: Hactenus de Versionibus Christianorum Orientalibus; quibus ea tantùm addemus, quæ de Græcis habet Joannes Tynmuthensis in Historiâ Aureâ MS. lib. 8. cap. 24. post narratam ex Aristeâ LXX. Versionis Historiam. De variis Translationibus semel dicere sufficiat. Ante Incarnationem Domini Annis 341. Interpretes LXX. floruerunt. Item post ascensionem Domini Anno 134. sub Adriano Principe Aquila transtu'it. Deinde post Annos 53. sub Commodo Principe Theodotion. Deinde post Annos 30. sub Severo principe Symmachus. Deinde post Annos 8. reperta est Jerosolymis Quinta Editio; quæ iccirco Vulgata dicitur, quia ejus Author ignoratur. Deinde post Annos 18. sub Alexandro principe Origenes transtulit cum asterisco & obeli, & postmodum sine his. Hi omnes de Hebræo in Græcum transtulerunt. De Græco autem in Latinum plures fuerunt. Ultimò tamen Jeronymus de Hebraeo in Latinum transtulit. Cujus Editio ubique, præterquam in Psalterio, ferè servatur. Ista autem παρέχως. Quas enim ante Origenem factas Tynmuthensis memoravit, Versiones à Judæis confectæ sunt: uti supra notavimus, Cap. I.
units.tr: So much for the versions of the Eastern Christians. To these we will add only what John of Tynmouth, in his manuscript Historia Aurea (book 8, chapter 24), says about the Greeks, after recounting the history of the Septuagint translation from Aristeas. It is enough to say a single word about the various translations. The Seventy interpreters flourished 341 years before the Incarnation of the Lord. Likewise, 134 years after the Lord's ascension, under the emperor Hadrian, Aquila translated. Then, 53 years later, under the emperor Commodus, Theodotion. Then, 30 years later, under the emperor Severus, Symmachus. Then, 8 years later, a Fifth Edition was found at Jerusalem, which is called the Vulgate because its author is unknown. Then, 18 years later, under the emperor Alexander, Origen translated, with asterisks and obeli, and afterwards without them. All of these translated from the Hebrew into Greek. Of translations from the Greek into Latin there were many. Last of all, however, Jerome translated from the Hebrew into Latin, and his edition is kept almost everywhere, except in the Psalter. These, however, [παρέχως] are incidental remarks. For the translations that Tynmouth mentioned as made before Origen were made by Jews, as we noted above, chapter 1.

units.la: In recensendis Occidentalium ante Reformationem editis, Cl. Armachanus præter alias à nobis supra diversis in locis memoratas, prætermisit Gallicam à Guarino Molinæo, Presbytero & Canonico Ariensi, Dioeceseos Teroanæ, ex vulgari Latino Anno 1294. confectam; cujus exemplar MS. in Bibliothecâ publicâ Genevensi asservatur, teste Richardo
units.tr: In listing the Western editions before the Reformation, the most distinguished Archbishop of Armagh, besides others that we have mentioned in various places above, passed over the French translation made by Guillaume Guarin Molinaeus, priest and canon of Arras, in the diocese of Thérouanne, from the common Latin in the year 1294. A manuscript copy of it is kept in the public library at Geneva, as Richard Simon attests

units.la: {k} Cap. 14. sect. 22, {l} Histoire Critique, I. 2. c. 24. {m} Vid. locum ab Usserio citatum ex Serm. 5. de curand. Græcor. affect. Simonio . Biblia etiam Moscovitica Illustrissimus Primas nequaquam viderat. Prodierunt ista typis impressa Ostroviae 1581. sol. characteribus Slavicis sive Cyrillianis. Praefigitur Interpretis Praefatio seu Oratio ad Deum Graecè & Moscoviticè; quà gratias agit Deo, qui vires ipsi dederit Versionem ad umbilicum perducendi ad honorem divini nominis. ἀλλ᾽ γὰρ σωσῆσαι τὰς ἀνθρώπους δυνάμεις, εἰ μὴ τῇ τῶν ἐντολῶν σου φυλακῇ, ὡς δύνασαι ἢ οὐ τῇ γενεᾷ ἀνθρώπων ἐπιγνῶναι, ἡ γὰρ μὲν ἱερᾷ σου ἡ, Θεοῦ ἀληθῶς γραφὴν πεφανῶς δ᾽ ἀπηγγέλλει, &c. Probè enim novi homines salutem aegre consequi, nisi observatione mandatorum tuorum; quae humano generi praescribere tibi placuit; & idcirco sacram tui ac divinam Scripturam palam omnibus praedicare. Nunc igitur tibi complacuit illam per me servum tuum ac peccatorem nostrae genti manifestare. Dein succedit Basilii Magni Ducis Admonitio. Κὰγὼ Κωνσταντῖνος Βασίλειος, &c. τοῖς διεσπαρμένοις παντα χῆ ἐν Σλαβανικῇ γλώσσῃ. Ego Constantinus Basilius, Dux Ostroviae, Beobodae, Kioviae, &c. omnibus ubique Catholicis linguam Slavicam scientibus versionem istam Bibliaque legenda commendo: Deoque gratias ago, qui in hunc finem me regno praefecit; ad opus istud aggrediendum incitavit; utque absolutum feliciter viderem, dedit; adeoque dignum habuit, qui vobis utrumque Testamentum typis impressum in lucem darem & in manus traderem; in civitate & Ducatu nostro Ostroviae, in Volhiniâ, Anno Orbis conditi 7809. Nativitatis Christi 1581. Denique in fine voluminis, Joannes Theodori filius, ex Magnâ Ruffiâ, qui Biblia ista Magni Ducis jussu typis excuderat; gratias Deo reddit; quòd dignus esset habitus, qui omnibus divinas Scripturas typis impressas publicaret.
units.tr: {k} Chapter 14, section 22. {l} Histoire Critique, book 1, chapter 24. {m} See the passage cited by Ussher from Sermon 5, de curandis Graecorum affectibus. Simon. The most illustrious Primate had by no means seen the Moscovite Bibles either. These were printed at Ostroh in 1581, in folio, in Slavonic or Cyrillic letters. Before it is a preface or prayer of the translator to God, in Greek and Muscovite, in which he thanks God for giving him the strength to bring the translation to completion, to the honour of the divine name. [ἀλλ᾽ γὰρ σωσῆσαι τὰς ἀνθρώπους δυνάμεις, εἰ μὴ τῇ τῶν ἐντολῶν σου φυλακῇ, ὡς δύνασαι ἢ οὐ τῇ γενεᾷ ἀνθρώπων ἐπιγνῶναι, ἡ γὰρ μὲν ἱερᾷ σου ἡ, Θεοῦ ἀληθῶς γραφὴν πεφανῶς δ᾽ ἀπηγγέλλει] and so on. For I know well that men obtain salvation only with difficulty, unless by keeping your commandments, which it has pleased you to prescribe to the human race; and therefore to proclaim your holy and divine Scripture openly to all. Now, therefore, it has pleased you to make it manifest to our nation through me, your servant and a sinner. Then follows the admonition of Basil the Great, Duke. [Κὰγὼ Κωνσταντῖνος Βασίλειος, &c. τοῖς διεσπαρμένοις παντα χῆ ἐν Σλαβανικῇ γλώσσῃ] I, Constantine Basil, Duke of Ostroh, Beaubodae, Kiev, etc., commend this version and the Bible to be read by all Catholics everywhere who know the Slavonic language. And I give thanks to God, who set me over the kingdom for this purpose, stirred me up to undertake this work, and granted that I should see it brought to a happy conclusion; and who thought me worthy to bring out and hand over to you both Testaments printed, in our city and duchy of Ostroh in Volhynia, in the year of the world's creation 7809, of the Nativity of Christ 1581. Finally, at the end of the volume, John, son of Theodore, from Great Russia, who had printed these Bibles at the command of the Grand Duke, gives thanks to God that he was deemed worthy to publish the divine Scriptures printed for all.

units.tr: {a} Catalogue des principales éditions de la Bible, chapter 6, page 531.

units.la: Addenda in Auctario.
units.tr: Addenda in Auctario.

units.la: De Versione Evangeliorum Saxonicâ.
units.tr: On the Saxon Version of the Gospels.

units.la: PRodiit Evangeliorum IV. Translatio Saxonica (quam Cl. Ussierius Alfredo Regi acceptam refert a) Londini 1571. 4°. Elizabethæ Reginæ à Joanne Foxo prolixâ Præfatione nuncupata. Non tamen Foxus sed Matthæus Parkerus, Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis, editionem procuravit; quod ipsemet Cantuariensis testatur in Præsatione suâ ad Asserii Menevensis Historiam de Vitâ Alfredi Regis. Eadem Versio castigatior prodiit, notisque doctissimis elucidata, à Thomâ Marshallo Anglo, Dordrechti 1665. 4°. unà cum Versione Evangeliorum Gothicâ vetustissimâ; quæ (ut id obiter moneam) & Cl. Armachano b, & Francisco Junio c, editore eruditissimo, judicibus, Ulphilæ Gothorum Episcopo debetur; & ex Codice Argenteo Monasterii Werdensis, de quo multa habet supra d Ussierius, evulgata est.
units.tr: PThe Saxon translation of the four Gospels appeared (which the distinguished Ussher traces back to King Alfred a) at London in 1571, in quarto. It was dedicated to Queen Elizabeth with a long preface by John Foxe. Yet it was not Foxe but Matthew Parker, Archbishop of Canterbury, who saw the edition through, as the Archbishop himself testifies in his preface to Asser of Menevia's History of the Life of King Alfred. The same version appeared in a more correct form, illustrated with learned notes, by Thomas Marshall, an Englishman, at Dordrecht in 1665, in quarto, together with the very ancient Gothic version of the Gospels. (I may note in passing that this Gothic version is owed to Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths, as Archbishop Ussher and Francis Junius, a most learned editor, judge; and it was published from the Silver Codex of the Monastery of Werden, about which Ussher has much to say above d.) b c

units.la: Antiquior videtur Versio Evangeliorum Saxonica ab Aldredo Presbytero confecta; quæ in celeberrimo Eadfridi Codice reperitur. Extat enim in Bibliothecâ Cottoniânâ nobilissimum Antiquitatis monumentum, Codex Quatuor Evangeliorum miræ pulchritudinis; qui inter pretiosissima Ecclesiæ Dunelmensis cimelia olim asservatus, plurimis (si Simeoni Dunelmensi fides,) miraculis enituit. Eum manu propriâ conscripsit Eadfridus Episcopus Lindisfarnensis, circa annum 680. juxta Seldeni calculum; Ethelwoldus autem Episcopus, & Billricus Anachoreta picturis, auro, gemmisque perornârunt; Aldredus denique Presbyter donavit Versione Saxonicâ interlineari, seu Glossâ (sic enim Versionem suam appellari voluit.) additâ ad calcem notâ, quâ libri Scriptorem, Pictorem, Ornatorem ac Glossatorem sigillatim indicat. Illam habes apud Seldenum loco citato g. Erravit itaque Cl. Ussierius h, quùm Versionem istam Evangeliorum Saxonicam Eadfrido tribuit. Oratio enim Dominica, quam ex Eadfridi editione Evangelistarum Saxonicâ desumptam memorat; ex illo ipso Codice descripta est. Habetur illa etiam in libro vernaculo, qui sub Camdeni Reliquiarum nomine circumfertur; cap. 3.
units.tr: The Saxon version of the Gospels made by the priest Aldred seems to be older; it is found in the famous Codex of Eadfrid. For in the Cottonian Library there survives a most noble monument of antiquity, a codex of the four Gospels of remarkable beauty. Once kept among the most precious treasures of the Church of Durham, it shone, according to Simeon of Durham, with many miracles e. Eadfrid, bishop of Lindisfarne, wrote it out with his own hand around the year 680, according to Selden's reckoning. Bishop Ethelwold and the anchorite Billfrith adorned it with pictures, gold and gems. Finally the priest Aldred added a Saxon interlinear version, or gloss (for so he wished his version to be called), and at the end added a note in which he separately names the writer, painter, decorator and glossator of the book. You have this note in Selden, in the place cited g. Therefore the distinguished Ussher was mistaken h when he attributed this Saxon version of the Gospels to Eadfrid. For the Lord's Prayer, which he cites as taken from Eadfrid's Saxon edition of the Evangelists, was copied from that very codex. It is also found in the vernacular book that circulates under the name of Camden's Remains, chapter 3.

units.la: Præter hanc Aldredi Versionem; alia Francisco Junio Glossarium Gothicum adornanti præstò fuit Glossa seu Versio Saxonica Evangeliorum
units.tr: Besides this version of Aldred, another interlinear Saxon gloss or version of the Gospels was available to Francis Junius when he was preparing his Gothic glossary; this one Junius called the Rushworth version, since it was lent to him by J. Rushworth, a lawyer, and was made by the priest Farmen of Harewood and Owen.

units.la: <bl>a</bl> Supra, pag 124. <bl>b</bl> Epist. ad Junium post Goth. Alphabet. <bl>c</bl> In Præfat. & Not. <bl>d</bl> Pag. 213, 214. <bl>e</bl> Hist. Dunelm. lib. 2. cap. 12. <bl>f</bl> Præfat. ad X. Scriptores Angl. <bl>g</bl> Fol. 16. <bl>h</bl> Supra, p. 105. interlinearis, quam Rufworthianam vocat, à J. Rufhworthio JC. sibi commodatam, à Færmenno Presbytero Harwoodensi & Oweno consecta. Penès eundem etiam fuit Glossa interlinearis Saxonica Proverbiorum Solomonis, ex Bibliothecâ Cottoniana descripta; & Psalterii Versio interlinearis, ab omnibus præcedentibus Psalterii Translationibus Saxonicis diversa, ex Bibliothecâ Isaaci Vossii; quin, ut id etiam adjiciam antiqua Versio Francica Harmoniæ Tatiani Evangelicæ; cujus editionem Eruditissimus Senex meditabatur.
units.tr: <bl>a</bl> Above, p. 124. <bl>b</bl> Letter to Junius after the Gothic alphabet. <bl>c</bl> In the Preface and Notes. <bl>d</bl> Pp. 213, 214. <bl>e</bl> History of Durham, book 2, chapter 12. <bl>f</bl> Preface to the Ten English Writers. <bl>g</bl> Folio 16. <bl>h</bl> Above, p. 105. The same owner also had an interlinear Saxon gloss of the Proverbs of Solomon, copied from the Cottonian Library, and an interlinear version of the Psalter, different from all the earlier Saxon translations of the Psalter, from the library of Isaac Vossius. Indeed, to add this too, there is also an ancient French version of Tatian's Evangelical Harmony, whose edition that most learned old man was planning.

units.la: Sunt, qui Versionem S. Scripturæ, his omnibus multò antiquiorem, apud Britannos fuisse volunt, desumpto opinionis argumento ex illis Chrysostomi verbis, χαὶ πεὸς τὰς Βρεταννικὰς νήσους ἐκείνας, quæ supra habes, pag. 331. Verùm cùm id ex illis nullâ arte exculpere potuissem, iis immorari nolui. Nec fœlicior videtur eorum conjectura; qui ex illis Bedæ verbis Lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. Angl. cap. 1. Hæc in præsenti juxta numerum librorum, &c. concludunt S. Scripturam Bedæ tempore in linguas Anglorum, Britonum, Scotorum, & Pictorum, vernaculas conversam fuisse. Conversam quidem negare nolim; me tamen nullo id artificio ex Bedæ verbis citatis colligere posse fateor.
units.tr: There are some who hold that a version of Holy Scripture existed among the Britons, much older than all these, and they base this opinion on those words of Chrysostom, "and to those British islands" [καὶ πρὸς τὰς Βρεταννικὰς νήσους ἐκείνας], which you have above, p. 331. But since I could not wring anything from those words by any skill, I did not want to dwell on them. Nor does the conjecture of those seem more fortunate who, from those words of Bede in book 1 of the Ecclesiastical History of England, chapter 1, "These things at present according to the number of books, etc.", conclude that in Bede's time Holy Scripture had been translated into the vernacular tongues of the English, the Britons, the Scots and the Picts. I would not deny that it was translated; yet I confess that I cannot by any artifice gather this from the words of Bede quoted.

units.la: De Versione Psalterii Gallicâ antiquâ supra, pag. 390.
units.tr: On the Old French Version of the Psalter, above, p. 390.

units.la: Parilis ætatis atq; elegantiæ Psalterium MS. Latinum, cum Versione interlineari Gallicâ, extat in Bibliothecâ Norfolciana, Cod. 230. 4°. In Angliâ, idque ante finem Sæculi duodecimi, scriptum esse, eadem suadent argumenta, quæ de Cottoniano Codice supra 1 protulimus. Norfolcianum autem cum illo Eadwini convenire fidem facit nota recenter præmissa cujusdam Eruditi Lectoris, qui Gallicam Versionem in quatuor prioribus Psalmis præ vetustate evanidam, ex altero Cantabrigiensi restituerat. Nos initia Psalmorum primi & quinti exinde descripta dedimus.
units.tr: A Latin manuscript Psalter of similar age and elegance, with an interlinear Old French version, is in the Norfolk Library, Cod. 230, quarto. That it was written in England, and before the end of the twelfth century, is supported by the same arguments which we brought forward above concerning the Cottonian codex. That the Norfolk codex agrees with Eadwine's is shown by a note recently prefixed by a certain learned reader, who restored from the other Cambridge copy the French version in the first four Psalms, which had faded with age. We have given from it the openings of Psalms 1 and 5.

units.la: Psalm. I. Beneurez hueme, qui ne allat el conseil des feluns, è en la veie des pecheurs ne stout, è en la chaere de pestilence ne sist.
units.tr: Psalm 1. Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of pestilence.

units.la: Psal. V. Les meies paroles atues orreilles receif, Sire; entent clamur lameie. Lentent alavoir de laoreisun lameie, limeus Reis & Deus limeus, vuiz elameie: kar ate io urrai, Sire, lematine orras.
units.tr: Psalm 5. Give ear to my words with your ears, Lord; consider my cry. Attend to the voice of my prayer, my king and my God, for to you I will pray, Lord; in the morning you shall hear.

units.la: De Saxonicæ linguæ usu post Normannorum adventum.
units.tr: On the use of the Saxon language after the coming of the Normans.

units.la: Paucula de hoc argumento adnotavi supra, pag. 388. Si quis integræ idiomatis Saxonici apud Anglos desuetudinis tempus scire velit; haud alibi certiora quam in antiquis Regum Chartis Latino-Anglicis inveniet.
units.tr: I have noted a few things on this subject above, p. 388. If anyone wishes to know when the full Saxon idiom fell out of use among the English, he will find nothing more certain anywhere than in the old Latin-English charters of the Kings.

units.la: 1 Loc. cit. inveniet. In his pro ætatis diversitate linguæ gradatim evanescentis vestigia clarissimè observare licet; præsertim in illis Chartis recentioribus antiquiorum confirmatoriis, quæ ab initiali vocabulo Inspeximus nomen sortiuntur. Quippe in his plurimæ Regum antecedentium Chartæ consimiles verbatim recenseri solent; ex quibus juxta positis linguæ in singulis usurpatæ collatio optimè institui potest. Plures ejusmodi Chartæ, Regum Henrici IV. Edwardi IV. Henrici VIII. &c. habentur in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, libertates & possessiones Chartasque antiquas Archiepiscopatûs Cantuariensis confirmantes. In his locum semper obtinent Chartæ Henrici I. Anselmo data, Stephani Regis, Henrici II. Henrici Regis filii ejus, Richardi I. &c. quæ deinceps confirmantur. Ex his tres priores in utrâque linguâ, Latinâ sç. & Anglicâ, exhibentur: reliquæ omnes Latinè solummodò conscribuntur. Hinc patet linguam Anglo Saxonicam in Chartis scriptisque publicis usurpari desiisse tempore Henrici II. Quin & eodem circiter tempore mutationem maximam subiisse, & in aliam fere linguam deflexam esse. Quùm enim idioma Chartæ Henrici I. ad veterem Saxonicam quàm ad hodiernam Anglicam multò propiùs accedit; illud Chartæ Henrici II. è contra multò magis ad hanc quàm ad illam accedit; Grammaticâ & terminationibus Saxonicis, quæ in priore retenta erant, in hodiernam ferè dialectum imminutatis. In illis quidem Chartis Confirmatoriis, antiquæ Chartæ non primævo sed neoterico charactere conscribuntur; adeò ut de Characteris Saxonici mutatione parum exinde constet. Verùm is defectus suppleri potest ex Chartis Originalibus; quarum duæ maximè insignes, sc. Henrici I. Willelmo Corbel, & Henrici II. Theobaldo Archiepiscopo datæ, in eâdem Bibliothecâ asservantur. Ex his Characterem etiam Saxonicum circa eadem tempora in communi usu esse desiisse non obscurè colligi potest. Cùm ex decem enim circiter Characteribus, quibus Saxonica Scriptura à Latinâ distinguitur, unicus in Chartâ Henrici I. immutetur; in illâ Henrici II. tres solummodò retinentur.
units.tr: 1 Loc. cit. In these, the traces of a language gradually fading away, according to the different ages, can be observed very clearly; especially in those more recent charters that confirm older ones and take their name from the opening word Inspeximus. In these, very many charters of the earlier Kings are usually copied out word for word, and by setting them side by side one can make a good comparison of the language used at each period. Several such charters, of Kings Henry IV, Edward IV, Henry VIII, etc., are held in the Lambeth Library, confirming the liberties, possessions and ancient charters of the Archbishopric of Canterbury. In these, the charters of Henry I granted to Anselm, of King Stephen, of Henry II, of Henry's son Richard I, etc., always have the place of honour, and they are confirmed in turn. Of these, the first three are set out in both languages, Latin and English; all the rest are written in Latin only. Hence it is clear that the Anglo-Saxon language ceased to be used in charters and public writings in the time of Henry II. Indeed, at about the same time it also underwent a very great change and was turned into an almost different language. For while the idiom of the charter of Henry I comes much closer to the old Saxon than to the modern English, the idiom of the charter of Henry II, on the contrary, comes much closer to the latter than to the former, the grammar and Saxon endings, which had been kept in the earlier one, having been reduced to the almost modern dialect. In those confirmatory charters, the old charters are written not in the primitive but in the newer script; so that little is established from them about the change of the Saxon letter-forms. But this defect can be supplied from the original charters; two of the most notable of these, namely the one given by Henry I to William Corbel and the one by Henry II to Archbishop Theobald, are preserved in the same library. From these it can be plainly gathered that the Saxon character also ceased to be in common use about the same time. For of the roughly ten characters by which Saxon writing is distinguished from Latin, only one is altered in the charter of Henry I, while in that of Henry II only three are retained.

units.la: De Armenis.
units.tr: On the Armenians.

units.la: De Armenorum consuetudine & eximio S. Scripturæ studio testimonium maximè insigne dedit Bonaventura Brocardus (Borchardum malè vocant libri editi Ordinis Prædicatorum; qui in Orientem iter suscepit circa Annum 1283. prout ipsemet in Itinerario suo k fidem facit. Ista autem de Armenis l refert; quæ quidem Thomas Rudburn, Monachus Anglus circa An. 1440. in Historiam Majorem suam MS. in Bibliothecâ Lambethanâ, nonnihil immutata, m transtulit. Solennissimo die in-
units.tr: Bonaventura Brocardus gives the most notable testimony to the customs of the Armenians and their remarkable devotion to Holy Scripture. (The printed books of the Order of Preachers wrongly call him Borchardus.) He set out for the East about the year 1283, as he himself attests in his Itinerary k. He reports these things about the Armenians l, and Thomas Rudburn, an English monk, about the year 1440 transferred them, with some changes, into his manuscript Historia Major m, preserved in the Lambeth Library. On a most solemn day I was present at their Mass, before the same Catholicos (as they call their patriarch), the King and the Queen. They have a very devout liturgy. They consecrate with unleavened bread and use the same words as we do. In their Masses they chant the same Epistles, the same Gospels, Prefaces, Sanctus, Pater Noster and Agnus Dei as we do, though in their own idiom.

units.la: {k} Par. 1. cap. 7. sect. 10. {l} Par. 2. cap. 2. sect. 9. {m} Lib. 5. cap. 2. terfui eorum Missæ coram eodem Catholico (sic Patriarcham suum vocant) & Rege & Reginâ; habentque Officium devotum valde. In azymo conficiunt, & eisdem verbis sicut nos. Easdem Epistolas, eadem Evangelia, Præfationes, Sanctus, Pater Noster, & Agnus Dei in missis decantant, sicut & nos; in suo tamen idiomate. Habent enim linguam vulgarem, propriam & literalem [Rudburn. cantant in Missa, sicut & omnes nos, sub idiomate suo. Scripturam habent, literam specialem, & linguam] — Reges Principesque Nobilesque ardenti animo audiunt divinos sermones. Propterea singulis diebus, horâ diei tertiâ Vatrapetæ (Monachi) Regis aut alterius Principis Curiam adeunt; ad quos statim accedunt Principes & Domini cum filiis ac potentibus suis; afferturque liber aliquis sacræ Bibliæ, legiturque in vulgari suo; & à Vatrapetis textus exponitur. [Rudburn. Reges & Principes & etiam omnes Nobiles audiunt libentissimè Verbum Dei. Unde cotidie ad horam tertiam, ubi Tapechæ sive Gapechæ seu Monachi ad Curiam Regis seu Principis alicujus advenerint; occurrunt eis statim ipsi Principes vel Rex cum filiis suis & omnibus de Curiâ suâ: & apponitur eis liber aliquis S. Scripturæ, & legitur coram eis in vulgari; quod linguam aliam nesciunt, sed linguâ & literis propriis utuntur.] Sæculares quando dubia proponunt; super hujusmodi à Vatrapetis instruuntur; & quæstiones per Sanctorum Expositiones solvunt. — Clerici & Laici in Ecclesiâ devoti admodum, nihil ibi operantur, nisi orare, legere, divina celebrare vel audire. Nunquam conspicies in Ecclesiâ ridentem vel vagum aut dissolutum, cujuscunque nationis exstat. Cæremoniala Missæ devotissima sunt apud eos. [Rudburn. Multùm devoti sunt in Ecclesiâ. Et Clerici & Laici nihil ibi faciunt; nisi aut orant, aut cantant & cætera quæ de jure facere possunt. Nunquam videbis eos in Ecclesiâ dissolvi nec ridere, nec Clericum nec Laicum; sive Græcus sit, sive cujuscunque alterius nationis. Officium Missæ devotissimum est apud eos.] — Et cantant Melodiam quandam, certè [Rudburn. valdè] devotam & dulcem, [Rudburn. dulcissimam] alternatim sibi invicem respondentes. Et id quidem [Rudburn. Istud absq; dubio] devotissimum est audire ac videre.
units.tr: {k} Par. 1. cap. 7. sect. 10. {l} Par. 2. cap. 2. sect. 9. {m} Lib. 5. cap. 2. I was present at their Mass, before the same Catholicos (as they call their patriarch), the King and the Queen; and they have a very devout office. They consecrate with unleavened bread and use the same words as we do. In their Masses they chant the same Epistles, the same Gospels, Prefaces, Sanctus, Pater Noster and Agnus Dei as we do, though in their own idiom. For they have a vulgar language of their own, and a literal one. [Rudburn: they sing in Mass, as all of us do, in their own idiom. They have Scripture, a special letter, and a language.] Kings, princes and nobles listen to the divine sermons with eager minds. Therefore every day at the third hour the vardapets (monks) come to the court of the King or of some other prince; the princes and lords come at once to them with their sons and powerful men; a book of the holy Bible is brought, it is read in their vernacular, and the text is expounded by the vardapets. [Rudburn: Kings and princes and also all nobles listen most gladly to the Word of God. Hence every day at the third hour, when the Tapechae or Gapechae, that is the monks, come to the court of the king or of some prince, the princes themselves, or the king with his sons and all of his court, meet them at once; and some book of Holy Scripture is set before them and read to them in the vernacular, since they do not know any other language but use their own language and letters.] When laymen put forward doubtful questions, they are instructed about such matters by the vardapets, and they solve questions through the expositions of the Saints. Clergy and laity in the Church are very devout and do nothing there except pray, read, celebrate or hear the divine offices. You will never see anyone in the Church laughing, wandering about or behaving loosely, of whatever nation he is. The ceremonies of the Mass are most devout among them. [Rudburn: They are very devout in church. Clergy and laity do nothing there but either pray or sing and the other things they may lawfully do. You will never see them, cleric or layman, dissolute or laughing in church, whether he be Greek or of any other nation. The office of the Mass is most devout among them.] And they sing a certain melody, certainly [Rudburn: indeed] devout and sweet [Rudburn: sweetest], answering one another in turn. And indeed [Rudburn: without doubt] it is most devout to hear and to see.

units.la: De Versionibus Anglicis.
units.tr: On the English Versions.

units.la: Cùm dixerim supra pag. 426. duos solummodo mediâ ætate (sc. inter Saxonum & Reformationis tempora) fuisse Interpretes S. Scripturæ Anglicanos, sc. Wiclefum & Trevisam; vellem duos solummodo notis conitare Authores integræ SS. Scripturarum Versionis Anglicanæ; qualis fuit illa, de quâ loco citato egimus. Id Lectorem monitum volui; ne incautum dicto laxiore in errorem inducerem.
units.tr: When I said above, on page 426, that in the middle age (that is, between the time of the Saxons and the Reformation) there were only two English interpreters of Holy Scripture, namely Wycliffe and Trevisa, I would have wished to note only two authors of a complete English version of the Holy Scriptures, such as the one of which I spoke in the passage cited. I wished to warn the reader of this, so that I might not lead him into error by a statement too loosely worded.
